en: Now begins the second section, the Bhūmikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa;
here is the first chapter. Om, salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
The sages said:
Listen, O highly fortunate Sūta, you who are skilled in the meaning of all truths;
O knower, we have fallen into a terrible doubt that destroys the intellect. 1.

O best of the twice-born, some read in the Purāṇas that Keśava was propitiated even by one who was only five years old, namely Prahlāda. How did he come to fight with Hari during the war between the gods and the asuras?
"Slain by Vāsudeva, he has indeed entered the body of Viṣṇu.
Sūta said:
"In ancient times, this was known by Kaśyapa and performed by the wise Vyāsa."
O twice-born ones, that which was previously told by Brahmā himself in the presence of the Lord Vyāsa,
that very thing I shall now declare before you;
the cause of your doubt has been severed by the divine Creator.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O highly fortunate Sūta, to that which was proclaimed by Brahmā regarding the birth of Prahlāda, as it has been heard differently even in the Purāṇas.
As soon as he was born, Prahlāda, the best among the great devotees of Viṣṇu and honored by the gods, took refuge in the Vaiṣṇava path of all happiness;
accompanied by his son, he went to the battlefield to fight with Viṣṇu.
Slain by Vāsudeva, he indeed entered the body of Viṣṇu.
Now hear from me about the creative state of this very Great Soul;
having encountered Saṃgara along with his sons and others, that powerful one [was absorbed] together with Viṣṇu.

Having entered the Vaiṣṇava splendor and attained it through his own luster, O highly fortunate one, he was born as he was in a previous kalpa, endowed with great prowess. I shall relate the account of that hero in brief.
At the edge of the western ocean is the great city named Dvārakā,
endowed with all prosperity and possessed of all supernatural powers.
In that city dwells eternally the Lord, the knower of yoga and the foremost among those who understand yoga.
There was one renowned as Śivaśarman, who was proficient in the meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras;
he too had five sons who were experts in the Shastras:
Yajñaśarman, Vedaśarman, and likewise Dharmaśarman.
The illustrious Viṣṇuśarman was surely skilled in that particular task.
The fifth was Somaśarman, who was devoted solely to his father; for, O best of the twice-born, there is no other dharma besides devotion to one's father. 14-15.
The great-souled ones do not know this, for they are permeated by that very state of being.
Observing their devotion, Śivaśarman, the best of the twice-born and possessed of great intelligence, reflected: "I shall draw forth these foremost of gods."
"That state of devotion toward one's father which did not reside in the minds of these [others], I shall now practice with deliberate intent as I understand it;
and by the grace of Viṣṇu, he attained all perfections. (17-18)

O best of the twice-born, that most excellent of Brahmins, possessing the power of asceticism, reflected upon the true nature of things and devised a means for the purpose of concealing [his form] through his illusory power (māyā). 19.
He, the knower of Brahman, being skilled in means, acted indeed by means of illusion.
Before them, Śivaśarman displayed this ruse:
he showed his mother as if dead from a severe fever.
Seeing their mother dead, they spoke these words to their father: (20–21)

"O highly fortunate one, we, having been nurtured within the womb of her body, have ourselves abandoned this physical frame and gone to the imperishable state. Having left it behind, she too has gone to heaven; O father, what more can be said? (22)
Having summoned his son Yajñaśarman, who was devoted to Śivaśarman, that best of brahmins spoke as follows. Śivaśarman said:
"With this very sharp and whetted weapon,
cut off all your limbs and cast them here and there. That son did exactly as he had heard his father's command.

Having returned once more, he spoke these words to his father: "O dear father, I have performed everything exactly as you commanded; furthermore, please instruct me regarding whatever task or purpose must be done today."
"O father, I shall accomplish all of that, however difficult it may be to conquer or hard to attain.
Having recognized him as one of great fortune and devoted to his father, and perceiving his supreme resolve, that twice-born man reflected upon a second course of action.
Having summoned Vedaśarman, he said: "Go at my command;
deluded by Kandarpa, I am unable to remain without a woman.
A woman endowed with every excellence of beauty has been shown to me through illusion."
"O Vatsa, having made a firm resolve for my sake, bring her here.
Being thus addressed, he replied, "I shall do what is most pleasing to you.
Having paid homage to his father, he departed from there and spoke to her.
"O Goddess, my father, tormented by the arrows of desire, entreats you;
therefore, O lady with a gracious countenance, show favor to him who is overcome by old age. O beautiful one, O lovely-limbed one, accept my father."
Having heard this from that Māyāvedasharman,
the woman said:
"Even though I am afflicted by old age, I never have such a desire."
"I now desire to enjoy the company of you, who are currently afflicted by a disease of the mouth accompanied by phlegm,
who are frail and distressed, and who are old;
I shall do what is most pleasing to you."

O giver of honor, we wish to hear: what will you do with that old man, when you yourself are adorned with beauty, fortune, and jewels of virtue, endowed with divine marks, possessing a celestial form and great majesty? 36.
"By becoming the object of my enjoyment, you shall obtain everything that is difficult to attain.
Whatever you desire, O Brahmin, I shall grant it to you; of this there is no doubt.
Having heard these great words, which were unpleasant and filled with wickedness, [he was struck with fear]. 37-38.
Vedaśarman said:
"O Goddess, do not speak such words to me, who am devoted to my father and innocent—words that are unrighteous, improper, and tainted with sin. (39)
"O auspicious lady, I have come for my father's sake and I entreat you: do not speak otherwise; worship my father.
O goddess, whatever you desire in the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile—"
"O auspicious one, you who possess such knowledge and whose doubt has been dispelled, you are superior even to the king of the gods.
(41) The woman said: "Since you are thus capable of granting [this] for the sake of my father..."
"Therefore, show us this very day those Indras and the Great Lords (Maheśvaras) who are equal to you;
for you are indeed capable of granting what is currently so difficult to obtain. O illustrious one, show us your own power! 42-43.
Vedaśarman said:
"Behold, O Goddess, behold my strength and the power of my asceticism! Summoned by me, Indra and the other foremost of the gods have arrived."
They said to Vedaśarman: "O best of the twice-born, what shall we do for you? O Brahmin, whatever you desire, we shall grant it to you without a doubt. (45) Vedaśarman said:
"O gods, if you are pleased, and if you are well-disposed with gracious faces, grant me pure devotion for the feet of my father alone.
"So be it," said all the gods; they departed just as they had come.
Seeing him thus, he said to him: "The power of your asceticism has been witnessed.
I have no business with the gods; if you wish to give me anything here, then do this kindness for me: take me to my preceptor."
Having indeed cut off his own head with his own hand, Vedaśarman said: "Today I have become blessed and truly liberated from the three debts. 49
"O auspicious lady, please accept, please accept my own head," said that best of the twice-born, as he took up a sharp-edged,
cold blade; then, having cut off his own head, he gave it to her while laughing.
Drenched in blood, she took hold of the sage and departed.
The woman said:
"O Brahmin, this was sent for your sake by the son of Vedaśarman."
"O tiger among the twice-born, take this head, severed by yourself from your own body; it has been offered by me, who am devoted to my father. For your sake, O best of brahmins, consume me thus."
When those brothers saw that act of violence by Vedasharman, their limbs began to tremble as they looked at one another;
for his mother, Dharmasādhu, had died through her steadfastness in truth.
"This illustrious and auspicious one has died for the sake of his father;
he is blessed, having attained the state of being blessed by performing a virtuous deed for his father's sake.
Thus was it spoken by those brothers who walk the path of merit.
Having heard the words of the twice-born and knowing him to be devoted to bhakti,
Dharmaśarmā then spoke to his son Vedaśarman, who had severed the head: "Now, take this head."
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Life of Śivaśarman," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Two.
Sūta said:
Then that great-souled one, out of devotion to his father, through his ascetic penances, and by the power of truth and uprightness, departed with haste;
and at that time, Dharmaśarman drew forth Dharma.
Drawn by the ascetic power of that wise one, Dharma was summoned; having approached Dharmaśarman, he spoke these words:
"O Dharmaśarman, why have you come here when summoned by me?"
"Tell me that task; I shall perform it without a doubt.
Dharmaśarman said:
"If you have unwavering devotion to the service of your guru, and if your austerity is firm... (4)
"By that truth, may this Dharma-Veda-Śarman live. Dharma said:
"O you of good vows, by self-restraint, purity, truth, and austerity—"
"O great-armed one, through devotion to his father, your brother Vedaśarman shall regain his life in this very way;
for I am pleased by this austerity and by his devotion to his father, O high-minded one."
"Choose a boon, O auspicious one; it is difficult even for those most proficient in the Dharma to obtain.
Having heard these well-spoken words, the highly illustrious Dharmaśarman addressed the high-souled son of Vivasvat.

When I am well-pleased, I shall grant him unwavering devotion to the worship of his father’s feet, as well as delight in dharma and liberation. Then Dharma said to him: "By my grace, this shall come to pass."
When these great sayings had been thus spoken, the highly wise Dharmaśarman then arose as if from sleep and said to Vedaśarman: "Brother, where has that queen gone? Where might our father be?"
Having been thus addressed in brief by his father,
Dharmaśarman, understanding it and being filled with joy, spoke to him: "O illustrious one, this very day, with my head and my life, [I am yours]."
"O brother of such splendor, who else like you exists on this earth?
Having thus addressed his brother, he, filled with longing for his father,
made up his mind to depart along with his brother Dharmaśarman.
Then those two, having approached their father Śivaśarman, who was there with a joyful mind and seated upon his two [vehicles], spoke to that most excellent one;
and Dharmaśarman then addressed his father, who was endowed with radiance.
"O highly fortunate one, by means of your austerity and even your life, Vedaśarman has been brought here this very day; O sir, please accept this son.
Then Śivaśarman was delighted, having recognized his devotion.
He said nothing to him, but again fell into reflection; then he addressed the high-minded Viṣṇuśarman, who was standing before him with humility: "Child, do as I say."
"Go now to the world of Indra and bring back the nectar from there.
I desire to dwell at this moment together with this beloved wife of mine—the nectar born from the ocean which destroys all disease. (19-20)
"O virtuous one, act quickly so that she desires me, just as I might obtain her; otherwise, she will go to another.
This young girl, though possessing a beautiful form, might despise you upon seeing that you are old."
"O Father, act in such a way that today, together with this beloved goddess, I may become faultless and free from disease throughout the three worlds; for you are my devotee on earth. (22-23)
Having heard these words of his high-souled father,
Viṣṇuśarman then spoke to his father of radiant splendor:
"I shall do all this for your supreme happiness."
Having spoken thus, the righteous and high-minded Viṣṇuśarman,
having bowed to his father and circumambulated him once more,
was endowed with great strength through his asceticism and self-restraint.
And as the wise one was proceeding, he went through the atmosphere with the great force of the wind, reaching toward the realm of Indra. 27.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Life of Śivaśarman," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. 2.
The third chapter.
Sūta said:
Having set out on that path, he entered into the midst of the sky.
Having observed this with his thousand eyes, the wise Lord of Gods, the sovereign of the deities, recognized his exertion and created an obstacle.
He spoke thus to Menakā: "Go, at my command."

"Go quickly and without hindrance, O fair-waisted one, and conduct yourself properly toward this son of the most excellent brahmin, Śivaśarman. Act in such a way— may you be blessed— that he does not come to my house."
Having heard these words, Menikā set out with haste.
Sūta said:
Endowed with beauty, nobility, and virtue, she was adorned with every ornament.
At the edge of the Nandana grove, she was seated upon a swing;
singing with a melodious voice a song resembling the tone of a lute,
that large-eyed woman of clever and beautiful eyes was seen by him.
"Having understood his resolve to be supreme and free from obstacles, she was sent by Indra; yet she has not brought about any good.
Realizing this, O best of the twice-born, he then departed with great haste.
Having been seen and questioned by her in that manner, O Mahāmati, Viṣṇuśarman then said to Menikā, who was free to go wherever she pleased:
"I shall go to the world of Indra, filled with haste for the sake of my father."

Pierced by the arrows of love, she spoke again these pleasant words to Viṣṇuśarman: "O tiger among the twice-born, I have come to you for refuge today; protect me, if you desire dharma in this world. (10)
As long as I have been seen by you with a mind agitated by desire,
so long I shall undoubtedly remain consumed by the fire of passion;
bewildered and tormented by lust, be gracious and look upon me with a favorable countenance.
Viṣṇuśarman said:
"O fair-faced one, the life-story of the God of gods is known to me; I am aware of yours as well, O auspicious lady, yet I am not such a person."

"O beautiful lady, Viśvāmitra and others are deluded by your splendor, form, and beauty, O Goddess; I am the son of Śivaśarman, who has attained perfection in yoga and success in asceticism, O frail one. (14)
"The great evils, beginning with desire, have already been conquered by me. O large-eyed lady, resort to another; I am going to the world of Indra.
Having spoken thus, that best of the twice-born then departed in haste. 15–16.
O twice-born ones, when Menakā was born fruitlessly, she was questioned by the wielder of the thunderbolt, Indra; he repeatedly showed her various terrifying forms,
just as heaps of grass are consumed by fire.
O best of men,
by the spiritual power of that brahmin who was devoted to his ancestors, those terrible and cruel terrors were utterly reduced to ashes and brought to destruction, O twice-born ones. (18–19)
The thousand-eyed Indra repeatedly manifested obstacles,
but the highly illustrious Brahmin destroyed them with his own splendor.
In this manner, he [overcame] the many obstacles presented even to that great-souled Indra.
The wise one destroyed them by means of the power of his asceticism.
When those obstacles— both dreadful and great— had been destroyed,
he recognized that they were the terrible and fearsome forms created by him [the demon].
Then the highly effulgent Viṣṇuśarman, the best of the twice-born and a man of great fortune, became enraged; with the corners of his eyes red with passion, he said to Indra:
"I shall cast Indra down from the world of Indra; it shall not be otherwise."

"Whoever creates an obstacle for one who is devoted to his own duty today, I shall inflict punishment upon him; indeed, he who strikes him shall himself be struck. Furthermore, I shall appoint another as the protector of the gods. 24-25.

O best of Brahmins, while that most excellent being was thus exerting himself for destruction, Indra, the lord of the gods and wielder of the thunderbolt, arrived at that very moment. "Ho there, O highly wise Brahmin! By means of your austerity and self-restraint..."
"In self-restraint, truthfulness, and purity, there is no other equal to you.
O best of beings, I have been moved by this devotion of yours toward your father; together with the gods, I ask that you forgive all my offenses."
"Choose a boon, O auspicious one; even that which is difficult to obtain, I shall grant you.
Then Viṣṇuśarman spoke to the king of the gods who had approached him:
"O Great Indra, the splendor of a Brahmin is unbearable even for the gods and deities."
O Lord of Gods, O All-pervading One, the devotion of one who is devoted to his father is difficult to withstand in every way.
No injury to the splendor of high-souled Brahmins should be done by you, even with all your sons and grandsons, nor by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or Hara. 30–31.

O best of the twice-born, there is no doubt that if you do not come today because you are angry, then this unsurpassed kingdom will perish through the power of your own asceticism and pass to another great-souled one. 32. You [must give it] to another high-souled being.
But having become desirous of giving [the boon], with eyes filled with anger he said:
"O Lord of Gods, you have arrived here today wishing to grant a boon; give me the nectar and likewise unwavering devotion to my father. (33-34)
"O slayer of enemies, if you are pleased, grant me such a boon as this. "I shall grant you this meritorious boon, joined with the nectar of immortality (amṛta).
Having spoken thus to that brahmin, he himself bestowed the nectar.
With a heart full of affection, he gave him a jar along with its contents.
"O Brahmin, may your devotion to your father remain steadfast forever.
Having thus addressed the Brahmin and dismissed him, the thousand-eyed Indra departed. (36-37)
Seeing that unbearable splendor of the Brahmin, Viṣṇuśarman became filled with faith; he then approached his father and spoke these words:
"Father, this nectar, which destroys disease, has been brought from Indra."
"By this, O illustrious one, may you always be free from disease;
through this nectar, may you attain supreme satisfaction this very day.
Having heard these great words of his son, Śivaśarman— 39–40.
Having summoned all his sons with a joyful heart, he said:
"O sons, you are devoted to your father and obedient to my word. O dear children, being well-pleased, choose a boon that is difficult to obtain on earth."
Having heard what he had thus spoken, all those who were highly esteemed listened. Then, after deliberating among themselves, they all spoke to their father:
"While we are still living, our mother has come to this house."
"O you of excellent vows, by the grace of the Goddess, may you become free from disease;
O father, may she be your mother, and we all, being performers of merit, may be your sons in birth after birth. (44)
Śivaśarman said:
"Even today, your mother, who is so affectionate toward her sons, has died; yet if she were alive, she would come here full of joy—of this there is no doubt."
When these auspicious words had been spoken by the sage Śivaśarman,
their mother arrived and, being greatly delighted, spoke these words:
"For this very purpose was this son of great heroism born."

Men desire a virtuous son who brings glory to their family and lineage; and women in this world—highly fortunate, meritorious, and devoted to virtue—everywhere desire a son of auspicious limbs who is a performer of merit. 48.
That woman of great merit, into whose womb the most meritorious embryo has entered and develops,
shall give birth to sons who are themselves meritorious, the upholders of family tradition, the pillars of the lineage, and the deliverers of their father and mother. 49–50.

"How can a woman obtain an excellent son without merits? By what kind of merits was this husband, who possesses great merit, born—one who is heroic in dharma, whose soul is dharma, and who is devoted to dharma? (51)
"By whose valor I attained [this state], and you, my sons, have become even greater than that.
Such is the power of merit; you, who are devoted to merit, have become my sons, entirely dedicated to filial devotion. (52-53)

In this world, through merits, a virtuous son is obtained; one after another, five more noble-minded ones were acquired, who were performers of sacrifices, of meritorious character, and possessed of ascetic power and prowess. 54.
Thus repeatedly nurtured by their mother,
those sons, filled with great joy, bowed down to their mother.
The sons said:
A mother is indeed obtained through great merits; she is a true mother and a true father.
You have become a merit-performing mother, brought forth by our good fortune, having entered our womb and been nurtured by great merits.
"In birth after birth, you two shall be my mother and father.
The father said:
"Listen, my sons, to this excellent boon which bestows merit."
While he was enjoying inexhaustible pleasures as the son of his father's satisfaction,
the sons said: "O Father,
if you are pleased with us and desire to grant a boon here," (59)
"Send us to Goloka, the realm of Viṣṇu, which is free from fire.
The father said:
"Go, you who are cleansed of all taint, to the realm of Viṣṇu. (60)
"By my grace, by your austerities, and by this devotion to your ancestors"—
when he had been thus addressed with these excellent words by that sage,
the Lord, holding the conch, discus, and mace in his hands and mounted upon Garuḍa, arrived there.
He spoke thus again and again to Śivaśarman and his son:
"O twice-born one, by you and your son, I have been conquered this very day through devotion. Come together with your four meritorious sons."
Śivaśarman said: "O my sons, go together with this virtuous wife who desires her husband to the supreme world of Viṣṇu. (64)
"For a certain time, I shall dwell upon the earth together with my wife and this excellent son, Somaśarman, the last of my offspring.
When these auspicious words had been spoken by the truth-telling Ṛṣi, [the gods departed].
Then the Lord of the Gods spoke to those excellent sons of Śivaśarman:
"Go to the world that grants liberation, which is free from burning and dissolution.
Having been addressed thus, O Brahmins, the four of them, whose minds were fixed on truth, [departed].
At that very moment, they all assumed the form of Viṣṇu;
with complexions like sapphire-blue, they bore the conch, the discus, and the mace,
endowed with the splendor of all ornaments, possessing the form of Viṣṇu, and great in majesty.
Richly adorned with necklaces and bracelets, and beautified by strings of jewels (69),
resembling the splendor of the sun and enveloped in flames of radiance, they entered the body of Viṣṇu as Śivaśarman looked on (70).
Just as lamps pass from one lamp to another, O Great-minded One, even so those best of the twice-born, having gone to the abode of Viṣṇu through devotion to their father, [attain that state].
(71) I shall now proclaim the truly wonderful power of Somaśarman. (72)
Thus ends the third chapter in the Śivaśarmopākhyāna of the Bhūmikhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Four.
Sūta said:
When they had departed for Goloka, the realm of Viṣṇu beyond darkness,
the highly wise Śivaśarman spoke these words to his youngest brother.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
O Somaśarman, you who are highly wise and devoted to your father,
protect this great jar of nectar now given by me; I shall depart on a pilgrimage to sacred sites together with this wife of mine.

"So be it, O illustrious one; we shall perform this auspicious protection. Having given the water-pot into the hand of that wise and high-souled one, he performed penance continuously for a period of ten years.
The righteous-souled one guarded the jar without weariness from day until night;
then the highly illustrious Śivaśarman returned,
that man of great wisdom, having employed a stratagem along with his wife and son.
Having become afflicted with the disease of leprosy, his wife likewise became so;
these two were born resembling mere lumps of flesh, created by illusion,
in the presence of that terrible Brahmin Somaśarman.
Seeing the two who had come together and were indeed deeply distressed on all sides,
the highly illustrious Somaśarman was overcome with supreme compassion;
bowing his head in devotion, he paid homage at their feet.
O one like you, endowed with the ascetic power of the Unseen (Anaśyatapas),
by what multitude of most meritorious virtues has this been brought about in you, that all the deities always attend upon you as if they were your servants? 9–10.

"O best of Brahmins, having received your command, they have been drawn here by your splendor. O foremost of Brahmins, tell me the cause: by what sin has this disease, accompanied by such agony, arisen in your body?"

"This meritorious woman, the daughter of a great sage and devoted to her husband, who by her husband's grace desires to create the three worlds—how can she experience suffering? Is there no fruit for asceticism? (12-13)
Having completely abandoned passion and hatred through various actions,
she who serves her beloved like a god and is devoted to him as to a guru— how could she incur suffering such as the most painful disease of leprosy? 14.
Śivaśarman said:
"Do not grieve, O illustrious one; the fruit born of karma is experienced by a person joined with action, consisting indeed of both sin and merit. (15)
"Perform purification for both of these who are afflicted by disease,
O highly fortunate one, if you desire merit here.
When these auspicious words had been spoken, the highly illustrious Somaśarman [replied].

"O best of the twice-born, I shall perform service for you two who are endowed with merit; for what else could be done by me, a wicked and miserable sinner? Indeed, one must worship one's guru this very day. (18)
Having spoken thus, pained by the suffering of both, he who was himself afflicted by grief cleansed the phlegm, urine, and excrement of both;
he likewise performed the washing of their feet and the massaging of their limbs.
Filled with devotion himself, that righteous and highly illustrious brahmin Somaśarman carried both of them upon his shoulders and led them to the sacred bathing place and other holy sites. 21.
That most excellent man, whose soul was devoted to dharma, carried them on his back to the tirtha.
Having bathed these two with his own hands using auspicious substances,

a knower of the Vedas should perform the ritual bathing according to the prescribed rules along with excellent mantras, as well as the libations for the ancestors and the worship of the deities. 22–23.

That virtuous soul constantly performed the fire-oblation himself with both of them; being well-pleased, he provided the two great gurus with unsurpassed food and offered them hospitality. 24. He honored these two as his supreme teachers.
The brahmin constantly causes them both to rest upon beds and seats;
he daily provides them with all things such as clothing and flowers,
and he offers both of them betel-leaf enriched with many fragrances.
The illustrious Somaśarman would also satisfy them both;
he would constantly provide them with roots, milk, and excellent food.
Indeed, the highly renowned Somaśarman would daily fulfill whatever those two desired.
By this sequential method, he should always remain serene.
Somaśarman, whose nature was virtuous, would worship his parents;
yet his father, being cruel, would call Somaśarman and revile him.

In the presence of sages, he would constantly strike his son with censured and harsh words, saying: "O defiler of the lineage, you have not done what is beneficial for me; though you have performed meritorious deeds, they were done only for the sake of your own ends. (30)
With such various kinds of harsh and painful words, Śivaśarman, who was always distressed, struck him with blows of his staff; yet, even when this was done,
the righteous-souled one did not become angry at all.
Being ever content through the threefold means of mind, speech, and action, he should likewise worship his father;
in that same manner, Somaśarman indeed worshipped his mother day after day.
Having known this, Śivaśarman beholds his own conduct [as follows]:
"Even nectar was brought for my sake by Viṣṇuśarman;
he is endowed with merit, a righteous soul, and always devoted to his father. (34-35)
When a great deal of time, numbering hundreds of years, had passed in this manner, Śivaśarman also, seeing his devotion and reflecting upon it as something inconceivable,
said to his excellent son named Yajña: "Indeed, this was previously stated by me."
"O son, cast these fragments of my mother here and there;
by that, my word shall be fulfilled and compassion shown toward your mother.
This is but a very slight suffering for one who desires to strike down the lifeless. (37-38)
I consider that act of violence committed by his son Vedaśarman to be even greater than this, because he did not waver for even a moment; indeed,
he would commit such violence again in the blink of an eye.
Furthermore, his power arising from austerity, which is perfected by truth,
is seen to be ever-increasing even through constant propitiation; therefore, an examination of his austerity was conducted at this opportune time.

Because of his state of devotion, even though he was real, the son did not perish; yet, through his illusory power (māyā), leprosy was manifested even upon his own body. Furthermore, he felt no disgust for phlegm, urine, or impurities.
The highly illustrious one constantly cleansed his own wounds with his own hand;
the great-minded one provided him with foot-massage and performed acts of purification, always enduring my unbearable and harsh words. 43–44.
Though he was always addressed with threats and blows, my high-minded son spoke only what was pleasing;
"By the grace of Viṣṇu, I shall take away this suffering.
Having reflected thus in his mind, the highly intelligent Brahmin Śivaśarman then performed an illusion so that the water was drawn back from the jar. 46-47.
Afterwards, having summoned Somaśarman, he said to him:
"I have given you the nectar that destroys disease;
give it back to me quickly so that I may drink it."
"By the grace of Viṣṇuśarman, may I become free from disease this very day.
When these words had been spoken by the sage Śivaśarman, Somaśarman rose up with haste and took his water-pot.

Seeing him thus empty and deprived of the nectar, Somaśarman became filled with anxiety and deeply distressed, wondering: "By whose sin was this done? By whom has such an unpleasant act been committed? (51)
"When I recount this account in the presence of my father,
then my preceptor, afflicted by disease, will fall into a rage.
Having reflected for a long time, the highly intelligent Somaśarman [spoke thus].
If there is truth in these words, if I have served my gurus,
and if austerity was previously practiced by me with a sincere heart; if truth, dharma, self-restraint, purity, and so forth were indeed protected by me— 54.
"Then this jar shall undoubtedly become filled with nectar"—
having thought thus, O highly fortunate one, as he looked, the jar once again became full of nectar. 55-56.
Seeing this, the highly illustrious Somaśarman, filled with joy,
went to his preceptor, paid his respects, and quickly took the jar, saying:
"O father, please accept this jar of milk that has arrived."
"O highly fortunate one, you shall soon be freed from this great disease.
Having heard these words—highly meritorious, truthful, meaningful, and sweet-syllabled—from his son, Śivaśarman [replied]. 58–59.
Overcome with great joy, he spoke these words.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Śivaśarman," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Five.
Śivaśarman said: "O good son, I am pleased with you today because of your austerity, self-restraint, purity, service to your guru, as well as your devotion and sincere disposition."
"Abandon this deformed appearance and receive happiness from me. Having spoken thus to his son, the Brahmin revealed that body;
he saw his parents standing exactly as they had been before.
Both of those great-souled ones were radiant, resembling the orb of the sun; with true devotion, he bowed at the feet of both those high-minded beings.
Then, filled with great joy, he addressed his son.
By the grace of Viṣṇu, that virtuous soul, together with his wife, went to Keśava through his own merits and the practice of yoga;
having entered the abode of Viṣṇu, that sage attained the state that is so difficult to reach.
That state which grants liberation is not attained through other merits or austerities;
Madhusūdana is seen only through meditations upon Viṣṇu, renunciation, contemplation, knowledge, hymns of praise, as well as gifts and pilgrimages to sacred fords.
Through the yoga of meditative concentration and knowledge, the supreme state is perceived,
just as a great yogi, O Brahmin, has entered the body of Viṣṇu.
Sūta said:

Then, the highly resplendent Somaśarman performed penance there; he regarded gold and ornaments as equal to stones and clods of earth. Having conquered his appetite, that righteous-souled one was entirely devoid of sleep.

Having abandoned all sense-objects, he resorts even to solitude (10). Seated upon a yogic posture, free from desire and without possessions— for him who has reached the time of death at its appointed hour— this [is the state] (11).
When the time of death arrived for Somaśarman, who had lived a life sustained by the practice of taking only what was offered and who subsisted on the bare necessities of life,
he went into the presence of [his teacher] at the great sacred field of Śāligrāma, which increases the merit of sages.
"Some are Daityas," others said, "Some are Dānavas.
Such a great clamor then reached the ear-cavities of that very best of brahmins, Somaśarman, after a long time. 14.
The fear born of the Daityas entered him who was absorbed in knowledge and meditation; yet, by that very meditation, his life-breaths departed swiftly due to that fear of the Daitya. 15.
And thus, the life-force of that great-souled one quickly passed away.
Overcome by fear of the Daityas, he fell under the power of death. Therefore, born in the house of the Daitya as the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu,
he was slain by the wielder of the discus in the great war between the gods and the Asuras.
Even by that high-souled Prahlāda, while engaged in battle,
the nature of Vāsudeva was clearly perceived, endowed with the universal form (viśvarūpa).
Through his previous practice of yoga, knowledge had already been attained by that great soul.
He recollected the entire previous life of Śivaśarman:
"Formerly, I was named Somaśarman; having entered this demonic body, when shall I [attain] from this body that pure and supreme abode? (19-20)

"By means of great merits known as knowledge, we shall go to that which bestows liberation; this was previously contemplated by the high-souled Prahlāda while he was dying in battle. O best of the twice-born, let this be heard. (21)
Thus has been narrated that which destroys all doubt.
Sūta said:
When Prahlāda had been slain in battle by the god of gods, the wielder of the discus, [the story continues].
That passionate woman, whose son had been slain, wept alone like a lotus-stalk.
But Prahlāda’s mother, the beloved wife of Hiraṇyakaśipu,
grieved day and night with great sorrow for Prahlāda.
To that illustrious Kamalā, devoted to her husband and dear to him,
who was weeping day and night, Nārada spoke:
"Do not grieve, O illustrious one, O partaker of merit, for the sake of a son."
"Your son, slain by Vāsudeva, shall return;
moreover, your high-minded son shall again be endowed with his own characteristic marks, and his name shall once more be Prahlāda. (26-27)
Deprived of asuric dispositions and endowed with divinity,
O auspicious one, you rejoice in the state of Indra, saluted by all the gods. O highly fortunate one, may you always be happy through that son indeed.
"O Goddess, this excellent secret must not be disclosed by you to anyone;
you should always keep it well-hidden from those who are ignorant.
Having spoken thus, Nārada, the best of sages, departed. 29–30.
Furthermore, O Brahmins, there was the birth from the womb of Kamalā;
his name was Prahlāda, and this is the narrative of that great-souled one.
Having reached the state of childhood, O sages, he meditated only upon Kṛṣṇa.
By the grace of Narasiṃha, he shall become a king of gods in heaven; having attained divinity, he shall reach the unsurpassed station of Indra,
and with his self consisting of knowledge, he shall go to liberation— the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.

"O best of the twice-born, all these numerous and immeasurable states of existence within creation have been described to you exactly as you asked; indeed, such delusion must not be entertained by high-souled men possessed of knowledge. (34)
"Ask another, O illustrious one; I shall dispel your doubt.
For the victory of the gods and the great destruction of the dānavas was indeed accomplished by the God of Gods, who established the three worlds. (35-36)
The sages said:
O Indra, from whom was this name born, which sustains the title of the gods?
By whom was it given? Tell us in detail, O best of the twice-born. (37)
Sūta said:
O best of beings, I shall relate in detail how this highly fortunate one attained [this state] through most meritorious means. 38.
When all those Daityas had been slain in that great battle and the wicked ones utterly destroyed by the high-souled Govinda,
then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Nāgas, and Vidyādharas, [rejoiced].
Then, with palms joined in reverence, they all spoke to Mādhava:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Hṛṣīkeśa, salutations to you!
We make this request of you; please attend to all of this."
O Keśava of the Kurus, you are our teacher, protector, and meritorious soul;
you are the king of merit and dharma, Indra, and the ruler of the world.
By taking refuge in you, the lord of the three worlds and the god of progeny, one may obtain happiness. 42.
Vāsudeva said:
O illustrious one, endowed with Vaiṣṇava splendor,
that best of brāhmaṇas has been made to dwell for a long time in my world.
O best of gods, the time for that great-souled brahmin, my devotee who dwelt in my world, was fully completed;
indeed, he became your protector through the very splendor of Viṣṇu. 44–45.
He will be a soul of true dharma and a delighter in the dharma; he will be a protector and a sustainer, that best of Brahmins.
He will be a soul of true dharma for the sake of being a refuge for you all.
And the son of Āditya, the high-minded one named Suvrata,
who possesses great strength and great heroism, shall indeed become Indra.
Sūta said:
O Lord of the Gods, having thus granted these supreme boons to the gods,
all the victorious deities, together with Viṣṇu, then went to see their father Kaśyapa and their mother. 48-49.
Those two high-souled ones, seated comfortably, were saluted by them;
and all, filled with great joy, spoke with palms joined in reverence:
"By your grace, indeed, we have attained divinity."
Overcome with great joy, he addressed these words to the gods.
Kaśyapa said:
"Indeed, you always abide by the dharma of truth."
"By our grace and through the power of your asceticism, you have attained divinity and the imperishable state. Filled with great affection, I grant them this boon. (52-53)
"O great Asuras, by my grace you shall become immortal, ageless, and indeed imperishable; your every desire fulfilled and endowed with all perfections, you shall become gods, nāgas, and gandharvas."
Viṣṇu said:
"Choose a boon, O auspicious one, O illustrious daughter of a god; whatever is desired by your mind, all that I shall certainly grant you."
Aditi said: "O Mādhava, by your grace, I have previously become possessed of sons—
immortals, free from decay, imperishable, and devoted to merit."
O Madhusūdana, hear how these sons were obtained by me through illness; and you especially, O Govinda, are the granter of the fulfillment of all desires.
You have dwelt within my womb, and you are the delighter of my heart. 57–58.
"O Keśava, just as you always fulfill the desires of Nandā, so too, O Lord, fulfill this great aspiration of yours through me, your son.
Vāsudeva said:
"For the sake of the work of the gods, you must descend into a human body;
then I shall certainly enter your womb when the twelfth age has arrived, in order to remove the burden of the earth."
"O Goddess, the son of Jamadagni, a supreme brahmin named Rāma,
endowed with prowess and splendor for the sake of slaying all the kṣatriyas,
shall become your son— the best among all wielders of weapons. (61-62)
O devoted wife, when the age known as Tretā arrives within the twenty-seventh cycle, I shall become your son, named Rāma;
listen further, O you who possess a store of merit, for I shall indeed become your son once again.
When the twenty-eighth [cycle] arrives at the end of the Dvāpara Yuga,
I shall undoubtedly become your son, known as Vāsudeva, for the sake of destroying all the Daityas and for removing the burden of the earth.

Now, O Goddess, having given birth to a beautiful son who is omniscient, endowed with all auspicious marks, and possessed of truth and righteousness, fulfill my words which are joined with dharma. 66.
"O Indra, I shall give you that; O Indra, he shall become a drinker of Soma.
Having heard these words spoken thus, she was filled with great joy, thinking, "By the grace of the God of gods, a son shall be born to Indra."
"O illustrious one, let it be so; I shall do as you say.
Then all those deities departed for their own abodes, filled with joy and free from fear, together with Hari.
Sūta said:
Having reached her season, the wise Aditi spoke to Kaśyapa:
"O Blessed One, let a son be granted who shall enjoy the position of the Lord of the Gods."
Having reflected for a moment, the brahmin spoke to that high-minded woman:
"So be it, O illustrious lady; you shall have a son who will be the creator of even the three worlds and the enjoyer of sacrifices."
Placing his hand upon her head, that best of the twice-born, radiant and endowed with truth and righteousness, performed austerities;
that glorious one named Suvrata shall dwell forever in the world of Viṣṇu.
O best of the twice-born, when his merit was exhausted, he fell from the world of Viṣṇu by the power of karma; thereafter, O best of the twice-born,
that Brahmin of great asceticism entered the meritorious womb of Aditi.

O Indra, for the sake of desiring to enjoy [the fruit], that goddess indeed conceived a child through the power of truthful merit and virtuous action; having gone to dwell in the forest, she performed penance without any indolence. (76)
A hundred divine years passed while the Mother of the Gods was performing her penance.
Then, as she performed that intense and difficult austerity, which is hard even for gods and asuras to achieve,
she became endowed with splendor through that asceticism and that radiant energy.
Resembling the splendor of the sun, she shone like a second sun, established in supreme meditation; at that time,
she attained even greater beauty through the power of her asceticism.
Then that ascetic lady, devoted to austerity and meditation, subsisting on air alone,
shone even more brilliantly than Dakṣa’s daughter.
All the Siddhas, the Ṛṣis, and the gods of great majesty were likewise filled with wonder.
They praised that illustrious lady and protected her with great devotion;
when a hundred years were complete, Viṣṇu arrived there.
He spoke to that illustrious Aditi, who was endowed with ascetic fervor.
The divine embryo is fully developed, and the time for birth is approaching.
Nourished by your very penance and increased by your splendor, release this fetus this very day, O illustrious lady! 83-84.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the Gods departed for his own abode;
and when the time of great prosperity had arrived, that goddess gave birth to a son,
a child endowed with radiance like a second sun.
He was fortunate, with beautiful limbs in every part, endowed with all auspicious marks;
he had four arms and a massive body, was the guardian of the world and lord of the gods, filled with the blaze of splendor, and held a discus and a lotus in his excellent hands. 86–87.
The high-minded one shone with a face resembling the orb of the moon,
endowed with great wisdom and the splendor of Viṣṇu,
and adorned with other divine marks and celestial qualities. 88.

Then those three gods, the sages who have mastered the Vedas, the Gandharvas, the Nāgas, the Siddhas, and likewise the Vidyādharas, arrived [before him] who was endowed with all auspicious marks, moon-like in appearance, and lotus-eyed. (89-90)
The seven divine sages of ancient times and great prowess,
as well as other holy munis who bestow merit and auspiciousness—
those high-souled ones arrived with their minds overflowing with joy.
When that illustrious and highly energetic one was born,
all the blessed deities arrived, as did the mountains, the ascetics, all the oceans beginning with the Ocean of Milk, and likewise the pure rivers. 92–93.
Then all of them, as well as all other beings, both mobile and immobile, and all the lords of the gods, being full of joy, celebrated with auspicious rites and great enthusiasm.
The throngs of Apsaras danced and the Gandharvas sang charmingly.
Then the gods and the Brāhmaṇas who had mastered the Vedas praised that high-souled son of Kaśyapa with Vedic mantras.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the Vedas themselves all assembled there.
O best of men, when that one of great luster was born, all beings in the three worlds who were endowed with merit assembled there together with their limbs and sub-limbs. 97.
When he of great luster was born, they gathered right there.
All performed auspicious rites with meritorious songs and great festivals.
Overwhelmed with joy, all those of great luster—Brahmā and the other three gods, as well as Kaśyapa and Bṛhaspati—offered worship. 98-99.
The karmic actions of that very same Great-Souled One were named Cakrin;
he was renowned as Vasudatta, and again, O son of Vasudeva, his name was Ākhaṇḍala, and furthermore, he was called Marutvān. 100.
You are Maghavan, Bṛhaspati, and Pākaśāsana;
you are also renowned as Śakra and Indra—these, O son, are the names of that very same Great Soul. 101–102.
All the deities, satisfied and joyful in their minds, caused the great asura to perform his ablutions and the purificatory rites;
having summoned Viśvakarman, they gave him ornaments.
Those divine merits were bestowed upon that great-souled one.
When that illustrious and high-minded Devarāja was born, all the gods of great power attained such joy. 104-105.

On an auspicious lunar day, under a favorable constellation and at a propitious moment, he was installed as Indra by the high-souled gods and consecrated with most auspicious rites. By the grace of that wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu), the station of Indra was attained by him.
The radiant Vasudatta, the lord of the gods, performed austerities,
endowed with fierce splendor and armed with the thunderbolt, the noose, and the goad.
Sūta said:
Beholding the entire power of his formidable austerity, Śukra spoke this verse:
"In the worlds, there shall be no other such as he; for he is indeed most beautiful to behold.
By the grace of Viṣṇu, this great-souled one has attained supreme divine sovereignty right here. (109-110)
"There shall be no one else in the worlds equal to him in the gravity of his ascetic power.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Coronation of Indra" in the Devāsura section of the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Six.
Sūta said:
There was another wife of Kaśyapa named Danu, an ascetic woman who, tormented by grief for her son, arrived at the abode of Aditi. 1.
Then, weeping and bowing down to his pair of lotus feet, Diti was overcome with great sorrow; Aditi then enlightened her.
Diti said:
"O illustrious lady, what is this cause for your weeping?
O daughter, noble women indeed become honored in the world by having even one son; you, O beautiful woman, possess even a hundred virtuous sons."
"O auspicious lady, you are the mother of the high-souled Śumbha and the others;
tell me the reason why this suffering has been experienced by you.
King Hiraṇyakaśipu and the very powerful Hiraṇyākṣa—"

"Since great suffering has arisen for you, whose two sons are high-souled and possessed of great strength and prowess, tell us the truth of that matter. Tell us the entire reason why this misfortune has now befallen you."
Having thus addressed the goddess, the high-minded Danu ceased speaking.
Danu said:
"Behold, behold, O highly fortunate one, the desire of your co-wife!"
That has been fully accomplished by that God of gods, the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu).
Just as in the past a boon was granted to Aditi by Viṣṇu, O Goddess, so now a great boon has been granted to his son.

From Kaśyapa was born a son renowned as the protector of the three worlds; O Indra, you were given to him by him, having been taken away from your own son. Thus Aditi, her desires fulfilled, experienced an increase in happiness.
Her youngest son, Vasudatta, now enjoys the station of Indra, which is so difficult even for the gods to attain. Diti said:
"O friend, why has my son Mahāmati fallen from his station? And how is it that the other Dānavas and Daityas have also been deprived of their splendor?
O illustrious one, tell me the cause of this in detail."
Having addressed her with these words, Diti, deeply distressed, fell silent;
Danu then spoke:
"All the gods and all the dānavas have gone to battle, filled with wrath. (14)
There a great battle took place, causing the destruction of the Daityas;
in that war with the gods and Viṣṇu, my sons were struck down. In the same way, those sons of yours were slain by the Discus-wielder, the God of gods.
Just as a lion dwelling in the forest roars by its own splendor,
so too have my sons slain that army led by Kālanemi— which was difficult for even gods and asuras to conquer— by the hand of Śaṅkhapāṇi. 16–17.
Just as fire consumes all the grass in a forest with its own flames— destroying, crushing, rending,
and disintegrating it— so too does Keśava utterly incinerate all the hosts of Daityas. 18.
O Goddess, my sons, the many Nandanas, have repeatedly been destroyed;
just as all moths meet their end upon reaching fire, so too have all those Dānavas met their destruction upon reaching Hari. 19–20.
Diti heard this dreadful account;
Diti said: "O blessed lady, how is it that you speak thus to me, like the falling of a thunderbolt?"
Having spoken thus to the queen, she fell down unconscious;
"Alas! Alas! This calamity has occurred, a source of great suffering and torment.
Then, deeply afflicted by grief for her son, she wept piteously.
Seeing her, those two best of sages spoke these auspicious words:
"Do not weep, O blessed one; for it is such as you—beings of great fortune, free from greed and delusion—who grieve in this manner. (23-24)
O sons of Kaśyapa, for an atheist in this saṃsāra, there is no goddess, no good kinsman, or anything else at all; hear all of that, O beloved.
You are the daughters of Dakṣa, beautiful ones, and likewise my own kin.

"O auspicious one, I am your husband, the fulfiller of your desires; O fair-faced one, I am your uniter, your protector, and your guardian. Why has enmity been waged against me by these cruel asuras who have not conquered their own selves? (26-27)
O highly fortunate one, your sons were devoid of truth and righteousness;
therefore, O auspicious lady, they have all been slain by Vāsudeva through that fault of theirs and indeed through your own fault, having been struck down by the gods.
Therefore, one should not give way to grief, for it destroys truth and liberation.
Indeed, grief destroys merit, and through the exhaustion of merit, one perishes;
therefore, O fair-faced one, abandon grief, which is the very form of an obstacle.
"By the power of their own faults, the Dānavas have met their death;
even the gods, though acting as mere instruments, were destroyed by their own karma.
Knowing this, O highly fortunate one, proceed toward happiness."

Having spoken thus to his beloved wife Tārā, who was sharing in her sorrow, that great yogi of vast intellect turned away from his despondency and ceased speaking. Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Lamentation of Diti," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The Seventh Chapter. Diti said: "O Lord, everything you have spoken is true; there is no doubt at all."
"O twice-born one, having abandoned my love for my husband due to the rivalry with a co-wife,
and being tormented by pride, sorrow, the loss of honor,
and great suffering, O best of men, I shall now release my life-breaths."
Kaśyapa said:
"Listen, I shall declare how peace will come to pass; for no one is anyone's son, nor mother, nor father, O auspicious lady. (3)
To whom is there no brother, no kinsman, nor any relatives?
Thus is the connection in saṃsāra, permeated by illusion and delusion.
O Goddess, one is oneself the father, oneself the mother, and oneself the kinsmen.

One's own kinsmen and one's own eternal dharma [are the true wealth]. O Goddess, through right conduct a person attains happiness; likewise, through misconduct and sin, one certainly meets with destruction. 5-6.

O Goddess, there is no doubt that a man thus goes to a cruel womb due to his delusion, having committed great sins through actions devoid of truth; such a mortal remains eternally established as an enemy toward all living beings.
Enemies will undoubtedly be present wherever he goes;
O beautiful lady, when a mortal conducts himself with friendliness toward the world, dear and auspicious ones, then friends will surely arise for him everywhere, O noble woman.
O Goddess, just as a farmer who has sown well-placed and well-covered seed reaps a fruit exactly corresponding to its nature,
so too have you and your virtuous sons vied with one another.
"Enjoy that well-established fruit of that karma which has come to you. O highly fortunate one, because your sons were devoid of austerity and tranquility,
they have all fallen from their great position due to that sin."
Knowing this, attain tranquility and abandon both suffering and pleasure; for whom are sons, friends, kinsmen, and relatives? Living beings live according to their own past actions. (13)
O Goddess, the wise who know the truth do not engage in thinking for the sake of others in vain;
there is no doubt about this.
They [know] that the body, composed of the five elements, is merely a collection of decaying joints. 14–15.

O Goddess, he has made himself his own friend for the sake of all happiness; he is the Great Merit (Mahāpuṇya), the All-pervading, and the Seer of All. He is the Success of All, the Soul of All, the Pure Being (Sāttvika), and the Giver of All Success. 16.
Thus, O Goddess, the one who is stainless wanders, consisting of all things.
O best of the twice-born, as he wanders in his formless state, four embodied beings—auspicious, possessed of great luster, and endowed with form—were manifested by him. 17–18.
The fifth was Śvasana, and Mitra was among the eastern ones;
then the Self arrived, providing assistance through knowledge. Having seen the virtuous ones, the Great-Souled One spoke to Knowledge and the Self.
"O Jñāna, go and ask those five who are consulting with one another, 'Who are you? Having heard these supreme words of the Great-Souled One, Jñāna understood their meaning. (20–21)
Then the Self said: "Why do you seek to propitiate me?
Tell me truly, O God; you are eternally pure at all times. (22) The Self spoke.

"O highly fortunate ones, these men are handsome and wise; having gone there, I shall show them to you. Let this knowledge be heard as it is spoken. I shall describe these auspicious beings who have attained the fifth state."
"Go on a mission as a messenger, O wise one, skilled in the duties of an envoy.
Jñāna replied, "O Self, listen to my words; I speak what is true, truly true."
"O dear one, you must never have contact with these five, O pure-souled one who desires what is auspicious;
for this [demon], O high-minded one, seeks your company out of delusion. (25-26)
The Self said:
"O wise one, tell me truly the reason why you prevent my association with these. (27)
Jñāna said:
"From the mere company of these, great suffering will arise; for these five are indeed the roots of misery, causing grief and torment. (28)
"So be it, O one of great wisdom; I shall do your bidding. Having spoken thus, Kaśyapa, endowed with knowledge, remained united with his own self through meditation. Kaśyapa said:
Then those five indeed saw that very Self there;
having summoned the intellect, they said to it: "O auspicious one, go to the Self itself and perform the duty of a messenger for us."
"The five great-souled ones, the auspicious sustainers of the universe, desire friendship with you. Having spoken thus to the high-minded one, he said:
"Having gone and understood [the situation], you must act; do not go further from here."
"So be it, O illustrious one; I shall perform this supreme task.
Having been addressed thus by them, he went and said to himself:
"O illustrious one, I am Intelligence (Buddhi), and I have come to you."
As their messenger, listen to the words from the presence of those great ones: "The five whose nature is the Self desire eternal friendship with you;
O one of great wisdom, establish friendship with the Kurus and cast away all anxiety far behind. (34-35)
Dhyāna said: "O Ātmā, you must not associate with these;
by merely coming into contact with them, great suffering will surely arise. (36)

"Deprived of my command, how will you perform your duty? You must not act in this way, nor should you have such an association with them; O Lord, they will lead you to dwell in a womb, and not otherwise."
"Deprived of knowledge by me alone, you will certainly go to ignorance. Having spoken thus to that high-minded one, the Self became silent.
Then the Self, being resolute, spoke to that Intellect which had approached Him.
"My two ministers, Jñāna and Dhyāna, who are high-souled and auspicious, are not fit for that vehicle;
therefore, O Buddhi, what shall I do?
Having heard this, the illustrious Buddhi then approached them.
He related that entire account of knowledge and meditation.
Then all those five [disciples] returned to themselves, saying,
"We indeed always accept only loving-kindness from you."
"Since you are pure, O Lord of the World, we have come to you;
having reflected upon this yourself, please grant us an answer. 43.
The Self said:
"You five have arrived; do you desire my friendship?
Tell me of your own qualities and power before me.
(44) The Earth said:
The structural arrangement of my entire body consists of skin and flesh,
with bones as its firm foundation, and is provided with nails and hair; O one of great wisdom, such is indeed the majesty within my very form.
The high-minded servant [said]: "O Gandharva, I am the one who goes to the nose. Ākāśa said: "I have arrived as the space within my body, possessing its power."
Listen, for I shall describe Him whose nature is the Supreme Brahman.
(47) I am like the void in the space both outside and within;
there, my two ministers, Tarkakarna and Ishravas, are stationed for the purpose of hearing. (48)
Vāyu said:
"I abide in five forms and thus perform both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Residing within the body of skin, O King, I experience the quality of touch."
Teja said:
"Residing constantly within the body, I always perform the process of digestion;
I manifest every substance, both internal and external, as one substance after another."
I send forth semen, marrow, saliva, and likewise that which resides in the skin and the joints;
I send forth blood as well, for I am stationed within the center of the body. Therein, the two eyes are my ministers, and the penis is the achiever of my purpose.
Thus, my supreme personal service has been described before you.
Water said:
"I shall constantly satisfy your body with nectar."
"Thus, O beloved, my function is in the city of the body (the nose). Know the minister to be the tongue, the supreme enjoyer of flavors.
Then the Nose spoke: [53]
"I shall also bring supreme nourishment to her body with fragrance;
having cast off its foul odor, I shall manifest a scent upon the body.
O noble one, she is endowed with intelligence and is permeated by that [fragrance]."
"I abide motionless within this body for the sake of my master's work;
know that fragrance, which is my quality, is twofold as it is set forth.
Śravaṇā and Śravantī said:

We shall hear the words spoken by people regarding what is to be done and what is not to be done, whether auspicious or inauspicious, true or false, pleasant or unpleasant—all while remaining within our own bodies.
For sound is said to be my attribute; it is indeed my very function.
"I shall unite them; there is no doubt when the intellect becomes fully perfected.
Tvak said:
"The wind, consisting of five forms, is established within this body. (58-59)
I know their activities truly, both external and internal:
cold, heat, sunshine, rain, and even the vibration of the wind;
I know every touch and the contact of men through their embrace and so forth.
"Touch alone is my quality; I tell you this as the truth. Thus indeed was his function explained by me. Then the two eyes spoke:
O best of beings, the forms in saṃsāra—whether belonging to those capable of liberation or incapable—are seen by the intellect when it is directed toward them, and not otherwise.
Dwell within the body; here, we two possess a form characterized by the guṇas.
O Mahāmati, in this way, the connection with activity within the body is such that the tongue, joined with the intellect, investigates the distinctions of egoity and its flavors. 64

I shall contemplate all things, such as alkaline and sour substances, as being tasteless; even through this activity, I remain eternally absorbed in equanimity. For this intellect is indeed the leader of all the senses.
Thus, O beloved, hear how the five senses arrived; they repeatedly declared their own respective functions. Then, the Intellect (Buddhi) arrived and spoke to that high-minded one.
"When the body is deprived of me, it perishes; it is not otherwise.
Therefore, O high-minded one, sustain yourself by taking recourse to me.
Then, the Self, having arrived through the power of karma, spoke as follows:
"I send you, who have come to the side of the Great-Wisdom Self (Mahāprājña-tattva), along that very path by which you have come here. Having heard all this, the Self spoke to them as follows.

"You yourselves are indeed possessed of the five elements and are common to all; why then do you desire friendship toward those who likewise consist of the five elements? Let everyone state the reason for this before me."
The five elements said:
"By association with our union, the physical body (piṇḍa) alone is produced;
in that body, O one of great intelligence, you dwell as one of excellent vows."
"Indeed, we all remain here by your grace;
for this reason, O Maitra, we desire your constant favor. Thus spoke the Self (Ātman).
"So be it, O highly fortunate one! I shall do exactly what is pleasing to you; there is no doubt in this, for friendship arises from affection.
Thus was the highly fortunate one addressed, even though he was being restrained by the high-souled one through his wisdom. 74–75.
And through his meditation, O Sūta, that Great-Souled One attained union with them;
deluded there by them through passion, hatred, and the like,
the Lord then assumed a physical body composed of the five elements.
When he has entered the womb, which is filled with feces and urine, fallen into a foul-smelling, slippery whirlpool, and joined with those [elements],
his body becomes agitated and his speech follows the nature of the five elements.
"O all you fivefold elements, listen to my words!
Bewildered by the great suffering arising from your association, I have fallen here into this slippery, terrible, and most fearsome place. (79)
The five elements said:
"O King, let it remain thus until the fetus is fully developed;
after that, your departure will certainly take place, there is no doubt."
"For you are our master, established in the land of Kāya.
The kingdom must be governed in this manner, and you shall become an enjoyer of happiness.
Having heard those words of theirs, he was tormented by grief. 81–82.
Desiring to depart from there, he became intent on flight. 83.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Account of the Bodies of the Lord of the Gods and the Asuras," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Eight.
Kaśyapa said:
"The virtuous soul became distressed while in the womb, suffering day by day;
overcome by sorrow, he was indeed tormented by every kind of pain."
Facing downward within the womb, bound by a web of delusion, overcome by mental and physical ailments, crying out "Alas!", he was rendered unconscious;
possessed by great suffering and tormented, he spoke with knowledge.
The Self said:
"O one of great wisdom, although your words were then disregarded by me, even as I was being restrained by meditation, I have fallen into the peril of delusion."
Therefore, from this most dreadful dwelling in the womb, O highly wise one,
I have spoken this knowledge to you; for I have indeed restrained you, yet you did not heed my words.
"By these five-fold, most cruel beings, you have been cast into the peril of the womb.
Now, go into meditation; from that you shall obtain happiness.
There will be liberation for you from dwelling in the womb; of this there is no doubt."
Having heard those words of his and having understood the true nature of ignorance, Dhyāna summoned him and said: "Listen to my words.
I have come to you for refuge; O Dhyāna, protect me always."
"O one of great wisdom, may it be so; I am the Great Intelligence (Mahāmati) who consists of meditation.
Having heard these words, he then attained the meditation of the Self (Ātmā);
for by means of that meditation, while remaining in the womb, he was freed from delusion.
For when the self has entered into deep meditation, the fear born of the womb is forgotten;
there, accompanied by both [the breaths], the self is freed from delusion (10),
constantly contemplating only the bliss that is the very nature of the self.
Immediately upon emerging from here, he cast off his five-fold body.
While the Lord was thus constantly reflecting, O fair-faced one, the time for birth arrived according to the ordinance of Prajāpati.
When the embryo is moved by the powerful vital wind (prāṇa),
the birth canal then expands to twenty-four finger-breadths;
when it reaches twenty-five finger-breadths, the embryo experiences pain due to that pressure.
Thus being tormented, O beloved, he fainted and fell upon the ground; yet, endowed with knowledge and meditation,
he was sustained by the divine wind of Prajāpati.
Upon the mere touch of the [lower] stages, knowledge and meditation were forgotten;
the self remained enveloped by the bonds of saṃsāra and shrouded in doubt, possessed by great delusion and overcome by both virtues and defects. 16.
Day after day, he desires all things such as food and drink. Thus, being nourished by these fivefold elements, the self is pervaded by all the senses and by objects that produce sin. 17–18.
O Goddess, through the delusion regarding kinsmen and likewise regarding his wife and others, he becomes increasingly agitated and distressed day by day.
Ensnared in the web of delusion, the lord is rendered bewildered by great infatuation.
Just as a fish caught by a fisherman is bound by nets and is not at all able to move, so too was the Self bound;
it was fettered by all those nets of delusion with very firm bonds. 20–21.
Thus, pervaded by such manifold elaborations, he is indeed deprived of both wisdom (*jñāna*) and discernment (*vijñāna*), struck down by passion, hatred, and the like;
he is likewise tormented by desire or by anger itself. (22)
By his very nature, through his actions, he became bound and was born as one who is utterly deluded.
Sūta said:
Thus, when that self is deluded, it falls under the sway of desire and anger.
Entangled by all those evil-natured things such as greed, passion, and the rest,
he is bound by this great delusion— the web of saṃsāra— thinking, "This is my wife, this is my son, this is my friend, this is my home. (24-25)
Then, agitated by various sufferings such as grief for his son,
and likewise seized by old age, diseases, and mental afflictions, his self was thus tormented by most dreadful miseries and delusions. (26)

Shattered by overweening pride, the loss of honor, and various miseries (27), and likewise afflicted by old age and infirmity, O Goddess, he constantly broods on his suffering, crying out "Alas! Alas! until he loses consciousness. (28)

O Goddess, day after day, one sees dreams at night and is devoid of consciousness during the day; thus, while wandering through the cycle of existence, one is pervaded by the impairment of the limbs [of the senses], and therein dispassion is revealed. 29.
To him—who was fearless, friendless, tranquil, and contented, and who was free from desire and anger—he then spoke:
"Who are you, appearing in the form of a naked mendicant; why do you not feel shame before your friends?"
"Since there are women here— old and young, as well as mothers—
you who are unclad do not fear passing into their midst.
Vītarāga said:
Who indeed could be seen here naked?
For even when one is well-restrained and fully clothed, one is never truly naked; O divine one, you appear naked because you are not naked. 33.133-34a.
Subservient to the power of the senses and objects and devoid of all restraint, he spoke thus: "O observer of excellent vows, tell me, what is the limit for a person?"
"If you, O one of great wisdom, know for certain, please explain in detail.
To him, the one of great intelligence, who was free from passion and possessed of great wisdom, replied:
"The mind always maintains firm stability amidst both pleasure and pain. (35-36)
One should abandon all those things that cause affliction in various circumstances;
now I shall speak of shame—that by which the mind is thoroughly restrained.
"I must not act thus today, standing naked and deprived of a place."
One who is consumed by remorse is called "ashamed," yet he is said to be devoid of shame.
To whom should one feel shame? There is always no second person [to witness]. And there is but one divine person (the Self) who can destroy nothing at all. 38–39.
Now I shall explain the worlds that have been mentioned by you;
just as a potter places a lump of clay upon a wheel,
causes it to revolve with a cord, and manifests various different forms.
Just as one established in his own will might create thousands of vessels according to his desire, so too does this Ordainer (Dhātṛ) create various forms and not otherwise;
subsequently, they meet their destruction for some reason or another.
One must show shame before those who are eternally established and the eternal worlds; they do not return to this earth. Space, wind, fire, earth, and water as the fifth—
These worlds shine forth, established everywhere.
These five are well-established within the limbs and regions of living beings; they exist everywhere—of whom should shame be felt? 44-45.
I shall now describe the form of women; listen, O father, at this moment.
Just as a single moon shines everywhere amidst thousands of water-filled jars, so do you shine. 46.
O Great-souled One, you have passed through thousands of births within the wheel of delusion;
likewise, O Bhava, you have entered through the door of the womb by means of sin consisting of the delusion of Māyā. 47–48.
She shines with her breasts, her hips, and her youth; indeed, an excessive growth of the flesh of the heart is seen here, without a doubt.
This form of delusion has been displayed for the downfall of the worlds.
That which you have proclaimed as "womanhood" does not exist at all.
For the sake of his own diversion, the Creator fashions it through his play;
just as there is womanhood, so too is the male soul situated everywhere. 50-51.
Those who are devoid of the womb of a woman are indeed always liberated while living; for a man is called *puruṣa*, while a woman is said to be *prakṛti*.
He truly delights with her [only when] liberated, never otherwise.
"You are seen among men as one joined with Prakṛti. Knowing this, who would feel shame toward whom? Go happily.
O fair-faced one, I shall speak of an aged woman who is always aged. (53-54)
O fair-faced one, even though her body had reached a state of decay through old age,
she was covered with white hair and grey locks; she was then devoid of strength, wretched, and overspread with wrinkles.

This woman would not be old, yet she is called "the Old One" (Vṛddhā). Her characteristic has been declared; now I shall describe the Young Woman (Yuvati), who dwells constantly by the side of the Jīva and increases through knowledge. 56–57.
She is proclaimed by the name Sumati; she is established eternally among all women and men, both old and young.
One must show her respect, and I shall tell you something else as well.
I shall indeed describe that which you have mentioned as the Mother;
she who always resides within the limbs and regions of living beings as consciousness, and who bestows supreme knowledge, is called Prajñā (Wisdom). 59–60.
She who is designated as Prajñāmātā exists for the protection of living beings, for their nourishment, or for their welfare throughout all worlds;
she is proclaimed by me as the Mother named Sumati. 61.
The gates and paths of saṃsāra are constantly appearing in the form of mothers; indeed, these reveal many forms of suffering.
This is declared to be the "mother-form"; what else shall I tell you?
The Self said:
"Who are you that have come here to destroy my torment? Tell me in detail your own true nature."
The one free from passion said:
"Because they are all devoid of desire, these very actions do not turn them back; due to their wickedness, they do not perceive this, nor is it otherwise. (65)
Hope never approaches his presence, nor do anger, greed, or delusion, for they have perished out of fear of him. "I am free from passion; may you be blessed; discrimination is my kinsman."
The Self said: "What is this brother of yours named Viveka like? O Self, tell me the characteristics of that brother and of yourself as well. (67)
Vītarāgā said:
"O highly fortunate one, I shall not describe his characteristics or form before you; rather, I shall issue a summons to that brother of yours."
"Oho! O brother Viveka, listen to these words of ours.
Come, come, O highly fortunate one, O great-minded one; [I speak] out of affection for me.
Thus spoke Kaśyapa.
Endowed with tranquility and forbearance, he is united with his two wives;
he is all-seeing, all-pervading, and devoted to the supreme reality of all principles.
He is the enemy of all doubts and is affectionate toward those who possess knowledge.
The great-souled Dhāraṇādhiśva had two daughters; his eldest son was Yoga, whose supreme teacher was Mokṣa. He was stainless, free from ego, devoid of expectations, and without possessions.
At all times his soul was serene, he had transcended dualities, and he possessed great intelligence (73). Endowed with discernment, he arrived adorned with the jewels of virtue;
his two high-souled ministers were the great-minded Dharmasatya and Mahāmati (74).
Endowed with patience and tranquility, and possessed of discernment, he who had arrived spoke thus to Vītarāga: "I have come here because I was summoned;
O brother, let the entire reason for this be told before me."
The Vītarāgas said: "O man, you who stand before us constrained by great fetters, it was on account of you that this invitation was made by us this very day. (76)
Confounded by the arrows of delusion and the bonds of saṃsāra,
this very Self of mine— though all-pervading and the Lord— is nevertheless enveloped by the five elements and devoid of knowledge and meditation. 77–78.
"Since you are an expert in the principles of reality, please ask him about this self.
Having heard these words from Vītarāga, Viveka spoke these words.
Viveka said:
"O Lord of the Universe, now that you have arrived, one dwells in happiness; O Deva, what happiness have you yourself experienced within this saṃsāra? (80) The Self said:
O one of great wisdom, I, being devoid of knowledge, have thus always experienced the great suffering of dwelling in the womb—unbearable and terrible;
indeed, having fallen away from knowledge, I have been born again and again within this body. 81.
In my state of childhood, O Lord, I performed both what ought to be done and what ought not to be done; in my youth, I engaged in play and indeed enjoyed many wives;
and having reached old age, I am thus tormented by grief for my sons and other such sorrows.
"O highly wise one, I am consumed day and night by the separations from my wife and others; scorched day after day by manifold sufferings, I find no happiness anywhere, by day or by night. (84)
"Thus intensely tormented by such sufferings, O high-minded one, what shall I do?
Tell me that very means by which I may indeed find happiness; release me today from this flood of the net of saṃsāra and from these firm bonds. (85-86)
Viveka said:
"O Lord of the World, you are pure, free from the pairs of opposites, and sinless; go to this great-souled one who is devoid of passion and bestows happiness. (87)
"Without doubt, you have seen one who is naked and devoid of proper conduct;
for this [state] is indeed the bestower of happiness and the destroyer of all torment.
Having heard this, the pure-souled one again attained freedom from passion (*vītarāga*).
Breathing heavily and dejected, he said to him, "Listen to my words:
show me that path by which I may find happiness. "So be it, O highly wise one; I shall do as you say. 89-90.
"Go back once more to solitude; for you have brought news of happiness, and this [result] shall belong to you as the speaker of the path of bliss.
Thus sent by the virtuous one who is free from passion, the Lord departed.
He spoke to that high-souled Viveka, who was of pure essence:
"Show me happiness, for I have been sent by one free from passion; having come for refuge to you, protect me from the terrible cycle of worldly existence. (92-93)
Viveka said: "O highly wise one, go to Jñāna; he will tell you everything. He who is called the Self has arrived where knowledge is established. 94
"O Knowledge, you of great splendor, who reveals all states of being!
I have come to you for refuge; show me the path to happiness.
Thus spoke Jñāna.

"I am your servant, O Lord of the World; you know me well, O observer of noble vows. Indeed, I previously restrained you again and again through meditation, yet you have fallen into calamity due to association with those consisting of the five elements."
