O one of great wisdom, you are the giver of the limbs of meditation and of happiness.
Since the self has been sent forth by knowledge and remains established by relying upon meditation, show me that meditation which is supremely blissful and perfectly accomplished. 97–98.
"Protect me, who have thus come for refuge to you.
Hearing those words spoken by him, he meditated and, becoming joyful, spoke again to that very self: 99.
"O father, I am certainly not to be abandoned, for I am firmly established in all duties.
Indeed, you yourself, being free from passion and possessed of discernment, should always remain engaged in meditation and behold the Self. (100-101)
Possessing self-mastery, become steady, free from distress, and devoid of conceptual construction;
just as a lamp situated in a windless place remains steady while emitting soot, so too, having burned away all defects, you shall indeed attain nirvāṇa. 102.
Staying in solitude, abstaining from food, and always eating sparingly; free from the pairs of opposites, devoid of sound, and remaining motionless while seated;
meditating upon the Self by means of the self with a mind fixed on me alone. 103–104.
"You shall attain the supreme station, that highest step of Viṣṇu.
(105) Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Inner Self," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Nine.
Kaśyapa said:
Thus enlightened there by means of self-meditation and other practices, that wise one then desired to abandon that fivefold activity.

Seeing only the signs and reaching those [objects], he departs; yet, having abandoned the body, he does not see it as it falls, devoid of characteristics. There is no connection between the vital breath and the body that have grown together.
And for what reason is there attachment to wealth, sons, and wife?
Knowing this, attain tranquility; do not yield to weakness, O beloved.
This alone is the Supreme Brahman; this alone is the eternal.
Abiding among the Daityas and gods in his own essential nature,
he is Brahmā, he is Rudra, and he is indeed the eternal Viṣṇu;
he creates all worlds and he protects all creatures.

This Janārdana, whose nature is both dharma and adharma, withdraws all things; O dear one, by him were the gods and the Dānavas produced. The gods were freed from unrighteousness, while your sons were devoid of dharma.

This is the duty of Mādhava, protected by all the gods at all times; O Goddess, one should contemplate righteousness and indeed protect righteousness. Viṣṇu, whose soul is united with righteousness, is always gracious toward him.
The gods were indeed sustained by righteousness, truth, and austerity. By those for whom Viṣṇu is pleased, dharma is protected here;
for this dharma is the body of Viṣṇu, and truth is his very heart. 9–10.
Viṣṇu is pleased with him who constantly protects truth and righteousness; however, he who would defile truth and righteousness would only foster sin.
Viṣṇu, being exceedingly powerful, would become enraged at him and destroy him.
The Dharma was protected by the Vaiṣṇavas, who were firmly established in austerity and truth. The righteous-souled one (Viṣṇu) was pleased with them and thus provided protection.
Your sons, the sons of Anu, as well as the sons of Siṃhika (the Rākṣasas), likewise [protected it].
Those of sinful mind, who had lived by unrighteousness and evil deeds,
were slain in battle by Vāsudeva, the wielder of the discus.
That very Self which was previously described by me before you—
This is Viṣṇu, of this there is no doubt; he is the righteous soul, the protector of all.
O Goddess, he who was established within the bodies of the Daityas and remained intent on evil—the high-minded one, filled with wrath, slew the Dānavas. 15–16.
O Goddess, having become both external and internal, your sons were struck down;
by the very one who created them, they have been brought to their fall.
You should not feel delusion regarding this; listen to my words.
"He who persists in evil shall surely go to his destruction. Therefore, casting aside delusion, always take refuge in righteousness.
Diti said:
"So be it, O illustrious one; I shall do as you say.
Having thus addressed Kaśyapa, the best of sages, she, though sorrowful, was enlightened by the sage and remained there, having cast off her grief. 20.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Address to Diti by the Devas and Asuras," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Ten.
The Sages said:
Then, O high-minded one, what resolve could all those Dānavas, led by Hiraṇyakaśipu, take after being broken in battle?
Tell us their unsurpassed conduct in detail as well.
"We all wish to hear from you now, O twice-born one.
Sūta said:
"At that time, they were all broken-spirited and devoid of strength."
Their pride gone and afflicted by great sorrow, those Daityas approached their father;
bowing with devotion, they all then spoke to Kaśyapa.
The Dānavas said:
O best of the twice-born, our origin is from your own vigor;
so too is that of the gods and the highly fortunate dānavas.
We are all dānavas, endowed with strength, heroism, and prowess.
"We are many, O father, and we are skilled in means, wise, and endowed with great effort;
whereas the gods are likewise few.
How is it that they all prevail while we have been defeated in the great battle?"
What then, O Father, is the cause that these [Daityas], though endowed with strength and splendor,
possess the power of each one equal to a thousand of my elephants, O Great-minded One, while such power does not exist among the gods? (7–8)
"O Father, since victory is seen thus even among the gods in this great battle,
you ought to explain all of that so as to dispel my doubt.
Kaśyapa said:
"Listen, all you sons, to the cause of Jayanta as well,
by which indeed all the gods became victorious in battle. The father is the one who pours forth the seed, and the mother is always this field."
For indeed, just as one acts toward a father, a son, or a friend in matters of support, protection, and nourishment, so too would one act toward an enemy for the sake of a purpose; in this matter,
it is action alone that is primary, and my intellect is thus resolved.
The connection with karma is twofold, arising from both sin and merit;
it is by relying solely upon truth that the supreme dharma is performed.
O sons, when joined with austerity and meditation, it is beneficial for one’s deliverance.
A downfall is declared to lead inevitably to a fall; of this there is no doubt at any time.
O sons, for a man devoid of merit, this power—consisting of strength, retinue, and noble birth—is rendered powerless. 14–15.
In the lofty mountain fastnesses, there are trees that are like good sons;
yet they fall by the force of the wind along with their very roots, just as those devoid of truth and dharma go to the inexhaustible realm of Yama. 16.

O good sons, this is the common duty of all living beings, by which a creature crosses over both in this world and in the next; yet that truth, endowed with righteousness, has been abandoned by you. 17–18.
"O sons, you have resorted to unrighteousness and are devoid of truth;
fallen from truth, dharma, and austerity, you have plunged into an ocean of suffering. The gods, however, are endowed with truth and possessed of excellence."
Endowed with austerity, tranquility, and self-restraint, they were highly meritorious and free from sin.
(20) Where truth, dharma, austerity, and merit reside, there Viṣṇu Hṛṣīkeśa is seen in victory. (21)
The eternal Vāsudeva became their companion;
therefore, those gods endowed with truth and righteousness achieved victory through that very assistance, strength, and likewise through human prowess. 22.
"O sirs, it is indeed well known that those sons who are devoid of austerity and truthfulness cannot prevail;
for those who know the Dharma understand that victory belongs only to him whose allies are Viṣṇu, as well as austerity and strength. (23-24)
"Deprived of dharma and devoid of austerity and truth,
you previously attained the station of Indra solely through force. O highly wise ones, [you did so] without austerity, without dharma, and without fame."
O sons, even the position of Indra cannot be attained through strength, pride, or virtues alone. Even after attaining the position of Indra, sons indeed fall from it;
therefore, O sons, you must all together perform penance.
Endowed with non-contradiction, joined with wisdom, and possessed of meditation,
you must never harbor enmity toward Keśava.
When your sons are of such a nature, you will become blessed.
"Then you shall all attain supreme perfection; of this there is no doubt.
(29) Having been addressed thus by the high-souled Kaśyapa, those Dānavas of great prowess listened to the words of their father. (30)
Having bowed with devotion to Kaśyapa and risen up with haste, the Daityas, united with one another, addressed Sumantra. Then King Hiraṇyakaśipu spoke to the Dānavas.
"We shall indeed perform austerities that are difficult to practice and grant all things. Then Hiraṇyākṣa said, "I shall perform fierce austerities;
thereafter, by means of my power, I will seize the three worlds—of this there is no doubt."
"Having conquered Govinda in battle, I shall slay this evil-minded one and, together with all the gods, go to the station of Indra. 34.
Bali said:

"O lords of the sons of Diti, it is not fitting for you to engage in enmity with Viṣṇu; such enmity is not a cause for liberation. [Rather, strive] through acts of charity, righteousness, merit, austerities, and the performance of sacrifices."
Having propitiated that Hṛṣīkeśa, human beings go to happiness.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"I shall never perform such worship of Hari."
Abandoning one's own nature, one practices the service of an enemy;
indeed, the wise bring that very act upon themselves as something worse than death.
The service of Viṣṇu is not to be performed by me, nor by others, nor by the demons. 37-38.

He spoke again to that high-souled grandfather of Bali regarding the counsel endowed with political wisdom (rājanīti) concerning the principal leaders of the enemy, as it has been observed in the treatises on dharma by sages who know the truth.
Recognizing oneself as weak and the enemy as powerful, one should go to his side and wait for the opportune time for victory;
just as darkness always remains by resorting to the shadow of a lamp. 40-41.
Just as even the great power of a lamp's light quickly fades upon seeing that its oil has reached its end, and darkness increases once more,
so too should one who desires grace explain the nature of affection according to reality.
Having established an alliance with the Asuras through righteous dispositions,
O Indra among kings, you who are self-possessed should perform your duty using that excellent mantra previously spoken by the sage Kaśyapa. 43–44.
Having heard those words of his, the powerful Daitya said:
"O grandson, I will not act in such a way as to cause the destruction of my own honor.
Then all the other kinsmen spoke to that one who was skilled in policy.
Bali said: "Whatever merit is pleasing to the gods, proclaimed as causing pride to Śakra, and terrifying to the Dānavas—all of us shall perform that very same unsurpassed austerity. (46-47)

"Having conquered the gods through austerity, we shall seize our own place. Having thus addressed one another and having cast aside Bali, those great asuras then harbored a great enmity toward Viṣṇu in their hearts.
Then they all performed austerities in mountain fastnesses and on mountain peaks. Thus all those Dānavas, having abandoned passion, were firm in their resolve;
free from desire and anger, abstaining from food, they conquered fatigue.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "Description of the Daityas' Penance," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Eleven.
The Sages said:
O Omniscient One, you have described the conflict between the Daityas and Dānavas;
now we wish to hear about the high-souled Suvrata.
Whose son was that man of great wisdom, and from which lineage did he originate?
"What was the austerity of that brahmin, and how was Hari propitiated by him?
Sūta said:
"I shall relate the story exactly as it was heard previously through the power of my wisdom."
Likewise, O Brahmins, by the grace of Viṣṇu, I shall relate before you the entire divine and purifying life-story of the high-souled Suvrata, which is Vaiṣṇava and brings about the highest good. 3-4.
In a former kalpa, O highly fortunate ones, in that excellent field which destroys sin,
on the most meritorious bank of the Revā at the sacred ford named Vāmana,
there was born to the family of Kauśika the best of the twice-born, Somaśarman.
Deprived of his son, he was beset by much suffering;
constantly tormented by the misery of poverty, he would contemplate means to obtain both a son and wealth day and night.

Once, however, his beloved wife named Sumanā, who was firm in her vows, observed that her husband was overcome with anxiety and had his face cast downward. Beholding her husband in that state, the ascetic woman spoke to him.

"O high-minded one, your mind has been overwhelmed by countless nets of suffering and utterly deluded by confusion. Abandon this anxiety; tell me of your sorrow, become composed, and proceed toward happiness."
There is no suffering equal to the anxiety of "it does not exist," for it truly withers the body; he who abandons such anxiety lives happily and rejoices.
Tell me, O Brahmin, the cause of this anxiety before me.
Having heard these affectionate words, Somaśarman spoke to his beloved.
Somaśarman said:
"O blessed lady, that which was desired by you has been achieved; anxiety is the cause of suffering."

I shall tell you all of that; having heard it, let it be understood. O lady of excellent vows, I do not know by what sin I have become destitute of wealth, nor why I am deprived of a son—this is the cause of my sorrow. (13-14)
Sumanā said:
"Listen, I shall declare that which destroys all doubt—the true nature of instruction, which reveals all knowledge. (15)

Greed is indeed the seed of evil, and delusion is its root; falsehood is its trunk, and illusion spreads out as its extensive branches. Hypocrisy and crookedness are its leaves, and it is always in bloom with wicked intellect.
Falsehood, its fragrance, and ignorance are its fruit (17). Deceit, heresy, valor, envy, the cruel, the fraudulent, and sinners—
these birds have taken refuge in the branches of the tree of delusion, which are composed of illusion (18).
Ignorance is its excellent fruit, and unrighteousness is indeed the juice of that fruit;
it is increased by the water of craving, and lack of faith is its beloved liquid.
Unrighteousness is its divine sap, which, though pungent, is experienced as sweet.
With whatever kinds of fruits the tree of greed bears such excellent fruit,
that man who takes refuge in its shade is completely satisfied and eats its well-ripened fruits day after day. (20–21)

Even if a mortal is protected by unrighteous means, he may be satisfied with the resulting fruits; yet such a person moves toward his own downfall. Therefore, having abandoned anxiety, a man should not yield to greed.
One should not harbor even a single thought concerning wealth, sons, or wife.
For the wise man who becomes a companion to fools inevitably follows their path;
the fool constantly worries, "How indeed shall this wealth be mine alone? (23-24)

"I have found a good wife here; how shall I obtain sons?"—thus he constantly thinks, deluded day and night. Yet, for even a single moment, he might perceive great happiness in the midst of his anxiety.
Furthermore, consciousness is afflicted by great suffering.
O twice-born one, abandon anxiety and delusion and follow [the path]; O high-minded one, there is no connection with anyone at all in this cycle of existence (saṃsāra). 17.26–27.
Friends, kinsmen, sons, fathers, mothers, servants,
relatives, and likewise wives, all truly exist [only through this connection].
Somaśarman said:
"O blessed lady, tell me in detail what kind of relationship it was,
by which all the kinsmen— wealth, sons, and other relatives— [were affected].
Sumanā said:
Some are related through debt, some are embezzlers of deposits, some provide profit, and others are indifferent;
likewise, sons, friends, and wives arise through these four types of distinctions. (30)
Wives, fathers, mothers, servants, kinsmen,
and relatives are all born on this earth through their respective connections with that person by whom they were treated as deposits or by whom they were misappropriated while on earth. (31-32)
The owner of the deposit shall become a son on earth, virtuous and handsome; there is no doubt that he will find in whose house the deposit was stolen by him.
Having experienced the suffering caused by the theft of the deposit, he attains a state of intense agony upon its restoration.
He became the son of Nyāsasvāmī, who had stolen the deposit;
endowed with virtue, beauty, and all auspicious marks, he manifested his devotion to him day after day as a son. (34-35)

Speaking kindly and sweetly, appearing free from disease, and displaying great affection, he took up his own property and generated the highest degree of love; just as in the past, by whatever means a deposit might have been given, it was [recovered] through its recovery. 36.
Such is this great and terrible suffering that destroys life.
Having become his son through his friendship and possessing great virtues, one likewise becomes short-lived and meets with death. (37-38)
Having repeatedly undergone birth after birth and having given such suffering, when he utters the lamentation, "O son!
O son!", then he surely laughs; for who is whose son, and who is whose father? 39.
"My deposit, which was my means of livelihood, has been stolen by him.
Even by the theft of this wealth, my life-breaths have indeed departed from me due to great and unbearable suffering in the past. (40-41)

"Having thus caused such suffering and having seized this excellent wealth, I shall depart today; for whose son am I, being such as this? Nor is he my father, nor was he ever before the son of anyone."
"Piśācha-hood has been bestowed upon this very wicked soul by me.
Having spoken thus, laughing again and again, he departs; having inflicted most terrible suffering, he goes away by this path.
Indeed, the sons of one who thus rescues from the *nyāsa* (debt) become beloved;
yet they are seen everywhere throughout this world of transmigration which abounds in suffering.
I shall now describe before you those sons who are connected by debt. 45–46.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Narrative of Suvrata," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Twelve.
Sumanā said:
I shall now describe before you the son who is connected through debt: he who, having taken a loan, indeed passes away;
that creditor, becoming his son, brother, father, or beloved wife.
That extremely wicked one always behaves as if he were a friend;
that cruel one of harsh appearance never perceives any virtue,
and he constantly utters harsh words even toward his own kin.
He eats only what is sweet, constantly enjoying sensual pleasures;
he is perpetually addicted to gambling and has a longing for the work of a thief.
He forcibly consumes the household property and becomes angry when restrained.
Day after day he reviles both his father and mother;
he is a rogue, a terror, and a speaker of many harsh words.
Having thus consumed that wealth, he remains at ease.
Through the birth-rites and others in childhood, the terrible [karma] seizes the substance;
furthermore, through various types of marriage relations, it manifests in many ways. Thus the substance is produced, and thus it is also given away.
"Without a doubt, everything— house, field, and so forth— belongs to me alone.
Day after day, he indeed strikes his father and mother with pieces of wood,
pestles, and all manner of most cruel blows."

But when that father or mother has died, he becomes exceedingly cruel, devoid of affection, and indeed harsh; of this there is no doubt. That wretched man does not perform the ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) nor offer gifts.
Such sons indeed arise upon the surface of the earth.
O bull among the twice-born, I shall now describe to you the enemy son;
having reached the stage of childhood, he always behaves with enmity.
While playing, he would strike his father and mother;
having struck them, he would depart laughing again and again, only to return in terror toward his father and mother once more. (13)
He constantly behaves with anger and reviles [others] again and again.
Thus he always persists in acts of enmity; and having killed his father and then his mother as well, 14–15.
Thus does that evil-minded one proceed, due to the influence of former enmity.
Now, therefore, I shall explain how that which is dear may be obtained:
as soon as he is born, one should make him dear through fondling and play in childhood.
Upon reaching adulthood, one should do what is pleasing immediately after [the service of] mother and father;
one should always satisfy them with devotion and gratify both of them with affection, with speech, and with pleasant conversation. 17–18.
Perceiving that his preceptor had died, he wept again out of affection; then,
afflicted by great sorrow, he performed all the funeral rites, including the offering of rice balls (piṇḍa) and other ceremonies, and provided for their journey.
Bound by the three debts, he constantly causes [the ancestors] to eat out of affection;
therefore, O wise one, having become a son, he undoubtedly bestows upon them whatever may be obtained through this very method. 20–21.

I shall now describe the indifferent one (udāsīna) to you, who is dear to me; he always conducts himself with an indifferent disposition. He neither gives nor takes, and he neither becomes angry nor is he pleased.
O best of the twice-born, having completely renounced all new attachments and remaining indifferent, I have told you everything before you: such is the destiny of sons;
as is the son, so too are the wife, the father, the mother, and kinsmen. (23-24)
Other servants have been mentioned, as well as cattle, horses, elephants, buffaloes, female slaves, and those related through debt; however,
no debt has been contracted by him with either of us.
"O beloved, listen: in a previous birth, no one indeed performed such a renunciation (nyāsa); nor did anyone hold a debt, O dear one;
and by no one was even enmity committed in a former life. (26-27)
"O best of sages, neither of us has ever abandoned one another;
knowing this, attain peace and abandon this useless anxiety. Whose sons are dear? Whose wife? Whose are one's own people and kinsmen? (28)
"It was not stolen by anyone, nor was it given away by you again.
How indeed did this wealth come to be? O Mādhava, I am filled with wonder.
O best of the twice-born, wherever a thing is destined to be obtained, it surely comes to pass."

That which is placed in the hands of one who exerts no effort is easily acquired; yet a man must exert great effort to protect his wealth. As he departs, his wealth follows him, but it remains right there where he leaves it.
Knowing this, attain peace and abandon useless anxiety.
Whose are sons and beloved wives? Whose are kinsmen and relatives? O best of the twice-born, in this cycle of existence, who belongs to whom? For all are without connection. 32-33.
Men deluded by great ignorance and possessed of sinful minds think:
"This is my house, this is my son, and these noble ones are indeed mine. Thus, the falsehood of worldly existence is perceived as a bond.
Thus addressed then by his beloved wife, the goddess, Somaśarman,
being well-disposed, spoke again to his dear wife, who was eloquent in wisdom.
Somaśarman said:
"O auspicious lady, you have spoken the truth, which destroys all doubt. Nevertheless, O beloved, virtuous and wise men desire a lineage;
my concern for my son is just as great as my concern for wealth."
"By whatever means possible, I shall produce a son.
Sumanā said:
"Through a son one conquers the worlds; a son delivers the lineage. (38)
O fortunate one, by means of a virtuous son, both father and mother—and indeed all living beings—are saved.
A single son who is excellent and learned is superior; what is the use of many sons devoid of merit?
One such son delivers the entire lineage, while others merely cause distress.

Previously, I have declared this to others who were concerned with their kinship: "By merit a son is obtained; by merit a noble lineage is obtained; and a virtuous conception is obtained through merits. Therefore, practice merit. (40-41)
For one who is born, death is certain; for one who dies, birth is certain.
A good birth is obtained through meritorious deeds, and likewise is death [under auspicious circumstances].
Through meritorious actions, happiness, wealth, and a beloved wife are enjoyed.
Somaśarman said:
"O beloved, tell me of the practice of merit as well as of other births.
O auspicious lady, what kind of person is highly meritorious? Tell me the characteristics of merit."
Sumanā said:
"I shall first proclaim merit, just as merit was heard by me;
how a man or a woman should always conduct themselves."
Just as one attains fame, beloved sons, and wealth through merits, O dear one, I shall describe to you the entire nature of merit:
through celibacy, truthfulness, and the performance of the five sacrifices. 45–46.
O beloved, one should thus fulfill Dharma by means of these ten factors: through charity, observances, forbearance, purity, non-violence, right exertion, and abstention from theft. 47.
Dharma becomes complete through its "swallowings," just as enjoyment is fulfilled within the belly.
The righteous-souled one creates Dharma by means of the threefold action; thus, his Dharma, being serene in nature, brings about merit alone. 48–49.
"Whatever a wise man contemplates, he attains even that which is difficult to obtain.
Somaśarman said: "O beautiful lady, what is the form of Dharma, and what are its limbs? (50)
Out of affection, she spoke in private, for a desire to hear had arisen in her;
Sumanā said:
"O best of the twice-born, by whom has the form of Dharma itself been seen in this world? (51)
His path is invisible, his nature is untruth, and he is unseen by gods and dānavas;
yet that twice-born one, born in the lineage of Atri as the son of Anasūyā, has always beheld that great Dharma through Dattātreya. 52.
These two high-souled ones, performing the most excellent penance and conducting themselves according to dharma, through austerity and power,
shall become superior even to Indra in their highly praised form. (53-54)
For ten thousand years, as long as they remained in the forest, those two of auspicious appearance became subsistent on air alone, abstaining from all food;
for that duration of ten thousand years, they accumulated the power of austerity.
And while those two were being perfected there, dharma was clearly manifested.
O best of the twice-born, the five-fire penance (pañcāgni) was practiced by the two for that duration;
likewise, they remained without food, having performed it three times a day.
While Dattātreya the ascetic and Durvāsas, the best of sages, remained thus in the midst of the water, emaciated by their penance,
that righteous-souled bull among sages grew angry regarding the matter of dharma.
When that most illustrious and best of sages was thus enraged,
Dharma then arrived in his own form; he was endowed with celibacy and other virtues, possessed of great wisdom, and rich in ascetic penances.

Truth is the foremost of the twice-born in the form of a brāhmaṇa, and likewise celibacy is the foremost; austerity is the best of the twice-born, as is self-restraint for the wise, the highest of the twice-born (61); and great wisdom is the rule, as is indeed generosity.
Indeed, they approached Ātreya in the form of the Agnihotra sacrifice; O best of the twice-born,
Kṣamā (Forgiveness), Śānti (Peace), Lajjā (Modesty), Ahiṃsā (Non-violence), and Akalpanā (Freedom from conceptualization)—
all these arrived there in female forms.
At that time, Buddhi, Prajñā, Dayā, Śraddhā, Medhā, Satkṛti, and Śānti—
these five sacrifices as well as the meritorious Vedas with their auxiliary limbs—
were all present, assuming their own respective forms and having attained perfection.
The rites beginning with the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*) and others such as the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) are meritorious; likewise,
[the women] were endowed with beauty and charm, adorned with all ornaments,
wearing divine garlands and garments, and anointed with divine perfumes.
Adorned with crowns and earrings, decorated with divine ornaments, radiant and handsome, they were enveloped in flames of splendor;
thus Dharma arrived, accompanied by his retinue.
"Where Durvāsas, wrathful like Time itself, resides. Dharma said:
"O Brahmin, why have you, who are endowed with ascetic power, become angry?"
Anger destroys prosperity; there is no doubt that it destroys even ascetic merit (tapas).
Since it causes the destruction of everything, one should therefore avoid anger in that state. Be composed, O best of the twice-born; the fruit of asceticism is supreme.
Durvāsas said: "Who are you that have arrived here together with these excellent brahmins?
Seven women of beautiful form, well-adorned, are standing there. (71)
"O Mahāmati, tell me this in detail.
Dharmā said:
"This one, endowed with all splendor, was in the form of a Brāhmaṇa. (72)
"With staff in hand and serene, likewise bearing a water-pot—
behold, this very person who has come before you is Brahmacharya. O best of the twice-born, look now at another who is radiant."
"O best of the twice-born, O righteous-souled one, behold this truth: Kapila with his reddish-brown eyes, who possesses a splendor equal to that of Vaiśravaṇa;
for the ascetic power which you abandoned, O Brahmin, has been taken up by all the gods. (74-75)
Behold him, O highly fortunate one, who has come to your side— he who is endowed with gracious speech and radiance, devoted to compassion for all living beings,
and likewise this Dama, who always nourishes you. 76.
He had matted hair, was harsh, tawny, extremely fierce, and a great lord (77).
O best of the twice-born, with sword in hand, he was the destroyer of sinners; yet he was peaceful, highly meritorious, and constantly engaged in his daily rites (78).
O best of the twice-born, a man of strict observances (niyamastu) arrived at your side;
he was unshakable, greatly radiant, resembling pure crystal, holding a water-pot in his hand, and carrying a tooth-stick. 79. He was a brahmin.
Having arrived here for the sake of purification in your presence,
this most virtuous and highly fortunate lady, adorned with truth as her ornament,
has come to serve you— she whose limbs possess the splendor of all ornaments. (80-81)
O best of the twice-born, this Gaurī, whose limbs are exceedingly steady and serene, whose face is graced with a gentle smile,
who holds a lotus in her hand, who has lotus-like eyes, and who is like a beautiful lotus-pond,
is endowed with divine ornaments and has attained self-control. 82.
Exceedingly peaceful, well-established, and endowed with many auspicious signs;
possessing a splendor created by divine jewels and adorned with celestial ornaments—O one of great wisdom, your peace, which is the very form of knowledge, has arrived. (83-84)
She was constantly intent on performing acts of benefit for others, filled with many truths,
moderate in speech, always free from conceptual construction, serene, endowed with patience, and adorned with every ornament. 85.
Seated in the lotus posture, of beautiful form, dark-complexioned, and renowned—
this illustrious Ahiṃsā has come to you,
her limbs the color of molten gold, sporting in red garments. 86–87.
Overwhelmed by the state of knowledge, that ascetic woman, whose hand was [marked] by merit, did not see anything there, even though she possessed very clear and excellent mantras;
she was richly adorned with pearl ornaments, stainless, and possessed a beautiful smile. 88.
O illustrious one, behold, behold this Śraddhā who has arrived!
She is possessed of great intelligence, filled with vast knowledge, endowed with a form attached to excellent enjoyments, well-established, and auspiciously beautiful. 89–90.
Endowed with all desired meditations, the mother of the world, illustrious,
rich in the beauty of all ornaments, with full hips and breasts,
fair-complexioned, she arrived adorned with garlands and garments. 91.
This Medhā, O you of great wisdom, is established solely within you—
resembling a swan or the moon, adorned with hanging pearl necklaces, decorated with every ornament, serene, and high-minded. 92–93.

Clad in white garments, seated upon a hundred-petaled lotus, and shining eternally with a book resting in her lotus-like hand—O fortunate one, this Prajñā has come to you. 94. O highly blessed one, she has arrived for the sake of your good fortune.
Her complexion was always as clear and bright as liquid lac;
she was adorned with garlands, necklaces, and armlets made of yellow flowers, and was further embellished with finger-rings, bracelets, and earrings. 95–96.
Clad in yellow garments, the Goddess always shines resplendent;
she is the peerless one for the sake of the welfare and nourishment of the three worlds. O best of the twice-born, her virtuous conduct has been celebrated forever.
"O best of the twice-born, she has arrived here at your side out of compassion;
O most wise one, this aged ascetic woman is my mother. O foremost of the twice-born, O you of excellent vows, I am your wife according to dharma. (98-99)
"Knowing this, attain peace and protect me in this way.
Durvāsas said:
"If indeed Dharma has now come into my presence," (100)
"Tell me this cause; what dharma of yours shall I perform? Dharma said:
O best of Brahmins, why are you angry? What unpleasant thing has been done by them? (101)
"Therefore, tell me the reason for this, O Durvāsas, if you so intend. Durvāsas said:
"O Goddess, listen to this very reason by which I have been provoked to anger. (102)

My own body has been purified by self-restraint, purity, and intense austerities; indeed, penance consisting of such practices was performed by me for a duration of one hundred thousand years. Do you see me thus? Out of compassion for you, I have acted in this manner.
"Therefore, being enraged, I shall this very day pronounce a curse upon you.
Having heard this, the highly intelligent Dharma then spoke to him. Dharma said:

"O one of great wisdom, when I am lost, the world will go to its destruction. O twice-born one, I shall utterly wither away that pride which is the root of suffering; I shall grant happiness later on, provided it does not abandon the truth. (105–106)
This sin is rooted in happiness, whereas merit is obtained through suffering;
a living being who thus practices merit gives up its life-breaths [only to attain merit]. (107) I shall surely grant great happiness in the next world as well; of this there is no doubt.
Durvāsas said:
"By that very means through which one attains happiness, one encounters supreme suffering;
having abandoned that [wealth], a mortal may enjoy it through another as well. (108)
Whoever knows that pleasure does not perceive certainty at all.
We do not see that as a true good; for what you have done is unjust.
By whichever body an action is performed, by that very same body its fruit is experienced, and not otherwise. 109–110.

One person commits the affliction, while another person experiences the pleasure; who then understands this injustice, or indeed the true Dharma? (111) One person commits the affliction, and yet another person experiences the pleasure.
A person enjoys all that merit joined with spiritual excellence;
indeed, one also experiences the fruit of this very merit.
Furthermore, merit being performed by one may be enjoyed by another.

All that which has been described as happiness, along with its characteristics as proclaimed in the treatises on Dharma, is experienced by them everywhere exactly as it was ordained, and not otherwise.
With whatever body they perform [actions], with that very body they endure suffering.
"Others enjoy by means of protection, and you likewise enjoy by this same means.
Having understood this, you, whose nature is righteous, should reflect upon it: how those great sinners, like thieves, must suffer together with their own bodies. 115–116.
"How indeed is there no intense and terrible suffering for happiness?
Dharma said: "By whatever body sinful people wander about committing transgressions... (117)
Therefore, they indeed endure suffering, which is the fruit of their sin; the wise have seen in the treatises on dharma that punishment alone is the ultimate remedy.
Know that very punishment to be preceded by righteousness through these principles. 118.
Durvāsas said:
"O Dharmarāja, I do not consider this to be right; listen to me, for I am enraged and shall otherwise bestow three curses upon you."
Dharma said:
"Since you have become angry with me, who am possessed of great wisdom, forgive me for this.
But if you do not forgive me, O best of Brahmins, then make me the son of a slave woman."
O great sage, he should indeed be made a king and a cāṇḍāla;
for Durvāsas was always well-disposed toward the Brahmin who bowed before him, yet he became enraged and cursed Dharma. 121–122.
Durvāsas said:
"O son, you were born from Dharmādya; it shall not be otherwise. Go now to the womb of a Cāṇḍāla, and depart according to your own will."
Having thus bestowed the three boons, that best of the twice-born departed;
and by this very occasion, it is said that Dharma was seen long ago.
Somaśarman said:
"O beautiful lady, tell me what kind of Dharma has arisen that the Great-Souled One cursed him; if you know it, please speak of its nature to me.
Sumanā said:
Yudhiṣṭhira was born into the lineage of the Bharatas as Dharma incarnate, while Vidura was the son of a slave-woman; this and other matters I shall now relate.
Furthermore, when King Hariścandra was tormented by Viśvāmitra—
Then that high-minded Dharma attained the state of a Cāṇḍāla;
thus was the fruit of his karma experienced even by the great-souled Dharma due to the curse of Durvāsas. This truth has indeed been spoken before you. 127–128.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Somaśarman and Sumanā," within the narrative of Somaśarman in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Thirteen. Somaśarman said:
"O beautiful lady, if you know it, tell me in detail the definition of brahmacarya and what that brahmacarya is like.
He whose constant delight is in truth, that virtuous soul attains contentment."
When her season has arrived, a man free from defects should approach his own wife;
he never abandons the virtuous conduct of his own family. This alone, O best of the twice-born, is declared to be the duty of a householder.

I have indeed declared the supreme celibacy for householders; now I shall proclaim that for ascetics—listen as I speak of it. It is characterized by self-restraint and truthfulness, and by being ever afraid of sin.
Having abandoned attachment to a wife and being established in meditation and knowledge, celibacy (brahmacarya) has been described before you for ascetics.
Now I shall speak of austerity (tapas); listen to me as I describe it.
One should proceed according to right conduct, free from desire and anger, established for the benefit of living beings, and enveloped in diligent effort.
Thus has austerity been fully described; thus do I speak the truth.
He whose mind does not become covetous upon seeing the possessions of others, nor likewise toward the wives of others,
is proclaimed to be truthful (satya).
I shall now explain the nature of giving (dāna), by which human beings live.
He who would grasp for his own happiness, whether in this world or the next,
should give even a great gift of food, for it is the certain source of happiness; likewise, even a single morsel should be given to one afflicted by hunger— of this there is no doubt.
One who eats dates always partakes of great merit and nectar. Every day, one should give according to one's means,
including grass for a bed, shelter, and very cool shade.
He who constantly provides for his own livelihood with land, water, food, and most excellent kind words, as well as a seat and conversation free from deceit; ||| 13 ||

He who, having thus honored the gods and the ancestors, bestows such gifts, indeed rejoices both in this world and likewise in the next. He for whom the day is not in vain through acts of giving, study, and ritual performance—[he truly lives]. 14–15.
Having become a human being, one may indeed become a god; there is no doubt in this.
I shall now declare the rule that is the supreme means for accomplishing dharma:
he who is truly devoted to the worship of the gods and the Brahmins.
O observer of excellent vows, this is proclaimed as the rule regarding constant engagement in self-restraint, acts of charity, sacred observances, beneficial services, and meritorious deeds.
Now I shall describe the nature of forbearance; listen, O best of the twice-born. (17–18)
Upon hearing the cries of others being struck by someone, he should not give way to anger;
nor, when struck himself, should he strike back. He should be patient and righteous in soul, for one who is thus does not fall into passion.

He enjoys supreme happiness both in this world and in the hereafter. (20) Thus has forbearance been fully described; now I shall speak of purity: he who is indeed pure within and without, and free from passion, (21) is truly pure.
One conducts oneself in worldly affairs through bathing, sipping water for purification, and similar practices;
thus is purity fully described. Now I shall speak of non-violence: even a blade of grass must not be cut by one who possesses discernment without a necessary purpose.
One should be devoted to non-violence toward others just as one is toward oneself. I shall explain peace alone; through peace one attains happiness.
Peace must indeed be practiced; one should never abandon it out of affliction.
Having thus abandoned enmity toward living beings, one should practice in this manner;
such is declared to be peace. Now I shall speak of non-stealing (asteya). One must never seize the property of another, nor likewise the wife of another.

O best of the twice-born, I shall now declare self-restraint (dama) to you; one should thus discipline the mind through thoughts, words, and physical actions. Self-restraint consists indeed in the subduing of the senses and even of the mind which is subject to transformation. (26-27)
He who possesses self-awareness should then destroy their restlessness through mastery; I shall now describe the kind of service that is prescribed in the Dharma-śāstras (28),
exactly as it was taught by the ancient teachers— of that very same [service] I speak thus.
One should accomplish a task for the guru through speech, body, and mind.
Where favor arises [from this], that is declared to be service (śuśrūṣā). O best of the twice-born, dharma with all its constituent parts has thus been fully explained to you. 29-30.
O Lord, I shall tell you something else if you wish to hear it: even in such a dharma as this, if a man always conducts himself thus,
his birth in this cycle of existence (saṃsāra) shall never happen again.
One goes to heaven by means of dharma; I tell you this as the truth, the absolute truth.
O highly wise one, knowing this, follow dharma alone;
for everything that is difficult to achieve on the surface of the earth is indeed obtained, my dear. 32-33.
"Therefore, out of faith in the Dharma, you must indeed do as I say.
Having heard the words of his wife, the highly intelligent Somaśarman spoke again to that virtuous wife who spoke of righteousness. (34-35)
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Sumanas," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the Śrī Padma Purāṇa, within the collection of fifty-five thousand verses.
Chapter Fourteen. Somaśarman said:
"How do you know, O blessed lady, such a supreme exposition of the Dharma of great merit, and from whom did you hear it?
Sumanā replied:
O high-minded one, I am born in the lineage of the Bhārgavas as your grandfather,
renowned by the name Cyavana and proficient in all branches of knowledge.
I am his beloved daughter, dearer to him even than his own life.
O observer of noble vows, wherever he goes— to sacred fords, groves,
assemblies of sages, or temples of the gods— I always go there alone, playing with him. (3-4)
Vedaśarman, of great intelligence and born of the Kauśika lineage, a friend of my father, arrived here by chance while wandering;
he was overcome with great sorrow and was reflecting upon it again and again. (5)
When that great-souled one had arrived, my grandfather said to him:
"O you of excellent vows, I know that you are tormented by sorrow; why have you become so distressed? Therefore, tell me the cause."

Having heard these words of the high-souled Cyavana, Vedaśarman, who was possessed of great wisdom and devoted to his vows, spoke to his father, the cause of all his suffering: 8. "O you of noble conduct, [speak] to that high-souled one regarding the cause of all my misery."
"My wife is a great virtuous woman, devoted solely to her husband; though she is childless, my lineage shall not perish. This is the reason I have told you, since I was questioned by you."
In the meantime, a certain perfected being (siddha) arrived;
my father likewise rose up along with Vedaśarman,
and that siddha was honored by both of them with devotion.
With offerings, various foods, and words of sweet syllables,
my righteous-souled father spoke to both of them— his friend and himself— regarding the internal matter previously mentioned by you. 12-13.
"I have indeed told you everything that is the cause of dharma;
for through dharma one obtains a son, wealth, grain, and likewise women.
Then, Vedaśarman performed dharma completely.

From that dharma, great happiness has been well produced for me along with my son. Through this connection, my mind has reached a firm resolve; therefore, I have spoken to you exactly as it was desired, for it is most auspicious. 15-16.
Therefore, having heard from the great Siddha that which destroys all doubt, always follow the dharma of the Brahmins. Somaśarman said:
"O beloved Dharmaja, tell me what kind of death and birth there is;
O handsome one, tell me all of that, for it is the characteristic of both.
Sumanā said:
I shall now describe the death of one by whom dharma has been protected through truth, purity, forbearance, tranquility, pilgrimage sites, merit, and so forth;
for such a person, no disease arises, nor does any affliction occur in the body.
There was neither fatigue nor exhaustion, nor sweat, nor even dizziness.
Having assumed divine forms, the Gandharvas and likewise the Brahmins were engaged in the recitation of the Vedas and were experts in the knowledge of song. 20–21.
Approaching his side, they offered incomparable praise;
he was indeed composed, seated upon his throne, and devoted to the worship of the deity.
The wise man, intent on dharma, also reached the holy ford for the purpose of bathing.
In the fire-sanctuary, in a cow-pen, and in temples; in a grove, at a pond, and wherever there is a holy fig tree (aśvattha),
a banyan tree (vaṭa), or likewise a brahma-tree or a śrīvṛkṣa.
When a man stands at a stable for horses, or has gone to an elephant stable, or stands leaning against an Aśoka tree or a mango tree,
or is in the presence of Brāhmaṇas, or has entered the royal palace; 25.
Having taken refuge on the field of battle where one might previously have died—
those places of death are meritorious and solely for the sake of dharma—
and having reached Gograha as well as Amarakaṇṭaka. (26–27)
Constantly performing pure deeds and being devoted to the Dharma by its very nature,
that best of men attains such a state when he encounters death; he beholds his mother and father in their merit.

He shall not see again his brother, nor any other kinsman or relative, who is joined with prosperity; nor shall he see again his mother, father, and so forth, while they are being praised repeatedly by virtuous bards.
The Gandharvas sang songs, and his devotees praised him with hymns; likewise, the Brahmins honored him with the recitation of mantras, and his mother worshipped him with affection.
His father, his kinsmen, and his circle of relatives [honored] that righteous and highly intelligent one.
Thus, O Lord, have the messengers and those holy places been described.
He beholds the messengers directly, filled with laughter and affection; he does not see them through a dream, nor through delusion, nor through anything characterized by distress. 32-33.
The highly wise Dharmarāja summons you:
"Come, come, O illustrious one, to where Dharma abides. For him there is no delusion, no confusion, no exhaustion, and no lapse of memory.
There is no doubt that this occurs; with a serene soul, he abides [in peace].
(35) Endowed with both knowledge and realized wisdom, remembering the Lord Janārdana, he indeed departs together with them, contented and joyful in mind. (36)
Upon leaving his own body there, he attains oneness;
resorting to the tenth door, his self departs. A palanquin comes for him, as well as a beautiful swan-vehicle.
He travels in a celestial chariot, or on a horse, or on an excellent elephant;
that meritorious soul is fanned on all sides by those very merits, with a parasol being held over him and with chowries and fans. 38–39.
The righteous-souled one was being sung of, while he was being praised by the learned, by bards,
by celestial singers, and by Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas;
he was extolled by holy men, endowed with every happiness.
Just as he obtains the fruit through the power of his giving,
there he proceeds with ease into the midst of gardens and groves,
surrounded by celestial nymphs and endowed with divine auspiciousness. 41–42.

Being praised by the gods, he beheld Dharmarāja; and the gods, endowed with righteousness, went directly before him. "Come, come, O highly fortunate one! Enjoy pleasures that are agreeable to the mind."
Thus beholding the Dharma in its gentle form,
that one of great intelligence enjoys heaven itself by the power of his own merit; and upon the exhaustion of those enjoyments, that righteous-souled one indeed undergoes rebirth.

O high-minded one, through faith in their own respective duties, the merit of a highly virtuous Brāhmaṇa, as well as that of a Kṣatriya, a wealthy Vaiśya, and even a highly virtuous [Śūdra], truly extends to their entire family. 46.
There he rejoices in righteousness and further performs meritorious deeds. 47.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Sumanas" in the *Aindra* section of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa*, within the glorious *Padma Purāṇa* consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
Chapter Fifteen.
Somaśarman said:
"O blessed lady, O beautiful woman, if you know it, tell me in detail what kind of characteristics are possessed by the death of sinners."
Sumanā said:
"Listen, for I shall relate what I have heard from that perfected being regarding the specific signs that appear at the death of sinners."
I shall now describe the place and the activity of those who have committed great sins: having reached ground filled with feces, urine, and impurities— a place associated with evil—
the extremely wicked-souled one abandons his life-breaths in great suffering.
Having reached the land of the Cāṇḍālas, he, being in a wretched state, meets his death;
having resorted to the house of a prostitute— a place frequented by donkeys—
and having gone to the home of a Kalpapālaka, he approaches his end.
Filled with bones, skin, and nails, and inhabited by sinful defilements—
having reached that [condition], that evil-souled one certainly goes to death. Having reached another [state] characterized by sinful conduct, he likewise goes to death.
Now, I shall describe the gestures of messengers who desire success:
those who are fierce, cruel, terrible, extremely dark, or large-bellied;
those with tawny eyes, or yellowish-blue, or exceedingly white, and large-bellied.
Seeing those who were exceedingly tall, terrifying, resembling dried flesh and fat,
with fierce fangs, formidable, lion-faced, and having serpents for hands—
one would tremble and be distressed again and again.
O high-minded one, all the messengers indeed release terrible, great roars like the howling of jackals right at his ears;
they bind him with nooses around the neck, as well as around the waist and the belly.

That which is repeatedly uttered by one who is being assailed and struck down, like a man speaking without cause while dying— that very thing I call lamentation (praṇapada). The seizing of another's property and the violation of another's wife—
Furthermore, whatever entire property of another was seized as a debt by wicked men,
yet never returned again due to greed and delusion by the taste of wealth— this is indeed another great sin, namely the acceptance of improper gifts (kupratigraha). 13–14.
When all those various sins previously committed by that dying person reach his throat,
they arrive at the base of his throat; for one who has committed great sin, this occurs and not otherwise.
These [worms] produce a terrible suffering through the constriction of phlegm;
with agonizing pains, his throat makes a gurgling sound, and he weeps and trembles excessively for his mother and father again and again. 16–17.
There, deluded by great sin, he remembers his brother, his wife, and his sons again and again, yet he repeatedly falls back into forgetfulness;
his vital breaths depart, overwhelmed by intense agony.
He trembles and faints again and again;
thus, joined with such torment, he experiences suffering, deluded as he is.
His vital breaths are shaken by great misery and extreme hardships. 19–20.
Listen, O beloved, as they depart by way of the anus;
thus the living being, utterly deluded and possessed by greed and delusion, is led away by the messengers of Yama—I shall now describe his suffering. 21–22.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Desire for a Sinful Death," in the Story of Sumanā within the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the collection of fifty-five thousand verses.
Chapter Sixteen.
Sumanā said:
Being dragged along a path strewn with heaps of glowing coals,
that wicked-souled one is scorched, struggling again and again;
there, the heat is most intense, tormented by the twelve suns.
Tormented by the rays of the sun, that evil-minded one is led along that path through mountains that are difficult to traverse and devoid of shade,
while being afflicted by hunger and thirst.
Being struck by the messengers with maces, swords, axes,
and beaten with whips, he is reviled by those messengers;
then, on the path of cold, he is again assailed by the wind.
Suffering from that cold, he arrives there without a doubt;
being dragged by messengers, he is led through various difficult terrains—
thus does the sinner, that evil-minded one who reviles gods and Brahmins.
One who practices all manner of evil deeds is led away by the servants of Yama;
that wicked-souled person beholds Yama, who resembles a mass of black collyrium.
He is fierce, cruel, and terrifying, surrounded by his formidable messengers.
O best of the twice-born, [he saw] the god Dharmarāja mounted upon a buffalo, surrounded by all manner of diseases and accompanied by Citragupta;
he was exceedingly fierce with terrifying fangs, and his mouth resembled the very God of Death.

The evil-minded one beholds Yama, who is of such a form and possesses a massive body; he wears yellow garments, holds a mace in his hand, is smeared with red sandalwood paste, is adorned with red garlands, and is terrifying. 10.
Seeing him arrived there, excluded from all righteous dharmas—
him who is wicked, most sinful, and a thorn in the side of dharma— Yama shall punish him with great sufferings and torments using wooden mallets.
For as long as the end of a thousand yugas, he is cooked;
he is cooked again and again in various kinds of hells. The evildoer indeed goes to a hellish womb among millions of worms.
He is cooked perpetually in impurity, crying out "Alas! Alas!", deprived of consciousness;
and thus that evil-souled one certainly undergoes death.
In this manner, the wicked-minded person experiences the consequences of his association with sin.
I shall further describe the rebirths he undergoes and the wombs into which he enters:
having entered a hundred births as a dog, he indeed experiences the consequences of his sin once more; then he becomes a tiger, and thereafter he enters the womb of a donkey. 16–17.
They enter the womb of a cat, a sow, and likewise that of a serpent;
again and again, they go into all the various species of animals, into sinful birds, and into other great [beings]. 17–18.
The sinner goes to the womb of a Cāṇḍāla, a Bhilla, or a low-born Pulinda;
thus has all this regarding the birth of sinners been declared to you. Now hear, O beloved, about their death and their most terrible conduct at the end of life. 19.
The practice of both sin and merit has been described by me before you.
O giver of honor, if you ask further, I shall speak of something else.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Sin and Merit," in the *Sumanopākhyāna* of the *Aindra-khaṇḍa*, within the *Pañcapañcāśat-sahasra-saṃhitā* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The seventeenth chapter.
Somaśarman said:
"O Goddess, you have fully explained the supreme establishment of dharma."
"How may I find a son who is omniscient and endowed with all virtues?

O illustrious one, O lady of excellent vows, if you know, please tell me about charity, dharma, and other such matters, O auspicious lady, for both this world and the next; of this there is no doubt. (1-2)
Sumanā said to Vasiṣṭha, "Go to that great sage, the knower of dharma; entreat him,
for from him you shall indeed obtain a son who knows the dharma and is devoted to righteousness."
Sūta said:
When these words had been spoken by her, Somaśarman, the best of the twice-born, replied: "O auspicious lady, I shall do exactly as you have said; of this there is no doubt."
Having spoken thus, Somaśarman, the best of the twice-born and a knower of all things, quickly approached the divine Vasiṣṭha, the foremost of those who practice austerity,
that excellent brahmin residing in his meritorious hermitage on the banks of the Gaṅgā.
Surrounded by a blaze of splendor like a second sun, that high-souled one was shining; he was a devotee of Brahman and the best among the twice-born.
Having prostrated himself repeatedly like a staff before that lord of brahmins with devotion, [he spoke].
The sinless son of Brahmā, possessed of great splendor, said to him: "O high-minded one, sit comfortably upon this auspicious seat.
Having spoken thus, that lord of yogis spoke again to the ascetic whose wealth is penance.
"O highly fortunate one, is there always well-being in your home, among your sons, your children, your wife, and your servants? Is there prosperity in your meritorious deeds and in your sacred fires?
Are your limbs free from disease, and do you always protect the Dharma?"
Having spoken thus, the one of great wisdom laughed again at Suśarman and said,
"O best of the twice-born, what dear service may I perform for you, that which is most pleasing to you?
Having addressed the Brahmin in this manner, the son of Kumbha ceased speaking.
When that illustrious Vasiṣṭha, the bull among sages, had spoken thus,
he addressed the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, the best of ascetics:
"O Blessed One, please listen to my words with a well-pleased mind."
O bull among sages, O best of the twice-born, since this is something dear to me, please dispel the doubt regarding the meaning of my question:
how is it that, due to some sinful act, there is no happiness from sons despite poverty? (14)
"O father, tell me this: from what sin does this doubt arise? (15) O twice-born one, utterly bewildered by great delusion, I was awakened by my beloved;
thus, being distressed, I have been sent by her to your side, O father. (16)
"Tell me all of that which destroys every doubt; may you become the giver of liberation for me from the bondage of saṃsāra.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Sons, enemies, brothers, and others who are one's own kin and relatives—
these five types of divisions arise for a man through conflict.
These have already been described by Sumanā previously in your presence.
O best of the twice-born, all those who are bound by debt are indeed bad sons;
I shall now proclaim before you the meritorious characteristics of a true son—
one whose soul is devoted to merit and who is always intent upon truth and righteousness.
Endowed with purity and wisdom, he was an ascetic and the best among those skilled in speech;
steadfast in all his actions, he was devoted to the study of the Vedas (21).
He was a knower of all the scriptures and a worshiper of the gods and Brahmins.
He was a performer of all sacrifices, a donor, one who practiced renunciation, and a speaker of pleasant words (22).

He was constantly devoted to the meditation on Viṣṇu, ever peaceful and self-controlled, always a friend to all, eternally devoted to his father and mother, and affectionate toward all his kinsmen (23).
A son who is wise, a savior of his family, and a nourisher of his lineage— one endowed with such qualities is a bestower of happiness;
others who are merely connected by kinship bring only sorrow and distress.
"What is to be done with such a person, who is devoid of fruit?
O best of the twice-born, they all come and go, inflicting most terrible suffering upon one another in this worldly existence in the form of sons. (25-26)
"I shall indeed recount all that merit performed in a previous birth which you have preserved; listen again to this wonderful account. Vasiṣṭha said:
"O highly wise one, you were a Śūdra in a previous birth; otherwise, how could this be? You were a farmer, devoid of knowledge, and possessed by great greed.
You always hated your only wife, yet you fathered many sons and gave nothing away. (28)

You have not understood the Dharma, nor have you heard the Truth. You have given no gift, nor have you studied the scriptures. O high-minded one, you have never even undertaken a pilgrimage to sacred fords. (29–30)
O best of the twice-born, you have thus repeatedly performed the tending of livestock, as well as the care of all the cows,
and likewise the tending of buffaloes and horses again and again. 31.
"O best of the twice-born, such was the vast wealth previously acquired by you alone through your own actions; yet, out of greed,
you never at any time spent it for the sake of great merit."

Seeing that this vessel is indeed weak, you have not given alms; yet, by showing compassion, let there be wealth for you. All the cattle, such as cows and buffaloes, that have been accumulated by you— [let them be yours]. 34.
O Brahmin, you have accumulated and sold vast wealth;
having sold buttermilk, ghee, milk, and likewise curd, you were deluded by the illusory power of Viṣṇu and worried about a time of famine. 35-36.
O best of Brahmins, you have prepared only very costly food here; however, you have never given any gift out of compassion. O Brahmin, you have never performed the worship of the gods.
Having obtained the festival days, you did not offer wealth to the Brahmins;
and when the time for the Śrāddha arrived, you did not perform it with faith. Your virtuous wife said to you, "This day has come. 38-39.
O high-minded one, this is the time for the ancestral rites (śrāddha) of your father-in-law and mother-in-law;
having heard those words of hers, you abandon your home and flee.
You have never seen the path of dharma, nor have you ever even heard of it.
Greed is one's mother, father, and brother; greed is one's kinsmen and relatives.
Having always abandoned unrighteousness and protected greed alone, you have therefore become miserable and are now excessively tormented by poverty. 41-42.
Day after day, great thirst increases within your heart;
whenever wealth enters your house, it grows even further. Thus, you are being consumed by that very thirst, which takes the form of fire.

At night you sleep soundly and remain fixed in thought; yet when day arrives, you are always pervaded by great delusions. When will this end? Will it be after a thousand, a hundred thousand, ten million, or even a hundred million [lives]? 44-45.
When will there be a *kharva* and a *nikharva* in my house?
Likewise, a thousand, a hundred thousand, ten million, and even an *arbuda*—
once a *kharva* and a *nikharva* have been acquired, thirst does not depart at all.
Having abandoned your body, it always attains growth;
yet you never gave [in charity], never offered [in sacrifice], and never fed the Brahmins.
You merely dug into the middle of the earth and buried it, so that your sons do not even know of it. 47–48.

Therefore, O wise one, always employ some other means for the sake of acquiring wealth; you should consult the world regarding alchemy, the art of digging for minerals, or the application of collyrium. 49. Furthermore, [consult them] regarding the science of metallurgy.
Wandering about, deluded by thirst, you alone ask questions;
constantly contemplating the touch of those who grant supernatural powers, you inquire well while thinking of entry into the openings of the subterranean caverns. 50–51.
Burned by the fire of craving, you find no happiness at all;
scorched by the fire of craving, you cry out "Alas! and lose your senses.
Thus deluded, O best of Brahmins, you have fallen under the sway of time.

"When your wife and sons asked about that wealth, you did not tell them the story at all; rather, you abandoned your life-breaths and went to Yama. Thus, I have related to you the entire account concerning your previous life."
By this karma, O Brahmin, you have become destitute and poor;
yet in this cycle of existence, you always possess virtuous sons who are indeed devoted, well-behaved, endowed with knowledge, and ever delighted in truth and righteousness. (55)
For him with whom Viṣṇu is pleased, these things arise in his home:
wealth, grain, a wife, and endless sons and grandsons; indeed, he alone enjoys them in the mortal world for whom Viṣṇu is well-disposed.
Without the grace of Viṣṹṇu, one shall not obtain a wife, sons, a good birth, or a noble family, O Brāhmaṇa; that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
(58) Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Sumanas," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. (17)
The eighteenth chapter.
Somaśarman said:
"O Sage, you have related to me the sin committed by me in a previous birth."
"O best of Brahmins, why was I abandoned by you in the state of a Śūdra? O most excellent of the twice-born, how did I indeed attain the status of a Brāhmaṇa?
O scholar of knowledge and realization, tell me the entire reason for that."
Vasiṣṭha said:
O twice-born one, I shall fully relate that deed based on dharma which was performed by you in the past; listen to it, if you so desire. 3.
There was a certain Brahmin, sinless, of virtuous conduct, and highly learned;
he was a devotee of Viṣṇu, righteous in soul, and eternally devoted to Viṣṇu. Under the pretext of visiting holy places, he wandered alone over the earth.
Wandering about, that highly intelligent one arrived at your house. O best of the twice-born, he requested a single place for his residence;
it was granted by your wife, along with you and your sons.
"O Brahmin, stay here at my auspicious home with ease," he said again and again to that meritorious Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇa;
"O you of noble vows, remain here comfortably, for this house is yours."
Today I am blessed; today I have come to this holy place.
Today the fruit of the pilgrimage has been attained through the sight of your two feet.
This excellent and meritorious abode of cows is offered for your residence.
Having performed a massage of his limbs and rubbed his feet, and having washed them again with water, he bathed with the water used for washing the feet.
He then immediately offered clarified butter, curd, milk, food, and buttermilk.
"O lady, you have thus satisfied this great-souled brāhmaṇa. Along with your wife, sons, and other highly fortunate ones, this Vaiṣṇava is truly learned in spiritual knowledge."
Then, when the morning had arrived on that auspicious day which bestows good fortune— the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, which destroys sins—
that day, which destroys all transgressions, duly arrived.
O twice-born one, having reached that [night] in which the Lord Hṛṣīkeśa enters into yogic sleep,
those people who were wise in intellect abandoned all household activities there, being intent on meditation upon Viṣṇu. 14–15.
They celebrated a supreme festival with songs and auspicious musical instruments;
all the brāhmaṇas offered praise with the Vedas and most auspicious hymns.
Having thus attained such a great festival, that best of brāhmaṇas—
On that day, while staying there, he heard the greatness of Ekādaśī being recited by a brāhmaṇa;
together with his wife, sons, and daughters, he listened to that unsurpassed dharma. 17–18.
Having heard this of great merit, urged by his wife and son, he said: "Through association with this brahmin, perform this very vow.
Having heard those significant words, which bestow all merit, [he acted accordingly].
With a mind firmly resolved, "I shall perform this vow," you went together with your wife and sons to the river and performed your ablutions;
then, with a joyful heart, you worshipped Madhusūdana, O Brahmin.
Having performed a night vigil with all kinds of offerings, merits, perfumes, incense, and the like, as well as with dance, song, and other such arts,
he then bathed again in the river on the occasion of a Brahmin’s visit.
The Lord of the Gods of gods was worshipped with auspicious offerings such as flowers and incense;
having bowed with devotion to Govinda and bathed him again and again, they gave such an offering (nirvāpa) to the high-souled Brāhmaṇa. 23–24.

Having bowed down to that brāhmaṇa with devotion, he gave him a generous sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and performed the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) together with his sons, wife, and others. He had been sent by you yourself with sincere devotion and a virtuous disposition.
O best of the twice-born, this vow was thus practiced by you through association with a Brahmin and by the grace of Viṣṇu;
you have attained the state of a Brahmin, endowed with truth and righteousness.
O one of great wisdom, it was by virtue of that vow that you attained a noble lineage among the gods on earth (brāhmaṇas), which is filled with truth and righteousness.
Therefore, [this gift] belongs to that very brāhmaṇa, a high-souled devotee of Viṣṇu.
Food that is well-prepared and given with faith and a sincere disposition—
by virtue of that gift, delicious food presents itself to him.
Yet, his mind is utterly deluded by great ignorance and pervaded by craving.

O Brahmin, in a previous birth, wealth was indeed accumulated for your sake alone; however, while dying out of greed for a son and a wife, you did not give it to Brāhmaṇas or to other distressed ones. 31. This was done by you as you were passing away.
Due to the presence of that sin, poverty has overtaken you.
Having abandoned the desire for a son and having cast away affection from afar, you have become sonless; this is indeed the fruit of that sin. 32–33.
A virtuous son, a noble family, wealth, grain, excellent women, a good birth, a good death, excellent enjoyments, happiness itself,
sovereignty, heaven, liberation, and whatever else is difficult to attain— [all these are obtained]. 34.
Through the grace of that god Viṣṇu, the Great-Souled One,
therefore, by worshipping Govinda Nārāyaṇa, the Untainted,
you shall attain the supreme abode, that highest station of Viṣṇu.

O Brahmin, I have related before you in its entirety all that was performed by you in previous births, which has resulted in your having excellent sons, wealth, grain, fine enjoyments, and happiness. 37. This has been fully explained by me in your presence.
"Knowing this, O illustrious one, become devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
Thus was that noble and eminent brāhmaṇa enlightened by the son of Brahmā; filled with joy, that high-souled man bowed there with devotion to Vasiṣṭha.
Having taken leave of the brahmin, he went home; having reached his wife Sumanā, he was filled with joy and said:
"Indeed, all that has happened—my former conduct—was brought about by that very brahmin through your grace.
O blessed lady, Vasiṣṭha has dispelled my delusion this very day."
"Indeed, by propitiating Madhusūdana, I shall attain liberation, that supreme state.
Having heard those most exalted, great, and highly auspicious words which bestow blessings, she was filled with joy and said to her beloved: "You are blessed; you have been awakened by the Brahmin."
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Story of Sumanas," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the collection of fifty-five thousand verses, in the section concerning Indra.
Chapter Nineteen.
Sūta said:

The highly wise Somaśarman, the best of beings, together with Sumanā, bathed at the confluence of the Kapilā on the exceedingly meritorious banks of the Revā, which bestows great merit; having bathed there, the intelligent one offered libations to the gods and the ancestors.
The tranquil-souled one performed austerities,
chanting the auspicious name of Nārāyaṇa with the twelve-syllable mantra; the high-minded one, firm in his vows, remained absorbed in meditation upon that very God of gods, Vāsudeva.
Remaining always steady and free from desire and anger, she beheld Keśava while sitting, lying down, traveling, or dreaming.
And she was a virtuous woman, highly fortunate, and devoted solely to her husband.
Even as he was devoted to the beloved Sumanā and engaged in ascetic penance,
fear was manifested before him by obstacles;
for virulent, black serpents would approach that high-souled one there.
As Somaśarman was thus being tormented at his side,
lions, tigers, elephants, and others created for him a state of fearlessness; likewise,
vetālas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, kūṣmāṇḍas, pretas, and bhairavas [did so].
These [beings] display a terrible fear that destroys life. Various kinds of most fearsome lions have gathered there;
with mouths formidable with fangs, they roar most dreadfully. 8-9.

Through meditation on Viṣṇu, the great-minded Somaśarman, whose soul was possessed of dharma, remained unmoved; though that bull among sages was shaken by well-entrenched and formidable obstacles, Somaśarman, the best of the twice-born, did not waver from his meditation.
10. Thus, the excellent brahmin Somaśarman did not move from his meditative absorption.
Greatly afflicted by stormy winds, cold, and heavy rain,
a most terrifying lion arrived there with a roar like a kettledrum;
seeing it, the twice-born man, trembling with fear, remembered Nṛhari.
[He saw] the god who resembles a sapphire, clad in yellow garments, possessed of great majesty, bearing a conch and a discus, and holding a mace and a lotus;
[he was adorned] with a necklace of great pearls that imitated the color of the moon. 13.
Janārdana was shining with the Kaustubha jewel;
his chest, adorned with the divine Śrīvatsa mark, gleamed, as did his limbs beautified by every ornament, and his eyes resembled lotus petals. 14–15.

With a face of beautiful smiles, exceedingly serene, and adorned with garlands of jewels, Hṛṣīkeśa was resplendent; by him, meditation was surely performed. O Kṛṣṇa, you alone are the refuge for those who have come to you for protection, you who are compassionate toward those seeking shelter.
Salutations to the God of gods; what fear will he cause me?
(17) Into the belly of that Great-Souled One, within whom the three worlds and the other seven exist, have I entered for refuge; where, then, can there be any fear for me? (18)
I have gone for refuge to Him who destroys all fears— the source from which powerful rites of sorcery and other such things proceed—
I have gone to him for refuge— he who is the protector of the devotees of Viṣṇu,
the refuge of all the gods, the high-souled Dānavas, and the path of yoga for the devotees of Kṛṣṇa. (20–21)
I, who possess knowledge, have gone for refuge to that one Indra in his true form, who is fearless and the destroyer of fear, and the destroyer of sin.
He exists in the form of medicine itself for the destruction of diseases.
I have taken refuge in Him who is free from disease and free from worldly joy.
(23) He is immovable, yet He can move the worlds; He is sinless and is knowledge itself.
Having attained refuge in Him, what fear will He do to me? (24)
I have gone for refuge to Him who is the protector of all holy men, who is free from ailment, who protects the universe, and who is the soul of the universe;
Having sought refuge in Him, I bow down to that Narasiṃha.
(26) A massive-bodied forest elephant, intoxicated with pride, approached the Lord who moves with the playful gait of an elephant and is compassionate toward those who have come for refuge. (27)
I have come for refuge to the elephant-faced one, endowed with wisdom, who holds a noose and a goad;
to Kālāsya and Gajatuṇḍa, I have gone for refuge. I have gone for refuge to the Boar, the slayer of Hiraṇyākṣa.
I have taken refuge in Vāmana, who is compassionate toward those who seek his protection.
(29) May the dwarfs, the hunchbacks, the spirits, the kūṣmāṇḍas, and others—all of whom assume the form of death—cease to show me fear. (30)
I have taken refuge in the nectar-like mantra; what fear can it cause me?
Hari is the friend of Brahman, the giver of Brahman, the Brahman itself, and consists of the knowledge of Brahman.
(31) I have taken refuge in Him as my shelter; what fear can it cause me?
He who is fearless, the destroyer of the world's fear, yet the giver of fear;
I have come before him whose very form is fear—what can he do to me?
He is the savior of all worlds and the destroyer of all sinners. 32–33.
I have sought refuge in that Janārdana, who is the embodiment of Dharma; he is the enemy of the gods, who assumes a wondrous golden form.
I shall always go to him for refuge; he is my ultimate resort.
The fierce and violent storm-torrent is intensely burning my body;
I have sought refuge in You, for You are my eternal resort.
The cold is extreme, the rain is excessive, and the sun’s heat is tormenting.
I have gone for refuge to that God who possesses their form; these protectors of mine, who grant fearlessness, have arrived in the form of Time (Kāla).
I have always sought refuge in these who possess the true nature of Hari.

I take refuge in him whom they call Nārāyaṇa, the primordial perfected one, the Lord of Siddhas, the supreme God of all gods, who is indeed the unique lamp consisting of pure knowledge. (39) Thus, meditating and constantly praising Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions.
Then, through his devotion, Hari was brought into the very heart of that man; having witnessed the exertion and valor of Somaśarman,
Hṛṣīkeśa manifested himself and spoke to him with great joy.
"O Somaśarman, O highly wise one, listen along with your wife: I am Vāsudeva, O best of brahmins; choose a boon, O observer of noble vows.
