Thus addressed by him, O best of brahmins, he opened both his eyes.
Having seen the Lord Viṣṇu, who is dark as a rain cloud and of great majesty (43),
whose limbs are adorned with the splendor of all ornaments, who is equipped with all weapons,
endowed with divine marks, and whose eyes resemble lotuses (44).
Clad in yellow garments, the illustrious one beheld the Lord of the Gods shining resplendently,
mounted upon Vainateya and bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace—
the great sustainer of Brahmā and others, and of this entire world. 45.
Filled with great joy, he prostrated himself like a staff before that Teacher of the World, who transcends this universe, who is beyond all forms,
endowed with splendor, and radiant with a brilliance equal to ten million suns. 46–47.
With palms joined in reverence, he addressed Jaya Mādhava, the bestower of honor, along with that Sumanā, saying, "Victory! Victory!
(48) "Victory, O Lord of Yogins, O Sovereign of Yogis! Victory, O You who recline upon the body of the serpent!"
Victory to You, the limb of sacrifice, the conqueror of sacrifice, the Lord of sacrifice, the eternal, the all-pervading!
(49) Victory to You, the Lord of all, the infinite, whose form is sacrifice; salutations be unto You!
Victory to You, the best among those possessed of knowledge; victory to You, the leader of knowledge! (50)

Victory to you, O Giver of All, O Omniscient One! Victory to you, O Creator of all beings! Victory to you, O Lord of the nature of the individual soul; great life to you, homage be to you! 51 Victory to you, O Source of Wisdom, O Embodiment of Wisdom! Victory to you, O Bestower of Life!
Victory, O Lord of merit who destroys sin! Victory, O Hari, Lord of merit!
52 Victory, O Lord whose nature is knowledge! Salutations to You, who are attainable through knowledge! Victory, O Lord with eyes like lotus petals! Salutations to You, the lotus-navelled one! 53
Victory to Govinda, the cowherd protector; victory to the stainless bearer of the conch!
Victory to the bearer of the discus, whose form is both manifest and unmanifest; salutations to You. 54. Victory to the one whose limbs possess the splendor of valor; victory to the leader of valor!
Victory to the one whose body is the play of the goddess Jayalakṣmī;

victory to the one whose limbs are the splendor of valor! Victory to the giver of the pride of enterprise; victory to the time of enterprise—salutations again and again to the one who is enterprise itself! 55-56.
Salutation to that Dharma, who is capable of victorious effort, who maintains the three types of exertion, and who is engaged in the endeavor of battle; salutation to you,
the golden-hued one, and salutation to you, the radiant one.
Salutations to the Supreme Self, whose nature is supreme splendor, who consists of all radiance,
who destroys the splendor of the Daityas, who removes the light of sin,
and who exists for the welfare of cows and Brahmins. 58–59.
Salutations to the consumer of oblations, who is called the eater of offerings;
salutations to the consumer of ancestral offerings, whose form is the *svadhā* call;
salutations to the sacrifice whose form is the *svāhā* call, the purifier—salutations again and again. 60.
Salutations to you, O Hara, who holds the Śārṅga bow in hand and removes all sins;
salutations to the one who impels both the existent and the non-existent, and who is endowed with supreme knowledge.
Salutations to the one whose very nature is the Veda, the purifier; salutations again and again.
Salutations to you, Harikeśa, who removes all afflictions;
salutations to Keśava, the supreme; salutations to you, the sustainer of the universe. Salutations to the performer of compassion; salutations to you, who consists of joy.
Salutations eternally to the Infinite One, the Pure One who destroys afflictions;
salutations eternally to the Blissful One, the Pure and Absolute One, whose feet are bowed to by Rudra and whose feet are bowed to by Brahmā. 64–65.
Salutations to him whose lotus feet are bowed to by the lords of the gods and demons;
salutations again and again to the Supreme Lord, the unconquered one, whose nature is immortality. Salutations to the dweller of the milk ocean, who is beloved of Padmā.
Oṃ, salutations again and again to the pure Oṃkāra, to the Immovable One (Acala).

Salutations again and again to the Pervasive One, to the All-pervading One, the remover of all misfortunes; salutations to the Boar (Varāha), and salutations to that Great Tortoise (Mahākūrma). 67–68.

Salutations to the Great Soul in the form of Vāmana; salutations to Nṛsiṃha. Salutations to the divine Rāma, the slayer of all the kṣatriyas. Salutations to the omniscient Fish-incarnation; salutations to that Rāma.
Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, the Buddha; salutations to the destroyer of the Mlecchas. (70) Salutations to the brahmin Kapila; salutations to that Hayagrīva.
Salutations to the one whose nature is Vyāsa; salutations to you who consist of all things. (71)
Having thus praised Hṛṣīkeśa, he spoke to Janārdana: "O Purifier, even Brahmā does not know the further shore of your qualities;
nor indeed can the omniscient Rudra, the thousand-eyed one, praise you in such a manner. (72)

O Lord, who indeed is capable of speaking such things? O Keśava, what kind of intellect do I possess that I could offer this hymn to You, both in Your aspect with attributes and Your attributeless nature?
O observer of noble vows, I am but a servant; may my speech, whether correct or incorrect, be forgiven.
"O Purifier, O Lord of the World, show me mercy birth after birth.
(75) Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Sumanas," in the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
Chapter Twenty.
Hari said:
"O twice-born one, by this penance, by this merit, by this truth, and also by this purifying hymn, I am pleased; let a boon be chosen."
"O illustrious one, grant a boon that is in accordance with your heart's desire; whatever wish you desire, I shall fulfill it for you.
Somaśarman said:
First, grant me this one supreme boon, O Kṛṣṇa, which I most desire:
that with a well-pleased mind, you may show me great compassion today; and having reached birth after birth, may I practice devotion unto you.
Show me that supreme, immovable abode which bestows liberation;
[show me] a son who shall be the savior of my lineage, endowed with divine marks, eternally devoted to Viṣṇu, and the sustainer of my family. 4-5.
He is omniscient, the giver of all, self-controlled, and endowed with the splendor of austerity;
he is the eternal protector and worshiper of the gods, the Brahmins, and the worlds;
he is a friend to the divine, meritorious in nature, a donor, and a scholar of wisdom.
"O Hara and Keśava, grant me such a son, even if he be poor. "Let it be so; there is no doubt. I choose this boon for myself," [he said]. Hari replied:
"So be it, O best of the twice-born; there is no doubt that this shall come to pass.
By my grace, you shall have an excellent son who will be the savior of your lineage. You yourself shall enjoy excellent pleasures, both divine and human, in this world."
Having beheld the supreme happiness and auspiciousness born from the birth of a son,
you shall not experience suffering for as long as you live as a brahmin;
you will be a donor, an enjoyer, and a grasper of virtues— of this there is no doubt.
"You shall also attain death at a sacred ford and reach the supreme goal.
Having thus granted this boon to the Brahmin and his wife, the Lord Hari vanished,
appearing like a dream.
Then that best of the twice-born, Somaśarman, joined by his daughter Asumā,
performed meritorious acts of charity at Amarakaṇṭaka, on the exceedingly holy bank of the Revā, a sacred and purifying tīrtha.
After a great deal of time had passed, that Somaśarman,
having performed his ablutions at the confluence of the Kapilā and the Revā, emerged; there the Brahmin saw before him a single white elephant.
It was brilliantly radiant, beautiful, divine, intoxicatingly charming, and endowed with exquisite marks;
its limbs were adorned with the splendor of various ornaments and possessed abundant majesty.
Its two temples shone with vermilion and saffron.
Adorned with blue lotuses on its ears and joined with flagstaffs,
there stood a divine person upon the elephant, firm and of excellent luster,
endowed with celestial marks and decorated with all ornaments. 17–18.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, anointed with divine perfumes and unguents,
most serene like the full moon and accompanied by an umbrella and chowries—
excellent as he was, he beheld him once more as he proceeded mounted upon an elephant.
Seeing that most auspicious person, beautiful and accompanied by an elephant, being praised by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Gandharvas,
Somaśarman, his mind filled with wonder, reflected: 20–21.
"Who is this one of divine limbs, who, having reached the path, proceeds with firm vows?
While he was thinking thus, [the traveler] arrived at his house.
As he was entering the gate of the house, [he saw] one of beautiful form and enchanting appearance.
Filled with great joy, Somaśarman, the best of the twice-born and a righteous soul, proceeded in haste toward his own home; yet,
as soon as he reached the door of his house, he did not see him there.
The high-minded and best of the twice-born, endowed with divine garments, scattered flowers that were naturally fragrant upon the courtyard;
it was further anointed with auspicious, sweet-smelling sandalwood and saffron. 25.25–26ab.
Seeing his own courtyard filled with dūrvā grass and unbroken grains (akṣata),
he was thus overcome with wonder and reflected again and again; then that wise man beheld Sumana, who possessed divine and auspicious splendor.
Somaśarman said:
"By whom were these divine ornaments given—this beauty, this charm, this good fortune, and the decoration of garments and jewelry? (28)
"Therefore, O blessed lady, tell me the reason for this without hesitation.
Having thus addressed his wife, the best of the twice-born ceased speaking.
Sumanā said:

Listen: a certain most excellent of divine beings arrived, mounted upon a white elephant, adorned with celestial ornaments, his limbs anointed with divine perfumes, and endowed with divine wonders. 30.
Indeed, that one God, served by Brahmins and Gandharvas, arrived while being praised by gods, Gandharvas, and Cāraṇas;
[he was accompanied by] women rich in meritorious beauty and endowed with the grace of form. 31–32.
Richly adorned with all ornaments and with all their desires fulfilled,
they, along with that high-souled man, filled the four-sided pavilion— which was endowed with every splendor— with jewels in my very presence.
There, I was indeed placed upon an auspicious seat by the brahmins;
they all gave me garments, ornaments,
and decorations, accompanied by Vedic auspicious songs and meritorious songs from the scriptures.
Having been consecrated by these smiles, they all vanished once more;
then, O best of the twice-born, they all spoke to me again from every side: "We shall indeed dwell in your house forever."
"O pure and auspicious one, you shall always remain together with your husband.
Having spoken thus, they all departed; indeed, it was by me that this was seen.
Having heard the account related by her, the high-minded one [reflected].
Then that highly intelligent Somaśarman, having fallen into reflection— thinking, "What is this? Is it created by the gods?"—
became engaged in the duties of a Brahmin, which are the highest dharma characterized by righteousness.
Therefore, that illustrious lady, steadfast in her vows, conceived a fetus;
with that fetus, the goddess then shone exceedingly, endowed with the blazing flames of the splendor associated with a radiant son.
Then, by means of his ascetic penance, Sāhi begot a son who resembled a god;
at that moment, divine drums resounded in the sky. The great gods blew their conchs, and the Gandharvas sang charmingly.
Then, at that time, all the Apsarases indeed danced for them.
Then, O best of the twice-born, Brahmā arrived together with the Asuras and,
being composed, gave him the name Suvrata.

Then, O gods, all those of great splendor departed after having performed the naming ceremony. When those gods had gone, Somaśarman, the best of the twice-born, performed for his son the rites beginning with the *jātakarma*.
O illustrious one, when a son was born who was firm in his vows and fashioned by the gods,
great fortune abounded in his house, filled with wealth and grain,
as well as elephants, horses, buffaloes, cows, gold, and jewels.
Just as the abode of Kubera shines with heaps of wealth, so too did the house of Somaśarman resplend;
that best of the twice-born performed his duties, such as meditation and meritorious acts. 48.
Having arrived there for the purpose of a pilgrimage to sacred sites, the Brahmin, filled with various merits,
performed other meritorious acts of charity there, O best of the twice-born, being wise and endowed with knowledge and virtue. 49-50.
Having thus accomplished his religious duties and protected them again and again,
that best of the twice-born performed the birth-rites and other ceremonies for his son,
and indeed celebrated his marriage with great joy.

Sons were born to his son, endowed with virtues and auspicious marks; they were possessed of truth, dharma, and austerity, and were always devoted to the practice of charity. Somaśarman performed meritorious deeds for them.
O highly fortunate one, he rejoices in the happiness of his grandsons;
free from old age and disease, he enjoys every kind of pleasure, and his body remains as if it were twenty-five years of age. 54.
The highly intelligent Somaśarman shone like the splendor of the sun;
and that noble lady Sumanā also shone with meritorious auspiciousness,
along with her sons and grandsons who were illustrious and restrained by their vows and self-control.
Possessing exceedingly large eyes and the merits of devotion to their husband and other virtues,
the two high-souled spouses, endowed with youth as if they were sixteen years of age, rejoiced in their beautiful and auspicious state.
Filled with joy, the two meritorious ones, Mahodaya and [his wife],
were thus [united]. O best of the twice-born, I shall now relate this account of theirs, which is endowed with virtuous conduct, as well as the practice of the vow of Suvrata.
Thus he propitiated Nārāyaṇa, the one who is free from all ailment.
(60) Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Origin of Suvrata," within the Legend of Sumanas in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the collection of fifty-five thousand verses.
Chapter Twenty-one.
Sūta said:
Once, the divine Vyāsa, filled with great wonder, questioned Brahmā, the Lord of the universe, concerning the entire narrative of Suvratā.
Vyāsa said: O Soul of the World, O Great Lord of the God of Gods, I now desire to hear the life-story of Suvrata, concerning the arrangement of the worlds.
Brahmā said:
O highly fortunate son of Parāśara, listen to this supreme and meritorious account concerning the practice of austerity by the virtuous and excellent Brahmin Suvrata. 3.
The wise Suvrata, even from his childhood reflecting deeply,
beheld within the womb the divine Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person;
through the practice of his previous deeds, he then attained meditation upon Hari.

One should meditate upon and contemplate that god who bears the conch and the discus, whose navel is a lotus, and who bestows great merit; O Gīti, he indeed [attains] knowledge through the recitation of this.
Thus, that best of the twice-born always meditated upon Lord Hari.

Thus that best of boys always played with the children; the wise, meritorious, and virtuous-souled one even made the name of the great-souled Hara known to the children. 7. He, the intelligent one, who was devoted to merit, performed this for them.
The high-minded one challenged his enemy by means of Hari’s name:
"O Keśava, come, come! O Mādhava, wielder of the discus, you alone are the Supreme Person; sport with me! 8–9.
"O Madhusūdana, we two must proceed in this very same manner;
likewise, O twice-born one, the invocation of Hari shall be performed by us using his names during play,
recitation, laughter, lying down, singing, and watching performances."

In his vehicle, his seat, his meditation, his mantras, his knowledge, and in his virtuous deeds, he sees Janārdana, the Lord of the World; he speaks thus, and he meditates solely upon Him, the Great Lord, the Sovereign of the Universe. 11–12.
Whether in grass, wood, stone, dry or moist, that righteous-souled one beholds Govinda, the lotus-eyed Keśava;
likewise in the sky, in the midst of the earth, on mountains, and in forests.
In water, on land, on stone, and among living beings— thus the high-minded,
virtuous, and well-disposed brahmin beholds Nṛsiṃha;
having attained the play of a child, he thus delights day after day.
And with songs of sweet syllables and divine melodies, accompanied by rhythmic beats, tempos, beautiful tones, and melodic modulations, they sang of Kṛṣṇa.
(16) Suvrata said:
I go for refuge to Madhusūdana, the Lord of Yoga, the destroyer of all sins, whom the knowers of the Vedas constantly meditate upon as the one in whose very body the entire universe resides,
and who alone pervades all the worlds and in whom all the worlds dwell. 17.
I perpetually bow to that Supreme Lord, who is free from all defects, and to His pair of feet alone.
(18) Those whose intellects are purified by the Vedāntas constantly recite the name of Nārāyaṇa, the treasury of virtues and of infinite prowess;
for the sake of crossing over this entire ocean of worldly existence—which is endless, bottomless, and difficult to traverse—I take refuge in Him as my sole protection. (19)

O Lord of Yogis, you who are the royal swan upon the lake of the minds of great souls, whose entire pure majesty is ever-present— grant protection to me, a wretched being, by means of your pair of stainless and expansive feet, O enemy of the Asuras!
20 And for the sake of shattering the darkness of suffering right here, I meditate upon the Lord, the Moon, who is the master of the entire world.

For the sake of protecting the world, I constantly sing of the one Lord of the universe at Śrīraṅgam—the preceptor of all worlds, the Lord of the gods, who has wedded Dharma and is endowed with truth;
who is the destroyer of ignorance, the peerless one, equal to the sun, the root of bliss, and possessed of all majesty. 21-22.
Thus, I sing with devotion to that storehouse of nectar, who is full in every way and skilled in song through melodies beyond all other tastes;
he, endowed with the instruments of his own yoga, perceives the eternal universe, including all things moving and unmoving, as the vision of the supreme reality.
Those of this world who are deeply sinful do not see him at all; therefore, one should always seek refuge in that Keśava.
Beating cymbals with his two hands and accompanied by rhythmic clapping,
he sings songs of praise to Kṛṣṇa and rejoices along with the boys.
Thus, ever devoted to play in his childhood state, he remains thus.
Suvrata, the son of Sumanas, was entirely devoted to meditation upon Viṣṇu.
As he was playing, his mother said to him, who possessed beautiful marks:
"O child, take your food; hunger is surely afflicting you."
The wise one spoke again to Sumanā’s mother:
"I am truly satisfied by the great nectar, the essence of meditation upon Hari;
I have ascended to the seat of food and behold the most delicious meal. (28)
This food is Viṣṇu himself; for the Self has taken refuge in food.
May that Viṣṇu, who dwells eternally in the Ocean of Milk, be satisfied by this food in his form as the Self. 29–30.
By this meritorious water, may Keśava attain satisfaction;
by these betel leaves, sandalwood, fragrances, and charming flowers—
may Keśava, who is satisfied by his own essential nature, attain satisfaction.
On his bed, the righteous-souled one should meditate upon that Kṛṣṇa;
I have gone for refuge to that Kṛṣṇa who is endowed with yogic sleep.
Thus, O twice-born one, [he should do so] during eating, dressing, sitting, and lying down. 32–33.
One should meditate upon that Vāsudeva and offer everything to him;
having attained youth, the righteous-souled one, indeed abandoning sensual enjoyments,
remains absorbed in meditation on Keśava on that most excellent mountain of lapis lazuli.
There is the Vaiṣṇava Liṅga Siddheśvara, which destroys all sins;
and having meditated upon Maheśvara, known as Rudra Oṃkāra, the God who was honored by Brahmā on the southern bank of the Narmadā. 35-36.
Having taken refuge at Siddheśvara, he reflected upon the nature of asceticism.
37. Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Narrative of Sumanas" within the Indra-section of the Bhūmikhaṇḍa, in the glorious Padma Purāṇa, consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
Chapter Twenty-two.
Vyāsa said:
O highly fortunate one, I shall now ask you a single question; please answer it, for you yourself previously spoke of the excellent vow dedicated to each Lord.
"By virtue of his former practice, he meditates upon the flawless Nārāyaṇa;
in what lineage was this man of excellent vows born in his previous birth?
Tell me that now, and how Hari was propitiated by him."
"O Lord of the Gods, by this [merit] as well, who is this person so filled with the abundance of merit?
Brahmā said:
"In the meritorious city of Vaidiśa, which is filled with all prosperity..."
There, the king was the powerful Ṛtadhvaja of great splendor; his son was the highly wise and famous Rukmabhūṣaṇa,
whose wife was the illustrious and lawful spouse Saṃdhyāvalī.
Having begotten upon her a son who was like himself,
the prince then gave him the name Dharmāṅgada;
he was endowed with all auspicious marks and devoted to his father.
This son of Rukmāṅgada, the best among the blessed,
gave his own head to Mohinī for the sake of his father’s happiness; indeed,
he was equal to Viṣṇu himself through his Vaiṣṇava dharma and devotion to his father.

Hṛṣīkeśa was exceedingly pleased; that knower of all duties, the Vaiṣṇava and best of the Sātvatas, was led to the abode of Viṣṇu. Dharmāṅgada was highly wise and proficient in both discernment and knowledge.
Remaining there, that highly wise one, Dharma, the ornament of righteousness,
enjoys divine pleasures that accord with his mind while rejoicing.
At the end of a full thousand yugas, Dharma indeed remains the ornament of righteousness.

The wise one performed austerities and became intent on meditation upon Viṣṇu. Having abandoned defects such as desire and anger, that best of the twice-born, having restrained the group of his senses, practiced penance continuously.
Having unified his mind and joined it with Viṣṇu in the presence of Siddheśvara on that most excellent mountain of lapis lazuli,
he remained thus for a hundred years through the meditation of this great-souled one.
The Lord of the World, Keśava, who holds the conch, discus, and mace, was exceedingly gracious;
together with Lakṣmī, he granted him another boon:
"O you of excellent vows, O righteous-souled one, best among the wise, take heed! (16-17)
"Choose a boon; may it be auspicious for you; Kṛṣṇa has come to slay him. Having heard these unsurpassed words of Viṣṇu, Medhāvī was filled with great joy upon seeing the Lord Janārdana.
Then, with his palms joined in reverence, he offered a salutation.
Suvrata said:
"The ocean of worldly existence is filled with the waves of a vast and great web of suffering, and with the surging currents of various accumulations of delusion."
Filled with my own faults and virtues, I have therefore quickly sought refuge in Janārdana;

O Madhusūdana, grant your hand to that wretched man for whom there is no vision because of the mass of delusion’s darkness and the heaps of my sins, while the great ocean of karma thunders, rains, and flashes with streaks of lightning. 20–21.

This dense forest of saṃsāra, though surrounded by many trees of manifold suffering and infested with lions of delusion, is ablaze; O Kṛṣṇa, protect it, for it is being incessantly scorched by the intense heat of the great fire of compassion. 22.
This tree of saṃsāra here is exceedingly decayed, yet it is lofty, with illusion as its trunk and the many sufferings of compassion as its branches.
O Enemy of Mura, the union with wife and others has borne fruit; O Blessed One, protect me who have fallen from that height.

23 I am constantly being burned by the fires of suffering, whose thick smoke consists of various delusions, and by sorrows resembling separation and death; O Kṛṣṇa, grant me liberation and always drench me thoroughly with the waters of knowledge. 24
O Kṛṣṇa, I have fallen into the great abyss called saṃsāra, which is covered by a veil of terrible darkness; I am constantly afflicted by fear and misery.
Therefore, having become detached from that world, I have come to you for refuge, O Great Lord who is ever-compassionate toward the virtuous.
(25) Those who, with minds fixed in constant devotion and endowed with a disciplined intellect, meditate upon You alone, attain the supreme state through their wisdom.

Having bowed to that pair of feet which possess great merit and which the hosts of gods and kinnaras constantly meditate upon—26—I speak of no other, I worship none other, I think of none other; I bow perpetually to Your pair of lotus feet.
O Kṛṣṇa, fulfill my desire this very day; let the mass of my sins depart far away. 27.
"I am your slave, O God; I am your servant, birth after birth. I constantly remember the pair of your lotus feet.
(28) "If you are pleased with me, O Lord Kṛṣṇa, grant me this boon: lead my mother and father, O Kṛṣṇa, to your own abode. (29)
"O Mahādeva, there is no doubt that you will not be able to endure me.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"In this way, your supreme task shall be accomplished; of this there is no doubt. (30)
Hṛṣīkeśa was pleased with him, being fully satisfied by his devotion;
he and the two others, Sumanā and Maśarmaka, along with Suvrata, went to the world of Viṣṇu, which is free from burning and dissolution. 31.
O high-minded one, for as long as two kalpas had elapsed, that twice-born man of excellent vows enjoyed divine worlds;
yet, for the sake of the gods' work, he returned once more to the house of Kaśyapa right here.
Having descended at the command of that wielder of the discus,
he who enjoys the station of Indra and indeed that of Viṣṇu through His grace,
is renowned as Vasudatta and is saluted by all the gods. 34.
He who now enjoys the station of Indra in heaven is Vāsava.
All this has been told to you regarding the cause of the creation;
I shall further explain that other matter about which you inquire.
Vyāsa said: O highly wise one, Dharmāṅgada, the mighty son of Rukmāṅgada, was born at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, at the time of creation, together with Vāsava. 37
Therefore, O Lord of the Gods, how is it that there is another Dharmāṅgada on earth and another King Rukmāṅgada, while this one is the lord of the thirty gods?
This doubt has arisen within me; you ought to explain it to me.
Brahmā said:
"Indeed, O best of the twice-born, I shall relate to you that which destroys all doubt; it concerns the divine play for the purpose of creation."
Just as days, fortnights, months,
and seasons come and go, and as years, Manus, and Yugas likewise return again, so too does the Kalpa arrive; thus I shall go to Janārdana.
O one of great wisdom, while I remain thus, all things moving and unmoving pass away; yet the Soul of Yoga creates the entire universe once more, exactly as before.
Again I am born, again the Vedas, and again those gods and twice-born ones.
Likewise, O highly fortunate one, all these kings who arise are immersed in their own conduct; the wise man is not deluded by them,
just as the highly fortunate King Rukmāṅgada was in a previous kalpa.
Likewise, this illustrious twice-born Dharmāṅgada has been born;
and the highly wise Rāma and others, as well as Yayāti, Nahuṣa, Manu, and other great souls, come into being and pass away. (45)
Kings devoted to righteousness enjoy the sovereign position of Indra, just as the heroic Dharmāṅgada enjoys his great station;
so too do the Vedas, the gods, and the Purāṇas, following the Smṛtis. 46–47.
O best of the twice-born, all this—the meritorious life-story of Suvrata which bestows a favorable rebirth—has been narrated to you.
O illustrious one, I shall now proclaim the Unmanifest before you. 48–49.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Narrative of Suvrata," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the Śrī Padma Purāṇa, within the collection of fifty-five thousand verses.
Chapter Twenty-three.
The Sages said:

"O best among speakers, this wonderful narrative you have related is meritorious, bestowing fortune, prosperity, and fame, and is said to remove all sins. You ought to tell us this account concerning the creation."
O son of Sūta, [you have asked] how creation occurred previously in detail.
Sūta said: I shall explain in detail the cause of creation and dissolution.

Merely by hearing it, even a person may attain omniscience. Hiraṇyakaśipu, having propitiated Brahmā through ascetic penance, obtained a boon that was exceedingly difficult to acquire, whereby he pervaded the three worlds.
From that highly fortunate god, [he obtained] immortality as well;
and having pervaded the worlds of the gods, sovereignty was acquired by him himself.
Then the gods, along with the Gandharvas and the sages who have mastered the Vedas—
The Nāgas, Kinnaras, Siddhas, Yakṣas, and others likewise,
placing Brahmā at their head, went to the Lord Nārāyaṇa,
who was sleeping upon the Ocean of Milk, having entered into yogic sleep.
Then, with palms joined in reverence, the gods addressed him with great hymns of awakening;
and when the Lord of Devas had become fully enlightened, they related the conduct of that evil-minded one to the one of great wisdom. Having heard it, the Lord of the World [acted].
Assuming the form of Narasiṃha, he slew Hiraṇyakaśipu;
again, in the form of a boar, he raised up the holy earth and then struck down the mighty Asura Hiraṇyākṣa.
He caused other Dānavas of terrible appearance to be slain; and thus,
when those great Dānavas and those other sons of Diti had been destroyed, at that time—
Furthermore, while the great gods had returned to their respective stations,
while all sacrifices and religious rites were being performed,
and while all the worlds were in a state of well-being, Aditi was tormented by suffering.
Tormented by grief for her son, crying out "Alas! Alas!", and rendered unconscious,
she then [beheld] her husband Kaśyapa— the high-souled giver, who resembled the sun and was endowed with the splendor of ascetic power.
Having prostrated with devotion, O best of Brahmins, he spoke to that high-minded one:
"O Blessed One, I am childless; all the Daityas and Dānavas have been struck down by the Lord who wields the discus, as well as by the gods. (15-16)
O best of sages, O Lord, I am consumed by the fire of grief for my son— my son who was the source of my joy, who eclipsed all splendor,
who was exceedingly strong, whose every limb was beautiful, and whose radiance equaled that of the king of the gods. 17–18.
He is the intelligent one, the most omniscient, the knower, and the wisest of all;
endowed with the splendor of austerity, possessed of strength, and marked by beautiful characteristics;
devoted to Brahman, a knower of wisdom, and a worshiper of the gods and Brahmins. 18-19.

"O twice-born one, O Lord, grant me a son who is a conqueror of all worlds, a bringer of joy to me, and endowed with every auspicious mark. Having heard these excellent words of hers, Kaśyapa [replied].
O best of the twice-born, his mind filled with compassion and feeling pity for her who was in distress, he, the highly fortunate one, spoke to that wretched woman of dejected mind;
intent upon her welfare, he placed his own hand upon her head.
"O highly fortunate lady, such a son as you desire shall be born.
Having spoken thus, he went to Meru, the best of excellent mountains,
where he performed penance without support, fulfilling his supreme vow.
In the meantime,
Aditi, who was wise in all dharmas, virtuous in her actions, and high-minded, became pregnant with that supreme embryo; she remained pure in heart for a period of one hundred years.
By her was born a son endowed with Brahmanic luster;
then Kaśyapa arrived, filled with great joy. That best of men gave his intelligent son a name.
"Strength," he said, "is the name of your son; he is truly great and worthy of that name. Having thus bestowed the name upon him, he then performed the rite of initiation (vratibandha).
He said to his son, "O highly fortunate one, accomplish the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya)."
"O best of the twice-born, O most excellent one, I shall do exactly as you have said;
I will perform the study of the Veda through the practice of celibacy. Thus, more than a hundred years passed for him as he engaged in ascetic penance.
Endowed with the splendor of ascetic power, he came into the presence of his mother;
Diti, filled with great joy, beheld her high-souled son’s divine celibacy, which consisted of the essence of penance and valor. 30–31.
He spoke to that high-souled son Bala, who was ascetic,
intelligent, great-souled, and proficient in wisdom and knowledge:
"O wise one, as long as you live, all my sons shall live."

Hiraṇyakaśipu and others were slain by the wielder of the discus; fulfill your enmity, my child, and slay the gods, your enemies, in battle. "O son, first quickly propitiate Indra, the lord of gods;
afterwards, let the other gods be struck down by him whose vehicle is Garuḍa.
Having heard this from them, that goddess Aditi, who held her husband as her deity, [acted accordingly].
Overcome by great sorrow, she spoke to her son Indra:

"O Brahman, this son of Diti, possessed of a massive body, is growing through spiritual power; indeed, he has performed austerities in the Nirañjana forest for the purpose of slaying the gods. (36-37)
"O Lord of Gods, know this if you desire my welfare here. Having heard those words of his mother, the subduer of Pāka,
the king of the gods, then fell into great sorrowful reflection.
Terrified by great fear, he then reflected thus:
"How shall I slay this one who reviles the dharma of the gods? Having thus resolved regarding the destruction of Bala, the Lord of the Gods [proceeded].
Once, that Ahibala also resorted to the ocean for the purpose of performing his twilight rites,
adorned with a divine black antelope skin and a wooden staff,
and by means of that pure and meritorious celibacy.
The subduer of Pāka (Indra) beheld him, perfectly tranquil, seated at twilight upon the shore of the ocean performing his recitation;
that son of the Sun was struck by that divine thunderbolt.
Seeing Bala fallen to the earth, having come as a living being,
the King of the Gods was then filled with great joy and rejoiced. Thus was that Daitya, the son of Diti, struck down.
The righteous-souled one ruled the kingdom with happiness like Indra, the subduer of Pāka.
45. Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Slaying of the Daitya Bala," in the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
Chapter Twenty-four.
Sūta said: Having heard that her sons Subala and Bala had been slain, Aditi wailed piteously, crying out, "Alas! Alas! What a tragedy for me! (1)
Having thus performed such a compassionate act for a long time, that illustrious ascetic woman went to Kaśyapa and spoke to him:
"Your son, O Indra, lord of the hosts of gods, has committed great sins."
Seeing that my strength was like the ocean and possessed the marks of Brahmā,
he struck him with a thunderbolt as he was at the very moment of twilight.
Having heard this, the son of Marīci then became enraged.
Overcome by great anger, that best of the twice-born blazed as if with fire; plucking out a single lock of matted hair, he said,
"I shall produce a son for the very purpose of slaying Indra."
Emerging from that sacrificial pit as if from the mouth of the fire-god,
he was endowed with the appearance of a heap of black collyrium; with tawny eyes and a terrifying form,
his mouth was formidable with fangs, bringing fear to the worlds.
Terrible with his great club, likewise bearing a sword and shield,
blazing with all-pervading splendor, powerful like a great cloud, he said to the Brahmin Kaśyapa, "Let a command be given to me."
"Tell me the reason why he was born as a Brahmin;
I shall accomplish that for you through your grace, O observer of good vows.
Kaśyapa said:

"O highly wise one, fulfill this very desire of mine, which has been my long-cherished wish: abandon the evil-minded Indra. Once the king of the gods has been slain, enjoy the station of Indra yourself."
Thus instructed by the high-souled Kaśyapa,
Vṛtra, endowed with manly vigor, made an effort toward the slaughter of that Indra and practiced the science of archery.
Having seen the strength, valor, kṣatriya prowess, and energy combined with fortitude of that hostile Daitya, the thousand-eyed Indra became distressed with fear;
he then reflected upon a stratagem against that evil-minded Vṛtra.
For the purpose of slaying him, the God of gods summoned the great sages and dispatched the seven Ṛṣis toward Vṛtra, the lord of the Daityas: "Go there, where Vṛtra resides. 15.
"O lords of sages, please establish a peace treaty with him.
Thus commanded by him, those seven sages, having been urged by the thousand-eyed Indra, then spoke to Vṛtrāsura.
"O best of Daityas, let friendship be established; let it be done.
Thus spoke the seven seers, knowers of reality, to the exceedingly powerful Vṛtra:
"O best of beings, let the highly wise thousand-eyed Indra be your friend."
You desire to act with friendliness; why then do you not do so?
O hero, enjoy the half of Indra’s station in true happiness; let the Asuras and the gods likewise abide by their respective halves. 19–20.
"May they all live happily, having indeed cast aside their enmity.
Vṛtra said:
"If, O best of beings, the noble Indra truly desires friendship with me..."
"Relying on truth alone, I shall act; of this there is no doubt.
But Indra, having resorted to deceit, might practice hostility toward me. "O Brahmins, what can be done then? For what confidence can there be in such a matter? 22.
"The sages have told me this; speak the truth regarding this matter. Tell us its reality if you desire friendship with us here.
Indra said:
If I were to act with falsehood or through deceit along with you, I would be tainted by sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, it was by resorting to such deceit that Indra committed the murder of Druhyu.
"I shall be tainted by sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; there is no doubt about this.
Thus spoke Purandara to you, O highly wise one.
"By this very proof, O great-minded one, establish friendship with me."
Vṛtra said:
"O best of the twice-born, by this truth and by the path taught by you, I shall indeed act with friendship toward him."
Vṛtra was brought to that place by the best of Brahmins.
Seeing Vṛtra arrived there for the sake of his friend, Indra rose quickly from his throne, taking the water of honor (arghya). 28-29.
O best of the twice-born, that unrighteous-souled one gave half [of his power] to Vṛtra, saying: "O highly wise Indra, enjoy this great position;
O best of Daityas, we two must live together in happiness. 30.
O best of the twice-born, while Vṛtra was thus being inspired with confidence by Maitreya, and those sages had departed for their own abodes,
that evil-minded one was constantly looking for a vulnerability in Vṛtra.
Even Indra, remaining vigilant, reflected day and night; yet he could find no flaw even in the high-souled Vṛtra. He then devised a stratagem for the very purpose of slaying him.
"O Rambhā, sent by him, delude that great asura (34).
O auspicious one, by whatever means possible, act so that you may obtain happiness after slaying him; thus bring about the delusion of the enemy of the gods (35)."
The forest was holy, greatly divine, frequented by virtuous trees,
endowed with many trees bearing fruit, teeming with deer and birds,
and adorned everywhere with divine celestial mansions.
It was always filled with the celestial music of the Gandharvas and swarms of bees;
it was everywhere made sweet and resonant by the holy cries of cuckoos, and everywhere thoroughly enlivened by the sounds of peacocks and deer. 37-38.
It was adorned everywhere with divine sandalwood trees and beautified by charming ponds, sacrificial pits, and lakes filled with water and blooming lotuses and hundred-petaled lilies. 39.
It shone with gods, Gandharvas, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Kinnaras; with divine sages and a most excellent celestial garden;
crowded with hosts of Apsarases and various wonders and auspicious sights.
It was crowded with golden palaces and adorned everywhere with staffs, umbrellas, chowries, jars, and banners; it was filled with the sound of the Vedas and resounded with the noise of songs. 42.
Thus, having reached Nandana, that charming-smiling woman,
full of playful energy, sports everywhere with the Apsarases as a graceful lady.
Sūta said:
Once, accompanied by Vṛtra and drawn away by the evening twilight, he went to the forest (44).
Together with several Dānavas and filled with supreme joy,
he wandered unobserved at the side of that very Great-Souled One (45).
O best of Brahmins, even the king of the gods, Vṛtra, though he was indeed seeking the vulnerabilities of his enemies,
was highly wise and trusted him in all matters; knowing Indra to be his supreme friend, he felt no fear of him.
Wandering about, he would see a forest that was supremely auspicious in every respect (47)—
a most delightful and wondrous grove, crowded with throngs of women,
where even the cool shade of the sandalwood tree bestowed great merit (48).
O illustrious one, having ascended a swing with her friends, the large-eyed and fortunate lady shines like a plantain tree;
she sings a melodious song that enchants the entire world. 49.
There, Vṛtra arrived with his mind agitated by desire,
having beheld Raṃbhā, who possessed beautiful, lovely eyes and was mounted upon a swing.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Deception of Vṛtra," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the Śrī Padma Purāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
The twenty-fifth chapter.
Sūta said:
"Indeed, this beautiful-eyed woman here sings, pervading the entire universe with her graceful gestures and amorous expressions."
One should utterly delude people with states that are exceedingly youthful, radiant, charming, and full of being.

Having seen her—whose gait is like that of a female elephant, whose eyes are as long as lotuses, whose breasts are full, whose limbs are smeared with saffron, whose face is like a lotus, and who is the abode of desire for me—one thinks: "This is not mere pleasure; she is most beautiful and enchanting."
"She possesses a perfect form, endowed with beauty, her conduct is devoted to the limbs of love, and her disposition is exceedingly virtuous;
I shall surely come under her power right here today, for I have been sent by the Mind-born [God of Love] this very moment.
Thus spoke the Daitya, possessed by deep reflection, deluded by passion, and impelled by it for a long time.

Anxious, he went there in haste and, with a dejected mind, spoke to that beautiful-eyed woman: "Whose daughter are you, O lovely one? By whom were you sent? What is your name? Tell me this most meritorious thing.
I am utterly infatuated by your form and your great splendor; O girl, come under my power."
When she had spoken thus to Vṛtra, who was overwhelmed by desire, the large-eyed Rambhā, O fortunate one, said:
"I have come with my companions to this most excellent forest,
the supreme Nandana grove, for the sake of sport."
"But who are you, and for what purpose have you come to my side?
Vṛtra said:
"Listen, O child; I shall tell you who I am that has come here."
"O auspicious one, I am born from the sacrificial fire, the son of Kaśyapa;
O lady of beautiful countenance, I am the friend of Indra, the god of gods.
O fair-hipped one, half of the station of Indra has come to be enjoyed by me."
"O Goddess, how is it that you do not recognize me as Vṛtra?
O lady of excellent complexion, the three worlds have come under his control. I have come to you for refuge out of desire; protect me, O lovely-faced one!"
"O large-eyed one, O beloved, enjoy me while I am thus agitated by desire.
Rambhā said:
"I shall indeed be under your control today; of this there is no doubt."
"O hero, whatever I tell you, that must indeed be done by you alone. "So be it, O highly fortunate one; I shall do all of that," he replied.
Having thus established this bond with her, the one of great strength [proceeded].
In that forest of great merit, the best of the Dānavas took his delight;
the exceedingly charming great Daitya was captivated by her singing, dancing, graceful laughter, and amorous dalliance.
He spoke to that illustrious Vṛtra, the best of the Dānavas:
"Drink the wine here; drink this honeyed Mādhavī liquor.
He then addressed the large-eyed Rambhā, whose face was like the moon. 15–16.

"I am the son of a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas; O auspicious lady, how could I commit the censurable act of drinking liquor? (17) Out of affection, that distressed and frightened lady forcibly gave him the liquor.
Then, out of a lack of self-restraint, he drank wine;
when he had become utterly deluded by that liquor and fallen from his wisdom, he was then struck down by Indra with his thunderbolt. 18–19.
Then Indra, smeared with sins such as the killing of a Brahmin,
was told by the Brahmins, "O Indra, a sin has been committed by you.
From these words, the very powerful one named Vṛtra became confident.
"O Hatā, it was precisely because of this spirit of trust that you committed such an evil deed.
Indra said:
"An enemy must always be slain by whatever means possible."
The slayer of gods and brahmins, a thorn to sacrifices and dharma—
this wicked Dānava, the leader even of the three worlds, has been slain.
That you were enraged for his sake is the very mark of justice.
"O best of the twice-born, you must first deliberate thus; afterwards, you may exercise anger, considering my conduct unjust. Thus were the Brahmins addressed by the high-souled Indra.
Enlightened by all the gods beginning with Brahmā,
those most excellent ones departed for their own abodes once the thorn of Dharma had thus been destroyed.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Slaying of the Asura Vṛtra," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Twenty-Six.
Sūta said:
Having heard that her son had been slain, Aditi was overcome with grief.
O best of the twice-born, consumed by that very grief for his son,
he spoke again to the high-souled Kaśyapa, the bull among sages,
for the sake of slaying even the most wicked Indra, O best of the twice-born.
"O Lord, grant me one son who is composed of Brahmanic splendor, fierce, and unbearable for all the gods; for I am very dear to you, O Beloved. Kaśyapa said:
"The two sons of Mamatā, Vṛtra and Bala, were both exceedingly powerful; yet they were slain by the wicked-souled god Indra through the employment of deceit.
Therefore, for the sake of their very slaughter, I shall grant you one son."
"O illustrious lady, remain pure for a hundred years.
Having spoken thus, that lord of yogis placed his hand upon her head and, together with Aditi, departed for Mount Meru, a forest of asceticism.

O best of the twice-born, the goddess, who dwells in the penance grove, having become ever pure, performed austerities for the sake of a son. Then the thousand-eyed god, having understood her exertion, [acted].
And thus, O highly fortunate one,
the Lord of the Gods, who resembles a deity, having assumed the form of a twenty-five-year-old Brahmin, became an observer of her inner state and approached her.
Having bowed to his righteous mother, who was endowed with ascetic power, the thousand-eyed one was addressed by her: "O best of the twice-born, who are you?
The thousand-eyed one said to her, "O beautiful lady, I am your son."
"O beautiful lady, I am a Brahmin learned in the Vedas and I know the Dharma.
I shall assist you in your asceticism; of this there is no doubt.
For she is serving her mother, a virtuous goddess endowed with austerity. (11-12)
Indra recognized him as a doer of evil when he arrived,
yet he perceived the son of Dharma as one who served her day after day.
He would massage the Queen's limbs and then wash her feet.
There, that righteous-souled one would always offer leaves, roots, fruits, bark,
and even deerskins to that goddess;
being constantly gratified by his devotion, she, being well-pleased, spoke to him.

"O highly fortunate one, since my son has been born with great merit and Indra has been slain, let the Kuru kingdom belong to my son by divine decree. "So be it, O highly fortunate one; through my grace, this shall come to pass."
And Indra, the subduer of Pāka, became intent on finding a vulnerability in her.
When less than a hundred years had passed, Acyuta saw his opportunity: Diti entered her bed without having performed the purification of her feet.
Placing her head at the edge of the bed, with her hair disheveled and extremely distraught,
she fell into a deep sleep; having entered her womb, Vajrapāṇi then cut the fetus into seven pieces.
O best of Brahmins, while that great embryo remained within Indra’s belly, he was pierced by a sharp-edged thunderbolt; and as it cried out, Indra spoke to that weeping great fetus again and again.
The one of great splendor, Śatakratu, spoke thus: "Do not weep!
Then Śakra, the king of the gods, cut that embryo—the son of a Diti—into seven parts again;
having cut each of those weeping fragments into seven more, he divided them.
Thus were those gods of great majesty born as the Maruts;
then, as they were addressed by Indra, they came to be known by those names.
Possessing extreme heroism and massive bodies, they were endowed with fierce luster and prowess.
Then those fifty Maruts became one less;
they are renowned by the name "Maruts," having taken refuge with Indra alone.
They cause the great host of all beings to rejoice.
In each of the lineages, Prajāpati Hari bestowed those kingdoms, beginning with Pṛthu, in due order;
he is indeed Sadeva, Puruṣa, Kṛṣṇa, the all-pervading Guru of the universe.
The conqueror through austerity, possessed of great splendor, the one Prajāpati of all—
Parjanya, Pāvaka, Puṇya, the Self of All, indeed, he is everything.
This entire world, both moving and unmoving, is his meritorious creation.
O best of the twice-born, for one who correctly understands this creation of beings, there is no fear of returning here; how then could there be fear of the next world?
This creation is highly meritorious, auspicious, and the remover of all sins. 29–30.
The man who hears this with devotion is liberated from all sins;
he is blessed, meritorious, and endowed with truth. He who hears of this creation attains the supreme goal.
With his soul purified of all sins, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu. 32.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Origin of Marut," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padmapurāṇa.
Chapter Twenty-Seven.
Sūta said: Then the Lord, the sovereign of all the worlds, consecrated Pṛthu,
the son of Vena, as the great lord over the entire kingdom.
Having sequentially considered the kingdoms of Brahmā for that one of mighty arms and massive body, who was like Indra, the lord of the gods,
he proceeded to bestow upon each whatever was appropriate to give.
The high-minded one consecrated Soma in the sovereignty over trees, Brāhmaṇas, and likewise over the planets and constellations; and [he consecrated him] over austerities, duties, sacrifices, merits,
and meritorious splendors.
O best of the twice-born, having likewise consecrated Varuṇa as the god of the waters, as well as the lord of the sacred fords and of jewels,
he further installed Vaiśravaṇa in the sovereignty over all other yakṣas.
The grandfather of the Ādityas thus established the highly wise Viṣṇu in the kingship for the sake of the welfare of all people; likewise,
he established Dakṣa Prajāpati over all meritorious deeds.
He installed Prahrāda— the knower of all dharmas, the lord of the hosts of Prajāpatis,
and endowed with the splendor of Viṣṇu— as the king over all the Daityas and Dānavas.
And having consecrated Yama Vaivasvata as Dharma in the kingdom of the ancestors;
and [having appointed him] over the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Piśācas, Uragas, and Sarpiṇīs,
over all the Yoginīs, and over the great-souled Vaitālas.
He is the lord of all skeletons and likewise of all kūṣmāṇḍas;
he is Giriśa, the wielder of the trident, of all earthly beings,
and of all mountains, being the great mountain Himavat himself.
O Lord of the Gods, in this divine kingdom, he established the meritorious ocean— the most excellent of all sacred fords (tīrtha)— along with rivers, lakes, ponds, pools, and wells. 12-13.
Then Brahmā, the lord of the gods, consecrated Citraratha as the king of all the Gandharvas and likewise over their merit;
and the four-faced one [Brahmā] [consecrated] Vāsuki as the king of the Nāgas of meritorious power.
Likewise, having consecrated Takṣaka as the king of the serpents,
he then anointed Airāvata as the king of the elephants,
and Uccaiḥśravas as the king of all horses.
Then Brahmā appointed Vainateya as the king of all birds, and he likewise assigned the lion to the sovereignty over wild animals; furthermore,
Prajāpati, having consecrated the bull among the cattle, [established him as their king].

Among all the lords of the forest, the Plakṣa tree alone was appointed by the Grandfather. Having thus established all the kingdoms, the Grandfather Brahmā, the most excellent being, then installed the guardians of the quarters.
Likewise, O best of beings, he consecrated Sudhanvan, the son of Vairāja, as the king and guardian of the eastern quarter;
and in the southern quarter, [he consecrated] the high-souled [son] of the Prajāpati Kardama.
He consecrated his son, named Śaṅkhapada, as king.
Likewise, in the western quarter, that Prajāpati Brahmā consecrated the son of the Prajāpati Varuṇa, named Puṣkara. 21–22.
In the northern direction, O Brahman,
he likewise consecrated Nalakūbara and the other guardians of the quarters (dikpālas) of great prowess,
by whom this entire earth with its seven islands and its cities was protected.
Even today, that realm is governed according to dharma.
Thus was that illustrious Pṛthu consecrated as lord of men,
having been anointed with all the great sacrifices, such as the Rājasūya.
According to the procedure seen in the Vedas, the lord of the earth ruled the kingdom of kings;
this occurred when the highly energetic and meritorious Manvantara named Cākṣuṣa had passed, O illustrious one, during that period which seeks the welfare of gods and the virtuous.
Then he assigned the sovereignty of the earth to Vaivasvata alone.
Furthermore, O best of Brahmins, if you wish to hear it without weariness, I shall explain in detail the history of the high-souled Pṛthu.
This great foundation has thus been proclaimed as meritorious;
indeed, this is always certain in all the Purāṇas.
It is auspicious, conducive to merit, fame, and long life, and it brings about residence in heaven. 29.
It is auspicious, purifying, life-prolonging, bestowing sons, and granting prosperity.
Whatever man listens to this with devotion, endowed with faith and meditation, he obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Royal Consecration," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
Chapter Twenty-Eight. The Sages said:
O highly fortunate one, we wish to hear once again in detail the account of the birth of that great-souled Pṛthu,
and how this earth was milked by that high-minded king.
Furthermore, it was [worshipped] by the gods, the ancestors, and the sages who know reality;
likewise by the Daityas, the Nāgas, the Yakṣas, the trees,
the mountains, the Piśācas, and the Gandharvas of meritorious deeds.
Just as it was previously milked by Brahmins, by perfected beings (siddhas), by Rākṣasas of terrifying prowess, and by other great-souled ones,
so too is there a specific distinction regarding the holding of the vessel for all of them.
O high-minded one, tell me also the procedure for milk and its specific qualities.
Why was the hand of the great-souled King Vena previously churned by the sages? For what reason did this occur here?
And being thus enraged, he spoke with a voice like that of the Sūta’s son;
this wonderful and meritorious narrative destroys all sins.
O highly fortunate one, those who desire to hear it never experience satiety.
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, [I shall describe] in full detail the birth, the valor, the lineage, and the manly prowess of Pṛthu, the son of Vena.
I shall proclaim in its entirety the life-story of that wise one. Listen, O highly fortunate ones, O best of the twice-born;
this must not be told to one who lacks devotion, nor to one who is faithless or deceitful.

O twice-born ones, [this should not be told] to one who is utterly foolish, to one who is deeply deluded, to a bad disciple, likewise to one devoid of faith, to a rogue, or to one destined for total ruin;
for he who recites it otherwise indeed goes to hell.

O venerable ones, endowed with existence and devoted to the true Dharma, I shall recount before you the entire narrative that destroys all sins in its entirety; listen, O best of the twice-born! (12-13)
O best of the twice-born, I shall proclaim this secret, which has been declared by the sages, which leads to heaven, brings fame, longevity, and prosperity, and is commensurate with the Vedas.
Whoever should constantly recite this detailed account of Pṛthu, the son of Vena—
Having paid homage to the Brāhmaṇas, one should not grieve over what has been done or left undone. Merely by hearing this, the sin accumulated over seven lifetimes is destroyed;
a Brāhmaṇa becomes a knower of the Vedas, and a Kṣatriya becomes victorious.
A Vaiśya shall become prosperous with wealth, and a Śūdra shall attain happiness;
such is the fruit one obtains from reciting or even hearing this sacred life-story of Pṛthu, which destroys all sins. (17)
A protector of the Dharma, possessed of great wisdom, and skilled in the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras; born in the lineage of Atri, a lord formerly equal to Atri himself;
the creator of all righteousness, he was the Prajapati named Anga. (18–19)
His son was the Prajāpati named Veṇa,
who always persisted in completely abandoning dharma.
O highly fortunate one, Mṛtyu had a daughter known by the name Sunīthā.
The illustrious Tāṭaṅga married Sunīthā;
upon her he begot Vena, the destroyer of dharma,
who, due to the fault of his maternal grandfather, was the son of the son of Kāla.
Abandoning his own duty, he became devoted to unrighteousness; out of desire, greed, and great delusion, he committed only sin.
O lord of men, having abandoned the dharma consisting of Vedic conduct, he acted thus.
Deluded by pride, intoxication, and delusion, he followed after evil.
At that time, people in the world proceeded without the study of the Vedas;
while that Prajāpati was their ruler, the subjects were devoid of Vedic recitation and the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*.
"The deities shall drink the soma offered at sacrifices that have commenced"—
thus that evil-minded one spoke constantly to the brāhmaṇas:
"One must not study, nor offer oblations, nor give gifts whatsoever."
"When the time for destruction had arrived, that Prajāpati made this cruel vow again and again: 'I am the one to be sacrificed to, I am the sacrificer, and I am the sacrifice itself. (27–28)
"I am Viṣṇu, the eternal; I have always said: 'The sacrifice is to be performed by me, and the oblation is to be offered by me.
I am Brahmā, I am Rudra, I am Mitra, I am Indra, and I am the ultimate goal."
"I alone am the enjoyer of both the *havya* and the *kavya*, without a doubt.
Then those sages of great power, becoming enraged,
all gathered together and spoke to that king of sinful mind.
The sages said:
"O Indra among kings, the king is the lord of the earth and always protects his subjects;
he is the very embodiment of dharma. Therefore, O king, one should indeed protect dharma. (32)
"We shall enter upon the twelve-year initiation for sacrifice;
do not practice unrighteousness through this sacrifice, for this is not the path of the virtuous.
O Great King, perform your duty; practice truth and merit."
"I shall protect the subjects"— this was the agreement made with them.
To all those great sages who were speaking thus,
the evil-minded Vena then laughed and spoke these meaningless words.
Vena said:
"Who else is the creator of dharma? Whose words should I listen to? And who on earth is equal to me in learning, heroism, austerity, and truth? (36)
"O you of deluded minds, you surely do not know me, the source of all beings and especially of all phenomena.
If I so desired, I could burn the earth or likewise submerge it with waters."
He shall indeed seize both heaven and earth; there is no need for hesitation here.
O King, when he cannot be removed through delusion and arrogance, then the great sages, becoming enraged, will deal with him.
Then, with great anger and their fury aroused, they forcibly seized Vena as he was struggling and churned his left thigh;
[from it emerged] one who resembled a heap of black collyrium, extremely short, and of strange appearance.

Those great-souled ones beheld him with a long face, deformed eyes, and the luster of a blue tunic; he had a protruding belly, wide-spreading ears, was exceedingly terrifying, and possessed a wicked stomach. Then they said to him, "Sit down. 41-42.
Having heard those words of theirs, he sat down, afflicted by fear;
The Bhramaras, the Capulidas, and whatever other Mleccha tribes there were—all those of sinful conduct—were born from that limb.
Then all those sages, with minds full of serenity, [spoke]. 44–45.
When that best of kings had thus become free from all taint,
they churned the right hand of that high-souled one;
and as his hand was being churned, sweat indeed arose.
Again, those brahmins churned his right hand;
from that hand was born a man resembling the twelve Ādityas, his limbs the color of molten gold, clothed in divine garlands and garments. 47–48.
His limbs were adorned with the splendor of divine ornaments, and he was anointed with divine fragrant unguents;
he shone with a crown the color of the sun and with two earrings.
Possessing a massive body and mighty arms, he was peerless in form upon the earth.
The great lord, bearing a sword and arrows, armed with a bow and clad in armor,
was endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament; that high-minded one possessed splendor, beauty, and a golden complexion.
Just as Indra shines in heaven, so did Vena shine upon his birth;
when that illustrious one was born, all the gods and the pure sages celebrated a festival for the sake of Vena’s son.
Blazing with his own body, radiant like Agni himself,
he took up the great and excellent bow named Ājagava,
as well as divine arrows for the sake of protection and armor of great luster.
O best of the twice-born, when that illustrious, great-souled hero was born, all beings were filled with joy; likewise,
all sacred fords and various holy waters rejoiced.
O best of Brahmins, at his consecration,
all the gods beginning with Pitāmaha, as well as various beings— both stationary and moving— proceeded and consecrated that lord of men. 56–57.

O best of the twice-born, having approached Pṛthu— the great hero and protector of subjects— while Vainya was in the sovereignty of kingship, the high-minded one was consecrated by all beings, both moving and stationary, as well as by the gods and the brahmins.
Just as the majestic Pṛthu, son of Vena, became the sovereign over all kings,
so too were all his subjects never before delighted by his father;
but being delighted by him, they truly rejoiced in happiness.
Out of devotion to that hero, O best of the twice-born, he was born with the name Nāma-rāja;
when that great-souled Suvīra set out toward the ocean, all the waters were solidified out of fear of him.
Having cleared away the difficult paths, they provided excellent roads from the mountains;
none of those mountains caused any obstruction to their banners.
The earth yielded crops without being ploughed, and everywhere there were wish-fulfilling cows.
The rain-god Parjanya showered down according to their desires, and all the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and others performed Vedic sacrifices and great festivals;
while that king was ruling, the trees bore fruits that fulfilled every wish.
There was no famine, no disease, and no untimely death among men.
All people lived happily, devoted to righteousness,
while that invincible and high-souled king of kings ruled.
At that very time, during that auspicious sacrifice of the Grandfather (Brahmā), the Sūta was born from the *sūti* (the sacrificial vessel) on a gentle and noble day;
and at that same great sacrifice, the wise Māgadha was also born.
The great seers summoned him there for the purpose of praising Pṛthu.
O best of the twice-born, I shall describe the characteristics of a Sūta, which are highly meritorious:
he is endowed with the topknot and the sacred thread, and is devoted to the study of the Vedas. (68–69)
He was a knower of the meaning of all the scriptures, devoted to the agnihotra sacrifice, endowed with charity and study, dedicated to the conduct of a brahmacārin,
and always intent on the worship of the gods and the brāhmaṇas. (70)
It is said that a beggar should indeed perform sacrifices with your merits and Vedic mantras;
always devoted to the conduct of a Brahmin and maintaining association with Brahmins—thus was Samāgadha born, though devoid of Vedic study. 71-72.

All bards and wandering minstrels (cāraṇas) who are devoid of Vedic conduct should be known as highly fortunate; they exist as panegyrists. For the purpose of praise, both the Sūta and the Māgadha were created as skillful ones.
Then all the sages said, "Let this king be praised,
for such is his deed as is his nature, O lord of men.
Thereupon, the two bards and the panegyrists spoke to all those sages.
"We two please both the gods and the sages through our own deeds;
yet no one knows his deed, nor his characteristic, nor his fame—by what deed we might compose a hymn of praise for this Great-Souled One. (76)
O best of Brahmins, you should know that this supreme among men is to be praised for his future meritorious qualities, for his virtues are not yet known;
likewise, one should praise him for the deeds that the highly illustrious Pṛthu has already performed.
All the sages spoke of the divine qualities of that great-souled one:
he is truthful, endowed with knowledge, wise, and renowned for his prowess;
he is ever heroic, appreciative of virtues, meritorious, generous, and possessed of excellent qualities.
He was righteous, truthful, and the best of sacrificial priests (80).
He was pleasant of speech, truthful, possessed of grain and wealth, virtuous,
a knower of virtues, one who appreciates virtue, a knower of dharma, and devoted to truth (81).
He is all-pervading and the knower of all; he is devoted to Brahman, a knower of the Vedas, and possessed of great wisdom.

He is endowed with discernment, possesses a melodious voice, and has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (Vedāṅgas). He is the sustainer and protector of all creatures, and he is victorious upon the field of battle.
O best of kings, he alone on this earth shall be the performer of sacrifices such as the Rājasūya, endowed with all virtues;
these qualities shall also belong to the limbs of that great-souled one.
Then, at the command of the sages, the Sūta and the Māgadha began to offer praise for that Great-Souled One with his past qualities and his future attributes.
From that time forth, O high-minded one, the worlds have indeed been pleased by their hymns of praise.
And from that time forward, O best of the twice-born, donors will appear before them in this world with praises of their virtues;
thus, in hymns of praise, blessings are invoked for them along with excellent wealth. 86–87.
To the Sūta, the Ābhīra, and the Bandin, he gave great prosperity; then to the Cāraṇa, he gave the excellent country of Tailaṅga.
And Pṛthu, the righteous-souled one, by his grace, gave the land of Haihaya as well.

O best of the twice-born, in ancient times, while performing sacrifice, King Pṛthu—the son of a king, a donor, and a giver of everything—made the banks of the Revā his city under his own name and gave it to the Brāhmaṇas;
he was omniscient, a giver of all things, possessed of the power of dharma, and the most excellent among men. 89–90.
All the subjects and the sages, pure with the power of their asceticism, beheld him and said to one another: "This is a meritorious and highly intelligent king,
the provider of sustenance for the gods and others, and especially for us."
He will indeed become a protector of the subjects, yet one who milks them of their livelihood.
This highly wise Dhātrī, it is said, was formerly sown as a seed; having been swallowed by the subjects for the sake of their subsistence, she became firm.
Then, O best of the twice-born, the subjects rushed toward Pṛthu, saying, "Provide for us a good livelihood. At those words of the sages,
Pṛthvī then became perfectly steady after having caused the grains to be swallowed [by them].
Seeing that great terror of the subjects, that best of kings,
at the word of the great seer, took up his bow along with arrows and,
filled with wrath, rushed with speed toward Pṛthvīdhvaja. 95–96.
Assuming the form of an elephant out of fear of him,
O best of the twice-born, the Earth wandered through forests and inaccessible regions, remaining hidden; yet that one of great wisdom did not perceive her ill-formed [disguise].
Assuming the form of an elephant, she spoke to the one of great wisdom. Then the king rushed toward her who was in the form of an elephant;
and being struck by him with sharp arrows, she— 98–99.
Assuming the form of Hari, he became intent on flight; assuming the form of Hari, the king rushed forward. He was exceedingly enraged, O highly wise one, his beautiful eyes reddened by fury.
With sharp, whetted, and keen arrows, he struck the earth;
then, overwhelmed and agitated by the impact of those arrow-wounds, [the demon], assuming the form of a buffalo, became intent on flight. 101–102.

O best of the twice-born, that wielder of the bow, with arrows in hand, rushed forward with great speed; having become a cow, she went surely to heaven and sought refuge with Brahmā and the high-souled Viṣṇu. 103.
The Rudras and the other gods found no place of refuge;
finding no protection at all, they sought out the son of Vena (Pṛthu), reaching his side once more while overwhelmed by the wounds of arrows. 104–105.
With her palms joined in reverence, she spoke these words to Pṛthu:
"Save me, save me, O Indra among kings! Thus she addressed the king.
"O illustrious one, I am Dhātrī, the Earth, the support of all."
When I was slain, O King, the seven worlds were also destroyed.
Then, with palms joined in reverence, she who is always to be honored by the three worlds spoke to that king: "O King, a woman is never to be killed. (107-108)
O Great King, the destruction of women is seen by the best of the twice-born to be a great sin;
the destruction of cows is seen by the best of the twice-born to be a great sin. Without me, how will you sustain your subjects?
When I am stable, O King, then all the worlds, both moving and unmoving,
attain stability; for when I have become stable,
these worlds, both moving and unmoving, would perish were I to vanish.
Then the subjects would perish when my destruction has arrived;
O King, how could you sustain the subjects without me? O King, the worlds are stable in me; by me this universe is sustained.

Without me, all subjects would undoubtedly perish; therefore, O protector of the earth, if you desire the welfare of your subjects, you ought not to kill me here. Listen to my words, which are like those of the gods. 114-115.
O illustrious one, undertakings attain successful accomplishment through skillful means; indeed, having observed the proper means, you shall bring forth progeny.
O Great King, by slaying me, you will always be capable of sustaining and protecting [the world].
"O King, O one of great wisdom, how will you sustain yourself and these subjects without me? Restrain your anger;
I shall become composed of food and I shall support these subjects. (116-117)
"I am a woman and therefore not to be killed; you shall instead undergo penance.
For they say that even a female belonging to the animal kingdom is not to be slain.
Having reflected thus, O Great King, you ought not to abandon dharma."
Thus addressed by the nurse with these various words, the lord of men, O Great King, indeed cast off his terrible anger.
"O Indra among kings, when you are pleased, then shall I become at ease. 119–120.
O best of the twice-born, having been addressed thus by her, King Pṛthu, the son of Vena and lord of creatures, spoke to that illustrious Earth.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Pṛthu," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Twenty-nine. Pṛthu said: "Even when one great sinner, a perpetrator of evil deeds, has been slain,"
The worlds live in happiness through the virtuous who perceive merit;
therefore, that one most wicked and evil-minded person must be struck down. Consequently, I shall indeed slay you, the destroyer of all living beings.

"All these seeds have now been destroyed by you; having made them your food, having become steadfast, and having destroyed the progeny, where will you go? When the wicked one of evil conduct is slain, the virtuous live in happiness."
Therefore, evil must be abandoned; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
Dharma must be protected with effort, for through it dharma increases. Otherwise, great sin arises which causes the destruction of the subjects.
For the sake of one person, one may slay either oneself or another;
having slain one who oppresses the world, there shall be no sin for him. Indeed, many will attain happiness when that evil person is killed.

When the wicked one who has stolen the cow of wealth is slain, there is neither a major sin nor a minor sin. For the sake of my subjects, I shall undoubtedly kill you yourself if you do not act according to these words joined with merit.
O Vasundharā, for the sake of the welfare of this world and because you have acted unrighteously,
I shall, at my word, strike you with sharp arrows when you turn your face away from me;
yet by your own splendor, you remain auspicious to the inhabitants of the three worlds.

"And I shall sustain the subjects through righteousness as well, of this there is no doubt. (10) Having established yourself in my command which is endowed with dharma, O Vasundharā, you must always sustain these subjects by my order. (11)
"O blessed lady, if you carry out this command of mine today, I shall be forever pleased with you and will protect you at all times.
There is no doubt that it is you alone— and no other supreme kings— who [shall receive my protection]."
In the form of a cow, her body adorned with arrows,
she spoke thus to Pṛthu, the son of Vena, the highly intelligent upholder of righteousness.
Dharaṇī said:
"O Great King, for the sake of the subjects, I shall undoubtedly carry out your command— which is joined with truth, merit,
and purpose— to the utmost degree, O Lord of Men, through exertion, merit, and skillful means."
Undertakings succeed, as do meritorious initiatives; therefore,
O Indra among kings, devise a means by which you may remain truthful and by which you may sustain and cause all these subjects to prosper.

"O King, these excellent arrows, whetted on stone, have become stuck in my limbs; pull them out yourself, for they pierce me most severely. O Great King, remain equanimous so that water may flow from me as it does from the earth."
Sūta said:
Driving away all those various and heavy mountains with his fierce bow, he then made them uniform in appearance. 19.
From that time forward, O best of the twice-born, the mountains attained growth;
and then, having extracted his own arrows from her body, the son of Vena, with a delighted mind, [honored them]. 20.
The pits and caves were leveled by the strikes of his arrows.
Thus, the increaser of merit made the entire surface of the earth even; having leveled it, the illustrious one fashioned a calf for her. 21–22.
O best of beings, after Manu Svāyambhuva had first been reflected upon again and again, then, throughout all the past Manvantaras,
the earth became uneven and the paths were obstructed in various places.
O best of the twice-born,
at that time, when the previous creation had occurred during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu, the surface of the earth became both level and uneven by its own nature. (24-25)
No boundaries were seen for villages, cities, towns, as well as for countries and sacred fields (kṣetra).
Neither agriculture, nor trade, nor cattle-rearing proceeded.
No one speaks untruth, nor is there greed or envy;
indeed, O best of the twice-born, no one ever commits pride or sin when the Vaivasvata interval has arrived. 27–28.
Before the birth of Vainya, there was the birth of the subjects themselves;

O twice-born ones, all these subjects then chose their dwelling places—sometimes on the earth, sometimes on a mountain, and sometimes on the banks of rivers. 29. At that time, they settled in various locations.
All the creatures made their dwellings in groves, at all sacred fords, and on the shores of the ocean by virtue of that merit; and their food became fruits, roots, and honey. 30–31.
O best of the twice-born, having observed the great suffering of his subjects, Pṛthu, the son of Vena, perceived that their sustenance was indeed obtained with extreme hardship.
Then, by that king, Svāyambhuva Manu was appointed as the calf.
O Mahāmati, he fashioned his own hand as a vessel;
then that tiger among men milked the earth, which was vast, and [obtained] milk consisting of all kinds of grain, containing every foodstuff endowed with all qualities. 33–34.
By that meritorious food, which was like nectar, those subjects brought satisfaction to the gods, as well as to the ancestors and others; indeed,
by the grace of that son of Vena, those subjects lived in happiness.
O best of the twice-born, after giving food to the gods and the ancestors,
and especially to the Brāhmaṇas as well as to guests,
all those meritorious subjects then eat.
And by means of sacrifices, others indeed worship and satisfy Janārdana;
and through that food, the deities attain satisfaction for the Lord of Gods (Deveśa).
Furthermore, Parjanya rains again, impelled by Mādhava.
From that [earth], auspicious and great medicinal herbs, which bestow great merit, came into being.
All varieties of grain were produced by Pṛthu, the son of Vena, the lord of creatures; by means of that food, all creatures have subsisted perpetually even until now.
