Thus, when the sages had gathered together, this earth was milked once more by the highly fortunate Brahmins, by those who speak the truth, and likewise by the gods;
Soma became the calf, and the Preceptor of the Gods himself was the milker. 41.
By the truth and merit of those for whom milk is a source of vigor and nourishment, by which the immortals live, all living beings subsist;
through that truth and merit, the earth yields its wealth when milked by the sages.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain how this earth was milked by the ancestors in ancient times, and by what ritual procedure that was done.
Having prepared a silver vessel, one should offer the milk of the *svadhā* oblation, which is filled with nectar.

O best of the twice-born, having imagined a calf, he became the milker and Death himself the drinker; then, using serpents as the milkers and Takṣaka as the calf, they took a gourd vessel and milked out poison as the milk.
Likewise, O best of the twice-born, the powerful Dhṛtarāṣṭra was the milker of the Nāgas;
by him the serpents and Nāgas were turned, and thus they became incomparable. O most excellent of the twice-born, it was indeed by that exceedingly fierce one that the Nāgas were turned.
And there were terrifying serpents with a dreadful form of poison;

they subsisted on that very [poison], being fierce, large-bodied, and possessed of great strength, having that as their food, that as their conduct, that as their vigor, and that as their prowess. 48–49.
Now, therefore, O best of the twice-born, I shall fully explain how the earth was milked by all the Asuras and Dānavas,
having fashioned a vessel made of iron that resembled food and fulfilled all desires.

Having fashioned milk that was composed of illusion for the destruction of all enemies, Virocana, the powerful son of them [the Daityas], became the calf; the twice-headed Madhu, the great strength of the Daityas, was the milker; and the officiating priest (ṛtvij) was the vessel. 51–52.
By that very illusion, the Daityas, who are exceedingly powerful,
possessed of great wisdom, massive bodies, and immense energy and prowess,
carry on their activities; it is by that strength and manliness of theirs that the Dānavas live.
O best of the twice-born, by that very illusion even today all illusions proceed; those of limited wisdom are thus deluded, for this is its power.
Likewise, that earth, the support of all, was milked by the Yakṣas.
Thus we have heard, O best of Brahmins, that in a former kalpa, this milk was placed in a very wide vessel made of iron by high-souled beings;
at that time, the highly wise Vaiśravaṇa was fashioned as its calf. 56.

Maṇidhara’s father was Puṇya, wise and the best among the intelligent. His son was Rajatanābha, who was high-minded, all-knowing, a knower of all dharmas, and powerful as the son of the king of Yakṣas. 57–58.
O best of the twice-born, he who had eight arms, great splendor, two heads, and performed immense penance was Yakṣāvarta; by him also, all the gods were milked.
Furthermore, this earth was milked again by the exceedingly powerful Rākṣasas.
Likewise, these Piśācas, tormented by the four [sufferings] and with their waters dried up, leaped up;
they were made of iron, possessing human skulls as their vessels, and—desiring to devour Suprajā—they were possessed of fierce anger and prowess. 60–61.
Among them, the one named Sumālī was the milker; he was of great strength, possessed a silver navel, had a calf named Vatsa, and milked blood as his milk.
From him were born the Rākṣasas, Yātudhānas, and the mighty Piśācas.
By that [milk], the Yakṣas and the fierce hosts of Bhūtas subsist;
furthermore, the Earth was milked by the Gandharvas and Apsarases, having made the highly learned Citraratha their calf once again. 63–64.
They milked her into lotus vessels, filled with the sounds of Gandharva songs;
among them was a highly intelligent Gandharva named Suruci,
O best of the twice-born, who was the most meritorious milker of that cow.
Then the great-souled Gandharvas milked pure song as their milk, and by that they, as well as the other Apsarases, live;
likewise, this earth was milked by the highly meritorious mountains. 66–67.

Various kinds of jewels and medicinal herbs comparable to nectar were [milked], and the highly fortunate Himavat was conceived as the calf; Meru became the milker, having made the mountain-born [vessel] his receptacle. 68.
All those mountains of great majesty were reared upon that milk.
Then they were milked again by the great, auspicious trees, such as the Kalpa-tree and others;
these brought forth a vessel made of Palāśa wood, from which the severed and burnt parts would grow back.
At that time, the Śāla tree became the udder, the Udumbara flower the limbs, and the Plakṣa tree became the calf; then this Earth,
the sustainer of all, who grants all desires, was milked by the Guhyakas, Cāraṇas, Siddhas, and hosts of Vidyādharas.

Whatever those worlds desire, she indeed gives them milk through various vessels and specific attributes; such is her true nature. This Earth is a nurse, but this [other] Vasundharā is the supreme creator.

Adorned by merits, she is this cow who milks all desires; she is the eldest, the foundation, the creation, and the progeny. She is the purifier, the giver of merit, the meritorious one, and the one who causes all crops to grow.
She is the foundation and the very source of all that is moving and unmoving.
This Mahālakṣmī is the eternal Vidyā, consisting of the entire universe;
she is the milch-cow who grants all desires and the one from whom all seeds sprout.
She is the mother of all blessings and the sustainer of all the worlds;
she is the manifestation and the very form of even the five elements.
This earth was once the ocean, and thus she is renowned as Medinī.
Because she was completely flooded with the fat (*medas*) of Madhu and Kaiṭabha,
she is called by the knowers of Brahman by the name *Medinī*.
Then, O best of men, from the acceptance [of her] by Pṛthu, the son of Vena, she became known as *Pṛthivī*.
O best of the twice-born, because she attained the status of a daughter to that king, this Earth is called Queen Pṛthivī; she is adorned with villages, houses, cities, and towns. 80.
O twice-born ones, the goddess Earth is thus always full of grain and mines, prosperous, and composed of all sacred fords;
O Indra among kings, such is her power as it is recited in the Purāṇas. 81–82.
The highly fortunate Pṛthu, son of Vena, who illuminates all actions,
is like Viṣṇu, like Brahmā, and like the eternal Rudra;
these three gods are to be saluted by the foremost of deities and by those who discourse on Brahman.
That best of kings is worthy of salutation by all Brahmins and sages;
he is the establisher of the social classes and stages of life, the sustainer of all the worlds, and [the ideal] for highly fortunate monarchs who desire sovereignty here on earth. 84-85.
The first king, the majestic Pṛthu, son of Vena, was worthy of homage by warriors seeking the science of archery and always desiring victory;
he was the great king worthy of homage, the provider of livelihood for all rulers of the earth. 86.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, I have described the distinctions among vessels (87),
as well as the specific qualities of calves and milkers before you; and I have also explained the distinctions regarding milk, just as they were pointed out by the king (88).

O best of the twice-born, he who hears this account of Pṛthu, the son of Vena, as it has been truly related by you here— this narrative is auspicious, conducive to fame, health, and merit, and it destroys all sin. (89)
For him, bathing in the Bhāgīrathī occurs day after day;
with his soul purified of all sins, he departs for the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Pṛthu," in the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
The thirtieth chapter.
The sages said:
"That Vena who was described by you, who lived according to sinful conduct—"

O twice-born one, what was the occupation of that sinner, and what fruit did he obtain? O best among the learned, tell us in detail his life story as it happened in the past; this is not something unknown to you, O high-minded one.
Sūta said: I shall duly relate the most meritorious life-story of that high-souled Vainya, son of Vena, as it was heard by me in the past.
O highly fortunate one, when that great-souled Pṛthu was born,
the king attained purity and once again attained the state of righteousness. All the great sins accumulated by the lowest of men [were likewise purified].
Through the occasion of association with holy places, their sin departs;
from the company of the virtuous, merit alone is produced—of this there is no doubt. But through the occasion of association with the wicked, only sin is produced.
Indeed, from conversation, sight, touch, sharing a seat, eating together,
and even from association with sinners, their guilt is transmitted; likewise, merit alone is transmitted among those whose nature is virtuous.
"Through association with great holy places (tīrthas), sinners are purified; it cannot be otherwise.
By this means, having shaken off all impurities, they attain a meritorious state.
The sages said:
O best of the twice-born, how do those sinners attain the supreme perfection?
Tell us that in detail; we have developed a desire to hear it.
Sūta said:
Hunters of great sin, as well as slaves and fishermen, were born there; they remained within the waters of the Revā, Yamunā, and Gaṅgā,
and having bathed both knowingly and unknowingly, they indeed sported in the water.
By the power of the great river, they attain the supreme goal;
having abandoned their state of servitude and the accumulation of sins, they all indeed go forth, having bathed in the contact with its holy waters.
O most excellent ones, by association with the Mahānadī, the sins of even great sinners are destroyed, as well as those of people of great merit;
there is no need for hesitation regarding this, whether it be through association, sight, or touch. 14.
In this regard, O Brahmins, an ancient history that destroys sin is heard;
today I shall relate it to you, for it bestows great merit.
In a vast forest, there was a certain deer-hunter named Sulobha.
Greedy for the taste of flesh, he constantly slaughtered deer with dogs, snares, nets, and likewise with bows and arrows.
Once, however, that evil-minded man, holding a bow and with an arrow in his hand—
Surrounded by dogs, he entered the difficult forest of the Vindhya mountains (18).
There, he killed many terrified deer, ruru-deer, and boars; then, having reached the bank of the Revā river, he became a killer of fish. (19)
Having killed the fish, he went out from the water; then the doe, terrified by the hunter's greed,
was intent on saving her life, distressed, frightened, and with a trembling mind.
Hurrying away and fleeing, she reached the very shore;
though agitated by dogs and distressed by the wounds from the arrows, even the hunter was easily overtaken by the force of the wind. 21-22.
The female deer came right behind him and ran ahead of him;
seeing her, the hunter, arrow in hand and prepared,
bent his bow with force and pursued that deer.
Just then, a hunter named Lobha arrived together with his dogs.
"She is mine; she must not be killed, for she has come to my hunt.
Hearing these words, the fish-eater, greedy for meat, [acted].
The mighty and evil-minded one discharged an arrow aimed at her; by that sharp arrow from the hunter, she was struck down. There, the female deer died from the arrows of those two wicked-minded men.
Attacked by the dogs' teeth, she fell down in haste;
from the mountain peak, she fell into the merit-bestowing, sin-destroying pool of the Revā.
And those dogs, running after her, fell into that pure pool.
Overwhelmed with rage, the hunter said to the fisherman:
"This deer belongs to me; why have you, O wicked one, killed it with your arrows?
To him, the fisherman spoke again to the slayer of the deer.
"This is mine, there is no doubt; you speak thus out of pride.
Then those two, O highly fortunate one, fighting each other out of anger and greed, fell into the pure water. 30-31.
At that time, O best of beings, there occurred a great festival that bestows a favorable rebirth,
coinciding with the new moon and granting the fruit of great merit.
All [the deities] fell at that very hour of that festival.

Those who were devoid of recitation and meditation, and bereft of the truth of inner disposition— 33 even the doe, the dog, and the hunter, by virtue of their association with bathing at the sacred ford,
were liberated from all sins and attained the supreme goal. 34
O best of the twice-born, by the power of sacred fords (tīrthas) and through association with the virtuous,
the sin of sinners is destroyed, just as fire burns fuel.
Sūta said:
Indeed, through such association with those high-souled sages,
and by their conversation, sight, and touch, the impurity of King Vena was destroyed; it is said that in ancient times, his sin perished through contact with the virtuous.
Through association with those of exceedingly great merit, the sin of evildoers perishes;
through association with those of exceedingly great sin, sin itself will spread.
By the fault of his maternal grandfather, he (Vena) became likewise tainted. 37–38.
The sages said:
What was the fault of the maternal grandfather? Tell us that in detail;
for he was Death himself, as well as Time, Yama, and Dharma. 39.
For no one here is a non-violent person, since even he who is established in this [state] sees that the worlds of moving and unmoving beings exist under the sway of their own karma;
they live and die, and likewise experience [the fruits] through their own actions.

The wicked behold that terrible [Yama] as a result of the ripening of their own karma (41). In all the hells, Yama— this most meritorious one— day after day binds and strikes them solely by means of their own actions (42).

In all these most meritorious deeds, that righteous-souled one, being so virtuous, engaged [himself]; no fault of his is seen. By what fault, like a sinner, did he become an outcast while still alive?
Sūta said:
Death is the eternal punisher of the wicked-minded who commit sins;
existing in the form of Time (Kāla), it examines their actions.

Even for one who has committed an evil deed, Yama may cause him to be slain by that very deed; having recognized his sin, Yama thus brings about what is beneficial. Indeed, one whose soul is characterized by good deeds shall attain heaven through that virtuous action.
Death itself unites all these people with its own messengers,

while they are filled with a state of great happiness and accompanied by the singing of auspicious songs; it likewise unites those of purified soul with acts of charity, enjoyment, and other such pleasures.
With various torments, afflictions, and dreadful wooden stakes, he would terrify and beat the Brahmins like Death itself;
for even his actions were thus directed toward them. 48–49.
O highly fortunate one, even from death, she was born through the merit of *lobha* (greed); she was born from the lineage of Sunītha as the daughter of that great-souled one.
Constantly playing, she would always reflect upon the deeds of her father.
He was the teacher and creator of living beings, the observer of merit and sin.
That highly fortunate maiden, Sunīthā by name, having reached the forest while sporting, was surrounded by her companions. 51–52.
There, amidst the clamor of singing, she then beheld that illustrious and excellent son of a Gandharva named Suśaṅkha,
whose every limb was beautiful, performing most intense penance.
He meditated upon Sarasvatī for the sake of perfecting his knowledge of music;
Suśaṅkha daily caused him only obstacles, yet he always forgave him and said, "Go, go."
She should not go where she has been sent, but should perform her duties without any obstacle.
Having been addressed thus by him, she, overcome with anger, struck the one established in asceticism.
Then Suśaṅkha, enraged and faint with fury, spoke to her.
"O you of wicked and sinful conduct, why have you suddenly created this obstacle? Great men respond to violence with non-violence;
they do not become angry when reviled—such is the established order of dharma. (57-58)
"I have been killed by you, O sinful woman, though I am innocent and endowed with ascetic merit.
Having spoken thus to the wicked Sunīthā,
that righteous-souled one ceased from his great anger, recognizing her as a woman and turning back.
Then, whether out of sin, delusion, or childishness, she spoke here to that high-souled Suśaṅkha who was established in asceticism: "O father,
you are the destroyer of me alone among all the inhabitants of the three worlds."
"One should always slay the wicked and protect the virtuous;
no fault shall accrue to him, for he shall live by means of great merit.
Having spoken thus, she departed and addressed these words to her father:
Struck by me in the forest, O Father, that son of a Gandharva,
who was performing austerities in constant solitude and free from desire and anger, was addressed by that righteous-souled man who was himself possessed of passion and wrath. (63–64)
"One should not strike one who strikes, nor should one revile one who reviles"—thus he spoke to me at the very end; tell me the reason for that.
O best of the twice-born, being addressed in this way, Mṛtyu [spoke] to Sunīthā.
Then the righteous-souled one did not say anything by way of reply to the question.
Having reached the forest where Suśaṅkha was staying,
that best of ascetics was then struck with blows of the hand out of malice.
O Brahmin, when Suśaṅkha was struck by the daughter of Mṛtyu, he became enraged; that man of great luster then cursed the slender-waisted girl:
"Since I am faultless, O wicked one, you have struck me yourself."
"Since I am established here in this forest, I shall therefore bestow a curse upon you:
listen, when you have entered the householder's life with your husband, you will have a son who is full of sinful conduct and a reviler of gods and Brahmins. 69-70.
"O you who delight in all sins, an evil one shall be born from your womb.
Having thus cursed him, he departed; and she too remained there, taking refuge in the penance grove.
When that illustrious one had gone, Sunīthā returned to her home.
With a distressed mind, she related everything concerning her high-souled father and how he had been cursed by that son of the Gandharvas;
all of that which had been spoken by Mṛtyu was heard by him.

"Why have you inflicted this injury upon me, who am free from fault and yet suffering? O daughter, it was not at all right for you to strike one as truthful as I. Having addressed him thus, the righteous-souled Mṛtyu was deeply distressed.
While he was thus reflecting, that [state] came to pass as ordained.
Sūta said:
There was a son of Atri, named Aṅga, who was possessed of great luster and prowess.
Once, O Brahmins, a certain virtuous twice-born man went to the delighter of the Brahmins (Nandana).
There he beheld that king of the gods, Indra, the subduer of Pāka,
accompanied by hosts of Apsarases, as well as Gandharvas and Kinnaras.

He was being sung to by singers with melodious voices in the seven musical scales, and he was being fanned on all sides with fragrant fans by women endowed with beauty who moved with the grace of swans.

I beheld the god of immeasurable splendor, shining with a swan-colored parasol that resembled the orb of the moon, adorned with all ornaments, possessing a thousand eyes, and engaged in amorous play. 79–80.

Beside him was the highly fortunate Paulomī, beautiful and auspicious, renowned for her beauty, splendor, and asceticism, shining with good fortune and the virtue of devotion to her husband. 81. She was that virtuous woman (Satī).
Accompanied by her, the thousand-eyed Indra entered the Nandana grove.
O best of the twice-born, beholding his splendor, Aṅga thought:
"Blessed indeed is this king of the gods, surrounded as he is by such attendants."
"Oh, how great is the power of this ascetic, by which such a high station has been attained!
When I shall have such a son as this, the sustainer of all the worlds, then I shall obtain great happiness; of this there is no doubt. (84)
Becoming absorbed in this thought, he returned home in haste. 85.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the *Vena-upākhyāna* of the *Bhūmi-khaṇḍa* within the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter Thirty-one.
Sūta said: O bull of great splendor, you then beheld the prosperity, enjoyment, luxury, and playful pastimes of that high-souled Indra.
"How might I have a son like Indra, endowed with righteousness?
Having reflected thus for a moment, Aṅga, the best among the upholders of dharma,
virtuous and devoted to truth, returned to his own home.
Bowing with his neck bent low, he questioned his father Atri:
"Who is this who enjoys such great prosperity through meritorious conduct, O Indra?
From what merit does his abundance arise, and what kind of deed was performed by him?"
"What kind of austerity did he perform in the past to propitiate him?
O best among those who speak the truth, tell me this in detail.
Atri said:
"Excellent, excellent, O illustrious one! Since you ask me thus, listen as I relate to you the life-story of Indra, my son.
Long ago, there was a most excellent Brāhmaṇa named Suvrata, who was wise and firm in his vows."
By him, Kṛṣṇa Hṛṣīkeśa was propitiated through ascetic penance; indeed,
by the grace of Viṣṇu, he again obtained a meritorious conception from Kaśyapa and Aditi, and thus became the king of the gods.
Aṅgā said:
"O you who are fond of your son, how might my son become equal to Indra? O best among the wise, please tell me the means for that. (9)
Atri said:
O high-minded one, listen briefly to the entire meritorious life-story of that very same great-souled one of excellent vows. 10.
Having observed the disposition, devotion, and meditation of that high-souled one, who had propitiated Hari through excellent vows and wisdom,
the Lord of the World indeed granted him the supreme state.
By the grace of Viṣṇu, the sustainer of the three worlds enjoyed the three realms— including Indra and all their riches— along with all moving and non-moving beings. Thus,
everything regarding the deeds of Indra has been narrated to you.
O best of men, Govinda is pleased by devotion and by meditation upon his true nature;
Hari, when satisfied and gratified by devotion, grants everything. Therefore, one should worship Govinda, the giver of all and the source of all.
He is the omniscient one, the knower of all, the foremost person among all.
Therefore, O Nandana, you shall obtain from him everything that you desire.
For he is the giver of happiness, the giver of the supreme goal, the giver of liberation, and indeed the Lord of the worlds.
"Therefore, go and propitiate him, my son; you shall obtain a son equal even to Indra.
Having heard these words, which were full of supreme truth and spoken by his well-wishing, high-souled Ṛṣi, he grasped the essence of that speech, bowed to him, and departed for the eternal one.
Having taken leave of his father, the high-souled Aṅga, who was equal to Brahmā and born of Brahmā,
reached the peak of Mount Meru, which was adorned with gold and jewels.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Legend of Vena," in the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
Chapter Thirty-two.
Sūta said:
His limbs were brilliantly illuminated by various jewels and also entirely covered with gold.
Shining like the sun with its own rays upon that best of mountains,
all the yogins, having reached the cool and comfort-bestowing shade of the Aśoka tree, sit upon firm seats in meditation.
In some places sages were performing penance; in other places kinnaras were singing.
The ṛṣis and gandharvas were contented, their hands occupied with lutes and rhythmic clapping, absorbed in the tempo, measure, and rhythm, accompanied by the seven musical notes.

On that best of mountains, the Gandharvas— experts in the essence of song and devoted to it— take refuge in the shade of sandalwood trees and sing a charming, clearly articulated melody, accompanied by the jewels of musical scales (mūrcchanās). 4–5.

There, upon that best of mountains, women dance for the gods; on that supreme mountain, the sweet sound of the Vedas is heard— a divine voice that destroys sin, bestows merit, and grants the highest welfare.
That best of mountains shines with sandalwood, aśoka, punnāga, śāla, tāla, and tamāla trees; it is resplendent with banyan trees resembling clouds,
with *saṃtānaka* and *kalpa* trees, and is thickly crowded with mango trees.
The lord of mountains shines everywhere with celestial trees in full bloom;
it is a mountain strewn with various minerals and abounding in heaps of diverse gems, endowed with many wonders and filled with manifold auspiciousness. 9.
It was well-frequented by hosts of Vedas and crowded with throngs of Apsaras; it shone with sages, munis, Siddhas, and Gandharvas,
and it resounded with the lion-like roars of elephants resembling mountains.
Adorned with śarabhas, intoxicated tigers, and cunning deer,
it shines everywhere with ponds, wells, and lakes filled with pure water and teeming with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks. 12.
It shines with golden lotuses, white lotuses, and red lotuses;
likewise with clusters of flowing rivers and pure waters, as well as with beautiful śāla and tāla trees, and with crystal-like elephants. 13–14.

Filled with vast, divine golden surfaces, radiant as the sun and fire, and with stone slabs, this king of mountains shines resplendently, adorned with the celestial palaces of the gods and magnificent mansions.
15. And with the palaces of the deities, it stands as the best of mountains.
Adorned with golden staffs resembling swans and the moon,
it was graced by palaces equipped with jars and chowries,
and beautified by hosts of gods delighted by its various virtues. 16–17.
Adorned everywhere by numerous hosts of gods, as well as by Gandharvas and Cāraṇas, Meru, the best of supreme mountains, shines with merit.
From it flows the Gaṅgā, the great river of highly meritorious and pure waters.
Abounding in holy fords where [sacred] waters flow forth, crowded with swans and lotuses,
and frequented by sages and throngs of seers— that great river flows through this best of mountains, which possesses such qualities and is auspicious with merit and wonder. (19-20)

The meritorious great sage Aṅga, the son of Atri, entered a very holy place on the bank of the Gaṅgā, in a secluded and beautiful cave. Having sat there, the wise man, free from desire and anger, [remained absorbed in meditation].
Restraining all his senses, that righteous-souled one meditated upon Hṛṣīkeśa, who dwells in the mind; he meditated on Kṛṣṇa, the Lord who removes all afflictions,
whether on his seat, his bed, his vehicle, or while in meditation— Madhusūdana.
One whose self is disciplined, who is absorbed in yoga, and whose senses are conquered, constantly beholds Keśava within all those living beings, both moving and unmoving;
Thus, as he performed austerities for a hundred years,
the Lord of the World, the wielder of the discus, observed that best of the twice-born and constantly manifested many most terrible obstacles for him. (25-26)
By the splendor of that high-souled god Nṛsiṃha,
that righteous soul, free from all fear, consumes [his sins] like fire consumes fuel;
O best of the twice-born, through observances, restraints, and other fasts.
As he was wasting away, he became resplendent with his own luster;
O dear one, he appeared thus, resembling the sun and fire.
In this manner, he remained deeply intent on austerity, meditating upon Janārdana.
Manifesting himself, the God said, "O giver of joy, choose a boon. And seeing Hṛṣīkeśa, Aṅga was supremely delighted; with a tranquil mind, he bowed down and praised Vāsudeva.
Aṅga said:
O source of all beings, O purifier, O soul of all beings, O Lord of all beings, salutations to you, the self of the qualities. 32.
Salutation to the one whose secret nature consists of qualities, yet who transcends all qualities;
salutation to the possessor of qualities, the creator of qualities, the one enriched by qualities, and the very essence of qualities.
Salutation to Bhava, the creator of worldly existence, and the remover of the cycle of birth for those devoted to him.
Salutations to the one who arises from existence, the secret path, and the destroyer of existence;
salutations again and again to the sacrifice, whose form is the sacrifice, and the Lord of sacrifice;
salutations to the one attached to sacrificial acts, and to the bearer of the conch. 34–35.
Salutations again and again to Hiraṇyagarbha; salutations to the bearer of the discus, to the Truthful One, to the embodiment of truth, and to Him who consists of all that is true.
Salutations to Dharma, to the creator of Dharma, and to the creator of all—salutations to Him.
Salutations to him who is the limb of Dharma, the excellent hero, and the support of Dharma.
(37) Salutations to the meritorious son, to the one who is truly sonless, to the Great Soul, to the destroyer of illusion and delusion, and to the creator of all illusions. (38)

Salutations again and again to the one who possesses the form of illusion, who is both embodied and unembodied; salutations again and again to Śaṅkara, who indeed assumes every form. 39. Salutations to Brahman, whose form is Brahman, and whose essential nature is the Supreme Brahman.
Salutations to You, the abode of all; salutations to the one who sustains the abode. 40 Repeated salutations to the auspicious Śrīnivāsa, the bearer of Śrī;
salutations to the one who dwells in the Ocean of Milk and to the one who is the nectar of immortality. 41

Salutations to the Great Medicine, to the Terrible One, to the Supreme Great Wisdom, to the Non-Cruel, to the Pure, and to the Lord of the impure. Salutations again and again to the Infinite, to the All-encompassing, and to the Sinless.
Salutations to You who manifest as space, who take the form of birds;

salutations to You who are the oblation, the consumer of the oblation, and the form of the sacrificial offering; salutations to You who are the awakened, the form of the wise, and eternally enlightened. 43–44.
Salutations to the one who is the utterance of *namas*, the utterance of *svāhā*, and the utterance of *svadhā*;
salutations to that pure, unmanifest, and great-souled one.
Salutations to Vyāsa, who is like Vāsava (Indra) and whose form is that of the Vasus.
Salutation to Vāsudeva, to the Universal One, to him who has the form of fire; salutation again and again to Hari alone, to Vāmana. 46.
Salutation to the divine Nṛsiṃha, to the protector of the virtuous; salutation to him. 47.

Salutations to Govinda, the protector of the cowherds; salutations to the one who consists of a single syllable, and salutations indeed to the one who consists of all syllables, to you who are in the form of the *haṃsa*. 48.
Salutations to you who are the three principles (*tritattva*), and salutations to you who are the five principles (*pañcatattva*).
Salutations to the one who is the support of the twenty-five principles and who is beyond the principles.
49. Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, whose form is dark, the Lord of Lakṣmī;
salutations to the one who has the petals of a lotus, to Bliss, and to the Supreme. 50.
Salutations indeed to the Sustainer of the Universe, salutations to the Destroyer of Sin; salutations to the Meritorious and Most Meritorious, salutations to You who are Truth and Dharma.
51 Salutations again and again to the Eternal and Immutable; salutations again and again to Him whose nature is the mass of light.
Obeisance to the lotus-feet of Keśava, who is the illustrious Padmanābha, the Great Lord (Maheśvara), and the immeasurable one.
O Vāsudeva, beloved of Lakṣmī, Lord of all, Īśa, Madhusūdana, grant me the state of servitude;
O conch-handed one, show mercy upon me birth after birth, and bestow upon me a state of peace. O Keśava, I bow at your feet. 52–53.

O Lotus-navelled One, O self-lord of worldly existence, who has assumed the form of my refuge for me in my distress— drench me with the cloud of wisdom, for I am scorched by the heat of the terrible fire of saṃsāra and by the many sorrows and torments arising from the death of sons and other kinsmen.
(54) Having thus heard this hymn of praise from the high-souled Tvaṅga as well...
Having revealed his own form— dark as a rain cloud,
possessed of great majesty, holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, with a lotus in his hand—
the Great Lord displayed his true nature, mounted upon Vainateya.
His limbs were beautified by all kinds of ornaments—necklaces, bracelets, and earrings—and he shone supremely divine and stainless with a forest garland;
Hṛṣīkeśa, possessing great luster, was resplendent at the forefront of his body. 57.
Having revealed his own body, which was marked with the Śrīvatsa, adorned with the auspicious Kaustubha gem, and composed of all the gods, Hari, the Janārdana,
spoke these words to that high-souled and most excellent of sages.
"O, O illustrious Brahmin, listen to these auspicious words!
Having addressed that best of the twice-born with a voice as deep as a thundercloud, [he said:
'I am pleased by this penance; choose an excellent boon.'"
Seeing Hṛṣīkeśa, the Lord of Kamalā, rejoicing—
blazing, resplendent, possessing a universal form, and the sovereign of all beings—
he prostrated himself again and again before his two lotus feet.

Overcome with great joy, he said to Janārdana: "O Lord of Gods, wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, I am your servant. You desire to grant me a boon; please grant me a son born of my own lineage."
Just as Indra shines in heaven, endowed with all splendor, grant me such a son, O God— one who is the protector of all the worlds,
beloved by all the gods, devoted to Brahman, and a scholar of dharma.
To Kṛṣṇa, the donor endowed with wisdom, possessed of the splendor of Dharma, the protector of the three worlds, the upholder of truth and righteousness,
the foremost among sacrificers, the peerless hero, and the ornament of the three worlds.
He was devoted to Brahman, learned in the Vedas, true to his word, and a master of his senses;
unconquered, yet the conqueror of all, he was Viṣṇu himself in the splendor of his brilliance—
a Vaiṣṇava who performed meritorious deeds, born of merit, and possessed of auspicious marks.

"Grant me such a son— tranquil, endowed with ascetic power, proficient in all scriptures, a knower of the Vedas, the best among yogis, and equal to you in virtues— as I desire to grant this boon. (69)
Śrī Vāsudeva said:
"Endowed with these qualities, O high-minded one, your son shall be the sustainer of this entire world and of the lineage of Atri."
He shall uplift his father through splendor, fame, and merits;
he who shall uplift his father and grandfather through truthful deeds will go to the station of Bhavānī, that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Having spoken thus, O twice-born one, the Lord of the Gods said to Aṅga: "Marry the virtuous daughter of someone of meritorious power;
through her, procreate a son who is auspicious, merit-bestowing, and dear."
"O Great-minded one, by my grace he shall become a righteous soul,
omniscient and all-knowing, exactly as you desired. Having thus granted this boon, Hari vanished from sight.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Granting of the Boon to Aṅga," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the account of Veṇu. Chapter Thirty-three.
The sages said:
"Having been cursed by the high-souled Gandharva Suśaṅkha, how did she come to be born because of that curse? And what deeds were performed by her?"
"O best of the twice-born, tell us in detail about what kind of son Śālibhikṣu had due to that curse, and the life-story of Sunīthā.
Sūta said:
Cursed by Suśaṅkha, that slender-waisted woman departed for her father’s abode; Sunīthā was deeply afflicted with grief,
and she revealed both her father’s conduct and her own.
O best among those who speak the truth, that righteous-souled Mṛtyu, though learned in the scriptures,
spoke thus to Sunīthā, his daughter who had been cursed by the high-souled one: "A wicked deed, a sin that destroys righteousness and splendor, has been committed by you."
O highly fortunate lady, why have you inflicted this beating upon Suśānta? This act,
devised by you, is contrary to the interests of all the world—
he who is free from desire and anger, perfectly tranquil, and devoted to righteousness.
Listen indeed to the sin of him who kills one who is absorbed in the path of austerity and established in the Supreme Brahman;
such a person becomes a sinful soul, O son, and incurs great demerit. 8.

Whoever strikes one who is being struck, or again makes one cry out who is already crying out, undoubtedly partakes of all the sin of the one who was struck; there is no doubt about this. He alone is peaceful and he alone has conquered his self who does not strike back at one who is striking him.
Even by one who has previously struck a faultless son,
if he should later, out of delusion and sin, strike that same faultless one;
or even by one who harbors groundless malice toward a faultless person— (10–11).

If one subsequently strikes an innocent person out of delusion due to some sin, that sinner incurs the sin born from the body of the innocent one. One who is innocent should indeed strike back that evil-minded assailant.
Rising again with impetuosity and through rashness, he acts with a sinful intent.
Whatever sin belongs to the wrongdoer passes over to the innocent one; therefore, one should never retaliate against a striker, even if that person is guilty of fault.
"O daughter, you yourself have nurtured great misdeeds;
you have been cursed by him this very day. Therefore, perform meritorious deeds and, having attained the company of the virtuous, always remain with them."
O Nandinī, by means of yoga, meditation, and knowledge, one undergoes transformation.
Association with the virtuous is of great merit and bestows manifold blessings;
O child, behold this well-illustrated example of the quality that comes from the company of the good.
O one of great intelligence, by touching, drinking, and bathing there, the sages attain perfection, being cleansed both externally and internally;
indeed, all these worlds, moving and unmoving, become pure. 18.

Waters that are tranquil, very cool, gentle to the body, and pleasing; pure, flavorful, endowed with merit, and removers of impurity—such virtuous waters should be known by you and diligently resorted to. (19-20)

Just as gold abandons its impurity through contact with fire, so too does a human being abandon sin through association with the virtuous. The fire of truth, when kindled, blazes forth with the splendor of merit.
He possesses a radiant splendor through truth and is perfectly pure through knowledge. He is intensely hot by the nature of his meditation and is untouchable by men born of sin;
moreover, through contact with the fire of truth, all evil is destroyed.
Therefore, you must by all means cultivate association with the virtuous; having cast off the burden of sin, take refuge thus in merit alone.
24 Sūta said:
Thus addressed by her father Sunītha, she was deeply distressed;
having paid homage at her father's feet, she departed for a secluded forest.
Abandoning desire, anger, and her childhood nature, the ascetic woman remained there.
Having abandoned delusion, pride, and deceit, she remained in solitude.
Her friends, full of playful charm, arrived there for the sake of sport;
those large-eyed women beheld Sunīthā, who was possessed by sorrow. (26–27)
To her who was meditating and lost in thought, those others, themselves absorbed in anxiety, said:
"O auspicious lady, why do you grieve, possessed as you are by this sorrow?
Tell us the cause of it, for this anxiety brings only suffering."
One thought alone is meaningful: that which is contemplated for the sake of the Dharma. A second thought is meaningful when it delights the yogi in the Dharma;
any other thought is purposeless, and one should not entertain it at all.
Anxiety, which destroys the body and diminishes strength and vitality, ruins all happiness and manifests the loss of beauty;
for anxiety brings about thirst, delusion, and likewise greed. (31)
One should not give rise to evil thoughts, for such thoughts, when entertained day after day,
manifest as diseases and lead to hell;
therefore, O beautiful one, abandon anxiety and follow me.
Whatever karma was previously acquired by a person himself, that very thing this living being experiences; even one possessed of knowledge should not reflect upon it.
Therefore, abandon anxiety regarding pleasure, pain, and the like, and speak.
Having heard those words of theirs, Sunīthā spoke these words.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Deeds of Sunīthā," in the Legend of Vena within the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. 33.
Chapter Thirty-Four.
Sūta said:
How they were previously cursed by the high-souled Suśaṅkha.
To those friends, that highly fortunate woman, being deeply tormented by grief, related everything concerning her own conduct;
then Sunīthā spoke.
Moreover, O friends, listen now as I speak further:
having beheld the excellence of my beauty, my youth, and the abundance of my virtues, my father has become filled with anxiety for no apparent reason. (2-3)
Desiring to give her to the gods and to the sages, that one of great renown took me by the hand and addressed these words to them all:
"This daughter of mine is endowed with virtues, youthful, immeasurable, and beautiful-eyed."
"I desire to give this blessing to the virtuous and high-souled one.
Then the gods and the sages heard those words of Death;
and the gods, led by Indra, spoke to him as he was speaking.
"This daughter of yours is rich in virtues and the supreme treasury of good conduct;
she has been defiled by only a single fault, namely that ṛṣi’s curse. Indeed, from her shall be born a son, by whose virility a man [shall be conceived]."
He will become a great sinner, a destroyer of his virtuous lineage.
A jar completely filled with the water of the Gaṅgā appears as such;
yet, if it is tainted by even a single drop of liquor, it becomes a jar of wine.
Through association with the wicked, a family becomes sinful, just as even a single drop of sour gruel, if it enters into the midst of milk,
subsequently destroys the milk and reveals its own nature. (10)
"In the same way, a wicked son will undoubtedly destroy his lineage.
Because of this very fault, let this sinful woman of yours be given to another; go! Thus was my father addressed by the gods. (11-12)
Abandoned by the gods, the gandharvas, and the high-souled sages, my father was tormented by grief;
even other virtuous people did not accept me.

"Thus, having performed such evil deeds and actions in the past, I am tormented by suffering and grief; I shall take refuge in the forest alone and practice asceticism, performing the emaciation of the body. (14-15)
"Indeed, you have asked me well regarding the very cause of my actions; that deed of mine, which follows from my thought, has now been revealed to you.
Having spoken thus to Mṛtyu’s daughter, the illustrious Sunīthā—
Afflicted by grief, she ceased speaking and said nothing further.
The friends said:
"O highly fortunate one, abandon this sorrow which destroys the body."
The gods attributed the fault of atheism to the family of that wicked one;
for in the past, he had spoken deceitfully in the presence of Brahmā, and though Brahmā was abandoned by the gods, he remained the most worshipful. 18–19.
O Lord, behold! Even that king of the gods, though guilty of the murder of a Brahmin, enjoys the three worlds together with the deities, O illustrious one;
for in former times he approached Ahalyā, the beloved wife of Gautama.
One who approaches the wife of another is reborn among the gods;
but Hara committed a terrible deed equal to the murder of a Brahmin, and even today he wanders about with the skull of Brahmā. 21–22.
The gods and the sages who have mastered the Vedas praise that God;
Āditya, joined with Kuṣṭha, illuminates the three worlds.
The gods and all beings, moving and unmoving, praise that God who is honored by the worlds.

Kṛṣṇa shall endure a great curse formerly inflicted by Bhārgava; having approached the wife of his preceptor, he will be born as a castrated man, yet he will become a king of kings, possessed of great luster and majesty. 24–25.
The son of Pāṇḍu, Yudhiṣṭhira, who is highly wise and righteous in soul, will speak a falsehood for the sake of slaying his preceptor. Thus, great sin resides within these very great men.
O fair-faced one, for which atheist would there not be the stigma of atheism? You have been defiled by a very slight fault;
O woman of excellent complexion, we shall indeed do you a favor. 27–28.
O auspicious one, such virtues as exist in your body are not seen even elsewhere among virtuous women, O fair-eyed one. O beautiful one,
for women, beauty itself is the primary virtue and ornament.
Virtue alone is the second, and truth is indeed the third; straightforwardness is the fourth, and righteousness itself is the fifth;
thereafter, sweetness is proclaimed as the sixth, O lady of beautiful countenance. (30-31)

Purity is the seventh vow for a girl; serving women both internally and externally is the eighth; indeed, service to one's father is the ninth; endurance is declared to be the tenth, and likewise, devotion to pleasure is the eleventh.
Then, O beautiful lady, the twelfth vow, that of devotion to one's husband (*pātivratya*), was proclaimed.
Adorned with these, O young girl of lovely countenance, do not fear;
by this means, he who upholds the true dharma shall become your husband.
"We ourselves shall indeed devise that means for your sake.
To them, those noble men said, "O friends, do not commit such a rash act.
Sūta said:
Thus addressed, Sunīthā spoke again to her praised companions:
"Tell me the means by which I shall have a husband.
To her, those beautiful-eyed noble women, Rambhā and the others, replied:
Endowed with the sweetness of form and increasing prosperity, she was terrified by the curse of Brahmā and came here;
they spoke to that large-eyed daughter of Mṛtyu, who possessed beautiful eyes. 37–38.
"O blessed lady, we shall bestow upon you a single lore that deludes men, which grants all auspiciousness to those who know all forms of illusion.
Then, by the power of this lore, these [goddesses] will grant him happiness. 39.
"O auspicious one, whomever you wish to delude in this way—be it a god or another—delude him immediately! Having been thus addressed, she did exactly so;
for when the vidyā was perfectly mastered, Sunīthā was greatly delighted. (40-41)
Thus wandering with her companions, she beheld men;
as she roamed about, she arrived at the most excellent Nandana forest. Then, on the bank of the Gaṅgā, she saw a Brāhmaṇa endowed with beauty.
Endowed with all the auspicious marks, possessing a radiance equal to the splendor of the sun,
peerless in form within the world like a second God of Love, he was of divine appearance, highly fortunate, blessed, and a bestower of good fortune. 43–44.
To that incomparable great-souled one, whose splendor is equal to the radiance of Viṣṇu, who belongs to Viṣṇu, who destroys all sins, and whose prowess is equal to Viṣṇu;
to him who is free from desire and anger, the ornament of the lineage of Atri. 45–46.

Seeing that one of beautiful form, the very embodiment of asceticism, possessed of divine power and yet burning with fervor, Rambhā, full of passion, asked her friend: "Who is this excellent, high-souled being dwelling in the heavens?
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Legend of Vena," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Thirty-Five. Rambhā said: Brahmā was born from the Unmanifest; from him Prajāpati was born.
"O blessed lady, this high-minded son of Atri, whose nature is identical to his father's, named Aṅga,
has come to this Nandana forest after beholding the supreme splendor and playful majesty of Indra."
Even for such a station as that of Indra, she felt no longing, thinking:
"Since I have such a son endowed with righteousness, my life shall be most auspicious, filled with honor and fame. (3)
Having propitiated Hṛṣīkeśa through austerities and observances,
and with Hṛṣīkeśa being well-pleased, he requested a boon:
a son equal to Indra, possessing the splendor and prowess of Viṣṇu.
"O Madhusūdana, grant me that Vaiṣṇava rite which destroys all sins;
for you have granted me such a son who upholds everything.
O best of Brahmins, from that time forward, he beheld a meritorious maiden.
"Just as you are beautiful in all your limbs, so does he perceive [the world].
Go to him, O lady of excellent hips; from him a son shall be born, a virtuous soul who knows righteous dharma and possesses the splendor and prowess of Viṣṇu."
All this has been explained to you as you have asked;
this husband of yours is worthy [of you], O Goddess, there is no doubt.
Even the curse of Suśaṅkha shall become void.
"O highly fortunate one, since a son devoted to the practice of dharma has been born from me, you shall become happy, O blessed lady; I tell you this as the truth, the absolute truth.
Just as a diligent farmer sows seed in a fertile field," so it shall be for you.
"O Queen, one reaps exactly as one sows;
otherwise, nothing would ever be produced, for everything must be like its cause.
This highly fortunate ascetic here possesses the power of merit."
From his own prowess he shall give birth to a son endowed with his very same perfection of qualities; a son of great splendor, the best among all embodied beings,
highly fortunate, self-disciplined, and a knower of the reality of yoga.
Having thus heard these words spoken by Arambhapriya, which bestow auspiciousness, the young woman reflected with her intellect upon their true meaning; for that was indeed the absolute truth.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter of the Bhūmikhaṇḍa in the Śrī Padma Purāṇa, within the narrative of Veṇu. 35.
Chapter Thirty-Six.
Sunīthā said:
"O auspicious lady, you have spoken the truth; I shall do exactly as you say."
"I shall delude the Brahmins with this ignorance, and not otherwise.
Give me your meritorious assistance so that I may proceed at once.
When she had spoken thus, he addressed that high-minded woman who was ready to begin.
"O beautiful lady, tell me what kind of assistance I may provide;
O auspicious one, go as a messenger to him right now.
When she had spoken thus, [he addressed] that beautiful-eyed Tārāmbā.
"In this very way, it was promised by the celestial woman Rambhā:
'I shall provide you assistance; let my command be given.
With sincerity, O large-eyed one, I who am endowed with beauty and youth [will do so].'"
Through her illusory power (*māyā*), that lady of beautiful countenance assumed a divine form, peerless in beauty within the world and enchanting the three realms;
she appeared upon the highly auspicious peak of Mount Meru, which possessed lovely caves.
It was strewn with various minerals and adorned with diverse jewels;
it was filled with celestial trees and graced by many flowers;
it was crowded with hosts of gods and frequented by gandharvas and apsarases.
In that charming and delightful place, filled with the cool shade of sandalwood and young *aśoka* trees,
the sweetly smiling lady ascended a swing, adorned with every kind of erotic ornament.
O best of the twice-born, that young woman of beautiful limbs, shining with a deep blue silken garment and a bodice the color of the bandhūka flower,
held a lute in her hands and kept time with her fingers. 10–11.
Surrounded by those charming young female companions who sang excellent songs in beautiful voices that enchanted the entire world,
the youth remained absorbed in meditation in the holy, secluded cave of Aṅga.
Free from desire and anger, he meditated upon Janārdana;
having heard that sweet, melodious, and most enchanting song, which was endowed with rhythm,
measure, and tempo, and which captivated all living beings.
The radiant one, deluded by the illusory song, wavered from his meditation;
rising quickly from his seat and looking again and again,
he went there with speed, his mind agitated by the illusion.
Beholding her seated upon a swing, her hand holding the neck of a lute,
laughing and singing beautifully with a face like the full moon, that one of great renown was enchanted by both her song and her beauty.
Struck by the arrows of the God of Love due to her lack of beauty, that best of the twice-born, the son of a rishi, his consciousness agitated and overwhelmed,
prattled on with extreme delusion and yawned again and again.
At that very moment, perspiration, trembling, and great distress arose within him; as if bewildered by profound delusions, exhausted and with a distracted mind,
he arrived there shivering and with his limbs throbbing.
Beholding that large-eyed, illustrious daughter of Death,

who was surrounded by her companions, the high-souled one then spoke to the sweetly smiling Sunīthā: "Who are you, O lady of beautiful hips, and whose daughter are you, surrounded as you are by these friends?"
"For what purpose have you arrived, and by whom were you sent to this forest? All your limbs appear beautiful here in this great forest;
tell me today, and be gracious with a favorable countenance. (22-23)

Deluded by the illusion of Māyā, even that great sage, though pierced by the arrows of the God of Love, did not perceive her actions. Having thus heard these significant words of the high-minded one, [he remained silent].
Looking at the face of her friend with a certain bashfulness,
she signaled to her companion Rambhā by means of a sign;
then Rambhā spoke respectfully to that brahmin.

This highly fortunate maiden, known as Sunīthā, is renowned for her perfection in all auspicious marks; she is the daughter of the great-souled Mṛtyu, and this young woman seeks a husband who is righteous and a treasure-house of asceticism.
Having heard such great words from him— who was tranquil, self-controlled, highly wise, and proficient in Vedic knowledge—
the great sage then spoke to Rambhā, the most excellent of the Apsarases.
"By my practice, Viṣṇu, Hari who pervades the entire universe, was propitiated; he granted me a boon called a son, which bestows all perfections.
For that reason, O blessed lady, I am constantly intent upon the sake of a son."
"I have always been reflecting upon a certain virtuous man's only daughter;
I have never before seen a truly excellent wife such as this. She is indeed the daughter of Dharma, a woman of righteous conduct and beautiful countenance. (31-32)
"Let her enjoy me alone if she desires me as her beloved here; whatever this young woman may wish for, I shall grant it to her without a doubt.
For the sake of her union, he said that even what is not to be given must be given."
"O best of the twice-born, listen; only one thing must be granted by you in this way.
Rambhā said: "O lord of brahmins, listen here; I shall now state my vow."
"This wife of yours by dharma must certainly not be abandoned by you;
never should her fault be taken up by you, nor her virtue.
O Brahmin, demonstrate proof of this matter in our very presence."
"O best of Brahmins, give with your own hand that which shall serve as a token of truth; 'So be it,' [I say], for her hand has indeed been given by me, without a doubt.
Sūta said:
Having thus established the relationship and made it a matter of solemn truth,
he married Sunīthā by the Gāndharva rite. Having given that Sunīthā to him with a heart as joyful as Rambhā, [he departed].
Having invited Sātā, they returned again to their own homes; with joyful hearts, the friends departed for their respective places.
O best of the twice-born, when all those friends had gone, [the sage remained].
Having begotten with his beloved wife a son endowed with all auspicious marks, Remitvaṅga gave that son the name Vena.
Then that son of Sunīthā, possessed of great splendor, grew up;
having studied the Vedas and the scriptures, as well as the science of archery along with its qualities, the intelligent youth reached the furthest limit of all branches of knowledge. 42–43.

Vena, the son of Aṅga, conducted himself according to the conduct of the Śiṣṭas; however, that best of Brāhmaṇas became devoted to the conduct of a Kṣatriya. Endowed with all splendor, he shone like Indra in heaven.

Thus that one of great wisdom shines by his own strength and valor. (45) When the Vaivasvata Manvantara arrived following the Cākṣuṣa interval, the subjects in the world constantly suffered due to the absence of a protector of the people. (46)

The sages, whose wealth was their austerity and who knew the true essence of dharma, deliberated upon a protector of the earth for the sake of progeny— one who knew the law and was a scholar of truth. O King,
they beheld him, Vena, endowed with all auspicious marks.
The best of the twice-born consecrated him at the holy site of Prājāpatya.
O highly fortunate one, when the son of Tvaṅga had been consecrated as king,
all those Prajāpatis departed for the forest of asceticism.
When all of them had departed, Vena ruled the kingdom.
Sūta said:
Having seen that her son was capable of governing the entire kingdom, Sunīthā [rejoiced].
"By the power of that great-souled one's curse,
my highly fortunate son will become a protector of dharma"—
thus she would constantly think, fearing on account of her former sins.

She showed her son the most meritorious limbs of Dharma; she revealed those virtuous qualities such as truthfulness and the like. For she said to her son: "O son, I am indeed the daughter of Dharma. 52-53.
"Your father knows the true essence of dharma; therefore, practice dharma"—in this way, that virtuous woman would constantly instruct her son.
He, in turn, should carry out the words of his mother and father, which are consistent with the welfare of their progeny.
Thus Vena was born as a protector of subjects upon the circle of the earth;
the world lived in happiness, for the subjects were delighted by his righteous rule. Such was the power of the sovereignty of that high-souled Vena.
While that king was ruling, the manifestations of Dharma proceeded.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the account of Veṇu.
Chapter Thirty-Seven.
The sages said:
Such was the creation of the high-souled Vena;
how could he, having abandoned righteous conduct, become one of sinful mind?
Sūta said:
The sages, endowed with spiritual knowledge and realized wisdom, who know the true nature of reality, declare that what is auspicious or inauspicious shall not be otherwise here on this earth. 2.
O Brahmins, how was the curse given by that high-souled Suśaṅkha while he was performing austerities brought about exactly as it happened?
I shall tell you everything regarding the sinful conduct of Vena.
While that great-souled protector of subjects, who knew the Dharma,
was ruling, a certain man arrived at that time, wearing a deceptive disguise; he was naked in form, possessed of a massive body, with a shaven head and great radiance.
Holding a broom made of peacock feathers in his armpit,
with a coconut wine-cup grasped in his hand,
he was indeed reciting false scriptures that defile the Vedic dharma.
Vena, the great king, arrived there with great haste; that wicked man entered his assembly hall. Seeing that he had arrived, Vena then addressed him with a question.
"Who are you that have arrived here, assuming such a form? Why have you come before me while I am presiding in this assembly?
What is your dress, what is your name, what is your dharma, and what is your work? Tell me."
What is the conduct of one who knows the Vedas? What is austerity? What is spiritual power? What is knowledge? What is your majesty? What is truth? What is the characteristic of dharma?
Tell me everything truly and accurately before me. (10–11)
Having heard those words of Avena, the sinner spoke these words:
Pātaka said, "O great fool, you are undoubtedly ruling this kingdom in vain. (12)

I am the entire essence of Dharma; I am the most worthy of worship by the asuras; I am knowledge, I am truth, and I am the eternal Creator. I am righteousness, I am liberation, for I indeed consist of all the gods.
Born from the body of Brahmā, he is true to his promise; it is not otherwise.
Know me to be the form of the Jina, the very embodiment of the True Dharma. Indeed, yogis intent on knowledge run toward me alone. 14–15.
Vena said: "What kind of action is yours, and what is your philosophical view? What is your conduct? Speak, indeed!"—thus was it addressed by that king.
Pātaka said:
Where the Arhat is seen as the deity and the Nirgrantha as the teacher, and where compassion is the supreme dharma—there liberation is clearly perceived. 17
In this system, I shall declare the practices free from doubt:

there is no performing sacrifices or officiating at them, nor is there the study of the Vedas; there is no twilight ritual, no austerity, no charity, and it is devoid of the utterances *svadhā* and *svāhā*. (18)
There is no offering of *havya* or *kavya*, nor indeed any ritual such as sacrifice; there is no libation for the ancestors, no guest-offering, and no *vaiśvadeva* rite.
For the mendicant, the worship of the Exalted One (*vara*) is supreme, and meditation upon the Arhat is the highest practice. (19–20)
This practice of dharma is seen in the path of the Jains;
all this has been declared to you as the characteristic of one's own dharma.
Vena said:

Where the dharma proclaimed in the Vedas—namely, rituals such as sacrifices, the libations for the ancestors, the *śrāddha*, and the *vaiśvadeva* offering—is not seen, there is neither charity nor austerity;
what then remains as the characteristic of dharma? 22.
"Speak the truth before me: what is the nature of the dharma of compassion?
Pātaka said:
"This body of living beings is indeed composed of the five elements."

This nature of the self is like the wind; for them, there is no possibility of attachment (24). Just as among beings in the waters, a union is observed that takes the form of bubbles, so too is the coming together of beings (25).
The earth-element resides in rajas, and water is situated right there;
light is seen therein, and wind exists within these three.
Afterwards, space envelops them, and the state of being a bubble is produced.
In the midst of the waters, a supreme, circular, and radiant light shines;
it may be seen for a mere moment, yet in the next moment it is no longer seen.
In that same way, the conjunction of the elements is observed everywhere.
At the time of death, the self departs; those five [elements] go into the five [others]. Thus deluded by ignorance, mortals revolve among one another.
Out of delusion, they perform the *śrāddha* and the libations for the ancestors on the anniversary of their passing.

"O best of kings, where does the deceased reside and what does he eat? What is his nature, and what is his knowledge? What is his body like, and by whom has he been seen? Tell me this. Furthermore, after being fed sweet food, how is it that the Brahmins depart satisfied? (30-31)
To whom should that faith be offered? That faith is indeed useless.
I shall speak further of another matter, the terrible ritual of the Vedas:
when a guest arrives at the house, a twice-born man might slaughter a great bull.
O king of kings, one should feed a goat as a guest.
O King, in the Aśvamedha sacrifice one should offer a horse, in the Gomedha a bull, in the Naramedha a man, and likewise in the Vājapeya, goats.
O Great King, in the Rājasūya there is the slaughter of many living beings;
in the Puṇḍarīka one should kill an elephant, and in the Gajamedha, an elephant;
in the Sautrāmaṇi, a sacrificial animal is seen to be a ram.
O prince, listen to [the account] regarding all these various forms.
The slaughter of animals of diverse species is recorded; as for the gift that is also given, what is the characteristic of that gift? 36–37.
That food which is left over after a great feast is considered impure;
for they kill those who are entirely free from fault in the great sacrifice—what dharma is seen there, O King, and what fruit is obtained therein? (38)

Wherever the slaughter of animals is prescribed by those learned in the Vedas, that [practice] is a destruction of dharma; it is neither meritorious nor a giver of liberation. For whatever dharma exists without compassion, that dharma becomes fruitless.
Wherever there is the protection of living beings, there is dharma; of this there is no doubt.

O best of kings, [where there is] the utterance of *svāhā*, the utterance of *svadhā*, austerity, and truth—[if these exist], there is dharma. But where there is cruelty and fickleness, there is indeed no dharma. 41.
These very Vedas would be non-Vedas where compassion does not exist.
One who is constantly devoted to compassion and charity should protect even his own life;
for whether he be a Caṇḍāla or a Śūdra, he is called a Brāhmaṇa by the gods.
That Brahmin who is merciless and devoted to the slaughter of animals is indeed utterly pitiless,
sinful, hard-hearted, and cruel-minded.
The Veda that is proclaimed by deceivers is a Veda devoid of true knowledge.
Wherever knowledge exists eternally, there the Veda is established.
O high-minded one, in those Vedas and Brahmins who are devoid of compassion, there is neither truth nor ritual action; such is the case with those Vedas and Brahmins. 45–46.

O Indra among kings, those Brahmins who do not know the Vedas and are devoid of truth have no fruit even from giving; therefore, no gift is given to them. Just as there is a specific mark for a śrāddha, so too is there a defining characteristic for a gift.
I shall now proclaim before you that Dharma of the Jina, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and which grants great merit;
first, it must be practiced with a mind that has become peaceful through compassion. 48–49.

One should propitiate the Jina, by whom the moving and non-moving world exists, through the heart alone; with a pure mind and disposition, one should worship the Jina as the One. 50. One must perform prostration to that Deva, and not otherwise.
One should never, under any circumstances, salute the feet of one's mother and father.
O best of kings, what need is there to speak of others?
Vena said:
These brahmins, teachers, and rivers such as the Gaṅgā likewise proclaim that these holy fords bestow great merit. Therefore, tell me the truth regarding this, if you desire righteousness here.
Pātaka said:
O great king, from the sky the clouds indeed rain down water; thus, the water falls everywhere upon the earth and the mountains. 54
Having bathed there, one should remain standing and cultivate compassion toward all beings.
Rivers are indeed floods of sin; how then can they be heard of as sacred fords (*tīrtha*)?
So too are reservoirs, great silver-lined ponds, and oceans.

The mountains and heaps of stones are indeed the supports of the earth; yet among these there is no holy ford (tīrtha) where the supreme merit of bathing in the waters of the Cloud exists—why, then, should it not exist among fish? 56-57.
Success is indeed attained through bathing; fish are purified, and not otherwise.
Wherever the Jina is, there is a sacred ford (tīrtha), and there resides the eternal Dharma.
All merit, such as austerity, charity, and the like, is established therein. 58–59.
O Indra among kings, there is no other supreme dharma or sacred ford (*tīrtha*) that encompasses all things like the One Jina;
therefore, this is the highest gain. By meditating upon Him constantly, you will become exceedingly happy.
[Thus he spoke,] having disparaged all dharma including the Vedas, as well as charity, merit, and the nature of supreme sacrifice.
"O King, you have been repeatedly awakened by many people of sinful nature, by that sinner who was the son of Aṅga.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Narrative of Vena," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
The thirty-eighth chapter.
Sūta said:
Thus enlightened, Vena indeed fell into a state of sinfulness.
Deluded by that most sinful man, Jaina,
he then prostrated at the feet of that very evil-minded one;
having abandoned the Vedic dharma, he performed rites such as those of the true dharma.

There would be a cessation of good sacrifices and likewise of the Vedas; at that time, dharma consisting of meritorious scriptures would not have been promulgated. By his rule, the world became filled with all manner of sins.
O Brahmins, while that king ruled, there were no sacrifices, no Vedas, and no study of the supreme meaning of the Dharmaśāstras; nor was there charity or Vedic study.
Thus, the destruction of Dharma occurred and great evil was set in motion.
Though restrained by his limbs, that evil-minded one acted most perversely; he even struck the feet of his father and mother.
"I alone am powerful, even compared to the sage Sanaka."
Though forbidden by his father and mother, that evil-minded one never performed any auspicious or meritorious act, such as visiting sacred fords or giving gifts,
for a long time, despite his great fame, acting instead in accordance with his own disposition.
Again, after everyone had deliberated thus, [they asked]: "Why was this sinner born?
How did he, the son of Prajāpati Aṅga, become a blemish upon his lineage?
Then the righteous-souled one questioned again the daughter of the great-souled Mṛtyu.
"Tell me truly, my dear, by whose fault has this arisen?
Sunīthā said:
"O Nandinī, [I shall tell you] my own history and my merit from before."
O Mahāmati, he related this in detail:
"In my youth, I committed a sin against the high-souled Suśaṅkha; though he was established in asceticism, I did nothing else for him. (11-12)
"O highly fortunate one, I know that because his father cursed him in anger, saying, 'May your progeny be wicked,' he has consequently fallen into wickedness.
Having heard this, the one of great splendor went to the forest together with her.
When that illustrious one had departed for the forest with his wife,
those seven sages likewise went to the side of Vena; having summoned him, they then spoke to the son of Aṅga.
The sages said:
"Do not act with rashness or violence; become the protector of creatures here.
By you, this entire world—the three realms with all things moving and unmoving—is sustained. (16)
"O highly fortunate one, everything is indeed established in Dharma alone;
therefore, abandoning sinful actions, practice meritorious deeds.
When this was said, he laughed and spoke these words to them.
Vena said:
"I alone am the supreme dharma; I alone am the eternal Arhat.
I am the creator, I am the protector, and I am the very meaning of the Vedas."
"I am the Dharma, possessed of great merit, the eternal Jaina Dharma. O Brahmins, worship me alone through your actions, for I am the very embodiment of Dharma. The sages said:
Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas—these three castes are the twice-born (dvijātayaḥ). This is the eternal Vedic revelation for all castes;
by following the conduct prescribed by the Vedas, living beings sustain their lives.

Born from the lineage of Brahmā, you were indeed a Brāhmaṇa; later, having displayed your prowess, you became the king of the earth. O Indra among kings, it is through the merit of the king that the twice-born live in happiness.

By the king's sin they perish; therefore, practice merit. O lord of men, you have honored righteousness and indeed performed it; such was not the case for the deeds of the Tretā age, nor likewise for the Dvāpara age. 23–24.
In the Kali age, men will indeed enter [this state],
having taken refuge in the Jaina dharma and being utterly deluded by sin;
abandoning Vedic conduct, those men will go toward wickedness.
Thus, O King, there is no doubt that the root of evil is indeed the Jaina dharma.
By this great delusion, O Lord of Kings, men have been cast down into a mass of sins; there is no other way for their destruction. 26–27.
Govinda shall indeed exist as the remover of all sins;
assuming a form at his own will, he will destroy [the world] from sin. When sins have thus accumulated, he will indeed act again for the destruction of the mlecchas.
The Lord Kalki himself will appear; of this there is no doubt.
Abandon the worldly dealings of the Kali age and take refuge in merit; conduct yourself with truth and become a protector of your subjects.
Veṇu said:
"I am the foremost among those possessed of knowledge; everything here has been known by me. Whoever acts otherwise shall certainly be punished. (31)
As that evil-minded king was speaking excessively,
all those high-souled sons of Brahmā became enraged. While the brahmins were thus incensed, O King, Vena [was addressed] by those great-souled ones.
Out of fear of the curse of the Brahmins, he entered an anthill. Then those sages, becoming enraged, searched for him everywhere;
having realized that the king had vanished, they found him now situated within the anthill.
The brahmins forcibly brought that cruel man of sinful mind;
and seeing him of wicked deeds, the sages, being well-composed,
became filled with wrath and wrung the king's left hand.

From him was born a great dwarf, dark-complexioned and terrifying; he was a barbarian with red eyes, holding an arrow in his hand and bearing a bow, and he became the leader of all the sinful Niṣādas. 36–37.
O high-minded one, seeing that man of evil deeds, the Ṛṣis— especially the kings who were the protectors of the realms and the Mlecchas—
wrested the right hand of the great-souled Vena.
From him was born that great-souled one by whom the earth was milked;
he was named Pṛthu, highly wise, a king of kings, and possessed of great strength.
Through the grace of his merit, Vena became skilled in the matters of dharma and artha.
Having enjoyed the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin) through the grace of that wielder of the discus,
he went to the world of Viṣṇu, that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Legend of Vena," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The thirty-ninth chapter.
The sages said:
How did Vena go to heaven, having cast away his sin far behind him?
Therefore, O best of speakers, tell me that here as well in detail.
Sūta said:
O best of the twice-born, [I shall speak] because of the merit of the sages' company and their discourse.
O twice-born ones, because his body was emaciated, his sin departed outside; thereafter,
that virtuous soul attained eternal knowledge and performed penance on the southern bank of the Revā.
In the sin-destroying hermitage of the sage Tṛṇabindu,
he remained for more than a hundred years, free from desire and anger;
by virtue of his fierce asceticism, the Lord who bears the conch, discus, and mace [appeared].
The illustrious one became pleased with the sinless king;
he said, "I am pleased; choose an excellent boon.
Vena replied:
"If you are indeed pleased with me, grant me this supreme boon: O Lord of the Gods, O illustrious one, I desire to go to your abode in this very body,
together with my father and my mother."
"By Your power alone, O God, that supreme abode of Viṣṇu [is reached].
Śrī Vāsudeva said: "O King, where has that great delusion gone, by which you were so deluded?"
"Overwhelmed by greed and joined with delusion, I have been cast down by the path of darkness.
Vena said:
"O Lord, I have been deluded by that sin which I committed in the past."
"Uplift me from this most terrible sin;
O Lord, please grant your grace and tell me what is to be chanted and what is to be studied.
The Blessed One said:
"O virtuous and illustrious king, that sin has been extinguished by him.
You have become pure through your austerity; therefore, I shall now recount your merit.
O dear one, it is just as you were asked by Brahmā in the past."
To him, my child, I shall tell all that which was spoken; once, while Brahmā was absorbed in meditation upon his navel-lotus,
O observer of noble vows, [I appeared] to grant him a boon.
Therefore, desiring great merit that destroys sin and bestows a happy rebirth, he requested that supreme and great hymn known by the name Vāsudeva,
which is the highest among all hymns. 13–14.
"O highly fortunate one, I shall always instruct you in that supreme [mantra] which bestows all happiness upon men who read and recite it, and which brings great pleasure to Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu said:
This entire world is pervaded by me in my unmanifest form; therefore, the sages devoted to Viṣṇu call me Viṣṇu. Wherever beings dwell, and wherever that all-pervading Lord dwells within them—
I, together with Vāsudeva, am to be known with reverence by the wise.
Because that all-pervading Lord withdraws all creatures into the unmanifest at the end of time, He is to be known by those who have come for refuge by the name Saṃkarṣaṇa. 17–18.
"By my own will, I am one who can assume any form at will through a mere gesture; therefore, I am to be known as Pradyumna by those wise men who desire sons.
In this world, apart from Īśa, both Hara and Keśava are lords of all."
"By the power of yoga, I have been restrained; therefore, I am like one who is restrained.
Known as Viśva, I am endowed with the knowledge and discernment of every world, yet I possess the egoism of 'I' and am agitated by the thoughts of the waking state. (20-21)

"I am Taijasa, consisting of the activity of the world and possessing the form of the senses; indeed, I have entered the state of dream, being fully endowed with knowledge and action. I am Prājña, the supreme divine self, whose sphere of experience is the substratum of Viśva."
I am the Fourth (Turiya), remaining like one indifferent to the world even while situated in deep sleep, free from conceptual construction;
I am changeless, devoid of the states of the qualities (guṇas), untainted, and my form is reflected as the entire universe, like a witness. 23–24.

"I am the manifestation of consciousness, the bliss of consciousness, composed of consciousness, and possessing the very nature of consciousness; I am eternal, imperishable, and of the form of Brahman—know me thus as Brahman itself.
Thus spoke the Blessed Lord.
Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu vanished in his true form before Brahmā;
he too, having realized the pervasiveness of the universe, became perfected in soul in an instant.
O King, you too are pure-souled, as is Pṛthu from his very birth.
"Nevertheless, O observer of noble vows, propitiate the All-pervading Lord with this hymn.
Viṣṇu, being pleased, addressed him, saying, "O giver of joy, choose a boon. Vena said:
"O Viṣṇu, grant me a good rebirth; deliver me from my evil deed!
I have come to you for refuge; tell me the cause of my miserable state.
Viṣṇu said:
Formerly, by this very noble-souled one of great fortune, I was propitiated; therefore, a boon was granted to him by me: "O highly fortunate one, you shall go to the supreme world of Viṣṇu. 29–30.
"O best of Brahmins, O illustrious prince, by virtue of your own meritorious deeds,
you may request a boon for your own sake.
Listen, O noble one, to this account of events from a former birth."
