O King, in former times, when you were but a child, the high-souled Suśaṅkha, being enraged, pronounced a curse upon Sunītha;
subsequently, I, who know the self, bestowed this body upon you. (32–33)
"O you who are fond of virtues, having spoken thus to your father, I said: 'I shall become your excellent son, desiring to uplift you,
and being born from your own body, I shall perform the protection of the world.'"
For as Indra shines in heaven, so do I abide upon the earth.
"The self is indeed born as the son"—this is the truth-bearing Vedic revelation.
Therefore, O dear one, you shall attain a happy state by virtue of my boon.

O King, O scorcher of foes, for the sake of your own welfare, perform this one act of giving: you who are like a sinner, having assumed the form of a naked mendicant, spoke to Sunīthā so as to lead you toward unrighteousness. (37)
Otherwise, the very words of Suśaṅkha would have been rendered false.
Therefore, O best of kings, both injunction and prohibition are indeed myself;
I am the bestower of fruits according to one's actions, perceived through the intellect as the grasp of the qualities. 38-39.
Giving alone is supreme and most excellent; giving is the source of all power.
Therefore, you must give; from giving, merit arises. (40) Through giving, evil is destroyed; therefore, indeed, you must give.
O best of kings, perform sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha;
indeed, bestow gifts such as land upon the Brāhmaṇas.
Through the gift of excellent things, enjoyment is obtained; through the gift of excellent things, fame is obtained. 41–42.
From generous giving, fame arises; from generous giving, happiness is attained.
Through giving, one reaches heaven and enjoys its fruit there, O best of beings, provided that the gift given is endowed with faith. 43.

When the proper time has arrived, one should go to a sacred ford; this indeed is the fruit of merit. Furthermore, he who, with a mind purified by faith and having fixed his devotion upon Me, gives a great gift to a Brahmin who is a worthy recipient—45.
To him, whose mind was entirely focused on Kalandā, he said: "Tell me, what kind of gift of time do you desire?
What are the characteristics of time? Vena replied: (46)

O Lord of the World, if you have compassion for me, please become gracious and speak at length regarding the nature of the sacred ford, the auspicious characteristics of the recipient, and the ritual procedure for giving. 47.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:

O King, I shall now describe the times for giving: the constant (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), and another, O Great King, the optional (kāmya), which furthermore leads to the attainment of the fourth [state].
At the time of sunrise, sin is destroyed in every way.
The sun in the sky, who causes the destruction of the terrible and excessive darkness of men, is my own portion, conceived as a treasury of splendors. 49-50.
By its very splendor, sins are consumed and reduced to ashes;
O King, what more need be said of him who, upon seeing my rising form, offers even a drop of water, for it eternally increases his merit? 51.
When that auspicious hour has arrived, a meritorious man,
having bathed and worshipped the ancestors and the gods, should again become a giver of gifts,
according to his capacity and by the power of a mind purified by faith.
Food, milk, fruit, flowers, clothing, betel, ornaments,
gold, gems, and so forth— the merit of one who gives these is infinite. O King, it is the same at midday as well as in the afternoon.
Whoever should offer me a heap of such [objects], his merit shall be infinite.
(55) [One should offer] food, drink, and the like, sweet ointments, perfumes, saffron, camphor and other substances, as well as garments and ornaments. (56)

Thus, I have described the auspicious daily time for those seeking the merit of giving and worship, which bestows uninterrupted enjoyment and happiness. Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the unsurpassed occasional rite (naimittika).
A gift must indeed be given at all three times of the day; of this there is no doubt. One who desires his own welfare should never let a day pass empty [of giving].
For at whatever time a gift is bestowed, O lord of men, [that very time becomes auspicious]. 58–59.
By its power, one becomes possessed of great wisdom, endowed with many capabilities,
wealthy, virtuous, intelligent, learned, and discerning;
even when no food has been given for a fortnight, a month, or as long as a day.
I shall indeed restrain that best of men from eating what is unfit for consumption;
and by not giving my own excrement, I shall produce a supreme seizure— an illness that obstructs all enjoyments.
In their bodies there arises a fever that causes great distress, accompanied by weak digestion and producing intense heat;
this occurs for those who have not offered [gifts] to Brahmins and gods during the three periods of the day.
He himself ate what was delicious; by that, a great sin was committed.
O Great King, one should purify him in this way through fierce penances, such as fasts that wither the body. 64–65.
Just as a pitiless leather-worker,
using astringent decoctions, cleanses a hide placed upon a frame and stretches it out,
so too do I cleanse the evildoer; of this there is no doubt.
Through the improper application of medicinal herbs, with bitter decoctions, certainly with hot water and torments— none other than by way of a physician—
others enjoy his fierce karmic fruits, which are meritorious and agreeable to the mind. 67–68.
And what can one who is capable do? One should bestow that supreme gift upon him;
otherwise, I shall torment him with great sin.
Just as the sinful always give gifts for their own sake, [so should you]. (69)
"O Indra among kings, that which was not given with a heart purified by faith—
such things I indeed cause them to consume through terrible means.
Vāsudeva said:
O best of men, I shall now declare before you the occasional rites, the proper times, and the meritorious acts; listen with focused attention and a well-disposed mind.
O great king, these include the new moon day (Amāvāsyā) and likewise the full moon day (Paurṇamāsī).
O Lord of Men, when there is a saṃkrānti, when a vyatīpāta occurs,
when a vaidhṛti is proclaimed, and when it is the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī);
likewise on Mahāmāghī, Āṣāḍhī, Vaiśākhī, and Kārtikī.
On the conjunction of the new moon with a Monday, on the anniversaries of the beginning of the Manvantaras and the Yugas (74),

as well as what is called Gaja-chāyā and likewise on the anniversary of the passing of one’s ancestors— by these, O best of kings, the occasional rites (naimittika) have been declared before you. (75)
To these [deities] a gift is given; I shall now declare the fruit of that gift, so listen, O best of kings. (76) A man who, with devotion, bestows [a gift] upon a Brahmin while dedicating it to me—
To him, I shall undoubtedly grant, O Great King, a home, happiness, heaven, liberation, and much else that is desired;
I shall now describe the time that yields the fruit of this gift. 77–78.
O King, the best of the twice-born have likewise declared the auspicious time for all vows, as well as for gods and others, and for the giving of gifts;
I shall now describe that very time which pertains to prosperity.
Among all sacrifices, the marriage ceremony is indeed unsurpassed (80).

Likewise, for a son as soon as he is born, the rites such as the tonsure and the investiture of the sacred thread, as well as the consecration and other rituals for temples, banners, and deities, [should be performed]. (81)

O King, at that time, the construction of ponds, wells, and tanks, as well as houses and dwellings, is declared to be conducive to prosperity, provided that the worship of the Mothers is performed there;
during that period, one should give gifts which bestow all success.
"O best of kings, this very time has been declared as conducive to worldly prosperity (ābhyudayika). Furthermore, O best of men, I shall describe that which wards off the affliction of sin,
when the time of death has arrived and one perceives the end."
In that regard, a gift should be bestowed which grants happiness on the path of Yama;
these include the regular (nitya), occasional (naimittika), optional (kāmya), and prosperity-seeking (abhyudayika) times. O Great King, the final time has now been described before you.
These times have been fully described as bestowing the fruits of one's own actions.
O King, I shall now declare before you the characteristics of a sacred ford (*tīrtha*); this Gaṅgā is the most excellent of all holy fords, and the Sarasvatī shines with merit. 86–87.
The Revā, Yamunā, Tāpī, as well as the river Carmaṇvatī, the Sarayū, Ghargharā, and Veṇā, which destroy all sins; the Kāverī, Kapilā, and another, the Viśālā, who delivers the universe. 88.
O best of men, the river known as Godāvarī, the Tuṅgabhadrā,
the Bhīmarathī which is constantly proclaimed to strike fear into sinners, the Devikā, the Kṛṣṇagaṅgā, and other such most excellent rivers exist. 89–90.
At the auspicious times for these [deities], there are numerous sacred sites (tīrthas) in villages or in forests; rivers everywhere are purifying.
In each of those places, rites such as ritual bathing and giving gifts should be performed.
O best of beings, O King, when the name of this sacred ford (tīrtha) is not known, one should utter the name "Viṣṇu-tīrtha.
Likewise, I myself am the presiding deity of that ford; of this there is no doubt. 92–93.

O prince, if a practitioner at a sacred ford among the gods should utter my name in this manner, the fruit of his merit arises under my name, O best of kings, for those sacred fords and deities who remain unknown.
94. O most excellent of monarchs, [this applies] to those holy sites and deities that are unrecognized.
O Great King, one should always utter the names of rivers during bathing and giving of gifts;
O Lord of Kings, these rivers were created by the Creator as the very queens of all sacred fords (tīrthas) among all meritorious places upon the circle of the earth. 95–96.

O King, wherever one performs acts such as bathing and giving charity, one obtains inexhaustible fruit through the grace of these excellent holy places (tīrthas). Indeed, the seven oceans themselves are of the nature of tīrthas and possess great merit.
Likewise, O King, those beginning with Mānasa are proclaimed as lakes;
waterfalls and ponds are said to be sacred fords (tīrthas) without a doubt. Even small rivers, O great king, are established as excellent sacred fords. 98–99.

Thus, among all these [features], with the exception of a well, there are mountains in the form of sacred fords (tīrtha) such as Meru and others upon the surface of the earth; likewise, the sacrificial ground and the sacrifice itself, as established in the Agnihotra. 100.
Likewise, the ground for ancestral rites (śrāddha), a pure place, a temple, and furthermore, a fire-offering hall (homashālā) is declared [auspicious]; as well as a room for Vedic study.
Among houses, a cow-pen endowed with merit is the most excellent. 101–102.
Where there is a tirtha established as a place for Soma-drinkers, where there is a meritorious grove, and where the Aśvattha tree stands;
where there is the Brahma-tree, and likewise the Vaṭa tree. (103)
Furthermore, this sacred site (tīrtha) is established in various other locations as well.
These are declared to be the sacred sites: where the father and likewise the mother [are present], where the Purāṇa is recited, and where the Guru himself resides. 104–105.

Wherever a virtuous wife resides, that is undoubtedly a sacred ford (tīrtha); wherever a good son resides, that is undoubtedly a sacred ford. These sacred fords have been fully described, as has the royal palace.
Vena said:
"O Madhava, O best of gods, please become gracious with a favorable countenance out of compassion for me, and tell me the characteristics of the recipient to whom a gift should be given. (107)
Vāsudeva said:
Listen, O King of great wisdom, to the excellent characteristics of a worthy recipient, to whom noble-souled men, purified by faith, should give a sublime gift. 108.
A Brahmin endowed with a noble lineage, devoted to the study of the Vedas, peaceful, self-controlled, engaged in austerity, and especially pure;
one who is wise, possessed of knowledge, and dedicated to the worship of the gods. (109-110)
One who is truthful, highly meritorious, a Vaiṣṇava, learned in knowledge,
knower of dharma, free from greed, and shunned by heretics—
such a person is declared to be a worthy recipient; now I shall speak of another.

"Know this son of your sister, O best of men, to be endowed with such qualities; know him, O great king, as the worthy recipient for your daughter's son, and as a son-in-law possessed of these very attributes."
O best of men, the guru, one who has been initiated, and one who is a worthy recipient—these alone are excellent vessels fit for giving, O most virtuous one.
One endowed with Vedic conduct is never satiated [with receiving gifts]. 114.
One should avoid a Brahmin who is a cheat, as well as one who is one-eyed or a great rogue (115).
O Great King, one should completely avoid one who is excessively dark or tawny;
one should also avoid one with crab-like eyes, one who is very blue-black, or one with black teeth (116).
O King, likewise one with blue teeth, one with yellow teeth,
a cow-killer, one with very black teeth, a barbarian, one who is excessively dusty, one with missing limbs, one with extra limbs, a leper, and one with deformed nails. 117.

O Great King, one should avoid a man with diseased skin or one who is bald. One should not give a gift to any Brahmin whose wife is devoted to unrighteousness, even if he were equal to Brahmā himself. 118–119.

O great-minded one, one should not give to one conquered by women; O lord of the earth, one should not give to a branch-rebel (one who has left his own school), nor to the sick, nor to those who eat the food of the deceased,
nor to a thief— even if he were equal to the three gods.

One should avoid giving to one who is insatiable; likewise, one should avoid giving to one who is excessively arrogant, and especially to one who is deceitful (121). [One should not give] to one who, though endowed with knowledge of the Vedas and scriptures, is devoid of good conduct (122).
O Indra among kings, when is it not appropriate to give at a *śrāddha*?
Now I shall describe the gift that is fruitful and bestows merit; it arises from the conjunction of the right time, the sacred site, worthy recipients, and faith. 123.
There is no merit equal to faith; there is no happiness equal to faith.
O King, for living beings in saṃsāra, there is no sacred ford equal to faith.
Endowed with the state of faith, one should thus constantly remember me alone. 124–125.
O best of kings, it should be given with the bowl in hand, even if it be very small;
the fruit of such a gift, when performed according to the prescribed rite, is infinite, and by my grace, one shall become happy. 126–127.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Vena," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. Chapter Forty.
Vena said:
"O Lord, I have previously heard from you the fruit of constant giving;
now, tell me also the fruit of occasional giving that has been bestowed."
"Tell me the fruit of that [merit] through your grace and with effort; I do not reach great satisfaction, for my faith continues to impel me to hear more. Viṣṇu said:
O best of kings, I shall now describe the occasional gift (*naimittika-dāna*) which one should offer with faith when a great festival (*mahāparvan*) arrives;
hear the fruit of the merit for him who has bestowed gifts upon worthy recipients (*satpātra*).
O best of kings, he who gives an elephant-chariot or even a horse,
that supreme king is born together with his servants in a holy land by my grace, O great monarch; of this there is no doubt.
He is born as a king who is righteous-souled, wise, powerful, intelligent,
invincible to all beings, and possessed of great splendor—
this is the case for one who bestows a gift of land when a great festival has arrived.
O Great King, by giving the gift of a cow, one becomes the lord of all enjoyments.
One who knows the proper recipients should diligently give gifts to a highly meritorious Brahmin,
and bestow great gifts at sacred fords and on auspicious festival days.
I shall now describe their characteristic marks: kingship arises for him who, when a sacred ford (tīrtha) or a festival day (parvan) arrives, gives secret charity.
There is the swift acquisition of treasures, and he becomes imperishable.
When a great festival (mahāparvan) has arrived, at sacred fords (tīrtha), and to a Brāhmaṇa,
one should give a great gift of fine clothing accompanied by gold;
O King, I shall now declare the meritorious fruit of that gift.
Many sons are born who are virtuous, masters of the Vedas,
long-lived, possessed of progeny, and endowed with fame and merit; and great, flourishing prosperity arises, O high-minded one.
He attains happiness and merit, and becomes a possessor of dharma.
When a great festival arrives, having gone to a sacred ford with diligence, one should give a golden Kapila cow to a high-souled Brahmin. 13–14.
I shall proclaim the merit of that gift, O Mahāmati:
King Kapilādya enjoys all forms of happiness for as long as Brahmā lives and remains there. 15.
When the great festival (Mahāparvanī) arrived,
he then adorned the earth with gold, as well as with garments, ornaments, and decorations;
O Indra among kings, I shall now describe the enjoyment of the fruit of that gift.
From this, great prosperity arises, abounding in both charity and enjoyment;
having become a master of all sciences, one indeed becomes a devotee of Viṣṇu.
That mortal shall dwell in the world of Viṣṇu for as long as the earth endures.

He who, having gone to a sacred ford (tīrtha), gives an ornament to a brāhmaṇa, enjoys vast pleasures and sports with Indra. When a great festival arrives, he likewise [gives] clothing to an eminent twice-born man.
Having given food accompanied by land into the hands of a worthy recipient with a mind full of faith,
he rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha, possessing prowess equal to Viṣṇu.
Having given gold along with clothing to a twice-born for the sake of his complete peace, [he likewise attains that state].
By his own will, he may dwell happily in Vaikuṇṭha like fire itself. One should fill a beautiful golden pitcher with ghee; its lid should be made of silver and adorned with garments and necklaces.
Then, having well-adorned them, he should give them to a high-souled Brāhmaṇa;
furthermore, sixteen cows with their cloths and bronze milking vessels,
four jars filled with water, and a sacrificial fee consisting of gold.
Likewise, twelve cows adorned with cloths and ornaments should be given to a Brahmin who is not related; of this there is no doubt.
O Prince, such gifts as these and others are to be given.
"Having reached a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) at the proper time, and likewise the dwelling of a Brahmin, one should give with a spirit of faith; this becomes the source of great merit.
Viṣṇu said:

Whatever gift is given with Viṣṇu as the intended recipient and is fashioned according to one's desire, a human being who is permeated by the disposition arising from that gift partakes of a corresponding fruit; of this there is no doubt. (29–30)
O best of the twice-born, I shall now declare that which leads to exaltation and proceeds from sacrifices and other rites; by that gift and through his faith,
one attains an increase of wisdom and does not experience suffering.
That righteous-souled one, while living in the present, enjoys pleasures;
having attained a divine state, he eternally enjoys the pleasures of Indra. He leads his own lineage to heaven for a thousand kalpas.
Thus has worldly prosperity been described; now I shall tell you how it is attained by them.
Having realized the decay of the body and being afflicted by old age, one should practice giving and should not harbor expectations toward anyone. 34.
"When I am dead, these sons, as well as my other kinsmen and relatives—how will they fare without me, their friend? Deluded by ignorance regarding them, he indeed gives nothing at all. (35-36)
The self goes to death while its friends and kinsmen weep; all of them, afflicted by suffering, are tormented by the delusion of Māyā.
They resolve to give gifts and they contemplate liberation.

When that great king had died and fallen into the delusion of Māyā, those whose souls were possessed by greed forgot their gifts; O Great King, he who was dead became deeply distressed upon the path of Yama. 38–39.

Overcome by thirst and hunger, and tormented by many sufferings, one should therefore give gifts oneself; of this there is no doubt. O best of kings, whose are the sons and grandsons, and whose is the wife?
To whom can one be an atheist within saṃsāra? Therefore, a gift is bestowed [upon him].
By one possessed of knowledge, these should be given by oneself without doubt: food, drink, betel, water, and likewise gold. 41–42.
O best of kings, he himself gave pairs of garments, umbrellas, and no doubt many water-vessels filled with water; as well as various mounts and vehicles, O high-minded one. 43.
O you who grant happiness on the path to Yama, sandals should be given along with various perfumes and camphor if one desires abundant happiness.
O great king, by these gifts, one indeed traverses the path to Yama with ease.
The two noble princes, adorned by the messengers of Yama, set forth. 46.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Vena," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. 40.
The forty-first chapter. Vena said:
"Tell me, how can a son, a wife, a father, and a mother be a sacred ford (tīrtha)?"
"And how is the Guru himself a holy place (tīrtha)? Tell me that in detail.
Śrī Viṣṇu said:
"There is the beautiful and great city of Vārāṇasī, joined by the Gaṅgā."
In that dwelling lived a certain Vaiśya named Kṛkala;
his wife was a great saintly woman, devoted to her husband, constantly intent on righteous conduct, and ever dedicated to her lord.
She was of auspicious limbs, possessing virtuous sons, beautiful and auspicious;
she always spoke the truth, was ever pure, pleasant in appearance, and dear to her beloved. Endowed with such qualities, she was fortunate and graceful in her conduct.
He was the best among all Vaiśyas, a knower of various dharmas, possessed of wisdom and virtue;
he was always intent on hearing the Purāṇas and the Vedic dharma,
and through the course of his pilgrimages, he bestowed much merit.
Having set out on a pilgrimage to holy sites that were meritorious and auspicious,
accompanied by that caravan leader and through the company of Brahmins,
she, a devoted wife, spoke to him as he had departed upon that path of dharma.
Deluded by affection, she spoke these words to her husband.
Sukalā said:
"O beloved, according to dharma, I am your wife; we are sharers of merit together."
"Waiting for my husband along the path, I worship him as my god.
O best of the twice-born, never shall I abandon your presence;
relying upon your shadow, I shall practice the highest dharma. (9-10)

This [account] called "Devoted to Her Husband" (Pativratā) is a destroyer of sins for women and bestows a supreme goal; it is said that in this world, only she who is solely devoted to her husband is a virtuous woman.
For young women, a separate pilgrimage site does not shine without their husband.

O best of beings, know that the right foot of the Lord is Prayāga and his left foot is Puṣkara; whatever woman performs [this visualization] grants happiness in this world and bestows heaven and liberation. 12–13.

From bathing in the water that has washed his feet, the merit of women becomes equal to bathing at Prayāga and Puṣkara; of this there is no doubt. The husband embodies all sacred fords; the husband is composed of all merit.

Whatever merit accrues to one initiated from the performance of great sacrifices, that very fruit he indeed attains through service to his master. And whatever merit comes from making pilgrimages to excellent holy sites such as Gayā and others— 15–16.
She obtains that very fruit through service to her husband;
I shall declare it to you in brief—listen as I speak.
Indeed, for these women, there is no separate dharma apart from service to their husband.
"Therefore, bringing you happiness by making you my beloved companion, I shall come having taken refuge in your shadow; it cannot be otherwise.
Viṣṇu said:
Having observed her beauty, character, virtue, devotion, and age,
and having likewise considered her delicacy again and again, Kṛkala thought:
"If I lead her along such a path that is difficult to traverse and full of great suffering," 19–20.
Her beauty will be destroyed by the buffeting of cold and heat;
her limbs, which resemble the interior of a lotus in complexion, will turn black from the cold, gale-force wind. (21)

The path is rough with sharp stones, yet her feet are very tender; she will experience intense agony and will not be able to walk. With her limbs overwhelmed by hunger and thirst, what will she become? 22–23.
She who stands at my left side, the one with the beautiful face, is my place of happiness, my constant beloved of life, and the eternal refuge of dharma;
when this young woman meets her destruction, my own destruction will surely follow here.
"This is my constant livelihood; this is the mistress of my very life.
Having reflected for a moment, the high-souled Kṛkala surely thought: "I shall not go to the eternal holy ford, nor shall I go alone. 25-26.
O best of kings, her state of being followed by his mind was thus known; then the illustrious lady spoke again to her husband as he was about to depart:
"O sinless one, O best of beings, listen to what must not be disclosed by men."
"O Mahāmati, such indeed is the root of Dharma for a person. Having understood this, O highly fortunate one, follow this very method now.
Thus spoke Viṣṇu.
Having heard all that much which was spoken for his benefit by his beloved,
Kṛkala laughed and spoke these words to her again:
"O dear one, a wife who has been obtained through dharma must certainly not be abandoned."
O fair-faced one, by him who abandoned his wife Sunītā, who was a practitioner of dharma, even that ten-fold dharma was abandoned;
therefore, O beloved, he will at some point abandon you as well for the sake of welfare.
Viṣṇu said:
"Having thus addressed his wife and having repeatedly awakened her,
he departed together with that caravan as soon as she was unaware of it."
When that illustrious Kṛkala of meritorious deeds had departed,
at the auspicious hour for divine rites and at a sacred time,
she of the beautiful countenance did not see her husband Kṛkala in her own home.
Rising up in haste, weeping and deeply distressed, she, overwhelmed by grief and sorrow for her husband, asked her companions:
"O noble ladies, has that Kṛkaloma been seen by you? (35)
"O my kinsmen, where has my lord gone?
O illustrious ones, if you have seen my husband—my protector, the performer of meritorious deeds, the all-knowing, and the truly wise Kṛkala—tell me now. (36-37)
When they spoke of the Great-Souled One, since that high-minded one had been seen,
having heard those words of hers, they said to that high-minded woman: "O auspicious lady, in the course of his religious journey, your lord Kṛkala [was seen]."
"O lady of excellent vows, why do you grieve so suddenly?
O beautiful one, having visited that great sacred ford, he will return; thus was she consoled by those trustworthy men. (39-40)
O King, having returned home once more, Sukalā, who speaks so beautifully, wept piteously in her grief; Sukalā was utterly devoted to him.
"Until my husband returns, I shall sleep upon the ground on a bed of straw."
"I shall not consume ghee or oil for a day, nor likewise curd or milk;
salt has been renounced, as have betel leaves, O King, and sweet things such as molasses. (42–43)
"Taking but a single meal, I shall remain without food until my husband's return occurs once again. Having spoken thus,
she became filled with sorrow and once more wore her hair in a single braid.
She became soiled, covered only by a single garment;
moreover, standing there clad in but one tattered cloth, she uttered cries of "Alas! Alas!", sighing deeply in great distress. 45–46.
Her body scorched by the fire of separation, bearing darkened limbs and impurities, practicing such conduct in sorrow, exceedingly emaciated and distressed,
she did not obtain sleep at night as she wept day and night.
O King, she did not find relief from her hunger, being utterly tormented by suffering.
(48) Then her friends arrived and asked Sukalā at that time: "O Sukalā, whose every limb is beautiful, why are you weeping now? (49)
"Therefore, O fair-faced one, tell me the cause of this suffering.
Sukalā said:
"My husband, who is devoted to dharma, has gone away for the sake of dharma, having abandoned me. (50)

Then, while wandering the earth on the occasion of a pilgrimage to sacred fords, my lord abandoned me— me who was faultless and free from sin— and departed. I am a virtuous woman of righteous conduct, ever meritorious and devoted to my husband.
"Leaving me behind, my husband has gone away, intent on performing his pilgrimage; O friends, because of that separation I am sorrowful and deeply afflicted.
Indeed, the destruction of life is better, and the consumption of poison is truly preferable."

"Better to enter the fire, better to destroy the body, than for a husband to depart so utterly cruelly, abandoning his beloved wife. O friend, it is better to abandon one's husband than to give up one's life."
"I am unable to endure this ever-cruel separation;
therefore, O friends, I am constantly distressed by this parting.
The friends said:
"Your husband, having gone on a pilgrimage, will return to you as your lord.
You are wasting away this body in vain; you are indeed grieving in vain.
You suffer in vain like a child, and you are abandoning enjoyments in vain. (56-57)
Drink your drink and eat what was previously given by yourself;
for whose master are the sons, and whose are the kinsmen and relatives? Indeed, in this world, who has no connection with anyone else, and by whom is there even any [lasting] bond? 58.
O fool, the fruit of saṃsāra is being devoured and consumed;
when a living being has died, who eats it, and who indeed witnesses that fruit? O fool, this fruit of saṃsāra is being drunk and consumed. 59–60.
Sukalā said: "That which has been proposed by you would not be in accordance with the Vedas, that a wife should indeed always remain alone and separate from her husband. (61)
Women who have become sinful, the virtuous do not honor;
their constant friendship with their husbands has always been seen in the Vedas.
This connection arises from the association with merit; of this there is no doubt.
In the scriptures, it is taught that for women, the husband is always their sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha).
Therefore, she should constantly invoke him through speech, body, and actions;
devoted to him with truthful intent, she should always worship him with her mind. 63–64.
The side of the husband is indeed always a great sacred site (tīrtha), his right limb;
whenever a housewife, resorting to that [side], performs acts of giving, she obtains the fruit of those gifts through the merit of her charity. 65.

That fruit which is obtained at Vārāṇasī and at the Gaṅgā is not found at Puṣkara (66); nor indeed does that woman ever obtain it at Dvārakā, nor at Avantī, nor at Kedāra, O Moon-adorned Lord, while performing sacrifice (67).
O friend, when will she obtain such a fruit as this: a handsome face, the good fortune of a son, bathing, charity, and ornaments;
clothing, jewelry, beauty, splendor, and the fruits [of merit] forever? 68.
A woman of excellent complexion attains fame, renown, and virtue;
by the grace of her husband, she obtains everything—of this there is no doubt. But if, while her husband is present, she practices another form of dharma, [she incurs sin]. 69–70.

The youth and beauty of women are certainly considered to be their very incarnation; yet for her, they become fruitless on this earth, and she is declared to be an unchaste woman, even if she has but a single husband. 71.
For the sake of that one husband alone on the circle of the earth—

A woman who possesses good sons, virtuous fame, and is always spoken of well by others is seen in this world as long as her husband is satisfied; of this there is no doubt. But a woman who is deprived of her husband shall remain so upon the face of the earth.
Whence could she have happiness, beauty, fame, or renown on this earth? She experiences great misfortune and intense suffering throughout the cycle of existence.
Indeed, she becomes a partaker of sin and her conduct is always miserable. (74)
When her husband was pleased, all the deities were also pleased. When the husband is pleased, the sages, gods, and humans are pleased;
the husband is the protector, the teacher, and the deity along with all the deities.
O prince, for women, the husband is their sacred ford, their merit, and their refuge;
he is their adornment, their ornament, their beauty, their complexion, and even their fragrance—
provided he remains constant, except on the auspicious festival days.

When her husband was present, she shone with ornaments and finery; yet without her husband, she appeared like milk in the mouth of a serpent. For the sake of her husband, that highly fortunate woman, firm in her vows, beautiful and auspicious, remained thus.
If a woman applies ornaments when her husband has departed, all that beauty and complexion turns into the form of a corpse;
people on this earth say she is an unchaste woman, without a doubt. (80)

Therefore, O noble ones, listen on this earth to the woman separated from her husband: even if she desires great happiness, it can never come to pass. For the husband is proclaimed in the scriptures as the supreme duty of a virtuous wife. 81-82.
Therefore, a wife must certainly not abandon this eternal dharma; thus I understand the dharma—how could a husband ever forsake her? In this regard, O friend, an ancient history is heard.
The most meritorious and sin-destroying life-story of Sudevā.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Life of Sukalā," in the Legend of Vena within the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. 41.
The forty-second chapter.
The friends said:
"O Sudeva, you have described her appearance; now tell us, what is her conduct?"
"O illustrious one, what you have spoken is indeed the truth.
Sukalā said:
"In Ayodhyā, there was a great king who was well-versed in dharma."

The illustrious son of Manu, Ikṣvāku by name, was devoted to the true meaning of all dharmas; he was omniscient and a worshiper of gods and brahmins. His wife was ever virtuous and dedicated to her husband.
Together with her, he should perform sacrifices and visit various sacred fords (*tīrtha*s) dedicated to the heroic Kāśīśa, the great-souled King of the Vedas.
Sudeva’s daughter was indeed a maiden devoted to truthful conduct.
O Great King, that lord of the earth, Ikṣvāku, married her;
Sudeva, whose every limb was beautiful and who was devoted to the vow of truth.
Together with her, the king, the leader of meritorious people, ruled over his kingdom.
That tiger among kings was always with his beloved wife; once, the great king went to the forest together with her. Having reached the Gaṅgā-forest, he used to sport there constantly in the hunt.
Having slain lions, boars, elephants, and likewise buffaloes,
as he was sporting, a boar approached before him,
accompanied by a large herd of swine and adorned with sons and grandsons.
Established by the side of her beloved Ekācaśūkarī,
she was surrounded by his boars and wild pigs;
and seeing that lord of kings, who was difficult to conquer and devoted to the hunt—
Relying on the support of a mountain, a boar stood alone with his mate;
having learned of the great slaughter of those deer by the Great King, he remained there with his sons, grandsons, elders, and young ones through his great valor.
The boar spoke to those sons, grandsons, and his wife:
"The mighty son of Manu, Vīra, the lord of Kośala, sports in hunting and slays many deer. (13)

"O Great King, having seen me, he will surely come here; of this there is no doubt. For other hunters, there is certainly no fear for their lives, but upon seeing my form, the king will not show any forbearance. (14-15)

Filled with great joy, wielding a bow and holding arrows in hand, that one of great splendor, accompanied by dogs and surrounded by hunters, will surely strike me as well; of this there is no doubt. (16-17)
The sow said:
"Whenever you see many hunters in the great forest, well-armed and in ambush, you flee far away along with these sons and grandsons of mine. (18)

"Having abandoned great courage, strength, and prowess, with a dejected mind due to even this great fear, what are you doing upon seeing the lord of kings, the supreme among the best of men? Tell me the reason for it, as a lover would.
Having heard her words, the boar-king spoke this reply to her.
O beloved, having heard of the boars, I have come from afar at night, fearing those greedy hunters;
(20) for those greedy hunters are evildoers and rogues, O beloved, who always commit sin in mountain fastnesses and caves;
they are ever wicked, constantly plotting many evils, and all are born into families of sinners. (21)
Indeed, I fear death at their hands; even when dead, I shall fall back into sin.
Fearing untimely death, I go far away to a mountain, a peak, or a cave in the wilderness.
For this holy one has arrived, O Lord of Men—the King who is Keśava, superior to the universe.
"I shall wage war in battle with that high-souled one through my own dear prowess and valor. If I conquer the king by my own splendor, I shall enjoy incomparable fame upon the earth;
or, struck down in combat by that best of heroes, I shall go to the world of Madhusūdana. (23-24)
"O Lord of the Earth, through the flesh and fat that have become my own limbs, the ruler shall attain supreme satisfaction;
the deities of the celestial realms shall be satiated, and from him has this Vajrapāṇi come. When his death occurs at the very hand of this man, O Sundarī, there will be for me the highest renown."
Therefore, O Yaśas, go from this earth to the world of Madhusūdana within the three worlds. (26) "I am not afraid in this way, nor am I agitated; I have gone to the mountain peaks.
Fearing sin, O beloved, I have departed; having seen Dharma, I have indeed remained [steadfast]. (27)
I do not know what sin was previously accumulated in another birth,
by which, through a heap of evils, I have entered the womb of a sow; I shall wash away that terrible accumulation of former sins.

With hundreds of most terrible, sharp, and whetted arrows, take my sons, grandsons, daughters-in-law, and the children of the household; go to the mountain and seize them, and abandon this delusion of mine. 29–30.
"Abandoning my affection for me, this Hari has arrived;
from his hand I shall depart to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. Even by fate, today the unsurpassed gate of heaven has been opened for me."
"But when the door is opened, I shall go to the great heaven.
Sukalā said: Having heard those words of that high-souled boar, she [departed].
Then, with her heart sinking, she spoke to her dear friends.
The sow said:
"In which herd are you the master, adorned by sons and grandsons?"
"By you alone, O highly fortunate one, has this herd been adorned;
with you it shines. Deprived of you, what will this herd become? (34-35)
Roaring even with their own strength, these boars roam the mountain; my young sons also wander there, free from fear due to your splendor, eating bulbs and roots that are good to eat. 36.
O mighty-armed one, on this mountain, in difficult terrains, forest thickets, villages, and cities, men do not experience intense fear from lions, for they are protected by your splendor. 37–38.
Abandoned by you, all these children and young boys will become wretched, distressed, and senseless;
for the children always find happiness upon seeing you on the road. (39)
Just as a woman who has lost her husband does not shine even though she is adorned with divine ornaments of gold,
with retinues, jewels, and garments, nor by her father, mother, and brothers; (40–41)
Deprived of her husband, she did not shine in the presence of her mother-in-law, father-in-law, or others,
just as a night without the moon, a family without its son,
or a house without a lamp never shines at all. 42.
O Giver of Honor, without you this herd would not shine at all (43).
Just as a mortal devoid of proper conduct, or like an animal lacking knowledge, or like a king deprived of his ministers, so too does this [herd] not shine at all (44).
Just as a boat on the vast ocean does not shine without a fisherman, nor does a caravan shine without its leader, so too an army does not shine without a commander. 45.
"O high-minded one, without you this army of boars will become as wretched as a twice-born man deprived of the Vedas;
for you are departing after having placed the burden of the family upon me. (46-47)
Knowing that death is easily attained, yet having made no such vow, O beloved Lord, I am unable to sustain my life-breaths without you; therefore,
O high-minded one, let us go together to heaven or to the earth.
"I shall even endure hell; I speak the truth, the absolute truth.
Or rather, O leader of the herd, take your sons and grandsons along with this excellent troop, and let us both go to that difficult-to-reach, pleasant cave. (49-50)
"Having abandoned the very means of life, one enters into battle; what kind of gain is seen there? Tell me, is death not improper in such a case?
Vārāha said:
You do not know the true dharma of heroes; listen now.
For a hero seeking battle must go before another hero and request it:
"Grant me combat in this assembly, for I have come seeking battle. (52)
O beloved, listen: when a man, out of desire, greed, fear, or even delusion, does not grant a battle when requested by another,
he shall dwell in the Kumbhīpāka hell for a thousand yugas.
For Kṣatriyas, there is no doubt that their supreme duty is to give battle.
When that battle is given by one who has indeed gone to the field of combat,
they enjoy the fame and glory of having conquered the enemy.
Fighting with great courage and utter fearlessness in the midst of a tumultuous battle,
he attains the world of heroes and enjoys divine pleasures for twenty-one thousand years; listen, O beloved.
He shall dwell in the world of heroes and be honored by the conduct of the gods;
this son of Manu has arrived as a hero, without a doubt. As he is requesting a battle, I must certainly grant him combat.
"The eternal Viṣṇu has arrived as a guest of war; O auspicious one, he must be honored by me in the form of battle. The sow replied:
"When the battle must be fought by you and the high-souled king, then I shall see what kind of manliness is in you. Having spoken thus, she hurriedly summoned her beloved sons.
He said: "O sons, listen to my words.
A guest of battle has arrived, the eternal one whose form is Viṣṇu.
I must go there where he shall indeed go."
"As long as I remain here as your protector, you must go far away to the face of a mountain cave, a place difficult of access. Live there happily, my children, avoiding those greedy hunters. (63-64)
I must go to that very place where he intends to go;
this brother of yours, the best among you, will provide protection for the herd. All these uncles of yours as well shall be your protectors.
"O good sons, all of you have gone far away from me through the air.
The sons said:
"This is indeed the best of mountains, abounding in roots, fruits, and water."
"There is indeed no fear for Bhayantu; he truly has a happy life.
For this terrifying thing has been spoken by you two quite unexpectedly. Therefore, O Mother, tell us the true reason for it right here. (67-68)
The sow said:
"This most fierce king, appearing like the form of the Kali age, has arrived;
having killed many deer in the forest, he is now sporting as a hunter. (69)
"The invincible Ikṣvāku, the son of Manu, who possesses great strength, will destroy it; O dear sons, the time for this has not yet arrived.
The sons said:
He who, having abandoned his mother and father, departs with an evil mind,
falls into a most fierce and terrible hell;
that pitiless man, having drunk the meritorious milk of his mother, has grown fat upon it.
"He who, being exceedingly weak, departs having abandoned his mother and father, goes here to the Pūyanaraka hell, which is crowded with worms and foul odors.
Therefore, we shall not go there, but shall remain right here, having abandoned our mother and our elder. (72-73)
Thus, a despondency born of their concern for dharma and artha arose within them;
having formed a battle array, they all stood there, bristling with strength and splendor. Endowed with daring and enthusiasm, they beheld the prince.
Roaring and endowed with manly prowess, they were then sporting in the forest. 75.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Deeds of Sukalā," within the Legend of Veṇu in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. 42.
Chapter Forty-Three.
Sukalā said:
"In this manner, all those boars have assembled for battle."
The hunters stood before the king as he sat there.
O Indra among kings, the great boar, having taken refuge on a mountain peak,
remained there, having formed a defensive array with his vast herd.

O King, Kapila—the boar with thick, stout limbs, large tusks, and a massive mouth, who was unbearable and roared most terrifyingly—was seen by the great king as he took refuge in the groves of śāla and tāla trees. 3. He beheld them there.
Having heard those words of theirs, the powerful son of Manu spoke thus to those heroes:
"Let this boar be seized; let him, who is arrogant in his strength, be pierced!
Having addressed them in this way, the powerful son of Manu, O twice-born ones, [proceeded].
Then all those hunters, infatuated by the intoxication of the hunt, set out fully armed and clad in armor along with their dogs;
the mighty king of kings was filled with great joy.
Mounted upon his horse and accompanied by a well-disciplined fourfold army,
he arrived at the bank of the Gaṅgā on Meru, the best of great mountains,
which is strewn with jewels and minerals and adorned with various kinds of trees.
Sukalā said:

That king of mountains shines, lofty and exceedingly high, composed of a mass of rays that are the abode of power, reaching even unto the sky, and beautified by the movements of various forest-dwelling creatures. 9.

The lord of mountains was endowed with great beauty, its rocky plateaus and surfaces everywhere washed white by pure water droplets resembling pearls, which rose from the breaking waves and ripples on the banks of the stainless Gaṅgā flowing in a stream a yojana wide;
it was surrounded by gods, Cāraṇas, Kinnaras, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Siddhas, hosts of Apsarases, sages, lords of Nāgas, and Vidyādharas. 10.
It shines with śrīkhaṇḍa, abundant sandalwood, sarala, śāla, and tamāla trees; with mountain-like rudrākṣas that grant excellent siddhis; and with wish-fulfilling kalpa-trees.
It is adorned with celestial chariots variegated with various minerals, with golden poles, and with beautiful women.
It shines with divine coconut groves, betel-nut trees, and celestial punnāga and bakula trees, adorned with clusters of plantains (13),
as well as with puṣpaka, campaka, ādri, pāṭala, and ketaka flowers.
It was adorned with various canopies of flowering creepers and padmaka trees,
decorated with many-colored blossoms and diverse trees;
it was filled with celestial trees and possessed crystal stone surfaces.
The mountain is graced by caves inhabited by perfected masters of yoga and lords of yogis, as well as by delightful waterfalls and many springs,
and it is further adorned by confluences refreshed by the flow of rivers.
With lakes, ponds, and pools bearing pure water,
the king of mountains shines alone, standing with its peaks,
adorned by śarabhas, tigers, and herds of deer. 17–18.
That king of mountains always shines with great elephants, buffaloes, and uru-deer, as well as with many divine beings;
[there dwells] the heroic lord of Ayodhyā, the descendant of Ikṣvāku and joy of Manu.
Accompanied by that beautiful wife and by a fourfold army, [he went] with hunters ahead and swift-moving dogs;
there stood the brave and powerful boar together with his wife. (20-21)
Then, protected by many boars— both large and small—
he took refuge on the slopes of Mount Meru, all around the banks of the Gaṅgā.
Sukalā said:
Filled with joy, the boar said to his very dear wife:
"O beloved, behold! The powerful lord of Kośala has arrived;
that highly wise king is hunting for my sake."
"I shall indeed wage a war that will bring great joy to both gods and asuras. Then the king, possessed of great splendor, bow in hand and arrow in grasp,
spoke with great delight to Sudevā, whose limbs were the very embodiment of truth and righteousness.
"Behold, my dear, this great boar of immense strength,
roaring and accompanied by its herd, which is difficult for hunters to withstand.
This very day, my dear, I shall slay it with my sharp, excellent arrows."
"Let this great hero come to me alone for battle.
Having spoken thus to his beloved wife, the hunter addressed the other hunters with these words:
"O great heroes, send forth the boar as if he were a mere common beast."

Then those heroes, endowed with strength, splendor, and prowess, being dispatched, rushed forward roaring with their strength, splendor, and prowess; they all now went toward Kola with the speed of the wind. 29.
Those forest-dwellers pierced the Boar,
who possessed a heroic form, with nets of sharp arrows, as well as with various weapons and missiles.
Sukala said:
Just as clouds rain upon the great mountain, so did the arrows and javelins released by the hunters fall;

thus, struck by those who dealt firm blows, the leader of the herd (yūthapālaka), along with his kinsmen, was utterly defeated in that battle. Having entered the fray, he slaughtered his own sons, grandsons, and relatives, while the hunters fell in the combat, struck down by his tusks.
As he stood there, his hands and feet fell off due to the whirling force of his speed; then that boar beheld the approaching one who roared with a greedy cry.
Struck by the tusk at the tip of its mouth and destroyed by its own splendor, he went to where that king desired to engage in combat.
The enraged lord of the boars, having violently terrified the great protector of the Ikṣvākus,
desired a battle with that Ikṣvāku in the forest, filled with the joy of combat. Furthermore,
that boar, skilled in war, desiring a struggle with his snout-tip and his very sharp teeth and claws, angrily agitated the earth.

O King, out of pride in uttering the syllable *huṃ*, he struck that stainless lord of the earth; and perceiving his prowess to be like that of Viṣṇu, the son of Manu was filled with joy and his hair stood on end.
(36) Beholding that incomparable manliness of the boar, the Lord of the Daityas, considering in his mind that the enemy of the gods was indeed Varāha, suddenly assumed the form of a boar.
Seeing that one of great strength, he quickly seized and repeatedly grappled the vast army of elephants joined together, in order to destroy them. (37)

And four extremely swift elephants and chariots were dispatched, carrying excellent arrows and swords, along with *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons and mallets; hunters with nooses in their hands rushed here and there intent on that task, yet the horses and elephants, once they had set out, did not stop even when obstructed.
In some places he was not seen, in some places he was clearly visible; in some places he displayed terror, and in some places he trampled the horses.

Having crushed the heroic soldiers, that warrior invincible in battle, his eyes red with rage, let out an unassailable roar; the heroic Lord of Kośala, seeing him who was so difficult to conquer in war—

Fighting with a massive body and emitting a sound like a cloud, he roars, moves through the battlefield, and sports with his own splendor; that steadfast hero shines and blazes like lightning flashing from the mouths of his fangs. 41–42.
Having seen his son likewise pierced one by one with sharp arrows by Kola and struck down along with his kinsmen by weapons,
the king said to his soldiers: "O heroes, why do you not seize him here with your might?"
"Fight there with sharp, whetted arrows against him as well!
(44) Having heard those words of the great-souled one, even though he was enraged, all those soldiers then stood ready for battle. (45)
Stationed at the edge of the forest in battle, they surrounded that boar from all directions with many thousands of warriors and pierced it in the fray. Then,
on the vast battlefield, it was struck by networks of arrows from excellent fighters wielding great discuses.
In some places struck by blows from discuses and in others by the falling of thunderbolts, that invincible one was slain by the great beings in battle.
Then, filled with fury, he, along with his boar, having severed the nooses in the fray, set forth;
he then proceeded together with the great boars, drenched by streams of blood.
The hero struck with his snout and severed the heads of heroic horses and elephants;

with the sharp tips of his tusks, he struck down the heroic foot-soldiers with displays of fury. Enraged, he struck the trunk of that elephant, and being delighted, he tore at the slain warriors with his claws.
Then all those boars and hunters, their eyes red with rage, engaged in combat with one another after declaring a battle;
the boars were slain by the hunters, and the hunters likewise by the boars.
Slain by the blood of the wounded, they fell to the ground, reddened by gore; having abandoned their lives, the hunters were struck down by the boars and fell upon the battlefield,
while the dead hogs and dogs there likewise gave up their breaths.

Wherever they fell dead upon the ground, many hunters of deer were struck down by the king with blows from his sword; some perished, some were wounded, and others, terrified of the boars, took refuge in the mountain fastnesses.
O best of kings, in the thickets, at the ends of the caves, and within the mountain caverns, certain hunters were killed by boars with their tusks bared;
though hacked into pieces, they cast off their lives and went to heaven. (55-56)
Snare-traps, nets, snares, cages,
and tubes had fallen upon the ground there, everywhere around him;
there the Boar stood together with his sole consort.
Proud of his strength, he went out for battle with his five or seven grandsons. Then the sow spoke again to her beloved boar who was departing: "Go, my beloved, together with me and these children."
The Boar, delighted, spoke to that beautiful beloved who was trembling:
"Where shall I go? I am broken; there is no place for me upon the surface of the earth.
O illustrious one, when I am lost, the herd of boars will perish."
A boar drinks water in the midst of two lions;
a lion does not drink water at all in the midst of two boars.
Thus, such supreme strength is seen among those of the boar species. 61-62.
Therefore, I shall surely destroy it when I go forth broken; O illustrious one, I know that dharma bestows many blessings.
Why should one who is fighting perish out of greed or even out of fear?
Having abandoned the Raṇatīrtha, he undoubtedly becomes a sinner;
yet, seeing the array of sharp weapons, he experiences great joy,
and having plunged into the river of the gods, he reaches the further shore of the sacred ford.
"He always goes to the world of Viṣṇu and uplifts men;
how then can I go broken before him as he approaches that battlefield, crowded with weapons and bringing joy to great heroes? (66)
Seeing him depart, he was greatly delighted; hear now the fruit of his merit:
at every step, the great merit of bathing in the Bhāgīrathī is produced for him.
Listen, my dear, to what happens when one who has been routed in battle returns home out of greed. (67–68)
One born of a woman is said to be "born of a female" because he reveals the faults of his mother;
here [in this land], the sacrifices, the sacred fords, and the gods of great majesty behold this wonder, O beloved, as do the sages, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas. 69.
The three worlds exist where the manifestation of heroes occurs;
seeing him broken in battle, all the inhabitants of the three worlds curse that pitiless sinner and laugh again and again. (70-71)
The King of Dharma will undoubtedly show him the miserable realms;
yet, if one drinks the blood from his own head in battle while facing the enemy, he enjoys the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice and goes to the world of Indra. 72.
O lady of beautiful countenance, when a hero conquers his enemies in battle, he then enjoys prosperity and various pleasures; of this there is no doubt.
When he gives up his life there, facing the foe and without any other support, [he attains the highest state]. 73-74.
"One attains the supreme state and enjoys celestial maidens;
thus I understand the dharma—how can I go away broken? I shall fight him in battle here; of this there is no doubt. (75)
"O fair-faced one, take these children and go; live happily with the steadfast King Ikṣvāku, the son of Manu.
Having heard his words, she said, "I am bound by your bonds."
"O dear one, O giver of honor, I shall give up these very life-breaths along with my sons— those who delight in playthings known as affection, pride, and passion.
Having thus conversed in this manner, those two, desiring each other's welfare, [remained there].
Having resolved upon battle, they both surveyed their enemies:
the heroic lord of Kośala, that Ikṣvāku of great intelligence,
who was like a cloud thundering in the sky during the rainy season with flashes of lightning.
In that very manner, roaring together with his beloved, he challenged the excellent horse with the tips of its hooves.
Seeing that single boar, who was roaring and endowed with manly prowess, the high-souled hero among men, steadfast and possessed of the speed of a horse, rushed toward him.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter in the Story of Sukalā within the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Forty-four. Sukalā said:

Seeing his own army, difficult to withstand, defeated by that Durdhara, the king grew furious toward the cruel and unbearable boar. Taking up his bow with speed, he drew an arrow resembling the fire of cosmic destruction.
He charged directly toward him with his horse;
when that lord of the boar herd saw the king, mounted upon his steed, endowed with excellent prowess and the slayer of enemies, advancing toward him upon the field of battle, he rushed forward.
When struck by a sharp arrow, the king’s horse fell at his feet;
yet, disregarding that very spot with a mind intent on speed, the excellent elephant rushed forward with fierce velocity.
Afflicted by the insect, the horse—its gait pierced and its strength exhausted—could not proceed further.
The horse fell to the ground, struck by the snout, and the king immediately mounted the light chariot. Amidst the sounds of the boar species, he roared;
then, having been struck with a mace by the king, that leader of the herd was killed while in the midst of the forest.
"Having abandoned his own body, it is better that he has gone directly to the abode of Hari.
Having fought in battle with that king, the king of the boars fell to the earth; and at that moment, the best of gods showered excellent flowers from the clouds.
Above him, a well-formed mass of flowers arose, fragrant as if from *saṃtānaka* trees;
and the gods, being highly pleased, created a rain of sandalwood mixed with saffron.
O King, when he was being reflected upon by the king along with his attendants, he too became four-armed.
Clad in divine garments and ornaments, with a celestial form, he shone by his own splendor like the sun.

When he went to heaven by means of a divine vehicle, being highly honored by the king of the gods and the deities, that king of the Gandharvas once again assumed his former body right here on earth. 10–11.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter in the Story of Sukalā within the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Forty-Five.
Sukalā said:
Then all those hunters approached the sow—brave, fierce, and terrifying, with nooses in their hands. 1.
Having made her four young ones stand nearby, the sow remained there;
then, seeing her beloved husband slain in the great battle,
she thought, "My husband's death has been brought about by the sages and the gods, who have honored him."
"By this heroic deed, that great-souled one has gone to heaven;
you too shall go to heaven by this same path while your husband remains there.
Having made this firm resolve, she reflected upon her sons.
As long as these four sons, the upholders of the lineage of this great-souled Kola, the hero Suvīra, remain alive,
Having become intent on this thought and seeing the narrowness of the mountain, she resolved,
"I shall go forth to emerge by way of that very wide path there.
Having made this firm determination, she reflected upon her sons.
He spoke to those sons who were utterly deluded:
"O sons, go quickly while I still remain. Among them, the eldest son said: "How shall I go, leaving my mother?"
"Having abandoned all attachment to life, alas, mother, my life is well-lived!
I shall avenge my father's enmity; I will slay the enemies in battle.
You, however, must take my three younger brothers to the mountain cave."
"Having abandoned his father and mother, that man of sinful intellect surely goes to hell, which is teeming with tens of millions of worms.
To him, she, afflicted by great sorrow, said: "O son, how can I [live] after abandoning you?"
"May we depart from this great sin; let these sons of ours go.
Thus, the three younger ones went into the interior of the mountain forest, while they [the others] watched them as they proceeded to the field of battle. 12–13.
Roaring again and again with their splendor and the strength of their vital breath,
As these two, mother and son, stood blocking the path,
hunters arrived there, bearing swords, arrows, and bows;
they then struck them with sharp javelins, discuses, and maces.
Placing his mother behind him, the son fought with them;
some were struck down by his fangs, while others were killed by his snout.
He also struck them with the tips of his hooves, and the heroes fell upon the battlefield.
The boar fought in battle, having been observed by the high-souled king;
knowing from his father that he was a hero, the son of Manu, possessed of great splendor and prowess, stood face-to-face with bow in hand. 18–19.
Struck by the high-souled king with a sharp arrow resembling a crescent moon, he fell to the earth with his chest pierced; that boar instantly died upon falling to the ground. 20.
Having reached a state of supreme delusion regarding her son, she herself flew up above him.
And by her, those brave hunters were struck down upon the earth with blows from her beak;
O King, many of those heroic hunters fell there, some dead and some nearly dead.
Then, with her tusk, the sow began to drag away that vast army,
just as a malevolent *kṛtyā* spirit arises to instill great terror.
Thereupon, the queen spoke to him, who resembled the son of the king of the gods.
"O King, indeed this great army of yours has been struck down by her; why do you disregard her? Tell me the reason for that.
To her, the great king replied: "I shall not kill this woman."
"O beloved, the killing of a woman has indeed been seen by the gods to be a great transgression;
therefore, one should not kill a woman, nor would I send anyone here. O beautiful one, I am afraid of the sin that would arise from her slaughter."
Having spoken thus, the king, the lord of the earth, then ceased;
meanwhile, the hunter named Jhārjhara beheld that female boar causing such carnage among them as was unbearable even for great warriors. (27-28)
Pierced by a sharp arrow with great force, she was drenched in blood by that arrow which remained lodged [in her];
radiant and filled with the splendor of a hero, she moved with haste. 29.
The water-jar was struck by her snout,
and again by her trunk; then, as that falling jar was struck by his sharp sword, it shattered and fell to the ground.
Sighing deeply and overwhelmed by fainting fits, she remained on the surface of the earth, possessed by great suffering, yet still alive.
(32) Thus ends the account of Sukalā’s life within the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Forty-Five.
Chapter Forty-Six. Sukalā said:
Seeing the sow panting and fallen down, who was so devoted to her young,
Sudeva, overcome with compassion, went toward that suffering creature and sprinkled her face with cool water.
Furthermore, she saw her beloved queen suffering in every limb upon the battlefield;
with holy, cool water,
she sprinkled her and spoke in a melodious human voice.
"O Goddess, if you have been consecrated, may there be happiness for you;
by your contact and by the sight of you, the accumulation of my sins has gone away.
Having heard those great words, which were endowed with a wonderful appearance, [he spoke].

"This which I have seen is wonderful; you have spoken these words free from affliction. Yet this woman, though belonging to the species of beasts, speaks with such clarity—endowed with vowels and consonants, my own excellent Sanskrit."
Filled with joy and wonder,
that illustrious lady, having performed a supreme act of courage while remaining there, spoke these words to her husband:
"Behold, O King, this unprecedented and great refined speech she utters!"
Even though she was born from an animal womb, she spoke just as a human would.
Then the king, the best among those possessing all knowledge,
heard that which was wonderful, of a wondrous form, and never before seen or heard by him.
Then the king spoke to his very dear queen Sudeva; he asked her, "O beautiful one, who might this auspicious woman be?
Having heard the king's words, she questioned the sow.
"Who were you, O blessed lady? Many wonders are seen in you.
Having entered the womb of a beast, you indeed speak human speech; you speak with elegance and endowed with knowledge, as if describing my own past deeds. (11-12)
O Great King, what was this great and heroic dharma of this high-souled warrior, your husband, by which he went to heaven through his valor?
Tell me everything concerning both yourself and your husband, following the sequence of events.
Having spoken thus, the highly fortunate beloved of the king fell silent. The female hog said:
"O blessed lady, if you ask me about this and that great-souled one,"
I shall relate all of that to you—their life story and their former deeds.
This highly wise one here is a Gandharva, an expert in song, named Raṅgavidyādhara, who is proficient in the meaning of all the scriptures. 15–16.
Resorting to Meru, the most excellent and best of mountains, with its beautiful caves and waterfalls, the highly effulgent Pulastya, the best of sages,
performed austerities with a sincere heart.
O lady of beautiful smiles, a Vidyadhara of great power arrived there of his own accord;
taking refuge on that best of mountains, he then practiced singing with excellent voice, accompanied by melody and rhythm.
Having heard the song, the sage’s mind was shaken from his meditation;
he spoke these words to that singing Vidyādhara:
"By your divine song, even the gods are deluded, and not otherwise."

O wise one of excellent vows, my mind has been drawn away from meditation by this song, which is melodious, highly meritorious, measured by the rhythmic *tāla*, endowed with *laya*, and accompanied by musical modulations (*mūrcchanā*). 21–22.
"Abandoning this place, go to another location. The two Vidyādharas said: "What need is there for us to go elsewhere? Our song is equal to the knowledge of the Self (ātma-jñāna). (23)
It causes suffering to no one and always bestows happiness upon men;
by this divine song, all the deities are gratified.
O twice-born one, it is for this reason that even Śambhu has been brought here by the sound of the song.

Song is said to contain all aesthetic flavors (rasas); song is the bestower of bliss. All the rasas, beginning with the erotic (śṛṅgāra), are established through song; even the four supreme Vedas attain their splendor through song. 25-26.
"All the deities attain satisfaction through song, and not otherwise;
yet you thus censure song and distract me in this way. O illustrious one, this great injustice is seen to reside in you alone. (27)
Pulastya said:
"What you have spoken today is true, for the meaning of the Gītā bestows great merit.
O high-minded one, do not abandon your pride; listen to my words."

I do not disparage song; rather, I honor song, and not otherwise. (29) These fourteen branches of knowledge, when offered with devotion and with a steady mind, bring about the spiritual perfection of living beings through their unification. (30)
Likewise, penance and mantras are well-perfected through one-pointed concentration;
yet the great multitude of the senses is considered by the wise to be hair-like in its instability, for it forcibly leads the self toward all objects of the senses. 31.
Having shaken off the mind from that very meditation, there is no doubt;
where there is neither sound nor form, and young women do not dwell, there the sages go, for they have indeed attained perfection through their austerities. 33.
"This song is sacred for you and bestows great happiness;
yet we do not see it, O Hero, as we remain established in the forest. Go to another place, or else let us depart."
Gītavidyādharā said:
That great-souled one by whom the host of the powers of the senses has been conquered is called a victor; he is a yogi, he is a hero, and he is an adept.

O Mahāmati, having heard such a sound or seen such a form, a steadfast practitioner of austerity does not waver from meditation; yet you have been overcome by your senses, for you are devoid of spiritual luster. (36–37)
"Even in heaven, I do not possess the power to overcome my song;
all those who are devoid of valor undoubtedly avoid the forest. This forest region, O Brahmin, is common to all, without a doubt."
"O gods, as it is with me, so it is for all living beings.
How can I depart, leaving behind this most excellent forest?
You may go or stay; whatever is destined to be shall not be otherwise."
When that wise Vidyadhara, skilled in song, had thus addressed the Brahmin, the sage listened to his reply and then reflected: "What virtuous deed should I perform? (41)
Having practiced forbearance, that best of the twice-born then went to another place.
The righteous-souled one performed austerities, always remaining in a yogic posture, having completely abandoned desire, anger, delusion, and greed. 42–43.
Restraining all the senses and keeping the mind perfectly equanimous, the yogi Pulastya, the best of sages, remained thus established. 44.
Sukalā said:

When that illustrious Pulastya, the bull among sages, had departed, that Vidyadhara, who had been commanded by Time, reflected for a long time: "He has not been seen for a very long time; he must have fled out of fear of me."
"Where has he gone? Or does he remain? What does he do, and how?
(46) Having learned that the son of the Lotus-born One was dwelling in the solitude of the forest, [Viṣṇu] went to his excellent hermitage in the form of a boar. (47)
O beautiful lady, seeing that high-souled one seated upon his throne, enveloped in a blaze of splendor, she caused a disturbance for that brahmin;
with wicked intent, she would surely have assailed the brahmin with the tip of her snout.
"O Great King, having recognized him as a beast, you should forgive his misdeed.
He urinates while standing before you, and then he defecates;
he dances and plays there, falling down and rising up again. 49-50.
O King, having recognized him as a beast, he was abandoned by that sage; however,
on one occasion, he returned again in that very same form,
and then laughter was once more provoked by his loud, boisterous laughter.
There, weeping was made and he sang songs in a beautiful voice.
O King, seeing that Vidyādhara who had arrived there, the Brahmin observed his behavior and thought, "This cannot possibly be Ghoṇi. 52–53.
"Having learned his conduct, he would thus deceive me;
this wicked and merciless one was abandoned by me once he was recognized as a mere beast. Knowing him to be such a high-souled [deceiver], he is indeed the lowest of Gandharvas."
The tiger among sages became enraged, and that highly intelligent one cursed him:
"Since you have thus provoked me while in the form of a boar,
therefore go to the womb of a boar, a most sinful birth resulting from great sin."
Having been cursed by that brahmin, O lady of beautiful countenance, he went trembling to the high-souled god Purandara and said to him:
"Listen to my words, O Thousand-eyed One; your business has been accomplished by me."
For that bull among sages was performing most formidable austerities;
therefore, having been moved and agitated by me through the power of his penance,
I was cursed by that brahmin, and my divine form was destroyed.
"Knowing the entire account of that Gīta-Vidyādhara, Indra went with him and spoke to that sage, saying, 'Protect Śakra, who has thus entered the womb of an animal.'"
"O Lord, let favor be bestowed; you are a knower of perfections, O best of the twice-born. May this be forgiven, O most excellent of sages, and let there be a release from the curse.
Thus was the Brahmin entreated by Mahendra, and he, with a joyful mind, replied: "Ah! 61-62.
Pulastya said:
"O Lord of Gods, at your word, this must indeed be forgiven by me as well; there shall be a mighty son of Manu, O Great King."
When death shall come from the hand of that righteous-souled Ikṣvāku, the protector of all dharma,
then he will regain his own body; of this there is no doubt.
This entire account regarding the boar has been related to you;
now I shall speak of myself along with my husband—listen indeed! Hear also of that terrible sin which was formerly committed by me, a woman of evil deeds.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter [and begins the forty-seventh chapter] in the Story of Sukalā within the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. Chapter 47.
Sukalā said to Sudevā,
who was beautiful in all her limbs: "O sow, having entered the womb of an animal, how is it that you speak refined Sanskrit?"
"Tell me, O lady, how did such great wisdom arise?
And how, O auspicious one, do you know the life-story of your husband?
The sow replied:

"O lady of excellent complexion, I have been robbed by the delusion that arises from the state of being an animal; struck by swords and arrows, I have fallen upon the head of a deer. O fair-faced one, I am overwhelmed by fainting and deprived of my senses."
O beautiful one, since I have been consecrated by you with that auspicious hand of yours,
my delusion has indeed vanished and left me, as I am consecrated by the cool, holy water held in your hand.
Just as darkness departs through the rays of light,
so too, O auspicious one, has my sin vanished through your consecration. By your grace, O beautiful lady, I have regained my ancient knowledge.
"I shall go to a meritorious state," O auspicious one, this was known by me.
Listen, for I shall relate my own former history, O blessed lady, as to the many evil deeds committed by me, a sinner. (7-8)

In the great country known as Kaliṅga, there was a city named Śrīpura, filled with all supernatural powers and inhabited by people of the four castes. There lived a certain twice-born man, renowned by the name Vasudatta.
Constantly devoted to the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya), dedicated to truth and righteousness, a knower of the Vedas and a knower of wisdom, pure, virtuous, and wealthy;
he was filled with riches and grain, and adorned by sons and grandsons. 10–11.
O Great-minded One, I was always beloved by him and by my father as well;
born with a matchless form, there is no such beauty in the cycle of existence.
Intoxicated by the pride of my beauty and youth, I was one of lovely smiles. (13-14)
"O lovely-faced one, I am a maiden of beautiful form, adorned with every ornament;
and when all the people and my own circle of kinsmen saw me,
they were thus entreating me for the sake of marriage."
"Requested by all the twice-born, my father did not give me away, O highly fortunate one.
Out of affection for me, that great-minded man was deluded; thus, I was not given away then by that high-souled father. (16-17)
When youth had arrived for me as a girl, my mother was deeply distressed upon seeing my beauty thus endowed with passion; she then said to my father, "Why is the daughter not being given away? (18)
"To which highly agitated, great-souled Brahmin shall I give this daughter, O illustrious one, now that she has reached her youth?
To this, Vasudatta, the best of the twice-born, replied: "O most excellent of the twice-born... (19-20)
O illustrious mother, listen to my words; O lady of excellent complexion, I have been deluded by great infatuation regarding my daughter.
Listen, O auspicious one, to what will become of me as a householder, a brahmin.
"I shall give my daughter to him as a son-in-law; of this there is no doubt.
She is as dear to me as my own life, O Sudeva; there is no doubt in this.
Thus did my father Sudatta speak for my sake.
Born in the family of Kauśika, he was proficient in all branches of knowledge;
endowed with the qualities of Brahmins, he was virtuous, possessed of merit, and pure.
He was perfected in the study of the Vedas and recited them with a beautiful voice.
Seeing him approaching for alms, deprived of father and mother, the high-minded father observed his appearance and spoke to him thus: "Who indeed are you, and what will become of you? (25-26)
"What is his name, family, lineage, and conduct? Speak now.
Having heard his father's words, he said to Vasudatta:
"He was born in the lineage of Kauśika and has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas."
"O Śivaśarman, I am devoid of both father and mother.
I have four other brothers who have mastered the Vedas; thus my lineage is described, as well as the conduct born of that family. (28-29)
Thus everything was related by Śivaśarman to his father,
when an auspicious moment had arrived— a favorable *lagna*, a propitious lunar day, and a constellation presided over by Bhaga.
O fortunate one, I was then given by my father to that very Brahmin.
I lived alone in my father’s house with that great-souled one;
at that time, I, a sinner, did not serve my husband, being utterly deluded by pride and the wealth of my father and mother. 31–32.
O auspicious one, never at any time have I massaged his limbs with a sense of pleasure, affection, or kind words; rather,
I have always looked upon him with a cruel mind and as a sinner.
O inauspicious one, through association with unchaste women, I have indeed come under their influence;
wherever I go, I do not perform what is beneficial for my mother, father, husband, or brothers. (34–35)
