Having thus seen my misdeed, my husband, the high-minded Śivaśarman, out of affection for his family of parents-in-law,
said nothing to me; he too forgives my transgression.
Though I was being restrained by my family, I remained such a great sinner.
Having learned of the virtuous character and goodness of Śivaśarman, my father, mother, and all [my kin] were distressed on account of my sin. (37–38)
Seeing his misdeed, the husband went out from his own house;
having abandoned that place and this village, he departed from there.
O father, when the husband had gone, she became filled with anxiety.
"My very self is pained by my suffering, as if afflicted by a disease.
(40) My mother spoke thus to her husband, who was tormented by grief: "O beloved, why do you brood over this sorrow before me? (41)
Vasudatta said to her mother: "O beloved, listen; my son-in-law, that brahmin, has gone away after abandoning his daughter in Nandana. This woman is of sinful conduct, merciless, and a doer of evil."
"Abandoned by this woman, the high-minded Śivaśarman—
out of courtesy toward his entire family, O beautiful one, this noble twice-born man does not speak ill of you at all. (43-44)
One who dwells with a gentle disposition, who neither censures nor reviles Sudevā despite her sinful conduct, is indeed a wise and intelligent person.
However, this wicked Sudevā shall become the destroyer of the family.
"I am leaving this place and departing, O dweller of the house.
The Brahmin woman said:
"O beloved, you have not yet recognized the fault in your daughter's character today."
Listen now: this [affection] is lost through delusion and attachment.
One should pamper a son until he is five years old; thereafter, O beloved, one should nourish him with a mind intent on discipline. 47–48.

Without a doubt, a father who is free from delusion always employs his beloved son in virtuous qualities, in true sciences, and in the practice of virtues by means of baths, garments, foods, edibles, and drinks. (49) He remains ever devoted to the training in those qualities.

In nourishing and supporting him, absolute delusion arises. She would not speak well of her son, but would revile him day after day; she would constantly speak harshly and torment him with her words. (50–51)
Just as one who is devoted to knowledge should constantly accomplish the true science,
having abandoned sin even from afar by means of the deception of self-conceit, so too skillfulness arises constantly in the sciences and in virtuous qualities. 52.
A mother may strike her daughter, and a mother-in-law may strike her daughter-in-law;
a teacher may strike his disciple—only then do they achieve success, and not otherwise.
Likewise, a husband may strike his wife, and a king his minister. (53–54)
O Lord, just as one might strike a horse born of disease day after day with the intent to train it, yet it attains mastery through both beating and protection; so too,
O Master, this [disease] has been destroyed by you at all times, without a doubt.
Together with you, the excellent Brahmin Śivaśarman, she has been rendered unrestrained by this household;
thus, O high-minded one, she has perished.
Listen to my secret words: one should indeed keep a maiden in the house for that long. 56-57.
As long as she remains in her father’s house, even after reaching eight years of age, a daughter who does not maintain herself with vigor incurs sin; indeed,
she incurs that sin for both of her parents.

Therefore, it is not ordained that she remain in her own father’s house once she is capable [of marriage]. Whomever she has been given to, she should be nourished in his house; staying there, she should win over her husband with devotion and virtuous qualities.
The family’s fame arises, and the father lives in happiness;
yet, whatever sin she commits while staying there, the husband suffers for that sin. While staying there, she always prospers through sons and grandsons.
O beloved, a father incurs infamy because of the excellent virtues of his daughter;
therefore, one should not keep a daughter with her husband in the house. Regarding this matter, O beloved, there is a historical account (itihāsa) that will be heard. 62-63.
O twice-born one, when the twenty-eighth Dvāpara Yuga has arrived,
I shall relate to you the great life-story of the heroic Ugrasena, the eldest of the Yadus and their lord; listen with a focused mind.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter in the Story of Sukalā within the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Forty-Eight.
The Brāhmaṇī said:
"In the beautiful region of Māthura, O best of kings, there is a Yādava renowned as Ugrasena, the slayer of enemy heroes, residing in Mathurā."

The king was a knower of the true meaning of all dharmas, a knower of the Vedas, learned, and powerful; he was a giver, an enjoyer, a perceiver of virtues, and one who understood the qualities of the good. Intelligent, he ruled the kingdom and protected his subjects with righteousness.
Thus was that highly effulgent and powerful Ugrasena. In the meritorious realm of Vidarbha lived the powerful Satyaketu;
his daughter was highly fortunate, lotus-eyed, and lotus-faced.
Named Padmāvatī, she was devoted to truth and righteousness;
endowed with the virtues of virtuous women, she was like a second daughter of the Ocean.
O King, that princess of Vidarbha shone with her own qualities, which were rooted in truth.
Māthura Ugrasena married Sulocanā.
With her, that illustrious and powerful king enjoyed happiness;
he was exceedingly fond of her virtues and lived happily with her.
Deluded by affection and love for her, the illustrious Lord of Mathurā came to regard the highly fortunate Padmāvatī as dearer to him than his own life;
without her he would not eat, and with her he would sport.
Without her, he did not experience even supreme happiness.
O best of the twice-born, thus they became mutually pleasing and unsurpassed, full of affection and bestowing happiness and joy upon one another. 10.
O Indra among kings, that illustrious Satyaketu remembered his daughter Padmāvatī; her mother was deeply distressed,
and the King of Vidarbha dispatched messengers toward Mathurā.
O best of the twice-born, with great respect, the messenger spoke these words to Ugrasena, the lord of men and heroes, the great king:
"The heroic ruler of Vidarbha, gladdening you with devotion and affection... (12-13)
"O Great King, Satyaketu speaks of his own welfare and inquires after yours; having thus inquired,
he has sent me to you to request that you send your daughter Padmāvatī to him so that he may see her."
If you consider this to be for your own pleasure, affection,
and welfare— O highly fortunate one, send your beloved wife who brings you joy;
O Great King, she remains full of longing and yearning for you.
Then, having heard those words of the high-souled Satyaketu with affection and love, the king Ugrasena,
O best of Brahmins, dispatched him out of courtesy.
The powerful Ugrasena sent his beloved wife Padmāvatī; O Indra among kings, that virtuous woman, filled with great joy, went first to her own home. 18-19.
Then, devoted to truth, that beautiful and auspicious lady bowed her head at her father’s feet;
and when Padmāvatī had arrived, O best of the twice-born, the great king [beheld her].
Overcome with great joy, the king, the lord of Vidarbha,
increased her gifts, honors, garments, ornaments, and decorations;
and Padmāvatī lived happily in her father’s house.
Accompanied by her friends, she moved about there without fear and took her pleasure;
Furthermore, that foolish woman, devoid of shame, conducts herself [improperly];
O Brahmin, she always moves about with her friends without hesitation, filled with great joy, though she was once a highly fortunate and devoted wife. 24–25.
"Indeed, happiness in my father's house is difficult to find in the house of my father-in-law; knowing this, when will my husband ever become like that again?"— thus,
with such deluded thoughts, the lovely-faced woman became addicted to her play.
"Always accompanied by her friends in the forests and groves at that time.
(27) Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the narrative of Veṇu, within the account of Sukalā’s life. The Forty-ninth Chapter.
The Brāhmaṇī said:
Once, O highly fortunate one, she went to an excellent mountain;
having seen a delightful forest adorned with groves of plantain trees.
With *śāla*, *tāla*, and *tamāla* trees, as well as abundant coconut palms;
with betel-nut trees, *mātulunga* citrons, oranges, and beautiful *jambuka* fruits;
and with auspicious *campaka*, *pāṭala*, and *kuṭaka* trees in full bloom, along with *vaṭa* banyan trees.
Endowed with Aśoka and Bakula trees and adorned with various other trees,
that meritorious mountain was seen everywhere delightful and filled with diverse minerals, its finest peaks covered in blossoms. 3–4.
A pond, auspicious on all sides and filled with holy water,
was shining with blooming lotuses, other fragrant flowers, golden lilies,
white lilies, and well-blossomed red lilies.
With blue lotuses, white water-lilies, swans,
and water-fowls, and with other aquatic birds, the lake was filled with various minerals and was bright on all sides, frequented by flocks of diverse birds.
Adorned on all sides by the sacred and melodious cries of cuckoos,
it resounds everywhere with sweet sounds;
it shines everywhere with the beautiful humming of bees.
On that delightful mountain, in that supreme celestial forest,
the princess of Vidarbha, the delight of kings, then beheld a lake auspicious on all sides while sporting there together with her companions.
Then, having beheld the holy forest filled everywhere with flowers,
Padmāvatī, together with her companions, was there on the shore of the lake by virtue of her fickleness, her power, her womanhood, and her playful charm.
Then, O Brahmin, that beautiful woman, having entered into water-sports, laughed and sang again; thus she sported in that very lake with great pleasure. 12–13.
Viṣṇu said:
There was a Daitya named Gobhila, a servant of Vaiśravaṇa, who was overwhelmed by all enjoyments even while traveling in a divine celestial chariot. 14.
Then Gobhila, the best of Daityas, traveled through the path of the sky;
there he beheld the large-eyed princess of Vidarbha, who was then free from fear, for she was indeed the beloved of Ugrasena and the most excellent among all women. 15.
"Unrivaled in beauty in this world, she shines with splendor in every limb.
Is she perhaps Rati, the beloved of Manmatha; or could she be the beloved of Hari? Or might she be the goddess Pārvatī, or even Śacī? (16-17)

Such as this woman, the most excellent among women, is seen, there is no other like her, a second one, upon the circle of the earth. Just as the full moon shines beautifully among the stars, so does she.
With her qualities, beauty, and arts, that lady of excellent countenance shone thus;
like a swan among lotuses, so did this sweet-smiling woman appear. Oh, how wonderful is her form! Oh, how wonderful is her nature as she is seen here! 19–20.
The Daitya Gobhila touched the lotus-faced Padmāvatī, whose breasts were beautiful, youthful, and shapely like those of a crow;
having reflected for a moment, he thought, "This will happen even to a brahmin like a crow."
Having recognized her through his great wisdom, there is no doubt that the princess of Vidarbha—
the beloved of Ugrasena, devoted to her husband,
and established by the power of her own self— is unattainable even for men. 22–23.
That great fool Ugrasena, by whom this girl was sent to her father’s house, is surely devoid of fortune; how could that man of deceitful mind ever live without her? 24.
Or rather, what man would be a king who would abandon her?
For upon seeing her, his soul instantly became filled with desire.
This young woman is devoted to her husband; she is difficult to obtain even for men.
"How shall I eat after going [to him]? Desire would torment me excessively.
If he should come while I have not eaten this [food], it would surely be my death. Indeed, there is no doubt that it will be this very day, for desire is exceedingly powerful."
Becoming absorbed in thought, Gobhila perceived with his mind that he would assume the illusory form of King Ugrasena,
exactly as the great king Ugrasena appeared, with all his limbs and ornaments.
Gobhila, having become such as he was, arrived and spoke in his own voice; appearing again in the same dress, the same attire, and the same age,
he wore divine garlands and garments and was anointed with divine perfumes.

Then, endowed with supreme illusory power (*māyā*) and a wealth of beauty and charm, he became like Ugrasena— the lord of Mathurā— with limbs as beautiful as all his ornaments. Thus, at that time, he took on the very form of the Daitya Ugrasena.
Taking refuge in the shade of an *aśoka* tree on a mountain peak,
the evil-minded Vīraka sat upon a stone slab, singing a song with a melodious voice that enchanted the entire world, using the neck of his lute as a staff. (33)

Enchanted by his form, that evil-minded one, standing on the mountain peak, sang a song accompanied by rhythmic measures and adorned with the seven musical notes, filled with great joy, O Brahmin. (34-35)

But Padmāvatī, of beautiful countenance, standing in the midst of her friends, heard a sweet song endowed with rhythm, measure, and tempo. "Who is this righteous soul singing that which bestows great happiness? she wondered.

Accompanied by her friends, the princess, filled with longing, went there and took refuge in the shade of an *aśoka* tree upon a spotless, beautiful stone slab; there she sang songs endowed with virtuous performance and imbued with every emotion. (37–38)

Padmāvatī, the devoted wife, beheld the destroyer of demons, Gobhila, appearing in the guise of a king, wearing flower garlands and divine garments, anointed with celestial perfumes, and his limbs radiant with every kind of ornament.
When did Mathureśa, devoted to righteousness, arrive?
While my high-souled lord, having abandoned his sovereignty, was reflecting from afar, she was [overcome] by that sinful man. 40–41.

"O my beloved, having been summoned, you have come here becoming distressed; why indeed, O dear one, did you become startled and apprehensive upon seeing that your husband had arrived? (42) She became ashamed and sorrowful, and then cast her face downwards.
"I am a sinful woman of wicked conduct, devoid of all shame," she thought; "O illustrious one, he will undoubtedly become angry.
While she was reflecting thus, that sinner also [thought the same]. 43–44.
"Summoned by me, O beloved, come, come!
Deprived of you, O goddess of lovely countenance, I am unable to sustain my life or hold onto that which is dear to me. (45)
"Out of affection for you, I am not greedy; having abandoned you, I cannot bear it intensely.
The Brahmin woman said:
"Having been addressed thus, she went and saw Sumukha, filled with shame."
Then that Daitya embraced Satī Padmāvatī;
having brought her to a secluded place, he then enjoyed her at his will, even though she was the daughter of Satyaketu, by means of the power of Gobhila. 47–48.
Sukalā said:
"O fair-faced one, I did not find the secret sign at his place of the scrotum;
grasping my own garment, she became indeed anxious and distressed. 49
Filled with anger, she spoke these words to Gobhila, the lowest of demons:
"Who are you, a man of sinful conduct, pitiless, and possessing the form of a demon?
Her eyes were agitated with grief as she stood prepared, intent on cursing him.
Trembling and oppressed by a heavy burden of sorrow, she said:
"O evil-souled one, having come here under the very guise of being my beloved, you have destroyed my foremost dharma—my unsurpassed devotion to my husband. (51-52)
"By weeping with such a sweet voice, you have brought about my birth;
behold my power here, for I shall pronounce a most terrible curse upon you.
Thus she spoke to Gobhila, desiring to curse him. (53-54)
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter in the Story of Sukalā within the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Fifty.
Sukalā said:
Having heard her words, Gobhila spoke these words: "O lady, you desire to curse me; tell me the reason why. (1)

"By what fault am I tainted that you are prepared to curse me? O auspicious lady, I am a Daitya named Gobhila, a soldier of Paulastya; I conduct myself according to the way of the Daityas, yet I know this unsurpassed science."
I am a knower of the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras, and furthermore, I am highly skilled in all the arts. Thus I understand everything; now hear from me about the conduct of the Daityas:
I enjoy the property of others and the wives of others by force, and not otherwise.
"O Daityas, having heard this, we shall now conduct ourselves according to the behavior of Daityas with a sense of wisdom;
I tell you the truth, the absolute truth.
For day after day, we observe the vulnerabilities of the Brāhmaṇas."
"O Goddess, we shall undoubtedly cause the destruction of their penance through obstacles;
having found a vulnerability, O auspicious one, we shall destroy them without a doubt. Listen, O lady of beautiful countenance, regarding the Brahmins and the sacrifice to the gods."
We shall destroy the sacrifices— there is no doubt— even the sacrifice of dharma,
by abandoning the true Brahmins and the Lord, the god Nārāyaṇa,
as well as the highly fortunate Sumati, who is devoted to her husband and faithful to him. 8.
They shall abandon it from afar and remain there; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, the Daityas are not capable of enduring the splendor of a virtuous Brahmin, nor that of the high-souled Hari, nor that of a woman devoted to her husband. 9–10.
Even by the power of a devoted wife, of Viṣṇu, and of a noble brāhmaṇa,
all the dānavas and the foremost of rākṣasas are destroyed and driven far away.
I, however, roam the surface of the earth according to the dharma of the dānavas.
"Why do you wish to curse me? Let this fault of mine be considered.
Padmāvatī said:
"My dharma and my good reputation have been utterly destroyed by you alone."

"I am a virtuous wife devoted to my husband, an ascetic who desires her spouse and remains steadfast on her own path; yet I have been utterly destroyed by your sinful illusion. Therefore, O wicked one, I shall surely consume you as well, without a doubt. (13-14)
Gobhila said:
"I shall proclaim dharma alone, if you, O lady, so desire; listen also, O daughter of a king, to the fire-sacrificing Brāhmaṇa. (15)
He who offers oblations to the deity twice a day and does not abandon the fire-sanctuary becomes an *agnihotrī*; he indeed performs sacrifice day after day.
Moreover, O lady of beautiful countenance, I shall likewise declare the duty of a servant.
O Goddess, he who is always pure in thought, deed, and speech;
who constantly carries out instructions and remains both behind and before [his master];
and who stands with his servants—he is called a partaker of merit, without a doubt. (17-18)
That virtuous son who, being wise and auspicious, protects his father and especially his mother through thought, word, and deed— for him,
the merit of bathing in the Bhāgīrathī arises day after day.
He who acts otherwise is indeed a sinner, without a doubt.
Furthermore, O beautiful lady, listen as I describe the unsurpassed vow of devotion to one's husband, which is practiced through speech, mind, and action. 20–21.
She performs service for her husband day after day;
when her husband is pleased, she is delighted and does not abandon him even if he is angry. She does not grasp at his faults, and even when struck, she is satisfied once more.

She always stood before her husband in all his duties; she was also described as a woman devoted to her vow of fidelity to her husband. Even though their father was fallen and possessed of many faults, he was [honored] by his sons.
Furthermore, for what reason should one not abandon even a father who is afflicted with leprosy or even one who is angry?
Indeed, sons who serve their father and mother in this manner go to the supreme world, that highest abode of Viṣṇu. 25.125-126.
For those servants who serve their master in this manner go to the world of their lord through the favor of that master.
A Brahmin should never abandon the sacred fire; he goes to the world of Brahmā.
A Brahmin who abandons the sacred fire is called the husband of a *vṛṣalī*;
a servant becomes a traitor to his master by abandoning his master—of this there is no doubt.
O auspicious lady, one should never abandon the sacrificial fire, one's father, or one's master.
A son, a servant, or a relative who is always unfaithful— I tell you the truth, the absolute truth—
those who abandon him and depart go to the ocean of hell, O Goddess, even if he be fallen, diseased, maimed, or afflicted with leprosy. 29–30.
A woman who desires her own welfare in this world should not abandon a husband who is destitute of all means of action and has lost his accumulation of wealth and property;
if she abandons her beloved and goes elsewhere, it is because she desires some other purpose in this life.
In this world, equanimity is like a harlot, excluded from all righteous dharmas.
When her husband has departed, that woman who, out of greed, pursues pleasure and ornamentation within the village is called a "harlot" by the people. (32-33)
I understand this Dharma to be thus, as it is agreed upon by the Vedic scriptures:
that at the very beginning, the Danavas, Rakshasas, and Pretas were created by the Creator.
I shall explain the entire reason for this here, without any doubt.

O beautiful one, the Brāhmaṇas, the Dānavas, the Piśācas, and the Rākṣasas have all studied this entire teaching for the sake of dharma; they all obtain everything, yet those Dānavas do not practice it. 35–36.
Deprived of knowledge, these men perform sacrifices devoid of ritual injunctions;
bereft of the prescribed rules, they proceed by unjust means. It is for the purpose of punishing them that these [beings] have been created, and not otherwise.
Those lowest of men who perform dharma devoid of the prescribed rules—we indeed punish them with severe punishment; for a cruel deed has been committed by you, most mercilessly. 38-39.

"Having abandoned the life of a householder, for what purpose have you come here? Even with your own mouth you speak thus; yet in deed, that devotion to your husband as a deity is not seen in you. 40. "Indeed, your divinity is centered solely in your husband. 41. "I am indeed devoted to my husband; I do not know any other god. I am a woman who has performed her duties, and I have come here for the sake of seeing my father-in-law. 42. "O lady, I am a servant of your father-in-law; I have come here for the sake of serving him. O virtuous one, I shall perform all the household duties according to your instruction. 43. "O beautiful one, I shall serve your father-in-law with great devotion. O lady, I shall perform all the household tasks according to your command. 44. "O beautiful one, I shall serve your father-in-law with great
"Having abandoned that husband of yours, for what reason have you come here?
(41) Having assumed this amorous appearance, ornaments, and attire, you stand here pitiless; tell me, for what purpose was this sin committed, and for whose sake? (42)

Listen, you who wander fearlessly and heedlessly in the mountain forest— you sinful woman, I have subdued you with a great punishment, for you are unrighteous and wicked, having abandoned your husband to come here. 43.
"Where is that devotion to her husband? Show it before me!
You women are unchaste, for by you your own husbands have been abandoned. When a woman sleeps separately on a bed, then she is considered unchaste. (44-45)
Within a distance of one hundred yojanas, she wanders about;
where does this woman, who follows the conduct of a harlot and is presided over by the gods, reside? O shameless, pitiless, and wicked one, what do you say to me face to face?
"Where is your asceticism? Where is your being, your splendor, and your strength?
Show me this very day your power, heroism, and prowess.
Padmāvatī said:
"Listen, O lowest of asuras:
though brought here out of affection by my father from my husband’s house, I did not go there out of desire, nor greed, nor delusion, nor envy. (48-49)

Having come here, I have abandoned my husband and remained established in the state of being his wife; yet I have been deceived by you yourself under the pretext of the husband's form. Knowing you to be Māthura, I have come before you.
"O lowest of Dānavas, when I recognize you as a magician,
I shall reduce you to ashes with a single roar of 'huṃ'!
Gobhila said:

Listen now: how can you, who are deprived of the eye of Dharma, recognize me here, you men who do not see those who lack physical sight? Listen to what happened when your disposition toward your father’s house arose. 52–53.

Having abandoned the meditation on the Lord, you have now lost the eye of knowledge through that meditation on liberation; indeed, it has clearly vanished from your heart. How can you recognize me on this earth, your eye of knowledge having been destroyed?
"Whose mother, father, or brother is there? Whose kinsmen and relatives are there?
For in every situation, the husband alone is the wife's [support], without a doubt.
Having spoken thus, Gobhila, that lowest of donors, laughed aloud. (55–56)
"No fear exists for you today; listen to me as well, O unchaste woman!
Why do you tremble in vain from my curse? Taking refuge in my house, enjoy pleasures according to your heart's desire."
Padmāvatī said: "Go away, you of sinful conduct! What do you say, you pitiless one?
I remain established in the state of a virtuous wife, devoted solely to my husband."
"If you speak thus, I shall burn you, O woman of great sin.
Having spoken thus, he sat down upon the ground in a secluded place;
then Gobhila spoke to her, who was overcome with great sorrow.
"O auspicious one, you have deposited your own well-performed vigor within your womb;
from that shall be born a son who will cause the three worlds to tremble. Having spoken thus, the Dānava Gobhila then departed.
When that evil-doing Dānava had departed,
the princess, afflicted by great sorrow due to her own sinful conduct, wept aloud.
Thus ends the account of Sukalā’s life within the Vena-legend of the Bhūmikhaṇḍa in the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Fifty-first Chapter.
The Brāhmaṇī said:
When that man of evil conduct, Gobhila, had departed, Padmāvatī then wept, overcome by great sorrow,
O best of the twice-born; and hearing her loud lamentation, all her friends [approached].
All those beautiful-faced women questioned that princess: "O lady, may it be well with you; tell us what has been done. Where has gone that great king, the lord of Mathurā?"
"By whom have you been summoned? Speak, O dear one," he said to her;
and she, weeping again and again with great sorrow, spoke.
She related everything that had occurred, including the origin of the transgression.
Led by them to her father’s house, trembling and deeply distressed,
she then related the matter to her mother in his presence;
having heard that, the queen went to her husband’s residence.
She indeed informed her husband of the entire account of her daughter;
having heard it, the king then became deeply distressed.
Having provided her with a vehicle, clothing, and provisions, he sent her away accompanied by her attendants.

O best of the twice-born, having concealed the fault of their daughter, the father and mother sent her to Mathurā; she went to the house of her beloved. Then the righteous Ugrasena welcomed Padmāvatī upon her arrival.
Seeing him, she rejoiced immediately and spoke these words again: "O fair-faced one, I am not able to live without you; I have always been greatly delighted by your virtues and character. (10)

Having addressed his beloved wife Padmāvatī with devotion, sincerity, and words of endearment, Ugrasena, the best of kings and lord of men, took pleasure with her in the company of those qualities that have the husband as their deity. 11–12.
The dreadful embryo, which portends fear for all the worlds, grew; Padmāvatī understood the cause of that embryo, reflecting day and night as it increased within her womb. 13.
"What is the use of this one who has been born as a true destroyer of the world?
Even with this wicked son, I have no business at present;
for she is asking everywhere for a herb that brings about the miscarriage of her fetus."
Day after day, she sought out great herbs and snakes,
and many means were employed for the very purpose of causing the miscarriage of the fetus;
yet that terrible fetus, which caused fear to all the world, continued to grow.
Then the fetus spoke to his mother Padmāvatī:
"O mother, why do you suffer day after day with these medicinal herbs?
Through merit life increases, but through sin, life becomes short."

They live and die according to the ripening of their own karma; some go forth as raw embryos, while others remain unripened upon the surface of the earth. Some die as soon as they are born, while others pass away even when endowed with youth.
Children, the elderly, and the young—all have fallen under the power of their lifespan;
all live and die through the ripening of karma.
Medicines, mantras, and deities may serve as instrumental conditions, of this there is no doubt. 20–21.
"Do you not know me? For such as I am, have you not seen or heard of me before—the mighty Kālanemi, the most heroic of the Dānavas, who strikes fear into the three worlds? (22)
"In the great war between the gods and asuras, I was slain by Viṣṇu in the past. To settle that enmity, I have come into your womb;
O mother, do not commit such rashness or exertion day after day."
Having spoken thus to the best of the twice-born, he ceased; and his mother, out of great sorrow, then abandoned all effort. As ten years passed, he attained full growth.
Afterwards, the highly effulgent and immensely powerful Kaṃsa was born (26),
by whom the inhabitants of the three worlds were terrified; he,
having been slain by Vāsudeva, attained liberation without a doubt (27).
Thus have I heard; it will surely come to pass.
This has been definitively declared to you in all the Purāṇas: a maiden who remains in her father's house shall meet with destruction in this way. 28.
"Do not allow yourself to be deluded by this exclusive passion for a maiden while living as a householder.
Abandoning this wicked woman, who is a source of great sin, remain steadfast;
for you shall surely experience the great sin and the most terrible suffering that must be endured."
"O beloved, enjoy this which brings the highest good to the world together with me.
Hearing these words of Sumantra, that best of brahmins, the boar, [spoke]. 31.
Summoned at that time, she set her mind on renunciation; listen, O auspicious one, how she gave me all my clothing and ornaments.
"By your own misconduct, the Brahmin Śivaśarman, the best of the twice-born—"

O wicked woman, you who act with such corrupt conduct, your husband has indeed gone to a state of uncertainty; go there without a doubt. Go to whatever place pleases you, and do exactly as you have been instructed. 33–34.

Having spoken thus, O illustrious one, I was abandoned by my father, mother, and kinsmen; shameless as I am, O fair-faced one, I have come here quickly, yet I do not find even a place to stay or any comfort, O auspicious lady. (35)
People revile me, saying, "This unchaste woman has arrived.
Wandering from place to place at the command [of my husband], I have come here, devoid of family honor, to the holy land of Gurjara, in Saurāṣṭra, to the temple of Śiva. 36-37.
Listen, O Goddess: at that time, I was exceedingly afflicted by hunger in the city well-known as Vanasthali, which was teeming with prosperity.
Taking an alms-bowl in my hand, I set out for the purpose of begging.
"I enter at the doorways of householders, deeply distressed.
O beautiful lady, people behold my form and revile me;
these wicked ones do not give me alms, saying, 'This woman has arrived.'"
Thus, due to the accumulation of such suffering and oppressed by poverty,
they wandered about until, by chance, they beheld a single unsurpassed house—
encircled by high walls and provided with a hall for the Vedas. 41.
Resounding with the sound of the Vedas, crowded with many Brahmins,
filled with wealth and grain, and adorned with male and female servants,
he entered that delightful house which was truly overflowing with prosperity.
Then Sudevā, afflicted by grief, said, "Give alms," at the house of that very Śivaśarman, which was auspicious on all sides (sarvatobhadra).
Then Śivaśarman, the best of the twice-born, heard the sound of the word for alms.
The righteous and high-minded Śivaśarman, smiling, spoke to his wife Maṅgalā, who was like Lakṣmī in form and possessed a beautiful countenance:
"This weak woman has arrived seeking alms and has come to the door. (45-46)
Having summoned her, he said, "O auspicious one, please give food to my beloved out of great compassion," knowing that I had arrived.
Maṅgalā then spoke to her husband: "I shall give the beloved food."
Having spoken thus to her husband, Maṅgalā, who was possessed of both auspicious and inauspicious qualities, again fed me, who was very weak, with delicious food;
then the great sage Śivaśarman, whose soul is righteous, spoke to me. 48-49.
"From where have you come here? Whom do you belong to? For what purpose do you wander throughout the world? Tell me everything before me.
Having thus heard those words of her high-souled husband, [she spoke].
Then, by her voice, I recognized my beloved, O sinful woman. When my husband was seen by me, I became bashful with my face cast down;
then Maṅgalā, beautiful in all her limbs, spoke thus to her husband: ||| 51-52 ||
"Tell me, who is this woman? Seeing her, even a serpent feels ashamed.
Please tell me out of your grace, who she might be.
Thus ends the [section] in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the account of Vena, in the narrative of Sukalā.
Fifty-first Chapter.
Fifty-second Chapter. Śivaśarman said:
O Maṅgalā, listen to my words if you are questioning me now;
O fair-faced one, understand that for which you have asked.
For this wretched woman, appearing in the form of a mendicant, has arrived here at this very moment.
This beautiful-eyed woman is the daughter of the Brahmin Vasudatta, named Sudevā, O auspicious one;
she is always dear to me as my wife,
yet for some reason she has come here after leaving her own country.
"O fair-faced one, she was consumed by grief for me due to our separation; knowing that I had arrived, she came to your house in the guise of a mendicant.
Knowing this, O auspicious lady, you have offered her a most splendid welcome."
"It must be done without doubt, for she desires what is very dear to me.
Having heard these words of her husband, Maṅgalā, who regarded her husband as a deity, was filled with great joy; being herself most auspicious, she [prepared to act]. 5-6.
O lady of excellent countenance, that devoted wife provided me with baths, clothing, and food, as well as ornaments set with jewels and gold;
for I was indeed adorned by you, O auspicious one, out of your desire for your husband.
O Goddess, by her I was honored with ornaments, baths, and meals; yet, O Goddess,
I have been slighted by my husband, and an endless sorrow has arisen within me—
a most intense anguish that threatens the destruction of all my life-force.
In that state, she beheld the suffering residing within herself;
thus, a thought as fierce as a mental affliction arose by which her life-breaths were departing. Never before had any auspicious word been spoken by me, that sinful woman.

While I was performing wicked deeds against this very best of Brahmins, I did not wash his feet, nor did I massage his limbs; indeed, I never offered myself in private service to that great-souled one. 11–12.
"How shall I, resolved upon sin, even speak with him?"— thinking thus, she then fell that night into an ocean of sorrow;
as I was contemplating in this way, my heart burst asunder.
Then, O fair-faced one, her life-breaths departed, leaving that body behind. At that time, the messengers of Dharmarāja arrived there—
heroic, formidable, and cruel, bearing maces, discuses, and swords.
Bound by them with heavy chains and firm fetters, O noble lady,
I was led to the city of Yama, weeping and deeply distressed;
being struck with mallets, I was tormented along a difficult path.
While being rebuked by those standing before him, I was ushered inside there.
I was seen by the high-souled King Yama, who was filled with wrath;
I was cast into a heap of glowing coals and hurled into a multitude of hells.
Having fashioned a man out of iron and heated it with fire, she was cast upon my chest as a means of deceiving her own husband;
tormented by various agonies and scorched by the fires of hell. 19.
Surrounded by a trench of boiling oil and upon sand of burning gravel (karambha),
they were cut by sword-leaves and driven by the water-mantra;
then they were cast by that Great-souled One onto the trees of the Kūṭa-śālmali.
O princess, by that very same great-souled one, I was cast into all the hells filled with pus, blood, and excrement, teeming with worms and accompanied by intense suffering. 22.
O princess, I was split by saws and struck violently with spears;
I was cast into other hells as well,
thrown into the pits of wombs, and fallen into a perilous mass of suffering.
By that King of Dharma, I was cast down into the hells; having entered a beautiful womb, I experienced most terrible suffering.
I went into the womb of a female osprey, and then again into the womb of a female dog.
Indeed, I entered the wombs of a hen, a cat, and a mouse; thus, I was cast into various specific wombs, those of sinful origin,
and tormented by the Lord of Dharma in every kind of birth.
O princess, by that very [act], the earth has been made into a field of merit;
O illustrious lady, there are many sacred fords (tīrthas) in your hand. O woman of excellent complexion, I have been sprinkled with that water by you yourself.
"O Goddess, O beautiful one, my sin has departed through your grace. O lady of lovely countenance, this knowledge has arisen in me due to the merit of your splendor;
now deliver me, who have fallen into the peril of hell. (29-30)

"O illustrious one, if you do not lift me up, I shall go once again to a terrible hell; save me, who am a partaker of suffering! Having fallen through my sinful nature, I am wretched and without refuge. (31)
Sudeva said:
"O auspicious lady, what meritorious deed, born of virtue, have I performed by which I might indeed deliver you? Tell me this now."
The sow said:
"O highly fortunate one, this king is an Ikṣvāku, a descendant of Manu. He is Viṣṇu himself, O wise lady; otherwise, you would not be Śrī."
O illustrious lady devoted to your husband, you are ever dedicated to your vows; O auspicious one, you are Satī, the beloved who embodies all sacred fords,
O Goddess, you are eternally composed of all things and always consist of all the gods.
O King, your beloved wife is the sole embodiment of the world of great devoted wives,
for she has served her husband day and night;
O fair-faced one, grant me the merit of even a single day.
"Even though you have been served by my husband, you now do what is pleasing to me. You alone are my mother and father; you are my eternal preceptor.
I am a sinner of wicked conduct, devoid of truth and knowledge. (37-38)
"O noble one, lift me up; I am terrified by the blows of Yama.
Having heard what she said, Sukalā then looked toward the king. (39)
"What shall I do, O Great King? What does this animal say?
Ikṣvāku said: "O auspicious lady, [release] this wretched woman who has indeed entered a sinful womb. 40
"By your merits, you shall uplift [others]; great welfare will come to pass.
Having been addressed thus, the excellent woman Sudevā, who was beautiful and auspicious, replied: "O fair-faced one, at the end of one year, my merit has been given by me."

As soon as these words were spoken by that goddess, at that very moment she was born with a divine body, endowed with beauty and youth, adorned with celestial garlands, and enveloped in a blaze of splendor.
Richly adorned with all ornaments and beautified by various jewels, she assumed a divine form and was anointed with divine perfumes and unguents.
Mounted upon a celestial chariot, she ascended into the sky.
Then, with her neck bowed low in prostration, she spoke to that queen:
"May it be well with you, O illustrious and beautiful lady! By your grace, I go from this sin, liberated, to the most meritorious and auspicious heaven."
Having thus bowed down as she departed for heaven, O Sudeva, best of beings, listen;
all this that was reported by Sukalā has been narrated to you.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Ascent to Heaven of Sudeva," within the Story of Sukalā in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The fifty-third chapter. Sukalā said:
"In this way, I previously heard this dharma in the Purāṇas."
"Deprived of my husband, how shall I live, you evil-minded woman? Without that beloved, how can I maintain life in this body?
Viṣṇu said:
Having thus spoken this supreme dharma, the unsurpassed vow of devotion to a husband,
those noble female friends, filled with great joy upon hearing that most meritorious dharma which grants women their ultimate goal, [listened].
O best of men, all the brahmins and gods praise that highly fortunate Sukalā, who is devoted to dharma;
they meditate upon her because of the power of her desire for her husband.
O Indra, Lord of the Asuras, having reflected deeply on this matter with extreme firmness,
and having thoroughly considered the supreme state of Sukalā,
the Lord of the Immortals might unsettle her fortitude and her love for her husband; of this there is no doubt.
Remembering the god Manmatha, the lord of the gods, the fish-bannered one, hastening and grasping his flower-bow, arrived accompanied by his beloved Rati,
who was endowed with great power.
Having joined his palms in reverence, he spoke to the Thousand-eyed One:
"O Lord, O Protector, why have you remembered me now? O Giver of Honor, let an instruction be given to me today with your whole being."
Indra said:
"O highly fortunate one, this woman is devoted to her husband;
listen, O Kāmadeva, and provide her with your supreme assistance."
"O highly fortunate one, extract Sukalā, who is meritorious and auspicious.
Having heard those words of Śakra, he then spoke to him:
"So be it, O thousand-eyed one; I shall do so, without a doubt."
"O Lord of the gods, provide assistance for the sake of your own curiosity.
Having spoken thus, the immensely radiant Kandarpa,
who is difficult even for sages to conquer and capable of defeating the gods, laughed at the best of ṛṣis.
How much more so, O friend of the gods, regarding the body of a passionate woman?
For I, O god, dwell constantly within the limbs of passionate women—on their foreheads, breasts, eyes, and the tips of their hair. (14)
In the navel, the hips, the region of the back, the loins, and the circle of the womb;
in the lower lip, the parts of the teeth, and the armpits—in these limbs and indeed in all the minor members, I dwell everywhere without a doubt. 15–16.
"O God, I always dwell there in the house of a woman; staying there, I kill all men without a doubt. O God, by my very nature, I torment women with my arrows."

Upon seeing her father, mother, or any other kinsman and relative—whether handsome or virtuous—a chaste woman struck by my arrows wavers; of this there is no doubt, and she does not consider the consequences. 19.
"The vulva of women throbs, O Lord of the Gods, as do the tips of their breasts; there is no steadfastness, O Lord of the Gods, and I shall destroy even a woman of good character.
Indra said:
"O Mind-born One, I shall become a man, handsome, virtuous, and wealthy; for the sake of curiosity, I shall move this woman. [He said:
"Neither out of desire, nor out of fear, nor out of greed, nor for any other reason."
"O you who are fond of truth, it is true, truly true that there is no delusion in her and no anger;
how is it that such great truth and devotion to her husband are seen in her? Having gone there, I shall extract the secret; delusion is surely the cause here. (22-23)
Having thus given his command as he desired, the King of the Gods himself departed; he was endowed with beauty and virtue, having manifested from his own transformation,
his limbs adorned with all ornaments and possessed of every enjoyment.
Filled with the play of enjoyments and always endowed with magnanimity,
O King, wherever the Goddess who is dear to Kṛkala resides, she displays her own divine play, her true form, her qualities, and her nature. 25-26.
She did not see that man endowed with beauty; wherever she went, O King, she saw only him.
With a longing mind, she beheld only him in this manner.
The Thousand-eyed One displayed amorous gestures before all those who were present.
Wherever the Goddess went—whether at a crossroads, on a path, or at a sacred ford—the Thousand-eyed One beheld her alone there. 28–29.
Sent by Indra as a messenger, she arrived before Sukalā and, smiling, addressed the highly fortunate Sukalā: "Oh, what truth!
Oh, what fortitude! Oh, what splendor! Oh, what forbearance! (30)
"In this formless saṃsāra, there is no woman with such a beautiful face.
Who are you, O auspicious one? To whom will you become a wife? He to whom you, endowed with such virtues, shall be a wife, will be the most fortunate and a partaker of merit upon this earth. (31–32)
Having heard her words, that high-minded woman said to her:
"Born of the Vaiśya caste, he is righteous-souled and devoted to truth;
indeed, I am the beloved wife of that wise man who is true to his word."

I shall speak the truth even regarding the Vaiśya Kṛkala: my husband, a wise and virtuous soul, has gone on a pilgrimage to sacred fords. Now that my illustrious husband has departed, [he remains] there. 34–35.
"Listen, three years have already passed;
since being separated from that great-souled one, I have become filled with sorrow.
Thus, I have related this entire account of my own life to you."
"Tell me, what will become of her? Thus you ask me, O lady.
Having heard the words of Sukalā, the messenger spoke again:
"O blessed one, you ask me this; I shall tell you all of that. 37-38.
"O lady of excellent complexion, my husband has gone away for the sake of some business;
listen, O fair-faced one, for I shall tell you, and having heard it, you must take it to heart. That merciless husband of yours has indeed abandoned you."

"What will you do with him who has killed his beloved? O sinful one, he who has departed after abandoning you, who are endowed with virtuous conduct— where has he gone, O young girl, and does he live there or is he dead?"
"What will he do with that?"—thus she grieves in vain;
why does she destroy her own limb, which is divine and possesses a luster like gold? For a human being does not attain [such a state] until the stage of childhood has been reached. 42.1–2.
O highly fortunate one, O auspicious lady, there is only one-sided happiness in childhood play; O lovely-faced one, in old age there is the onset of suffering as decay destroys the body,
whereas in youth all enjoyments are experienced with ease.
As long as youth remains, so long do human beings enjoy all things such as pleasure and enjoyment; a person delights according to his own will.
As long as youth remains, so long do they partake of worldly enjoyments.

O noble lady, when youth has passed away, what will one do? O goddess, when old age has arrived, no purpose whatsoever is accomplished; an elder person constantly broods and does not attain happiness.
Just as a bridge is constructed when the water has receded,
so too does this body become such [a vessel] once auspicious youth has passed away.
Therefore, enjoy yourself in happiness and drink the sweet wine of spring.
"O lady with beautiful eyes, my body is being consumed by the arrows of desire.
This one man has arrived, handsome and virtuous; for he is a tiger among men, all-knowing, endowed with merit, and wealthy. (49-50)
"O woman of excellent complexion, you are eternally bound to me by affection for my sake.
Sukalā said:
"In this life there is no childhood, nor is there youth in this existence. (51)
He has no old age; he is self-perfected and the bestower of perfect success.
He is immortal, free from decay, all-pervading, perfectly accomplished, and the supreme knower of all.
Free from desire, he exists in the form of the Self as the fulfiller of desires in the world.
Just as the structure of a house is seen, so too is the body perceived;
just as a carpenter constructs a temple with a measuring line, using an assembly of many timbers and a collection of various woods. 53–54.
One should apply clay and water all around;
once it has been plastered by the plasterers, the wood becomes variegated by the painters.
First, it assumes its form when it has been laid out with threads.
And they themselves nourish it daily by applying ointments. A house that is constantly buffeted by the wind becomes soiled;
this is described as the intermediate stage of a house's life. 56–57.

There will be a loss of beauty for that house; however, the master of the house may apply ointments according to his own desire, and the master of the house may bring the house to a state of possessing beauty.
O messenger, the youthfulness of that house is thus described.
Through the accumulation of wooden masses over a long period of time, it reaches a state of decay.
Fallen from their positions, they are born [as new growth] and they sway at the roots and tips; yet, together with the plaster, it remains supported by its foundation.
O messenger, this old age of the house has been described; listen:
seeing the house falling, the master of the house abandons it and proceeds with haste to enter another house. 61.
Likewise, there is childhood, youth, and old age for men.
In childhood, he manifests as a child devoid of knowledge; he may even paint his body with garments, ornaments, and decorations.
Through ointments such as sandalwood and other products like betel-leaf,
the body attains youthfulness and becomes exceedingly beautiful;
one should nourish it both internally and externally with all kinds of juices.

Nourished by the state of being sustained by that [food], it comes into being; O King, the growth of flesh arises from the essences of the food, and the limbs, being replenished, attain great expansion. 65–66.
Indeed, through their respective vital essences, the individual limbs attain their own specific forms:
the teeth, lips, breasts, arms, waist, back, both thighs,
as well as the palms and soles of the feet, likewise attained growth.
By both of these, those very limbs indeed attain growth;
through the blood and flesh of the limbs, they become well-formed.
O messenger, by means of those physical forms, the mortal becomes bound by passion.
"O messenger, by what means can a mortal be called handsome and beloved in this world? This body is merely a vessel for feces and urine;
it is an impure body that constantly flows with filth, O merciless one. (70)
O auspicious lady, how can its form be described? It is like a bubble on water.
It remains firm for only fifty years;
thereafter, its decline occurs day by day.
The teeth become loose and saliva flows from the mouth;
one cannot see with the eyes nor hear with the ears, O messenger, and one is unable to move with the hands and feet. 73.
The body becomes incapable, oppressed by the fire of old age;
its essence withers, dried up by the heat of the fire of aging. It becomes powerless—by what means is beauty desired? 74–75.

Just as an old house inevitably goes to ruin, so too, without a doubt, does this body go to decay in its state of old age; my own form has likewise come to pass day by day, like the fading of a color.
By what am I joined with form, and by what is your own form desired?
By whom did that powerful man go to an old house, for whose sake this messenger has arrived, and whom does she praise? (77–78)
"Tell me now, what have you seen upon my body?
For there is nothing here lacking a limb, nor is there anything extra, O messenger.
As you are, so is he; as he is, so am I—of this there is no doubt."
Whose form does not exist? There is no one on the surface of the earth who possesses a form [that is eternal].
O auspicious one, even trees and mountains, which are characterized by height, end in falling;
when oppressed by time, they perish, and living beings are no different. (80–81)
O messenger, the formless one who possesses form, the divine self, all-pervading and pure, dwells alone within all things, both stationary and moving,
just as a single pure water-jar contains the same water. 82.
Through the destruction of the jar, that which was one attains oneness; yet you do not perceive this.
Through the destruction of the body, this Self becomes uniform;
this single form has been constantly perceived by me while dwelling within saṃsāra. 83–84.
"Knowing him for whom you have come here, speak thus: 'If you wish to eat here, show me something unprecedented,' [saying this] to one who is afflicted by disease and obstructed by phlegm. (85)
The blood moves away from its [proper] limb and becomes displaced from its location.
Within all the joints of the limbs, it becomes like a stone; it perishes on one side and abandons its own natural form. 86–87.
It quickly turns into excrement and indeed becomes infested with worms;
likewise, one should abandon even that which causes suffering once it has lost its own form.
Listen: thereafter, it arises as a mass of worms, foul with stench.
Indeed, lice or worms are born there, without a doubt. Accompanied by worms, it produces boils and a most dreadful itching;
the louse causes pain and makes the entire body tremble. 89–90.
Just as an itch is pacified when rubbed by the tips of the nails, so too is it with those [pleasures] of sexual union; hear this, there is no doubt.
A mortal indeed enjoys flavors and drinks excellent foods.

By means of that wind, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the food consumed by living beings is led to the place of digestion. Once it has reached the place of digestion, all that food is covered over there, and the wind indeed causes the waste matter to fall away.
The essence of its sap is produced there as blood;
being stainless and possessing pure potency, it proceeds to the station of Brahmā (the brain).
Drawn upward by the samāna wind, it is carried further by that very air.
It finds no stable place and exists in a state of instability due to its flickering nature.
Indeed, there are five types of worms within the skulls of living beings;
two of these are at the root of the ears, and then again, two are in the location of the eyes. 95–96.
O messenger, those with red tails are measured by the span of the little finger;
those with black tails have the color of butter—of this there is no doubt.
O auspicious lady, listen as I recite their names from my own mouth.
Piṅgalī and Śṛṅkhalī are the two worms located at the roots of the ears;
Capala and Pippala are these two located at the tips of the nose; and Śṛṅgalī and Jaṅgalī are the other two situated within the eyes. 98–99.
Without a doubt, fifty-six such worms are situated at the end of the forehead,
all the size of a mustard seed;
they all afflict the skull-disease, without a doubt.
O messenger, listen: two hairs are found in his mouth;
know that at that very moment the destruction of living beings occurs, without a doubt, even while he remains stationed in his own place within the face of Prajāpati. 101–102.
That semen falls there in the form of rasa; of this there is no doubt.
He drinks the semen with his mouth, and by that he becomes intoxicated.
It remains in the region of the middle of the palate with a state of agitation.
The channels known as Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumṇā are situated there.
Even with great strength, within that cage-like network of his channels, there is indeed the itch of desire for all living beings, O messenger. 104–105.
O messenger, the male organ throbs for the man and the womb for the woman;
when the man and woman are both overcome with passion, they then proceed to union.
Indeed, the physical friction of body against body arises from sexual intercourse.
The pleasure in the body lasts but a moment, and then there is itching just like that;
such indeed is the nature of a messenger seen everywhere. Go now to your own place, for there is nothing extraordinary here. 107–108.
"I possess nothing unprecedented; I simply act, of this there is no doubt.
(109) Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Story of Sukalā," within the *Veṇu-upākhyāna* of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* in the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*. 53.
The fifty-fourth chapter.
Viṣṇu said: Thus addressed by that messenger, Sukalā, she then departed.
Having attentively grasped what had been well-spoken in brief,
and having reflected upon her speech— which was consistent with truth and righteousness, as well as her courage, fortitude, and wisdom— Puraṃdara [remained silent].
Indeed, who on the surface of the earth, having become a woman, could speak such words—
words that are well-instructed in the form of yoga and cleansed by the waters of logic?
This illustrious lady is undoubtedly pure and the very embodiment of truth.
"She would be capable of bearing the burden of the entire three worlds.
Having reflected upon this very matter, Jiṣṇu said to Kandarpa:
"I shall go with you to see that beloved of Kṛkala."
Proud of his strength, Manmatha replied to the thousand-eyed one:
"O Lord of Gods, go to that place where that devoted wife resides;
her honor, heroism, strength, and fortitude consist in her true devotion to her husband."
"O Lord of Asuras, how much shall I destroy once I have gone there?
Having heard these words of Manmatha, the Thousand-eyed One said:
"O Naṅga, listen; you have spoken excessively and in vain."
"By virtue of his most firm truthfulness and heroism, and being well-established in righteous deeds, this wicked age is invincible; indeed, your manliness does not exist here.
Having heard this, Manmatha then became enraged and spoke to Indra.
"The power of the sages and the gods has been destroyed by me. Tell me, how much strength does he possess? O Lord of Gods, watch as I destroy that woman for you. (10-11)
Just as butter, upon seeing the heat of fire, melts away, so shall I cause this [earth] to melt by means of my own form and splendor.
Go there; a great task has certainly now presented itself.
"Why do you revile this splendor that destroys the three worlds?
Viṣṇu said:
"Having heard these words of the Mind-born One, I know that this woman is unattainable by you through desire."
Summoning her fortitude, he beheld her—whose body was meritorious, who was holy through merit, and whose conduct was full of virtue.
"I shall see your manly prowess and fierce valor; having gone from here, you must indeed do so with that archer.
With those words, he went once more toward that devoted wife, accompanied by Rati and his messenger.
With one shoulder bared, seated in her own home, and focused through meditation on the feet of her husband—
just as a skilled yogi, having fixed his mind, remains free from conceptualization and does not imagine anything else—
Sati then assumed a most wonderful form endowed with infinite splendor, causing great wonder.

Seeing that great-souled man of beautiful playfulness moving about with such amorous passion— blue-clad, endowed with serpents for ornaments, bearing the fish-banner, and resembling Purandara himself—
the wife of that high-souled Vaiśya [fell in love] with him who was possessed of such beauty and discerned his virtues. 17–18.
Just as a water drop fallen upon a lotus leaf attains the reputation of being a pearl,
so too did the character of that devoted wife become renowned for its perfect truthfulness.
By this [character], she had previously sent a female messenger to me, saying, "This youth is a connoisseur of virtue."
He shall manifest to me his entire nature as Līlā, his manifold self-existence.
Having considered my own powerful Time, that wicked one has come before me with his solitary qualities;
how indeed can he live, being crushed by the weight of the true stone along with Rati? 20–21.

"May my beloved live on for some time longer, endowed with his excellent intellect, having taken hold of my very being; for this body of mine is now empty, devoid of movement, and truly like one who is dead.
(22) "The inhabitants of the village of the body have perished; I have taken up the activity known as 'great transformation'."
Even though he was my superior, that lustful one brought his lovely body to a state of upward splendor;
when he, powerful and full of joy, danced about with his own eyes as if intoxicated, he spoke thus of a marvel: "Whoever desires me even wishes to consume me. (23-24)
Having reflected thus, that great virtuous woman, whose mind was firmly bound by the rope known as Truth, then entered her own home in order to ascertain his state of being with certainty.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Story of Sukalā," in the *Venu-upākhyāna* of the *Bhūmi-khaṇḍa* within the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The fifty-fifth chapter.
Viṣṇu said:
Having understood her intention, the king of the Asuras spoke to Kāma, who was standing before him.
And she, being incapable of being forgotten due to her splendor,

stood ready for battle like a hero possessed of a proud and valorous nature— having taken up in her own hand the bow called Dharma and the excellent arrow named Knowledge, she remained there, well-sharpened by the power of her truthfulness. 1-2.

Desiring victory, you exert your human effort solely for the sake of your own self-interest; yet you are not capable of defeating me in battle today. Whatever is destined to happen must be contemplated right here and now. You were previously consumed right here by the high-souled Śambhu; do not enter into conflict with him.
Having rendered that wrongful act fruitless, you have indeed been born as the bodiless Smara; this is the truth.

Just as you performed an action in the past, O Smara, so too have you received its intense fruit; you will certainly attain a most despicable womb, for you are being addressed here even now along with this virtuous woman.

Those men in the three worlds who, despite possessing knowledge, harbor enmity toward high-souled beings, consume only the fruit of their own evil deeds—a result fraught with suffering and the destruction of their physical form. Having proclaimed our departure, go to Vraja as you please; leave this virtuous woman behind and proceed.

"In former times, through an association with Satī, I obtained an unbearable fruit consisting of sin. You alone know this history; I was cursed by that Gautama as well, and my testicles have always been those of a ram. Now that you have gone there, leaving me behind—" (7–8)

Indeed, the power and majesty of virtuous women is incomparable; even the Creator, the Sun himself, is not capable of enduring this most despicable form, for it was formerly cursed by a sage upon Anasūyā.
Thus, she obstructed the sun with her splendor as it rose with great velocity and blazed intensely.

Did you not hear long ago how the three gods were brought to the state of being the sons of Atri’s beloved wife—who was devoted to her husband through her vow of fidelity—even as they were warding off the death of their master, the curse of Māṇḍavya, and the [curse] of Kauṇḍinya? Indeed, virtuous women who are always endowed with refinement possess such power. 10–11.
Sāvitrī, the daughter of Dyumatsena, brought back her beloved who had been taken away;

she likewise recovered the noble son of Aśvapati right here from Yama. Such is your renowned devotion to your husband. Who would touch the crest of fire, or who, being deluded, would attempt to cross the ocean?
"Who could possibly subdue a virtuous woman who is free from passion, even if she were bound by her arms to a stone slab set upon pebbles?

(13) When Indra had spoken these words, full of many maxims, for the purpose of thoroughly instructing Kāma, the fish-bannered god, having heard those words, spoke this very same thing in reply to the Lord of the Gods. (14)
Kāma said:

"By your command I have come; yet you have abandoned fortitude, friendship, and even the goals of human endeavor (puruṣārtha), and for their sake you discourse upon this [world] which is devoid of essence and filled with many fears. (15)
"I shall go forth with a troubled mind; in the midst of the world, my infamy will perish.
Even though I am devoid of marriage, everyone will say that I have been conquered by this woman.
Indeed, those hosts of gods and dānavas who were previously conquered, as well as the lords of sages engaged in asceticism—"
"This formidable god of love, conquered by this noble lady, will immediately cause even me to laugh.
Therefore, O Lord of the Gods, I shall go with you alone; otherwise, he will destroy her strength, pride, splendor, and fortitude. Why, O Śakra, do you fear him here? (17-18)
Having thus awakened the Lord of the Asuras, who held a bow with an arrow and beautiful flowers, he said to her who stood before him, having assumed that illusory form: "O lady, go to Sukalā,
the virtuous and highly meritorious wife of the Vaiśya, who abides in truth and knows both dharma and virtue."

"O dear friend, having come here, I have stated the task to be performed and the manner in which you may assist; now listen. After Manobhava (the God of Love) had finished his speech, he then called upon Prīti (Affection), who was standing before him, saying: 'This is my supreme task; you must attend to her with great affection.'"

"O dear friend, listen! Having seen Indra, this woman with beautiful eyes will surely become filled with affection for him; therefore, by means of various powers and words endowed with virtue, you must certainly bring him under her control.
O friend, go quickly and accomplish this illusory form of the Nandana grove."
Abounding in flowers and preeminent in fruit, resounded with the songs of cuckoos and bees,
[Spring] summoned the Hero Makaranda— who was endowed with the quality of sweetness as a veritable elixir—
and dispatched him once again toward Kama, accompanied by the Wind and others engaged in their respective duties.
Having thus commanded his great army, desiring to cause the delusion of the three worlds,
he set out together with the king of the gods for the very purpose of deluding that great virtuous woman.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Story of Sukalā," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The fifty-sixth chapter.
Viṣṇu said:
For the sake of destroying her truthfulness, Manmatha, together with the lord of the gods, [approached].
Having set out for Sukalā, Satyavat then spoke of dharma:
"Behold, O highly wise one, the workings of Manmatha (the god of love),
which concern your own interest, as well as that of yourself and even of my own great merit."
I shall abandon this great site, the form of a dwelling that brings about happiness—
namely Satya, Supriya, and Sudeva, the most excellent of houses.
This Desire, with its heedless intellect, goes there and destroys it.
He is an enemy in the form of a friend, a most wicked soul; of this there is no doubt for us.
(4) My husband is a brahmin rich in asceticism, and my wife is a virtuous woman devoted to her husband.
My king is truly righteous; of this there is no doubt regarding my home. (5)

Wherever I have grown and flourished, there my residence shall be for one's welfare; there merit arrives and sports together with faith. Those endowed with forgiveness and tranquility come to my abode.
Where there is truth, self-restraint, compassion, and friendship;
where one is endowed with wisdom, free from greed, and established in purity of nature— there indeed I abide, and there these kinsmen of mine are found.
"Non-stealing, non-violence, forbearance, and the increase of [virtue] have come to my house; hear this, O King of Dharma!
Service to gurus and Viṣṇu accompanied by Lakṣmī [are here]."
The gods, led by Agni, come to my abode;
endowed with the radiance of knowledge, I illuminate the path to liberation.
Together with these, I dwell among virtuous and righteous women.
Among all these virtuous ones who always take the form of houses, I dwell together with you, even with the family members you have mentioned.
Those beings of virtuous form were made my household by the Creator.
"O illustrious one, we wander at our own will with playful ease.
And the Lord, the Master of the World, the three-eyed one whose vehicle is the bull,
dwells in my house in his own form, accompanied by Śivā."

This very essence of worldly existence, the great lord Śaṅkara in the form of a house known as Sadana, was indeed destroyed by Manmatha while the high-souled Viśvāmitra was performing supreme penance. 15.15-16a.

In ancient times, this Kāma, relying upon Menakā, conquered [the sage Viśvāmitra]. Furthermore, the virtuous and auspicious Ahalyā, the devoted wife of Gautama, was led astray from her truth by that evil-minded Manmatha. 16–17.
These sages who know truth and dharma, and these women devoted to their husbands— these, all of them, are my household, yet they have been set ablaze by the fire of lust.
This [lust] is difficult to restrain, unbearable, pervasive, and exceedingly cruel toward those established in truth.
"For one who constantly perceives me in this way, where can truth remain?
Knowing me to be equal [to all], that sinful archer with arrow in hand shall come and destroy my house, even by means of those things called Vedic fires. (19-20)
Those cruel ones who are full of even a trace of evil, as well as others who take refuge in heresy—
all those who are harmful in their intellect indeed enter the abode of Truth. By that [king], the commander-in-chief, though dishonest, was won over through deception.
That wicked and evil-minded one might strike down and destroy my house with weapons;
that sinful Mahābala, born of lust, might thus assault me.
Consumed by his splendor, I shall surely go to utter ruin.
"We desire a new house called 'Woman,' with the husband as its king;
this Śivamaṅgalā is dear even to the merit of Kṛkala. Thus, that sinner prepared to burn that house known as Sukalā.
"This powerful one, possessing a thousand eyes, was accompanied by Kāma;
for what reason does he not know his former history concerning Kāma?
It was through the incident with Ahalyā that this ram-like organ was produced. (25-26)
Having witnessed the manly power of the sage and the transgression of Satī,
the king of the gods, perishing through the fault of lust, remained there in terror;
having endured a terrible curse, he was filled with great sorrow.
"This Sukalā, who performs meritorious deeds, is the beloved of Kṛkalāsya.
This thousand-eyed Indra is striving to kill her, filled with lust.
Act in such a way that this desire of his does not succeed against Indra. (28-29)
"O Dharmarāja, you are of great wisdom and the best among the intelligent.
Dharmarāja said:
"I shall diminish your splendor and likewise bring about the death of Kāma."
"Let her behold that single means which has not been seen by me right here; for she is a bird-like woman of great wisdom, and let her announce my husband’s auspicious arrival by her cry. 31.
By the power of the bird and by the arrival of her husband,
those who had been ruined by wicked men will undoubtedly become healthy in mind once again;
sent forth by his wisdom, that Sukaḷā has gone to her home.
Making a great sound as she beheld the God, she shone forth,
honored and revered with wisdom, incense, lamps, and other offerings at that time.
She asked the Brahmin Sukalā, "What does she say to me?"
The Brahmin said:
"O fortunate one, tell me of your husband's arrival; remain steadfast.
Within seven days he will come; it shall not be otherwise."
Having thus heard these most auspicious words, she suddenly became filled with great joy, for that virtuous and righteous beloved had arrived, as indicated by the omen.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Story of Sukalā," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The fifty-seventh chapter.
Viṣṇu said:
Assuming the form of a playful Satī, she went to the home of that beautiful woman devoted to her husband.
When she had arrived, the virtuous woman, endowed with the nature of truth, spoke these words with respect to her who was blessed and honored by her most meritorious speech; then, laughing,
she spoke a reply consistent with truth and wisdom— a playful artifice that follows illusion and deludes the entire world.

"Listen, my husband—a lord, a knower of virtues, steadfast, learned, endowed with greatness, virtuous, and of holy fame—has abandoned me, a woman of very sinful nature, and departed; yet he was my protector. Having heard all these words, which were meritorious and consistent with her own feminine nature, she spoke of her many arts.
"O Sundarī, why has our protector departed today with his mind so utterly purified? Leaving behind your exceedingly beautiful form, tell me everything regarding your excellent husband;
absorbed in meditation, he treats even a friend who has come to his house as if she were his own self."
In playful jest, she said: "Listen to this true nature of my husband’s character:
I am ever devoted to him who is dear to me, and I console him according to his every wish.
I perform all that is most meritorious at the command of my excellent husband, remaining ever intent upon meditation."

"O Goddess, it is through service that corresponds to my solitary virtue and good qualities that this very same [result] occurs for me here and now; for this, the ripening of my past karma, manifests at this very moment, since my husband has abandoned me, one so unfortunate, and departed. (7-8)
A wife should sustain her life and even her own body with her husband;
how can women who are bereft of their husbands live well, being devoid of compassion?
Beauty, grace, good fortune, happiness, and prosperity exist [only] through him, and not otherwise.
"For indeed, in the scriptures, the husband of women is proclaimed as highly fortunate.
Having heard all that she had said in jest at that time, and having understood her true intent, she then spoke these words to Menā. 10-11.
To those who were full of trust, that illustrious one, the goddess-like wife of Sukalpa,
spoke again all her words concerning her own actions; she related in brief the account of her former life.

Just as her husband had set out on a journey intent on performing meritorious deeds, O wise lady, she perceived her own suffering to be truly like penance; thus consoled by her in playful words, that devoted wife was comforted. 13–14.
Sūta said:
On one occasion, she spoke in jest to Sukalā: "O friend, look at this beautiful forest adorned with divine trees. 15
There is a supreme, most meritorious holy site (tīrtha) there that destroys all sins,
adorned with various spreading creepers and beautiful flowers.
O fair-faced one, we two must also go there for the sake of merit.
Then,
having heard this, she entered that divine forest, which was like the Nandana grove,
endowed with flowers of every season and resounding with the songs of hundreds of cuckoos, accompanied by Sukalā and Māyā.
It was filled with the holy sounds of bees humming with most sweet notes and of auspicious birds warbling;
it was resplendent with fragrant trees such as sandalwood.
Completely filled with all enjoyments, it was indeed fashioned by Mādhava in the month of Vaiśākha for the sake of enchanting Sukalā;
she entered that forest, which possesses every excellence, together with her.

O Lord of Men, beholding that divine forest together with her, he perceived its merit-bestowing bliss and found no trace of illusion (māyā). Then Śakra also arrived there, resplendent in his divine form.
Having arrived there together with that messenger, Kāma met her;
becoming the lord of all enjoyments and overwhelmed by the play of passion, he addressed Kāmā, saying, "This is she who has come from a noble family. 23–24.
"O highly fortunate one, strike! This Māyā, who stood before you during our play, was brought here by that very game into your presence.
Show your prowess this very day; if it exists, do so with certainty."
Kāma said:
"O Thousand-eyed One, show me your own form, skillful and endowed with playfulness, by which I may strike her with my five arrows."
Indra said:
"O fool, where is that manliness of yours by which you mock the world?
Having become dependent on my support, you now desire to fight."
Kāma said:
"Even by that God of gods, Mahādeva, the wielder of the trident, my form was taken away long ago; it does not exist anywhere."
Listen now: whenever I desire to kill a woman, I manifest my own form by taking possession of a man's body;
or, O thousand-eyed one, I take possession of a man's body for the sake of a woman's purpose.
When a man repeatedly contemplates a woman previously seen, the form of that woman [becomes] his constant object of thought;
however, relying upon one never before seen, I drive that man to madness.
Nevertheless, O Lord of the Gods, there is no doubt that even by the mere remembrance of my name, "Smara," I cause such women to lose their composure; having seen her,
I take refuge in a body of such exquisite form.
By the radiance of my own splendor, I shall enter into the state of the subduer and the subdued;
assuming the form of a woman, I will utterly delude even a steadfast man. But by resorting to a man, I manifest myself as a woman.
"O Indra, I am devoid of form; let him take recourse to my form.
By taking recourse to your form, he shall accomplish his desired goal.
Having spoken thus to the lord of the gods, [he entered] the body of that great-souled one. 35–36.
Relying upon Sakhāsaumādhave as well, the flower-armed god (Kāma) remains eager to slay that very same virtuous and highly meritorious wife of Kṛkala;
he stands watching her body with his eyes as the target for his arrows. 37–38.
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter in the Story of Sukalā within the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Fifty-Eight.
Viṣṇu said:

Sukalā, the slender wife of a Vaiśya who had entered the forest while engaged in play, beheld that entire charming and dense grove; then that virtuous woman questioned her friend: "O friend, whose is this excellent, most meritorious, divine, and mind-delighting forest?"
All those excellent Siddhas, desiring happiness, joyfully questioned that friend of Sukalā.
Krīḍā said:
"This forest is endowed with divine qualities through the contemplation of the nature of the Siddhas."
Behold all this, crowded with flowers and provided with the fruits of desire, belonging to the one whose banner is the makara.
Having heard these words, she was filled with great joy upon beholding that great display of the wicked-souled Kāma.
As that fragrance was being carried by the wind, he inhaled it;
yet the wind itself was naturally endowed with that same fragrance.
Then his arrow entered her nose with effortless ease, just as it had done before.
That lady of beautiful countenance did not accept the fragrance of the flowers, nor did that great virtuous woman taste their sweet flavors;
