she remained with her friends, having utterly defeated the God of Love as he sought to sport with her.
Ashamed, he turned his face away and fell to the ground with his garments;

for, though adorned with clusters of flowers from well-ripened fruits, he was surpassed by the beauty of that fruit which had fallen to the earth. 8. That fruit, having fallen to the ground, surpassed him in its brilliance.
Then Makaranda, his soul deeply dejected, falls from the fruit back onto the ground;
just as one who has died in battle is devoured by flies, so too he,
being devoured by flies, is carried away by the current.
Moving very slowly indeed, birds are present there;
they move about happily with various cries, filled with intense joy.
Out of affection, the birds situated on the trees in the middle of that forest [behave] thus.
For this [Nala], having been won by Sukalā, has indeed taken to a downward path.
Rati, the wife of Kāma, accompanied by Prīti, went there and, laughing, said to Sukalā: "Blessings upon you! Welcome, O auspicious lady; enjoy yourself with pleasure, charming to the eye."
"O Indra, even for a high-souled one such as you, this [gift] is desired and stainless;
whatever else is desired by you, tell me that, and I shall surely bring it about—of this there is no doubt.
Sūta said:
Having seen or heard the well-spoken words of the two women, they said:
"My husband, who is highly intelligent, has gone away after accepting his pleasure; wherever my husband goes and stays, there I shall remain, united with my lord. (15)
"Therein is my desire, my joy, this source and my refuge.
Having heard both these words, Rati and Prīti departed bashful and ashamed, leaving that place where Kāma, of great power, remained.
They spoke to that great hero, who was stationed within Indra’s body, drawing his bow and visible to the eye, possessed of great strength:
"O highly wise one, this [city] is invincible; abandon your own manliness."
"O illustrious lady, you who are devoted to your husband and ever faithful to him.
Kāma said:
"By her, the beauty of this great-souled Indra is surpassed."
"If this is indeed so, then I shall kill him, without a doubt.
(20) Or rather, the Lord, the sovereign of the gods, assuming a great form and disguised as a hunter, then quickly followed her with supreme ease. (21)
Surrounded by all kinds of enjoyments, adorned with every ornament,
wearing divine garlands and garments, and anointed with divine perfumes,
he was joined by that Rati where her god-like husband resided.
He replied to the illustrious Sukalā, who was devoted to truth:
"O blessed lady, you were previously sent by me with affection in the presence of the messenger; why do you not welcome me, O auspicious one, as I have come here to seek you?"
Sukalā said:
"I am well-protected by my high-souled sons, O blessed one; even when alone, I have no fear of anyone, whether with or without companions. (25)
Guarded on all sides by brave men who appeared like heroes, she was so preoccupied with his work that she did not speak much;
O high-minded one, for as long as her eye remained fixed upon him, for that duration of time—
"Why are you not ashamed, O Lord, while being insulted by me? Who are you that have come here, fearless even of death?
Indra said:
"For I see you thus, come here into the midst of the forest.
You have described to me the heroic sons of my husband; how then may I see them? Show them before my eyes. (28-29)
Sukalā said:

Having established his own entire circle of kinsmen in sovereignty, and having entrusted Dhṛti, Mati, Gati, and Buddhi with the task of praising the Truth, that great-souled one—who was ever devoted to all immutable dharma, whose nature was dharma as firm as a mountain, and who was self-controlled—always protected me. (30)

While Dharma thus protects me with these virtues—purity, truth, tranquility, and forbearance—and while the immensely powerful and far-famed Bodha stands ever before me, accompanied by peace and patience, why does he not release me? I am bound by firm fetters born of my own qualities;
yet here they have come into my presence, and now all of them, including Truth and the rest, are engaged in guarding me.
"All those who gain merit through dharma and the like possess this same wisdom and prowess.
Indeed, they protect me in this way; why do you seek me by force? Who are you, having become fearless, that have come here together with a messenger? (32-33)
Truth, righteousness, merit, and likewise powerful qualities such as knowledge—
these are the companions of my husband, and they protect me in this dwelling. I am constantly endowed with protection, devoted to self-restraint and tranquility.
Even the Lord of Śacī himself would not be able to conquer me;
or even if the powerful Manmatha were to approach, I am always armored with truth—this is the truth, and not otherwise. (35–36)
His arrows will become useless, of this there is no doubt;
for these great warriors, Dharma and the others, will surely slay you. Go far away and flee; do not remain here at present.
If you persist in this despite being forbidden, you shall be reduced to ashes.
When you gaze upon the immortal form without your husband, I shall consume you with fire just as wood is burned; it shall not be otherwise.
Having heard this, the thousand-eyed one [Indra] looked directly at Manmatha and said:
"Behold his manliness; fight with your own prowess!
Then all of them, distressed by the fear of the great curse, departed just as they had come.

Then, O Great King, Indra and the other gods departed each to their own respective abodes. When they had all gone, Sukalā, that devoted wife endowed with merit, returned to her own home while meditating upon her husband.
Then, O King, that wife, who regarded her husband as a deity, arrived at her own home, which was endowed with merit, consisting of all sacred fords (tīrthas), and containing all sacrifices.
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Story of Sukalā," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the narrative of Veṇu.
The fifty-ninth chapter.
Viṣṇu said:
Having visited all the holy fords, Kṛkala was returning toward his home.
Setting out with the caravan leader, he was filled with great joy. As he reflected constantly in this way: "My worldly existence has become fruitful;
my ancestors, being satisfied, will surely go to heaven, and not otherwise."
Then, having bound his ancestors before him in visible form, he spoke; by that, his supreme merit was increased.
Possessing a divine form and a massive body, Kṛkala addressed these words to him: [3]

"There is no fruit from those holy places; you have merely performed labor in vain. You obtain satisfaction for yourself, but not the highest merit. Having heard this, the Vaiśya Kṛkala was then afflicted with grief.
Who are you that speaks thus? Why have my grandfathers been bound? By the power of what fault has this occurred? Tell me the reason for that.
Why is there no fruit from sacred pilgrimage sites? And why is it that my journey [there] has not taken place?
"Tell me everything clearly, if you know it.
Dharma replied:
"He who departs, leaving behind his own wife, who is pure and most meritorious—"
All the fruit of his merit becomes entirely in vain, and not otherwise.
[He who abandons] a wife who is devoted to righteous conduct, meritorious, dedicated to virtuous vows, intent on devotion to her husband, endowed with good qualities, and fond of merit— (8-9)

If one abandons even that [wife] and proceeds to perform religious duties, all the dharma performed by him becomes in vain; it is not otherwise. She should be devoted to all proper conduct and intent upon the means for accomplishing dharma.
She who is constantly devoted to her husband, always fond of knowledge,
and possesses such virtues as these— a meritorious and great satī— such a wife belongs to him in whose house the gods of great majesty always reside.
The ancestors residing within his house desire his welfare;
for him, the Gaṅgā and other holy rivers, as well as the oceans, are present there—of this there is no doubt.
In whosever house a virtuous and faithful wife dwells, devoted to truth, [there too they reside].
Therein are sacrifices and cows, and therein are the sages; it is not otherwise.
Therein are all sacred fords and various merits;
through union with a wife, all these abide there—it is not otherwise.

Through the practice of a virtuous wife, the state of householdership arises; there is no second dharma on this earth superior to householdership. The home of a householder is meritorious and endowed with true merit.
Containing all sacred fords, O Vaiśya, and accompanied by all the gods;
having taken recourse to the householder’s stage of life (gārhasthya), all living beings subsist—such another supreme stage of life we do not see at all. 17–18.
In the house of that man where the sacred mantras, the fire-sacrifice, the gods, all eternal dharmas, and the practices of charity prevail,
even so, the home of one who is deprived of his wife becomes like a forest.

Sacrifices and various kinds of gifts do not succeed for a man who is deprived of a wife; neither does the great vow, nor any religious duties, nor various meritorious acts, succeed for such a man. 20-21.

There is no sacred ford equal to a wife for the purpose of accomplishing dharma; listen, for there is no other dharma for a householder in the three worlds. Where there is a wife, there is a home for a man, and not otherwise.
Whether in a village or in a forest, there is no means for accomplishing all dharma equal to a wife; there is no sacred ford (tīrtha) equal to a wife, no happiness equal to a wife,
and no merit equal to a wife for the sake of crossing over [saṃsāra] and for one's welfare.
"O lowest of men, having abandoned your virtuous wife who was devoted to dharma, where do you dwell now that you have forsaken both home and dharma? Where is the fruit of your dharma?
Since you performed śrāddha and gave gifts at sacred fords while apart from her," 25 ||| "When [you did so] without her..."
"Indeed, on account of this very fault, your ancestors of former times were bound; and you too are a thief, as are these others who, being excessively greedy,
have consumed the food of the śrāddha offered by you in such a manner without her."
I shall now describe the merit of that virtuous son endowed with faith who offers the śrāddha-oblation, even when the piṇḍa is given by his wife;
just as the satisfaction of men arises from drinking nectar. (28)

Nevertheless, I tell you the truth, the absolute truth: regarding the ancestral rites for the ancestors and the duty of the householder, the wife is the mistress. You have deceived her; this act of yours, like that of a foolish thief, is in vain. 29–30.

These ancestors are like thieves; they consume that food even without her [the wife]. If the wife herself, with her own hand, offers food resembling nectar, then the ancestors eat that very food with delighted minds. 31.
By that alone they attain satisfaction and become contented.
Therefore, without a wife, dharma is not accomplished for a man; there is no sacred place (tīrtha) equal to a wife that bestows a good rebirth upon men.
"Whatever dharma one performs without a wife, that very same [dharma] shall become fruitless.
(34) Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Story of Sukalā," in the *Vena-upākhyāna* of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* within the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter Sixty.
Kṛkala said:
"O Dharmarāja, tell me now in detail: how is success attained by me, and how is the liberation of my ancestors achieved?"
Dharma said:
"Go home, O highly fortunate one; without you, she experiences great sorrow.
Console your own wife Sukalā, who walks the path of righteousness."
"Go to the house of the one performing the *śrāddha* and perform it with his own hand;
remembering the holy pilgrimage sites (*tīrtha*), worship the best of the gods.
Thus, the success of your pilgrimage will indeed be yours."
But he who in this world desires to accomplish dharma without a wife,
having utterly ruined the householder’s life, shall wander alone in the forest; his efforts become fruitless in the world, and the gods do not honor him.
Sacrifices attain success only when there is a wife in the house;
for he who is alone is not capable of accomplishing the goals of dharma and artha.
Viṣṇu said:
Having spoken thus to that Vaiśya, Dharma departed as he had come; and the righteous-souled Kṛkala also set out for his own home.
Upon reaching his home, the wise man saw that devoted wife.
Having reached his own home, that wise caravan leader,
seeing his husband— who was skilled in dharma— reunited with her,
then performed auspicious and meritorious rites upon his arrival.
The virtuous-souled one also related the deeds of Dharma; having heard her husband’s speech, which brought joy and was full of righteousness,
the illustrious lady praised those words of dharma and likewise gave her consent.
Viṣṇu said:
Then the Vaiśya Sakalaka,
staying in the temple of the deity, performed a most meritorious śrāddha ceremony together with her, out of faith.
The Pitṛs, gods, and Gandharvas arrived together in their celestial chariots;
likewise, the sages praised that noble couple.
And I, as well as Brahmā and Maheśvara joined by the Goddess, did the same.
All the gods, together with the Gandharvas, assembled there in their celestial chariots; then I, Brahmā, and Maheśvara, joined by the Goddess, [were present].
All the gods, along with the Gandharvas, were satisfied by her truth.
Those two great-souled ones, who were knowers of dharma, truthful, and wise, said:
"May it be well with you; O observer of excellent vows, choose a boon together with your wife.
Kṛkala said:
"O best of gods, by virtue of whose merit and asceticism have you all come together to grant a boon to him along with his wife?
Indra said:
This Asatī is highly fortunate, virtuous, graceful, and auspicious. We are truly pleased with her and desire to grant you a boon;
thus has her former history been told to you in brief. 17–18.
Having heard the greatness of her conduct, the righteous husband was filled with joy; his eyes overflowing with delight,
he bowed to all the deities and spoke again and again.
If you three great-souled eternal gods, and other meritorious sages, are pleased, then having shown compassion toward me, may I thus practice devotion to the gods in birth after birth. 20–21.

"O gods, by your grace, may I find delight in the truth of the Dharma; thereafter, O you of great majesty, if you are pleased, I wish to go to the world of Viṣṇu together with my wife and my ancestors. (22)
The gods said: "So be it, O illustrious one; everything shall come to pass.
Then, O King, they rained down a shower of flowers upon the two of them.
Then they sang a song of great merit, charming and melodious;
the Gandharvas, who knew the essence of song, and the hosts of Apsaras danced.
Thereafter, O best of kings, the gods along with the Gandharvas returned each to his own abode.
Having granted the boon, they departed while praising that devoted wife;
I shall now tell you of another well-known sacred site (tīrtha).
O King, the man who hears this is liberated from all sins.
A woman who listens with faith to this supreme narrative called Sukalā is never deprived of good fortune, truthfulness, sons, or grandsons. (27-28)
She shall be happy with her husband, possessing moderate wealth and grain;
she shall be a devoted wife (pativratā) birth after birth, and not otherwise. A Brāhmaṇa shall be learned in the Vedas, and a Kṣatriya shall be victorious.
Wealth and grain shall indeed be present in the house of a Vaiśya; of this there is no doubt.
O King, a Śūdra becomes a knower of dharma, possesses good conduct, and becomes happy; he attains happiness and prospers with sons and grandsons. 30–31.
From this, vast prosperity arises, adorned with wealth and grain.
32. Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Life of Sukalā," in the Legend of Veṇu within the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Sixty-one.
Vena said: "The Bhāryātīrtha has been fully described as the most excellent among all holy places. Now, tell me of the Pitṛtīrtha, the supreme means of salvation for sons."
Viṣṇu said:
In the great sacred field of Kurukṣetra, there was a Brāhmaṇa named Kuṇḍala;
the son of that high-souled Kuṇḍala was a virtuous man named Sukarman.
His two gurus were very old, knowers of dharma, and experts in the scriptures; these two great souls were afflicted by old age. He then attended upon them with supreme devotion.
Day and night, without ceasing, he was devoted to the knowledge of dharma and possessed of true being;
therefore, he studied the Vedas and his father’s various scriptures,
becoming proficient in all conduct, skillful, a knower of dharma, and fond of wisdom.
He himself performed the massage of his parents' limbs,
as well as the washing of their feet, and attended to the acts of bathing and eating; with devotion and sincerity, he became absorbed in them through meditation upon them.
O great king, one should cause service to be rendered to one's mother and father.
Sūta said:
O best of kings, in that present time, there were [these practices].
A certain Brahmin named Pippala, belonging to the high-souled Kaśyapa,
performed austerities while abstaining from food, having conquered his self and subdued his envy; endowed with compassion, charity, and self-restraint, he had completely mastered desire and anger.

The wise and high-minded one, having gone to the ten forests, devoted himself to knowledge and tranquility; restraining all his senses, he performed austerities. By the power of his austerity, living beings [appeared] with bodies capable of moving at will.
They lived there in that golden age as if they were from one womb;
seeing his penance, those sages were filled with wonder,
for no one else had ever performed such austerity as this sage was practicing.
The gods, headed by Indra, were filled with supreme wonder:
"Aho! How intense is his austerity, his tranquility, and his restraint of the senses!
He is free from perturbation, devoid of agitation, and liberated from desire and anger. (13)
Enduring cold, wind, and heat, he remained with his lower lip [unmoving];
indifferent toward sense objects, that wise and courageous best of the twice-born did not hear the sound of anyone, as if it were past all grasping. 14–15.
Having assumed such a posture and remaining with a one-pointed mind,
he became absorbed in meditation upon Brahman, his lotus-like face filled with bliss;
becoming as still as stone or wood, he remained motionless like a mountain.
He appeared like a pillar, steadfast and devoted to dharma;
his body was emaciated by asceticism, yet he was full of faith and free from malice.
In this manner, one thousand years passed for that wise man.
Upon a heap of earth brought by many ants,
he stood with his great body inside an anthill, his own dwelling,
as if rendered motionless within the belly of the ant-hill. 19.
Thus that brahmin Pippala performed great austerity;
that best of the twice-born was coiled all around by black serpents, and those snakes, fierce with virulent poison, bit that brahmin of intense splendor.

Having reached the vital points of his body, the poison did not spread; by the power of that Brahmin’s splendor, the serpents then attained peace. From his body there arose flames of blazing brilliance.
O best of men, they are seen individually in many diverse forms;
just as the rays of fire are exceedingly sharp, and just as the sun, having entered the interior of a cloud, shines with its beams. 23–24.

Likewise, O best of kings, a brahmin residing in an anthill is protected by the great splendor of the pippala tree; even when serpents bite that brahmin out of anger with their fangs, they do not pierce him, for their fang-tips merely cut through his skin.
O Indra among kings, as that high-souled sage performed such ascetic penance for one thousand years— enduring cold,
rain, and heat while practicing his observances three times a day— a great deal of time passed.
O Great King, time passed for that high-souled Pippala; likewise, that great soul practiced subsisting on air alone. Three thousand years passed while he was performing those austerities.
Then, upon his head, the gods showered a rain of flowers.
"O highly fortunate one, you are a knower of Brahman; you are a knower of Dharma, without a doubt.
You have become composed of all knowledge through your own past actions."

"Whatever desire you wish for, that you shall obtain; it shall not be otherwise. You yourself shall become one whose every desire is fulfilled. Having heard these great words, the high-minded Pippala—

Having bowed to all the deities with devotion and his neck bent low, he, filled with great joy, replied with these words: "So that this entire universe, this whole world, may come under my control. (32-33)
"O lords of the gods, act accordingly so that I may become a Vidyādhara.
Having spoken thus, O best of kings, the wise one became silent.
Then the gods said to that foremost of the twice-born, "So be it."
Having granted this boon, O highly fortunate one, they departed for that great-souled one.
(35) When those gods had gone, Pippala, the best of the twice-born, constantly practiced devotion to Brahman and meditated upon the subduer of the universe. (36)
From that time forward, O Indra among kings, the best of the twice-born, Pippala,
having attained the station of a Vidyādhara, is honored as one who travels at will.
Thus did that brahmin Pippala reach the rank of a Vidyādhara.
Born as the lord of the world of the gods, he was proficient in all the scriptures.
Once, that one of great splendor, Pippala, reflected: "Everything shall be under my control; I have been granted the most excellent boon. (38-39)
To produce that conviction, the eminent brahmin prepared himself;
whatever he intended to do, he brought that very thing under his control. When such conviction had arisen, he reflected within his mind as follows.
"There is no second person in the world who is my equal, the Supreme Being.
Sūta said:
Thus did the high-souled Pippala reflect.
Having understood his mental state,
O King, the crane, standing on the bank of the lake, spoke to Pippala with a melodious voice, endowed with refined articulation and full of elegance. (42-43)
Why do you thus carry such pride regarding the Supreme Self?
For I certainly do not consider this accomplishment—which consists of bringing all under one's control—to belong to you alone.
This act of subjugation is merely inferior and is praised only as something temporary.

"You do not know what lies beyond; indeed, O Pippala, you are dull-witted. Since you have performed austerities for three thousand years, why then, O twice-born one, do you indulge in such vain pride? (45-46)
The son of Kuṇḍala was the wise Sukarman, who was free from disease and possessed of excellent intellect;
he brought the entire world under his control—listen now to this. That intelligent man indeed knew both the near and the far.
"In this world there is no great knower equal to him; hear this, O Pippala.
You are not the equal of Sukarman, the son of Kuṇḍala;
for he gave no gift, nor did he ever contemplate [the acquisition of] knowledge."

O Brahmin, he never at any time performed rituals such as burnt offerings (*huta*) or sacrifices (*yajña*), nor did he go on pilgrimages to sacred sites (*tīrtha-yātrā*), nor did he practice the worship of the sacred fire. However, he once performed the supreme service of dharma for the sake of serving other brahmins.
Moving according to his own will, he was the very embodiment of knowledge, always devoted to his father, mother, and friends;
he was accomplished in the study of the Vedas and skilled in the meaning of all the scriptures—
such indeed was the wisdom of that boy of virtuous deeds.
"You possess no such knowledge; you bear pride in vain. Pippala said: "Who are you that, in the form of a bird, should thus revile me? (53)
"Why do you disparage my knowledge? What is that which is beyond (parācīna) like?
Tell me that in detail; how can knowledge of that be attained through you?
[Tell me] now about all the paths leading toward the beyond."
"O best of birds, speak at length and with prior knowledge:
will you become Brahmā, or Viṣṇu, or Rudra?
The crane replied:
There is no essence to austerity that has not been practiced, nor is there any fruit for such [unpracticed] austerity;
now hear how even the merit of one who has not performed penance can arise, as in the case of the earrings and even of a young son. (56–57)
"Thus, that consciousness has indeed been fully understood by him, yet not that state.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, even after going from here, you should ask me about my form; that righteous-souled one will surely explain all knowledge to you."
Viṣṇu said:
Having heard all that which was spoken by Sārasena,
he departed with great speed for the great hermitage of Daśārṇa.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the narrative concerning Vena. Chapter Sixty-two.
Viṣṇu said:
Having gone to the hermitage of Kuṇḍala, which was filled with truth and righteousness,
he then beheld Sukarman, who was devoted to his father and mother,
serving his high-souled preceptor, and whose prowess was rooted in truth.
He saw him seated at the feet of his parents— one of great form, great splendor, and filled with great wisdom;
endowed with great devotion, peaceful, and a vast treasure-house of all knowledge.
Seeing the high-minded Pippala arrived at the gateway, the noble-souled Sukarman, the son of Kuṇḍala,
quickly rose from his seat and performed a formal welcome.
"Come, O highly fortunate one, O great-minded Vidyādhara!
The high-minded one gave him a seat, water for the feet, and the respectful offering (arghya), saying:
"O one of great wisdom, you are free from obstacles; you proceed with skill."
The Nirāmaya then questioned Pippala who had arrived:
"I shall tell you everything regarding the reason for your arrival today. For three thousand years, penance was performed by you."
"O highly fortunate one, you have thus obtained a boon from the gods;
you have attained subjection to me as well as the power to act according to your will. Therefore, you do not know me, and you carry pride in vain."
Having observed all their conduct, the high-souled Sārasa told me his name and his unsurpassed knowledge.
Pippala said:
That Lord, the All-Knowing Master, who has bestowed upon me this essence of the Yogaśāstra on the bank of the Viprasarit river— what other being could possibly surpass him?
Sukarman said:
"O Lord, that crane who spoke to you on the bank of the river—know him to be Brahmā, the possessor of great knowledge, the Supreme Lord.
What else do you wish to ask? Speak, and I shall tell it to you."
Viṣṇu said:
"O son of a king, having been thus addressed by that righteous-souled Sukarman, Pippala spoke.
(13) Pippala said:
"We have heard on this earth that you alone can surely subjugate the entire world;
therefore, O Brahmin, show me that wonder through your own effort.
Behold today the very wonder of how you bring even the inevitable under your control."
The righteous Sukarman spoke to Pippala;
then, in order to provide proof, Sukarman called to mind the gods—
the world-protectors beginning with Indra, and the deities led by Agni.
Then the various Vidyādharas who had assembled and been summoned, as well as the gods led by Agni, spoke to Sukarman:
"O Brahmin, for what reason have we been remembered by you? Tell us the purpose of this."
Sukarman said:
"This very Pippala, the Vidyadhara, has arrived;
he speaks thus to me, O Brahmin, regarding the cause of subjugation and the means of being subdued."
"Having been summoned for the sake of this very Great Soul,
go each to your own respective abodes," he said to the gods.
Then the gods spoke to that high-minded one of virtuous deeds.
"O Brahmin, our vision never goes in vain;
choose a boon—may prosperity be yours—whatever is pleasing to your mind.
"Whatever that may be, there is no doubt," they said, O best of gods.
Having prostrated with devotion before the gods, that best of the twice-born made this request:

"O Indra, Lord of the Gods, grant me unwavering and auspicious devotion accompanied by true feeling, as well as constant devotion toward my mother and father; let this indeed be my unsurpassed boon. (22-23)
"O Lord of Gods, let my father alone go to the world of Viṣṇu; this is the supreme boon. Likewise, let my mother [go there], but do not ask for any other boon. 24.
The gods said:
"O best of Brahmins, you are devoted to your father; O twice-born one of virtuous deeds, we have been won over by your devotion.
Listen with affection to our words, for we are accompanied by the gods.
Having spoken thus, O prince, the gods departed for the celestial realm.
By means of this, his entire sovereignty was displayed before him.
Pippala also witnessed that most wonderful marvel;
then that righteous-souled one spoke to Pippala, the son of Kuṇḍala.
"What is this form that is near, and what is the nature of that which is far?
O best among speakers, tell me also of the power of both.
Sukarman said:
I shall describe the very sign of His transcendent form,
by which the worlds— including Indra and all things moving and unmoving— rejoice.
This alone is the Lord of the universe, the omnipresent Sovereign.
The form of this [Self] has not been seen by anyone, even by a yogi;
for the Śruti itself speaks thus, as if hesitant to speak of it:
"It is without hands, feet, or nose; it is without ears and devoid of a mouth. (30–31)

He indeed beholds all the karma performed by the inhabitants of the three worlds; he hears what they have spoken, being the witness who provides testimony. Though devoid of movement, he goes, for he is seen everywhere.
Though deprived of hands he grasps; though deprived of feet he runs.
O Brahmin, he is seen everywhere as all-pervading, yet devoid of feet—him whom even the lords of the gods and the sages who perceive reality do not see. 33–34.
He beholds all of them established in the states of truth and untruth—
the pervasive, stainless, perfected one, the bestower of perfection, the leader of all—
whom the great yogi Vyāsa, skilled in the meaning of Dharma, knows. 35.
That form is a mass of splendor, the sky itself, of a single color and infinite.
This stainless form has been declared with certainty by the Śruti; Vyāsa indeed knows that state, as does Mārkaṇḍeya. 36–37.
I shall now describe the subsequent period; listen with a one-pointed mind.
When the Soul of all beings, having withdrawn [the universe], proceeds alone, he takes his seat upon the waters, established upon the throne of the serpent Śeṣa.
Relying upon that, Janārdana alone sleeps for a long time.
The great sage Mārkaṇḍeya, scorched by the darkness of the waters, being weary of his wandering and desiring a place of rest, became absorbed in yoga. 39-40.
While wandering about, he beheld the Lord reclining upon the couch of Śeṣa,
resembling ten million suns, adorned with divine ornaments,
wearing celestial garlands and garments, the all-pervading Sovereign. 41.

O best of the twice-born, a certain highly fortunate woman, resembling a mass of black collyrium, with a terrifying form and a face made fearsome by protruding fangs, approached her beloved who was fallen into yogic sleep and bore the conch, discus, and mace. 42–43.
Thus addressed by her, that best of sages, the great muni, said,
"Do not fear. Then Mārkaṇḍeya was placed upon a very broad lotus leaf by the Great Goddess, a leaf five yojanas in length.
"Even while Keśava is fast asleep, there is no danger for you here.
To her, that lord of yogis said: "Who are you, O beautiful lady? You alone have become swollen with pride now that he has been conquered?"
O Brahmin, having been thus questioned by the sage, the Goddess respectfully replied:
"Keśava lies here upon a couch marked by the coils of a serpent;
I am his Vaiṣṇavī power, known here as Kālarātri."
"O best of brahmins, know me thus to be endowed with all powers of illusion (māyā).
In the Mahāmāyā-purāṇas, I am described as such for the purpose of deluding the world.
Having spoken thus, the goddess vanished right there, and Pippala likewise disappeared. 48–49.
While Mārkaṇḍeya was looking on, as the Goddess followed him,
a lotus with the luster of gold sprang forth from his navel;
from that was born Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, endowed with great splendor.
Therefore, all the worlds, both stationary and moving, came to know [the truth].
O King, Indra and the other guardians of the world, as well as the gods led by Agni, have indeed been shown by me in their manifest forms. 51-52.
This one whose nature is proximate is remote and without support;
when he reveals his body, you shall become embodied in the form of that body.
(53) Brahmā and all the worlds are indeed proximate, like the fruit of the pippala tree.
Those worlds within the three realms of existence are directed toward this side (arvācīna),
whereas that Self of all beings is directed beyond (parācīna); yogis clearly behold Him as the supreme state in the form of liberation, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman.

The unmanifest, imperishable *haṃsa*, pure and endowed with perfection—whatever is the form of that which transcends [the world], O Vidyādhara, you have seen it before me. 56 All this has been explained by me; what else shall I tell you?
Pippalāda said:
"O you of excellent vows, from where did this great knowledge arise for you,
who know the path of the recent as well as the path of the remote?"
The supreme knowledge of the three worlds revolves within you alone.

O observer of excellent vows, I do not see any higher culmination of austerity than this: that you have performed sacrifice, officiated at sacrifices, visited sacred fords, and practiced penance. (58–59)
"Tell me thus of his power; by what means was all this knowledge attained by you?
Sukarman said:
"I do not know of any austerity performed, nor of any emaciation of the body. (60)
I do not know the means of sacred pilgrimage sites through performing sacrifices or officiating at them;
nor have I accomplished meditation born of meritorious time and good deeds.
I clearly know only one thing: the worship of my father and mother.
With my own hands, I constantly perform the meritorious washing of the feet for both my mother and father,
as well as massaging their limbs, bathing them, and providing food and other necessities.
Absorbed in meditation throughout the three periods of the day, I accomplish this day after day:
I receive the water from their feet and likewise honor my mother and father every single day with a spirit of devotion and a pure heart.

"O Pippala, as long as my two gurus remain alive, for that long indeed an incomparable prosperity shall arise for me. I worship these two at the three times of day with a mind of pure devotion. (65–66)
Moving about at my own will in playful sport, I indeed dwell here on this Pippala tree;
what need have I for other austerities, or for the emaciation of my body? What use have I now for pilgrimages to sacred sites or for other meritorious deeds?
O twice-born one, whatever fruit is obtained from all sacrifices,
that very fruit has been seen by me even in the service of my father;
likewise, the service of the mother grants the same goal to sons.
In all actions, service to one's mother is the very essence and the most precious asset in the three worlds;
through it, even greater merit than that arises from service to one's father. (70)

There is the Gaṅgā-Gayā tīrtha, and there is Puṣkara itself; where the mother and father reside, there is no doubt that they are present for their son as well. There are also other various and meritorious tīrthas located there.
O Brahmin, these qualities arise for a son even from the service rendered to his father; indeed, the fruit of that service, of giving, and of austerity belongs to him.
For a virtuous son, O Brahmin, any other religious duty becomes mere labor.
Through service to his father, a son obtains unsurpassed merit;
indeed, one's own mother and father are both gurus while living, representing the entirety of one's own duty in this world and the next. 74–75.
Listen to the fruit of the merit of him who becomes a son and serves [his father]:
the gods and the sages who are fond of merit are pleased with him;
indeed, the three worlds are satisfied here by his service to his father. (76)

He who daily washes the feet of his mother and father indeed attains the merit of bathing in the Bhāgīrathī day after day. Likewise, he who honors his father and mother with meritorious offerings of sweet food and drink [attains the same].
I shall now declare the merit of one who constantly feeds [him] with devotion:
the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice is born for his son. (79) Likewise, by means of betel-leaves, coverings, drinks, and foods, [he attains this merit].
By honoring his two gurus with devotion, food, and merit, he too shall become all-knowing and attain glory and fame;
having seen his mother and father, the son should address them with joy. 80–81.
The treasures remain contented with him; they abide in his house, and cows come to him with affection, always bestowing happiness upon his son.
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Holy Places of Mother and Father," within the Legend of Vena in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The sixty-third chapter. Sukarman said: And when those two, his mother and father, the best of the twice-born, had also bathed...
When drops of water fall upon every limb of even a son,
a bath equal to all sacred fords (tīrthas) is effectively accomplished for that son as well—
[even] for one who is fallen, infirm, aged, or incapable of performing any ritual acts.
I shall describe the merit of that son who attends upon his father afflicted with leprosy, as well as his mother in such a state;
Viṣṇu becomes pleased in spirit toward him— of this there is no doubt.
He indeed goes to the world of Viṣṇu, which is difficult even for yogis to attain. Yet,
this son of evil mind abandons his parents— who are distressed, wretched, aged, and burdened by a great disease— even though they are his gurus.
Having become his son, he now enters the terrible Putranaraka hell, which is teeming with worms;
summoned here by his two aged elders,
he does not depart— of that sin I shall speak.
The fool who eats excrement is born as a village pig without a doubt (7).
Furthermore, for as many as a thousand births, he is born again as a dog while his aged mother and father remain at home with their son (8).
If a son eats food himself without first feeding those two,
he shall eat urine and excrement for as many as a thousand births;
that sinful one shall become a black serpent for two hundred births.
Disregarding his mother and father when they are old, he acts with arrogance;
even after hundreds of millions of births, such a wicked person becomes a crocodile.
Such a son reviles those two parents even with harsh words.
Even if he were to become a sinful tiger, he is later born as a bear;
that son of wicked intellect who does not honor his mother and father shall dwell in the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as a thousand yugas.
There is no spiritual ford equal to a mother, and for sons, none equal to a father.
For the sake of crossing over, for welfare, and indeed for both this world and the next,
O one of great wisdom, I therefore worship the father as a god.
I became one with all the gods, like a yogi in union with the Goddess who is the mother of all deities;
through the grace of my mother and father, this supreme knowledge was born within me, and this entire triple world has come under my control. 15.
O high-minded one, I know the inward-moving course of this great-souled deity Vāsudeva, and all his outward-moving knowledge has arisen through the grace of his father and mother. 16–17.
What wise man truly honors his father and likewise his mother through those Vedas,
along with their limbs and sub-limbs, and endowed with the Śruti scriptures?
O Brahmins, what is the use even of the Vedas if the father has not been honored by them?
For him by whom his mother has not been honored, the Vedas are useless. (19) What is the use of sacrifices, asceticism, O Brahmin, or gifts and acts of worship?
All these go to waste for him by whom his mother has not been honored. (20)
That by which one remains alive and established in the home while honoring the barber—
this is the duty of a son, as well as his pilgrimage here among men;
this indeed is the liberation of a son, and likewise the auspicious fruit of his birth.

For such a son, this sacrifice is indeed the act of giving; of this there is no doubt. He who constantly honors his father with devotion and a dedicated spirit has already accomplished all that was previously described.

By him who has served his mother, the fruit of giving, the fruit of visiting sacred fords, and the fruit of performing sacrifices have been obtained; there is no doubt of this. By him who has constantly served his father with true devotion, [the same fruits are attained]. 24.
For him, all ritual acts such as sacrifices that bestow merit are fully accomplished.
It is for this purpose that the Dharmaśāstra has been understood and heard by me; therefore, O Pippala, a son should always be devoted to his father. 25–26.
Listen now to what great suffering was formerly experienced by King Yadu when his father was pleased, and what great sin was formerly incurred when his father was enraged (27).
Even Ruru, the descendant of Puru, was cursed upon the earth by his father.
"Thus has this knowledge been attained by me, because these two were worshipped by me.
And through their grace, this unsurpassed fruit has been obtained.
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Pilgrimage Site of Mother and Father," within the Legend of Vena in the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The sixty-fourth chapter.
Pippala said:
Indeed, by the grace of his father, Vyāsa experienced supreme happiness.
Tell me in detail how that was obtained and how it was well-eaten;
O best of the twice-born, why does one experience the power of sin? O son of Kuṇḍala, tell me all of this at length.
Sukarmā said:
Listen, for I shall relate the sin-destroying life story of the highly meritorious Nahuṣa and the great-souled Yayāti. 3.
Born from the lunar dynasty, Nahusha was a lord of the earth who performed many incomparable acts of charity and dharma;
he indeed sacrificed a hundred of the most excellent horse-sacrifices.
Having performed a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices as well as various other sacrifices in manifold ways,
he attained the world of Indra through the power of his own merit;
he then made his son, endowed with the qualities of dharma, the protector of his subjects.

King Yayāti, endowed with truthfulness, possessing the vigor of dharma, and great in intellect, attained the station of Indra; his son [Pūru] then occupied his own place. Yayāti, perfected in truth, protected his subjects according to dharma.
He himself beheld those very deeds performed by his subjects;
having heard the unsurpassed dharma, that knower of dharma caused sacrifices to be performed,
and he undertook all the merit of sacrificial fords and the like, as well as acts of charity.
The wise prince ruled the kingdom according to truth and righteousness for eighty thousand years;
such was the duration of the reign of that great-souled Yayāti.
He had four sons, equal to him in heroism, strength, and valor.
I shall state their names; listen with a one-pointed mind.
His eldest son was named Tururu, who possessed great strength.
Puru was the second by name, Kuru was the third,
and the fourth son of the king was Yadu, who was righteous in nature.
Thus were the four sons of the high-souled Yayāti.
In splendor and even in manly prowess, they were equal to their father in valor. Thus was the kingdom governed by that righteous Yayāti;
his fame and glory became abundant throughout the three worlds.
Viṣṇu said:
Once, O King, Nārada, the best of the twice-born and son of Brahmā, went to the world of Indra to see Purandara. 16.
Then the thousand-eyed god beheld the Brahmin approaching, who was equal in radiance to the fire, omniscient, and a scholar of wisdom;
with his neck bowed in devotion, he honored him with offerings such as the madhuparka.
Having seated him upon a meritorious seat, he questioned that bull among sages.
Indra said:
"From where have you come today, and for what purpose have you arrived here?"
"O great sage, what very dear service may I perform for you today?
Nārada said:
"Everything has been done by the King of the Gods, and whatever was spoken was done with devotion."
"I am satisfied, O one of great wisdom; I shall now give the answer to your question.
Having arrived from the world of the earth, I have now reached your abode, having come here specifically to seek you out after seeing Nahuṣa. (20-21)
Indra said: "King Akopa always protects his subjects with truth and righteousness; he is endowed with all virtues, learned in the scriptures, possessed of wisdom, and full of excellence. (22)
"There is no king on earth more excellent than he— he who knows the Vedas, is dear to the Brahmins,
is devoted to Brahman, is a knower of the Vedas, is heroic, a performer of sacrifices, a giver, and full of true devotion.
Nārada said:
Endowed with these qualities, the powerful son of Nahuṣa—
by whose truth and valor all the worlds are sustained— is indeed like Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, in this world of mortals.
You exist both in heaven and on the surface of the earth as one who increases prosperity.
O Great King, Yayāti, the lord of the earth and the best of fathers, likewise performed a hundred horse-sacrifices and a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices. 25–26.
With devotion, he gave gifts of many kinds:
thousands of lakhs of cows and hundreds of crores of cows; furthermore, he performed ten million fire-sacrifices (koṭihomas) as well as one hundred thousand fire-sacrifices (lakṣahomas).
He who gave gifts such as land and other offerings to the Brahmins,
by whom indeed the entire nature of dharma was protected—
Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, was thus endowed with such virtues. 28–29.
That best of kings ruled the kingdom with truth for eighty thousand years, just as the powers of heaven exist here on earth. 30.
Sukarman said:

Having heard this from Nārada, the lord of sages, the wise Indra reflected upon it; fearing that Nahuṣa might protect righteousness through the power of his hundred sacrifices, he thought, "Indeed, Nahuṣa shall become my equal."
In ancient times, the heroic Devarāja, having attained the station of Indra, became [the king];
by the power of Śacī’s intellect, he who had fallen from that position was born as this great king, equal to his father in prowess. 32–33.
"He will attain the station of Indra; of this there is no doubt, no uncertainty.
By whatever means possible, I shall lead that king to heaven.
Thinking thus, the Lord of the Gods became afraid of him.
O best of kings, out of great fear of King Yayāti,
the lord of the gods then dispatched a messenger to bring Nahuṣa [back], along with his celestial chariot that fulfills all desires.
Accompanied by his charioteer named Mātali and his celestial chariot, Mātali went to that place where the son of Nahuṣa was,
having been dispatched by the king of the gods to bring back that high-minded one.
Just as Indra shines while presiding over his assembly, so did the righteous-souled Yayāti resplend in his own assembly.
[The sage] spoke to that high-souled king, whose ornament was truth. 38–39.
"O King, listen to my words as the charioteer of the king of the gods: I have been dispatched by the king of the gods to your presence at this moment.
Whatever the king of the gods tells you, perform all of that with a well-disposed mind. (40)
"O God, you must indeed come to the world of Indra; it cannot be otherwise.
Having abdicated the kingdom to his son and performed the final supreme sacrifice, the immensely radiant King Ilā, the son of Nahuṣa, has departed. (41-42)
Purūravas of great heroism, the high-minded Vipracitti, Śibi, Anu, and King Ikṣvāku resided right there;
as did the wise Sagara and your father Nahuṣa.
Ṛtavīrya, Kṛtajña, the high-minded Śantanu, Bharata, Yuvanāśva, and Kārtavīrya, the lord of men— these kings,
having performed various sacrifices, now rejoice in heaven. 44–45.
Moreover, all those four kings who were devoted to the performance of sacrifices rejoice in heaven with Indra by virtue of their own deeds;
yet you, on the other hand, are a knower of all dharmas and are firmly established in all dharmas.
"O Lord of the Earth, rejoice together with Śakra in the heavenly world.
Yayāti said: "What deed was performed by me, because of which you have made this request of me?"
"Tell me all that regarding Indra, the king of the gods.
Mātali said:
"O King, for eighty thousand years that you have [reigned]..."
The merit of charity and other such deeds has been fully accomplished through sacrifices (yajñas).
O Great King, O Lord of the Earth, go to heaven by virtue of your own actions;
establish friendship with the King of the Gods and proceed to the abode of the immortals. 49–50.
O high-minded one, abandon this body composed of the five elements upon the earth;
assuming a divine form, enjoy pleasures that are agreeable to the mind.
Just as sacrifices, gifts, and austerities were performed by you on this earth, [so shall it be].
"O Lord of Men, they pray for the enjoyments of heaven in whatever manner [is required].
Yati said:
"By which body on earth are good deeds and evil deeds accomplished?"
"Mātali, how could he go, having abandoned this world he had acquired?
Mātali said:
"O King, [he went] to that very place where this body, composed of the five elements, was acquired."
Having abandoned everything right there, they proceed to that [state] by means of the divine alone. All other human beings, who are the performers of both sin and merit,
also indeed abandon the body and proceed either downward or upward.
Yayāti said:
"O Mātali, having produced both good and evil deeds with this body composed of five elements, men indeed depart from here, both downwards and upwards. (56)
O Sūta, a specific distinction exists: one who knows the Dharma may cast off the body upon reaching that stage;
however, the falling away of the body occurs due to the power of sin and merit.
An example of this is seen directly in the mortal realm.
I do not perceive any distinction whatsoever between greater sin and greater merit.
(58) Why indeed would a mortal man abandon that very body by which he accumulates actions such as truth and righteousness? (59)
"Both of these—the self and the body—are of the nature of friends;
yet, having abandoned the body, the friend, the self departs with complete certainty.
Mātali said:

"O King, you have spoken the truth; having abandoned the body, he departs. There is no connection between that body and the self, because this [body] is of the nature of the five elements and is always worn out by the joints. (61)
Afflicted by old age and constantly tormented by various diseases,
he is broken by the defects of senility; no longer desiring to remain here,
his life becomes agitated and utterly distraught, and having abandoned it, he departs.
Neither by truth, nor by dharma and merit, nor by gifts, nor by restraints and self-control, nor by sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha, nor by pilgrimages and mortifications,
nor by other highly meritorious good deeds, is old age ever overcome.
"O Great King, by means of sins, that very body indeed runs away.
Yayāti said: "Why has old age arisen? Why does it afflict the body?"
"O best of beings, you ought to describe this to me in detail.
Mātali said:
"Indeed, I shall describe to you the remedy for old age."
And because this [body] has arisen within the midst of the body, O best of kings— since the body consists of the five elements and is supported by the five sense objects,
O King, when the Self abandons it, that body will be completely consumed by fire. (67–68)
O King, being ignited by fire, the lake blazed forth;
from that, smoke was produced, and from the smoke, clouds were born. From the clouds, waters flow forth, and from the waters, the earth is fashioned.
Just as a virtuous woman who has reached her menses does not approach [her husband], so too water comes [to the earth].
From that, O best of kings, fragrance is produced; from fragrance, taste; from taste, food arises; and from food, semen—of this there is no doubt. (70–71)
From semen the body is born, and the body is indeed of an ugly form;
just as the earth produces fragrances and moves upon the surface of the world through its juices, so too the body always moves, for it is entirely supported by the juices.
From that, fragrance is born; from fragrance, beauty arises once more.
From that, the great fire was produced. Behold this illustration, O King:
just as fire comes from wood and in turn illuminates the wood.
From the essence of the bodily fluids, fire is produced in that very same way;
it moves there constantly and nourishes the body, O King. As long as there is an abundance of the essence, for so long does the living being remain at peace.
Having performed such conduct, that fire exists in the form of hunger (76).
Intense in its desire, it seeks food accompanied by milk;
and it receives the gift of food as well as water, O King (77).
Fire consumes the blood, and in the same way it consumes the semen; of this there is no doubt.
From that, the disease of consumption arises, which destroys the entire body.
O King, either there is an excess of the vital fluids (rasa), or else the digestive fire is extinguished.
When pressed by the *rasa*, it arises in the form of fever (79).
The digestive fire (*vahni*) remains obstructed in the neck, back, waist, anus, and indeed in all the joints; thus the fire manifests within the body (80).
If that [rasa] should always flow in excess, it nourishes the body in every way;
then the rasa attains firmness and becomes strength and form. However, if it is excessive, it would indeed displace the vital organs (marmas) by means of its vigor.
From that very [desire], O King, lust is born; it becomes like a thorn.
It is declared to be the fire of lust, O King, which destroys one's strength. Through indulgence in sexual intercourse, there is destruction of the body. 82–83.
A living being afflicted by the fire of desire, intoxicated by the pursuit of sexual union, and emaciated by lust, may resort even to a woman;
yet his body becomes devoid of luster and a loss of strength arises.
When it is devoid of strength, being weakened by the fire, that fire circulates through the body the blood and the semen;
from the destruction of the semen and the blood, the body becomes empty. 85–86.
An exceedingly fierce wind arises, terrible in appearance;
he becomes pale, tormented by suffering, and his intellect becomes vacant. Having seen or heard of a woman, his mind is constantly distracted by her.
Satiety does not arise in the body when the path of the mind is greedy;
and whether one is deformed or handsome, one becomes middling through meditation when, due to the depletion of flesh and blood, one is devoid of strength and desire. 88–89.
Gray hair arises on the body due to the black fire of desire;
therefore, having become old day by day, the lustful man thinks of women in sexual union, just as a usurer thinks of his wealth. 90.
In that very manner, O Lord of Men, there occurs a loss of his vital energy;
from that, decay is produced, and he encounters the form of destruction.
Fire is born once more in the form of old age—of this there is no doubt.
A terrible fever arose among living beings in the form of consumption; all things, both stationary and moving, were tormented by this fever.
Afflicted by manifold suffering, they all came to their destruction.
"All this has been told to you; what else shall I tell you? (94) Being addressed thus, the great king spoke these words to Mātali.
(95) Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Pilgrimage Site of Parents," within the Legend of Vena in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The sixty-fifth chapter. Yayāti said:
"O Mātali, this body is the protector of dharma along with the self."
"Since you have set out seeking heaven, tell me the reason for this.
Mātali said:
"O King, there is no association even with the five elements."
They exist together with the self, yet they do not manifest through association.
Therein, the entire collection proceeds within the village of the body;
when afflicted by old age, they all depart to their respective abodes.
Just as the great king Rasādhika prepared the earth with juices, O Lord of the Earth, the earth, moistened and spread with those juices, attained softness; it was even pierced by ants and mice.
Just as hollows and large-ant-hills with vast interiors are produced,
so too do goiters, scrofula, and ringworms arise upon the body; and this body, O best of men, is being torn apart by worms.
Then, growths (tumors) arise there, causing immediate pain.
O son of Nahuṣa, O lord of men, how can this body, joined with these defects, go to heaven through its union with the vital breath? 7.
The earthly portion of the body is established for the sake of common purposes;
the body does not go to heaven, for it remains just as the earth does.
All this has been explained to you regarding the multitude of defects belonging to the earthly [nature]. 8–9.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Pilgrimage Site of Parents," within the *Vena-ākhyāna* of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter Sixty-six. Yayāti said:
"O Mātali, we hear that this body falls from sin and from dharma;
yet we do not perceive any distinction on the surface of the earth regarding merit. Furthermore, just as there was a previous falling away, so too is the body born again."
"How does the body arise? Tell me that in detail.
Mātali said:
"Now, for those men who belong to the hell-realms, it arises solely from unrighteousness (adharma)."
In a mere instant, a body arises from the elements;
likewise, by means of a single dharma, the divine,
spontaneously born body of the gods is produced immediately from the essence of the elements.
The body of great-souled beings, which arises from unmixed karma,
should be understood as being of four kinds according to its transformation of form:
those born from sprouts are to be known as the immobile, consisting of the forms of grass, shrubs, and so forth.
O King, worms, insects, moths, and other such beings are born from moisture;
all birds, serpents, and crocodiles are egg-born; and humans, as well as quadrupeds, are to be known as womb-born.
There, the ground, moistened by waters or ripened by heat and being fanned by the wind, receives the seed in its fields;
just as seeds, once sown, are again moistened by water.
Having approached, they attain softness and proceed to the state of being a root (9).
From that root arises the sprout; from the sprout, the birth of leaves; from the leaves, the stalk; from that, the stem; and from the stem, there is further production (10).
From [the cow] comes milk, and from milk arises rice;
from rice, likewise, cooked medicinal herbs are produced.
Seventeen types, beginning with barley and ending with śāli rice, are recorded as the most excellent.
Herbs rich in the essence of their fruits are proclaimed as the remaining minor ones (12).
These have been crushed by sages and previously prepared using winnowing baskets,
mortars, vessels, and the like, along with cooking pots, water, and fire (13).

O King, through the mutual combination of their juices, they undergo a sixfold transformation according to their distinct natures, attaining a variety of tastes— namely, that which is to be chewed, swallowed, drunk, licked, sucked, and crunched. (14)
Their divisions are the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), and their qualities are the six flavors beginning with sweet (madhura).
That food, when consumed by embodied beings in the form of morsels, mouthfuls, and gulps, establishes all the vital breaths (prāṇas) sequentially within the stomach, which is the root of food. 15–16.
The vital air (vāyu), having entered the midst of the food, divides the uncooked meal into two parts; having made it cooked, it separates its various qualities.
It places water above the fire and that food upon the water.
The self-sustaining vital breath (prāṇa), situated beneath the water, gently fans the fire;
the fire, being fanned by the wind, makes the water extremely hot, and that food is then cooked on all sides by means of that heat. 18–19.
When that [food] is digested, it becomes twofold: the waste matter (*kiṭṭa*) separately and the nutrient essence (*rasa*) separately.
The waste matter, divided by the twelve impurities (*mala*), goes out from the body.
These are: the ears, eyes, nose, tongue, teeth, lips, genitals, and anus.
Then sweat, impurities, feces, and urine are discharged; these twelve are recorded [as the outlets].
All the channels are connected on all sides to the lotus of the heart;
at their openings, the subtle prāṇa establishes that essence.
The prāṇa again fills the channels with the essence (rasa);
those filled channels then nourish the body on all sides.
Then, that essence situated within the midst of the channels [is processed] by the bodily heat.
Furthermore, there would be two acts of cooking for that which is being cooked and that which has been cooked.
Skin, flesh, bone, marrow, fat, and blood are produced;
from blood arise hair and flesh, and from flesh arise hair and sinews.
From the sinews, marrow, and bones arise fat, marrow, and bone-products;
from marrow comes deficiency, and semen is of the nature of procreation.
Thus, the twelve transformations of the tranquil [element] have been proclaimed.

Semen is its transformation; from semen arises the birth of the body. When, during the fertile period, the faultless semen is situated in the womb, then, impelled by the vital wind (vāyu), it attains oneness with the female blood.

At the time of the emission of semen, the individual soul (jīva), joined with its cause and constrained by its own past actions, constantly enters the womb. Within one day, the semen together with the blood becomes the embryo (kalala).
Within five nights, the *kalala* becomes a bubble;
then, within a month, it becomes flesh and further develops into five parts:
the neck, the head, the shoulders, the spinal column, and the abdomen.
Likewise, the hands, feet, sides, hips, and limbs, as well as the joints,
gradually come into being within two months.
Within three months, hundreds of sprouts and articulations are produced.
In four months, the fingers and other limbs are produced in due order;
in five months, the mouth, nose, and ears are formed,
as well as the rows of teeth, the tongue, and the nails.
Within six months, there shall be an opening in the ears; furthermore, the anus, the penis, the generative organ, and the phallus are produced.
And those joints that are in the limbs are formed within seven months.
Complete with all major and minor limbs and endowed with hair on the head,
with distinct and clearly defined parts, it becomes manifest again in the eighth month;
joined with the five elements, it remains fully developed.
By the potency of the mother’s food and by the six kinds of tastes, [the embryo] grows day by day, bound to the umbilical cord.
Then, when this body is fully formed, the living soul (jīva) regains its memory.
One perceives pleasure and pain, sleep, dreams, and past deeds.
"I have died and been born again; I have been born and died again. Thousands of various wombs have been seen by me in many ways. (39-40)
"Having just been born and having already received the sacraments, I shall thereafter perform that which is most beneficial, so that there may be no further birth from a womb.
While still within the womb, he reflects thus; and once emerged from the womb—
I shall entreat the Supreme Knowledge that brings an end to saṃsāra.
Oppressed by the great suffering of the womb, the individual soul, dwelling there under the power of karma, should contemplate the means to liberation. 42–43.
Just as someone oppressed by a great mountain remains in suffering, so too the embodied being, distressed, remains in pain due to the fetal membrane (jarāyu).
Just as one who has fallen into the ocean remains agitated in misery, so does he remain. 44.
With his limbs drenched by the fluids of the womb, he remains thus with a distressed mind. Just as someone cast into an iron cauldron is cooked by fire,
so too is one cast into the cauldron of the womb cooked by the digestive fire.

The suffering that arises when one's body is pierced without interval by needles the color of fire— that very suffering in the womb is eight times greater than that. There is no dwelling place anywhere more painful than dwelling in the womb.
The suffering of embodied beings is incomparable, most terrible, and even perilous.
Thus has the suffering of the womb been fully described for all living beings—both moving and stationary—in accordance with their respective wombs. 48–49.
For the embodied being who is being born, there arises from the womb a suffering ten million times greater than that caused by the crushing of a mechanical press,
as he faints while being squeezed like a sugarcane under the pounding of the hammer of sin. (50)
As one emerges from the womb, a great suffering arises due to the powerful winds of labor; finding no protection,
one is squeezed by the birth canal like sugarcane being pressed in a machine until all essence is extracted.
Likewise, this bodiless [fetus], situated in the womb, is cast out through the pressure of the birth canal;
it is bone-like, spherical in shape, encircled by the binding of tendons, smeared with blood, flesh, and fat, and a vessel for the substances of feces and urine. 53.
Covered with hair, body-hair, and nails, this supreme abode of disease has the face as its single great door, adorned by eight windows;
it possesses two lips as its door-panels and is provided with teeth, tongue, and throat as its internal fittings. 54–55.
It is flooded with the flow of sweat from the channels and overwhelmed by phlegm and bile;
it is seized by old age and sorrow, situated within the fire of the mouth of Time;
it is assailed by desire and anger, and crushed by the vital breaths. 56.
Afflicted by thirst for enjoyments, hidden, and subject to the power of passion and hatred;
with its major and minor limbs fully formed and enveloped by the fetal membrane, it emerges through the narrow and impure path of birth. 57–58.
In this body, one should know that there is a mass of skeletal framework, its limbs drenched in feces, urine, and blood, arising from the six sheaths;
it consists of three hundred and fifty [bones] and five hundred muscles. 59.
It was covered on all sides by three and a half crores of body-hairs,
both coarse and fine, visible and invisible;
it was endowed with these millions of fleshy channels.
Indeed, by means of that [body], which contains internal impurities such as sweat,
thirty-two teeth are proclaimed and twenty nails are recorded;
likewise, one kuḍava of bile (pitta) and half an āḍhaka of phlegm (kapha) are to be known.
Fat is known to be five hundred palas, half of that (two hundred and fifty) for the gall-bladder;
five hundred million palas are to be known for the flesh, and ten palas for the fat.
The mahārakta is three palas, and the marrow is four times the amount of the blood.
The semen should be known as half a kuḍava; half of that is the strength of embodied beings.
The flesh, taken as a single mass, is said to be one thousand palas.
Blood should be known as one hundred palas; feces and urine are of no fixed measure.
Thus, O King, the dwelling of the Self is eternally within the house of the body. Though the Self is pure, this [dwelling] is impure, being fashioned by the bondage of karma.
Somewhere, a body is born from the union of semen and blood. (66–67)
Because it is constantly joined with feces and urine, this body is remembered as impure;
for just as a jar filled with excrement is considered pure both inside and out [only after cleaning],
so too this body remains impure even when being purified by ritual cleansing.
Upon reaching which even the most purifying five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and sacrificial oblations (havīṃṣi) quickly attain impurity;
therefore, this body is impure. Even delicious foods and fragrant drinks, upon reaching it, [become so]. (69–70)
Impurity quickly reaches another, and from that, the other becomes impure;
O people, do you not see that which flows out day after day?
The filth follows the body, so how can its support be pure? 71.
Even when being purified with the five products of the cow and water infused with *kuśa* grass,
the body does not attain purity, just as charcoal does not become clean even when scrubbed;
for its channels flow constantly like those of a mountain.

How can this body, which is impure with phlegm, urine, and other such things, ever be purified? Not even a single spot of this body, which is a storehouse of all impurities, is found to be pure, even if one were to search for it. (74)
Even though the hand is cleansed with clay and water by day and by night, it does not thereby become pure; likewise, people do not turn away from food.
Even when this body is carefully refined with the finest incense and other offerings, [it remains impure]. (75–76)
For just as a dog's tail does not abandon its nature when bent down,
so too, a black woolly fiber by its very nature never becomes white.
Likewise, even when being thoroughly cleansed, a physical form does not become pure.

Even while smelling his own foul odor and seeing his own filth, this world does not become dispassionate, even though it afflicts its own nose; oh, the power of delusion, by which the entire world is utterly infatuated! 78–79.

Smelling and seeing the defects of his own body, a man does not become disenchanted with it; indeed, no other cause for disenchantment could be taught than the foul odor of one's own body. (80) What else can be taught as a cause for his disenchantment?
The entire world is pure, while the body alone is supremely impure. (81) Because it becomes impure through contact with its filthy parts, even that which is clean becomes unclean;
therefore, purification of the body is prescribed for the removal of odor and stains. (82)
After the departure of duality, one becomes pure through the purity of one's inner state;
for this mortal body, though smeared with all the waters of the Ganges and with loads of clay, does not become pure if it is corrupted by its own nature and foul with odors. (83)
A person of wicked soul is not purified by bathing at sacred fords or by austerities;
rather, one's own form attains purity when washed at a sacred ford. However, for one whose inner disposition is corrupted, even entering the sacrificial fire [does not bring purification]. 84-85.
Neither heaven nor liberation exists for one who burns the body; purity of intention is the supreme purification and the standard for all actions.
Otherwise, a beloved wife is embraced with one feeling, while a daughter is embraced with another.
The mental function is divided even among things that are not distinct;
for instance, one might think of a son in one way and a husband in another, according to the specific nature of each, O illustrious one, as has been illustrated. 87–88.
Even when embraced by his wife, a man should not cause her to be devoid of emotion; he should not eat various kinds of food, nor delicious and fragrant things, if she lacks feeling.
Therefore, in the absence of emotion, a man [is powerless]; thus, emotion is the cause in all matters.
Purify the mind with effort; what is the use of other external purifications?

One whose self is pure and clean through inner disposition attains heaven and liberation. Furthermore, by means of the stainless water of knowledge and the clay of dispassion, [the wise man purifies himself]. 90–91.
The stains of ignorance, passion, feces, and urine are removed by means of purifications;
thus indeed, they know this body to be impure by its very nature. One should understand it to be without essence and devoid of substance, like the core of a plantain tree.
Having thus understood the body to be full of defects, the wise man who becomes detached transcends saṃsāra; he who holds fast remains bound.
Thus has this great misery of the suffering of birth been proclaimed. 93–94.
Due to the fault of ignorance and the power of various karmas, the consciousness that a person possessed while dwelling in the womb perishes upon birth;
this occurs because one is intensely stupefied by the suffering of being crushed within the mechanism of the birth canal.
When the external wind touches the bodies of embodied beings through attachment to delusion,
a terrible fever arises as soon as they are touched;
by that great fever, a profound delusion is produced.
For one who is thus deluded, a loss of memory quickly arises once again;
and due to that loss of memory, as well as by the power of his prior karma, attachment is produced in that very birth for that living being. (98)
Deluded by passion, this world engages in what ought not to be done;
it does not recognize itself, nor others, nor the divine; it hears not the highest good, and though possessing eyes, it does not see. 99–100.

Walking slowly along the same path, as if stumbling at every step, he does not recognize the truth even when being enlightened by the wise. Thus, that man, following the power of greed, suffers in saṃsāra. 101.
And because there is an absence of recollection of the womb, Śiva has declared this scripture for the purpose of describing that suffering, which accomplishes both heaven and liberation;
for when that Śiva— the means for accomplishing dharma, kama, and artha— is known [102-103].
That they do not perform what is for their own welfare is a great wonder here;
moreover, due to the unmanifest state of their senses and intellect, there is great suffering in childhood.
Even though he desires it, he is unable to speak or act with propriety.
There is great suffering at the eruption of teeth, as well as from the wind due to restlessness (105).
There is affliction from various childhood diseases and even from the seizures of childhood demons;
with his body overcome by thirst and hunger, he sometimes stands and sometimes moves about (106).
Out of delusion, a child may engage in such acts as eating excrement and urine;

likewise, during childhood, one experiences suffering through the piercing of the ears and the beatings administered by mother and father, as well as through the study of the alphabet and other tasks under the discipline of teachers and elders. (107)

For one whose senses are unrestrained, who is tormented by desire and passion, and who is constantly afflicted by disease—how indeed can there be happiness in youth? Through envy arises great suffering, and from delusion, suffering is born. (108–109)
Remaining there, like one who is enraged, he experiences only the suffering of passion;
exhausted by the fire of desire, he finds no sleep at night. And how could there be happiness even by day, given the anxiety of acquiring wealth? (110)
The drops of semen belonging to a man whose body is exhausted by women should not be considered sources of happiness;
they are like drops of sweat produced from a leper or a commoner being tormented by worms. 111-112.

The wise know that the pleasure found in women is like the pleasure derived from scratching an itch or the heat of a fire; just as one considers the happiness gained from the anxiety of acquiring wealth,
so too should it be regarded regarding women— nothing more exists.
That very sensation of a mortal being is that by which the mind finds no peace.
Therefore, what was previously experienced as mutual [pleasure] becomes quite the opposite in the end.
Thus, even that which is dear is seized by old age and afflicted by disease.

Who else is more senseless than he who, seeing himself as never before— oppressed by old age— does not become dispassionate? Even a living being overcome by old age [is supported] by kinsmen such as wife, sons, and others.
Due to his lack of capacity, he is treated with contempt by servants of ill-conduct.
One joined with old age is not able to accomplish dharma, artha, kāma, or mokṣa; therefore, one should practice dharma while young. 117–118.
The imbalance of wind (vāta), bile (pitta), phlegm (kapha), and so forth is called disease;
this body is proclaimed to be a collection of wind and the other humors.
Therefore, this body of the self should be known as consisting of disease.

Because diseases and the cage [of the body] are not distinct from wind and the other humors, the embodied being undergoes manifold sufferings through various kinds of illnesses; these are to be known by one's own self—what more shall I say? (120–121)
One hundred and one deaths are established within this body;
among them, one is joined with Time (inevitable), while the rest are known as adventitious.
Those which are declared here to be adventitious are pacified by medicines.
Through recitation, fire-offerings, and gifts, untimely death is pacified;
or rather, untimely death may not occur from the consumption of poison without apprehension, nor does it come from excessive men; therefore, he fears untimely death.
Various diseases, as well as creatures such as serpents, poisons,
and malevolent spells, are the gates of death for embodied beings.
Even one afflicted by all these diseases and other ailments, Dhanvantari himself [protects].
One cannot restore to health that which has reached its time, nor can it be otherwise.
Neither medicine, nor austerity, nor charity, nor mother, nor kinsmen are able to protect a man afflicted by Time. 126–127.
If one does not attain peace through great-souled beings perfected in alchemy, austerity, recitation, and yoga, one will meet untimely death;
having died, one is born again among the worms of the womb by the power of karma. 128.

When one perceives the separation from a particular body due to the exhaustion of karma, that is designated as death; it is not, in the ultimate sense, a destruction. This occurs when one has entered into great darkness while the vital organs are being severed.
The suffering that a living being experiences at death has no comparison anywhere in this world;
crying out in extreme distress, "O father! O mother! O beloved!"—the entire world is swallowed by death like a frog by a serpent. 131.
Abandoned by his kinsmen and surrounded by those he loved,
sighing long and hot breaths from a parched mouth,
he rolled upon his bed and fainted again and again.
Utterly deluded, he throws his hands and feet about here and there; from the bed he seeks the ground, and from the ground the bed again, and then the earth once more (134).
Helpless and stripped of shame, he is smeared with urine and excrement.
With his throat, lips, and palate parched, he begs for water;
reflecting on his own possessions— wondering whose these will be once he is dead—
he is led away by the messengers of Yama, dragged along by the noose of Time.
Thus, even as they look on, the living being dies; like a leech moving from one blade of grass to another, it gradually enters one body after another.
