It attains the subsequent limb while still leaving the previous body.
For those possessed of discernment, the suffering arising from longing is indeed greater than that of death.
The pain of death is momentary, whereas that produced by longing is infinite; it was because of his state of being a petitioner that Viṣṇu, the Lord of the worlds, assumed the form of a dwarf.
What greater insult than this could there be, that my teacher should now become a cause for the lightness [of my status] through death? I have realized this today;
I shall not again entreat him, for craving is the cause of one's own degradation. 140.

Suffering at the beginning, suffering in the middle, and terrible suffering at the end—such is the succession of sufferings for all beings by their very nature. These are the sufferings that are currently occurring and those that have passed. 141–142.
A person should not grieve over birth, for one does not become dispassionate through that alone.
Excessive eating causes great suffering, while eating little brings the opposite; the throat is strained by food, so how can there be happiness in eating? 143.
Among all diseases, including those caused by hunger and poison, this [disease] is considered the most severe.
It is pacified for a mere moment by the application of cooling medicinal ointments; however, the pain of the disease of hunger is intensely acute and utterly destroys all strength. 144–145.
Overcome by it, a man dies just as he would from other diseases;
what pleasure, then, is there even in that *rasa* when it merely rolls upon the tip of the tongue?
Having reached the throat, it returns after half a moment's time.
Thus, for those tormented by the disease of hunger, food is considered to be like medicine. (147) Wise men should not consider that to be true happiness from the perspective of ultimate reality;
for he who lies down like a corpse, devoid of all activity, is merely as if dead. (148)
Even there, where is the happiness for one whose self is impelled by darkness?
And even upon waking, where is the happiness for one whose self is exhausted by labors such as agriculture, trade, service, and the protection of cattle? 149.
In the morning they are oppressed by urine and excrement; at midday by hunger and thirst;
at night, living beings are overcome by sleep and by the pursuit of sensual desires.
There is suffering in the acquisition of wealth, and suffering in the preservation of what has been acquired. (150–151)
One must destroy sorrow and exhaust sorrow; for where is happiness in wealth?
Those possessed of wealth face constant fear from thieves, from water, from fire, from their own kinsmen, and even from kings—just as embodied beings face the fear of death.
On the earth, the flesh of the wealthy man is devoured by sky-dwelling birds and by beasts of prey;
likewise, in the water, he is devoured by fish. Thus, everywhere, prosperity deludes him and holds him back from calamities. (153–154)

Those who seek wealth cause distress at the time of its acquisition, whereas those whose needs are met bring happiness; the master of wealth is anxious at first, but later becomes indifferent to all possessions.
Between these two, the master of wealth is miserable, while the other is happy, his mind detached from worldly things.

In the heat of spring and summer it is terrible, and likewise during the rains and festivals; with wind, sun, and rain even at the proper time, where is there any happiness? There is suffering in the elaborate preparations for marriage, and again in the carrying of the fetus. 156–157.
"I am suffering from the pains of difficult childbirth and the toil of clearing excrement; alas, what shall I do in this misery of my son's toothache and eye disease?
The cows are lost, the farming is ruined, and my wife has run away. (158)
"These guests have arrived at my home seeking safety;
what will I do for cooking while my wife is with her young child?
And at the time of the girl's marriage, what kind of groom will there be? (159–160)
Whence can there be happiness for householders overcome by such anxieties?
For a man distressed by the cares of his family, all his learning, character,
and virtues perish along with his body, like water poured into an unbaked clay jar.
Even in a kingdom, where is there happiness when one is consumed by anxiety over peace and war? Where there is fear even from one's own son, what kind of happiness can there be?
For almost all embodied beings, fear generally arises from those of their own kind.
Like dogs vying for a single piece of meat, no king on earth has ever been renowned for entering the forest;
for who, having cast aside everything, can remain happy and fearless? (164-165)
In battle, the powerful son of a sage brought down the thousand arms of the illustrious Kārtavīrya to the earth;
and Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, [brought down] the son of that sage.
He struck down the incomparable, upward-striving prowess of that great-souled one.
Jarāsaṃdha destroyed the fame of Rāma by his own splendor;
Bhīma destroyed that of Jarāsaṃdha; and the son of the Wind-god [Hanumān] destroyed even that of him.
Hanumān, too, was cast down by the Sun and fell upon the earth;
the illustrious Arjuna slew all the Nivātakavacas, the Dānavas who were arrogant in their strength, yet he was utterly defeated by the cowherds.
Even the sun, though endowed with scorching heat, is sometimes shrouded by clouds;
the cloud is scattered by the wind, yet the power of the wind is overcome by mountains;
the mountains are burned by fire, and that fire is extinguished by waters. (170–171)
That water is dried up by the suns, and the suns together with the waters perish along with the entire triple world at the day of Brahmā;
even Brahmā, together with the gods, is withdrawn once again.
At the end of two parārdhas, by Śiva, the Supreme Self, it was said:
"In this manner, there is nothing whatsoever in the cycle of existence that possesses the most excellent power, except for the one Lord of the World, the imperishable Supreme Self. (173-174)

Having understood this supreme excellence, one should abandon all pride; for in this world, who is there—be they a god or even a scholar—who is omniscient, nor yet anyone who is entirely ignorant? (175)

As long as one truly understands, for that long one is considered wise in that regard. (176) However, in terms of meditative concentration, power is considered equal everywhere; yet, due to the excellence of wealth, the power of some [is manifest] in certain places. (177)
The gods were conquered by the Dānavas, and they in turn were conquered by the gods;
thus the world is dependent upon one another through fortune, victory, and defeat. Likewise, the kings possess but a pair of garments and food consisting of only a prastha of water.

Vehicles, beds, and seats—even these result in nothing but suffering; in the seventh house as well, the possession of even a mere bed leads to an expansion of distress and exhaustion far exceeding that of thousands of water-jars. (179–180)
At dawn, along with the city-dwellers, there is the sound of musical instruments;
for me, however, this that is sounded in my house is merely the pride of sovereignty. Indeed, every ornament is a burden, and every ointment is but filth.
All singing is mere prattle, and all dancing is the behavior of a madman.
(182) Thus, when one reflects, where is there happiness for kings in the enjoyment of sovereignty? They are burdened with anxiety regarding war and their mutual desire for victory. (183)
Generally, great kings such as Nahuṣa and others, having reached heaven due to the intoxication of their splendor, have fallen; who can find happiness through prosperity?
Even in heaven, where is there any happiness, having seen the blazing splendor of others? 184.
In the heavens, where the gods stand in a state of mutual excellence, one above the other,
the fruit of their merit is consumed by men until its root is severed;
no further karma is performed there, and thus that fault is most terrible.
Just as a tree whose roots have been severed falls to the earth within days,
so too do the denizens of heaven fall due to the exhaustion of their merit.
For those who are intent upon the desire for pleasure, there is an abundance of enjoyments and the like.

Sudden-falling suffering is a hardship even for the dwellers of heaven in the celestial realm. (188) Thus, upon reflection, there is no happiness even for the gods in heaven; furthermore, there is the exhaustion of the merits required for enjoyment in heaven when the objects of the senses fail to be attained. (189)
There, for embodied beings in the fires of hell, there is great suffering and intense hardship through various terrible conditions arising from speech, mind, and body;
[they endure] the severe cutting with axes and the scraping of their bark-like skin.
The falling of leaves, branches, and fruits by violent winds; being uprooted by rivers, elephants, and other embodied beings;
and suffering from forest fires, frost, and desiccation—such is the misery among the stationary species.
Likewise, for the serpents and snakes, there is terrible suffering in their anger;
for the wicked in this world, there is execution and binding with nooses;
and for insects, there is birth and death again and again, occurring all at once.
For the classes of crawling creatures, there are likewise manifold sufferings of this kind:
for animals, there is the subduing of themselves, being beaten with sticks, terror caused by piercing the nose, and being severely lashed with a goad. (194–195)

The binding of limbs with cane, wood, and other fetters, or with a goad; the affliction of begging, youth, and so forth through mental distress; separation from one's own herd; and being led away by force or bound. 196.
Thus do animals with small bodies experience manifold sufferings (197).
For birds and beasts, there is suffering from rain, cold, and heat, and great hardship;
thus do those with bodies afflicted by affliction and pride experience manifold sufferings (198).
For human beings, there is the great suffering of dwelling in the womb, as well as the suffering of birth;
the suffering of early childhood and ignorance, the discipline of the teacher in youth, and furthermore, the suffering arising from desire and passion in youth, as well as envy. (199)
Through agriculture, trade, service, and other such activities, as well as through occupations such as cattle-rearing;
and due to being tormented by old age and diseases in the state of decrepitude; and at the time of death there is great suffering, which is even greater than the longing for it. (200–201)

There is great fear from kings, fire, floods, calamities, thieves, and enemies; there is fear in the acquisition and protection of wealth, and again, fear in its loss or expenditure. (202) There is stinginess, envy, and pride, yet when wealth is excessive, there is great fear.
For those without wealth, there is constant engagement in improper actions and suffering;
there is the life of a servant, usury, slavery, and dependence on others, as well as the pursuit of the pleasant and unpleasant, and thousands of such unions. 203–204.
Famine, misfortune, folly, and poverty; the state of being inferior or superior, the torments of hell, and the tyranny of kings;
mutual subjugation, suffering, and great fear from one another. 205.
Furthermore, mutual provocation brings suffering to kings among those who hold the earth;

for embodied beings who have performed actions driven by desire, there is impermanence regarding their states due to the piercing of each other's vital points and the mutual oppression of one another’s hands. 206–207.
Since all that moves and is stationary is terrified by such sufferings as greed, the distinctions of sin, and devouring one another—
from the hells up to the human realm— the wise person should renounce them all. 208.
Just as one who shifts a burden from one shoulder to another considers himself to have found rest,
so too all this suffering in the world is stilled only by means of further suffering;
for the floods of sensory enjoyments are always characterized by mutual excess.
Due to the exhaustion of merit, the suffering of the gods remains established;
through the depletion of their virtue, they undergo birth among thousands of various wombs.
Furthermore, diseases of manifold forms are recorded even in the world of the gods.
Indeed, the head of the sacrifice was severed and then restored by the Aśvins;
because of that defect of the sacrifice, it has always suffered from headache.
Likewise, Mārtaṇḍa Bhānu suffers from leprosy, and Varuṇa suffers from dropsy.
The loss of teeth was proclaimed for Pūṣan, the paralysis of the arm for Śacīpati (Indra),
and a very great wasting disease for Soma;
and there was also a very great fever for Dakṣa, the Prajāpati.
In every kalpa, even the great gods undergo destruction;
at the end of two parārdhas, even Brahmā is subject to impermanence.
Furthermore, Brahmā lusted after the granddaughter of Dakṣa’s daughter.
Out of anger, the Lord cursed the goddess Jayā, who was skilled in yoga:
"Wherever lust and anger reside, there the defects consisting of them shall abide;
all miseries likewise reside there, without a doubt. (217)
The destruction of birth and death, the state of devouring all things, and being the consumer of oblations;
the killing of a woman, addiction to desire, and acting as a charioteer in the army of the Pāṇḍavas; the burning of Tripura by Rudra, and the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice. (218–219)
From the birth of Skanda, from the [conflict] with Śukra, and from his thousands of sports and other deeds—
it is thus that even the three gods are possessed of defects such as passion and the like. Beyond these is the Lord, who is peaceful, perfectly complete, and the bestower of liberation.

Thus, having realized that this entire world exists in a state of mutual competition and is agitated by sufferings, one should attain supreme detachment (*nirveda*). From detachment arises dispassion (*virāga*), and from dispassion arises the birth of knowledge (*jñāna*).
Through that knowledge, one attains supreme knowledge, auspiciousness, and liberation; then, freed from all suffering, with a self established in its own state, one becomes happy,
omniscient, and perfectly complete— this is what is called "liberation."
Mātali said: "All this that was asked by you has been explained;
for the discernment between dharma and adharma arises from all-encompassing knowledge."
"One must go to the world of Indra by the command of the King of the Gods.
(225) Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Tīrtha of Father and Mother," within the Vena-legend of the Bhūmikhaṇḍa in the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Sixty-seven.
Yayāti said:
"O charioteer of Śakra, it is by the power of our good fortune that I have obtained the sight of you; this is an incomparable blessing for me."
"O Mātali, tell me now of the ripening of the karma of those who commit terrible sins in the world of mortals and in the world of the immortals. Mātali said:
Listen, for I shall describe the characteristics of one who follows sinful conduct;
when such conduct is heard, great ignorance arises in this world. They practice censure of the Vedas and revile the conduct of Brahmanas.
This should be understood as a great sin (mahāpātaka) by those wise in knowledge. Indeed,
whoever inflicts suffering upon any of the virtuous shall likewise proceed toward a great sin and must undergo atonement.

Abandoning the conduct of one's own family and following the conduct of others— this is declared by those who know what ought to be done to be a terrible sin. Likewise, reviling or striking one's mother and father, or [striking] one's sisters, [is a grave offense].
Furthermore, reviling one's father’s sister is certainly a sin;
likewise, when the time for the śrāddha has arrived, it is a sin to neglect a son-in-law or a daughter’s son who resides within a distance of five krośas.
When one sets aside one's own sister or sister's son and,
out of desire, anger, or fear, feeds another instead,
neither the ancestors nor the gods will eat.
This is a sin for him equal to the murder of a father.
Even when the time for giving has arrived and a Brahmin has indeed come, why is abundant charity abandoned and given instead to only a few?
If a gift is given to one person and not to others,
this is remembered as a terrible sin that causes the failure of the act of giving.
[One should avoid] those Brāhmaṇas who reside in the house of the sacrificer as his servants.
The measure of a gift is that which is given after abandoning all sense of shame; such is the defining characteristic of giving.
O King, one should support with every means and with many excellent gifts that brahmin who has sought refuge, being endowed with righteous conduct. 13-14.
O King, one should never disregard a learned man; a Brāhmaṇa who is supported always becomes endowed with all merits through many excellent gifts.
Having honored that learned Brāhmaṇa when he has arrived, one should always offer him due respect.
Having abandoned that [gift], one should give it to another Brāhmaṇa;
what was given to him becomes as if offered (into the fire), and there is no doubt that it is fruitless.
[This applies to] a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, and the Śūdra as the fourth.
On all auspicious occasions, one should honor a twice-born man who has taken refuge [in the path], whether he be a fool or a scholar; hear now the fruit of his merit.
The fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice is produced for him. (18)
For what reason, O King, should one not perform [the rite] even after reaching Śakya?
At that time, during the śrāddha ceremony, another brāhmaṇa arrived;
he then honored both of them there with food and clothing. 19–20.
The ancestors of that person are delighted by the betel leaves and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).

Whatever should be given to one who has eaten at a śrāddha, that gift and the dakṣiṇā must always be bestowed. If the performer of the śrāddha does not give these, it becomes equivalent to the sin of killing a yogin.
Therefore, O best of kings, one should worship these two with faith;
indeed, due to the power of poverty, one should worship even one of them when Vyatīpāta or Vaidhṛti occurs, O supreme among monarchs. 22–23.
O King, on the new moon day and likewise on the anniversary of a death during the dark fortnight,
the Śrāddha ceremony should be performed in this manner by the three varṇas beginning with the Brāhmaṇas. O Great King, likewise at a sacrifice, one should appoint officiating priests (ṛtvij).
In this manner, Brahmins should always be selected for the giving of śrāddha.
An unknown Brahmin should never be chosen by one who does not know him; however, he whose lineage and family, extending back three generations, are well known [may be accepted]. 25–26.
O King, one should invite that Brahmin who possesses such conduct;
for the lineage of one is not known, one should judge him by his conduct. Indeed, even a fool who is pure should be engaged in the performance of the Śrāddha offering.
A Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas may remain unrecognized;
therefore, O best of kings, one should invite such a Brahmin and perform the Śrāddha offering, providing unprecedented hospitality. 28–29.
Otherwise, the sinner will certainly go to hell;

therefore, a Brahmin should be engaged in giving and at śrāddha ceremonies on the sacred festival days (parvan). First, one should examine the Brahmin, and then cause him to perform the giving at the śrāddha.

The ancestors do not eat in the house of one who excludes a Brahmin; having uttered a curse, they depart from that śrāddha performed without a Brahmin. Even if he were equal to Brahmā himself, he would become a great sinner.

O best of men, he who abandons the ancestral conduct of his forefathers should be known as a great sinner, excluded from all dharma. Those who likewise abandon the Śaiva or Vaiṣṇava conduct that bestows enjoyment [are likewise fallen].
Those who revile the Brāhmaṇas and the Dharma should be known as increasers of sin.
Those who abandon the conduct of Śiva, who hate the devotees of Śiva, who revile Hari, and who are always haters of Brahman are indeed sinful. 34-35.
These revilers of right conduct are the greatest of those who have committed heinous sins (mahāpātaka),
for they disparage the primordial, worshipful, supreme knowledge, as well as the meritorious Bhāgavata,
the Vaiṣṇava, the Harivaṃśa, or the Matsya and Kūrma Purāṇas.
I shall declare the welfare of those who worship the Pādma;
for by you, O King, the god Madhusūdana has been worshipped directly.
Therefore, one should indeed fully honor Vaiṣṇava knowledge, which is dear to Viṣṇu. 38.
O King, the Vaiṣṇava manuscript should always be kept in the temple;
when that is worshipped, the Lord of Kamalā (Viṣṇu) is worshipped, and the Brahmins are worshipped.
Those who sing or write the knowledge of Hari without having worshipped Him [do so in vain].

Without knowing [the truth], they bestow [it], listen to it, and recite it; they sport with it out of greed and through adherence to false knowledge, and they establish it at will in unconsecrated places. 40–41.
One should reveal the knowledge of Hari, which is as secure as direct perception;
yet he who, though having studied and being capable, acts with negligence, and he who is impure and teaches or listens in an impure place—[these are to be avoided]. 42.
In brief, all this is considered equal to the censure of knowledge.
(43) He who desires to hear the scripture without having first worshipped the guru, and who fails to perform service while intentionally violating his commands; (44)
He does not welcome those words, he offers no reply,
and he shows indifference even when a heavy task is to be accomplished. Likewise, he disregards his teacher when the teacher is afflicted, incapacitated, or about to depart for a foreign land.
I shall now describe the sin of that evildoer who abandons one who is being oppressed by enemies while he is reciting the Purāṇa:
he shall dwell in the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as fourteen Indras reign.

That evil-minded person who disregards his first preceptor incurs a terrible sin that yields rebirth in hell for a long time; likewise, he who shows contempt toward his wife, sons, or friends [incurs the same]. 48.
This is to be known as a great sin, equal to the reviling of one's guru.

The killer of a Brahmin, the thief of gold, the drinker of liquor, the violator of the Guru’s bed—these are the perpetrators of the great sins (mahāpātakas), and the fifth is he who associates with them. 49–50.
One who, out of anger, hatred, fear, or greed— especially toward a Brāhmaṇa—
cuts into the vital parts [of another], is proclaimed a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa (brahmaghna). Furthermore, he who, having summoned a Brāhmaṇa who is destitute and begging, [refuses him]...
O King, he who later says "it does not exist" is indeed a slayer of a Brahmin (brahmahā). Furthermore, he who, out of pride in his own learning,
humiliates a twice-born man who is indifferent in the midst of an assembly is proclaimed a slayer of a Brahmin.

Furthermore, he who elevates himself by means of false virtues and opposes his guru is indeed remembered as a slayer of a Brahmin (brahmahā). [This applies even] to those whose bodies are tormented by hunger and thirst and who desire food and drink.
He who creates obstacles for one practicing [virtue] is called a slayer of a Brahmin (brahmaghātaka). He who is a slanderer of all people, intent on searching for their faults,
causing agitation, and cruel— he indeed is remembered as a slayer of a Brahmin.
He who seizes land previously given to the gods, the twice-born, or cows—
even if it has been lost over time— is called a slayer of Brahmins (brahmaghātaka). The seizure of a twice-born’s wealth, even that acquired through a formal deposit, is likewise [a grave sin].

This supreme sin of his should be known as equal to the killing of a Brahmin. He who abandons the Agnihotra and the rites of the five sacrifices, and he who gives false witness against his mother, father, or teachers—[these are likewise equal]. 58–59.
Doing what is displeasing to the devotees of Śiva, eating forbidden foods,
and the senseless slaughter of innocent living beings in the forest; setting fire to cow-pens, forests, cities, and villages.
Thus, these terrible evils— equivalent to the drinking of liquor—
include the seizure of all one's property, as well as the abduction of another's wife, elephants, horses,
cattle, land, silver, clothing, medicinal herbs, and liquids. 61–62.
The theft of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, and fine garments,

as well as the misappropriation of deposits, is recorded in tradition as equal to the theft of gold. Not giving a maiden who is fit for marriage to a suitable groom [is likewise considered a grave offense].
Sexual intercourse with one’s son, a friend, a female relative, or a sister; the violent assault of a maiden;
and consorting with women of the lowest castes (antyajās)—these are recorded as equal to violating the bed of one’s guru when committed with a woman of the same caste.

Those sins which have been described as equal to the great transgressions (mahāpātaka) are designated by the term "transgression" (pātaka); that which is less than those is a minor transgression (upapātaka). Furthermore, he who promises wealth to a twice-born man but does not give it to him—

In that regard, the Brahmin who forgets [the teachings] commits an equal minor offense (upapātaka). Stealing the property of a twice-born, transgressing established boundaries, excessive pride, excessive anger, hypocrisy, and ingratitude—these are likewise [minor offenses]. 67–68.
Attachment to other objects, stinginess, deceit, envy, approaching the wives of others, defiling virtuous women and maidens, being superseded in marriage by a younger brother (parivitti),
being the one who supersedes (parivettṛ), and he by whom the supersession is performed; 69.
Giving away one's daughter to those two, officiating at their sacrifices, and likewise abandoning sons, friends, wives, masters,
and wives in their absence, as well as abandoning virtuous ascetics— [these are forbidden]. (70–71)
The killing of cows, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, women, or Śūdras;
the destruction of trees in a temple of Śiva or the ruin of a sacred grove; and whoever should inflict even the slightest harm upon those dwelling in a hermitage—[these are grave offenses].
The theft of their servants, retinues, cattle, grain, or forest produce;
the stealing of crops, grain, or livestock; performing sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice; and the sale of a sacrifice, a grove, a tank, a wife, or a child. (73–74)
Those women who live off the wealth of women— derived from pilgrimages, fasts, vows, and virtuous deeds— are utterly consumed by the fortune of women.
That man who sells his own dharma and praises what is unrighteous [is likewise lost].
One who speaks of the faults of others, one who looks for the weaknesses of others,
one who covets the property of others, and one who gazes upon the wives of others— these,
O Prince, should be known as equal to cow-slayers. (76–77)
He who is the author of all scriptures, yet is a stealer of cows and a seller of them;
he who is exceedingly merciless toward his servants and a tamer of cattle;
and he who speaks false words and listens to others [in that manner]. (78)
One who betrays his master, betrays his guru, is deceitful, fickle, and fraudulent;
one who eats while leaving his wife, sons, friends, children, the elderly, the emaciated, the sick, servants, guests, and kinsmen hungry—[these are the ones who fall]. 79–80.
They eat what has been well-prepared and give to one who does not ask;

such a person is to be known as a "separate-cooker" (pṛthak-pākī), condemned among those who discourse on Brahman. Those who, having themselves undertaken religious observances, abandon them with their senses unsubdued— [are likewise condemned].
Those who are associated with those who have abandoned the life of renunciation, those who drink intoxicants,
and those who do not diligently protect cows whose limbs are afflicted by consumption or distressed by thirst and hunger—
these are remembered as cow-killers destined for hell. 82–83.
Those who are devoted to every kind of sin, those who divide the four-footed [animals] or the boundaries of fields, those who strike a virtuous person, a Brahmin, a teacher, or even a cow;
and those who beat an innocent woman who stands in the path of the righteous—[these go to hell]. 84.
He whose entire body is bound by laziness sleeps again and again;
they do not nourish the weak, nor do they seek out those who have perished; they oppress them with excessive burdens and compel even the wounded to carry loads. 85–86.
Those who are devoted to all kinds of sins, and those who eat [the flesh of] a cow that has broken limbs, is afflicted by wounds and disease, and is emaciated and tormented by hunger—
even if they do not protect her with effort, such people are known as denizens of hell. 87.
Those men who kill bulls or castrate them, and those who harass calves, become inhabitants of the great hells; likewise, those who,
having encountered one who has arrived seeking food, is afflicted by hunger, thirst, and fatigue— [88-89]
Those who do not honor a guest surely go to hell;
those fools who show no compassion for the helpless, the disabled, the wretched, the child, the aged, or the severely afflicted, they go to the ocean of hell. 90.
One who keeps goats, sheep, or buffaloes, or a Śūdra who is the husband of a Vṛṣalī;
a Śūdra who conducts himself according to the conduct of a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya; artisans, craftsmen, physicians, and likewise those men who serve as temple-priests (Devalakas). 91–92.

Those who perform the work of ministers for wages go to all the hells; he who, having transgressed what has been ordained, collects taxes according to his own will, and he who inflicts punishment in vain, shall be cooked in the hells.

That king whose subjects in his kingdom are oppressed by bribe-takers, officials, and thieves is cooked in the hells; so too are those twice-born who accept gifts from a king who walks the path of sin.
They too undoubtedly go to terrible hells;
for whatever terrible sin belongs to adulterers, thieves, and even to a king who fails to protect, that king incurs it by accepting [the kingdom].
Furthermore, if a king should act without investigation—regarding one who is not a thief as a thief, or conversely, regarding a thief as one who is not a thief—he too shall go to hell;
[as shall he who confiscates] ghee, oil, food, drink, and so forth, as well as honey, meat, wine, and liquor. 97–98.
Molasses, sugarcane, milk, vegetables, curd, roots, and fruits;
grass, wood, flowers, leaves, and even a bronze vessel (99);
sandals, an umbrella, bracelets, a palanquin, and a soft seat.
Copper, lead, tin, bronze, and things produced from water such as conch shells;
musical instruments such as flutes and pipes, as well as household utensils; and wool, cotton, silk, dyes, and lotus-fiber products. 100–101.
Those who, out of greed, steal fine cotton or delicate garments,
as well as other various items such as these—
even if they are of small value— shall quickly go to the hells after having stolen them. (102)
Whether it be that or another substance, even if only the size of a mustard seed, a man who steals it goes to hell; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, even a great deal or a small amount belonging to another is treated as "mine" [by the thief]. 103–104.

Having committed such acts as stealing from a man, there is no doubt that he goes to hell; through these and other such sins, immediately after departing [from this life], a person assumes a previous form for the purpose of having his body destroyed.
By my command, these people, while still in their bodies, go to the realm of Yama (Yamaloka),
being led by the most terrible messengers of Yama and suffering great misery—
those among gods, animals, and humans whose souls were fixed in unrighteousness. 106–107.
The King of Dharma is remembered as the teacher through various most terrible punishments for those who are engaged in disciplined conduct yet become negligent and defiled in soul;
the Guru is the teacher through expiatory rites, and Yama is not seen by means of those.
The king is declared to be the punisher of adulterers, thieves, and those who act unjustly; and for those who are concealed [from his sight], the King of Dharma (Yama) is the punisher.
Therefore, one should perform the expiation for the sin committed.
There is no destruction of an action that has not been experienced even in hundreds of millions of eons;
whoever performs an action themselves, causes it to be done, or approves of it— whether by body, mind, or speech— the result for them is a downward rebirth.

Thus, the various types of sins have been briefly described as threefold. Now, the diverse destinies of men who perform sinful deeds shall be told. O King, this fruit of dharma has been explained in great detail. 112–113.
"O best of men, what else shall I tell you? Tell me that;
the fruit of unrighteousness has been declared, and now I shall also give you the fruit of righteousness.
Having spoken thus, Mātali addressed the king, who was affectionate toward all beings.
In that context, this was narrated by the Great-Souled One as an incidental discourse on Dharma.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Pilgrimage Site of the Ancestors" within the Yayāti-caritra of the Vena-upākhyāna in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The sixty-eighth chapter. Yayāti said:
O Sūta, O Lord, I have heard all about the fruit of unrighteousness.
"Tell me also the fruit of dharma; I have a great curiosity to hear it.
Mātali said:
"Now, these four types of people go to the world of Yama because of their sins."
It is terrifying and inspires great dread; all embodied beings, rendered helpless,
must go there— beings dwelling in the womb, those being born, children, the young, the middle-aged, men, women, eunuchs, and the elderly.
There, the fruits of the auspicious and inauspicious deeds of embodied beings are scrutinized by Citragupta and all others, who are impartial and all-seeing.
There are no living beings there who go to the abode of Yama.
Indeed, action that has been performed must necessarily be experienced; this has been well-considered.
Those there whose actions were virtuous, who possessed gentle minds and were endowed with compassion, go by a gentle path to the abode of Yama.
He who gives wooden sandals or shoes to Brahmins goes happily to the abode of Yama by means of a great celestial chariot;
through the gift of an umbrella, embodied beings travel along the path under a cloud.
Those who give fine garments go to one who is clothed in divine raiment;
by the gift of a palanquin, one shall travel happily in a celestial chariot (vimāna); and by the gift of a comfortable seat, they go happily to the abode of Yama.

The builder of a grove shall go happily in the cool shade; those who donate a flower-grove travel by means of a floral celestial vehicle (puṣpakayāna). Furthermore, the builder of a temple for the gods or of a hermitage for ascetics [attains great merit].
He who provides excellent playhouses for the pavilions of the destitute;
who honors the gods, the sacred fires, the gurus, the brahmins, and his mother and father;
and who, with faith, gives even a small amount to brahmins who are poor yet endowed with virtues.
The virtuous declare that giving at a *śrāddha* ceremony brings all desires within reach in this world. Even if it be only the size of a hair-tip, a gift given with faith is to be highly esteemed;
for among those four factors beginning with the recipient, faith is always my foremost concern. 13–14.
Therefore, faith is always to be trusted, for from faith its fruit arises;
he who gives even dwellings to the poor who are endowed with virtue,
O King, goes to the abode of the Grandfather (Brahmā) where all desires are fulfilled.
Even if only a single *kākiṇī* coin is given with faith to a Brahmin,
that donor becomes a divine guest among kings and gods, increasing their fame;
therefore, gifts should be given by those endowed with faith, for the fruit thereof is certain.
Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Pilgrimage Site of the Ancestors" within the Narrative of Yayāti, in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Sixty-Nine. Mātali said:
Now, the dharmas spoken by Śiva— the supreme scriptures of the Śivadharma—
are to be known as manifold according to the various divisions of *karmayoga*.
They are free from defects such as violence and devoid of affliction and exertion.
Beneficial to all beings, pure, subtle in their practice, and yielding great fruit; possessed of infinite branches yet rooted solely in Śiva;
rich with the beautiful flowers of knowledge and meditation—such are the eternal Śiva-dharmas.
Because they uphold auspiciousness and because they are upheld by the words spoken by Śiva, these are remembered as the Śivadharma-s; therefore, they are the means for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra.
For likewise, [they consist of] patience, truthfulness, modesty, faith, and restraint of the senses.
Charity, sacrifice, austerity, and giving—this tenfold set is the means for accomplishing Dharma.
(5) Now, whether these Śaiva dharmas are performed individually or collectively, once they have brought about complete absorption in Śiva, only one single goal is ordained. (6)
Just as the earth is remembered as the common abode for all beings,

so too is the city of Śiva remembered as equal for all devotees of Śiva. Just as the enjoyments of all beings here in this world are remembered as being characterized by degrees of excellence, [so it is there].
Likewise, in the city of Śiva, enjoyments arise through various specific merits;
yet all embodied beings experience both the fruits of good and evil deeds,
whereas there, the fruit of the single Śivadharma alone is enjoyed.
Whatever merit one may possess, according to the specific nature of the object of faith,
one’s auspicious enjoyments in the city of Śiva should be known as being correspondingly superior. Furthermore,
the attainment of that station is equal [to others], yet the enjoyments there remain characterized by supreme peace.
Therefore, one desiring to attain great enjoyments should perform great merit;
for that alone, cultivated by the best of gods, surpasses all else.
One shall become a sovereign over one's own enjoyments, while Śiva is the Lord of the entire universe.
Some people there are described as being devoted to the yoga of knowledge,
while others, intent on worldly enjoyments, revolve again in saṃsāra.
Therefore, one who desires liberation should abandon attachment to enjoyments.

One who is dispassionate and whose mind and self are tranquil shall attain the knowledge of Śiva. And those beings who, even if their hearts are not fixed on the Lord, worship the Lord incidentally—to them too the Lord grants a station according to their disposition. 14–15.
There, to those who worship Rudra even once and whose sins have been utterly severed,
the Lord grants enjoyments even in the worlds of the Piśācas.
All embodied beings, tormented by the burden of suffering, die.
The giver of food is declared to be a giver of merit, a giver of life, and indeed a giver of everything.
Therefore, by the gift of food, one obtains the fruit of all possible gifts: whatever jewels, enjoyments, women, and vehicles exist within the three worlds.
The giver of food obtains all the fruits of his merit both in this world and the next;
for he whose limbs are nourished by another's food and drink performs a store of merit, half of which belongs to the giver of that food and half to the doer—of this there is no doubt. (19)
The body is the supreme means for attaining dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. Its sustenance depends upon food and drink; therefore, food is the means for everything.
Food is Prajāpati himself, food is Viṣṇu, and food is Śiva himself. (20–21)
Therefore, there has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift equal to food.
Water is remembered as the life-force of all three worlds. Divine water is pure, holy, and a panacea for all things.
Food, drink, horses, cows, clothing, beds, thread, and seats—
these eight gifts are especially praised in the world of the departed (preta-loka).
By such specific acts of giving, a person [attains] the city of Dharmarāja.
Therefore, one should practice dharma with the greatest possible ease; however,
O Prince, those who perform cruel deeds and are devoid of the restraint of sin experience terrible suffering in hell.
In that same way, only those who practice giving enjoy happiness;
for those whose minds are devoted to the yoga of action, happiness arises through divine celestial chariots that fulfill all desires and possess immeasurable qualities. (26-27)
That city is pervaded by countless beings who bring benefit to all living creatures;
it is divine, possessing a thousand moons and a splendor equal to the radiance of the sun.
It is called Rudraloka, endowed with every excellence.
That city is proclaimed for all devotees of Śiva.

And for those who have died in the sacred field (kṣetra) of Rudra—whether they be mobile beings or immobile things—whoever worships Śaṅkara with devotion for even a single day, [attains that state]. 29–30.
Having slept, he went to that most auspicious place; how much more so, then, those Vaiṣṇavas who are devotees of Viṣṇu and intent upon meditation on Viṣṇu?
They too go to Vaikuṇṭha, into the presence of the Lord who wields the discus.

The expounder of Brahman, whose soul is established in dharma, goes to the world of Brahmā; the performer of meritorious deeds goes to the world of merit by means of that great merit. Therefore, one should always cultivate devotion toward the Lord within one's own self.
O Great King, even one who is disciplined in self and possesses knowledge himself must,
therefore, through all-encompassing inquiry and by examining the defects of mental states,
[act] thus through the power of Viṣṇu and even through distinguished ritual action.
Having attained this station of men in accordance with their regional dispositions (35),
this other great and glorious Śivapura has been described;
it is remembered as the place of return for embodied beings devoted to ritual action (36).

Above the city of Śiva, one should know the supreme world of Viṣṇu; those devoted to the meditation on Viṣṇu go there as divine human beings (mānava). But the best of men, the Brāhmaṇas of virtuous conduct, go to the world of Brahmā.
All those who perform sacrifices and are proficient in the principles of reality go to that city. Likewise, kṣatriyas distinguished by their prowess in battle go to the world of Indra,
and others who perform meritorious deeds go to the worlds of merit.
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Story of Yayāti at the Pilgrimage Site of the Ancestors," within the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the Śrī Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Seventy. Mātali said:
I shall now describe the suffering in Yama’s realm, which is exceedingly intense and most dreadful;
all those wicked ones, the cruel slayers of Brahmins, experience it there.
In some places, the sinners are cooked by a fierce fire of chaff.
In some places there were lions, wolves, tigers, gadflies, and dreadful insects;
in some places great leeches, and again in others pythons;
in some places fierce flies, and in some places serpents with virulent poison.
With herds of intoxicated elephants, preeminent in strength and destructive;
with great bulls possessing sharp horns that tore up the path;
and with buffaloes having massive horns that afflict those with wicked bodies.
Tormented by fierce ḍākinīs, by terrifying rākṣasas,
and by most dreadful diseases,
they proceed mounted upon a great scale that is being scorched by a fire below.
They were violently shaken by a fierce wind of great velocity,
split apart on all sides by a rain of massive boulders,
and struck by falling meteors as terrible as the roar of thunderbolts.
Being struck by a rain of blazing coals, they proceed on;
being filled by a great rain of dust,
those men of evil deeds go to the realm of Yama, where they experience terrible suffering for their sins.
Thus, according to their specific sins, the most wicked evildoers experience hell, which is filled with manifold torments. All this has been told to you as the discernment between merit and sin.
"What else shall I proclaim to you, this unsurpassed Dharmaśāstra? (11).
Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Pilgrimage Site of the Ancestors" within the "Story of Yayāti," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. Chapter Seventy-one.
Yayāti said: Although you have explained all this most excellent dharma and adharma,
as I listen, my lack of faith is arising once again.
"Tell me of the worlds of the gods, which are proclaimed to be innumerable, and by what connection with merit they were attained by him, O Mātali. Mātali said:
I shall describe the arrangement of the worlds of the gods, which is attained through yoga and austerity, and which bestows the enjoyment of happiness;
I shall also separately describe the nature of dharma as it is acquired through various efforts.
And [I shall describe] the nature of the worlds above, in their proper sequence.
There, the eightfold sovereignty of the flesh-eating beings is earthly;
therefore, it is remembered as being equal to that of men who have attained immediate liberation (sadyogata).
The power of the Rākṣasas is sixteenfold, and that of the kings (Pārthivas) is of the same kind; thus, without exception, whatever remains belongs to those of noble lineage and splendor.
Furthermore, the power of the Gandharvas is known to be of the nature of wind, and that of the Yakṣas is entirely of the nature of fire.
The great body of Indra consists of the five elements and possesses forty qualities.
That of Soma is mental, divine, belonging to the Lord of All (Viśveśa), composed of the five elements,
gentle, and characterized by a predominance of the qualities of Ahaṃkāra, O Lords of Prajāpati.
The supreme sovereignty of Baudha is sixty-four times that of Brahmā;
the sovereign power of Viṣṇu is based on primordial nature (pradhāna),
while the station of Brahmā is [the sovereignty] in the divine city of Śrīmat-Śivapura, which fulfills all desires.
The sovereignty of Śiva possesses infinite qualities and is a great attribute of his own self;
it is devoid of beginning, middle, or end, pure, characterized by ultimate reality, illuminating all things, subtle, incomparable, and higher than the highest. 10–11.

For one who has attained whatever state that is fully complete, free from worldliness, and brings liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu-pāśa), his enjoyment consists of that very nature;
and by the grace of the Lord, his celestial vehicle (vimāna) shall likewise be equal to it.
These millions of Tārās of various forms are seen;
indeed, twenty-eight of them are thus blazing for those of virtuous nature who offer salutations to the Lord here and there. 13–14.
Through association, curiosity, or greed, they obtain that celestial chariot;
or even he who, through mere circumstance, utters the name of Śiva,
or offers him a salutation— for him there shall be no dissolution [into rebirth].
These are the great paths therein for the performance of auspicious deeds (śivakarma).
Even through internal action, by virtue of their state as lords of men, those persons who—even incidentally—should perform the remembrance of Śaṅkara [attain these]. 16–17.
By them incomparable happiness is to be attained; how much more so by those who are devoted to Him?
With their minds absorbed in meditation, they perform contemplation upon Viṣṇu. They go to the supreme abode, that highest step of Viṣṇu.
O best of men, the form of Śiva and the form of Viṣṇu are one and the same form. There is no difference between these two great-souled ones; they are of a single nature.
To Śiva who has the form of Viṣṇu, and to Viṣṇu who has the form of Śiva.

Viṣṇu is the heart of Śiva, and Śiva is the heart of Viṣṇu; the three gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—are a single form. There is no difference between the three; they are proclaimed as such only through the distinction of their qualities (guṇas). 21.
"O Indra among kings, you are a devotee of Śiva, and indeed a devotee of the Bhagavān.
Because of that, O King of noble vows, the gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—are pleased with you; they are well-pleased to grant boons for your deed."

O giver of honor, having arrived from the region of Indra, go now to the presence of Indra; thereafter, go to the station of Brahmā and Maheśvara. Go also to that of Viṣṇu, which is free from burning and dissolution.

By means of this divine celestial chariot that travels everywhere, you shall possess a divine form; therefore, having ascended the Puṣpaka chariot which moves with ease, enjoy delightful divine pleasures. 25–26.
Sukarmā said:
Having spoken thus to the best of the twice-born, Mātali then became silent before King Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, who was a knower of the essence of dharma.
Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Holy Places of Parents," within the Story of Yayāti, in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Seventy-two. Pippala said:
Having heard the words of Mātali, what did that highly wise king, the son of Nahuṣa, do? Tell me that in detail.
This meritorious story, consisting entirely of virtue, is a destroyer of sins.
"I desire to hear, O wise one; I am never satiated.
Sukarman said:
"Yayāti, the best among all upholders of dharma, was the most excellent of kings."
He spoke to that messenger who had arrived, Mātali, the charioteer of Śakra.
Yayāti said: "I shall not abandon my body; I will not go to heaven again."
Without a body, there is no doubt that there is no king among messengers.
Even though these great defects have been proclaimed as belonging to the body alone,
you have previously explained all its virtues and faults.
"I shall not abandon this body, nor shall I go to heaven again"—
go and report this to Purandara, the God of gods.
O high-minded one, [I say this] even though I am alone with this living body.
Thus, in this very world, one does not attain even worldly success;
for indeed, the body cannot exist without the vital breath, nor can the living soul exist without the body.
O Indra, I shall lead both of them to destruction, as they possess no true friendship.

"O messenger of the gods, knowing this, you must not enjoy the pleasures of heaven; for it is solely through his grace that this life-breath of yours experiences happiness and other enjoyments that follow the mind. (9)
Greatly wicked diseases that cause suffering arise;
O Mātali, they are born indeed from sin and from the defect of old age.
Behold this body of mine, endowed with merit, appearing sixteen years of age.
From birth, a single body proceeds for fifty years;
nevertheless, even for the body, a new state arises.
O messenger, my time has passed away, and the years have gone on infinitely and unsurpassedly.
Just as the body of a sixteen-year-old man shines with beauty,
so does my body shine, endowed with strength and vigor;
there is no exhaustion for me, nor hunger, nor fatigue, nor diseases, nor old age.

O Mātali, even within my body, there increases through the zeal for Dharma that which consists entirely of immortality—a divine medicine, the supreme medicine. Indeed, this which is called Dharma was created in the past for the purpose of destroying the disease of evil. 15.
Therefore, my body has been purified, yet a certain defect remains.
The meditation upon Hṛṣīkeśa and the supreme utterance of His name—this is the elixir of immortality, O messenger; I perform this constantly. 16–17.
By that, those diseases— the defects such as sin and the like— have gone to their destruction;
for while the great medicine of Kṛṣṇa's name exists in this world,
men afflicted by the disease of sin pass away from death.
Great fools do not drink the elixir of Kṛṣṇa’s name. O Mātali, by means of that meditation, knowledge, devotion in worship,
truthfulness, and the merit of charity, my abode is free from all affliction.
From the pursuit of sinful wealth, diseases and afflictions arise for embodied beings;
from these afflictions, death is born for living creatures—of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, dharma must be practiced by men who take refuge in merit and truth.

The body consists of the five elements and is worn out by its veins and joints; thus mortals are joined together like a goldsmith with his crucibles. Therein shines the great fire, which is always moving among the bodily constituents.
O Pippala, that wise man who joins together even a hundred fragments by means of the divine name of Hari and through good fortune is truly wise. Indeed,
those five constituent parts, shattered at their hundred joints, [are joined].
By that [merit], all [the constituent elements] are sustained and the body becomes uniform with the element [of the deity].
Through the ritual offerings to Hari, through meditation, through observance of rules, through truthfulness, and through charity, a new body is born. 25–26.
The defects of the body and diseases perish; listen, O Mātali, for through the internal and external purity [of this practice], a foul odor never arises.
O Sūta, one then becomes pure by the grace of that wielder of the discus.
"I shall not go to heaven; I shall make this very earth into heaven.
By means of austerity, devotion, and my own duty, through the grace of that Wielder of the Discus, I shall transform the surface of the earth into the likeness of heaven. (28-29)
"Knowing this, proceed and speak to Purandara.
Sukarman said:
"Then the charioteer listened to the speech of the king."
Having greeted him with blessings and taken leave of the king, he departed; then he reported everything to the high-souled Indra.
Having heard this from the high-souled Yayāti, the thousand-eyed one [Indra]...
Then he reflected upon how to bring [her] from heaven.
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Holy Places of Mother and Father" within the Legend of Vena in the Yayāti-carita of the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Seventy-three.
Pippalāda said:
After that illustrious one had departed, what did the righteous-souled Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa, do next with regard to Indra’s messengers?
Sukarman said:
When that messenger of the best of gods had departed, the son of the lord of men reflected;
then, having quickly summoned his foremost messengers, he commanded them with words endowed with righteousness and purpose. 2.

"Let the foremost messengers go to the best of cities, to all regions, to all islands, and throughout the worlds; let them carry out my righteous command, and let the people walk upon the excellent path of Hari. [Let them do so] through most meritorious dispositions, through meditations comparable to nectar, and through knowledge, worship, and austerities."
O Madhusūdana, let them abandon the objects of the world and worship You alone through sacrifices and gifts;
let them behold the one Enemy of the Asuras everywhere— in the dry and the moist, in the stationary,
in the clouds, on the earth, in all moving and non-moving things, and even in their own bodies as the form of the living soul.
"Offering gifts for the sake of the gods, through hospitality and ancestral rites, worship Nārāyaṇa, the best of gods; you shall soon be liberated from all defects.
That man who, out of greed or even delusion, does not act upon these words of mine here in this world,"
"That merciless one will surely face punishment, just like a base thief before me.
Having heard these words of the king, all the messengers, filled with joy,
proclaimed throughout the entire earth this royal decree issued by the monarch to the subjects.
"O mortals, beginning with the Brahmins, this most meritorious nectar has been brought by the King of the World;
drink this merit-bestowing nectar called Vaiṣṇava, which is free from defects and has a desirable result.
[Drink] Śrī Keśava, the remover of afflictions, the most excellent, whose form is bliss, and who is the supreme reality."
The nectar of His name, which removes all defects, has indeed been brought by the divine command; let the worlds drink it!

(10) To Him who holds a sword in His hand, known as Madhusūdana, the abode of Śrī, possessed of all virtues, and the Lord of the gods—the nectar of His name, which removes all defects, has indeed been brought by the divine command; let the worlds drink it! (11)

The illustrious Padmanātha, lotus-eyed, the foundational form of the worlds and the Great Lord—this nectar of His name, which removes all defects, has indeed been brought here by the noble king; let the people drink it!
(12) It dispels sin, takes the form of the destruction of disease, bestows bliss, and is the annihilator of Dānavas and Daityas.
The nectar of the Name, which removes all defects, has indeed been brought by the Great King; let the worlds drink it!

(13) The nectar of the Name, which takes the form of the limbs of sacrifice, whose hand holds the discus, which is a mine of merit, and which is infinite bliss, has indeed been brought by the Great King; let the worlds drink it! (14)

The nectar of the Name—the abode of all, stainless, the ultimate repose, known by the name Rāma, the lover, the enemy of Mura—has indeed been brought here by the good king; let the worlds drink it, for it removes all defects.
It is the form of the Sun, the destroyer of darkness, and the eradicator of the bonds that fetter the lotuses of the intellect. 15.
The nectar of the Name, which removes all defects, has indeed been brought by the King of Gods; let the worlds drink it!

(16) This nectar of the Name is true and most meritorious; the high-souled man who is a devotee of Viṣṇu, having studied this with self-restraint at the time of dawn, attains liberation—of this there is no doubt. (17)
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Pilgrimage Site of the Ancestors within the Narrative of Yayāti," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Seventy-four. Sukarman said:
The messengers proclaimed in all the villages, islands, regions, and cities:

"O people, hear the command of the king! Worship Hari with all your powers, with gifts, with many sacrifices, with austerities, with a desire for righteousness, with offerings, and with your whole hearts."
The people meditated upon Madhusūdana according to the command of that king. When all these meritorious words were thus proclaimed, they were heard by the people throughout the surface of the earth;
from that time forward, mortals sacrifice to Viṣṇu, meditate upon him, sing his praises, and recite his names.

With their minds fixed upon him, they [worshipped] Śrī Keśava with well-composed Vedic hymns and mantras, with most meritorious praises comparable to nectar, and through vows, fasts, observances, and gifts;
having abandoned all faults arising from their own body, mind, and speech, they were entirely devoted to love.

They worship Śrī Vāsudeva, the abode of Lakṣmī and the dwelling place of the worlds. Thus, by the command of that king, all people on the circle of the earth abide with a Vaiṣṇava disposition; may they be victorious!
Those proficient in knowledge worship Viṣṇu by means of His names and deeds;
they are absorbed in meditation upon Him, devoted to Him, and solely intent on the worship of Viṣṇu,
as long as the entire circle of the earth exists and as long as the sun shines.
At that time, all those human beings became devotees of the Lord (Bhāgavatas).
Through the power of meditating upon Viṣṇu, and by means of worship, hymns of praise, and the chanting of His names,
those humans then became free from mental anguish and physical disease.
Free from sorrow and meritorious, they all became possessors of ascetic wealth and devotees of Viṣṇu through the grace of that discus-wielding Brāhmaṇa;
they were devoid of diseases and abandoned by faults and passions.
Then, by the grace of that deity, all human beings became endowed with every sovereignty, free from all diseases,
immortal, ageless, and possessed of wealth and grain. 11–12.

O highly fortunate one, by the grace of Viṣṇu, those mortals who are adorned with sons and grandsons will always have most meritorious wish-fulfilling trees at the doors of their houses, which grant the fruits of all desires. 13.
In their meritorious homes there exist cows that yield all desires and likewise wish-fulfilling gems that grant every wish;
they are adorned with sons and grandsons born as both gods and humans.
By the grace of Viṣṇu, they were entirely free from all defects;
endowed with every auspicious fortune, they were possessed of merit and blessings.
(16) They were perfected through highly meritorious gifts and were devoted to knowledge and meditation.

While that king, who knew the Dharma, was ruling, there was no famine, no disease, and no untimely death among men. At that time, all the human beings were devotees of Viṣṇu, entirely dedicated to the vows of Viṣṇu.
Absorbed in that meditation, they all became intent upon the state of non-existence;
O best of the twice-born, their dwellings were divine and meritorious, indeed adorned with very white banners and conchs. 19.
The houses, resembling celestial chariots (*vimāna*), shone with walls painted by skilled artists, featuring flags marked with maces and constantly adorned with discs and lotuses. (20–21)
O best of the twice-born, at the doors of all houses and in sacred places, there are divine forests, auspicious and lush with green grass, containing groves of tulasī and temples of Keśava. 22.
The divine abodes of merit of living beings always shine forth;
O friend, everywhere on the earth, the auspicious nature of Vaiṣṇavas is seen in abundance, along with the sounds of conchs mingling with the sounds of joyful shouts. 23–24.
O best of Brahmins, it is heard that there, on the doors and walls of the houses, conch shells, svastikas, and lotuses— which destroy faults and sins—
were drawn by women out of devotion to Viṣṇu, O foremost of the twice-born. (25)
With songs in beautiful melodies, accompanied by golden ornaments and excellent tones through *mūrchanās* and *tānas*,
the people, devoted to meditation on Viṣṇu,
sang of Keśava; others affectionately proclaimed Hari, Murāri, Keśava, Ajita, and Mādhava.
Those who chant the names of the glorious Nṛsiṃha, the lotus-eyed one, Govinda alone, and Kamalāpati;

who worship Kṛṣṇa, the refuge of all, with prayers, and Rāma with recitations; and who bow down to Viṣṇu with prostrations like a staff—engaged in meditation upon Him, they are the supreme Vaiṣṇavas. 28-29.
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Pilgrimage Sites of Parents," within the Story of Yayāti, in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Seventy-Five. Sukarman said:
Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, Hari, Rāma, Mukunda, Madhusūdana,
Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇurūpa, Nārasiṃha, Acyuta,
Keśava, Padmanābha, Vāsudeva, and Vāmana.
Vārāha, Kamaṭha, Matsya, Hṛṣīkeśa, the Lord of the Gods;
Viśveśa, Viśvarūpa, Ananta, the Sinless, the Pure;
Puruṣa, Puṣkarākṣa, Śrīdhara, Śrīpati, and Hari. 2–3.
"Śrīnivāsa, Pītavāsa, Mādhava, Mokṣada, Prabhu"—
indeed, by uttering these names, all men, including children, the elderly, and young girls, always perform this recitation.
Women, always engaged in household duties, sing of Hari;
on their seats, beds, vehicles, during meditation, and in their speech, they [speak of] Mādhava.
Likewise, even while playing, those children bow down to Govinda.
Day and night they utter the very sweet name of Hari;
O best of the twice-born, the chanting of Viṣṇu’s name is heard everywhere.
By the power of Viṣṇu, mortals wander upon the surface of the earth.
Upon the tops of the temple domes and in the shrines,
the wheels shine just like the orbs of the sun;
the state that is seen in Vaikuṇṭha is now present upon the surface of the earth.
Thus, the merit performed for the Brahmins by that high-souled king brought even the surface of the earth to an equality with the world of Viṣṇu;
so too did Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, who was devoted to Viṣṇu.
The existence of both worlds became one with the surface of the earth;
indeed, no distinction at all was seen between the earth and Viṣṇu.
Just as Vaiṣṇavas utter the name of Viṣṇu in Vaikuṇṭha, so it was here.
O Brahmin, when human beings on the surface of the earth perform such an utterance, a single state is observed for both worlds;
there is no fear of old age or disease, and men became free from death.

The power of their giving and enjoyment is seen to be even greater on earth (verse 14). Furthermore, O best of men, human beings on earth enjoy the happiness and merit arising from their sons, as well as that born of their grandsons, with great ease (verse 15).
By the granting of Viṣṇu’s grace and by his instruction,
men are always liberated from all diseases and become Vaiṣṇavas; indeed,
the power of the heavenly realm has been established on the surface of the earth by the King.
O best of kings, all men lived for a measure of twenty-five years; they were free from diseases, devoted to knowledge and meditation,
dedicated to sacrifice and charity, and possessed of a compassionate nature.
Devoted to helping others, meritorious, fortunate, and vessels of fame,
they were all intent on dharma and dedicated to meditation upon Viṣṇu;
instructed by that king, they became Vaiṣṇavas on this earth.
Viṣṇu said:
"O tiger among kings, listen to the life-story of that monarch. Nahuṣa was eternally devoted to all duties and a constant devotee of Viṣṇu. (20)
Even for him who had lived a hundred thousand years on earth,
his body appeared as if it were twenty-five years old; at that time,
he shone with the appearance and the vigor of one twenty-five years of age.
By the grace of that Wielder of the Discus, those who are powerful and endowed with maturity do not go to Yama after taking birth on the human plane;
they are liberated from passion and hatred and freed from the snares of affliction.
O King, through the merit of their gifts, those people become happy and devoted to all dharmas; they all expand through their progeny,
just as dūrvā grass and banyan trees spread across the surface of the earth.
Just as all these men, expanded through their sons and grandsons,
are freed from the defect of death and indeed live for a long time— 26—
possessing stable bodies, happy, and devoid of old age and disease.
All those on the surface of the earth appeared to be twenty-five years of age;
they were all devoted to truthful conduct and dedicated to the meditation upon Viṣṇu— such was the state of all mortals through the grace of that wielder of the discus.
All of them were free from pride and devoted solely to the enjoyment of gifts; O best of men, not a single mortal was heard to have died in that world,
nor did they experience grief or fall into any fault.
O best of men, by the grace of that wielder of the discus, the very nature of the heavenly realm and the nature of the earthly realm became one and the same;
those messengers of Yama were cast down and struck by the messengers of Viṣṇu. 30–31.

Weeping, they all approached Dharmarāja and recounted to one another everything that had been done by the messengers regarding the king. (32) O Bhāskara, through his acts of charity and enjoyment, the surface of the earth has become as if free from death.
Even by Nahuṣa’s own son, the meritorious Devayāti, who was a devotee of Viṣṇu, heaven itself was manifested. All of this was heard by Dharmarāja at that time.
Then the King of Dharma (Yama), having heard the full account from the messengers and having thus heard this conduct of the king, reflected upon all matters.
Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Pilgrimage Site of Parents" within the Legend of Yayāti, in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The seventy-sixth chapter.
Sukarman said:
Thus, accompanied by all the messengers of Sauri, he went to heaven.
There, he saw the thousand-eyed Indra surrounded by hosts of gods;
then the king of the asuras beheld Dharmarāja approaching, and rising up with haste, he offered him the most excellent *arghya*.
He asked about his arrival: "Tell me everything before me. Having heard those great words spoken by the king of the gods, Dharmarāja related the entire, magnificent life-story of Yayāti.
The King of Dharma said:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, let it be heard why I have come;
I shall tell you here the reason for which I have arrived before you."
Even by the high-souled son of Nahuṣa, who was a devotee of Viṣṇu,
those on the surface of the earth who were made immortal by Vaiṣṇavas [were transformed]; the form of the mortal world indeed became equal to that of Vaikuṇṭha.
Born as immortals and humans, they are free from old age and disease; they do not commit sin, nor do they speak untruth. Devoid of desire and anger, they are free from greed and delusion.
Those great-souled ones, devoted to charity and virtue, were all intent upon the Dharma;
through all dharmas, they worshipped the flawless Nārāyaṇa by means of that Vaiṣṇava dharma on the surface of the earth. 8–9.
Free from disease and devoid of sorrow, all of them possessed stable youth;
like dūrvā grass or banyan trees, O Lord, they spread across the surface of the earth through sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons. Thus did they attain expansion.
Through their sons and grandsons, they passed from one generation to another.
Thus, indeed, the entire mortal world was rendered free from old age and death by that son of Nahuṣa, the devotee of Viṣṇu.
"I have fallen from my station and am deprived of my duties;
all this has been told to you as the cause of the destruction of my merit.
Knowing this, O Thousand-eyed One, act for the welfare of this world."
"All this has been told to you exactly as I was questioned by you.
For this reason, Indra has come into your presence.
Indra said:

Previously, O King of Dharma, a messenger was sent by me to that great-souled one; and what was spoken by his messenger was this: "I have no desire for the pleasures of heaven, nor shall I return to the celestial realm again. (15-16)
"I shall make this entire circle of the earth take on the form of heaven," so the protector of the subjects declared as he ruled the kingdom;
and by the power of his righteousness, I remain constantly in fear.
Dharma said:
"O illustrious King of the Gods, by whatever means possible, bring that lord of the earth here, if you desire my pleasure."
Having heard these words of Dharma, O King, the wise Indra, the lord of the gods, reflected upon the matter in its entirety;
he then summoned Kāmadeva and the Gandharvas.
"O Great-minded One, O God, bring Makaranda and Rati here;
act in such a way that the king indeed comes. Commanded by me, you all must go to the mortal world without a doubt."
Kāma said:
"I shall undoubtedly perform what is pleasing and meritorious for you both; behold the king and me standing here together in the battle."
Having said, "So be it," they all went to where King Sāhuṣi was;
O twice-born one, all those [gods] beginning with Kāma, having assumed the forms of actors through their power, greeted him with blessings and spoke of a fine drama. 23-24.
Having heard those words of theirs, the wise King Yayāti, lord of the earth, convened an assembly hall of divine appearance with highly learned men;
the self-born king himself arrived, skilled in both theoretical knowledge and practical wisdom.
While King Nahuṣa was watching their drama, he beheld the life of Vāmana, who had manifested in the form of a brahmin;
his beauty was peerless in the world, and his excellent singing was melodious.
O King, while singing, she appeared in the form of an aged noble woman;
by means of her song, her grace, her laughter, her charm,
her sweet speech, and the illusion of Kandarpa.
Enchanted by that state of being a thief and by his divine conduct,
he assumed the form of Bala as it was before, and likewise the form of Vindhya-valī as it was in the past, and he made Māra assume the form of Vāmana. 29-30.
The Sūtradhāra himself was Kāma, and the Pāripārśvaka was Vasanta;
the actress who appeared in the dress of Rati had become Sarati, whose lover was delighted.
O King, she moved within the tiring-room during that performance of dance.
The highly wise Makaranda agitated the king; for as the lord of the earth beheld that supreme dance and listened to the song,
so did that noble-souled one delude the king by means of the performance presented by the dancer.
Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Story of Yayāti at the Pilgrimage Site of Parents," within the *Vena-upākhyāna* of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter Seventy-Seven. Sukarman said:
Deluded by the singing, dancing, laughter, and graceful charms of Kāma in the form of a dancer, Pippala, the king of kings,
that son of Nahuṣa, discharged urine and excrement.
Without having performed the purification of his feet, he sat down upon a seat. Having found that opportunity, O best of kings, Jarā moved about Indra’s body at will and performed a beneficial task.
When that drama had concluded and those arrows had departed, the king—
overcome by old age, righteous in soul yet with a mind attached to desire—
was deluded by the delusion of passion, agitated, and his senses were impaired.
Extremely simple-minded yet righteous in nature, he was nonetheless led astray by sensory objects. Once, however, the king, afflicted by the addiction to hunting,
went out and sported in the forest, having fallen under the sway of delusion and passion.
While the high-souled king was sporting in the lake, O King,
a single incomparable deer with four horns arrived;
it was beautiful in every limb, O King, and its body-hair was like gold.
With his limbs beautifully adorned with radiant jewels, handsome and captivating,
he rushed forward with great speed, bow in hand and arrows in his grasp;
thus did that intelligent Daitya, Kopa, approach.
Drawn far away by the deer even as he pursued it,
the king went with the speed of his chariot, exhausted by fatigue;
yet even as he looked on, the deer vanished from sight.
There he beheld a forest, incomparable and wonderful, filled with beautiful trees and graced by the five elements;
it was adorned with noble, holy sandalwood trees and clusters of plantain groves. 11–12.
With Bakula, Aśoka, Puṃnāga, coconut, and Tinduka trees;
with betel-nut trees, date palms, Kumudas, and Saptaparṇakas;
with Karṇikāras in bloom and various trees that bear fruit at all times.
Then,

O great king, as he gazed upon it, he beheld that most excellent lake, five yojanas in extent, filled with holy water and covered with ketakas, pāṭalas, and other flowers endowed with blooming fragrance.
It was crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, made resonant by water-birds, gladdened by lotuses, and adorned with white water-lilies;
it shone with red water-lilies and was decorated with golden lotuses. 16.
It was illuminated by blue lotuses, exceedingly beautified by white water-lilies, and resounded everywhere with the humming of intoxicated bees;
thus Sārva beheld that most excellent place, endowed with every excellence. 17–18.
The lake Sarvatobhadra was five yojanas wide and ten yojanas long, adorned with divine features;
[the king], exhausted by the speed of the chariot and somewhat oppressed by fatigue, [arrived there]. 19.
He sat down there in the very cool shade of a mango tree.
Having bathed and drunk the cool water, which was scented with the fragrance of lotuses, which allayed every fatigue, and which was truly like nectar itself. (20–21)
Then, while the king was seated there in the shade of a tree,
he heard the sound of singing being sung exactly as it was;
this divine sound was heard just as a woman would sing.
The great king, who was fond of music, fell into deep reflection. While that righteous soul, overwhelmed by anxiety, was contemplating for a moment,
a certain wretched woman appeared, with full hips and breasts.
While the king was looking on, she arrived in that forest, her limbs adorned with all ornaments and endowed with the perfection of character and auspicious marks;
having come to that forest, she stood before the king.
The great king said to her: "Whose wife will you become?
For what purpose have you come here? Tell me the reason for that.
When she was thus questioned by him, O Pippala, she did not say anything at all.
Smiling, the fair-faced woman, holding the neck of her lute in her hand, spoke both auspicious and inauspicious words to the king; then that weak woman departed quickly.
At that time, the lord of kings was pervaded by great wonder.
"Though addressed by me, she did not give me an answer.
Then King Yayāti, the lord of the earth, fell once more into reflection regarding that golden,
four-horned deer which had been seen by him.
"Therefore, that which has arisen from a woman does not appear as truth;
this form of illusion will become the truth for the Dānavas.
Having reflected thus for a moment, King Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, [departed].

O Brahmin, while the king was thus reflecting, that woman vanished in the great forest; laughing, she disappeared from the sight of the prince. In the meantime, that same melodious song was heard once again.
He heard a supreme, divine sound, joined with melodic modulations and musical scales; the king went quickly to where that great sound of song arose.
There, at the edge of the water, was an excellent thousand-petaled lotus.
Above him was a supreme woman, endowed with virtue, beauty,
and excellent qualities; she was perfected with divine marks, adorned with celestial ornaments,
and shone with divine splendors, her hand holding the neck of a lute.
Singing a sweet song endowed with rhythm, measure, and tempo,
she enchanted all mobile and immobile beings— gods, hosts of sages, daityas, gandharvas, and kinnaras— by the power of that song. 37.
Having seen that large-eyed woman, resplendent with beauty and splendor, he thought:
"In this world of the moving and the unmoving, there is no other woman like her. Long ago, a dancer afflicted by old age [entered] the very body of the king. (38-39)
Then, as that great desire was stirred, it became manifest, just as fire arises when ghee is touched by the sun's rays.
And upon seeing her, desire likewise became manifest from her body.
His heart possessed by the god of love upon seeing Sītā with her beautiful eyes,
the king reflected for a moment— his mind deeply attached to desire— that he had never before seen a young woman of such form who could enchant the entire world.
Even in her absence, the king then became greedy for her;
burning with the fire of passion and afflicted by the fever of desire, he thought: "How might she be mine? How will our union come to pass? (43)
"When this young woman with the face and eyes of a lotus hides me away,
if she can be obtained, then my life would become fruitful.
Thinking thus, the righteous-souled Yayāti, the lord of the earth, departed.
