He spoke to that woman of beautiful hips: "O auspicious one, has any woman ever been seen by you before who, having been seen once, was seen again? O righteous-souled one, who is this woman standing by your side? whom he questioned.
"O auspicious one, tell me everything; for I am indeed not the son of Nahuṣa. O beautiful lady, I am born of the Lunar dynasty and am the sovereign of the seven continents;
my name is Yayāti, O goddess, and I am renowned throughout the three worlds."

"O auspicious lady, since you desire such a state of mind for the sake of union with me, grant me your company; indeed, do what is most pleasing to me. Whatever you desire, O blessed one, I shall grant it to you without a doubt."
"O lady of excellent complexion, I have been struck down by Kāma, who is difficult to conquer.
Therefore, protect me, who am utterly wretched and have come to you for refuge; [protect] my kingdom, the entire earth, and even my own body."
"I shall give this very triple world to you as a gift upon our union.
Having heard these words of the king, that woman with a lotus-like face spoke to her friend Viśālā: "Go and tell the king that I have arrived."

"O auspicious one, tell me her name, her place of birth, and her father and mother; and with single-minded devotion, declare my own intention before her. Then, having ascertained her desire, [inform] the king of Viśālā. (53-54)
He spoke with sweet words: "O prince, listen! This Kāma was formerly burnt by Śambhu, the god of gods," Viśāla said. 55.
Deprived of her husband, Sāratī wept with a beautiful voice out of grief;
at that time, Sāratī was dwelling in this king of lotuses.
Hearing those very lamentations of hers, so melodious and full of compassion—
O King of kings, having heard this, the gods, filled with supreme compassion, spoke these words to Śaṅkara:
"O Mahādeva, restore the Mind-born one to life once again. (57-58)
"O highly fortunate one, what will this wretched woman, deprived of her husband, become even if she is united with Kāma? Out of affection for us, please bring this about.
Having heard those words, he replied, "I shall restore the Mind-born (Kāma) to life."
Even though deprived of his body, this five-arrowed Mind-born one will undoubtedly become the friend of Mādhava once again;
he will exist with a divine body, and not otherwise. 60–61.
O best of men, by the grace of Mahādeva, the fish-bannered god has been restored to life; having thus greeted the Goddess with blessings, he said, "Go, O Kāma,
and sport eternally with your beloved."
Thus I spoke, O one of great splendor, the agent of preservation and destruction.
Again, Kāma reached the lake where Rati dwells in sorrow; this, O King, is the Lake of Kāma, and here Rati is well-established.
O highly fortunate one, when the six [sages] were burnt, the fire— born from the wrath of Rati and overcome by the pain of love— assumed a terrible form; by that fire,
Rati was excessively scorched and fell into a swoon of delusion.
Then, O best of men, she who was bereft of her husband shed tears;
from her eyes, drops of water fell, and from them arose a great sorrow that destroyed all happiness. (66-67)

O best of kings, after old age had arisen from tears, there was born the dull-witted one named Separation (Viyoga); from him was born the destroyer (Praṇāśaka). Then, both the terrible Affliction (Duḥkha) and Torment (Saṃtāpaka) were born.
From that,
O Great King, there arose fainting— a terrible destroyer of happiness— along with grief, the fever of passion, or delusion, as well as incoherent speech, agitation, insanity, and even death. (69–70)
And from her teardrops were born the Viśvanāśakas;
they all emerged from the side of Rati, possessing squinting eyes, O Great King, embodied and endowed with the quality of true being. 71.
"O King, it was said by someone at that time: 'Kāma has arrived here.
Upon seeing Kāma arrive, she was filled with great joy, and drops of tears fell from her eyes which were overflowing with tears. (72-73)
O Great King, from Cāpalya, offspring were born in the midst of the waters.
From him was born Prīti, O best of men; from her, Khyāti and Lajjā.
From them, O best of kings, Mahānanda and Śānti were born.
Two auspicious daughters were born, O King, who bestow the enjoyment of happiness; their union with Līlā in playful sport was truly great.
Indeed, from the left eye of Rati, drops of tears fell out of joy. (75–76)
O King, from that [lotus] which had fallen into the water, a beautiful lotus was born;
and from that beautiful lotus, O best of men, this woman of lovely countenance was born, the daughter of Rati named Aśrubindumatī. 77.
Out of love for her, O King, I always remain near her, providing her happiness; ever joyful in my nature as her friend, I am auspicious at all times.
I am known by the name Viśālā, O monarch, and am the daughter of Varuṇa.
"And at its conclusion, out of affection, I shall always remain devoted to her;
all this has been told to you regarding her and myself.
O Indra among kings, that lovely-faced woman, desiring a husband, performed austerities.
The king said: "O auspicious one, you have explained everything; it has been understood by me. Listen, O fair-faced one:
let this daughter of Rati worship me in this manner."
"Whatever this fool desires, I shall grant it all to him. Act accordingly, O auspicious lady, so that he may come under my control.
Viśālā said:
I shall proclaim its vow; listen to it, O King:
[one should choose] a man endowed with youth, omniscient, possessing the marks of a hero, equal to the king of the gods, O King, and fully possessed of righteous conduct. 83–84.
O King, he was radiant and possessed of great wisdom; a generous donor and the best among those who perform sacrifices;
a knower of virtues and the nature of dharma, a vessel of merit, equal to Indra among men, and devoted to righteousness through excellent sacrifices. 85.
Endowed with all sovereign powers like another Nārāyaṇa, he was eternally beloved by the gods and exceedingly dear to the Brāhmaṇas;
devoted to the Brahman, a knower of the truth of the Vedas, his prowess was renowned throughout the three worlds. (86–87)
"Endowed with such qualities, honored by the three worlds, wise, very dear, and handsome— such a beloved one does my mind desire.
Yayāti said:
"Know me to have come here endowed with such qualities;
I am undoubtedly created by the Creator as a husband worthy of her.
Viśālā said:
"O King, I know you to be one whose merit has increased throughout the three worlds;
all the qualities previously mentioned by me exist in you. Yet, because of even a single fault, this serpent does not trust you. (90)
"O King, this doubt has arisen in them regarding you, who are composed of Viṣṇu.
Yayāti said:
"Explain the great fault for which they do not approve of me."
"O you whose every limb is beautiful by nature, become gracious and look upon me with a pleasant countenance.
Viśālā said:
"O Lord of the World, why do you not recognize your own fault?"
"Because your body is pervaded by old age, she does not honor you with this.
Having heard these harsh words, the lord of the earth, the king, overcome with great sorrow, spoke to her again. 93-94.
O noble lady, this defect of old age did not arise in me through contact with anyone at any time; nor did I ever experience this onset of aging among people.
For whatever she desires, O auspicious one, even if it be difficult to obtain in the three worlds—
"O Tamasā, if you desire to go to the other world, choose an excellent boon.
Viśālā said:
"When you become free from old age, then she shall be very dear to you."
This is certain, O King; I speak the truth, the absolute truth.
Śruti declares thus, O King: "In whomsoever old age is transferred—to a son, a brother, or a servant—it shall circulate within that person's own body. (97–98)
Having taken his youth and given him old age in return, a beautiful conversation of mutual affection arises between the two through Suruci.
Just as one might give out of compassion for the merit of having given oneself away.
O King, the fruit of that [merit] arises for the one who acted for the benefit of others; there is no doubt in this.
(100) Indeed, when merit acquired with great difficulty is bestowed upon another, it becomes exceedingly meritorious for that person, and he enjoys the fruit of that merit. (101)
"O King, let youth itself be given to your son; therefore, O Lord of the Earth, return having taken hold of beauty. O King, whenever you wish to enjoy [it], then you may do so. 102
Having spoken thus to the king, Viśālā ceased. 103.
Sukarman said: Having heard this, the lord of kings then spoke to Viśālā.
The king said: "So be it, O illustrious one; I shall do your bidding. Thus spoke Yayāti, the lord of the earth, who was deluded and attached to sensual desires.
Having gone home, he summoned his sons and spoke these words:
"O Turu, Pūru, Kuru, and Yadu, who are devoted to your father, O sons, by my command you must ensure my happiness. (105-106)
The sons said: "The words of our father must be carried out by us, whether they be auspicious or inauspicious. O father, let it be spoken quickly; know that it has been done, without a doubt. (107)
Having heard these words of his sons, the lord of the earth, his mind overflowing with joy, spoke to them once again.
Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Pilgrimage Site of Mother and Father," within the Legend of Yayāti, in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The seventy-eighth chapter. Yayāti said:
"O sons, let this old age, which brings misery, be taken up by one of you."
"O wise ones, let youth be granted to me from among yourselves.
For this excellent form of mine, O illustrious ones, is my own;
yet my mind is now scorched, excessively fickle, and attached to women."
Just as fire causes water contained in a vessel to boil away, so too, O sons, has my mind been set ablaze by the fire of desire.
O sons, let one of you take upon himself this old age that brings such suffering.
"Give me your own youth; I shall move about according to my desire. That best of sons who effects the removal of my old age shall enjoy my kingdom and uphold the lineage of the bow."
He shall possess happiness, great prosperity, wealth, and grain; he shall have an extensive lineage, as well as fame and renown.
The sons said:
"O King, you are devoted to dharma and protect your subjects with truth; why has such a state of mind arisen in you, characterized by natural fickleness?
The king replied:
"Previously, dancers came to my city and performed for me;
from them arose this singular infatuation, and such delusion as this has been born within me.
My body is pervaded by old age, yet my mind is possessed by the god of love."
Agitated and overwhelmed by desire, he begot excellent sons.
"O sons, I saw a certain woman of divine form and beautiful face; I spoke to her, O sons, but she did not say anything to me."
Her friend, Cāruvicakṣaṇā, who was named Viśālā, spoke these auspicious words to me, which would bring me happiness:
"When you are free from old age, she will become very dear to you. (11)
Having thus accepted the words spoken by her, he returned home. "For the sake of removing my old age, that was exactly what was proposed by me;
knowing this, O good sons, you must act so as to bring me happiness."
Turu said:
"O King, a body is obtained by sons through the grace of their father and mother; and with that body, O wise one, dharma is performed. (14)
"O lord of men, sons must especially perform service to their parents;
this is not the time for the bestowal of youth. O King, worldly objects should be enjoyed by humans during the first stage of life."

Now this very time has arrived for you at present. O son, having bestowed upon your father the great state that ends in old age, you may enjoy happiness afterwards; otherwise, your life itself would not endure. 16–17.
"Therefore, O Great King, you shall not do this again.
Thus did the eldest son, Tura, then address the king.
Upon hearing those words of Tura, the king became enraged.
The righteous-souled Turuṃśa, his eyes red with anger, said:
"O evil-minded one, you have violated this command of mine; therefore, O sinner, may you become excluded from all dharma. (19-20)

"You shall be shorn of your topknot, devoid of the Vedas and scriptures, and bereft of all proper conduct; of this there is no doubt. You are a slayer of a Brahmin, a wicked one toward the gods, a drinker of liquor, and abandoned by truth."
"You shall become a performer of fierce deeds, the lowest of men.
Devoted to liquor, hungry, sinful, and a killer of cows, you shall be one with foul skin, with disheveled hair, a hater of Brahmins, and an outcast. (22-23)
"You shall always be one who approaches the wives of others, exceedingly fierce, lecherous,
an eater of all things, and evil-minded. You shall take pleasure in women of the same lineage, you destroyer of all dharma."
Deprived of merit and wisdom, you shall become a leper (25). Your sons and grandsons, too, will undoubtedly be like this— Mlecchas who destroy all merit and are thoroughly defiled (26).
Having thus cursed Yadu, he then spoke to his son Pūru: "Indeed, take upon yourself this old age here; enjoy the kingdom free from all thorns.
With palms joined in reverence, King Pūru addressed the king.
Yadu said:
"O father, I am unable to bear the burden of old age; therefore, have mercy.
Cold, travel, bad food, and women who have passed their youth—[these are what I cannot endure]."
And mental aversion—these are the five causes of old age.
O King, I am unable to ward off the suffering of old age while I am still in my youth;
for who indeed is capable of averting it? Therefore, please forgive me now.
O best of the twice-born, the great king, being enraged, cursed him:
"Your lineage shall never again be worthy of sovereignty;
it shall be devoid of strength, splendor, and forbearance, and utterly abandoned by the dharma of the kshatriyas. (31)
There is no doubt that he who turns his back on my teaching will come to ruin. 32.
Yadu said:
"O Great King, I am faultless; why have you now cursed me?"
"Have mercy on me, who am wretched; be gracious and look upon me with a favorable countenance.
(33) The King said: "O son, Mahādeva indeed exists within your lineage even by his own portion."
"And when he performs the emission [of semen], then your lineage shall be purified.
Yadu said: "O Great King, I am your blameless son; you have cursed me."
"If you have compassion for me, let some favor be granted.
The king said:
"He who would be an eldest son, a remover of his father's sorrow—"
He indeed enjoys the inheritance of the kingdom and becomes the bearer of its burden;
yet by you, no dharma has been practiced, so there is no doubt that you are one who should not be spoken to.
By you, my command has been destroyed, and those who strike have been punished with a great rod.
Therefore, there is no favor [to be granted]; do as you wish.
As Yadu said:
"O King, since my kingdom, lineage, and beauty have been consumed by you... (38)

"Therefore, O King, I shall become corrupted; yet, there will be various branches of kṣatriyas within your lineage. To them [I shall grant] villages, excellent lands, women, and whatever jewels indeed exist. (39)
They will eat [them], there is no doubt— those fierce and mighty ones born from my lineage in the form of Turuṣkas and Mlecchas—
who were all devoured by you and cursed with most terrible curses. 41.
O best of kings, when he had thus spoken to the king while being greatly enraged,
the great monarch, filled with anger, again uttered this curse:
"Listen, all those born of your lineage shall be destroyers of my progeny."
As long as the moon and the sun, the earth, the constellations, and the stars endure,
so long shall the Mlecchas be cast into Kumbhīpāka and Raurava;
then, having seen the boy Kuru playing there, endowed with auspicious marks.
Knowing him to be a mere infant, the king abandoned that son, the joy of the monarch;
then the Lord of the World summoned that virtuous Pūru, the son of Śarmiṣṭhā. 45.
Having summoned him, he spoke again: "O Jarā, take back [the body];
enjoy the most meritorious kingdom given by me, with its thorns removed.
Pūru said:
"The kingdom must be enjoyed by you, O King, just as it was enjoyed by your father.
I shall carry out your command; O King, let your old age be given to me, so that today I may possess youth and a beautiful form. (47–48)
"O illustrious one, enjoy pleasures and perform good deeds with a mind attached to sense objects; sport with her as long as you desire.
Father, as long as I live, I shall carry [the burden] until old age."
Thus addressed by that Pūru, the lord of the earth,
filled with great joy, replied to his son: "Since you, my child,
have indeed carried out my command here."

Therefore, I shall bestow upon you that which grants great happiness, since you have surrendered your own youth to me who am seized by old age. O high-minded one, enjoy the kingdom; it has been granted to you by me.
O lord of the earth, having been addressed thus by that king, the noble Supūru gave his youth to him and received old age from him, O monarch; then,
after the exchange of the ages of father and son had been made, [the king departed].
Therefore, Pūru appeared older in all his limbs; the king attained such youthfulness that he seemed like a sixteen-year-old. Endowed with great beauty, he was like a second Manmatha.

The great king gave to that high-souled Pūru the kingdom, the bow, the parasol, the fly-whisk, the throne, the elephant, the treasury, the territory, the entire army, the chowrie, and likewise the chariot. (56–57)

Attached to desire yet devoted to dharma, the son of Nahuṣa, constantly thinking of that woman, went with swift strides to that lake called Kāma, which resembled the ocean, where Aśrubindumatī had gone. 58.
Having seen that large-eyed woman with beautiful, full breasts and a broad figure,
O Great King, his mind was drawn away by Kandarpa.
The king said:
"I have come, O illustrious one, O lady with large and beautiful eyes. O auspicious one, I have cast off old age and am endowed with youth;
having become young, I have now arrived before them."
"Whatever she desires, that he shall surely grant her; of this there is no doubt.
Viśāla said: "When you arrived, having abandoned this wicked old age... (62)
"You are tainted by a single fault, yet you do not consider yourself so.
The king said: "If you know it for certain, then tell me my fault. (63)
"I shall abandon that fault of the thread; there is no doubt that it will take the form of a virtue.

(64) Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Pilgrimage Site of Parents" within the Legend of Vena, in the Story of Yayāti, in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. Chapter Seventy-Nine.
Viśālā said:
"O King, since Śarmiṣṭhā is the wife of him [Yayāti] and Devayānī, the fair-faced one, is his daughter-in-law, prosperity is indeed seen there; otherwise it would not exist."
Therefore, O illustrious one, how could you have become her husband through the power of destiny, established as her lord despite the hostile feelings born of a rival wife?
O Great King, you were like sandalwood upon the earth even while accompanied by a serpent.
O King, just as a great sandalwood tree is indeed encircled by serpents,
so too are you surrounded by snakes known as your co-wives; yet for you,
entering the fire would be better, or even falling from the tip of a flame would be preferable.

She did not regard you, an ocean of virtues, as her beloved, even though you were endowed with beauty and splendor and accompanied by a wife; for she instead cherished such a lover who was joined with poison through his wife. Therefore, she does not honor you.
The king said:
"O fair-faced one, Devayānī and Śarmiṣṭhā have come here for a single purpose;
behold this, which is consistent with the dharma of the virtuous."
Aśrubindumatī said: "O King, I am the enjoyer of your kingdom and the mistress of your body;
O Lord of the Earth, whatever I say must certainly be done by you."
"For this purpose, O lover of dharma, extend your own hand,
which is endowed with many virtues and possessed of beautiful marks.
The king said:
"O lady of excellent complexion, I shall not take another wife than you; O fair-faced one,
enjoy the kingdom, the entire earth, my body, and the treasury— O lovely-limbed one,
this hand of mine is offered to you."
"O blessed lady, I shall do exactly as you say.
Aśrubindumatī said: "By this very act, O illustrious one, I shall become your wife. (11)
Having heard this, O best of men, King Yayāti, the lord of the earth, his eyes agitated with joy, married that auspicious daughter of Manmatha by the Gāndharva rite.
Together with her, the high-souled prince Vīramati wandered along the shores of the ocean, in forests and groves, on delightful mountains, and by rivers. 13–14.
O Indra among kings, while that lord of the earth, the great-souled Yayāti, was thus devoted to pleasure, twenty thousand years passed by in his youth. 15.
O Indra among kings, such was the time spent by that high-minded monarch.
Viṣṇu said:
"O high-minded one, thus was the great king Yayāti then deluded by her, through the stratagem of Kandarpa, for the sake of Indra."
Sukarmā said:
Thus was that King Yayāti, the lord of the earth,
[delighted] by her through enchanting desire, passion, and grace.
Deluded by the daughter of Kāma, he did not distinguish between day and night.
Once, when King Yayāti was thus infatuated, the beautiful-eyed daughter of Kāma spoke to him as he stood bowed, humble, and under her control.
Aśrubindumatī said: "O beloved, my pregnancy longing has arisen; fulfill this desire of mine:
O Lord of the Earth, perform the Aśvamedha, the most excellent of sacrifices. (20)
The king said: "So be it, O illustrious lady; I shall do what is pleasing to you. Having summoned my eldest son, who is indifferent to the enjoyments of sovereignty," 21.
Summoned, he arrived with his neck bowed in devotion;
having joined his palms in reverence, he then offered his salutation. With his neck bowed in devotion, he then prostrated at her feet.
"O King, let an order be given; summoned by you, I have arrived. What shall I do, O illustrious one? I am your servant and I bow before you.
The king said:
"O son of Pūru, prepare the requisites for the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Having been thus addressed, the highly effulgent and supremely righteous Pūru summoned the meritorious twice-born priests and the protectors of the earth. 24–25.
Together with that daughter of Kāma, he received the excellent initiation as described by the Great-Souled One,
having given various kinds of gifts in the sacrificial enclosure of the Aśvamedha.

O Great King, Yayāti, the lord of the earth, gave infinite and abundant gifts to the Brāhmaṇas; he gave especially to the poor. And at the conclusion of the sacrifice, O Great King, he spoke to that lovely-faced woman.
"O young girl, tell me what else is dear to you; what shall I do? O goddess, O lovely-faced one, I shall accomplish all of it, whether it be possible or impossible.
Sukarman said:
Thus addressed by that king, she replied to the monarch:
"O King, O sinless one, grant me that which has arisen as my desire;
[lead me] to the world of Indra, the world of Brahmā, and likewise the world of Śiva. (30)
"O Great King, I desire to see the beloved world of Viṣṇu. O illustrious one, show it to me, for it is very dear to you.
Having been addressed thus by her, the king spoke to that Supriyā.
"Excellent, excellent, O lady of noble form! You speak only of merit,
yet due to the nature of women, O fair-faced one, because of fickleness and curiosity— O highly fortunate one— that which has been spoken by you appears impossible to accomplish."

That which is to be accomplished may be achieved through the gift of merit, or even by sacrifice and austerity (34). Otherwise, O fair-faced one, that which you have spoken would not be achievable; yet what you have described is impossible because it is mixed with merit (35).
"O lady of beautiful hips, even with this very body from the world of mortals,
that man who has heard [this] or seen [it] has gone to heaven today, having performed great merit. Therefore, O lady of excellent form, what you have spoken to me is impossible to achieve."
"I shall do something else that is pleasing to you; tell me what it is, O beloved. The Goddess said:
"O King, there is no doubt that this would be impossible for other men to accomplish."
O Great King, I tell you the truth, the absolute truth:
that which is to be accomplished by you cannot be achieved by penance, fame, kṣātra duties, gifts, or sacrifices; for there is no other mortal man like you in the world of mortals. 38–39.
"The power of a Kṣatriya and great splendor—all this is established in you;
therefore, O son of Nahuṣa, you must act in such a way as to do what is pleasing to me.
Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Pilgrimage Sites of Mother and Father" within the Legend of Yayāti, in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The eightieth chapter. Pippala said:
O best of the twice-born, when the king married Kāmakanyā...

Furthermore, what did those two former wives of his, who were highly meritorious— namely the illustrious Devayānī and Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan— do then? Tell me all of their conduct in my presence.
Sukarmā said:
Since that king brought the maiden Kāmakanyā to his own home, the high-minded Devayānī has been excessively competitive with her. (3)
When her purpose was thwarted, she, her soul agitated by anger, cursed her two sons;
then the illustrious lady summoned Śarmiṣṭhā and raised a clamor.
[She did so] on account of [Śarmiṣṭhā’s] beauty, splendor, generosity, as well as her truthfulness, merit, and vows.
Śarmiṣṭhā and Devayānī were indeed competing with one another;
she (the mother) also perceived their wicked disposition born of passion, and at that very moment, she related everything to the king here.

Then, O great king, the enraged monarch summoned Yadu and said: "Go and bring Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Śukra, here; she must be executed. My dear child, do what is most pleasing to me if you consider it to be for your own welfare."
Having thus heard those words of his father,
Yadu then replied to that lord of kings, his father who bestows honor:
"I will not kill my mother and father, who are free from fault."
The killing of a mother is declared by the learned in the Vedas to be a great sin;
therefore, O Great King, I shall not carry out the execution of these two.
For even if a mother were stained by a thousand sins, [she must still be protected].
"A sister, a daughter of a great king, and likewise again—
neither by sons nor by brothers should she ever be killed.
Knowing this, O Great King, do not kill my mother."
Upon hearing those words of Yadu, King Yayāti, the lord of the earth, became enraged; he then cursed his son, saying:
"Since even you, O sinner, have now disregarded my command."
"Since you have been defiled by my curse, you must take your mother's portion.
Having spoken thus to his son Yadu, the illustrious King Yayāti, lord of the earth, having cursed his son, departed with her.
Intent on the meditation of Viṣṇu, she enjoyed the pleasures of delight;
and that beautiful-eyed Aśrubindumatī, her every limb lovely, enjoyed meritorious enjoyments that were agreeable to the mind along with him. 16.
When that high-souled Yayāti had thus passed away,
all other subjects became free from decay and undecaying; likewise,
O illustrious one, all the worlds became solely devoted to the meditation upon Viṣṇu.
"O Pippala, O highly fortunate one, through austerity, truthfulness, and meditation upon Viṣṇu, all the worlds become happy for those who serve the virtuous.
(19) Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sacred Places of Mother and Father within the Legend of Yayāti," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the Śrī Padma Purāṇa.
The eighty-first chapter.
Sukarman said: O one of great wisdom, just as Indra was always afraid of that Great-Souled One, so too was he.
Having observed Yayāti’s great prowess, his generosity, merit, and other virtues,
he dispatched the Apsaras Menakā on a mission as a messenger, saying: "Go, O blessed and highly fortunate one, and deliver my command."
"Go to the city of Amita and speak the words of the King of the Gods;
by whatever means possible, bring the king here.
Having heard this, Menakā, who had been sent there, arrived.
She related all of that which had been spoken by the king of the gods. Having been thus addressed and urged, Menakā departed;
and when Menakā had gone, the high-minded daughter of Rati remained there.
The illustrious lady replied to King Dharmasaṃketa:
"O King, in the past, I was brought [to you] by your word of truth; your own hand was placed within mine, and I was led to your palace."
"O King, whatever I say must indeed be done by you. Since you,
O hero, have not acted according to my words, I shall therefore abandon you and go to my father's house."
The king said:
"O blessed lady, I shall undoubtedly do for you exactly as you have stated;
however, O Goddess, having set aside what is impossible, tell me that which is possible."
Aśrubindumatī said:
"For this very purpose, O beloved of the earth, you have been chosen by me—endowed with all auspicious marks and possessed of all virtues. (10)
Knowing him to be the accomplisher of all things and the sustainer of all,
the creator of all dharmas and the originator of meritorious deeds; knowing him to be the achiever of the three worlds and truly peerless within the three worlds— 11.
"I know him to be a devotee of Viṣṇu, the greatest among Vaiṣṇavas. With this hope, I previously accepted you as my husband;
for he who possesses the grace of Viṣṇu may wander everywhere.

O Indra among kings, O observer of noble vows, there is nothing difficult to attain in all the three worlds, including the mobile and immobile beings, nor in any of the auspicious realms; for by the grace of Viṣṇu alone, you possess this supreme movement through the sky.
O lord of the earth, having arrived at the world of mortals, you yourself have made people free from old age and grey hair, and even free from death,
at the doors of every house of mortals, O bull among men. (15-16)
By you alone have many wish-fulfilling trees (kalpadrumas) been fashioned for those mortals in whose homes sages and wish-granting cows (kāmadhenus) reside.
O King, they were sent by you alone and have been made to remain forever stable.
All men have been made happy by you with all their desires fulfilled.
Within a single house, a thousand noble-born ones are seen;
thus has the increase of the lineage of men been brought about by you.
O best of men, by opposing even Yama and Indra,
you have made the mortal world free from disease and sin;
through your own splendor and ego, the surface of the earth has been transformed into heaven.
It has been shown, O Great King, that there is no sovereign equal to you. Indeed, no man like you has ever been born, nor will one ever be born;
thus do I know you to be the illuminator of all dharma. 21–22.
"Therefore, you have been made my husband by me; speak thus before me. O Indra among kings, having spoken jestingly, you must now speak the truth before me.
O lord of men, if truth exists here for you, let dharma exist for you."
In the worlds of the gods, there is no higher course than this sky-faring [of yours].
(24) But when you abandon truth and do not go to heaven, then your word will undoubtedly become false; of this there is no doubt. (25)
"For whatever merit was previously performed will be reduced to ashes.
The King said:
"O blessed lady, you have spoken the truth; there is nothing for me to accomplish, nor anything impossible for me. (26)
O Lord of the World, by your great grace, all this world is easily attainable for me;
O Goddess, hear now the sole reason why the gods do not come to this mortal realm. (27) Indeed, the deities will not grant permission to enter the world of mortals.

"Therefore, O fair-faced one, all these human beings and all creatures shall be joined with death when deprived of me; there is no doubt about this. I have no desire to go to heaven; this is the truth I have spoken, O fair-faced one. (28-29)
The Goddess said:
"O Great King, having seen the worlds, you shall indeed return again; fulfill my present and most incomparable faith. (30)
The king said,
"I shall do everything exactly as you have stated, without a doubt," and having thus spoken,
the highly effulgent Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa, looked around.
Having spoken thus to his beloved, the king then reflected:
"Even a fish dwelling within the water is caught by a net;
even a deer possessing speed equal to the wind meets with capture."
A bird perceives bait situated at a distance of thousands of yojanas, yet,
deluded by fate, it does not see the noose already caught around its neck;
Time makes the even uneven, and Time is the destroyer of honor.

Time, which brings about humiliation, wherever it may abide, makes a man a donor and then again a petitioner; so too does it affect all beings, whether stationary or otherwise, in heaven or on earth. 35.
Time encompasses everything; indeed, Time alone is this entire universe. (36) Without beginning or end, Time is the sustainer and the supreme cause of the world;
Time ripens the worlds like fruit placed upon a tree. (37)
Neither mantras, nor penance, nor charity, nor friends, nor kinsmen are able to protect a person afflicted by Time.
Three snares created by Time cannot be overcome.
Marriage, birth, and death—whenever, wherever, and by whomsoever they occur; just as clouds are driven through the sky by the wind, so too is this world driven by time joined with karma. 39–40.
Sukarman said:
"Time, when conjoined with action, is worshipped by men;
time impels action, and time itself performs that [action]. (41)

Accidental injuries, the faults of violence, serpents, and diseases— all these are appointed by karma and they operate among human beings. Furthermore, those means which are the causes of happiness are mixed with merit.
They would see all those joined with their karma, whether auspicious or inauspicious; for in this world,
karma is the inheritance, and karma-bound kinsmen urge a person toward happiness or suffering.

Just as gold or silver is determined according to its specific form, so too is a living being bound by the power of its own karma. These five [elements] are produced here even while the embodied being is still in the womb.
Life-span, karma, wealth, knowledge, and even death— just as a maker fashions whatever he desires from a lump of clay,
so too does previously performed karma follow after the doer. 46–47.
Divinity, humanity, the state of a beast, a bird,
as well as the condition of an animal or an immobile being, is attained through one's own actions; he alone experiences that accordingly, as it has been eternally ordained by himself.

The suffering ordained by oneself and the happiness ordained by oneself—beginning from the bed of the womb, beings experience the results of their previous bodily actions; on this earth, men never abandon their own karma. 49–50.
Whether by strength or by wisdom, those capable of acting otherwise enjoy the fruits of their well-performed deeds, both suffering and happiness;
yet, having encountered a cause, a man is constantly bound by the fetters of karma. 51.
Just as a calf finds its mother among a thousand cows, so do auspicious and inauspicious karmas follow the doer;
for them, there is no destruction except through experience. 52–53.
Who is able to alter past karma, that bond? Even as one runs with great speed, destiny pursues him; it lies down together with him, according to how his past actions were performed.
As he stands, it stands near him; as he walks, it follows him.
As he performs an action, it conforms to the doer, just as shadow and sunlight are eternally and intimately bound to one another.
In the same way, the doer of karma and the wheel [of destiny] are well-bound to one another;
subsequently, planets, diseases, poisons, serpents, *śākinīs*, and likewise *rākṣasas* afflict the person who has already been tormented by his prior karma. (57)
Wherever one is destined to experience pleasure or even pain,
there one is led by force, as if bound with a rope, by destiny;
for destiny is the master over all beings in the production of pleasure and pain.
One thing is thought of by a person while awake or even while sleeping, yet it happens otherwise; thus, O wise one, destiny seeks to destroy one's efforts.
That which ought to be protected from weapons, fire, poison, and difficult terrains, destiny protects instead.
Truth remains unguarded; thus it is protected by destiny.
But for that which is destroyed by destiny, no protection is seen, just as seeds sown upon the earth or even riches [perish]. 61–62.
In the same way, actions abide within the self and emerge from it; just as a lamp reaches extinction when its oil is exhausted,
so too does a living being meet destruction of the body upon the exhaustion of karma.
The wise who know reality have declared that death occurs through the exhaustion of karma. (64) Various living beings are the causes of that death and of disease;
likewise, this is the ripening of my own past actions, and not otherwise. (65)
"He has arrived here; there is no doubt about this. He is in the form of a woman, without a shadow of a doubt.
Where is the house for us who have come as actors, dancers, and performers?
Through association with them, old age has taken hold of my body."
"I firmly believe that everything has been accomplished by my own actions;
therefore, action is paramount, and other means are useless.
Long ago, for my sake, the best of messengers was sent by the King of the Gods."
"Sent by him, Mātali spoke these words to Nakṛta;
now the ripening of that karma of his is seen by me. Thinking thus, he became absorbed in reflection, overcome with great sorrow.

"If I do not grant this at all out of affection for the serpent's words, then both truth and dharma will depart from me; there is no doubt that what has come upon me through my own actions is now manifest. (70-71)
"There will be no doubt; for destiny is indeed difficult to overcome.
Having become thus absorbed in thought, Yayāti, the lord of the earth, went for refuge to Hari, the god Kṛṣṇa, the remover of afflictions.
Having meditated upon and praised Madhusūdana with his mind, he said:
"Protect me, O beloved of Kamalā; I have come to you for refuge.
Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Story of Yayāti," within the description of the Tīrthas of Parents in the Legend of Vena, in the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The eighty-second chapter.
Sukarman said:
While the king, who was exceedingly unrighteous, was thus reflecting, [the following occurred].
Then that goddess, the daughter of Rati, with her beautiful countenance, spoke:
"O King, O high-minded one, what are you reflecting upon here? Generally, all women are fickle; of this there is no doubt."
"I do not cause you to waver in this way out of fickleness,
O best of kings; for I am not acting thus today out of desire for another woman, as others in the world might speak out of capriciousness."
O Indra among the lords of kings, those who are greedy and lustful commit improper acts out of delusion. You have been born merely for the sake of being seen by the world;
for the sight of the gods is meritorious and indeed difficult for mortals to obtain.
O King, tell me if there is any fault or evil-creating consequence that might arise from my association with them, such that I should not allow you to see them; for in this way,
you would suffer as any other ordinary person would.
Just as one terrified by great fear, or as one fallen into a pit of delusion—O Great King, abandon your anxiety; you must go to heaven. Whatever causes suffering to arise, that I shall never do.
Thus addressed by the king, he spoke to that lovely-faced lady:
"O Goddess, listen now to that which has been contemplated by me;
O beloved, I have never seen my own pride shattered."
"When I have gone to heaven, O beloved, there will be suffering for the subjects and others. This evil-minded one will terrify the people with diseases.
O lady of beautiful countenance, I shall go to the heavenly world together with you."
Having spoken thus, the king summoned his eldest son, Pūru, who was a knower of all dharmas, possessed of great intelligence, and burdened with old age:
"Come, come, O knower of all dharmas; you know dharma with certainty."
"O you whose soul is devoted to dharma, by my command you have preserved dharma. Father, give me back my old age and take back your youth;
rule this kingdom of mine, complete with its treasury, army, and mounts."
"O highly fortunate one, enjoy the earth, filled with jewels and extending to the ocean, given by me along with its villages, forests, and cities.
O sinless one, you must always perform the meritorious duty of protecting your subjects."
"The constant punishment of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous must always be performed by you,
O highly fortunate one, according to the authority of the scriptures of dharma and by means of your own duties prescribed by rule. (16-17)

One must perform protection with devotion, for he is worthy of worship in the three worlds; O wise one, look toward his treasury on the fifth and seventh days, and always honor his strength with favors, wealth, and food.
Be one whose eyes are spies; be constantly devoted to giving. Be self-restrained in the mantra, which must always be kept secret by the truly wise.
Be disciplined in soul, my son, and do not go hunting.
Trust should not be placed in anyone, nor in women, nor in a sword, nor in great power;
however, you should gather all the vessels and all the arts. By worshipping Hṛṣīkeśa with sacrifices, may you always be a person of meritorious soul.
Day by day, crush all thorns that afflict the subjects;
day by day, grant all that the subjects desire. O son, you must ensure the happiness of the subjects and nourish them. 22–23.

One should establish one's own lineage; do not set your mind on the wives of others, nor on the wealth of others; always follow the ancestors. Indeed, one should always contemplate the Vedas and all the scriptures. 24.
Do exactly this, my child; always remain devoted to the practice of weapons. Always be content, my child, and intent upon your own bed [of discipline];
always practice with the elephant, the horse, and the chariot.
Having thus addressed his son and honored him with blessings, he placed the weapon given by himself into his hand with his own hand;
having taken back his own old age and bestowed youth upon him.
Then, desiring to go to heaven, Yayāti, the lord of the earth, departed.
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Account of the Pilgrimage to Mother and Father," within the Story of Yayāti in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Eighty-three.
Sukarman said:
Having summoned all the subjects of the continents, the lord of the earth, filled with great joy, spoke these words. 1.
O best of beings, I shall go to the world of Indra, the world of Brahmā, and the world of Rudra beyond that,
as well as to the realm of Viṣṇu which destroys all sins and grants the ultimate goal to living beings;
of this there is no doubt, for I am going along with her.
"O Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras,
my subjects, you must dwell upon this earth with ease along with your families.
This highly fortunate Puru shall be your protector here."
"O King, the steadfast Ustimayālokārāja has been established along with his staff.
Having been addressed thus, all those subjects spoke to the king:
"O best of kings, it is heard in all the Vedas and Purāṇas—"
By whom indeed was such a Dharma seen in the world before? This Dharma,
which possesses ten limbs and is beloved by Truth, was seen by us in the great house of Nahuṣa, born of the Lunar dynasty.
Endowed with hands, feet, and a face, he was the practitioner of all proper conduct;
he was perfected in both theoretical knowledge and practical wisdom, a great treasury of merits,
a mine of virtues, O Great King, and a scholar of truth.

Those who possess great luster and are devoted to truth perform this supreme dharma. We have seen that dharma in you, who can assume any form at will, who are the fulfiller of desires, and who are such a speaker of truth.
"By all three kinds of karma, we are unable to abandon you;
wherever you go, there we shall go, for that place will be most happy and meritorious. Even if it be in hell, wherever you are, there we shall be—of this there is no doubt."
Of what use are wives, wealth, enjoyments, life, or even this very existence?
O Great King, there is no reason for this other than you; O Lord of Kings, we shall go with you alone, and not otherwise. (12-13)
Having heard these words of those subjects, the lord of the earth,
filled with great joy, spoke these words to his people:
"Let all the most meritorious regions come along with me."
The king, having ascended his chariot together with that maiden of his desire,
proceeded with her in a swan-colored chariot resembling the lunar disc,
while being fanned with chowries and fans, his distress now gone.
Shining with that banner of merit,
pure and most exalted, he appeared like the god Purandara, the king of the gods;
while being praised by sages, as well as by bards and celestial minstrels.
Being praised by his subjects, Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, [departed].
Then all the subjects, mounted on vehicles—elephants, horses, chariots, and others—set out toward heaven to accompany the lord of men. 18–19.
The Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and other common people—
all the worlds were Vaiṣṇavas, devoted solely to the meditation upon Viṣṇu.
Their banners were white and adorned with golden staffs.
All were marked with conchs and discs, and all carried staffs and banners. Among the multitudes of subjects, their banners fluttered in the wind;
they all wore divine garlands and were adorned with tulasī leaves. 21–22.
With their limbs smeared with divine sandalwood and anointed with celestial perfumes,
adorned with the beauty of divine garments and decorated with divine ornaments,
all those people of beautiful form approached the king.
Hundreds of thousands of subjects, as well as hundreds of lakhs and crores,
and thousands of arvaks and kharvas— these people all followed the king; they were all devotees of Viṣṇu and performers of meritorious deeds.
All were intent on meditation upon Viṣṇu and devoted to the practice of recitation and charity.
Sukarman said:
"Thus they all set forth, filled with great joy. (26)

Having consecrated his son Pūru in his own kingdom, O Great King, Yayāti, the lord of the earth, then departed for the realm of Indra; this was due to his splendor, merit, righteousness, and asceticism at that time. 27.
All those Tejans set out for the supreme realm of Viṣṇu.
Then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and Cāraṇas,
together with the king of the gods, arrived before them at that time.
O best of kings, while they were honoring that very lord of men, Indra said:
"Welcome to you, O great king; enter my abode. 30.
"Enjoy here the divine pleasures that follow your heart's desire.
The King said: "O thousand-eyed one, O highly wise one, [I seek] your pair of lotus-feet. (31)
"I pay homage to the gods; I am going to the world of Brahmā.
Being thus praised by the gods, he went to the world of Brahmā, where the lotus-born one of great splendor was then together with the best of sages.
He offered him hospitality with water for the feet, respectful offerings (arghya), and excellent seats;
he said, "Go indeed to the world of Viṣṇu by virtue of your own deeds.
When the Creator had spoken thus, [the sage] went to the abode of Śiva.
Śaṅkara, together with Umā, performed the rites of hospitality for him;
and to that very lord of kings, he spoke these words:
"O Indra among kings, you are a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, and you are very dear to me as well."
"Therefore, O Indra among kings, dwell in my palace;
enjoy all pleasures that are difficult for mortals to attain. There is no difference between me and Viṣṇu, O Indra among kings—of this there is no doubt. (36-37)
He who exists in the form of Viṣṇu is undoubtedly Rudra; O King, he who is known as Rudra is the eternal Viṣṇu. There is no difference between the two; therefore, I speak thus.
"I myself shall grant a place of residence to you, a meritorious devotee of Viṣṇu.
Therefore, O sinless great king, you must remain here.
Having been addressed thus by Śiva, Yayāti, the beloved of Hari, departed.
Having bowed with devotion to Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods, with my neck bent low, [I said:
"O Mahādeva, all of this has now been spoken by you;
there is no difference between you two, for the one form has become twofold."
"I wish to go to the realm of Viṣṇu; I bow at your feet.
"So be it, O Great King; go now to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus commanded by Śiva, the lord of the earth departed. 42-43.
Then, by those great meritorious Vaiṣṇavas, beloved of Viṣṇu,
who were dancing before that king,
[the place was filled] with the sounds of conchs that destroy great sins and with abundant lion-roars.
He was honored by excellent bards with the sounds of the *jagāmanī* lute (45),
while reciters learned in the scriptures sang with melodious voices. Before him, the Gandharvas, devoted to song, sang their praises (46).
Being praised by the sages and accompanied by hosts of gods,
and being served by beautiful apsaras,
the son of Nahuṣa was attended by gandharvas, kinnaras, siddhas, and cāraṇas of auspicious merit.

The great king was being praised on all sides by the Sādhyas, the Vidyādharas, the Ādityas, the Maruts, and likewise the Vasus; by the Rudras, the hosts of Ādityas, the world-protectors, and the lords of the directions, as well as by the three worlds.
O King, he beheld the incomparable and painless realm of Viṣṇu,
adorned with golden celestial chariots that were suffused with every splendor,
and graced by vehicles as white as swans, kunda flowers, and the moon.

With palaces a hundred stories high, resembling Mount Meru and Mandara, with peaks scraping the celestial vault and adorned with gold, and with brilliantly blazing finials, that most excellent city shines forth. 51-52.
Just as the sky is illuminated by clusters of stars, that world of Hari shines with the splendor of its radiance;
it gazes, as it were, with blazing flames of light as if they were eyes, and with various jewels as if they were smiling teeth. (53)

O Indra among kings, by means of the banners— those charming tips of the flags, with their excellent sprouts moving at the top, swayed by the wind— they seemed to summon those meritorious Vaiṣṇavas who are beloved of Viṣṇu. 54–55.
It was adorned everywhere with golden staffs and bells,
and further embellished with gate-towers and watchtowers radiant as the splendor of the sun,
as well as with windows, lattices, and charming casements.
With the illumination of the city gates, with ramparts adorned with golden figures (57), with archways and beautiful banners, with various most auspicious sounds,
and with the tops of water-pots and discus-marks possessing a luster equal to the sun’s orb (58).
With excellent palaces having a hundred stories, resembling waterless clouds,
adorned with staffs, umbrellas, and jars,
and graced by mansions shaped like monsoon clouds; 59.
With those beautiful jars, the surface of the earth became like the sky with its constellations of stars;
with their networks of staffs and banners possessing a luster equal to a cluster of stars,
they appeared like crystal forms, resembling the moon and the conch in their brilliance.

Haripattana shines with tens of billions of celestial chariots (*vimāna*), numbering in the hundreds of millions, which are crowded with golden palaces and composed of various precious minerals, and are endowed with every object of enjoyment.
Those men by whom the Lord, the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, has been propitiated, dwell by His grace within their own homes and in all divine,
meritorious abodes rich in enjoyments.
The Vaiṣṇavas, performers of meritorious deeds whose every stain has been washed away,
[inhabit] that temple of Viṣṇu adorned with such holy dwellings;
it is filled with various trees and forests beautified by sandalwood.
O King, it was adorned everywhere with the fruits of all desires,
beautified by ponds, pools, and lakes graced by cranes, swarms of *haṃsa* and *kāraṇḍava* birds, and splendid with white water-lilies (*kalhāra*). 66–67.
Vaikuṇṭha, rich in every splendor and adorned with divine gardens, shines with hundred-petaled great lotuses, with ponds resplendent with lotuses and water-lilies, and with golden lotuses. 68.
Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, beheld Vaikuṇṭha, the unsurpassed abode of liberation, filled with divine splendor, graced by the Vaiṣṇavas,
and crowded with hosts of gods. 69–70.
He entered the beautiful city, which was entirely free from fire; there he beheld the healthy Nārāyaṇa, the destroyer of all afflictions,
resplendent with celestial chariots and adorned with every ornament.
He is the Lord of the World wearing yellow garments, marked with the Śrīvatsa, and possessed of great splendor;
mounted upon Vainateya, endowed with Śrī, he is higher than the highest, the Supreme Lord who is the ultimate goal for all the worlds of the gods. 72–73.
Hari shines forth in the form of supreme bliss as absolute liberation (kaivalya), served by great worlds and by most meritorious Vaiṣṇavas;
he is crowded with hosts of gods and attended by throngs of Gandharvas. 74.
Then the king, together with his wife, bowed down to the high-souled Hari, Nārāyaṇa, who removes the affliction of suffering;
and all the human beings there, being devotees of Viṣṇu, prostrated before Madhusūdana.
O high-minded one, as soon as he had departed, all the Vaiṣṇavas, together with the king,
bowed with devotion at his two lotus feet; they paid homage to that great-souled king of radiant splendor.
Hṛṣīkeśa said to him: "I am pleased, O you of firm vows! Choose a boon, O Indra among kings, whatever dwells in your mind;
I shall grant it to you without doubt, for you are my devotee, O high-minded one. (78-79)
The king said:
"O Madhusūdana, Lord of the gods of gods, if you are pleased with me,
O Lord of the universe, grant me forever the status of being your servant."
Viṣṇu said: "So be it, O illustrious one! You are my devotee without a doubt; O great king, you must remain in this world together with her."
Having been addressed thus, the great king Yayāti, the lord of the earth, by the grace of that deity, has attained the realm of Viṣṇu;
this monarch now dwells in the supreme world of Viṣṇu. 82–83.

Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Ascent of Yayāti to Heaven," within the Story of Yayāti, in the Description of the Pilgrimage Sites of the Ancestors, in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Eighty-four.
Sukarman said:
All this history has been narrated to you; it is divine, a destroyer of sins, a savior for sons, and a bestower of great merit.
This account of Yayāti’s life, once heard, is visibly perceived in the world.

Through Pūru, a great kingdom was obtained; Turu fell into misfortune through his father’s favor and his own anger, yet he was restored to his former state again. This [account] is meritorious, conducive to fame, and bestows wealth and grain upon sons.
These two words joined with a curse are most terrible and difficult to endure;
there is nothing equal to father and mother that bestows the desired fruit. With a longing heart, the father should summon his son.
Listen to the fruit of his merit: when a mother calls out, "O son, O son," and the son, filled with great joy, goes toward his mother, he shall obtain the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā. (5-6)
O highly illustrious one, the son who washes their feet enjoys the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas) through the grace of those two;

The son who supports his guru with food, clothing, and bathing attains merit equal to the gift of the entire earth; for the mother is indeed Gaṅgā, the embodiment of all sacred fords—of this there is no doubt. 8–9.
"Just as the ocean consisting of much merit is established in the world,
so too do the ancient poets know it to be established in this hair-pore.

Furthermore, that son who insults or causes harm to his father or mother goes without doubt to the hell named Raurava.
Likewise, the householder who does not support his aged mother and father [is likewise condemned].
He shall go to hell with his sons and will certainly experience intense suffering. When a wicked-minded son reviles his guru,
no atonement for that has ever been seen by the poets of the Purāṇas.
Knowing this, O Brahmin, I worship my mother and father every single day with constant devotion, my neck bowed low;
and having summoned me, my guru would instruct me in what ought and ought not to be done. (14)
O Pippala, I perform that [service] without hesitation according to my ability;
by that, supreme knowledge which grants liberation has arisen in me, and through the grace of these two, I do not wander further in saṃsāra. 15–16.
Whatever humans dwelling on earth perform,
and whatever proceeds in heaven, I, as a householder, know it all; O Pippala, even while staying here, I know the conduct of the Nāgas.
"O best of Vidyādharas, it is by the grace of these two that the three worlds have come under my control; you should worship Mādhava.

Thus urged by him on account of his own past actions, Pippala bowed to that best of the twice-born and, though filled with shame, departed for heaven; and Sukarman, O King, being righteous in soul, continued to serve his preceptor.
All this concerning the ancestral pilgrimage sites (pitṛtīrtha) has been narrated by me to you; I shall speak further regarding the Vadava [site], O high-minded one. 21.

The eighty-fifth chapter. Vena said:
"O Blessed One, O Lord of the gods, by your grace toward me..."
The Bhāryātīrtha is well-known, as is the unsurpassed Pitṛtīrtha;
O Hṛṣīkeśa, the Mātṛtīrtha bestows great merit.
Becoming gracious and well-disposed, please tell me now about the Guru-tīrtha.
The Blessed Lord said:
O King, I shall describe the unsurpassed Gurutīrtha, which is declared to be the remover of all sins and the bestower of the ultimate goal upon disciples. 3.
It is the supreme merit for disciples, the eternal form of Dharma, the highest sacred ford, the supreme knowledge, and the bestower of perceptible fruit;
by whose grace, O Lord of Kings, one enjoys the fruit even in this very life. 4.
By his grace, O Indra among kings, one enjoys happiness in the next world and attains fame and renown;
indeed, through that high-souled Guru, the entire triple world with its mobile and immobile beings is seen directly by his disciples. 5-6.
O prince, the disciple attains proficiency in worldly transactions, conduct,
and specialized knowledge, and indeed proceeds toward liberation;
for he is the illuminator of all the worlds, just as the sun is.
The Guru is the illuminator; likewise, he is the supreme refuge for his disciples.
O best of kings, it is during the night alone that the Moon shines;
by its splendor, it accomplishes every function pertaining to the moving and the unmoving.
O best of kings, a lamp illuminates a multitude within a house and destroys all the dense, turbid darkness with its radiance; likewise,
the guru illumines the disciple who is enveloped by the darkness of ignorance.
O Mahāmati, through the illuminations of instruction for disciples, [he shines]. The sun is the illuminator by day; the moon is the illuminator at night;
and the lamp is the constant illuminator of the house that destroys darkness. 11–12.
Day and night, within the confines of his home, the Guru always destroys all the darkness known as ignorance for his disciple;
therefore, O Lord of the Earth, the Guru is the supreme sacred ford for disciples.
Having understood this, the disciple should always worship him;
knowing the Guru to be composed of merit, one should do so through the three kinds of action.
In this regard, O Brahmin, an ancient historical narrative is heard.
It is declared that this [rite] removes all sins; it belongs to the high-souled Cyavana.
Born in the lineage of Bhārgava, Cyavana was the best of sages. O best of kings, once a reflection arose in his mind.
"When shall I become perfected in knowledge upon this earth?
(17) Thus did that best of sages, seeking knowledge, reflect day and night;
as that high-souled one was contemplating in this way, an idea arose in his mind. (18)
"I shall set out on a pilgrimage to sacred fords that bestows desired fruits,
having renounced my home, fields, and so forth, as well as my wife, son, and wealth. Then, in the course of that pilgrimage, I wandered over the earth.
O King, that lord of sages performed the pilgrimage following the direction of the hair on the Ganges, and likewise on the Narmadā, the Sarasvatī,
all rivers such as the Godāvarī, and the ocean. 20–21.

O best of kings, under the pretext of pilgrimage, he wandered to all other holy fords, sacred sites, and the meritorious liṅgas of the gods. As he was thus wandering among those supreme tīrthas, [he encountered...]

His body became stainless, possessing a radiance equal to the splendor of the sun. Cyavana, his soul purified by that deed, shone with brilliance as he wandered and arrived at that most excellent of sacred fields. 23–24.
On the southern bank of the Narmadā, he beheld the great temple complex named Amarakaṇṭaka, which grants the ultimate goal to all;
having bowed to, praised, and fully worshipped the Great Lord Siddhanātha.
Then, having beheld Jvāleśvara and also Amareśvara,
as well as Brahmeśa, Kapileśa, and the excellent Mārkaṇḍeśvara,

he then heard a sound uttered by a bird.

It was endowed with divine speech and possessed both knowledge and realization. There lived there a single parrot who had lived for a very long time; he was a righteous soul named Kuñjala, who had four sons and a wife.
He had four sons who delighted their father;
O Indra among kings, I shall recount their names before you:
the eldest was named Ujjvala, and the second was Samujjvala.

O high-minded one, these were the four sons of that meritorious Kuñjala, who were devoted to their father and mother. 32-33.
They wandered through mountain thickets and islands, remaining composed, yet agitated for the sake of food and tormented by hunger;
[they sought] to satisfy the hunger within their own bellies with gentle fruits resembling nectar. 34.
O best of kings, they quench [the thirst] with water as sweet as nectar.
Having given ripe mango fruits for the sake of food, those good sons diligently place them before the husband and wife. 35–36.
For the sake of their mother, those highly fortunate ones, endowed with a spirit of devotion,
being satisfied, produce food, eat it, and recite [the scriptures].
There, all of them, delighting in play, sport and take pleasure.
Recognizing that it was the time of twilight, they came diligently into the presence of their father, bringing food for the sake of their guru,
while the high-souled Brahmin Cyavana looked on.
O high-minded one, all the birds returned to their father’s beautiful nest; they bowed down before both the father and the mother,
and having brought food for them, they stood in their presence.
O King, all those excellent sons were addressed by their father and honored by him; likewise, they were treated with compassion by their mother with words full of affection,
and at that time, they were cooled by the cool breeze from the wings of their parents.
O King, those two birds performed the nourishment of them both,
having greeted the two good sons with blessings;
they then provided them with well-nourished food, like nectar.

O best of the twice-born, those two indeed felt great affection for one another as they drank the pure water arising from ten million sacred sites (tīrthas), having returned to their own abode with minds contented in happiness. 44–45.
They both recounted a divine, highly meritorious, and sin-destroying story.
Viṣṇu said: "The radiant son was questioned by his father with even a mere handful of water. (46)
"Where have you been today, my son? What unprecedented merit have you seen or heard there? Tell me that, O joy of my heart.
Having heard these words of his father Kuñjala, Sujjvala [replied].

Ujjvala said:
"O illustrious one, O high-minded one, I go constantly to Plakṣadvīpa for the sake of food despite great effort. O great king, there are many regions in Plakṣadvīpa. (49-50)

The mountains, rivers, gardens, forests, and lakes, as well as the villages and other towns, were filled with joyful and virtuous people; the inhabitants lived there, ever content and delighted in happiness. 51.

O great king, in Plakṣadvīpa there was a man always possessed of merit, endowed with charity, virtue, and the chanting of prayers, and filled with the spirit of faith; he was the righteous-souled Divodāsa, and his son was Anūpamā. 52–53.
Endowed with virtues and beauty, virtuous, charming, and auspicious,
she was renowned as the divine goddess, peerless on earth in her form; though she possessed such beauty, youth, and auspiciousness, she was overlooked by her father.
In her very first youth, Cārumaṅgalā was conducting herself [properly].
Then, having seen his daughter—the divine goddess—before the eyes of the virtuous, Dāsa thought:
"To which noble and great-souled man should this maiden be given?"
Having become absorbed in such thoughts and looking about, that best of men,
the lord of the earth, beheld the king of Rūpadeśa;
and having summoned the high-souled Citrasena, that best of men spoke.
That high-souled one gave his daughter to the wise Citrasena. O King, when the time for her marriage had arrived,
Citrasena indeed passed away according to the law of time.
Then the righteous King Divodāsa,
the son of a monarch, summoned the excellent brāhmaṇas and questioned them:
"At the time of her marriage, Citrasena has departed for heaven."
"Tell us, what kind of karma will befall her?
(61) The Brāhmaṇas said: "O King, the marriage of the maiden is seen to be according to the prescribed rites."
If her husband goes to his death or enters into union with another woman, he is seized by great mental and physical afflictions and departs having abandoned her; O King,
it is seen in the treatises on dharma that he becomes an outcaste.
The wise perform the marriage of an unmarried maiden until she reaches her menses; no other husband is ordained for her.
A father should perform the wedding according to the prescribed rule; of this there is no doubt.
"O King, thus has the Dharmaśāstra been declared by wise men.

Then the righteous Divodāsa, impelled by the words of the twice-born," (65-66)
O Great King, O best of the twice-born, the king again made an effort for the sake of marriage through the gift of Dattātraya;

When the king, the lord of the earth, has fallen subject to the law of death,
O highly fortunate one, whenever the husband of the divine queen dies at the appointed time, it always occurs when the *lagna* (ascendant) has been reached. 68–69.
"O father, twenty-one husbands have died one after another over time;

The lord of the earth made great preparations for the *svayaṃvara*. The kings of Plakṣadvīpa were summoned by that high-souled one;

Deluded by her beauty, the kings were incited by Death;
those fools engaged in battle and perished on the field of combat. Thus, O dear one, the destruction of the high-souled Kṣatriyas occurred.

"O Father, tell me that cause in full detail.

Chapter Eighty-six.
Kuñjala said:
O child, I shall tell you of the deeds of that divine goddess; listen as I recount everything she did in her previous birth. 1.
There is a meritorious city named Vārāṇasī, which destroys all sins;
in it dwells one of great wisdom known by the name Suvīra,
born of the Vaiśya caste and possessed of abundant wealth and grain.

His wife, named Citrā, was renowned for her great wisdom; yet, having abandoned the conduct of her family, she lived according to improper behavior. She did not respect her husband and acted according to her own independent will.
Devoid of merit from dharma, she practices only evil;
she constantly reviles her husband and is always fond of quarreling. She constantly dwells in the houses of others and wanders from one home to another.

"O good son, that divine lady enjoys widowhood; thus, O son of a noble family, I have related to you all this conduct of the divine lady. What else do you wish for me to tell you here, regarding that which you ask?"

"The illustrious lady weeps alone in the great forest.

"O son, my knowledge has now been lost due to my state as an animal;

By means of which one obtains knowledge and turns back from the state of liberation— 52— I shall proclaim that unsurpassed instruction on the path to liberation,

O highly wise one, through meditation on that Great-Souled Hari, sin is quickly destroyed for sinners, just as the nature of fire becomes pure through contact with a calf;
indeed, through recitation, burnt offerings, and vows, the sin of the wicked goes to its destruction.
Just as an elephant always abandons its pride out of fear of a lion,
so too does that sin depart at the mere utterance of Kṛṣṇa’s name,
like serpents deprived of their venom by the splendor of Garuḍa.
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin go to destruction, and not otherwise;
by the utterance of the name of that wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu), they likewise depart.
When the hundred names, which destroy heaps of evil, [are recited]...
Having become steady through the practice of recitation, free from desire and anger, and having restrained all the senses, she should protect herself through the knowledge of the Self;
thus absorbed in meditation, she became one-pointed and composed. (58–59)
When one recites that supreme knowledge, then one attains liberation, provided that one is absorbed in that state, with the mind fixed thereon, and joined in yoga. Ujjvala said:
"Tell me now my supreme knowledge regarding the Supreme,
as well as the meritorious vow of meditation and the hundred names [of the Lord] right here.
Kuñjala said:
I shall proclaim the supreme knowledge which has not been seen by anyone;
listen, my son, to this absolute liberation that is entirely free from impurity.
Sūta said:
Just as a lamp situated in a windless place, motionless and free from air,
burning brightly, O Mahāmati, would dispel all darkness;
even so does the Self, when freed from defects, become truly without support.
Hopeless, stainless, and like a calf toward its mother, he has no enemy at any time.
He is neither subject to sorrow nor joy, neither greed nor envy;
alone, he is liberated from both dejection and exultation, as well as from pleasure and pain.
One should also withdraw the senses from all their objects;
then, having become solitary, the state of solitude arises.
Just as a lamp dries up its oil through the process of burning, so too [the senses are withdrawn].
O Indra among kings, when the wick is held steady and free from wind, O high-minded one, it subsequently emits soot even from the oil;
O great-minded one, a black line is seen in front of the lamp. 67–68.
Just as oil drawn out by its own heat becomes pure,
so too the wick of the body dries up the oil of karma;
having turned the objects of the senses into collyrium, it reveals them directly before one's eyes.
Having become stainless, one should generate [the light] and manifest it by oneself (70).
Completely freed from the winds known as afflictions, such as anger and the like,
and having become desireless and immovable, one should blaze forth by one's own splendor (71).
Remaining in his own abode, he perceives the entire three worlds by his own splendor;
this one, whose nature is absolute knowledge (kevalajñāna), has been described by me. I shall now explain the two-fold meditation (dhyāna) of that wielder of the wheel (cakrin).

He is perceived through the eye of knowledge in the form of absolute knowledge (kevalajñāna). Those great souls who are disciplined in yoga and devoted to the supreme truth behold Him while remaining wakeful; that is the austerity which reveals all things.
O son, though devoid of hands and feet, he moves everywhere and grasps the entire triple world, both the stationary and the moving;
and though devoid of nose and mouth, O prince, he smells.
Though earless, He hears everything; He is the witness of all, the Lord of the world.
Though formless, He is connected with forms and has come under the sway of the fivefold group [of senses].
He who is the life-breath of all the worlds is worshipped by all things moving and unmoving. (76–77)
O son, though tongueless, he speaks everything in accordance with the Vedas and Shastras;
and though skinless, the sensation of touch arises for him in all things. He is eternally blissful, detached in soul, uniform in nature, and without dependence.
He is free from decay, free from possessiveness, righteous, virtuous, stainless, and free from possessiveness.
He is independent, yet the master of all; he is the giver of everything and the supreme knower of all.
There is no creator of him, for he is the All, the omnipresent Lord who consists of everything.
He who thus beholds this meditation consisting of all things belonging to the Great Soul (Mahātman) goes to the supreme state, which is formless and like unto the immortal.
Now I shall describe the second meditation of this Great Soul.
He who possesses form yet is formless, who is without blemish, and whose latent impression perfumes the entire incomparable universe with its embodied appearance—
he, my son, is therefore called Vāsudeva. 82–83.
It would possess the color of a rain-showering cloud;
it resembled the splendor of the sun, had four arms, and was the Lord of the Gods.
On his right side shone a conch shell, adorned with gold and jewels.
A discus with the appearance of the solar orb is established upon a lotus; and on the left hand of that Great-Souled One, the Kaumodakī mace, the destroyer of great asuras, shines resplendent. 85–86.
The beloved of Kamalā, adorned with weapons, always remains resplendent with a great lotus rich in fragrance held in his right hand.
His neck is like a conch, his face is round, and his eyes resemble lotus petals.
O son, Hṛṣīkeśa shines with teeth resembling jewels; he whose lower lip has the appearance of coral is Puṇḍarīkākṣa, who is resplendent even with his crown. 88–89.
Janārdana shone with his vast and most radiant form, adorned by the Kaustubha gem;
he was resplendent with two earrings that rivaled the brilliance of the sun. 90.
Hari shines forever with the merit of the Śrīvatsa mark;
Vijaya, the best among victors, blazes with his body adorned with armlets, bracelets, and pearl necklaces resembling stars. 91-92.
Govinda also shone with a golden-colored garment, and he was resplendent with fingers adorned with rings set with jewels;
Hari was fully equipped with all divine weapons and ornaments.
Mounted upon Vainateya, the Creator of the World and Lord of the Universe—
by meditating thus on Him constantly with an undistracted mind,
a person is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
All this regarding the meditation upon the Lord of the Universe has been narrated to you; now I shall proclaim the vow that wards off all sins. 96.
Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Holy Site of the Guru," within the Legend of Vena in the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. 86.
The seventy-eighth chapter. Kuñjala said:
I shall proclaim the various types of vows by which Hari is propitiated.
Jayā and Vijayā, Jayantī the destroyer of sin, Trispṛśā, Vañjulī, another, Tiladagdhā,
Akhaṇḍā, Cārakanyā, Manorathā, and Suputrakā.
"O son, there are many different varieties of Ekādaśī;
there is also Aśūnyaśayana, another, and the great vow of Janmāṣṭamī.
By means of these highly meritorious vows, sin goes far away."
"There is no doubt regarding this for living beings; I speak the truth, the absolute truth.
Kuñjala said:
"I shall proclaim his hymn of praise, which destroys the heap of sins."
This collection known as the "One Hundred Names of the Good Son" bestows a favorable destiny upon men.
O best of sons, I shall now proclaim this supreme hymn consisting of the one hundred names of that Lord Kṛṣṇa; listen to it.
O highly fortunate one, I shall now declare the seer and the meter of the hundred names of Viṣṇu, as well as the deity who purifies all sins.
For the hundred names of Viṣṇu, Brahmā is proclaimed to be the seer.
The deity is said to be Oṃkāra, and the meter is likewise Anuṣṭubh.
Its application is for the complete attainment of all desires as well as for liberation. [This is] of this hymn of the hundred names of Viṣṇu.
Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), Viṣṇu is the deity (devatā), and Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chanda).
The application (viniyoga) is for the fulfillment of all desires and for the destruction of all sins. 9.
I bow to Hṛṣīkeśa, Keśava, and Madhusūdana.
The destroyer of all Daityas, Nārāyaṇa, the one free from ailment; Jayanta, Vijaya, Kṛṣṇa, Ananta, and then Vāmana;
Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Universe, the meritorious, the support of the universe, worshipped by the gods. 10–11.
The sinless one, the destroyer of sins, Narasiṃha, the beloved of Śrī,
the Lord of Śrī, the bearer of Śrī, the giver of Śrī, the abode of Śrī, the one of great prosperity;
Śrī Rāma, Mādhava, Liberation, the embodiment of forgiveness, Janārdana.
The omniscient one, the knower of all, the giver of everything, the leader of all; Hari, the enemy of Mura, Govinda, Padmanābha, the Lord of creatures;
bliss itself, endowed with knowledge, the giver of knowledge, the leader of knowledge. 13–14.
I bow to Acyuta, the one of infinite power, the Moon, the wielder of the discus, the supreme and the inferior,
the support of the ages, the source of the world, the Great Lord whose form is Brahman;
to Mukunda, the excellent Vaikuṇṭha, the one of singular form, the Lord of the universe.
To Vāsudeva, the Great-Souled One, who is devoted to Brahman and dear to the Brāhmaṇas;
who is fond of cows and beneficial to cows; who is the sacrifice itself, the constituent parts of the sacrifice, and the increaser of the sacrifice;
who is the excellent enjoyer of the sacrifice as well, and has reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary branches.
To him who knows the Vedas, whose form is the Veda, the abode of knowledge, the lord of the gods;
to that unmanifest Great Swan, the ancient one with a conch in his hand;
to the Puruṣa with lotus-like eyes, the Boar who upholds the earth. 18.
Pradyumna, Kāmapāla, Vyāsa, Vyāla, Maheśvara;
Sarvasaukhya, Mahāsaukhya, Mokṣa, and Parameśvara; Yogarūpa, Mahājñāna, the beloved bestower of the goal for yogins. 19–20.
To Murāri, the guardian of the world, who holds a lotus in his hand and bears a mace;
who dwells in the cave, who is the abode of all, the abode of merit, and possesses mighty arms; the lord of Vṛndā, of vast body, the purifier, and the destroyer of sin.

I bow with unwavering mind, speech, body, and action to Gopīnātha, the friend of the cowherds, the protector of the cows, the refuge of the herds of cattle, the Supreme Self, the Lord of the supreme, Kapila, who has assumed a human form for his own purpose. 22–23.
