Even he who performs great merit and praises Kṛṣṇa with a steady mind by means of even a hundred names, being purified by his merit, leaves behind these worlds and goes to the realm of Madhusūdana.
This hundred names is of great merit and is the purifier of all sins.
One should recite [the mantra] with a one-pointed mind and meditate, endowed with concentration;
by doing so constantly, a person obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā through merits. Therefore, becoming well-steadfast and with a composed mind, one should recite it. 25–26.

If a mortal, remaining self-restrained and established in his vows, recites this three times a day, he obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice; of this there is no doubt. (27) He who, having fasted on the Ekadashi day, [recites it] before Madhava...
I shall now declare the merit of that mortal who performs recitation while awake:
such a person obtains the fruit of the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice.
Furthermore, the man who stands in the presence of Tulasī and performs recitation with his mind [focused] attains the same.

A human being enjoys the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice even by [staying] for a year where there is both a Śālagrāma stone and a Dvārāvatī stone; one who desires happiness should perform the chanting of prayers in the presence of both.
Having enjoyed great happiness for a hundred and one generations of his family,
that mortal who performs the ritual bath in Kārttika and worships Madhusūdana shall deliver himself along with them. 31–32.
He who, being self-restrained, recites this hymn attains the supreme goal; likewise,
one who bathes in the month of Māgha, worships Hari— the slayer of Madhu— with devotion,
and meditates upon Hṛṣīkeśa, or chants or hears [this hymn], [attains the same].
Having abandoned sins such as the drinking of liquor, a man reaches the supreme state;
O son, he proceeds to Janārdana without any obstacle.
For that mortal who, at the time of a Śrāddha ceremony, [stands] before the Brahmins while they are eating—
One should recite this hymn of one hundred names, which destroys all sins;
the ancestors attain satisfaction and, being satisfied, reach the supreme goal.
A Brāhmaṇa becomes a knower of the Vedas, and a Kṣatriya gains the earth.
The Vaiśya who constantly recites [this] enjoys wealth and prosperity;
the Śūdra enjoys happiness and attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa. Having obtained another birth, O child, he masters the knowledge of the Vedas.
This hymn, which bestows happiness and liberation, should undoubtedly be recited;
by the grace of Keśava, a man shall attain all perfections. 39.

Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Deeds of Cyavana," within the Description of the Holy Places of the Guru, in the Legend of Vena, in the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. 87.
The eighty-eighth chapter. Kuñjala said:
O good son, [I shall tell you] the vow, the hymn, the great knowledge, and the meditation.
I have thus described before you this [account] of Viṣṇu which destroys all sins. Indeed,
when one performs these four meritorious acts,
he goes to the world of Viṣṇu, which is difficult even for the gods to attain.
Having gone there, awaken the divine goddess Vatsā;
tell her of this king of vows named Aśūnyaśayana (the Unempty Bed), and deliver the illustrious princess from great sin.
"What you asked has been told by me; it bestows merit and destroys sin.
Go, go, O highly fortunate one! Having said this, he became silent.
Śrī Viṣṇu said:
Thus addressed by his father with tears in his eyes,
the righteous and high-minded Ujjvala bowed at the feet of his mother and father, O King, and departed in haste for Plakṣadvīpa.
That mountain, Sarvatobhadra, was filled with various minerals and adorned with lofty peaks composed of diverse gems;
O King, it was further graced by waters of brilliant clarity flowing in various streams.
On that best of excellent mountains, there are rivers of clear water;
there, O King, the Kinnaras and Gandharvas sing with melodious voices,
while the place is crowded with Apsarases and surrounded by hosts of gods.
Resounding with the voices of perfected beings and celestial musicians (cāraṇas), adorned by throngs of sages,
and made to echo on all sides by the cries of various birds—
having thus reached that mountain, Ujjvala moved with quick strides.
Even with a sweet voice, that maiden wept upon that mountain. As she was wailing piteously, the wise man spoke these words: "Who are you, O auspicious lady? Why are you weeping now? (11-12)
"O illustrious lady, who has done you this displeasure? Tell me today, for it is the cause of all my sorrow. (13) The divine lady said:
"O fortunate one, this is now the ripening of my own karma;
I remain here in suffering, possessed by widowhood. Who are you, O fortunate one, who, being pained by compassion for me," [have come here?]. 14.
Assuming the form of a bird, he addressed Vatsa with joy. Having heard all that speech, the princess said: "O noble one, I am a bird; I am pained by you out of compassion."
"O auspicious lady, I am not a perfected being (siddha), nor do I possess supernatural knowledge;
I merely saw you here weeping with loud lamentations. Therefore, O goddess, I ask you: tell me the reason for this."
She reported everything concerning her own conduct and her life in her father’s house exactly as it had happened,
all of which was painful; having heard it in its entirety, I became radiant and joyful in spirit.
The great bird spoke to that divine lady who was deeply distressed:
"Just as at the time of your wedding your husbands met their death,
so too have the kṣatriyas perished for the sake of your *svayaṃvara*."
All these deeds of yours have been related by me as told by my father;
O fair-eyed one, the sinful karma you committed in another birth has been compassionately described before me by my father. 21–22.
"O fair-faced one, you have become smeared and nourished by that very fault;
all this reason has been explained by your father.
Now, endure the ripening of your past karma and take heart. (23)

Having heard these words spoken by that radiant youth, the maiden replied once more to the high-souled bird who was speaking, with humble and piteous speech: "O bird of the Kurus, show me mercy! (24-25)
"By your grace, please tell me the atonement for that sin—
a most meritorious expiation that purifies my transgression—
by which I may go to the realm of merit, purified and with my stains washed away. (26)
"O highly fortunate one, please tell me this expiation through your grace.
Ujjvala said:
"O highly fortunate one, it was for your sake that I questioned my father."
Therefore, the father has explained this unsurpassed expiation (prāyaścitta).
O highly fortunate one, perform this reality which purifies all sins;
meditate here upon Hṛṣīkeśa and chant His hundred names. 28-29.

The virtuous-souled one fully explained that unsurpassed, meritorious vow known as Aśūnyaśayana, which destroys sins, is eternal, and illuminates all knowledge, while enjoining the supreme observance of Bhavajñāna. 30.
Knowledge, hymns of praise, vows, and meditation upon the high-souled Viṣṇu—
Viṣṇu said:
"Therefore, she indeed grasped them while remaining in the lonely forest."

Free from all dualities, established in the heat of asceticism, she undertook a vow; having conquered her appetite, she remained without support and endured great suffering. Devoid of desire and anger, she constantly restrained the group of senses. 32–33.
O Great King, having cast aside the great delusion of the senses,
when the fourth year had arrived, Janārdana became well-pleased;
desiring to grant him a boon, that Lord of Boons arrived.
The Lord, the bestower of boons, revealed his true form to him.
Sūta said:
[He was] dark-complexioned like an indranīla gem or a rain cloud, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
To the Great Lord, richly adorned with all ornaments and holding a lotus in his hand, she—
trembling, without support, and with palms joined in reverence—
bowed down and spoke with faltering words to Madhusūdana. (36-37)

Indeed, I am unable to stand before this divine splendor; who are you, possessing such a divine form, appearing out of compassion before me? Tell me, by your grace, what is the cause of your presence here? 38.
O Mahāmati, speak everything with confidence;
O Lord of the World, through your splendor and your gestures, I understand you thus, yet those devoid of knowledge do not know your form or your name. 39–40.
"Are you Brahmā, or are you Viṣṇu, or indeed Śaṅkara himself?
Having spoken thus and prostrated herself like a staff upon the earth, she bowed down.
O King, the Lord of the World spoke to that Nandinī as she lay prostrate.
The Blessed One said:
"O beautiful-faced one, there is no difference between even these three gods; by whomsoever Brahmā or Śaṅkara is worshipped, [he is worshipped by all]. 42.
Therefore, I am constantly worshipped by him; there is no need for hesitation in this matter. (43) These two are eternally non-different from me and possess three forms;
indeed, those by whom I am worshipped have also well-worshipped these two. (44)

"I am Hṛṣīkeśa, the God; out of compassion for you, I have come here because of this meritorious hymn of praise, as well as your vow and your observance. You have become free from all impurities; choose a boon, O beautiful one."
The divine goddess said:
Be victorious, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Kṛṣṇa, remover of afflictions!
I bow to Your pair of feet; O Lord of the gods, lift me up.
O wielder of the sword and discus, I desire this boon; be gracious to me! O sinless one, grant me devotion even toward Your own pair of feet.
O Lord of the World, show me the path to liberation that is free from all affliction. 47–48.
"O Janārdana, if you are pleased, let there be servitude to your body in Vaikuṇṭha.
The Blessed Lord said: "So be it, O highly fortunate one; go, your sins having been washed away."

"Go, go now to the supreme Vaiṣṇava world, which is always difficult for yogis to attain— go to that highest realm by my grace. When these words had been spoken by the high-souled Mādhava, [he departed].
Divyādevī became manifest, possessing a splendor equal to the divine radiance of the sun;
while all the worlds were looking on, she was adorned with divine ornaments,
endowed with a divine garland, and graced by hanging divine necklaces.
He went to the world of Viṣṇu, which is free from burning and dissolution;
then the bird returned to his own home filled with joy. That best of beings related all of that to his father. 53-54.
Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the episode of Cyavana, concerning the holy ford of the Guru.
Chapter Eighty-Nine. Viṣṇu said:
Then Kuñjala spoke these radiant words to his son:
"O son, tell me, what unprecedented thing have you seen?
Tell it to me with joy; I am now desirous of hearing it."
Having thus instructed his son, Sakunjala ceased speaking.
Then the son, Samujjvala, bowing low with humility, replied to his father.
Samujjvala said:
"O father, I am going to Himavat, the best of mountains, which is frequented by hosts of gods,
for the sake of food for myself. I shall behold there a marvel never seen nor heard of before."
The region was crowded with throngs of sages, graced by celestial nymphs (apsarases),
rich in the splendor of many wonders, auspicious, and endowed with auspicious things; it was further adorned with various forests yielding the fruits of great merit.
O father, there I beheld something unprecedented near Lake Mānasa that bewildered my mind with its manifold wonders:
a single swan arrived, surrounded by many other swans.
Thus, O illustrious one, some black ones have gathered there;
others have white bodies with beaks and feet that are not white (i.e.,
dark), while others, O high-minded one, are blue like that, and others are white.
There, four noble women appeared, fierce in form and terrifying;
they were cruel, with mouths formidable with fangs, with hair standing erect, and inspiring dread.
They subsequently arrived at that Mānasa lake.
The black swans, having bathed in the Mānasa lake before me,
became bewildered by another who had also bathed there in that Mānasa;
O dear one, those women laughed with loud and harsh laughter.
From that lake emerged a single swan of great body;
afterwards, three others emerged, and they disregarded me as they departed through the path of the sky, disputing with one another. (12-13)
Those three women, most terrifying, wandered all around on the sacred peaks of the Vindhya mountains like birds in the shade of trees;
they all sat there, consumed by most dreadful sorrows.
While they were looking on closely, a certain Bhilla arrived (15).
Having harassed the deer, he— bow in hand and arrows in his grasp—
sat down comfortably, having taken recourse to a stone slab (16).
Afterwards, the Bhillī arrived, bringing food along with water;
she beheld her own beloved king endowed with joyful marks,
yet seeing her husband transformed and enveloped in splendor, she looked upon him as someone entirely different.
Overcome by divine splendor like the sun situated in the sky, she recognized him as another man; abandoning him, she departed.
Vyādha said:
"Come, come here, my dear; why do you not look at me? I am tormented by hunger and I gaze upon you.
Having heard his words, the hunter quickly approached. 19-20.
Having approached her husband’s side, she was then filled with wonder, thinking, "Who is this deity of such radiant conduct who would summon me?
Then Vyādhī spoke to her husband, who was blazing with splendor.
"O hero, what has been done here? Who are you, possessed of divine marks?
Sūta said:
Thus addressed by the hunter's wife, the hunter spoke to his beloved.
"O beloved, I am indeed your lover, and you are my dear wife. Why do you not recognize me? How has such doubt arisen?
Even one tormented by hunger awaits water and food. (23-24)
Vyādhi said:
"My husband is a barbarian, dark-complexioned, red-eyed, and wearing a black tunic;
such is he who causes terror to all living beings. (25)
"Who are you? Tell me, 'I am so-and-so,' and call upon me as 'Beloved.
This doubt has arisen in me; speak the truth before me.
[Tell me] your lineage, your name, your village, your playthings, your body, your son, and your daughter."
She related [the matter] before her beloved for the sake of gaining his confidence. With a joyful heart, she, Vyādhī, replied to her husband:
"Why is your body like this, wearing a white tunic? (27-28)
"How was he born? Tell me, for a great wonder is unfolding.
Thus questioned by his wife, the hunter spoke.
Sūta said:
Having heard those words of his beloved, which were full of humility, Narmadā replied: "O lady of excellent vows, there is a confluence on the northern bank;
O very dear one, my life has become distressed by the heat."
At this very secluded confluence, exhausted by fatigue, I went there in haste; having bathed and drunk water, I returned afterwards.
From that time forward, you have been alone, enveloped in such splendor.
Having become as if born, joined with garments, and attained a pure whiteness,
he likewise abides through the families and positions of the previously mentioned signs.
Then, having observed his own beloved one and understood the arising of merit—
Then he replied to his husband, "Show me a place where I may bathe;
afterwards, O hunter, you may give me food along with drink.
Thus addressed by his beloved, the hunter went in haste.
Then, O highly fortunate one, that destroyer of sins pointed out the confluence; the birds, possessing swift prowess,
flew up together and all went with her to the supreme confluence of the Revā.
While those birds were looking on and I was watching,
my husband was bathed by her, and she herself was bathed again; both of them then assumed divine bodies, endowed with celestial splendor.
With wings fully grown, adorned with excellent divine garments and ointments,
wearing divine garlands and clothes, and anointed with divine perfumes,
they boarded the vehicle of Viṣṇu, being honored by sages and Gandharvas. 39.

I beheld those two high-souled ones, husband and wife, being honored by the Vaiṣṇavas as they went to the world of Viṣṇu; they were being praised as they traveled along the path to heaven, while birds sang melodiously. 40–41.
Then, having beheld that supreme king of holy places (Tīrtharāja), those four black swans, with words manifesting their joy at the confluence that destroys all sins,
bathed; purified by that devotion, they once again attained their radiant splendor.
Having bathed and drunk water there, they emerged once again outside;
at that moment, those women died from the mere sight of Kṛṣṇa's bathing, wailing and writhing, shaken by cries of "Alas! Alas! (Hāhākāra).
O father, when those who had gone to the realm of Yama were seen by me,
the swans flew up from there and returned to their own abode.
Thus, O father, what was seen by me has been told to you directly.
"O Kṛṣṇa, please tell me by your grace who those women praised as the Dhārtarāṣṭras with great bodies will be;
and tell me of those Dhārtarāṣṭras who have emerged from the midst of Lake Mānasa."
"O father, tell me now, what will become of them?
Why have I attained such deep blackness, while they, though pure, have become so at that very moment? And why, O father, have those women died?"
"O Father, such a terrible doubt has arisen in my heart;
you, who are expert in knowledge, ought to sever it this very day. Be gracious and look upon me with a favorable face, for I am ever bowing before you."
Having thus addressed his father, the radiant one fell silent;
then that parrot named Kuñjala began to speak.
Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Life of Cyavana," within the Description of the Holy Places of the Preceptor in the Legend of Vena, in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The Ninetieth Chapter.
Sūta said: Having thus heard all that was spoken by Samujjvala, [the sages asked:]
The righteous-souled Kuñjala replied to his son.
Kuñjala said:
"O dear one, I shall explain it; listen with a steady mind."
This account, which destroys all doubts and annihilates sin,
began to circulate in the world of Indra; it was a conversation full of divine wonder that took place in the assembly hall of that high-souled god, Indra.
Nārada went in haste to see the thousand-eyed Lord Indra; seeing him approaching with a radiance equal to the splendor of the sun, the high-minded Indra rose up, overcome with joy.
With a mind bowed in devotion, he offered water for the feet and the respectful arghya;
then, with palms joined in reverence, he prostrated himself.
Having seated the best of the twice-born upon a soft and auspicious seat, he paid his respects.
Bowing down and filled with supreme faith, he asked: "For what reason have you come today? Tell me the cause at once. Thus addressed by the king of the gods, the great sage replied.
Indra, the lord of the earth, has come to see you;
having bathed with great faith in sacred regions and holy fords, and having worshipped the gods and ancestors and visited numerous shrines. (8-9)
"All this that was previously asked by you has been explained.
Devendra said:
"O Muni, you have seen the holy tirthas and the auspicious sacred fields."

By reaching which holy ford (tīrtha) would a slayer of a Brahmin be liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin; how could a drinker of liquor be freed from that evil, as well as a killer of cows or a thief of gold?
O highly fortunate one, how can a woman who betrays her master or a murderer of women find happiness?
Nārada said: O Lord of the Gods, regarding whatever holy places there may be, such as the Gaṅgā and others,
I do not know which among them possesses the specific power to destroy sin.
"O Purandara, I know all these excellent, divine, merit-bestowing, sin-destroying, and equal holy fords (tīrthas) without distinction;
indeed, at this moment, I perceive no difference between them. (13–14)
"Let the deities be made to grant their assurance regarding the bestowal of the goal [of liberation] for the holy fords (tīrthas).
Having heard these words of the high-souled Nārada,
the holy fords situated on earth were summoned by Indra.
By his command, divine forms arrived, O observer of excellent vows;
they were joined with palms in reverence, adorned with beautiful ornaments, wearing celestial garments, and radiant with luster. 16–17.

O Lord of Men, the specific forms of women and men were created with particular care; they possessed divine forms, shining like gold, sandalwood, and kasha grass, and gleaming with the luster of pearls. 18.

There, indeed, some were the color of molten gold and others were reddish; some within that assembly hall were white and bright yellow, while others, possessing physical forms, resembled lotuses. 19–20.
Within that assembly hall, other splendors shine forth—some possessing the brilliance of the sun’s radiance, some equal to the flash of lightning, and others like the glow of fire;
Adorned with necklaces, bracelets, armlets, and garlands, and well-anointed with excellent sandalwood paste—
divine, fragrant, and heavy with sandalwood—
their water-pots held in their hands, they entered the interior of the assembly hall.

The Gaṅgā, the Narmadā, the Puṇyā, the Candrabhāgā, the Sarasvatī, the Devikā, the Bimbikā, the Kubjā, the Kuñjalā, the Mañjulā, and the Śrutā; the Raṃbhā, the Bhānumatī, the Puṇyā, the Pārā, and the Sughargharā. 24.
The Śoṇā, Acasindhu, Sauvīrā, Kāverī, and Kapilā; the Kumudā, Vedanadī, Puṇyā, Supuṇyā, and Maheśvarī; the Carmaṇvatī, as well as the renowned Lopā, and others such as the Kauśikī. 25–26.
Suhaṃsī, Haṃsapādā, Haṃsavegā, Manorathā,
Suruthā, Svāruṇā, Veṇā, Bhadraveṇā, Supadminī, Nāhalī, Sumarīcā, another Puṇyā, and another Pulidikā. 27.
Hemā, Manorathā, Divyā, Candrikā, Vedasaṃkramā;
Jvālā, Hutāśanī, Svāhā, Kālā, Kapiñjalā; Svadhā, Sukalā, Aliṅgā, Gambhīrā, and Bhīmavāhinī. 28–29.
Devadrī, Cīvīravāhā, Lakṣahomā, Aghāpahā, Pārāśarī, Hemagarbhā, Subhadrā, and Vasuputrikā—
these, O Lord of Men, are the great meritorious goddesses who have today appeared here in embodied form. (30)
Richly adorned with all ornaments, holding water-pots in their hands, and well-worshipped—
Prayāga, Puṣkara, Arghadīrgha, Manoratha, and the highly meritorious Vārāṇasī, which destroys even the sin of killing a Brahmin. 31–32.
Dvārāvatī, Prabhāsa, Avantī, Naimiṣa,
Caṇḍaka, Mahāratna, Maheśvara, Kaleśvara, Kalijara, Brahmakṣetra, Māthura, and Mānavāhaka. (33)
Likewise, other divine and various [beings] such as Māyākāntī,
the sixty-eight excellent holy sites (sūtīrtha), and hundreds of millions of rivers headed by the Godāvarī, all arrived there at his command. 34–35.
Then all the great and excellent holy sites (tīrthas) of the continents,
bearing forms and lingas, gathered together before the thousand-eyed Lord of the Gods, ready to carry out his command. 36.
With their heads bowed, they prostrated themselves in every way before the Lord of the gods of gods.
Sūta said:
Those great holy places spoke thus to the illustrious King of the Gods.
"Why have you not been summoned by me, you whose voice is like that of the God of gods?
Tell us the full reason for this; salutations to you, O Lord of the Suras! Having heard these words, the King of the Devas replied:
What great holy place (tīrtha) is capable of removing the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa,
the great sin known as the killing of a cow, the unsurpassed sin known as the killing of a woman, that which arises from treachery toward one's master, and the terrible sin of drinking liquor? 40.
Who is capable of destroying that which arises from stealing gold, as well as that produced by reviling one's guru,
the most terrible sin of foeticide, and the great evil of treason against the king, which brings about manifold suffering? 41-42.

Betrayal of friends, as well as other acts of treachery against those who trust one; causing division among the gods, and furthermore, causing division among the *liṅgins*; the destruction of the livelihood of Brahmins, and the obstruction of the movement of cattle. 43.
The burning of a dwelling and likewise the setting fire to a house—
these sixteen are great sins, as is sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached, deserting one's master, and fleeing from the field of battle. 44–45.
"Who indeed among you is capable of destroying these [sins] certainly without penance, O best of holy places?
While the deities and Nārada look on."
"Let all of you speak after reflecting and deliberating thus with firm resolve.
When these auspicious words had been spoken by the high-souled King of the Gods, the Lord of Tīrthas consulted [his attendants] and spoke to Śakra, who was present in the assembly. 47–48.
The holy fords said:
"Listen, O King of the Gods; we shall speak to you. Salutations to you! Indeed, there are all manner of holy fords that remove every sin. 49
"O Lord of the Gods, we are not at all able to destroy the most terrible and blazing great sins such as the killing of a Brahmin that you have mentioned.
[Yet] Prayāga, Puṣkara, and the unsurpassed Arghatīrtha— "
Vārāṇasī is highly fortunate, capable, and the destroyer of sins.
(51) For the sake of destroying great sins, there are four of immeasurable prowess; for the sake of destroying minor sins, there are four of immeasurable prowess. (52)

"O Lord of the Gods, Puṣkara and the other great powerful Tīrthas were created by the Creator. Having heard those words of the Tīrthas, the King of the Suras was then filled with great joy and offered them praise.
Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, titled "The Life of Cyavana," within the "Guru-tīrtha-māhātmya" section of the *Vena-upākhyāna* in the *Bhūmi-khaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter Ninety-one. Kuñjala said:
In ancient times, when the thousand-eyed Indra was overcome by the sin of killing a Brahmin due to his illicit union with the beloved wife of Gautama—
a grave transgression that had occurred— he was abandoned by both the gods and the Brahmins.
The thousand-eyed one performed penance, without support and without refuge.
At the conclusion of his penance, all the gods, sages, yakṣas, and kinnaras performed a consecration for the sake of honoring the king of the gods.
Having led his excellent son to the land of Mālavaka, the illustrious king of gods caused him to bathe with jars filled with water.
First, he was led to Vārāṇasī himself in order to perform the ritual bathing.
Then,

O best of the twice-born, that high-souled one was personally bathed by the thousand-eyed Indra at Arghatīrtha in Prayāga, and again at Puṣkara by all the gods beginning with Brahmā and by hosts of sages.

O best of the twice-born, at that time, the king of the gods was bathed by the Nāgas, trees, Nāgas and serpents, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras, and was well-consecrated with Vedic mantras by the sages who destroy all sins.
When that illustrious and great-souled thousand-eyed one was purified,
his sin of killing a Brahmin vanished, as did his sin of approaching a woman who should not be approached; thus,
through the [atonement for] approaching a forbidden woman, the sin of Brahmin-murder was destroyed.
On the surface of the earth, the thousand-eyed Indra, being highly pleased, granted a boon to those [waters] along with that terrible sinner: "O you,
you shall undoubtedly become kings of sacred fords (tīrtharāja)."
"Since I have been liberated from this most terrible sin by you pure ones through my grace, [I am purified]. Having thus granted them a boon, he gave a boon to Mālava as well. 12.
"Since you have today carried my burden, which was so exhausting, you shall, by my grace, become fully provided with food, drink, wealth, and grain;
of this there is no doubt, there is no uncertainty."
"Free from the most terrible ages, you shall become one possessed of great merit.
Having thus granted him this boon, Purandara, the king of the gods,
[bestowed upon him] all sacred fields, all holy fords, as well as the region of Mālavaka.
Together with Ākhaṇḍala, they returned to their own abodes.
Sūta said: From that time forward, the four [sages]—Prayāga and likewise Puṣkara—[became famous]. 16.
Having reached the Argha-tīrtha at Vārāṇasī, he attained supreme sovereignty. Kuñjala said: There was a kṣatriya named Vidura in the Pañcāla countries.
In that very delusion, a Brahmin was previously killed by him;
though now devoid of his topknot and sacred thread, and bereft of his sectarian mark, he wanders about for alms—he who has arrived here as a slayer of a Brahmin. (18-19)
"Let food obtained as alms be given to those who have killed a Brahmin, those who drink liquor, and those who eat the food of a mendicant.
Thus he wandered and begged in all those houses;
having thus roamed through all the sacred fords (tīrthas), he returned.
O best of the twice-born, even though he was burdened by the sin of killing a Brahmin,
Vidura, filled with misery and grief, remained there with a burning heart, taking refuge in the shade of a tree. 21-22.
Then the brahmin Candraśarman, afflicted by great delusion and having become a slayer of his guru,
dwelt in the land of Māgadha;
that evil-minded man was abandoned by his own kinsmen and circle of relatives.
Accompanied by his attendants, he arrived where that Vidura was staying;
though devoid of the topknot and sacred thread and shunned by the brahmins, he was then questioned by that evil-minded Vidura. 24–25.
"Who are you that have arrived here with such a wretched appearance and a scorched mind? Why do you wander the earth, deprived of your sacred thread?
As soon as he was addressed thus by Vidura, Candrāśarman, the lowest of the twice-born, [spoke].
He related everything exactly as it had been done by himself previously—
both the most terrible sin committed while living in the teacher’s house, and that which was done while overcome by great delusion and agitated by anger. (27–28)
"Previously, the murder of my guru was committed; by that, I am now consumed.
Having related this entire account, Candraśarman asked: "Who are you, so full of sorrow, who has taken refuge in the shade of this tree?"
Vidura had thus briefly confessed his own sin.
Then a certain third twice-born man arrived, emaciated by fatigue and burdened with a great accumulation of sins; he was named Vedaśarman.
Questioned by both of them, "Who are you, appearing so sorrowful? Why do you wander the earth today?
Tell us of your own condition," Vedaśarman then related everything regarding his own conduct.
They both told him that they had committed the act of approaching a woman who should not be approached.
Reprimanded by all the people, as well as by other kinsmen and relatives, he said: "Tainted by that sin, I wander thus upon this earth. (33-34)
A Vaiśya named Vañjula, who was a drinker of liquor and specifically a killer of cows, arrived there; he was questioned by them just as before,
and he reported all the sinful deeds he had previously committed.
All that he had spoken was heard by them and by others as well.
Thus, these four most sinful men came together in one place; yet not one of them had any contact with another, even regarding food or clothing.
They conversed with one another regarding the most exalted news of Kṛṣṇa; they did not sit down together, nor did they sleep upon the same bed.
Thus, overcome by sorrow, they went to various sacred fords (tīrthas).
But their evil and terrible sins perish, O Nandana;
the holy fords have no power to destroy such great transgressions.
Then Vidura and the others went to Mount Kālañjara.
Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "The Life of Cyavana at the Sacred Site of the Guru," within the *Veṇu* sub-narrative of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* in the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter Ninety-Two. Kuñjala said:
Having reached Kālañjara, they dwell there in extreme misery, scorched by great sins, crying out "Alas! Alas!", and deprived of their senses. Then, a certain highly renowned Siddha arrived there.

Questioned by him, they said, "O highly wise one, you who are expert in all knowledge, we are afflicted with great suffering; by whom have we been made miserable? Having understood their great sin, that most meritorious one showed them compassion.
Siddha said: "Prayāga at the conjunction of the new moon and Monday, Puṣkara,
and Arghatīrtha as the third, while Vārāṇasī is the fourth."
"Go there, you four who are defiled by sin; when you have bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā, you will then be liberated from your sins. There is no doubt that you will attain purity."
Commanded by him, they all bowed down to him with great effort.
Then, afflicted by sin, those best of the twice-born departed quickly from Kālañjara; having reached Vārāṇasī, they bathed there.
Having reached Prayāga, Puṣkara, and the excellent Arghatīrtha on the day of the new moon falling on a Monday, O best of men, they departed for that great city;
Vidura, Candraśarman, and Vedaśarman as the third.
There was a Vaiśya named Vañjulaka, an evil-minded drinker of spirituous liquor.
When that festival arrived, O twice-born one, he bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā;
by the mere act of bathing, he was liberated from his sins, such as the killing of cows.
Tainted by the sins of killing a Brahmin, killing a guru, drinking liquor, and other such crimes,
these holy places wander across the earth.
Puṣkara is a half-tīrtha, while Prayāga is the destroyer of sin.

O best of the twice-born, having smeared their bodies with ash in Vārāṇasī on the fourth lunar day, they all attained a dark hue and wandered about in the form of swans; those best of the twice-born performed their ablutions in all the excellent holy fords.
O Great King, they shall not incur blackness through their sin; rather, having bathed again in all the excellent holy fords (tīrthas),
O best of the twice-born, whatever specific ford they visit, they obtain the merit of all holy fords.
In the form of swans, they indeed travel together with them, while their wives, who are embodiments of sin, wander about in great distress. Thus,
in the form of swans, they roamed through the sixty-eight excellent holy places (tīrthas).
Together with those great kings and the great sacred fords, they returned once more to Lake Mānasa, their minds agitated by sin. Having bathed there, O great king, one abandons that sin.
To those whose minds were overcome with shame, he appeared in the form of a swan;
then, he who was previously seen by you as having a dark body became manifest.
Thereafter, they went to the northern bank of the Revā, which destroys all sins.
O best of the twice-born, by merely bathing at the confluence of the Kubjā, which is frequented by gods and siddhas, they were liberated from their sins;
casting off this very [human] caste, they returned to their state of merit.
To whichever holy ford these swans went, they proceeded to bathe;
seeing this, those women laughed, saying, "Sin does not depart at all by water, nor even by fire; rather, the sin of Kubjā alone is superior. 21-22.
Then those women were praised as having become immortal,
while the sins of killing a Brahmin, killing a guru, drinking liquor,
and violating the preceptor’s wife were reduced to ashes, destroyed by the power of Revā and Kubjā.
O highly fortunate one, those [waters] were indeed slain and became immortal on the riverbank.
Then, in the form of a swan, he arrived together with those sixty-eight excellent holy sites; know that you are indeed that swan, Mānasa.
There are four black swans; hear their names:
Prayāga, Puṣkara, the unsurpassed Arghatīrtha, and Vārāṇasī as the fourth—these four are the destroyers of sin.

Overwhelmed by the sin of killing a Brahmin, the four of them wandered about. O high-minded one, as they wandered from one sacred ford to another, that terrible sin did not leave them, my son. (27-28)
It is said that at the confluence of the Kubjā, one is purified and liberated from sin;
indeed, it is esteemed here as the most meritorious of all sacred fords (tīrthas). It is said that King Prayāga was born before Indra.
Let the holy fords roar as long as Revā is not seen;
she has been established for the destruction of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin at the confluence of the Kapilā and likewise at the confluence of the Revā. 30–31.
The Revā is everywhere difficult to attain; she is greatly meritorious and highly auspicious at the confluence with the Meghanāda, as well as at the union with the Ūru.
She is likewise [sacred] at Oṃkāra, at Bhṛgukṣetra, and at the confluence of the Narmadā and the Kubjā.
In Āmāhiṣmatī, which is difficult even for the best of gods and non-humans to attain,
at the confluence of the Viṭaṅkā, at the meritorious Śrīkaṇṭha, and at Maṅgaleśvara, the Revā— filled with the merit of the gods— is everywhere hard to find. 33–34.

The Great Goddess Tīrthamātāmahā, who destroys the lower heap [of sins], is present wherever she may be between the two banks; there, a man is happy. By a single bath, a human being enjoys the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
"All this which you have asked has been explained to you;
it is meritorious, destructive of all sins, and a bestower of the supreme goal for those who hear it.
Having spoken thus, the one of great wisdom addressed his third son.
Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "The Life of Cyavana at the Sacred Site of the Guru," within the *Venopākhyāna* of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* in the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter Ninety-Three. Kuñjala said:
"O observer of noble vows, what unprecedented thing have you seen while wandering the earth that is so full of wonder? Tell me that.
From here, I am intent on traveling to another region for the sake of food."
"O best of sons, tell me everything wonderful that you have seen.
Vijvala said:
"On the ridge of Mount Meru, there is a forest named Ānanda."
It was always filled with divine trees consisting of fruits and flowers;
it was crowded with hosts of gods, accompanied by sages and perfected beings (siddhas),
and by beautiful apsaras, gandharvas, kinnaras, and uragas.
The meritorious Ānandakānana shines with divine splendors through its ponds, wells, lakes, rivers, and springs;
it is illuminated by tens of millions of celestial chariots resembling swans, kunda flowers, and the moon.
Resounding with the delightful clamor of songs and the thundering roar of clouds, it was made sweet everywhere by the humming of bees;
it was surrounded by sandalwood trees, mango trees, and flowering campaka trees.
Thus the supreme Ānandavana shines with various trees,
filled with the great clamor of the songs of diverse birds.
In this way, that most beautiful Ānandana was seen by me there.
And that lake, O dear one, shines like the ocean, pure and filled with holy water;
it is strewn with auspicious fragrant lotuses and water-lilies, and is frequented by swans and kāraṇḍava ducks. 9–10.
Thus it was that in the center of that forest there was a lake,
adorned by throngs of sages and crowded with gods and gandharvas;
it shone brilliantly with kinnaras, uragas, gandharvas, and cāraṇas.
"O father, it is impossible for me to describe the wonder that was seen there.
O best of men, it was adorned with divine palanquins and water-jars, and it shone brilliantly with parasols, staffs, and banners."
O observer of excellent vows, he shone while being sung to by kinnaras, gandharvas, and apsarases, even though they were distracted by all manner of enjoyments;
and he was praised by great perfected sages who knew the ultimate reality.
Incomparable in beauty in this world, such a being was never seen anywhere; his limbs were radiant with the splendor of all ornaments and graced by a divine garland,
and a necklace made of great jewels shone upon his chest.
And standing near him, a certain woman with a beautiful face was seen,
adorned with golden necklaces, pearls, bracelets, and bangles;
she was dressed in divine garments and anointed with fragrant sandalwood pastes and lovely unguents.
While being praised and sung of, a man arrived there; he was accompanied by a woman of exquisite form, with swelling hips and breasts,
her limbs radiant with every ornament and endowed with such perfection of beauty and song.
These two, whom I have never seen before, have arrived even by means of a celestial chariot;
they possess beauty, charm, and sweetness that eclipse all other splendor. Having descended from their celestial chariot, they have come near the lake.
The two high-souled ones, a man and a woman with lotus-like eyes, having bathed and grasped great weapons,
fell there upon the bank of the lake as a couple in such a state, like two corpses.
Then those two lotus-eyed ones, a woman and a man, shone forth;
O highly fortunate one, both corpses were of such beauty that they resembled celestial forms,
just like the living man.
Whatever form he had, such a [corpse] was seen there;
and according to the form of his wife, a second corpse appeared likewise.
Then, having cut off the flesh of that female corpse with a weapon, he ate it.
He devours their flesh, which is drenched in blood;
likewise, a man, overcome by distress, devours the flesh of a corpse. Oppressed by hunger, those two devour the flesh of one another.

They ate meat until they were fully satisfied; then, having drunk water from the lake, they became happy. After staying there for some time, they departed once again by means of a celestial chariot (vimāna). 27–28.
On another day,
he went out to hunt; there, in that great forest, he saw two women endowed with beauty and good fortune, possessing auspicious marks, who had devoured his father’s flesh.
Then they will laugh at me here with loud, boisterous laughter;
moreover, those two will constantly devour their own flesh while I look on,
even as I perform my ablutions and other rites there.
O illustrious one, two other women, endowed with fierce forms and possessing mouths terrifying with fangs, spoke there in that most fearsome place, saying again and again, "Give! Give! (32).
"O Father, while living in the vicinity of the forest, I have seen this:
these two [creatures] constantly tear out and eat the very flesh of corpses;
yet their bodies become fully restored once again. (33-34)
"O Father, I have witnessed this marvel: that those who have already crossed over, as well as others, even while seeing me, perform the very same actions as previously described. (35)

"O Father, that which was asked by you—the very marvel that was seen—has been related by me before you, which indeed removes all causes of doubt. Speak [more], for my heart is filled with joy through your grace. (36-37)
O best of the twice-born, he who has arrived in a celestial chariot together with a woman,
possessing a divine form and lotus-like eyes— he is a certain man, O illustrious one,
And when one’s father has arrived and, having approached, eats [the food], then the father might laugh at the two women, or they might speak with a voice like their father's, saying, "Give! Give!
thus repeatedly. (39–40)
"O you of excellent vows, please explain to me this matter concerning these two most terrifying women; O dear one, you ought to sever this doubt of mine.
Having spoken thus, O great king, that bird [the son of Aṇḍaja] fell silent.
Thus questioned by his third son, Vijvala,
he related the entire account while Cyavana was listening as well.
Thus ends the section on the conduct of Cyavana within the Gurus Tīrtha of the Vena Legend in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The ninety-third chapter;
the ninety-fourth chapter. Kuñjala said:
Listen, my son, I shall explain the entire cause for which those two were born as eaters of their own flesh;
there is no doubt that in all cases, karma— whether auspicious or inauspicious— is the cause.

Through meritorious action, a man enjoys happiness as his son; likewise, through action joined with sin, he experiences suffering here. Having thus reflected upon the subtle path with the eye of knowledge of the scriptures— 3.
Having clearly perceived the gross nature of the object and having reflected upon it again and again,
a person should undertake the work with a skillful mind,
just as a sculptor brings a figure possessing form to completion.
O son, by the brilliance of the fire and its flames on all sides,
the mineral, being heated slowly by the fire, becomes liquefied;
just as food that has been well-cooked is poured out, O child.
A calf of such a form is born, without a doubt;
for as the action is performed, so it is experienced.
Karma alone is primary, which exists in the form of the year.
O dear one, whatever kind of seed a farmer sows in the fields, he reaps that very kind of fruit; there is no doubt about this. Whatever kind of action is performed, that very kind is experienced.
Karma is the cause of his destruction; we all exist under the sway of karma.
Karma is our inheritance, time is our relative, and karma is our kinsman in this world.
It is karma that impels a person toward happiness and suffering in this life.
Just as gold or silver is cast into whatever form [is intended],
so too is a living being cast [into a body], following the power of its past karma.
These five [stages] are seen here even while the embodied being is still within the womb.
Lifespan, karma, wealth, knowledge, and even death— just as a maker fashions whatever he desires from a lump of clay,
so too does the fruit of one's actions return to the doer.
Through their own actions, a living being attains the state of a god, a human, an animal, a bird, or likewise the state of a beast or an immobile object;
it is that very same being who thus constantly experiences what has been ordained for itself.
Suffering is ordained by oneself, and happiness is ordained by oneself;
from the time one enters the bed of the womb, one experiences the results of actions performed in previous bodies.
O Supreme Person, no one else [experiences] the karma created in a previous body.

Whether by strength or by wisdom, one is capable of making things otherwise. (17) One experiences only those very sufferings and pleasures created by oneself; yet, for various reasons or causes, one is afflicted by the sense of ego (ahaṃkāra). (18)
Just as a calf finds its mother among a thousand cows, even so does good and evil karma follow the doer.
For that which has no destruction apart from experience [does not perish]. 19.
Who is able to alter past karma, which is a bond from former lives?
Destiny pursues one who runs very swiftly;
it shines forth through the convergence of conditions, exactly as it was performed in the past.
As he stands, it stands; as he moves, it follows;
as he performs an action, it conforms to him like a shadow.
Just as shadow and sunlight are eternally and intimately bound to one another.
Calamities arising from external objects, as well as those such as old age and the like,
afflict a person later on, even after he has been afflicted by his prior karma.
Whatever suffering or happiness is to be experienced by someone, wherever it is to be experienced, that is what occurs.
There, bound as if by a rope, one is led away by force by destiny;
they say that destiny is the bringer of pleasure and pain for all beings.
That destiny is inconceivable, whether one is awake or even asleep, and it acts otherwise than one's own karma.
Otherwise, destiny indeed rises up to strike and seeks to kill;
one must guard against weapons, fire, poison, and difficult terrains, just as one protects the seeds, trees, shrubs, and even the grasses upon the earth.

In the same way, actions abide within the self and arise from it; just as a lamp reaches extinction when its oil is exhausted, so too does the body of a living being meet its destruction through the exhaustion of karma. 28.
Death occurs through the exhaustion of karma; this has been declared by the knowers of reality. Various diseases of living beings are recorded, along with their causes;
therefore, for living beings, karma alone is indeed the primary principle.
Whatever karma was performed in the past is experienced right here;
and as for that which you have just seen and asked about, O father,
its meaning has been explained by me, so let these two enjoy it now.
Their faces were filled with joy as they witnessed that most terrible deed.
I shall describe their actions as they spoke; listen, O child.
This is the land of action (karmabhūmi), my dear; other lands are for the sake of enjoyment.
The Greatly Wise One enjoys the fruits of his merit through the creation and other cosmic cycles;
Sūta said:
"In the land of Cūla, O Greatly Wise One, there was a king named Subāhu. (34)
There is no one on earth like him— possessed of beauty, virtue,
and wisdom; a devotee of Viṣṇu, highly intelligent, and very dear to the Vaiṣṇavas—
who meditates upon Madhusūdana through all three types of action.
O King, he performed all the sacrifices, such as the Aśvamedha and others. His priest was a Brāhmaṇa named Jaimini;
having summoned Subāhu, he spoke these words to him.
"O King, give excellent gifts by which you may enjoy happiness;
for by means of gifts, a man who has gone to the next world overcomes difficult realms. Through giving, one attains happiness and obtains eternal fame. (38)
Through charity, incomparable fame arises within the circle of mortals. As long as that fame remains here, so long shall the donor dwell in heaven.
They say that such charity is difficult to perform; it is not at all easy to give. 39-40.
Therefore, men should always give with every effort.
Subāhu said: Between the two—giving and austerity—which is more difficult to perform? 41.
"Or what great fruit is there after death? Tell me that, O best of the twice-born.
Jaimini said:
"There is nothing on earth more difficult to perform than giving. (42)
O King, it is directly perceived and witnessed by the world that men,
deluded by greed for the sake of wealth, abandon their dear lives and enter the ocean as well as the forest. 43.

They resort to service, which is considered a livelihood for dogs; likewise, they formerly practiced agriculture, which consists mostly of violence and involves great suffering—even though that wealth was acquired with hardship and is dearer to them than their own lives. 44–45.

O tiger among men, the renunciation of wealth is extremely difficult, especially for a great king, when that wealth has been acquired through righteous means; yet there is no end to the merit of what is given with faith, according to the rules, to a worthy recipient. 46.
She is the goddess Śraddhā, the daughter of Dharma, the purifier, and the one who carries all across;
she is Sāvitrī, the progenitor, and the one who delivers beings from the ocean of saṃsāra.
Dharma is accomplished through faith, not by vast heaps of wealth. 47–48.
O best of kings, there are sages who possess nothing and have gone to heaven through the dharma of faith; they perform many kinds of various gifts.
Among these, O giver, there is no gift for living beings superior to the gift of food.
Therefore, food should be given accompanied by milk and accompanied by sweet and meritorious words;
for there is no gift superior to food, both in this world and in the next. 50-51.
For the sake of crossing over, for welfare alone, and as a cause for the attainment of happiness,
One should give morsel by morsel, fistful by fistful, or prastha by prastha; of this there is no doubt.
That gift becomes inexhaustible and yields great fruit;
yet for a human being, neither a prastha nor a fistful would ever fail to be possible.

O Lord of Creatures, by the power of not being an atheist, a man who has reached a sacred festival day (parvan) should, with faith and devotion, feed even a single Brāhmaṇa, provided he offers at least one principal portion of food. 55. Even for a single principal meal, O Lord of Creatures.
Having attained another birth, one constantly enjoys food;
whatever was given with devotion by men to a worthy recipient even once in a previous life, having attained another birth, one enjoys that very thing perpetually. (56-57)
Those men who give food constantly to Brāhmaṇas enjoy sweet food and drink; indeed, the Ṛṣis who have reached the further shore of the Vedas declare that food alone [is the essence]. 58.
There is no doubt that food is the very life-force, for it arises from the nectar of immortality. Indeed, by one who has offered food, life itself has been given;
therefore, O Great King, you should diligently practice the gift of food. 59–60.
Having thus heard the words of the high-souled Jaimini of the Vairāja lineage,
he again questioned that Brahmin Jaimini, who was learned in wisdom.
Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Deeds of Cyavana," within the "Guru-tīrtha-māhātmya" of the *Vena-upākhyāna* in the *Bhūmi-khaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The ninety-fifth chapter. Subāhu said:
O best of the twice-born, tell me now of the qualities of heaven.
"O best of the twice-born, I shall perform all this naturally.
Jaimini said:
"The various delightful and divine [gardens] such as Nandana,"
There, the meritorious gardens were endowed with all objects of desire;
they were beautiful on all sides with trees bearing fruits that grant every wish,
and there were most divine celestial chariots frequented by hosts of apsarases.
Everywhere there were various objects that moved at will and were subject to one's control,
possessing the color of the rising sun and adorned with lattices of pearls; they were as bright as the orb of the moon and featured couches and seats of gold.
Abounding in all desired objects and free from all suffering,
virtuous men wander there just as they do on earth; neither atheists nor those who have not conquered their senses go there.
Those men who were not cruel, not backbiting, not ungrateful, and free from pride;
who were truthful, established in austerity, heroic, compassionate, and devoted to forgiveness;
and who were performers of sacrifices and of a generous disposition—they went there.
There is no disease, nor old age, nor death; there is no sorrow, nor cold, nor heat. There is neither hunger nor thirst, and no exhaustion is found there.
These and many other such qualities belong to heaven, O King.
Now hear from me the faults that exist in that very state:
the entire fruit of a virtuous deed is experienced right there, and no further action is performed here; this is considered a great fault in that regard. 10.
And dissatisfaction arises upon seeing the blazing prosperity of others. Likewise, there is the sudden downfall of those whose minds are permeated by pleasure.
Whatever action is performed here, its fruit is experienced right there. 11–12.
"O King, this is the land of action; that is known as the land of fruition.
Subāhu said: "But you have described these great defects of heaven. (13)
"O twice-born one, you speak of these worlds as being faultless and eternal.
Jaimini said:
"O King, from the abode of Brahmā downwards, there are indeed faults. (14)
Therefore, the wise do not desire the attainment of heaven;
for that supreme abode of Viṣṇu is above the realm of Brahmā. They know it to be the auspicious, eternal light, the Supreme Brahman. (15)
Foolish men whose nature is centered on sense-objects do not go there;
they are driven by hypocrisy, delusion, fear, malice, anger, and greed.
[Only those] free from possessiveness, free from egoism, free from dualities, and with senses fully restrained [go there]. 16–17.
"Virtuous people, devoted to the yoga of meditation, go there. All this that you asked me has been explained to you.
Having thus heard the qualities of heaven, Subāhu, the lord of the earth, [proceeded].
He spoke to that high-souled Jaimini, the best among speakers.
Subāhu said:
"O Sage, I shall not go to heaven, nor do I even desire it."
Because falling is said to result from that, I shall not perform such an act.
O highly fortunate one, I shall certainly never give even a single gift; for it is through giving and through greed for the fruit thereof that a man indeed falls. 20–21.
Having spoken thus, the righteous Subāhu, lord of the earth,
resolved through the yoga of meditation that he would worship the Lord of Gods, the beloved of Lakṣmī,
and said: "I shall go to the world of Viṣṇu, which is free from burning and dissolution."
Jaimini said:
"O King, you have spoken the truth, which is filled with all that is most auspicious;
kings of virtuous character perform great sacrifices."
O prince, all kinds of gifts are bestowed in sacrifices. At the outset of the sacrifices, they offer food, clothing, and betel-leaf;
they also bestow gifts of gold, land, and cows.
Through well-performed sacrifices, those best of men go to the world of Viṣṇu;
through giving, they attain satisfaction, and the protectors of the earth remain contented. Thus do the high-souled ascetics constantly perform sacrifice.

Having requested alms in a land of plenty, they returned to their own place; O King, for the sake of that [alms], they divided the portions, O high-minded one, giving one share to the Brahmin and a mouthful of fodder to the cow. (27-28)
The ascetics bestow one [portion] upon those who dwell near Supārśva;
by the gift of that food, human beings enjoy its fruit:
free from hunger and thirst, they indeed go to the world of Viṣṇu. 29.

Therefore, O Indra among kings, you too, having attained knowledge through the giving away of wealth earned by righteous means, shall reach perfection through that knowledge. That mortal who hears this unsurpassed and meritorious narrative [shall likewise attain it].
For him there shall be the accomplishment of all goals, and all his sin is dissolved;
liberated from all sins, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu. 32.
Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Life of Cyavana at the Sacred Site of the Guru," within the Legend of Vena in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. 95.
The ninety-sixth chapter. Subāhu said:
By what kinds of actions do men go to hell after death?
"You ought to tell me what kind of people go to heaven after death.
Jaimini said:
"Those twice-born ones who, deluded by greed, abandon their meritorious Brahminhood—"
Those who subsist on evil deeds are indeed destined for hell. Atheists, those who have broken the bounds of propriety, those intent upon lust and sensual objects,
hypocrites, and the ungrateful— they too are indeed destined for hell.
Those men who, having promised wealth to Brahmins, do not give it,
and those who seize the property of Brahmins, go to hell;
likewise, men who are backbiters, arrogant, and speakers of untruth [go to hell].
Those who engage in incoherent chatter go to hell;
those who steal the property of others, those who point out the faults of others, and those who approach the wives of others—these indeed go to hell. (5–6)
Those men who are always devoted to harming the lives of living beings,
and those who are likewise devoted to censuring others, indeed go to hell,
O scorcher of foes, [as do those who destroy] good wells, tanks, and water-stations.
Men who destroy ponds go to hell;
those who treat their wives, children, servants, and guests with hostility,
and who have abandoned the worship of ancestors and gods, go to hell.
Those who defile the life of renunciation, those who harm kings, those who corrupt the stages of life (āśramas), and those who betray their friends— these indeed go to hell.
[One should worship] the Primordial Person, the Lord, the Great Sovereign of all the worlds.
Even those who do not think of Viṣṇu go to hell;
likewise, those who revile the *prayāja* offerings, sacrifices, daughters, friends, virtuous people, and teachers go to hell. 11–12.
Those who obstruct paths with wood, or even with stakes, or likewise with empty stones, are indeed destined for hell.
Those who lack trust toward all living beings, as well as those afflicted by lust, are likewise [destined for hell].
Those who are deceitful toward all living beings are surely destined for hell.
Those who refuse entry to Brāhmaṇas who have arrived seeking food and are emaciated by lack of livelihood are surely destined for hell. 14–15.
Those men who destroy fields, livelihoods, and homes, who destroy joy,
and who destroy hope, indeed go to hell;
as do those who manufacture weapons, arrows, and bows.
O Indra among kings, those who sell [such things] go to hell.
Those fools who show no compassion for the helpless, the distressed, the wretched, the afflicted by disease, or the elderly—they indeed go to hell. 17–18.
Those who, having previously undertaken the restraints, later transgress them due to their fickleness because their senses are unsubdued—they alone are destined for hell. 19.
Thus, O King, these men who go to hell have been described.
Learn from me those people who are destined for the heavenly world:
those men who follow righteousness through truth, austerity, patience, charity, and Vedic study are the ones who go to heaven. 20–21.
Those high-souled men who are devoted to burnt offerings, study, and the worship of the deities, and who take [only what is rightfully theirs], go to heaven.
Those who are pure, dwelling in a pure place, and are solely intent upon Vāsudeva, [go to heaven].
Those people who recite and sing of Viṣṇu go to heaven.
(23) Those people who always respectfully serve their mother and father and avoid sleeping during the day go to heaven. (24)
Those men who have desisted from all violence, who associate with the virtuous,
and who are intent upon the welfare of everyone, go to heaven. Those men who have desisted from all greed and who are patient toward all, [go to heaven].
Those men who have become the refuge of all, who go to heaven by means of service and austerities, and who give honor to their gurus while refraining from accepting gifts—
by these means those men go to heaven. 26–27.
Those who provide for thousands, likewise those who give thousands,
and those who are protectors of thousands— such men go to heaven.
[They save] those who are emaciated by fear, sin, penance, grief, poverty, and disease.
Those beings who release [living creatures] from slaughter, O Bhārata, go to heaven. Those who possess self-nature, those who are in the prime of youth,
and those wise ones who have conquered their senses— those men go to heaven.
O Bhārata, those men who give gold, cattle, land, food, and clothing go to heaven;
likewise, those who rejoice when asked for something and speak kindly after giving what is dear to them.

Those men who have abandoned the desire for the fruits of their giving go to heaven. O scorcher of foes, those men who give away houses, grain, and people after producing them themselves go to heaven.
Those men who never speak of the faults even of their enemies, but rather proclaim their virtues, go to heaven; likewise,
those who, upon seeing the prosperity of others, do not burn with envy.
Rejoicing and offering praise, those men go to heaven (35).
Furthermore, those great-souled men who practice both the path of worldly engagement and the path of renunciation exactly as prescribed in the Vedas and the scriptures go to heaven (36).

Those men who do not know how to speak unpleasant words to others, but are experts only in speaking pleasant words, go to heaven. Those who, though afflicted by hunger, thirst, and fatigue, set aside portions of their own food [for others], [go to heaven].
Those men who give the cry of "Haṃta! go to heaven;
those men who construct step-wells, wells, tanks, water-stations, houses, and groves go to heaven. (38–39)
Those men who are truthful even toward the untruthful, upright even toward those lacking uprightness, and who are well-disposed even toward enemies, go to heaven;
regardless of which family they were born into, they possess many sons and live for a hundred years.
Those men who are compassionate and of virtuous conduct go to heaven;
those men who always make their days fruitful through the single practice of dharma and constantly observe vows go to heaven. 41-42.
Those men who look with equanimity upon one who reviles and one who praises,
whose minds are peaceful and who have conquered pride, go to heaven.
And those who [protect] Brahmins and likewise women who are terrified by fear, [they too go to heaven].
Those men who protect traveling caravans go to heaven;
those men who offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to their ancestors at the Gaṅgā, at Puṣkara, and especially at Gayā, go to heaven. 44–45.
Those men who remain established in self-restraint regarding the nine openings of the senses,
having abandoned greed, fear, and anger— they are the ones who go to heaven.
(46) [They do not harm] living beings such as lice, bedbugs, and gadflies that bite the body.

Those men who protect [others] like their own sons go to heaven; those men who, even out of ignorance, accumulate [merit] according to the prescribed rule and endure all dualities in this world go to heaven. 47–48.
Those pure men who do not take pleasure in the wives of others through action, thought, or speech, and who abide in goodness, go to heaven;
they do not perform censurable acts, but perform those that are prescribed. 49.

Those men who understand their own power go to heaven. Thus, O King, everything has been told to you by me in accordance with the truth: how both an evil state and a good state are attained through one's actions. 50-51.
A man who acts in opposition to others goes to a terrible and most dreadful hell;
for a man who always lives in accordance with others, liberation that brings happiness stands not far away.

Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Life Story of Cyavana," within the "Greatness of the Guru as a Holy Place" section of the Legend of Vena in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The ninety-seventh chapter. Kuñjala said:
Having thus heard what was spoken by the sage at that time, the king [listened].
He spoke thus to the Sage, who had reached the ultimate end of all paths of dharma and adharma.
Subāhu said:
"O best of the twice-born, I myself shall practice dharma; I myself shall perform meritorious deeds."

O Sage, he shall worship Vāsudeva, the source of the universe, most intensely; he should honor Madhusūdana through fire-offerings and recitation alone. Having performed sacrifice and practiced austerity, that king [shall attain] the world of Viṣṇu.
Honored with all his desires, he quickly attained joy; yet, when that great world had vanished, he did not see the God of gods. Intense hunger arose within him, and an extreme thirst set in.
And for those two as well, O one of great wisdom, there was much suffering for their lives;
the king also, together with his beloved, afflicted by hunger and thirst and possessed by great misery, did not see Hṛṣīkeśa.
Sūta said: Thus, O best of beings, the king, together with his beloved wife, became deeply distressed and agitated, being severely afflicted by hunger.
The lord of the earth ran here and there with great speed,
his limbs adorned with all kinds of ornaments, garments, and sandalwood paste;
his body was further graced by flower garlands, necklaces, earrings, and bracelets.
With his limbs beautifully adorned by the luster of jewels, that lord of the earth proceeded on;
thus, following a course of sorrow while being praised by reciters,
and overwhelmed by pain and grief, he spoke these words to his beloved wife.

"O beautiful one, I have reached the world of Viṣṇu along with you, O radiant lady, being praised by sages even as I travel in a celestial chariot. By what action, however, does this hunger of mine increase so excessively?"
"Having reached the world of Viṣṇu, Madhusūdana was not seen by me.
O blessed lady, what could be the cause of this? I have not failed to enjoy the great fruit of my own past actions; yet this suffering has come upon me."
Having heard those words, she spoke thus to the king: The wife said:
"O King, you have spoken the truth; indeed, there is no fruit of dharma."
Those Brāhmaṇas who study the Vedas, the Śāstras, and the Purāṇas,
having shaken off sorrow and grief in this world, are liberated from all defects by the utterance of the name of the divine Viṣṇu, the wielder of the excellent discus.
"O meritorious and highly fortunate ones, you who meditate upon Janārdana— the Lord who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace— have indeed propitiated him. Yet,
as declared by the twice-born, you have not bestowed gifts of food and other necessities upon the Brahmins."
"I know the fruit of that [merit], yet Madhusūdana has not been seen by me. (18) "O King, hunger oppresses me and thirst indeed dries me up.
Kuñjala said:
Thus addressed by his beloved, the king’s senses became overwhelmed with anxiety. Then he beheld a most meritorious hermitage that dispels fatigue,
filled with divine trees and adorned with ponds.

O son, the hermitage shines with ponds, wells, and lakes filled with sacred waters, crowded with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks, and adorned with kahlāra lotuses; it is graced by sages who know the ultimate truth.
It was filled with divine trees and graced by herds of deer;
it was strewn with various flowers and permeated with heart-pleasing fragrances;
it was crowded with twice-born ones and siddhas, and thronged with the disciples of the ṛṣis. 22–23.
Resounding with the voices of lords of yogis, adorned by hosts of gods, and graced by dense groves of plantain trees laden with excellent fruit;
it was filled with various kinds of trees and endowed with everything that fulfills all desires. 24.

It was always adorned with sandalwood trees of lovely fragrance and beautiful fruit. Thus, that meritorious place, filled with such splendors and endowed with the marks of Brahmā, was visited by King Subāhu together with his beloved wife.
He entered that forest of great merit, which grants all desires, where he who resembles the sun dwells, illuminating all directions with supreme radiance like the sun itself. 27.
Shining with great splendor, he was resplendent like the sun.
Seated upon a yogic posture and girt with a yogic belt (28),
Vāmadeva, the best of sages and likewise the foremost among Vaiṣṇavas,
was meditating upon Hṛṣīkeśa, the bestower of worldly enjoyment and liberation (29).
Having seen that high-souled Vāmadeva, the best of sages,
the king, together with his beloved wife, went quickly and prostrated before him.
Then Vāmadeva, seeing that best of kings bowing down, [spoke].
Having greeted the king, who was accompanied by his beloved wife, with blessings (31),
he seated Subāhu, that best of kings, upon an auspicious seat; and then, with water for the feet, the arghya offering, and other forms of worship (32).
The king, who had not been honored by the sage, arrived together with his beloved; then he questioned that most exalted devotee of the Lord.
Vāmadeva said:
O Indra among kings, through divine knowledge I recognize you as Viṣṇu, the knower of dharma, the devotee of Viṣṇu, and the best of men; and I know you, O lord of the earth, to be the son of Ula.
You have arrived free from ailment together with your wife, the daughter of Tārkṣya.
The king said:
"I have come free from ailment, having attained the supreme abode of Viṣṇu;
for by my supreme devotion, Janārdana, the God of gods, [was propitiated]."
"The Lord of the World has been propitiated and is pleased by my devotion, O Lord of the Gods;
why then do I not see that God, the Lord of Kamalā? My father, hunger afflicts me, and my thirst is exceedingly terrible. (36-37)
"O best of sages, we find neither peace nor happiness because of those two; this is the cause of the sorrow that has arisen within me.
Therefore, tell me the reason for it, and by your grace, become gracious-faced toward me. (38)
Vāmadeva said:
"O Indra among kings, you have indeed always been a devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
Madhusūdana has been propitiated by you with supreme devotion."
The Lord of the worlds was not worshipped with devotion, nor with services such as ritual bathing, nor with perfumes, flowers, and the like, nor with food offerings and fruits; yet,
O Indra among kings, upon reaching the tenth day, you always performed these very acts yourself.
A single meal of excellent food was not given by you to a Brāhmaṇa;
having reached the Ekādaśī day, no meal was taken by you. No meal was offered by you to a Brāhmaṇa for the sake of Viṣṇu.
Food always exists upon the earth in the form of nectar.
O Great King, you have never specifically given the gift of food; now hear of the various kinds of medicinal herbs that are praised. 43–44.
O King, pungent, bitter, astringent, sweet, sour, and alkaline substances, as well as all various kinds of condiments such as asafoetida and the like—
all these medicinal herbs that cause nourishment were born from the nectar.
Having well-prepared the food, accompanied by medicinal herbs and condiments (vyañjana), it is offered with the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "To the gods who are forms of Viṣṇu";
and it is placed in the hand of the Brāhmaṇa for the ancestors who are forms of Viṣṇu. 46–47.
Having given that [food] to guests, O Lord, one should feed one's dependents;
thereafter, one should eat that food, which is like nectar, oneself.
After death, there is no suffering for such a person, O King, but rather happiness. 48.
O King, the Brahmins are the ancestors and the gods, appearing in the form of Kṣatriyas.
Just as a certain farmer always performs good cultivation, so too should a mortal perform cultivation in the field that is the mouth of a Brahmin, O King. (49-50)

One should constantly pierce the bull [of the senses] with the ploughshare of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), as well as with the weapon of faith; likewise, discernment (*buddhi*) and austerity (*tapas*) are the goad, while the Lord who experiences truth and knowledge is the pure self (*śuddhātman*). 51.
In the great field named Vipra, one should offer salutations and take leave;
O King, just as a farmer daily breaks up the soil, so too should one who is intent on the cultivation of the field and desires Viṣṇu please Him by constantly dispelling his impurities. 52–53.
In the same way, one should propitiate the Brahmins with auspicious and meritorious words. When the time for reaching mountain pilgrimage sites arrives, like a cloud raining down,
the field-plotter (the seeker) should desire to sow [seeds] and then cause them to be sown in that field.
In the same way, O Great King, when a gift is bestowed upon a Brahmin who has won the favor of the monarch,
the giver enjoys the fruit just as the owner of the field enjoys the harvest from the seed sown therein. 55-56.
And after death, one becomes eternally satisfied right here, and not otherwise; for the Brāhmaṇas, the ancestors, and the gods are undoubtedly of the nature of the field (kṣetra),
O great king, and they grant [the fruits] sown by men.
Thus, there is no doubt that the fruit will certainly be exactly as it is [in its cause].
O King, from something bitter, sweetness does not arise; likewise, from that which is called sweet, bitterness does not arise again. 58–59.

Whatever kind of seed one sows, such is the fruit one reaps; he who does not sow the field does not enjoy its fruit. In the same way, O Brahmins, the gods and the ancestors are the very form of the field.

O King, they manifest the fruit of even that which has been given; of this there is no doubt. Whatever kind of action—whether auspicious or inauspicious—you yourself have performed, O King, experience the corresponding result; it does not happen otherwise.
Then, with a devout mind, she gave delicious food and drink to the gods, the Brahmins, and the ancestors;
she provided them with excellent, refined, and sweet foods, as well as things to be chewed and drunk.

"O Great King, you have not given any of the delicious foods you yourself ate to anyone else; since your own body has been nourished by you with food resembling nectar, therefore hunger arises. (64-65)

O King, O illustrious one, karma alone is the cause of happiness and suffering, as well as of birth and death for human beings; therefore, enjoy this fruit of your own karma. Even the great-souled ones of old attained heaven through their own actions.
Furthermore, having returned to the world of mortals when the time for the exhaustion of their merit arrived,
Nala, Bhagīratha, Viśvāmitra, and Yudhiṣṭhira—
O King— attained heaven solely through their actions at the proper time.
"O King, for one receives happiness or suffering according to that destiny which is one's past karma; indeed, who—even if he were the Lord—is capable of transgressing it? 69.
Then, O best of kings, even though he had gone to heaven, it happened to him...
Therefore, that impulse arising from hunger and thirst is indeed a corrupted action for you.
O best of kings, if the remedy of sugarcane is truly desired by you, then go and eat your own body situated in the Forest of Bliss (Ānandāraṇya). 70–71.
"And this great queen of yours appears extremely emaciated by hunger.
Subāhu said: "For how long must this deed be performed together with my beloved? (72)
Tell me that, O highly fortunate one; when is such favor seen, and by the gift of what substance is what merit obtained, O best of sages? 73.
Tell that, O one of great wisdom, if you are pleased with me now.
Vāmadeva said:
O high-minded one, through the gift of food and water, mortals enjoy great happiness and indeed do not suffer from those very sins; they go to heaven. 74.
Whatever has not been given by humans as a gift, even when the time of death has arrived, everyone gives it as a gift;
therefore, food accompanied by water should be given right at the outset. 75–76.
He who bestows these eight gifts— a fine umbrella and sandals, a beautiful water-vessel, land, excellent gold, and a cow—
shall not be born in heaven subject to the occurrence of hunger, thirst, and other such afflictions. (77)

O King, by the gift of food, one who was previously afflicted by hunger becomes fully satisfied; by the gift of sandals and the gift of an umbrella, O Lord of the Earth, one who was previously tormented by intense thirst becomes forever free from thirst. 78–79.
O best of kings, a giver indeed obtains shade and a vehicle;
by the gift of sandals, I shall tell you something else.
O highly fortunate one, through the gift of land, one may obtain all desires.
O Great King, by the gift of a cow, a man shall always be nourished with the finest essences;
enjoying all pleasures, he shall dwell in the heavenly world.
There is no doubt that the giver becomes truly satisfied through the gift of a cow. 81–82.
Free from disease, endowed with happiness, contented, and possessed of wealth, he is born with gold and fine gold; of this there is no doubt.
Such a man becomes illustrious, handsome, generous, and an enjoyer of jewels.
When the time of death has arrived, he who bestows a gift of sesame seeds becomes the lord of all enjoyments and goes to the world of Viṣṇu; thus,
through this specific kind of giving, supreme happiness is attained.
O Indra among kings, while you were alive, you did not give the gift of cows, nor the gift of land, nor food and water to a brāhmaṇa;
even at the time of death, nothing was given, and therefore this hunger prevails.
"This is declared to be the cause for what has arisen following the power of karma;
whatever kind of karma was performed, that very same kind is experienced.
Subāhu said:
"O best of sages, how may my hunger be pacified?
For this body, withered by her, is exceedingly tormented.
O foremost of the twice-born, tell us the atonement for our hunger. (88-89)
Vāmadeva said:
"O best of kings, there is no atonement for this terrible karma except through its experience."
"O King, you shall enjoy the entire fruit of this deed while remaining in your own state, wherever this body and that of your beloved fall;
