for there is no doubt that both of you must depart from here. (91)
"O King, both of us must eat from this body, for it is indeed imperishable; there is no doubt that each shall eat their own portion together with you and your beloved.
The king said:
"For how long must I enjoy [this] together with my beloved? O illustrious one, please instruct me on that duration. Vāmadeva said:

This great hymn to Vāsudeva destroys even the most heinous sins. (94) When you hear this meritorious [hymn], then you shall attain liberation. All this has been told to you; go now, O King, and enjoy [the fruits of your merit]. (95)
Having heard this, the king, together with his beloved wife, would again eat the flesh of his own body along with her; thus,
O highly wise one, his body would always remain full.
The king, the queen, and their son were constantly devouring [the flesh].
As the king and [the others] devoured the body, that ignoble woman would always laugh; I shall now describe their state of mind. 97–98.

The conduct of that king’s great and virtuous wife, Prajñā, who was never-failing in her devotion, constantly caused him to laugh; for, though urged by Prajñā, he did not give [the gift] with faith. 99.
Having properly resolved upon it for the Brahmins and dedicated it to Viṣṇu,
he thus constantly eats the flesh of his own body; likewise,
the woman also consumes her own body with juices that are like nectar.
Then, at the end of a hundred years, O observer of excellent vows, having remembered the great sage Vāmadeva, he reproached himself, saying:
"Never have I given [offerings] to the ancestors, the gods, or to Brāhmaṇas."
For he has not given to guests, nor especially to the elderly;
he has not given out of compassion to the wretched or to the sick.
Thus he eats his own flesh, censuring his own actions. (103–104)
O King, when Subāhu was thus eating his own flesh along with his beloved wife,
Prajñā and Śraddhā, those two women, seeing him,
laughed; for he was of a virtuous nature due to the ripening of that karma.

O evil-minded one, through the attachment to my company, you have committed what was not given; yet, by those words of wisdom, the king laughs at you once more. "Where has that great delusion gone, by which you were so infatuated, O King? (106-107)
O King, by greed joined with delusion, one is cast into the pit of darkness;
having fallen there, I myself have fallen into a crisis of suffering, having abandoned the path of generosity and followed the path of greed. 108.
"Eat together with your wife; you are greatly afflicted by hunger. Thus, O son, Prajñā laughed at Subāhu who was accompanied by his beloved; this is the entire reason for their laughter. 109–110.
Then, as the king was being devoured, his two bodies, filled with suffering, cried out, "Give! Give! for they were constantly begging;
O highly wise one, they were hungry, thirsty, of terrible form, and fearsome.
"Request from the lord of kings food mixed with milk. (112) "All this that was asked by you has been told; what else shall I tell you? Speak, O high-minded one! (113)
Vijvala said:
O father, tell me that hymn named Vāsudeva, by which a king may attain liberation and reach that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. 114
Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Life of Cyavana," within the "Guru-tīrtha-māhātmya" section of the "Vena-upākhyāna" in the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Ninety-eight.
Sūta said:
When these auspicious words had been spoken by the high-souled Vijvala,
Kuñjala, the best among speakers, uttered this meritorious hymn,
having meditated upon and bowed to Hṛṣīkeśa, the destroyer of all afflictions.
This hymn of Hari has been proclaimed as the bestower of all that is most auspicious;
it is known by the name Vāsudeva, and it grants all supreme welfare.
It is the door to liberation, endowed with bliss, bestowing peace, and increasing nourishment.
This hymn to Vāsudeva, which bestows all desires, grants knowledge, and increases wisdom, was revealed by Vijvala;
it is named after Vāsudeva, is immeasurable, and increases merit.
Having understood everything from his father, Vijvala, the best of birds,
O King, then set out to go to his father's side. Thus,
knowing that Vijvala, who had reached the further shore of knowledge, was resolved to go, [the father spoke].
The righteous-souled Kuñjala spoke to his son, who was intent on performing a service:
"O son, listen; I know that king has committed a great sin."

"Go and recite this while Subāhu listens; in whatever measure he hears this supreme hymn, to that same extent he shall become filled with knowledge of Śrī Vāsudeva—of this there is no doubt. By his grace, what I have spoken shall be most auspicious."
Then, having taken leave of his guru and flying with swift prowess,
Vijvala reached the holy Ānandakānana forest;
taking refuge in the shade of a tree, he sat down filled with joy.
Seeing the king again arriving by means of a celestial chariot (vimāna), [he thought]:
"When will this King Subāhu come with his beloved?
When shall I release him from his sin by means of this hymn of praise? ||| 11-12 ||
At that moment, a celestial chariot arrived, adorned with a network of tinkling bells,
filled with the sound of bells, accompanied by lutes and flutes,
resounded with the voices of Gandharvas, and attended by Apsaras.
Though possessing all his desires fulfilled, he was nevertheless deprived of food and water.
King Subāhu, standing in that vehicle with his beloved wife, descended from the celestial chariot along with his son, Tārkṣya, and his wife.
Just as he took up a sharp weapon and was about to cut that corpse, Vijvala then issued a challenge:
"O tiger among men, O you who are like a god, this [is for you]! 16.

O tiger among men, it is not possible for cruel and merciless people to perform such a heartless deed; this reversal of fate is something that cannot be done, for a wicked, rash, and blameworthy act is always condemned throughout the worlds. (17-18)
"Why have you begun this work here, being devoid of Vedic conduct? Tell me the entire reason for that exactly as it is.
Thus was it spoken by that high-souled Vijvala.
Having heard this, the great king spoke these words to his beloved wife:
"O dear one, for a hundred years I have lived as a doer of evil deeds; when and by whom was such a thing ever spoken of me, that he should speak of me in this way?"

O beloved, as I was thus tormented by hunger, my heart went out to you in longing, O dear one, and peace arose within my mind. (22) [This occurred] as soon as I heard his words, which grant relief from all suffering.
"O lady of beautiful smiles, such delight continues in my heart.
Who is this god? Or will he be a Gandharva? Or perhaps he will be the thousand-eyed Indra? Let the words spoken by the sage in the past come true for these sages. (23-24)
Having heard these words spoken by her beloved, his wife, who was devoted solely to her husband, then replied to the king:
"O Lord, what you have said is true; this is a supreme marvel. (25)
"Just as this beloved one behaves toward me, so too does she act again within my heart.
"Who is this that, assuming the form of a bird, asks [this] like a well-wisher?
Having heard these words spoken by his beloved, the lord of the earth [replied]. (26-27)
With palms joined in reverence, he spoke these words to the bird.
Subāhu said: "Welcome to you, O highly wise one; O Lord, you who have assumed the form of a bird. (28)
With my head, together with my wife, I bow at your two lotus-like feet; may there be merit for us through your grace.
Who are you, appearing in the form of a bird, who speaks such meritorious words?
O best of beings, whatever karma— whether good or evil— is performed by the previous body, that very same thing is experienced right here in this world. Then,
he reported his own conduct before him.
"Just as it was previously heard by my father Kuñjala, tell me your own story: who are you that speaks to me?
Thus did the best of birds then address these words to Subāhu.
Vijvala said:
"Born of the Śuka lineage, my father was named Kuñjala;
I am his third son, Vijvala by name."
"O mighty-armed one, I am neither a god, nor a nāga, nor a gandharva, nor a siddha;
I simply behold this most terrible karma perpetually. For how long must I endure this great deed, joined with such acts of reckless violence?"
"O Great King, tell me now what I shall do.
Subāhu said: "That which was previously mentioned by the brahmins, namely the one named Vāsudeva—" (36)
O auspicious one, when I shall hear what has been spoken by that meritorious sage of restrained self, then I will attain my own destination;
at that time, I shall undoubtedly be liberated from sin. 37.
Vijvala said:
"O best of beings, listen as I shall now declare that eternal truth which my father told me when he was questioned by you."

Oṃ. Of this hymn named *Śrīvāsudeva*, Nārada is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chandaḥ*), and Oṃkāra is the deity (*devatā*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of destroying all sins and for the attainment of the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*) during recitation.
Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva—this is the mantra.
I bow to that Praṇava, the supreme purifier, the highest merit, the knower of the Vedas, the abode of the Vedas, the repository of knowledge, and the support of existence.
(40) It is without dwelling, formless, brilliantly luminous, and of great exaltation.
I bow to the supreme Praṇava, which is devoid of qualities yet bound by qualities;
I bow to that which is most beautiful, possessed of great energy, the destroyer of great delusion, the creator of the entire universe, and transcendent beyond all qualities. 41–42.
Having become the source of all existence, the increaser of the prosperity of beings, I bow to the auspicious Praṇava, which is inseparable from the mendicant and bestows fearlessness;
it is the Gāyatrī, sung by the Sāma singers, the song itself, dear to song, and pure. 43.
I bow to the Praṇava, the enjoyer of the songs of the Gandharvas;
I bow to that Oṃkāra, who is the investigation [of truth], whose form is the Veda, who abides in the sacrifice, who is kind to his devotees, and who is the source of the entire world. 44-45.
I bow to Hari in the form of the Praṇava, who shines as a boat for the deliverance of all beings submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra;
he who dwells in all worlds in a single form, yet manifold ways. 46
I bow to Śiva, the Praṇava, who exists in the form of the absolute state (kaivalya);
who is subtle, subtler than the subtle, pure, devoid of qualities yet the lord of qualities; who is free from all material states and is the abode of the Vedas. 47–48.
I bow to that Oṃkāra, who is always free from the separations of gods and demons, who is the object of meditation for the gods and yogis,
the all-pervading knower of the universe, the supreme and auspicious consciousness. 49.
I bow to the auspicious Lord Praṇava, who possesses auspicious qualities and is peaceful.
(50) I salute him, having entered whose Māyā even the gods and demons, beginning with Brahmā, do not find the supreme, pure gateway to liberation. (51)
Salutations to Him whose intellect is pure, the root of bliss, the pure Swan, the one who is both supreme and inferior;
salutations to that Leader of the Gaṇas, the illustrious Vāsudeva of great splendor.
(52) He who shines with the glorious Pāñcajanya conch and with the Sudarśana discus, radiant as the sun.
I take refuge this very day in that Lord who shines even with the lotus-marked mace. 53.

I take refuge in that Vāsudeva, who is the secret of the Vedas, who possesses all qualities, who is the support of the qualities of all things mobile and immobile, and whose splendor is equal to the sun and the fire. 54.

I take refuge in that Vāsudeva, the treasury of hunger, who is stainless, beautiful, and resplendent with the measure of bliss; having attained whom the worlds of the gods and others live, he who constantly effects the destruction of dense masses of darkness by his own rays and is the cause of all purification. 55.
I take refuge in that Vāsudeva, who is resplendent with the blazing splendor of the sun.

(56) I take refuge in that Vāsudeva, who shines everywhere with the radiance of the sun, who causes desiccation and bestows moisture, and who dwells within the vital breaths of all living beings. (57)
I take refuge in that Vāsudeva, who, like a boat for the purpose of crossing over, sustains all the worlds and their protectors according to his own will;
he who, existing within, eternally cooks the moving and unmoving beings composed of the world. 58.
I take refuge in that Vāsudeva, who is the cause of the host of gods headed by Svāhā.

59 I take refuge in that Vāsudeva, who is gentle, whose nature is to bestow qualities, who nourishes all things in the world with most meritorious juices, and who is the source of food through his pure splendor. 60
There truly exists everywhere the cause of destruction, the support of all, consisting of all, and that All itself;

he who enjoys the objects of the senses even without the sense organs—to that Vāsudeva I go for refuge. (61) In the form of the individual soul (jīva), he sustains the worlds, including his own manifestations, both moving and unmoving.
I take refuge in that Vāsudeva, who is absolute, consisting of pure knowledge, and perfectly stainless.

(62) I take refuge in that Vāsudeva, the destroyer of demons, the root of the destruction of suffering, the peaceful, the supreme, the embodiment of power, the vast one, by attaining whom the gods attain humility. (63)

I take refuge in Vāsudeva—the end of happiness, the giver of happiness, the Lord of the gods, the ocean of knowledge, the best of sages, the Lord of the gods, the refuge of truth, and who is established in truthful qualities;
he whose form is the limbs of sacrifice, whose form is the supreme reality, who is endowed with *māyā*, and who is the fierce merit of the Lord of the earth. 64.
I take refuge in Vāsudeva, the singular consciousness, the abode of all worlds.
(65) His bed lies in the midst of the ocean upon the vast coils of the body of the serpent; I bow eternally to those two lotus feet of that Vāsudeva. (66)

The two lotus feet of that Śrī Vāsudeva— endowed with merit, ever attended by Śaṅkara, and served by numerous sacred fords— are indeed the destroyers of sin; those lotus feet resemble great red lotuses and are fit for the victory over the excellent signs of worldly existence.
I bow eternally to the feet of Śrī Vāsudeva, which are adorned with anklets and seals;
(68) those lotus-feet of Śrī Vāsudeva, which are always praised with true devotion by the gods, the perfected ones (*siddhas*), the sages, and the lords of the serpents—I bow to them eternally. (69)
I take refuge in that Vāsudeva, in whose foot-water even those sages who are submerged become purified and go to heaven free from sin; being well-satisfied, they attain liberation.
Wherever the water from Viṣṇu’s feet remains, there the Gaṅgā and other sacred fords always abide along with their presiding deities.
Even those whose bodies are stained with sins, by drinking it, go purified to the beautiful abode of Murāri.
Even those whose bodies are smeared with terrible sins, by being sprinkled with even the water from His feet, attain liberation from the Supreme Lord; I perpetually bow at His very feet. 71–72.
By merely consuming the well-prepared food offering (naivedya) of that great-souled Lord who wields the beautiful discus,

men obtain the fruit of the Śrī Vājapeya sacrifice and become endowed with all goals of life. [They worship] that Nārāyaṇa, the destroyer of the depths of hell, who is free from illusion and the knower of all qualities.
I take refuge in that Vāsudeva, meditating upon whom beings attain a happy rebirth.

(74) I bow with devotion to his two most excellent and purifying feet—the feet of him who is worthy of salutation by the hosts of ṛṣis, siddhas, and cāraṇas, and who is eternally worshipped by the gods; he who is the Lord of Brahmā and the other deities, acting as the cause for the creation of the universe; and he who is compassionate, the one who rescues those fallen into the great ocean of saṃsāra. (75)

I bow to that supreme, purifying pair of lotus-feet of Śrī Vāmana, who was seen by the hosts of gods in the sacrificial pavilion chanting the Sāman hymns; he who, as the sole Lord of the three worlds, inspired the throngs of deities with joyful curiosity through his singing; and who, with his auspicious glances, brought sinlessness to the eyes of those in his army.
He shone in the assembly of the twice-born at the commencement of the sacrifice, adorned with the glory of Brahman, and possessed a divine splendor like a sapphire.
I bow to the Lord Vāmana, who, out of a desire for the welfare of the gods, begged even the son of Virocana, saying, "Give me three paces of land.

(77) I praise the incomparable prowess of that Lord, the wielder of the excellent discus, who was seen by hosts of sages in the solar orb as he ascended to heaven, and who, at the interval between the setting of the sun and moon, covered the heavens with a single step; it was by that very body of his, the universal and unbounded banner, that the hosts of gods attained their dissolution. (78)
Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Life of Cyavana," within the "Greatness of the Guru-tīrtha" section of the "Story of Vena" in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Ninety-nine.
Viṣṇu said:
Having heard this hymn—which is purifying, supreme, ancient, a destroyer of sins, meritorious, auspicious, blessed, well-composed, and most excellent for recitation—the king became happy;
his thirst and hunger departed, and he became like a god. 1.

Both of them, though endowed with beautiful forms, were joined by their wives and had fallen into the bondage of sin. Then the Lord, surrounded by gods, brahmins, and perfected beings (siddhas) devoted to Hari, arrived; He who bears the conch, discus, lotus, mace, and sword, came to that king whose impurities had been removed.
Śrī Nārada, Bhārgava, Vyāsa, and the meritorious son of Mṛkaṇḍu arrived there;
the sage named Vālmīki, a devotee of Viṣṇu, arrived, as did Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā;
the high-souled Garga, endowed with devotion to Hari, Jābāli, Raibhya, and Kaśyapa also came.
Accompanied by Hari, these most excellent devotees of Viṣṇu arrived;
they were meritorious, highly fortunate, and cleansed of all taints. Devoted to the beautiful lotus feet of Hari, they stood surrounding Śrī Vāsudeva and praised the Lord in various ways.
All the gods, headed by Agni the consumer of oblations, as well as Brahmā, Hari, and the most divine goddesses,
along with the Gandharva kings and other excellent singers, sing a divine, sweet, and captivating song.
The sages praise Him with hymns that are well-composed, consistent with the supreme truth, and highly meritorious.
Seeing the king, his husband, Lord Hari spoke these enchanting words:
"O King, choose whatever boon you desire; since I am well-pleased, I shall grant it to you.
Hearing Hari’s speech and seeing the Enemy of Mura speaking before him, the king—
The Lord who resembles a blue lotus, the slayer of Mura, who bears the conch, discus, sword, and mace;
who is endowed with Śrī, the Supreme Sovereign, resplendent with jewels, adorned with bracelets and necklaces;
possessing the brilliance of the sun, well-served by hosts of gods, and beautifully decorated with ornaments of highly precious necklaces—10.

With divine fragrances and excellent unguents, the king, having descended to the earth with sentiments of true devotion, constantly prostrated himself with staff-like salutations; then that great monarch worshipped him with the words, "May you be victorious," saying, "I am your slave, I am your servant; may I always possess devotion before you and the highest state of being."
O Hari, protect me who have come here accompanied by my wife; I have sought refuge in you.
Blessed indeed are those Mādhava-devotees, the twice-born, whose minds are always dissolved in meditation upon you.
13. Uttering "Bhava-Mādhava," they depart from here to Vaikuṇṭha, utterly purified.
Those men who bear upon their heads the holy water flowing from your very lotus feet,
they become bathed in the waters arising from all sacred pilgrimage sites and attain the supreme abode of Hari.
(14-15) I possess neither yoga, nor devotion, nor knowledge, nor ritual action.
"By attachment to what merit do you offer me this boon?
(16) Hari said: "That which is named Vāsudeva is the destroyer of great sins."
O King, you have heard this from the merit-bestowing Avijvala;
therefore, you have become a partaker of liberation, of this there is no doubt. Enjoy divine pleasures, agreeable to the mind, as my lord in my world.
The king said:
"If a boon is indeed to be granted by you to me, who am not in need, then grant first to Vijvala this most excellent boon. (19)
Hari said:
O King, Vijvala’s father was the meritorious Kuñjala, adorned with knowledge; he constantly recited the great hymn to Vāsudeva. 20.
"Accompanied by his beloved wife and sons, he shall go to my abode;
I shall grant this fruit to one who constantly recites this hymn.
When these auspicious words were spoken, the king addressed Keśava.
"O Keśava, may this hymn of great merit be fruitful for you in Kurukṣetra. Hari said:
"O Great King, when men shall offer praise in the Kṛta Yuga..."

Then they shall attain liberation at that very moment; of this there is no doubt. (23) In the Tretā age, [they attain it] in just one month; in the Dvāpara, in six months; and in the Kali age, those men who perform the recitation attain it in a single year. (24)
O Indra among kings, those Brāhmaṇas who, having bathed, recite [this] either three times a day or once a day, go to heaven— that destination which bestows the state of Viṣṇu.
Whatever desire they may wish for, that shall indeed be theirs.
A Kṣatriya attains victory, adorned with wealth and grain;
a Vaiśya shall become prosperous and happy; and a Śūdra shall likewise become happy. Whoever causes even an outcaste to hear this shall be liberated from sin.
By the grace of this hymn to me, a disciple shall never behold the terrible hell; he shall become a master of all accomplishments (sarvasiddha).
He shall recite it while Brahmins are being fed during the time of a Śrāddha ceremony.

O King, the ancestors will go to the world of Viṣṇu, fully satisfied. At the conclusion of the libation (tarpaṇa), whether a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya should perform the recitation (japa); his ancestors, with delighted minds, drink the nectar (amṛta). 29-30.
If a person recites this with devotion in their home or in the midst of a sacrifice, no obstacles shall arise there; all success will be attained.
Even in difficult places, in inaccessible regions, or in the perilous presence of a predatory tiger, [no harm shall come].
When one has fallen into danger from thieves, one should recite this hymn there;
O Great King, there will be peace, of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, for other auspicious occasions, such as when a man has gone to the king’s gate—33.
A person who has purified themselves through celibacy and is free from anger and greed should recite the mantra named Vāsudeva ten thousand times;
then, they should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with sesame seeds and rice grains mixed with clarified butter (ājya) in a quantity equal to one-tenth of the recitation.
Having worshipped Vāsudeva, one should offer [the gift] with a restrained mind;
then, for every verse, men should perform a fire-oblation (homa) while meditating. To them, I shall never leave their side, remaining ever by their side like a devoted servant. 35–36.
When the Kali age has fully arrived, one shall attain the state of a servant through this hymn; even if it is given to anyone whatsoever on the occasion of breaking the Veda,
he shall indeed become one whose purpose is fulfilled with all desires.
Listen, O King, to this hymn which I have composed so that it may bear fruit:
it was created by Brahmā and formerly chanted by Rudra;
by it, Indra was liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin and freed from his transgression. 38–39.
The gods, sages, secret ones, siddhas, vidyādharas, and immortals,
as well as the nāgas, having worshipped this hymn, attained their desired perfections (siddhi).
He who recites it shall become meritorious, fortunate, a donor, and possessed of sons.
"He shall recite this hymn; there is no need for hesitation here.
"Come with your wife to my abode, O best of kings," [said Hari];
and the hand of that monarch was taken by Hari. 41–42.
There, the kettledrums resounded, the gandharvas sang charmingly, the foremost apsaras danced, and they showered down a rain of flowers;
all the gods and sages praised him with Vedic hymns. 43.
Then the king went with his beloved to Hari (44). While He was being praised by hosts of gods and Siddhas, the blazing king, with a joyful mind,
arrived and stood where his father and mother were, he of great power and speed (45).
Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Life of Cyavana at the Sacred Site of the Guru," within the *Vena-ākhyāna* of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter One Hundred. Viṣṇu said:
On the beautiful bank of the Narmadā, his father indeed resided under a banyan tree; Vijvala also arrived there and, having prostrated before his father,
that high-minded one [began] the hymn named Vāsudeva.
The virtuous-souled one related the greatness of his father before him:
how Viṣṇu, having arrived, granted him an auspicious boon;
he recounted all of that with a very joyful heart.
Having heard the account of Kuñjaloṭhī from the king,
Vijvala was filled with great joy; embracing his son, he said, "O child,
a meritorious deed has been performed by you for the sake of the high-souled king."
"Great merit is gained from the recitation of Vāsudeva’s deeds. Having thus addressed his son, having greeted him with blessings,
and having praised his son— who was endowed with divine qualities— again and again, [he departed].
Standing on the beautiful bank of the river while Cyavana looked on,
all this conduct of those high-souled Vaiṣṇavas has been narrated to you, O great king; what else shall I tell you?
Vena said:
"The nectar was offered to me for the purpose of drinking in a conch vessel;
therefore, what mortal on the surface of the earth would have the confidence to drink it?"
The supreme Vaiṣṇava knowledge is indeed always the foremost among all drinks here; yet,
as you speak thus, no satiety arises in me as a drinker,
for my faith to hear it, O Lord of the God of Gods, increases ever further.
Out of your grace, please tell me of the conduct of Mekuñjala as well;
what was said by that great-souled one to his fourth son?
O Lord, out of compassion, please relate that truth to me in full detail.
The Blessed Lord said:
Listen, for I shall relate the life-story of Kuñjala and the life-story of Cyavana, which is endowed with great spiritual merit.
O best of men, this meritorious narrative destroys sin.
The man who listens to it with devotion shall obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Thus ends [the section on] the greatness of Gurus as a sacred ford within the Legend of Vena in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The One Hundredth Chapter in the Life of Cyavana.
The One Hundred and First Chapter.
Sūta said:
Hṛṣīkeśa, the God of gods, spoke to the son of Aṅga, that best of kings,
concerning the narrative called Mahāśreya, which destroys all sin.
"Listen, I shall relate this account which bestows prosperity."
And [he told] the account of the high-souled brāhmaṇa Kuñjala.
Viṣṇu said:
"The righteous Kuñjala, moreover, [gave] his fourth son..."
Being thus summoned, Udāyuka spoke to that Kapiñjala: "O son, what unprecedented thing have you seen? Tell me. O best of sons, for what purpose have you come here from there to seek food?"
"O highly fortunate one, tell me that which was seen, which bestows great merit.
Kapiñjala said: "O dear one, I shall relate to you that unprecedented matter about which you have asked."
"That which has not been seen or heard by anyone, and which I myself have never heard before—that very thing I shall now proclaim here; let it be heard even now, O father!
Listen, all you brothers, and you, mother, listen now."
Kailāsa, the best of mountains, is white like the moon;
it is filled with various minerals, adorned with diverse trees,
and washed on all sides by the auspicious, holy waters of the Gaṅgā, O Father.
Thousands of divine and various rivers,
as well as thousands of water-filled lakes on the great mountain, have their waters produced from you, O Father. 9.
In that best of mountains, there are vast rivers frequented by swans and cranes, which bestow merit and destroy sin;
and there are various forests filled with blossoming flowers and fruits. 10–11.
It was filled with various trees providing green and auspicious fruits;
it was joined by throngs of kinnaras and crowded with apsarases;
it was beautifully adorned by gandharvas, cāraṇas, siddhas, and hosts of gods.
It was endowed with groves of celestial trees and filled with divine splendors;
it was richly adorned with various jewels and divine fragrances of exquisite beauty, and it was most beautiful with white slabs of crystal. 13–14.
O King, it was filled with splendors like the radiance of the sun, and was adorned everywhere with sandalwood trees of lovely fragrance, with *bakula* trees bearing blue blossoms,
and with various trees laden with diverse flowers.
With the soft warbling of birds and the divine, it becomes sweet;
with the humming of bees and the multitude of trees, it is made pleasant;
and with the songs of cuckoos, this mountain and its groves shine forth beautifully.
There stands a temple of Śiva, crowded with tens of millions of attendants,
white with rays of light, meritorious, and like a mountain-peak of accumulated virtue.
It is further [surrounded] by roaring lions, buffaloes, and elephants.
It resounded on all sides with the deep roars of the world-elephants (diggajas),
was filled with various wild beasts, crowded with swarms of monkeys,
and echoed through its caves with the cries of peacocks. 19–20.
It was resplendent with caves, clay slopes, peaks, and ridges; endowed with various springs and shining with medicinal herbs;
divine, possessed of celestial qualities, meritorious, and filled with holy abodes. 21.
That great mountain, a mass of merit frequented by those in the worlds of virtue,
and that best of mountains inhabited by Pulindas, Bhillas, and Kolas,
shines as the king of mountains with its formidable peaks and summits. 22–23.
With various other merits, auspicious ceremonies, and propitious rites,
as well as with the great sound of the flowing waters of the Gaṅgā,
I proceeded to Śaṅkara’s abode there on Kailāsa.
There, I beheld a marvel such as has never been seen before nor heard of at any time.
Listen, for I shall relate everything that was spoken by him from the auspicious and highly exalted peak of Meru, the king of mountains. 25–26.
O highly fortunate one, a stream of snow, milk, and gold falls upon the earth from the Ganges, adorned with the roar of its great velocity;
having reached the summit of Kailāsa, it spreads out there.
There, a great Ganges pool measuring ten yojanas in extent shines with vast, holy, and pure water;
having attained that state which is auspicious in every respect, it is graced by great swans.

O high-minded one, on its bank, upon a rock, the daughter of the Himalaya dwells; there the swans warble with divine and sweet voices, resonant with the chanting of the Sāman hymns, and it shines because of that sound. 30.
Seated with her hair loose, she was radiant with the wealth of beauty;
endowed with a divine form and possessing divine qualities and characteristics,
she shone upon its bank adorned with divine ornaments.
I do not know whether she is the daughter of the King of Mountains or of the great ocean,
nor whether she is the wife of Brahmā, or if she will be Svāhā;
or perhaps this highly fortunate lady will be Indrāṇī or Rohiṇī.
Such a perfection of form is not seen among other young women, nor indeed among any other most divine women, O dear one, as is this abundance of beauty,
qualities, and character that is observed here. (34-35)
O dear one, does any among the apsarases possess such marks of beauty as that which I have seen—
those limbs which enchant the entire world?
Seated upon the stone slab, she was overwhelmed even by her own suffering.
The young women, deprived of their many kinsmen, weep with piteous cries;
O high-minded one, they shed many pure tears that shine like pearls as they fall into this lake. (37–38)
Drops resembling pearls fell into the great waters; from them arose beautiful and fragrant lotuses, O high-minded one—lotuses that were born from those tears of the eyes. 39.
Those who have fallen into the waters of the Gaṅgā with great speed are indeed countless;
they cross over [to liberation] while being well-served by flocks of swans in the midst of the Gaṅgā’s current. 40-41.
The stream of the Bhāgīrathī emerged from that place and,
reaching the peak of Kailāsa, entered the beautiful cave named Ratna;
there it remains full of water, extending for two yojanas.
It was crowded with flocks of swans and teeming with aquatic birds;
there, in that place frequented by hosts of sages, were lotuses of various distinct colors, rendered pure by the flowing current. 43–44.
Those lotuses which were born from her tears became fragrant and magnificent at dawn, as if drenched in the waters of the Gaṅgā;
they floated upon the current, which was filled with pure water. 45.
In the midst of it all, it resounded with the cries of swans and water-birds.
Sūta said:
On that mountain named Ratna, the Great Lord Maheśvara resides as Ratneśvara.
"O father, he who is always well-worshipped by gods and daityas remains there.
There, O father, I saw a certain meritorious sage,
burdened by a mass of matted hair, naked, and carrying a staff."
Supportless and without food, he was exceedingly weakened by austerity; though his limbs were emaciated, they were but a collection of bones wrapped in mere skin.
All the limbs of that great-souled one were merely smeared with ashes.
He ate dry leaves that were withered and fallen;
seated in devotion to Śiva, he was a man of great austerity and formidable matted locks. From his tears there arose fragrant lotuses. 50–51.
Having brought water from the Gaṅgā, the highly fortunate one, skilled in song and dance, should worship the God of gods, Ratneśvara;
he sings and dances while standing at the gateway of that enemy of Tripura.

"O best among speakers, O dear one, this unprecedented sight has been seen by me as I arrived at the monastery; the righteous-souled one is rejoicing even with melodious sounds. If you know the cause, please tell it to me out of your grace. (53-54)
"O noble lady, why does my father weep all of a sudden? Why does he worship the Great Lord Maheśvara along with the gods and men?
Tell me that in detail, for it is the cause of all my doubt."
Thus addressed by his son Kapiñjala, the highly wise Kuñjala spoke at length before the listening sage, O Muni.
Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "The Life of Cyavana," within the "Guru-tīrtha-māhātmya" section of the "Vena-upākhyāna" in the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The one hundred and second chapter. Kuñjala said:
"O child, I shall explain everything that you have just told me."
O best of the twice-born, since that which was born from the play of both [deities] occurred,
once the great goddess Pārvatī, the most excellent of women,
while sporting, spoke these words to the high-souled Īśvara.
"O Mahādeva, O Great Lord, show me before my eyes that great forest, the best of forests, which has arisen from your own breast and for which I have a great longing. Śrī Mahādeva said:
"So be it, O Great Goddess! I shall show you that holy place, crowded with gods, frequented by the twice-born and the Siddhas.
Having thus addressed the Goddess, he then departed with her and his attendants.
The god, eager to go, went indeed to the Nandana grove—
everywhere beautiful, divine-backed, adorned with ornaments,
joined with garlands of bells, and garlanded with clusters of small tinkling bells. 5–6.
Mahādeva, mounted upon a bull that resembled a swan or the moon and possessed beautiful characteristics, was adorned with chowries, silk threads, and strings of pearls,
and was surrounded by ten million attendants.
Nandī, Bhṛṅgi, Mahākāla, Skanda, Caṇḍa, Manohara,
Vīrabhadra, Gaṇeśa, Puṣpadanta, Maṇīśvara,
Atibala, Subala by name, Meghanāda, and Ghaṭāvaha. 8–9.
Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Cakālida, Pulida, Vīrabāhuka, Keśarī, the one named Kiṅkara, Caṇḍahāsa, and Prajāpati—
these and many others, such as Sanaka and his brothers, possessed the power of asceticism.
Surrounded by hosts numbering in the tens of millions,
Mahādeva, accompanied by Śiva and the Goddess, entered the Nandana grove, which was frequented by gods and kinnaras. 11–12.
The Lord of the Gods showed to Girijā that most beautiful place, abounding in various trees and filled with many flowers;
it was strewn with divine *raṃbhā* vines and with flowering *caṃpaka* trees. 13.
It was crowded with clusters of jasmine and beautifully blossomed *mallikā* flowers,
and it shone with excellent groves of *pāṭala* trees whose branches were perpetually in bloom,
as well as with great sandalwood trees of lovely fragrance.

It was filled with forests of *devadāru* trees and crowded with lofty trees; likewise, it abounded with *sarala*, coconut, and betel-nut trees, as well as divine date and jackfruit trees, all bent down by the weight of their fruit. 16.16–17a.
It was filled with large trees emitting a rich fragrance,
beautifully adorned with *saptaparṇa* trees that shone like the brilliance of fire, and with *rājavṛkṣa* and *kadamba* trees that were always graced with the splendor of flowers. 17–18.
It was filled with great jambu and nimba trees, mātulunga fruits, nāraṅgas, sindhuvāras, priyālas, śālas, and tindukas;
it was adorned with udumbaras, kapitthas, and jambu trees. 19.

It was filled with *lakuca* trees fragrant with blossoms and with blooming *nāga* trees; it was crowded with mangoes—the kings of fruits—and with dark trees resembling dense clouds, as well as divine groves of blue *śāla* forests and thickets of *jāla* trees. 20–21.
It was graced by vast *tamāla* trees resembling the sun, and adorned with all other trees like dark blue forests; thus was the holy Nandana grove revealed by Śiva.
22. And it was beautified by other trees, all resembling dark blue woods.
The Nandana grove was adorned with wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*) of great merit, which yield auspicious fruits and are endowed with the fruits of all desires;
it resounded with the sweet calls of various birds. 23–24.
It resounded with the holy songs of cuckoos and the humming of honey-bees, and was filled with the warbling of birds eager for the makaranda nectar;
it was crowded with various trees and teeming with diverse herds of wild animals. 25.
With various fragrant flowers fallen from the trees onto the ground, that earth shone, O son, as if honored by perfumes;
there were also most meritorious ponds, pure with the fragrance of lotuses. 26–27.
It was filled with lakes resembling oceans, honored by the fragrance of their waters, and frequented by swans and ducks; there,
the great Nandana grove shone, filled with all the hosts of Apsarases.
With celestial chariots, auspicious pitchers, and beautiful golden staffs,
and with palaces plastered with white lime, the king of the Nandana forest shone everywhere, filled with great throngs of Kinnaras.
O best of the twice-born, that sacred abode of Nandana shone everywhere with Gandharvas and beautiful Apsarases, with the diversions of the gods, and with throngs of sages and excellent yogis. 31-32.

Having thus observed [the place], the high-souled Bhava, the Great-Souled One, together with Sudevī, beheld Śrīnaṃdana— the abode of the meritorious, a source of happiness, endowed with the quality of tranquility,
possessing a luster equal to the splendor of the sun, shining with hosts of rays like gold. 33.
Endowed with flowers, fruits, and all objects of desire, even the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpadruma*) in the Nandana grove is not its equal.
Beholding such a sovereign of trees, the Goddess spoke to Śiva: "O Lord, tell me the name of this most meritorious mountain, which is itself a source of merit for all. (34–35)
Among the radiant ones, Śiva spoke to the Sun, the best of luminaries, who was surrounded by gods and goddesses.
Śiva said: "His installation shall be great and known as auspicious; and Madhusūdana is the foremost among the gods. (36)
Just as the Creator is the author of the creation of the principal rivers, the Asuras, and the celestial streams;

just as the Moon is the bringer of happiness to all beings; just as the Earth is the foremost among the elements; just as the King of Mountains is the chief of mountains; and just as the Ocean is the preeminent among reservoirs of water—37.
O Goddess, as food is among great medicinal herbs, and as Himavat is among the mountains;
as the knowledge of the Self is among all sciences, and as the lord of men is among all people in the worlds;
even so is this king of trees preeminent—he who is the guest of all and beloved by the Lord of the Gods. (38–39)
Śrī Pārvatī said: "O Śambhu, please proclaim the auspicious and most meritorious qualities of this lord of trees.
Having heard the words of the Goddess, the Lord spoke everything concerning the benefit of that excellent tree. 40.

Whatever those most meritorious gods, who resemble gods and are the best of deities, desire in their hearts, that very thing this tree named Kalpadruma, the most excellent, bestows upon them for their benefit.
From this merit all things arise; it is difficult to attain here even by those with great ascetic power.
The most eminent gods enjoy that exceedingly divine jewel, which is superior even to life itself.
Having reflected in her mind upon the wondrous words of Śiva, the Goddess, with his approval, prepared for him a single jewel among women— one of excellent qualities and beautiful form.
With lotus-like faces and lotus-hands, they possess beautiful lotuses; their forms are like fine gold, and their radiance is likewise pure and full of splendor.
Their playful brilliance is exquisite, their hair is beautifully curled and bound with very fine strands, and they are anointed with fragrant flowers. 45–46.
With her hair firmly bound by a strong lock, the young woman shone with a most excellent form;
and on the parting of her hair, a string of pearls appeared like a row of trees.
At the base of the parting, the illustrious lady’s tilaka-mark gleamed like the radiant preceptor of the Daityas at sunrise.
On her forehead, the splendor arising from the lotus of musk shines forth;
the radiance of the tilaka at the parting of her hair reveals the beauty of her form in this auspicious world.
Upon her hair, her pearl ornaments, and her forehead, it eternally creates exquisite loveliness. 48–49.

Just as the new moon shines with a luster that appears beautiful through its very activity, so too does the full moon shine with a canopy of moonlight and a web of cool rays; in that same way, her face shines, creating splendor and being renowned throughout the world. 50. Even the moon, though possessed of digits, wanes as it is eternally deprived of its fullness;
yet her face was always perfectly full, joyful, and entirely stainless.
Beholding its own fragrance and blossoming, the lotus found no happiness therein.

This lotus-faced woman, endowed with all virtues, was fashioned by my own creative powers; behold her own fragrance, for the wind of the world blows from her mouth. (53) Overcome with shame, she suddenly took refuge in the water and remains there forever.
With an intellect that was somewhat uncertain, they spoke of the treasury of King Sumadana as being like the ocean through its various arts;
[she] was endowed with the jewels of her beautiful teeth and the playfulness of her smiles, her face shining with a reddish-brown bimba-fruit-like lower lip.
Her eyebrows were beautiful, her nose was lovely, and her ears, adorned with jewels, were exquisite.
The two cheeks, endowed with a luster like that of gold, are possessed of radiance.
Three lines, beautifully situated upon the neck, shine forth;
indeed, these three lines here signify good fortune, virtuous character, and elegance.

Her breasts, firm, full, and resembling spherical forms, were fashioned like two jars of Kandarpa for the purpose of consecration; her shoulders shone exceedingly, being symmetrical and endowed with pride. 58.
His two arms were rounded, smooth, golden, and endowed with auspicious marks;
his lotus-like hands were perfectly symmetrical, lotus-colored, very cool,
possessed of divine characteristics, and marked with the signs of the lotus and the svastika.
The fingers are straight, joined with lotuses, and endowed with nails;
the nails are very sharp and resemble drops of water. The complexion produced from his body resembles the interior of a lotus.
That beautiful woman, Padmagandhā, shone like a lotus in every limb; endowed with all auspicious marks, she was as radiant as a celestial maiden.
Her feet, resembling red lotuses, were smooth and exceedingly beautiful.
The nails arising from the tips of her feet possess the appearance of radiant jewels;
as described in the scriptures, so too are they seen upon her limbs.
Her body is beautified by all manner of ornaments—necklaces, bracelets, and anklets.
She shone with the sound of her girdle and waist-string; the auspicious lady attained supreme beauty with a dark blue silk garment,
and she was endowed with excellent qualities by means of a divine, deep-red bodice.
Having attained great prosperity through the extraordinary power manifested by Pārvatī,
she received joy from the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma) and spoke these words to Śaṅkara: "O Lord,
the tree has been seen by me exactly as you described."
"In whatever manner a thing is conceived, in that very manner it is perceived.
Sūta said:
Then she, whose every limb was beautiful, approached the side of the two of them.
Then, with devotion, she bowed at the lotus feet of you both, O Bhava and Bhavānī.
At that time, she spoke words that were affectionate, pleasing, and charming:
"O Lord, O Mother, tell me the reason why I was created by you. (69-70)

The illustrious goddess said: "O auspicious lady, out of curiosity regarding the tree, I have indeed performed a test; immediately, O blessed one, the fruit has been obtained through the perfection of your beauty."
"Undoubtedly, my daughter, endowed with all auspicious fortune, shall attain renown in the world by the name Aśokasundarī,
just as the god Purandara is celebrated among the Somavaṃśas. (72)
"O Indra among kings, one named Nahuṣa shall become the worshiper of that deity. Having thus granted her the boon, the Daughter of the Mountain,
filled with supreme joy along with Śaṅkara, departed for Mount Kailāsa.
Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, titled "The Life of Cyavana," within the "Guru-tīrtha-māhātmya" section of the *Vena-upākhyāna* in the *Bhūmi-khaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter One Hundred and Third. Kuñjala said:
Then Aśokasundarī, born from the best of all women, rejoiced in the auspicious Nandana grove, which was endowed with every desirable quality; she,
possessing a beautiful smile, was accompanied by well-formed, lovely daughters of the gods.
Enjoying all pleasures and being skilled in song and dance,
Vipracitti’s son Huṇḍa— fierce, always intense,
acting according to his own will, and possessed of great lust— entered Nandana.

Seeing Aśokasundarī adorned with all her ornaments, the Daitya was pierced by the arrows of Kāma at the mere sight of her. That great-bodied one said to her, "Who are you, O auspicious lady, and to whom do you belong?"
"And for what reason have you come here to the supreme abode of Śiva?
Aśokasundarī said:
"Listen now; I am the daughter of the most meritorious Śiva."
"I am the sister of Skanda and the daughter of my own maternal uncle; in my childhood, I arrived here at will in this Forest of Delight. Who are you, and for what reason do you question me thus?"
Huṇḍa said:
"I am the son of Vipracitti, endowed with all virtues and characteristics;
I am renowned by the name Huṇḍa, arrogant with the pride of strength and heroism."

"O fair-faced one, among the Daityas I am also the foremost; there is no Rākṣasa equal to me in the worlds of gods and mortals, nor in the various worlds of the Nāgas, in terms of ascetic merit, fame, wealth,
or enjoyments."

"O large-eyed one, having been struck by the arrows of Kandarpa upon seeing you, I have come to you for refuge; be gracious and look upon me with a favorable countenance. Become my beloved wife, dear to me as my own life."
Aśokasundarī said:
"Listen, I shall tell you the cause of all these connections; for in this world, it is destined for every man and woman who is born."
A woman must likewise have a husband who is equal to her in qualities;
this is the path of the world in the cycle of existence (saṃsāra). Listen, Huṇḍa, according to the rule:
there is indeed a cause for this, by which I become as I am.
O lord of the Daityas, O possessor of a noble wife, listen with a focused mind:
"O high-minded one, when I was born from the king of trees at the proper time, I was fashioned by Pārvatī after she had perfectly grasped the essence of Śambhu."
"By the will of the divine Anumati, he shall indeed be the husband of me, the goddess;
in the lineage of Soma, that one of great wisdom shall be righteous in soul. Victorious, equal to Arjuna in prowess, and like fire in splendor, he shall be."
He was omniscient and true to his word, equal to Vaiśravaṇa in generosity;
he was a performer of sacrifices and a lord of charity, and in beauty he was like the god of love.
That righteous-souled Nahuṣa was a great treasury of virtues and good character. (17–18)
"The god has granted me a husband who shall be renowned;
therefore, I shall obtain a beautiful son endowed with all virtues, equal to Indra and Upendra in this world, a Yayāti beloved by the people. (19)
"By the grace of Śambhu, I shall slay that wise one in battle. I am a devoted wife, and especially the wife of another hero;
therefore, O Huṇḍa, abandon this delusion by all means and depart from here."
Laughing, he spoke these words to Aśokasundarī;
Huṇḍa said:
"What you have said is certainly not appropriate, neither for a goddess nor for a god."
In the Lunar dynasty (Soma-vaṃśa), there will be a righteous-souled one named Nahuṣa;
among you, he shall be the eldest, for the youngest is not joined with [the status of] the first-born.
A younger sister is indeed praised, but a younger brother is not praised.
"O blessed lady, when will that base man become your husband? Thus, both your maturity and youth shall surely come to an end;
for even by the power of their youth, women are always considered beautiful. (24-25)
O woman of excellent complexion, youth brings about the state of being beloved by men;
for youth, O fair-faced one, is the great root of young women. By means of its support, they enjoy pleasures and desires that follow the mind.

"O blessed lady, listen to me: when will the son of Āyu come to you? Youth is passing away this very day, and it will surely become useless. Consider how childhood, infancy, and boyhood have already passed. (27-28)
"When will he reach youth and become a suitable match for you?
By the power of your youth, drink the honeyed wine of spring (29). Together with me, O large-eyed one, enjoy yourself in pleasure."
Having heard the words of Huṇḍa, the daughter of Śiva, filled with trepidation,
spoke again to that lord of the Dānavas when the twenty-eighth age known as the Dvāpara Yuga had arrived.
The remaining incarnation will be the righteous-souled Balarāma, the son of Vasudeva;
he shall take as his wife the divine daughter of Revata.
She too was born, O fortunate one, in that most excellent of ages known as Kṛta-yuga.

By the measure of three *yugas*, she will also be the eldest by virtue of her strength; she became the beloved of Bala as Revatī, equal to his very life, and when the future *dvāpara* age arrives, she will exist here once more.
The excellent daughter of a Gandharva, born in the city of Māyāvatī,
was carried off and restrained by Śambara, the foremost of the Dānavas.
He is known as her husband, the powerful son of Mādhava.
The lord of heroes named Pradyumna, the son of the Lord of the Yādavas, will appear in that age;
this was foreseen by the ancient, highly fortunate, and wise-souled sages such as Vyāsa and others. (36-37)

Thus indeed was the speech of the Daitya seen as it was uttered by the Goddess, the mother of the world, the daughter of Himavat, at that time: "But you, greedy with greed and desire, speak what is wicked. (38)
One who is possessed by sin and devoid of the Vedas and Shastras—
whatever is destined for a person, whether auspicious or inauspicious, that certainly comes to pass for him in accordance with his past karma. (39-40)
Whatever well-spoken words emerge from the speech of the gods and the Brahmins,
if they are true, they never become otherwise.
(41) It is solely by my good fortune that this has been understood regarding both him and Nahuṣa.
Having thus reflected upon this union, it was spoken by the Goddess and by Śiva:
"Knowing this, one attains peace; cast away the delusion residing in the mind. You are certainly not capable of moving my mind, O Daitya. 42–43.
"O you whose mind is firm in devotion to your husband, I am not able to move you; I shall consume you with a great curse. Go from here, O great asura!
Having heard those words, the powerful Dānava Huṇḍa—
He reflected in his mind, "How might she become my wife? (45) Having thus deliberated, the illusory Huṇḍa vanished; then, leaving her behind, he departed from that place with speed.
When another day had arrived, the noble Dānava created a darkness-filled illusion; having assumed a divine form composed of *māyā*,
he then took the form of a maiden through his illusory power, O delighter of the Manas.
Then, from that place where the joyful lady’s residence was located, Māyā arrived in the form of a beautiful woman of noble hips, endowed with laughter and playful charm;
she spoke these affectionate words to Aśokasundarī.
"O fortunate one of Kāśī, why do you dwell here in this penance grove?
O girl, for what purpose do you perform this asceticism that withers desire? Tell me, O blessed one, what is the cause of this most difficult practice? (49-50)
Having heard those inauspicious words spoken by the Dānava,
who was concealed in a deceptive form and filled with desire, she quickly related the account of her own creation as it had occurred in the past.
Deeply distressed, she related the entire cause of her asceticism; however,
out of friendship, she did not reveal the deceptive form of that evil-minded Dānava, Upaplava.
Huṇḍa said:
"O Goddess, you are devoted to your husband; you are well-established in virtuous vows, possessed of excellent character and conduct, of noble behavior, and a great satī. (54)
"O auspicious lady, I am a devoted wife, dedicated to my husband; O beautiful one, I, a great satī, perform penance for the sake of my husband. My husband has been slain by that evil-minded Huṇḍa."
"In order to prevent his destruction, we shall perform great and formidable penance.
"Come; let us dwell in my own meritorious hermitage on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Thus was she addressed with other charming words that inspired confidence.

Deluded by Huṇḍa’s feigned friendship, the daughter of Śiva was violently dragged away; utterly bewildered by great infatuation, she was brought to his own divine, incomparable, and most beautiful home. 58.
On the peak of Mount Meru, there is a supreme city named Vaiḍūrya;
it is endowed with all virtues, exceedingly auspicious, and known as Kāñcana, crowded with lofty palaces, pinnacle-domes, banners, and chowries. 59–60.
It was beautified by forests filled with various trees, resembling dense clouds in their deep green hue,
and by ponds, wells, lakes, rivers, and reservoirs of water;
it was further adorned with great jewels and encircled by ramparts bound together with gold.
Then Aśokasundarī beheld that beautiful city, which was filled with the fulfillment of all desires for the sake of the donor;
she said, "Tell me, my friend, whose abode is this? (62-63)
He said: "O illustrious one, that foremost of Dānavas is the abode of him whom you have never seen before;
O woman of excellent complexion, I have brought you here by means of my illusory power."
Having addressed her, he led her to a most beautiful golden house,
adorned with various chambers and resembling a peak of Mount Kailāsa; having seated the beautiful woman there upon a swing, he was tormented by desire.
Then, O Lord of Daityas, having returned to his own form and being tormented by the arrows of desire, he joined his palms in reverence and spoke these words:
"O blessed lady, whatever you wish for, that very thing shall be yours; of this there is no doubt."
"O large-eyed one, you who worship me, worship me, for I am tormented by desire.
The Goddess said: "O Lord of the Dānavas, you are not able to move me at all."
"Even in my mind, I cannot conceive of this delusion that has come upon me.
I am difficult to attain even by gods like you, who are great sinners, or by the lowest of demons; of this there is no doubt. Speak to me again and again."
Joined with the ascetic power of Skanda’s younger sister and blazing with great wrath,
she, desiring to destroy him who was surrounded by dānavas, quivered like the tongue of Time; then that goddess spoke again thus to that lowest of dānavas.
A fierce deed was committed by you,
a wicked soul, for the sake of destroying yourself, your lineage, and these kinsmen of yours, when the blazing flames of fire were brought into your own home. (72-73)
Just as the inauspicious *kūṭapakṣin* bird, having arisen from all sorrows,
enters the house of whomever it finds and brings about their destruction— of all one's kinsmen, along with one's wealth and family. (74)
Just as one who desires the destruction of good Brahmins enters their house [only to bring ruin],
so too have you entered this house seeking my destruction—
now for the sake of your sons, your wealth, your grain, and your lineage. (75-76)
Having destroyed for you your life, family, wealth, grain, sons, grandsons, and everything else, I shall depart; of this there is no doubt.
Just as I was brought by you while I was performing supreme penance, [so shall I go]."
"O Dānava, even as she who desired Nahuṣa, the son of Āyu, [was destroyed], so shall my husband destroy you. Indeed,
this means for your destruction was previously seen by the Lord on my account."

This worldly verse is indeed true, which wise people sing: "In this world, it is seen directly that those of evil intellect find whatever suffering, happiness, or the like they are to experience, and wherever they are to enjoy it. (80)
He alone shall eat there; of this there is no doubt. (81) "Enjoy the fruit of your own action upon the surface of the earth;
you shall go to the place of hell because of violating another's wife. (82)
Just as one might strike with the tip of a finger a very sharp, well-edged, and pleasant sword, so now pierce me with your anger,
having gone before the roaring lion in his fury. 83.
With a violent gesture, he seized the hair from the face of Kolūnāti.
"He who desires to devour me—she who is endowed with truth, conduct, self-restraint, and discipline, and established in asceticism—indeed wishes for my death. (84-85)
He desires to seize the life of a black serpent while it is still alive, for he was sent at the wrong time;
but you, O fool, have been sent at the wrong time, deluded by Time.

Have you not seen that such a wicked thought has arisen in you? For who else here would look upon [him] except for Āyu’s son? Indeed, another would meet his death from the mere sight of his immortal form. (87–88)
Having spoken thus, she went to the bank of the Gaṅgā, filled with grief, agitated by suffering, and observing both prescribed and optional vows;
there she performed the terrible penance she had previously practiced out of longing for her husband.
Desiring the destruction of you, she will again practice a terrible penance when you,
the wicked one, have been slain by the high-souled Nahuṣa with sharp arrows resembling thunderbolts and like venomous serpents. 90-91.
"I shall go to my husband when I behold him fallen on the battlefield, his hair disheveled, bloodied, and lifeless. Having made this firm vow, she went to the unsurpassed bank of the Gaṅgā.
Intent on the destruction of Huṇḍa, she remained steadfast, bringing joy to Śiva.

Just as a blazing flame of fire, radiant with its own brilliance, might consume the beautiful worlds, so did the daughter of the Lord of the Gods, inflamed with wrath, perform difficult penance on the banks of the Gaṅgā. 93–94.
Kuñjala said: Having been addressed thus, O illustrious one, the daughter of Śiva went to the waters of the Gaṅgā; having bathed there, she returned to her own city named Kāñcana. 95.
The slender-limbed young woman, beautiful as an *aśoka* tree, performed penance for the sake of slaying Huṇḍa, endowed with truthfulness.
Huṇḍa, too, became distressed, his mind consumed by the curse.
He reflected, greatly distressed by the fires of her words (97). Then, having summoned his minister named Taṅkaṃpana, he spoke to him;
he related the entire great account concerning the origin of her curse (98).
"I have been cursed by Aśokasundarī, the daughter of Aśiva:
'You shall die at the hands of my husband, Nahuṣa.
Furthermore, that noble child was not yet born, and Āyu’s wife was still pregnant."
"Since she has been falsely praised despite her untruthfulness, inflict upon her a curse accordingly.
Kaṃpana said:
"Having carried off his beloved wife, bring her back to Āyu as well."
Even by this means, your enemy is not produced. Nor should you cause her fetus to fall with terrifying threats;
even by this means, your enemy is not produced. (101-102)
"Wait for the time of birth of the evil-minded Nahuṣa; having seized him and brought him here, abandon that sinful-minded one. Thus did the Asura consult with Kaṃpana.
There arose a despondency in Nahuṣa regarding his destruction.
Viṣṇu said:
"O illustrious one, there is a lord of the earth named Āyu, the son of Elā."
That universal monarch was a virtuous soul, devoted to the vow of truth;
by his asceticism, fame, and strength, as well as by his highly meritorious gifts, sacrifices, truthfulness, and self-restraint, he was equal to Indra, the lord of the gods.
That best of kings, who knew all dharmas and was the ornament of the Lunar dynasty, ruled the earth under a single umbrella; yet,
because he did not obtain a son, the king became sorrowful.

The righteous-souled lord of the earth, Āyu, fell into deep reflection: "How may a son be born to me? Thus he became absorbed in thought and, with great concentration, made the supreme effort for the sake of a son.
There, the high-souled son of Atri, the great sage Dattātreya,
was sporting with a woman, his eyes reddened by wine;
intoxicated by *vāruṇī*, his virtuous soul was surrounded by throngs of women.
Having taken up Aṅkeyuvati, the most excellent and auspicious of all women,
that supreme lord of great yogis, the Brahmin, sang, danced, and drank wine profusely, even without his sacred thread (yajñopavīta). 111–112.
Anointed with sandalwood and agallochum, the lord of sages shone resplendent with divine flower garlands and ornaments of pearl necklaces;
having gone to his hermitage, the king beheld that best of the twice-born.

With his mind perfectly composed, the son of Atri, whose nature was righteous, prostrated himself with his head like a staff before the best of kings. Having beheld the king who had arrived before him with devotion, he then established himself once more in meditation.
O best of men, when a hundred years had passed in this manner for that king, his mind became unwavering, attained peace, and was solely intent on devotion.
Having summoned him, [the deity] said this: "O King, why do you afflict yourself?"
I am devoid of the conduct of a Brahmin; I never possess the nature of a Brahmin.
I am greedy for wine and meat, and I am always attached to women.
By virtue of the boon granted to me, I have the power to command another Brahmin to serve me. (117–118)
Āyu said: "O highly fortunate one, there is no best of Brahmins like you; you are the supreme lord in the three worlds, the granter of all desires. (119)

O highly fortunate one, in this lineage of Atri, you, Govinda, the Supreme Lord whose banner is Garuḍa, have appeared in the form of a Brāhmaṇa. Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods; salutations to you, O Supreme Lord.
I have come to you for refuge, O you who are compassionate toward those who seek shelter.
Lift me up, O Hṛṣīkeśa; having employed your illusory power (māyā), you remain established as the wise leader of all beings and creatures in the universe. 121–122.
"I know you, O Lord of the World, to be Madhusūdana; protect me alone, O Govinda! Salutations to you, whose form is the universe! (123) Kuñjala said:
When a great deal of time had passed, Dattātreya, assuming an intoxicated form, spoke to the best of kings:
"Give me wine from your skull-cup and a meal of cooked meat."
Having heard those words, King Cāyu,
eager for the skull-cup, swiftly brought the wine;
and having quickly cut up well-cooked meat with his hand, he acted with haste.

O best of kings, he then bestowed [the boon] upon Dattātreya; for that bull among sages had become gracious in mind, having witnessed his devotion, his power, and his supreme service to his guru. 127.
He spoke to that lord of kings, whose mind was bowed in prostration:
"O auspicious lord of the earth, choose a boon, even one difficult to obtain on this world;
I shall grant you everything that you desire right now."
The king said:
"O best of sages, you are truly the most excellent of givers; out of compassion, grant me a son who is endowed with virtues, omniscient, and possessed of all noble qualities. (130)
He possessed divine vigor and supreme luster, being unconquerable by gods, dānavas, kṣatriyas, fierce rākṣasas, dānavas, and likewise by kiṃnaras;
he was especially devoted to the gods and brāhmaṇas, and was a protector of his subjects. 131.
He was a performer of sacrifices, a lord of charity, and a hero; he was affectionate toward those who sought his protection.
He was a donor and an enjoyer, a high-souled being, and learned in the Vedas and Shastras.
He was skilled in the science of archery and devoted to the sacred scriptures.

"O noble lady, grant me a son of great fortune who shall uphold my lineage— one who possesses an unassailable intellect, who is steadfast, unconquered in battles, endowed with such virtues, and handsome in form. (134)
"Or rather, O Lord, if a boon is to be granted by you out of compassion," Dattātreya said, "So be it, O highly fortunate one; you shall have a son."
In his home, he was a merit-bestowing progenitor who practiced compassion toward all living beings.
Endowed with these qualities and possessed of a portion of Viṣṇu, he was a sovereign emperor, a lord of men equal to Indra. 136–137.
"Having thus granted the boon, he gave that unsurpassed fruit; 'O great yogi, let it be given to my noble wife.
Having spoken thus, he dismissed Āyu, who stood bowed before him. (138)
Having greeted him with blessings, he indeed vanished from sight.
139. Thus ends the one hundred and third chapter, titled "The Deeds of Cyavana," within the "Guru-tīrtha-māhātmya" section of the "Vena-upākhyāna" in the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter One Hundred and Four.
Kuñjala said:
O great king, when that illustrious and great sage Dattātreya had departed, Āyu returned toward his own city. 1.
Delighted, he entered Indumatī’s palace, which was endowed with splendor,
filled with all objects of desire, and resembled the abode of Indra.
The wise king ruled his kingdom just as Purandara rules in heaven.
O best of the twice-born, together with Indumatī, the daughter of Svarbhānu,
that queen Indumatī conceived a child endowed with divine luster, according to the word of Dattātreya, through the eating of fruits.
O noble father, Indumatī saw an unsurpassed dream during the night that was accompanied by [visions] during the day, bestowing many blessings;
she saw a man resembling the sun entering the interior of her house.
The brahmin was adorned with a pearl necklace and graced by a white garment;
a garland made of white flowers shone upon his neck,
his limbs were beautified by all kinds of ornaments, and he was anointed with divine fragrant unguents.
Four-armed, with a conch in his hand and bearing a mace, a discus, and a sword,
he was resplendent with great majesty, adorned with divine ornaments, and shaded by a parasol that resembled the orb of the moon.
Adorned with necklaces, bracelets, armlets,
and anklets, and resplendent with two earrings that resembled the orb of the moon—
such a man of great wisdom arrived there.
Then, having summoned Indumatī, that beautiful woman was bathed again and again with milk from a conch shell, white as the moon,
which was filled to the brim and adorned with gems and gold.
He [beheld] the white Naga of beautiful form, possessing a thousand heads and a hood;
he was radiant with great jewels and filled with the blaze of his own splendor.
Then, a pearl was cast by him into the corner of his mouth and offered once again.
Then, having placed that lotus in the hand of this highly illustrious Indumatī at her throat, the Lord of the Gods departed for his own abode.
Such was the great dream she beheld, foretelling an excellent son.
The illustrious lady related it all to the long-lived lord of the earth.
Having heard this, the great king reflected once more,
and afterwards, having summoned his preceptor, he recounted that excellent dream.
The King said to the highly fortunate Śaunaka, the omniscient one and the best among the wise:
"O best of the twice-born, this very night, my wife, O illustrious one... (17)
"Entering the house at dawn, he was seen; what could be the cause of this dream?
Śaunaka said: "A boon had previously been granted to you by the wise Dattātreya. (18)
"The king had previously commanded that an excellent fruit be given for the sake of a son;
O King, what was done with that fruit, and to whom was it offered by you?
"It was given by me to a virtuous wife," were the words spoken by the king.
Having heard these words, the highly wise Śaunaka, the best of the twice-born, said:
"By the grace of Dattātreya, an excellent son shall be born in your house, endowed with a portion of Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt. (20-21)
O King, I have thus told you the cause of this dream;
a son equal to Indra, possessing divine prowess, shall be born to you. He will be a soul of all righteousness and the enhancer of the Lunar dynasty.
"He shall become proficient in the science of archery (Dhanurveda) as well as in the Vedas.
Having spoken thus, Śaunaka departed for his home;
the king, filled with great joy, remained together with his beloved wife.

Thus ends the one hundred and fourth chapter [and the beginning of the one hundred and fifth chapter] in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the narrative of Cyavana, concerning the greatness of the Guru-tīrtha. Kuñjala said:
Having gone to the Nandana grove with her friends to play,
she then heard a great and unpleasant speech from her father,
as it was being uttered by delighted Cāraṇas and well-attained Siddhas.
"Your son shall be the best of men, possessing great vigor, immense heroism, and prowess equal to Viṣṇu; he will bring about the end of Huṇḍa.
Such were these great words, unpleasant and causing him pain.
Having heard what was reported by her father’s messenger,
she related that which caused him sorrow in brief before him;
then, having heard it, her father spoke in his presence, filled with wonder.
He recalled the curse previously pronounced by Aśokasundarī;
for her sake, this Asura had always performed penance so that the fetus of Indumatī might be destroyed.
The wicked and evil-minded one, drawn by Time, made an effort to find a flaw; thus, he constantly sought out a weakness in Indumatī.
Whenever he saw that queen, who was endowed with beauty, nobility, and virtue, [he was overcome].
Endowed with divine splendor and protected by the power of Viṣṇu,
she was possessed of celestial luster and resembled the orb of the sun;
O highly fortunate one, he stood constantly at her side for the sake of her protection.
From afar, the wicked Dānava constantly displayed various kinds of fierce and terrifying spells to her;
yet she was protected by the splendor of Viṣṇu and endowed with the power of the embryo.
Fear never arose in him, nor did dejection ever occur again.
(11) The gift became fruitless and his effort was rendered useless; not even the slightest desire of the evil-minded Huṇḍa was fulfilled. (12)
Thus, as he gazed for a full hundred years,
she then gave birth to a son— the offspring of Svarbhānu—
during the night; that best of sons was born to her in the very night.
He shines exceedingly with splendor, like the sun in the vault of the sky.
Sūta said:
Then a certain very wicked maidservant came to the lying-in chamber.
Engaged in impure conduct and speaking words of great ill omen,
the base Dānava Huṇḍa, having learned everything about her,
entered the body of that maidservant and thus entered the palace of Āyu.
While the great multitude was fast asleep and overcome by a profound delusion,
that lowest of Dānavas carried off the son, who shone like the offspring of a god, and went outside; he reached his own city named Kāñcana.
Having summoned his beloved wife Vipulā, he spoke these words:
"Slay this great sinner, my enemy in the form of a child;
afterwards, let him be placed in the hands of the cook for the sake of food."
"O highly fortunate one, cook [it] mercilessly with various methods and variations from the hands of the cooks; afterwards, he shall eat it—of this there is no doubt.
Upon hearing these words of her husband, Vipulā was struck with amazement.
Why does my husband, so cruel and utterly heartless, act with such ruthlessness?
Whose son— endowed with every auspicious mark and resembling the offspring of a god—
is being devoured by whom, for what reason, this man devoid of patience and extreme in his cruelty?
Thinking thus, filled with compassion, she questioned her husband again: "Why do you devour the child?
Why are you so enraged and utterly shameless? (23)
"O Lord of the Danujas, tell me everything in truth regarding the cause of this;
relate in brief your own fault, the account of events,
and the curse pronounced by Aśokasundarī as well as by the evil-minded Huṇḍa."
She understood all that to be the reason for the Dānava’s death:
"This child will truly kill our husband, whether he is true or not.
Having reflected thus, Vipulā was overwhelmed with rage.
Then, having summoned Mēkalā, the maidservant, she spoke these words:
"O Mēkalā, cast out this wicked boy today into the kitchen;
place him in the hands of the cook for the sake of feeding Huṇḍa."
Taking the Mekalā boy, he summoned the cook and said, "Carry out the king's command today; indeed, cook this boy.
This was heard by that high-souled cook as well.
Taking the child from his hand and raising a weapon, he stood ready; yet,
protected by the splendor of Dattātreya, the god of gods, Āyu’s son laughed again and again.
Seeing him laughing, the cook was filled with compassion;
the maidservant (sairandhrī), likewise moved by pity, addressed the cook in reply:
"O wise cook, this child is not to be killed by you."
"Endowed with divine marks, whose son is he born into such a noble family? (33) The cook replied:
"O blessed lady, you have spoken the truth; these words are filled with compassion."
Whose child is this boy, endowed with the marks of royalty and possessed of such beauty?
Why shall this evil-souled Huṇḍa, the lowest of Dānavas, enjoy [the kingdom]—he by whom the lineage was previously protected through his own meritorious deeds? 34-35.

Even in calamities and difficult straits, one who possesses action as his companion shall live and not otherwise; whether carried away by the force of a river or entered into the midst of fire, he lives—of this there is no doubt. (36)

Therefore, one who is endowed with the merit of ritual action (karma-dharma-puṇya) is highly esteemed; because of that, long-lived men proclaim him to be happy. For that [merit], which is the savior and the protector, guards him and remains ever watchful.

He who performs beneficial acts endowed with the merit of generosity, accompanied by pleasant speech, and joined with helpfulness, becomes a constant bestower of liberation and a provider of a state of friendship. (39) When he acts as a doer of good, he is possessed of such qualities.
One protects that very karma at all times; of this there is no doubt.
Impelled by one's own karma, one enters another womb.
What can a father, a mother, or other kinsmen and relatives do? 40–41.
But he who was struck down by his own karma did not survive for even a moment.
Sūta said:
By that very same karma, however, the son of Añjana was protected. 42.
Therefore, a cook endowed with compassion was born, following the course of his past karma;
likewise, a *sairandhrī* was born, impelled by that same karma. From these two alone, a son was born, protected by the wind and endowed with beautiful marks.
That very night, he was brought from that house to the great hermitage;
at the auspicious door of the leaf-hut in that same great hermitage, in the holy hermitage of Vasiṣṭha, by the cook-maid of virtuous deeds.

After the deer had gone home with its life-breath departed, the Daitya lord Huṇḍa placed that best of young ones there; then, having had the meat cooked by a cook after killing the deer, he fed it [to his wife] and became delighted.
Filled with great joy, the Asura Huṇḍa, the lord of the Dānavas, spoke these words to Kuñjala, having rendered the curse upon Aśokasundarī infallible.
47. Kuñjala said:
When the pure dawn had broken, the righteous-minded Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages,
went outside and looked from the door of his hut;
seeing the boy there, complete and endowed with divine marks.
"Behold this beautiful child with lovely eyes, resembling the full moon," said Vasiṣṭha; "all you sages, having come here, look upon him. 50.

"By whom was this one, who resembles the offspring of a god or a gandharva and is endowed with the marks of royalty, brought here at night to my doorway? Let the sages behold him, stainless and like ten million gods of love."
Then those best of the twice-born, filled with great wonder and rejoicing,
beheld the son of the high-souled Atri;
and Vasiṣṭha, that righteous soul, having perceived the boy through his spiritual knowledge, [was filled with joy].
The son of Brahmā, having risen out of compassion for that young boy who was well-known as Āyuputra and endowed with virtuous conduct, [related] the account of that wicked and evil-minded Huṇḍa. 54.
