As soon as that most excellent of the twice-born took [the vessel] with both hands,
the gods showered a rain of flowers upon the son; meanwhile,
the Gandharvas and Kinnaras sang a charming song in melodious tones.
The sages praised the prince with Vedic mantras;
then, beholding him, Vasiṣṭha granted him a boon:
"The name 'Nahuṣa' shall become renowned for you in the world."
O lord of men, he was not at all delighted by that, nor even by his childhood ways. Therefore, O Nahuṣa, you shall become one worthy of worship by the gods.
The best of the twice-born performed for him the rites beginning with the birth-ceremony (jātakarman).

Having completed the vows and the formal dismissal, having studied the Veda in its entirety along with the six auxiliary limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) and the Pada and Krama recitations, and having studied all the Śāstras from that best of the twice-born teacher— 60.
From Vasiṣṭha, the high-minded one learned the science of archery along with its secret doctrines (61),
as well as divine weapons and missiles together with the methods for their seizing and releasing, the sciences of knowledge and logic, and the qualities of royal policy (62).
And the son of Āyu, being devoted, became a disciple of Vasiṣṭha;
thus was the exceedingly handsome son of Nahuṣa perfected in every way.
By the grace of Vasiṣṭha, he became a wielder of the bow and arrows.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Life of Cyavana," within the "Guru-tīrtha-māhātmya" section of the "Vena-upākhyāna" in the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter One Hundred and Sixth. Kuñjala said:
Not seeing her very young son, who was like a god and peerless, the noble and long-lived wife of Svarbhānu wept, raising a great cry of lamentation. 1. She, of excellent complexion, wept aloud.
By what characteristics was this boy, endowed with auspicious marks, brought here?
O son, through penance, gifts, sacrifices, and difficult observances, and again through great and terrible hardships, have you been obtained by me? 2-3.
"By whom has the son, granted by the meritorious and great-souled Dattātreya who was well-pleased, been taken away? Ruru, filled with compassion, [cried]:
'Alas, my son! O you who were like a cow to me! Alas, child, temple of virtues!'"
"By whom have you been stripped away from me? Let my name be restored!
You are, without a doubt, the ornament of the entire Lunar dynasty.
By whom have you been removed from me, while still endowed with life?"

"Endowed with divine and auspicious marks of a king, that lotus-eyed child—by whom has he been carried away today? What shall I do? Where shall I go? Clearly, I recognize the karma I have committed in another birth."
"Whose loss of the deposited [merit] has been caused? Therefore, my son has been taken away from me.
Or what deception was practiced by whom in a previous birth?
Otherwise, I would not be experiencing the suffering resulting from that karma. (8-9)
The jewel of a son has been taken from me by one who steals jewels; therefore, it must be by fate that this divine child, a mine of incomparable virtues, has appeared.
Or perhaps this is the unforeseen fruit of some past action, O Brahmin.

"I have undoubtedly attained this state, which is intensely filled with grief for my son. Or perhaps some hostility toward an infant was committed by me in a previous birth; I am now experiencing such a fruit of that sinful karma."
And while he was thus begging, before the performance of the Vaiśvadeva rite,
no food whatsoever had been offered by the twice-born, nor had it been sacrificed with the Vyāhṛtis.
Thus, due to the pride of Sudeva, at that time [the food] of Svarbhānu’s son [was consumed].
Overwhelmed with compassion by the grief for the illustrious Indumatī,
she fell down in a swoon; overcome by sorrow,
she became agitated and sighed like a cow deprived of her calf.

King Āyus, overcome by great grief and sorrow upon hearing that his son had been carried away, abandoned his fortitude. He thought, "There is no fruit of asceticism; indeed, there is no fruit of giving."
Since my son has been carried away in this manner, there is no doubt that he does not exist [any longer].
However, in the past, Dattātreya, out of his grace, granted me a boon:
a son who was invincible, endowed with victory, and possessed of all virtues. 17–18.
Thinking, "How indeed did an obstacle arise to that granting of the boon? the king, overcome with anxiety and filled with grief, wept bitterly. 19.
Thus ends the [section on] the greatness of the Guru-tīrtha within the narrative of Cyavana, in the Legend of Vena, in the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The one hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Nahuṣa.
Chapter one hundred and seventh. Kuñjala said:
Then that Nārada, having come from heaven, approached King Āyu; having arrived, he said: "O King, why do you grieve?
O high-minded one, the abduction of your son has occurred today; ill fortune has befallen you."
O Great King, having understood this regarding the gods and others, do not grieve.
Your son shall come, omniscient, endowed with all virtues, possessed of all specialized knowledge, and perfected in all arts.
"O Great King, he by whom this boy— equal to the gods— was abducted today has undoubtedly brought his own life to its end;
for he who is of great heroism and great strength shall surely bring about his destruction."
O King, he will approach Satvā along with the daughter of Śiva;
he will become a son equal to Indra and Upendra by his own splendor,
and he too shall enjoy the status of Indra through his own meritorious deeds.

Having thus addressed the king, the best of divine sages departed suddenly while he and his followers were looking on. When that highly fortunate Nārada, who was equal to a god, had gone, [the king remained].
Āyu, having approached Queen Āgatya, reported all of that to her:
"The son who was granted by Dattātreya, the most excellent among the best of gods—he is indeed well, O Queen, by the grace of Viṣṇu. (8–9)
"O fair-faced one, even if my son is unkind,
he will take his head and return once more;
O blessed lady, do not grieve," so said Nārada.
And she abandoned that great delusion which destroys one's duty and purpose. Then, having heard these words of her husband, Queen Indumatī was filled with joy regarding the arrival of her son.

As spoken by the divine sage, so shall it be: "Dattātreya has granted me this boon; casting off old age and death, I shall become free from them—of this there is no doubt. Indeed, this very thing appears clearly to him.
Having reflected thus, he bowed to that bull among the twice-born:
"Homage to him, the bestower of complete success, the noble son of Atri;
by whose grace I have obtained this excellent son, who is steadfast, virtuous, and highly meritorious."
Having spoken thus, the queen Aditi, deeply distressed,
ceased speaking as she perceived that her son Nahuṣa was approaching once more.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Narrative of Nahuṣa," within the "Life of Cyavana" in the "Guru-tīrtha-māhātmya" section of the "Vena-upākhyāna" in the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The one hundred and eighth chapter. Kuñjala said:
Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā, possessed of great splendor and the best among those who perform austerities, spoke.
Having summoned Nahuṣa, he spoke these words: "Go quickly to the forest and bring back abundant forest produce. Hearing the sage's words, Nahuṣa went to the forest.
There, the powerful Nahuṣa heard a certain account of virtuous conduct: "This is that very one named Nahuṣa, a heroic soul of righteous nature,
the highly wise son of Āyu, who was separated from his mother since childhood."
Due to this very separation, his wife Āyu is weeping.
O Aśokasundarī, she has performed most difficult penance;
when will that queen see her auspicious son Indumatī?

The daughter of Śiva, the most excellent woman, who was previously abducted by the Dānavas, performed penance without support; she was the young Aśokasundarī, for the sake of the son of Āyu, the knower of dharma named Nahuṣa. 6.
"By this association with a mere servant, you shall come to be so.
Thus did that righteous-souled Nahuṣa, overcome by delusion, hear these worldly words spoken during his deliberation in heaven.
Having gone there and taken forest produce, that righteous-souled one presented the forest offerings to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha;
then, with palms joined in reverence and his neck bowed in devotion, he stood before him.
He spoke to that highly wise Vasiṣṭha, the best among those who practice austerities:
"O Blessed One, please hear these unprecedented words uttered by the Cāraṇa:
'This man, named Nahuṣa, the son of Āyu, has indeed been separated [from his celestial status].'"
O Preceptor, for the sake of this wise Nahuṣa, Indumatī, the daughter of Himālaya, performed a most difficult penance amidst thousands of hardships caused by the Dānavas.
12. For the sake of this wise one, O Preceptor, as it was with Nahuṣa.
All that was thus spoken by them was heard by me. Who was that righteous-souled Āyu? Who was the auspicious Indumatī from the sky? Who was Aśokasundarī, and who is said to be Nahuṣa? 13–14.
This doubt has arisen within me; you ought to dispel it.
O highly wise one, who else could there be, and where is that Nahuṣa?
Tell me all of that, my father, for it must surely have some other underlying cause.
Vasiṣṭha said: King Āyu was a righteous soul, the powerful lord of the seven continents;
his wife was Indumatī, who was truthful in nature and renowned for her fame.
In her, you were born as a son, a temple of virtues and an ornament of the Lunar dynasty, by King Āyu;
she was a daughter of Hara, possessed of beautiful hips and adorned with qualities and beauty. 17–18.
Named Aśokasundarī, she was fortunate and possessed a beautiful smile; for his sake, she performed penance in the forest of asceticism, remaining without support.
By the decree of the Creator, you have been ordained as her husband through the power of destiny.
Resorting to the bank of the Gaṅgā, she took refuge in the yoga of meditation.
Then Huṇḍa, the lord of the Dānavas, saw that virtuous woman alone,
blazing with ascetic power, beautiful, and lotus-eyed.
Afflicted by the arrows of desire, he approached her— who was endowed with the quality of magnificent beauty— and spoke to her, saying, "Become my wife.
Having heard these words of his, that ascetic woman replied to him.
Do not commit such a rash act; do not speak thus again and again.
O hero, I am unattainable by you, especially as I am another's wife. By destiny, this son of great strength was created for me long ago. 23-24.
"There will undoubtedly be one named Nahuṣa who is wise;
he, being of great splendor, will act otherwise than you have done toward Devadatta. Therefore, I shall pronounce a curse by which you will be reduced to ashes."
Having heard those words, he was tormented by the arrows of desire; though she had been brought to his own palace by him under a pretext, that illustrious one,
realizing this, cursed that lowest of Dānavas.
"Your death shall come at the very hand of Nahuṣa; just as you were born when Ajas was already born, so it shall be. You, that heroic son of Āyu, have been carried off by the wicked Huṇḍa."

"Protected by the cook and sent by the maidservant to my hermitage, you were seen in the middle of the forest by the Cāraṇas and Kinnaras; that which was proclaimed by them, O child, has been told to you by me once again. (29-30)
Wipe away the tears that she sheds from her eyes as she abandons the wicked Dānava named Huṇḍa, the doer of evil.
Go from here and behold the mighty Gaṅgā-tīra.
"Having slain that lord of the Dānavas, bring him from the prison;
indeed, become the husband of Aśokasundarī. All this has been told to you as the reason for this question. (32-33)
Having addressed Nahuṣa, the high-minded Brahmin ceased speaking.
Having heard everything uttered by the sage— which was truly wonderful— and reflecting upon it,
the son of Āyu, desiring alone to bring about its end, then gave way to anger.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Cyavana," within the "Greatness of the Guru-tīrtha" section of the "Story of Vena" in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter One Hundred and Ninth. Kuñjala said:
Having prostrated and propitiated Vasiṣṭha, the best among those who practice austerity,
he took his leave and departed, bow in hand and arrow in grasp. That boy, protected by her through her own intelligence, had the venison well-cooked and was fed.
Āyu’s son was virtuous, handsome, god-like, and endowed with divine qualities.
With that very meat— well-prepared, seasoned, cooked, and flavorful— the cook, having addressed that wicked Daitya, then fed him with great joy.
The Dānava, filled with joy, ate meat endowed with delicious flavor;
then, his mind overcome by lust, he quickly went to Aśokasundarī and spoke to her.
"O auspicious lady, your husband Āyuputra has been devoured by me; he is indeed yours.
O lovely-limbed one, devote yourself to me alone and enjoy pleasures that accord with your heart. What will you do with him, a mere mortal whose life has come to an end?"
Having heard this, the ascetic daughter of Śiva replied:
"My husband has been granted by the gods—eternal and free from all defects;
even by the high-souled deities, his death has not been seen."
Having heard those words,
the Dānava of wicked conduct laughed again and again and said to that large-eyed woman:
"O beautiful one, today I have already eaten the flesh of Āyu’s son."
Having heard these words of the wicked-minded Nahuṣa as soon as he was born,
she, who was firmly established in truth and purified by asceticism, became exceedingly enraged and spoke again.
"I have indeed performed this austerity with my mind and through self-restraint; by truth alone, O son, you shall be long-lived.
Go from here, O man of evil conduct, if you wish to live."
"Otherwise, I shall curse you again, without a doubt.
(12) Having heard this from her regarding the king, the cook said:
"O Great King, abandon her and resort to another. (13)

Sent by the cook, the evil-minded Daitya Huṇḍa went out in great haste toward his beloved wife, unaware of the deed that had been committed by the maidservant and the cook. 14. He did not know at all what the servant and the cook had done.
And he reported all that had occurred regarding his beloved to him. Sūta said: And that Aśokasundarī, it is said, through her great asceticism...
Tormented by grief and sorrow, the ascetic woman became emaciated;
thinking of her beloved husband, she meditated upon him again and again.
What indeed will the Daityas not do, even with various means? (16–17)
"O best of the Danujas, those who possess knowledge of means always act with constant intelligence and exertion at all times through various stratagems.
Previously, I was carried away by that sinner through the employment of illusion and yoga."
Likewise, O son, there will be no harm whatsoever;
having seen by the power of destiny that he shall be free from disease,
one might look upon him even with great effort, wondering whether he will perish or not.
What indeed is the supreme effort, or what is the fruit born of that action? How might a future state be destroyed? That is where the Veda stands firm.
How could that specific destiny ordained by the gods ever become otherwise?
While she of such great fortune was thus reflecting again and again,
there appeared a Kinnara named Vidūra, of large lineage and massive body, with a human torso from the navel upward, yet entirely devoid of wings. 22–23.
Two-armed, holding a flute in his hand, adorned with a necklace and bracelets,
and his body anointed with divine perfumes, he arrived together with his wife. He spoke to her, who was joyless and accompanied by her son, for she was indeed the consort of Śaṅkara.
"For what reason do you grieve? Know that I, a Kinnara devoted to Viṣṇu, have arrived here sent by the best of gods. You should not feel such sorrow regarding Nahuṣa. (25-26)

O auspicious lady, Huṇḍa, of evil conduct, performed every possible rite for the sake of slaying that wise one, yet the son’s life was taken away by the gods through various stratagems. He was indeed protected by the gods through diverse means.

"O fair-eyed one, O auspicious lady, Huṇḍa indeed understands thus: 'The son of Āyu has been carried off by me; he has been devoured,' O beautiful one. Having made this known to you all, that lowest of Dānavas has departed. (28-29)
O you of great renown, even though he is devoid of merit, your husband lives solely by the ripening of his own karma acquired in a previous birth. Indeed,
it is by the power of merit alone that the lifespan of those beings has been ordained.
The slayers, evil-minded and greatly sinful, wishing to extinguish the glory of the illustrious Svarjit— who defiles the splendor of others—
devised deceptions day after day for the purpose of destroying his fame. 31–32.
Then, by various means such as poisons and weapons,
they seek to kill that meritorious one who is protected by his virtuous deeds;
and the sinners, such as Huṇḍa and others, [seek to harm him] through delusion, paralysis, and other such spells.
They afflict those of great sin with various kinds of violent torments;
however, O highly fortunate one, through the application of merit earned in a previous birth, even a meritorious person is well-protected by that very merit. 34–35.
O auspicious one, the stratagems of those sinners— be they mechanical devices, rituals, mantras, weapons, fire, poison, or imprisonment— all come to naught;
for the Great-Souled One is well-protected by the merits of the gods.
The perpetrators go to ashes, while he alone remains as the possessor of merit.
O auspicious one, may all the deities who are the protectors of Vīrasena’s son, and the entire accumulation of his merit, as well as the storehouse of his austerities, remain intact. 37–38.
Therefore, let not the hero Nahuṣa— the best among the strong—
be harmed by that truth, austerity, merit, self-restraint, and discipline;
do not inflict cruel suffering upon him, and abandon this groundless grief.
The righteous-souled one lived happily even without his mother and father;
he dwelt alone in a penance grove, protected by ascetics,
knowing the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and having reached the further shore of the science of archery.
Just as the moon shines with its own digits by means of its own luster,
so too does he shine with his own digits, O slender-waisted one,
through his branches of knowledge, great merits, ascetic penances, and fame. 42.

The slayer of enemy heroes, the destroyer of foes, beloved by the gods, will shine forth after killing Huṇḍa, the lord of the Daityas; for he shall obtain you alone as his consort, and together with you and this woman, he shall be the sole sovereign on earth. 43–44.
O blessed lady, you shall obtain an excellent son who will become a great yogi, just as Vāsava is in heaven—
he who is named Yayāti, a knower of dharma and devoted to the protection of his subjects. 45.
Likewise, there are also a hundred maidens endowed with beauty, nobility,
and virtue, by whose merits, O Great King, you shall go to the world of Indra;
and, O Lord, Nahuṣa, whose prowess is meritorious, shall enjoy the status of Indra.

"O great king, your son will be named Yayāti, a righteous soul, a protector of subjects, a great monarch, and one devoted to compassion for all living beings. He shall have four sons of great majesty."
Endowed with strength and heroism, they were masters of the science of archery (dhanurveda).
The first was named Catura, the second was named Puru,
the third was named Uru, and the fourth was the heroic Yadu.
Thus, those sons will be of great heroism, radiant, and possessed of great strength; they will be high-souled and endowed with all splendor.
And the heroic sons of Yadu will possess prowess equal to that of lions.
Listen now as I tell you their names:
Bhoja, Bhīmaka, Andhaka, and Kuñjara; likewise, the one named Vṛṣṇi will be a virtuous soul and a supporter of truth. 52–53.
The sixth was Śrutasena, and the seventh was Śrutādhāra; then Kāladaṃṣṭra, who was of great heroism and powerful enough to conquer Death itself in battle.
O lady of beautiful countenance, these sons of Yadu were known as the Yādavas and possessed great prowess.
Their sons and grandsons shall be born by the thousands.
Thus, O Goddess, will the lineage of Nahuṣa continue;
therefore, casting aside this sorrow, proceed with happiness.
"O lady of auspicious countenance, your husband, possessed of great wisdom, will come; having slain the Dānava Huṇḍa, he will marry you.
Indeed, tears born of sorrow fall hot from his eyes."
The giver of honor will wipe away the tears of Indumatī;
having removed the suffering of Āyu, he will deliver his own lineage.
Having made his father happy, he will become a protector of his subjects.
"All this narration of the gods has been told to you, O auspicious one;
casting aside sorrow and grief, proceed with happiness.
Aśokasundarī said:
"When will my husband come here, as ordained by the gods?
Tell me truly, O knower of dharma, and increase my happiness.
Vidura said:
"O beautiful one, you shall see your husband before long; listen thus.
Having spoken these words, the Gandharva then departed for the abode of the gods.
And Aśokasundarī indeed performed penance there.
"O daughter of Śiva, completely renounce desire, anger, and greed as well.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Cyavana within the Legend of Nahuṣa," in the section on the Greatness of the Guru-tīrtha, within the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter One Hundred and Tenth.
Kuñjala said:
Having taken leave of all the sages and Vasiṣṭha, the best of ascetics, Nahuṣa, being eager and desirous of going toward the Dānava, departed. 1.
Then all those sages, Vasiṣṭha and the others whose wealth is asceticism,
greeted that mighty son of Āyu with blessings.
In the sky, all the deities joyfully beat their celestial drums.
They caused a rain of flowers to fall upon the head of Huṣa.
Then the thousand-eyed god arrived together with the deities and bestowed upon him weapons and missiles that were like the splendor of the sun.
O best of the twice-born, that tiger among kings received those divine weapons from the gods and became like one of celestial form.
Then all those deities spoke to the thousand-eyed Indra.
"O Lord of the Asuras, let a chariot be sent for this Nahuṣa.
O twice-born one, having ascertained the will of the gods, the wielder of the thunderbolt summoned his charioteer Mātali and gave him this command.
"Go to this great-souled one on his chariot adorned with banners; let him, the highly wise Āyudha, who is prepared for battle, be bewildered.
He replied to the thousand-eyed Indra, "I shall carry out your command."
Having spoken thus, he quickly approached the son of Hyāyu, who was prepared for battle.
He addressed the king with the words of the King of the Gods:
"O knower of dharma, may you be victorious in this combat by means of this chariot."
"O lord of kings, the thousand-eyed Indra spoke thus: 'Abandon this evil-minded Dānava, Huṇḍa, in battle!
O king of kings, upon hearing this, his hair stood on end with joy."
"By the grace of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, the god of gods,
I shall slay in battle the evil-minded Dānava,
who has especially oppressed the gods through my illusory power."
When these great words had been spoken by the high-souled Huṣa,
the Lord himself arrived, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Uprooting a massive discus from his own, which resembled the orb of the sun, he appeared.
Blazing with radiant splendor, well-rounded at the rim, and bringing auspiciousness—this trident, indeed, the God gave to Nahuṣa with great joy;
Śambhu gave him that very sharp weapon, endowed with fiery energy. 15–16.
With that excellent spear, he shone as he prepared for battle, appearing like a second Śaṅkara, the Lord who destroyed Tripura. Brahmā gave him the Brahmāstra, and Varuṇa gave him the supreme noose.
Indra gave him a conch that resembled the splendor of the moon and was auspicious with its sound;
likewise, Vāyu gave a bow together with arrows, and Agni gave the Āgneya weapon to that great-souled one. 18–19.
The high-souled gods gave many various divine weapons and missiles to that king of great power. Kuñjala said:
Then Āyu’s son,
honored by the gods and gladdened by the blessings of the sages who know the truth,
ascended a divine, radiant chariot adorned with garlands of jewels.
Resounding with the ringing of bells and crowded with small tinkling bells,
King Nṛgada shone upon that divine and beautiful chariot as he traveled along the path of the sky, like the sun indeed by its own splendor.
Scorching the heads of the Daityas with his splendor,
he proceeded swiftly with great speed, like the ever-moving wind,
to where that wicked Dānava stood accompanied by his own forces.
Together with that high-souled charioteer Mātali...

25. Thus ends the one hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Nahuṣa" within the Life of Cyavana, in the Section on the Greatness of the Preceptor as a Holy Site (Gurutīrtha-māhātmya), in the Legend of Vena, in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter One Hundred and Eleventh.
Kuñjala said:
As that hero Nahuṣa, who was equal to the king of the gods, was departing for battle, all the women there followed him, accompanied by songs of curiosity and auspiciousness. 1.
O best of beings, the excellent goddesses, as well as Rambhā and the other apsarases, and the kinnarīs, eager with curiosity, sang with beautiful voices;
likewise, the wives of the gandharvas, endowed with exquisite forms and ornaments, [sang].
Out of curiosity, they went there where the king was staying.
The city named Mahodaya belonged even to the evil-minded Huṇḍa;
it was adorned everywhere with divine groves like the Nandana garden.
That best of cities was adorned with houses possessing seven courtyards, beautified by jars, and shining with great flagstaffs bearing banners;
it was further graced by lofty peaks resembling the summit of Kailāsa that seemed to touch the heavens.
That supreme city was radiant with divine splendors endowed with every glory;
it was graced by forests and celestial groves, and by lakes resembling the ocean,
filled with water and beautifully adorned with lotuses and red water-lilies.
It was adorned with ramparts made of great jewels, hundreds of watchtowers,
and moats filled to the brim with clear water;
it was further resplendent with other great jewels, as well as elephants and horses.
The best of kings, the great hero Nahuṣa, beheld that city of great prosperity, which was crowded with beautiful women and men of great luster, and which shone with various divine powers. 9-10.

At the edge of the city was a divine forest adorned with celestial trees; the great hero, whose soul is righteous, entered it with Mātali on his chariot, just as an immortal enters the Nandana grove. 11.
Together with Mātali, that virtuous-souled one proceeded by means of the chariot.
Having entered the middle of the forest on the bank of a river, that lord of kings beheld there noble and divine beings endowed with celestial forms who had assembled;
those Gandharvas, experts in the essence of song, sang songs for the best of monarchs.
All the bards and panegyrists praised that best of kings, the son of Āyu, who was resplendent like the sun;
meanwhile, Nahuṣa heard the sweet singing uttered by the Kinnaras. 14–15.

Thus ends the one hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Narrative of Nahuṣa" within the Life of Cyavana, concerning the Greatness of the Guru-tīrtha, in the Legend of Vena, in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter One Hundred and Twelfth. Kuñjala said:
Having heard that very song sung by the celestial nymphs, and being moved by those constant melodies, the daughter of Śambhu there became deeply agitated with anxious thought;
rising quickly from her seat, she was filled with great enthusiasm.
The woman of excellent limbs, endowed with the spirit of asceticism, went quickly;
having seen him who resembled a god, possessing a divine form and equal radiance,
his body anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with divine garlands.
The prince was adorned with divine ornaments and garments, radiant like the sun and endowed with divine marks;
"Could he perhaps be a god of great wisdom, or a gandharva? [they wondered].
Is he perhaps the son of Anāga, or could he be a Vidyādhara? Among the gods I do not see anyone like him; from where could he be born among the Yakṣas?
By this playful display, even the thousand-eyed Indra himself might be born as a hero.
"Could this be Śambhu? Or could it be Manobhava (the god of love)?
Or perhaps this might be my father’s friend, the lord of wealth, the descendant of Pulastya?
While she was reflecting thus, that sovereign of beauty and virtue [appeared] with great haste.
Having come together with her great friends, the Rambhās, she laughed and spoke to that daughter of Śambhu.

Thus ends the one hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Nahuṣa within the Life of Cyavana, concerning the Greatness of the Guru-tīrtha," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter One Hundred and Thirteen.
Rambhā said:
"O auspicious one, why do you look upon this [man] after abandoning your asceticism? Indeed, even by merely thinking of a man, there would be a loss of ascetic merit."
Aśokasundarī said:
"My mind is fixed upon this ascetic even against the desire of Nahuṣa;
neither gods, asuras, nor great serpents are able to move me from him."
"O highly fortunate one, having seen him, my mind is greatly agitated;
I desire to go and sport with him, for I have become so full of longing.
Thus, O best of gods, there was this reversal in my mind in this excellent forest."
Tell me the reason for that, if there exists some supreme knowledge.
I am the wife of Āyu’s son, created by the high-souled gods; why does my mind feel such longing, and why does it yearn only for him?
Rambhā said:
"O illustrious lady, O beautiful one, in all these forms of bodies,
the Self itself— the eternal Brahman whose nature is knowledge— dwells."

Although bound by the helpful senses which are tied to the process of material nature and consist of the snares of delusion, he remains forever established; yet he does not know even a fraction of the power of knowledge and realization belonging to primordial nature.
O beautiful one, when this knower of dharma is pure and realizes the Self,
even seeing this great-minded one, they experience mental anguish; thus abandoning sin, he hastens toward truth alone.
"This husband is the son of Āyu; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
Upon seeing another man marked by evil characteristics, he would become suspicious.
Such was the decree made by the gods, binding him with the tether of truth.
"O son of Āyu, that he shall also attain the status of being her husband—
having heard this, O blessed one, and having personally understood that true connection of their feelings, O beautiful lady, he himself remained there. (11-12)
She does not know another state of being, yet she finds the son of Āyu; O Goddess, Nature (Prakṛti) does not even know her husband has arrived.
Knowing this, the Supreme Self (Puruṣa) runs toward you this very day.
The Self knows all; the Self is the eternal deity.
(14) This very one is the heroic Indra, the powerful one named Nahuṣa;
he comes here to you because he desires a true alliance. (15)
"O blessed lady, having known that the son of Āyu does not go to another,
all this which is eternal has been told to you, as it dwells in your mind.
Having slain the most terrible Huṇḍa, the lowest of Dānavas, in battle,"
He will lead you to your own abode, the supreme home of Āyus.
This lord of heroes, remaining only through his own merit, has been carried away by the Daitya;
indeed, from childhood, this lord of heroes has been separated from his kinsmen.
"Deprived of father and mother, having gone to the great forest,
he will surely go to his father's house right now along with you.
Having heard these words spoken by Raṃbhā, Śivanaṃdinī—
Overcome with great joy, she spoke to that daughter of the ocean:
"This very one is my husband, truly possessed of great valor;
he delights my mind, which has been exceedingly distressed and overwhelmed by grief."
"O lady of beautiful smiles, the god who is equal to the mind knows this with perfect certainty;
this truth has been seen by me, which is most wonderful. [I have seen] a man possessing divine marks who is equal to the god of love. (22)
"O friend, having seen him, she does not run away as she did before; O blessed one, she no longer regards any other man. We two must go home with our friends; indeed, this is where we must go."
Having spoken thus, Rambhā prepared to depart for the presence of Nahuṣa;
perceiving her to be eager to go, she said to her: "O Goddess, why do you not proceed? (25)
Sūta said:
Accompanied by my friend Bhayā, I approached Nahuṣa, who possessed the marks of a hero;
having reached his presence, I sent that friend of mine [forward].
"O illustrious one, go to this Huṣa, who possesses a divine form.
Tell him this story, for we have come here for his sake.
Rambhā said:
"O you of excellent vows, I shall thus make you my dear friend.
Having spoken thus, Arambhā approached the prince Nahuṣa,
who was a hero bearing a bow and arrows, like a second Indra.
With her efforts ceased, Rambhā replied with these excellent words to the son of Āyu: "O illustrious one, I am Rambhā; I have come before you, sent by the heroic daughter of Śiva."
Long ago, for your sake, the God of gods created through the Goddess this excellent and most superior form of a wife, which is difficult to find in the worlds,
unattainable even by the best of men, or by gods led by Indra, or by those whose wealth is their asceticism. (31-32)
Listen now: for your sake, the Gandharvas, Pannagas, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas of meritorious characteristics have come here of their own accord.
O highly wise one, she is a jewel among women, perfect and fashioned by merit.
Named Aśokasundarī, she is established in the austerity of silence;
she has performed exceedingly great penance and always desires you.
Knowing this, O illustrious one, please accept her who worships you.
"Except for you, O noble lady, she does not ask for any other man.
Having heard those words spoken by Nahuṣa, Rambhā reflected upon his speech and then gave this reply: "O Lord, please hear my words."
"I understand all of that which has been spoken by you before me.
Previously, it was told in my presence by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha; I know it all, as well as her supreme penance. (37-38)
"Listen, O blessed lady, to the reason why happiness will come to pass:
I shall not go, O beautiful woman, without having slain the Dānava Huṇḍa.
I indeed know this entire account of events exactly as it is."

"Your birth was brought about for my sake, and penance was performed by you; you have become my wife, of this there is no doubt, having been created by destiny. Having made a firm resolve for my sake, penance was performed by you."
O Goddess, from that very heart, by means of that most wicked Dānava who was possessed of self-restraint,
I was indeed carried away from the maternity chamber while still in my childhood and deprived of both father and mother. 42.
"Therefore, I shall slay that Hunda, the lowest of the Danavas; afterwards, O blessed one, I will lead you to the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha.
Thus did he speak to Rambhā, who was intent on doing what was pleasing to him."
Thus dismissed by him, she returned quickly and spoke to Queen Aśokasundarī and to him as well;
O best of the twice-born, Rambhā related everything in brief exactly as it had occurred.
Having attentively heard these well-spoken words of the heroic Nahuṣa, Aśokasundarī was filled with joy;
she then remained there together with her dear friend Raṃbhā.
"I shall always observe what kind of prowess my husband possesses.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Nahuṣa," within the "Life of Cyavana" and the "Greatness of the Guru-tīrtha" in the *Vena-upākhyāna* of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter One Hundred and Fourteen.
Kuñjala said: Now, all these Dānavas, the attendants of Huṇḍa,
shall relate to you the conversation between Nahuṣa and Rambhā exactly as it was heard.
They reported everything that the lord of the Daityas, Huṇḍa, had eloquently spoken;
having heard it, he became enraged and then spoke these words to the messenger:
"Go, O hero, at my command, and find out about that man."
That man conversed together with that daughter of Śiva. Having heard the command of his master, the swift-moving Dānava went to the secluded place and spoke these words to the heroic Huṣa: 3–4.
"Having heard the command of his master, the swift-moving Dānava went to the secluded place and spoke these words to the heroic Huṣa."
He stands ready in a divine chariot with horses and a charioteer;
indeed, he is terrifying in the assembly hall with his bow and divine arrows. For what purpose has he been sent by whom, and by whom have you been sent?
"By this other daughter of Śiva who has been brought here today—
tell me clearly everything that was said by her. O Devamarda, why is it that you do not fear Huṇḍa?"
"Tell me all this, if you wish to live; go quickly and wait upon the unbearable lord of the Dānavas.
Nahuṣa said:

Know that this son of mine, the destroyer of all the Daityas, is the famous one named Nahuṣa, who was once King Āyu, the powerful lord and sovereign of the seven continents, and a worshiper of the gods and Brahmins. 9.
"O Dānava, this girl was carried off by Huṇḍa from her childhood while you were her protector. Previously, this daughter of Śiva was also abducted by the Daitya;
she is now performing severe penance for the sake of slaying even Huṇḍa."
I, that very child who was brought from the lying-in chamber by you and given into the hands of a maidservant and even a wicked cook—
listen, O sinful one, I have now arrived here for the purpose of killing you.
"I shall indeed lead this wicked Huṇḍa Daitya of evil deeds, as well as other terrible Dānavas, to his destruction. Know me to be such a one; thus did I speak to that most sinful Dānava. (13-14)
Having heard all this from the high-souled Nahuṣa,
that evil-minded one went to Huṇḍa and reported his speech. Upon hearing it from his mouth, the lord of the Daityas quickly became enraged.
"Why was he not killed by that wicked cook or by this maidservant? This very disease, which I have neglected, has now reached full growth; I shall now destroy it with this daughter of Śiva. (16-17)
"Kill Khala, the son of Āyu, in battle with these arrows sharpened on stone"—
having thought thus, he spoke these words to his charioteer:
"Harness the chariot with excellent and auspicious horses."
Summoning the commander-in-chief, he spoke to him in great distress:
"Prepare my army; marshal the heroic elephants with their riders, the warriors on horseback, and provide them with banners, parasols, and chowries."
"Quickly mobilize my fourfold army today! Having heard this from Huṇḍa, the highly wise commander-in-chief promptly carried out everything according to the prescribed rites.
Surrounded by that great army consisting of four divisions, he went toward the heroic Nahuṣa, who was equipped with bow and arrows in battle,
mounted upon Indra’s chariot, and was the foremost among all wielders of weapons.
The gods of great majesty, stationed in their celestial chariots in the sky, beheld that hero, difficult for even the gods and dānavas to overcome,
as he rose up in battle like a second sun enveloped in flames of splendor. 24.
Sūta said:
Then all those Dānavas showered him with excellent arrows,
swords, nooses, great spears, javelins, and battle-axes.
They fought in battle with that high-souled Nahuṣa;
enraged and roaring like clouds against a mountain,
the powerful son of Āyu beheld his prowess.

O Brahmin, the great-souled Nahuṣa drew his bow, which was equal to Indra’s weapon, producing a twanging sound from its string; the noise of that bow was like the crash of a thunderbolt, striking terror into the Dānavas.
At that great roar, the Dānavas trembled;
their hearts were overcome by dejection and their courage was broken in that great battle.

Thus ends the one hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Nahuṣa," within the Life of Cyavana, concerning the Greatness of the Guru-tīrtha, in the Legend of Vena, in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The one hundred and fifteenth chapter. Kuñjala said:
Then that high-souled Saṃyati, shining brightly, stood ready with his bow raised.

Just as Time, when enraged, desires to destroy the worlds, so too did he desire to destroy the Dānavas. With nets of great weapons, blazing and equal to the sun, he struck down the Dānavas; just as the wind uproots trees here on earth, even so did the king strike down the Dānavas.
Just as the wind, by its own strength and power, scatters a mass of celestial clouds,
so did that king destroy the asuras, who were intoxicated with pride, with his most excellent and sharp arrows.
All the dānavas were unable to withstand the rain of arrows from that great-souled one.
Some were killed, some fled, and some perished from that great battle.
Sūta said:
[He was] possessed of great splendor, of great wisdom, and the destroyer of the great Dānavas.
Seeing that prince, the evil-minded Huṇḍa became enraged; having approached him while he stood there, he addressed him in battle, saying: "Stay, stay!
Today I shall lead you before Yama, the son of Āyu."
Nahuṣa said:
"I stand here in battle; behold me, for I have come to slay you.
I shall now kill you, O Dānava of sinful mind!"
Having spoken thus, he took up his bow and arrows resembling tongues of fire;
with a parasol being held over him, he shone resplendent in that battle.
He then addressed these words to Mātali, the divine charioteer of Indra:
"Drive my chariot today to face Huṇḍa!"—
having been addressed thus by that hero,
Mātali, swift in his prowess, urged on the horses whose speed was like that of a great wind.
Then the mounts sprang up like swans in the sky;
with his moon-colored umbrella and his bannered chariot,
he reached the vault of heaven and shone like the sun.
Then Āyuputra appeared with such immeasurable splendor and prowess; likewise,
Huṇḍa, though mounted on a chariot, shone by his own majesty,
equipped with all weapons and established in the vow of a hero.
Then the battle between those two heroes was astonishing to the gods; it was fierce, terrifying, and [the work] of the highly wise one.
With sharp, whetted, excellent arrows, heron-feathered and stone-tipped shafts, [they fought].
Then Huṇḍa struck the king between his two arms;
pierced by five arrows in his beautiful forehead, he then became enraged.
Pierced by those arrows, the king shone even more brilliantly.
Rising with his rays like a garland of lotuses, the sun appeared;
meanwhile, the king shone like the sun in the sky of a former age, his limbs smeared with blood and golden arrows fixed upon his body. 17.
Seeing his lack of manliness, he spoke these words to the Dānava: "Stay, stay for a moment, O Daitya! Let me see your agility once more.
Having said this, he struck the Daitya in battle with ten arrows.
Struck by the blow from Mukhabhāla’s mouth, he fell down unconscious; then,
while the divine gods were looking on from above, that one of great strength was greeted with a cry of joy arising from the gods, Cāraṇas, and Siddhas.
"Victory! Victory!"—thus, O Indra among kings, they blew their conchs again and again.
That tumultuous sound, accompanied by a great clamor raised by the gods, entered the ear-cavities of the swooning Huṇḍa. 21-22.

Hearing this, he took up his bow and an arrow resembling a venomous serpent and cried out: "Stay! Stay! I am dead; I have been slain by you! Having spoken thus, he rose once more, endowed with great agility.
Again, he struck Nahuṣa with twenty-one arrows;
one in the middle of his fist, four in the middle of his arms,
four at his great horses, and one indeed at his umbrella.

The Dānava pierced Mātali’s chariot-seat with five arrows, the flagstaff with seven, and the wicked-souled one’s grip on the reins and his aim at the target with three sharp, feathered shafts like fire. 26.
Seeing his agility, the deities were filled with wonder.
Observing that supreme Dānava’s prowess, the king said:
"You are a hero, you are accomplished in learning, you are courageous, and you are skilled in battle."
Having spoken thus, the king, acting with swift prowess, drew his bow and pierced that Dānava with ten arrows;
he then cut down his banner with three, and it fell to the surface of the earth.
With four of his arrows, he of swift prowess struck down his horses; with one, he cut off his parasol;
and with ten, he dispatched his charioteer to the abode of Yama.
Having cut through Daṃśana with ten arrows and shattered him,
he pierced the lord of the Asuras in all his limbs with thirty shafts.
His horses slain and deprived of his chariot, he stood with bow in hand, arrows in grasp, wielding his weapon.
He rushed forward with great speed, showering him with sharp arrows.
The Daitya, wielding a sword and shield, charged at the king;
as he was charging, the monarch cut off Huṇḍa’s sword.
The king cut through his armor with sharp, razor-edged arrows;
then Huṇḍa, that wicked-souled one, having looked all around, quickly seized a mallet and hurled it with swift prowess.
Then the king beheld Vajravega approaching;
by his own prowess, he brought down that thundering mallet from the sky with ten sharp, razor-edged arrows. (36-37)
Seeing the mallet fallen on the ground in ten pieces, he raised his mace with great force and rushed toward the king; then,
with a sharp-edged sword, he severed his arm.
Then,
having let out a great roar like the crashing of a thunderbolt, he fell to the ground with his armor, armlets, and bracelets, his limbs smeared with blood as he ran about in that great battle. 39-40.
Possessed by great anger and desiring to devour the king, he approached that monarch, having become impossible to restrain. Then the Dānava was struck in the heart by Nahuṣa with a mighty spear.
He suddenly fell to the ground like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
When that Daitya had gone to the earth, the other Dānavas arrived;
some entered various difficult terrains, while others took refuge in the netherworld (Pātāla).
The gods, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas attained great joy when that great sinner Huṣa was slain by the high-souled [Indra].
When that best of Daityas was killed at the great sacrifice, all the gods experienced supreme delight.
Having regained her, who was of divine form and increased by ascetic penance, the son of Āyu was filled with joy.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Nahuṣa," within the "Life of Cyavana" in the "Guru-tīrtha-māhātmya" section of the "Vena-ākhyāna" in the *Bhūmi-khaṇḍa* of the *Śrī Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter One Hundred and Sixteen.
Kuñjalā said:
Delighted by the commencement of Aśokasundarī’s meritorious undertaking, that ascetic woman, having approached the valiant Nahuṣa, spoke to him. 1.

"O Hero, according to the law of *ahantā*, this ascetic woman has been ordained as my wife by the gods; marry me if you desire righteousness here. While established in penance, I have always been meditating upon you."
"O best of kings, it is through my devotion to Dharma that you have been obtained by me.
Nahuṣa said:
"O blessed lady, if you remain steadfast in austerity for my sake,"
"By the word of my guru, within a moment I shall become your husband.
O beautiful lady, let us go together with this Rambhā;
having placed that enchanting Rambhā upon the chariot."
With that very same excellent chariot, the highly illustrious one went swiftly toward the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha together with those two.
Having beheld that brahmin who had arrived at the hermitage, he bowed down to him.
Endowed with great splendor and filled with immense joy,
he reported everything regarding how the battle had occurred in the field and how that lowest of Dānavas was slain, to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha.
Vasiṣṭha, having heard of Nahuṣa’s undertaking,
was filled with great joy and honored him with blessings. Then,
when an auspicious lunar day and a favorable moment had arrived, that bull among sages [performed the rites] for the two of them.
He caused the marriage to be performed in the presence of the sacred fire and the Brahmins.
Having thus congratulated the couple with blessings, he sent them away, saying,
"O high-minded one, go quickly and see your mother and father."
"And upon seeing you, O observer of noble vows, let your mother and father attain an increase of joy, like the ocean on a full-moon day.
Thus was that hero dispatched by the sage, the son of Brahmā.
With that very same excellent chariot, he of swift prowess departed;
having paid homage to that lord of brahmins,
Mātali then took him to his own city to see his father and likewise his mother.
Sūta said:
Then, sent by the gods from among the companies of Apsarases, Menakā approached Āyu’s wife, who, out of great sorrow, had fallen into an ocean of grief. 15
She spoke to that illustrious queen Indumatī:
"O noble lady, abandon your grief; behold your son together with his wife.
Having slain the wicked Dānava who abducted your son," [she continued].
And as he entered the assembly hall endowed with heroic splendor,
Cemenikā reported to Indumatī how Nahuṣa had conducted himself during their union. 17-18.
Having heard the words of Menikā, she was filled with great joy and spoke in a faltering voice: "Friend, you speak the truth. These words were like nectar, most dear, and inspiring to her mind. 19.
"Life and all else that belongs to me must indeed be given by me to you.
Having spoken thus, the goddess said this to the king:
"Your mighty-armed son has indeed arrived right now."
O Great King, having thus addressed her husband, this most excellent Apsaras, filled with great joy, became silent. Having heard what was praised, the lord of men spoke to his beloved.
O highly fortunate one, it was indeed previously declared by the sage Nārada:
"O King, you must never experience grief on account of a son;
having slain that Dānava with his own valor, your son shall attain heaven. 23-24.
"What has been spoken by the sage in the past is indeed true;
O Goddess, how could his word ever be otherwise?
Dattātreya, the best of sages, will become a god in person."
O Goddess, you were served by me through penance in the past;
therefore, he has granted you a jewel of a son who upholds the portion of Viṣṇu. He shall always slay the supreme Dānava of sinful mind.
"The destroyer of all Daityas, the protector of subjects, and one of great strength—
this most excellent son, a portion of Viṣṇu, has been granted to me by Dattātreya.
Having thus addressed Queen Indumatī at that time, the king [spoke].
Then he held a great festival in anticipation of his son's arrival; filled with immense joy, he indeed called Viṣṇu to mind once again—
the one who is endowed with all things, accompanied by the hosts of gods, the embodiment of bliss, and the singular ultimate reality.
It removes the afflictions of men, bestows happiness, and grants supreme liberation to true Vaiṣṇavas. 31.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Nahuṣa," within the Life of Cyavana, in the Section on the Greatness of the Guru as a Sacred Site, in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter One Hundred and Seventeen.
Kuñjala said: Nahuṣa, together with his beloved wife Saraṃbhā, traveled by means of that excellent,
divine chariot belonging to Indra.
He arrived at the city named Nāga, endowed with every splendor, graced with divine auspicious objects, and beautified by palaces;
it was furnished with golden archways and adorned with banners.
It was graced by the sounds of various musical instruments and adorned by bards and panegyrists; it was further embellished by meritorious men resembling gods in form,
as well as by women of celestial beauty, elephants, horses, and chariots.
Then, amidst various auspicious sounds, the resonance of the Vedas, the noise of songs and musical instruments, and the melodies of lutes and flutes,
he entered that preeminent city, which was filled with every kind of splendor.
Honored by the Vedic auspicious chants and by the Brahmins,
the hero beheld his father and his most virtuous mother;
filled with great joy, he prostrated at his father’s feet.
With a heart full of devotion, that fair-faced woman bowed again and again at the feet of both Aśoka and Suṃdarī; then Rambhā also bowed and displayed her affection toward them.
Having bowed and addressed his own guru, the prince inquired after the health of his mother and father. Thus addressed,
the illustrious man was filled with joy, his hair standing on end.
Āyu said:
"This very day, O son, diseases have been destroyed and both suffering and grief have departed; by the sight of you, the world rejoices with great satisfaction."
"I have become one who has accomplished his purpose now that you, of great luster, have been born;
having performed the upliftment of my own lineage, I myself have been truly delivered.
Indumatī said:
O highly fortunate one, just as the great ocean attains increase upon seeing the splendor of the moon when it reaches its full phase on a parvan day, so do I attain growth through the sight of you;
I have grown, I am greatly delighted, and I am overwhelmed with joy.
"O wise one, by seeing you, I have become blessed; O giver of honor!
(14) Having spoken thus, he embraced his son, that most excellent of offspring, and smelled the crown of his head, just as a cow sniffs her own calf. (15)
Then Queen Indumatī, the virtuous one, honored her son Nahuṣa— who had arrived with a divine form— by welcoming him and bestowing blessings upon him.
Sūta said:
Then the son, the highly illustrious one, related to his virtuous mother, Queen Indumatī, the account of how he had been carried away,
as well as the birth and recovery of his wife.
The battle fought by Huṇḍa and the downfall of Huṇḍa itself—
this entire account has been related by me in brief, exactly as it happened between mother and father, bringing them joy. 18–19.
Having heard of their son’s valorous exertion, his parents were filled with great joy, their hearts becoming full. Then Nahuṣa, taking up the bow, [set out] indeed in the chariot of Indra.
He conquered the entire earth with its seven continents and its cities;
he offered the wealth-filled earth to his father,
constantly gladdening his father through acts of charity and virtuous deeds.
Then they caused their father to perform sacrifices such as the Rājasūya,
along with great sacrifices, gifts, vows, restraints, self-control,
noble charities, glorious merits, and sacrifices of great auspicious results.
Then the two parents were made fully satisfied by the son of Āyu.
Next, the gods, having assembled at the excellent city named Nāga,
consecrated the high-souled Nahuṣa, the crusher of heroes.
Having been consecrated in his own kingdom by that king Āyu, together with the sages, the perfected ones (siddhas), and the daughter of Śiva,
the highly illustrious King Āyu, accompanied by his wife, remained in his own body.
The righteous-souled one went to heaven, highly honored by the gods and the siddhas.
Having abandoned the station of Indra, he went again to the world of Brahmā;
then, worshipped by the gods and the sages, he proceeded to the world of Hara.
By his own deeds and by the great splendor of his son, this king has gone to the realm of Hari through his merits and dwells there;
such is this supreme merit known as "meritorious action" performed by men. 29.
"O highly fortunate one, what need is there for other causes of grief?
Just as he was born, that Nahuṣa is a righteous soul who delivers his father;
Nahuṣa is the sustainer of the entire lineage and is wise with knowledge. (30-31)
All this history of that king has been narrated to you;
O son of Kapinjala, what else shall I tell you?
Such is this meritorious, pure, and glorious account.
Even a mortal who hears of the son of Āyu, having enjoyed those pleasures, attains the state of Murāri. 33.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Nahuṣa" within the Life of Cyavana, concerning the Greatness of the Guru-tīrtha, in the Legend of Vena, in the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter One Hundred and Eighteen.
Kapiñjala said:
O dear father, at the mouth of the Gaṅgā, a noble woman is weeping,
and drops of tears fall from her two eyes into the great waters.
In the middle of the Gaṅgā, lotuses emerge— divine in form, fragrant, and large;
O father, for what reason do they fall from her two beautiful eyes?
O noble one, his pure teardrops are like the waters of the Gaṅgā;
though he remains with only bone and skin remaining, wearing matted hair and bark garments, he nevertheless gathers those fragrant lotuses. 3–4.
"O one of great intelligence, tell me: who is that woman who, having brought divine golden-colored [offerings], worships Śiva with them?
And why does she, after having worshipped Śiva, subsequently weep?"
"Tell me all of this, if I am dear to you.
Kuñjala said:
"Listen, my child, I shall relate the account ordained by the gods."
This is the life-story of the high-souled Viṣṇu, which destroys all sins. That Huṇḍa of great prowess was slain by Nahuṣa in battle;
his son, the famous Vihuṇḍa, has now resorted to ascetic penance.
Having heard that his father, along with his ministers and retinue, had been slain by the heroic and powerful son of Āyu, Nahuṣa,
out of anger, performs austerities and prepares to destroy the gods.
All the gods knew that the prowess of that wicked one, who had been strengthened by asceticism, was unbearable on the field of battle;
for Huṇḍa’s son, Vihuṇḍa, was intent on destroying the three worlds. 10–11.
"I shall avenge my father's enmity; I will slay these gods and men! Thus resolved, that sinner—a thorn to the gods and Brahmins—began his depredations and oppressed all living beings.
Burned by his very splendor, the gods, led by Indra,
went for refuge to the high-souled Viṣṇu,
the God of gods, the Lord of the universe, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.
And they said, "Protect us constantly from the great fear of Vihuṇḍa.
Śrī Viṣṇu said:
"May all the gods, O Maheśvaras, prosper with great happiness. (15)
"I shall destroy Vihuṇḍa, the most wicked thorn in the side of the gods.
Having spoken thus to the gods and having employed his illusory power (māyā), Janārdana,
the highly illustrious one, himself remained there in Nandana.
Then she created a form consisting of illusion, endowed with the three qualities (guṇas), in the likeness of a woman.
The illustrious Māyā of Viṣṇu, who deludes the entire universe, assumed an incomparable form; Viṣṇu’s Māyā, the deluder, took on that form.
For the sake of slaying Vihuṇḍa, Kuñjalā, endowed with beauty and charm,
went by a divine path for the purpose of destroying the gods. 19.
Then, at the edge of the Nandana grove, the lord of the Daityas beheld Māyā;
deluded by her, his heart pierced by the arrows of desire, the demon did not realize that this beautiful woman was the very form of Time (Death) leading to his own destruction.
Seeing her, who possessed the luster of molten gold and was radiant with the wealth of beauty, the wicked-souled Vihuṇḍa became lustful and spoke to that excellent woman:
"Who are you, O beautiful lady, who agitates my heart? (21-22)
"O auspicious one, O lady of beautiful countenance, protect me, protect me from this union!
O Goddess of gods, whatever you desire at present through this union with me, O highly fortunate one, that I shall grant you, even if it be difficult for gods and dānavas to obtain."
Māyā said:
"O Dānava, if you truly desire to enjoy me, then give me my dowry;
worship Śaṅkara with seven crores of flowers."
"O highly fortunate one, place upon my neck a garland made of those flowers— divine, fragrant, born of the Kāmoda tree, and difficult even for the gods to obtain— and grant this gift to me. (25-26)
"Then I shall become your beloved wife, without a doubt. Vihuṇḍa said: "O Goddess, I shall do exactly so; I grant the boon you have requested. (27)

The lord of the gods, overcome by the god of love, wandered through those divine and meritorious forests, yet he did not see that tree. Having gone here and there himself, he asked one named Kāmodaka.
"Great people say that there is no tree called Kāmodya," they said.
Thus questioned, that evil-minded man, tormented by the arrows of desire, went to Bhārgava and, with his neck bowed in devotion, made his inquiry. 29-30.
"O beloved, plant the Kāmodaka tree, which is beautiful and laden with flowers.
Śukra said: "O Dānava, there is no such tree as the Kāmoda; it exists only for women. 31.
When she laughed out of joy during that conversation,
from that laughter there arose fragrant and excellent divine flowers, which undoubtedly possess great fragrance. (32)
Even with a single flower that is pleasing to the heart, not yet faded, and endowed with fragrance, he who worships Śaṅkara— Śaṅkara fulfills his desired great wish. 33–34.
From its weeping, Daityas arise; of this there is no doubt.
Such flowers are likewise red and large, but one should not allow contact with them, for they lack fragrance. 35.
Having thus heard these words spoken by Śukra, she said, "O son of Bhṛgu,
where is Kāmadā?
Śukra replied:
At Gaṅgādvāra, which is of great merit and the destroyer of great sins, there is a city called Kāmoda built by Viśvakarman;
in that city of Kāmoda, women are adorned with divine enjoyments. 37–38.
Thus, she shines with ornaments and is well-honored by all the gods;
you must go there and honor that excellent Apsaras, O Dānava, even by means of some meritorious stratagem to make her laugh. 39.
Having spoken thus to the Dānava Śuka, that lord of yogis, possessed of great splendor, ceased speaking and became intent upon his own task.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Kāmodā," within the Life of Cyavana, in the Section on the Greatness of the Guru as a Holy Place (*gurutīrtha-māhātmya*), in the *Vena Upākhyāna* of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The one hundred and nineteenth chapter. Kapiñjala said:
O father, by whose laughter indeed do friends become truly dear?

"O high-minded one, why do all the deities desire these divine-scented flowers that are difficult even for the gods and asuras to obtain? Śaṅkara attains happiness when he is well-worshipped with these fragrant flowers."
Tell me in detail what the qualities of that flower are,
and how Kāmadoṣā, the daughter of Kātu and an excellent woman,
came to be; for from her laughter, O illustrious one, beautiful flowers arise.
"Tell me all about his qualities and his story in detail. Kuñjala said:
"In ancient times, the gods and the great Daityas established a most excellent friendship."
Exerting themselves for the sake of the nectar of immortality, they churned the ocean of milk.
From that churning of the gods and demons, four jewels of maidens emerged,
first revealed by Varuṇa and likewise again by Soma.
Afterwards, the merit was revealed as the nectar situated within the jar;
previously, the four maidens desired the welfare of the gods.
One of them was named Sulakṣmī, and the second was Vāruṇī.
They proclaim that among those [daughters], the one who was not so named was Kāmodā.
Among them, O Mahāmati, she who was born first was the most excellent and best; therefore, she is renowned in the world as Jyeṣṭhā and is always honored.
From the foam of the milk, there arose the one known as Kāmadā, who was like the drink of Varuṇa and possessed waves of nectar. Likewise, King Soma and Lakṣmī were both born from that very nectar.

Soma, the ornament of the three worlds and beloved of Śaṅkara, was born; likewise, Vāruṇī, the destroyer of death and disease, was born; and Jyeṣṭhā, the bestower of great merit, was born for those desiring the welfare of the worlds. 11–12.
The goddess named Kāmodā, who arose from the nectar and bestows merit,
shall exist for the pleasure of Viṣṇu and will assume the form of a tree;
she shall indeed always be a source of delight to Viṣṇu.
There is no doubt that the merit of the name of Tulasī shall arise;
there is no doubt that the Lord of the World will take pleasure with her.
Whoever, having taken even a single leaf of Tulasī, shall offer it to Kṛṣṇa—
"Thinking constantly, 'What can I give to him for his services? one will become dear to him.
Thus was she who was formerly born from the ocean named Kāmodā.
When the goddess laughed, speaking with a voice faltering with joy (17),
fragrant blossoms fell from her mouth; indeed, as he stood ready, he caught those unfading, beautiful flowers (18).
One should worship the god Śaṅkara, as well as Brahmā and Mādhava;
the gods become well-pleased with him and grant whatever he desires. When she, afflicted by some sorrow, wept, [the gods granted her wish].
From the tears of the eyes, they arise and fall;
O highly fortunate one, those flowers are indeed heart-pleasing and very large.
Yet, he who worships Śaṅkara with them without fragrance— 20–21.

For him, suffering and torment arise; there is no doubt about this. If a person of sinful mind worships the gods even once with such flowers, the gods inflict suffering upon him; there is no doubt about that.
Thus has this entire, supreme narrative of Kāma been related to you.
Then Kṛṣṇa, having reflected and observed the prowess and audacity of the wicked Vihuṇḍa, as well as his undertaking and that very boldness at that time— 23–24.
He dispatched Nārada, saying, "Delude this one who is difficult to overcome. Then,
having heard the words of the high-souled Viṣṇu, Nārada followed that wicked-minded Dānava as he was departing for Kāmodā.
Having gone there, Nārada spoke to that lord of the Daityas as if laughing:
"O lord of the Daityas, where are you going so hurriedly and agitated? For what purpose now, for whose sake, and by whom have you been urged?"
Having paid homage to the son of Brahmā with palms joined in reverence, he replied:
"O best of the twice-born, I have set out for the sake of *kāmoda* flowers. That righteous-souled one said to him: "What is the purpose of your need for flowers?"
The best of brahmins spoke again concerning the cause and effect of his own situation:
"In a certain region of the forest, upon merely seeing a woman of beautiful countenance belonging to Nandana, I fell under the sway of desire. (29–30)
O best of brahmins, she said to me: "Worship Mahādeva with seven crores of flowers produced from the Kāmada tree;
then you will undoubtedly become my beloved wife. 31.
For her sake, I am setting out today toward the city named Kāmoda.
I shall now desire that daughter of the ocean;
furthermore, with the delights of my mind and great laughter, I shall cause her to laugh again.
Being delighted, the illustrious lady will laugh again and again;
that laughter of hers, O Brahmin, will be faltering and will increase my distress.
From that laughter, divine flowers will fall.
"With these very things, I shall now worship the beloved of Umā.
By the offering of that worship, Śaṅkara— the Lord of all beings and the creator of the worlds— will be pleased and grant me the fruit."
Nārada said:
"O Daityas, you must go there to that supreme city named Kāma;
there dwells the highly intelligent Viṣṇu, who brings about the destruction of all the Daityas."
I shall tell you the means by which these flowers known as Kāmoda will come into your hand, O Dānava;
there is no doubt that divine [flowers] will fall into the waters of the Gaṅgā. 38.
"Divine waters, carried by the wind, shall arrive right now;
you must accept them, for they are pleasant and great. Having taken those flowers, accomplish what you desire. 40
Then, having deluded that best of Dānavas, Nārada once again—thereupon, that righteous-souled one reflected further:
"By what means might she, being so distressed, shed tears? (41)
While Vānara was thus reflecting for a moment, an idea arose in him: "I shall go to the city named Kāmodā.

Thus ends the one hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Kāmodā," within the account of Cyavana’s life, concerning the greatness of the Guru-tīrtha, in the Vena-episode of the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The one hundred and twentieth chapter. Kuñjala said:
There is a divine city named Kāmoda, crowded with all the gods.
Then, not seeing the fulfillment of all his desires, Nārada,
that best of the twice-born, reached the house of Kāmodā and entered it;
having then seen Kāmodā, who was filled with every object of desire.
Having been honored by her with auspicious words such as "welcome" and the like, that best of brahmins sat upon a divine seat and questioned her:
"O blessed lady, born from the splendor of Viṣṇu, are you dwelling in comfort?"
Having greeted them with blessings, he asked after their well-being.
Kāmado said:
"By the grace of you and Viṣṇu, I am living in happiness."
O one of great wisdom, tell me the reason for this question and answer:
O bull among sages, a great delusion has arisen in my limb,
pervasive throughout all the worlds, which destroys my intellect.
Therefore, O sage, sleep arose and took its course among mortals; while I was asleep, a terrible dream was seen by me,
which someone approached and spoke to me in my presence, O best of the twice-born.
"O Hṛṣīkeśa, he will enter into worldly existence while remaining unmanifest.
From that time forward, O Great-minded One, I have been pervaded by suffering;
therefore, you, the best among the wise, must tell me the cause of this."

Nārada said: "O blessed lady, among human beings, dreams arise—those born of wind (vātika), those born of bile (paittika), those born of phlegm (kaphaja), and those born of the combination of all three (sānnipātika); of this there is no doubt."
O beautiful one, neither sleep nor dreams occur among the gods;
however, at the time of sunrise, an excellent dream is seen. Indeed, such a true dream bestows the fruit of merit upon human beings.
I shall now explain another cause of dreams, O auspicious one.
O lady of beautiful countenance, when the water is shaken by great gusts of wind, minute droplets of water break off from that mass of water. 12–13.
O auspicious lady, just as these pure drops of water fall outside and then return to their dissolution, becoming visible and then invisible;
even so, O beautiful woman, listen as the nature of a dream is described.
The Self is pure, dispassionate, and free from attachment and aversion;
having indeed transcended those composed of the five elements, it remains perfectly steady and shines resplendent among the twenty-six principles. 15-16.

When the pure, eternal, and isolated Self comes into contact with Prakṛti, and when it moves from its station due to those states of being which have the nature of air, then a light resembling that of the Self is produced. 17.
From the Self and from the fiery [element], a counter-light is born.
O auspicious lady, that which is called the "inner self" (antarātman) is declared to be the impurity of that very [self].
Just as drops of water become distinct from milk, O auspicious one, so too is the inner self described as being distinct from the radiance of the Self. 18–19.
Earth, fire, wind, space, and water—
Having attained union with that [deity], they indeed reach oneness;
yet, O fair-faced one, through the defect of their own nature, they destroy it. Desiring another body, O beautiful-faced one, they seek it again and again. 21–22.
This play and recreation of theirs is the cause of the creation of the universe;
just as a wave arises from water and dissolves back into it,
so too does such a being undergo repeated birth and repeated destruction.
Just as that was the illustration for the form of water, so it is for these [other elements] without a doubt.
O Goddess, the self does not perish; fire and wind do not perish; earth and space do not perish, and water likewise does not perish. 24–25.
O blessed lady, these five, beginning with the self, arise and depart together with the self; for they are indeed eternal in nature, without a doubt.
Even the physical body is born and perishes along with them.

O twice-born one, when the vital breaths— composed of the five elements— are struck by the great defects of the sense objects, such as passion, hatred, and the like, they depart from the physical body (piṇḍa).
At the end of the body, the self (ātman) remains in a form that is its very counterpart.

Just as a spark from a fire shines forth, so does the inner self (antarātman) manifest; appearing and disappearing, it is born again and again. The pure self (śuddhātman), which is the Supreme Brahman, remains eternally awake at all times.

But the inner self, bound by the great qualities of *prakṛti*, proceeds happily when nourished by the food of *anna*. From that great happiness arises delusion (*moha*), and because of that, the mind becomes bewildered. (30–31)
Afterwards, tamasic sleep arises, which increases the quality of inertia (tamas).
When the sun, traveling through the path of the channels (nāḍīs), passes over Mount Meru, then night is produced until the sun rises again. 32.
Freed from the darkness of sense-objects, the inner self shines forth.
(33) By means of the dispositions consisting of the principles—the five elements nourished and existing as the aggregates from previous births—the inner self is grasped. (34)

O Mahāmati, the inner self (antarātman), bound by defects, is led through various high and low states in the cycle of existence (saṃsāra). The individual soul (jīvātman) protects the body, while remaining situated in the middle.
The udāna rises with great intensity, and from it that sound is produced.
Just as a bellows filled with air produces a breath when blown, so too does the udāna forcefully produce the breath by the power of the sound. 36–37.
By the power of the self (ātman), however, udāna becomes strong;
thus the body becomes utterly stupefied and is born as if dead.
Likewise, it is established in the heart, the throat, the mouth, and at the tip of the nose.
Having contracted the arms, one should remain with the breath fixed in the heart or the navel region;
by the power of the self, this wind is called udāna. 39-40.
He produces a great and intense obstruction of the vital force;
just as one who holds a wooden wedge remains bound by a rope, so too the vital air (prāṇavāyu) is firmly attached to the self, without a doubt. 41.
But the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*), O fair-faced one, is attached to the inner self (*antarātman*). O blessed lady, when it is led by the intellect (*buddhi*), the inner self runs forward;
remembering the impressions (*vāsanā*) acquired in previous births, it runs toward them. (42–43)
Established therein, O one of great wisdom, he sports again according to his own will;
Likewise, one sees mountains that are very difficult to traverse and various high and low elevations; know that this indeed is the vātika [dream].
Now I shall describe the kaphaja [dream] in the same way: one sees water, a river, a pond, and reservoirs of water. 45–46.
O Goddess, if one sees fire and much excellent gold, know that to be of the bilious (paittika) type; and I shall now describe what is to be considered auspicious.
A dream seen at dawn may be either auspicious or indeed inauspicious.
O lady of excellent hips, he who is joined with karma reveals gain and loss;
O woman of noble lineage, even the state of dream has been described by me, as well as its future manifestation for Viṣṇu, O lady of excellent hips. 48–49.
"It was for that reason that you saw that evil dream, which has now been observed [by me].

Thus ends the one hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Kāmā," within the "Life of Cyavana" section of the "Greatness of the Guru-tīrtha" in the "Story of Vena" of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter One Hundred and Twenty-One.
Kāmoda said:
"All the deities do not know the end or even the form of that in whom all this [universe] is dissolved; and he is proclaimed as the one Self."
O Nārada, hear how this saṃsāra is indeed the expansion of Māyā;
why does my Lord, the Master of the Universe, enter into saṃsāra? A man is bound by actions, both by sins and by great merits.
"O Hari, tell me why he wanders through saṃsāra.
Nārada said:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall tell you what was done by that wielder of the discus."
"I shall perform the protection of the sacrifice as previously promised by Bhṛgu.
At Indra’s word,
Govinda immediately departed from Bhṛgu’s excellent sacrifice to fight with the Dānavas.

When the god had departed after abandoning the sacrifice, that entire sacrifice was subsequently destroyed by those foremost of Dānavas, who were evil-minded. Then the lord of yogis, Bhṛgu, being enraged at Hari, uttered a curse.
"Defiled by my curse, you shall undergo ten births;
Janārdana will experience the fruit of his own karma. It was for that reason, O Goddess, that you beheld that evil dream."
Having spoken thus, the brahmin Nārada departed for the world of Brahmā;
and she, too, became distressed with profound sorrow for Kṛṣṇa. The young girl wept piteously, crying out "Alas! Alas! again and again.
Listen, O Nandana: seated on the bank of the Gaṅgā at the edge of the water, Sunetrā likewise shed tears out of sorrow;
those shed tears fell into the waters of the Gaṅgā. 10–11.
And her teardrops sink into the water;
from them, O Father, lotuses are born again, which indeed proceed as full-blown flowers carried along by the waters of the Gaṅgā. 12.
Deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu, the best of the Dānavas did not recognize the birth born of sorrow, even though it had been described by the sage;
overcome with great joy, that asura accepted it. 13–14.
Deluded by the illusory power of Viṣṇu, that lord of the Daityas also worshipped the beloved of the Daughter of the Mountain with seven crores of blossoming lotuses.
Then, becoming enraged, the Mother of the World spoke these words to Śaṅkara: 15.
Behold, O high-minded one, the improper conduct of this Dānava:
these lotuses born from his grief that have fallen into the waters of the Gaṅgā, he now seizes with a mind agitated by lust. (16–17)
How could there be any great welfare for one of wicked soul who worships me with flowers born of suffering and grief— those things which cause sorrow and torment?
Even with whatever disposition one may have, one should worship me alone.
"Even with such a disposition, his success will come to pass.
Though he is devoid of true meditation, his mind has become free from desire; having become one of sinful conduct, O Goddess, depart by your own splendor. (19-20)

Having thus heard those words of the high-souled Śambhu, the Goddess, desiring his destruction, spoke: "O Śambhu, by your command, I shall bring about his end. Having spoken thus, she then [prepared] for the sake of slaying him.
Indeed, he reflected upon the means for the slaughter of Vihuṇḍa. Having assumed the illusory form of a high-souled Brāhmaṇa,
