he would worship the Lord Śaṅkara with excellent flowers born of the Pārijāta tree.

Then the sinful Dānava, agitated by lust, afflicted by great suffering, and absorbed in that state with his mind intent upon it, approached and destroyed the divine worship of Viṣṇu’s Great Māyā, which he had previously seen. 24. And the Dānava [approached] the Great Māyā of Viṣṇu, which had been seen before.
Afflicted by the arrows of desire, that wicked Dānava remembered her;
merely by the recollection of her, he was overcome by powerful passion and, tormented by the suffering of separation, wept again and again. (25-26)

Drawn by Time, that wicked-souled one arrived having gathered those flowers born of the *aśoka* tree, desiring to worship Maheśvara. He performed the worship of the Goddess with beautiful flowers born of the *pārijāta* tree.
Having destroyed them through great greed, one should worship with tears born of sorrow.
O child, those drops produced from the tears of that wicked man then fall incessantly upon the top of the *liṅga*. 28–29.
Then, assuming the form of a brahmin woman, she said to him, "O high-minded one, who are you that always worships the god with a mind agitated by grief?
Tears born of sorrow fall from you upon the head of the god."
"Tell me this matter before me: who are these impure women?
31 Vihuṇḍa said: "Previously, I saw a woman endowed with all the wealth of good fortune."
She was endowed with all auspicious marks and was a great abode of desire. Unconsumed by delusion, yet overcome by passion for her, he said: "Grant me this excellent body for our union. (32-33)
Worship Maheśvara with flowers produced from the Kāmoda tree;
place a garland made of those flowers around my neck. Worship Maheśvara with seven crores [of such flowers].
For that purpose, I worship the Lord who bestows the fruit [of my desires],
with flowers produced from the Kāmada tree, which are difficult even for gods and demons to obtain.
Śrī Devī said:
Where is the devotion, where is the meditation, and where is the wisdom of that evil-souled one?
You indeed have no connection whatsoever even with the Lord;
tell me now, what kind of excellent form does Kāmada possess? 36–37.
"Excellent flowers have been obtained, and they have arisen from her laughter.
Vihuṇḍa said: "I do not know her disposition or her meditation; I have never seen her at any time. (38)

"I constantly take up only those [flowers] found in the waters of the Gaṅgā; with them, I worship the One, whom I proclaim as Śaṅkara. O Brahmin, this was told before me even by the high-souled Śukra.
"By his command, I worship the Lord of Gods day after day. [40] "All this that I have been asked by you has now been told. Śrī Devī said:
With those flowers born from weeping out of desire, which arise from suffering, you should worship the *liṅga* every day at the dawn of the wicked night;
indeed, with whatever disposition and with whatever kind of flowers you [possess]. 41–42.
"Since you have worshipped the Lord of the Gods of gods, may you obtain such a fruit;
yet, having destroyed the divine worship, you now worship with flowers of grief. This most terrible fault has arisen from you alone today. (43)
"Therefore, I shall inflict punishment upon you; eat the fruit born of your own karma.
Having heard his words, Kāla, drawn by fate, spoke: "Ho there, you wicked one of evil conduct, you defiler of my work!"
"I shall kill you here with this sword; of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus to that Brahmin, the evil-minded Dānava took up his sharpened sword and rushed forward, desiring to slay him.
That supreme goddess, assuming the form of a Brahmin and filled with rage, said:
"I shall slay you here with this sword; of this there is no doubt.
Seeing that he had returned to his own place, she uttered the syllable "Hum."
By that sound of "huṃ," the lowest of Dānavas fell;
rendered motionless by his will-form, he was like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
When that destroyer of all worlds, the Dānava, had fallen, 48–49.
All the worlds have attained well-being and are freed from the heat of suffering;
for this reason, my child, she laments like a woman in distress, her mind agitated by grief on the banks of the Gaṅgā, O lady of beautiful limbs. 50.
"All this that you have asked has been explained to you.
Viṣṇu said:
Having spoken thus to his good son, Kuñjala, the lord of birds—
The highly wise one ceased and said nothing at all, O King.

(52) Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Narrative of Kāma" within the Life of Cyavana, in the Section on the Greatness of the Guru-tīrtha, in the Legend of the Hunter, in the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter One Hundred and Twenty-Two.
Viṣṇu said:
"O Kuñjala, you are a partisan of dharma. Having spoken thus to his sons, the highly wise one ceased speaking and said nothing further to them.
The best of the twice-born, seated beneath the banyan tree, said to that great parrot: "Who are you who speaks of dharma while existing in the form of a bird?
Are you a god, or a gandharva, or perhaps a vidyādhara?"
"By whose curse has this sinner attained this womb of a crow? O Śuka, from where does such super-sensory knowledge as yours arise?
Is it the fruit of some great merit or of what ascetic penance?"
"O Mahāmati, who are you in this disguised form? Are you a perfected being (siddha) or a god? Tell me the reason for this.
Kuñjala said:
"O Siddha, I wish to know your lineage, your excellent clan, your knowledge, and the power of your asceticism, by which you wander the earth.
O Brahmin, I shall tell you everything; welcome to you, O observer of noble vows."
Having sat down upon a meritorious seat, cooled by the shade of a sheltering tree— Brahmā, whose origin is unmanifest, from whom Prajāpati was born;
and from him was born the twice-born Bhṛgu, a Brāhmaṇa endowed with virtues and equal to Brahmā himself.
He had a son named Bhārgava, who was a knower of the true meaning and essence of all dharmas; in his lineage you were born, O Brahmin, renowned on earth as Cyavana.
"I am not a god, nor a Gandharva, nor again a Vidyādhara."
Listen as I, who am about to speak extensively, relate this to you.
In the lineage of Kaśyapa, there was a certain most excellent brāhmaṇa, who knew the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary branches, and who illuminated all ritual acts. 10–11.
Renowned as a Vidyādhara and endowed with noble lineage, character, and virtues, that brahmin then shone with splendor through his conduct and asceticism. To that Vidyādhara, three sons were born.
There were three of us named Vasuśarman, Aśarma, and Dharmaśarman.
Among them, I was the youngest, Dharmaśarman, and devoid of virtues;
my brother Vasuśarman was an expert in the meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras. (13–14)
Furthermore, Nāmaśarman was well-endowed with proper conduct and excellent qualities such as learning; he was highly wise and likewise possessed of superior virtues.
O best of beings, listen: I alone was born as a great fool.
When shall I hear of the supreme power of the sciences, their auspicious purpose,
and the unsurpassed abode of my guru?
Then my father would have thought of me in this way.
"The name of this son, Dharmaśarman, has become meaningless; he was born upon the earth as one devoid of learning, though I am a mine of virtues.
Having reflected thus, the righteous-souled king, deeply distressed, spoke to me.

"Go and accomplish your studies at the house of the preceptor of Vraja's sons. Having heard those auspicious words of his father, I said: "O Father, I will not go to the house of the preceptor; it brings great suffering."
O best of beings, listen to what happens there by the power of karma: where there is constant beating, crying out with knitted brows and other gestures, and where food is not seen;
there, neither day nor night is there sleep, nor is there any means for happiness.
"Therefore, O daughter, go to the house of the guru; it is full of suffering. I am eager for play, and I shall perform my studies.
By your grace, O father, I shall eat, sleep, and engage in play. (22-23)
Day and night, along with his children, he remained unwearied;
yet, perceiving me to be deluded, that righteous soul, deeply distressed, spoke to me.
(24) The Vidyādhara said:
"O son, do not act rashly; make an effort for the sake of knowledge.
Through knowledge, happiness is attained, as well as incomparable fame and glory.
Knowledge leads to heaven and liberation; therefore, strive to master knowledge."
"Though it may be very painful at first, knowledge bestows happiness in the end.
Therefore, fulfill your duty as a son and go to the house of a teacher for learning.
Not following my father's words, I remained thus day after day. (26-27)
Wherever I stayed, I constantly caused the loss of wealth; people mocked me and reviled me as a brahmin. At that time, shame arose within me, which brought about the destruction of my livelihood.
"O Brahmin, striving for the sake of knowledge, I pray to my preceptor.
Thus he became lost in thought, overwhelmed by pain and grief: "How shall I acquire knowledge? How shall I attain these virtues? 29-30.
"How can heaven be born for me? How shall I attain liberation?"—thinking thus, O Brahmin, I again reached old age.
Once, while seated in a temple of the gods, I was filled with sorrow.
Impelled by my good fortune, a certain Siddha arrived;
he was without shelter, abstaining from food, ever blissful, free from desire, dwelling in solitude, disciplined in yoga, and having conquered his senses. 32-33.

Absorbed in the Supreme Brahman and possessed of knowledge, meditation, and samādhi— that wise one of great intelligence, whose form is wisdom— I have taken refuge in him with a pure disposition and with my neck bowed in devotion. 34.134-135a.
Having paid homage to that Great-Souled One, I stood before him;
for I had become wretched in appearance and likewise unfortunate. Then that Brahmin asked me: "Why do you grieve? (35-36)
"O best of Brahmins, I was then told by that wise yogi: 'By what intention does one indeed experience only suffering? To him, I, being utterly deluded, related his very past history. (37)
"How can one who has been instructed in all this thus attain omniscience?
For this purpose, you have always been my refuge, O Greatly Afflicted One.
He, the Great-Souled One, told me everything that is the cause of knowledge. 38–39.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second chapter in the *Cyavana-caritra*, within the *Guru-tīrtha-māhātmya* of the *Vena-upākhyāna* in the *Bhūmi-khaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter One Hundred and Twenty-Three. The Siddha said:
Listen, I shall describe the nature of knowledge before you: Knowledge has no body, nor does it have hands, feet, or eyes; it has neither nose nor ears, and it possesses no collection of bones.
By whom indeed has that knowledge been seen, and what are its signs?
It is eternal and devoid of form; it knows everything, and thus it is the All-Knowing.
By day the sun is the illuminator, and by night the moon shall illuminate.

A lamp illuminates a house, yet these [beings] situated in the midst of the world do not see that state; hear, O best of men, by what light it is seen. Indeed, those fools who are deluded by the *māyā* of Viṣṇu do not find it.
The knowledge situated within the center of the body is radiant through meditation and incomparable.
That state can be seen by that [knowledge], yet it is not seen by the moon, the sun, or other such lights;
it is devoid of hands and feet, and lacking eyes and ears.
O best of Brahmins, its movement is universal; it grasps everything, sees everything, smells everything, and likewise hears everything—of this there is no doubt.
There is no lamp equal to this knowledge for the destruction of all darkness.
It is seen in heaven, on earth, in the netherworld (pātāla), and in every place.
Those of evil intellect do not perceive the knowledge situated within the body;
I shall now describe the locus of knowledge from which knowledge arises.
O twice-born one, that which is eternally and always situated within the hearts of living beings—
desires and other such great enjoyments, as well as great delusions and the like—
he constantly seeks to burn them all with the fire of discernment.
Having become the source of all peace, one should crush the objects of the senses.
Then, knowledge arises that reveals the meaning of all principles; this knowledge, rooted in reality, is stainless and all-seeing. 11–12.

Therefore, practice that peace which increases all happiness; be impartial toward enemy, friend, and others just as you are toward yourself. Be ever self-restrained, having conquered your food and mastered your senses.
One should not practice even friendliness; one should utterly abandon enmity.
Having become free from attachment and free from desire, and having resorted to a solitary place, you will become a knower who illuminates all things and a seer of all.
"Staying in one place, O Vatsa, you shall know through my grace every event that will occur in the three worlds; of this there is no doubt. Kuñjala said:
By that Siddha, the nature of supreme wisdom was revealed;
remaining constantly within his words and cultivated through that very disposition, I abide in a single place even while existing throughout the three worlds. 17.
I understand all this through the grace of that true guru.
Thus, I have related to you my entire life story;
O best of the twice-born, tell me what else I shall speak for you.
Cyavana said:
"O best among the wise, how did you come to be born in the womb of a Kiri? Tell me the reason for this, which shall destroy all my doubts. (20)
Kuñjala said:
"Sin is born from association, and indeed merit is born from association;
therefore, one who is pure and worthy should avoid that which is contrary [to dharma]. (21)
A certain wicked hunter, having captured a young parrot and brought it along, was intent on selling it;
and he beheld it as it was charming, handsome, and eloquent in its speech.

"O best of the twice-born, it was taken by one Brāhmaṇa and handed over to me out of affection for me. Constantly established in knowledge and meditation, I myself held it in my hand out of curiosity, as if it were a child's plaything. (23-24)
O best of the twice-born, I was not deluded by his curious words, for my mind was constantly fixed on Śuka, who had taken the form of a son;
he too would speak to me thus: "Father, stay. (25)
"Go to bathe, O illustrious one; worship the deity now.
With such flattering words as these, he would address me;
and through the diversion of his speech, my supreme knowledge was forgotten.

"I went to the forest for the sake of flowers and for the enjoyment of fruits, yet I was led away by a cat to become the cause of my own sorrow. All my companions who associate with me are practitioners of virtue."
"The bird was killed by a cat; indeed, it was devoured by that very creature.
Hearing that the parrot, who had been so full of endearments, had met his death, the Brahmin was exceedingly distressed with a state of great sorrow and unhappiness. 29-30.

O best of the twice-born, though deluded by his suffering and severely tormented even by intense pain, bound by the great net of delusion, I cried out, "Rāmacandra! O King of Parrots! O Wise One! (31)
O King of Ślokas, his mind having become agitated by great delusion,
he was thereafter tormented by sorrow due to his own karma;
O best of Brahmins, listen now to [the account] of the separation from Śuka.

O Bhārgava, listen as he, tormented by grief, constantly lamented like a calf for its mother, remembering that parrot who used to speak so sweetly and who had revealed the forgotten knowledge of the Self even to him, though he was already a perfected one (siddha).
"O child, who else but you will now awaken me with sentences composed of prose and verse, joined with refined Sanskrit syllables,
and with most wonderful stories, while I am propitiating the King of Birds?"
"Having left this secluded garden, where have you gone?
Tainted by what fault am I? Tell me that now. Thus deluded by those compassionate words of his, [I remained there].

Lamenting in this manner and deeply tormented by grief, I died; yet even by that delusion, I was further bewildered by the thought of his state. Whatever my disposition was at the time of death, and whatever my mental state was then— (38–39)
O best of the twice-born, even by such a state of being, I was born; and that which brings about knowledge and memory was attained by me while in the womb.
My own previously performed actions were remembered as they were actually carried out.
"What indeed have I, a sinner, deluded and of unrefined soul, done?
(41) Now that I am again mounted upon the union within the womb, I contemplate that [Lord]; by that, stainless knowledge, which perceives all things, has truly arisen in me. (42)
By the grace of that Guru, I have indeed attained the supreme knowledge;
and by the pure waters of his words, the impurity of my body—
both external and internal— has been washed away and rendered stainless.
I attained the state of an animal, born into the species of a parrot.
When death was imminent for that parrot,
at that moment he died as a Brahmin, having been permeated by that very disposition.
I have been born again on this earth in the form of a boar;
for whatever state arises for living beings at the time of death, such indeed do those beings become, taking that very form and being devoted to it. 46.
O best of brahmins, his qualities, his very nature, and his states of being indeed become one with him;
O great-minded one, there is no doubt that even by this state of mind at the time of death, I have attained incomparable knowledge here. 47–48.
Therefore, O Greatly Wise One, I perceive with my knowledge all that has been, all that will be, and all that is present;
for even while remaining here, O High-Minded One, I know everything—of this there is no doubt. (49)
O twice-born one, for humans wandering in saṃsāra, there is no ford equal to the Guru that severs worldly bonds;
all this has been told to you, so listen, O son of Bhṛgu. 50–51.
O Brahmin, all that you have asked has been revealed to you:
just as every external impurity is destroyed by land-born or water-born [substances],
so too does the pilgrimage to the Guru destroy the sins committed in previous births.
"Indeed, for the sake of crossing over saṃsāra, he is the supreme moving tīrtha.
Viṣṇu said: "O Śuka of great wisdom, thus [he spoke] to the high-souled Cyavana."
Having thus revealed the truth, O best of kings, he ceased speaking.
"All this has been narrated to you regarding the supreme moving tirtha.
Choose a boon—may prosperity be yours—whatever dwells in your mind."
Veṇu said:
"O Janārdana, I do not desire the kingdom, nor do I crave anything else; I wish to enter your body with this very body."
"O Lord, I would consider this a boon if you wish to grant it here.
Viṣṇu said:
"O King, perform the Aśvamedha and the Rājasūya sacrifices. (57)
O high-minded one, perform the gift of cows, land, gold, water, and grain;
through such giving, even terrible sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are surely destroyed.
Furthermore, the fourfold aims of human life are accomplished through giving; of this there is no doubt.

Therefore, O King, a gift should be made with me as its object. Whatever state of being one possesses when giving while having me as the object, I truly bring about that very same state for him. 59-60.

"By the sight and touch of the sages, your accumulation of sins has been destroyed; you shall come to my body at the conclusion of the sacrifice, without a doubt. Having addressed Tvaṣṭṛ thus, Hari vanished from sight. 61-62.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Completion of the Greatness of the Guru-tīrtha and the Conclusion of the Life of Cyavana," within the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the section concerning the narrative of Vena.
Chapter One Hundred and Twenty-Four.
Sūta said: When Viṣṇu had vanished, the high-minded King Vena became consumed with anxiety, wondering, "Where has the Lord of the gods gone? 1.
Overcome with great joy and having reflected, that best of kings summoned Pṛthu, the most excellent of monarchs, and addressed that high-souled one with sweet words,
filled then with great delight.

"O son, by you I have been delivered from great sin in this world of mortals; O child Pṛthu, my lineage has now been brought to brilliance. That which was ruined by me through vices has been made radiant by you through your virtues."
"I shall perform the Aśvamedha sacrifice and give various gifts many times over;
today, by your grace, I shall go to the world of Viṣṇu. O illustrious one, O best of kings, prepare the necessary materials."
"O illustrious one, summon the Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas. Thus commanded by that high-souled one,
the high-souled Pṛthu replied with respect to his father.
"O Great King, enjoy the Kuru kingdom and pleasures that follow your heart's desire, whether divine or human; perform meritorious sacrifices to worship Janārdana.
Having spoken thus, he bowed down to his father, who was devoted to the knowledge of reality.
Taking up his bow along with an arrow with great care, the lord of the earth commanded all his soldiers:
"Proclaim throughout my realm that no sinful deed whatsoever must be committed by any of the three types of action."
Whatever sin they may commit by transgressing the command of King Vena, he shall indeed meet his death; of this there is no doubt. (11) One should give gifts and worship Janārdana with sacrifices.
"O all you men, perform sacrifices with focused minds and free from envy.
Having thus given this instruction and having entrusted the kingdom to his servants, O Brahmins, that son of Vena departed for the forest of asceticism in order to practice penance.
Having abandoned all faults and restrained the senses from their objects, he remained without food for a duration of one hundred years. Brahmā, being pleased by his austerity, spoke to Pṛthu.
"O ascetic, why do you practice penance? Tell me the reason for that.
Pṛthu said:
"O highly wise one, this Vena is my father, the increaser of my fame."
"May that lowest of men who commits evil while in this kingdom have his head severed by the god Janārdana;
and may Hari himself become his punisher with invisible great discuses. (16-17)
"O Lord of the Gods, listen to this which I consider a boon from you: may the heads of those who desire to commit sin through mind, action, or speech shatter like ripe fruit from a tree. (18)
O Grandfather, may I not be tainted by the defects of my subjects;
act accordingly, O Lord of Gods, if you wish to grant me a boon. Grant me this supreme desire, O Four-faced One; salutations be unto you! 19–20.
Brahmā said: "So be it, O illustrious one! Your father has attained purification; he was commanded by Viṣṇu, my child, and likewise by you, O Pṛthu."
Having thus granted such a vast boon, the All-pervading Lord departed; Pṛthu himself returned and remained established in the duties of kingship.
O best of Brahmins, in the kingdom of Vainya, no one at all practiced unrighteousness.
Whoever contemplates evil through any of the three types of action shall have his head severed as if cut by discus-weapons; from that time forward, no one at all shall commit sin. 23–24.
Thus, all the worlds constantly followed the conduct of that great-souled Vainya according to his commands;
devoted to all duties, they proceeded with acts of charity and enjoyment.
By the grace of that king, they prospered with all forms of happiness. 26.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fourth chapter in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the narrative of Veṇu.
Chapter One Hundred and Twenty-Five.
Sūta said: Having received the command of Vena, the most righteous Pṛthu,
the son of the king, prepared all the necessary materials for various meritorious rites.
Having invited all the brāhmaṇas, even those born in various lands,
that king performed the Aśvamedha sacrifice; moreover,
he bestowed gifts of many kinds and in great numbers upon the brāhmaṇas.
That lord of the earth, his body intact, went to the realm of Viṣṇu; that righteous soul now dwells eternally together with Viṣṇu. Thus has this entire life-story of that king been narrated to you.
The pacifier of all sins and the destroyer of all suffering, King Pṛthu himself, whose nature is righteousness,
rules over the earth today; that best of kings milked the earth today together with the three worlds.
The subjects were delighted by him through his meritorious deeds and righteous actions.
All this has been narrated to you; this is the unsurpassed Bhūmikhaṇḍa, while the first is the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa and the second is the Bhūmikhaṇḍa.
I shall again recount the majesty of the Bhūmikhaṇḍa;
that best of men who hears even a single verse of this section has the sins of one entire day utterly destroyed.
O best of the twice-born, listen as I declare the merit of that wise man who, joined with both male and female bodies, hears this chapter on a holy festival day,
equal to the merit of giving a thousand cows to Brahmins.
Whatever fruit may arise from that, Viṣṇu is pleased with him who constantly recites this Padma Purāṇa. Indeed, in the Kali age, no obstacles shall arise for such a man.
Vyāsa said:
O Lotus-born one, why do various most terrible obstacles arise for a meritorious man who listens [to this], even in the Kali age? 12.
Brahmā said:
"O dear one, that fruit which is proclaimed as belonging even to the horse-sacrifice (Aśvamedha) is seen,
O father, in the Purāṇa known as the Padma."
The meritorious horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha) does not take place in the Kali age.
Therefore, tell me that Purāṇa which is indeed equal to the Aśvamedha,
and which possesses the merit of the Aśvamedha that bestows the fruits of heaven and liberation.
O best of beings, sinful men established on wicked paths do not enjoy the merit of this ancient and meritorious work known as the *Padma Purāṇa*; in the Kali age,
men do not enjoy its merit, which is equal to that of a horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
In the Kali age, men shall go to the ocean of hell due to their sins.
Why then would they listen to that merit which accomplishes the four goals of human life—by means of hearing this meritorious Purāṇa known as the Padma? 17–18.
Indeed, everything that accomplishes the four aims of human life was accomplished by him;
therefore, O high-minded one, sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha have perished in the Kali age and have gone to heaven along with all the Vedas, including their auxiliary branches and accents.
Whosoever is endowed with goodness, possessed of faith, devoted to the Blessed One, and righteous in soul, desires to hear [this] together with his son and wife;
for him, a great faith arises prior to the hearing. 20–21.
O best of the twice-born, even for a man who listens, great obstacles shall not prevail; yet first, lack of faith arises in the listener, and greed also arises in that man who recites.
The god Viṣṇu dispatched the most terrible Great Delusion (Mahāmoha). While he was constantly listening, it brought about his destruction;
for corrupters, revilers, and sinners began to appear day after day. 23–24.
"O Vyāsa, it must be understood by one of keen intellect that an obstacle has now arisen for me;
seeing this, one should perform a fire-sacrifice (homa) with Vaiṣṇava mantras and the highly meritorious Viṣṇu-sūktas. || 25 ||

One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) in this manner with the mantra "Viṣṇorarāṭam," with the "Sahasraśīrṣaka" [Puruṣasūkta], repeatedly with the excellent mantra "Idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," with the "Ābrahmaṇa" [mantra], and with the "Tryambaka" mantra. 26–27.
With the Bṛhat-sāman, with auspicious mantras, and with twelve-syllable mantras,
one should perform the oblation for whichever deity using that deity's specific mantra (verse 28).
One should also offer oblations with sesame seeds and clarified butter, as well as with fuel-sticks of the Palāśa tree, numbering one hundred and eight.
O twice-born one, the installation and worship of the planets must also be performed (verse 29).
There, one should worship Vighneśa, Śāradā the queen of the gods,
Jātavedas, Mahāmāyā, Caṇḍikā, and the Lord of the Field (Kṣetranāyaka) (verse 30).

With sesame seeds, rice grains, and clarified butter, while the mantras are being recited, the fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed in this manner; one should give wealth to the Brāhmaṇas, O beloved, as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) accompanied by a cow, according to one's means. 31.

Then obstacles shall perish and one shall attain ancient perfection (siddhi). (32) Now, I shall declare the obstacle that befalls him who does not act in this manner: a disease arises in his body, which brings about great suffering. (33)
Grief for a wife, grief for a son, and loss of wealth arise;
one suffers from various kinds of great diseases—of this there is no doubt. He in whose house there is no wealth should observe a fast.
Having reached the Ekādaśī, one should worship Madhusūdana with the sixteen types of offerings and a mind endowed with devotion; thereafter,
one should feed the Brāhmaṇas according to one's means.

Having offered the oblation accompanied by the resolve (saṃkalpa) to Keśava, the wise man should then himself partake of a meal together with his kinsmen, sons, and wife; thus he shall attain perfection. 37.

Those devoted to dharma should listen to the complete Purāṇa-saṃhitās; for them, the accomplishment of the four aims of life arises, and not otherwise. Now hear of the one hundred and twenty-five thousand [verses] known as the Brahma, which is the Puṣkara. 38–39.

O twice-born one, in the Kṛta Yuga, men are free from sin; they hear half of a hundred thousand verses, and thereafter the entire Purāṇa known as Padma, consisting of two thousand verses plus more. 40.
Likewise, when the Tretā Yuga has arrived,
those humans who shall hear [this] will enjoy the fruits of the four aims of life and then go again to Hari.
There are twenty-two thousand verses in the collection known as the Padma.
In the Dvāpara age, the supreme Brahman himself proclaimed the collection known as Padma, consisting of twelve thousand verses; in the Kali age, men devoted to Viṣṇu shall recite it.

O best of Brahmins, that single purpose and single essence which has been set forth in all four [Vedas] exists within the *Saṃhitās* themselves; O most excellent one, the extensive narrative known as the *Śeṣa* will likewise meet its destruction along with the twelve thousand verses.
When the Kali age has arrived, this Bhūmikhaṇḍa will indeed appear first; by hearing it, a man is liberated from all sins.
He is released from all miseries and is freed from all diseases.
Abandoning everything else—recitation, charity, and likewise sacred learning—one should indeed listen with diligence to this work called Padma, which destroys sin.
Its first section is the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, and the second is the Bhūmikhaṇḍa. 47–48.
The third is the Svargakhaṇḍa, and the fourth is Pātāla;
the fifth is the Uttarakhaṇḍa, which destroys all sins. That man who listens with devotion to these five sections in their proper order—
A human being obtains the fruit of a thousand gifts of cows; O Brahmins, these five sections, which are attainable through great fortune,
grant liberation when heard— this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fifth chapter (125) in the Venopākhyāna of the Bhūmikhaṇḍa within the Śrī Padma Purāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
This second section, the Bhūmikhaṇḍa, is complete. 2.
Thus ends the second section, the Bhūmikhaṇḍa, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the third section, the Svargakhaṇḍa, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Om, salutations to the remover of obstacles; Om, salutations to the illustrious one.
First Chapter.

I bow to the lotus-feet of Govinda, which are honored by Indirā (Lakṣmī), supremely wealthy, seated in the hearts of the people of the world, the sole refuge for great men, and the highest of the high. 1.
Once,
all those sages who dwelt in the Himalayas— sages who had mastered the Vedas,
high-souled knowers of the three periods of time, and repositories of various merits— resembled blazing fires.
Those who dwell on Mount Mahendra, those who delight in the Vindhya mountains, those devoted to the Aruṇa forest, those residing in the Puṣkara forest,
those devoted to Śrīśaila, and those dwelling in Kurukṣetra; 3–4.
Those who delight in the forest of Dharma, those who dwell in the Daṇḍaka forest,
those who take pleasure in the path of the Jambū tree, and those who reside in Satya—
these and many other stainless sages, together with their disciples, [are present].
They arrived at Naimiṣa, eager to see Śaunaka.
Having honored him according to the prescribed rites, they too were well-honored by him and seated in due order upon various seats, such as grass mats (bṛsī) and the like.
Seated upon the seats provided by Śaunaka, those ascetics,
devoted to Kṛṣṇa, then spoke to one another of meritorious stories. At the conclusion of those stories of the sages of purified souls, [the following occurred].
Then the Sūta of great splendor and immense luster arrived there;
he was the disciple of Vyāsa, known by the name Romaharṣaṇa, and was a knower of the Purāṇas.
Having saluted them according to custom, he was likewise honored by them in return.

When Sūta Romaharṣaṇa, the disciple of Vyāsa, was seated comfortably according to custom, the great sages headed by Śaunaka— those highly fortunate ones whose wealth is their austerity— questioned him.
The sages said: O you of great vows, O son of Romaharṣaṇa, O one of great intelligence well-versed in the Purāṇas, we have heard from you these highly meritorious ancient stories of the Purāṇas.
Now we have become intent upon the story of Hari,
for devotion to Adhokṣaja is the supreme dharma for all men;
therefore, relate once more the Purāṇa, which is filled with accounts of Hari.
Conversations concerning anything other than Hari are remembered as being like a cremation ground;
it has been heard that Hari himself dwells there in the form of sacred fords (tīrtha). Therefore, indeed, proclaim the names of those sacred fords which bestow merit.
From what has this world arisen, and by whom is it sustained?
(16) Into what does this world of moving and non-moving beings dissolve? Which fields are meritorious, and which mountains are worthy of worship? (17)
"O highly fortunate one, tell me all of this in due order: the rivers, the peaks, and the other auspicious places that remove the sins of men.
Sūta said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate ones! Well asked, O you whose wealth is penance!

Having bowed to him, I shall proclaim the Purāṇa known as Padma—the son of Parāśara, the Supreme Person, the sole source of all that is to be known by the universe, the repository of knowledge, the bestower of vast intelligence, and he who is to be known through the Vedas and Vedānta. (19)
I perpetually bow to Vedavyāsa, whose fame is widespread, who is eternally peaceful, who is the object of his own intellect, who is vast with pure splendor, and whose glory is extensive.
(20) Salutations to that blessed Vyāsa of immeasurable luster, by whose grace I shall relate this narrative of Nārāyaṇa. (21)
I shall proclaim the highly meritorious Purāṇa known as the Padma,
consisting of one thousand and fifty-five [verses] and endowed with six sections (khaṇḍas).
Among them, first there is the Ādi-khaṇḍa, and after that, the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa.
After that is the Brahmakhaṇḍa, and then the Pātālakhaṇḍa;
after that is the renowned Kriyākhaṇḍa, and the final section is the Uttarakhaṇḍa.
This is indeed the great and wonderful Mahāpadma, of which the entire universe is composed. 24.
Therefore, because it takes as its subject matter that account, it is called the *Pādma* by the wise;
this is the stainless Purāṇa, the supreme majesty of Viṣṇu, which Hari, the God of gods, formerly narrated to Brahmā. (25)
Brahmā taught it to Nārada, and Nārada [taught it] before our guru. Vyāsa repeatedly taught all the Purāṇas, along with the Itihāsas and the Saṃhitās, to me, his most beloved disciple.
I shall now proclaim to you that ancient Purāṇa which is exceedingly difficult to obtain;
by hearing it, a person is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, and he who hears it indeed obtains the merit of bathing in all sacred fords.
Bestowing liberation by the mere hearing [of it] through supreme faith and devotion;
even one who hears it without faith obtains a store of merit.
Therefore, with every effort, make the Lotus the guest of your ears. 29-30.
In this regard, I shall describe the first section, which is meritorious and destructive of sins;
let all you sages, together with your disciples who are present here, listen.
31. Thus ends the first chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. 1.
The Second Chapter.
Sūta said:
O best of the twice-born, I shall now describe the primary creation.
By which the Blessed One, the Supreme Self, the eternal, is known:
O best of the twice-born, after the dissolution of the creation, nothing at all existed;
there was only one light called Brahman, the cause of all.
Eternal, stainless, peaceful, pure, and eternally immaculate; a clear ocean of bliss which those seeking liberation desire;
omniscient because its nature is knowledge, infinite, unborn, and undecaying.
It is indestructible, eternally pure, infallible, all-pervading, and great.

But when the time for creation arrived, having recognized that [universe] as being of the nature of knowledge and dissolved within itself, He began to bring about its manifestation through modification. 4–5.
From that, Pradhāna manifested; and from that, Mahat also came into being.
Mahat is threefold: Sāttvika, Rājasa, and Tāmasa.
Indeed, it is enveloped by Pradhāna, just as a seed is covered by its skin.
The Vaikārika, the Taijasa, and the Bhūtādi which is Tāmasa—
this threefold Ahaṃkāra was born from the principle of Mahat.
Just as the Mahat is enveloped by Pradhāna, so too is it enveloped by the Great Principle (Mahat).
Then Bhūtādi, undergoing transformation, created the subtle element of sound (śabda-tanmātra);
from that subtle element of sound, he created space (ākāśa), which is characterized by sound.
Thus, Bhūtādi completely enveloped space, which consists of sound alone.
Likewise, he created space as mere sound and wind as mere touch.
The powerful wind came into being, and touch is considered its quality.
Space, consisting of mere sound, then enveloped mere touch.
Then Vāyu, undergoing transformation, emitted the subtle element of form (rūpa-mātra); light is produced from Vāyu, and that is said to have form as its quality.
Vāyu, which consists of the subtle element of touch (sparśa-mātra), indeed enveloped the subtle element of form.
And light, undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of taste (rasamātra). From that, the waters (ambhas) came into being;
those waters consist of the subtle element of taste. And the waters enveloped the subtle element of form (rūpamātra).
The waters, undergoing transformation, produced mere fragrance;
from that was born this earth, which possesses the qualities of all the elements. Since it is a combination [of elements], fragrance is considered its specific quality.
Because it consists of that alone in each respective case, it is known as "tanmātra" (the state of being that alone).
These tanmātras are the non-specific (aviśeṣa); the subsequent ones are the specific (viśeṣa). This creation of the elements and the tanmātras proceeds from the tāmasa ego (ahaṃkāra). 16–17.
Thus, O best of sages, those whose wealth is austerity have briefly described them;
they say that the ten organs of sensation are the deities born of *vaikārika* [sattva],
and the eleventh, the mind, is also proclaimed here by the contemplators of reality.
The five organs of perception and the five organs of action are here;
I shall describe them and their functions, O purifiers of your lineage.
Hearing, touch, sight, taste, and the nose as the fifth—these are the organs of perception. (19–20)
For the sake of accomplishing the cognition of sound and the other [objects], the five organs endowed with intellect are indeed proclaimed:
the anus, the generative organ, the hands, the feet, and speech as the fifth.
Their functions are remembered as excretion, pleasure, grasping, movement, and speaking.

O Brahmins, space, wind, fire, water, and earth are joined with their respective qualities, beginning with sound; being of diverse potencies and existing separately, they are thus unable to act without a combination. (22–23)
They were unable to create living beings without coming together in their entirety; then, having come together and entered into mutual union with one another,
they formed a single mass, possessing common characteristics, having attained complete unity.

And because they are presided over by the Puruṣa and through the favor of Pradhāna, the principles beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas produce the Egg; that [Egg], having grown in sequence like a bubble on water, remains eternal. 25–26.
O highly wise one, from the elements arose that egg, ancient and resting upon the water;
it is the primordial, unsurpassed abode of Viṣṇu in his form as Brahman. Therein dwells that Lord Viṣṇu, the Sovereign of the Universe, whose true nature is unmanifest.
Assuming the form of Brahmā, he himself became established [therein].
From that Great Self, the egg was born from his sweat, the mountains were the chorion, and the oceans became the amniotic fluid. 28–29.
Within that egg, everything came into being— including the mountains, islands, and oceans, as well as the collection of worlds with their luminaries— along with the gods, asuras, and humans;
it had arisen from the navel of Viṣṇu himself, who is indeed without beginning or end.
That lotus became the golden egg by the will of Śrīkeśava.
The Lord himself, assuming the form of Brahmā and possessing the quality of rajas, being devoted to Hari, proceeds to create the world. 31-32.
He emits [the world] and casts it down in every age until the end of the kalpa-cycle; then, in the form of Narasimha and other manifestations, as well as in the form of Rudra, he shall withdraw it.
Desiring to protect the entire universe, that Great-Souled One emits it again in the form of Brahma.
Assuming the form of Rāma and others, he went forth as Rudra to devour this universe.
34. Thus ends the second chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Three.
The sages said:
"Tell us in their entirety the names of the rivers and mountains,
as well as those of the provinces and whatever others are situated upon the earth."
"O best of men, please describe in its entirety the extent of the earth known by those who understand the means of valid knowledge, as well as all the forests on every side.
Sūta said:
O one of great wisdom, the wise declare that these five great elements, through their combination, comprise everything existing in the world;
they are earth, water, wind, fire, and space.
All these [elements] possess increasing qualities; among them, earth is primarily the ground [of these qualities].
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—these are declared by the seers who know reality to be the qualities of earth. 4–5.
O Brahmins, water has four qualities; smell is not found there.
Sound, touch, and form—these are the three qualities of fire.
Sound and touch belong to air, while in space there is only sound.
O Brahmins, these five qualities exist within the five great elements in all worlds, upon which all beings are established;
they do not exceed one another, and at that time, there is indeed a state of equilibrium.
When they enter into mutual disharmony with one another, then embodied beings emerge from their bodies, and not otherwise. They perish in succession and are born again in succession.
All these [elements] are immeasurable, and their form is divine.
Wherever they are seen, the beings composed of the five elements run toward them; regarding those, humans declare various means of knowledge through logical reasoning.
Indeed, those entities which are inconceivable should not be established through logic;
O best of sages, I shall now describe the island of Sudarśana.
O illustrious ones, that island is circular and shaped like a wheel.
It was bounded by river waters and by mountains resembling oceans;
it was likewise filled with cities of various forms, delightful provinces,
and trees endowed with flowers and fruit, and it was abundant in wealth and grain.
Surrounded on all sides by the salt ocean,
the continent of Sudarśana appears like a circular disc, just as a man might see his own face in a mirror. 15.
Twice that portion is the Pippala tree, and twice that again is the great Śaśa;
having gathered all medicinal herbs and being surrounded on all sides, the waters beyond those are not to be known [individually], and thus the remainder is stated in brief. 16–17.
The sages said: O Sūta, you have duly explained the summary of that [Purāṇa] to us; since you are a knower of the truth of everything, O wise one, tell us its detailed account. 18.
"Tell us the measurement of this extent of ground that is visible upon the moon, marked with the hare; after that, you shall speak of the pippala fruit.
Thus questioned by them, the charioteer then spoke these words.
Sūta said:
O highly wise ones, these six jewel-mountains extend from east to west;
they are indeed immersed on both sides in the eastern and western oceans.
Himavān, Himakūṭa, and Niṣadha, the best of mountains;
Nīla, which consists of lapis lazuli, and Śveta, which resembles the moon; and the mountain named Śṛṅgavān, covered with all kinds of minerals. 21-22.
O Brahmins, these very mountains are frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas;
the distance between them, measured across their breadth, is many thousands of yojanas.
Therein, O best of men, are the meritorious regions and those varṣas.
All these various kinds of beings dwell everywhere within them.
This is the land of Bhārata; beyond it lies Haimavata, and beyond Hemakūṭa, they declare the region to be Harivarṣa.
To the south of Nīla and to the north of Niṣadha, extending toward the east, is the highly fortunate mountain named Mālyavat. Beyond that Mālyavat mountain is the mountain Gandhamādana.
In the center of those two is Mount Meru, a mountain of gold, with a circular form;
it has the brilliance of the young sun and is like a smokeless fire, rising eighty-four thousand yojanas in height. 27–28.
O best of the twice-born, it stands eighty-four yojanas below, encompassing the worlds above, below, and across. On its sides, O brahmins, these four continents are situated.
Bhadra, Śvaḥketumāla, and Jambūdvīpa are the most excellent;
likewise, the Northern Kurus are the refuge for those who have performed meritorious deeds.
It is said that Vihangasumukha was the son of Supārśva.
Seeing those golden crows, he reflected:
"Since this [gold] makes no distinction between the superior, the middling, and the inferior birds, therefore I shall abandon it."
The Sun, the best among luminaries, constantly revolves around it;
as do the Moon together with the constellations, and the Wind, O highly wise ones, along with the mountain adorned with celestial flowers, all moving in a clockwise direction.
O Brahmins, on that mountain, which is entirely covered with beautiful palaces made of gold,
hosts of gods, Gandharvas, Asuras, and Rākṣasas,
accompanied by throngs of Apsarases, always sport.
There, Brahmā, Rudra, Śakra, and the lord of the Asuras,
having assembled, perform various sacrifices accompanied by manifold sacrificial fees;
as do Tumburu, Nārada, Viśvāvasu, Hāhā, and Hūhū.
Having approached the best of the immortals, the high-souled seven ṛṣis and Kaśyapa, the lord of creatures, praise him with various hymns;
they go there on every auspicious festival day— may prosperity be yours.
Thus, on his summit, Uśanas Kāvya is honored by the Daityas.
His golden treasures and his various jewel-mountains belong to him;
from those, the blessed Kubera receives a fourth part.
Then, having taken a portion of that consciousness, he bestows it upon men.
Within the mountain is a divine and delightful forest of Karṇikāra trees, filled with flowers of all seasons and rising high with clusters of rocks.
There, Paśupati himself, the Lord who brings all beings into existence, accompanied by Umā, sports surrounded by divine beings;
he wears a garland made of Karṇikāra flowers that hangs down as far as his feet. 42–43.
Illumined by his three eyes as if by three risen suns,
Maheśvara is beheld by the perfected ones (siddhas) who are fierce in austerity, firm in their vows, and speakers of truth; he cannot be seen by those of evil conduct.

O best of the twice-born, from the peak of that mountain, the auspicious Gaṅgā Bhāgīrathī— possessing a universal form, immeasurable, with a terrifying roar, and frequented by those who are both meritorious and most sinful— flowed forth as a stream of milk. 45–46.
And Plavaṃtī, with great force, entered the auspicious lake of Candramas;
by her, that meritorious lake was produced, resembling the ocean. At that time, he held her, who was difficult to be supported even by mountains.
O best of the twice-born, for a hundred thousand years the wielder of the Pināka bow bore [the earth] with his head alone. O twice-born ones, on the western side of Meru,
in that very region of Jambūdvīpa, lies the great Janapada known as Ketumāla.

The lifespan of the virtuous people there is ten thousand years; the men are golden-colored, and the women are equal to the Apsarases. They are free from disease and sorrow, with minds perpetually joyful.
There, human beings are born with the luster of refined gold.
On the peaks of Gandhamādana, Kubera, the lord of the Guhyakas, rejoices together with the Rākṣasas and surrounded by hosts of Apsarases. 51-52.
On the side of Gandhamādana, however, there are others who are free from sin;
their maximum lifespan is eleven thousand years.
There, the Kṛṣṇas, Naras, and Brahmins are endowed with splendor and possess great strength.

And all the women there have the luster of lotus petals and are exceedingly beautiful to behold. O Brahmins, the white region called Hiraṇyaka is superior to Nīlotpala; it is the excellent region of Airāvata, filled with various provinces.
O highly fortunate one, between the two Varṣas, Dhanuṣkhaṇḍa and Ketumāla, lies Ilāvṛta in the center; these indeed constitute the five Varṣas.
Each subsequent Varṣa among these is superior to the preceding one in its qualities.

The lifespan, health, and righteousness of all those beings were endowed with both spiritual merit and worldly desire. Thus, O most excellent ones, this highly fortunate earth was covered with mountains. 57–58.
The very great Hemakūṭa is the mountain named Kailāsa;
there the god Vaiśravaṇa rejoices together with the Guhyakas.
To the north of Kailāsa, toward the Maināka mountain, there is [another].
There is a very great, divine mountain with golden peaks, composed of jewels. Beside it is a vast, divine, and bright lake called Viṣṇusaras, with sands of gold, where King Bhagīratha dwelt.
Having seen the Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā, he dwelt there for many years;
there the sacrificial posts were made of jewels and the altars were made of gold.
Having performed sacrifices there, the highly illustrious Sahasrākṣa attained perfection.
Where the eternal Lord of beings, the Creator, of fierce splendor, is worshipped by all the worlds on every side;
where Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, Manu, and Sthāṇu as the fifth [are present].
There, the divine triple-pathed river (Ganges), having first descended from the world of Brahmā, becomes established in seven streams:
the Vaṭodakā, the Asā, the Nalinī, the Pārvatī, and the Sarasvatī.

The Jambūnadī, the Cakṣu, the Sītā, the Gaṅgā, the Sindhu, and the seventh; that [river] is endowed with inconceivable, divine names and powers, where a sacrificial session (*satra*) is performed at the transition of a thousand yugas. (66–67)
In various places there, Sarasvatī becomes visible and invisible;
these are the seven divine Gaṅgās, renowned throughout the three worlds.
On Himavat dwell the Rākṣasas, and on Hemakūṭa the Guhyakas.
The serpents and nāgas dwell in Niṣadha, and Gokarṇa is a forest of asceticism.
Śveta is said to belong to all the gods and asuras;
the gandharvas reside eternally in Niṣadha, and likewise the brahmarṣis in Nīla.
Śṛṅgavān, O highly fortunate ones, is the place of the retreat of the gods;
these, O highly fortunate ones, are the seven regions respectively, where beings—both mobile and immobile—are established. 71.
Their supernatural power is seen to be manifold, both divine and human; it is impossible to enumerate it all, yet it is adorned with qualities worthy of faith.
O Brahmins, ask me about that celestial one who possesses the form of a hare.
O Brahmins, it is said that in the two years of the Lord of the Quarters (Śiva), there were the islands of Karṇa to the south and north;
furthermore, Nāgadvīpa and Kāśyapadvīpa,
Karṇadvīpa, Śila, and the glorious Malaya mountain.
This second island is seen situated like the moon.
Thus ends the third chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Four.
The sages said: O Sūta, tell us now in its entirety about the regions to the north, west, and east of Meru,
as well as the mountain Mālyavān, which is greatly renowned.
Sūta said:
To the south of Nīla and likewise on the northern side of Meru, O brahmins, lie the meritorious Uttarakurus, frequented by the Siddhas. 2.

There, O best of the twice-born, the trees were always laden with flowers and fruits; their flowers were fragrant and their fruits were flavorful. Some of those trees there bore fruit that granted all desires as their sustenance.
O best of the twice-born, there are milk-yielding trees there that constantly exude milk resembling nectar; moreover,
garments and ornaments are produced from their fruits.
The entire ground is composed of jewels and consists of fine golden sand;
it possesses the pleasant touch of all seasons, O you whose wealth is penance, and is free from fruitless toil.
All those who fall from the world of the gods are born there as human beings.
Endowed with pure lineage and all very pleasing to behold, they are born as pairs; the women are like celestial nymphs (apsarases). They drink the milk of those milky trees, which is like nectar.
In due time, a pair is born and grows equally on all sides; it is endowed with identical form and qualities, and likewise possesses a symmetrical appearance,
O twice-born ones— a single, matching pair resembling a cakravāka bird.
The three worlds were free from disease, and their minds were eternally joyful. Those fortunate ones lived for ten thousand and one thousand years, and they never killed one another.
There are birds called Bhāruṇḍas, with sharp beaks and great strength; they carry off those who have died here and cast them into caves.
O Brahmins, the Uttarakurus have thus been described to you in brief.
I shall now describe Merupārśva exactly as it is.
O you whose wealth is asceticism, its summit is consecrated by the Bhadrāśva;
there lies the Bhadraśāla forest and the great trees known as Kālāmras. 13–14.

There are highly fortunate *kālāmra* trees that are always auspicious with flowers and fruit; these trees are one *yojana* in height and are frequented by *siddhas* and *cāraṇas*. There, those men are white-complexioned, endowed with splendor, and possessed of great strength.
The women were the color of white water-lilies, beautiful and pleasing to behold;
they were moon-colored, possessed of the four complexions, with faces resembling the full moon,
their limbs as cool as the moon, and they were experts in dance and song.
O best of the twice-born, the lifespan there is ten thousand years;
having drunk the juice of the black mango, they remain eternally youthful.
To the south of Nīla and to the north of Niṣadha—
There is an eternal great jambū tree named Sudarśana,
which yields the fruits of all desires, is meritorious, and is frequented by siddhas and cāraṇas;
after its name, this eternal continent is called Jambūdvīpa.
O best of the twice-born, on the eastern peak of Mālyavat, extending for one thousand and one hundred yojanas, lie those regions that follow the east;
O twice-born ones, Mālyavat itself measures fifty thousand yojanas.
The humans born there resemble great silver;
they have all descended from the world of Brahmā, and all are exponents of the Veda.
They perform divine austerities and remain perpetual celibates.
For the sake of protecting all beings, sixty thousand and sixty hundred of them enter the sun;
they proceed in front of Aruṇa, surrounding the sun.
For sixty thousand and sixty hundred years, scorched by the heat of the sun, they enter the lunar orb. Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. 4.25–26.
The Fifth Chapter.
The Sages said:
O most excellent one, [tell us] the names of the regions and the mountains as well.
"Tell us truly who those are that dwell upon the mountain.
Sūta said:
"To the south of Śveta and to the north of Niṣadha..."
There, human beings are born in a place named Varṣaramaṇaka;
they are all endowed with pure lineage, handsome in appearance,
and free from rivals.
Those highly fortunate ones, with minds ever joyful, live for twenty-five thousand years.
To the south of Nīla and to the north of Niṣadha—
There is a region named Hiraṇmaya where the river Hairaṇvatī flows;
there, O wise ones, dwells this king of birds, the best of winged creatures,
along with excellent Brahmins who follow the sacrifices, skilled archers of pleasing appearance.
The people there are of great strength, with minds delighted by the Brahmins;
those whose wealth is penance live for eleven thousand years,
reaching a lifespan of fifteen hundred years.
O best of the twice-born, there are indeed three pure peaks:
one there is made of jewels, another is wonderful gold,
and the third consists of all kinds of gems and is adorned with palaces.
There, O best of the twice-born, the goddess Svayaṃprabhā, who is ever-shining, dwells; and to the north of Mount Śṛṅgavat, at the edge of the ocean,
lies the region named Airāvata, which is beyond that mountain.
There, the movement of the sun does not exist, nor do human beings age. The moon, together with the constellations, is enveloped in light itself.
[The inhabitants] possess the radiance of lotuses, the color of lotuses, and eyes resembling lotus petals.
The humans born there possess the fragrance of lotus petals;
they are free from unfulfilled desires, devoid of foul odors, abstinent from food, and have their senses conquered.
O twice-born ones, all of them, being free from passion, fall from the world of the gods to be born there.
O best of the twice-born, at the end of thirteen thousand years,
those men who are preeminent among the righteous live for that span of life;
likewise, the Lord [resides] to the north of the ocean of milk.

Lord Hari, Vaikuṇṭha, remains upon a golden chariot that has eight wheels, is yoked with living beings, possesses the speed of thought, is fire-colored, endowed with great splendor, and adorned with gold. 16.
It is of the color of fire, possessed of great majesty, and decorated with jāmbūnada gold.
O best of the twice-born, he is the lord and the all-pervading master of all beings;
he is both the creator and the instigator of them in their contraction and expansion—namely earth, water, space, air, and fire, O most excellent ones. 17–18.
He is the sacrifice of all beings, and the consumer of oblations is his mouth. 19.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Svarga-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Six.
The sages said:
"Explain to us all that which is this Bhārata-varṣa, which is meritorious and the bestower of merit; for you are considered by us to be wise."
Sūta said:
In this regard, I shall proclaim to you the most excellent Bhārata-varṣa,
belonging to Priyavrata, the god, and to Manu Vaivasvata.
[The glory] of Pṛthu Vainya, the wise, and likewise of the high-souled Ikṣvāku;
of Yayāti, Ambarīṣa, Māndhātṛ, and Nahuṣa; and likewise of Mucukunda, Kubera, and Uśīnara.
Of Ṛṣabha, of the Tathāgata, and likewise of King Nṛga;
of the royal sage Kuśika, and of the high-souled Gādhi;
and of the royal sage Soma, and likewise of Dilīpa.
O highly fortunate ones, this excellent Bhārata is dear to all other powerful Kṣatriyas and indeed to all living beings. Thereafter,
O twice-born ones, I shall describe the region as it was heard by me.
Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimat, Ṛkṣavat,
Vindhya, and Pāriyātra— these seven are the principal mountain ranges (kulaparvatas).
O Brahmins, thousands of other mountains surround them.
O twice-born ones, there are others who are unknown, full of essence, vast, and possessed of variegated peaks; yet there are others who are well-known, short, and subsist upon what is short—
these men, O brahmins, are a mixture of noble and barbarian natures.
They drink from the river Gaṅgā of pure form, the Sindhu, and the Sarasvatī; 10.
the Godāvarī, the Narmadā, and the great river Bahūdā;
the Śatadru, the Candrabhāgā, and the great river Yamunā. 11.
[He visited] the Dṛṣadvatī, the Vitastā, the Vipāśā with its clear sands, the river Vetravatī, and the river Kṛṣṇaveṇī; as well as the Irāvatī, the Vitastā, the Payoṣṇī, and the Devikā.
The Vedasmṛti, the Vedaśirā, the Tridivā, the Sindhu, the Lākṛmi;
the Karīṣiṇī, the Citravahā, and the river Trisenā;
the Gomatī, the Dhūtapāpā, and the great river Candanā. 13–14.
O best of the twice-born, [he visited] Kauśikī, Tridivā, Hṛdyā, Nācitā, Rohitā, Araṇī, Rahasyā, Śatakuṃbhā, Sarayū,
Carmanvatī, Vetravatī, Hastisomā, and Diśā.
The Śarāvatī, the Payoṣṇī, the Bhīmā, and the Bhīmarathī; the Kāverī, the Culukā, the Tāpī, and the Śatamālā;
as well as the Nīvārā, the Mahitā, and the river Suprayogā. 16–17.
Pavitrā, Kṛṣṇalā, Sindhu, Vājinī, Puramālinī,
Pūrvābhirāmā, Vīrā, Bhīmā, Mālāvatī,
Palāśinī, Pāpaharā, Mahendrā, and Paṭalāvatī.
O best of men, [he saw] the Karīṣiṇī, the Asiknī, the Kuśacīrī, and the Mahānadī;
also Menā, the foremost of rivers, the Hemā, the Ghṛtavatī, the Anāvatī, the Anuṣṇā, the Sevyā, and the Kāpī. 19–20.
[He saw] the Sadāvīrā, the Adhṛṣyā, the Kuśacīrā, the Mahānadī,
the Rathacitrā, the Jyotirathā, the Viśvāmitrā, and the Kapiñjalā; also the Candrā, the Vahaphalā, and the Ambuvāhinī with its beautiful groves.
The Vainadī, Piṅgalā, Veṇā, and the great river Tuṅgavegā; the Vidiśā, Kṛṣṇaveṇā, Tāmrā, and Kapilā;
as well as the Dhenu, Sakāmā, Vedasvā, Haviḥsrāvā, and Mahāpathā.
The Śiprā, the Picchalā, the river Bhāradvājī, the river Kaurṇikī, the Śoṇā, the Bāhudā, and the Candrabhāgā;
the Durgā, the Antaḥśilā, the Brahmamedhyā, and the Dṛṣadvatī.
[He crossed] the Parokṣā, the Atharohī, and likewise the Jambūnadī;
also the Sunāsā, the Tamasā, the Dāsī, the Sāmānyā, the Varaṇā, the Asi, the Nīlā, the Dhṛtikarī, and the great river Parṇāśā. 25–26.
O bulls among the twice-born, there are the Mānavī, Vṛṣabhā, Bhāsā, Brahmamedhyā, and Dṛṣadvatī; these and many other great rivers,
which are eternally free from affliction, dark-hued, slow-moving, and gentle-flowing.
And [they saw] Brāhmaṇī, Mahāgaurī, and Durgā, O best of men; likewise Citrotpalā, Citrarathā, the incomparable Rohiṇī,
Mandākinī, Vaitaraṇī, Kokā, and the great river.
The Śuktimatī, the Anaṅgā, and likewise the one called Vṛṣa; the Lohityā, the Karatoyā, and likewise the Vṛṣakātvayā; the Kumārī, the Ṛṣitulyā, the Māriṣā, and the Sarasvatī.
The most excellent ones [honored] the highly meritorious Mandākinī and the entire Gaṅgā;
likewise, all the mothers of the universe, who yield great fruits,
as well as rivers of great renown by the hundreds and thousands.
Thus, O Brahmins, these rivers have been fully described according to tradition; hereafter, learn from me as I speak of the provinces (janapadas).
Among them are the Kurus, the Pañcālas, the Śālvas, the Mātreyas, and the Jāṅgalas.
The Śūrasenas, Pulindas, and likewise the Baudhas and Mālas; the Matsyas, Kuśaṭṭas, Saugandhyas, Kutsapas, Kāśis, and Kośalas;
the Cedis, Matsyas, Karuṣas, Bhojas, Sindhus, and Pulindakas.
The Uttamas, Daśārṇas, Mekalas together with the Utkalas,
the Pañcālas, Kośalas, and the Nāikapṛṣṭhas and Yugandharas; the Bodhas, Madras, Kaliṅgas, Kāśayas, and Parakāśayas.
The Jaṭharas, Kukuras, Sudāśārṇas, and Susattamas; the Kuntis, Avantis, and likewise the Aparakuntis;
the Gomantas, Mallakas, Puṇḍras, Vidarbhas, and the Nṛpavāhikas. (37–38)
The Aśmakas, the Sottaras, the Goparāṣṭras, the Kanīyasas, the Adhirājyas, the Kuśaṭṭas, the Mallarāṣṭras, the Keralas,
the Mālavas, the Upavāsas, the Cakrāvakrālayas, and the Śakas. (39)
The Videhas, Magadhas, Sadas, Amalajas, and Vijayas; likewise the Angas, Vangas, Kalingas, and Yakṛllomas;
as well as the Mallas, Sudeṣṇas, Prahlādas, Mahiṣas, and Śaśakas. 40–41.
The Bāhlikas, Vāṭadhānas, Ābhīras, Kālatoyakas,
Aparāntas, Parāntas, Paṅkalas, Carmacaṇḍikas,
Aṭavīśekharas, and the excellent Merubhūtas. 42.
The Upāvṛtas, Anupāvṛtas, Surāṣṭras, and likewise the Kekayas;
the Kuṭṭas, Aparāntas, Māheyas, Kakṣas, Sāmudras, Niṣkuṭas, and many Andhas, O Brahmins, as well as those from Antargiri; 43–44.
The Bahirgiryas, Oṅgas, Maladas, Magadhas, Mālavas, and Arghaṭas;
the Sattvataras, Prāvṛṣeyas, and Bhārgavas, who are the best among the twice-born;
the Puṇḍras, Bhārgas, Kirātas, Sudeṣṇas, and Bhāsuras.
The Śakas, Niṣādas, Niṣadhas, as well as the Ānartas and Nairṛtas; the Pūrṇalas, Pūtimatsyas, Kuṇṭalas, and Kuśakas;
the Tarigrahas, Śūrasenas, Ājiikas, and Kalpakāraṇas. 46–47.

The Tilabhāgas, the Asāras, the Madhumattas, the Kakundakas, the Kāśmīras, the Sindhusauvīras, the Gāndhāras, and likewise the Darśakas; the Abhīsāras, the Kudrutas, the Saurilas, and the Bāhlikas. 48.
The Darvīcamālavādās, the Darvāvātajāmarathoragas (49), the Balaraṭṭas, as well as the Vipras, Sudāmānas, Mumallikas,
Bandhākarīkas, Kaṣās, Kulidās, and Gandhikas (50).
The Vanāyus, Uddeśas, Pārśvaromas, Kuśabindus, Kācchas, Gopālakacchas, Jāṅgalas, Kuruvārṇakas,
Kirātas, Barbaras, Siddhas, Vaidehas, and Tāmraliptikas. 51.
The Auḍras, Mlecchas, Sairindhras, and the excellent mountaineers; then other regions of the south, O bull among sages: the Dravidas, Keralas, the Prācyas, the Ūṣikas, and the Bālamūṣikas.
The Karṇāṭakas, Āmāhiṣakas, Avikaṃdhas, Mūṣikas,
Jhallikas, Kuṃtalas, Sauhṛdas, Analakānanas,
Kaukkuṭakas, Bolas, Kokaṇas, and Maṇivālakas. (54)
Samaṅga, Kanaka, Kuṅkura, Aṅgāra, Māriṣa;
Dhvajinī, Utsava-saṃketa, Trivarga, Mālya, Senaya; Vyūḍhaka, Koraka, Proṣṭha, and Saṅgavegadharas. (55–56)
Likewise, the Vindyarulikas along with the Pulindas and Balvalas,
the Malavas, the Amlaras, and likewise the Aparavartakas; the Kulidas, the Kaladas, the Candakas, and the Kuratas.
The Muśalāstana-vālās, the Satīrthas, the Pūtisṛñjayas,
the Anidāyas, the Śivāṭas, the Tapanas, the Sūtapās, as well as the Ṛṣikas, the Vidarbhas, the Taṅgaṇas, and the Parataṅgakas. (58–59)
And other Mleccha peoples to the north, O bull among sages,
such as the Javanas, the Kāmbojas, and fierce tribes of Mlecchas; as well as the Sakṛdgrahas, the Kulaṭyas, and the Hūṇas together with the Pārasiakas.
Likewise, there were other delightful regions such as Daśamālikā;
and the settlements of Kṣatriyas, as well as the families of Vaiśyas and Śūdras;
and the Śūras, Ābhīras, Daradas, and Kāśmīras, together with their cattle.
The Khāṇḍīkas, the Catuṣārās, the Padmagas, the Girigahvaras, the Ādreyas, the Sabhirādajas, as well as the Stanapoṣakas, the Droṣakas, the Kaliṅgas, and the various tribes of Kirātas. 63.
The Tomaras, the Ahanyas, and likewise the Karabhajakas—
these and other provinces, both eastern and northern,
have been described by me in brief, O twice-born ones.
And according to the strength of one's virtues, there is likewise the great fruit of the three aims of life (trivarga).
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Seven.
The sages said: O Sūta, tell us the measurement of the lifespan, as well as the strength and the auspicious or inauspicious qualities, of this Bhārata-varṣa and likewise of Haimavata-varṣa.
"O best of men, tell us in detail about the future, the past, and the present, as well as Harivarṣa. Sūta said:
O best of sages, O most excellent of the twice-born, there are four yugas in Bhāratavarṣa: Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Tiṣya (Kali).
First was the age named Kṛta, and then, O twice-born ones, came the Tretā Yuga.
After that, the Dvāpara age follows, and then the Tiṣya (Kali) age proceeds.
O best of sages, O you whose wealth is penance, the lifespan in the Kṛta Yuga is reckoned by the sages to be four thousand years.
Likewise, they know that in the Tretā age the lifespan is three thousand years;
in the Dvāpara age, it stands at two thousand years at present.
O bulls among sages, the duration of his stay shall indeed remain at that same measure.
Some die here while still in the womb, and likewise some die as soon as they are born;
yet others, possessed of great strength, great being, and endowed with the qualities of wisdom,
are born and continue to be born by the hundreds and thousands.
In the Kṛta Yuga, O twice-born ones, the Brahmins were powerful, pleasing to behold,
and gave birth to sons who were sages whose wealth was their asceticism;
they were full of great energy, high-souled, righteous, and speakers of truth.

Handsome, possessing beautiful bodies, of great heroism, and wielders of the bow—such Kṣatriyas, esteemed as heroes, are born for battle in the Tretā age; indeed, at that time, all Kṣatriyas are universal emperors (cakravartins). 10–11.
And in the Dvāpara age, all the social orders (varṇas) are born always possessing great energy and prowess, yet desiring to slay one another; indeed,
those men are joined with a blindness of splendor and are prone to anger.
O twice-born ones, in the Tiṣya age, beings are born greedy and indeed untruthful; O best of men,
envy, pride, anger, deceit, malice,
passion, and greed arise among living beings in the Tiṣya age.
O Brahmins, in the middle of the Dvāpara Yuga,
the region of Haimavata exists as superior in quality, and beyond that is Harivarṣa.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
The Eighth Chapter.
The Sages said:
O most virtuous one, you have duly described here the region of Jambūkhanda.
Tell us truly the measurement of Viṣkambha; O you who perceive without flaw, tell us correctly the extent of the ocean,
and speak to us of Śākadvīpa and the righteous Kuśadvīpa.
[He described] Śālmala truly, and likewise Krauñcadvīpa.
Sūta said:
O Brahmins, there are very many islands by which this world is pervaded.
I shall describe the seven islands; listen, O best of the twice-born! O foremost of the twice-born, the diameter of Mount Jambū is eighteen thousand and six hundred full yojanas.
The diameter of the salt ocean is recorded as being double [that of Jambūdvīpa];
it is filled with various inhabited regions and adorned with jewels and coral,
and it is beautified by mountains variegated with many kinds of minerals.
The circular ocean is crowded with Siddhas and Cāraṇas. O best of men, O righteous ones, listen now as I duly describe Śākadvīpa according to its proper order, as I speak.

O bulls among the twice-born, O highly fortunate ones, the ocean of milk, by which [the island] is surrounded, is twice the size of Jambudvīpa in its breadth, according to its divisions, O tigers among sages. (8)
In that place, there are no regions lacking merit, and people do not die there. Indeed, how could there be famine in that land which is endowed with patience and splendor?
O best of sages, this is a brief account of Śākadvīpa as it truly is.
"O highly fortunate ones, this has been told; what else shall I relate to you? 10.
The sages said:
"O righteous one, tell us here the summary of Śākadvīpa exactly as it is."
"You have spoken; O one of great wisdom, explain this in detail according to the truth.
Sūta said:
"O Brahmins, in that same manner, there are seven mountain ranges here consisting of jewels."
I shall describe the names of those oceans and rivers which are mines of jewels.
O righteous ones, you ask about that reality which is exceedingly virtuous;
first, Meru is said to be joined by celestial sages and Gandharvas. 12-13.
To the east of Āyato is the highly fortunate mountain named Malaya;
from there the clouds arise and originate in every direction. Beyond that, O sages, is the great mountain Jaladhāra.
From that, Vāsava constantly takes up the supreme water;
from that, O best of the twice-born, rain arises during the rainy season, whereon Mount Raivataka stands eternally firm. 15–16.
O best of brahmins, the constellation Revatī was the day of birth for Pitāmaha’s ordinance;
to the north, however, is the great mountain named Śyāma, which possesses the luster of a fresh cloud, is lofty, glorious, and has a radiant form. (17)
Since they have attained a dark complexion yet possess joyful minds,
the sages said: "O Sūta, this very great doubt has arisen within us because of what you have said."
"O Sūta, how did the subjects here attain this dark complexion?
Sūta said:
"O most wise ones, O bulls among sages, it is thus in all the continents."
O twice-born ones, Gaura and Kṛṣṇa are birds;
from the mixture of their colors, the Śyāma [mountain] originated, and for this reason it is known as Śyāmagiri.
Beyond that, O best of sages, is the great and exalted mountain Durgaśaila.
From where the wind blows forth, it is joined with the Keśarī and Keśara [mountains];
their width is twice that [of the central range], according to their respective divisions. O best of Brahmins, the regions (varṣas) within them have been described by the wise.
Mahāmeru, Mahākāśa, Jalada, Kumudottara, Jaladhāra, Mahāprājña, and Sukumāra are recorded as his [Revata’s] sons;
while the sons of Revata are Kaumāra, Śyāma, Maṇi, and Kāñcana. 23–24.

O best of Brahmins, beyond the Keśara mountain lies the great Manuṣyaka island; it is surrounded by Jambūdvīpa, and its dimensions—both in length and breadth—are equal to those of Jambūdvīpa. In its center stands a great tree.
O highly wise ones, his subjects, known as the Śākas, were accompanied by their followers. There, the regions are meritorious, and there Śaṅkara is worshipped;
there the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and deities go.

All the subjects were righteous, and the four castes were free from envy; they were devoted to their own duties, and no thief was seen there. They were long-lived, highly wise, and devoid of old age and death.
There the subjects flourish like rivers flowing to the ocean during the rainy season.
There are rivers of holy water there, and the Gaṅgā has arrived in many forms: Sukumārī, Kumārī, Śītā, and likewise Śītodakā. 29–30.
O Brahmins, the Mahānadī, the Maṇijalā river, and the Ikṣuvarddhanikā are likewise remembered as rivers by the best of sages (31).
From there, most beautiful rivers of meritorious waters have issued forth.
Even if Vāsava were to rain for hundreds of thousands of years,
it would not be possible to remember or enumerate the names of those excellent, meritorious rivers. 32–33.
Then there were four meritorious provinces, world-renowned:
Mṛga, Maśaka, Mānasa, and Mallaka.
Among them, the Mṛgas were predominantly Brahmins, twice-born ones devoted to their own duties.
In Maśakēṣu, the Kṣatriyas are unrighteous yet grant all desires;
the highly fortunate Vaiśyas live according to the dharma of their class, are endowed with all objects of desire, are heroic, and are resolute in matters of dharma and artha. 35–36.

O best of Brahmins, there the Śūdras constantly ate from the vessels of the Mallakas, as they were men of unrighteous character; there was no king there, nor punishment, nor those who inflict punishment.
Knowing the dharma, they protected one another solely through their own duty.
Only this much can be spoken regarding that island;
and only this much should be heard concerning the highly powerful Śāka-dvīpa.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Svarga-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
The Ninth Chapter.
Sūta said:
O Brahmins, the following account is heard regarding the northern continents.
Listen now as the highly fortunate one speaks thus:
there is an ocean of ghee, another with water of curd-cream,
the ocean of wine, and likewise yet another, the ocean of milk.

O best of the twice-born, O highly wise ones, all the islands and mountains increase twofold from one another, and they are surrounded by oceans. In the middle of the island, however, is the great mountain Gaura, which is composed of red arsenic.
O twice-born ones, on the western side is the mountain Kṛṣṇa, the friend of Nārāyaṇa.
There Keśava himself guards the divine jewels;
being well-pleased, he bestows happiness upon the people there.
O twice-born ones, in the midst of the country on Śaradvīpa there is a clump of kuśa grass, and on Śālmalidvīpa the śālmali tree is worshipped;
on Krauñcadvīpa stands the great mountain Krauñca, a mine of heaps of jewels.
O best of Brahmins, he is constantly worshipped by the four castes.
O Brahmins, there is a very great mountain named Gomanta, rich in all minerals,
where the glorious, lotus-eyed Lord dwells eternally.
Lord Nārāyaṇa, Hari, is eternally associated with those seeking liberation.
O best of Brahmins, in Kuśadvīpa there is a mountain composed of coral;
the second is the golden mountain named Sudurdharṣa.
O best of Brahmins, the third mountain is named Dyutimat;
the fourth is named Puṣpavat; the fifth is Kuśeśaya;
and the sixth is Harigiri—these six are the most excellent of mountains. 10–11.
The diameter between them is double [the width of each], divided proportionately:
the first region is Audbhida, the second is Reṇumaṇḍala,
the third is named Suratha, and the fourth is known as Lambana.
The fifth region is Dhṛtimat, the sixth is Prabhākara, and the seventh is Kāpila;
these seven are the Varṣalaṃbakas.
O twice-born ones, the gods, Gandharvas, and subjects there are joyful.
People dwell and take delight there, and no one dies among them.
O best of men, there are no bandits there, nor any of the Mleccha tribes, nor even [low] twice-born castes;
all the people are predominantly fair-skinned and very delicate.

O best of the twice-born, O highly wise ones, I shall now describe all that remains as it has been heard; listen to it being recounted, O brahmins. (16) O fortunate ones, in Krauñca-dvīpa there is a great mountain named Krauñca.
Beyond Krauñca is Vāmana, and beyond Vāmana is Andhakāraka. O Brahmins, beyond Andhakāraka is Maināka, the best of mountains; and beyond Maināka, O Brahmins, is Govinda, the supreme mountain. 17–18.
Beyond Govinda is the great mountain Puṇḍarīka,
and beyond Puṇḍarīka is said to be Dundubhisvana.
O best of sages, the width of each of these is double that of the preceding one.

I shall now describe those regions; listen as I speak of them. O you whose wealth is asceticism, the region of Krauñca is Kuśala, that of Vāmana is Manonuga, and the region beyond Manonuga is named Uṣṇa. 20–21.
Beyond Uṣṇa is Prāvaraka; beyond Prāvaraka is Andhakāraka; and beyond the region of Andhakāraka, the region of Munideśa is remembered. Beyond Munideśa, indeed, is proclaimed Dundubhisvana.
