The land of Gaura is known to be mostly inhabited by Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
These regions have been described as frequented by gods and Gandharvas.
In Puṣkara, there is a mountain named Puṣkara, which abounds in jewels and gems.
There, the divine Lord Prajāpati himself constantly moves about;
all the gods and great sages perpetually attend upon him, and the best of the twice-born honor him with words that are pleasing to the mind. 25.
O best of sages, from Jambūdvīpa various kinds of jewels are brought forth to all those islands for the sake of the people,
through the celibacy, truthfulness, and self-restraint of the Brahmins. 26–27.
O best of brahmins, from that point on, the lifespan and the measure of health double successively in those regions;
these are the excellent countries on those continents where the singular Dharma prevails. Thus have the countries been described.
O best of sages, O brahmins, the Lord Prajāpati himself, having raised his rod of punishment,
remains forever protecting these islands—
he who is the King, Śiva, the Father, and the Grandfather.
O best of the twice-born, O wise brahmins, he protects his subjects;
and here, O leaders of the vipras, food is presented to him by the subjects themselves. O highly fortunate ones, they always eat that which is thus prepared.

Beyond that, O highly wise one, the great mountain Lokasaṃsthiti is seen; it is four-cornered and perfectly circular on all sides. There, O best of Brahmins, four mountains stand, honored by the world.
The world-elephants— the best of sages— Vāmana, Airāvata, Añjana,
Supratīka, and likewise Vipra, with their temples and faces streaming with rut—
I do not venture here to calculate his dimensions.
Innumerable and eternal, they exist always across, above, and below.
There, O best of sages, those twice-born ones restrain the winds coming from all directions—east, west, and so forth—even though they are unrelated [to them]. 35-36.
With lotus-like trunks of great luster,
they repeatedly draw them in and then instantly release them a hundredfold; they constantly exhale through their mouths and nostrils like the winds from the elephants of the quarters.
The best of the twice-born come there, and indeed the subjects dwell there.
Having heard this measurement of the earth—which was described by me as it was ordained, including this entire creation—and which is merit-bestowing and pleasing to the mind; 39.
O best of Brahmins,

for him who listens to this being narrated on the lunar festival days while observing his vows, prosperity increases, as do his goals accomplished, his standing among the virtuous, his lifespan, his strength, his fame, and his splendor. 40.
His ancestors and likewise his grandfathers are pleased. 41.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Ten.
The sages said:
"O highly fortunate one, having heard from you the dimensions of the earth, its configuration, and likewise its rivers, it is as if we have drunk nectar itself."
O highly wise one, we wish to hear from you in detail about those sacred fords on earth that purify us, as we have heard of them; tell us all of them and how they yield their fruits. (2)
Sūta said:
O you whose wealth is penance, this great narrative, which is indeed meritorious and auspicious, has been asked;
I shall relate it according to my understanding, as is appropriate, and as I have heard it. 3.
O best of the twice-born, listen to this ancient dialogue between the divine sage Nārada and Yudhiṣṭhira.
At that time, the sons of Pāṇḍu, those great chariot-warriors, had been deprived of their kingdom and were dwelling in the forest.
The highly fortunate Pāṇḍavas dwelt together with Draupadī on Mount Nyavaśanti.
Then they beheld there the high-souled celestial sage Nārada,
blazing with Brahmanic splendor and possessing a brilliance equal to a kindled fire.
Surrounded by his brothers, the illustrious joy of the Kurus shone with radiant splendor like Indra among the gods in heaven;
and just as Sāvitrī attends upon the gods, so did Yājñasenī attend upon her husbands.
O Pārtha, he could not have cast down Dharmarāja from his state, just as the light of the sun cannot cast down Mount Meru.
Then, having accepted the worship, the venerable sage Nārada comforted the son of Dharma with words that were both appropriate and pleasing.
He spoke to the high-souled Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira:
"Speak, O best among the upholders of dharma; what is it that you desire? I shall grant it to you.
Then the king, the son of Dharma, together with his brothers, bowed down.
With palms joined in reverence, he spoke these words to Nārada, who was equal to a god:
"O illustrious one, honored by all the worlds, since you are pleased, everything has indeed been accomplished through your grace, O observer of noble vows."
O sinless one, if I am worthy of favor along with my brothers,
you ought, O best of sages, to sever the doubt residing in my heart. [For] he who,
devoted to sacred fords, performs a circumambulation of the earth—
"O Brahmin, you ought to tell me in its entirety what the fruit of that is.
Nārada said:
"Listen attentively, O King, to how it was formerly performed by Dilīpa."
All of this was indeed heard from the presence of Vasiṣṭha:
formerly, on the banks of the Bhāgīrathī, Dilīpa, the best of kings, dwelt like a sage, having undertaken a righteous vow. (15–16)
O Great King, in that auspicious and meritorious place, Gaṅgādvāra, which is honored by divine sages and frequented by gods and gandharvas,
the one of supreme luster and great majesty offered libations to the ancestors and the gods.
He gratified the sages according to the rites prescribed by the rules. Then,
after some time, while he was engaged in silent recitation, that high-minded one beheld the supreme sage Vasiṣṭha, who appeared like a living being.
Seeing the family priest shining as if with splendor,
he experienced incomparable joy and attained the highest wonder; O descendant of Bharata, he honored the one who had arrived, O great king.
That best of those who uphold dharma, purified and with a restrained mind, having taken the arghya offering upon his head according to the prescribed rite,
proclaimed the names of that most excellent of brahman-sages.
"O Dilīpa, may it be well with you!
O you who are devoted to the Vasus, by the mere sight of you I have been liberated from all sins.
Having spoken thus, O Great King, Dilīpa, the best among men, [departed].

Restraining his speech and joining his palms in reverence, Yudhiṣṭhira remained silent (24). Seeing that Dilīpa, the best of kings, emaciated by his disciplined observances and Vedic study, the sage became pleased in heart (25).
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Eleven. Vasiṣṭha said:

"O highly fortunate one, I am entirely satisfied by this devotion to the knowledge of Dharma, by your self-restraint, and by your truthfulness. Since you possess such Dharma as this, your ancestors have been delivered by you."
"Therefore, behold me, O son; you are worthy of my sacrifice, O sinless one.
My joy increases toward you today; tell me, what may I do for you?
Whatever you shall say, O best of men, I am its giver, O sinless one."
Dilīpa said:
"O knower of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, honored by all the world!
It is as if it has already been accomplished by others, since I have beheld you, O Lord."
"If I am worthy of your favor, O best among the upholders of dharma,
then you should dispel this doubt residing in my heart that I shall ask; for,
O Blessed One, I have a certain doubt regarding the dharma concerning the goal of liberation (tīrtha)."
Therefore, I desire to hear from you their individual glorification.
O best of the twice-born, O brahmin-sage, O one rich in asceticism, tell me what fruit belongs to him who circumambulates the earth. (6–7)
Vasiṣṭha said:
"I shall tell you that which is the refuge of the sages;
listen with a one-pointed mind, my son, to what the fruit is in sacred fords."
He whose hands, feet, and speech are well-restrained, and who possesses knowledge, austerity, and fame, enjoys the fruit of the holy ford.
One who has turned away from accepting gifts, who is contented, self-controlled, and pure, [attains that same fruit].
And one whose egoism has ceased enjoys the fruit of the holy ford.
He who is free from guile, abstains from food, does not obtain food [yet remains steadfast], has conquered his senses, and is liberated from all defects—he enjoys the fruit of the holy ford. (10–11)
O Indra among kings, one who is free from anger, truthful in character, firm in his vows,
and who treats all beings as himself, enjoys the fruit of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites.
Sacrifices have been proclaimed by the seers even among the gods in their proper order.
And the fruit, according to its true nature, both hereafter and in this world, in every respect.
(13) O Lord of the Earth, sacrifices cannot be attained by a poor man, for sacrifices require many implements and an extensive collection of materials. (14)
O King, these goals are attained by prosperous monarchs or by monkeys in certain cases, but never by groups of men who are destitute, solitary, and lacking in means. Yet,
O Lord of Men, there is a way that can be achieved even by the poor.
O Lord of the Earth, understand that it is equal in merit to the fruits of sacrifices;
O best among the upholders of dharma, this supreme secret of the sages—that the meritorious pilgrimage to sacred fords excels even sacrifices—is now revealed. 16–17.
By failing to observe the three-night fasts and by not visiting sacred fords (tīrthas),
and by not giving gold and cows, one is born poor.
Having performed sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma with abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), [one does not become poor].

One does not obtain that fruit by visiting other sacred fords which one obtains by reaching Puṣkara, the ford renowned throughout the three worlds, which is a ford of the world of gods within the world of men; having reached the ford of Puṣkara, one becomes equal to the God of gods. 19–20.
O Lord of the Earth, descendant of the Solar dynasty, ten thousand crores of sacred fords (tīrthas) are present at Puṣkara during the three junctions of the day;
there the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas, and the hosts of Maruts reside.
O Lord, the Gandharvas and Apsarases were also present there;
and where the gods, Daityas, and Brahman-sages, O great king, having performed austerities and attained divine yoga through great merit, became twice-born [divinities]. 22–23.
Even for a wise person who merely desires the Puṣkara lakes in their mind,
all sins are purified and they are honored in the heights of heaven.
O highly fortunate one, the Grandfather (Brahmā) dwells eternally at this sacred site.
Residing there with supreme joy, honored by gods and dānavas,
O highly fortunate one, the gods, preceded by the ṛṣis, attained the highest perfection, endowed as they were with great merit. 25–26.
The wise declare that he who, devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods, performs an ablution there, gains ten times the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
Even if one residing in the Pushkara forest feeds but a single Brahmin, [he gains great merit].
Therefore, he who, with palms joined in reverence, remembers these highly honored Puṣkara lakes situated in the abode of Brahmā at both evening and morning,
O King, has effectively performed ablutions in all sacred fords.
Whatever sin has been committed by a woman or a man since birth, it is entirely destroyed as soon as one arrives at Puṣkara.
Just as Madhusūdana is the primordial source of all the gods, so too is Puṣkara the foremost among all sacred fords.
In that very way, Puṣkara is said to be the foremost of all sacred fords (tīrthas). Having stayed at Puṣkara for twelve years, self-restrained and pure,
one obtains the merit of all sacrifices and goes to the world of Brahmā.
He who maintains the *agnihotra* sacrifice for a full hundred years, and he who dwells for even a single day at Puṣkara on the full moon of Kārttika—these two are equal.
It is difficult to go to Puṣkara; it is difficult to perform penance at Puṣkara.
Giving at Puṣkara is difficult, and giving there a physical object is even more difficult.
There are three white peaks and three springs; we do not know the reason why Puṣkara is the foremost of sacred fords (tīrthas). 34–35.
Having fasted for twelve years, self-restrained and restricted in diet, one is liberated from all sins and obtains the fruit of all sacrifices. 36.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Puṣkara Tīrtha," in the Svarga-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. 11.
Chapter Twelve. Vasiṣṭha said:
Having performed a circumambulation, one should enter the Jambūmārga.
Having entered Jambūmārga, which is worshipped by the ancestors and the celestial sages,
a man obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the world of Viṣṇu; having stayed there for five nights, he partakes of food at the sixth meal-time.
He does not fall into an evil state of existence and attains unsurpassed success;
having turned back from Jaṃbumārga, he should go to the Duliḳāśrama hermitage.
He does not fall into an evil state of existence and is honored in the heavenly world.
Having reached the hermitage of Agastya, O King, one who is devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods and fasts for three nights obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice; or,
subsisting on vegetables or fruits, one attains the supreme state of Kumāra.
O bull among kings, having reached the hermitage of Kanyā, which is prosperous, nourishing, and honored by the world—
that meritorious and primordial Dharmāraṇya—
merely upon entering it, one is indeed liberated from all sins.
Having worshipped the ancestors and the gods, being self-restrained and restricted in diet,
he enjoys the fruit of a sacrifice that fulfills all desires; then,
having performed a circumambulation, he should proceed to the place where Yayāti fell.

One obtains the fruit of the horse-sacrifice (hayamedha); one should indeed go from there to Mahākāla, self-restrained and with a regulated diet. Having touched the waters at Koṭitīrtha, one shall obtain the fruit of the horse-sacrifice.
Then, the knower of dharma should go to the sacred ford of the Lord of Umā,
known by the name Bhadravaṭa, which is renowned throughout the three worlds.
Having approached the Lord of the East (Īśāna) there, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Through the grace of Mahādeva, O best of men, one shall attain the status of a Gaṇapati— prosperous, without rival, and endowed with glory—
upon reaching the river Narmadā, renowned throughout the three worlds.
Having gratified the ancestors and the gods, one shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. 13.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Thirteen.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Vasiṣṭha described to Dilīpa that supreme sacred ford known as the Narmadā, which shatters the mountain of sins.
Furthermore, O Nārada, best of the twice-born, I wish to hear again from you the greatness of the Narmadā as spoken by Vasiṣṭha. How did this highly meritorious river become renowned everywhere?
"O Nārada, tell me about her who is renowned by the name Narmadā.
Nārada said:
"The Narmadā is the best of rivers, the destroyer of all sins."
It delivers all beings, both the stationary and the moving.
O Great King, this entire majesty of the Narmadā as spoken by Vasiṣṭha, which was heard by me, I shall now relate to you in its entirety.
The Gaṅgā is sacred at Puṣkara, Nakhala, and Kurukṣetra;
the Sarasvatī is sacred in a village or in a forest; and the Narmadā is sacred everywhere.
The water of the Sarasvatī [purifies] in three days, while that of the Yamunā does so in seven days.
The Narmada, originating from the Ganges, purifies instantly by its mere sight.
In the western half of the Kaliṅga country, on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka, there is a holy place, auspicious in the three worlds, delightful and enchanting. 7–8.
O great king, the ṛṣis, together with the gods, asuras, and gandharvas, who possess the wealth of asceticism, having performed penance there, attained supreme perfection.
Having bathed there, O great king, remaining under restraint and with senses conquered, [one attains the same].
By observing a fast for a single night, one may deliver a hundred generations of one's lineage.
When a man bathes at Janeśvara and offers the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) according to the prescribed rite,
his ancestors remain satisfied until the dissolution of all beings.
Ten million Rudras are established all around the mountain;
whoever performs a bath there with perfumes, garlands, and ointments,
those ten million Rudras will be pleased with him— of this there is no doubt.
At the western end of the mountain, Lord Maheśvara himself resides.
Having bathed there and become pure, remaining celibate and with senses subdued, one should perform the ancestral rites (pitṛkārya) according to the procedure prescribed by the rules. 13–14.
O Pāṇḍava, by offering libations of water mixed with sesame seeds right there, one satisfies the ancestors and the gods; his lineage remains in heaven for seven generations,
and he is honored in the heavenly world for sixty thousand years.
Surrounded by throngs of Apsaras and attended by celestial women, anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with divine ornaments,
he then falls from heaven and is born into a noble family.
He is born again wealthy, charitable, and indeed righteous;
he remembers that pilgrimage and performs it there once more.
Having delivered a hundred generations of his lineage, he goes to the world of Rudra.
O king of kings, that best of rivers is said to be slightly more than a hundred yojanas in length;
its width, however, is two yojanas. It contains sixty thousand and sixty crore sacred fords (tīrthas).
On all sides of Mount Amarakaṇṭaka, they stand,
having become pure celibates, having conquered anger and subdued their senses,
having desisted from all violence, and being devoted to the welfare of all beings. 21.
Thus, with all conduct in accordance with this, one should wander among the guardians of the fields (Kṣetrapālas).
O King, listen attentively to me as I describe the fruit of his merit:
for a hundred thousand years, O son of Pāṇḍu, he shall rejoice in heaven.
Crowded with throngs of Apsarases and attended by celestial women, anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with divine ornaments,
he sports in the world of the gods and rejoices together with the deities.
Then, having fallen from heaven, he becomes a powerful king;
he obtains a home adorned with various jewels,
featuring divine pillars made of gems and embellished with diamonds and lapis lazuli.
Adorned with paintings, divine, and provided with male and female servants,
that gate was agitated by the sounds of rutting elephants and the neighing of horses, like the palace of Indra.
The illustrious Lord of Kings, beloved by all women—
having dwelt in that house, endowed with play and enjoyment,
he shall live for more than a hundred years, free from all diseases. (28-29)
Such shall be the enjoyment of him who has died at Marakaṇṭaka,
whether by entering fire, or likewise in water, or by fasting;
his destination is from which there is no return, like that of a mountain in the sky.
O lord of men, that man who falls [from his vow] falls [to a lower state);
yet, three thousand maidens remain in his house, each one of whom seeks to be sent as a messenger to him. 31-32.
Born with divine enjoyments, he sports for inexhaustible time;
on this earth as far as the oceans, no one else is ever born such as this best of men on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka. 33.
Koṭitīrtha should be known as being on the western side of the mountain.

There is Rudra, named Jāleśvara, renowned throughout the three worlds; by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) there and by performing the rite of twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana), [one attains great merit]. 34–35.
Your ancestors have been gratified for ten years;
to the south of the Narmadā is the great river named Kapilā, situated not far away and covered with Sarala and Arjuna trees. 36.

O Yudhiṣṭhira, that auspicious and highly fortunate place is renowned throughout the three worlds; O King, it is heard in the Purāṇas that there are more than a hundred million holy sites (tīrthas) there, and everything becomes ten-million-fold in merit. 37-38.
Moreover, those trees on its banks that have fallen due to the passage of time,
being joined with the waters of the Narmadā, they too attain the supreme goal. O highly fortunate one, the second [tirtha] is the auspicious Viśalyakaraṇa.
A person who bathes there on the bank becomes free from all afflictions in an instant.
There, all the hosts of gods, along with the Kinnaras, Mahoragas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, and sages whose wealth is their asceticism, [reside].
All of them gathered there on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka;
and having assembled with all those sages whose wealth is their asceticism,
[they established] the holy Narmadā by the name Viśalyā.

O King, having bathed there, a man who is a celibate student with controlled senses and who fasts for one night shall deliver a hundred generations of his lineage; that highly auspicious place destroys all sins. 43-44.

O best of kings, it is heard that Kapilā and Viśalyā were described by the Lord in ancient times out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds. By bathing there, O King, a man obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
O lord of men, he who performs a fast at that tīrtha becomes purified of all sins and goes to the world of Indra;
this is what was heard by me in the Purāṇa regarding the Narmadā, O king of kings. 46–47.
Having bathed at each of those various places, a man shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice; those who dwell on the northern bank [of the Sarasvatī] reside in the world of Indra.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, [this applies to] the Sarasvatī, the Gaṅgā, and the Narmadā.
Śaṅkara has told me how equal are the gift and the bath;
he who gives up his life on the Amarakaṇṭaka mountain is honored in the world of Indra for more than a hundred crores of years. 49-50.
The holy water of the Narmadā, adorned with foam and waves, is pure and worthy of being saluted with the head; by it, one is liberated from all sins.
The Narmadā is meritorious in every way and is the remover of the sin of killing a Brahmin.
By fasting for a day and night, one is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Thus, O son of Pāṇḍu, this meritorious and beautiful great river Narmadā purifies even all the three worlds.
In Vaṭeśvara, the great merit-field, at Gaṅgādvāra, and in the penance-grove—
among all these places, it is heard that the merit for those who have fasted while firm in their vows is tenfold at the confluence of the Narmadā and the ocean. 54
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Fourteen. Nārada said:
The Narmadā is the best of rivers, meritorious and most holy among the three [worlds],
divided by highly fortunate sages who longed for dharma; its sacred sites,
O Pāṇḍava, have been distributed as far as the length of a sacrificial thread.

O Indra among kings, by bathing in them, one is liberated from all sins. O son of Pāṇḍu, listen as I describe the origin of that holy place known as Jaleśvara, which is renowned throughout the three worlds.
In former times, all the hosts of sages, along with Indra and the hosts of Maruts,
praised that high-souled Maheśvara, the God of gods. While they were thus offering praise, they arrived at the place where the Lord Maheśvara was present.
The hosts of Maruts, led by Indra, informed the Lord of the Gods, saying:
"O Lord, protect us who are agitated by fear from Virūpākṣa!
Īśvara said:
"Welcome, O best of sages! For what purpose have you come here?
What is your sorrow, what is your distress, or from where has fear arisen?
Tell me, O highly fortunate ones; I desire to know this."
Thus addressed by Rudra, those sages of immeasurable vows spoke.
The sages said:
"Even though he is terrible, of great heroism, and a Dānava arrogant with strength,"
There was one renowned by the name Bāṇa, whose city was Tripura.
It dwelt in the sky, divine and wandering by his splendor;
terrified of him, O Virūpākṣa, they have come to you alone for refuge.
"Save us from great suffering, for divinity is indeed the supreme goal.
O Lord of Gods, O Śaṅkara, you ought to show such grace toward all of us, by which the gods, being well-pleased, may prosper in happiness."
"They shall attain supreme bliss; you ought to bring that about.
The God said:
"I shall do all this; you must not despair."

"Before long, I shall bring about that which will bring you happiness. Having thus consoled them all, O Pāṇḍava, the Lord of All stationed himself on the bank of the Narmadā and reflected upon his slaughter.
"By what means and in what manner must Tripura be destroyed by me?
Having reflected thus, the Blessed One then remembered Nārada; and by that very remembrance, Nārada arrived and stood before him. 14.
Nārada said: "Command me, O Mahādeva; for what purpose have I been remembered? O God, tell me what task must be performed by me. (15)
Ishvara said:
"Go, Narada, right there where that city of Tripura is; go quickly to the presence of Bana, the lord of the Danavas, and perform that task."
Their husbands are radiant like deities, and their wives are like apsarases;
by their splendor, the triple city (Tripura) revolves in the sky.
O best of brahmins, having gone there, employ another mantra.
Having heard the words of the god, the sage, moving with swift strides,
entered that city for the purpose of destroying the hearts of the women.
That divine city shone, adorned with various jewels.
It was one hundred yojanas wide and twice that in length; there he beheld Bāṇa, arrogant in his strength,
resplendent with garlands, earrings, armlets, and a crown.
Covered with necklaces of jewels and adorned with the luster of the moon, the women there were rich in gems and the men were decorated with gold;
seeing Nārada, the exceedingly powerful lord of the Dānavas rose from his seat. 21-22.
Bāṇa said:
"O best of the twice-born, since the divine sage has himself arrived at my house just now, let the guest-offering (arghya) and water for the feet (pādya) be provided according to the rule."
"The Brahmin has arrived after a long time; let him depart from this seat.
Having thus honored Nārada who had approached, his wife, the great queen named Anaupamyā, [spoke]. (24-25)
Anaupamya said:
"O Blessed One, by what vow, observance, gift, or even austerity do the gods not indeed become satisfied in the world of men? (26)
Nārada said:
He who gives a sesame-cow to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas, it is as if the entire earth with its oceans and nine islands has been given by him. 27.
Adorned with royal edicts, he rejoices for an inexhaustible period of time and for a very long duration in celestial palaces that resemble ten million suns and fulfill all desires.
[There he finds] mangoes, wood-apples, plantains, and groves as well.
There were kadamba, campaka, and aśoka trees, as well as many various other trees.
(29) The eighth, fourth, and twelfth lunar days, both equinoxes, the sun’s passage into a new sign, and likewise the "mouths" of the days— (30)
For those women who observe all these meritorious fasts and are endowed with righteousness, there is no doubt that their residence shall be in heaven;
they are liberated from the Kali age and freed from all sins. 31.
"Ascetics do not approach noble women who are devoted to fasting. Having heard this, O lady of beautiful hips, you should do as you wish.
Hearing the words of Nārada, the queen spoke these words: [32-33]
"O best of Brahmins, show me favor; accept as you desire gifts such as gold, gems, jewels, garments, and ornaments.
O Brahmin, I shall give those to you, as well as whatever else is difficult to obtain."
"O best of the twice-born, accept this; may Hari and Śaṅkara be pleased.
Nārada said:
"O blessed lady, let it be given to another brahmin whose means of livelihood are exhausted."
"Let us go; we are perfected in virtue, yet devotion is being practiced by me.
36. Having thus captivated the minds of all those women and having instructed them, the best of the Bharatas returned once more to his own abode. 37.
Thereupon, their minds being drawn away and their thoughts fixed elsewhere, a vulnerability arose in the great-souled Bāṇa.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. 14.
Fifteenth Chapter.
Nārada said:
O son of Kuntī, listen and understand that which you ask me.
In the meantime, Rudra was stationed on the bank of the Narmadā at the place known as Hareśvara, renowned throughout the three worlds; there,
Mahādeva was contemplating the destruction of the Tripuras.
Making Mount Mandara the bow and Vāsuki the string,
making Vaiśākha his stance and Viṣṇu the supreme arrow,
he established Agni at the front and assigned Vāyu to the tip.
The four Vedas were the horses, and the chariot was composed of all the gods.
The two Aśvin deities were the two wheels, and the wielder of the discus himself was the axle.
Indra himself was at the end of the bow, and Vaiśravaṇa stood as the arrow.
Yama was on the right hand and the terrible Kāla was on the left;
the world-renowned Gandharvas were stationed upon the spokes and the rims of the wheels.
Brahmā himself was the charioteer of that preeminent chariot of Prajāpati.
Having thus fashioned the chariot composed of all the gods, O Lord of Gods,
he stood there as motionless as a pillar for a thousand years,
until the three [fires] that move through the intermediate space had come together.
Then, impelled by Rudra toward Tripura, that arrow pierced those three cities with its triple-pointed shaft.
Their splendor was lost, they became women, and their strength shattered.
Thousands of portents appeared in that city.
Then, for the destruction of Tripura, forms like those of Death manifested,
as well as wooden figures emitting loud, boisterous laughter.
They perform the acts of closing and opening their eyes through the power of their wondrous arts,
and in dreams they see themselves adorned in red garments. Furthermore,
in dreams they likewise perceive various things that are contrary to reality.
Those people who were stationed there beheld these portents;
their strength and intellect were destroyed by the wrath of Hara.
Then a great wind named Saṃvarta arose, resembling the end of a Yuga.
The best of fires, being fanned by the wind, torments their heads; the trees there blaze up, and their peaks fall down.
Everything there becomes utterly agitated, filled with cries of "Alas!", and rendered unconscious. 15.
All the gardens were shattered and quickly burst into flames;
by that very fire, everything was set ablaze, burning with fiery arrows—the trees, the groves, and various kinds of houses. 16–17.

This blazing carrier of oblations has spread throughout the ten directions; consequently, the rocks are being cast forth from each of the ten quarters. The fires are flaming with thousands of most fierce crests of flame.
The entire city appeared ablaze, resembling a mass of *kiṃśuka* flowers;
it was impossible to move from one house to another because of the smoke.
Scorched by the fire of Hara’s wrath, the city wailed in extreme distress. (19–20)
The city of Tripura was burning, ablaze in every direction;
the peaks of its palaces were shattering by the thousands, as were the celestial chariots variegated with various jewels in many ways. 21.
And even delightful houses are being consumed by the blazing fire;
it afflicts the clusters of trees as well as the dwellings of people, and it blazes and burns intensely within all the temples of the gods. 22–23.
Touched by the fire, they sink down and cry out with various sounds;
there, heaps of glowing coals resembling mountain peaks are seen.
They praise the Lord of the gods, saying, "O Lord, save me!"
Embracing one another there, the Dānavas, tormented by the fire,
were being burnt by the hundreds and thousands;
it was like a lotus pond filled with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks, along with its lotuses.
The cities, gardens, and ponds were being consumed by fire,
yet they remained covered with unfading lotuses spread over hundreds of yojanas.
There, the palaces, adorned with jewels, resembled the peaks of mountains.
They fell like clouds of water being consumed by fire;
driven by the wrath of Hara, the merciless fire burned through women, children, the elderly, cattle, birds, and horses alike. 28–29.

And many people, including their wives, were fast asleep; embracing their sons tightly, they were being consumed by the Enemy of Tripura. Then, in that blazing city, there were women who resembled celestial nymphs (apsarases).
Struck by the flames of the fire, they fell there upon the surface of the earth.
A certain young woman with large eyes, adorned with a string of pearls, was overwhelmed by the smoke; she woke up, tormented by the cresting flames.
Another woman, possessing a golden complexion and adorned with blue gems, fell to the surface of the earth while reflecting upon what she had heard; yet another,
overwhelmed by smoke, fell to the surface of the earth.
But another, whose hand was not grasped by her friends, was burned by the children;
another, of divine form, having been seen and deluded by intoxication, placed her joined palms to her head and addressed the Fire-god. 34-35.
If you desire enmity toward men who have done you harm,
what offense have these women committed, who are but cuckoos in the cage of the household? O sinful, merciless, and shameless one, why do you direct your anger toward women?
"Neither courtesy, nor shame, nor truth, nor purity exists in you. 37 You are rich in many forms and colors; having found me, speak! Have you not heard in the world that all women are inviolable? 38"
But these virtues of yours, O Consumer, are directed toward the destruction of others; you possess neither compassion, nor mercy, nor even courtesy toward women.
Even barbarians show pity upon seeing women before the fire.
Even for the Mlecchas, you are miserable, uncontrollable, and indeed devoid of consciousness.
These very qualities of yours are directed toward burning and destroying; why then do you seek to strike down even these women of ill-conduct? 40-41.
"O you who are wicked, merciless, shameless, a fire of misfortune,
and hopeless! You heartlessly burn these girls of ill conduct!"—
thus they lamented and spoke in many voices.
Others, deluded by grief for their child, cried out in great anger:
"The pitiless fire burns like an enraged enemy;
it blazes in the lotus pond, in the water, and likewise even in the wells. (43-44)
"Having burned us, you will lead us to what state, O Mleccha?
To those who were thus lamenting, the Fire spoke these words.
Vaiśvānara said:
"I shall not bring about your destruction by my own will;
I am merely the executor of the command, for it is He who bestows grace. 46. It is only when possessed by anger that I wander here according to my own inclination."
Then Bāṇa, possessed of great splendor, seeing Tripura set ablaze,
spoke thus while remaining on his throne: "I have been destroyed by the gods, who are of little substance and wicked conduct, having been reported to the Lord."
Indeed, I am unexamined and yet consumed by the high-souled Śaṅkara;
no other enemy than Maheśvara is capable of slaying me.
Raising my head, I bow with reverence to the Lord of the three worlds.
Having personally abandoned his friends, he departed from the city gate;
taking various wonderful jewels and diverse women, he placed them upon his head as he entered the circle of the city.
I praise Śiva, the Lord of the gods and sovereign of the three worlds;
since I have been consumed by you, O Śaṅkara, let me be slain.
By your grace, O Mahādeva, let my *liṅga* perish.
"O Mahādeva, although I am always worshipped by you with supreme devotion, if I am to be slain by you, let my *liṅga* not perish;
for having obtained this, O Mahādeva, I have attained the grasping of your feet. (53-54)
"O Great God, throughout birth after birth I have been devoted to your feet;
having thus praised the Supreme Lord in the Toṭaka meter— Oṃ! Salutations to Śiva, the Beneficent One, the Doer of All; salutations to Bhava, Bhīma, Maheśa, and Śiva."

Salutations to the one who brought about the destruction of the body of the flower-armed god (Kāma), the destroyer of Tripura, and the crusher of Andhaka; salutations to the one who is beloved by women, who dispels desire and delusion, and who is bowed to by hosts of gods and Siddhas;
salutations to him who is accompanied by Gaṇas with faces like horses, monkeys, lions, and lordly elephants, and with faces that are exceedingly short or very long.

O Blessed One, salutations to you who bear the digit of the immovable moon; you were not distressed by the asuras, who are exceedingly difficult to perceive, even though they bowed with many hundreds of bodies and great devotion.
O Conqueror, may I, along with my sons, wife, family, and wealth, always remember you. 58.

I am tormented; through many hundreds of bodies, I have been led to the path of the great hells. This course of mine, born of sin, does not turn back; it abandons even that which is purified by pure deeds.
Compassion pities me, yet I wander and wander, lost in all directions; may this delusion be restrained by right understanding.
To whoever recites this divine *Ṭoṭaka*, being self-restrained and pure in mind, Rudra shall become the granter of boons, just as he was to Bāṇa.
Having heard this most divine hymn, the Lord Maheśvara—
When he had thus offered his praise with a serene mind, Lord Maheśvara himself appeared.
The Lord said: "O Dānava, you who stand here as Suvarṇa, you need not fear."
"From this day forward, together with your sons, grandsons, co-wives, wife, and servants, you shall possess the state of Bāṇa, being invulnerable even to the gods; furthermore,
O Pāṇḍava, a boon was granted to him by the God of Gods."
Inexhaustible and undecaying, Hanumān wandered through the world fearlessly;
then he likewise warded off the seven-flamed [fire] that Śaṅkara had sent forth,
which was protected by the high-souled Mahātman.
It wandered constantly through the sky by the power of Rudra’s splendor.
Thus, the triple city, blazing with garlands of flames, was burnt by the high-souled Śaṅkara and fell upon the surface of the earth.
One [image] of him was installed at Śrīśaila by Tripurāntaka;
the second was installed there on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka. O King, when Tripura had been burnt, ten million Rudras were established.
Because that blazing [fire] was cast down there, it is remembered as Jvāleśvara.
As its divine flame ascended upward and reached the heavens, a cry of "Alas! Alas! then arose from the gods, asuras, and kinnaras.
Rudra would have restrained that arrow at that supreme city of Maheśvara;
thus, O son of Pāṇḍu, one should go to that mountain Amarakaṇṭaka and, having fully enjoyed the fourteen worlds, [attain liberation].
For thirty-three thousand million years,
he remains there; then, having reached the surface of the earth, he becomes a righteous king who enjoys the earth under a single umbrella— of this there is no doubt.
O Great King, this Amarakaṇṭaka is meritorious in every respect;
those who go to Amarakaṇṭaka during solar or lunar eclipses, the wise declare, receive ten times the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. (74)
Having beheld Maheśvara there, one attains the heavenly world. They say that when the sun is eclipsed, those who come to Saṃnihati obtain all that merit on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka. 75–76.

A person obtains the fruit of the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice there on the mountain named Amarakaṇṭaka, where the deity Jvāleśvara resides. Having bathed there, those who die go to heaven and are not subject to rebirth.
O Great King, he who should renounce his life at Jvāleśvara—listen now with devotion to the fruit thereof during an eclipse of the moon or sun:
those gods known as the Amaras reside on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka. (78–79)
One attains the world of Rudra until the dissolution of all beings,
on the waters at the foot of the mountain of the god Amareśvara;
there, millions of preeminent sages of virtuous vows perform austerities.
O King, for a distance of one yojana all around, the sacred field of Cāmarakaṇṭaka—
whether free from desire or possessed of desire— one who bathes in the auspicious waters of the Narmadā is liberated from sins and goes to the world of Rudra. 81–82.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Sixteen.
The Sage said:
All those great-souled persons, led by Yudhiṣṭhira, as well as the ṛṣis whose wealth is asceticism, questioned Nārada:
"O Blessed One, tell us truly of the great confluence at the Kāverī."
For the welfare of the worlds and for our own prosperity,
may those men who are constantly devoted to sin and who commit evil deeds be liberated from all their sins and go to the supreme state.
"I wish to know this, O Blessed One; you should deign to speak.
Nārada said:
"Listen all together, led by Yudhiṣṭhira."
Having performed a great sacrifice here and reached this sacred ford, Kubera, whose valor is truth, became superior even to imperial sovereignty;
O Great King, listen as I describe how he attained perfection.
There, at the world-renowned confluence of the Kāverī and the Narmadā,
Kubera— the lord of the Yakṣas, whose valor is truth— having bathed and become pure,
performs great divine penance for a hundred years.
Mahādeva was pleased with him and said, "O Yakṣa of great courage, grant you an excellent boon! Speak whatever you desire;
tell me your purpose as you wish, or whatever dwells in your mind. (7)
Kubera said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to me, let me be the first creator and the sovereign lord of all yakṣas."
Having heard the words of Kubera, the Lord Maheśvara was pleased; having said, "So be it," he then vanished right there.
That Yakṣa, too, having obtained the boon, quickly went to the assembly of Yakṣas.

Honored by all the lords of the yakṣas, that king was consecrated there at the confluence of the Kāverī, which destroys all sins; those men who do not recognize it have undoubtedly been deceived. 10–11.
Therefore, with every effort, a person should bathe there;
for both the Kāverī, which is highly meritorious, and the great river Narmadā are present there.
Having bathed there, O lord of kings, one should worship the Bull-bannered Lord (Śiva).

Having obtained the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice, one is glorified in the world of Rudra. Śaṅkara has declared that for one who enters the fire or who practices fasting unto death, there is a state from which there is no return. 13–14.
Served by excellent women, he rejoices like Rudra in heaven for sixty thousand years, and likewise for another sixty crores;
established in the world of Rudra, he rejoices wherever he goes.
Falling away due to the exhaustion of his merit, he becomes a righteous king (16),
one who possesses enjoyments, is virtuous in character, and is born into a great family;
by drinking the water there properly, one obtains the fruit of the Cāndrāyaṇa vow (17).
Those mortals who drink the auspicious water go to heaven;
whatever fruit those men attain by bathing in the region between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, that same fruit is produced for him who bathes at the confluence of the Kāverī. 18.
Thus, O Indra among kings, there is that great confluence of the Kāverī, renowned as Patreśvara, which is the supreme remover of all sins. 19.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. 16.
The seventeenth chapter.
Nārada said: On the northern bank of the Narmadā, there is a sacred site (tīrtha) extending for one yojana.
It is renowned as Patreśvara, the supreme destroyer of all sins.
Having bathed there, O King, a man rejoices together with the gods;
assuming a form at will, he sports for five thousand years.
Then one should go to Garjana, where clouds gather;
by the power of that holy site (tīrtha), one obtains the name Indrajit. Then one should go to Megharāva, where the clouds thunder.
There, Meghanāda’s host attained the state of being endowed with excellent qualities.
Then, O lord of kings, one should go to the place known as Brahmāvarta;
there, O Yudhiṣṭhira, Brahmā is eternally present.
O Indra among kings, having bathed there, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā; thereafter,
being self-restrained and restricted in diet at the Aṅgāreśvara Tīrtha,
one whose soul is purified of all sins goes to the world of Rudra.

Then, O lord of kings, one should go to the supreme Kapilātīrtha. Having bathed there, O King, a man obtains the fruit of the gift of a cow. Then one should go to Kāñcītīrtha, which is frequented by hosts of divine sages.
O King, having bathed there, a man shall attain Goloka;
from there, O lord of kings, he should proceed to the excellent Kuṇḍaleśvara.
There, Rudra dwells in close proximity together with Umā.
O Indra among kings, having bathed there, one becomes incapable of being slain even by the gods;
thereafter, one should go to Pippaleśvara, which destroys all sins.
Having gone there, O Indra among kings, one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Then, O Indra among kings, one should go to Vimala-Vimaleśvara;
there, a beautiful peak of the mountain was struck down by Īśvara.
By renouncing one's life there, one shall attain the world of Rudra.

Thereafter, one should go to Puṣkariṇī and perform a bath there; by the mere act of bathing there, a man shall obtain half of Indra’s throne. Narmadā, the best of rivers, has issued forth from the body of Rudra. 13–14.
May he, the Great-Souled Lord, the God who transcends all gods, deliver all beings, both the stationary and the moving;
for he has declared this to the assemblies of sages, and especially to us.
Indeed, this river Narmadā, the most excellent of rivers, is praised by the sages;
having issued forth from the body of Rudra out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, she is eternally the remover of all sins and is saluted by all living beings. 16–17.
Salutations to you, praised by the gods, gandharvas, and likewise by the apsarases; salutations, O primordial one with meritorious waters; salutations to you who flow toward the ocean.
Salutations to you, who have issued from the body of Śaṅkara and are honored by the hosts of ṛṣis.

Homage to you, O refuge of the Dharma; homage to you, O sole object of worship for the hosts of gods. Homage to you, the purifier of all that is pure; homage to you, who are most highly honored by the entire world.
That person who daily recites this hymn with a pure mind— (19-20)
A Brāhmaṇa attains the Veda; a Kṣatriya becomes victorious;
a Vaiśya obtains profit; and a Śūdra indeed attains an auspicious state. One who seeks food certainly obtains food simply by constant remembrance.
The Lord Maheśvara himself constantly resorts to the Narmadā;
therefore, that river of merit should be known as the remover of the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa. 22.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. 17.
The eighteenth chapter.
Nārada said:
From that time forward, the sages headed by Brahmā, whose wealth is their austerity, [began to practice].
O King, those who worship the Narmadā while being free from desire and anger—
having seen the trident of the God fallen upon the earth there—
the great-souled Śaṅkara proclaimed its merit.
There is a great and most meritorious sacred site (tīrtha) renowned as Śūlabheda;
having bathed there, one should worship the God and obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
O lord of men, he who observes a fast for three nights at that tīrtha—
Having worshipped Mahādeva, one is not subject to rebirth.
Then one should go to Bhīmeśvara, the excellent Narmadeśvara, and the highly meritorious Ādityeśvara, along with Ajya and Madhu. 4-5.
Having worshipped Mallikeśvara, the fruit of one's birth is fully attained;
thereafter, one should behold Varuṇeśvara and the supreme Nīrājeśvara. By the sight of these five shrines (pañcāyatana), one obtains the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Then, O lord of kings, one should go to the place where the battle was indeed fought;
it is the famous Koṭitīrtha, where the Asuras were contended against,
and where, O King, those Dānavas arrogant in their strength were slain by him.
Seizing their heads, they were struck down; having assembled there, they installed the trident-bearing god Maheśvara. Ten million were slain there by him, and thus he is remembered as Koṭīśvara.
By the mere sight of that sacred ford (tīrtha), one may attain heaven even with the body.
At that time, because Indra was small-minded, he pinned it down with a vajra-stake;
from that moment on, the attainment of heaven by the worlds was obstructed.
Having offered a bilva fruit with ghee and having performed a circumambulation at the conclusion, one should take it up with the head while reciting the Sahadeva mantra and wear it;
thus, O Pāṇḍava, the king becomes fulfilled in all his desires. 12.
O Mṛtyu-rudra, he attains you; he is not born again here on earth.
Having gone to heaven and ruled there, he then returns to the celestial realm. Thus, by worshipping Mahādeva on the thirteenth lunar day, a human being [attains this].
A man who has merely bathed there obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.
Thereafter, O lord of kings, one should go to the most beautiful and supreme holy site, Agastyeśvara, for the destruction of the sins of men. 14–15.

Having bathed there, O King, a man is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika. Remaining in meditative absorption and with his senses subdued, he should bathe the deity with ghee.
One who is endowed with twenty-one generations of his lineage shall be liberated from the state of Īśvara.
By giving cows, sandals, an umbrella, as well as a blanket and food to the Brahmins, all of it becomes multiplied ten-millionfold. 17–18.
Then, O lord of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed hymn of praise to Ravi;
having bathed there, O king, a man shall attain the state of sitting upon a lion-throne. On the southern bank of the Narmadā is the famous tīrtha of Śakra.
Having observed a fast for one night, one should perform a ritual bath there.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rule, one should worship Janārdana; he obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
From there, one should go to Ṛṣitīrtha, which removes all sins for men;
merely by bathing there, a man is glorified in the world of Śiva. And right there is the most beautiful tīrtha of Nārada.
A man who has merely bathed there obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows.
23. From there, one should go to Devatīrtha, which was created by Brahmā in ancient times;
having bathed there, O King, a man is glorified in the world of Brahmā. 24.
From there, one should go to Amarakaṇṭaka, which was established by the immortals in ancient times;
merely by bathing there, a man obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows.
Then, O lord of kings, one should go to the excellent Vāmaneśvara.
Having seen Vāmanaka there, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin (brahmahatyā).
From there, a man should certainly go to Ṛṣitīrtha and then to Īśāneśa;
having seen Vaṭeśvara thereafter, the fruit of his birth is fully realized.
Then one should go to Bhīmeśvara, which destroys all diseases;
O King, merely by bathing there, a man is liberated from all suffering.
Then, O Indra among kings, one should go to the excellent Vāraṇeśvara.
Having bathed there, O King, a person is liberated from all suffering.
Then one should go to Somatīrtha and behold the most excellent Candra; having bathed there, O King, endowed with supreme devotion, a person [attains the highest state]. 29–30.
At that very moment, established in a divine body, he rejoices for a long time like Śiva himself;
for sixty thousand years, he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Then, O lord of kings, one should go to the supreme Piṅgaleśvara.
By fasting for a single day and night, one obtains the fruit of a three-night fast.
O Indra among kings, for him who gives a tawny cow (kapilā) at that sacred ford,
as many hairs as there are on her body and on the bodies of those born in her lineage, [so many years shall he dwell in heaven].
O King, he who gives up his life there is honored in the world of Rudra for thousands of years;
he rejoices for an inexhaustible period of time, as long as the moon and the sun endure.
Those men who dwell taking refuge on the banks of the Narmadā go to heaven upon death, just like those of meritorious deeds. One should go to Surabhikeśvara and Koṭikeśvara, which wards off hell.
On that day, there is no doubt that the descent of the Gaṅgā is meritorious;
from there, one should go to Nanditīrtha and perform a bath there. By doing so, Nandīśa is pleased, and one is glorified in the world of Soma.
Then one should go to the island-lord Vyāsatīrtha, a grove of asceticism (tapovana).
There, the great river, having been turned back from the city out of fear of Vyāsa, was sent toward the south by Vyāsa’s utterance of the syllable "Huṃ. 38-39.
O lord of men, he who performs a circumambulation at that sacred ford (tīrtha) shall find Vyāsa pleased with him and obtain his desired fruit.
He who should encircle the radiant Lord together with His altar with a thread...
For he sports for an imperishable time, just like Rudra himself. 41.
Then, O lord of kings, one should go to the excellent Eraṇḍī-tīrtha;
by bathing at the confluence, a person is liberated from all sins. 42.
The Eraṇḍī is renowned throughout the three worlds as the destroyer of sins;
or else, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, a man, having become pure and having bathed, should be devoted to fasting. 43–44.

Having bathed at the confluence of the Eraṇḍī, colored by a spirit of devotion, one should feed a single Brāhmaṇa; it is as if ten million have been fed. Placing a piece of mother-of-pearl upon one's head, one should indeed immerse oneself in the water.
One who bathes in water mixed with the waters of the Narmadā is liberated from all sins.
O lord of men, he who performs a circumambulation at that sacred ford has,
by that act, circumambulated the earth with its seven continents.
Then, having bathed at Suvarṇatilaka and given gold,
one is glorified in the world of Rudra by means of a golden celestial chariot (vimāna).
Thereafter, descending from heaven at the appointed time, one becomes a powerful king.
From there, O lord of kings, one should go to the confluence of the Ikṣunadī;
it is divine, renowned throughout the three worlds, and Śiva is ever-present there.
Having bathed there, O King, a man shall attain the status of a leader of the Gaṇas.
Then one should go to Skanda-tīrtha, which destroys all sins;
it removes the sin committed since birth by merely bathing there. (51) Then one should go to Āṅgirasa and perform a bath there.
He is honored in the world of Rudra with the merit of giving a thousand cows.
Then one should go to Lāṅgalatīrtha, which destroys all sins;
having gone there, O lord of kings, one should perform a ritual bath.
One is liberated from the sins committed in seven lifetimes; there is no doubt about this.
Thereafter, one should go to Vaṭeśvara, the most excellent of all holy places (tīrthas).
Having bathed there, O King, a man obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows.
Then one should go to Saṅgameśvara, the supreme destroyer of all sins. Having bathed there, a man obtains a kingdom; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, O Bhadra, whatever gift a man gives after reaching Bhadratīrtha, [it becomes inexhaustible].

By the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha), everything becomes ten millionfold. Furthermore, if any woman should perform her ritual bath there, she will become equal to Gaurī and go to the realm of Indra; of this there is no doubt.
Then one should go to Aṅgāreśvara and perform a ritual bath there;
merely by bathing there, a man is glorified in the world of Rudra.
On the fourth lunar day falling on a Tuesday, one should perform a bath there.
Having received the command of Murāri, he rejoices for an inexhaustible period of time;
having bathed at Ayonisamgama, he shall not behold the abode of a womb again. Having gone to Pāṇḍaveśvara, one should perform a ritual bath there.
He rejoices for an inexhaustible time, incapable of being slain by gods or asuras.
Having gone from there to the world of Viṣṇu, endowed with play and enjoyment,
and having experienced great pleasures there, he is born as a king among mortals.
One should go to Kāmbhojikeśvara and perform a ritual bath there;
if one so desires when the northern solstice has arrived, that [desire] shall be fulfilled for him. Then one should go to Candrabhāgā and perform a ritual bath there.
A man who has merely bathed there is glorified in the world of Soma. 64.
Thereafter, O lord of kings, one should go to the famous shrine of Śakra, which is honored by the king of the gods and saluted even by the deities. 65.
O King, having bathed there and given a gift of gold,
or whoever should release a bull of blue hue—
the hairs on that bull's body [are equal in number] to those born in his family.
For that many thousands of years he shall dwell in the city of Narohara;
thereafter, having descended from heaven, he becomes a powerful king, O lord of men, possessing a thousand white-colored horses.
By the power of that sacred ford, he becomes a lord among mortals;
from there, O Indra among kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Brahmāvarta.
Having bathed there, O King, a man should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods.
Having fasted for one night and offered a funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) according to the prescribed rite when the sun has entered the sign of Virgo, whatever has been accumulated becomes inexhaustible;
then, O lord of kings, one should go to the supreme Kapilā-tīrtha.

O King, that man who bathes there and bestows a Kapila cow shall obtain the same fruit as one who has given away the entire earth. Narmadeśvara is a supreme sacred site; it has never existed before, nor will it ever cease to exist.
O King, having bathed there, a man obtains the fruit of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha).
O King, one who dies there is reborn on earth as a sovereign, endowed with all auspicious marks and free from all diseases.

On the northern bank of the Narmadā is a most beautiful tīrtha, a delightful sanctuary of Āditya consecrated by Īśvara. Having bathed there, O Indra among kings, and having given gifts according to one's ability, [one attains great merit].
By the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha), whatever is given becomes inexhaustible.
Those who are poor, those who are diseased, and those who have performed evil deeds—
all are liberated from every sin and proceed to the world of the Sun.
When the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha has arrived,
he who dwells in the sanctuary, selfless and with senses subdued,
shall not be born diseased, nor blind, nor deaf at the time of his death.
Endowed with good fortune and beauty, he becomes beloved by women. (79) This highly meritorious Tīrtha was described by Mārkaṇḍeya;
those men who go there, O lord of kings, have been deceived—of this there is no doubt. (80)
Then one should go to Māseśvara and perform a ritual bath there;
as soon as a man has bathed there, he shall attain the heavenly world (svargaloka).
He rejoices, residing in all the worlds, for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
Then, O lord of kings, having stayed nearby that penance grove of Nāgeśvara and having bathed there, becoming pure and composed,
he sports for eternal time with many daughters of the nāgas.
One should go to the abode of Kubera, where Kubera resides;
it is the supreme holy site of Kāleśvara, where Kubera was gratified.
O Indra among kings, having bathed there, one shall obtain all prosperity.
Thereafter, one should go to the supreme abode of Maruta in the west.
Having bathed there, O king of kings, and having become pure and composed, the wise man should then give gold and food according to his capacity. 85-86.
By means of the Puṣpaka vimāna, he goes to the world of Vāyu;
from there, O Yudhiṣṭhira, he should go to my tīrtha in the month of Māgha,
and perform his bath there on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
Then one should eat only at night and avoid entering the narrow passage of rebirth (the womb).
Next, one should go to Ahalyā-tīrtha and perform a bath there; as soon as a man has bathed there, he rejoices with the Apsarases. 88–89.
Having performed penance for the sake of the Supreme Lord, he attained liberation from Ahalyā;
when the month of Caitra arrives, on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight— that day being the festival of Kāmadeva— one should worship Ahalyā.
Wherever such a man may be born, he shall be beloved there;
he shall be dear to women, prosperous, and like a second Kāmadeva.
Having reached Ayodhyā, one should visit the famous tīrtha of Śakra. 91–92.
A man who has merely bathed there obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows;
from there he should go to Somatīrtha and perform the mere act of bathing. By merely bathing there, a man is liberated from all sins.
O Indra among kings, it brings about the destruction of sins.
O lord of men, the Soma-tīrtha, renowned throughout the three worlds and yielding great fruit, is where one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. 94–95.
One whose self is purified of all sins goes to the world of Soma,
whether by entering fire, or likewise by [drowning] in water, or by fasting unto death (anāśana). He who dies at Somatīrtha is not born again among mortals.
From there, one should go to Stambhatīrtha and perform a ritual bath there;
merely by bathing there, a man is glorified in the world of Soma.
Then, O lord of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Viṣṇutīrtha. 97–98.
There is the unsurpassed Viṣṇutīrtha, renowned as Yodhanīpura; there, crores of Asuras were fought by Vāsudeva. That Tīrtha arose there, and Viṣṇu becomes pleased here.
By fasting for a day and night, one dispels the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Thereafter, O Indra among kings, one should go to the excellent Tāpaseśvara, known as Amohaka; there one should offer libations to the ancestors.
On the full moon day and the new moon day, one should perform the śrāddha rite according to the prescribed rules;
having bathed there, O King, a man should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to his ancestors. There, stones in the form of elephants are established in the midst of the water.
One should offer a funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) there, especially during the month of Vaiśākha;
the ancestors remain satisfied as long as the earth endures.
Then, O Indra among kings, one should proceed to the unsurpassed Siddheśvara.
Having gone there, O lord of kings, one should proceed to the presence of Gaṇapati;
from there, O lord of kings, one should go to where Janārdana exists as a Liṅga.
Having bathed there, O lord of kings, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
On the southern bank of the Narmadā is a most beautiful tīrtha (106).
There, the great Kāmadeva himself performs penance; for a thousand divine years, he worships Śaṅkara (107).
But having been consumed by the fire of Samādhi by the high-souled Śaṅkara,
it became like the White Mountain (Śveta-parvata), resembling a sacrificial fire on the bright fortnight.
All these [deities] residing at Kusumeśvara were thus burnt for you.
After a thousand divine years, Maheśvara was pleased with them;
accompanied by Umā, the gratified Rudra, the bestower of boons,
liberated them all as they stood upon the bank of the Narmadā.
By the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha), he has returned to the state of a god;
and by your grace, O Mahādeva, let this excellent tīrtha extend for half a yojana in every direction. 111.

Having bathed at that tirtha and being devoted to fasting, a man is glorified in the world of Rudra in the form of Kusumāyudha (the Flower-Armed One). [He is likewise glorified] by Vaiśvānara, Yama, Kāmadeva, and Vāyu. 112–113.
O King of kings, having performed penance there in ancient times, those who had arrived at that very place—
near, yet not too far from the blind man—
performed bathing, giving gifts, feeding, and the offering of funeral cakes right there.
O Agniveśa, whether in water or even by fasting,
the destiny of one who dies within half a yojana of this place is such that there is no turning back.
A preeminent man should bathe [the deceased] with the water consecrated by Tryambaka.
Even by offering a funeral cake (piṇḍa) according to the prescribed rite at the root of the Andhona tree,
his ancestors remain satisfied as long as the moon and sun endure. Furthermore,
whoever performs a ritual bath there when the winter solstice (uttarāyaṇa) has arrived—
Whether a man or even a woman, one who dwells pure in the sanctuary of the god Siddheśvara attains the goal of the virtuous by worshipping at dawn—
a goal that cannot be reached by all the great sacrifices. 118–119.
When one becomes handsome and fortunate at the time of death,
he becomes a king among mortals, ruling as far as the limits of the ocean;
yet he shall not behold Kṣetrapāla or the mighty Daṇḍapāla.
"His journey would be in vain without seeing Karṇakuṇḍala.
Having realized this fruit of the sacred ford, all the gods assembled; they released a rain of flowers and praised Kusumeśvara. 122
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. Chapter Nineteen.
Nārada said:
Then one should go with devotion to Bhārgaveśa,
where the Dānavas were sent to their destruction by the Lord Viṣṇu with a roar of "Huṃ.
O Indra among kings, having bathed there, one is liberated from all sins.
O son of Pāṇḍu, listen now to the origin of Śuklatīrtha. It is situated upon a beautiful peak of the Himavat, variegated with various minerals,
resembling the rising sun, and like unto molten gold.
There, upon a surface of variegated silk-stones with steps made of diamond and crystal,
adorned with divine lotuses made of Jāmbūnada gold,
sat the Great God, the omniscient, sovereign, and immutable Lord.

Mārkaṇḍeya questioned the Lord— who bestows grace upon the world, who is tranquil, who is surrounded by hosts of attendants, and who is accompanied by Umā— along with Skanda, Nandin, Mahākāla, Vīrabhadra, Gaṇeśa, and others.
O God of gods, Mahādeva, Indra, you who are praised by Kāma and others; I am terrified by the existence of saṃsāra—tell me the means to happiness.
O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, [grant] that which destroys all sins.
"O Lord, tell me here of that supreme holy place among all holy places.
The Lord said: "Listen, O highly fortunate Brahmin, you who are learned in all the scriptures."
Surrounded by hosts of sages, go forth to perform your ablutions and other rites.
Manu, Atri, Yājñavalkya, Kaśyapa, Aṅgiras, Yama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Kātyāyana, and Bṛhaspati—[these are the seers]. 9–10.
Nārada and Gautama, desiring to know the Dharma, asked about the meritorious Gaṅgā, Kanakhala, Prayāga, Puṣkara, Gayā,
and the holy Kurukṣetra when the sun was eclipsed by Rāhu.
Whether by day or by night, Śuklatīrtha yields great fruit (12).
Through seeing it, touching it, bathing in it, meditating upon it, performing austerities,
offering oblations, and fasting, the merit of Śuklatīrtha is immense (13).

The highly meritorious Śuklatīrtha is situated upon the river; there the royal sage named Cāṇikya attained perfection (siddhi). This sacred field (kṣetra) has arisen and extends for a circumference of one yojana.
The Śuklatīrtha is of great merit and is the destroyer of all sins.
By merely seeing its tip with the foot, one removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
O best of sages, I shall dwell here together with Umā.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the pure month of Vaiśākha,
I indeed depart from Kailāsa and am present there;
likewise, gods, kinnaras, gandharvas, siddhas, and vidyādharas [are present].

The Gaṇas, Apsarases, Nāgas, and all the gods have assembled; stationed in the sky, they remain in celestial chariots that fulfill all desires. O Indra among kings, those desiring merit have arrived at Śuklatīrtha.
Just as a washerman makes a garment white with water,
so too does one cast off the sins accumulated since birth at Śuklatīrtha,
O Mārkaṇḍeya, best of sages; bathing and giving gifts there yield great merit.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a holy ford superior to Śuklatīrtha.
Having committed sinful deeds in his earlier years,
a human being wipes them away by fasting for a day and night at Śuklatīrtha.
Neither through austerity, celibacy, sacrifices, nor again through gifts, nor even by hundreds of rituals, can that nourishment be attained which is obtained by the gift of a deity.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika—

Having fasted, one should bathe the Supreme Lord with ghee; thus, accompanied by twenty-one generations of his lineage, he shall not fall from the station of Ishvara. Shuklatirtha is a supreme sacred site, frequented by sages and perfected beings. 24–25.
Having bathed there, O King, one is no longer subject to rebirth;
having bathed at Śuklatīrtha, one should worship the Bull-bannered Lord (Śiva).
One should perform a vigil there with auspicious rites such as dance and song.
At dawn, at Śuklatīrtha, one should perform ablutions and the worship of the deities (27). Then, being pure and devoted to the vow of Śiva, one should feed the preceptor;
one should provide food according to one's means and must not practice stinginess regarding wealth (28).
Then, having performed a circumambulation, one should slowly approach the presence of the deity;
listen now to the fruit of the merit of him who acts in this manner:
mounted upon a divine vehicle, he is praised by hosts of apsarases.
Endowed with strength equal to Śiva, he remains until the dissolution of all beings. Furthermore,
whatever woman gives auspicious gold at Śuklatīrtha,
she should bathe the God with ghee and worship Kumāra.

Listen to the fruit of the merit of one who performs [this rite] with such devotion: she rejoices in the world of the gods for as long as fourteen Indras endure. On the fourteenth day of either solstice, at the transit of the sun, and likewise at the equinox—
Having bathed, fasting, with self-restrained mind and concentrated focus, one should give gifts according to one's ability so that Hari and Śaṅkara may be pleased;
by the power of Śuklatīrtha, everything becomes inexhaustible. 33-34.
Listen to the fruit of merit for him who marries at a sacred ford (tīrtha) a Brahmin who is destitute or in distress, whether he be otherwise without a protector or indeed possessed of one:
as many as are the hairs on his body, so many [years] shall it endure for the families of his progeny.
For that many thousands of years he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
36. Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. Chapter Twenty.
Nārada said:
Thereafter, one should go to Naraka and perform a ritual bath there; as soon as a man has bathed there, he beholds Naraka itself.
O son of Pāṇḍu, listen to the majesty of this Asya-tīrtha; O lord of kings, whatever bones one may cast into that tīrtha,
they all go to dissolution, and that man is born endowed with a beautiful form.
Then one should go to Gotīrtha; having seen it, one is liberated from sin.
Then, O lord of kings, one should go to the supreme Kapilātīrtha;
having bathed there, O King, a man obtains the fruit of [giving] a thousand cows.
Especially on the fourteenth day when the month of Jyeṣṭha has arrived,
that man who, fasting there with devotion, bestows a tawny cow (kapilā),
lights a lamp with ghee, and bathes Śiva with ghee;
Having offered a *śrīphala* fruit with clarified butter and performed the circumambulation at the conclusion,
the man who bestows a tawny cow (*kapilā*) adorned with bells and ornaments becomes equal to Śiva and is not born here again.
When Tuesday arrives, especially on the fourth lunar day,
one should bathe Śiva with devotion and provide a meal for the Brahmins. Likewise, on a Tuesday falling on the ninth lunar day or the new moon (amāvāsyā), one should do the same.
One should bathe [the Liṅga] there with effort; one will then become handsome and fortunate.
By bathing the Liṅga with ghee and worshipping the twice-born with devotion, one shall travel in the Puṣpaka celestial chariot, surrounded by thousands [of attendants].
He attains the state of Śiva; there is no returning from that place again.
He rejoices for an inexhaustible period of time, just as Rudra does himself.
But when, through the connection of his past karma, he returns to the world of mortals, [he is born as a king].
He becomes a most righteous king, handsome and powerful. Then, O Indra among kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Ṛṣitīrtha,
where the sage named Tṛṇabindu remains, consumed by a curse.
By the power of that sacred ford, the twice-born man was liberated from sin;
thereafter, O lord of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Gaṇeśvara on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight when the month of Śrāvaṇa has arrived.
A man who has merely bathed there in the world of Rudra is glorified.
By performing the libation for the ancestors, he is released from the three debts.
Near Gaṇeśvara is the supreme Gaṅgāvadana.

Whether free from desire or possessed of desire, that human being who bathes there is liberated from the sins committed since birth; of this there is no doubt. One should always perform a ritual bath there on the days of the lunar festivals (parva).
By performing the libation for the ancestors, one is liberated from the three debts.
Whatever merit is seen at Prayāga by the high-souled Śaṅkara,
that same entire merit is found at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Arka.
Not very far from that very place, situated toward the west,
is the site renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Daśāśvamedhika; having fasted there for one night during the month of Bhādrapada, [one attains merit].
On the new moon day, a man, having bathed, should go to where Śaṅkara resides. He should always perform his ablutions there on festival days;
by performing the libation for the ancestors, he shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
To the west of Daśāśvamedha, Bhṛgu, the best of Brahmins,
remained in worship of the Lord for a thousand divine years;
he stayed within an anthill as his southern dwelling.
A great wonder arose for Umā and Śaṅkara. Gaurī then asked the God: "Who is this stationed here? Is he a god or a dānava? Tell me, O Maheśvara. (24-25)
Īśvara said:
O beloved, Bhṛgu, the best of the twice-born, the foremost of sages and ṛṣis, being established in meditative absorption, meditates upon me and prays for a boon. 26.
There, the goddess Aprahasitā addressed Īśvara:
"From the mass of smoke and flames that arose, you have not yet been satisfied even today; you are difficult to propitiate by Asita—there is no need for further deliberation on this point. (27)
The god said: "O Mahādeva, you do not know that I have acted out of anger; I shall show you the truth as it is, and I shall do what is pleasing to you. 28.
Then the bull, whose form is dharma, was reminded by the God of gods;
and by that very remembrance of the God of gods, the bull quickly appeared.
He spoke in human speech: "O Lord, let your command be given."
"O Brahmin, covered as he is by anthills, strike him down to the ground! (30) Then, remaining established in yoga and meditating upon that, he was struck down by him;
at that very moment, inflamed with anger, he raised his hand toward the bull. (31)
Speaking thus, he said: "O bull, where are you going? Today, O bull, I shall visibly strike down your sin.
Then, having been thus provoked, the brahmin went into the intermediate space toward the bull.
He gazed further into the sky at this supreme wonder. Then, as Rudra laughed, the sage standing before him beheld the third eye and, overcome with shame, fell to the ground.
Having prostrated like a staff upon the ground, he praised the Supreme Lord;

having bowed down before you, the Lord of beings and the source of existence, I, who am terrified of worldly rebirth, O Lord of the universe, shall make a certain request concerning what has occurred. 35.
O Lord, what human being has the power to describe the multitude of Your virtues?
Even this Vāsuki, were he ever to possess a thousand mouths, would be unable to do so.
O Śaṅkara, Lord of the World, even for one whose mouth is made eloquent by devotion to You, the task of praising You remains difficult.
O Lord, be gracious to me who have fallen at your feet; forgive me, for you are the very nature of that which is to be worshipped.
O God, you are Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas in the maintenance, creation, and destruction [of the world];
O Lord of the universe, O Sovereign of the worlds, there is no deity whatsoever in the universe other than you. 37–38.
Neither the observance of restraints and disciplines, nor sacrifices, nor gifts, nor the diligent mastery of Vedic study, nor even devotion to you, is worth a thousandth part of this [attainment];
nor indeed is the perfection of superior elixirs, mercurial potions, swords, collyrium, sandals, and so forth. 39.
The marks of those who have bowed down to you are clearly visible in this birth, O Lord. Even if one bows with deceit, you grant [the fruit] to those who desire dharma;
devotion that severs worldly existence has been fashioned for liberation, O Protector. 40-41.
O Supreme Lord, protect me, who am tormented by the humiliation and intense grief of being devoted to another's wife and another's wealth, who am intent on gazing at the faces of others,
and who am consumed by false pride in the fleeting display of transient prosperity. 42 O God!

O Lord of Gods, protect me, for I have fallen upon a cruel and evil path. 43 Even though my hopes are filled with a multitude of wretched senses and kinsmen—yet so trivial—why, O Śaṅkara, do you mock me, a fool? 44
"Quickly take away my thirst and grant me the eternal Lakṣmī dwelling within my heart;
sever the bonds of pride and delusion, and deliver me, O Mahādeva!
This divine hymn named *Karuṇābhyudaya* bestows spiritual perfection."
"May Śiva be pleased with him who recites this endowed with devotion, just as he was pleased with Bhṛgu. 46. The Lord said: "O best of Brahmins, I am pleased with you; ask for whatever you desire."
"Accompanied by Umā, the God should grant him a boon.
Bhṛgu said:
"O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to me,"
"O Rudra, let it become an altar; accomplish this for me.
(48) The Lord said: "So be it, O chief of Brahmins; it shall become a place of wrath."
And from that time forward, the barber and his son will always speak with one voice.
Then, beginning from that moment, all the gods, including Brahmā and the Kinnaras,
shall worship the holy ford of Bhṛgu, where Maheśvara is pleased.
By the mere sight of that sacred ford, one is instantly liberated from sin;
there, living beings—whether against their will or by their own choice—meet their death. Their destination shall be the secret of secrets, of this there is no doubt.
