This field is exceedingly vast and destroys all sins. Having bathed there, those who die go to heaven and are not born again.
At that time, sandals, an umbrella, food, and gold should be given.

Whatever food one gives according to one's ability shall become inexhaustible for him; likewise, whatever gift one gives according to one's desire during a solar eclipse, and whatever gift of bathing at a sacred ford (tīrtha) one gives, that too shall become inexhaustible for him. 54.
O King, during lunar and solar eclipses, the release of a bull is unsurpassed;
yet deluded men, bewildered by the māyā of Viṣṇu, do not know of the divine Vṛṣatīrtha situated on the Narmadā. 55-56.
The man who hears the majesty of Bhṛgutīrtha even once is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Rudra.
Thereafter, O lord of kings, one should go to the excellent Gautameśvara.

Having bathed there, O King, a man devoted to fasting is honored in the world of Brahmā by means of a golden celestial chariot. Thereafter, he should go to Dhautapāpa, where [the sin] was washed away by the Bull.

O King, situated on the Narmadā is that which destroys all sins; by bathing at that sacred ford (tīrtha), a man casts off even the sin of killing a Brahmin. O great king, he who gives up his life at that sacred ford—
He shall become four-armed, three-eyed, and equal in strength to Rudra;
he shall dwell for more than ten thousand kalpas with prowess equal to Rudra, and after a long time, having attained his goal, he shall become the sole sovereign of the earth.
From there, O Indra among kings, one should go to the excellent Eraṇḍī-tīrtha;
whatever fruit is seen at Prayāga, as described by Mārkaṇḍeya,
that fruit a human being obtains simply by bathing there, O King.
Having fasted for one night on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the months of Bhādrapada and Āśvina, one should perform a ritual bath there; thus,
one will not be tormented by the messengers of Yama and shall go to the world of Indra.
Then, O lord of kings, one should go to where Janārdana is perfected,
the famous Hiraṇyadvīpa, which destroys all sins. Having bathed there, O king, a man shall become wealthy and handsome.

Then, O lord of kings, one should go to the great holy site of Kanakhala. O ruler of men, Garuḍa performed penance at that holy site, which is renowned throughout all the worlds; there, a Yoginī resides.
There he sports with yogis and dances together with Śiva;
having bathed there, O King, a man is glorified in the world of Rudra. 69. Thereafter, O Indra among kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Īśa-tīrtha.
Liberated there, the Lord ascended upwards; of this there is no doubt.
(70) Then, O Indra among kings, one should go to where Janārdana, the inconceivable Supreme Lord, dwells having assumed the form of a boar. (71)
Having bathed at Varāhatīrtha, especially on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī),
a man attains the world of Viṣṇu and does not go to hell.
Thereafter, O lord of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Somatīrtha.
One should especially perform a ritual bath there on the full moon day;
having prostrated before Īśāna, Bali becomes pleased with him.
The divine city of Hariścandra is seen in the intermediate space.
At that place, which was surrounded by the banner of the discus and frequented by the Ruru-kaccha region due to the force of the Narmadā’s waters,
Viṣṇu made his residence and spoke to Śaṅkara.
Having bathed at Dvīpeśvara, a man should obtain much gold. Then, O lord of kings, he should go to the confluence of the Rudrakanyā;
merely by bathing there, a man shall attain the abode of the Goddess. 76–77.
From there, one should go to Devatīrtha, which is saluted by all the gods;
having bathed there, O lord of kings, one rejoices together with the deities.
Then, O lord of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Śikhitīrtha.
Any gift given there becomes ten millionfold in merit.
(79) On the new moon day of the dark fortnight, one should perform a ritual bath there;
by feeding a single Brāhmaṇa, it is as if ten million have been fed. (80)
O Indra among kings, ten million sacred fords (tīrthas) are established at Bhṛgutīrtha;
whatever man bathes there, whether free from desire or possessed by desire,
attains the merit of a horse sacrifice and rejoices together with the gods.
There, Bhṛgu, the bull among sages, attained perfection;
an incarnation was thus made by that high-souled Śaṅkara. 82.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. 20.
The twenty-first chapter.
Nārada said:
O lord of kings, one should then proceed to the supreme Vihageśvara.
O Indra among kings, by the mere sight of it, one is liberated from all sins.
Thereafter, O Indra among kings, one should go to the supreme Narmadeśvara;
having bathed there, O King, a man is glorified in the heavenly world.
Then one should go to Aśvatīrtha and perform an ablution there; that man becomes fortunate, handsome, and wealthy. Then one should go to Pitāmaha, which was created by Brahmā in ancient times.
Having bathed there with devotion, a man should offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to his ancestors;
he should also cause water mixed with sesame seeds and darbha grass to be offered.
By the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha), everything becomes inexhaustible.
Having reached the Sāvitrī-tīrtha, whoever performs an ablution there,
having shaken off all sins, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
And right there is the Manohara-tīrtha, which is supremely beautiful.
Having bathed there, O King, a man is glorified in the world of the ancestors (pitṛloka).
Then, O lord of kings, one should go to the supreme Mānasa-tīrtha;
having bathed there, O King, a man is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Then, O lord of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Kratutīrtha,
which is renowned in all the worlds as the destroyer of all sins. Whatever desires one prays for— be they cattle, sons, or wealth— they are attained there.
O lord of men, having bathed there, one shall obtain all those [fruits].
Thereafter, O Indra among kings, one should go to the place renowned as Tridaśadyotin;
there, those daughters of sages of excellent vows perform austerities.
May the imperishable Lord and Master be the protector of them all;
may Mahādeva Hara, assuming a fierce form, be pleased with them. Having arrived at that sacred bathing place (tīrtha), he appeared with a deformed face and a loathsome appearance.
There, O Great King, is the supreme lord Varāya; he who serves the prosperity of Kanyā and bestows the gift of a maiden, that sacred ford is renowned, O Great King, as Daśakanyā. 13–14.
Having bathed there and worshipped the God, one is liberated from all sins.
Then, O lord of kings, one should go to the place known as Svargabindu.
Having bathed there, O King, a man does not behold an evil rebirth.
Then one should go to Apsareśa and perform a ritual bath there;
residing in the world of the Nāgas, one sports with the Apsarases and rejoices.
Then, O Indra among kings, one should go to the supreme Tīrtha called Naraka.
Having bathed there, one should worship the God; such a person does not go to hell. Then, devoted to fasting, one should proceed to Bhārabhūta.
Having reached this sacred ford (tīrtha), one should indeed visit the descent of Śambhu.
Having worshipped Avirūpākṣa, one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Having bathed at that tīrtha belonging to the Great-Souled Bhārabhūta, even for one who dies anywhere else, the goal of Gāṇeśvarī is certain.
Having worshipped Maheśvara during the month of Kārttika,
the wise declare that the merit is a hundred times greater than that of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. One should offer a hundred lamps filled with ghee.
He travels by means of celestial chariots as radiant as the sun to where Śaṅkara dwells.
He who gives a bull resembling a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon,
goes to the world of Rudra in a vehicle yoked with bulls.
O lord of men, at that sacred ford, one should offer a single *caru* oblation consisting of milk-rice mixed with honey and various kinds of edible foods;
O Indra among kings, one should feed others according to one's ability along with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
By the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha), everything becomes ten million times more meritorious.
Having sprinkled the water of the Narmadā and having worshipped the Bull-bannered Lord (Śiva),
they do not behold an evil state of existence due to the power of that sacred ford.
O lord of men, he who reaches this sacred ford (tīrtha) and gives up his life there becomes purified of all sins and goes to where Śaṅkara dwells; likewise,
he who enters the water at that sacred ford [attains the same].
He goes to the world of Rudra by means of a vehicle yoked with swans.
As long as the moon and the sun endure, as long as the Himavat and the great ocean, and as long as the Gaṅgā and other rivers flow, for so long he is glorified in heaven. 28–29.
O lord of men, O Indra among kings, the man who performs a fast at that sacred ford (tīrtha) is never again born into a womb.
Thereafter, O lord of kings, one should go to the supreme Aṭavī-tīrtha.
Having bathed there, O Indra among kings, a man shall obtain half the throne of the Lord. Then one should go to Śṛṅgatīrtha, which destroys all sins;
by merely bathing there as well, the state of Gaṇeśvara is certain.
The confluence of the Eraṇḍī and the Narmadā is world-renowned;
there is a sacred ford (tīrtha) of great merit that destroys all sins. Having become intent on fasting and constantly devoted to Brahman, [one should dwell there].
Having bathed there, O lord of kings, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin. From there, O lord of kings, one should go to the confluence of the Narmadā and the ocean,
known as Jamadagni, where Janārdana attained perfection.
O King, by bathing at the confluence of the Narmadā and the ocean, where Indra became the lord of the gods after performing many sacrifices,
a human being obtains the fruit of three times an Aśvamedha sacrifice. (36)
It bestows union with the Western Ocean and opens the door to liberation.
There, the gods along with Gandharvas, sages, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas worship Vimaleśvara, the Lord of Gods, at the three junctions of the day. 37–38.
With his soul purified of all sins, O Rudra, he is glorified in the world.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a supreme sacred ford (tīrtha) like Vimaleśvara. Those who observe a fast there and behold Vimaleśvara [attain the highest state].
With their souls purified of all sins, they go to the world of Rudra.
Then, O lord of kings, one should go to the supreme Keśinī-tīrtha; having bathed there, O King, a man devoted to fasting [attains the highest goal]. 40–41.

Having fasted for one night, self-restrained and restricted in diet, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin by the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha). Furthermore, whoever beholds Sāgareśvara obtains the merit of bathing in all sacred fords.
Within the distance of one *yojana*, Śiva resides established in the whirlpool (*āvarta*).
Having seen him, all sacred fords (*tīrtha*) have been seen; of this there is no doubt.
Liberated from all sins, one goes to where that Rudra dwells.
O Great King, between the confluence of the Narmadā and Amarakaṇṭaka, there exist ten million holy fords situated within the water;
wandering from one sacred ford to another is the practice cultivated by ten million sages.
O Indra among kings, she was served by those devoted to the Agnihotra sacrifice, by divine beings, and by all who are intent on knowledge; she bestows the desired objects upon them.
Furthermore, whoever would constantly recite this or listen to it with devotion— 46–47.
O Pāṇḍava, all the Taṇtu-tīrthas consecrate him; furthermore, Narmadā shall always be pleased with him—of this there is no doubt. Rudra and the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya will also be pleased with him.
A barren woman obtains sons, and an unfortunate woman becomes fortunate.
A maiden finds a husband; whatever fruit one desires, that very thing one obtains entirely—there is no need for hesitation in this matter. 49-50.
A Brāhmaṇa attains the Veda, a Kṣatriya becomes victorious, a Vaiśya obtains grain, and a Śūdra attains a good state— indeed,
even a fool acquires knowledge— whoever recites this at the three junctions of the day.
One shall not see hell, nor does one go to a base womb. 52.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the Svarga-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Twenty-two.
Nārada said: Thus, O King, has been described to you the supreme Narmadā-tīrtha, and the terrible danger arising from the curse of the Gandharva maidens in ancient times. 1.
That [sin], O Great King, was destroyed by the fire of the drops of Revā’s water;
by the touch of the drops of Revā’s water, a human being becomes liberated.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Blessed One, how and from where did the curse come upon so many maidens?
Whose offspring were they, what were their names, and what was their age? How did the touch of the waters of the Revā lead to the ripening of that curse?
"O Lord, tell me everything: from where did those liberated ones bathe? The majesty of the Narmadā tīrtha is truly wondrous;
it is said that even by hearing of it, the impurity of sins is destroyed. (4-5)
Whoever utters the words "Narmadā, Narmadā," for them there is eternal liberation as long as the moon and stars endure. You have previously described the supreme majesty of the Revā.

Nevertheless, let that virtuous conduct which has been practiced be told. Furthermore, since the highest discourse is to be cultivated by the wise, I ask you, O best of Brahmins, about the supreme majesty of the Revā.
It is a history, radiant with the conduct of those who have renounced worldly attachments through dialogue.
Nārada said:
"O tiger among kings, listen to another tale pregnant with dharma."
Just as fire resides within the fire-drill, so too did Dharma reside within Brahmā, like a sun.
There was a Gandharva named Śuka, whose singing was enchanting; he had a daughter who was utterly captivating.
She was Suśīlā, possessed of excellent character, belonging to Suśīla, who was himself a knower of the science of musical notes and possessed a beautiful voice.
O King, these were the excellent names of those apsarases: Sutārā, Candrakāntā, Candrikā, Suprabhā, and [the fifth].
All five of them were maidens, moreover, beautiful in their youth.
And they always spoke to one another like sisters;
they had emerged from the moon, as radiant as moonlight,
with faces like the moon, beautiful hair, and as brilliant as the moonstone.
Among the gods, these playful women are like moonlight among white water-lilies; possessing divine forms that captivate the mind, they seem as if formed from a mass of pure loveliness.
With the lotuses of their budding breasts in full bloom, they are like ketakī flowers in the month of Mādhava.
With the sprouts of the forest-creepers of their beloveds’ youth having emerged,
they were fair as gold, radiant with a golden luster, adorned with golden ornaments, wearing garlands of golden campaka flowers, and clothed in garments of golden brilliance. 15–16.

In the various melodies (*mūrcchanā*) of the scales (*svaragrāma*), in the playful delights of cymbals and percussion, in the playing of the flute and the lute, and in the rhythmic cycles (*laya*) of the *lāsya* dance accompanied by the sound of the drum; 17.
Expert in diversions such as painting and in the fine arts,
they were thus endowed with excellent pastimes;
cherished by their parents, they all lived in the abode of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
Once, during the month of Mādhava, five women gathered out of curiosity and wandered from forest to forest, gathering mandāra flowers;
on another occasion, celestial nymphs went to the Acchoda lake to propitiate Gaurī.
Taking from there again excellent golden lotuses along with choice blue lilies,

they bathed at the Ghaṭṭa where the pavement was made of pure vaidūrya and crystal; having put on their garments in silence, they fashioned an image of the Goddess upon a pedestal on the sacrificial mound, adorned with gold and pearl ornaments.

Having worshipped Gaurī with sandalwood paste, fragrant scents, and saffron, and having honored her with choice lotuses and various offerings, the young maidens— inspired by pure devotion— performed a dance accompanied by rhythmic movements.
Then, resorting to the art of music, they sang that song with supreme melody, harmonized by the natural resonance of their voices.
Those women, with eyes like those of a doe, sang with sweet voices, their notes rising in high pitches and their movements perfectly in harmony.

While they were thus overflowing with joy, raining down the essence of aesthetic sentiment (*rasa*) through their deeply moved mental states, the elder son of the sage Veda-nidhi arrived at that time at the sacred bathing place of Acchoda to perform his ablutions. 24–25.
In appearance, that youth with the excellent face was boundless; with eyes like full-blown lotuses, a broad chest, fine arms, and a most beautiful dark complexion, he was indeed like another Kāma.
Adorned with a topknot and a staff, he shone as a fellow student of Brahmā, like the God of Love equipped with his bow.
Clad in a deerskin, wearing a golden-colored girdle of muñja grass around his waist, and supreme, he was Samudradhṛk.
Seeing that brahmin on the shore of the lake, those young girls were filled with wonder and rejoiced, thinking, "He shall be our guest."
Having abandoned singing and dancing, they were longing to behold him;
like female deer pierced by the arrows of a hunter, they were struck by Kāma. Uttering "Look! Look! with fivefold agitation, those charming women were filled with excitement.
Upon that best of brahmins, they fell into the delusion of being Kāmadeva;
repeatedly honoring him with their eyes as if with lotuses,
the apsarases thereafter began to deliberate among themselves.
If this were Kāmadeva, how could he be devoid of Rati? Or perhaps it was both the Aśvin deities, who move as a pair;
or a Gandharva, a Kinnara, or a Siddha, assuming any form at will. (32)
Whether he be the son of a seer or some eminent man,
this person has surely been created by the Ordainer for our sake,
just as a treasure is placed by previous karmas for the benefit of those who are fortunate. (33–34)
Likewise, for us maidens, this most excellent bridegroom has been brought by Gaurī,
whose heart was moistened by the surging waves of the water of compassion; he was chosen by me, and he has been chosen by you, and likewise by her.
O best of kings, while the five maidens were speaking thus (36), the wise king, having heard their words and performed his midday rites there, reflected:
"What deed must be done so that merit may arise? (37)
Even those twice-born ones such as Gādhisambhava Parāśara and others, headed by Kaṇḍu and Devala,

though possessed of yogic power, were wonderfully deluded by the women through their effortless charms— by the sharp arrows of their glances, discharged from the firm bows of their creeper-like eyebrows.
Whose mind does the deer of desire, struck by the archer Cupid, not cause to fall? (39) Only so long does the wisdom of policy shine; only so long does fear of the people persist;
only so long is there intense stability of mind; and only so long is there concern for calculation. (40)

Only so long does men possess the boldness for austerity and only so long do they practice self-restraint, as long as they are not intoxicated by the swift-acting liquors of the glances of beautiful women. Women delude and intoxicate the passionate man with their charming and captivating graces.
They delight me, they gladden me—these women who, by their own qualities, are intent on protecting their own dharma.

(42) In the bodies of women, which are composed of flesh, blood, filth, and urine, and are devoid of merit and impure, those whose minds are utterly deluded imagine beauty and enter into them with lustful desire. (43)
"Since these women have been described as dangerous by serpents, and as unwholesome by wise men of pure intellect,
I shall go to my own home while they are still near the temple.
Before those excellent women arrive in his presence," 44.

By the power of Viṣṇu, that twice-born man then vanished; through the force of his yoga, he became invisible to the king. Having witnessed that miraculous deed of the Vaiṣṇava brahmacārī, [the king was amazed].
With eyes trembling like those of a young female deer, and filled with terror,
they gazed vacantly at the ten directions with eyes transfixed.
The maidens said:
"He clearly understands Indra's net, or rather, he knows it to be an illusion;
though seen, he has become one whose form is unseen," they said to one another. At that very moment, their hearts were pervaded by the fire of separation.
Just as a lush forest is abandoned by a blazing forest fire,
abandon this illusory magic (jālikā-vidyā) immediately and show yourself to your beloved.
It is not fitting for you to be like a fly, consumed first in his mouth.

"Alas! Why have you been shown to us? By what creator were you fashioned? It is now understood that you were created by our own self as a cause for great torment. Is your heart merciless? Do you have no regard for us? (51)
Are you cruel here in this solitary place? Do you perhaps steal our minds?
(52) Do you have no trust in us? Do you perhaps test us? Are you by nature devoid of possessiveness? Are you an expert in illusion? (53)
Do you know the agility of consciousness as it enters the mind? Do you not know the means of its exit, much less its origin?
Why indeed do you become angry with us without any fault on our part? (54)
I hope you do not experience the suffering of deceiving others? (55) Without the sight of you, our lords of the heart have now perished;
we neither live nor yet do we live, for we live only in the hope of seeing you again. (56)
"Go quickly to that place where you have gone; there, the Creator, who has stolen the sight of you, has brought about the destruction of the sprout of my joy.
By all means, show yourself; by all means, practice compassion."
The virtuous people could not see the end of anyone [in this world].
Having lamented thus and waited for many moments, those maidens then began to go home quickly out of fear of their father. 58-59.
Bound by the fetters of love for him and deeply distressed by separation, they somehow summoned their courage and returned to their respective homes;
having arrived, they all fell down before their mothers.
"What is this? Why has such a lapse of time occurred?"—thus were they questioned by their mothers.
While sporting together with the Kinnarīs, they remained at Saṅgataka on Lake Acchoda; because of that, the day was not noticed by them.
"O Mother, our bodies are weary from the journey; because of this great distress and delusion, none of us has the strength to speak.
Having said this, the young maidens rolled there upon the jeweled floor.
Concealing their true forms, those young women engaged in charming conversation with their mothers;
one was dancing a toy peacock, while another,
out of curiosity, was teaching a parrot in its cage.
She would fondle the mongoose but not the other [pets], and she would coo to the sarika bird but not to others; she would play with the cranes who were exceedingly innocent, but not with others.
She found diversion in new things, yet she did not even frequent her own palace.
They did not converse with their kinsmen, nor did they play upon the vīṇā lutes.
Whatever flowers there were from the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa), all that was like fire to them;
yet they drank the sweet honey, fragrant as the mandāra flower.
These maidens were indeed like yoginīs, with their eyes fixed on the tips of their noses,
their continuous stream of meditation imperceptible, and their minds intent upon Puruṣottama;
they were in a mountain cave concealed by moonstone gems from which water was trickling.
For a moment they stand at the window, for a moment in the fountain-house; for a moment they prepare a bed with lotus petals from the pond,
while being fanned by their friends with cool lotus leaves.
Thus those celestial women passed a night equal to an eon,
somehow maintaining their composure while trembling and as if consumed by fever;
then, seeing the sun— the jewel of the sky— in the morning, they considered themselves to have returned to life.
Having informed their respective mothers, they went to worship Gaurī.
Having bathed according to that rite and having performed the worship of the Goddess with flowers and incense, they remained there singing.
In the meantime, that brahmin also arrived at this Acchoda lake from his father’s hermitage to bathe;
just as female lotuses see their friend at the end of the night.
Seeing that celibate student, their eyes blossomed with joy;
having gone right there to the side of the celibate student, those maidens formed a noose of arms by binding them from left to right and right to left.
"O you who are dear to the sword, you departed yesterday; it is not possible for you to go today. You have surely been chosen by us; there is no doubt about this.
Thus addressed, the Brahmin, held fast by the noose of her arms, laughed and said:
"You have spoken auspicious, agreeable, and pleasing words;

however, for one established in the first stage of life who is devoted to the practice of learning, how could this vow not be destroyed, since he has not yet reached the further shore within the lineage of his guru? (79–80)
"O highly learned ones, this dharma pertaining to the three stages of life must be protected;
therefore, I consider this marriage to be dharma for young maidens.
Having heard these words of the Brahmin, the excellent women spoke to the Brahmin:
Just as the cuckoo longs for the month of Mādhava, so do all sounds long for Him;
thus the wise, possessing certain knowledge, describe how from Dharma comes Artha, from that Artha comes Kāma, and from Kāma arises the fruit of happiness. 82–83.
"Because of the abundance of dharmas that accord with their desires, this pure land has arisen before them; therefore, let it be enjoyed with various pleasures.
Having heard those words of theirs, he spoke with a profound voice:
"What you have said is true, but I too have a necessary vow.
Having obtained my teacher’s permission, I shall perform the marriage rite; otherwise, not.
Thus addressed, they replied again: 'O handsome one, you are clearly a fool! (85-86)

O Sage, by means of righteous conduct (*dharma*), a wise person should cultivate these which have come together: a perfected medicine, the elixir of immortality through the intellect of Brahman, success, a treasure, excellent women from noble families, sacred mantras, and likewise a perfected alchemical elixir.
(87) If a task, having been undertaken by chance, reaches completion, those who follow the path of policy do not neglect it.
Since equanimity does not yield fruit again, its prolongation is praised.
(88) Even from poison, one should take the nectar; even from filth, gold;
even from a low person, the highest knowledge; and even from a base family, a jewel of a woman. (89)

"Men of noble birth, pure, with hearts moistened by intense affection, possessing sweet speech, and endowed with beautiful forms and lovely youth—only such fortunate men as these obtain maidens in self-choice (svayaṃvara); indeed, no others do.
(90) Where are we, mere celestial beauties, and where are you, a young ascetic student?"
One who brings about the accomplishment of what is difficult to achieve is truly wise.
Therefore, you should now accept us through the Gāndharva form of marriage; otherwise, there shall be no further livelihood for us. 91–92.
Having heard those words, the brāhmaṇa, the most knowledgeable in dharma, then said:
"O deer-eyed one, how can dharma be abandoned by men whose wealth is dharma?
Dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—this is the fourfold aim."
As it has been said: "That which is performed according to the rules should be known as yielding fruit; that which is contrary [to the rules] is fruitless.
(94) A practitioner of vows should not take a wife at an improper time; he who does not know the proper time for an action does not obtain the fruit of that action. (95)
"Since my mind is thus occupied with this inquiry into dharma, therefore, O maidens, listen; I do not myself desire a svayaṃvara.
Having understood his intention and having looked at one another, [they spoke]. 96.
Then Pramohinī released one hand from his hand and seized his foot;
Suśīlā and Susvarā both grasped his arms; Sutārā embraced him, and Candrikā kissed his face. 97–98.
Nevertheless, though he was changeless and resembled the fire of universal dissolution,
that celibate student, utterly overcome by rage,
cursed them: "Since you have clung to me like a female demon (piśācī), you shall all become female demons."
Having been thus cursed by him, they abandoned him and stood before him, saying:
"What is this sinful deed you have committed through your conduct toward one who was innocent?
Having done what is unpleasant to one who had done you kindness, you have become a destroyer of righteousness. (100-101)
"We have heard that for a man who acts with hostility toward those who are devoted, faithful, and friendly, happiness in both worlds comes to an end.
Therefore, you too shall quickly become a piśāca due to our curse."
Having spoken thus, O King, those girls, sighing and agitated by anger,
through that very mutual agitation at the edge of that lake,
all those maidens and the celibate student attained the state of Piśācas.
Together with the male and female piśācas, they cry out most piteously as they exhaust those ripenings of the karma previously acquired;
for what was acquired in the past, whether auspicious or inauspicious, inevitably comes to fruition in its own time.
O King, like one's own shadow, they are difficult even for the gods to ward off.
Their fathers cry out here and there, as do their mothers and the brothers of those children; indeed, destiny is insurmountable.

From that point upward, those Piśācas, extremely distressed for the sake of food, dwell on the banks of the lake, running hither and thither. (108) Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. 22.
The twenty-third chapter.
Nārada said:
Thus, after a great deal of time had passed, Lomaśa, the best of sages, [arrived].
Then a highly fortunate sage arrived there by chance.
Upon seeing that brahmin, all the piśācas, agitated by hunger,
gathered together in a herd and ran toward him, desiring to devour him.
Being scorched by that intense splendor of Lomaśa,
they were all unable to stand before him and remained at a distance.
There, by the power of his past karma, a piśāca was present along with the twice-born man.
Having observed Lomaśa, O King, and having prostrated before him with all eight limbs,
she spoke these truthful words while joining her palms in reverence upon her head:
"The company of the virtuous occurs only through the dawning of great fortune."

A man may bathe in all the holy pilgrimage sites such as the Gaṅgā, yet for him who associates with the virtuous, association with the good is superior; O Brahmin, association with gurus yields both seen and unseen fruits on this earth.
"Bestower of heaven, remover of disease, dispeller of anxiety—thus he was regarded.
Having spoken thus, he related the wonderful past events:
"O Sage, these are the daughters of the Gandharvas whom I, the son of a twice-born, saw."
"O best of sages, we have all been deluded by mutual curses in the form of piśācas; with dejected faces, we stand before you.
By the sight of you, our deliverance shall come to these children."
"Upon the rising of the sun, would the mass of darkness not surely dissolve in the lotus pond?
Hearing these words of Lomaśa, his mind moistened with compassion,
the one of great luster replied to that grieving son of the sage.
"By my grace, let memory suddenly arise in all of you, and let them abide in righteousness (dharma) so that the mutual curse may come to an end. 12.
The Piśāca said:
"O Great Seer, let the dharma be told so that I may be released from this sin;
for this is no time for delay, since the fire of the curse is terrible.
Lomaśa said:
"Perform the ritual bath with me according to the prescribed injunctions;
he will surely be liberated from the curse, for there is no other atonement.
Listen attentively, O Brahmin, for this is the certain destroyer of men's sins."
"By bathing in the Revā, this shall be produced"—such was my firm conviction.
The sin committed in seven lifetimes, as well as present transgressions, the bath in the Revā consumes them all, just as fire consumes a heap of cotton. 15-16.

Whatever sin, even that which is demonic, for which one sees no atonement—that all perishes merely by bathing in the waters of the Narmadā. Therefore, bathing in the Narmadā produces knowledge, and thus it indeed has liberation as its fruit. 17.
The sacred fords (tīrthas) of the Himavat indeed remove all sins.
This [place] was fashioned by the exponents of Brahman as a bestower of the world of Indra; it is celebrated as the fulfiller of all desires and the giver of liberation. 18–19.

The *āplāva* at the Narmadā destroys sin, removes evil, grants the fruits of all desires, and bestows the world of Viṣṇu; it is the destroyer of sins. The excellent *āplāva* at the Yamunā leads to the world of the Sun.
It destroys the flow of the Sarasvatī and bestows the fruit of the world of Brahmā (21).
Viśālā is said to grant vast fruits; it is a forest fire for the fuel of sins and removes the karma that causes rebirth in the womb (22).
The Narmadā is proclaimed as leading to Viṣṇuloka and liberation;
likewise the Sarayū, Gaṇḍakī, Sindhu, Candrabhāgā, Kauśikī, Tāpī, Godāvarī, Bhīmā, Payoṣṇī, and Kṛṣṇaveṇikā. (23)
The Kāverī, the Tuṅgabhadrā, and other rivers flowing to the ocean—
O twice-born one, it is said that among them, the Revā alone bestows the world of Viṣṇu; she is attained only through the merits performed in previous births.

O son of a sage, the gods dwelling in heaven constantly sing of this immersion at the end that grants freedom from rebirth. When the Revā comes into one's sight, what harm could there be? Having bathed there, men do not experience the pain of the womb; behold, they remain in the presence of Viṣṇu. 25–26.
Those men who daily bathe here in the waters of the Revā, though clothed in many sins, sink into hells according to the law;
yet they move about in heaven like gods.
In ancient times, the Creator placed them on a scale together with severe vows, gifts, austerities, and sacrifices. (27)
There, between the two—Revā and Piśāca—the Revā was swift, and she was the one who brought about their liberation.
Nārada said: Having heard these words of Lomaśa, the Piśācas...

Together with him, they went quickly for the purpose of bathing in the Revā. Then, by chance, a breeze arose on the bank of the Revā, bestowing drops of water upon their limbs as they were touched by its current.
"By the touch of a drop of Revā’s water, they were liberated from their state as Piśācas;
at that very moment, assuming divine bodies, they praised the Narmadā. Then, by the word of Lomaśa, those Gandharva maidens—
Having married them, he lived happily for a very long time on the bank of the Narmadā with that brahmin, through bathing, drinking, and immersion in its waters.
Having worshipped the Narmadā there, they all went to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus, O King, has this history (itihāsa) concerning the virtues of the Narmadā been told to you; it is highly meritorious and destroys sin through its mere hearing. 34.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. 23.
The twenty-fourth chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Now, tell me of other sacred fords (tīrthas) spoken of by Vasiṣṭha."
"O Nārada, having heard [of them], even great sins go to destruction.
Nārada said:
"Listen, O King, to the holy places (tīrthas) spoken of by Vasiṣṭha."
Having reached the Southern Sindhu, a student of sacred knowledge who has conquered his senses attains the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and ascends a celestial chariot;
having reached the Carmaṇvatī, being self-restrained and moderate in diet, he likewise attains these rewards.
Permitted by Rantideva, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice; from there,
O knower of dharma, one should go to Arbuda, the son of Himavat, where,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, there was formerly a fissure in the earth.
Therein lies the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha, renowned throughout the three worlds;
by staying there for a single night, O lord of men, one obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows.
Having touched the waters at Piṅgatīrtha while observing celibacy, O king, one gains that same reward.
O tiger among men, one would obtain the fruit of [giving] a hundred tawny cows;
from there, one should go to Prabhāsa, renowned in the world and known for its righteousness,
where the Fire-god himself is eternally present.
O Hero, Anala, who has the wind as his charioteer, is the mouth of the deities. Having bathed in that best of holy places, pure and with a restrained mind,
a human being obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma and Atirātra sacrifices.
Then, having gone to the confluence of the Sarasvatī and the ocean, one obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows and is glorified in the heavenly world,
O bull of the Bharatas, shining eternally with splendor like a blazing fire.
Having bathed at the sacred ford of the Lord of Waters with a restrained mind,
and having stayed there for three nights, one should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
such a person shines like the moon and attains the merit of a horse sacrifice.

O best of the Bharatas, O Yudhiṣṭhira, one should then go to the Tīrtha Varadāna, where a boon was granted to Viṣṇu by Durvāsas. By bathing at Varadāna, a man obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows.
Then, self-restrained and with a regulated diet, one should go to Dvāravatī. Having bathed at Piṇḍāraka, a man shall obtain much gold.
At that sacred site (tīrtha), O Great King, [there are those] marked with the signs of a lotus.
Even today, O subduer of enemies, those mudrās are still seen; this is truly wonderful.
O descendant of Kuru, lotuses marked with the sign of the trident are seen there;
O bull of the Bharatas, the presence of Mahādeva is indeed in that very place.
O descendant of Bharata, having reached the confluence of the Sāgara and the Sindhu, and having bathed at that sacred ford of the lord of waters with a restrained mind,
one should offer libations to the ancestors, the gods, and the sages, O bull among the Bharatas.
Attaining the world of Varuṇa, he shines with his own splendor.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the wise declare that by worshipping the god Śaṅkukarṇeśvara, one obtains ten times the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Having circumambulated it clockwise, O bull of the Bharatas,
one should go to the sacred ford (tīrtha) renowned throughout the three worlds as the best among the foremost of Kurus—
famous by the name Timi and the liberator from all sins. 21.
Where Śakra and the other gods worship Maheśvara,
having bathed there and worshipped Rudra who is surrounded by hosts of gods, a person destroys the sins committed since birth. 22–23.
O best of men, having bathed there at Timirāra, which is praised by all the gods, one obtains the merit of a horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha).
O highly wise one, it was there that Viṣṇu, having conquered the son of Aditi, [established his presence].
O King, having previously performed the purification after slaying those thorns that were like obstacles to the gods,
one should then go, O knower of dharma, to the celebrated Vasudhārā.
By merely going there, one obtains the merit of a horse sacrifice.
O best of the Kurus, having bathed there with a self-controlled mind and having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, a person is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
O bull of the Bharatas, there is also another sacred ford (tīrtha) there belonging to the Vasus.
Having bathed and drunk there, one becomes esteemed by the Vasus.
Known as Sindhutamas, it is the destroyer of all sins;
having bathed there, O best of men, one obtains much gold.
Having reached Brahmatunga, pure and with a restrained mind,
that virtuous man, free from passion, attains the world of Brahmā.
This is the shrine of Kumārikā belonging to Śakra, frequented by the Siddhas.
Having bathed there, O best of men, one shall attain the world of Śakra.
Furthermore, at that very place is the tīrtha of Reṇukā, frequented by the gods;
having bathed there, a brahmin becomes as stainless as the moon.

Then, having gone to Pañcanada, one who is self-restrained and restricted in diet obtains, in due order, the five sacrifices which have been proclaimed. Thereafter, O knower of dharma, one should go to the supreme abode of Bhīmā.
O best of the Bharatas, having bathed there at Anyeyī,
O King, a man shall become the son of the Goddess, possessing earrings as his ornaments,
and he shall obtain the great fruit of giving a hundred thousand cows.
Having reached Girikuñja, which is renowned throughout the three worlds,
one obtains the merit of donating a thousand cows by bowing to the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Then, O knower of dharma, one should go to the supreme and stainless holy site (Tīrtha) of Vimala.
Even today, O best of men, where golden and silver fish are seen, by bathing there one obtains the merit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
with a soul purified of all sins, one shall go to the supreme goal. 37-38.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Twenty-Five. Nārada said:
O Bhārata, having reached the Vitastā and having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, a man obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
In Kāśmīra itself is the abode of the Nāga Takṣaka.
The place renowned as Vitastā is celebrated for liberating one from all sins.
Having bathed there, a man will certainly obtain the merit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
with his soul purified of all sins, he shall attain the supreme goal.
Then one should go to Aṭamalada, renowned throughout the three worlds;
having performed ritual ablutions according to the rules during the evening twilight,
O King, one should offer *caru* oblations to the seven-flamed fire according to one's capacity.
The wise declare that this is an inexhaustible gift for the ancestors.
A vessel of oblation for the seven-flamed fire is superior to a hundred thousand cows, a hundred Rājasūya sacrifices, and a thousand Aśvamedha sacrifices.
Having turned back from there, O Indra among kings, one should then enter the abode of Rudra;
having approached Mahādeva, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Having reached Maṇimanta, being composed and observing celibacy, one should remain there.
O King, having stayed for one night, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Then, O Indra among kings, one should go to Devikā, world-renowned,
where the origin of the Brahmins is heard of, O bull of the Bharatas.

O bull of the Bharata race, having bathed in the Devikā and worshipped Maheśvara according to one's ability, a man should offer oblations there at that place of the Trident-bearer which is renowned throughout the three worlds.

One obtains the fruit of a sacrifice in which all desires are fulfilled. There is the sacred ford (tīrtha) of Rudra called Kāma, esteemed by gods and sages; having bathed there, O Bhārata, a man quickly attains perfection.
Having gone to Yajana, Yājana, and likewise Brahmavālaka, and having touched the Puṣpanyāsa, one does not grieve over death thereafter. [It is] half a yojana in width and five yojanas in length.
They say that this much is the meritorious Devikā, esteemed by the celestial sages.
Then, O knower of dharma, one should proceed in due order to Dīrghasatra,
where Brahmā and the other gods, as well as the Siddhas and supreme ṛṣis, reside.

O Indra among the lords of gods, O subduer of enemies, by merely going there, people who have been initiated for long sacrificial sessions and are observant of fixed vows obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices. 16.16–17a.
Then, with his diet restricted, he should go resolutely to Vināśana.
While traveling, Sarasvatī remains invisible for a yojana; however, she is seen at Merupṛṣṭha, Camasa, Śivodbheda, and Āgodbheda. 17–18.
Having bathed at Camatodbheda, one obtains the fruit of an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice;
having bathed at Śivodbheda, a man obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows;
and having bathed at Nāgodbheda, a man attains the world of the Nāgas.
O Indra among kings, having reached that difficult-to-attain sacred ford where,
O Bhārata, the lotuses are concealed in the form of hares on the Sarasvatī for a full year, O highly fortunate one. (20–21)
O best of the Bharatas, those who always bathe there on the full moon day of Kārttika,
having bathed there, O tiger among men, always shine like Śiva; and one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows, O bull of the Bharatas.
O descendant of Kuru, having reached Kumārakoṭi, one becomes free from all doubt;
there, intent on the worship of the ancestors and the gods, one should perform an ablution.
One obtains the merit of ten thousand cows and uplifts one's entire lineage. 23-24.
Then, O knower of dharma, one should go with a concentrated mind to Rudrakoṭi,
where in ancient times, O great king, ten million sages were assembled with focused minds for a year, longing for a vision of the God.
"I shall see the bull-bannered Lord first, I shall see him first!"—
thus, O King, O descendant of Bharata, did the sages set out.
Then, O lord of the earth, the Lord of Yogins also resorted to his yogic power.
For the sake of pacifying the anger of those sages of purified souls,
I created ten million Rudras who stood before the sages;
they each thought individually, "Hara was seen by me first."
O King, Mahādeva, being pleased with those ṛṣis of fierce splendor,
granted them a boon out of supreme devotion:
"From this day forward, there shall be an increase in your righteousness."

Having bathed there at Rudrakoṭi, O tiger among men, a pure man obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and uplifts his entire lineage. Thereafter, O lord of kings, one should go to the world-renowned confluence.
On the Sarasvatī, one should worship Janārdana, which is of great merit;
where, O Indra among kings, Brahmā and the other gods, as well as ṛṣis, siddhas, and cāraṇas, go on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra.
Having bathed there, O tiger among men, one who gives much gold becomes purified of all sins in soul and goes to the world of Śiva; it was there,
O lord of men, that the sacrificial sessions of the sages were completed.
Having reached the conclusion there, one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. Chapter Twenty-six.
Nārada said:
Thereafter, O lord of kings, one should go to the highly praised Kurukṣetra;
all living beings who have gone there are liberated from their sins. 1.
"I shall go to Kurukṣetra; I shall dwell in Kurukṣetra"—whoever should constantly speak thus is liberated from all sins.
O lord of men, a wise man should dwell there for a month on the banks of the Sarasvatī.

O lord of the earth, O descendant of Bharata, where Brahmā and the other gods reside, and where the celestial sages, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Apsarases, Yakṣas, and Pannagas dwell— that most meritorious field of Brahman— go there.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, even for one who merely desires [to go] with their mind, sins perish at Kurukṣetra and they go to the world of Brahmā.
For having gone to Kurukṣetra endowed with faith, O best of the Kurus—
A person obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
Then, O King, there is the gatekeeper Mattarṇaka of great strength;
by saluting him, one indeed obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.

Then, O Indra among kings, one should go to the unsurpassed abode of Viṣṇu, the knower of dharma, where Hari is eternally present. Having bathed there and having beheld Hari, the source of the three worlds;
One obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. 9. Thence one should go to Pāriplava, a tīrtha renowned throughout the three worlds;
there a person obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma and Atirātra sacrifices. 10.
Having reached Tīrtha on the earth, one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows;
then, O lord of men, the pilgrim having gone to Śālvikinī and bathed at Daśāśvamedhika, he obtains that same fruit.

Having reached Sarpanīvi, the supreme tirtha of the Nāgas, one obtains the merit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and goes to the world of the Nāgas. From there, O knower of dharma, one should go to Dvārapāla Matarṇaka. 12–13.
Having stayed there for one night, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows;
then, having gone to Pañcanada, self-restrained and restricted in diet, one obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice by touching the waters at Koṭitīrtha.
Having come to Aśvinī-tīrtha, one is born endowed with beauty.
Then, O knower of dharma, one should go to the supreme Vārāha-tīrtha,
where in ancient times Viṣṇu remained in the form of a boar.
Staying there, O tiger among men, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice;
thereafter, O lord of kings, one should enter Somatīrtha at Jayantī. Having bathed there, a person attains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Having bathed at Ekahaṃsa, a man obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows. O best of the Kurus, the pilgrim who reaches Kṛtaśauca attains the Puṇḍarīka and becomes purified.
Then, having stayed for one night at the place named Muñjāvaṭa belonging to the wise Mahādeva, one shall obtain the status of a leader of the Gaṇas.
And in that very place, O great king, is Jayā, renowned throughout the world.
O Indra among kings, having bathed and approached [that place], one shall obtain all desires.
O bull of the Bharatas, that is the renowned gateway to Kurukṣetra;
the pilgrim, having performed a circumambulation, returns fully restored.
O King, by remembering the Puṣkara lakes, bathing there, and worshipping the ancestors and the gods,
one becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose and attains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice, when summoned by the high-souled Rāma, the son of Jamadagni. 23.
Thereafter, O lord of men, the pilgrim should go to Rāmahrada,
where, O king of kings, Rāma— possessing blazing splendor and prowess—
having eradicated the kṣatriyas by his might, resorted to five lakes.
"O tiger among men, we have heard that you have filled [the vessels] with blood;
thus all the ancestors and likewise the great-grandfathers have been gratified.
Then those ancestors, being pleased, spoke to Rāma, O lord of the earth. (25-26)
"O highly fortunate descendant of Bhṛgu, we are pleased with you because of this devotion to your father and because of your prowess, O sinless one.
Choose a boon—may it be well with you—what do you desire, O high-minded one? (27)

Thus addressed, O lord of kings, Rāma, the best among eloquent speakers, spoke with palms joined in reverence to his ancestors stationed in the sky: "If you are pleased with me, and if I am worthy of your favor... (28-29)
"By the grace of my father, I desire once again to nourish myself through asceticism; for that constellation which was destroyed by me while overcome by anger—
may I be released from that sin through your splendor."
"May these lakes become famous on earth as sacred pilgrimage sites.
Having heard these auspicious words of Rāma, his fathers then replied to him, filled with supreme joy and satisfaction.
"May your ascetic power increase even further, especially through your devotion to your father;
for that constellation which was destroyed by you while overcome by anger—
thereby you are released from that sin, and they have been slain by their own karma."
These lakes will undoubtedly attain the status of sacred fords (tīrthas).
Whoever bathes in these lakes and offers libations to the ancestors, his ancestors, being pleased, shall grant him that which is difficult to obtain on earth.
"Having thus granted the boon of his heart's desire— the eternal world of heaven— O King, Rāma’s ancestors, being pleased, took leave of Bhārgava and then vanished on the spot. (36)
O king of kings, having bathed in these holy lakes of Rāma— the lakes of the high-souled Bhārgava— a celibate student observing auspicious vows and having worshipped Rāma, shall obtain much gold.
O best of the Kurus, having reached Vaṃśamūla, the pilgrim should uplift his own lineage;
O King, by bathing at Vaṃśamūlaka, he attains purification of the body. O most excellent of the Bharatas, having reached the holy site of Kāyaśodhana— 38–39.

Having bathed there, one undoubtedly attains purity of body; with a purified body, one goes to the auspicious and unsurpassed worlds. Thereafter, O lord of kings, one should go to the sacred ford that is difficult to find even in the three worlds.
Formerly, the worlds were rescued by the all-powerful Viṣṇu. Having reached the world-rescuing Tīrtha, renowned throughout the three worlds,
O King, one who bathes in that best of Tīrthas rescues his own people.
Having reached Śrītīrtha, one obtains supreme prosperity; and having reached Kapilātīrtha, being a celibate student and composed in mind,
one should bathe there and likewise worship the gods and the ancestors.
A person obtains the fruit of a thousand Kapila cows by reaching Sūryatīrtha, bathing with a restrained mind,
honoring the ancestors and the gods, and being devoted to fasting. 44–45.

The pilgrim who visits the sacred sites in due order attains the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and goes to the world of the Sun; having reached the abode of cows, he obtains the merit of a thousand cows for performing an ablution there. 46.
O lord of men, having reached the Gaṅgā-tīrtha, a pilgrim who bathes there obtains supreme vigor. Then, O Indra among kings, one should go to the gatekeeper Lavaṇaka. 47–48.
At that sacred ford on the Sarasvatī, which belongs to the high-souled Indra,
a man who bathes there, O King, obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Thereafter, O knower of dharma, O lord of men, he should go to Brahmāvarta.
Having bathed in Brahmāvarta, a man shall attain the world of Brahmā. From there, O knower of dharma, one should go to the unsurpassed Sutīrthaka,
where the ancestors are eternally present together with the deities.
There, one devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods should perform an ablution;
he obtains the merit of a horse sacrifice and goes to the world of the ancestors.
Then, the knower of dharma, having reached another sacred ford (tīrtha) in due order—
O best of the Bharatas, having bathed in the sacred fords of the Lord of Kāśī,
one is liberated from all diseases and is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
And right there, O King, is the Mātṛ-tīrtha, where one who has bathed [attains the same].
O King, by increasing one's progeny, one shall attain the heavenly realm;
thereafter, self-restrained and restricted in diet, one should go to Śītavana.
O great king, that sacred ford (tīrtha) there is another that is difficult to find elsewhere.

O King, by the mere sight of this [Daṇḍa], one is purified; even those with hair as long as a reed become pure here, O Bhārata. Furthermore, there is another excellent tīrtha there known as Snātalokārtihan.
O best of the twice-born, they remove their bodily hairs through breath-control (prāṇāyāma);
O king of kings, having purified their souls, they attain the supreme goal at that very holy site, Daśāśvamedhika, O lord of the earth. 59–60.
O tiger among men, having bathed there, they go to the supreme goal. Thereafter, O lord of kings, one should go to Mānuṣa, which is renowned in the world.
There, O King, black deer were afflicted by the arrows of a hunter.
Having plunged into that lake, those who have attained human form [are purified]. Having bathed at that sacred ford (tīrtha), a man who is celibate and composed,
his soul cleansed of all sins, is glorified in the heavenly world.
O Lord of the Earth, one krośa to the east of Mānuṣa is a river not widely known, frequented by siddhas; there,
the man who offers food made of śyāmāka grain—
Aiming for the gods and the ancestors, the fruit of that dharma is great. When one Brahmin is fed there, it is as if ten million have been fed.
Having bathed there and having likewise worshipped the deities and the ancestors, [one obtains great merit]. 65–66.
Having stayed for one night, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice;
from there, O Bhārata, one should go to the supreme abode of Brahmā,
known as Brahmānusvara, which is radiant upon the earth.
O bull of the Bharata race, O lord of kings, having bathed there in the seven sages' pools (Saptarṣikuṇḍas) and at Kedāra as well as at the site of the high-souled Kapila,
one should then approach Brahmā, pure and with a restrained mind.
With his soul purified of all sins, he attains the world of Brahmā;
having reached Kapiṣṭhala’s Kedāra, which is very difficult to attain,
he achieves invisibility, his impurities burnt away by austerity.
Then, O lord of kings, one should go to Sarvaka, renowned throughout the world.
By approaching Vṛṣadhvaja on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
one indeed obtains all desires and goes to the heavenly world.
There are thirty million sacred fords (tīrthas), O joy of the Kurus, and among them, the most excellent;
likewise, there is Rudrakoṭi at the well, and Samantaka in the lakes, as well as the Ilāspada tīrtha right there, O best of the Bharatas. 72–73.
Having bathed there and having worshipped both the deities and the ancestors,
one does not meet with an evil fate and obtains the merit of a Vājapeya sacrifice. O Lord of the Earth, what gift should a man give after bathing there, and what should he recite?
A man who, possessing faith and with his senses subdued, sips water at Kalaśī, obtains immeasurable merit from both charity and sacrifice;
such a person attains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
To the east of Saraka is the auspicious tīrtha of the great-souled Nārada, O best of the Kurus, renowned as Rāmajanma.
Having bathed in that tīrtha and having cast off his life-breaths there, O Bhārata, a man [attains liberation].
Permitted by Nārada, he attains worlds that are difficult to reach;
on the tenth day of the bright fortnight, one should enter Puṇḍarīka.
Having bathed there, O King, a man obtains the fruit of the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice.
Thence one should go to Triviṣṭapa, renowned throughout the three worlds. There flows the meritorious river Vaitaraṇī, which liberates one from sin;
having bathed there and worshipped the trident-bearing Lord whose banner is the bull, [one attains the highest goal].
With his soul purified of all sins, he shall attain the supreme goal;
from there, O lord of kings, he should go to the excellent Phalaki forest.
There, O King, the gods have taken refuge in the Phalaki forest together with their wives.
They perform extensive austerities for many thousands of years. Having bathed at Dṛṣatpāna and offered libations to the deities,
a man obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma and Atirātra sacrifices.
O best of the Bharatas, O lord of kings, by bathing at the sacred ford (tīrtha) of all the gods, a human being obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Having bathed at the place known as Pāṇi and having offered libations to the deities, a man [obtains that same fruit].
By performing the Rājasūya sacrifice, one attains [the fruit thereof] and goes to the world of the Ṛṣis (85).
Thence, O knower of dharma, one should go to the world-renowned Miśraka;
there, O lord of kings, the tīrthas have been mixed together by the Great-Souled One (86).

O tiger among kings, we have heard from Vyāsa that whatever merit a man gains by bathing in all the sacred fords (tīrthas), a man who bathes in the Miśraka [tīrtha] gains that same merit. Therefore, with self-restraint and a regulated diet, one should go to the forest of Vyāsa.
Having bathed at Manojavana, a man obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Having gone to Madhuvana, the abode of the Goddess, a pure man,
being self-restrained and clean, should bathe there and worship the gods and the ancestors.

O Bhārata, he who, permitted by the gods and men, bathes at the confluence of the Kauśikī and the Dṛṣadvatī while restrained in diet, shall obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows and be liberated from all sins.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, it is at Vyāsasthalī that the wise Vyāsa, tormented by grief for his son, resolved to abandon his body; however, he was restored to life once again by the gods. 91–92.
By visiting Abhigamyasthala, one obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows;
and by reaching Ṛṇāntakūpa and offering a prastha of sesame seeds, O lord of men, one is liberated from debts and attains supreme perfection.
Having bathed at the Vedītīrtha, a man obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
O King, there are two Tīrthas difficult to attain, namely Ahaḥ and Sudina;
by bathing in those two, an excellent man attains the world of the Sun.
Then one should go to Mṛgadhūma, renowned throughout the three worlds;
having bathed there at Rudrapada and worshipped the high-souled wielder of the trident, a person obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. 96.
Having bathed at Koṭitīrtha, a man shall obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Or else, having gone to Vāmanaka, which is renowned throughout the three worlds,
and having bathed there in Viṣṇupada and duly worshipped Vāmana— 97–98.

With his soul purified of all sins, he shall attain the world of Viṣṇu; by bathing there, a man purifies his lineage, and that man sanctifies his own family. Having gone to the lake of Pavana, the supreme tīrtha of the Maruts, [he attains the same].
Having bathed there, O tiger among men, one is glorified in the world of Vāyu.
Having bathed at the feet of the immortals and having duly worshipped the Lord of the Immortals,
one is glorified in the heavenly world through the power of the immortals.

O Indra among kings, O best of men, having bathed according to the prescribed rites at Śālisūrya in the Śālihotra [river], one obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows. O best of the Bharatas, there is also the holy site of Śrīkuñja on the Sarasvatī.

O King, having bathed there, a man obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. Then, O Indra among kings, having reached the Naimiṣa grove which is very difficult to attain, it is said that the sages of Naimiṣa, whose wealth is their austerity, [reside there].
In ancient times, having set out on a pilgrimage to the sacred fords, they went to Kurukṣetra;
then, O best of the Bharatas, Kuñja was created upon the Sarasvatī so that there might be a great and pleasing space for the sages. 105.
Having bathed in that Kuñja, a person shall obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
106. Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. Chapter Twenty-Seven.
Nārada said: From there, O knower of dharma, one should go to the unsurpassed Kanyātīrtha;
by bathing at Kanyātīrtha, a man obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
From there, O tiger among men, one should go to the supreme abode of Brahmā;
having bathed there, even a man of inferior caste attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa,
while a Brāhmaṇa of purified soul attains the highest goal.
Then that tiger among men should go to the unsurpassed Somatīrtha;
having bathed there, O King, a man shall attain the world of Soma.
Next, O lord of men, he should go to the Saptasārasvata Tīrtha.
Seeing the entire universe, the great ascetic, the brahmin-sage Kila, was overcome with joy; with eyes wide with wonder, he began to dance.
Then, as he danced, everything—both the stationary and the moving—began to dance as well.
Both dances were bewildered by the splendor of that hero;
then, O lord of men, Mahādeva was petitioned by the gods, headed by Brahmā, and by the sages whose wealth is asceticism, for the sake of the rishi.
"Just as this god does not dance, so you ought to act.
Then the god, seeing the sage dancing with a heart filled with joy, spoke to him out of a desire for the welfare of the steadfast.
"O great sage, knower of dharma, for what reason are you dancing? Or for what reason, O bull among munis, is there this cause for your joy? The Rishi replied:

"O best of the twice-born, O Brahmin, do you not see that the vegetable juice mixed with blood has been spilled by me, who am an ascetic established on the path of dharma? Seeing this, I have indeed begun to dance, overwhelmed by great joy."
Laughing, the god spoke to that rishi who was deluded by passion: "O Brahmin, I do not feel any astonishment; behold me here as I am.
Having spoken thus to the best of men, Mahadeva [did this]. 13–14.
O sinless lord of kings, when his own thumb was struck by the tip of his finger, O King,
ashes resembling snow issued forth from the wound;
seeing which, O King, the sage was filled with shame and fell at [the king's] feet.
O Rudra, I do not consider any other god to be greater than you;
you are the refuge of the world of gods and asuras, O wielder of the trident.
This entire universe, the three worlds with all things moving and unmoving, was created by you. 16–17.
O Blessed One, at the end of the eon, everyone enters into you alone; even by the gods you cannot be fully known, so how could you be known by me?
O sinless one, all the gods, beginning with Śakra, are seen within you.
"You alone are the constant creator and the one who causes all these worlds to be created.
By your grace, all the gods rejoice here, free from fear from any quarter.
Having thus praised Mahādeva, the sage bowed down and spoke.
"O Mahādeva, by your grace, may this penance of mine not perish.
Then the God, with a delighted soul, spoke thus to the Brahmarṣi: "O Brahmin, by my grace, may your penance increase a thousandfold."
"O great sage, I shall dwell here in this hermitage together with you.
Those who bathe in the Saptasārasvata and worship me—for them, nothing whatsoever will be difficult to attain, either in this world or in the next. (22-23)
One shall go to the world of Sarasvatī; of this there is no doubt. Having spoken thus, Mahādeva vanished right there.
Then, one should go to Auśanasa, which is renowned throughout the three worlds.

O Bhārata, there, at the three junctions of the day, the gods headed by Brahmā, the sages whose wealth is asceticism, and the blessed Kārttikeya would indeed maintain their presence out of a desire to please Bhārgava.
The Kapālamocana tīrtha destroys all sins;
having bathed there, O tiger among men, one is liberated from all evils. Then, O bull of the Bharatas, one should go to Agnitīrtha and bathe.
One attains the world of Agni and uplifts one's lineage.
O best of the Bharatas, right there is the tīrtha of Viśvāmitra; having bathed there, O great king, one is born into the status of a Brāhmaṇa. 28–29.
Having reached Brahmayoni, pure and with a restrained mind, one who bathes there, O tiger among men, attains the world of Brahmā;
he purifies his lineage up to the seventh generation— of this there is no doubt.

Then, O lord of kings, one should go to the tirtha renowned throughout the three worlds, known as Pṛthūdaka belonging to Kārttikeya, O monarch; there, devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods, one should perform an ablution. 31-32.

O Bhārata, whatever inauspicious karma has been committed by a person of human intellect— whether through ignorance or knowledge, whether by a woman or by a man— all that perishes for one who has merely bathed there.
One obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) as well as heaven itself.
They say Kurukṣetra is meritorious; [more so than] Kurukṣetra is the Sarasvatī; [more so than] the holy fords of the Sarasvatī are Pṛthūdaka among all holy fords. 34–35.
He who, devoted to silent recitation (*japa*), should cast off his body at Pṛthūdaka— the most excellent of all sacred fords— shall never again undergo the cycle of worldly existence;
thus it was sung by Sanatkumāra and by the high-souled Vyāsa.
O King, one should go to Pṛthūdaka, which is not restricted by the Vedas.
O best of men, there is no sacred ford more meritorious than Pṛthūdaka;
it is pure, holy, and purifying—of this there is no doubt.
O best of men, the wise say that even people who have committed sins go to heaven after bathing there at Pṛthūdaka;
and right there, O most excellent of the Bharatas, is the sacred ford known as Madhusrava.
Having bathed there, O King, a man obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows.
Then, O best of men, one should proceed in due order to the world-renowned confluence of the Sarasvatī and the Aruṇā, which belongs to the Goddess. 40–41.
Having fasted for three nights and bathed, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin and obtains the fruit equal to that of the Agniṣṭoma and Atirātra sacrifices;
he purifies his lineage up to the seventh generation— of this there is no doubt.
O scion of the Kuru lineage, there is also the Avakīrṇa tīrtha, created in ancient times by Darbhi out of compassion for the Brahmins;
[therein] a twice-born man [is purified] by means of the vows, the initiation ceremony, or fasting. 43–44.

A Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with ritual actions and mantras becomes [perfected], of this there is no doubt; even one devoid of ritual actions and mantras, O bull among men, becomes a twice-born who has fulfilled his vows by bathing there—
this has been seen in ancient times.
Furthermore, the four oceans were brought together by Darbhi;
having bathed there, O tiger among men, one shall not meet with an evil fate, and he obtains the fruit of four thousand cows.
From there, O lord of kings, one should go to the two world-renowned tīrthas, Śatasahasraka and Sāhasraka;
by bathing in both, a man obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Whether it be charity or fasting, it shall become multiplied a thousandfold.
Thereafter, O lord of kings, one should go to the supreme Reṇukā-tīrtha;
there, devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods, one should perform an ablution. 49-50.
With his soul purified of all sins, he who has conquered anger and mastered his senses obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice upon touching the water at Vimocana;
he is completely liberated from all sins incurred through the acceptance of gifts.
Then, having gone to Pañcavaṭa as a celibate student with senses subdued,
one endowed with great merit is glorified in the heavenly world;
for there stands Sthāṇu himself, the Lord of Yogins, whose banner is the bull.
By worshipping that Lord of Gods, one attains perfection simply by going there;
the Taijasa-Vāruṇa Tīrtha shines with its own splendor,
where the gods led by Brahmā and the sages whose wealth is penance [reside].
Then Guha was consecrated as the commander-in-chief of the gods.
O best of the Kurus, to the east of Taijasa is the Kurutīrtha;
having bathed at Kurutīrtha, a man who is celibate and has conquered his senses [attains merit].
With his soul purified of all sins, he attains the world of Rudra; then,
self-restrained and moderate in diet, he goes to the gate of heaven and attains the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice as well as the world of Brahmā.
From there, O lord of men, the pilgrim shall go to Anaraṇya;
having bathed there, O King, a man shall not meet with an evil fate, for Brahmā himself is eternally glorified there along with the gods. 58–59.
O best of kings, O upholder of the lineage of Rudra, by the arrival of those tigers among men who have attained the state of Nārāyaṇa, and by their very presence at the Vedic altar of Rudra,
one shall not meet with an evil fate after approaching that goddess.
And right there, O Great King, by approaching Mahādeva, the Lord of the Universe and Consort of Umā, one is liberated from all sins;
and by approaching Nārāyaṇa, the lotus-navelled one, O subduer of enemies—
O great king, as soon as one has bathed in the sacred fords (tīrthas) of all the gods, one becomes radiant and attains the world of Viṣṇu;
entirely freed from all suffering, he shines forever like Śiva.
Then, O lord of men, the pilgrim should go to Asthipura.
Having reached that purifying tīrtha, he should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
thus, O Bhārata, he obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
O bull of the Bharatas, there is the Gaṅgā-hrada and a well at that very spot; three crores of sacred fords (tīrthas) are magnified within that well.
Having bathed there, O King, a man attains the world of Brahmā.
Having bathed in the Āpagā river and worshipped Maheśvara,
a man attains the supreme goal and uplifts his lineage;
thereafter, he should go to Sthāṇuvaṭa, which is renowned throughout the three worlds.
Having bathed there and stayed for the night, one shall attain the world of Rudra;
from there, one should go to the grove of Badarīs and then to the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha.
There, a man who has fasted for three nights may eat the Badarī fruits.
O lord of men, he who eats badarī fruits for twelve full years and likewise fasts for three nights shall be equal [to the merit of visiting Indra’s path].
O lord of men, having reached Indra’s path, the pilgrim [attains this]. 70–71.
By fasting for a day and a night, one is glorified in the heavenly world;
having reached [this place] for even a single night,
a man who is self-restrained and truthful in speech is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
O Indra among kings, one should likewise go to that tīrtha renowned throughout the three worlds, where the hermitage of the high-souled Āditya, a mass of splendor, is located;
having bathed in that tīrtha and having worshipped Vibhāvasu, a man [attains merit]. 73–74.
O best of the Kurus, by bathing at the Soma-tīrtha, a man who frequents sacred fords goes to the world of Āditya and uplifts his entire lineage;
such a man attains the world of Soma— of this there is no doubt.
From there, O lord of men, one should go to the most meritorious tīrtha of Dadhīca, who was a knower of dharma— O King, it is purifying and world-renowned—
where that treasure-house of asceticism attained perfection through his penance on the banks of the Sarasvatī. (76–77)
Having bathed at that tirtha, a man obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice and also attains Sarasvatī-like intelligence; of this there is no doubt.
Then, having gone to Kanyāśrama with self-restraint and celibacy, he should remain there.
O King, having stayed for three nights devoted to fasting,
one obtains a hundred divine maidens and goes to the world of Brahmā.
From there, O knower of dharma, one should go to the Tīrtha called Saṃnihitī.
Where Brahmā and the other gods, as well as the sages whose wealth is austerity, endowed with great merit, shall assemble month after month;
having performed ablutions at Sannihitī when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu.
By him, a hundred horse-sacrifices have been eternally performed.
Whatever sacred fords exist on earth and those that move in the intermediate space, as well as wells, O Brahmins, and holy shrines— [all these he has visited]. 82–83.
O lord of men, O tiger among men, O lord of the earth, there is no doubt that on the new moon day every month,
the gods will assemble here; because of this gathering at the sacred ford, it has become renowned throughout the world as Sannihitī.
Having bathed and drunk there, one is glorified in the heavenly world.
(85) Now hear the fruit of the merit of that mortal who performs a śrāddha on the new moon day, as well as when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu. (86)

A man who performs a śrāddha and sips water obtains the very same fruit that results from a thousand horse-sacrifices properly performed. Whatever evil deed has been committed by a renunciant, a woman, or a man— [it is all purified]. 87.
As soon as one has bathed, all that perishes; of this there is no doubt.
By means of a lotus-colored vehicle, he goes to the world of Brahmā.
Then, having saluted the doorkeeper named Mucukunda by name—
O best of the Bharatas, right there is the Gaṅgāhrada tīrtha; O knower of dharma, one who is self-controlled and observant of celibacy should bathe there,
and that person obtains the fruit of both the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
Naimiṣa is sacred on earth, and Puṣkara is sacred in the intermediate space;
yet Kurukṣetra excels all three worlds.
Even the dust particles of Kurukṣetra, when wafted by the wind, [purify].
Moreover, they lead even one who has performed evil deeds to the supreme goal—
those who dwell to the south of the Sarasvatī and to the north of the Sarasvatī; those who dwell in Kurukṣetra dwell in Triviṣṭapa.
"I shall go to Kurukṣetra; I shall dwell in Kurukṣetra. Even by uttering this single speech, one is glorified in the heavenly world.
Kurukṣetra is the sacred altar of Brahman (*brahmavedī*), a holy place frequented by the Brahman-sages.
O King, those who dwell there are not to be grieved for in any way.

The space between the Taraṇḍaka and Karaṇḍaka [lakes], and between Rāmahrada and Cakrūka—this is Kurukṣetra, known as Samantapañcaka, which is said to be the northern altar (uttaravedi) of Pitāmaha. 96.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Twenty-Eight. Nārada said:
From there, one should go to the ancient Dharmatīrtha, known to those who know the Dharma,
where the highly fortunate Dharma performed supreme penance. By him, that meritorious tīrtha was established and marked with his own name.

O King, having bathed there, a man of virtuous character who is composed in mind purifies his lineage up to the seventh generation; of this there is no doubt. Thereafter, O knower of dharma, one should proceed to the supreme Kalāpavana forest.
Having traveled with great difficulty and bathed there with a concentrated mind,
one obtains the merit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
O King, from there, that person should go to the Saugandhika forest.
Where the gods headed by Brahmā, the sages rich in asceticism,
the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, along with the great serpents (Mahoragas) reside—
merely upon entering that forest, one is liberated from all sins.
Then, O King, there is the Sarasvatī, the best of rivers, the most excellent of streams, known as Plakṣādevī; she is highly meritorious.
One should perform an ablution there in the water that has emerged from an anthill.
Having worshipped the ancestors and the gods there, one obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
That Tīrtha, named Īśānādhyuṣita, is very difficult to attain;
it is certain that its merit is sixfold at places where anthills and the like have fallen.
O tiger among men, having bathed there, one obtains a thousand tawny cows and the merit of a horse sacrifice; this was seen by the ancients,
O Bhārata, as well as [the merit of] Sugandhā, Śatakumbhā, and Pañcayajña.
Having approached that best of men, one is glorified in the heavenly world.
(11) Having reached that rare holy ford (tīrtha) there called Triśūlapātra, one devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods should perform an ablution there. (12)

Without a doubt, he shall attain the status of a Gaṇapati after casting off his body; thereafter, he should go to Rājagṛha, the station of the Goddess that is very difficult to reach. She is renowned as Śākambharī, famous throughout the three worlds.
