O descendant of Bharata, O lord of men, it is said that for a thousand divine years she took food only once every month in the form of potherbs; meanwhile,
sages rich in asceticism who were devoted to the Goddess arrived there.

O Bhārata, because hospitality was offered to them with vegetables (śāka), the name Śākambharī became established for her. Having reached Śākambharī, one who is self-controlled and observant of celibacy—
Having stayed there for three nights, self-restrained and pure, one should subsist on vegetables.
O Bhārata, whatever fruit is obtained by one who subsists entirely on vegetables for twelve years, that same fruit belongs to him who acts by the will of the Goddess.
Then one should go to the place called Suvarṇa, renowned throughout the three worlds,
where in ancient times Kṛṣṇa propitiated Rudra for the sake of obtaining grace and received many boons that are difficult even for the gods to attain. 19.
O Bhārata, it was said by the gratified destroyer of Tripura:
"Moreover, O Kṛṣṇa, you shall become dearer than one's own self in this world; and the entire universe shall have its face turned toward you—of this there is no doubt. (20-21)

O Indra among kings, having gone there and worshipped the bull-bannered god (Śiva), one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and attains the status of a leader of Gaṇas. Then, a man should go to Dhūmāvatī and stay there for three nights.
One obtains the desires prayed for by the mind; of this there is no doubt.
O lord of men, the Rathāvarta is located in the southern half of the Goddess's [domain];
having gone there, O knower of dharma, one who is faithful and has conquered his senses [attains these fruits]. 23–24.
O bull of the Bharatas, by the grace of Mahādeva, one shall go to the supreme goal; having performed a circumambulation,
one should proceed to the place named Dharā, O highly wise one, which destroys all sins.
Having bathed there, O tiger among men, one does not grieve, O lord of men.
Then, O tiger among men, having paid homage to the great mountain, one should proceed to Gaṅgādvāra, which is equal to Svargadvāra; of this there is no doubt. (26–27)
There, being composed in mind, one should perform an ablution at Koṭitīrtha;
one obtains the Puṇḍarīka [merit] and indeed uplifts one's entire lineage.
By staying there for a single night, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.

One should offer libations at Saptagaṅgā, Trigaṅgā, and Śakrāvarta according to the prescribed rites for the gods and ancestors; thus one is glorified in a meritorious world. Then, having bathed at Kanakhala and fasted for three nights, a man [attains the same].
O lord of men, the pilgrim who goes to Kapilāvaṭa obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the heavenly world;
by staying there for a single night, he gains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
O Indra among kings, O best of the Kurus, there is the holy site of the high-souled Nāga king Kapila,
renowned throughout all the worlds; there, O lord of men,
one should perform an ablution at the Nāga-tīrtha.
A human being obtains the fruit of [giving] a thousand tawny cows. 33.
Thereafter, O King, one should go to the excellent shrine of Śaṃtanu called Lalitaka;
having bathed there, a man shall not meet with an evil fate. 34.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Twenty-nine. Nārada said:
From there, O lord of kings, one should go to the supreme Kālindī-tīrtha;
having bathed there, O King, a man shall not meet with an evil fate.
[This applies even as if he had bathed] at Puṣkara, Kurukṣetra, Brahmāvarta, or Pṛthūdaka.
A person obtains the fruit known as the "Golden Avimukta";
O best of men, one attains that same fruit at the Yamunā for those whose minds are truly indifferent toward the enjoyments of heaven. 2–3.

O best of men, for those who desire longevity, health, prosperity, beauty, youthfulness, and virtuous qualities, the waters of the Yamunā must not be forsaken, especially through bathing and giving gifts therein.
Those who fear hell and other such realms, and those who suffer from poverty in this world—
by all means, they should strive with diligence to immerse themselves there [in that lake],
for the purpose of washing away the mire of poverty, calamity, and misfortune.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, there is no other [merit] like that of the Yamunā;
indeed, rituals devoid of faith are considered to yield only half their fruit, whereas the mere act of bathing in the Yamunā bestows the full result. 7.
O King, whether free from desire or possessed of desire, one who is pure through the waters of the sage does not see any sufferings in this world or the next;
for like the moon, he wanes and waxes during both fortnights.
There, sin is destroyed by bathing and merit increases. Just as various kinds of jewels easily enter the ocean, so too do longevity, wealth, wives, and prosperity come into being there. 9–10.
Just as the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) grants whatever is desired and the wish-granting gem (Cintāmaṇi) grants what is thought of, so too does bathing in the Yamunā grant every heart's desire.
In the Kṛta age, supreme knowledge was the highest; likewise, in the Tretā age, sacrificial worship was supreme.
In the Dvāpara and Kali ages, O King, the auspicious Kālindī always bestows merit upon all castes and stages of life;
indeed, immersion in the Yamunā rains down dharma like a continuous shower. 12–13.
In this land of Bhārata, specifically in this field of action (karmabhūmi),
the birth of those men who do not bathe in the Kālindī is declared to be fruitless. It is like the absence of splendor in the sky, or like the lunar orb on the new-moon day.
In the same way, this [world] does not shine without immersion in the Yamunā of virtuous action (satkarma).
Hari is not so pleased by vows, gifts, or austerities as He is by that mere immersion alone; thus Keśava is gratified. 15–16.
There exists nothing whatsoever equal to the splendor of the sun;
likewise, ritual acts born of sacrifice are not equal to bathing in the Yamunā, which is for the pleasure of Vāsudeva and for the removal of all sins. 17.
A person should perform an immersion in the Kālindī for the sake of attaining heaven.
What is the use of preserving this body—though well-nourished, powerful, and exceedingly beautiful—if it is transient and lacks immersion in the Yamunā? (18-19)
It has pillars of bone, bonds of sinew, and is plastered with flesh and blood;
it is a foul-smelling fortress covered with skin, filled with urine and excrement,
pervaded by old age, grief, and calamity— a sickly abode of disease.

It is rooted in passion, impermanent, and the locus of all defects; it is characterized by helping others [only for gain], sin, distress, malice toward others, and envy; it is greedy, slanderous, cruel, ungrateful, and likewise momentary. 21–22.
It is cruel, difficult to restrain, wicked, and corrupted by the three defects;
it is impure, foul-smelling, and deluded by the three types of suffering.
By its very nature, it delights in unrighteousness and is agitated by hundreds of cravings.
This body, which stands at the gateway to hell through desire, anger, and great greed,
and which brings about the qualities of transformation into worms, excrement, and ashes— such a body is indeed useless without bathing in the Yamunā. 24–25.
Like bubbles in water or like eggs among birds, those who have not bathed in the Yamunā are born only for death.
A Brāhmaṇa who is not a Vaiṣṇava is as good as dead; likewise, a Śrāddha ceremony performed without the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍas) is as good as dead.
The Kṣatriya is destroyed by unrighteousness; the family is destroyed by lack of proper conduct. Dharma is destroyed by hypocrisy, and austerity is destroyed by anger.
Knowledge is destroyed by instability, and sacred learning is destroyed by negligence.

A woman struck by devotion to another, a celibate student struck by a woman, an oblation offered in a fire that is not kindled, and equanimity (sāmāyika) struck by a lack of devotion; a daughter struck by being made a means of livelihood, and the act of cooking performed for one's own sake—[these are all ruined]. 29.

The food of a Śūdra is destroyed by [the recipient's] attachment; the wealth of a miser is destroyed. Knowledge is destroyed by lack of practice; understanding is destroyed by one who creates discord. A sacred pilgrimage site is destroyed for the sake of livelihood; a vow is destroyed for the sake of mere existence. (30–31)
A mantra is destroyed by speaking untruth, by falsehood, and likewise by one who speaks maliciously;
it is destroyed when heard by six ears. Recitation is destroyed by a distracted mind. A gift is destroyed when given to one ignorant of the Vedas, and the world is destroyed for the nihilist.
Everything performed for the sake of the next world that is struck down by lack of faith is lost;
O King, just as this world is lost to men who are poor, so too is the birth of human beings lost without bathing in the Kālindī. 33–34.
O King, all minor offenses, all major sins, and even the great transgressions— all are reduced to ashes by immersion in the Yamunā. All sins tremble when a man has gone to the Yamunā.
If one bathes in the water, there is the destruction of all sins; those best of men who bathe in the Yamunā blaze like fires,
liberated from all evils like the moon from the clouds.
Whether moist, dry, light, or heavy, committed through speech, mind, or action—therein, bathing burns away that sin just as fire consumes sacrificial fuel.
Whatever sin is committed through negligence, and whatever is done whether knowingly or unknowingly; [all that is destroyed by this bath].

O best of kings, by merely bathing in the Yamunā, one is freed from sin; the sinless go to heaven, while even the most wicked attain purity. One should have no doubt regarding bathing in the waters of the Yamunā. (39-40)
O King, all who are devoted to Viṣṇu are indeed eligible for this;
for everyone at all times, this Goddess Yamunā is the destroyer of sins.
This alone is the supreme mantra, and this is the supreme austerity.
Furthermore, bathing in the Yamunā is the supreme expiation.

O King, just as proficiency in spiritual knowledge arises from practice over many lifetimes, so too does the inclination toward immersion in the Kālindī arise through the practice of previous births. 42-43.

O King, those who bathe there at that supreme bathing place in the Yamunā— which is skilled at washing away the smearing of the mire of saṃsāra and is the purifier of purifiers— obtain the fruits of all their desires. 44.
They enjoy auspicious pleasures comparable to the sun, the moon, and the planets.
(45) Yamunā is said to bestow liberation when joined with Mathurā;
in Mathurā, Kālindī increases one's merit even further. (46)
Elsewhere, the river Yamunā removes great sins and bestows devotion to Viṣṇu; however, when she has joined with the goddess Mathurā, she becomes even more so.
If one who is endowed with a spirit of devotion should immerse themselves in the Kālindī, [the result is unsurpassed].
Those men who dwell in the presence of Hari for thousands of millions of kalpas surely attain liberation, even if they are devoid of Sāṃkhya;
his ancestors, being satisfied, remain gratified in heaven for hundreds of kalpas. 48–49.
For those men who drink the auspicious waters of the Yamunā, what need is there for the consumption of thousands of *pañcagavya*?
What need is there for the visitation of thousands of millions of sacred pilgrimage sites (*tīrtha*)? 50.
Therein, both charity and the fire-oblation shall all become ten millionfold in merit.
51. Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Thirty.
Nārada said: O King, in this regard I shall relate to you an ancient history concerning the excellent city of Niṣadha in the former Kṛta Yuga.
There was a Vaiśya named Hemakuṇḍala, who resembled Kubera;
he was well-born, performed virtuous deeds, and was a worshiper of the gods, the twice-born, and the sacred fire.
He was a practitioner of agriculture and trade, engaged in various kinds of buying and selling.
He was intent on rearing livestock such as cows, horses, camels, and buffaloes; [he dealt in] milk, curd, buttermilk, cow dung, grass,
wood, fruits, roots, salt, fresh ginger, and long pepper.
He was constantly selling grains, vegetables, oils, various kinds of clothing, minerals, and products of sugarcane; thus,
the Vaiśya employed these and other diverse means.
He constantly accumulated eight crores of gold;
thus, though he possessed such great wealth, he eventually became gray-haired at the ears.
Afterwards, he reflected within his own mind upon the transience of worldly existence.
With one-sixth of that wealth, he performed acts of dharma;
he built a temple for Viṣṇu and a house for Śiva. He had a vast reservoir dug, resembling the ocean.
By him, many step-wells and lotus ponds were caused to be constructed;
he then created groves of banyan, holy fig, mango, *kaṃkola*, rose-apple,
and neem trees through his own effort, as well as a beautiful flower garden.
From sunrise until sunset, he established extremely beautiful water-stations (prapās) for food and drink outside the city in the four directions.
O King, those gifts which are well-known in the Purāṇas—
Then that righteous soul, constantly devoted to giving,
bestowed these gifts; he performed penance for the sins committed throughout his life, remained eternally intent on the worship of the gods, and was always a host who honored guests.
While he was living in this manner, O King, two sons were born to him,
well-known by the names Śrīkuṇḍala and Vikuṇḍala. Having abandoned his home at their heads, he went to the forest for the sake of asceticism.
There, having propitiated the supreme deity Govinda, the Lord who grants boons,
his body emaciated by ascetic penance and his mind ever fixed on Vāsudeva, he attained the world of Viṣṇu, reaching which one no longer grieves.
Then, O King, his two sons were endowed with great pride; they were young, possessed of beauty, and arrogant with the conceit of wealth.
They were ill-behaved, addicted to vices, and indifferent to dharma, ritual action, and other such duties.
They disregarded the words of their mother and likewise the advice of the elders;
they were followers of evil paths, wicked-souled, obstructers of their father and friends, devoted to unrighteousness, and corruptors who approached the wives of others. 18–19.

Devoted to song and instrumental music, delighting in the lute and the flute, and accompanied by hundreds of courtesans, the two of them then lived there singing; skilled in the arts of love, they were joined by men who offered flattering words, and they were experts in the charms of women with lips like the *bimba* fruit.
Well-dressed in beautiful garments, anointed with exquisite sandalwood paste (21),
likewise enriched with fragrant garlands and marked with spots of musk,
they were resplendent with various ornaments and captivating with pearl necklaces (22).
Then, sporting with a multitude of elephants, horses, and chariots,
those two— intoxicated by the drinking of wine and infatuated with pleasure in the wives of others—
squandered their paternal wealth and gave away thousands for hundreds.

They remained in their own beautiful home, constantly devoted to sensual enjoyments. In this manner, that wealth was squandered by the two of them on improper expenditures upon courtesans, libertines, actors, wrestlers, minstrels, and bards.
This wealth was given to one who is not a worthy recipient; it is like seed sown in barren soil.
It was not given to a true vessel, nor was it offered into the mouth of a Brahmin.
Viṣṇu, the sustainer of all beings and the destroyer of all sins, has not been worshipped.
In no long time, that wealth of both of them came to an end.
Then, having fallen into misery and reached a state of extreme wretchedness, they grieved and were bewildered, oppressed by the pain of hunger and suffering.

While those two remained standing there, whatever was eaten by their kinsmen, relatives, all their servants, and dependents was done so while they were being disregarded in the city due to the lack of wealth. 29. Thus they were left behind and thought upon.
O King, thereafter they began to commit theft in the city; then, terrified of the king and the public, they fled from their own city and, being oppressed by everyone, took up residence in the forest.
The two fools constantly struck various birds, boars, deer, rohitas, as well as rabbits, porcupines, monitor lizards, and many other beasts of prey with sharp arrows smeared with poison. 32.
O scorcher of foes, those two— Mahābala and Udbilla— were always engaged in hunting with their arms;
thus, subsisting on a diet of meat and other sinful food, one of them reached a mountain while the other entered the forest.

O King, on a single day, the eldest was killed by a tiger and the youngest was bitten by a snake; both, being most sinful, met their end. Then, bound by the messengers of Yama, they were led to the abode of Yama because of their sins.
Having gone there, all those messengers addressed the two sinners:
"O Dharmarāja, these two have been brought here by your command; give an order to your servants, be gracious, and tell us what we should do. (36-37)
Having reflected upon this, Yama spoke to Citragupta and his messengers:
"Let one hero be led to hell, which is filled with intense agony; let the other be established in heaven, where indeed there are unsurpassed enjoyments."
O King, having heard the command of Kṛtānta (Yama), the eldest was swiftly cast by the swift-acting messengers into the terrible Raurava hell;
then one of those excellent messengers spoke these sweet words.
"Come to heaven together with Vikuṇḍala and Maya; I grant it to you. Enjoy the most divine pleasures, which have been earned by your own karma.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter of the Svargakhaṇḍa in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
The thirty-first chapter.
Nārada said:
Then, with a joyful mind, he questioned that messenger on the path.
Holding doubt in his heart, he was struck with supreme wonder;
reflecting within himself, "For what reason is heaven the fruit for me?
Vikuṇḍala said:
O supreme one, I ask you about my doubt regarding the questions of the departed:
though our births were in equal families and our deeds were likewise performed,
our deaths were equally wretched, and Yama was seen by us both in the same way.
"How was my elder brother, who performed the same deeds as I, cast into hell? And how did he attain heaven? Cut through this doubt of mine;
O divine messenger, I do not see the cause for his lack of heaven."
The divine messenger said:
"O Vikuṇḍala, mother, father, son, wife, sister, and brother—these designations exist for a living being solely for the sake of experiencing the fruits of one's karma. (5)
Just as birds gather together upon a single tree,
whatever action a person performs according to their prior disposition, they always experience the fruit of that very action.
I tell you the truth out of affection: O Vaiśya, men experience their own performed actions—both auspicious and inauspicious—at every moment, again and again.
One alone performs the deeds; one alone enjoys their fruit.
One is never smeared by the actions of another anywhere;
your brother has fallen into hell due to his own most cruel sins, while you, O knower of dharma, attain eternal heaven through righteousness. 9.
Vikuṇḍala said:
"O messengers, from my childhood my mind has been devoted to sinful acts rather than meritorious ones;
indeed, in this birth, many evil deeds have been committed by me. (10)
"I know that my own karma was well-performed; if you know of my merit, please tell it to me out of compassion. (11) The divine messenger said:

"Listen, O Vaiśya, I shall declare how much merit has been earned by you; I know all of that, whereas you certainly do not know it. (12) "The son of Harimitra is the Brahmin Sumitra, a master of the Vedas."

There was a holy hermitage on the southern bank of the Yamunā. O best of people, your friendship with him arose in that forest; through association with him, you likewise bathed for two months of the month of Māgha.

O lord of the people, by means of this single [visit] to that supreme holy place— renowned in the world as Kālidīpa, a sacred water that removes all sins and destroys evil— you have been liberated from all transgressions.

O sinless one, by the merit of the second Māgha, heaven has been attained by you; by the power of that merit, rejoice forever in the celestial realm. As for your brother, he undergoes great torment due to his sins in the hells.
Being cut by sword-leaves, pierced by mallets,
ground to powder on the surface of rocks, and roasted upon glowing embers—
having heard these words of the messenger, he was pained by the suffering of his brother.
With his entire body covered in horripilation, humble and full of modesty,
he spoke these sweet and skillful words to the divine messenger: "O virtuous one, the seven-step bond of friendship among the good bears excellent fruit."
Considering our friendship, you ought to assist me;
therefore, I wish to hear this, for in my view, you are omniscient. (21) By what action do human beings avoid seeing the world of Yama?
"Tell me out of compassion what it is by which they go to hell.
(22) The divine messenger said: "O Vaiśya, you have asked well; you are now indeed freed from sin."

In those whose hearts are purified, wisdom regarding the highest good arises. (23) Even though there is no occasion for me to serve another, nevertheless, out of affection for you, I shall speak according to my understanding. (24)
Those who never cause harm to others through action, mind, or speech at any time or in any state do not go to the abode of Yama;
nor can they be reached by means of the Vedas, nor by gifts, nor by austerities, nor by sacrifices.
In some way or another, even men who harm living beings may attain the heavenly realm. Non-violence is the supreme dharma; non-violence indeed is the supreme austerity;
non-violence is the supreme gift—thus the sages have always declared.
Compassionate men regard mosquitoes, reptiles, gadflies, lice, and other such creatures, as well as human beings,
by comparing them with themselves.
[They likewise avoid] glowing coals, iron spikes, wine, and the river of the dead.
By that [merit], those people do not go to an evil state at all, even when facing the God of Death (Kṛtānta).
Those beings here who harm creatures moving in water or on land, even for the sake of their own livelihood, go to the Kālasūtra hell and to an evil state. 29–30.
There they eat the flesh of dogs, drink pus and blood, and wallow in the mire of fat, bitten by insects with their heads turned downward;
devouring one another in the darkness, they strike each other down.
Crying out a terrible sound for many seasons resembling the springtime,
they enter hundreds of births as worms and remain as stationary beings for a long time; thereafter, those cruel ones wander through hundreds of animal births.
Those humans who harm living beings are subsequently born blind, one-eyed, humpbacked, lame, impoverished, and deformed in their limbs.
Therefore, O Vaiśya, hereafter [you must refrain from such acts] through deed, mind, and speech.
One who knows the Dharma and desires happiness in both worlds should not practice that [violence].
Those who harm living beings do not find happiness in either of the two worlds;
for those by whom beings are harmed do not fear anything at all.

Just as rivers, whether flowing straight or winding, enter the ocean, so do all dharmas firmly enter into non-violence (ahiṃsā). He has bathed in all sacred fords (tīrthas) and has been initiated into all sacrifices.
O best of the twice-born, those Vaiśyas who have granted fearlessness to all beings here,
and who carry out the duties prescribed in the scriptures— whether mixed with dharma or adharma— under my command, do not go to the abode of Yama. (38-39)
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic—
all who are devoted to their own respective duties dwell upon the back of heaven.
All those belonging to the various castes and stages of life who act according to what has been prescribed [attain this state].
Those who have conquered their senses go to the eternal world of Brahmā.
Those who are devoted to sacrificial rites and charitable works, those who are intent on the five daily sacrifices,
and those who are constantly endowed with compassion— these do not behold the abode of Yama.
Those Brahmins who are incapable of turning away from the objects of the senses, who are proponents of the Vedas, and who are constantly devoted to the worship of fire, go to heaven;
they are brave, with faces free from dejection, even when surrounded by enemies. 43.
For those who perish in battles, the Sun is their path.
Those Vaiśyas who give up their lives for the sake of a protectorless woman or a Brāhmaṇa, or for the protection of one who has sought refuge, do not fall from heaven. 44–45.
Those Vaiśyas who always nourish the lame, the blind, children, the elderly, the sick, the protectorless,
and the poor, always rejoice in heaven. Having seen a cow sunk in mud, as well as a twice-born man overwhelmed by disease, [they rescue them].

Those men who rescue [cows from distress], their world is that of those who perform the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha). Those who give a mouthful of grass to cows, those who always serve cows, and those who ride upon the backs of cows, dwell in the heavenly world (svarga-loka). 47–48.
Those men who have made even a mere pit where a cow might become thirsty go to the heavenly realm without beholding the world of Yama.
Those who are devoted to the worship of fire, the worship of gods, and the worship of their guru [attain the same].

Those brahmins who are constantly devoted to the worship of the twice-born go to heaven. There is no end to the merit of constructing step-wells, wells, ponds, and the like, wherein aquatic and terrestrial creatures drink at their will. 50–51.
O best of the Vaiśyas, he who is constantly devoted to giving is described even by the gods as such;
for just as living beings drink water in great abundance, so too does his inexhaustible heaven increase through his sense of dharma.
Water is the life of living beings; indeed, all vital breaths are established in water. Even those men who are sinners are purified by daily bathing.
Morning bathing, O Vaiśya, removes both external and internal impurity.

By bathing at dawn, a man becomes free from sin and shall not go to hell; however, that man who eats without bathing is always an eater of impurity. The ancestors and the deities turn their faces away from that man who does not bathe.

A man who neglects bathing is sinful; a man who neglects bathing is impure. One who does not bathe experiences hell and is reborn among male insects and the like. Furthermore, those who perform a bath in a flowing stream here on a sacred festival day— 56–57.
By that alone, O best of Vaiśyas, men do not go to hell nor are they born into evil wombs;
their bad dreams and wicked thoughts always become fruitless through the morning bath of purified men. 58.

Having offered sesame seeds, vessels of sesame, and a prastha of sesame according to the prescribed rite upon the ground for the Lord of the Departed (Yama), men never go anywhere [to a lower realm]. By giving land, gold, and a cow, as well as the sixteen types of gifts, [one attains the same].
O Vikuṇḍala, having gone there, they do not return from the heavenly world;
on auspicious lunar days, during the Vyatīpāta yoga, and at the sun’s passage into a new sign, the wise man who bathes and gives whatever he can does not sink into an evil rebirth.
Givers do not at all tread upon the terrible path of Raurava; rather, they are born in this world into a family devoid of wealth. As for that man who is truthful, always silent, and speaks kindly—

Free from anger, of upright conduct, not given to excessive speech, and free from envy; always endowed with courtesy, always possessed of compassion for all beings, a protector of others' secrets, and a speaker of others' virtues. (63–64)
One should not, even in thought, take another's property, even if it be as small as a blade of grass; for by doing so, O best of men, they do not see the torments of hell.
One who slanders others and is a heretic is considered worse than even those who commit sins.
O best of people, one who speaks harsh words should be considered as having gone to hell; he is cooked there until the dissolution of all beings,
and there is no doubt that he shall again go to a miserable state of existence.

There is no atonement for an ungrateful person through pilgrimages or austerities; such a man suffers terrible torments in hell for a long time. As for those tirthas that exist upon the earth, the man who immerses himself in them [is purified].
One who has conquered the senses and is moderate in diet does not go to the abode of Yama.
One should not commit a sin at a sacred ford (tīrtha), nor should one live off the merit of a tīrtha.
Accepting gifts at a tīrtha must be abandoned, as must the sale of dharma.

A sin committed at a sacred ford is difficult to digest, as is the acceptance of gifts at a sacred ford; indeed, everything done at a sacred ford is difficult to digest—such a person shall go to hell. One who has bathed even once in the waters of the Gaṅgā is purified by the water of the Gaṅgā.

Even one who has committed a heap of heinous sins does not go to hell; we have heard that vows, gifts, austerities, sacrifices, and other purifying acts are not equal to being sprinkled with even a drop of water from the Gaṅgā. 72-73.
O Vaiśya, that lowest of men who says that the Gaṅgā is equal to any other river goes to the great and terrible Raurava hell;
for she is the essence of dharma, the seed of the waters, fallen from the feet of Viṣṇu.
The pure water of the Gaṅgā, which was held upon his head by Maheśa, is indeed Brahman itself—beyond doubt, devoid of qualities, and beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
With what else within the scope of the cosmic egg could it possibly be compared? 75–76.

Even if one were to say "Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā" from across hundreds of yojanas, that man would not go to hell; what else could be equal to that? No other action instantly burns away [sin] as does the rite that grants liberation from hell. (77)

Men should bathe in the waters of the Gaṅgā with great effort; that twice-born man who desists from accepting gifts, even if he were capable of doing so, shines for a long time in heaven in the form of the Vaiśyā-tārā. 78.
Those who rescue cows from the mud and protect those afflicted by disease, and those who die within a cow-pen—for them, the stars in the sky [are their lot];
devoted to the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), they do not behold the realm of Yama. 79.
Moreover, even those who have committed evil deeds, having their sins destroyed by these very [practices],
purify even a direct slayer of a Brahmin when sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) are performed daily, day after day, like those of a Vaiśya. 80.
Whatever austerities are performed, whatever vows and observances there are,
and even the gift of a thousand cows— prāṇāyāma is equal to all of them.
A man who might drink a drop of water from the tip of a blade of kuśa grass month after month [is not equal to one who performs prāṇāyāma].
A single breath-control (prāṇāyāma) is equal to more than a hundred years [of other practices]; likewise,
a man reduces all great sins as well as minor offenses to ashes in an instant through breath-controls.
Those best among men who regard the wives of others as their own mothers never, O best of men, go to the torments of Yama;
he who does not even in his mind consort with the spouses of others.
Along with the two worlds, existence itself is supported by the earth held by the Vaiśyas.
Therefore, those endowed with dharma must abandon the pursuit of another's wife; for the wives of others lead one to twenty-one hells. 85–86.
O best of Vaiśyas, those whose minds do not give rise to desire for the wives of others go to the world of the gods, and certainly not to that of Yama; likewise,
he who is not overcome by anger amidst the constant causes of wrath [attains the same].
A man on earth who has conquered heaven should be regarded as one who is free from anger;
he who honors his mother and father like gods does not go to the abode of Yama before reaching old age. 88-89.
O best of the people, those men who honor their father with even greater devotion than their teacher become guests of Brahmā in this world;
and here on earth, women are blessed by the preservation of their virtuous conduct.
For women who break their vows of conduct, the world of Yama is most terrible.
(91) Women must always protect their virtue by avoiding association with the wicked; for through virtue alone, O Vaiśya, women attain the supreme heaven—of this there is no doubt. (92)

For a Śūdra, a miserable state is ordained through the performance of *pākayajña* sacrifices and the practice of forbidden acts; for a Vaiśya, that same fate is a descent into hell. Those who investigate the scriptures and those who are devoted to the study of the Vedas [attain a higher state]. 93.

Those who recite and read the Purāṇa-saṃhitās, those who explain them, those who preserve the Smṛtis, and those who awaken others to dharma—those who are established in the Vedāntas; by these, this world is sustained. 94–95.
Through the greatness of their respective practices, all these people, their sins destroyed,
go to the world of Brahmā, where delusion does not exist.
(96) He who gives knowledge arising from the Vedas and Śāstras to one who is ignorant—
Even the Vedas praise that which tears asunder the bonds of worldly existence.
Listen, O best of Vaiśyas, to this wonderful secret, which is esteemed by Dharmarāja and bestows immortality upon all the worlds. 97–98.
"O Vaiṣṇavas, you surely do not see Yama, the world-protector, nor the beings of terrible appearance; this which I have spoken is the truth, the absolute truth.
Thus indeed did my brother always say to us again and again. 99.
"O Vaiṣṇavas, you must certainly avoid those who would not come within my range of vision.
Those beings who remember Keśava even once,
even by chance, having all their masses of sins destroyed, go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu."
Even if he is of evil conduct and a doer of wicked deeds, yet if that man is devoted to virtuous conduct and worships Viṣṇu, he should always be accepted by you.
Furthermore, those in whose house a Vaiṣṇava eats and who have the company of Vaiṣṇavas [should likewise be honored]. 102.
"Even they should be avoided by you, for their association destroys one's merit.
Thus does the divine Lord, the eternal wielder of the rod of punishment, instruct us Vaiśyas;
therefore, we do not go to the capital city of Yama.

O best of Vaiśyas, for sinful men there is no other means, nor any other way, to cross the ocean of hell except through devotion to Viṣṇu. Even a Vaiṣṇava Vaiśya who is beloved in the worlds should not look upon a dog-eater (outcaste).
Even one who is outside the pale of the Vaiṣṇava castes purifies the three worlds.
This much alone is sufficient for the removal of the sins of men: the chanting of the qualities, deeds, and names of the Blessed Lord.
For even Ajāmila, though he was a sinner, attained liberation at the moment of death by crying out "Nārāyaṇa! while calling his son. 106–107.

Those who were previously submerged for a long time in hell within the two families [of their ancestors], they go to heaven at that very moment when they joyfully worship Hari. Those who are servants of a devotee of Viṣṇu and those who eat the food of a Vaiṣṇava—[they too attain the same]. 108.
Those who have performed four sacrifices go, free from agitation, to the state of a Vaiśya.
A wise person should diligently seek the food of a Vaiṣṇava for the sake of purification from all sins; in its absence, one should drink water.
If a person dies anywhere while chanting the mantra "Govinda," he shall not see Yama; nor do we have the power to behold him.
[This mantra] is complete with its limbs, its ocean [of syllables], its meditation, its seer, its meter, and its deity.
Having been initiated according to the prescribed rites, one should recite the twelve-syllable mantra.
Those best among men who recite the eight-syllable lord of mantras—
by seeing them, even a killer of a Brahmin is purified and shines forth like Viṣṇu himself.

Having become bearers of the conch and the discus, those men who enter within the Brahman dwell in the world of Viṣṇu in the form of Viṣṇu himself— whether they meditate on Him in the heart, in the sun, in water, or upon an image or a sacrificial altar. 114.
Having fully worshipped Hari, men go to that very abode of Viṣṇu.
Alternatively, Vāsudeva should always be worshipped by those seeking liberation in a Śālagrāma stone, a jewel, or a discus formed by a vajra-insect.
O Vaiśya, that sacred site of Viṣṇu is the destroyer of all sins,
the bestower of all merit, and the giver of liberation to everyone.
Whoever worships Hari in the form arising from the Śālagrāma stone—
By worshipping the Śālagrāma stone, men obtain the merit of performing a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices every single day;
they always attain the Vedānta, the liberation of Brahman, and the imperishable state—
this grace comes to people through the worship of the Śālagrāma stone.
Just as fire situated within a large log manifests in the sacrificial arena,
so too does the all-pervading Hari manifest in the Śālagrāma.
Even those of sinful conduct who are ineligible for ritual action [attain liberation through it].
Vaiśyas who worship the Śālagrāma do not go to the abode of Yama.
(121) Neither does Hari delight so much in Lakṣmī nor in His own city as He always delights in the discus-marked stone of Śālagrāma. (122)
By him who has worshipped Hari arising from a Śālagrāma stone, the Agnihotra sacrifice has been performed and the earth with its oceans has been gifted.
I shall declare the merit of him by whom [this] has been worshipped according to the rules:

whatever merit would arise from worshipping twelve crores of Liṅgas with golden lotuses at twelve different times throughout a single day, that same merit shall be attained [by this worship]. 124–125.

Furthermore, he who worships with devotion a hundred Śālagrāma stones dwells in the world of Hari and is born as a universal monarch (cakravartin). [In that world] where the lowest of men are pervaded by desires, anger, and delusions... 126.
He too goes to the world of Hari by worshipping the Śālagrāma stone.
That man who joyfully worships Govinda at the Śālagrāma does not fall from heaven until the dissolution of all beings.
O Vaiśya, without holy fords, without gifts, without sacrifices, and even without spiritual wisdom, men attain liberation through the worship of the Śālagrāma stone. (129) [Otherwise,
they face] hell, dwelling in a womb, rebirth as an animal, or birth in the womb of a worm.
Even a Vaiśya who is not free from sin, if he worships the Śālagrāma stone, is liberated.
He who knows the mantras for the rite of initiation and offers oblations to the discus (Cakra) attains success.
The Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, Revā, and other rivers are the bestowers of liberation.
All [the goddesses] reside together within the water of the Śālagrāma stone;
one should worship the Śālagrāma stone with various food offerings, flowers, incense, lamps, and ointments, as well as with songs, instrumental music, hymns, and the like. 132.
That man who in the Kali age is devoted to worship attains such a state;
he rejoices in the presence of Hari for thousands of millions of kalpas.
Whatever fruit is obtained by seeing ten million lingas or by worshipping them, [that is attained here]. 133-134.
The fruit that is obtained by [other means] in a single day is attained in one day by worshipping even once a Linga produced from a Śālagrāma stone;
such men surely attain liberation, even if they are devoid of Sāṃkhya knowledge.
Wherever Keśava resides in the form of the Śālagrāma stone,
there dwell the gods, the asuras, the yakṣas, and the fourteen worlds.
Furthermore, that man who performs a śrāddha ceremony at the Śālagrāma stone [attains great merit].
His ancestors remain in heaven, satisfied for a hundred kalpas, those men who daily drink the water from the Śālagrāma stone;
what need is there for the consumption of thousands of *pañcagavya*? 138

What is the use of visiting thousands of millions of holy fords (tīrthas), if one should drink the sacred water originating from the body of the Śālagrāma stone? Wherever there is a Śālagrāma stone, that place is a holy ford for three yojanas around.

In that regard, both charity and fire-offerings performed there shall all become ten millionfold in merit for one who drinks even as much as a single drop of water from the Śālagrāma stone; such a man,
a partaker of Viṣṇu, shall never again drink the breast-milk of a mother.
Within a distance of one krośa all around the vicinity of Śālagrāma,
even a worm that dies goes to the supreme abode of Vaikuṇṭha;
he who gives the gift of the Śālagrāma stone discus performs the highest of gifts.
The man who establishes a price for a Śālagrāma stone would, by that act, be giving away the entire earth-circle along with its mountains, forests, and groves.
This applies to the seller, the one who approves, and whoever rejoices in the examination [of the stone]. (144)
They all go to hell until the dissolution of all beings.
Therefore, one should avoid buying and selling for a Vaiśya; what is the use of much speaking? A Vaiśya who fears sin must perform his duty. 145–146.

The remembrance of Vāsudeva, the remover of all sins, yields that same fruit which one attains by performing severe austerities in the forest with restrained senses, after bowing down to the one whose banner is Garuḍa. 147.
Even after committing many sins, a man possessed by delusion does not go to hell if he goes to Hari, the remover of all sins;
for whatever holy places and meritorious shrines exist upon the earth, [they are all contained within Him]. 148–149.
One attains all of these simply by chanting the names of Viṣṇu—
those who have taken refuge in the divine Viṣṇu, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, as their supreme resort. For them, there is no world of Yama, nor shall they ever be inhabitants of hell.

A Vaiṣṇava man who reviles Śiva shall not find the world of Viṣṇu; he goes instead to a great hell. Even if a person observes the Ekādaśī fast only once, even by chance, [he attains such merit]. (151–152)
"I have heard from Lomaśa that there is no suffering in Yama’s realm;
indeed, nothing so purifying as this exists in the three worlds.
Both the day and the night of the Lotus-navelled One destroy all sins. (153)
O best of the people, sins dwell in this body only so long as a living being does not fast on the auspicious day of Padmanābha;
[for that day] is equal to thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Rājasūya sacrifices.
The merit of fasting on Ekādaśī is not equaled by even a sixteenth part [of its own];
whatever sin has been committed by human beings through the eleven senses, O Vaiśya,
all of that shall go to destruction by means of fasting on Ekādaśī.
There is no merit found in the world equal to Ekādaśī (157). Even those who observe it under a pretext come under the control of the Sun;
indeed, this [vow] bestows heaven and liberation, and grants health to the body (158).
Neither a virtuous wife, nor the gift of a living son,
nor the Ganges, nor Naga, nor Gayā, nor Vaiśya, nor Kāśī, nor Puṣkara,
nor even the sacred field of Viṣṇu, is equal to the day of Hari (Ekādaśī). 159.
On the day of Hari, which is equal to a hundred thousand Yamunās and Candrabhāgās,
by means of which the state of Vaiṣṇava is attained here without effort—
having kept a vigil at night and having fasted on the day of Hari.

In the ten paternal lineages and the ten maternal lineages, he certainly uplifts his beloved wives and those of the Vaiśya caste; they have abandoned all dual attachments and have made their home in the homeless state. 162.
Adorned with garlands and wearing yellow garments, they proceed to the abode of Hari.
O best of the Vaiśyas, whether in childhood, youth, or even old age, one who fasts on Ekādaśī certainly does not fall into a miserable state. 163-164.

Having fasted for these three nights and performed ablutions at sacred fords (tīrtha), men who give gold, sesame seeds, and cows go to heaven. Those Vaiśyas, however, who do not bathe in the sacred fords and by whom no gold has been given, [do not attain such merit].
They would perform no austerity at all and would be miserable in every respect. (166) Dharma has been briefly described, as well as the description of hell:
non-injury toward all beings through the actions of speech, mind, and body. (167)

The restraint of the senses, charity, service to Hari, and the constant performance of the duties of one's caste and stage of life according to the rules— these are always for the sake of heaven; however, a Vaiśya seeking heaven should never proclaim his own austerities or gifts.
One should give according to one's ability, desiring one's own welfare.
Sandals, clothing, food, a leaf for a seat, roots, fruits, and water—these should not be given in vain on any day, even by a poor person, O Vaiśyaka. (169–170)
Neither in this world nor in the next does that which was not given remain with one; indeed, the givers do not experience those various torments of hell.
Yet, they become long-lived and wealthy here again and again.
What need is there for much speaking on this? By unrighteousness men go to a miserable state; by righteousness they ascend to heaven at all times and in all places.
Therefore, from childhood onwards, one should undertake the accumulation of dharma.
"Thus everything has been told; what else do you wish to hear?
Vikuṇḍala said:
"O gentle one, having heard your words, my mind is indeed thus pacified."
The water of the Gaṅgā instantly destroys sin, and the speech of the virtuous likewise removes evil.
(175) It is the innate quality of the good to act for the benefit of others and to speak kindly; by whom could the moon, with its orb of nectar, be made cool? (176)
"O messenger of the gods, out of compassion, please tell me who am asking:
how can my brother’s immediate deliverance from hell be brought about?
Having heard these words of his, the messenger of the gods spoke.

Having observed his meditative state and contemplated for a moment, he said: "Bound by the rope of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), give all that merit which you accumulated during your eighth birth as a Vaiśya to your brother, if you desire that he attain heaven. (178–179)
Vikuṇḍala said:
What is that merit? How did it arise? And what was my former birth?
O messenger, let all of that be told; then I shall give [the gift] immediately. (180)
The divine messenger said:
Listen, O Vaiśya, I shall explain that merit along with its cause.
Formerly, in the holy Madhu forest, there was a sage named Śākuni. 181
Endowed with austerity and sacred study, and equal to Brahmā in splendor,
nine sons were born to him by his wife Revatī, like so many planets:
Dhruva, Śīla, Budha, Tāra, Jyotiṣmat, and Utapa as the fifth.
For these were devoted to the *agnihotra* sacrifice and took delight in the duties of householders.
Yet, free from delusion, having conquered desire, possessing the treasury of meditation, and preeminent in virtue, these four sons of the twice-born became detached from domestic life. 183–184.
Having entered the fourth stage of life, they were free from desire for all objects of pleasure; though residing in a village, they were all unattached and without possessions,
devoid of expectations and free from effort, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal.
Clad in whatever was available and eating whatever was available, they were always intent on meditating upon Viṣṇu;
they had conquered sleep and conquered their appetite, and they were enduring to the winds and the cold. 186–187.
Beholding the entire world, including all moving and non-moving beings, as the form of Viṣṇu,
they wander upon the earth today with ease, maintaining silence toward one another; for these yogis perform no action whatsoever, being intent only on the ultimate reality.
Possessing direct knowledge and free from doubt, they were experts in the transformations of consciousness.
Thus, O Brahmin, in your eighth previous birth, while you were living in the Middle Country with wife, children, and family; 189–190.
At midday, thirsty and craving sugar-cane juice, they came to your house;
at the time of the Vaiśvadeva offering, they were seen by you in the courtyard of the home,
[addressing you] with voices choked with emotion, eyes filled with tears, yet full of joy and agitation.
Having prostrated like a staff with great reverence,
having bowed at her feet with his head and joined his palms in *añjali*,
they were all then greeted by her with words that were kind and true.
Today my efforts have borne fruit, and likewise my birth and life have become fruitful;
today Viṣṇu is pleased with me, and today I am protected and purified. Today I am blessed, my home is blessed, and today my family members are blessed.
Today my parents are blessed; blessed are our cows and our wealth of sacred learning (195).
Since I have beheld your feet, which remove the threefold suffering, your sight is indeed like that of the blessed Hari (196).
Having thus performed worship and likewise washed his feet, O best of the Vaiśyas, he then placed [the water] upon his head with supreme faith;
for where the water from the feet is borne on the head with faith by a Vaiśya.
Having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, incense, and lamps, preceded by meditative devotion (198), they were likewise fed with delicious food;
those supreme *paramahaṃsas*, being satisfied, rested in the temple during the night (199).
O best of men, meditating upon the Supreme Brahman, that light which is considered the light of all lights,
the merit born of their hospitality—
which has arisen for you— is indeed such that I am not able to describe it even with a thousand mouths.
Among beings, those with breath are the best; among those with breath, those who live by their intelligence; among the intelligent, the gods are the best; among men, those born of the Brahman caste;
among Brāhmaṇas, the learned; and among the learned, those whose intellects are fixed on righteous deeds. 201–202.
Among those who have perfected their intellect, they are the true doers; among doers, they are the knowers of Brahman.
For this very reason, they are most worthy of worship; therefore, they are the most excellent in the three worlds.
O best of Vaiśyas, association with them destroys even the greatest of sins.

Those who have found rest in the homes of householders, who are contented and know Brahman, truly destroy in an instant the sin accumulated from birth; indeed, they destroy whatever sin has been accumulated by a householder until the end of life. 204–205.

"A mendicant who has fasted for a single night completely burns away all that [evil]; give this merit to your brother, and he will be liberated from hell. Having heard these words of the messenger, he quickly gave the merit.
With a joyful heart, that brother also emerged from hell;
honored by the gods with a rain of flowers, they both ascended to heaven. Having been properly honored by them, the messenger departed just as he had come.
Having heard the words of the divine messenger, which brought awakening to the entire world and were equal to the declarations of the Vedas, the son of the Vaiśya,
having delivered his brother by means of the gift of his own performed merit, went together with him to the excellent realm of the Lord of the Gods.
O King, let one who is a ruler read or even hear this history.
One obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows, free from sorrow.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter of the Svargakhaṇḍa in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Thirty-Two.
Nārada said:
From there, O lord of kings, one should go to Sugandha, which is world-renowned;
with his soul purified of all sins, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā. 1.
O lord of men, a pilgrim should then go to Rudravartana;
having bathed there, O King, a man is glorified in the heavenly world. O best of men, [there is also the confluence] of the Gaṅgā and the Sarasvatī.
Having bathed there, one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the heavenly world.
Having bathed there in Karṇahrada and worshipped the god Śaṅkara,
one does not meet with misfortune and goes to the heavenly world.
Then, O lord of men, the pilgrim should proceed in due order to Kubjāmraka; he obtains the merit of a thousand cows and goes to the heavenly world.
Next, the pilgrim should go to Arundhatīvaṭa.

Having touched the waters of the ocean and fasted for three nights, a man obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows and goes to the heavenly world. Thence, one who is self-controlled and observant of celibacy should go to Brahmāvarta.
One obtains the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice and goes to the heavenly world;
having approached the Yamunā-prabhava and performed ablutions in the waters of the Yamunā,
one attains the fruit of an Ashvamedha and is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Having reached the ford known as Darvīsaṃkramaṇa, which is renowned throughout the three worlds,
one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the heavenly world.
Having gone to the source of the Sindhu river, which is frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas, [one attains the same].
Having stayed there for five nights, one should give much gold;
then, having reached the goddess who is extremely difficult to attain,
a man obtains the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice and goes to the destination of Ushanas.
O descendant of Bharata, having reached the Ṛṣikulyā and Vasiṣṭha,
all castes become twice-born by passing beyond Vasiṣṭha;
a man who bathes in the Ṛṣikulyā attains the world of the sages.
O King, if one subsists here for a month on a diet of śāka vegetables,
and having reached Bhṛgutuṅga, one obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice (vājimedha).
Having gone to Vīrapramokṣa, one is liberated from all sins.
Having reached the sacred ford (tīrtha) of the months of Kārttika and Māgha, which is difficult to attain,
the performer of meritorious deeds obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma and Atirātra sacrifices. Then, having arrived at the Sandhyā, one reaches the unsurpassed Vidyātīrtha.
By touching [the water] at all these places of learning, one becomes a master of all sciences;
one should dwell for one night at Mahāśrama, which liberates one from all sins. By fasting for one meal-time, one dwells in auspicious worlds.
By fasting at Mahālaya for a month on the sixth lunar day,
one who has crossed over delivers ten ancestors and ten descendants;
having beheld this supreme merit of Maheśvara, which is saluted by the gods.
Having accomplished his purpose in all his duties, he shall never grieve over death; with his soul purified of all sins, he shall obtain the Bahusuvarṇaka [Tīrtha].
Or else, he should go to Vetāsikā, which was frequented by Pitāmaha.
One obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and shall go to the supreme goal.
Then, having reached the Sundarikā Tīrtha, which is frequented by the Siddhas, one becomes a possessor of beauty; this has been observed by the ancients. 21-22.
Then, having gone to Brāhmaṇikā with a concentrated mind as a celibate student,
one attains the world of Brahmā by means of a lotus-colored vehicle. Then, one should go to the meritorious Naimiṣa, frequented by the twice-born.
There, Brahmā dwells eternally together with hosts of gods.
For one who merely desires to go to Naimiṣa, half of their sin is destroyed;
but upon entering it, a person is liberated from all sins.

There, O Bhārata, the wise man devoted to that sacred site should dwell for one month at Naimiṣa; for whatever sacred sites exist on earth, they are all present at Naimiṣa. Having performed his ablutions there, self-controlled and restricted in diet, he attains the fruit of his merit.
That man obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice;
O best of the Bharatas, he purifies his lineage up to the seventh generation who, devoted to fasting, gives up his life at Naimiṣa. 27–28.

O best of kings, the wise have said that Naimiṣa is eternally pure, auspicious, and meritorious, as if one were already situated in the heavenly realm. Having reached Gaṅgodbheda, a man who fasts for three nights—
He obtains the Vājapeya sacrifice and shall forever become one with Brahman.
Having reached the Sarasvatī, he should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
he rejoices in the worlds of Sarasvatī—of this there is no doubt.
Then one should go to the holy Carajanī, frequented by meritorious people;
devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods, one obtains the merit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Having reached Vimalāśoka, one shines like the moon.
Having stayed there for one night, one is honored in the heavenly world;
from there, one should go to Gopratāra, the supreme sacred site on the banks of the Sarayū, where Rāma went to heaven along with his servants, army, and mounts.
Having abandoned his home and the city, O King, by the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha),
by the grace of Rāma, and through his own resolve, O Bhārata— having bathed in that tīrtha at Gopratāra, O lord of men (36–37).
O descendant of Kuru, having bathed at Rāmatīrtha on the Gomatī, a man whose soul is purified of all sins is glorified in the heavenly world;
he attains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and sanctifies his own lineage.

O best of the Bharatas, there is a sacred ford (tīrtha) there called Śatasāhasraka; having performed ablutions there, being self-restrained and restricted in diet, one obtains the merit of a thousand cows, O bull of the Bharata race. 39-40.
Then, O knower of dharma, a man should go to the unsurpassed Ūrdhvasthāna;
having bathed at Koṭitīrtha and having worshipped Guha, O King, he obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows and becomes endowed with splendor. 41.
Then, having gone to Vārāṇasī and worshipped the Bull-bannered Lord (Śiva),
and having bathed in the Hrada of Kapilā, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
O Indra among kings, having reached the difficult-to-attain Tīrtha of Mārkaṇḍeya— 42–43.
At the world-renowned confluence of the Gomatī and the Gaṅgā,
one obtains the merit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and uplifts one's entire lineage.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter of the Svargakhaṇḍa in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Thirty-three.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
You have related the greatness of Vārāṇasī in brief.
"O Sage, speak in detail; it pleases my mind.
Nārada said:
"In this regard, I shall relate an ancient history concerning the virtues of Vārāṇasī."

By the mere hearing of which one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin. Formerly, on the peak of Mount Meru, the Goddess, seated upon her divine throne, questioned the Great God, the Lord Īśāna, the enemy of Tripura.
The Goddess said: O Mahādeva, God of gods, destroyer of the afflictions of your devotees, how does a person behold you, the Divine, in such a short time? 4

O Śaṅkara, Sāṃkhya-yoga, as well as meditation, Vedic karma-yoga, and whatever other practices there are in this world that involve great exertion— by what means do the yogis and even the performers of ritual action attain a state where their minds are at rest?
For the Lord is indeed visible as subtle within all embodied beings.
This most secret knowledge is profound and practiced by Śakra and others;
for the welfare of all creatures, speak it, for it destroys the fire of desire.
Īśvara said:

I shall declare to you, according to its true nature, that knowledge which is inexpressible, which is known by the wise, and which has been excluded by the ignorant—just as it was spoken by the supreme seers. 8.
Vārāṇasī, my city, is the most supreme and secret field;
it carries all living beings across the ocean of saṃsāra.
There, O Great Goddess, those who abide by my vow with devotion—
High-souled beings dwell there, established in supreme discipline.
That which is the best of all sacred fords (tīrthas), the best of all places,
and the highest knowledge among all forms of knowledge— that is my supreme Avimukta.

There are sacred places, holy fords, and shrines located in various other sites, situated even in cremation grounds as well as in divine lands; my abode is in the intermediate space, directly connected with the world of earth (bhūrloka). 12.
Those who are not liberated perceive it as such there, while those who are liberated perceive it with their consciousness.
This place is renowned as a cremation ground, heard of as Avimukta;
having become Time (Kāla), O beautiful one, I withdraw this entire world here. 13-14.
O Goddess, this is the station of all secrets, most dear to Me; My devotees go there and enter into Me alone.
Whatever has been given, chanted, offered in sacrifice, performed as a rite, practiced as austerity, or whatever else has been done [therein], [all that becomes infinite].
Meditation, study, and knowledge— all these become inexhaustible there.
Whatever sin was previously accumulated over thousands of other births,
all of it goes to destruction for one who has entered Avimukta.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those of mixed castes;
women, Mlecchas, and others who are of mixed origin and born of sinful wombs; even insects, ants, and whatever other beasts and birds there may be—(all these were present). 18.

O fair-faced one, those who meet their death in time at Avimukta are born as men in my city, O Goddess; they possess crescent moons upon their crests, have three eyes, and ride upon great bulls. 19–20.
No sinner who dies in Avimukta goes to hell; for all those favored by the Lord attain the supreme goal.
Considering liberation to be very difficult to obtain and worldly existence to be most terrifying, [one should strive for it].
A man should dwell in Vārāṇasī even after breaking his feet with a stone;
for, O Supreme Goddess, that destination which grants liberation from saṃsāra to one who dies anywhere else is difficult to attain even through ascetic penance. 22-23.
O daughter of the lord of mountains, through my grace, one is born correctly;
yet those deluded by my māyā do not perceive me while still unevolved.
They dwell again and again in the midst of feces, urine, and semen.
Even if he is being struck down by hundreds of obstacles, the wise man who continues to dwell [in this practice] goes to the supreme state, reaching which he no longer grieves;
freed from birth, death, and old age, they go to the supreme abode of Śiva.
For those who desire liberation, there is no goal higher than this state of non-returning to death; having attained it, the wise consider their task accomplished.
(27) Not by gifts, nor by austerities, nor by sacrifices, nor even by knowledge [is this attained].
An exalted state is attained, yet liberation is not obtained.
There are those of various complexions and discolored, such as the Cāṇḍālas and others who are loathsome, their bodies filled with sins and likewise with distinguished transgressions. 28–29.
The wise know that for them, Avimukta is the supreme medicine;
Avimukta is supreme knowledge, Avimukta is the supreme state, Avimukta is the supreme reality, and Avimukta is supreme auspiciousness. 30.

To those who, having taken the vow of perpetual celibacy (naiṣṭhikī-dīkṣā), dwell in Avimukta, I grant supreme knowledge at the end and the highest state. [Likewise for those in] Prayāga, Naimiṣa forest, Śrīśaila, and Mahābala. 31-32.
Kedāra, Ambha, Karṇa, Gayā, and Puṣkara;
Kurukṣetra, Bhadra-koṭi, the Narmadā, and Āmrātakeśvarī; Śālagrāma, Kubjāmra, and the unsurpassed Kokāmukha. 33.
Prabhāsa, Vijayeśāna, Gokarṇa, and Bhadrakarṇaka—
these are the meritorious places renowned here in the three worlds;
yet they do not lead one to the supreme reality as does death in Vārāṇasī.
In Vārāṇasī especially, the Gaṅgā, flowing through the three paths,
destroys the sin committed over hundreds of previous births once she has entered [the city].
Elsewhere, the Gaṅgā is easily accessible, as are śrāddha, charity, austerity, and recitation.
All these vows are indeed very difficult to obtain elsewhere than in Vārāṇasī.
A man who remains in Vārāṇasī constantly subsisting on air, should always mutter prayers, offer oblations, give gifts, and worship the immortals. 37–38.
Whether a man be sinful, whether he be deceitful, or whether he be unrighteous,
upon reaching Vārāṇasī, he purifies his entire lineage.
Those who worship and indeed praise Mahādeva in Vārāṇasī—

Those who are completely liberated from all sins should be known as lords of the gaṇas. Otherwise, that supreme state is attained through the practice of yoga and knowledge, or through renunciation, or by some other means, only after a thousand births.
Those who dwell in Vārāṇasī, O Lord of the gods, attain supreme liberation in a single birth alone;
for there, yoga as well as knowledge and liberation are achieved in one lifetime. 42.
Having reached that Avimukta, one should not desire any other forest of asceticism (tapovana).
Because it has not been abandoned by me, it is therefore remembered as Avimukta; that indeed is the secret of secrets, and this is called the supreme knowledge. 43–44.
O fair-browed one, that goal which is known for those established in knowledge or ignorance who desire supreme bliss— that same state belongs to one who has died in Avimukta.
Furthermore, whatever [signs] are seen in the body of one who has not yet been liberated [from the body], in their entirety—
Even more auspicious than the cities and places of Vārāṇasī is that place where Mahādeva himself, the Lord, at the end of one's physical existence,
personally imparts the Tāraka Brahman for the sake of liberation from saṃsāra. 46-47.
That supreme reality which is known as Avimukta,
one may attain in Vārāṇasī in a single birth alone.
[It is located] between the eyebrows, in the center of the navel, in the heart, and likewise in the head.
Just as the eternally liberated Sun is situated at Ādityeśvara in Vārāṇasī, so too is the city of Vārāṇasī situated between the Varaṇā and [the Asī];
right there, the eternally liberated reality itself is established. 49–50.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a place superior to Vārāṇasī,
where the divine Nārāyaṇa, Mahādeva, the Lord of Heaven, resides.
There, the gods dwell together with the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas.
The Grandfather, the God of gods, constantly attends to this city. O Goddess, even those who are great sinners and the most wicked among evildoers, upon reaching Vārāṇasī, attain the supreme goal.
Therefore, one desiring liberation should dwell in Vārāṇasī with self-restraint until death; having obtained knowledge from Mahādeva, one is liberated.
However, obstacles will arise for those whose minds are afflicted by sin.
Therefore, one should never commit sin through body, mind, or speech (55).
O lady of excellent vows, this secret of the ancient gods and the knowledge that takes refuge in Avimukta is not known by anyone in its true essence (56).
Nārada said: While the deities, the ṛṣis, and the supreme beings were listening,
the God of gods spoke that which destroys all sins.

Just as Nārāyaṇa is the best among the gods and Puruṣottama, and as Giriśa is the lord of lords, so is this place the most excellent among all sacred sites. O Rudra, by those who have propitiated him in a previous birth, [this place is attained].
They also know this supreme field, Avimukta, the abode of Śiva.
For those whose intellect has been stolen away by the impurities born of the Kali age,
it is not possible for them to know that station of the Supreme Lord.
For those who always remember and speak of this city,
their sins perish quickly both in this world and the next. Whatever sins they may commit here while residing [in this city], [they are likewise destroyed].
Śiva, the God whose body is Time, shall destroy all of those [sins].
One should come to this very place, frequented by those who desire liberation,
so that for the deceased there shall be no further rebirth in the ocean of worldly existence.
Therefore, with every effort, a person should dwell in Vārāṇasī—
whether they be a yogi or not a yogi, a sinner or the most virtuous of doers—
not out of the words of the world, nor from the command of parents, nor even from the instruction of a guru.
"One's mind should not waver toward a destination other than the Avimukta [state].
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Thirty-four.
Nārada said:
There is this pure, auspicious liṅga named Oṃkāra, by the mere remembrance of which one is liberated from all sins. 1.
This is the supreme knowledge, the most excellent Pañcāyatana,
which is constantly practiced by sages in Vārāṇasī as the means of liberation.
There, Mahādeva himself is present in the form of the fivefold abode (Pañcāyatana).
The Blessed Lord Rudra, the bestower of liberation upon living beings, delights [in this].
This is the knowledge of Pāśupata, which is said to have five abodes; it is this very stainless *liṅga*, established as the syllable *Oṃ*. 3–4.
Śāntyatītā, Śānti, Vidyā—the higher and lower—and Pratiṣṭhā and Nivṛtti: these five constitute the Ātman of the Īśvara-liṅga.
It is the common refuge for the five liṅgas, beginning with Brahmā.
The *liṅga* that awakens the syllable *Oṃ* is called the fivefold abode (*pañcāyatana*).
One should meditate upon the Lord as the imperishable *liṅga* of the fivefold abode;
at the end of the body, the wise one enters the supreme light of bliss.
There, in former times, the celestial rishis, the perfected ones (siddhas), and likewise the brahmin rishis,
having worshipped the Lord Ishana, attained the supreme state. On the auspicious banks of the Matsyodarī is that most secret and beautiful sacred place.
O King of kings, [the area] the size of a cow's hide contains the supreme Oṃkāreśvara;
the Kṛttivāseśvara Liṅga, the supreme Madhyameśvara, as well as Viśveśvara, Oṃkāra, and Kandarpaśvara. 10.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, no one here in Vārāṇasī knows these secret signs except by the grace of Śambhu;
thus, O King, hear the majesty of Kṛttivāseśvara.

In that place, in former times, a Daitya, having become an elephant, came into the presence of Śiva in order to kill the Brahmins who were constantly engaged in worship there; at that moment, the three-eyed Mahādeva manifested from their *liṅgas*.
For the sake of protecting his devotees, Mahādeva, who is affectionate toward his devotees,
killed the Daitya in the form of an elephant with his trident as if in sport; he then made the elephant's hide his garment, and thus became Kṛttivāseśvara.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, those two sages attained supreme perfection there;
indeed, by means of that very body, they reached that highest state as the Rudras known as the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyā) and the Lords of Ignorance (Avidyā), who are celebrated as Śivas. 15–16.
Knowing the Kali age to be terrible and abounding in unrighteousness, people remain constantly taking refuge at the Kṛttivāseśvara Liṅga;
they do not leave Kṛttivāsa, for by that they have achieved their life's purpose—of this there is no doubt. 17.
Liberation may or may not be attained even after a thousand previous births;
however, liberation is obtained here at Kṛttivāsa in a single birth. Indeed, they say this place is the abode of all the Siddhas. 18–19.
It was concealed by the God of gods, Mahādeva Śambhu;
for in every age, self-controlled Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas worship that Great Soul here and recite the Śatarudriya.

They constantly praise the god Tryambaka, clad in animal skins; they meditate in their hearts upon the god Sthāṇu, the auspicious one who dwells within all. The Siddhas indeed sing songs, as do the Brahmins who reside in Vārāṇasī.
Then, among them, liberation would come to those who have taken refuge in Kṛttivāsas.
Having attained birth in the families of Brahmins— a birth that is most difficult to obtain and is desired by all the worlds—
they, as ascetics, having concentrated their minds in meditation, chant the Rudra-mantra while meditating upon Maheśa in their hearts.
The lords of sages dwelling within Vārāṇasī propitiate the Lord, the Sovereign;
free from worldly desire, they worship Him with sacrifices, praise Rudra, and bow down to Śambhu.
24. "Obeisance to Bhava, the abode of the yoga of immortality; I take refuge in Sthāṇu, the ancient Giriśa."
"I remember Rudra entered within my heart; I know Mahādeva, who possesses manifold forms.
(25) Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Thirty-Five.
Nārada said:
Then, O King, there is another supreme Liṅga there called Kapardīśvara;
having bathed there according to the prescribed rite and having offered libations to the ancestors, [one should worship it].
One is liberated from all sins and attains both liberation (mukti) and worldly enjoyment (bhukti).
Beyond that stands another sacred site named Piśācamocana.
There resides the wondrous Lord, the bestower of liberation and the destroyer of all defects.
A certain Daitya, a tiger among beasts assuming a terrifying form,
came there to devour a certain doe at the supreme shrine of Kapardin-Īśvara. There, with a heart full of fear, she performed circumambulation again and again.
Running in great agitation, they fell into the power of the tiger;
then that mighty tiger, having torn her with his sharp claws,
went to another secluded place upon seeing the lords of sages.
Immediately upon her death, that young girl appeared before Lord Kapardī as a doe;
she possessed a great flame in the sky with a radiance equal to the sun,
was three-eyed and blue-throated, and her hair was marked by the crescent moon.
Surrounded by men likewise mounted upon bulls, the sky-dwellers released a rain of flowers from all sides;
at that very moment, she herself became the Mistress of the Gaṇas (Gaṇeśvarī). Thus it was seen.
Having seen that most excellent wonder, the gods and others offered praise.
By merely remembering that supreme *liṅga* of Maheśvara known as Kapardīśvara, one is swiftly liberated from the entire multitude of sins.
All defects such as lust, anger, and the like, as well as all obstacles for the residents of Vārāṇasī, perish through the worship of Kapardīśvara.
Therefore, one should always behold the supreme Kapardīśvara.
It should be worshipped with diligence and praised with Vedic hymns.
For yogis who meditate here constantly with tranquil minds, the perfection of yoga shall arise within six months; of this there is no doubt. 12–13.
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are destroyed by worshipping him;
for peace is attained by one who has bathed in the Piśācamocana pool.
Formerly, in that sacred field, there was a Brahmin ascetic of rigid vows.
Known as Śaṅkukarṇa, he worshipped Śaṅkara;
he chanted the Rudramantra and the Praṇava, which is the very form of Brahman,
incessantly with flowers, incense, and other offerings, along with hymns, prostrations, and circumambulations.
Having performed the perpetual initiation (*naiṣṭhikī dīkṣā*), he practiced yoga there;
yet once, he beheld a deceased spirit that had arrived, overcome by hunger, its limbs bound together by skin and bone, sighing again and again. (17)

Seeing him, that best of sages was filled with supreme compassion and said: "Who are you, and from what country have you come to this place? To him, the piśāca, tormented by hunger, spoke these words.
In a previous birth, I was a Brahmin endowed with wealth and grain,
possessed of sons, grandsons, and so forth, and intent on maintaining my family;
yet I did not worship Mahādeva, nor cows, nor guests.
Never has merit been performed by me, whether it be small or great.
Once, the Blessed Lord, whose vehicle is the bull-king, the Lord of the Universe, was seen, touched, and saluted by me in Vārāṇasī. 21–22.
Then, after a short time, I met my death;
yet, O Sage, that most terrible abode of Yama was not seen by me. Now, overcome by thirst, I do not distinguish between what is beneficial and what is harmful.
"O Lord, if you see any means to deliver me, please do so; salutations to you, for I have come to you for refuge.
Having been addressed thus, Śaṅkukarṇa then spoke these words to the Piśāca: 24–25.
There exists no one else in this world who has performed such supreme merit as you,
for you previously beheld the Blessed Lord Śiva, the Sovereign of the Universe;
having been touched by him and honored by him repeatedly, who else on earth is equal to you?
"By the ripening of that karma, you have come to this place. Perform your bath quickly with a concentrated mind in this pool, by which you shall swiftly cast off this contemptible womb. (27-28)
Thus addressed by the compassionate sage, he remembered the three-eyed Lord of gods, Kapardīśvara, the Sovereign; and having composed his mind, he entered into meditative absorption.
Then, immersed in the presence of the sage, Māra appeared, adorned with divine ornaments.
Invisible, resembling the sun, with a beautiful crown marked by the sign of the moon,
that Lord Rudra shines in the sky, attended by the gods and borne by immeasurable yogis such as the Vālakhilyas, like the Sun, the God of all, at his rising. 30–31.
The hosts of gods, beginning with the Siddhas, offered praise; the delightful celestial Apsarases danced;
and the Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Kinnaras, and others released a rain of flowers mixed with water.
Then, being thus extolled by the assemblies of the lords of sages, he attained enlightenment through the grace of the Blessed One.
He entered this supreme maṇḍala, consisting of the three Vedas, wherein Rudra shines forth.
Having seen even the Piśāca-bhūta liberated, the sage was delighted in his mind;
reflecting upon Rudra—the one Seer and the Fire—he bowed down and praised that Kapardin.
Śaṅkukarṇa said:
I go to you, the one with matted hair, who is beyond the beyond, the sole protector, the ancient Puruṣa, the Lord of Yoga, the fulfiller of desires, the Sun, the Fire, mounted upon Kapila. 35.
I go for refuge to you, Rudra, who are seated in the heart as the essence of Brahman, the golden one, the primordial yogi, dwelling in heaven, the great sage, composed of Brahman, and pure.
You are endowed with a thousand feet, eyes, and heads, possessing a thousand forms, beyond the darkness.
I bow to that Śambhu, the shore beyond Brahman, the Lord of Hiraṇyagarbha, the three-eyed one;
I perpetually take refuge in that Blessed Lord, the shore beyond Brahman, in whom is the origin of the world and by whom all this is pervaded through his auspiciousness. 38
I shall bow to You, who are beyond the reach of the senses, whose form is devoid of light, who are self-effulgent, the Lord, the singular form,
the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Ishvara— than whom nothing else exists. (39) To You,
whom the yogis, having abandoned seeded yoga and attained samādhi, become one with the Supreme Self...
I bow eternally to that Lord Paśyanti-deva, the ultimate shore of Brahman, the supreme essential nature (40)—
