in whom there is no construction of distinctions such as names and so forth, whose essential nature does not appear as an object of sight,
and who stands as the shore of Brahman; I take refuge in you, the Self-existent One (41).
I perpetually bow down to that Brahman, the further shore, whom those devoted to the Vedas perceive as the one, non-dual realization of Brahman, yet who appears as Your manifold form;
from whom the ancient Puruṣa sustains both Pradhāna and Tejas, and before whom the gods prostrate themselves. 42.
I bow to that great Time, established in the light, which is your own essential nature. 43 I go for refuge eternally to Guheśa; I seek shelter with Sthāṇu, the ancient Giriśa.
I seek refuge with Śiva; I go for protection to you, Hari, the moon-crested wielder of the Pināka bow. 44
Having thus praised the Lord who wears his hair in matted locks, Śaṅkukarṇa prostrated himself on the ground like a staff, uttering the supreme Praṇava.
At that very moment, the supreme Liṅga, whose essence is Śiva, manifested.

Knowledge, which is supreme bliss and resembles a fire with millions of flames—[this] Śaṅkukarṇa, having then become liberated, being of that nature, all-pervading, and stainless, merged as it were into the stainless Liṅga;
that was like a marvel. 46–47.
Thus has been told this laughable majesty of the one with matted hair (Kapardin); no one knows it, for even a learned man is deluded here by darkness.
Whoever should daily hear this story that destroys sin—

One whose soul is purified by having abandoned all evil shall attain proximity to Rudra. Furthermore, being pure, he who constantly recites this great hymn to Brahmā at dawn and at midday shall attain the supreme yoga.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Vārāṇasī," in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Thirty-six.
Nārada said:
In Vārāṇasī, O Great King, at that supreme place known as Madhyameśa, Mahādeva, the Great Lord,
dwells together with the Goddess; there the Blessed One eternally rejoices, surrounded by the Rudras.
There, at first, Hṛṣīkeśa, the soul of the universe and son of Devakī,
Kṛṣṇa, dwelt for one year constantly accompanied by the Pāśupatas—
his entire body smeared with ashes and intent upon the recitation of the Rudra-mantras.
Worshiping Śambhu by performing the Pāśupata vow,
Hari had many disciples devoted to the practice of celibacy;
having received knowledge from his mouth, they beheld Maheśvara.
To him, the Lord Mahādeva, Nīlalohita, appeared in person and,
as the bestower of boons, granted this supreme boon to Kṛṣṇa:
"Those who are my devotees and worship Govinda according to the prescribed rites, [they shall attain me]."
Then, that divine knowledge consisting of the universe will arise within them;
they shall be worthy of salutation, worship, and meditation by people devoted to the Supreme. By my grace, there is no doubt that these twice-born ones will become so.
O Lord of Gods, those who, having bathed, behold the God who wields the Pināka bow here,
their sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are swiftly destroyed.
Even those mortals who, though devoted to sinful deeds, shall cast off their lives [here], [their sins are likewise destroyed].
That supreme state belongs to them; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Blessed indeed are those who, having offered water in the Mandākinī, have worshipped the Great Lord, the Sovereign Madhyameśvara. 10.
Knowledge, giving, austerity, the ancestral śrāddha, and the offering of the funeral cake—
each of these acts performed here purifies one's lineage up to the seventh generation.
Having touched the waters at Sannihatya when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, [one attains the same merit].
Whatever fruit one obtains by matricide, ten times that is obtained here;
thus has been told the majesty of Mahārāja at Madhyameśvara—he who hears this with supreme devotion goes to the highest state. 13.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, concerning the majesty of Vārāṇasī.
Chapter Thirty-Seven.
Nārada said:
O Yudhiṣṭhira, hear now of other great royal tīrthas that purify, situated here in Vārāṇasī; Prayāga is a supreme and most auspicious tīrtha, even greater than [the general] Prayāga.
Likewise, Viśvarūpa, the Tīrtha, and the unsurpassed Tālatīrtha;
the great Tīrtha called Ākāśa, the supreme Tīrtha of Ṛṣabha, the great Tīrtha Sunīla, and the unsurpassed Gaurītīrtha. 2–3.
Prājāpatya, likewise Atīrtha, Svargadvāra,
and that which is called Jambukeśvara, as well as the supreme tīrtha named Dharmākhya; Gayātīrtha, the highest tīrtha, and the Mahānadī tīrtha.
The supreme Nārāyaṇa-tīrtha, the unsurpassed Vāyu-tīrtha;
the most secret Jñāna-tīrtha, the excellent Vārāha-tīrtha;
the meritorious Yama-tīrtha, and the auspicious Sammūrtika-tīrtha.
O Great King, there is Agnitīrtha and the most excellent Kalaśeśvara;
likewise Nāgatīrtha, Soma-tīrtha, and Sūrya-tīrtha;
as well as the great secret known as Parvata and the unsurpassed Maṇikarṇikā.
Ghaṭotkaca, the excellent Tīrtha, Śrītīrtha, and Pitāmaha;
Gaṅgātīrtha, Deveśa, and the supreme Tīrtha of Yayāti; Kāpila, Someśa, and the unsurpassed Brahmatīrtha. 8–9.
At that time, Viṣṇu installed that Īśvara-liṅga there, just as Brahmā had come to stay at Liṅgapura.
Having bathed there and returned, Brahmā spoke to Hari.
"Why have you installed this linga brought by me?
(11) Viṣṇu said to him: "O Rudra, my devotion to you is even firmer than yours;
therefore, this installed linga shall be known by your name. (12)
Likewise, O Yudhiṣṭhira, there is Bhūteśvara Tīrtha, the Tīrtha originating from Dharma, the most auspicious Gandharva Tīrtha, the excellent Vāhneya Tīrtha,
Daurvāsika Tīrtha, Vyoma Tīrtha, and Candra Tīrtha.
The holy tīrtha of Cintāṅgadeśvara, Vidyādhareśvara (14), Kedāra-tīrtha known as Ugra, the unsurpassed Kālañjara,
Sārasvata, Prabhāsa, and the auspicious Rudrakarṇahrada (15).
The great holy site named Kokila, the holy site Mahālaya,
Hiraṇyagarbha, Goprekṣa— an unsurpassed holy site—
and Upaśānta, Śiva, and the unsurpassed Vyāghreśvara. 16.
The great pilgrimage site Trilocana, Lokārka known as Uttarāhvaya (17),
the Kapālamocana tīrtha which destroys the sin of killing a brahmin,
the highly meritorious Śukreśvara, and the supreme Ānandapura (18).
"Such holy places as these, situated in Vārāṇasī, cannot indeed be described in detail even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Greatness of Vārāṇasī," in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
The thirty-eighth chapter.
Nārada said:
O Lord, [tell me] the majesty of Vārāṇasī and the holy fords within it.

These sacred fords have been described in brief; now hear of others. Then, O descendant of Bharata, having reached Gayā while remaining celibate and composed, one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice merely by going there.
O Lord, where the tree named Akṣayyavaṭa is renowned throughout the three worlds,
what is given there for the ancestors becomes inexhaustible.
Having touched the waters of the Mahānadī river, one should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods.
One shall attain inexhaustible worlds and uplift one's entire lineage; thereafter,
having reached Brahma-saras, frequented by the forest of Brahmā,
one attains the Puṇḍarīka [world], just as the night reaches its dawn.
There, the Sarasī Brahmin erected an excellent sacrificial post;
by circumambulating that post, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Thence, O Indra among kings, one should go to Dhenuka, which is world-renowned.
O King, having stayed for one night, one should give a sesame-cow;
with one's self purified of all sins, one will certainly go to the world of Soma.
O Great King, the sign of this remains there even today, without a doubt.
Indeed, O Bhārata, that Kapilā cow used to roam upon the mountain together with her calf; even today, O Indra among kings, O best of monarchs, her footprints are visible there.
Having touched water at those footprints, O lord of kings, [one attains merit].
Whatever inauspicious or sinful act has been committed, O Bhārata, that is utterly destroyed.
Thereafter, one should go to Gṛdhravaṭa, the abode of the trident-bearing God; having approached the Bull-bannered Lord there, one should bathe with ashes.
The twelve-year vow shall have been performed by the Brāhmaṇa,
and for the other castes, all sin is destroyed. Then one should go to Mount Udyanta, which resounds with songs.
O bull of the Bharatas, the footprint of Savitṛ is seen there;
a Brāhmaṇa of firm vows should perform his twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) there, for by doing so,
his saṃdhyā worship becomes equivalent to twelve years' worth.
O bull of the Bharatas, the Yonidvāra is also renowned in that very place;
by approaching it there, a person is liberated from the narrow passage of rebirth.
A man who would dwell at Gayā during both the bright and dark fortnights [attains this].
O King, he purifies his lineage up to the seventh generation; of this there is no doubt.
One should desire many sons, so that at least one might go to Gayā, or perform a horse sacrifice, or set free a dark-colored bull.
Thereafter, O King, the pilgrim who serves the sacred fords should go to Phalgu, O lord of men; he obtains the merit of a horse sacrifice and attains supreme perfection.
Then, O Indra among kings, one should proceed with a concentrated mind to Dharmapṛṣṭha.
O Great King Yudhiṣṭhira, wherever Dharma is eternally established,
one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice by approaching that Dharma.
From there, O Lord of Kings, one should go to the supreme tīrtha of Brahmā.

There, O Bhārata, one who is firm in his vows should approach and worship Brahmā; he obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices. Thereafter, O lord of men, the pilgrim should proceed to Rājagṛha.
Having sipped water there, Kakṣīvān then rejoices. A pure man who goes there before the fire to the Yakṣiṇī is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin by the grace of the Yakṣiṇī.
A man who eats the daily offering at Maṇināga shall go from there to heaven and obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows; moreover,
O King, the venom does not spread within one who has been bitten by a poisonous snake there.
Having stayed there for one night, one is liberated from all sins.
Then, O King, one should go to the forest of the Brahman-sage Gautama; having bathed at the site of Ahalyā, one shall attain the supreme goal. 25–26.
O King, having approached Śrī, one obtains supreme prosperity; there is a well there, O knower of dharma, renowned throughout the three worlds.
One who performs an ablution there shall obtain the merit of a horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
There is the well of the royal sage Janaka, worshipped by the thirty gods (28).
Having performed an ablution there, one shall attain the world of Viṣṇu;
from there, one should go to Avināśana, which grants liberation from all sins (29).

Having reached the Gaṇḍakī, which arises from the waters of all sacred fords (tīrthas), one obtains the merit of the horse sacrifice (vājimedha) and goes to the world of Soma. One obtains the merit of the Vājapeya sacrifice and goes to the world of the Sun.
Then Dhruva, the knower of dharma, entered the penance grove;
there he rejoiced among the highly fortunate Guhyakas, of this there is no doubt.
Having reached the river Karmadā, which is frequented by the Siddhas, [he dwelt there].
One obtains the Puṇḍarīka merit and goes to the world of Soma;
then, having reached the river Viśālā, which is renowned throughout the three worlds,
one obtains the Agniṣṭoma merit and goes to the heavenly world.
Then, O lord of men, having reached the Dhārā of Māheśvarī,
one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and uplifts one's lineage;
and a pure man, having reached the Puṣkariṇī of the gods, [obtains the same].
He does not fall into an evil state of existence and obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
moreover, being self-controlled and observant of celibacy, he shall go to the station of Maheśa.
Having bathed in the station of Maheśvara, one obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice (Aśvamedha).
There, O bull of the Bharatas, are ten million famous holy fords (tīrthas), O lord of kings;
they were being carried away by a wicked-souled asura in the form of a tortoise, but were recovered, O King, by the powerful Viṣṇu. 37–38.
O lord of men, one should perform an ablution there at Tīrthakoṭi;
one obtains the Puṇḍarīka [merit] and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. Then, O best of men, one should go to the abode of Nārāyaṇa.
O Bhārata, Hari dwells there, ever present; where Brahmā and the other gods, as well as the sages whose wealth is austerity,
and the Ādityas, Vasus, and Rudras, worship Janārdana.
Having approached the Śālagrāma, renowned as Viṣṇu of wondrous deeds— the Lord of the three worlds, the granter of boons, the infallible Viṣṇu—
one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. 42.
There, O King of kings, is the well known as Udapāna, which liberates one from all sins;
there are always four oceans present within that well, and by performing ablutions there, O Indra among kings, one shall not fall into an evil state of existence. 43–44.
Having approached the great god Viṣṇu, the giver of boons and the imperishable one,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, he shines like the moon freed from its debts;
remembering his former births, he touches the water, pure and with a restrained mind.
Having bathed there, one attains the memory of past births; of this there is no doubt.
Having gone to Vaṭeśvarapura and having worshipped Keśava, one obtains the desired worlds through fasting; of this there is no doubt.
Then, having gone to Tuvāmana, which destroys all sins,
and having paid homage to the god Hari, one shall not encounter misfortune.
Having gone to the hermitage of Bharata, which releases one from all sins...
One should then resort to Kauśikī, which destroys great sins;
a person obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Thereafter, O knower of dharma, one should go to the excellent Campakāraṇya.
Having stayed there for one night, one obtains the fruit of donating a thousand cows;
then, having reached the highly esteemed holy site of Govinda,
one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice by fasting for one night.
Having beheld Viśveśvara there together with the Goddess,
O bull of the Bharatas, one shall attain the worlds of Mitra and Varuṇa;
having fasted there for three nights, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
O bull of the Bharatas, having approached the abode of virgins and being self-restrained with a regulated diet, one attains the worlds of Manu Prajāpati.
O Bhārata, those who bestow even a very small gift upon a maiden [attain the same].
The sages of firm vows declare that it is inexhaustible.
Having reached Niṣṭhāvāsa, which is renowned throughout the three worlds,
one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Moreover, O tiger among men, those people who bestow gifts at the time of death go to the healthy world of Brahmā;
there is the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha, renowned throughout the three worlds.
One who performs an ablution there shall obtain the merit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Having reached Devakūṭa, which is frequented by hosts of gods and sages,
one obtains the merit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice and uplifts one's entire lineage.
From there, O lord of kings, one should go to the lake of the sage Kauśika;
it was there that Viśvāmitra, the son of Kuśika, attained supreme perfection.
O bull of the Bharata lineage, it is there that the wise one resided by the Kauśikī river.
One obtains in a single month that merit which belongs to the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
Furthermore, he who dwells at that great lake, the best of all sacred fords (tīrtha), shall not fall into an evil state; one should know him to be possessed of much gold.
Then, having approached Kumāra, who dwells in the hermitage of Ābhīra,
one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the world of Śakra. And having reached the well at Nandinī, which is frequented by the gods, [one attains the same].
O best of the Kurus, one obtains that merit which belongs to the human sacrifice (naramedha) by bathing at the confluence of the Kālikā, where the Kauśikī and Aruṇā meet; there,
a wise man who has fasted for three nights is liberated from all sins.
Having reached the Urvaśī-tīrtha and likewise the hermitage of Soma, O wise one, and having bathed at the hermitage of Kumbhakarṇa, a man is honored on earth;
likewise, having bathed at Kokāmukha, being self-controlled and observing celibacy.
One attains the memory of past births; this has been observed by the ancients.
(67) Having reached the river even once, the twice-born becomes one who has accomplished his purpose;
with his soul purified of all sins, he goes to the heavenly world. (68)
Having reached Ṛṣabhadvīpa and served the destroyer of Krauñca,
and having sipped the waters of the Sarasvatī, one shines resplendent seated in a celestial chariot.
Audyānaka is a great royal tīrtha frequented by sages.
One should perform an ablution there; one is liberated from all sins.
Having reached the meritorious Brahma-tīrtha, frequented by Brahmanical sages, a man obtains the Vājapeya sacrifice; of this there is no doubt.

Then, having reached Campā and performed the water-libation in the Bhāgīrathī, one obtains the merit of donating a thousand cows upon reaching Daṇḍārpaṇa. Thence, one should go to the holy Lāviḍhikā, which is frequented by the meritorious.
He attains the Vājapeya sacrifice and is honored while seated upon a celestial chariot.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of Gayā and Other Holy Places," in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Thirty-nine. Nārada said:
Then, having reached the excellent sacred ford (tīrtha) known as Savidyā at the time of twilight (saṃdhyā),...
A wise man who touches [the water] here becomes a knower of the Self; there is no doubt about this.
By the grace of Rāma, that king of tīrthas was made in ancient times; having reached that Lauhitya, one should know it as Bahusuvarṇaka. 1-2.
Having reached the Karatoyā and fasted for three nights,
a man obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the world of Śakra.
Furthermore, O Indra among kings, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean—
The wise declare that [the merit of bathing there] is ten times that of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha).
O descendant of Bharata, he who reaches the further island of the Gaṅgā and bathes there,
having fasted for three nights, O King, shall obtain all his desires.
Then, having gone to the river Vaitaraṇī which liberates one from sin,
and having reached the holy ford Viraja, he shines like the moon;
and by the power [of that place], having purified his lineage, he casts off all evil.
Having obtained the merit of a thousand cows, that man purifies his own lineage. Dwelling at the confluence of the Śoṇa and the Jyotirathyā,
pure and having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, he obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.

O bull among the Kurus, by touching the Vaṃśagulma at the source of the Śoṇa and the Narmadā, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice. O lord of men, having reached the Ṛṣabha Tīrtha in Kośalā, [one obtains the same].

A man who has fasted for three nights obtains the merit of a horse-sacrifice (vājimedha). Having reached Kālatīrtha in Kośalā, he should touch its waters; there is no doubt that he receives the merit of eleven bulls as a sacrificial gift.
Having touched the waters at Puṣpavatī and fasted for three nights, a man shall obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows and uplift his entire lineage.
Then, with a restrained mind, having bathed at the holy ford of Badarī, he [should proceed].
One attains long life and goes to the heavenly world. Then, having reached Mahendra, frequented by the son of Jamadagni, a man who bathes at Rāmatīrtha obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice. 13-14.
O bull of the Bharatas, right there is the field of Mataṅga;
having bathed there, O King, a man obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows.
Having reached Śrīparvata, one should perform ablutions at the riverbank.
One obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and attains supreme perfection.
On Śrīparvata, the greatly effulgent Mahādeva dwells together with the Goddess, supremely delighted, as does Brahmā surrounded by the thirty gods.
Having bathed there in Devahrada, pure and with a restrained mind,
one obtains the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice and attains supreme perfection. Having gone to Mount Rishabha, which is worshipped by the gods at Bhāṇḍeṣu...
One obtains the Vājapeya sacrifice and rejoices upon the back of Nāka. Thence one should go to the Kāverī, which is surrounded by hosts of Apsarases;
having bathed there, O King, a man obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
There, at that sacred ford of the ocean, one should perform ablutions at Kanyātīrtha; having performed ablutions there, O Indra among kings, one is liberated from all sins.
Then, having reached Gokarṇa, which is renowned throughout the three worlds.
O Indra among kings, in the midst of the ocean is that which is honored by all the worlds;
there dwell Brahmā and the other gods, sages whose wealth is their asceticism,
as well as bhūtas, yakṣas, piśācas, kinnaras, and great serpents.
Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, humans, as well as Pannagas,
rivers, oceans, and mountains, all worship the Lord of Umā. Having fasted there for three nights and having duly worshipped Īśāna, a man [attains his goal].
One obtains the merit of ten horse-sacrifices and attains the status of a leader of the Gaṇas (Gāṇapatya).
By fasting for twelve nights, a man becomes one who has accomplished his purpose;
for in that very place is the station of Gāyatrī, renowned throughout the three worlds.

Having stayed there for three nights, one obtains the merit of a thousand cows; O lord of men, this is a visible manifestation before the eyes of the Brahmins. Furthermore, that twice-born man born of mixed lineage who recites the Gāyatrī [attains the same].
O King, for one who recites verses, songs, or hymns, [the merit] is lost;
for a non-Brahmin who recites the Sāvitrī, it perishes, even after reaching the difficult-to-attain lake of the brahmin-sage Saṃvarta. 28–29.
One becomes possessed of beauty and is born fortunate; then, having reached the Veṇā, one should satisfy the ancestors and the deities.
That man obtains a celestial chariot (vimāna) yoked with peacocks and swans.

Then, having reached the Godāvarī, which is constantly frequented by the Siddhas, one attains the Gavāmaya sacrifice and goes to the world of Vāyu. Having bathed at the confluence of the Veṇā, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Having bathed at Varadāsaṅgama, one obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows.
Reaching Brahmasthūṇā, a man who fasts for three nights shall find the merit of giving a thousand cows and goes to the heavenly world.
Having reached Kubjāvana, being self-restrained and composed,
one who fasts for three nights and bathes shall obtain the merit of giving a thousand cows.
Then, having bathed in Devahrada, which arises from the waters of the Kṛṣṇaveṇā, [one obtains the same].
O King, there is also the Jyotirmātra lake and likewise the Kanyāśrama,
where the king of the gods, having performed a hundred sacrifices, ascended to heaven;
by merely going there, one obtains the merit of a hundred Agniṣṭoma sacrifices.
Having bathed in the lake of Sarvadeva, one obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows.
Having bathed in the lake of Jātimātra, a man becomes a rememberer of his past births.
Having gone to the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga and that of the high-souled Śuka, [one attains the same]. 37–38.
One devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods shall obtain the merit of giving a thousand cows;
having reached Daṇḍakāraṇya, O great king, one should perform ablutions.
Having gone to the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga and that of the high-souled Śuka, [one obtains great merit].
A man does not fall into an evil state of existence and purifies his own lineage.
(40) Thereafter, a man should go to Sūryāraka, frequented by Jamadagni; having bathed at Rāmatīrtha, he shall obtain much gold. (41)
Having bathed at Saptagodāvarī, being self-restrained and restricted in diet,
one obtains great merit and goes to the world of the gods. Then, being self-restrained and restricted in diet, one should go to Devapatha.

A human being obtains that merit which belongs to a sacrifice for the gods (devasatra) by reaching Tuṅgakāraṇya. In ancient times, Sārasvata, a celibate with his senses subdued, taught the Vedas there to the sages.
O Bhārata, when the Vedas had been lost there, the son of the sage Aṅgiras sat upon the upper garments of the great sages and,
according to the rule, correctly uttered the syllable *oṃ*.
Whatever had been practiced by him previously presented itself before him.
There were the sages and the gods, Varuṇa, Agni, Prajāpati, the god Hari Nārāyaṇa, and likewise Mahādeva. 46–47.
And the illustrious Grandfather, together with the gods,
appointed the highly resplendent Bhṛgu to perform the sacrifice.
Then that blessed one duly performed it for the sages.
Furthermore, for all of them, the re-establishment of the sacred fires was performed through a rite witnessed by the gods.
By means of the *ājyabhāga* offering, they were gratified according to the prescribed rule; thus the gods departed for the three worlds, and the sages went as they pleased. 49–50.
O best of kings, for one who has entered that forest of Tuṅga,
whether a woman or a man, sin is destroyed instantly.
A wise person, self-restrained and restricted in diet, should dwell there for a month.
O King, he goes to the world of Brahmā and purifies his lineage once again. Having reached Medhāvana, one should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
one obtains the merit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and attains memory and intelligence.
Having gone there to Kālañjara, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows;
O King, one should perfect the self there on Mount Kālañjara. Such a man shall be honored in the heavenly world; of this there is no doubt.
Then, O lord of the people, having reached the Mandākinī river— which liberates one from sin— at Citrakūṭa on that best of excellent mountains,
one who performs ablutions here and is devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods [attains great merit].
One obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and attains the supreme goal;
from there, O lord of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed abode of Guha,
where the god Mahāsena is eternally present, O monarch.
A man becomes a supreme person simply by going there.
Having bathed at Koṭitīrtha, a man obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows;
then, having performed a circumambulation, he should proceed to Yaśaḥsthāna.
Having approached Mahādeva, one shines like the moon;
there, O great king, O bull of the Bharata race, is the famous well where the four oceans reside, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

Then, O Indra among kings, having sipped water and performed a circumambulation, a man of self-restraint, purified, shall go to the supreme goal. Thereafter, O best of the Kurus, one should go to the great city of Śṛṅgavera-pura.
O one of great wisdom, where formerly Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, crossed over;
there, a man who bathes in the Gaṅgā while practicing celibacy and controlling his senses becomes cleansed of sin and obtains the merit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Then one should go to the place of the wise god, Muñjavaṭaṅga (64).
Having approached Mahādeva and worshipped him, O lord of men,
and having performed a circumambulation, one shall attain the status of a Gaṇapati (65).
Then, O lord of kings, one should go to Prayāga, which is praised by the sages, where Brahmā and the other gods, the quarters along with their presiding deities,
the world-protectors, the Siddhas, and likewise the ancestors, are ever devoted.
Likewise, the great seers headed by Sanatkumāra, as well as the nāgas, suparṇas, siddhas, and those who uphold the seed (the *śukradharas*),
along with the rivers, oceans, gandharvas, and apsarases.
And there the Lord Hari resides, preceded by Prajāpati;
and there, between those two, is the triple pool (Triveṇī),
where the Gaṅgā flows after having passed beyond Prayāga, honored by all sacred fords.

There, the daughter of Tapaṇa (Yamunā), renowned throughout the three worlds, joined with Gaṅgā, bringing light to the world. The region between Gaṅgā and Yamunā is remembered as the hips of the Earth.
The sages know Prayāga to be the end of the hips and the vulva;
both Supratiṣṭhāna and Prayāga, as well as Kaṃbala and Aśvatara,
and the sacred ford Bhogavatī, are declared to be the altar of Prajāpati.
There, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the Vedas and sacrifices took embodied form (73),
and the ṛṣis of great merit worshipped Prajāpati;
likewise, O King, the gods and those who bear the discus performed sacrifices with ritual offerings (74).
"Therefore, O Bhārata, there is nothing more meritorious in the three worlds than Prayāga; it is superior in power to all other tīrthas, O Lord.
Even by hearing the name of that tīrtha or by its mere recitation..."
Or even by bowing one's head there, one is liberated from all sins.
He who, firm in his vows, performs an ablution at that confluence,
obtains the great merit of both the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
For this is the sacrificial ground even of the gods; what need then to speak of others?
O Bhārata, even a very small gift given there becomes great. Not by the word of the gods, my dear, nor even by the word of the world [is this so].
Your mind should be directed toward death at Prayāga;
for it has been proclaimed here, O joy of the Kurus, that ten thousand holy sites and sixty crores of others have their presence in this very place.
Whatever merit lies in the four Vedas and whatever merit lies in those who speak the truth,
one obtains that very merit simply by bathing at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
After that is the supreme sacred site named Bhogavatī, belonging to Vāsuki.
Whoever should perform an ablution there would obtain the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
There, O descendant of Kuru, is the tirtha known as Hamsaprapatana, renowned throughout the three worlds,
as well as Dashashvamedhika on the Ganges.
A bath taken at Gaṅgādvāra is equal to Kurukṣetra; there is no distinction [between them], yet Vaikuṇṭhanakhala is superior, and Prayāga is the greatest of all.
Even if one has committed a hundred wrongful acts, if service to the Gaṅgā is performed, [they are all purified].
The water of the Gaṅgā burns away all that [evil], just as fire consumes fuel;
the water of the Gaṅgā burns everything away like fire consumes a heap of cotton.
All merit is found in the Kṛta Yuga, while Puṣkara is remembered as the source of merit in the Tretā Yuga. 85–86.
Kurukṣetra is remembered as the foremost in the Dvāpara age, and the Gaṅgā in the Kali age;
one should perform penance at Puṣkara and bestow gifts at Mahālaya. One should ascend the fire on Mount Malaya, and seek death by fasting at Bhṛgutuṅga.
At Puṣkara, Eka-tuṅga, Kurukṣetra, and in those places situated within the waters of the Gaṅgā, a living being is instantly delivered, as well as seven generations of ancestors and descendants.
Merely by hearing its name, it purifies sin; by seeing it, it bestows merit.

Having bathed and drunk [the water], one purifies even one's lineage unto the seventh generation; O King, as long as a man’s bones touch the water of the Gaṅgā, so long is that person honored in the heavenly world.

Just as one who attends upon holy fords (*tīrtha*) and sacred shrines (*āyatana*) according to their merit obtains merit and becomes a partaker of the world beyond, there is no ford equal to the Gaṅgā, nor any deity superior to Keśava. 91–92.
"There is nothing superior to the Brahmins," so said the Grandfather (Brahmā).
O Great King, wherever the Gaṅgā is present, that place extends for a yojana;
it should be known as a field of perfection (siddhakṣetra) situated along the banks of the Gaṅgā.
This truth [should be recited] in the minds of the twice-born and the virtuous;
one should whisper liberation into the ear of a disciplined disciple who follows him.
This is righteous, this is pure, this leads to heaven, and this is happiness. 94–95.
This most meritorious, delightful, purifying, and supreme dharma is the secret "Head of the Earth," which liberates one from all sins;
by studying it in the midst of the twice-born, one attains stainless purity. 96.
This glorification of the lineage of holy fords (tīrthas) is auspicious, leading to the heavenly realm, bringing great merit, and subduing enemies. It is the foremost producer of intelligence;
indeed, one without a son obtains a son, and one without wealth shall obtain wealth. 97–98.
A king conquers the earth, a Vaiśya acquires wealth, and a Śūdra attains his desired objects by reciting this; and a Brāhmaṇa becomes one who has reached the further shore of all knowledge.
He who constantly hears this merit-bestowing account of the sacred fords shall always remain pure.
One attains the memory of past births and rejoices upon the heights of heaven.

(100) One should visit, even in thought, those sacred fords that have been described as accessible as well as those that are inaccessible, with the intention that all sacred fords are present there. (101)
These were performed by the Vasus, the Sādhyas, the Ādityas, the Maruts, the Aśvins,
and the god-like Ṛṣis, who sought to achieve meritorious deeds;
even so, O Kauravya of noble vows, you too [should act] according to this rite.

One who travels to sacred fords (tīrthas) with self-restraint increases their merit through that merit. (103) Having first purified their faculties through faith and the study of the scriptures, these sacred fords are attained by the virtuous who follow the example of the wise. (104)

O descendant of Kuru, no man who has not performed his duties, whose soul is not disciplined, who is impure, who is a thief, or whose mind is crooked, bathes in sacred fords; yet you, by contrast, have always followed the right conduct and perceive both dharma and worldly purpose.
"O father, the ancestors have been gratified, as have all the great-grandfathers,
the grandfathers led by the Pitāmaha, and likewise the gods along with the hosts of sages.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"And you, O knower of dharma, having been constantly gratified by him through righteous conduct, shall attain great and eternal fame on earth like that of Dilīpa. Nārada said:
Having spoken thus and granted permission, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha,
being pleased with a joyful mind, vanished right there,
O tiger among the Kurus; for Dilīpa, through his perception of the true meaning of the scriptures—
And following the words of Vasiṣṭha, he indeed traversed the earth.
Thus, O highly fortunate one, this pilgrimage to the sacred sites (tīrthayātrā), which is immensely meritorious and liberating from all sins, is established at Pratiṣṭhāna.
Whoever shall wander the earth according to this rite will,
after death, enjoy the fruit of more than a hundred horse-sacrifices. Furthermore, O Pārtha, you shall obtain eight times that supreme merit.
Just as King Dilīpa obtained [the fruit] in former times, O Pārtha,
because you are the leader of the sages, therefore you shall obtain eightfold the fruit.
These sacred fords (tīrthas), O Bhārata, are strewn with hosts of Rākṣasas.
O joy of the Kurus, there exists no other path for those who have attained immortality than this account of the deeds of the divine sages, which encompasses all sacred fords.
Whoever rises at dawn and recites this shall be liberated from all sins.
The foremost sages were always there: Vālmīki, Kaśyapa, Ātreya, Kauṇḍinya, Viśvāmitra, Gautama, Asita, Devala, Mārkaṇḍeya, and Gālava. 115–116.
The sage Uddālaka, disciple of Bharadvāja,
as well as Śaunaka with his son, Vyāsa— the best among those who possess the power of penance— and Durvāsas, the foremost of sages, and Jābāli of great asceticism. 117.
"All these excellent sages, whose wealth is asceticism, are to be honored by you. O illustrious one, travel along these sacred fords together with them;
you shall attain great fame, just as King Mahābhiṣa did."
Just as the righteous-souled Yayāti, and as King Purūravas, so do you act, O tiger among the Kurus; you shine by your own dharma. Just as King Bhagīratha, and as the renowned Rāma.
Just as in the past the slayer of Vṛtra, the king of the gods, having burnt all his enemies,
protected the three worlds free from anxiety,
so shall you, having brought about the destruction of your foes, protect your subjects.
"O lotus-eyed one, having obtained the earth acquired through your own dharma,
you shall attain renown for your valor like that of Kārtavīryārjuna.
Sūta said:

Having thus addressed the king, the venerable sage Nārada took leave of the great monarch and vanished on the spot. Yudhiṣṭhira, the righteous-souled one of excellent vows, remained there together with the sages.

The lord of the earth went with reverence to all the sacred fords (tīrthas). O sages, whoever reads or even hears this narrative concerning the pilgrimage to the sacred fords as told by me shall be liberated from all sins. 125–126.
"I have explained the entire truth; what more do you wish to hear?
Regarding these sages of meritorious fame, there is indeed nothing further that remains for me to say.
Thus ends the description of various sacred fords (*tīrtha*) in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious *Padma Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter Thirty-nine: The Thirty-Ninth Chapter on Names.
Chapter Forty.
Sūta said:
"O you of virtuous vows, these sacred fords have thus been described as the very body of Viṣṇu;
by association with any one of these, a human being becomes liberated.
Blessed is the hearing of the accounts of these sacred fords, and blessed is the service rendered to them."
In the Kali age, there is no other means for the destruction of the heap of sins than residing at a sacred ford (tīrtha) and likewise touching that sacred ford;
he who speaks thus every day attains the supreme, great state.
Sins perish merely by speaking of sacred fords (*tīrtha*);
indeed, O observers of good vows, sacred fords are blessed and worthy of being served.
By the very service of sacred fords, the Lord himself becomes served.
Nārāyaṇa is the creator of the world; there is no state higher than the sacred ford (tīrtha).
A Brāhmaṇa, Tulasī, the Aśvattha tree, a collection of sacred fords, and Viṣṇu the Supreme Lord must always be served by men.
O best of sages, the foremost of the twice-born know that the specific service of Brāhmaṇas is superior to bathing in all sacred fords and other such acts.
Therefore, the feet of the twice-born are directly auspicious and consist of all sacred fords.
A wise person should worship [these] daily; therein, it becomes superior to all other holy places (tīrthas).
One who performs circumambulation of the Aśvattha tree, Tulasī, and cows, having obtained the fruit of all tīrthas, is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.

Therefore, one should destroy the effects of evil deeds by resorting to sacred fords (*tīrtha*); otherwise, one goes to hell, for [the fruit of] karma is exhausted only through its experience. The residence of sinners is in hell, while the virtuous enjoy heaven.
Therefore, a wise person should indeed cultivate merit at this sacred ford (tīrtha).
The sages said:
O observer of excellent vows, we have indeed heard of the various sacred fords and their great majesties.
"Now we wish to hear the specific details concerning Prayāga. Previously, O Sūta, you spoke of Prayāga only in brief; we desire to hear it in detail, so let it be told by you, O Sūta. (12-13)
Sūta said:
O highly fortunate ones of excellent vows, you have asked well regarding Prayāga;
indeed, I shall now provide a detailed description of Prayāga. 14.

This was related by Mārkaṇḍeya in the past to the son of Pāṇḍu, when the Bhārata war had concluded and Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pṛthā, had obtained the kingdom. During this interval, King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī—
Tormented by grief for his brother, King Duryodhana, the commander of eleven armies, reflected again and again: "Having caused us much distress, he has now met his death along with all of us. (16-17)
Having taken refuge in Vāsudeva, how did the five remaining Pāṇḍavas [cope with] Droṇa, Bhīṣma, and the exceedingly powerful Karṇa,
as well as King Duryodhana together with his brothers and sons?
"All the kings have been slain, as well as all those others who considered themselves heroes.
Without the kingdom, what is to be done with enjoyments or even with life?
Alas, what misery!"—thinking thus, the king fell into a state of agitation. 19-20.
Then, motionless and devoid of energy, he remained for a while with his face cast downward;
when the king regained consciousness, he reflected again and again:
"With what rite, yoga, observance, or even pilgrimage site shall I proceed? (21)

By what means may I be quickly liberated from the taint of great sins? Where, having bathed, a man goes to the unsurpassed world of Viṣṇu? How shall I ask Kṛṣṇa about this, by whom this great [work] was caused to be made? 22–23.
"How shall I question Dhṛtarāṣṭra, whose hundred sons have been slain?
How shall I question Vyāsa, by whom the destruction of his own lineage was brought about?
Thus did Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, fall into a state of despondency.
All the Pāṇḍavas, overwhelmed with grief for their brother, wept;
as did all those high-souled ones who had gathered there seeking refuge with the Pāṇḍavas, including Kuntī and Draupadī, and whoever else was assembled there.
Having fallen to the ground, they all wept on every side;
however, Mārkaṇḍeya recognized Yudhiṣṭhira in Vārāṇasī by the way he was overcome with distress,
weeping, and deeply afflicted with sorrow.
In a very short time, Mārkaṇḍeya, the great ascetic,
arrived at Hastināpura and stood at the king’s gate;
seeing him, the gatekeeper quickly informed the king.
"Desirous of seeing you, the sage Mārkaṇḍeya stands at the door.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, being intent upon that purpose, quickly went to the door and spoke.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

Welcome to you, O one of great wisdom; welcome to you, O great sage. Today my birth has become fruitful; today my lineage has been purified. Today my ancestors are satisfied, O great sage, now that you have been seen by me.
Having offered him a lion-throne, water for his feet, and performed worship and other honors, the high-souled Yudhiṣṭhira paid homage to that sage.
Then, being thus honored by him, O Lord, Mārkaṇḍeya said to him: "I have been worshipped by you."
"O King, why are you in such haste? For what reason have you become so distressed? Tell me the truth before me.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O great sage, you have come here having learned all that has occurred regarding our kingdom; thus it is, O Blessed One.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O mighty-armed King, to where dharma is established: no sin is seen in a wise man fighting in battle,
much less so for a Kshatriya who follows the specific duties of his royal order.
Therefore, keeping this in your heart, you should not contemplate sin.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, bowing his head to the sage, said:
"O best of sages, I ask you—who always perceive the three periods of time—this."
"Tell me in brief, so that I may be liberated from sin.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Listen, O King, O highly fortunate descendant of Bharata, to that which you ask of me."
Thus, O Yudhiṣṭhira, regarding Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and the various Tīrthas—
how much more so, O Lord, has the journey to Prayāga been proclaimed by the meritorious Brāhmaṇas of old as the most excellent for men of virtuous deeds?
Thus ends the fortieth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Forty-one.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Blessed One, I desire to hear how it was situated in a former kalpa; what is the manner of men’s journeying to Prayāga, and what is it like there?
What is the destiny of those who die there, and what is the fruit for those who bathe there?
"What indeed is the fruit for those who go to Prayāga?
Tell me all this; I have a great curiosity. Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O dear child, I shall tell you whatever is desired and whatever is its fruit,
as it was heard by me in the past when it was being recounted to the sages and the brahmins,
from Prayāga to Pratiṣṭhāna, and from Dharmakī to Vāsukī-hrada.
The two nāgas Kambala and Aśvatara are there with many medicinal roots.
This is the field of Prajāpati, renowned throughout the three worlds;
having bathed here, those who die go to heaven and are not born again.
There, Brahmā and the other gods stand together performing protection,
as do many other sacred fords that destroy all sins;
they cannot be fully described, O King, even in hundreds of years.
I shall briefly proclaim the glorification of Prayāga:
sixty thousand *dhanus* protect the Jāhnavī, while the Sun, whose vehicle has seven horses, always protects the Yamunā. 7–8.
Vāsava himself especially protects Prayāga; Hari, together with the gods, protects the Mandala as is well agreed upon.
Maheśvara, the wielder of the trident, constantly protects that banyan tree.
The god protects that auspicious abode which removes all sins.
O lord of men, when the world is seized by unrighteousness, even one who possesses only a very small or even smaller amount of sin goes to that place.
For one who remembers Prayāga, everything goes to complete destruction;
by the sight of that sacred site, or even by the chanting of its name, or by taking up its clay, a person is liberated from sin. 12.
O King of kings, among these five sacred pools (kuṇḍas) flows the Jāhnavī.
When one has entered Prayāga, sin perishes at that very moment.
That man who remembers the Gaṅgā even from thousands of yojanas away [is purified].
Moreover, even one who has performed evil deeds attains the supreme goal; by chanting [her name] he is freed from sins, by seeing her he beholds auspiciousness,
and by bathing in and drinking [the water of her stream], he purifies his lineage up to the seventh generation.
One who speaks the truth, has conquered anger, is firmly established in non-violence,
follows the dharma, knows the reality, and is devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins—
having bathed in the middle of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, such a person is liberated from sin.
One obtains in abundance all the desires conceived by the mind; then, having gone to Prayāga, which is protected by all the gods,
one should dwell there for a month as a celibate student and offer libations to the ancestors and the gods.
One obtains one's desired wishes and is reborn in various [auspicious] places.
Wherever the illustrious river Yamunā, the daughter of the Sun and renowned throughout the three worlds, has joined with other rivers, [that place is sacred]. 19–20.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, there at Prayāga— which is difficult for mortals to attain— the Lord Maheśvara himself is eternally present in person. There,
gods, dānavas, gandharvas, ṛṣis, siddhas, and cāraṇas [reside].
Having sipped water there, O Indra among kings, one is glorified in the heavenly world.
22. Thus ends the forty-first chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Forty-Two.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen again, O King, to the majesty of Prayāga, by going to which one is liberated from all sins; of this there is no doubt. 1.
For those who are afflicted, for the poor, and for those of firm resolve,
there is no place that can ever be as inexhaustible as Prayāga. Having reached the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, whoever should renounce their life there [attains that state].
In a celestial mansion with the luster of blazing gold and the brilliance of the sun,
that man rejoices in heaven amidst Gandharvas and Apsarases; the preeminent sages declare that he obtains all his desired wishes.
Amidst divine objects made of every kind of jewel, crowded with various banners,
and surrounded by beautiful women endowed with auspicious marks, he rejoices;
and while asleep, he is awakened by the sounds of singing and musical instruments.
As long as one does not remember their birth, for that long they are honored in heaven.
Then, having fallen from that heaven and descended due to the exhaustion of their karma,
they are born into a prosperous family filled with gold and jewels.

One should remember that very holy place; by remembering it, one goes there—whether staying in one's own country, in the forest, in a foreign land, or at home. Even he who merely remembers Prayāga and then gives up his life [attains the highest goal].
The preeminent sages declare that one attains the world of Brahmā; there,
in that world where the seers, munis, and perfected ones go, lies a golden earth abounding with the fruits of all desires.
On the auspicious bank of the Mandākinī, delightful and crowded with thousands of women, he rejoices together with the ṛṣis by virtue of his own deeds performed here;
he is honored by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, and the gods of heaven.
Then, having fallen from heaven, he shall become the lord of Jambudvīpa.
Then, reflecting again and again upon auspicious deeds, he becomes virtuous and endowed with wealth in this world; of this there is no doubt.
One who, established in untruth and unrighteousness through deed, mind, or speech,
bestows gifts between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā—
be they gold, jewels, pearls, or even grain received as a gift— [does not attain the fruit]. (14)

Whether in one's own work, in the work of one's father, or even in the worship of the deities, that sacred ford (tīrtha) becomes fruitless for him as long as he enjoys its fruit; thus one should accept [the gift] at a sacred ford and in holy shrines. 15–16.
A twice-born man should remain vigilant regarding all such signs;
he who bestows at Prayāga a milch cow of Kapila or pale-red hue, with horns tipped in gold, hooves in silver, and a cloth around her neck, [attains the highest reward]. 17.
Having caused a virtuous śrotriya from Prayāga— one who wears white garments, is tranquil, knows the dharma, and has mastered the Vedas— to accept [the gift] according to the prescribed rite,
a cow should be given to him at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
O best of men, for as many hairs as there are on the body of that cow, for that many thousands of years he is honored in the heavenly world with garments of great value and various kinds of jewels.
Wherever that bull obtains a birth, there he is born again;
by that deed, he does not behold the terrible hell,
but having reached the Northern Kurus, he rejoices for imperishable time.
One should give a single milch cow in exchange for hundreds of thousands of other cows; by means of that one cow, one may deliver one's sons, wife, and servants across [the ocean of rebirth].
Therefore, among all gifts, the gift of a cow is preeminent.
"In this difficult, uneven, and terrible place where great sins arise, the cow alone provides protection; therefore, she should be given to a twice-born man.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter of the Svargakhaṇḍa in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. 41.
Chapter Forty-Two.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Just as the greatness of the sage Prayāga has been described by you, [so too describe that of]...

In that very way, one will undoubtedly be liberated from all sins. O Blessed One, by what procedure should one proceed according to the certainties of Dharma? Tell me that procedure which has been proclaimed for Prayāga, O Great Sage.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O child, I shall describe to you the sequence of the rules for the pilgrimage;
go, O best of the Kurus, to Prayāga, which is frequented by the gods. 3.
Listen also to the fruit for him who is mounted upon a bull;
he dwells in a terrible hell, in the most dreadful wrath of cows,
and the ancestors of that embodied being do not accept even water.

He who bathes his sons and likewise his children, and causes them all to drink [the water] just as he does for himself, and bestows gifts upon Brahmins; or that man who, out of greed for power or through delusion, should travel by means of a vehicle [to the pilgrimage site]; 5–6.
That sacred ford (tīrtha) is fruitless for him; therefore, one should abandon [going there].
However, he who gives away his daughter between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā according to the Ārṣa rite, in accordance with his means, [attains success].
By that deed, he does not behold the terrible Yama or hell;
having gone to the Northern Kurus, he rejoices for an imperishable time.
He obtains sons and wives who are righteous and endowed with sound conduct.
There, one should give gifts according to the extent of one's wealth;
by that alone, the fruit of the sacred ford increases—of this there is no doubt. O Indra among kings, such a person dwells in heaven until the dissolution of all beings.
Whoever should abandon their life-breaths while taking refuge at the foot of a banyan tree transcends all worlds and goes to the world of Rudra; there, O Rudra,
the twelve Ādityas dwell, performing austerities while taking refuge in you.
They burn the entire world, yet the root of the banyan tree is not burned.
When the moon, sun, and wind have perished and the world has become a single ocean,
Viṣṇu sleeps right here, being born again and again.
Gods, dānavas, gandharvas, ṛṣis, siddhas,
and cāraṇas always frequent that sacred ford at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā; they go there, O lord of kings, as well as to Prayāga where they are united.
There were Brahmā and the other gods, the lords of the directions,
the guardians of the world, the Sādhyas, and the ancestors esteemed by the world;
likewise, there were the supreme ṛṣis headed by Sanatkumāra.
And likewise the other Brahman-sages, headed by Aṅgiras;
as well as the Nāgas, Siddhas, and those Suparṇas who move through the sky;
the rivers, oceans, mountains, Nāgas, and Vidyādharas. 17–18.
And the Lord Hari dwells there, preceded by Prajāpati;
the region between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā is remembered as the hips of the Earth. O tiger among kings, Prayāga is renowned throughout the three worlds.
O Bhārata, there is nothing more meritorious than that in the three worlds;
by hearing of that tīrtha, by the chanting of its name, or even by touching its clay, a person is liberated from sin.
O dear one, he who, firm in his vows, performs an ablution there at the confluence, obtains a fruit equal to that of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices;
this is from the words of the Vedas, not merely from the words of the world.
Your mind is inclined toward going to Prayāga.
O descendant of Kuru, ten thousand and sixty crores of holy places (tīrthas) have their presence right here through mere mention. 23–24.
The destination attained by a wise man who is disciplined in yoga and established in truth is the same as that of one who gives up his life at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
By that [merit], O Yudhiṣṭhira, they live wherever they may be in this world.
Those who have not reached Prayāga, which is renowned throughout the three worlds— having thus beheld that supreme sacred site of Prayāga,
one is liberated from all sins, just as the moon is released by Rāhu.
The two nāgas Kambala and Aśvatara [reside] on the southern bank of the Yamunā;
having bathed and drunk there, one is liberated from all sins. Having gone there, one reaches that abode of the wise Mahādeva.
A man delivers all ten preceding generations and ten future generations;
having performed the ablution, that man obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice and attains the heavenly world until the dissolution of all beings.
O Bhārata, on the eastern bank of the Gaṅgā,
there is a well known as Sāmudraka and a famous place called Pratiṣṭhāna;
he who stays there for three nights as a celibate student, having conquered his anger, [attains great merit].

With his soul purified of all sins, he shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice. To the north of Pratiṣṭhāna and to the east of the Bhāgīrathī is the sacred ford named Haṃsaprapatana, renowned throughout the three worlds.
O Bhārata, for one who has merely bathed there, the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice is attained;
he is glorified in heaven for as long as the moon and the sun endure, upon the delightful, vast, and pale-white sandy bank of the Urvashī, frequented by swans. 34.
O lord of men, he who, free from envy, offers libations of water to the ancestors there,
dwells in the heavenly world together with his ancestors for sixty thousand and sixty hundred years.
There he is constantly worshipped by ṛṣis, gandharvas, and kinnaras;
then, having fallen from heaven, his merit exhausted and descending by the power of destiny,
he obtains a hundred maidens resembling Urvaśī.
O King, he becomes the enjoyer of hundreds of thousands of cows;
while asleep, he is awakened by the sound of waist-bands and anklets,
and having enjoyed vast pleasures, he attains that sacred ford once again.
Constantly holding a seat of kusha grass, self-restrained and with senses controlled, one who eats but once a day shall for a month become a lord of enjoyments;
he obtains a hundred women adorned with golden ornaments.
On this earth, as far as the oceans, he shall become a lord of great enjoyments;
he shall be a ruler of the land who enjoys ten thousand villages, endowed with wealth and grain, and a constant giver. 41–42.
Having enjoyed abundant pleasures, he remembers that sacred ford again;
then, at that beautiful banyan tree, a celibate student who has conquered his senses, having fasted and being absorbed in yoga, shall attain the knowledge of Brahman. 43.

Whoever reaches Koṭitīrtha and gives up their life there is honored in the heavenly world for ten million thousand years. Then, having fallen from heaven and descended when his karma is exhausted, he returns to earth.
Born into a family enriched with gold, jewels, and pearls, he will be handsome in form;
then, having gone to Bhogavatī to the north of Vāsuki, there will be another sacred ford (tīrtha) there called Daśāśvamedhaka.
Having performed the consecration, that man shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice. He becomes wealthy, handsome, capable, generous, and righteous.
Whatever merit exists in the four Vedas and whatever fruit belongs to those who speak the truth—[he obtains all that]. 47–48.
But as for the dharma that arises from non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), it occurs simply by its attainment;
wherever one immerses oneself in the Gaṅgā, that place becomes equal to Kurukṣetra. Wherever the Sindhu river meets [the Gaṅgā], it is ten times more meritorious than Kurukṣetra.
Wherever the highly blessed Gaṅgā, rich in many sacred fords and ascetic merit, flows—that should be known as a field of perfection (siddhakṣetra); no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
She delivers mortals from the earth and likewise delivers the Nāgas from the netherworld.
Because she leads the gods to heaven, she is remembered as the three-pathed river;
for as many thousands of years as the bones of that embodied being remain in the Gaṅgā, so long is he honored in the heavenly world.
She is the supreme sacred ford among all sacred fords, the most excellent river among all rivers. She grants liberation to all beings, even to those who have committed great sins;
though the Gaṅgā is easily accessible everywhere, she is difficult to attain at these three specific places.
At Gaṅgādvāra, at Prayāga, and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, those who bathe there go to heaven; once dead, they are not born again.
This applies to all beings whose minds have been afflicted by sin.
For those seeking a destination, there is no goal equal to the Gaṅgā;
she is the most purifying of purifiers and the most auspicious of auspicious things—
falling from the head of Maheśvara, she is the remover of all sins and the source of well-being.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Greatness of Prayāga," in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter Forty-four]
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen again, O King, to the majesty of Prayāga, by hearing which one is liberated from all sins; of this there is no doubt. 1.
Having fasted for three nights at that sacred ford named Mānasa on the northern bank of the Gaṅgā, one shall obtain all desires;
a man shall obtain whatever fruit he would gain by the gift of cows, land, and gold.

One obtains this fruit and remembers that sacred ford again. Whether free from desire or possessed of desire, whoever passes away at the Gaṅgā becomes established in heaven after death and does not behold hell.
Awakened by the musical performances of hosts of Apsarases,
he proceeds in a celestial chariot yoked with swans and cranes;
O Indra among kings, he enjoys these pleasures for many years— six thousand in total.
Then, having fallen from heaven and descended due to the exhaustion of his karma,
he is born into a great family rich in gold, gems, and pearls.
There are sixty thousand and sixty hundred sacred fords [in that lineage].
Whatever fruit is obtained from the proper gift of a hundred thousand cows at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā during the month of Māgha,
that same fruit is obtained by bathing for three days at Prayāga during the month of Māgha.
He who practices the austerity of the five fires between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā becomes free from defects in his limbs,
free from disease, and endowed with all five senses;
as many as are the pores on the body of that embodied being, [so many years shall he dwell in heaven].
For that many thousands of years he is honored in the heavenly world;
then, having descended from heaven, he becomes the lord of Jambūdvīpa.
Having enjoyed vast pleasures, that man resorts to that sacred ford once again.
Whoever should enter the water at the world-renowned confluence is liberated from all sins, like the moon when released from being seized by Rāhu;
he attains the world of Soma and rejoices together with Soma. 12–13.
For sixty thousand and sixty hundred years,
he attains the heavenly world, served by sages and gandharvas; then, having descended from there, O lord of kings, he is born into a prosperous family.
A man who drinks [the nectar] with his head downward and his feet upward is honored in the heavenly world for a hundred thousand years;
O Indra among kings, when he eventually falls from there, he becomes a man who maintains the sacred fire (agnihotrī).

That man who, having enjoyed vast pleasures, resorts to that sacred ford and offers his own body to the birds— listen now to the fruit obtained by him as he is devoured by the winged creatures. 17.17-18a.
He is honored in the world of Soma for a hundred thousand years.
Then, having descended from heaven, he becomes a righteous king,
virtuous, endowed with beauty, learned, and possessed of a very pleasing body.
Having enjoyed vast pleasures, he returns once more to that sacred ford on the northern bank of the Yamunā and to the south of Prayāga;
that supreme sacred site is known as Ṛṇapramocana.
Having stayed there for one night, one is liberated from all debts;
one attains the world of the Sun and shall forever be free from debt.
Thus ends the section on the Greatness of Prayāga in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Forty-Four.
Chapter Forty-Five.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Having heard this account of Prayāga that you have narrated,
my heart has become completely purified by the glorification of Prayāga.
O Blessed One, tell me what kind of fruit is obtained there through fasting unto death.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Listen, O King, O Lord, to the kind of fruit that a wise and faithful man obtains at Prayāga by fasting unto death. 2.
Free from physical defects and disease, and endowed with all five senses,
he shall attain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice at every step; O King,
he shall deliver ten preceding and ten succeeding generations of his lineage.
One is liberated from all sins and shall go to the supreme state.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "O illustrious one, you are a knower of dharma; O Lord, tell me about the gift."
"By means of *alpena* alone as the primary factor, one may attain many dharmas;
yet the Aśvamedha sacrifice is attained here through many meritorious deeds.
Explain this doubt of mine to me, for my curiosity is great. (5-6)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O King Mahāvīra, to what was spoken by the Lotus-born One in the presence of the sages; it was heard by me as it was being told previously.
Entering that region of Prayāga, which extends five yojanas in width,
he performed the Aśvamedha sacrifice at every step upon that ground—
seven for those who have passed away and fourteen for those yet to come.
A man who gives up his life saves all;
knowing this, O lord of kings, one should always be devoted to faith. Those men who lack faith have their minds struck by sin.
They do not reach that place, Prayāga, which was created by the gods.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Whether out of affection, or out of greed for wealth, or those who have fallen under the sway of desire..."

How do they obtain the fruit of the sacred ford, and how do they acquire merit? For one who sells all kinds of goods and does not distinguish between what should and should not be done, what is his destiny at Prayāga? Tell me this, O great sage. (11-12)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O King, to this great secret that destroys all sins, concerning one who dwells for a month at Prayāga with his senses restrained, O lord of kings. 13.
One who is pure, self-restrained, non-violent, and endowed with faith is liberated from all sins, just as ordained by the Self-born;
Now hear the fruit for those who betray trust at Prayāga:
one should bathe at the three times of day and subsist on alms; after three months, one shall be liberated from [the sin], of this there is no doubt. 15–16.
He who performs pilgrimages and other such rites here with wisdom becomes fulfilled in all his desires and is glorified in the heavenly world;
he obtains a permanent abode, teeming with wealth and grain.
Thus, one who is filled with such knowledge always becomes a possessor of enjoyments.
By him, his fathers and great-grandfathers have been delivered from hell,
O knower of truth, as you ask again and again in accordance with the Dharma.
"For the sake of your pleasure, this eternal secret has been fully declared.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Today my birth has become fruitful; today my lineage has become fruitful."
"I am pleased, O deity; I am graced this very day by your sight alone.
By the sight of you, O righteous-souled one, I have been liberated from all sins.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"By good fortune your birth has become fruitful; by good fortune your lineage has been delivered.
Through its recitation, merit increases, and when heard, it is the destroyer of sin.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O great sage, what is the merit and what is the fruit of [bathing] in the Yamunā?
Tell me all of this exactly as it was seen and exactly as it was heard.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The daughter of the Sun, the goddess Yamunā, renowned throughout the three worlds, that highly fortunate river arrived at the very place from which Gaṅgā had emerged.
Thus, Yamunā came by the same path as Gaṅgā.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, by chanting [her name] for thousands of yojanas, one destroys sin;
having bathed and drunk there at the Yamunā, one obtains merit through chanting and beholds auspiciousness upon seeing her. 24–25.
One who bathes there and drinks its water purifies his lineage up to the seventh generation;
he who gives up his life there attains the supreme goal. This is the famous Agnitīrtha on the southern bank of the Yamunā.
To the west of Dharmarāja is remembered the excellent tīrtha of Hara (27). Having bathed there, those who die go to heaven and are not born again.
Thus, there are thousands of tīrthas on the southern bank of the Yamunā (28).
To the north, O Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall describe the sacred ford named Viraja, belonging to the high-souled Āditya,
where the gods together with Vāsava constantly perform their twilight worship.
The gods and other wise people likewise resort to that holy ford (tīrtha).
Having become devoted to faith, perform your ablutions at the holy ford;
there are many other auspicious holy fords as well that remove all sins.
Having bathed in them, those who die go to heaven and are not born again;
both the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā are remembered as yielding equal fruit.
However, the Gaṅgā alone is worshipped everywhere due to her superior nature.
O Kaunteya, perform in this manner the ritual ablution at the heavenly tīrtha;
the sin committed throughout one's entire life perishes in that very instant for whoever, having risen at dawn, reads or hears this during the Kalya period.
One is liberated from all sins and goes to the heavenly world. 35.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Yamunā," in the Svarga-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. 45.
The forty-sixth chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"I have heard that which was spoken by Brahmā in the Purāṇa, which is commensurate with merit."
Thousands, hundreds, and millions of sacred fords (tīrthas) are all meritorious, pure, and are remembered as the supreme goal;
yet Naimiṣa is meritorious on earth, and Puṣkara is meritorious in the intermediate space.
"Kurukṣetra is superior even to Prayāga for all people; having abandoned all others, why do you praise only one?
This which has been declared is without authority, untrustworthy, and not supreme."
"The supreme, divine state and enjoyments exactly as desired—
why do you praise such manifold dharma through a minor yoga?
Explain this doubt of mine as it has been seen and heard."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: One should not speak what is unbelievable, even if it is something witnessed by one's own eyes,
to a man who lacks faith and whose mind is afflicted by sin.

For those who lack faith, who are impure, wicked-minded, and have abandoned auspiciousness—all these are sinners; it was because of them that this was spoken by me. Now listen to the majesty of Prayāga exactly as it was seen and heard.
Whatever else may occur, whether perceptible or imperceptible,
just as other things were previously seen or heard by me,
one honors the yoga of the self by taking scripture as the authority. 8–9.
Another person may suffer there and never attain yoga;
for men, yoga may be obtained after thousands of other births,
or as yoga may be obtained by men through a thousand yogas.
But he who bestows all kinds of jewels upon the Brahmins— by that gift being given, yoga is attained by human beings;
for one who has died at Prayāga, all this comes to pass, and not otherwise.

O Bhārata, listen with faith as I shall explain the primary cause, by which [Brahman] is seen everywhere indeed within all beings; there is nothing that exists apart from Brahman, yet this is spoken for the sake of explanation. 13.13–14a.
Just as Brahman is worshipped everywhere among all beings,
so too is Prayāga worshipped by the wise in all the worlds;
this is the truth regarding the King of Tīrthas, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Even Brahmā constantly remembers Prayāga, the most excellent of holy places;
having reached this king of tīrthas, he desires nothing else at all.
For who, having attained divinity, would wish for the state of a human?
"By this very inference, O Yudhiṣṭhira, you shall understand it;
just as merit and demerit exist, so too have they been described by me.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
I have heard that which was spoken by you, and I am amazed again and again.
How is the attainment of that [liberation] through yoga, while the heavenly world is attained through ritual action?
Then one enjoys pleasures there, and the earth is the fruit of those actions.
"We ask again about those deeds by which the earth is obtained.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Listen, O mighty-armed King, how the earth is attained through the performance of the prescribed rites. (20)
O lord of men, he who reviles a cow, fire, a Brāhmaṇa, the scriptures, gold, water, women,
his mother, or his father— Prajāpati has declared that there is no upward ascent for such people.
Thus is the attainment of yoga, a state that is extremely difficult to reach. By this [lack of it], men who are doers of evil go to a terrible hell.
[They lose] elephants, horses, cattle, oxen, gems, pearls, and gold. 22–23.
Those who take [wealth] in secret and later offer a gift do not go to heaven, where the donors enjoy their rewards;
joined with such karma, these base men are cooked in hell. 24.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, regarding this yoga, this dharma, and the giver—
whether it be true or false, whether the fruit exists or does not exist—
I shall now declare the definitive explanation so that one may personally attain it.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, concerning the Greatness of Prayāga;
[followed by] the forty-seventh chapter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen again, O King, to the majesty of Prayāga,
as well as Naimiṣa, Puṣkara, and the confluence of the Gaṅgā with the ocean at Sindhusāgara.
Kurukṣetra, Gayā, and the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean—
these and many other meritorious mountain peaks,
as well as ten thousand tīrthas and thirty crores of others.
The wise have always said this regarding those established at Prayāga:
there are three fire-pits (agnikuṇḍas) in the midst of which the Jāhnavī, preceded by all sacred fords (tīrthas), emerges from Prayāga. 3–4.
The goddess, the daughter of Tapaṇa, renowned throughout the three worlds,
dwells together with the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, bringing light to the world. The region between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā is considered the hips of the Earth.

They do not equal even a sixteenth part of Prayāga, O tiger among kings. Vāyu has declared that there are thirty-five million sacred fords (tīrthas) in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space; all of them are contained within the Gaṅgā.
Prayāga is the presiding seat, as are both Kambala and Aśvatara;
furthermore, Bhogavatī is the sacrificial altar of Prajāpati.
There, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the gods and the sacrifices exist in embodied form.
The ṛṣis whose wealth is their asceticism worship Prayāga;
likewise, kings with vast riches sacrifice to the gods with solemn rites.
Therefore, O Bhārata, there is nothing more meritorious than this in the three worlds.
O Lord, by its power it excels all other holy fords;
there are ten thousand, three crores, and further [others] besides. Where the highly blessed Gaṅgā flows, that region is indeed a grove of asceticism.

That place situated on the bank of the Gaṅgā should be known as a field of accomplishment (siddhakṣetra). This truth should be whispered into the ear of the twice-born, the virtuous, one’s own son, friends, or a devoted disciple. 12–13.
This is auspicious, this leads to heaven, this is to be cultivated, this is beautiful;
this is meritorious, this is delightful, this is purifying, and this is the supreme dharma. (14) This is the secret of the great seers, which destroys all sins.
Having studied and reflected upon this, a twice-born man shall attain purity.
Whoever constantly hears this meritorious and eternally pure sacred text (tīrtha) shall obtain the memory of his past lives and rejoice in the heights of heaven.
These sacred fords (tīrthas) are to be reached by the virtuous who perceive the goals of the righteous; bathe in these tīrthas, O Kauravya, and do not be of crooked mind.
Since you have questioned me properly, O Lord, I have thus related this to you.
All the fathers have been delivered, and all the grandfathers have been delivered;
yet they are not worth even a sixteenth part of Prayāga.
Such is the knowledge, the yoga, and the sacred ford itself, O Yudhiṣṭhira. 18–19.
By being joined with many afflictions, they then attain the supreme goal;
by the mere remembrance of Prayāga, people go to the heavenly world.
Thus ends the section on the majesty of Prayāga in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Forty-seventh Chapter.
Forty-eighth Chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O great sage, this entire narrative of Prayāga has been told; now tell me everything as it is, so that it may deliver me. Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O King, I shall proclaim this entire world as it has been described:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and likewise Īśāna are the immutable lords of the deities.
Brahmā creates all beings, both the stationary and the moving.
In the world beyond, Viṣṇu protects these subjects;
at the end of the kalpa, Rudra indeed withdraws that entire universe.
He neither gives nor takes away, and he never perishes.
He who sees the Lord of all beings truly sees;
by the northern [path], having established himself, he now abides as Brahman.
Having become a banyan tree, Maheśvara, the Supreme Lord, remains there.
Then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Siddhas, and supreme ṛṣis,
eternally protect that supreme [place] from those who are devoted to sinful deeds; and others who remain there do not attain the supreme goal.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Have I heard the truth exactly as it is regarding how these [virtues] abide? For what reason indeed do they abide, being honored by the world?"
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara dwell here at Prayāga;
I shall explain the reason for this, so listen to the truth, O Yudhiṣṭhira."
The precinct of Prayāga, extending five yojanas in width,
stands for the purpose of protection and for the warding off of evil deeds; indeed,
even a very small amount of sin therein will cause one to fall into hell.
In this way, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Great Lord Śiva remain at Prayāga; likewise,
the seven continents, the oceans, and the mountains on the surface of the earth remain supported there until the dissolution of all beings.
And all those others, O Yudhiṣṭhira, who dwell there in great numbers,
[are present] at this place on earth fashioned by the three gods;
this field of Prajāpati is renowned as Prayāga.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this Prayāga is meritorious and purifying;
O Indra among the Kurus, rule your own kingdom together with your brothers.
Thus ends the "Greatness of Prayāga" in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Forty-eighth Chapter. Forty-ninth Chapter.
Sūta said:
All the Pāṇḍavas, firm in their resolve for righteousness, together with their brothers,
offered salutations to the Brāhmaṇas and gratified the preceptors and the gods.
At that very moment, Vāsudeva also arrived there.
Being honored by all the Pāṇḍavas together with Mādhava,
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, was likewise consecrated in his own kingdom by all those high-souled ones together with Kṛṣṇa.
In the meantime, the high-souled Ārkaṇḍeya,
having said "May it be well," returned to the hermitage from his visit.
Yudhiṣṭhira, the righteous one, was also there together with his brothers.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, who bestows great bliss, [spoke].
He who, having risen at dawn, recites or hears this,
is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Vāsudeva said:
Out of affection for you, I tell you this: you must carry out my word;
remaining free from all anxiety, be constantly devoted to sacrifice at Prayāga.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, O lord of kings, by constantly remembering Prayāga along with us,
you shall yourself attain the eternal world of heaven. Or, whatever man should go toward Prayāga, or even dwell there;
With his soul purified of all sins, he goes to the heavenly world.
One who abstains from accepting gifts, who is contented, self-controlled, pure,
and free from egoism, enjoys the fruit of sacred pilgrimage sites.
