O King of kings, one who is free from anger, truthful in speech, firm in his vows,
and who treats all beings as himself, enjoys the fruit of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites.
Sacrifices have been proclaimed by the sages and also by the gods in their proper order.
O Lord of the Earth, sacrifices cannot be performed by one who is poor;
for sacrifice requires many implements and involves the bustling preparation of various materials,
which can only be obtained by those who possess diverse wealth or by men of great prosperity.
O lord of men, that which can be attained even by the poor and the unlearned— listen now, O ruler of people, to that [attainment] through the merit of the fruits of sacrifice.
This, O best of the Bharatas, is the supreme secret of the sages.
Visiting sacred fords is meritorious and even excels [the merit of] sacrifices.
O bull among men, ten thousand crores and another thirty crores of people will go to the Gaṅgā during the month of Māgha.
"O Great King, having enjoyed a kingdom free from all thorns, you shall become healthy; O Lord of Kings, you shall see me again, especially while performing a sacrifice. 17.
Thus ends the "Glorification of Prayāga" in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
The forty-ninth chapter;
the fiftieth chapter.
The sages said:
"Everything that has been asked and whatever else has been told by you has now been heard; O Mahāmati, tell us one more thing:
what fruit indeed does one obtain from resorting to these sacred fords?"
"Indeed, by performing which single action among all can [the goal] be attained? O Omniscient One, tell us this: how does such karma function?
Sūta said:

O highly fortunate ones, it is said that the yoga of action (karmayoga) is prescribed for the social classes (varṇas), beginning with the twice-born; therein, there are many varieties, yet one stands preeminent:
devotion to Hari performed by means of the mind, speech, and voice. 3–4.
By him [Hari] it is conquered, by him it is conquered; of this there is no doubt.
Hari alone is to be propitiated, the Lord of all the lords of gods.
By the great mantras of Hari’s name, the demon of sin shall perish.

Those of pure heart who perform even a single circumambulation of Hari obtain the merit of bathing in all sacred fords; of this there is no doubt. Furthermore, by beholding an image of Hari, one obtains the fruit of all sacred fords.
O best of the twice-born, by chanting the name of Viṣṇu, one obtains the fruit of all mantras; and having smelled the Tulasī granted by Viṣṇu’s grace,
one does not behold that fierce and terrifying face of Yama.
One who has performed even a single prostration to Kṛṣṇa shall never again drink his mother’s milk. Eternal salutations to those whose minds are fixed upon the feet of Hari—
even if they be Pulkasas, Śvapacas, or any other outcaste tribes.
Even they are highly fortunate and worthy of worship, being the sole servants at the feet of Hari;
how much more so, then, the meritorious Brahmins, the devotees, and likewise the royal sages!
By performing devotion to Hari alone, one does not behold rebirth in a womb.
O Brahmins, a man who dances loudly before Hari while chanting His names purifies the world just as the waters of the Gaṅgā and other rivers do;
this occurs through seeing him, touching him, or even hearing him speak with devotion. 12–13.

A man who performs the circumambulation of Hari while loudly chanting His name is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt. He should employ hand-claps and the like, singing with a beautiful voice and melodious sounds.
Even sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are struck down by that very act. 15.
That man who, having spoken of the stories of devotion to Hari, listens to the narrative, becomes purified merely by the sight of him. 16.

O bulls among sages, O great seers, what need is there even to mention the fear of sins for him? The name of Kṛṣṇa is the supreme holy site among all holy sites; those who have taken up the name of Kṛṣṇa make the entire world a sacred place.
Therefore, the best of sages know that there is no merit greater than this.
Having consumed or worn upon his head the remains of the offerings (nirmālya) that have pleased Viṣṇu,
a mortal becomes Viṣṇu himself, the destroyer of the sorrow of Yama.
Hari alone is undoubtedly worthy of worship and salutation;
for those who perceive Mahāviṣṇu, the unmanifest, or even the god Maheśvara with a sense of oneness, there is no rebirth.
Therefore, behold Viṣṇu alone—the beginningless and endless, the imperishable Self—and likewise worship Hari. Those who perceive Hari as equal to other deities [fall]. 21–22.
A wise person should not count those terrible hells as being high or low;
for whether he be a fool or a scholar, a Brahmin or a favorite of Keśava, or even a dog-eater (outcaste), Nārāyaṇa himself, the Lord, liberates him. 23.23-24.1.
There is none higher than Nārāyaṇa; he is the forest fire that consumes the heap of sins.
Even after committing a terrible crime, one is liberated by the name of Kṛṣṇa.
He himself is the god Nārāyaṇa, the teacher of the worlds by his own name. 24–25.

Those of firm vows established their own power as superior; however, because they saw it as involving little effort, they disputed among themselves. Due to the weight of their fruits, they too go to many hells.
Therefore, one should be devoted to Hara and intent upon the name of Hari.
The Lord protects the worshipper at his back and the bearer of the Name upon his chest;
the great thunderbolt of Hari’s name is for shattering the mountain of sins.
His two feet, however, are fruitful, for they possess the power of movement for that purpose;
those two hands alone are declared blessed which perform worship.
His head is indeed the most excellent limb, yet it remains bowed before him.
That tongue which praises Hari is the mind following in His footsteps (30). Those hairs are said to be such because they stand on end at His name;
and those eyes shed tears through association with Acyuta (31).
In this world, those who are utterly deceived by the fault of fate do not indeed worship Him,
the giver of liberation, through the mere utterance of His name.
Deceived and defiled, they are so due to their attachment to the company of women.
Those whose body hairs do not stand on end at the mention of the name "Kṛṣṇa" are indeed fools of unrefined soul; overwhelmed by grief for their sons and the like,
they weep with many lamentations instead of chanting the syllables of Kṛṣṇa’s name.
Even having obtained a tongue in this world, if one does not chant the name of Kṛṣṇa,
they fall away with ease despite having attained the very staircase to liberation.
Therefore, a human being should diligently worship Viṣṇu through the yoga of action.
Viṣṇu, when worshipped through the yoga of action, becomes truly pleased; it is not otherwise.
(36) The worship of Viṣṇu is said to be a sacred site superior even to all other sacred sites, surpassing all holy waters through bathing, drinking, and immersion. (37)
Whatever fruit a mortal obtains [from other means], that fruit is obtained from the service of Kṛṣṇa; blessed indeed are those men who worship Hari through the yoga of action (karmayoga).
Therefore, O sages, worship Kṛṣṇa, the supreme auspiciousness. 38-39.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Praise of Devotion to Viṣṇu," in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Fifty-one.
The sages said:
O Sūta, tell us how the yoga of action is performed and by what means Hari is propitiated; O highly fortunate one, best among speakers, please explain this to us.
Tell us that by which the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, is propitiated by those seeking liberation;
likewise, speak of the protection of all the worlds and the compendium of dharma—
that very *karmayoga* which exists in the form of Sūta as you yourself.
Thus the Brahmins, desirous of hearing, stood before him.
Sūta said:
"In this very manner, Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, was questioned in the past."
Vyāsa spoke to those sages who resembled fire; listen.
Vyāsa said:
"Listen, all you sages, to that which is eternal and about to be declared."
Manu, the Lord of Creatures, formerly declared this entire Karmayoga— which bestows the ultimate fruit upon Brāhmaṇas,
is established by the Vedas, and is intended for the benefit of Brāhmaṇas—
while the sages were listening.
"Listen with concentrated minds as I speak of that which removes all diseases, which is meritorious, and which is practiced by the assembly of sages.
Having performed the initiation ceremony, the best of the twice-born should study the Vedas. (7)
In the eighth year from conception, or in the eighth year itself, according to the procedure prescribed in his own sūtras,
he becomes a sage (*muni*), carrying a staff, a girdle, a sacred thread, and wearing a black antelope skin;
subsisting on alms, devoted to his guru, and gazing at the face of his guru.

In ancient times, Brahmā fashioned from cotton for the purpose of the sacred thread (upavīta) a threefold cord for Brāhmaṇas, or it may be made of kuśa grass or even cloth. A twice-born man should always wear the sacred thread and always have his topknot tied.
Otherwise, an action performed in one way becomes as if it were not performed at all.
He should wear either an unwashed garment or a cotton cloth dyed with astringent decoctions; that same garment, when washed and white, made of excellent thread, is fit to be worn.

Furthermore, the sacred tradition prescribes a garment or a beautiful black antelope skin; in its absence, even a cow-hide or a goat-skin is ordained. Having raised the right arm, it is placed upon the left arm.
The sacred thread (upavīta) should always be worn over the left shoulder; when it is suspended around the neck, it is called nivīta.
O twice-born ones, when the left arm is raised and it is held over the right shoulder, it is termed prācīnāvīta, and one should employ it in rites for the ancestors (pitrya). 14–15.
One should likewise avoid it in the fire-sanctuary, in a cow-pen, during a fire-oblation,
while engaged in Vedic study, while eating, always in the presence of Brahmins, in the service of gurus, during the two twilights, and in the company of the virtuous. 16.

One should always wear the sacred thread; this is the eternal rule (17). One should make the girdle for a Brāhmaṇa out of muñja grass, triple-stranded, even, and smooth; in the absence of muñja, they say it may be made of kuśa grass with one or three knots (18).

A twice-born man should carry a staff made of bamboo or palāśa wood, reaching to the tip of his hair; or else one made from a tree suitable for sacrifice, which is handsome and free of blemishes. In the evening and in the morning, the twice-born man, with a concentrated mind, should perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā).

Having abandoned her out of lust, greed, fear, or delusion, one becomes fallen. Then, with a tranquil mind, having bathed, one should perform the fire-ritual in the evening and morning, and likewise offer libations to the gods, the sages, and the hosts of ancestors.
One should perform the worship of the deities with flowers, leaves, barley, and water;
one should always be habituated to saluting elders according to the dharma,
properly preceded by a full prostration and saying, "I am so-and-so, O venerable sir."
Free from sloth and other defects, he should be long-lived and healthy;
thus says the Brahmin when greeting: "May you be long-lived, O gentle one! And at the end of his name, the syllable *om* should be uttered with the preceding vowel protracted.

A learned man who does not know how to return a greeting should not be greeted by one who knows; he is just like a Śūdra. The clasping of the teacher’s feet should be performed with the hands crossed.
The left [hand] should be touched with the left, and the right with the right.
Whether it be worldly, Vedic, or even spiritual knowledge, one who has acquired such knowledge should first be saluted.
One should not carry alms-food, flowers, sacrificial fuel,
or similar items for the sake of rites dedicated to the gods.
One should ask a Brāhmaṇa about his welfare (*kuśala*) and a Kṣatriya about his health (*anāmaya*).
Having approached a Vaiśya for security, and a Śūdra for health alone;
[one should likewise approach] a teacher, a father, an elder brother, and a protector from fear;
as well as a maternal uncle, a father-in-law, and one's maternal and paternal grandfathers. 29–30.
The highest caste, the paternal uncle, and other men are remembered here as gurus;
likewise, the mother, the maternal grandmother, the mother’s elder sister, and the brothers of one’s father and mother [are gurus].
(31) The mother-in-law, the paternal grandmother, the elder sister, and the nurse are the female gurus.
O twice-born ones, this group of gurus beginning with the mother and father must be known;
one should follow them through the actions of mind, speech, and body.
Upon seeing the gurus, one should rise and salute them with palms joined in reverence.
One should not sit together with these, nor should one dispute with them for one's own sake;
even for the sake of one's life, one must never engage in conversation with teachers out of hatred. Even if one is distinguished by other virtues, one who hates the teacher falls downward.
Among all gurus as well, five are especially worthy of worship.
Of these, the first three are the most excellent; among them, the mother is most highly honored—she who nourishes, she who gives birth, and she by whom knowledge is imparted.
The eldest brother and the husband—these five are remembered as gurus.
One who desires prosperity must honor these five especially, with every effort or even at the cost of one's life. 37.
As long as both father and mother remain free from change, so long should the son, renouncing everything else, be devoted solely to them;
provided that both father and mother are well-pleased by the virtues of their son. (38–39)
By that deed, one together with one's sons shall attain the entirety of Dharma;
there is no destiny equal to a mother, and there is no teacher equal to a father. Furthermore, no repayment whatsoever can ever be made for them.
One should always perform what is pleasing to those two through action, mind, and speech.

Without being permitted by them, one should not practice any other duty, with the exception of that which has liberation as its fruit, as well as the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites. 41–42.

The essence of the Dharma has been fully declared; it bestows infinite fruit after death. Having properly propitiated the teacher and being dismissed by his permission, the disciple enjoys the fruit of that knowledge after death and attains heaven.
The fool who disregards his eldest brother, who is equal to a father,
goes to a terrible hell after death because of that transgression;
for a man, the husband is always to be honored as one established upon the path.
In this world, even more than for one’s mother, respect arises from the benefit she provides; likewise,
one should rise and salute maternal uncles, paternal uncles, fathers-in-law, officiating priests, and teachers, saying, "I am so-and-so."
One who has been initiated should not be addressed by name;
even if he is younger, the knower of dharma should address him using the honorifics "bho" or "bhavat.
Furthermore, he should be saluted, honored, and bowed to with the head. 47–48.
Brahmins desiring prosperity should always respectfully avoid saluting Kṣatriyas and others;
nor should Kṣatriyas and others ever be saluted by a Brahmin, even if they are endowed with knowledge, ritual action, and virtues, and are highly learned. 49.
"The Brāhmaṇa shall bring well-being to all castes; such is the Vedic revelation.
(50) "Salutation must indeed be performed by one of the same caste toward those of the same caste.
The fire is the preceptor of the twice-born, and the Brāhmaṇa is the preceptor of all castes. (51)

For women, the husband is the preceptor; everywhere, the guest is the preceptor. Learning, occupation, age, kinship, and wealth is the fifth—these they call the five bases for respect, each preceding one being weightier than the succeeding one. 52.

Among the three castes, those who possess the five qualities in abundance and in great strength are worthy of honor here, even if they are Śūdras who have reached the tenth stage of life. The path must be yielded to a Brāhmaṇa, just as it is to women and to a king who possesses clear vision.
Having collected alms daily from the houses of virtuous people for one who is elderly, burdened by a load, diseased, or weak, he should,
being pure and restrained in speech, offer it to his teacher and eat only with his permission.
The best of the twice-born should go for alms using the word "bhavat" (lady) at the beginning;
a Kṣatriya should place it in the middle, while a Vaiśya should place it at the end.
[He should seek alms from] his mother, or a sister, or his mother’s own sister. 56–57.
He should beg for alms at first, and he should not insult the one from whom he begs; he should seek them only in the houses of those of his own caste, or even among all castes.
This is declared to be the practice of begging for alms, excluding those who are outcasted and the like.
A student, being pure, should daily collect alms from the houses of those who are not deficient in Vedic study and sacrifices and who are praiseworthy in their own duties;
he should not beg for alms at the family of his teacher, nor among his own kinsmen, relatives, or friends.
If houses belonging to others cannot be found, he should avoid each preceding one in the sequence;
or, if none of those previously mentioned are available, he may wander through the entire village.
Restraining his speech and remaining diligent, he should not look toward the cardinal directions.
Having collected alms-food according to his needs without deceit, he should always eat with self-restraint, controlled speech, and a mind focused on nothing else;
one who observes the vow should always subsist on alms and never become dependent on a single person's food.
The livelihood of one who subsists on alms is declared to be equal to fasting;
he should always honor his food and eat it without disparaging it.
Upon seeing it, he should rejoice, become serene, and welcome it in every way.

Excessive eating is detrimental to health, longevity, and the attainment of heaven; it is meritless and loathed by the world, therefore one should avoid it. One should eat food facing either the east or toward the sun.
One should always eat facing north; this is the eternal rule.
Having washed both hands and feet, while eating, one should sip water twice (perform *ācamana*). Sitting in a clean place, after having eaten, one should again sip water twice.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Exposition of Karma-yoga," in the Svarga-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Fifty-two.
Vyāsa said:
Having eaten, having drunk, having slept, having bathed, upon approaching a road,
after touching the lips or body hair, and after changing one's garment— (1)
Upon voiding feces, urine, or excrement; upon speaking untruths;
after spitting; at the commencement of Vedic study; and likewise upon the onset of coughing or labored breathing;
as well as having stepped upon a crossroads or a cremation ground, the best of the twice-born [should perform purification].
Likewise, at both twilights, even one who has already sipped water (ācānta) should sip water again;
so too when conversing with a Caṇḍāla or a Mleccha, when speaking with a woman or a Śūdra while they are impure from food,
upon seeing a person who is impure from food, or likewise when seeing food that is in such a state.
One should sip water (perform *ācamana*) upon the falling of tears, likewise upon the appearance of blood;
after eating, during the two twilights (*saṃdhyā*), after bathing, after drinking, after voiding urine or excrement;
or upon returning [from a journey], after waking from sleep, and once for each other occasion.
Upon touching fire, cattle, or even one who is impure;
or upon touching women or oneself; or after putting on a soiled garment—one should touch water, wind, grass, or the earth itself.
When touching his hair, his own body, or a garment that has slipped off,
he should sip water according to the law— water that is not warm, free from hair, and pure. For the sake of purification, he should always sip water while seated, facing either the east or the north.

One should not be impure on the road without having washed one's feet, nor should a wise man perform the *ācamana* rite while covering his head or neck, with his hair loose, or even with his topknot untied; likewise, he should not do so wearing shoes, standing in a vehicle, or wearing a turban. 9–10.
Nor should one perform it while standing under streams of rain, nor with water drawn up [in vessels], nor with water held in a single hand, nor without the sacred thread,
nor while wearing sandals or sitting on a seat, nor with the knees outside [the legs].
One should not bathe while talking, laughing, looking around, or lying down upon a bed (12).

Nor should one bathe with water that is unobserved, or that is mixed with foam and the like, or released by a Śūdra who has failed to perform purification rites, or likewise with water that is salty (13).
One should not make a sound with one's fingers, nor with a distracted mind; nor with water corrupted by color or taste, nor with water from a crack in the ground (14);
nor with water agitated by the hand, nor indeed with anything that has an external odor.
A Brahmin is purified by [water] reaching the heart; a Kṣatriya becomes pure by water reaching the throat;
likewise, a Vaiśya by water that has been swallowed; and a woman or a Śūdra by contact with the water at the end.
The area between the root of the thumb and the line is called the Brahma-tirtha. 15–16.
The space between the thumb and the forefinger is called the *tīrtha* for the ancestors (*pitṛs*); behind the base of the little finger, they declare the *prājāpatya*;
the tips of the fingers are remembered as the *daiva*, and that same [space] is proclaimed as the *ārṣa*.

The *daiva* and *ārṣa* [tīrthas] are at the root, while the *āgneya* is remembered as being in the middle. That very same [tīrtha] is the *saumika*; knowing this sacred ford (*tīrtha*), one is not deluded.
A twice-born man should always perform his ritual sipping (*upaspṛśet*) using the *brāhma* tīrtha alone.
Or rather, O twice-born ones, he should offer the oblation with the *daiva* rite and not with the *pitrya*; first, being self-restrained, he should sip water three times with the *brāhma* formula,
and then he should touch his mouth, rubbing it with the root of the thumb.
Then, one should touch the two eyes with the thumb and the ring finger;
next, one should touch the two nostrils by joining the index finger and the thumb,
and touch both ears by joining the little finger and the thumb.
With all his strength, he should touch his heart with the *tanu* [mantra], and likewise touch his head and both shoulders with his thumb.
He should drink three mouthfuls of water; by that, the deities are pleased with him.
We have heard that Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa become [pleased];
Gaṅgā and Yamunā are pleased by the act of cleansing, and when the two eyes are touched, the Moon and the Sun are pleased. 24–25.
When the two nostrils are touched, the Nāsatyas and Dasras are pleased;
likewise, when the two ears are touched, Vāyu and Agni are pleased.
And when his heart is touched, all the deities are pleased.

By touching the head [of another], that person becomes pleased. (27) Drops of water that fall from the mouth do not make one impure; likewise, food stuck between the teeth is like the teeth themselves, and one remains pure even if the tongue touches it. (28)

Drops that touch the feet of one who is offering water for rinsing to others should be known as equal to dust on the ground; there is no impurity from them. This applies during the *madhuparka* offering, at a *soma* sacrifice, and when chewing betel.
Manu has declared that there is no fault regarding fruits, roots, or stalks of sugarcane (30).
A man walking while carrying food, drink, or other articles in his hand should set those items on the ground, perform ācamana, and then sprinkle them with water. (31)
If a twice-born man, having taken a metallic vessel, should become impure by leaving food remnants,
he should place that object on the ground, sip water for purification, and then sprinkle it with water.
Whatever object one takes up, if one becomes possessed of food remnants, [the same procedure applies].
If one leaves this object unburied on the ground, it becomes impure;
there may be an option regarding clothes and such, for one should not touch them here. [This applies] in a desolate forest, at night, or on a path infested with thieves and tigers.
Having discharged urine or feces with a substance still in one's hand, one does not become defiled,
provided one places the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) over the right ear and faces north;
during the day one should discharge feces and urine thus, but at night, facing south.
Having concealed the earth with wood, leaves, clods of earth, or grass,

and having covered his head, he should perform the voiding of feces and urine; nor should he do so in the shade, in a well, by a river, in a cow-pen, at a sacred shrine, in water, on a path, or on ashes.
One should not void feces or urine in fire, nor in a cremation ground;
nor on cow-dung, nor on wood, nor at a large tree, nor on a grassy plot (38).
One should not do so while standing, nor naked, nor on a mountain range.

One should never [perform these acts] in a dilapidated temple, nor on an anthill; one should not go there, nor should one perform them among living beings, in pits, or upon husks, charcoal, or potsherds, and likewise on the royal highway. 39–40.
Nor on a field, nor in a pit, nor at a sacred bathing place, nor at a crossroads; nor in a garden, nor near water, nor on barren soil, nor in a city dwelling.
(41) Nor with shoes on, nor with sandals, nor with an umbrella, nor in the open air.
Nor indeed should one look directly at women, teachers, Brahmins, or cows; nor ever at gods, temples, or water; nor while gazing at the celestial luminaries, nor with one's face turned away. 42–43.
Having taken earth from a bank that removes dirt and odor— facing the sun, facing fire, and likewise facing the moon—
one should perform purification with pure, drawn-up water, remaining free from sloth.

A Brahmin should not take earth that is dusty, nor that which is mixed with mud (45). He should not take it from a path, nor from a saline wasteland, nor from what has been used for purification by another, nor from a temple, nor from a well, nor from a dwelling, nor likewise from water (46).
Then one should always perform the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśet) according to the previously stated injunctions. 47.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Exposition of Karma-yoga," in the Svarga-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. 52.
Fifty-third Chapter. Vyāsa said:
Thus, endowed with the staff and other [emblems], and possessed of purity and proper conduct, [he should proceed].
When summoned, he should perform his teaching while gazing at the face of his guru.
He should always have his hand raised, be of virtuous conduct, and well-restrained.
When told, "Be seated," he should sit facing the guru.
One should not engage in responding or conversing while lying down;
nor should one do so while sitting, eating, standing, or with one's back turned. His bed and seat must always be lower than those of his guru.
In the presence of the guru, one should not sit as one pleases within his field of vision. One should not utter his name alone, even when referring to someone else,
nor should one imitate his gait, speech, or gestures.

Wherever slander or even censure of the guru arises, one should either cover one's ears or depart from that place to another. Standing at a distance, one should not honor him; nor should one do so when he is angry, nor in the presence of women.
One should never speak back to him, nor sit near him;
one should always bring for him a water-pot, kusha grass, flowers, and sacrificial fuel,
and should constantly perform his cleansing and the anointing of his limbs.
One should never step upon his discarded flower-garlands, bed, wooden sandals, or shoes, nor upon his seat, his shadow, or similar things.
One should prepare the tooth-sticks and other necessities for him, and whatever is obtained, one should offer it to him.
One who is devoted to the beloved’s welfare should not go anywhere without first taking leave.
One should never, in his presence, stretch out one's feet, nor yawn, nor laugh, nor cover the neck with a garment. (10–11)
One should always avoid staying in his presence [engaging in idle talk] as well as cracking one's fingers;
one should study at the proper time as long as the teacher is not distracted.
Seated below and to the side of the teacher, one should serve him with a fully concentrated mind.
He should never sit, lie down, or travel in the same vehicle as [his teacher].
He should run after him when he runs, and follow behind him when he walks;
likewise when he is on a cow, a horse, a camel, a carriage, a palace, or even on a lower seat.
He should always dwell together with his guru upon stone slabs or wooden planks;
he should be one who has conquered his senses, whose self is perpetually under control, free from anger, and pure. He should always employ speech that is sweet and beneficial.

Perfumes, garlands, desire, gambling, the use of shells, and the killing of living beings; 16. Anointing the body, collyrium for the eyes, massage, the carrying of an umbrella, as well as lust, greed, fear, sleep, singing, instrumental music, and dancing; 17.
One should diligently avoid threatening others, reviling them, gazing at or touching women, harming others, and backbiting.
[One should also collect] a water-pot, flowers, cow dung, earth, and kusha grass.
He should collect as much food as needed and go out for alms every day.
He must avoid all ghee and salt, as well as anything that has been kept overnight.
He should constantly refrain from watching dances and remain free from desire for songs and the like.
One should not gaze at the sun, nor should one practice the cleaning of the teeth; one should avoid solitude with women and conversation with Śūdras and others who are impure.
One should use the remains of the teacher's food as medicine, but not out of desire for its taste.
One should never perform a ritual bath for the removal of impurities [if it involves disrespecting the guru]. One must by no means commit the mental offense of abandoning the guru;
whether out of delusion or greed, having abandoned him, one becomes fallen.
Whether it be worldly, Vedic, or even spiritual knowledge, one should never act with malice toward the person from whom that knowledge is received.
Even if a teacher is arrogant and ignorant of what ought and ought not to be done, [one should not harm him]. 24.
He taught the abandonment of following one who has set out upon a wrong path.
(25) When the teacher’s own teacher is present, he should behave toward him as toward his own teacher;
having bowed and been permitted by that teacher, he may then salute his own teachers. (26)

Toward teachers of knowledge, toward yogis who are constantly engaged in practice, and toward those who restrain one from unrighteousness while instructing one in what is beneficial—one should always behave exactly as toward one's own guru. 27. One should always maintain the same conduct toward these as toward one's own teacher.

A young boy should show honor to the noble sons of his teacher, as well as to the teacher’s own kinsmen (28). Or, if he is already disciplined in ritual action, when teaching the teacher’s son, he deserves honor just like the teacher himself (29).
He should not perform the massaging of the limbs, the bathing,
or the eating of the leftovers for his teacher’s son, nor should he perform the washing of his feet. Women of the same caste as the teacher should be honored like the teacher himself.
Those of a different caste should be honored by rising from one's seat and by salutation.
However, the anointing, bathing, massaging of the limbs, and the dressing of the hair of the teacher’s wife must not be performed [by the pupil]. 31–32.
One should salute the feet of the young wives of the guru by prostrating on the ground, saying, "I am so-and-so.
Upon returning from a journey, one should perform the salutation preceded by grasping their feet.
Remembering the dharma of the virtuous, one should behave toward the wife of the guru as one would toward the guru himself.
A mother’s sister, a maternal uncle’s wife, a mother-in-law, and a father’s sister are to be honored like the wife of the guru; they are equal to the wife of the guru. 34–35.
He should clasp the hands of his brothers' wives who are of a different caste even day after day;
likewise, when traveling abroad, he should clasp the hands of women who are his kinsmen or relatives.
He should also clasp the hands of his father’s sister, his mother’s sister, and his wife’s sister.
One should behave toward her as toward a mother; a mother’s affection is indeed greater than that of others. 37.
One should constantly teach the Veda, the Dharma, the Purāṇas, and the Vedāṅgas to one who is thus endowed with good conduct, self-possessed, and free from deceit. 38.
If a teacher, having accepted a disciple for a year, does not impart knowledge, he takes upon himself the sins of that disciple who has lived with him (39).
A teacher’s son who is obedient, pure, righteous, and a giver of knowledge [is also fit to be a teacher].
A virtuous man who is capable, joyful, and like a cloud [in providing for needs],
who has mastered his throat [is eloquent], is free from malice, is intelligent,
serves his guru, is trustworthy, and is dear— these six types of twice-born men should be taught according to the prescribed rule. 40–41.

In these cases, one should give a gift to the Brāhmaṇas as is appropriate; otherwise, having sipped water and being self-restrained, one should always study while facing north, having clasped the teacher's feet and gazing at the teacher's face. 42.
One should say, "Recite, sir," and one should pause when saying, "Let there be a pause.

Purified by three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) while sitting upon grass-blades with their tips pointing eastward and holding sacred grass-bands (pavitra), the purifier (the teacher) is then worthy to utter the syllable Om.
O twice-born ones, a Brāhmaṇa should utter the Praṇava at the end [of the recitation] according to the rules;
he should always perform the teaching preceded by the Brahmāñjali.
For all beings, the Veda is the eternal eye.
One should study this constantly; otherwise, one falls from the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
One should daily recite the Ṛg-verses; by offering the oblation of milk, one gratifies the deities at all times, and the deities, being invoked with their desired objects, are satisfied.
By studying the Yajus verses with self-restraint, one daily gratifies the deities with offerings of curd;
by studying the Sāmans, one gratifies them daily with oblations of clarified butter;
and by constantly studying the Atharva-Angirasas, one gratifies the deities with honey.

One should satisfy the gods with these ancient limbs of Dharma consisting of meat. Having gone to the forest, being self-restrained and composed, one should recite the Gāyatrī morning and evening, following the obligatory rite.

One should constantly recite the Gāyatrī mantra, which has a maximum of one thousand syllables, a middle of one hundred, and a minimum of ten; this is proclaimed as the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña).
Furthermore, the Lord weighed the Gāyatrī and the Vedas on a scale.
On one side are the four Vedas, and on the other side is the Gāyatrī;
having placed the syllable *Oṃ* at the beginning, followed by the Vyāhṛtis, one should then recite the Sāvitrī with single-minded concentration and endowed with faith.
In a former age, there arose the three eternal Great Utterances (Mahāvyāhṛtis)— Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svaḥ— which destroy all that is inauspicious.
[They represent] Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Kāla, as well as Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Maheśvara.
The three syllables *sat*, *vaṃ*, and *raṃ* are known as the *vyāhṛtis* in their respective order. The syllable *oṃ* is that supreme Brahman, and following it is the *Sāvitrī*.
This mantra is the great yoga; it is declared to be the essence of essences.
The celibate student who studies this Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas, day after day, having understood its meaning, attains the supreme goal.
Gāyatrī is the progenitor of the Vedas; Gāyatrī is the purifier of the worlds.
Knowing this, it is said that there is no other recitation superior to the Gāyatrī.
O best of the twice-born, the commencement of Vedic study (upākaraṇa) is prescribed for the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa,
or on the full moon days of Āṣāḍha or Bhādrapada.
O Brahmin, during the five and a half months when the sun moves toward the south, a student, pure and composed, should study in clean places; however,
in the month of Puṣya, the twice-born should perform the *utsarjana* ceremony outside.

When the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa has arrived, during the forenoon, the twice-born man should begin the study of the Vedas; indeed, a twice-born man should study the Vedas during the bright fortnight, while a wise man should study the Vedāṅgas and the Purāṇas during the dark fortnights.
One who is studying, as well as one who is teaching or diligently practicing [the Veda], should always avoid these occasions of non-study (anadhyāya):
when the wind is audible to the ear at night, and during the day when there is a cloud of dust.
During the simultaneous occurrence of lightning, thunder, rain, and great meteors,
Prajāpati has declared that these constitute an untimely suspension of Vedic study;
one should recognize these as having arisen when the sacred fires have been kindled.

Then, one should know that these occasions— ignorance [of the Vedas], the appearance of clouds out of season, untruth, the sight of lightning, a thunderclap, an earthquake, and the eclipses of the luminaries—
are times when study is prohibited, even during the rainy season.

When the sacred fires have been kindled, and when there is the sound of lightning and thunder, there shall be a suspension of study for as long as the light remains; in the remaining cases, it is like the rule for the night during the day. In villages and in cities, there shall always be a suspension of study.
For those desiring proficiency in the Dharma, there is a suspension of study at all times when there is a foul odor,
when a corpse is present within a village, in the proximity of a *vṛṣala*,
and during the rising of clouds at the time of rain.
One should not even mentally contemplate discharging feces or urine in water or at midnight (70),
nor should a learned twice-born man who has received the fee for a *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, while still impure from a meal or having eaten at a *śrāddha*, contemplate such things even in his mind (71).
One should not perform the *brahma-yajña* for three days during the impurity (*sūtaka*) of a Brahmin or a king, nor during an eclipse (*rāhu*),
as long as one partakes of food from a single source and as long as oil remains on the body. For a learned Brahmin, one should not recite the Veda as long as these conditions persist.

One should not study while lying down, with feet raised, or having placed one's knees upon a cloth (avasakthikā). Nor should one study after eating meat, or food from a Śūdra’s funeral feast (śrāddha),
nor during a mist, nor when there is the sound of an arrow, nor during either of the two twilights.

On the new moon and the fourteenth days, on the full moon and the eighth days, as well as at the commencement (upākarma) and the conclusion (utsarga) of the Vedic studies, a three-night fast is prescribed.
On the Aṣṭakā days and during the nights at the end of the seasons, a fast of one day and night is required.
In the months of Mārgaśīrṣa, Pauṣa, and likewise Māgha,
three Aṣṭakās are proclaimed by the wise in the dark fortnights;
[one should avoid] the shade of the Śleṣmātaka, the Śālmali, and the Madhuka trees.
One should never study under a *kovidāra* or a *kapittha* tree, nor when one's fellow student (*sabrahmacārin*) has died,
nor likewise when one's teacher (*ācārya*) has passed away; in those cases, a fast of three nights is prescribed.
These are proclaimed as the defects that constitute unfit times for study (*anadhyāya*) for the wise.
During these times, Rākṣasas cause harm; therefore, one should avoid them.
However, there is no such unfit time for the daily obligatory rites (*nityaka*), nor for the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*). 79–80.

At the conclusion of the *upākarma* fire-sacrifice, and likewise in the midst of the sacrifice, one should not recite even a single verse (*ṛc*), a single sacrificial formula (*yajus*), or even a single chant (*sāman*). Furthermore, one should not study during the *aṣṭakā* festivals or when the wind is blowing violently.
But there is no suspension of study for the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas), nor for the Itihāsas and Purāṇas;
nor for the other Dharmaśāstras—one should avoid all these [other occasions] during their study.
This dharma of the student (brahmacārin) has been proclaimed in brief. 82–83.

Formerly, it was declared by Brahmā that a twice-born man who, without having studied the Śruti, exerts effort in other matters, is utterly deluded; he is not to be conversed with by the twice-born, for he is outside the Veda. (84)
A twice-born man should certainly not be satisfied with the mere recitation of the Vedas;
he who terminates his study at the mere recitation sinks like a cow in the mud.
Having studied the Veda according to the prescribed rules, he who does not reflect upon the meaning of the Veda [is likewise lost]. 85–86.
One who is deluded and behaves like a Śūdra does not attain the status of being a fit recipient; however, if he desires to dwell permanently with his guru,
he should serve him with devotion until the release of the body.

Having gone to the forest, he should offer oblations into the sacred fire according to the prescribed rules (88). Furthermore, being established in Brahman and composed in mind, he should constantly study the Sāvitrī, the Śatarudriya, and especially the Vedāntas.
One should practice this constantly, disciplined and devoted to subsisting on alms.

This supreme and ancient ordinance, which was correctly proclaimed here in the Vedas and Āgamas, was spoken of old by the divine Manu, the son of Svayambhū, when he was questioned by the foremost of the great seers. 89–90.
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Exposition of Karma-yoga," in the Svarga-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
[Now begins] the fifty-fourth chapter.

Vyāsa said: O twice-born ones, having studied the one Veda, two Vedas, or likewise all the Vedas, and having mastered their meaning, the best of the twice-born should then perform the ceremonial bath (snāna).
Having given wealth to his guru and with his permission, he who has completed his vows and whose mind is disciplined may bathe; or, if he is unable, he may bathe [at the conclusion of the vow].
He should carry a bamboo staff and wear an inner garment as well as an upper garment.
He should carry two sacred threads, a water-pot with water,
an umbrella, a stainless turban, wooden sandals, and leather shoes; he should wear golden earrings, keep his hair and nails clipped, and remain pure.
Except for gold, a Brahmin should not wear a garland made of red flowers;
he should always wear white garments, be fragrant, and be pleasant to behold.
He should never wear worn-out or dirty clothes when he has the means to do otherwise.
One should not wear a garment that is dyed red, nor one that is excessively bright, nor one worn by another; likewise, one should not use earrings, sandals, a garland, or wooden shoes.
One should display the sacred thread, ornaments, and the black antelope skin.
He should not wear his garment over the right shoulder, nor should he wear one that is discolored;
he should take a wife according to the prescribed rules— one who is suitable for himself, auspicious, endowed with beauty and auspicious marks, and free from defects of lineage.
A Brāhmaṇa should take as his wife one who is not born of his father’s lineage, who is not of a non-human lineage, and who is endowed with good character and purity;
he should approach her during her fertile period until a son is born.
One should diligently avoid the prohibited days:
the sixth, the eighth, the fifteenth, the twelfth, and the fourteenth; one should always remain celibate, as well as on the three days of birth [of the planets].
One who has established the marriage fire should offer oblations into Jātavedas. These purifiers, a Snātaka should always perform;
he should constantly carry out his own duties as ordained by the Veda, remaining free from sloth.
One who fails to perform these falls swiftly into most terrifying hells;
therefore, one should diligently study the Veda and not neglect the great sacrifices (mahāyajñas).
One should also perform the domestic rites and the worship at the twilights (saṃdhyopāsana).
One should form friendships with those who are equal or superior; one should always approach a lord. One should visit deities and provide for the maintenance of one's wife.
A wise man should not proclaim his own dharma, nor should he conceal his sin.

One who is compassionate toward all beings should always perform what is beneficial for oneself, acting in accordance with one's age, occupation, learning, and lineage; one should always conduct oneself by conforming to the customs of the region, speech, and intellect.
One should practice that conduct which is proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti, which is rightly followed by the virtuous, and never anything else;
[one should follow] that path by which one's fathers have gone, and by which one's grandfathers have gone. (18–19)
By that path one should go; going by it, one does not incur fault.
One should be constantly devoted to the study of the Vedas, always wearing the sacred thread, truthful in speech, having conquered anger, and free from greed and delusion.

A householder who is devoted to the recitation of the Sāvitrī, who performs śrāddha rites, and who is intent on the welfare of his mother and father, as well as devoted to the welfare of a brāhmaṇa, is liberated. One who is a giver, a performer of sacrifices, and a devotee of the gods is glorified in the world of Brahmā. 21–22.
One should constantly pursue the three aims of life and perform the worship of the gods every single day; with a restrained mind, one should always pay homage to the deities.
One should always be disposed toward sharing, endowed with forgiveness, and compassionate.
One is called a householder not merely by living in a house; rather,
forbearance, compassion, wisdom, truthfulness, self-restraint, tranquility, constant devotion to the inner self, and knowledge— these are the characteristics of a Brāhmaṇa.
Therefore, the best of the twice-born should not be negligent, especially while practicing dharma according to his capacity; he should avoid those things that are censured.
Having shaken off the turbidity of delusion and attained the unsurpassed yoga, [he should remain steadfast].
A householder is liberated from bondage; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
(27) Forgiveness is the endurance of faults arising from anger toward others—such as insults, defeat, provocation, injury, imprisonment, and physical assault. (28)
The sages have declared that compassion toward one's own sufferings and benevolence toward the sufferings of others is the direct means for accomplishing Dharma;
indeed, the mastery of the fourteen branches of knowledge is for the sake of others. 29.

That by which dharma increases is called *vijñāna* (higher knowledge). Having studied the sacred lore according to the rules and having understood its meaning, one should perform the duties of dharma; this indeed is called *vijñāna*. (30–31)
One conquers the world through truth; truth is that supreme state.
The wise declare that truth is non-negligence regarding things as they truly are.
Self-restraint is the cessation of bodily impulses; tranquility arises from the clarity of wisdom.
The knowledge of the imperishable within the self, having attained which one does not grieve—
by which that blessed Lord, the Supreme, the very Hṛṣīkeśa himself, is known— that is celebrated as true knowledge. 33–34.
The learned Brahmin who is devoted to that, intent on that, eternally free from anger, pure,
and dedicated to the great sacrifices, attains that unsurpassed state. One should protect the body with effort, for it is the abode of dharma.
Without the body, the Supreme Viṣṇu is not perceived by men.
A twice-born man, being self-restrained, should always apply himself to virtue, wealth, and pleasure;
he should not even mentally contemplate pleasure or wealth that is devoid of virtue. 36–37.

Even while suffering, one should not practice unrighteousness, for Dharma is the Blessed Lord, the God who is the refuge for all living beings. One should act for the benefit of all creatures and not set one's mind on deeds that harm others. (38)
One should not revile the deities of the sacrificial offerings, nor should one dwell with those who do so.
However, that mortal who, being self-restrained and pure, recites this chapter on Dharma,
or teaches it, or causes others to hear it, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Fifty-Five. Vyāsa said:
One should not harm any living beings, nor should one ever speak untruth;
one should not utter what is harmful or unpleasant, nor should one ever be a thief. Whether it be grass, or even vegetables, or earth, or even water— [one should not take these without permission].
One who steals the property of another goes to hell.

A wise man should not accept gifts from a king, nor from a Śūdra, nor even from one who has fallen from his caste; nor from anyone else unless he is unable to obtain them otherwise, for he should avoid those who are censured.
One should never be a perpetual beggar, nor should one ever beg from that same person again;
for such a beggar takes away the very life of that foolish man.
One should not be a stealer of another's wealth, especially so in the case of the best of the twice-born.
One should never, even in times of distress, seize the property of a Brāhmaṇa.
They say that poison is not truly poison; it is the property of a Brāhmaṇa that is called poison.
Therefore, one should always avoid the property of the gods with great effort.
"Manu, the Lord of Creatures, has declared that taking flowers, vegetables, water, wood, as well as roots, fruits, and grass that have not been given constitutes theft.
A twice-born man may take flowers for the purpose of worshipping the gods."
A wise person should not take grass, wood, fruit, flowers, or even light from a single source alone, unless it has been specifically permitted;
they say this is for the sake of dharma alone, otherwise one becomes fallen. 8–9.

Those standing on the path who are hungry may take a handful of sesame, mung beans, barley, and so forth; it is not otherwise for Brahmins, O sages, nor for those seeking merit and the like—this is the established rule.
One should not perform a vow under the pretext of dharma after having committed a sin.
A Brahmin who, while performing a vow, conceals his sin by practicing deceit toward women or Śūdras,
is censured by those who discourse on the Veda both in this world and after death; for a vow performed through hypocrisy goes to the Rākṣasas.
He who adopts a livelihood by wearing the dress of a religious student (aligī) incurs the sin of a student-breaker and is born into the womb of an animal.
Begging, forming matrimonial alliances, living together, and conversing [with such a person must be avoided].
One who commits [such acts] shall fall eternally; therefore, one should avoid them with great effort. One should not commit an offense against the gods, nor likewise an offense against the guru.
An offense against the guru is many millions of times more grievous than an offense against the gods.
Public scandal and atheism are each ten million times more detrimental than that; likewise,
families that are deficient in dharma fall from noble status to ignoble status through cattle-rearing, service to deities, service to Brahmins, agriculture, or service to kings.
Through evil reflections, the omission of prescribed duties, the failure to study the Vedas,
the neglect of Brahmins, falsehood, adultery, and the eating of forbidden food, noble families fall into a state of ignobility. (17–18)
A family perishes quickly by practicing the dharma of those who do not belong to a [spiritual] lineage (agotra),
and likewise by giving gifts to those who are not learned in the Vedas (aśrotriya) or to outcasts (vṛṣala).
A family perishes quickly when it lacks those who follow the prescribed conduct.
One should not dwell in a village surrounded by unrighteous people, nor in one abounding in disease; nor should one live in a kingdom ruled by Śūdras, nor in one filled with heretics.
The region between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, extending from east to west, is auspicious.
A twice-born man should not dwell anywhere except in regions between the two oceans,
or where the black antelope naturally roams at all times;
or he may dwell there where there are rivers renowned for their sanctity.
Having avoided a riverbank within half a *kośa*, the best of the twice-born should not dwell elsewhere;
nor should he live near a village of outcastes (*antyaja*), nor with those who have fallen from their caste (*patita*), nor with *caṇḍālas* or *pulkasas*. (23–24)

One should not share a bed, a seat, a row, a vessel, or the mixing of cooked food with fools, the arrogant, others, or those intent on women; likewise, one should avoid sacrificing for them, teaching them, sexual union with them, and eating together with them. 25.25–26a.

Studying together is the tenth, and officiating at sacrifices together is the eleventh; these are declared to be the defects arising from intermixture. By living in close proximity, sin is transmitted among men.
Therefore, with every effort, one should avoid confusion;
for those who sit in a single row and touch one another, there would be no confusion among them if a boundary has been established by means of ashes. 28.
By fire, by ashes, by water, by scratching,
by the door, and by the path— by these six, a row is divided.
One should not engage in dry enmities, nor dispute, nor slander.
One should never point out a cow wandering in another's field; one should not live with a slanderer, nor should one ever pierce the vital spots of others.
One should not gaze at a halo around the sun, nor at Indra’s bow (a rainbow) appearing in the afternoon.
A wise man should speak of the moon or gold to others;
he should not engage in conflict with many people, nor even with his kinsmen,
and he should never do to others what is disagreeable to himself.

The best of the twice-born should not speak of the lunar day of the fortnight, nor should he point out the constellations; he should not address a woman in her courses, nor one who is impure. He should not prevent anything being given to the gods, to his teacher, or to Brahmins.
One should not praise oneself, nor should one avoid censuring others.
One should diligently avoid censuring the Vedas and censuring the gods.
That twice-born man who censures the gods, the sages, or the Vedas—35–36.
O lords of sages, no atonement for such an act is seen in the scriptures here; a man who reviles his guru, the deity, the Veda, or its supplementary texts (Upabṛṃhaṇa),
is cooked in the Raurava hell for more than a hundred crores of kalpas.
One should remain silent during censure and should not utter any reply; one should depart after covering one's ears and should not even look at the censurer.
A wise person should avoid disclosing the secrets of others and refrain from reviling them. (38–39)
A superior twice-born man should never engage in dispute with his own kinsmen; he should not speak of sin to sinners, nor of sinlessness to them.
A fault equal to that of untruth would arise from speaking the truth, and one becomes guilty of a fault by speaking what is untrue. 40.
The tears shed from the weeping of men who have been falsely accused fall upon the children and livestock of those false accusers;
[the sins] of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, and violating the teacher’s wife [fall upon them]. 41–42.
The elders have declared that there is no purification for one who makes a false accusation;

one should not look at the rising sun or the moon without a specific reason, nor at them when setting, nor when reflected in water, nor when touched by the rays, nor when they are at the meridian. 43.43-44ab.
One should look at that which is reflected, following its path in a mirror or similar surface (44).
One should never look at a naked woman or a man, nor at urine or feces, nor at one engaged in sexual intercourse (45).
A wise man, while impure, should not look at the planets such as the sun and the moon;
nor should he speak to another, nor remain with his mouth full of food remnants, nor with his head covered.
He should not look at one who has touched a corpse, nor at the face of a teacher when he is angry.
One should not look at the shadow of one’s own tail or water, nor at a row of people while they are eating (47).
One should not look at a person whose bonds have not yet been released, nor at a mad elephant; one should not eat together with one's wife, nor look at her while she is eating (48).
A wise man should never look at his own reflection— whether auspicious or inauspicious— in water while he is sneezing, yawning, not seated on a seat, or as he pleases;
nor should he ever step over it.

A wise man should not give a Śūdra a command, nor rice mixed with sesame, nor milk-rice, nor curd (50); nor should he give him the remains of food, nor honey, nor ghee, nor a black antelope skin, nor an oblation. Furthermore, he should not explain a religious vow to him, nor should he discourse upon dharma (51).
One should not fall under the sway of anger; one should abandon hatred and passion, as well as greed, hypocrisy, deceit, malice, and the disparagement of knowledge.
One should completely avoid envy, intoxication, sorrow, and delusion.

One should not cause pain to anyone, yet one may strike a son or a disciple. One should not serve those who are base, nor should one ever have a mind consumed by craving. One should not despise oneself, and one should diligently avoid dejection.
A wise man should not treat another who is not superior as if they were inferior, nor should he disparage himself due to his latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
He should not scratch the earth with his fingernails, nor should he lie down while treading upon a cow.
He should not speak of one river when among rivers, nor of one mountain when among mountains.
One should not abandon a traveling companion at a lodging or while eating. One should not enter water without a garment, nor should one step over a fire.
Furthermore, one should not smear the body with oil remaining after anointing the head. 56–57.
One should not play with snakes or weapons, nor touch one's own nails; one should not go about with unrefined people, nor expose one's private parts.
One should not indulge in the fickleness of hands, feet, speech, or eyes. 58.

One should not exhibit fickleness regarding the genitals or the belly, nor should one ever do so with the ears (69). One should not make a sound by scratching the body, nor should one drink from joined palms;
one should never strike water with the feet or with the hands (70).
One should not destroy roots or fruits with bricks; one should not learn the speech of Mlecchas, nor should one drag a seat with the foot.
One should not tear one's nails, clap the hands, cut anything, or scratch oneself.
A wise person should perform massage, but never do so fruitlessly and without cause.
He should not eat food while sitting on his haunches, nor should he engage in useless exertion; he should not dance, nor sing, nor play musical instruments.
One should not scratch one's own head with hands that are not joined together;
nor should one seek to please the gods, even those of the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati), with worldly praises.
One should not play with dice, nor run about, nor void excrement or urine in water.
One should never lie down while still impure from food, nor should one bathe naked. One should not recite [sacred texts] while walking, nor should one touch one's own head.
One should not cut one's nails or hair while they are growing, nor should one wake a sleeping person.
One should not expose oneself to the morning sun, one should avoid the smoke from a funeral pyre, one should never sleep in an empty house, and one should not remove one's own sandals.
One should not spit without cause, nor should one cross a river using only one's arms.
One should never wash one's feet with the foot itself;
a wise man should not warm his feet over a fire, nor should he scrub them on a bell-metal vessel.
Furthermore, one should not stretch out one's feet toward a deity, a Brāhmaṇa, or even a cow.
Being impure, one should never at any time perform sleeping, drinking, Vedic study, bathing, eating, or going outside while facing the wind, fire, a king, a Brahmin, the sun,
or the moon.

One should always avoid sleeping, studying, bathing, applying unguents, eating, and walking during both twilights as well as at midday. A Brahmin who is impure from eating should not touch with his hand a cow, a Brahmin, or fire.
One should not move the feet upon a deity’s image; one who is impure should not tend the fire, nor should one invoke the gods or the sages.
One should not plunge into a bottomless body of water, nor should one enter it without a valid reason.

One should lift up water with the left hand and drink it from the mouth; one should not cross [a body of water] without having performed the ritual sipping (ācamana), nor should one discharge semen into water,
nor [enter water that is] smeared with impurity, fit for sacrifice, blood, or venomous creatures.

One should not cross a flowing river, nor should one engage in sexual intercourse in water; one should not cut down a sacred tree (caityavṛkṣa), nor should one discharge phlegm into the water. One should not [step on] bones, ashes, potsherds, hair, or thorns.
A wise person should never step upon husks, charcoal, or dried cow-dung. He should not leap over the fire, nor should he ever place it beneath himself.
He should not hold it at the level of his feet, nor should he blow upon it with a winnowing basket.
One should not climb a tree, nor should one ever look at anything impure; one should not throw fire into fire, nor should one extinguish it with water.
Furthermore, one should not inform others merely of the death of a friend, nor of one's own.
A wise man should not engage in selling what is unfit for sale or counterfeit goods. He should not, while impure, kindle fire with the breath from his mouth;
nor should he carry fire across sacred sites, water sources, or boundary lines.
One should never violate a previously established agreement;
one should not cause wild beasts, tigers, or birds to fight one another; and one should not inflict harm upon others by means of water, wind, heat, or other such elements. 82.
Having had difficult tasks performed by his elders, he should not later deceive them.
(83) Every evening and morning, he should bolt the doors of the house for the sake of protection.
He should avoid wearing garlands or perfumes outside [the home], and he should eat only together with his wife. (84)
Having engaged in a contentious dispute, he should avoid entering [the village]; a wise Brāhmaṇa should not stand eating from his fingernails, nor should he speak or laugh.
He should not touch his own fire with his hand, nor should he remain in water for a long time.
One should not blow upon the fire with one's breath when it is without fuel, nor with a winnowing basket, nor with the hand.
One should kindle the fire with one's mouth, for it was born from the mouth.
A wise man should not speak of another's wife, nor should he officiate at a sacrifice for one who is unworthy of sacrificing.
A Brahmin should never wander alone, and he should avoid large crowds; he should never go around a temple in a counter-clockwise direction (apradakṣiṇa).
He should not wear his garments so as to cause distress, nor should he sleep in a temple.
One should not set out on a journey alone, nor with unrighteous people (89),
nor with those afflicted by disease, nor with Śūdras, nor with outcasts, nor without shoes, nor likewise without water and such provisions (90).
A twice-born man should never at any time step across the path of a dog,
nor should he revile yogis, perfected beings (siddhas), those observing vows, or ascetics. A wise man should likewise [respect] the temples of the gods and the sacrificial grounds of the gods.
One should not intentionally step on the shadow of Brahmins or even of a cow (92).
Nor should one cause one's own shadow to be stepped upon by those who have fallen [from their status], the diseased, or others;
nor should one ever stand upon charcoal, ashes, hair, or similar things (93).

A twice-born man should avoid the dust raised by a broom, the water from a bathing cloth, and the water remaining in a jar; he should not eat what is unfit to be eaten, nor drink what is unfit to be drunk. (94) Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. 55
The fifty-sixth chapter. Vyāsa said:
A Brahmin should not, out of delusion or desire, eat the food of a Śūdra.
He who eats [the food of another] when there is no distress enters the womb of a Śūdra.
That twice-born man who eats the censurable food of a Śūdra for six months becomes a Śūdra while still alive;
once dead, he is reborn as a dog.

O lords of sages, he whose stomach is filled with the food of a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, shall, upon death, enter the womb of that same caste. [One should avoid] the food of a king, the food of a quail-keeper, the food of a eunuch, and the food of leather-workers.
One should avoid the food of a *gaṇa*, the food of a courtesan, and the six types of food [already mentioned].

Likewise, one should avoid the food of those who live by their vehicles, a washerman, a thief, and a liquor-seller, as well as the food of a musician and a blacksmith, and the food of a funeral feast. 4–5.

The food of a potter, a painter, a usurer, one who has fallen from his caste, the son of a remarried woman, a student by profession, one who is cursed, a goldsmith, an actor, a hunter, a eunuch, and one who is afflicted by disease; 6. [these are those whose food should not be eaten].

The food of a physician, of an unchaste woman, and of a jailer; the food of a thief, of an atheist, and of one who reviles the deities; the food of a seller of Soma, and especially that of a dog-cooker (outcaste)—[these should be avoided].

The food of one who is conquered by his wife, of one in whose house there is a paramour, of one who has renounced the world but remains at home, of a miser, and likewise of one who eats the leavings of others; the food of a most sinful man, the food of a multitude, and indeed the food of one who lives by the sword.

The food of one who is frightened, weeping, or crying out; that which is defiled by injury; the food of one who hates the Vedas, of one who delights in sin, and of one who is dead; the food of a meal cooked for no sacred purpose, the food of a house in mourning, and the food of one who is ill—[these should be avoided]. 10–11.
One should especially avoid the food of childless women, of the ungrateful, and likewise of artisans, as well as that of those who sell weapons (12).
One should also avoid the food of drunkards, of bell-ringers, and of physicians.

The food of one who has procreated through a learned man, as well as that of a *parivitti* (one superseded in marriage), and especially that of a *punarbhū* (a remarried woman) and the husband of a *didhiṣū* (a younger sister married before the elder);
food treated with contempt, rejected, or accompanied by anger and wonder. (13-14)
One should not eat even the food of a guru if it is devoid of the proper consecratory rites (saṃskāra),
for all the evil deeds of a person reside within their food. Whoever eats the food of another, eats that person's sin.

The Ardhakākula, a friend, a cowherd, a charioteer, and a barber—these are among Śūdras whose food may be eaten; one should also offer oneself [as a servant] to them. Furthermore, the actor, the potter, and the field-laborer [are also such]. 16–17.
Among these Śūdras, the wise should not eat the food of one who possesses very few virtues;
however, milk-rice cooked with ghee, cow's milk,
barley meal, oil-cake, and oil may be accepted from a Śūdra by the twice-born.

One should avoid eggplant, the nālikā vegetable, safflower, and bhasmaka; likewise, one should avoid onion, garlic, fermented liquids, and resinous exudations; as well as mushrooms, village pigs, boiled milk, and fresh colostrum.
One should avoid those buds that are facing downward or are withered,
as well as *gṛñjana*, *kiṃśuka*, and likewise *kūṣmāṇḍa*.
Having eaten *udumbara* or *alābu*, a twice-born man indeed falls from his status.
Likewise, kṛsara, saṃyāva, upāyasa, and apūpa;
unprepared meat, the food of the gods, and sacrificial oblations;
gruel, mātuluṅga, and even fish that have not been prepared [for sacrifice]. 22–23.
One should carefully avoid the *nīpa*, *kapittha*, and *plakṣa* fruits,
as well as oil-cake from which the oil has been extracted, and likewise grains offered to the gods.
At night, one should diligently renounce all things associated with sesame.

One should not eat buttermilk with milk, nor should one consume forbidden foods. One must always avoid food infested with worms, food that is morally tainted, food mixed with earth, and food fallen into by insects or worms, as well as anything that causes distress to friends.
Furthermore, food that has been smelled by a dog, prepared by a Caṇḍāla, or likewise gazed upon by a Caṇḍāla;
food smelled by a woman in her courses, by outcasts, or even by a cow;
food that is unwholesome, stale, or always cast away.

That which has been touched by crows or cocks, or even come into contact with worms; that which has been smelled by humans, or touched by one afflicted with leprosy; that which is offered by a woman in her menses, by an unchaste woman, or by one who is diseased. (28–29)
One should also avoid the milk of a woman in her courses, or one whose clothes are soiled; likewise, the milk of a cow that has lost its calf, and that of a sheep within ten days of birth (30).
Manu declared that the milk of a ewe and the milk of a cow in heat (sandhinī) are unfit for drinking.
The crane, the swan, the dātyūha, the sparrow, and likewise the parrot;
the kurara, the cakora, the web-footed bird, and the cuckoo; the crows, the wagtails, the hawk, and likewise the vulture. 31–32.
An owl, a ruddy goose, a hawk, a pigeon, a turtle-dove, and likewise a village cock;
a lion, a tiger, a cat, a dog, and a boar. 33.
One should not eat jackals, monkeys, or donkeys (34).
One should not eat snakes, deer, peacocks, or other forest-dwelling creatures, nor any animals that move in water or on land; such is the established rule (dhāraṇā) (35).

The iguana, the tortoise, the hare, the rhinoceros, and the porcupine—these five-clawed animals are always fit for consumption; so says Manu, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati). One may eat fish that have scales, as well as the meat of the ruru deer.
It should be offered to the deities of the sacrificial oblation and to the Brahmins, and not otherwise.
(37) The peacock, the partridge, the pigeon, the francolin, the rhinoceros, the crane, the fish, the swan, and the parājitā—these are edible. (38)
O best of the twice-born, the śapharī, siṃhatuṇḍa, pāṭhīna, and rohita fish are likewise declared to be edible.
One may eat the meat of these when it has been consecrated by sprinkling (prokṣita) for the sake of a brahmin.

One who eats meat according to the prescribed rule—even at the risk of one's own life—and who eats only what remains, is not tainted. Nor is one tainted when eating for medicinal purposes, when lacking strength, by command, or for the sake of a sacrifice. (40–41)
If one who has been invited to a *śrāddha* for the ancestors or the gods should discard meat, he falls into hell for as many years as there are hairs on the animal's body.
Likewise, that which is unfit to be given, unfit to be drunk, or even unfit to be touched [is likewise forbidden].
"It is the established rule that liquor is always unfit for the twice-born to look upon.
Therefore, one should always avoid liquor with every effort;
for by drinking it, a twice-born man falls from his religious duties and becomes one with whom others must not converse. (43-44)
Even after consuming what is unfit for consumption or drinking what is unfit for drinking, a twice-born man shall not regain his status until he has discharged that [impurity] from below. Therefore,
one should always avoid things unfit for consumption with great effort.
O Brahmin, these are indeed unfit for drinking; if one drinks them, he goes to the Raurava hell.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Rules Regarding Edible and Non-edible Foods," in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
The fifty-seventh chapter. Vyāsa said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the unsurpassed dharma of giving.
Formerly, this was declared by Brahmā to the sages who discourse on Brahman:
"The faithful bestowal of appropriate objects upon a worthy recipient is designated as 'giving' (dāna), which yields the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation."

I consider that gift which one endowed with supreme faith gives to those who are most distinguished; everything else belongs to someone else. Giving is said to be of three kinds: constant, occasional, and for a specific desire.

The fourth is declared to be Vimala (the Stainless), the most excellent among all gifts. Whatever is given daily with constancy to a non-benefactor Brahmin, without aiming for any fruit, is therefore called Nityaka (the Constant). 4–5.
That which is given into the hands of the learned for the sake of pacifying evil is designated by the virtuous as the unsurpassed *naimittika* (occasional) gift.
That which is bestowed for the sake of offspring, victory, sovereignty, or happiness—
That gift which is given for the sake of a specific desire is called "kāmya" by the sages who contemplate dharma.
But that gift which is bestowed upon those who know Brahman for the sake of pleasing the Lord,
with a mind joined to dharma— that gift is stainless and auspicious.

One should practice the duty of giving as much as one is able, having encountered a worthy recipient; that recipient is to be honored who delivers one from all [suffering]. One should give what remains after providing for the family’s food and clothing.
Whatever is given otherwise is not a gift that yields fruit.
(10) It should be given with devotion to one who is learned in the Vedas, of noble birth, humble, ascetic, observant of vows, and poor. (11)

But he who would give land with devotion to a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires goes to the supreme abode, having reached which he does not grieve. [Land] endowed with sugarcane, barley, wheat, and rice—
He who gives [land] to one learned in the Vedas is born again and again.
Or, he who bestows even a piece of land the size of a cow-hide upon a poor Brāhmaṇa is liberated from all sins. 13–14.
There is no gift whatsoever found here superior to the gift of land;
one should know that the gift of food is equal to it, and the gift of knowledge is greater than that.
(15) He who [gives] to a Brāhmaṇa who is peaceful, pure, and of virtuous character...
One who bestows knowledge according to the prescribed rite is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
(16) He who gives gold daily with faith to a celibate student, being liberated from all sins, shall attain the abode of Brahmā. (17)

A person obtains the fruit of giving food to a householder; indeed, food alone should be given to him, for by giving it, one attains the supreme goal. On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, [one should feed] seven or five Brāhmaṇas.

Having fasted according to the prescribed rite, being tranquil, pure, and of restrained mind, he should worship with black sesame seeds and especially with honey, while keeping in his heart the thought:
"May Dharmarāja be pleased. (19–20)

Whatever sin has been committed throughout one's entire life perishes in that very instant for one who places sesame seeds upon a black antelope skin and gives it, along with gold, honey, and clarified butter, to a brahmin; such a person overcomes all evil deeds.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha especially, by offering food with ghee and a water-pot dedicated to Dharmarāja and to the Brahmins, one is released from fear;
likewise, by giving [gifts] consisting of gold and sesame seeds to seven or five Brahmins.
He should satisfy [the ancestors] with vessels of water and thus removes the sin of killing a Brahmin;
having fasted on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Māgha,
wearing white garments, he should offer oblations of black sesame seeds into the fire.
Being composed, he should give sesame seeds for the sake of praise to the Brahmins;
by doing so on the new moon day (amāvāsyā), the twice-born man transcends all sin committed since his birth. (25-26)
Whoever should give a fast unto the Lord of the gods, dedicating it to Keśava, [with the prayer]:
"May the eternal Lord Viṣṇu, Hṛṣīkeśa, be pleased"—
the sin committed during seven lifetimes perishes at that very moment.
He who, having bathed on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
worships the Lord who wields the Pināka bow through the mouth of a twice-born, shall not undergo rebirth; especially so on the eighth day of the dark fortnight when he honors a righteous brahmin.

Having bathed and worshipped according to the rules by washing his feet and other rites, [one should pray]: "May Mahādeva be pleased with me; may he grant his own wealth. Thus liberated from all sins, one attains the supreme goal.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, and especially on the eighth day,
as well as on the new moon day, Trivikrama should be worshipped by the twice-born and by devotees.
Having fasted on the eleventh day, one should worship Puruṣottama on the twelfth day.
One should worship through the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa and shall go to the supreme state;
this Vaiṣṇavī guest is indeed the twelfth day of the bright fortnight. On that day, one should diligently propitiate the Lord Janārdana.
