O ascetic, whatever is given to a pure Brahmin with reference to Lord Īśāna, or even to Viṣṇu himself, that is recorded as having infinite fruit. For whatever deity a man may wish to propitiate, [that gift is offered to him].
One should diligently honor the Brāhmaṇas and satisfy them with wealth;
for the deities always reside within the bodies of the twice-born.
When Brāhmaṇas are unavailable, they are sometimes worshipped by them in images and other such forms.
Therefore, by one who desires the fruit [of their efforts], effort should be made toward images and the like;
the deities should always be worshipped especially among the twice-born.
One who desires prosperity should constantly worship Indra.

One who desires spiritual luster should worship Brahmā; one desiring knowledge, Viṣṇu; one desiring health, the Sun; one desiring wealth, the Fire-god; and one desiring the successful accomplishment of ritual acts, one should worship Gaṇeśa. 39.
One who desires enjoyment should worship the Moon; one who desires strength, Vāyu;
and one who seeks liberation from the entire cycle of worldly existence should diligently worship Hari.
Likewise, one who seeks yoga, liberation, and divine knowledge [should worship Him]. 40–41.
Those who desire great enjoyments and also [desire] knowledge should worship Virūpākṣa, the Lord of the Gods, with diligence;
those who seek enjoyment likewise worship Bhūteśa and Keśava, the Great Lord. 42.
The giver of water obtains satisfaction; the gift of water is superior even to that. The giver of oil obtains desirable offspring, and the giver of a lamp obtains excellent vision.
The giver of land obtains everything, and the giver of gold obtains long life. (43–44)

The giver of a house attains an excellent residence; the giver of a beautiful woman attains the highest form; the giver of clothing attains the same world as Candra (the Moon); the giver of a horse attains an excellent vehicle; the giver of food attains his desired prosperity; and the giver of a cow attains the realm of Brahman.

The giver of vehicles and beds attains a wife; the giver of fearlessness attains sovereignty. The giver of grain attains eternal happiness; the giver of the Veda attains eternal Brahman. One should also bestow grains upon Brahmins according to one's ability. (46-47)
By bestowing [wealth] upon those distinguished by Vedic knowledge, one enjoys heaven after death;
and by the gift of food to cows, one is liberated from all sins.
By the gift of fuel, a man becomes possessed of a blazing fire.

One should always joyfully give fruits, roots, drinks, and various kinds of vegetables to the Brāhmaṇas; likewise, one should provide medicine, oil, and food for the sick in order to alleviate their illness. 49–50.

The man who gives an umbrella and shoes crosses the path of the Sword-Leaf Forest (Asipatravana), which is filled with razor-sharp edges, and passes through intense heat free from disease, happy, and long-lived.
Whatever is most beloved in the world and whatever is desired in one's home, that very thing should be given to a virtuous person by one who desires that [gift] to become inexhaustible;
especially during the solstices, the equinoxes, and during the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
What is given during times such as the solar transits (saṃkrānti) becomes inexhaustible; likewise,
by giving at sacred pilgrimage sites like Prayāga, in holy sanctuaries, and at rivers and springs, one attains inexhaustible merit.
There exists no dharma for living beings higher than the dharma of giving;
therefore, the twice-born should give to a Brahmin learned in the Vedas,
if they desire heaven, prosperity, and likewise the pacification of sin.
A seeker of liberation should give daily to the Brāhmaṇas; however,
that unrighteous soul who, out of delusion, prevents what is being given to cows, Brāhmaṇas, fire, or the gods, shall go to the womb of an animal.
But he who, having performed the rite of *dra-vyārjana*, does not honor the Brahmins and the gods—having confiscated all his property, the king shall banish him from the kingdom.
And he who does not provide food and provisions during a time of famine... (58-59)

When Brahmins are dying, a virtuous Brāhmaṇa should not accept gifts from them, nor should he even dwell with them; for by that [association], he too would be censured. Having identified such a person, the king should banish him from his own kingdom.
If a man here gives his own wealth, which is a means for practicing dharma, to the virtuous only after [giving it] to others, he is a sinner even greater than those before him and is cooked in hell.
Those Brahmins who possess Vedic study, who possess learning, and whose senses are conquered—[to them he should give]. 61–62.
O best of the twice-born, one should give to those who are endowed with truth and self-restraint;
even if he has not eaten for ten nights, one should feed a learned and righteous Brahmin, but not a fool who does not abide by proper conduct. 63.
He who, bypassing a nearby *śrotriya*, gives [a gift] to another,
becomes a sinner by that act and destroys his lineage down to the seventh generation— unless that other Brahmin himself should be superior in character, learning, and other such qualities.
One should give to him with effort, even bypassing what is at hand; one who receives a gift should do so with honor, and one should likewise give with honor.
Both of them go to heaven, but in the opposite case, they go to hell.
One should not give [these] to an atheist, nor to a rationalist, nor to any heretic, nor to one who does not know the Vedas, even if he claims to know the Dharma. [These are:
silver, gold, a cow, a horse, land, and sesame seeds. 67–68.
An ignorant man who accepts [a gift] is reduced to ashes like wood; therefore, O best of the twice-born, one should seek wealth from commendable members of the twice-born classes,
even from a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, but never from a Śūdra.
One should seek the contraction of one's livelihood and not strive for the expansion of wealth; for one who is addicted to the greed for wealth falls away from his very Brahminhood.
Even after studying all the Vedas and performing all sacrifices in their entirety, [one who acts thus is lost].

Through contentment, one attains the state of the bowed (the gods); that which one might obtain [through other means] should not be sought through a desire for receiving gifts. One should not accept food from a Śūdra. A Brāhmaṇa who accepts more than what is necessary for his subsistence goes to a low state.
He who does not attain contentment is not a fit vessel for heaven. He who causes distress to living beings is just like a thief.
One who desires to uplift his teacher and dependents, and who gratifies the gods and guests, [is a true seeker]. 73–74.
One should accept gifts from all quarters, yet one should not satisfy oneself with them;
thus, the householder who is disciplined in soul, a worshiper of deities and guests, and who lives with self-restraint, attains that supreme state. 75.

Having entrusted his wife to his sons and gone to the forest, the knower of reality should always wander alone, indifferent and composed. O best of the twice-born, this dharma of householders has thus been declared to you.
Having known [the Lord], one should remain steadfast and likewise cause the twice-born to perform the practice regularly.
(77) Thus, one should worship the beginningless, singular Lord with the dharma of the householder perpetually;
having transcended Prakṛti, the source of all beings, he goes to the Supreme and does not undergo birth again. (78)
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Determination of the Duties of a Householder," in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Fifty-Eight.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus remained in the stage of the householder for the second portion of his life,
he should proceed to the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) together with his wife and his sacred fires.
Having entrusted his wife to his sons, he may then go to the forest; or else,
having seen the offspring of his offspring and with his body worn out by old age,
he may depart during the forenoon of the bright fortnight and under the auspicious northern course of the sun.
Having gone to the forest, one who observes restraints should perform austerities with a concentrated mind.
He should always take pure fruits and roots as his food;
with whatever food he may have, he should worship the ancestors and the gods.
One should always honor the guest, and having bathed, one should worship the gods;
taking food from the house, one should eat eight mouthfuls with a concentrated mind. One should always wear matted hair and should not discard the nails or body hair.
One should perform the private recitation of the Vedas in every way and restrain one's speech from other matters.
One should offer the Agnihotra oblation and perform the five great sacrifices with various kinds of pure offerings, or with vegetables, roots, and fruits.
He should always wear garments of bark, bathe three times a day, remain pure,
have compassion for all living beings, and avoid accepting gifts.
The twice-born man should constantly perform the New Moon and Full Moon sacrifices.
One should perform the *ṛtviṣṭi*, the *āgrayaṇa*, and the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices; likewise, the *uttarāyaṇa* and the *dakṣiṇāyana* in their proper sequence,
using sacrificial materials grown during the spring and autumn, which are pure and gathered by oneself.

One should offer sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas) and cooked rice (carus) separately according to the rules to the deities and the ancestors, having presented the most pure oblation. Then one may partake of the remainder and salt prepared by oneself.
One should avoid liquor and meat, as well as mushrooms growing from the earth; likewise, bhūstṛṇa grass, śaṣpaka grass, and the fruits of the śleṣmātaka tree.
One should not eat food grown by the plow, nor even that which has been discarded by anyone.
One should always attend upon the sacred fire according to the very rite prescribed for Śrāvaṇa, using flowers and fruits that have grown in the village even if they are wild.
One should not bear malice toward any living beings; being free from the pairs of opposites, one should be fearless.
One should not eat anything at night; during the night, one should be devoted to meditation.
With senses conquered and anger subdued, contemplating the knowledge of reality, one should always remain a celibate student and should not even resort to a wife. 15–16.
If a twice-born man, having gone to his wife’s forest-dwelling, should engage in sexual intercourse out of lust, his vow would be violated and he must perform penance.
Any child conceived therein is not to be touched by members of the twice-born caste.
Indeed, he has no right to the Veda, and it is the same for his offspring as well.
He should always sleep on the ground, be intent upon the recitation of the Sāvitrī, be a refuge for all beings, and always devoted to the distribution of gifts to the virtuous. 18–19.
He should avoid slander, false speech, sleep, and idleness;
he should maintain a single fire, remain homeless, and take refuge on ground that has been sprinkled with water.
Self-controlled, he should wander with the deer and dwell together with them.
He should sleep on a stone slab or on gravel, remaining well-composed.
He may be one who washes away his impurities immediately, or one who stores for a month; or he may store for six months, or even for a year.

One should eat food brought according to one's ability at night and during the day; or one may observe the fourth meal-time, or even the eighth meal-time. Or, by means of the Cāndrāyaṇa rules, one should avoid [food] during both the bright and dark fortnights.
Day after day, he should eat boiled barley gruel only once;
or, remaining steadfast in the doctrine of the Vaikhānasas, he should always subsist solely on flowers, roots, and fruits that have fallen naturally of their own accord.
He should either roll about on the ground or stand on his tiptoes for a day; he should pass his time by alternating between standing and sitting, never relinquishing his fortitude.
In the summer he should practice the "five-fire" penance, and during the rains he should live under the open sky.
Wearing wet clothes during the winter, he should gradually increase his austerity.
He should perform ablutions three times a day, offer libations to the ancestors and the gods,
stand on one leg, and constantly drink the rays of the sun.
He may subsist on the smoke of five fires, on cow-urine, or on steam; he may drink Soma juice, or drink milk during the bright fortnight and cow-dung during the dark fortnight.
Alternatively, he may subsist on withered leaves or constantly pass his time through various *kṛcchra* penances.
One should be devoted to the practice of yoga and always remain absorbed in meditation on Rudra (30).
One should study the Atharvaśiras Upaniṣad, be intent upon the practice of Vedānta,
and constantly observe the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas) without weariness (31).
Alternatively, having consigned the sacred fires into his own self and being intent on meditation,
he may become a forest-dweller (muni) without fire or fixed abode, devoted to liberation;
he should obtain alms for his sustenance from brahmins who are ascetics.
While living in the forest, he should eat eight mouthfuls of food brought from a village from other householders or twice-born men who wander the woods;
he should receive it using only his cupped hands, his palms, or a fragment of a leaf.
For the sake of self-perfection, he should recite various Upaniṣads (35),
as well as specific Vidyās, the Sāvitrī, and likewise the Rudrādhyāya;
or he may undertake the Great Departure or fasting unto death.
"Or else, remaining steadfast in the rite of offering to Brahman, he may enter the fire.
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Duties and Conduct of the Vanaprastha Stage of Life," in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Fifty-nine. Vyāsa said:
Having thus remained in the forest hermitage for the third part of his life, he—
One should gradually spend the fourth part of one's life in renunciation (saṃnyāsa). Having established the sacred fires within himself, the twice-born becomes a wandering mendicant (pravrajita),
devoted to the practice of yoga, tranquil, and dedicated to the knowledge of Brahman.
When one has attained mental perfection and detachment toward all things, then one should desire renunciation;
otherwise, one would be fallen. Having performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice, or alternatively the Āgneyī sacrifice, [one may then renounce].
Self-controlled and wearing the white saffron robe, he should enter the stage of the Brahmacarya (the student).

4. Some are known as renunciants through knowledge (*jñāna-saṃnyāsins*), others as renunciants through the Vedas (*veda-saṃnyāsins*), and yet others as renunciants through action (*karma-saṃnyāsins*); thus they are proclaimed to be of three kinds. 5.
He who is liberated from everything, free from dualities, and fearless,
is called a renunciant of knowledge (jñāna-saṃnyāsī), established in the Self alone;
he should constantly study the Veda, being free from desire and without possessions.
One who has renounced the Vedas, who desires liberation, and whose senses are conquered, is called a renunciant of the Vedas (7).

But that twice-born man who, having internalized the sacrificial fire, is intent on offering everything to Brahman and is devoted to the great sacrifices— he should be known as a renunciant of action (8).
Among these three as well, the man of knowledge is considered superior;
for that wise one, there is no duty to be performed, nor any outward mark.
He is free from possessiveness, fearless, peaceful, beyond dualities, and subsists on leaves.
He should wear a worn-out loincloth or remain naked, intent upon meditation; observing celibacy and having conquered his appetite, he should collect food from a village;
he should delight in the supreme self, being indifferent and free from desires.
One should wander in this world for the sake of happiness with oneself alone as one's companion;
one should neither rejoice in death nor rejoice in life.
One should simply await the time, just as a servant awaits his dismissal.

One should never study, recite, or listen [to such things]. Thus, the yogi devoted to knowledge becomes fit for absorption into Brahman. Whether the wise man wears a single garment or even merely a loincloth for cover, he attains this state.
He may have a shaven head or a top-knot, or he may carry three staffs; he should be without possessions, always clad in saffron robes, and devoted to meditation and yoga.
He should dwell at the edge of a village, at the foot of a tree, or even in a temple.
He should be equal toward enemy and friend, as well as toward honor and dishonor.
He should always subsist on alms and never, under any circumstances, eat the food of a single person.
If an ascetic, out of delusion or for any other reason, should eat the food of a single person, [he incurs a fault].
No atonement whatsoever for such a person is seen in the treatises on Dharma;

rather, one whose self is free from passion and hatred, who regards a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal, who abstains from harming living beings, who observes silence, and who is devoid of all longing [should be the one]. 18.18–19a.
One should place one's foot down purified by sight; one should drink water purified by a cloth.
One should speak words purified by truth and act with a mind that is pure. A mendicant should not dwell in a single place for more than the rainy season.

Having bathed daily while observing the rules of impurity, pure and holding a water-pot in his hand, he should remain constantly devoted to celibacy and intent on dwelling in the forest. He should be dedicated to the scriptures of liberation, wear the sacred thread, and have his senses fully subdued.
Free from hypocrisy and egoism, and devoid of censure and backbiting,
if one endowed with the quality of self-knowledge should attain liberation,
one should constantly practice the eternal God known as the Praṇava. 22–23.
Having bathed and sipped water according to the prescribed rules, being pure in temples and other sacred places,
wearing the sacrificial thread (yajñopavīta), with a tranquil mind, holding kusha grass in his hand, and composed;
clad in washed saffron robes, his body hair covered [with ash].

One should constantly mutter the Brahman pertaining to sacrifice, that pertaining to the deities, and that pertaining to the self as declared in the Vedānta. Furthermore, whether living among his sons, as a celibate student, a forest-dweller, or a silent sage; 25–26.
One should constantly study the Veda alone; by that, one attains the supreme goal.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and supreme austerity—patience, compassion, and contentment—are his specific vows above all. 27.
Established in the knowledge of Vedānta and composed in mind, he should perform the five great sacrifices (pañcayajña) every day after bathing;
indeed, for the sake of alms alone, he should daily recite the sacrificial mantras at the proper times with a concentrated mind. 28–29.
One should perform one's daily recitation every day, chant the Sāvitrī at the two junctions of the day (sandhyā),
and constantly meditate upon the God, the Supreme Lord, in solitude. One should always avoid eating food from a single source, as well as desire, anger, and possessiveness.
Wearing one garment or two, with his hair unshorn and possessing the sacred thread, holding a water-pot in his hand, the wise man, carrying a triple staff, proceeds toward that supreme goal.
Thus ends the description of the duties of ascetics in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Fifty-nine.
Chapter Sixty. Vyāsa said:
Thus, for ascetics established in their hermitage who have restrained their selves, subsistence by means of alms or even by fruits and roots has been prescribed;
one should wander for alms at a single time of day and should not become attached to abundance.
For an ascetic who is overly attached to begging becomes attached even to sense-objects.
He should wander for alms at seven houses; if he receives nothing, he should wander again.
A mendicant should wait with his face cast downward for a period of time equal to the milking of a cow.
Having said "Bhikṣā" (alms) repeatedly, he should remain silent, restrained in speech, and pure; having washed his hands and feet and sipped water according to the rule,
he should show the food to the sun and eat facing the east.
Having offered the five *prāṇāhuti* oblations, being composed, he should eat eight mouthfuls.
Having sipped water (*ācamya*), he should meditate upon Brahmā, the Supreme Lord.
[He should use] a vessel made of gourd, wood, clay, or likewise of bamboo.
Prajāpati has prescribed four times for the recitation of the *Yatisūkta*:
at the first watch of the night, at midnight, at the last watch of the night, and likewise during the twilights; one should constantly meditate upon the Lord with this specific recitation.
Having placed within the abode of the heart-lotus the Self known as Viśva, the source of the universe,
which stands beyond the darkness of all beings,
the unmanifest support of all, blissful, and imperishable light; 8–9.
[He saw] the auspicious fire, the ether beyond both Pradhāna and Puruṣa;
the Lord who is the limit of all existents and whose form is Brahman.
Or else, having reached the Self within the Supreme Self at the end of the syllable Om.
One should meditate upon the Lord Īśāna as situated in the midst of space (ākāśa).
By meditating on Viṣṇu, the Ancient Puruṣa—the cause of all existents and the sole refuge of bliss—one shall be liberated from bondage. 11–12.

Or rather, having meditated upon the Supreme Ether— the sole cause of all beings, the life-force of all creatures, and that into which the world dissolves— within the Cave, the primordial Prakṛti, the abode of the world’s delusion. (13)

The bliss of Brahman, which is subtle and which those seeking liberation behold—within that [lotus] is established the absolute Brahman, characterized by pure knowledge, infinite, true, and sovereign; having meditated upon this, remain with speech restrained. 14–15.

This knowledge, the most secret of secrets, has been declared for ascetics; he who remains constantly established in it attains the sovereign yoga. Therefore, one should always be devoted to knowledge and intent upon the science of the Self.
One should practice that knowledge of Brahman by which one is released from bondage.
Having realized the Self as entirely distinct from everything else, solitary, blissful, and imperishable, one should meditate upon that knowledge which is even beyond that. 17–18.
Because all beings come into existence from Him, and knowing this one is not born again, therefore He is the Lord, the Divine One, who presides over that which is beyond.
That within which this movement occurs is eternal, auspicious, and imperishable.
He for whom this is directly perceived is indeed the true God, the Great Lord (Maheśvara).
Whatever vows belong to the mendicants, these same vows apply to him as well; for the transgression of each one, an expiation is prescribed. 20–21.
Having approached a woman out of lust, one who is composed and pure should perform the *sāṃtapana* penance accompanied by *prāṇāyāma*.
Then, with a restrained mind, he should perform the *kṛcchra* penance according to the prescribed rules.
Returning again to the hermitage, the mendicant should practice with unwearied diligence.
"Indeed, untruth joined with dharma does no harm," so say the wise;
nevertheless, one must not indulge in such a practice, for it is terrible.
Having spoken a falsehood, an ascetic seeking dharma must perform a fast for one night and likewise a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
Even when fallen into the greatest distress, he must not commit theft from another.
"There is no unrighteousness greater than theft," so says the Smṛti.
Furthermore, there is another form of violence: craving, which destroys self-knowledge.
That which is called "wealth" consists of these very vital breaths moving outside [the body]. (26-27)
"He who takes away the wealth of one whose life-breaths he has spared— having acted thus, that evil-souled man, fallen from his conduct and deviated from his vow,
shall again fall into despondency and wander as a mendicant without sloth. (28)
If a monk should commit violence even unintentionally,
he should perform the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penance or perhaps the Cāndrāyaṇa.
If a man, upon seeing a woman, should stumble due to the weakness of his senses, [he must likewise atone].
Therefore, sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) should be maintained;
however, O wise ones, if one commits an offense against the Skandas during the day, one must perform a hundred prāṇāyāmas for three nights.
Likewise, this applies to eating food from a single source, consuming honey or meat, and at a funeral rite (śrāddha).
Regarding the direct perception of salt, it is said that the *prājāpatya* penance is the means of purification (32).
For one who is constantly established in meditation, all sin is destroyed;
therefore, having meditated upon Nārāyaṇa, one should remain intent upon His meditation (33).
That supreme light of Brahman which has entered the imperishable and immutable,
that inner self which is the Supreme Brahman— he is to be known as Maheśvara.
This god is Mahādeva, the absolute, the supreme Śiva.
That very syllable is non-dual, that is the eternal, supreme state.
Therefore, because he is greater than the gods in his own abode known as knowledge, through the yoga of the Self and by virtue of being the Supreme Reality, he is remembered as Mahādeva. 35–36.

He perceives no other god as distinct from Mahādeva; he who follows that very Self attains the supreme state. Those who consider their own selves to be separate from the Supreme Lord [do not attain it].
Those who do not behold that God have their efforts in vain.
The one supreme Brahman alone is to be known as the imperishable reality;
he who knows that Great God, Mahādeva, is not bound. 38–39.
Therefore, a self-controlled ascetic should strive with constant discipline, having a restrained mind,
delighting in the yoga of knowledge, being peaceful, and devoted solely to Mahādeva.
O Brahmins, this auspicious stage of life for ascetics has thus been described to you.
This was previously proclaimed by the all-pervading Grandfather, the Sage:
"One should not impart this unsurpassed knowledge—spoken by the Self-born, auspicious, and based on the duties of ascetics—to anyone who is not a son, a disciple, or a yogi. (41-42)
Thus has been declared this ordinance for those various rules, which serves as the sole cause for the gratification of the best of gods;
yet there is neither arising nor destruction for these [rules], for those of steady mind practice them eternally.
43. Thus ends the sixtieth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. 60.
The sixty-first chapter.
Sūta said:
O Brahmins, having been addressed in this manner in the past by Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor, [the sages asked].
Having spoken thus and comforted all the sages, the Blessed Vyāsa, son of Satyavatī, departed as he had come. I have now related to you this exposition of the rules for the castes and stages of life.
By acting in this way, one indeed becomes dear to Viṣṇu and not otherwise.
O best of the twice-born, listen as I shall declare the secret therein;
these are the duties prescribed here, which are bound to the system of castes and stages of life.

O twice-born ones, devotion to Hari is equal to even a minute fraction of a fraction of a portion of [other] beneficial acts; indeed, O best of Brahmins, in the Kali age, devotion to Hari alone can be accomplished by men,
whereas in other ages, dharma must be practiced by a person with great effort.
He who worships the god Nārāyaṇa in the Kali age partakes in righteousness—
he who holds within his heart Dāmodara, Hṛṣīkeśa, the eternal Puruhūta, the supreme and most peaceful one; by him alone are the three worlds conquered.
Having drunk the nectar of devotion to Hari, a twice-born man transcends the poison of the serpent of the Kali age, the sin arising from the Kālakūṭa [poison].
If the name of Śrī Hari is grasped by men, what need is there for other recitations? 7–8.
What is the use of ritual baths for one who bears the water from Viṣṇu’s feet upon his head?
What is the use of sacrifice for one who holds the lotus-feet of Hari within his heart? And what is the use of charity for one who has manifested the deeds of Hari in the assembly?
He who, having heard the multitude of the qualities of Hari, rejoices again and again—
his goal is that state of one whose mind is fixed on Kṛṣṇa and who is delighted by meditative absorption (samādhi).
In that regard, those who are skilled in the talk of heretics are said to be creators of obstacles.
Women and those who associate with them are destroyers of devotion to Hari;
even for the gods, the command of women's eyes is difficult to overcome.
He by whom this has been conquered in the world is called a devotee of Hari.
Even the sages at the end of the age are here lusting after the conduct of women.
O twice-born ones, how can men possess devotion to Hari when they are devoted to women?
O twice-born ones, these are Rākṣasīs in the guise of amorous women who roam the world.
Those who are ever devoted to their own welfare constantly consume the intellect of men as if it were a morsel of food.
(14) Only so long does learning prevail, only so long does knowledge proceed, and only so long does the perfectly pure intelligence exist that upholds all the scriptures. (15)
So long is there chanting and austerity, so long is there resorting to sacred fords, so long is there service to the guru, and so long is there the mind intent on crossing over [saṃsāra].
So long indeed does awakening and discernment persist. 16.16

O Brahmins, as long as there is no swaying of the tremulous eyes of women with parted hair, so long will the virtuous have a taste for their vows and a longing for the ancient ways; [otherwise], O Brahmins, there would be a total destruction of all dharma among the people.
Among them, those who have been graced by even a drop of the nectar from the lotus feet of Hari—
indeed, for them, the casting of glances by the tremulous eyes of women would be a source of power.
O twice-born ones, this applies to those by whom the service of Hṛṣīkeśa has been performed birth after birth.

Offerings were made into the fire by the twice-born, yet there was a lack of interest here and there. Indeed, what is it that they call the beauty of women? It is merely the glitter of their ornaments and garments. 20-21.
How can the form of a woman, which is devoid of knowledge of its own nature as consisting of moisture, be remembered [as beautiful]?

For that body is composed of pus, urine, feces, blood, skin, fat, bone, and marrow; how then can there be any beauty in it? 22. Indeed, that is merely called a "corpse. 23. How indeed can there be beauty here?
Thus, having touched that very [water] which is distinct and inconceivable, and having bathed, one becomes pure.
O twice-born ones, the body joined with those [elements] is indeed seen as beautiful by people; alas, what a miserable state for men, fashioned by ill fortune! 23-24.
When a man perceives a woman’s body as covered by breasts, he acts [with desire]; yet when there is inquiry, what woman is there, or what man, or anything at all?
Therefore, a virtuous person should avoid association with women with his whole being. 25.
Having approached what kind of woman does one attain accomplishment on this earth?
One should abandon even the company of a passionate woman who is attached to passion; that from such association comes only distress is directly perceived. 26–27.
Out of ignorance, people there, greedy and deceived by fate, cook women and men directly in this hellish pit;
from whatever part of the earth they came, to that very place they shall return again.

Since urine, semen, and excrement constantly flow forth from it, people take delight in that very place; who, then, could be more impure than that? Alas! What a terrible thing in this world! Oh, what a mockery of fate! 29-30.
To indulge in it again and again—what shamelessness this is on the part of men!
Therefore, a wise man should reflect upon the many host of faults inherent in women.
From sexual union comes a loss of strength, and sleep acts like a youth.
A man whose knowledge is stolen by sleep becomes short-lived;
therefore, a wise and intelligent person should strive to look upon a woman as his own death, and fix his mind on the lotus feet of Govinda. 32–33.
Fie upon that service of Govinda’s feet which yields happiness in this world and the next!
What great fool, abandoning it, would serve the feet of a woman? For service at the feet of Janārdana indeed grants freedom from rebirth. 34.
Through the pursuit of women's wombs, one creates a constriction of the womb;
falling into the womb again and again like something pressed out by a machine, he would desire that very same thing once more—know this to be his mockery. (35–36)
With arms raised, I speak; listen to my supreme word:
place your heart in Govinda, and do not enter into a womb that is subject to rebirth. He who, having abandoned union with women, undergoes transformation [of the body], [attains liberation]. 37.
At every step, that man obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
(38) If a virtuous woman, having been married to men by the power of fate, should give birth to a son there, he who [the husband] should completely avoid association with her. (39)
The Lord of the World is indeed pleased with him; of this there is no doubt.
For those who know the Dharma, association with women is proclaimed to be association with the wicked.
When that [association] exists, devotion to Hara does not arise at all, even if it were very firm.
Having renounced all attachments, one should practice devotion to Hari.
(41) Devotion to Hari is indeed difficult to find in this world, even for the wise; in my opinion, he who possesses devotion to Hari has achieved his life's purpose—of this there is no doubt. (42)
One should perform whatever action by which Hari is indeed pleased; when He is satisfied, the world is satisfied, and when He is gratified, the world is gratified.
The birth of men without devotion to Hari is proclaimed to be in vain. 43.
Who would not worship that Nārāyaṇa, the unmanifest, whom Brahmā, Śiva, and the other gods worship for the sake of their own gratification?
Fortunate indeed is his mother, and great is his father. 44–45.
Those mortals who utter these words— "O Janārdana, you who are worshipped by the world and are compassionate toward those who seek refuge— may the pair of Janārdana’s feet be held within my heart"—
have no destination in hell. (46)
Brahmins especially should worship Hari in his manifest form according to the proper rites; thus Hari becomes pleased with them.
Viṣṇu wanders this earth in the form of a Brahmin. 47–48.
Indeed, without a Brāhmaṇa, one never attains the perfection of ritual action;
for by those who have drunk the water from a twice-born’s feet with devotion and applied it to their own heads, the ancestors are gratified and the self itself is truly liberated. 49.

That which is given sweetly and with honor into the mouths of Brahmins is indeed given directly into the mouth of Kṛṣṇa; Hari himself partakes of that. Oh, how difficult it is for people to find a Keśava in the form of a visible Brāhmaṇa! 50-51.
In the absence of such [qualified recipients], one should serve them through images and the like,
for it is said that the earth is blessed by the presence of Brāhmaṇas. Whatever is given into their hands is offered into the hand of Hari.

Indeed, for one who offers salutation to them, there is a rejection of sin; by greeting a Brahmin, one is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin. Therefore, a Brahmin should be propitiated by the virtuous with the realization that he is Viṣṇu himself.
If even a little is given to this hungry twice-born man,
he shall be sprinkled with streams of nectar for ten million kalpas even after death;
for the mouth of a twice-born man is a great field, free from salt and thorns.
If one performs even a small act of worship there, one shall obtain a fruit of millions upon millions; moreover, by giving him food with ghee, one rejoices for an entire kalpa.
He who gives various kinds of delicious food for the satisfaction of the twice-born [attains this]. 56–57.
His worlds shall be of great enjoyment, granting liberation until the end of ten million kalpas;
having placed a Brāhmaṇa at the forefront, one should daily listen to the Purāṇa as recited by that Brāhmaṇa—a fire for the great forest of sins. (58)
The Purāṇa is said to be the most excellent sacred site among all sacred sites (59).
By hearing even a single quarter-verse of it, Hari himself becomes pleased;
indeed, Hari moves about for the sake of illumination, having assumed a form like that of the sun (60).
For the sake of illumination for all the worlds,
and likewise for the sake of inner light, Hari, in the form of the Purāṇa, wanders here among all beings as the supreme purifier. 61.
Therefore, if the mind is set upon generating devotion to Hari, men should listen incessantly to the Purāṇa which is the very form of Kṛṣṇa;
it should be heard by one who is peaceful and devoted to Viṣṇu, for such an opportunity is indeed difficult to attain.
O Brahmin, that Purāṇa which is stainless, the supreme purifier,
and in which the meaning of the Vedas was extracted by Hari in the form of Vyāsa— therefore, one should be devoted to that Purāṇa above all else.

The Purāṇa is the determined Dharma; Keśava himself established that Dharma. Therefore, when the Purāṇa is heard in the Kṛta age, Viṣṇu himself becomes present; O Brahmin, Hari is manifest therein, and the Purāṇa is likewise of such a nature.
Having attained the union of these two, a man indeed becomes Hari himself;
likewise, by sprinkling the water of the Gaṅgā, he shall destroy his own sins.
Keśava, in the form of the ocean, delivers the earth from evil.
A Vaiṣṇava is one who desires the worship of Viṣṇu and conducts himself accordingly. He should perform the pure sprinkling of Gaṅgā water, which is a means of purification;
for the goddess Gaṅgā is celebrated on earth as the bestower of devotion to Viṣṇu.
Gangā is indeed the form of Viṣṇu, the one who causes the expansion of the worlds.
Therefore, men should practice causeless devotion toward Brāhmaṇas, the Purāṇas, Gaṅgā, cows, and the Pippala tree, regarding them with the thought that they are Nārāyaṇa himself. (70–71)
Since these have been ascertained by those who know the truth established by the direct manifestation of Viṣṇu's form,
they should therefore be constantly worshipped by one who desires devotion to Viṣṇu.
Without devotion to Viṣṇu, the birth of men is said to be fruitless.
The ocean of the Kali age is crowded with the crocodiles of sin; it has the whirlpools of immersion in sense-objects and is thick with the foam of ignorance;
it is terrifyingly formidable, filled with the great and wicked serpents of evil men. (73–74)
Those who are established upon the boat of devotion to Hari cross over even that which is difficult to cross;
therefore, let the world strive to accomplish devotion to Viṣṇu. What happiness does a living being obtain by attending to false news?
One becomes attached through the narration of the wonderful pastimes of Hari;
indeed, the minds of men, which are otherwise mixed with various sense-objects, must surely be made to listen to His diverse stories. (76–77)
O twice-born ones, even if the mind is directed toward Nirvana,
Hari becomes pleased by hearing [His names] even with indifference; for though Hṛṣīkeśa is beyond action, He performs various deeds.
He who is affectionate toward his devotees is found for the benefit of those who desire to hear him,
even more so through devotion than by means of a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices or ten thousand Rājasūya sacrifices. (79–80)

That state which is to be cultivated by the mind and repeatedly practiced by the virtuous—the essential means for crossing the ocean of worldly existence—take refuge in that foot of Hari. O you base and cruel men, greedy for sense-objects! 81.
In the Raurava hell, whom will you cause to fall upon yourselves by your own hands?
(82) If you desire to cross over sufferings without effort, there is no way other than serving the gentle feet of Govinda. (83)
Worship the feet of Kṛṣṇa, which are the cause of non-rebirth;
for from where has a mortal come, and to where would he go again? Having reflected thus, a wise person should take refuge in the collection of Dharma.
If a person, having risen from falling into various hells,
should obtain a body as an immobile being or the like, and then, by the power of fortune, should again attain human birth, therein the dwelling in the womb is exceedingly painful. 85–86.
Then, O twice-born ones, if a living being is born on earth by the power of karma, he becomes afflicted by many defects such as childhood and the like;
and even upon reaching youth, he is tormented by poverty.
Due to a severe illness, or likewise from drought and other such calamities,
or through old age, one may suffer indescribable affliction here and there;
then, from the agitation of the mind caused by disease, one shall meet with death.

No suffering greater than that is experienced even within saṃsāra; therefore, by the power of karma, a living being is tormented in the world of Yama. Having endured extreme agony there, one is born once again.
A living being is born and dies; it dies and is born again.
(91) Such is the condition for one who has not propitiated the feet of Govinda: death without effort and life with great effort. (92)
Wealth does not arise for one who has failed to propitiate the feet of Govinda;
even if wealth should exist in the home, what is the fruit of its preservation? When he is dragged away by the messengers of Yama, what wealth would follow him? (93)
Therefore, the honoring of the twice-born is a source of wealth that bestows all happiness;
charity is the staircase to heaven and the destroyer of sin;
and the practice of devotion to Govinda increases great merit.
If a mortal possesses strength, he should not spend it in vain;
rather, he should perform dance and song before Hari without indolence.
Whatever little belongs to men, that one should offer unto Kṛṣṇa.
That which is offered to Kṛṣṇa bestows auspiciousness, while that offered to others bestows unhappiness.
With one's eyes, one should behold the images and other representations of Śrī Hari alone; with one's ears, one should constantly, day and night, take in the qualities and names of Kṛṣṇa. 97–98.
The wise should taste with their tongue the water from the feet of Hari;
they should smell with their nose the tulasī leaf from the lotus-feet of Govinda; they should touch with their skin a devotee of Hari, and meditate upon His feet with their mind. 99.
A living being becomes one who has accomplished his purpose; there is no need for deliberation on this point.

(100) The wise man should have his mind fixed on That, and likewise his inner disposition should be directed toward That; at the end, the world departs toward That alone—there is no need for deliberation on this point. (101)

Who would not serve Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning or end, who grants his own abode even to one who has merely meditated upon him with the mind? One whose mind is constantly disciplined should, for the sake of devotion, perform service to him according to their capacity, directed toward the lotus feet of Viṣṇu.
One should bestow devotion and delight upon her two feet; for such a person shall indeed attain honor in the world of men. 103.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Sixty-two.
Sūta said:
Such is the greatness of that Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord who assumes various forms, which is the cause of the liberation of the worlds in this universe.
This single ancient form is indeed the supreme and great Padma Purāṇa;
the Brāhma Purāṇa is the head of Hari himself, while that named Padma is his heart.
The Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa is the right arm of the Great Lord, and the Śaiva Purāṇa is his left.
The *Ūrubhāgavata* is said to be the two thighs; the *Nāradīya* is the navel.
The *Mārkaṇḍeya* is the right foot, while the *Āgneya* is called the left. The *Bhaviṣya* is the right knee of the high-souled Viṣṇu. 4.
The one known as the Brahmavaivarta is said to be his left knee;
the Liṅga Purāṇa is his right ankle, and the Vārāha Purāṇa is his left ankle. The Skanda Purāṇa is his body hair, and the Vāmana is remembered as his skin.
The Kūrma Purāṇa is declared to be the back; the Mātsya is proclaimed to be the fat. The Garuḍa is said to be the marrow, and the Brahmāṇḍa is sung as the bone.
In this very manner, Viṣṇu, Hari, became the constituent parts of the Purāṇas in ancient times.
In that very heart is the lotus, by hearing which one partakes of the nectar;
this *Pādma Purāṇa* is indeed Lord Hari himself.
By teaching even a single chapter of it, one is liberated from all sins.

Therein, having heard this first section on heaven— the bestower of the fruit of all the *Padmas*— even those who are great sinners are liberated from their sins, just as snakes cast off their worn-out skins. 9-10.
Moreover, even one of very wicked conduct who has been excluded from all righteous duties shall obtain that fruit which one attains by hearing of the primordial heaven;
having heard this account of the primordial heaven, a person obtains its fruit.

By bathing daily at Prayāga during the month of Māgha, a person is liberated from sin; indeed, this occurs simply through hearing [of it]. By him, a balance of gold was given, and the entire earth was likewise given.
Generosity was practiced by him, and whatever debt was incurred toward the poor was repaid;
indeed, the thousand names of Hari were recited by him repeatedly, and likewise all the Vedas were studied and their respective rites performed. 14.
And many teachers were established by him through the granting of livelihoods (15).
O twice-born ones, he likewise granted fearlessness from all fears to the world; those who were virtuous, possessed of knowledge, and endowed with righteousness were honored by him (16).
Between the signs of Aries and Cancer, he gave very cool water for the sake of Brahmins and cows, and indeed, he sacrificed his own life for them. Furthermore,
many other virtuous deeds were performed by that wise man.

By whomsoever the Ādi-khaṇḍa has been heard, seen, or likewise recited; having thoroughly studied the Svarga-khaṇḍa, he enjoys manifold pleasures and awakens while sleeping happily amidst the women of the inner apartments. 18-19.
By the resonant tinkling of small bells and likewise by sweet speech,
one enjoys half of Indra’s throne and shall dwell for a long time in the world of Indra. From there, one shall go to the abode of the Sun, and from there to the world of the Moon.
Having enjoyed the pleasures in the abode of the Seven Sages, he then goes to the Pole Star (Dhruva). From there, having reached the world of Brahmā with a body composed of light,
he attains knowledge right there and reaches supreme liberation (nirvāṇa).
A wise man should dwell with the virtuous, perform his ablutions at sacred bathing places, always engage in conversation with the good, and listen to authentic scriptures.
Among these, the *Padma* is a great scripture that bestows the fruit of all the Vedic traditions (*āmnāyas*).
Within that, the Svargakhaṇḍa bestows the fruit of great merit. Worship Govinda; bow down to Hari, the one supreme among gods. You shall go to worlds of exceedingly pure enjoyments.
Listen, O people! Utter the incomparable name of Hari alone, if you desire the easy crossing of the waves of worldly desires and the attainment of cherished blessings. 25
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. This first section, also known as the Ādikhaṇḍa or the Svargakhaṇḍa, is complete.
May there be auspiciousness; may there be prosperity.
Thus ends the third section, the Svargakhaṇḍa, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. Now begins the fourth section, the Brahmakhaṇḍa, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Salutations to Śrī Vedavyāsa.
The First Chapter. Śaunaka said:
O Sūta, now that the Kali age has arrived, by what action do living beings [attain their goals]?
"Therefore, let there be an exposition; speak it before me.
Sūta said:
"Excellent, excellent, O best of sages! You are the foremost among those of meritorious soul."
And there is a constant desire for the welfare of all people.
O Vaiṣṇava, listen to that which the omniscient Vyāsa— the Brahmin honored by all— spoke when he was questioned by Jaimini in the past.
Having prostrated himself like a staff before his preceptor Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, who has reached the further shore of all knowledge, that bull among sages questioned him. Jaimini said:
"O Lord, tell me how liberation can indeed be attained by men in the Kali age,
since mortals therein possess short lifespans and achieve merit only in small measure.
Vyāsa said:
O Lord, from association with the virtuous comes the hearing of the scriptures;
from that arises devotion to Hari, from that comes knowledge, and from that, the ultimate goal. Indeed, the story [of the Lord] does not please the most sinful person on this earth.
A Vaiṣṇava should be known as the most excellent among the twice-born even if he is a sinner.
Having heard the stories of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, one indeed becomes a Vaiṣṇava;
however, he who speaks of them as untrue when they are true should be known as the greatest of sinners.
In whatever place the story of Kṛṣṇa is being told, Jagannātha never departs from that spot; yet that lowest of men who creates an obstacle at the commencement of the story of Kṛṣṇa [is lost].
There is no liberation from hell for those who, having heard portions of the Purāṇas, indeed revile and mock them, even for a period of a hundred Manvantaras; for them,
hells that cause manifold afflictions shall remain forever within the palm of their hand.

Even the sin accumulated over previous births perishes in that very instant for one who merely forms the desire to hear the life-story of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Likewise, the man who performs the narration of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s life with devotion [attains the same].
I do not know what destiny will await him upon hearing this.
The sin of killing a Brahmin and other such evils, as well as untimely death, the drinking of liquor, and theft—all these perish for the sinner. 13–14.

If a mortal, having committed a sin, should later turn away from that evil, his sin shall go to destruction like a heap of cotton in a fire. O Brahmin, let the book containing the life-story of Śrī Kṛṣṇa be established in one's home.
The servants of Yama approach the vicinity of his house.
Jaimini said:
"O Guru, tell me which Vaiṣṇavas they speak of; please satisfy my curiosity."
"Now, in order to understand their supreme majesty," Vyāsa said:
"O twice-born one, he who with devotion [applies] the water from the feet of a Vaiṣṇava to his head..."
What need has he for bathing at sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrtha) who performs the sprinkling of water (karotisecana)?
O twice-born one, if one should associate with the virtuous for even a moment or half a moment, his sins, including those such as the killing of a Brahmin, are destroyed. 18-19.
In whichever family there is even a single Vaiṣṇava, that family, though joined with sins, indeed attains liberation. So too those men who are free from violence, hypocrisy, lust, and anger.
O twice-born one, those who have completely abandoned greed and delusion should be known as Vaiṣṇavas.

Those who are devoted to their ancestors, endowed with compassion, intent on the welfare of all living beings, free from envy, and speakers of truth—these indeed should be recognized as Vaiṣṇavas. (21–22)
Those who are devoted to the worship of the Brahmins, who are like eunuchs toward the wives of others, and who are intent on the vow of Ekādaśī— they should be known as Vaiṣṇavas;
they sing the names of Hari while wearing garlands of Tulasī.
O Brahmin, those whose feet are sprinkled with the water from the feet of Hari, and who are difficult to recognize, are indeed to be known as Vaiṣṇavas.
(24) O Brahmin, those on whose ears or heads an excellent leaf of Tulasī is ever seen are to be known as Vaiṣṇavas. (25)
Those who water the Tulasī plant while remaining free from association with heretics and devoid of hatred toward Brahmins— those men should indeed be known as Vaiṣṇavas.
(26) Those who worship Hari and those who honor Him with Tulasī [are likewise so].
Those who delight in giving their daughters in marriage, those who truly honor guests,
those who listen to the deeds of Viṣṇu, and those in whose home a Śālagrāma stone is well-established— these men should be known as Vaiṣṇavas. (27–28)
Those who purify the abode of Hari, who initiate the ancestral sacrifices (pitṛyajña), and who are endowed with compassion for the distressed—these indeed should be known as Vaiṣṇavas.
(29) Those who view the property of others and the wealth of Brāhmaṇas as poison... [30]
Those who do not eat food offered as an oblation to Hari (harinaivedya) should be known as Vaiṣṇavas. Those who are devoted to the Vedas and Śāstras, those who protect Tulasī groves,
and those who are intent on the vow of Rādhāṣṭamī— they too should be known as Vaiṣṇavas.
Those who offer a lamp with faith at the waters of Śrīkṛṣṇapura and do not engage in censuring others should be known as Vaiṣṇavas.
Sūta said:
Thus questioned by Jaimini, Vyāsa spoke as follows in due order: "O Brahmin, this which was heard by me from my guru on that occasion is now being told by me.
Those best of men who listen to this chapter with faith—" (33)
For one who is completely liberated from all sins, there is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. 34.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Vyāsa and Jaimini," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Two.
Sūta said: Listen, O Śaunaka, I shall relate another ancient dharma—the dialogue between Vyāsa and Jaimini—which destroys the sins of those who hear it. 1.
Jaimini said:
"O Guru, tell me first how even a sinful man reaches the abode of the Lord of the World through ritual action; O Lord, please explain that to me. (2)
Vyāsa said:
That man who applies ointment in the temple of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is liberated from all sins and, being weary, goes to the abode of Hari. 3.
And he who should offer water and ointment— listen briefly to that, O Jaimini— I shall describe his merit in the temple of the Lord of the World (4).
As many particles of dust as are seen there, O best of the twice-born, [so many years shall he dwell in heaven].

He shall dwell in the abode of Viṣṇu for as many thousands of kalpas as [the syllables of the name]. Formerly, in the age known as Dvāpara, there was a thief named Daṇḍaka who struck fear into the world; he was a plunderer of the property of Brahmins and a slayer of his friends.
He was a speaker of untruth, cruel, and devoted to approaching the wives of others; he ate beef, drank liquor, and associated with heretics (pākhaṇḍas).
He was one who cut off the livelihood of the twice-born and likewise a stealer of deposits.
A slayer of those who have sought refuge, and one greedy for the amorous dalliances of prostitutes;
once, that man of deluded intellect went to the temple of Viṣṇu belonging to a certain eminent brāhmaṇa in order to steal the wealth of Viṣṇu.
Then, having entered the doorway with his feet covered in mud,
he smeared the entire floor of the temple with it;
by that very act, the ground became low-lying and hollowed out.
Quickly and joyfully opening it with two iron rods,
he entered the abode of Hara, which was adorned with excellent canopies,
enriched by lamps of gems and gold, and where all great darkness had been dispelled.
Abounding with the fragrance of various flowers, filled with various vessels,
and completely suffused with the scent of well-perfumed oil— then,
upon this beautiful couch provided with a canopy;
He saw Acyuta, clad in yellow garments, lying together with Rādhā.
Having prostrated before the Lord of Rādhikā, he then became free from sin, thinking:
"Shall I take him away? Or shall I not take him away? What would happen to me by this? (14-15)
"Unable to perform service and always a thief by nature, I set my mind on taking wealth because I have a need for it.
Having cast the silken garment of the Lord of Kamalā upon the ground, [he departed].
O Jaimini, having taken all those various objects belonging to his father into his hands, he trembled;
then, making a most terrible sound, they indeed fell down by the power of the illusion of Viṣṇu, the Lord of Māyā. 17-18.
Abandoning their deep sleep, they ran out crying, "Alas!

Alas! and many people arrived; the thief also fled with great speed, terrified, having abandoned both his wealth and himself. 19. Having left his riches behind, the thief, too, being afraid, went off somewhere.
Bitten by a black serpent, that sinner was dead;
at the command of Yama, his messengers—fanged, clad in skins, and bearing nooses and mallets in their hands—arrived to take him away. (20-21)
They bound him with a leather noose and led him along a difficult path;
seeing this, Śamana became enraged and questioned his minister.
(22) Yama said:
"O wise one, tell me in my presence what karma this man has performed— whether it be sinful or meritorious— I shall burn it away along with its very roots. Citragupta said:
"Whatever evils have been created upon the surface of the earth by the Creator, they have all been committed by this fool; this which I have spoken is the truth.
However, O Lord of the World, listen: he also possesses some merit."
"O brother, I believe this [river] has destroyed all my sins.
Dharmarāja said:
"O minister, what merit exists in me that you speak of it as being so substantial?"
"Having heard this, I shall act in such a way that he becomes fit for it.

O twice-born one, having heard these words of Yama, Citragupta, filled with fear, joined his palms in reverence and said to his master: 26-27. "I shall do so; wherever he may be fit, there I shall place him. Having heard Yama's speech, Citragupta, overcome with fear, joined his hands in *añjali* and spoke to his own master, O twice-born one.
Citragupta said: O King, this foremost of sinners went for the purpose of seizing Hari’s wealth; he was cast away from the very threshold of Hari’s feet like a heap of mud. 28.
By the power of that merit, the earth became free from stains and devoid of holes, pits, and cavities; his great sin was cast out, and he, now fit for Vaikuṇṭha, emerged from your punishment. 29.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard his words, Yama gave him a seat made of gold; having been honored there, he sat down upon it. 30.
Bowing his head to him with humility,
Yama said:
"Today my abode has been purified by the dust of your feet."
"I have achieved my purpose, I have achieved my purpose, I have achieved my purpose; of this there is no doubt.
Now go, O virtuous one, to the supreme abode of Hari, which is endowed with manifold enjoyments and wards off birth and death. (32)
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, that Dharmarāja placed him, whose sins were gone, upon a divine chariot made of gold and yoked with royal swans, and departed.
He sent [him] to that abode which bestows all happiness upon the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu).
Having thus entered Vaikuṇṭha, he remained there happily for a long time. Those who anoint the temple of Hari with devotion likewise attain this state.
O best of the twice-born, I do not know what will become of them;
yet whoever hears this with devotion or reads it with a concentrated mind, the sin accumulated over ten million births is surely destroyed—of this there is no doubt. (36-37)
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Greatness of Smearing the Temple of Hari," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Three.
Śaunaka said:
O Sūta, tell me in my presence the greatness of Kārttika;
what is the fruit of that vow, and what is the fault for one who does not perform it? 1.
Sūta said: O best of sages, once Jaimini asked this of Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī; it was then related by that sage. 2.
Vyāsa said:
He who abandons sesame oil and sexual intercourse during the auspicious month of Kārttika is liberated from the sins committed over many births and goes to the abode of Hari. 3.

He who abandons fish and sexual intercourse during the month of Kārttika will certainly become a deluded pig in every birth. One should indeed worship Janārdana with Tulasī leaves in the month of Kārttika.
In every leaf, that person obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
He who worships Madhusūdana with *muni* flowers during the month of Kārttika attains liberation, which is difficult even for the gods to achieve, through the grace of Hari.

O best of men, that man who eats *kārttika-śāka* (the potherb of the month of Kārttika) for a year destroys the sins committed throughout that year by means of that single vegetable dish. Furthermore, he who eats its fruit in the month of Kārttika, which is dear to Hari, [attains great merit].
O Brahmin, by giving this to Hari, one’s sins accumulated over ten million births are destroyed.
Furthermore, he who gives to Hari clarified butter mixed with ghee shall be liberated from all sins and go to the abode of Hari.
One who offers even a single lotus to Kārttikeya or to Hara shall go to the abode of Viṣṇu at the end, freed from all sins. Indeed,
that man who performs the morning bath during the month of Kārttika, which is dear to Śrī Hari—

Whatever fruit one might obtain by bathing in all the sacred fords (tīrthas), that same fruit he obtains [by this act]. O twice-born one, the man who offers a lamp in the sky to Kārttikeya shall be liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and go to the abode of Hari.

O best of Brahmins, Hari is always pleased with him who, for the sake of pleasing Hari, offers even for a single moment a lamp in the sky during the month of Kārttika. And that twice-born man who offers a lamp with ghee in the house of Kṛṣṇa—

In the month of Kārtika, there shall be the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice day after day. O best of the twice-born, listen with a concentrated mind as I describe the specific greatness of the lamp, along with its ancient history. 14–15.

Formerly, in the Tretā Yuga, there was a pure brahmin named Vaikuṇṭha, by the power of whose association even a sinner becomes liberated. Once, during the month of Kārttika, he also placed a lamp before Hari.

Having given it, the brahmin, that best of the twice-born, went home with the vessel full of ghee. O bull among the twice-born, while the mouse had come from the direction of the lamp and begun to eat that ghee, he was awakened by that very lamp. 17–18.
The mouse fled from that place with great speed out of fear of the fire;
by the grace of Hari, all the sins of the rat were destroyed. Bitten by the serpent, the rat gave up its life.
Then, by his command, messengers with nooses and mallets in their hands arrived to bring him; they bound him with leather thongs just as those who bear the conch,
discus, and mace intended to lead him away.
The four-armed messengers of Viṣṇu arrived, mounted upon Garuḍas;
and in the sky appeared a beautiful celestial chariot drawn by royal swans,
fashioned of pure gold and moving at will through the grace of Hari.
Then, having severed the noose, the messengers said to those servants of Yama:
"O fools, even though he is a devotee of Viṣṇu, you have bound him in vain.
Go, messengers of Śamana, if you have any desire for life! (23-24)
Hearing this, they remained as if unshaken; filled with humility, they asked: "By what power of merit are you being led to the city?
You are great sinners against Viṣṇu; you ought to explain that. (25)
The messengers of Viṣṇu said:
"A lamp was lit before Vāsudeva;
by that very deed, O messengers, we shall go to the abode of Viṣṇu."

Even if one performs the lighting of a lamp for Viṣṇu unintentionally, having abandoned the sins accumulated over ten million births, one goes to the abode of Hari. Whoever offers a lamp with devotion during the days of Hari in the month of Kārtika [attains the same].
No one, except for Hari, is capable of fully describing the merit of that person who, with devotion, offers a lamp filled with ghee in the temple of Hari;
what need has he for a thousand horse-sacrifices? (29)
He who performs the horse sacrifice goes to heaven on the day of Hari;
and he who offers a lamp in the month of Kārtika shall go to the abode of Hari.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard this, those messengers departed just as they had come;
but the messengers of Viṣṇu, having placed him in their chariot, went to that abode of Viṣṇu,
and in the very presence of Viṣṇu, a hundred manvantaras passed for him.
Then, by the grace of Hari, she became the daughter of a mortal king;
endowed with sons and grandsons, she enjoyed worldly pleasures for a long time. Thereafter, through her service to Hari, she departed once more for Goloka.
Sūta said:
That mortal who listens with devotion to this supreme majesty of Dvīpa,
being liberated from all sins, goes to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Gift of Lamps," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Four.
Śaunaka said: O Sūta, when is the greatness of Jayantī performed by people? Tell me, for you are indeed a boat in the ocean of worldly existence. 1.
Sūta said:
Listen, O best of Brahmins; since you have asked me, I shall explain that which was formerly asked by Nārada from Brahmā in the abode of the gods.
Nārada said: O Grandfather, tell me the greatness of Jayantī, hearing which I shall go to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. 3.
Brahmā said: Listen attentively, O Brahmin; I shall speak before you. By fasting on Jayantī, one goes to the world of Viṣṇu. 4.

O Sage, the sin accumulated over seven births is consumed by the mere remembrance and chanting of Jayantī; how much more so, then, for one who observes the fast! Furthermore, the auspicious Janmāṣṭamī and Navamī in the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra—

The fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Kṛṣṇa, the full moon of Kumbha, the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Meṣa, the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, and the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina conjoined with the Śravaṇā nakṣatra—
these six are proclaimed as the Jāyantīs, which are highly meritorious and bringers of auspicious victory.
This Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī, celebrated on the preceding day, is renowned as the destroyer of sins;
it is equal to ten million sacrifices and equal to tens of thousands of holy pilgrimage sites.
It is equal to one who gives a thousand cows every single day.
One obtains that same fruit by fasting on the Jayantī day;
one obtains that same fruit by fasting on the Jayantī day as one would by giving a thousand bhāras of gold at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse.
One obtains that same fruit by fasting on the Jayantī day as is obtained from giving thousands of black antelope skins and hundreds of sesame-cow gifts;
indeed, it is equal to the fruit of giving thousands of millions of maidens.
One obtains that same fruit by fasting on the Jayantī day;
(12) one obtains that same fruit by fasting on the Jayantī day which one obtains by giving away this entire earth together with its oceans. (13)
One who constructs ponds, wells, tanks, and the like, or builds a temple for a deity,
obtains that same fruit by fasting on the Jayantī day. Furthermore,
he who is endowed with devotion toward his mother, father, and teachers [attains the same].
One obtains that same fruit by fasting on the Jayantī day.

Whatever merit belongs to those of truthful vows who, for the sake of removing calamities, have devoted themselves to visiting sacred pilgrimage sites—that merit is obtained by fasting on the Jayantī day. (15–16)
Whatever merit is found in the Gaṅgā, the Narmadā, or the waters of the Sarasvatī,
one obtains that same merit by fasting on the Jayantī day;
and whatever merit belongs to those who perform śrāddha for their ancestors during the waning of the moon.
One obtains that same fruit by fasting on the Jayantī day.
Nārada said:
O Grandfather, tell me who performed this in the past, and by whom?
Brahmā said: In former times,
it was performed by Kārtavīrya, Karṇa, the wise Kumāra, Sagara, Dilīpa, and Rāma of the Kakutstha lineage.
Formerly practiced by Gautama, Gārgya, the wise Jāmadagnya, Vālmīki, and the virtuous Draupadeya, this eighth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada bestows all desired objects.
The eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) specifically conjoined with the Rohiṇī asterism (Prājāpatya-ṛkṣa) should be observed every year for the sake of pleasing the wielder of the discus (Cakrapāṇi).
In a mere moment, the sin accumulated over ten million lifetimes is dissolved.
Having kept a vigil at night and having first completed the concluding rites with his senses subdued,
he should worship [the deity] individually with perfumes, flowers, and food offerings.
O Brahmin, he who thus observes the Jayaṃtī fast— 23–24.
Sin accumulated over ten million births, whether committed knowingly or unknowingly,
dissolves in half a watch through the grace of the Son of Devakī— yet those lowest of men who eat when the Jayantī lunar day has arrived [are lost]. 25–26.
There is no doubt that he experiences the sins born of the three worlds; however,
for those who perform the Jayantī vow, all the sacred sites beginning with the oceans and all the places of liberation reside within every limb of their bodies.
All sacred fords (tīrthas) and deities reside within her.
O great sage, I have not seen in the Vedas, the Purāṇas, or anywhere else that a man who worships Jayantī, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, with devotion [obtains anything greater]. 28–29.
Any man who does not perform the Kṛṣṇa-Rādhā-aṣṭamī vow with devotion— whether it be equal to or even greater than that [other merit]— shall become a cruel Rākṣasa.
O twice-born one, that deluded soul who eats on the day of Jayantī...

Just as one consumes [the sins of] a great hell on the day of Hari, so indeed, by eating on the Jayantī day, one hundred and one generations of one's family— both past and future— shall surely fall into a terrible hell.
O tiger among sages, when Jayantī falls on a Wednesday in conjunction with the Rohiṇī asterism, what can be achieved by performing ten million other vows during the Kṛta,
Tretā, Dvāpara, or Kali ages?
The Jayantī, when observed according to the correct ritual procedure, is the destroyer of sins.
He who recites a Purāṇa during the vigil for Padmanābha burns away the sins accumulated since birth, like a heap of cotton.
O Sage, that man who listens with devotion to the Purāṇa on the day of Hari (Ekādaśī) has his sins accumulated over ten million births destroyed at that very moment.
On the day of Padmanābha, one should honor the reciter.
Having uplifted ten million members of his lineage, he is honored in the world of Viṣṇu (37). That man who,
being averse to this [observance], fasts on the Jayantī day,
is utterly devoid of all merit and certainly goes to hell (38).
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps filled with ghee,
and with feelings of devotion, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin. O Brahmin, whoever performs the Jayaṃtī festival according to this rite—

A man who, out of devotion, delivers twenty-one persons [to this state] shall experience neither misfortune nor widowhood; there shall be no strife in his home, nor shall he witness discord among his progeny or the depletion of his wealth. 40–41.
Whatever desires one who observes the Jayaṃtī fast may wish to accomplish,
he attains them all in their entirety and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Those whose minds are fixed on the Jayaṃtī vow are eternally devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu.
Blessed are they, noble are they, lords are they, and wise are they—those who observe the day of Jayantī.
Whatever holy fords, vows, and observances there may be, they do not equal even a sixteenth part of that very day. 43-44.
He who, together with his wife, observes the Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa-aṣṭamī on both fortnights of the month of Bhādrapada, O child, attains the presence of Hari;
and he who always performs this meritorious vow of Hari [attains the same].
One who fasts on the Jayantī day attains Vaikuṇṭha, the eternal abode of Viṣṇu.
Jayantī, the beloved of Hari, swiftly destroys the sin of one who is devoid of proper conduct, fallen from his lineage, lacking in fame, or born of a low womb.
One who fasts on the Jayantī day completely consumes all sins, even those equal to Mount Meru, such as the killing of a Brahmin;
one seeking a son obtains a son, and one seeking wealth obtains wealth.
One who seeks liberation attains liberation by fasting on the Jayantī day.
For those whose minds are supremely intent upon performing the Jayantī vow, even Yama constantly fears them; they go to the supreme goal. 49–50.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus to Nārada, he departed as he had come.
O Brahmin, O Muni, I have also related that which I was asked by you.

O Brahmin, those who listen with a spirit of devotion to the greatness of Jayantī, as well as to the reciter of the Purāṇa and the observer of the Jayantī vow, they too go to the supreme abode, liberated from all sins.
52. O Brahmin, [one should honor] the reciter of the Purāṇa and likewise the one who observes the Jayantī vow.
Those sinful men who behold [this] go to the supreme state. 53.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Jayantī Vow," in the Brahmakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada. 4.
The Fifth Chapter. Śaunaka said:
O one of great wisdom, please tell me how a person may become deprived of sons.
"By what action did he become the son of a charioteer, and by what [action]?
Sūta said:
"In the past, this was asked of Brahmā by the high-souled Nārada."
"O bull among sages, listen now to that which was said by him at that time.
Nārada said:
"O Grandfather of great wisdom, you who have reached the further shore of the meaning of all principles!"
O Lotus-born One, by what karma does a mortal become childless?
Or by what sin does a woman become barren? Tell me this before my very eyes, O You who are devoted to the welfare of all living beings, as I listen. (3-4)

By what karma is a daughter born, or how does one become a eunuch? By what cause does one have stillborn children, or become a woman who has lost her children and is deeply afflicted by grief? O Brahmin, tell me: by what merit can a son be born again? (5)
Brahmā said: I shall tell it to you in brief; listen attentively to that account which you ask about, for it will surely produce wonder in those who hear it. 6.

That mortal who, in a previous birth, would obstruct a Brāhmaṇa’s livelihood or seize his property, shall indeed become childless in this life. Furthermore, that mortal who, in this birth, listens to the Purāṇas...
One endowed with faith should indeed make a gift of land for cultivation;
by giving a golden cow of many virtues that yields much milk, along with a priestly fee (dakṣiṇā) and a golden image, his son will certainly be born. 8–9.

A woman who, through deceit, causes the killing of another's child in a previous birth will certainly be deprived of her children. A woman endowed with faith who makes a gift of a golden image [attains a different fate].
One should respectfully offer a drink and water for washing the feet to a Brāhmaṇa;
one should listen to the Purāṇas and indeed give abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). She shall have many children and her living children shall survive; of this there is no doubt. 11-12.
He who, seeing a child submerged in water, does not rescue him,
will certainly remain sonless in this life, whether he be a man or a woman. [Likewise, one who fails to give] a bull, a pumpkin, gold, and clothing [as a gift].
One should give gifts to a Brāhmaṇa and perform the auspicious *bāla-vrata*;
likewise, for one who listens to the Purāṇas, a son is born who destroys all sins. 14–15.

O twice-born one, a mortal who, being devoid of hope, should treat a guest with anger and inflict punishment upon him, will certainly be childless. One should perform the worship of a Brāhmaṇa guest with devotion.
The gift of food, the gift of water, and likewise the construction of a beautiful temple for the gods—(these are meritorious). 17.
That woman who in a previous birth committed the murder of an embryo, or that man who did so, shall certainly become one whose children die at birth, or one whose children are born dead. 18.
That woman who observes the day of Hari (Ekādaśī) together with her husband shall possess good sons and be fortunate with her husband in every birth.
That Śūdra who, being deluded, would cause illness or loss of wealth [to others]... [19]

Or, by the act of abducting a Brahmin woman, one becomes a eunuch. However, O twice-born one, he who commits such a sin but subsequently performs meritorious deeds shall, through the power of that merit, have a daughter born to him in this world.
In the Tretā Yuga, O twice-born one, there was a king named Śrīdhara who possessed great wealth;
he was childless, and his wife was Hemaprabhāvatī.
[He approached] Vyāsa, the knower of all scriptures and the seeker of the welfare of all the world.
Having arrived, he asked, "O twice-born one, why have I come?
Having heard the king's humble words, he spoke;
and a seat fashioned from gold and other precious materials was offered by the king.
Having washed the feet of that king and queen, the two were filled with joy; having drunk the water from those feet, which destroys all sins, both of them [were purified]. Vyāsa said:

"O King, listen to that which you have asked: by what karma did this queen of yours become childless, as did you yourself, even though she was devoted to the vow of a single husband? In a previous birth, you were known by the name Varatanu, O Moon."
His wife was named Śubhrāṅgī, who was known as Vaiśaṅkarī. Once, while traveling on the road, they saw their low-born son submerged in water; having passed him by with indifference, he met his death.
"By the power of much merit, you two—queen and king—have come together;
yet by the ripening of that karma, no son shall be born to you both.
The king said:
"O Lord, by what merit is a son born?
For the life of men who are childless is indeed meaningless.
Vyāsa said:
Give a pumpkin with its skin intact and a bull adorned with gold as a gift to a Brāhmaṇa; likewise, perform the Bālavrata. Give away a daughter as Gaurī, and listen to the Purāṇas.
"Indeed, a son shall be born there, which destroys all sins. 32.
Brahmā said:
Having heard this supreme gift described by Vyāsa, the king then [acted].
Having thus cleansed his sins, he listened to the Purāṇas. Then, in the middle of the year, a son was born who was honored by all;
he became a universal monarch, handsome, and the leader of his lineage.
Sūta said:
