He who hears this with devotion performs a supreme gift;
even one without a son obtains a son. This has been told by me in brief. 35.
O twice-born one, that woman who, having heard this with devotion, performs the worship of a Brāhmaṇa according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, shall always possess excellent sons.
[She should offer] gold, silver, clothing, flowers, garlands, and sandalwood.
Whoever would devoutly give this book, which destroys all sins,
[attains merit]. O twice-born one, he who was a fool in a previous birth and a killer of Brahmins or children will have a cruel son for seven subsequent lifetimes.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Ripening of Karma," in the Dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada within the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Six.
Śaunaka said: O Sūta, by what merit is Vaikuṇṭha attained? Tell me that, for you are a boat to me as I listen, in this ocean of worldly existence. 1.
Sūta said:
"Excellent, excellent, O best of sages, you who bring about all auspiciousness!
I shall relate in brief that which destroys the sins of those who listen."
O best of the twice-born, listen to the merit of that man who constructs a house out of clay and gives it to a Brahmin devoted to Viṣṇu;
that Brahmin, freed from all sins, shall dwell in the world of Viṣṇu.

He shall dwell eternally in a celestial mansion and be honored in the world of Viṣṇu. He who gives a house with a mansion to a Brāhmaṇa for the sake of Viṣṇu will certainly become a resident of heaven after reaching the abode of Hari.
O twice-born sage, having gone at last to the city of Viṣṇu accompanied by ten million kinsmen,
and dwelling in a golden palace, one may enjoy pleasures as one pleases. O Bhīma, such is the merit that arises from the installation of a Brāhmaṇa.
But even he who is capable of creating all things is unable to count it;
for while the drops of rain can be counted by others,
the fruit of establishing [others] in Brahman cannot be counted even by the Creator.
In ancient times, Brahmā was questioned by Nārada regarding the origin of worldly existence;
the Creator explained it to him—listen to that, O great sage.
Long ago, O Brāhmaṇa, in the Dvāpara age, there was a very beautiful woman named Vāranārī.

She who has beautiful hair, eyes like a doe, a slender waist, and a lovely smile— she whose sidelong glances are restless was once known by the name Cañcalā; she departed for another land at some time, and those joined with all manner of sins cause her to fall into hell.
Desiring to go to the temple with her companions, she went there;
having sat down for a moment, she consumed betel leaf.
Out of curiosity, she placed the remaining lime-powder on the wall of the palace and then departed.

Then, desiring a paramour for the sake of wealth, she suddenly made an appointment with a certain lover. Having gone to that rendezvous at night, the prostitute became utterly infatuated in the forest.
The Vaiśya woman, having arrived at the trysting place and looking about, became suspicious: "How is it that my beloved has not come? Has he been devoured by snakes or tigers?
Or why has he abandoned the trysting place and gone away, perhaps overwhelmed by passion? (15)

O twice-born one, having reflected thus within her heart, she did not enter the city out of fear of the Koṭapāla, as the public roads were blocked by those [guards]. Would she ever have felt desire for another man’s wife? (16–17)
In the meantime, O twice-born one, a tiger capable of assuming any form at will, sent by the God of Death (Kāladeva), arrived and forcibly devoured him.
Then, the messengers of Yama’s brother, who rain down terrors, [arrived].
O twice-born one, those of evil deeds arrived to seize her— beings with mountain-peak-like bodies,
crooked feet, distorted faces, high noses, and many fangs,
carrying leather thongs and mallets, and covered in dust. (19–20)

Those who bear the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and wear forest garlands, being sent by the God of gods who is affectionate toward his devotees, bound the intoxicated courtesan with leather ropes. 21.
Resembling dark clouds, with shimmering lotus-like faces,
wearing rows of ornaments and beautiful noses, and adorned with divine earrings, they saw the messengers of the high-souled Viṣṇu traveling along the path.
The messengers of Viṣṇu said:
"Who are you, appearing with such deformed and variegated forms?
Having seized this most excellent woman, the beloved of Viṣṇu, where are you going?"
Having heard these words, they departed quickly from their presence.
Then those mighty messengers of Viṣṇu, filled with wrath,
struck the messengers of Yama, the lord of the world.
O twice-born one, all the soldiers of Kṛtānta, who possessed the splendor of ten million suns and were equipped with multitudes of weapons such as discuses, fled while crying out;
terrified, they reported the entire incident to Yama.
Having heard that account, Yama spoke to Citragupta: Yama said: "O minister, by what merit has this woman attained liberation?"
"Tell me all this as you deem appropriate, for I ask you.
Citragupta said:
"By her, very many sins were accumulated from birth."
But listen, O Lord of the World: if there be any merit in this, [hear it].
Once, a courtesan adorned with all the ornaments of Dharmarāja went swiftly to a certain city, desiring a lover and seeking wealth. (29–30)
Remaining there in that temple and having consumed some betel,
she out of curiosity applied the remaining powder upon the wall.
By the power of that merit, the courtesan was freed from her sin.
"Having emerged from your staff, she has gone toward Vaikuṇṭha.
Sūta said:
O twice-born one, having heard these words, Yama then [spoke] to the messengers.
Meanwhile, that courtesan directed her mind elsewhere;
yet she too, having ascended a divine chariot yoked with royal swans,
went to the world of Viṣṇu, surrounded by the servants of Viṣṇu.
By the command of Śrī Viṣṇu, she remained in a palatial mansion accompanied by ten million members of her family, and she enjoyed various pleasures, O Brahmin.
Indeed, whoever with devotion diligently offers powdered incense in the temple of Hari, [attains such rewards]. 35.
O bull among the twice-born, I do not know what merit might accrue to him;
however, he who recites this chapter with devotion or listens to it with respect, being liberated from all sins, goes to the abode of Hari. (36-37)
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada.
Chapter Seven. Śaunaka said:
O one of great wisdom, tell me by what action a person goes to Goloka; O intelligent one, how does one cross over the difficult-to-traverse ocean of saṃsāra?
And [tell me] the supreme majesty of Rādhā’s Aṣṭamī festival. 1.
Sūta said:
O great sage, in former times Nārada questioned Brahmā regarding this;
listen to that in brief, O twice-born one, as he asked it.
Nārada said: O Grandfather, O one of great wisdom, O best among those who know all the scriptures, please describe to me the ritual of Rādhā-janmāṣṭamī. 3.
O Lord, what is the fruit of its merit, and by whom was it performed in the past?
O twice-born one, what sin would accrue to those people who do not perform it?
By what specific procedure should that vow be observed, and when?
"Tell me from the very beginning why Rādhā was born so devoid of essence.
Brahmā said:
"O child, listen with a well-composed mind to the account of Rādhā’s Janmāṣṭamī."
I shall relate it in brief, for without Hari it cannot be told in its entirety;
even Nārada is unable to describe that meritorious fruit.
Great sins accumulated over ten million births, such as the killing of a Brahmin and the like, [are destroyed].
For those who perform this even once with devotion, that merit perishes in an instant;
yet the merit of the Rādhā-Janmāṣṭamī is a hundred times greater than the fruit that a man obtains from a thousand Ekādaśīs. 8.
Whatever fruit is obtained by giving gold equal in weight to Mount Meru,
a hundred times more than that is gained by observing the Rādha-aṣṭamī even once;
and whatever merit is attained by people through the gift of a thousand maidens— [that is surpassed by this].
On the eighth day [dedicated] to the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu,
people obtain that same fruit which one would receive by bathing in sacred fords such as the Gaṅgā;
on this eighth day, so dear to the life of Kṛṣṇa, a human being attains that fruit.
O child, even a sinner who performs this vow, whether with negligence or even without faith, shall go to the abode of Viṣṇu accompanied by ten million members of his lineage.
Long ago, in the Kṛta Yuga, there was a most beautiful woman.
She had a slender waist, eyes like those of a doe, beautiful limbs, and a lovely smile;
with beautiful hair and charming ears, she was known by the name Līlāvatī. By her, many very grave sins were committed.
Once, desiring to perform a spiritual practice,
he departed from his own presence and went to another city; there, in a beautiful temple, he saw many wise people devoted to the Rādhā-aṣṭamī vow.
Worshipping the supreme form of Rādhā with devotion through perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, various garments, and diverse fruits,
some sang, some danced, and some recited the excellent hymn of praise. 17.
Some joyfully played upon cymbals, flutes, and drums.
Seeing them in such various states, she was filled with curiosity; she approached them and, full of humility, questioned them.
"O virtuous souls, what are you doing so full of joy? O meritorious ones, tell me, for I am filled with humility.
Having heard her words, those who were devoted to the welfare of others [replied].
Those devoted to the Vaiṣṇava vow began to speak as follows. The observers of the Rādhā-vow said:
"Since Śrī Rādhikā was born on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada..."
Even for one who, through lack of effort, fails to perform the rites on the eighth lunar day and other such occasions,
[the sins of] killing a cow, theft, killing a Brahmin, abducting another's wife, and violating the Guru’s bed are destroyed. 22–23.
The eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī), when duly observed, quickly destroys for men these [sins]: that born of treachery against trust and likewise that produced by the killing of a woman.
Having heard their words, which destroy all sins...
Reflecting again and again, "I shall do it," she performed that supreme vow together with other practitioners of vows; then,
by fate, she met her death through the bite of a serpent, purified.

Then, by that command, messengers with nooses and mallets in their hands arrived to bring her; they bound her with great difficulty. (27) When they set their minds on taking her toward the abode of Yama, [the messengers acted].
Then the messengers of Viṣṇu arrived, bearing conchs, discs, and maces;
they fashioned a noose from the edges of their discs and, filled with haste, [prepared] a beautiful golden celestial chariot yoked with royal swans. 28–29.
They placed that woman, whose sins had been removed, upon a chariot and led her to the beautiful city of Viṣṇu known as Goloka;
there she remained with Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā by virtue of the grace of her vow.
O father, a person of deluded intellect should not fail to observe the Rādhāṣṭamī vow;
for there is no liberation from hell even after hundreds of millions of kalpas for those who do not perform this auspicious vow, nor for women who do not observe it. 31–32.
It brings delight to Rādhā and Viṣṇu and destroys all sins;
yet at the end, having gone to this city, men fall into hell for a long time. Having obtained birth on earth once again, they certainly become widows.
Once, having been struck by wicked herds of cattle as if they were calves,
she became a cow and, being extremely distressed,
approached me; weeping again and again, she reported her suffering.
Having heard those words, I went into the presence of Viṣṇu; and Kṛṣṇa was quickly informed of the entire mass of suffering upon the earth.
He said, "Go, O Brahmin, to the surface of the earth along with the gods."
"I shall go there as well, followed by my hosts.
Having heard that, he arrived upon the surface of the earth together with the gods;
then Kṛṣṇa summoned Rādhā, who was dearer to him than life itself.

"O Goddess, I shall go to the surface of the earth for the destruction of the world's burden; you, however, go from here to the solar orb. (39) Having heard this, Ārādha also then returned to the earth.

In the month of Bhādrapada, during the bright fortnight, on the lunar day known as the eighth (Aṣṭamī), she was born from the sacrificial ground of Vṛṣabhānu; and when that ground had been purified for the sake of sacrifice, she was seen possessing a divine form. 40–41.
Having become one who subdues the king and having reached her own home, she took that queen and gave her [to him]; and she protected her. 42.
Thus, O child, that which was asked by you has been told to you.
"It must be guarded, guarded, guarded with great effort.
Sūta said: "Whoever should hear this with devotion, which bestows the fruits of the four aims of life,"
And being completely liberated from all sins, he goes at the end to the abode of Hari. 44.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Śrī Rādhāṣṭamī," in the Brahmakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada. 7.
The Eighth Chapter. Śaunaka said:
O Sūta, why was the churning of the ocean performed in the past, O Teacher?
"A curiosity has arisen in my heart; tell me, O Cāmaras, so that I may hear it. Sūta said: "O Brahmin, I shall tell you in brief the cause of the churning of the ocean."
Listen to this historical narrative of the conversation between Durvāsas and Indra.
Once, the great ascetic Durvāsas, possessed of great luster and born from a portion of the Lord,
that Brahman-sage departed for heaven to see Indra.
At that time, he saw the Lord of Śacī mounted upon an elephant;
having seen him, the great sage gave him the Pārijāta garland. Having taken that garland, Indra placed it upon the head of the elephant.
The king of the gods, Brahmā, set out toward the Nandana grove with his army.
And the elephant, having seized that garland and cut it, cast it upon the surface of the earth; then, being greatly enraged, the great sage spoke to him thus.
"Since you, who are endowed with the sole glory of the three worlds, treat me with contempt, that glory of the three worlds shall surely perish for you; of this there is no doubt.
Then Śakra departed quickly and returned once more to his own city while [the other] was still asleep.
The Mother of the worlds herself vanished;
when she had disappeared, the three worlds were lost to her sight,
and everyone, afflicted by hunger and thirst, cried out incessantly.
The clouds ceased raining, the reservoirs became dry,
and all those trees withered, stripped of both fruit and flowers.
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, they all went into the presence of Brahmā.
They all related that suffering and grief to their grandfather.
(11) Having heard the words of the gods, the Creator, together with the hosts of deities and the sages headed by Bhṛgu, went to the Ocean of Milk. (12)
On the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk, he worshipped Viṣṇu,
chanting the eight-syllabled mantra while meditating upon the Lord of the Universe.
Then the Blessed One became pleased with all the inhabitants of heaven.
Having mounted Vainateya, the compassionate Lord arrived.
Seeing him—the Lord of the worlds, with eyes like lotuses, wearing yellow garments, four-armed, and bearing the conch, discus, and mace—[he was filled with joy]. 14–15.

With eyes overflowing with tears of bliss, they praised Viṣṇu—the boat for crossing the ocean of worldly existence, adorned with a forest garland, his chest marked by the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha gem—and they bowed down incessantly with shouts of "Victory! (Jaya). 16.
The Blessed Lord said: "O gods, choose a boon! For what reason have you come here? I am the giver of boons; speak that, and I shall grant it to you, for it shall not be otherwise."
The gods said: "O Lord, by the curse of Brahmā, the three worlds—along with their gods, asuras, and humans—are bereft of prosperity and afflicted by hunger and thirst. (18)
"Protect all these worlds; we have come to you for refuge.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O gods, Indirā has vanished due to the curse of Brahmā."
By whose mere sidelong glance the world is endowed with sovereign power—
then all you gods, having uprooted Mount Mandara, the golden mountain,
making it resound and encircling it with the king of serpents; 20.
"O gods, together with the Daityas, churn the Ocean of Milk!
From it, O deities, Lakṣmī, the mother of the world, will arise;
delighted by her, you shall become highly fortunate—of this there is no doubt. (21-22)
"I myself shall support the mountain on all sides in the form of a tortoise," having said this, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu vanished;
O twice-born one, all the gods and asuras then proceeded with the churning of the ocean. 23.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Effort for the Churning of the Ocean," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Nine.
Sūta said:
Then those hosts of immortals, along with the Gandharvas and the Dānavas,
having uprooted Mount Mandara, cast it into the ocean.
Thereupon, the eternal, glorious, and compassionate Lord of the World—
O twice-born one, they supported the base of the mountain from behind with their backs in the form of a tortoise;
having encircled Ananta there, they churned the ocean of milk.
As it was being churned on the eleventh day, the first thing to emerge appeared.
Upon seeing the Kālakūṭa poison, they all fled;
then, seeing them fleeing, Śaṅkara spoke this: "O hosts of immortals, you must take the poison with respect!"
"I shall quickly ward off the great poison Kālakūṭa.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Pārvatī meditated upon Nārāyaṇa within his heart,
and having recited the great mantra, he took up the terrifying poison.
By the power of this great mantra, even the most potent poison is digested and neutralized.
One who is disciplined and devoted should recite these three names of Hari—Acyuta, Ananta, and Govinda—preceded by the syllable Om and ending with "Namaḥ. (7)
Likewise, for that creature born from the fire of the enjoyment of poison, there was no fear of death. Then, with joyful minds, the gods churned the Ocean of Milk;
from it arose Alakṣmī, dark-faced and red-eyed.
Bearing a body with coarse, tawny hair,
that eldest woman spoke to the gods, "What must be done by me? The gods then spoke thus to that goddess, who was a vessel of sorrow.
To those men in whose house quarreling breaks out,
we grant a place there, O eldest sister, provided they are endowed with auspiciousness;
as well as to those men who speak harsh words and those who speak untruths.
Those who eat here during the twilight hours shall dwell in misery in that house where skulls,
hair, ashes, bones, chaff, and charcoal are found;
there, O Jyeṣṭha, shall be your place— of this there is no doubt.

Those lowest of men who eat without having washed their feet—[in] their house, [the goddess] who bestows misery and poverty shall always remain, [as if made] of sand, salt, and charcoal; they perform the cleaning of their teeth with these. 14–15.

In their houses, Kālī, the giver of misery, always dwells together with them— those lowest of men who eat mushrooms and leftover jackfruit. Their abode is in the house of that eldest [wife] who bestows impurity.
Those of sinful intellect who eat sesame paste, bottle-gourd, garlic, *gṛñjana*, the leaf of *potikā*, *kalaṃbuka*,
or onion— there shall be no doubt that your residence will be in their house. 17–18.
O inauspicious one, you always dwell where there is no honor for gurus, gods, or guests, where there is no sacrifice or charity, and where the sound of the Vedas is absent;
where there is constant quarreling between husband and wife, and where there is no worship of the ancestors or the gods.
Where those devoted to gambling always remain engaged in various [vices], O auspicious one;
where there are those devoted to the wives of others and those who steal the property of others;
and where no worship exists for Brahmins, virtuous people, or elders.
"Remaining there, she shall dwell as one who bestows sin and poverty.
Having thus addressed the eldest of the Asuras, the beloved of the Kali age,
they all, being well-composed, once again performed the churning of the Ocean of Milk.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Churning of the Ocean," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka.
Chapter Ten.
Sūta said:
From him were born Airāvata, as well as the horse Uccaiḥśravas, Dhanvantari, the Pārijāta tree, Surabhi, and the origin of the Apsarases.
Then, at the time of dawn on the twelfth day, when the sun had risen,
the goddesses of Dharma beheld that great goddess, their mother Mahālakṣmī, who was endowed with all auspicious marks and possessed of splendor.
The cool-rayed moon, the brother of Lakṣmī, was born from the nectar of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who dwells in the hearts of all living beings;
and then Tulasī, the wife of Hari and the purifier of the world, arose. 3–4.
Having restored that mountain as it was before, their desires fulfilled,
they gathered together, praised their Mother, and recited the supreme Śrīsūkta.
Then, the Goddess, being pleased, spoke to all the gods.
"Choose a boon, may there be prosperity; I am the giver of boons, O best of gods.
The gods said:
"Be gracious, O Goddess Kamalā, Mother of All, beloved of Hari!"
"Without you, the world is empty; protect the lives of all beings.
Thus addressed, Mahālakṣmī, the beloved of Nārāyaṇa, replied:
"Now I shall effect the protection of the lives of all creatures."
Then the glorious Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Universe, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace,
appeared suddenly out of compassion.
Thereupon, the gods, having prostrated before the Lord of the Worlds, offered him praise.
With palms joined in reverence and voices faltering with joy, they said:
"O Viṣṇu, accept your mother, your beloved queen Lakṣmī, who shall never depart from you for the sake of protecting the world."
As long as she did not withdraw her vow,
Lakṣmī spoke to Hari: "O Madhusūdana, why do you refuse to marry the elder sister, Alakṣmī?"
Having heard this, Viṣṇu then granted Lakṣmī to Uddālaka along with the gods, in accordance with the words of the Vedas; thereafter,
the glorious Nārāyaṇa accepted Lakṣmī.
Then all the hosts of gods bowed down again and again.
Then all those [gods], superior in strength, struck all the asuras; and they, crying out in distress, fled in the ten directions.
By the command of Śrī Viṣṇu, all the gods formed a row in due order to consume the nectar;
they all spoke to one another, saying, "You give it! You give it! You give it! (16).
"I am not capable, I am not capable, I am not capable," they said.
Then Viṣṇu arose and assumed a female form; he placed that nectar into a golden vessel and served it.
O best of the twice-born, while Rāhu was consuming the nectar, that Rākṣasa arrived there by means of his magical power;
then the Lord of the World, becoming enraged, struck him with his golden vessel.
His head fell upon the earth and became known by the name Ketu (20).
Then Rāhu and Ketu both departed quickly, overwhelmed with distress;
on that very day, the Moon and the Sun now engage in battle. (21)
If Rāhu should swallow a morsel [of food] at that moment, it would become difficult to obtain;
all water is equal to the Gaṅgā, and twice-born ones are equal to Vedavyāsa.
By bathing at Vāyasa-tīrtha, one obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
Through this gift, merit shall become inexhaustible, as well as the [merit] accumulated over ten million births;
likewise, sin will be destroyed along with its very root—how much more so by ten million sacrifices?
One seeking knowledge obtains knowledge, and one seeking a son obtains a son. (23–24)
One who seeks liberation attains liberation, and the perfection of mantras will certainly be achieved. Thus, O Brahmin, the churning of the ocean has been described to you. 25.
Thus ends the churning of the ocean in the *Brahmakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka and others.
The Tenth Chapter, titled "The Names.
The Eleventh Chapter.
Śaunaka said:
Now I desire to hear; tell me according to the truth,
O son of Ahaṅkāra, O Hesiuta, you who act for the benefit of the world, as instructed by Vedavyāsa himself in the form of Hari.
By what means does a woman become auspicious, and by what does a sinful woman become most ill-fated?
By what does she become beloved by her husband’s body and like nectar to his eyes? And by what is prosperity born? Tell me that, O one rich in asceticism. (2–3)
Sūta said:
O venerable one, listen as I relate in brief, according to the prescribed rules, this meritorious account which has been set forth and is most difficult to attain. 4.

In the age known as Dvāpara, there was a king named Bhadraśravas who resided in the country of Saurāṣṭra; he was a master of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas. His wife was born with the name Suraticandrikā.

To that illustrious king were born seven charming sons. Then, O best of Brahmins, there was a daughter born of noble lineage, Sundarī by name, who was truthful in speech and dark-complexioned; she brought joy to her father.
Then one day, on the sands of the Āśyā river which were like gold dust,
she joyfully went to the foot of a *nīpa* tree— extremely difficult to reach— to play with her friends who possessed hidden, enchanting jewels.
In the meantime,
O Brahmana, Vipralakṣmī, the savior from worldly existence and the servant of the world's moral order, arrived there in person before them, assuming the form of a Brāhmaṇa woman with grey hair.
"Since there is no destruction for all the worlds except that of the king,
to whose most insignificant house shall I go now?
Having reflected thus in her mind, she went to the royal palace.
Having passed through the main gate, which was joined with golden walls and adorned with banners, he then spoke to the female doorkeeper:
"O doorkeeper endowed with auspicious marks, open the gate! (12-13)
"I see the queen Suraticandrikā as if by the force of a river.
Hearing those words of hers, which were uttered like the song of a cuckoo, Ratnadaṇḍa the Rākṣasa attained supreme joy. 14.
The doorkeeper said:
"O old woman, what is your name? Who is your husband?
Why have you come, and what business do you have with the queen?"
"O Brahmin, why do you speak thus? I have a great curiosity to hear it.
The elder said:
"Listen, O King, to what happened when Daṇḍaka was the wife of Poṣya."
"You have a curiosity to hear the reason for my arrival.
(16) I am well-known by the name Kamalā; my lord of life is renowned as Bhuvaṇeśa, and my city is Dvāravatī. (17)

In that very place, the Lord of my life has not yet returned from his journey; therefore, I have come with a jeweled staff in hand—listen to my curiosity. Indeed, I shall now speak before you of the purpose of my arrival. 18–19.

Formerly, there was a queen born of a Vaiśya family who was distressed by the words [of her husband]. One day, a quarrel was raised by her husband against her dependents; then that ignoble woman, suffering and oppressed by her husband, [acted].
Barhiṣmān quickly emerged from the house, weeping again and again;
hearing her lamentation, I approached her side. I inquired about the entire situation, and it was related to me exactly as it had happened.
Then, because of her, I gave her the instruction on this most excellent vow.
By my instruction, she joyfully performed that excellent vow; through its grace, O gatekeeper, she became happy.
Once, when the wife born of a Vaiśya family had fallen under the power of death,
the Lord Dharmarāja dispatched his servants, Caṇḍa and others— who were capable of performing every act of slaughter— to bring her back from there.
At the command of Yama, the fear-inspiring messengers of Yama arrived;
with iron mallets in their hands, they bound the two of them with leather nooses and made an effort to go toward the refuge of Yama. 25-26.
In the meantime, the messengers of Lakṣmī, who were devoted to Viṣṇu and bore conchs, discs, and maces, arrived there to bring her back.
Upon seeing them in such a state, the messengers of Yama fled.
Likewise, the noble-souled Lakṣmīdūta, Svaprakāśa, and the others,
having severed their bonds and ascended a chariot yoked with royal swans, all went suddenly through the path of the sky to the city of Lakṣmī.
Having performed that excellent vow as many times as she was a Vaiśya woman,
they both remained in Kamalapura for thousands of kalpas;
now, for the sake of enjoying the remainder of their merit, they have been born into a royal lineage.
"Having forgotten their vow and being arrogant due to the king's wealth,
they have come for the purpose of giving instruction even to you.
The gatekeeper said:
"O Mother, by what procedure was this excellent vow performed when you were old?
In which month is this supreme vow observed, and which deity is worshipped?
You ought to tell me, who am asking, exactly as it is. (32)
Kamalā said: When Kārttika had passed and Mārgaśīrṣa had arrived,
having fasted in that month on the day known as Thursday (Guru-vāsara), 33.
Then, at the time of forenoon, surrounded by all those observing the vow, one should worship Lakṣmī together with Nārāyaṇa;
[one should do so] with sweet foods consisting of milk-rice mixed with sugar-candy.
One should satisfy Lakṣmī and send her away; then one should pray as follows:
"O Goddess worshipped in the three worlds, O Kamalā, beloved of Viṣṇu! Just as you are eternally established in Kṛṣṇa, so may you abide in me. (35-36)

O sinless goddess, take refuge in the lotus of the Lord; having commanded Lakṣmī with various offering materials, you should satisfy her. One should worship the Goddess, accompanied by great festivals, with the sacred scriptures.
Then, having given the remnants of the food offering to the most excellent of Brahmins (38),
one should provide for oneself, one's husband, one's sons, dependents, and other servants.
Now listen, O beautiful lady, to the special procedure for the second lunar day dedicated to the Guru (39).
One should satisfy Goddess Kamalā with deep devotion by offering *bhrāṣṭras* made of wheat, which are excellent and decorated with various powders;
on the third day, one should offer an oblation of rice mixed with curd and sugar-candy.
In the fourth [period], one should joyfully worship Goddess Lakṣmī with the essence of śyāmāka and śāli rice; then, with effort, one should offer a jeweled staff (ratnadaṇḍaka).
For the pleasure of Goddess Lakṣmī, one should honor the Brāhmaṇas with wealth. 41–42.
Nourished with garments, ornaments, food, and various kinds of fruits, she said, "O Vṛddhā, stay right here at my command; you are truly moon-like in your beauty. (43)
"I shall inform her; do not be angry, O best of beings.
Having spoken thus, that woman of beautiful limbs went into the presence of the queen.
Placing her joined palms upon her head, O Brahmin, she spoke to her protector from the very root.
From the beginning up to the conclusion of the ritual with its constituent parts, whatever the lotus-dwelling goddess had spoken,
she related all of that to Queen Suraticandrikā.
Having heard the words of the female gatekeeper, Queen Suraticandrikā— (45–46)
The proud Sundarī went to the side of the Brahmin woman and laughed; the queen said: "O old Brahmin woman, what has happened? For what purpose have you come to give me instruction? (47)
"Tell me for a long time, casting aside all fear, as you please.
The Brāhmaṇī said:
"Having seen your lack of policy, I, fickle-minded, wish to depart. (48)
"O wicked woman, I shall tell you of that most rare vow which you,
a Cāṇḍāla, have performed today on the day of Indirā. O wicked one, that has now been seen by me in your proud house."
Having heard those words of the Brahmin woman, her eyes bloodshot with anger,
she struck the aged Brahmin woman with a blow; thereupon, the old Kamalā fled while crying out.
Then, while she was playing, the young ascetic girl heard the sound of the Brahmin woman’s lamentation;
having heard it, she approached her. The young girl Śyāmā said:
"O old woman, tell me, by whom was such a thing given to you?
Speak! Having heard her words, O best of the twice-born, Kamalā related the entire account with a voice choked with grief.
Then, having heard of that most difficult vow from Śyāmābālā,
he performed it with faith and devotion according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures;
when three cycles were completed and the fourth day arrived, (54–55).

Having received that [garland], which was perfected through the marriage rite by the grace of the fortune of the twice-born, Mālādhara— the son of King Śrīsiddheśvara, who possessed royal splendor— went home. 56.
Now, O Brahmin, listen with curiosity to what happened regarding her disappearance:
all the many various articles that were in the queen's house had been taken away by someone, yet they remained unknown, O protector of the earth. (57-58)
Devoid of livelihood, lacking intelligence, and destitute of both food and clothing,
she sat down; yet, even in that state, she sent her husband to her daughter's house for the sake of making some request.
After some time, O Brāhmaṇa, Mālādhara also entered that village on the bank of the lake with great difficulty;
his servants arrived there to fetch water from it.
Seeing him, the best among those suffering, they asked him with compassion.
The female servants said:
"Who are you? From where have you come, being devoid of flesh and blood?"
"Tell me all of that, O voice with rough limbs and rough hair.
The poor man said:
"I am a young man from Saurāṣṭra, and my father was dark-complexioned."
"O servants, tell him this in the presence of the dark-complexioned girl.
Having heard those words of his, they all, filled with curiosity,
turned their faces toward one another and laughed as they returned to their own city.
O twice-born one, having heard all that Śyāmā and Bālā had related, he dispatched servants with flower-essence oil, divine garments, sandalwood, and betel leaves. 65.
Having likewise given the horse to her father, Sundarī then went toward him; thereafter, all those servants, having dressed in excellent attire,
led the dark-complexioned girl to a house resembling the palace of the King of the Gods.
Then Śyāmābālā, with great effort, fed her father— the foremost among those in distress— with rice mixed with ghee. O ascetic, when four days had passed, [she continued to serve him].
Having given him wealth placed in a secret vessel, they sent him away.
Then, having entered his own house, he saw that the wealth which had been in another vessel was now a heap of charcoal; deeply distressed, he wept.
Having come out from the house, he departed to go to his daughter’s dwelling;
and there, at the edge of the lake, the sorrowful woman entered. Thus she was brought back, as dear to him as his own life.

In that very manner, out of maternal affection, the devoted wife continued her worship. At that time, the demon Lakṣmīvasara resolved in his mind to transform his mother into a dark-complexioned young girl.
Her mother was poor; having eaten alone even in a secluded place, she was filled with indignation at the leftovers of the disciples.
Thus, three days passed for Indirā as well.
On the fourth day, she had that [palace] constructed very firmly.
Having arrived at the city, Queen Suraticandrikā saw the house, which was thus divine by the grace of Indirā.
O best of Brahmins, Śyāmābālā once again went to her mother’s house at a certain time, desiring to see Aiśvaryā. Then, seeing Śyāmābālā from afar, she became enraged.
"I do not see her face," she said, and remained there unnoticed.
Then, having gone into the interior of the house and taken some rock salt,
she returned to her own home, somewhat silently and full of grace.
The king and the master asked that virtuous woman, who regarded her husband as a god:
"O beloved, what have you brought? Tell me before me.
The beloved replied:
Having said, "I shall show you the very essence of sovereignty during this meal," she then prepared a dish without salt and gave that food and other items to King Mālādhara.

Then King Mālādhara, having eaten the food—which was devoid of salt and possessed of certain defects—was overcome by a sense of unease; yet he gave her the essence of his kingdom. Then, O twice-born one, the king, being delighted in mind, took his meal.
They praised that woman, saying, "Blessed! Blessed!
[They said: "That woman who does not perform this vow with great devotion shall be poor and unfortunate in birth after birth. (84)

Whoever hears this with devotion, or whoever recites it with a concentrated mind, shall be liberated from all sins and attain the world of Lakṣmī. One should not perform the vow without having heard this narrative of the vow.
His fruit of the vow indeed perishes; of this there is no doubt. 86.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Twelve.
Śaunaka said: O Sūta, by what other merit does a man go to the abode of Hari, freed from sin? Tell me that out of compassion. 1.
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, that mortal who protects the life of a Brāhmaṇa by means of wealth, or his wealth by means of his own life, goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
In the age known as Tretā, there was a powerful Vaiṣṇava named Purārāja, who was a priest and yet remained childless.
Once, filled with humility, the king questioned Gālava.

"By what merit may one be born as a son who is an ocean of compassion? Tell me, O tiger among sages; by your command I shall perform it, for the life of those men who have no son is indeed meaningless. (4-5)
Gālava said:
O King, listen attentively to that which I have been asked by you;
I shall relate in brief the cause of the birth of your son.
"O best of kings, perform the sacrifice known as the Naramedha;
then your progeny shall indeed be endowed with all auspicious marks.
The king said:
"O twice-born one, tell me, O preceptor: what kind of man shall I bring for this great sacrifice of human immolation, the most excellent of all sacrifices?
Galava said:
One who possesses beautiful limbs and a handsome face, and is a knower of all the scriptures, if born into a noble family, then becomes fit for sacrifice.
One who is deficient in limbs, dark-complexioned, and foolish, is certainly not fit.
When Gālava had spoken thus, O lord of men,
the king dispatched messengers with the sage’s words, and after giving much wealth to the brahmins headed by Gālava, he sent them forth.
Then, by the king's command, messengers who had mastered all the scriptures set out joyfully from place to place;
O best of the twice-born, they went to every village and even to every city with focused intent. 12.12-13ab.
Having failed to find [such a place] anywhere, he then went to a region known by the name Daśapura, O Brahmin, which was filled with virtuous twice-born men,
where the women had beautiful hair and eyes like those of young fawns.
Upon seeing him, men became bewildered, for he was like the moon itself; in that delightful city lived a twice-born man named Kṛṣṇadeva together with his three sons and his virtuous wife.
He was a Vaiṣṇava, pleasant in speech, and always devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu.
He maintained the sacred fire, was devoted to his ancestors, and acted for the benefit of the Vaiṣṇavas.
Then the messengers made their request to that best of the twice-born on behalf of the king.
"O best of Brahmins, say 'Give me a son,' 'Give me a son'—
for the king has no son, O foremost of the twice-born, who might destroy his anguish. For that purpose, he has been initiated into the sacrifice known as the Naramedha.

"O Brahmin, we shall take your son to be offered as a sacrifice in our great ritual; bring four hundred thousand gold pieces with a focused mind. If he is to be given away easily, then do not [cling to him] out of longing for a son. (19-20)
"By that power we shall go; we are the executors of the king's command.
Having heard the words of the messengers, the two brahmins became overwhelmed with grief, their minds filled with uncertainty as if they were bereft of life. (21)
"What is the use of wealth, gold, livelihood,
or even a home?"— thus that brahmin spoke these words to the king's officers.
The brahmin said:
"O messengers, since you have come to bring back my son, who dispels the darkness of grief, listen certainly to my words:
Who, remaining on this earth, would wish to violate the command of a king? (23)
"Leaving aside your son, why do you take me, an old man, O twice-born one? Hearing these words of his, the messengers, filled with rage,
forcibly cast the gold pieces into that house.
When they resolved to take that son away, it is said that the virtuous brahmin, having bound his hands in añjali and weeping, spoke in anger:
"Leaving aside my eldest son, you cannot take any other excellent son of mine."
"O people, the words 'let him lead [her] away' do not even come to my mouth to be spoken.
Having heard the words of the twice-born man, the messengers spoke to the virtuous weeping Brāhmaṇī: "O best of women, give us your younger son."
Having heard those words of theirs, the Brāhmaṇī then fell from the ground along with the whirlwind, like Rambhā, being deeply afflicted by grief.
Taking up a mallet, she forcefully struck it against her own head.
"O messengers, I shall by all means give my youngest son.
At that moment, O Brahmin, the middle son of the Brahmin,
overcome with humility, bowed to his parents and spoke while weeping.
"If a mother gives poison, if a father sells his son,
and if a king seizes all one's property— who then shall be the protector?
Having spoken thus, his son bowed his head at his father's feet.
Then, messengers went in haste to that king who was about to be initiated;
meanwhile, those two Brahmins, their minds distressed by the separation from their son, wept again and again until they reached a state of blindness.
Then, as they were traveling along, they reached the hermitage of the sage Viśvāmitra, which was inhabited by his disciples and frequented by young deer.
Seeing the sages, the king’s men questioned them with respect.
"O Keyūya, where has he gone? Tell us what his conduct was. (36) The royal messengers said:
"Listen attentively, O Brahmin; no son is born to the king."
"For that purpose, the king has been consecrated for a sacrifice known as the Naramedha.
We shall take this young son of a Brahmin there for the sake of the sacrificial offering.
Upon hearing these words of theirs, that Brahmin became compassionate.

"May they attain life, and may the child become well. For the sake of the child, for the sake of the twice-born, and for the sake of their master, those people here who renounce their lives like blades of grass shall attain eternal worlds."
Reflecting thus within his heart, that sage, the best among the twice-born, spoke:
"O messengers, leave me behind and take this brahmin boy quickly to the sacrifice; for this child is most excellent."
Having attained birth in this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), no happiness has been found here; how will this child die? When he has arrived home, his parents will become distressed by messengers.
"Surely, having reached this state of ill fortune, you have come to the very house of Yama.
Having heard these words of his, the messengers then spoke to the twice-born man: "O Brahmin, without the command of the king, the protector of the distressed, [we cannot take you]. 43-44.
"O wise one, how shall we lead you, who have turned grey, into delusion?
Having spoken thus, those messengers then went to the king's city.
Accompanied by the assembly of messengers, the sage went to the sacrificial hall.
The messengers reported the Brahmin's conduct to the king.
Having heard that, his mind filled with apprehension, he spoke these words to the sage: "O sage, even if a son is born to me for the sake of this sacrifice... (46-47)
"O Lord Brahmā, even without strength, lead that son of a Brahmin there.
The sage said:
"O King, by your performing this sacrifice, a great son shall be born to you."

"Let there be no doubt in this matter; even a sight [of you] is not in vain. Having heard these words of his, the king was exceedingly joyful and, together with all the sages, performed the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) in the sacrifice.
Then, that most excellent sage, taking with him the son of the brāhmaṇa, went at that time to the city named Daśapura; having reached his residence, the sage spoke these words.
"O Sage, you remain standing here as if lifeless, having lost your footing.
The king has taken my son away by force; what shall I do?
Now that our son has gone, O Brahmin, what will become of us two, husband and wife?"
And his eyes too had fallen into blindness due to his lamentations;
then that tiger among sages, beholding his son,
spoke thus to those two brahmins who were filled with joy.

"Having made the son the cause, these two have come outside in an instant. (55) Due to the fulfillment of the sage's word, their vision immediately regained its light at that very moment from the sight of their son. (56)

O brahmins, having drunk in the lotus-face of their son with eyes resembling bees for a long time, and having bowed to that sage again and again, the two Brahmin priests, who spoke kindly, addressed these words.
"O sage, the gift of life to us two is indeed a meritorious act.
Having heard those very words of theirs, the sage, an ocean of compassion,
gave them his blessing and departed for his own hermitage.

Having placed the supreme state of Viṣṇu within his hands, the highly fortunate sage performed austerities that were difficult even for the gods to attain. O Brahmin, when some time had passed, a son was born to that king.
Handsome and worthy of kingship like the moon in the ocean of milk,
that king of Brahmins also enjoyed himself on earth like a god, free from sorrow and filled with joy at the festival of his son's birth, after having bestowed wealth upon the brahmins.
He who protects the Brahmins by giving them even his own life and wealth goes to the abode of Viṣṇu,
from which rebirth is difficult to attain. Those who recite this narrative here with devotion, or listen to it from a Brahmin, [attain the same].
Even those who recite a single verse of this narrative go to the abode of Viṣṇu.
(64) Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Protection of Brāhmaṇas," in the Brahmakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. (12)
The Thirteenth Chapter. Śaunaka said:
O Sūta, [tell me] the supreme majesty of Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī on that day.
"O one of great wisdom, tell [me] and deliver [us] from the great ocean.
Sūta said:
"O Brahmin, that man who observes Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī with devotion..."
O twice-born one, at the end [of his life], he goes to the city of Viṣṇu accompanied by ten million members of his lineage.
O best of the twice-born, the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī) occurring on a Wednesday or a Monday,
when conjoined with the Rohiṇī asterism, grants liberation to ten million members of one's family.

Even one joined with great sins who performs this supreme vow becomes liberated from all evils and, at the end, goes to the abode of Hari. O Brahmin, that lowest of men who does not observe Kṛṣṇa-janmāṣṭamī [is lost].
She experiences suffering in this world and, after death, she shall go to hell. That woman who does not observe the Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī vow year after year is deluded; she goes to a terrible hell.

On the day of Janmāṣṭamī, that man of deluded intellect who eats food indeed consumes a great hell; I speak the truth, the absolute truth. Formerly, Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, was questioned by Dilīpa.
Listen to that, O one of great wisdom, which destroys all sins.
Dilīpa said:
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, Janārdana was born.
Therefore, O great sage, I desire to hear this; please tell me:
how was the Blessed One Viṣṇu, the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, born in the womb of Devakī? For what purpose and by what cause did he take birth there?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, O King, I shall explain why Janārdana was born on earth after abandoning the third heaven; I shall tell it to you. 11.
Formerly, the earth was indeed oppressed by kings such as Kaṃsa; struck by a messenger of Kaṃsa who was arrogant in his own authority, she went about crying out, her eyes rolling in distress.
12. As she cried out again and again, she proceeded with trembling eyes.
Wherever the Lord of Gods, the bull-bannered beloved of Umā, was stationed,
those women— disregarded by Kaṃsa, pale and weeping tears— rained down showers of tears to inform him [of their plight]. 13-14.
Beholding her weeping, his lower lip quivering with rage,
Mahādeva— accompanied by Umā and followed by all the hosts of gods— came in anger to the abode of the Creator.
Having gone there, he spoke to Brahmā for the sake of destroying Kaṃsa:
"O Brahmā, let a plan be devised by you together with Viṣṇu.
Having heard those words, the self-realized one (Brahmā) said that he would go.
While Vaikuṇṭha was sleeping upon the serpent in the Ocean of Milk, the Creator (Brahmā),
having mounted the back of a swan, went into the presence of Hari.
Having arrived there, the Creator [was joined] by hosts of gods led by Hara.
Endowed with eloquence, that best among those skilled in speech was praised with gentle words:
"Obeisance to the lotus-eyed Hara, the Supreme Self;
obeisance to you, the protector of the world and the beloved of Lakṣmī. (19-20)
Having heard this praise from them, Janārdana replied to all those gods whose faces were distressed: "How have you come here?
Brahmā said:
Listen, O Lord of the World; since this has come upon us, I shall tell you, O Best of Gods, O Creator of the World:
King Kaṃsa is difficult to overcome, being intoxicated by the boons granted by the Wielder of the Trident.
Afflicted by the blow of his hand, which struck like the earth itself, [he said]:
"O Bhava, although I was previously deceived by your illusion (māyā) after you had granted me a boon, my death shall come through the destruction of my nephew. 23–24.
"Therefore, go yourself to slay Kaṃsa, who is difficult to approach; having taken birth in the womb of Devakī and gone to Gokula.
Thus urged by Brahmā, the Lord replied to the wielder of the trident (Śiva).

"O Lord of Devas, having stayed for a year with Pārvatī, he will depart. Then the lotus-seated one, bearing the conch, discus, and mace, set out on his journey toward Mathurā together with Umā and Lakṣmī. 26–27.
There, the wielder of the mace (Gadādhara) took birth in the womb of Devakī;
meanwhile, the deer-eyed Śarvāṇī resided within the belly of Yaśodā for nine months and nine days.
In the month of Bhādrapada, during the dark fortnight, on the lunar day known as the eighth (Aṣṭamī),
joined with the Rohiṇī asterism and resounding with deep thunder,
on that night the Lord of the World, the enemy of Kaṃsa and son of Vasudeva, was born.
Yaśodā, the wife of Nanda, the lord of the Vairāṭas, gave birth to a daughter;
yet [the child] was a son with lotus-hands, a lotus-navel, and eyes like lotus petals.
Then, seeing him, Ānakadundubhi began to rejoice.
Then Devakī, terrified by the fear of the demon Kaṃsa, said: "O Lord, go to Vairāṭī; it is said that the son has been returned. Having given the boy to Yaśodā, bring back her daughter. 32–33.
Having heard his words, Vasudeva, also distressed,
took the infant in his arms and went toward Vairāṭī;
on that path, in the middle of the way, he encountered the Yamunā river filled with water.
It was terrible, vast, and long, filled with a deep flood of water.
Having seen this and standing upon the bank gazing at the Yamunā,
Vasudeva, afflicted by grief, lamented with great anxiety.
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? For I have been deceived even by fate; how shall I go from here to the house of Nanda in Vairāṭī?
Thus spoke Hari, who had there joyfully deceived his father through his illusory power (māyā).
Standing on the bank for a mere moment while gazing at the Yamunā, he saw that even she had, in an instant, become knee-deep; seeing her thus,
he rose up in joy and proceeded toward his destination.
Having created an illusion, the Lord of the World fell from his father's lap into the water;
seeing his son fallen, he cried out "Alas! Alas!
and was deeply distressed, for he had been deceived by that very fate (Vidhi) who intended to employ a great stratagem once more.
"O Lord of the worlds, protect me; O best of gods, guard my son! 41.
Seeing his father's lamentation, the enemy of Kaṃsa was repeatedly moved by compassion;
having finished his water-play, he went once more into his father's lap. 42.
In this manner, the best of the Yadus went to the palace of Nanda;
having given his son to Yaśodā, he brought back her daughter. Then, having reached his own residence, he restored the daughter to his wife.
When the enemy of the asuras received news that Devakī had given birth,
he dispatched messengers at once to bring his son and daughter.
Having arrived, those messengers of Kaṃsa proceeded to take away the daughter.
Having forcibly dragged her away from Devakī and Vasudeva,
she was seized by Kaṃsa’s messengers and handed over to the enemy of the gods.
O Great King, upon seizing her, that invincible one became filled with fear.
Seeing her, who possessed the luster of pure gold, whose face resembled the full moon,
whose laughter was sweet, and whose eyes flashed like lightning, Kaṃsa,
the foremost of the Asuras, commanded: "Take her and kill her upon a stone!"
Having received this command, those asuras set out to crush her;
meanwhile, Gaurī, with the speed of lightning, went into the presence of Śaṅkara.
Gaurī said:
"Listen, O King, I shall tell you where that supreme enemy resides; hidden in the abode of Nanda, that best of asuras is your slayer.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, the daughter of the cowherd went to her own home.
Then, having heard those words of the goddess, King Kaṃsa was deeply distressed.
He said to his sister Pūtanā, "Go to the house of Nanda."
"Having killed my son by means of deception, he is surely going to obtain much that he desires.
O auspicious one, go very quickly to slay my enemy. Having received this command, that rākṣasī set out toward Gokula.
Having entered Gokula there in the form of a beautiful woman through her illusory power (māyā), she approached with the intent to kill, having seized [the child] in her breast;
she was then perceived as having entered the door of the cowherds' houses. 54.
Having gone there, He raised up the infant from within, gave him the breast, and [attained] the state of the lowest of men;
then, having overturned the cart and performed the crushing of Tṛṇāvarta and others, and having subdued Kālīya, He then went to Madhupurī.
Having gone there, the cruel Kaṃsa was slain; he defeated the wrestlers of Kaṃsa.
O King, this vow for the birth-day of Viṣṇu has been told to you.
By hearing it, sins are destroyed; who would not perform it? What will happen [to those who do]?
Whatever mortal man or woman performs this vow of Hari,
having attained incomparable sovereignty in another birth according to their desire, they should not perform the third lunar day joined with the second (pūrvaviddhā), nor indeed the sixth. 58-59.

Those who desire dharma, pleasure, wealth, and auspiciousness should diligently avoid the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī) when it is joined with the seventh (saptamī), even if it falls on the eighth, eleventh, or fourteenth. However,
the eighth lunar day joined with the ninth (navamī) should be observed even if it lacks a favorable lunar mansion (ṛkṣa).
If the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī) rises for even a moment and the ninth (navamī) is complete,
and Rohiṇī is joined with it for even a single Muhūrta, then the eighth becomes full.
If the eighth is joined with Wednesday and accompanied by Rohiṇī, [it is likewise auspicious].
O King, what is the use of performing ten million vows?
On the ninth lunar day, when the moon has risen just slightly, even on a Wednesday, that [merit] may be obtained—
even in a hundred years— or it may not be obtained at all.
The eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) joined with the ninth (Navamī) should not be observed without the constellation Revatī.
However, the eighth day joined with Rohiṇī should be observed even if it is overlapped by the seventh (Saptamī).
When even a fraction, a minute (kāṣṭhā), or a moment (muhūrta) of the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī tithi occurs [on the seventh], it must be accepted.
The ninth day itself should not be observed when conjoined with the seventh;
how much less so when joined with Wednesday, and especially with Monday? How much more so when joined with the ninth, for it grants liberation to ten million families!
"O Indra among kings, one should abandon the eighth lunar day because of its contact with the seventh,
just as a jar of Ganges water is defiled by a single drop of liquor.
Dilīpa said:
By whom was this first composed, and by whom was it revealed?
What is its merit, and what is its fruit, O God? Tell me, O Great Sage.
Vasiṣṭha said:
The great king Citrasena was a man of immense and supreme wickedness;
he committed sexual intercourse with forbidden women, stole the gold of a twice-born brahmin,
was constantly addicted to liquor, and was always devoted to eating meat in vain.
Thus, constantly joined with such evil and always delighting in the slaughter of living beings, he always engaged in conversation with outcasts and those who had fallen from their caste;
it was for such a king that his mind became intent upon hunting.
Having recognized a tiger in the forest and having surrounded it on all sides, he spoke these words to all his soldiers with great caution:
"I alone shall slay this beast; whoever else strikes at it shall be punished."
There was no doubt that he was to be killed; thus the tiger followed the path of the king.
Then the king, though filled with shame, followed behind the tiger, intent upon slaying it despite its many hardships and sufferings.
Afflicted by the distress of hunger and thirst on the bank of the Yamunā at twilight, they thought:
"Today is the eighth lunar day conjoined with the Rohiṇī asterism; that day is the anniversary of his birth. Tomorrow, O lord of men, the maidens will perform the vow at the Yamunā. || 75 ||
With various offerings, substances, and beautiful incense and lamps (76),
and seeing fragrant flowers, pleasing substances such as saffron, and food of many qualities, his mind became agitated with the desire to eat (77).
The king said,
"Due to the lack of food, my vital breaths will surely depart this very day.
The women said:
"O King, O sinless one, you must not eat on the Janmāṣṭamī day of Hari.
There is no doubt that he who eats on the birthday of Kṛṣṇa has consumed vulture flesh, donkey meat, crow meat, beef, and even excrement. (78-79)
O King, there is no deficiency whatsoever that has not arisen for men dwelling in saṃsāra,
by which the Jayantī festival was not observed while the vital breath remained in the body; for one who has failed to observe it, the command of Yama’s abode awaits.
"Whatever is offered daily to the ancestors according to the prescribed rites, they do not accept it;
all the ancestors have been cast down when the meal is prepared on the Jayantī day.
Having heard this, O lord of men, the king then undertook the vow.
Bringing some flowers, some incense, and a garment, he was filled with joy; having performed this vow, the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) occurred at the end of the lunar day.
By the power of this vow, Citrasena went to the abode of Hari. 83.

The fruit that is obtained by ascending a divine celestial chariot and going with one's ancestors [to heaven] is attained by a person through the vow of Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī, by going to Mathurā and beholding the lotus-face of Kṛṣṇa. 84.
Whatever fruit is obtained by going to Dvārakā and beholding Hari, the Lord of the Universe, that same fruit is attained by the humble by performing the Janmāṣṭamī vow. 85.
Thus ends the majesty of the Hari-Janmāṣṭamī vow in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
The Thirteenth Chapter [ends].
The Fourteenth Chapter. Śaunaka said:
"O one of great wisdom, O ocean of compassion, please tell me out of kindness the greatness of the Brāhmaṇa, who is the best among all castes. Sūta said:
O best of the twice-born, the Brāhmaṇa is indeed the preceptor of all castes;
he should be known as the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself, the refuge of all the immortals. He who offers salutation to a Brāhmaṇa with the thought that he is Hari [attains great merit].
O best of the twice-born, through devotion, his wealth and other prosperity increased.
Even when he saw a Brāhmaṇa, though he was proud, he would bow down;
yet Hari always desired to cut off his head.

Those of sinful intellect who hate a Brahmin who has committed an offense should be known as haters of Hari; they go to a terrible hell. He who sees a Brahmin who has come to make a request with anger—
Kṛtānta indeed thrusts a red-hot needle into the eyes of that foolish, lowest of men who reviles a Brahmin;
and the messengers of Yama place molten iron into his mouth.
In whosever home this ascetic, the lord of the earth, eats,
there Kṛṣṇa himself eats along with the gods;
all sins, including the killing of a twice-born, perish in those homes.

If a man partakes of even a mere drop of the water from the feet of a Brahmin, O Brahmins, he is liberated from all sins. I tell you the truth: that man who devoutly washes the feet of a twice-born with his own hands is released from every transgression.
A woman bereft of sons, one whose children have died, and even a woman who has lost her husband,
all gain life through their children by serving the lotus feet of the twice-born. Whatever sacred fords exist in the universe, all those sacred fords are present in the ocean.
All holy places that exist in the ocean reside at the feet of the twice-born;
he whose head is constantly sprinkled with the water from the feet of the twice-born has bathed in all sacred fords and is liberated from all sins. 12.

Listen, O Śaunaka, I shall tell you this greatness that destroys sin. (13) O ascetic, I shall relate the history of the water from a Brahmin’s feet. Long ago, O best of the twice-born, there was a man devoted to the livelihood of a Vaiśya. (14)
In the Dvāpara age, Bhīma was a Śūdra who had committed a thousand instances of brahmin-slaughter; he was cruel, yet always pleased with everyone, and he even consorted with a Vaiśya woman.
Furthermore, that Bhīma had fallen from proper conduct as a Śūdra and had violated the bed of his guru.
"I shall describe each one, O tiger among sages; there is no end to the number of sins of that wicked-minded robber Bhīma.
Once, he went to the house of a certain Brāhmaṇa."
Having gone there, he resolved to take [the wealth] from his house;
he stayed outside near the gate of the Brahmin's residence and spoke these words of distress to that earth-lord who was rich in asceticism.
"O Master, listen to my words; you appear as if compassionate.
I am afflicted by hunger; give me food, for my life-breaths are departing quickly.
The Brahmin said:
"Afflicted by hunger, listen to me; I have no means to prepare food.
Take these rice grains and eat them as you please.
I have no father, no mother, no son, and no brother. (21)
"My wife, mother, and kinsmen are gone; all have departed from me.
I remain alone in this house, inactive, devoid of fortune, and like a guest to Hari. I am truly unable to live without them. (22-23)
Bhīma said:
"O best of the twice-born, there is no one who serves me, nor even a Śūdra; having abandoned my home, I shall remain here forever. (24)
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of his, that joyous protector of the earth (the king) then quickly prepared the cooked food and gave it to the one whose wealth is austerity (the sage). 25.
Filled with joy, he remained there in the brahmin’s dwelling, performing charming service full of affection for the god among men; thinking,
"Today or tomorrow, I shall acquire wealth for myself as well as for him."
"When I shall bring [the water], I will not fail to bring it; of this there is no doubt.
Having thus reflected within his heart and performed the ritual action for him, he should wash the guest's feet and so forth, with his own head bowed to remove all sin. 27–28.
Having sipped water for ritual purification, the twice-born man would daily receive the water from his feet under a pretext.
Once, a certain food-bearer arrived to fetch goods;
at night, he entered the interior of that house through a small opening.
Seeing Abhīma approaching for the purpose of striking him, Daṇḍahasta quickly fled after severing his head with a sword. Then Viṣṇu’s soldiers arrived, bearing conchs, discs, and maces.

O twice-born one, they arrived to lead Bhīma there, free from all sin; and a divine chariot drawn by royal swans arrived as well. Having ascended it, he went to the abode of Viṣṇu, which is indeed difficult to attain.
Thus has the majesty of the god of the earth been proclaimed by me; whatever man hears this with devotion, his sins shall be destroyed. 33.
Thus ends the "Majesty of the Brāhmaṇas" in the Brahmakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka.
The Fourteenth Chapter, titled "The Name.
The Fifteenth Chapter.
Śaunaka said:
"O highly fortunate one, tell us the greatness that destroys sin;
what is the fruit of Ekādaśī, and what is the transgression for one who does not observe it?
Sūta said:
What can I say now regarding the greatness of Ekādaśī?
Upon hearing of Ekādaśī, even the messengers of Yama become apprehensive;
there is no doubt in this matter, for they are terrifying to all living beings.
Of all vows, the auspicious Ekādaśī is the most excellent;
having fasted upon it, one should keep a vigil and perform a grand decoration for Viṣṇu.
Indeed, that mortal who performs the worship of Hari with Tulasī leaves [attains great merit].

O twice-born one, by fasting on a single Ekādaśī, one obtains the fruit of ten million sacrifices; furthermore, whatever sin is proclaimed to arise from approaching those who should not be approached, that sin goes to destruction through fasting on Ekādaśī.
O twice-born one, he who offers a lamp filled with ghee on the day of Viṣṇu goes to the city of Viṣṇu at the end, having destroyed darkness by his own splendor;
blessed indeed are those regions, and blessed is that lord of the earth.

In the kingdom of Hari’s son, there is a great festival on the Ekādaśī day; those who remain without food especially on the Prabodhinī day, when Nārāyaṇa lies down and turns upon his side, [attain the highest state].
"Do not bring living beings who possess merit into my presence," the Lord of the Ancestors commanded his messengers day and night:
"The eleventh day is dear to the Lord of the World; it increases merit."

Viṣṇu indeed burns away the body of those who eat that food; fie on their life, fie on their prosperity, fie on their beauty, and fie on their conduct—those most sinful ones who eat food on the Ekādaśī day, becoming consumers of excrement. 11.
O best of the twice-born, on the eleventh day, many various sins remain, relying solely upon worldly enjoyment;
just as great impurity arises for women at their union during the new moon.
Likewise, by eating food on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), sin is incurred; living beings who eat its food become diseased, as well as those with lameness, cough, skin diseases, and leprosy. 14.
Thus do creatures become through the consumption of that food.
O best of the twice-born, by eating that food, one indeed becomes a village pig and falls into poverty; whatever sins exist in this world, O Brahmin, they are incurred on the day of Hari. 15–16.
Those who remain subsisting on water alone according to the injunctions shall be liberated from all sins and the hells; however, for those men who eat on the day of Hari, there is no atonement.
17. There is no atonement for men who eat on the day of Hari.
Those men who eat various foods on the day of Hari incur the sin arising from ten million killings of Brahmins for every morsel of food.
I speak again, I speak again: listen, listen, O men! 18–19.
"One must not eat, one must not eat, one must not eat on the day of Hari.
Whatever fruit is obtained by bathing in sacred fords such as the Gaṅgā, fasting on the day of a lunar or solar eclipse, and on the Ekādaśī, [is attained by eating on this day]. (20)
Having worshipped the Lord of Kamalā (Viṣṇu) with garlands of lotuses according to the prescribed rites,
and having performed the breaking of the fast on that [Ekādaśī], O twice-born one, he performs the decoration of the house of Hari on the eleventh day, which is the vessel for his mother's womb.
Having attained the supreme goal, they shall abide in the abode of Viṣṇu; those who, having observed Ekādaśī, remain without food,
their residence in the city of Viṣṇu shall be eternal— of this there is no doubt.

Those whose minds shine, being fully absorbed in devotion to Tulasī, go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt. Furthermore, those in whom no desire for the wealth of others exists [attain the same].
Even those whose minds are contented [attain] Viṣṇu’s city for certain;
and those best of men who, having encountered a time of famine, give food to living beings, reach the abode of Hari— of this there is no doubt.

Those who give up their lives for the protection of cows, the twice-born, or their own masters and wives, O Madra, certainly attain the city of Viṣṇu. The tenth lunar day (Daśamī) should never be observed as a fast by living beings when it overlaps with the eleventh day.
O best of the twice-born, one must avoid the proximity of a wicked person; likewise,
if the tenth lunar day (daśamī) should coincide with the time of dawn,
then the eleventh day (ekādaśī) should be observed as a fast, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the thirteenth day (trayodaśī).
If the dawn (aruṇodaya) should be joined with the remainder of the tenth day,
the Vaiṣṇava must not perform the Ekādaśī vow on that day;
the four ghaṭikās in the morning are called aruṇodaya.
For ascetics, this time of dawn is considered equal to the waters of the Gaṅgā;
however, if the tenth lunar day is seen at the time of sunrise,
the eleventh day should not be observed there, as it destroys virtue, desire, and wealth.
A wise man should avoid even a very slight overlap with the tenth day (daśamī) on Ekādaśī;
just as one would discard a jar of ghee due to contact with a drop of liquor.
Where there is a full Ekādaśī, and that same [Ekādaśī] recurs on the twelfth day (dvādaśī), [one should observe it].
A householder should fast on the preceding Ekādaśī when it is joined with the Uttarāyana; provided that the Dvādaśī does not extend beyond [the following day],
he should perform the pāraṇa on the Trayodaśī, which yields the merit of a hundred sacrifices.

If the Ekādaśī is lost [to the night] and the following day is joined with the Dvādaśī, one should fast on the full Dvādaśī if one desires the supreme goal. Where the Ekādaśī is complete and it recurs again at dawn, [that is the time for fasting]. 36–37.
If the twelfth day (dvādaśī) occurs after the following day for all [the Ekādaśīs],
then for those men whose minds are fully absorbed in the vow of Ekādaśī, heaven is indeed their dwelling, or else they go to the abode of Hari.
There is no means for attaining the next world superior to Ekādaśī.
Even one burdened with many sins who observes the day of Hari becomes liberated from all sins and goes to the abode of Hari. 39-40.

She who offers a lamp before Hari with a spirit of devotion, along with her husband, shall become a woman possessed of a good son, a fortunate mistress, and after death, she goes to the abode of Hari. (41)
O best of the twice-born, the measure of the merit of Hari’s day cannot be known. O brahmin, that woman who, together with her husband,
performs a vigil for Hari shall dwell for a long time in the abode of Hari along with her husband.

O twice-born one, whatever object anyone offers with devotion on the day of Hari, his merit is indeed inexhaustible for all time. (44) Formerly, there was a man named Vallabha in the city called Kāñcana.
O twice-born one, that lord of wealth shone even with abundant riches, and his beloved was of great beauty, named Hemaprabhā;
yet there, the fault of the Kali age, namely loquacity, oppressed him most severely. 45–46.
O ascetic, she would constantly engage in quarrels with her husband; she would perpetually and at will revile her elders with vulgar speech.
That impure woman would always eat alone in secret from the cooking vessel.
She should daily give the remnants of her food to her elders.

O Brahmin, she should always say, "I am a virtuous wife," even though her mind is constantly fixed on a paramour; she is always a source of mental agitation for her husband due to his quarrels. 48-49.
O twice-born one, once her husband saw her returning and rebuked her; he struck her, for she was possessed of every sin. Filled with rage, she went indeed to an empty house.
Sleeping and remaining unaware of her situation, she did not eat any food or water.
O Brahmin, by chance on that day, it was the Ekādaśī vow— the side-turning of Viṣṇu— which destroys all sins.
Then, at dawn, that woman arrived there on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism, her mind overflowing with anger;
she had remained without food for two days and had become stainless.
O twice-born one, she passed away at night on the day of Jayantī.
Then, by the command of Yama, terrifying messengers arrived with nooses and mallets in their hands to take her away in that state. (54–55)
When he resolved to bind her and lead her to the abode of Yama,
the messengers of Viṣṇu, bearing conchs, discs, and maces, arrived; they then cut the noose and led her, free from sin, upon a divine chariot.
They caused her, who was stainless, to ascend to the abode of Hari.
Then, surrounded by those gods who had arrived, she attained that auspicious and rare day of Viṣṇu.
O best of the twice-born, the majesty of that day of Viṣṇu has thus been recounted to you.

Even one who acts without desire would go to the abode of Hari; moreover, a mortal who goes to the house of Hari on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) to offer a lamp gains a fruit greater than that of the horse-sacrifice at every step.

Those who listen to or recite the Purāṇas on the day of Hari obtain the fruit of the gift of a tawny cow for every single syllable. Thus ends the narration of the majesty of the Day of Hari within the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka.
The Fifteenth Chapter on Names.
Chapter Sixteen. Śaunaka said:
"O Sūta, by what action and by what means does the destruction of sins occur?
May there be the grace of Śrī Hari; please tell me that out of compassion.
(1) Sūta said:
Listen, O Śaunaka, I shall speak that which destroys the sins of those who hear it, by which the grace of Viṣṇu— indeed, that which causes the destruction of all evil— may be obtained.
On the full moon day, however, whichever brāhmaṇa is endowed with a state of devotion...
O Sage, one should perform various kinds of worship for the Lord of the Universe;
his sins accumulated over ten million lifetimes shall perish, and the grace of this Śrī Rāmaṇa will certainly arise within him. 3-4.
Whoever should devoutly offer food to a twice-born on the twelfth day,
his sins perish just as darkness does at the rising of the sun.
O twice-born one, that man who should perform the ceremonial bathing of Śrī Hari with milk—
Devotion to Śrī Hari [is attained] immediately on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) by means of sugar and other offerings. Indeed,
that donor who gives a flower like a stone to Śrī Hari without a mantra goes to a downward state.
Whatever gift a man may give to one who is like a stone— a fool among those who dwell upon the earth— no merit whatsoever accrues to him.
A twice-born man devoid of learning who, out of delusion, accepts a gift, is a person of foolish intellect.

Just as one who has consumed the fire of time (kālānala) perishes, so too shall he go to hell. O best of Brahmins, just as there may be an elephant made of wood or a deer made of painting, so are those Brahmins devoid of learning; they are merely bearers of the name. 10.
Just as water situated on a path is purified by wind and the sun, so too,
upon seeing a Pārṣada with devotion, one's sin is destroyed. Furthermore,
that man who, in the month of Āśvina, on the full-moon day, [offers] oblations of ghee...
One should offer parched grains (lāja) to Śrī Hari, and even a single cowrie shell for His amusement.
Through devotion, such a person goes to the abode of Hari, from which there is no return;
however, if a man does not give out of delusion, Hari is not pleased with him.
Whoever steals even a single cowrie on the full moon day will certainly dwell in the abode of Hari for that many days during the month of Āśvina.
Long ago, there was a man in Karavīrapura who was a Śūdra and utterly merciless.
Known by the name Kāladvijodvijaśreṣṭha, he was a sinner who inspired fear;
though intent on his own affairs, he was a destroyer of his master’s work.
Once, having met his death, the terrifying messengers of Yama arrived.
They arrived to lead him to the abode of Yama;
having bound him and brought him there, Yama saw him and questioned his minister.
(17) Yama said:
"O wise Citragupta, tell me in full detail what deeds— whether auspicious or inauspicious— this man has performed as a minister.
Citragupta said:
"O King, let this sinner of evil conduct, who has destroyed his master's work, be cooked in hell for a hundred manvantaras; he possesses not even an atom of merit. 19.
"O King, let this cruel man remain in the womb of a serpent for a hundred manvantaras."
Having attained birth as a stone, he remained there in the house continuously.
Sūta said: O Brahmin, after that period of time, he fell into hell.
After that, he was born in a very miserable state within the womb of a serpent in a stone house.
Once, O twice-born one, on the full moon day of the month of Āśvina,
he cast parched grain and cowries outside from the serpent's hole.
Having fallen at the feet of Hari, Hari himself—
the compassionate destroyer of suffering— quickly destroyed his sin.
Once, when the time had come, he departed to the state of death.
O twice-born one, the messengers of Yama arrived many times to bring him [there]; when they bound him and set out to lead him toward the abode of Yama,
then the messengers of Viṣṇu, bearing conchs, discs, and maces, arrived.
Having cut the noose, he then ascended that divine chariot, his sins having been removed;
the messengers of Yama fled, and he caused him to be placed there.
Then the serpent, surrounded by them, went to the abode of Viṣṇu.
There he remained before Hari, freed from rebirth.
O twice-born one, I do not know what certain merit would accrue to him who, with devotion, offers parched grain with ghee and even a single cowrie shell to Hara. 27–28.
