Whoever should hear this chapter, which destroys sin, his sins shall perish through the grace of Śrī Hari as well. 29.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. 16.
The Seventeenth Chapter. Śaunaka said:
"Tell me also of the greatness of the water from Viṣṇu’s feet, which destroys all sins."
"O ocean of mercy, O one of great wisdom, tell me [this] with its root.
Sūta said:
"The auspicious water from the feet of Viṣṇu destroys all sins."
He who carries even a mere drop [of it] shall obtain the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrtha). O Brahmin, the water from Viṣṇu’s feet destroys sin through its very touch;
there is no such thing as untimely death, and one obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
O Brahmin, the sinner who drinks the water from Viṣṇu’s feet—his sin residing within the body undoubtedly goes to destruction; there is no doubt.
O twice-born one, [this applies when] the water from Viṣṇu’s feet is joined with a Tulasī leaf.
If one carries [the water] on one's head with devotion and, having sipped it, goes to the house of Hari,
that fruit which is obtained by giving gold equal to Mount Meru is attained by men simply by touching the water from Hari’s feet.
The fruit that men obtain by giving thousands of millions of cows,
that fruit is certainly attained by touching the water used for washing the feet. (7) The fruit that is obtained by performing thousands of millions of sacrifices—

By touching the water from Hari’s feet, men obtain ten million times that merit. O twice-born ones, the fruit obtained by people through the gift of ten million maidens is surpassed by the fruit gained from touching the water from Viṣṇu’s feet.

The fruit that a mortal obtains by giving seven crores of tusked elephants, he obtains by touching the water from the feet of Hari. (10) The fruit that a mortal would obtain by giving away the seven continents along with their crops—
By touching the water from Viṣṇu’s feet, one obtains even more than that from the brāhmaṇa. Listen, O brāhmaṇa, I shall tell you further in brief:
having touched the water from Viṣṇu’s feet, even a sinner goes to the abode of Hari. 11–12.
Śaunaka said: O Sūta, tell me out of compassion how, in the past, which living being attained the abode of Hari after merely touching or drinking [the water]? 13.
Sūta said:
Formerly, in the Tretā Yuga, there was a wicked brāhmaṇa named Sudarśana; that best of twice-borns would always eat on the day of Janārdana. 14.
He constantly reviled the scriptures and always disparaged religious vows;
he knew nothing other than his own belly.
Once, when his time had come, that twice-born man met his death.
The messengers of Yama arrived, bound him, and brought him to the abode of Yama.
Seeing him, Yama’s brother asked his minister in anger: "O Minister, tell me thoroughly what merit or what sin this man has."
"This brahmin is a great sinner and appears to be one of cruel deeds.
Citragupta said:
"Listen to his sin; there is not even a particle of merit in him."
O Lord, he always took his meal even during the day. O King,
that lowest of men who eats during the day of the Lord of Kamalā (Viṣṇu) would be eating excrement and goes to a terrible hell.
For a hundred Manvantaras, this embodied being shall remain in hell;
thereafter, he will take birth in the womb of a village pig.
Sūta said:
Then, by the command of Yama, that brahmin was cast into excrement by terrifying messengers for more than a hundred manvantaras;
thereafter, he was released as a village pig upon the earth.

One shall suffer in hell for a long time due to eating on the day of Hari (Ekādaśī). Then, O Brahmin, when his time had come, he met his death and was reborn in the womb of a crow, always eating excrement.
One day, O Brahmin, having drunk the water from the feet of Śrī Hari that was standing at the doorway, he was freed from all sins. On that very same day, a crow fell upon the hunter.
Having reached the stage of timely death, whether through disease or even by a crow, when that auspicious divine chariot yoked with royal swans arrives,
the crow ascends it and departs for the abode of Hari.
The greatness of the water from the feet, which destroys sin, has been told; the sinful man who hears it has his sin destroyed. 28.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Water from the Feet," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. 17.
Chapter Eighteen. Śaunaka said:
"If one who is utterly deluded should perform the act of approaching a woman who should not be approached, or [if he should approach her] during the period of birth-impurity (sūtaka)..."
"Tell me from the very root, by what means can his purification be achieved?
Sūta said:
O best of the twice-born, if a man approaches a Caṇḍāla or a Śvapākī..."
One should observe three fasts and then perform a *prājāpatya* penance; furthermore, one should undergo a tonsure including the crest-lock (*śikhā*) and give away two cows.
By giving a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's means, the virtuous twice-born attains purification.
Whether it be a Kṣatriya, a Cāṇḍāla, or a Vaiśya who goes [to the cremation ground],
he should perform the Prājāpatya penance and a Sakti-cchra, and give two pairs of cows. O ascetic, if a Śūdra or even a dog-cooker (Śvapākī) follows [the corpse], [he must likewise perform these].
One should give four pairs of cattle and perform the Prājāpatya vow. If,
being deluded, one should approach his mother, sister, daughter, or daughter-in-law, he should then perform three Kṛcchra penances.
Having performed three *cāndrāyaṇa* penances, one should then give away three pairs of cattle;

having shaved one's head including the top-knot (*śikhā*), one should thereafter drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). O ascetic, even after the fire has been offered in sacrifice, one becomes pure in this manner.
If one approaches out of delusion the wife of a father, the wife of the best of the twice-born, or likewise a mother’s sister;
or the wife of a guru, a maternal aunt, a brother’s wife, or a woman born of one’s own lineage,
one should perform two Prājāpatya penances.

O Brahmin, by performing three Cāndrāyaṇa penances and giving five pairs of cows as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the brāhmaṇas, one is purified; of this there is no doubt. Furthermore, that fool who approaches a cow should observe a fast for three days.
By giving a cow and likewise food, one becomes purified; of this there is no doubt.
O twice-born one, having pulled a prostitute, a she-ass, a sow, a monkey, or a buffalo up to their necks from the mud of cow-dung and water, [one is purified]. 11-12.
One should remain there without food; by three nights alone one becomes pure.
Having shaved one's head including the top-knot, one should fast for three nights.
By staying in water for one night, one becomes pure; of this there is no doubt.
But when a man, deluded by lust, approaches a Brahmin woman,
he should perform three Prājāpatya penances and likewise three Cāndrāyaṇas; furthermore, O ascetic, he must give away three cows to attain purification.

A twice-born man who has had intercourse with a Brahmin woman should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for five nights and give two cows as a sacrificial fee; he is purified thereby, of this there is no doubt. When one approaches another's wife, he should perform the Kṛcchra-sāntapana penance.

As is a bolt, so is a woman; therefore, one should avoid her. If a man should even once have intercourse with a woman of low caste or one who is base, he should perform the Prājāpatya penance; by this he is purified, without a doubt. (17–18)
A woman is like glowing coals and a man is like a pot of clarified butter;
O Brahmin, one should never stand near her.
That woman who, through a paramour, conceives a child is the destroyer of her lineage.
O Brahmin, she must be abandoned in every way; no fault whatsoever exists in that.
(20) A woman who departs from her home even after abandoning her own kinsmen—having been ruined and fallen from her family—there shall be no reunion with her again. (21)

If a woman, being deluded, should approach another man for the sake of solicitation, she should perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra penance and thereafter drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). She should then give two cows as a gift; thus she is purified, without a doubt.

O Brahman, if a foolish woman, deluded by another man, should come [to him], she must be abandoned by people; no fault is found in this. If a Brahmin, a king, or a priest, deluded by lust, should violate a Brahmin woman, [he too must be abandoned]. 23–24.
One should then give cow-hoof-shaped pieces [of gold]; one is purified thereby, of this there is no doubt.
24. Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Nineteen.
Śaunaka said:
O twice-born one, listen as I describe how purification occurs for those who have unknowingly consumed feces or urine, or who have again touched liquor. 1.
O Sage, one should perform two Prājāpatya penances, visit sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrthas),
give the gift of eleven cows along with a bull, and then have the hair shaved including the top-knot (śikhā).
Having gone to a crossroads, one should likewise perform the entire Prājāpatya vow.
Then one should give two cows, and thereafter drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

After feeding the Brāhmaṇas, one becomes pure; of this there is no doubt. This applies even to the case of eating the food of a Cāṇḍāla or drinking their water, whether done intentionally or in times of distress.

If any man eats [forbidden food], he should perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances; having shaved his head including the top-knot, he should then drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). One, two, three, or four cows should be given to Brahmins in successive order.
If one eats the food of a *vṛṣala*, the food of one in a birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), the food of those whose food is forbidden, or water [from such sources],
or when one eats the leavings of a *śūdra*— whether intentionally or during times of distress—
one should perform two *prājāpatya* penances as well as three *cāndrāyaṇas*.
Then he should give two cows and drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
having offered oblations into the fire and fed many Brahmins, he will certainly become pure.
O twice-born one, if food has been eaten by a rat, a mongoose, or a cat...
Having sprinkled [the person] with water containing sesame seeds and *darbha* grass, he becomes pure; of this there is no doubt.
O Brahmin, the man who eats onion, garlic, *śigru*, bottle-gourd, *gṛñjana*, or meat must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
A Brahmin should avoid from afar that Śūdra who is fond of liquor and meat and follows base occupations, just as one avoids a dog-cooker; however,
those who are devoted to the service of the twice-born and abstain from liquor and meat [should be accepted].
Those who are devoted to their own duties of giving should be known as the best among the *vṛṣalas*.
(12) If a Brahmin eats during a period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or death-impurity (*mṛtaka*) out of ignorance, he becomes pure by reciting the *Gāyatrī* ten thousand times. (13)

O ascetic, a Kṣatriya becomes pure by [drinking] five thousand [units] of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and a Vaiśya by five thousand; even a Śūdra becomes pure in this way. However, a person of low caste who drinks ghee, water, curd, or milk contained in a vessel belonging to such a person [is purified by the same penance].
Even if [this] varṇa [has intercourse] out of ignorance, he should perform the Prājāpatya vow (15). He should give abundant gifts and become purified by the fire according to the rule;
for Śūdras, there is not even a fast, but they are purified by giving alone (16).
O twice-born one, that man who has been struck with a staff or other such lowly instruments should have his hair shorn along with the top-knot and observe a fast for a day and night;
he should then perform either the Prājāpatya vow or the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.

He should then undergo a tonsure including the top-knot and drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). Thereafter, he should give two cows as a gift and offer food and other oblations into the fire.
This applies even if a Brahmin intentionally or by chance drinks liquor in his own home. 18–19.
If any man eats [the food of such a person], he too must be cast out from his family; likewise one who destroys cattle or seeds, one who cuts down trees, and one who is lazy.
A thief of gold shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance and observe three *prājāpatya* vows.
Having performed a tonsure including the top-knot, he should likewise drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having offered oblations into the fire according to the prescribed rite, he should likewise give three cows as a gift.
O ascetic, his food and even his water may be accepted.
One should eat in the morning for three days, in the evening for three days, and for three days one should not eat at all; this is the Prājāpatya vow.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with kuśa grass— The output should be only the translation, no additional text.
O Brahmin, having fasted for one night, one should drink [the decoction] for two days;
this Sāntapana Kṛcchra, which removes all sins, is thus remembered by the Sage.
Furthermore, one should eat a single morsel each for three days in the morning, evening, and as an unasked meal.
One should fast for three days; this is the vow known as Atikṛcchra.
O twice-born sage, one should drink hot water, milk, and ghee, each for three days respectively; bathing once a day is declared to be the Taptakṛcchra, which removes all sins.
Abstaining from food for twelve days is the *kṛcchra* penance that destroys sin; it is known as the *parāka*, O ascetic, and is well-established in tradition.
One should increase the number of mouthfuls by one each day during the bright fortnight and decrease them during the dark fortnight.
It is recorded that during the waning of the moon, one should not eat; this is known as the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
A self-controlled Brahmin should eat four morsels in the morning when the sun has risen, and four when the sun has set; this is recorded as the Śiśu-Cāndrāyaṇa.
A woman who has killed a pumpkin gourd should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for three days;
she should give five pumpkin gourds along with gold and clothing, and her food should be accepted without restriction, O ascetic. (30)
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Twenty. Śaunaka said:
"What meritorious deed did he perform such that, having done it, those who are like frogs in the dark well of ignorance during the Kali age will cross over the ocean of saṃsāra?
Sūta said:
O Brahmin, in the month of Kārttika, which is dear to Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, she should perform her morning ablutions;
with a concentrated mind and devotion, she should worship Rādhā-Dāmodara,
having abandoned meat and other forbidden foods, and being solely intent on service to her husband.
She goes to the exceedingly rare abode of Śrī Hari known as Goloka (3).
She who offers incense and lamps to Rādhā and Dāmodara during the month of Kārtika goes to the abode of Viṣṇu, having cast off all her sins (4).

Any woman who, during the month of Kārttika, gives a garment at the temple to Rādhā and Dāmodara, shall dwell for a long time with Śrī Hari. She who offers fragrant flowers and garlands to Rādhā and Dāmodara [shall likewise dwell there].
She who gives perfume and an offering of sugar and other sweets to Rādhā and Dāmodara on this day in the month of Kārtika shall indeed go to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha. 6-7.

O Brahmin, whatever one gives to a twice-born person during the month of Kārttika for the pleasure of Rādhā and Dāmodara, its merit shall be inexhaustible. O twice-born one, that woman who with devotion worships Rādhā and Dāmodara in Kārttika—
If she does not perform the morning worship until evening, she shall dwell in hell for a long time.
In some future birth, she may become a widow in her own birthplace and, having previously been beloved by her husband, she may even become unloved by him.
Long ago, in the Tretā Yuga, there was a certain Śaṅkara named Vipravṛṣala who resided in the country of Saurāṣṭra; his wife was named Kalipriyā,
who always desired a paramour and regarded her husband as no more than a blade of grass.
Thinking, "This husband is my worthy master,
my lord, and my supreme person," that utterly deluded woman always gave him her leftovers; due to association with the base, she even ate meat and liquor.
She may constantly subject her master to reproaches and even be harsh at will;
she may become a tethering rope for his feet, or perhaps he might even die from some cause. Once he is dead, I shall enjoy him as I please.
Having reflected thus,
O twice-born one, he then made a secret agreement with that single Jāra, saying, "We two shall go to another country.
At night, while the master was asleep, the twice-born man cut his throat.

Having cut off her hair, she went to the appointed place for her lover; O twice-born one, seeing that the man who had come as her lover had been devoured by a leopard, she wept aloud and fell down in a swoon.
Having recovered her breath after a long time, she lamented piteously and deludedly.
Kalipriyā said:
"Having killed my own husband, I have come to another man."
"By fate, a tiger has devoured that husband of mine; what shall I do? Where shall I go? I have been deceived by the Creator.
(19) Sūta said:
Then, O Brahmana, Kalipriyā returned to her own home; having offered her face to her husband at the doorway, she lamented.
Kalipriyā said:
"O Lord, tell me at least this much: what extremely cruel deed have I, a servant of Hānātha, committed?
To which world shall I go? Please speak these words to me. Let me be reviled as I wish, but let me be censured. (21)
"O Lord, nothing new remains for me to say.
Sūta said:
He bowed at his feet and departed toward another city.

Having entered there, O twice-born one, those women saw many meritorious people— Vaiṣṇavas intent on their morning ablutions in the Narmadā— and even the women in that river committed an offense against Dāmodara.
Having seen him, she, filled with devotion and humility, performed worship with conch blasts and great festivals,
using perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, various garments, fruits,
and mouth-fresheners.
He asked, "Tell me, O women, what is this that you are doing?
The women said:
"Everything was well with us until the two auspicious ones, Rādhā and Dāmodara, arrived."
O Mother, having performed this auspicious worship that removes all sins, the sin accumulated over ten million births was destroyed and our abode was attained; for she,
having abandoned meat and other offerings, performed this worship on the day of Hari.
O twice-born one, having attained the state of death on the full moon day, her stainless servants quickly went toward the abode of Yama;
filled with rage, they bound her with leather ropes in order to lead her away.
Then the messengers of Viṣṇu arrived in a celestial chariot made of gold;
bearing conchs, discs, maces, and lotuses, and adorned with forest garlands,
they struck the messengers of Yama with the edges of their discs until the latter fled.
Mounted upon a golden celestial chariot adorned with royal swans, she arrived at the temple of Viṣṇu surrounded by them;
there she remained for a long time, enjoying pleasures as she desired.
O Brahmin, he who performs the worship of Rādhā-Dāmodara in the month of Kārttika goes,
freed from all sins, to the enchanting realm known as Goloka.
And whatever woman listens to this with devotion and a concentrated mind, [she too attains that same state].
The sin accumulated over ten million births of that very person is destroyed. 34.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of the Worship of Rādhā-Dāmodara," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka.
Chapter Twenty-One.
Śaunaka said: O Sūta,
son of Muni, you should tell us correctly the entire procedure for the most excellent month of Kārttika, as well as its specific observances.
Sūta said:
O best of the twice-born, with a concentrated mind, one should perform the vow of Kārttika on the full moon day of Āśvina, until the Udbodhinī [full moon] occurs.
During the day, a wise man should void urine and excrement facing north, remaining silent; at night, O twice-born one, he should do so facing south,
provided it is not near a path, water, a cow-pen, a cremation ground, or an anthill.
One who observes a vow must never perform the voiding of urine or feces;
one should not discharge excrement or urine in the most excellent places.
Having taken pure earth, one should then wash the left hand.
First, twenty applications of water and clay should be made for the sake of purification;
five on the anus,
ten on the left hand, ten on both hands, and three each on the two feet.
Then one should perform the purification of the mouth and the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the bath. Having meditated upon Dāmodara in the heart, one should then recite this mantra:
"O Janārdana, I shall perform the morning bath in the month of Kārtika. (7-8)
For the sake of pleasing Dāmodara, [I offer] this sin-destroying [offering] along with Rādhā; obeisance to the lotus-navelled one, to Śrī Kṛṣṇa who reclines upon the waters. 9.
Obeisance to You; together with Rādhā, accept this arghya and be gracious to me.
Then, O Brahmin, one should perform the ritual bath and apply the *tilaka* according to the prescribed rules.
Whatever action a person performs while devoid of the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, all that action is fruitless; this which I speak is the truth.

That body of human beings which is devoid of the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* should not be looked upon; having seen it, one should gaze at the sun. On whose forehead the auspicious white *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* made of clay is seen—

Even a Cāṇḍāla whose soul is purified is indeed worthy of worship; of this there is no doubt. However, those lowest of men who apply the flawless vertical *puṇḍra* mark, on their foreheads there is always the footprint of a dog—of this there is no doubt.
Having completed the rituals performed at dawn,
O Brahmin, one should worship with devotion Tulasī, the beloved of Hari and the destroyer of sins;
then, with a mind fixed on Śrī Hari, one should listen to the Puranic narrative.
Then, with devotion and observance of vows, one should worship that Brahmin according to the prescribed rites.
One should always avoid another’s seat, another’s food, another’s bed, and another’s wife; especially so during the month of Kārttika.
One observing the vow in Kārttika should always avoid *sauvīraka*, black gram, meat, honey, and *rājamāṣa* (mungo beans) and the like; likewise,
O twice-born one, one should avoid the citron fruit, meat, flour, and food that has been left overnight.
Dhānyamāṣa and masūrikā are said to be non-meat; the milk of cows is non-meat; salt produced from the earth is non-meat, O Brahmin; and indeed, the limbs of living beings are meat.
All juices purchased from a twice-born man and water situated in a small pond [are likewise considered meat].

O tiger among the twice-born, one should practice celibacy during the fourth period of life and eat from the leaves of the *patra* tree; one should also avoid anointing oneself with oil. One must likewise avoid mushrooms, lotus stalks, asafoetida, onions, and the leaf of the *pūtika* plant. (20–21)
Garlic, radish, drumstick, as well as the fruit of the bottle gourd,
wood-apple, eggplant, pumpkin, eating from a bell-metal vessel,
food cooked by two people, food from a woman who has recently given birth, fish, and a menstruating woman’s bed. 22.
One observing the Kārtika vow should avoid eating food more than twice a day and refrain from sexual union with women.
(23) A householder Brāhmaṇa should always avoid the dhātrī fruit during the time of the sun; by eating kūṣmāṇḍa, there will be loss of wealth, and by eating bṛhatī, one shall not remember Hari. (24)
In the *paṭola* there is an increase in boils; in the *mūlaka*, there is a loss of strength;
in the *kalañjī*, one becomes deformed; and in the *vilva*, one is born into the animal realm.
In the *nimbu*, there is rebirth as an animal; in the *tāla*, there is the destruction of the body; and in the *nārikela*, there is foolishness.
One who eats the *tuṃbī* gourd incurs a sin equal to that of eating cow's flesh; the consumption of *kalindaka* is equivalent to the killing of a cow.
The *śimbī* bean is said to cause sin, while the *pūtikā* is a killer of Brahmins.
By eating the eggplant (*vārtāka*), there shall be the loss of one's children, and by eating black gram (*māṣaka*), one becomes chronically ill.
There is great sin in eating meat; one should avoid it on the first lunar day (pratipad) and other such days.
O twice-born one, he who avoids food for some time for the pleasure of Lord Hari should, at the conclusion of his vow, give that [food] to a Brahmin and then eat himself.
The messengers of Yama flee from a Brahmin who observes the Kārtika vow and acts according to the injunctions, just as elephants flee upon seeing a lion; O Brahmin,
the vow of Viṣṇu is supreme, and a hundred sacrifices are not equal to it.
Having performed the ritual, the observer of the Kārtika vow goes to heaven and Vaikuṇṭha; whatever evil deed, born of the mind, speech, or body,
he may have committed against a Brahmin, it dissolves in an instant upon seeing one who observes the Kārtika vow.
Even the four-faced Brahmā would not be capable of describing the merit of one who observes the Kārttika vow as prescribed,
by performing which all impurity departs in ten directions like a bird.
"O twice-born one,

on both full-moon days of the month of Kārttika, one who observes the vow should give food, clothing, and other gifts according to one's ability for the pleasure of Śrī Hari, and should also feed brāhmaṇas. (34)
The observer of the vow should keep a vigil at night with dancing, singing, and other such activities;
whoever hears this with devotion, their sin is destroyed.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter of the Brahma-khaṇḍa in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka.
The twenty-second chapter.
Śaunaka said:
O omniscient one, tell us the majesty that destroys the sins of those who hear it.
Out of incomparable compassion for the welfare and benefit of all living beings.
Sūta said:
O twice-born one, he whose grove stands in the vicinity of Tulasī—

Because the home possesses the nature of a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha), the servants of Yama do not come there. O Brahmin, men who plant the auspicious grove of Tulasī, which removes all sins, are the best of men; they behold the Son of the Sun (the Lord).

O best of the twice-born, for one who performs the planting, protecting, serving, seeing, and touching [of the Tulasi plant], all sin shall be destroyed. Those who worship Hari with tender Tulasī leaves—
Noble-minded brāhmaṇas go to the abode of Kāla;
the Ganges and other excellent rivers, as well as Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Maheśvara,
along with the gods and holy places such as Puṣkara, all abide within a tulasī leaf.
The sinner who, joined with *tulasī* leaves, gives up his life-breaths, goes to the abode of Viṣṇu; this which I have spoken is the truth.
One who is smeared with the earth of *tulasī*, even if joined with hundreds of sins, [attains the same].
The man who gives up his life shall go to the abode of Hari.
O Brahmin, sin does not touch the body of one who wears the sandalwood paste from Tulasī wood; he goes to the supreme state.
He who wears a garland of Tulasī wood around his neck,
even if he is impure or of improper conduct, shall go to the abode of Hari through devotion.
A garland made of Dhātrī fruits or produced from Tulasī wood [is likewise auspicious].
On whosever body this is seen, that man is indeed a Bhāgavata. He who wears a garland made of Tulasī leaves around his neck,
especially one that has been offered as the remains of Viṣṇu’s food, is worthy of the salutations of the gods.
Furthermore, he who places a garland of *tulasī* around his neck and worships Janārdana obtains the merit of ten thousand cows for every single flower.
Those who, being motivated by mere worldly reasons and possessed of sinful minds, do not wear this garland—
Those who have been burnt by the fire of Hari’s wrath do not return from hell.
One should never abandon a garland of tulasī, especially a garland of dhātrī, which destroys great sins and bestows dharma, kāma, and artha. 14–15.
As many hairs as one touches with the wind from the garland worn by the nurse of men, for that many thousands of years does he dwell in the abode of Keśava.
Having offered a garland made of tulasī wood to Keśava, [one attains this merit].
That man who wears [it] with devotion—indeed, for him there is no sin.
Seeing a garland made of Tulasī wood, the messengers of the King of the Dead flee far away, like a leaf driven by the wind. 17–18.
O best of the twice-born, when a superior man offers funeral cakes (piṇḍa) in the shade of a Tulasī, a non-poisonous plant (avipina), or a Dhātrī tree, his ancestors attain liberation.
O twice-born one, [one should offer water] upon the hand, the head, the throat, the two ears, and the mouth.
He who wears the *dhātrī* fruit should be known as Hari himself.
O Brahmin, O twice-born one, if one worships Śrī Hari with *dhātrī* leaves and fruits, the sins accumulated over ten million births perish in a single act of worship. 20–21.
O twice-born one, the gods, sages, and sacred fords always reside in Kārtika by taking refuge in the Dhātrī tree.
In Kārtika, on the twelfth day, [one should offer] a Dhātrī leaf and a Tulasī leaf.
He who goes to another's house shall go to hell, which consists of agonizing torments.
O Brahmin, the sin arising from the contact with food that a man incurs by eating in the shade of a Dhātrī tree during the month of Kārtika perishes for him for an entire year.

O best of the twice-born, if one performs the worship of Hari in the month of Kārtika in the midst of a Tulasī grove or at the root of a Dhātrī tree, he certainly goes to Vaikuṇṭha; even if he is situated merely at the base of a Tulasī plant, O foremost of the twice-born.
The sinner who devoutly takes upon his head the water dripping from a Tulasī leaf goes to the abode of Hari;
having bathed in all sacred fords, he goes to the abode of Hari at the end.
O great sage, in former times during the Dvāpara age, there was a certain best of the twice-born who, having bathed and offered water with tulasī leaves, went home;
by virtue of his merit, he became known as Āditya in name and like Mārtaṇḍa in splendor. 28.
A certain eater, afflicted by thirst and burdened with great sin, arrived;
having drunk water from the very roots of the Tulasī plant, his sins were destroyed.
Then, a hunter named Yaśāsimardana also arrived in haste. (29-30)
He said, "I ate the food, and having eaten, I went away after breaking [the vessel].
Having placed it in a cooking pot, I have indeed come back to you, O destroyer. He pierced him, for he was destined to go to his life's end by the command of Yama.
The servants of Yama arrived, enraged, with nooses and mallets in their hands;
having bound him, they intended to take him away. Then the servants of Viṣṇu arrived, and having cut his leather noose, they placed him in a beautiful chariot.
They quickly helped him mount [the vehicle] and, filled with humility, asked:
"O holy ones, by what merit indeed is he being led away?
They replied: "This man was formerly a king who performed exceedingly great meritorious deeds."
In some places, he took away Suṃdarī, a beautiful woman;
by this sin, the king went indeed to the inexhaustible realm of Yama.
There, by the command of Yama, you were made to undergo suffering.
O King, having slept with a woman made of copper, he engaged in play upon a red-hot iron bed; through his own actions, he experienced such distress that,
by the command of Yama, he was placed upon a terrifying, heated iron pillar.

Then, having remained there, embraced, and eaten, the king suffered misery for a long time; he was drenched with streams of caustic water by others in the abode of Yama. Thereafter, when his portion in hell was exhausted, he repeatedly entered sinful wombs.
Having attained birth and experienced long-lasting suffering through one's own karma,
one who drinks the water from the root of a *tulasī* plant goes to the abode of Hari.
Now, having heard those words, the messengers departed as they had come.
Together with him, the messengers of Viṣṇu went to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
O Sage, I do not know what might happen for those who perform service with devotion to Tulasī, whose sin-destroying majesty has been described by Brahmā. 41–42.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Greatness of Tulasī," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka.
Chapter Twenty-three.
Śaunaka said: O Sūta,
out of compassion, please tell us the majesty of Muni which destroys all impurities, even regarding the remaining five days of the month of Kārttika.
Sūta said:
Listen, O Śaunaka, to that greatness which destroys sins, concerning which you have asked;
I shall indeed recount it regarding the month of Kārttika and its remaining five days.
O tiger among sages, the Viṣṇu-pañcaka is the most excellent among all vows;
he who worships Śrī Hari along with Rādhā therein with devotion,
using perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, garments, and various kinds of fruits— 3.
One who is free from all sins goes forever to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Whether he be a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic,
one does not attain the supreme station without performing the Viṣṇu-pañcaka.
The Viṣṇu-pañcaka is renowned as meritorious and the remover of all sins;
whoever performs a bath there obtains the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
O Brahmin, it is situated in front of Śrī Hari and near the Tulasī plant.
Whoever, out of a spirit of devotion, offers a lamp filled with ghee for the pleasure of Śrī Hari in the sky, goes to the abode of Viṣṇu;
even a sinner reaches the realm of Hari— this which I have spoken is the truth.

One should bathe Acyuta with devotion using honey, milk, ghee, and so forth; to that virtuous person, Hari, being pleased, shall surely grant his grace. One should offer the supreme food (paramānna) as a sacrificial offering (naivedya) to the Lord of the gods.
Even the four-faced Brahmā is indeed unable to calculate his merit.
Having worshipped Hṛṣīkeśa on the eleventh day with a concentrated mind,
one who has properly obtained cow-dung should attend upon Him according to the mantras.
The observer of the vow should consume cow’s urine with the recitation of mantras on the twelfth day,
likewise milk on the thirteenth, and curd on the fourteenth;
having thus fasted for four days for the sake of purifying his sins.
On this fifth day, having bathed and worshipped Keśava according to the prescribed rites,
one should devoutly feed the Brāhmaṇas and give them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). Thereafter,
one should eat only at night, consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) consecrated with mantras.
O Brahmin, he who is unable to do this should indeed offer fruits and roots,
or even sacrificial food (haviṣya), according to the prescribed injunctions;
or he may perform the "Five-fold Rite" (pañcaka) for Śrī Hari with tulasī leaves.
One should worship him, for he is to be known as the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself.
(16) In ancient times, during the Tretā Yuga, there was a Śūdra devoted to the livelihood of a bandit named Daṇḍaka, who constantly reviled righteousness. (17)
One who speaks untruths, a betrayer of friends, one greedy for the amorous dalliances of a prostitute,
a stealer of a Brahmin’s property, a cruel man, one devoted to approaching the wives of others, a slayer of those who have sought refuge, and one who associates with heretics. 18.
O best of the twice-born, having observed that he was always an eater of cow-flesh, a drinker of liquor, a constant reviler of others,
a betrayer of trust, and one who cut off the livelihood of his kinsmen— having seen him to be so utterly wicked— the Brahmin [left] his house. (19-20)
His kinsmen, having arrived and being incensed by his devotion to sin, said:
"O fool! O you of wicked conduct! You are being led toward your own destruction!"
"O best of the twice-born, because he has acquired unprecedented infamy within our stainless lineage," thus spoke they in anger; and out of fear of ill-repute,
they all abandoned that foremost of sinners from their midst.
Then, having lost all his wealth and power, he went to the great forest and engaged constantly in the work of a bandit together with his followers.
Out of fear of them as they traveled along the road, O Brahmin, [the people] did not even dare to eat their own nails.
Having obtained a little, those who were afflicted by hunger went toward another place.
O Brahmin, having entered there, they all saw many holy people— excellent twice-born Vaiṣṇavas— standing at the foot of a Dhātrī tree.
All these sages had departed; Daṇḍakara also went to their vicinity and indeed offered them his salutations.
Daṇḍakara said:

"O best of the twice-born, afflicted by hunger, my life-breaths will surely depart; give me something to eat, for I have come to you for refuge. Having heard his words, those who were devoted to dharma spoke.
"You are renowned as the remover of all sins during the Viṣṇupañcaka. Why do you desire to eat food today on the day of Hari? Tell me the specific reason; what is your name now? (28-29)

"O wise ones, I have uttered improper speech; though I have offered food and am free from taxes, I am burdened with all manner of sins. How can my liberation be achieved? They said to him, "Perform the most excellent vow, the Viṣṇu-pañcaka."
At the command of the brahmins, Vipra performed the Viṣṇu-pañcaka rite. Then, ascending the excellent chariot of Hari and attaining the form of Śrī Hari, he remained there, freed from rebirth.
Whoever listens with devotion to this narrative that destroys sin,
the sins accumulated over ten million births perish for them instantly.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Viṣṇu-Pañcaka," in the Brahma-Khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka.
The twenty-fourth chapter. Śaunaka said:
O best among the learned, O knower of reality, O high-minded one, please tell me.
O Sage, now [describe] the greatness of these gifts in their proper order.
Sūta said:
O best of sages, the gift of land is considered the most excellent among all gifts.

By whomsoever this gift is made, it is considered to possess the fruit of all gifts. O best of the twice-born, he who gives land abounding in crops to a Brāhmaṇa enjoys happiness in the world of Viṣṇu for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
Having obtained birth upon this earth as a sovereign monarch,
that king shall enjoy the entire world for a long time and then indeed go to the abode of Śrī Hari.
He who bestows even a piece of land the size of a cow-hide upon a twice-born man [attains the same].
Freed from all sins, he goes to the abode of Hari.
Where one hundred cows and one bull stand restrained, the great sages declare that land to be the measure of a *gocarma*. 5-6.
Both the one who leads to the land and the one who gives the land go to heaven;
therefore, wise twice-born men should accept land even while abandoning hundreds of other gifts. That ignorant Brahmin who, being deluded, would abandon his land, [is lost].
In every birth, that brahmin shall experience extreme suffering.
However, he who, having obtained land from another, gives it to a twice-born man—
to him the Lord of the World grants the supreme state.

O twice-born one, he who seizes land given by himself or given by another, along with ten million members of his lineage, goes to a most dreadful hell. Indeed, he who seizes land from a Brahmin, a god, or even another Brahmin [suffers the same].

O Sage, there is no atonement for that [sin] even in hundreds of millions of kalpas. O twice-born one, when a king protects land that has been given to another, the merit of that protection becomes ten million times greater than the merit of the original gift itself.
O twice-born one, whatever merit is obtained by giving away the earth with its seven continents, that same merit a mortal shall obtain who gives a cow to a member of the twice-born class,
and he who gives a bull to a poor family man.
Freed from all sins, he goes to the world of Śiva. He who gives gold the size of a sesame seed to a Brāhmaṇa goes to the abode of Hari, accompanied by ten million members of his lineage.
Whoever should give silver to a virtuous Brahmin,
a protector of the earth, attains the world of the Moon and shall drink nectar there forever.
Likewise, coral, pearl, diamond, and gem—

O best of the twice-born, he who gives gold goes to the heavenly world. Whatever merit a person obtains through the gift of a *tulāpuruṣa*, one obtains ten million times that merit by giving a *śālagrāma* stone. 17–18.
Whatever merit one obtains by giving away the earth consisting of seven islands, along with its mountains, forests, and groves, that indeed is obtained by the giver of a Śālagrāma stone.
Whoever gives a Śālagrāma stone to a brāhmaṇa, [obtains that same merit].
Therefore, O bull among the twice-born, for him who performs the Tulāpuruṣa gift, fourteen worlds bestowed by Nārāyaṇa are his;
and for his mother, there shall be no further rebirth.

The man who gives away the daughter of an excellent brahmin adorned with ornaments shall go to the abode of Brahmā; for him, there is no rebirth. There is no escape from hell for one who sells a daughter.

For one who performs the gift of a daughter in marriage, there is no returning from heaven again. He who gives a pair of sandals and an umbrella to a twice-born man goes to the city of Indra after death and shall dwell there for four kalpas.

O best of the twice-born, he who gives divine clothing to a virtuous Brahmin shall dwell for a long time in heaven wearing celestial raiment. O twice-born one, he who gives an old cow and worn-out clothing [attains the same merit].
Likewise, one who approaches a young girl who has not yet reached puberty goes to hell.
O Brahmin, a wise man should not even look at a seller of girls;
if he sees one, whether intentionally or through ignorance, he should gaze upon the sun.
O best of the twice-born, the giver of fruit shall go to heaven free from disease;
there he enjoys for thousands of kalpas a fruit that is like nectar. O twice-born one, the mortal who offers vegetables at the temple of Śiva—
For two kalpas, he enjoys the milk-rice (pāyasa), difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Furthermore, one who gives ghee, curd, buttermilk,
or milk goes to the abode of Viṣṇu and partakes in the drinking of nectar (sudhā).
The mortal who gives perfumes and flowers goes to the abode of the gods;
adorned with perfumes and flowers, he shall dwell there for thousands of yugas. He who gives to a Brāhmaṇa the gift of a bed, which is the essence of all gifts—
He who gives a seat shall dwell for a long time in the abode of Brahmā, reclining upon a couch. The giver of a pedestal and the giver of a lamp are freed from all evil deeds;
surrounded by rows of blazing lamps, he shall sit upon a lion-throne in heaven.
The excellent man who gives betel-leaf as a gift enjoys the entire earth in happiness;
having slept in the lap of celestial nymphs in heaven, he indeed eats betel-leaf there.
That best of men who performs the supreme gift of knowledge [attains the same].

After death, O best of the twice-born, he shall remain in the proximity of Viṣṇu for three hundred yugas. Having attained there that knowledge which is difficult to obtain, O twice-born one, he attains liberation through the grace of Śrī Hari, which is likewise difficult to attain.
The best of men who causes a helpless and suffering Brahmin to recite [the scripture] goes to the abode of Śrī Hari, freed from rebirth.
That man who, endowed with devotion and faith, gives a book [as a gift], [attains the same].
For every grain [of salt], one obtains the merit born from the gift of ten million tawny cows (kapilā).
A mortal who gives honey and molasses likewise goes to the ocean of sugarcane juice; and the man who bestows salt goes to the world of Varuṇa. 38–39.
O best of the twice-born, among all gifts, food and water have been proclaimed as the most excellent by all the sages who know the truth.
O foremost of the twice-born, he who has given food and water on this earth—

Therefore, O bull among the twice-born, all gifts that have not been given are [as nothing]; a man who gives food, O Brahmin, is proclaimed to be a giver of life. Consequently, among all gifts, the giver of food obtains the fruit.
Just as food is, so too is water; these two are declared to be equal.
O best of the twice-born, without water, food cannot be prepared. O tiger among the twice-born, hunger and thirst are likewise declared to be equal.
Therefore, food and water have been declared by the wise to be the most excellent.
O Brahmin, those best of men on earth who perform the gift of food are liberated from all sins and go to the abode of Hari. 44–45.
O ascetic, as many morsels of food as one bestows upon the earth,
so many instances of the killing of a Brahmin are surely destroyed;
and for those who give gifts of food, even their own bodies are freed from sin.
O Śaunaka, they suddenly depart, leaving behind those who grasp at their limbs. Therefore, the wise do not accept food from the most sinful;
those fools who accept it out of delusion become partakers of sin. 47–48.
O best of the twice-born, one should cause even a single drop of water to reach the earth;
liberated from all sins, he shall go to the abode of Hari.
O foremost of the twice-born, one should diligently accumulate wealth.
O Brahmin, one should disperse accumulated wealth through the act of giving (verse 50). Those who, out of miserliness, do not spend their wealth are exceedingly miserable;
at the end, having abandoned all their wealth, they depart destitute, O fearsome sage (verse 51).

O tiger among the twice-born, those men who give this gift constantly—whether having given it or not—are known as the lords of the world of men; yet they are poor and wretched, while the thieves [of virtue] are the great lords.
In the next world, O tiger among the twice-born, which is devoid of the self-restraint of the virtuous, [they suffer].

That which is given neither to the merciless nor to the friendless does not remain with the giver. A man who possesses wealth but neither eats it nor gives it away should be known as one who is truly poor; after death, he shall only release a sigh.

"Even charity has been declared by the seers of truth to be superior to austerity; therefore, O best of the twice-born, one should perform the act of giving with great effort. A donor should never give a gift to a member of the twice-born after having cast it aside."

[One goes] forever to the terrible hell that brings fear to all living beings. (56) If neither the giver nor the recipient remembers the gift, nor does the recipient ask for it, both shall dwell in hell as long as the moon and sun endure. (57)
"O best of the twice-born, whatever sins such as the killing of a Brahmin exist, they are destroyed by giving; therefore, one should practice the act of giving.
Thus ends the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Twenty-four.
Chapter Twenty-five. Śaunaka said:
This "Śrīpada," the life-story of Viṣṇu, destroys all calamities,
effects the destruction of all sins, wards off malevolent planets,
grants proximity to Viṣṇu, and bestows the fruits of the four aims of human existence.
The man who hears this with devotion at the conclusion [of the ritual] shall go to the abode of Hari.
The greatness of the utterance of the Name is heard to be most wonderful;
by the mere utterance of it, a person may attain the supreme state.
"In that same way, tell me now the procedure for the naming ceremony (*nāmakīrtana*).
Sūta said: Listen, O Śaunaka; I shall relate the dialogue which is a means to liberation."

Nārada previously asked Kumāra; I shall tell you that. Once, he questioned Sanatkumāra, who was seated on the bank of the Yamunā with a tranquil mind, while Nārada stood with his hands joined in reverence.
Having heard various kinds of dharmas as well as the violations of dharma,
Śrī Nārada said: "That which was described by the Blessed One as the violation of dharma for human beings— "
"How can there be its destruction? Tell me, O beloved of the Blessed One.
Śrī Sanatkumāra said:
"Listen, O Nārada, you who know the dharma of Govinda and are dear to Govinda."
That which was asked— the cause of liberation from the world, that which is beyond darkness (tamas)—
is [the state] where those who are devoid of all conduct, deceitful-minded, outcasts, deceivers of the world,
devoted to hypocrisy, egoism, drinking, and backbiting, and those who are sinful and cruel, [no longer exist]. 8-9.
O twice-born one, even those others who are devoted to wealth, wives, and sons— all those base ones indeed become pure by taking refuge in the lotus feet of Śrī Govinda.
He is the supreme bestower of liberation, the source of divine hands, the mine of compassion, and the ancient moving and unmoving being.
We bow down to those who, even when committing offenses, do not abandon their devotion to Hari;
for one who takes refuge in Hari is liberated even from every offense.
But he who commits offenses against Hari is the lowest of men.
The basis of one's name may sometimes be transcended by being free from that very name;
for through the transgression against all friends that is the name, one falls downward.
Śrī Nārada said:
"O best of Brahmins, what offenses committed against the name of the Blessed Lord destroy the natural disposition of men and lead them toward unrighteousness? Śrī Sanatkumāra said:

Since the censure of the virtuous constitutes the supreme offense, how could one endure the reproach of Him who is renowned as the auspicious Śrī Viṣṇu, whose every quality, name, and so forth [is the source of all]?
One who utters the name of Hari should perceive it as inseparable from his own intellect; indeed, such a person brings benefit to all.

(15) Disrespect toward the guru, reviling the Vedas and the scriptures, treating the explanatory passages (arthavāda) as mere literalities regarding the name of Hari, and the perception of sin in the Name—these do not exist for him; for his purification is achieved through the restraints (yamas). (16)
Neglecting one's religious vows and abandoning all auspicious deeds such as fire-offerings, as well as negligence,
lack of faith, turning away from the teachings, not listening to the instruction, and even hearing it, being devoid of joy— these are offenses against the Name of Śiva.
(17) He who, despite having heard the greatness of the Name, remains devoid of love is the lowest of men.
Even he who is the supreme offender regarding "I" and "mine" [is purified];

thus, O Nārada, this supreme name of the Blessed One, which brings happiness to me and to the sages, was spoken by Śaṅkara out of compassion— one that should always be avoided with great effort [by those unworthy].
Those who, despite knowing [the power of the name], suddenly avoid the ten offenses against the Name,
and who, refusing food, cause even their angry mother distress, suffer like children. Indeed,
one who is free from offense should always practice the chanting of the Name.
"O divine sage, by this name alone everything will be accomplished for you, and not otherwise.
Śrī Nārada said:
"O Sanatkumāra, [this is for those] who are fond of rash acts and devoid of discernment and detachment."
"How can we, who are devoted solely to our bodies, pleasures, and self-interest, remain free from offense?
(21) Śrī Sanatkumāra said: "If an offense has somehow occurred due to negligence,"
One should always chant His name and become solely dependent upon it.
For those who have committed offenses against the Name, the names themselves remove their sin;
when applied without ceasing, they alone are effective in accomplishing one's purpose. 22–23.

It is true that even a single name, whose mark has entered the path of memory or reached the root of the ear— whether its syllables are pure or impure, and whether it is separated by other sounds or not— certainly delivers one,
provided it is not situated amidst the heresy born of greed for the body and wealth.
O Brahmin, that which has been deposited here will very quickly produce its fruit.
This supreme secret was heard by Nārada from Śaṅkara in the past; it removes all inauspiciousness and wards off transgressions. 24–25.
O Nārada, even those men who are intent on committing offenses against Viṣṇu shall attain liberation simply by reciting His name;
for the entire majesty of the Name is celebrated throughout the Purāṇas. 26.
Therefore, O bestower of honor, you ought to hear the entire Purāṇa.
For him who possesses daily faith in hearing the Purāṇa, O brother,
Śiva and Viṣṇu, along with their attendants, shall become visibly pleased.
The fruit that one obtains by bathing at the holy site of Puṣkara, at Prayāga, or at the confluence of the Sindhu— twofold that fruit belongs to him who listens with faith.
Those who read the Purāṇas and listen to them with concentrated minds, [attain the same].
They obtain the fruit born from the gift of a tawny cow for every single syllable.
One without a son obtains a son; one seeking wealth obtains wealth;
one seeking knowledge obtains knowledge; and one seeking liberation shall attain liberation.

Those who listen to the Purāṇas, having indeed destroyed the web of sins accumulated over ten million births, go to the abode of Hari. One should worship the Brahmin who recites the Purāṇas with a spirit of devotion.
O Sage, with cows, land, gold, garments, perfumes, flowers, and so forth,
he who is filled with joy [should offer] a vessel fashioned from bell-metal as a water-vessel,
as well as an earring and a ring made of gold.
O ascetic, one should likewise offer a seat, flowers, and garlands; one must not practice stinginess regarding wealth, for a gift given with such parsimony yields inferior fruit.
A Brahmin should recite the Purāṇa for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals.
One who gives gold, silver, clothing, flowers, garlands, or sandalwood with devotion,
or a book, shall go to the abode of Hari;
those who complete a book according to this rule [shall likewise attain that goal].
O twice-born one, Citragupta shall record their names according to their worship.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. 25.
The twenty-sixth chapter. Śaunaka said: O wise one, I desire to hear this; tell it to me with its very root.

O Sage, what sin is there in breaking a promise? Or what merit is there in keeping one? What would happen, O Ocean of Mercy, if one were to show compassion by granting a servant as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) after taking a false oath? Or what would happen if it were a true one? 1-2.
Sūta said:
Listen, O tiger among sages, I shall relate this from the very beginning;
for you are the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas and are devoted to the welfare of all the worlds. 3.

O twice-born one, the merit obtained by a man who gives a hundred cows is surpassed ten-millionfold by the merit in fulfilling one's promise. Through the breaking of a promise, a fool goes to a terrible hell.
He is cooked there for as long as one hundred *manvantaras*; of this there is no doubt.
Then, having obtained birth here in the house of a poor man, he shall be destitute of food and clothing and afflicted by suffering due to his own karma.

One should take an oath by truth in the presence of the gods, the fire, and one's preceptor; as long as Viṣṇu’s lineage is not destroyed, that [oath] indeed burns the body. O Brahmin, what shall I say now regarding a false oath? 7.124.105–106a.

O Brahmin, for a hundred *manvantaras* one suffers in hell for speaking falsely; how much more so for touching the *nirmālya* (remnants of worship) of Śrī Hari? O best of sages, having truly taken [the *nirmālya*], seven generations of men are cooked in hell for a long time.
O Brahmin, having attained birth at some time, one may become a leper in every subsequent birth;
this happens through truth—what then is said regarding falsehood? That mortal who, having given a gift, protects his hand [from returning it] [is likewise affected].
O Kṛṣṇa, its attainment would be black; I tell you the truth, the absolute truth. As long as a mortal, having given his hand [in marriage], does not fulfill his word, the ancestors undergo torment.
But even if he himself goes to a most terrible hell, O tiger among sages, he will undoubtedly be delivered by ten million men after death. Śaunaka said:
"O Sage, tell me with respect— I wish to hear— how Kṛṣṇa was obtained by someone in the past through the protection of his right [hand]. Sūta said:
Formerly, in a certain city, there was a Śūdra named Vīravikrama;
he was a heavy eater with a large frame, possessed many tongues, and was exceedingly handsome.
He was wealthy, had sons, was refined, learned, and beloved by all people.
He was always a worshiper of Brahmins and guests;
O best of the twice-born, he was devoted to his ancestors, a keeper of his vows, a protector of the speech of his elders, and a servant of Hari. 16–17.
Once, a young and wise Śvapaca named Sundara, assuming the guise of a Brāhmaṇa, arrived at his house under a pretext.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"Listen to these wise words of mine; O immortal one, I am inauspicious.
Out of compassion, tell me today: what shall I do, and where shall I go?
A man should perform a marriage, especially with a Brāhmaṇa. (19)
"What is the use of gifts? What is the use of holy fords? What is the use of sacrifices or millions of vows?
(20) Having heard this, Vīravikrama spoke to the Brahmin: "Listen to my words, O Brāhmaṇa; I have a young daughter. (21)
"If you desire it, O Brahmin, I shall give [it] according to the prescribed rites;
I will take your right hand, for otherwise I will not.
Having heard these words of his, he took his right hand.
Filled with joy, the dog-cooker (śvapaca) spoke these words: 23.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"Having made an auspicious moment for me, give your daughter, who is endowed with auspicious qualities."
"In the scriptures it is certain that there will be many obstacles if there is delay.
Vīravikrama said, "O Brahmin, I shall give my daughter to you tomorrow; it cannot be otherwise."
That lowest of men would not perform [the rite] after placing his right hand [upon it].
Sūta said:
O Sage, having summoned the Brāhmaṇa Kṛṣṇaśarman, he spoke to him.

O twice-born one, he spoke all this to the domestic priest: "O Brahmin, since you wish to give your daughter to a Śūdra, how can that be? Do not give her, especially to one who is unknown and of low birth. (26-27)
O ascetic, all those born of that lineage, Janaka and the others, said:
"O father, O hero of valorous prowess, listen to our words.
The family, country, lineage, and wealth of this man are not known. (28)
"Because of his virtuous conduct and his youth, his kinsmen and relatives do not give him a maiden in marriage.
He said: 'O best of the twice-born, the fee given to me as my hand was taken must never, under any circumstances, be made otherwise.'"
Having spoken thus, he proceeded to give the maiden to them along with the brahmins;
seeing this, all the kinsmen were struck with wonderful amazement.
Hearing those true words, the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace [bestowed her].
O sage, he suddenly appeared, having mounted Garuḍa.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Blessed is your lineage, blessed is your dharma, and blessed are your mother and father."
Blessed is your truthful speech; blessed is your right hand.
Blessed is your deed and your birth, which is indeed not found elsewhere in the three worlds.
O virtuous one, by such action as this, you shall uplift your lineage.
Sūta said:
While Śrī Kṛṣṇa was speaking thus, a celestial chariot made of gold arrived, accompanied by hosts of attendants of Hari, and bearing the banner of Garuḍa everywhere. 35.
O Brahmin, Hari himself, the bearer of the conch and the lotus, placed his entire family— including even the outcaste dog-cooker who served as their priest— upon the chariot;
having taken them all, Hari went to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
Having remained there for a long time and having enjoyed that which is so difficult to obtain,
he who violates this command or who disregards the right hand— along with his entire lineage—
he goes to hell; I tell you the truth, the absolute truth.
O Brahmin, his food and water must not be accepted by the ancestors or the deities;
O best of the twice-born, even Dharma abandons his house out of fear. A person of deluded intellect who, having offered hope, creates despair, [is likewise forsaken].
Taking ten million people along with their kinsmen, he shall go to hell.
He who violates a word [of promise] finds his own dharma violated;
by kings, fire, and thieves—he is destroyed. O Brahmin, this is the truth, the truth, most certainly so. 40–41.

Having properly heard this *Svargottara*, one shall go to the supreme abode called Kṛṣṇa, being liberated while living in this world and the next. Thus ends the [section] in the *Brahmakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka.
The twenty-sixth chapter [ends].
Thus, the Brahma-khaṇḍa, also known by the name Svargottara, is complete.
Thus ends the fourth Brahma-khaṇḍa in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the fifth section, the Pātālakhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa;
Chapter One.
Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa! Homage to the venerable family deity!
Salutations to the lotus feet of the venerable Guru.
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the best of men, as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, one should then utter the word "Jaya. 1.
The sages said:
"O highly fortunate one, we have now heard from you the entire captivating Svargakhaṇḍa; O long-lived one, tell us now the life-story of Śrī Rāma."
Sūta said:
Now, on one occasion, Vātsyāyana, the best of sages, questioned the Lord of Serpents, the support of the earth, regarding this most pure narrative. 3.
Śrī Vātsyāyana said:
From you [I have heard] all remaining narratives concerning the creation and dissolution of the universe,
as well as the terrestrial globe, the celestial globe, and the determination of the circle of luminaries.

O sinless one, you have related the distinct determination of the principles (tattvas) such as the Great Principle (mahat-tattva) and other creations, as well as the various accounts of the deeds of kings,
including the wonderful history of the monarchs born of the Solar dynasty.
In that regard, there is the account of how Rāma, the destroyer of many great sins,
established a grove; I have heard from you in brief the story of that hero Rāma’s horse sacrifice, and I desire it in full detail.
"Even when merely heard, remembered, recited, or spoken, she removes great sins;
she bestows desired objects and grants satisfaction to the hearts of her devotees.
Śeṣa said:
Blessed are you, O best of the twice-born, for your mind is such as this—
eager for the nectar of the pair of feet of the hero of the Raghus.
All sages declare that association with the virtuous is the most excellent of all things.
Since this story of Raghunātha, which brings about the destruction of sins,
has come forth, you have bestowed a grace upon me by reminding me once again of Rāma, whose feet are illuminated by the jewels in the crowns of hosts of gods and demons. 10–11.
How insignificant am I, compared to the fire at the end of the Rāvaṇa-foe’s (Rāma’s) story,
wherein even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, are deluded and do not understand it?
Nevertheless, O Lord, I shall speak to you according to my own capacity.
Birds fly through the vast expanse of the sky by relying upon their own flight;
likewise, those whose intellect is of a certain capacity recount the life of Raghunātha according to that same extent, though its full scope extends for hundreds of millions of verses.
"The fame of Raghunātha’s virtuous wife will, through her own contact, make my intellect stainless, just as fire makes gold pure.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus to that best of sages, his eyes motionless in meditation,
he beheld with his wisdom a most auspicious and transcendent narrative;
his voice faltering and his limbs marked by great joy.
They again related the clear story of the son of Daśaratha.
Śeṣa said:
When the Lord of Laṅkā, the bringer of sorrow to gods and demons, had been slain...
When the moon-like splendor of the lotus-faces of the hosts of Apsarases was eclipsed by Him, all the gods, led by Indra, attained happiness;
having attained that happiness, they offered praise and bowed down like servants. 18–19.
Having established Vibhīṣaṇa, who was devoted to righteousness, upon Laṅkā,
Rāma, accompanied by Sītā, boarded the Puṣpaka chariot;
he was then joined by Sugrīva, Hanumān, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa.
Bibhīṣaṇa also followed with his ministers, eager for the departure; beholding Laṅkā with its walls and gateways shattered in many places,
and seeing there the Aśoka grove— the site where Sītā had stayed— he fainted.
He saw *śiṃśapā* trees there, in full bloom and covered with buds,
crowded with ogresses who had died out of fear of Hanumān. Having quickly observed all this, Rāma set out toward the city.
Accompanied by Brahmā and the other gods in their respective celestial chariots, the best of the Raghus was honored with the sounds of divine drums, which brought delight to the ears,
as well as by the dances of the Apsarases.
Showing Sītā the paths, sacred fords, hermitages,
and the sages, the sons of sages, and the chaste wives of sages— wherever they had previously made their dwellings with the wise Rāma. (26)
Accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, he showed them all;
while Rama was thus showing them his own city,
he beheld it, and furthermore, he saw the village of Nandigrāma near it.
There, King Vaibhara, established in righteousness,
protected the realm while bearing many marks of the sorrow born from the separation from his brother;
he slept on the ground, lived as a celibate student, and was endowed with matted hair and bark garments.
With his slender body emaciated and afflicted by suffering, he repeatedly recounted the stories of Rāma.
He did not even eat barley-gruel, nor did he drink water frequently;
and having offered salutations to the rising sun, he spoke as follows: (30–31)
O Lord of the gods, the eye of the world, destroy my great evil deeds!
For my sake, even Rāmacandra, who is worshiped by the entire universe, went to the forest, having entered the wilderness attended by Sītā, whose limbs are so delicate. (32)
Sītā, who once sat sorrowful upon a couch of blue lotuses,
and who never before experienced the scorching heat of the sun—
alas, that very Janakī now wanders through the forest for my sake! 33-34.
That Sītā who was never before seen by hosts of kings with longing eyes is surely now being gazed upon by Kirātas who have the form of Death;
she who once ate sweet food is no longer hungry.
"Ah! She desires the fruits of the stations beginning with Sāsīta and ending with Yavana.
Thus, every day after performing the ritual worship of the Sun, the great king Bharata, the beloved of Rāma, would speak these words morning after morning.

When his ministers— wise, learned in the scriptures, experts in policy, and sharing equally in his joy and sorrow— spoke thus to him, the king said to them: "O ministers, why do you speak in this way to me, an unfortunate man, the lowest of men?"
"For my sake, the eldest brother Rāma has reached the forest and is suffering.
Out of respect, I shall perform the purification of the sin of my unfortunate mother by repeatedly remembering the lotus-feet of Rāmacandra, O good ministers. (39-40)
Blessed is Sumitrā, the mother of a hero and beloved by her husband, whose son daily serves the feet of Rāma.
In that village surely resides Bharata, who is devoted to his brother. 41.
He beheld that village, where [Rāghava] was loudly uttering lamentations. 42.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Vision of the Village of Nandi in the Direction of Bharata’s Residence by Raghunātha," in the *Aśvamedha* section of the *Padma Purāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. 1.
The second chapter. Śeṣa said:
Now, with his mind overwhelmed by the longing to behold Him...
Again and again remembered was his brother Bharata, the foremost of the righteous;
he spoke to the powerful Hanumān, the son of the Wind,
while the darkness [of his face] was dispelled by the moon-like luster of his gleaming teeth.
"Listen, O hero Hanumān, to my words spoken by your brother,
which are faltering and distressed due to his long-standing separation.
Go, O hero, son of the Wind-god, to your brother."
He forcibly bears a body with a slender frame emaciated by separation from me;
he wears bark garments and maintains matted locks upon his head, and,
distressed by our parting, he would not even consume fruits.
To him, the wives of others will be like clods of earth and gold like a blade of grass; he, knowing his duty, will protect his subjects like his own sons, as if they were his own kin.
His body shall be consumed by the flames of the fire of grief born from separation from me.
Sprinkle [him] quickly with the rain of milk that is the message of my arrival—
[sprinkle] Rāma, who is accompanied by Sītā and joined by Lakṣmaṇa, along with Sugrīva and the other lords of monkeys, the Rakṣasas, and Vibhīṣaṇa.
"Report that he has arrived comfortably, seated upon the Puṣpaka throne,
so that this younger brother of mine may quickly find happiness through my arrival.
Having heard these words of the wise hero of the Raghus, [Vibhīṣaṇa] then...

Carrying out his command, he went to the village named Nandigrāma. Having gone to Nandigrāma, the wise one beheld Bharata, who was surrounded by elderly ministers and remained deeply distressed by the separation from his brother.
While the elder ministers were recounting the narrative of Rāmacandra, Bharata—
who was completely filled with the nectar of the lotus-feet of that [Lord]—
He was created by the Creator himself from a portion of his own being.
Seeing him, Bharata quickly rose with palms joined in reverence and said, "Welcome; tell me of Rāma's welfare. 14.
As he was speaking thus, his right arm throbbed;
his heart was freed from sorrow, and his face was filled with tears of joy. Seeing the king in such a state, the Lord of Monkeys replied:
Know that Rāma, along with Lakṣmaṇa, has arrived nearby.
My body drenched in the nectar of the news of Rāma’s arrival, I feel as if I have become thousand-mouthed to express the flood of my joy. 16–17.
"I have no sense of 'mine' regarding that which is being given to you by me; I am your servant until the end of my life, a messenger for Rāma’s commands.
Vasiṣṭha, having accepted the water-offering (arghya), was greatly delighted along with the elder ministers.
He beheld Rāmacandra, shown the way by Hanumān;
seeing from afar the charming Rāmacandra approaching, seated in the midst of the Puṣpaka chariot together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa. 19–20.
Rāma, seeing Bharata approaching on foot,
wearing matted hair, bark garments, and a loincloth,
and seeing his ministers likewise dressed in the attire of ascetics with matted hair, [was moved]. 21.
He saw that his form was emaciated due to being constantly afflicted by ascetic penance.
Seeing the king in such a state, Rāma also reflected: "Alas! This is the son of the wise Daśaratha, the king of kings."
My son has arrived on foot, wearing matted hair and garments of bark;
"O, look! This brother, a friend dearer than life itself—having heard that I have arrived nearby, Bharata has come with the joyful elder ministers and accompanied by Vasiṣṭha to see me. (25-26)
Speaking thus, the lord of men,
having been shown respect by Vibhīṣaṇa, Hanumān, and Lakṣmaṇa,
quickly descended from the Puṣpaka chariot into the courtyard of the sky, his heart moistened with longing due to their separation.

Seeing Rāmacandra, accompanied by the gods, having safely crossed over, the wise Bharata beheld him who was parched by the separation from his brother, repeatedly crying out, "Brother! Brother! Again, brother! Brother! Brother! (28).
Shedding tears of joy, he prostrated himself like a staff.
Seeing him fallen on the ground like a staff, Raghunātha, filled with a look of joy, raised him up and embraced him with both arms. 29–30.
Although he was lifted up vigorously, he did not rise, weeping repeatedly,
his arms clinging to the lotus feet of Rāmacandra.
Bharata said:
Have mercy on me, who am of evil conduct, wicked, and a sinner; O mighty-armed Rāmacandra, O ocean of compassion, show me grace through your kindness.
For even he who considered the touch of Sītā’s hand to be cruel— [32] — [may you have mercy on me].
"For my sake, he wandered through the forest of Rāma's feet.
Having spoken thus, his face distressed with tears, he embraced him again and again and stood before him with palms joined in reverence, his countenance overwhelmed with joy.
Raghunātha, that ocean of compassion, embraced his younger brother,
bowed respectfully to the chief ministers, and after taking leave of them with due honor,
took his seat upon the Puṣpaka chariot together with his brother Bharata.
Bharata beheld his brother’s irreproachable wife Sītā;
he regarded the daughter of Janaka as a devoted wife, like Anasūyā of Atri or Lopāmudrā of the Pot-born Sage (Agastya), and he addressed her by name.
"O Mother, forgive whatever sin has been committed by me, who am lacking in wisdom;
for women like you are devoted to their husbands and perform what is virtuous for all.
Even the highly fortunate Jānakī, having seen her brother-in-law with respect... (38)
Then, having addressed them with blessings, he inquired after their well-being.
Mounted upon that excellent celestial chariot, they all, in an instant, beheld from the expanse of the sky the city near their father’s abode.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Vision of Rāma’s Royal Capital," in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana within the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Three.
Śeṣa said:
Having beheld the capital city inhabited by his own people, the exceedingly heroic Rāma rejoiced greatly, having long yearned for the sight of it. 1.
Bharata also dispatched his own friend, the minister Sumukha, toward the city for the purpose of preparing the city’s festivities.
Bharata said:
Let the people quickly prepare a delightful festival for the arrival of the Lord of the Raghus in every house, adorned with wonderful paintings and festive decorations;
let the royal highways be cleared of dust and sprinkled with sandalwood paste.
Filled with joyful and well-fed people gathered for the sake of the abundance of flowers,
their entire courtyards decorated with banners of various colors,
let the monkeys behold them as if they were rainbows appearing at the arrival of the clouds.
Let them cause the houses of all people to be perfumed with aloe-wood incense,
so that upon seeing its smoke, the peacocks may dance with playful ease.
Let there be elephants for me, resembling mountains and well-restrained by their mahouts.
Let the horses, swift as thought, be painted many times over with various minerals such as red ochre and others; let them shine most beautifully,
so that at the mere sight of their speed, even the horse of the gods abandons its pride.

Thousands of beautiful maidens, adorned with all ornaments and mounted upon elephants, should scatter pearls; and Brahmin women, holding vessels in their hands containing dūrvā grass and turmeric, [should likewise proceed].

Let those married women perform the lustration ceremony for the great king Rāma. Let Kausalyā, who is distressed by the news of her son’s union [with Sītā], attain joy—she who is exceedingly emaciated yet intensely longing for that sight. 10-11.
Thus, with such arrangements intended to beautify the city, the people made preparations for the arrival of Rāma, who brings joy to the hearts of men.
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words, Sumukha, the most excellent among those who know mantras,
set out for the city to have festive arches erected. Then, having reached that city, the one named Sumukha, the master of mantras, indeed—
He proclaimed to the people the great festival of Rāma’s arrival. Having heard that the Lord of the Raghus had reached the city, the people were filled with joy—
those who previously, due to his separation, had abandoned all enjoyments, pleasures, and the like.

The Brāhmaṇas, perfected in the Vedas, pure, with *darbha* grass in their hands and draped in washed upper garments, went to the illustrious Lord of the Raghus. The Kṣatriyas, most heroic, bearing excellent bows and arrows, [also followed].
Victorious heroes who had many times won in battles also went toward him.
Wealthy Vaiśyas, their hands adorned with rings and wearing bright white garments, approached the lord of men. 17–18.

Those Śūdras who were devoted to the twice-born and firmly established in their own conduct, as well as those devoted to Vedic practice— they too went to the lord of the city. Likewise, all those people who provided their livelihood remained steadfast in their respective duties.
Taking their own belongings, they went to King Śrī Rāma.
Thus, by the command of the king, filled with a flood of joy and accompanied by various curiosities, they arrived before the lord of men. 20–21.
Śeṣa said:
Raghunātha too, surrounded by all the deities mounted upon their respective vehicles, entered the city of Mohanā with great splendor. 22.
The monkeys, endowed with the power of leaping and traveling through the paths of the sky,
their bodies adorned with their respective splendors, followed after that supreme city.
Having quickly descended from the Puṣpaka chariot, he then ascended another swift vehicle.
Accompanied by Sītā and surrounded by his retinue,
Rāma then entered Ayodhyā, which was adorned with festive arches,
crowded with joyful and well-fed people, and embellished with celebrations.

Resplendent as he was, being loudly accompanied by the sounding of lutes, drums, kettledrums, and other musical instruments, and being praised by sūtas, māgadhas, and bards who cried out, "Victory to Rāghava! Victory to Rāma! Victory to the ornament of the solar dynasty! (26) "Victory! "O Aṅgada! "Victory!"
"Victory to the son of Daśaratha! O God, victory to the Leader of the World!
