(27) Hearing these auspicious words of the citizens, whose bodies were thrilled with joy and who were beautified by the bristling of their hair arising from the sight of Rāma, (28) he [proceeded].
He entered the excellent road, which was adorned with market-streets and crossroads,
sprinkled with sandalwood water, and strewn with flowers and sprouts.
At that time, some women of the city took refuge at the openings of their windows.
Then, their desire awakened by the sight of Raghunātha’s true form, the women of the city spoke:
The Women of the City said:
"O, blessed indeed was that Bhilla maiden in the forests, whose lotus-face was the very mouth of the garden [of delight]!"
Thus, these women, whose great prosperity was born of their own good fortune, drank in [the sight] with the blue lotuses of their own eyes.

31 Blessed is the lotus-eyed face of the illustrious Lord Rāma, the abode of heroism, the sight of which even the gods, headed by Brahmā, have attained; yet, oh, we here are endowed with such great fortune! 32
"Behold this face with its lovely smile, its head graced by a resplendent crown,
possessing lips that bestow a luster surpassing the bandhūka flower, and a prominent nose.
Having spoken thus, she gazed at them with eyes like lotus petals, her vision overflowing with a weight of affection.
The Teacher of All, delighted that his body had returned from its journey, desired to go to the city of his birth, where the world of men was filled with a weight of no small affection.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Entry of Raghunātha into the City," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
The Fourth Chapter. Vātsyāyana said:
O Lord of the lords of the serpent-kings, capable of supporting the earth!
Please tell me out of compassion this one doubt of mine:
ever since the time the Lord of the Raghus departed for the forest,
I have remained with a body, yet with a mind that is empty.

How did she rejoice, what happened, and what were the signs there— Sumukhā, whose body was emaciated and distressed by the pain of separation from him, having heard from the minister that the Lord of the Raghus had arrived?
"What did she say to the messenger of Rāmacandra?
Cut through this doubt of mine, which concerns the manifestation of the virtues of the Lord of the Raghus;
by your grace, relate it to me exactly as it happened as I listen."
Śeṣa said: O illustrious one, honored by the best of the twice-born, you have asked well. Listen with a single-minded focus as I relate it to you directly. 6.
Having drunk again and again that nectar of the news of Rāma’s arrival, which had fallen from the lotus-face of Sītā, she became overwhelmed, her limbs paralyzed with joy.
"Is this a dream for me, a deluded woman? Or is it a deceptive word? she wondered.
"How shall I, unfortunate as I am, behold Rāma’s face again?
Having attained this infant son through great ascetic toil,
he has once more been separated from me by some sin of mine."
"O good minister, is Rāma well, together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa?
How does that hero, who now wanders the forest, remember me, so deeply afflicted?
Thus she lamented loudly, her mind fixed on the memory of the Lord of the Raghus.
Deluded, she did not report anything belonging to another;
and Sumukha, seeing his mother thus deeply distressed,
fanned her with the tips of his garments, and she regained consciousness once more.

He repeatedly spoke gentle and joy-inspiring words to his mother. Delighted by the news of Raghunātha’s arrival, he further addressed her: "O Mother, know that Raghunātha has reached our home along with Lakṣmaṇa."

"Behold him together with Sītā and greet him with blessings"—having heard these truthful words spoken by Sumukha, I do not know what kind of joy he might have attained. 14. Indeed, I cannot fathom such joy.
Rising up and reaching the courtyard, her body’s hair standing on end,
her limbs overwhelmed with joy and shedding tears, she gazed at Rāma; meanwhile, the lord of kings, Rāma, arrived mounted upon a man-borne chariot.
Having reached his mother Kaikeyī’s palace, the virtuous Rāma stood before her; she, bowed down by the weight of shame,
did not say anything at all to him as he stood there, for she was repeatedly overcome by great anxiety.
Seeing his mother ashamed, Rāma, the banner of the solar dynasty,
spoke to her with words mixed with humility, consoling her.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Mother, I went to Māyāvana and acted exactly as instructed. Now, O Mother, what shall I do by your command?
Ah, have I done anything deficient that you will not look upon me again?"

"Having greeted him with blessings, look upon Bharata and me," O sinless one; having heard those words of her father, she, with her face bowed down, slowly replied: "O Rama, you may go to your own abode."
Having heard the words of his mother, Rāma, the best of men and a treasure-house of compassion, paid his respects and went to the home of Sumitrā.
Seeing Rāma together with the son of Sumitrā, the high-minded Sumitrā [was filled with joy].
"Live long! Live long! he exclaimed with blessings;
and Rāmabhadra, having prostrated at his mother's feet, embraced her and, being full of joy, spoke these words again: ||| 24 ||
"O Ratnagarbha, no one else, not even my brother,
has done for me what this wise man has done in dispelling my sorrow.
Since Sītā was abducted by Rāvaṇa, it is he who has recovered her again for me."
"O Mother, tell me all of Lakṣmaṇa's activities.
Having received the blessing bestowed by Sumitrā upon his head, he,
surrounded by the gods, departed for the palace of his own mother.
Seeing his mother, who was thrilled with joy and longing for the sight of him,
Hari descended from his vehicle and took hold of her feet.
His mother’s mind was overwhelmed by the intense yearning for that vision of him.
Embracing Rāma again and again, she attained great joy;
at that moment, her body experienced a thrill of horripilation, her speech became faltering, and warm tears of delight flowed forth in a continuous stream.
Seeing his mother— devoid of her two earrings,
her body stripped of bracelets and anklets,
yet appearing somewhat delighted by the sight of him— she, with her slender limbs, was overcome with grief.
Thinking, "This is the source of suffering," he spoke to the two women.
(33) Śrī Rāma said: "O Mother, for a long time I have not served your feet."

Therefore, forgive the offense of me, who am indeed destitute of fortune. (34) O Supreme Mother, those sons who are not intent upon serving their mother and father must be considered as mere insects born of semen. (35)
"O Janaka, what could I do when I went to the Daṇḍaka forest under your command? Even there, by the side-glance of your compassion, I crossed the ocean of suffering.
Sītā was abducted by Rāvaṇa and taken again to Laṅkā."
"By your grace, I have slain that lord of the rākṣasas.
O Sītā, here is this devoted wife, fallen at your feet; please honor her, for she is pure, anxious, and has fixed her mind upon your feet. (37-38)
Having heard those words, the two addressed their devoted wife, the daughter-in-law, who had fallen at their feet; bestowing blessings upon her, they spoke to that lady of noble character:
"O Sītā, O beautiful woman, may you sport for a long time together with your husband."
O purifier, give birth to a son who shall sanctify your own lineage.
(40) It is not true in the three worlds that women like you—who are devoted to their husbands and share in their joys and sorrows—should become partakers of misery. (41)

O daughter of Videha, your own family has been sanctified by you yourself, as you follow the pair of Rāma’s lotus feet into the great forest. What is surprising in this, that men are indeed the destroyers of millions of enemies? 42.
"In whose house there is a virtuous wife who desires the welfare of her husband"—
having spoken thus to the lotus-eyed wife of Raghunātha,
she became silent, thrilled, with the hair on her body standing on end. 43–44.
Then his brother Bharata presented to the wise Rāmacandra his own great kingdom, which had been bestowed upon him by their father; meanwhile,
those ministers, their limbs thrilled with joy, [consulted] the astrologers who were experts in counsel.
Having summoned him at an auspicious moment, they questioned him with great reverence (46). On an auspicious day, at a favorable hour joined with a propitious lunar mansion,
they prepared and performed his consecration for the great kingship (47).

Having depicted the earth with its seven islands upon a beautiful tiger skin, the lord of kings, the great monarch, sat resplendent upon it. From that very day, the minds of the virtuous attained great joy.

The minds of the wicked, who tormented others, became despondent. But the women, devoted to their husbands and dedicated to the vow of fidelity, O Sage, never committed a sin even in their thoughts. 49-50.
The Daityas, Devas, Nāgas, Yakṣas, Asuras, and Mahoragas—
all, established upon the path of justice, received the command of Rāma upon their heads (51). They were intent on assisting others and were contented in the happiness of their own dharma.
The auspicious moments of their days and nights were spent in the diversion of sacred knowledge;
even a powerful wind could not forcibly carry away the garments of those standing on the path, for there was no talk of thieves there. 52–53.
Rāma, the giver of wealth to those who seek it, compassionate and a treasure-house of mercy, together with his brothers, constantly performed the praise of the Guru and the Deity. 54.
Thus ends the section on Rāma’s Horse Sacrifice in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
Chapter Four, titled "The Coronation of Raghuvara.
Chapter Five. Śeṣa said:
Then the gods, bowing down with minds delighted by the slaying of the lord of Daityas named Rāvaṇa, praised Rāma who had been consecrated. The gods said:
Victory to the son of Daśaratha, the destroyer of the afflictions of the gods! Victory to the burner of the lineage of the Dānavas!
Victory to the one whose hands are ever busy seizing the wives of his enemies—the foremost among the celestial women!
O Lord, poets are eager to describe your destruction of the king of the Danujas.
O Lord of the World, you who by your divine play swallow again the multitudes of worlds at the time of dissolution—victory to you!
O Acyuta, who are free from birth, old age, and other sufferings, and who are the powerful deliverer;
victory to you, O Unfallen One, born in the ocean of the lineage of Dharmakara, yourself ageless and immortal! 3–4.
Even those who have committed many sins are purified by the names of you, the best of gods; how much more so those preceded by virtuous brahmins who have assumed human form in their beautiful bodies?
O Lord, the pair of your feet, praised by Hara and Viriñci, grants the fulfillment of all desired wishes.
We mentally long for that which is beautifully fashioned with marks such as the *hrīṃ* syllable, the *pavitra*, and barley;
for if you, who bear a splendor that eclipses the form of Madana, do not grant fearlessness to the world, O Purifier full of compassion, how indeed could the hosts of gods experience happiness? 6–7.
Whenever those who grant us suffering abandon us, O Lord, you shall take birth upon this earth again and again;
though you are unborn, immutable, and the supreme Lord, O All-pervading One, you assume your own inherent nature when worshipped by your devotees.
Having strewn the surface of the earth with virtuous deeds that destroy sin and are like nectar for the dead—
Praised by non-human beings who extolled his virtues, he quickly entered his own abode once again.

May He—beginningless yet the first, bearing a form that is ageless, wearing a garland and a crown, resembling the god of love, the slayer of enemies, whose lotus feet are served by the enemy of Smara (Śiva)—victoriously and forcefully destroy all foes. 9–10.
Having spoken thus, all those gods, headed by Brahmā and Indra,
repeatedly bowed down to the Leader of the Raghus, who was gratified by the destruction of his enemies.
Thus, the highly illustrious Lord of the Raghus was exceedingly delighted by this praise.
Seeing those gods bowing with their necks bent low,
Śrī Rāma spoke to them: "O gods, choose some boon, however difficult it may be to obtain."
"Whosoever—whether a god, a demon, or a yakṣa—attains [this] with devotion.
The gods said:
"O Lord, we have obtained everything most excellent from the Blessed One."
Since this enemy of ours, the Ten-faced one, has been slain;
whenever, O sirs, an asura inflicts harm upon us, then and there this much must be done for the destruction of the foe. 14–15.
Having said "So be it," the heroic descendant of Raghu, Śrī Rāma, spoke again: "O gods, listen to my words with full respect. (16)
The person who repeatedly recites this wonderful hymn composed by you and woven from my own deficiencies— whether at dawn or once at night—
shall not suffer terrible defeat by his enemies. (17)
There shall be for them no association with poverty, nor any defeat by disease;
indeed, through recitation, there will arise within the hearts of those men a great devotion to my pair of feet, filled with joy. 18–19.
Having spoken thus, that crest-jewel of kings became silent; all the gods, greatly delighted, departed to their respective worlds.
And Raghunātha, protecting his wise brothers like a father, [remained].

The Lord of the World looked upon his subjects as if they were his own sons. (21) While he ruled, there was no untimely death among men, nor was there any great affliction by disease or other misfortunes in their homes. (22)
No calamity shall ever be seen, nor any fear from enemies;
the trees shall always bear fruit, and the earth shall abound with grain.
One’s life shall be made secure, blessed with sons, grandsons, and a full circle of kinsmen.
With the fatigue of separation dispelled by the joys born of union with their beloveds,
they are constantly eager for stories of the lotus feet of the illustrious Raghunātha;
never do their words become subject to the censure of others.
Even the artisans, alas, never committed any sin in their minds,
for they were constantly apprehensive of the pain of being struck by the hand of the Lord of the Raghus;
with their eyes fixed and motionless upon beholding the face of Sītā’s husband.
The worlds were constantly filled with compassion;
the kingdom was attained without rival, abounding in troops and vehicles,
and made delightful by sages who were joyful, well-nourished, and adorned with golden ornaments.

It was enriched by those who constantly performed their desired rites of charity and public works; it possessed ever-abundant crops, excellent fields with good soil, a favorable location, a virtuous population, stability, abundant fodder, and great wealth in cattle. 29.
It was a fine country, blessed with good subjects, secure, rich in grass, and full of herds of cows.
It was adorned with rows of divine temples; there, the villages were completely full and resplendent with great wealth and prosperity,
possessing artificial gardens of beautiful flowers and trees bearing sweet fruits.
Wherever there are lands with lotus-filled ponds and rows of *rājataru* trees, and wherever there are rivers free from deceit and where the people are never unrighteous;
(32) there alone are the families of the noble-born, and not among those who lack wealth.
In that realm, there was never any delusion among women, nor ever among the learned; the rivers did not flow in crooked courses, nor were the subjects crooked-minded;
and in those many nights, the people were never possessed by darkness.

Where women were free from passion, where men were not dominated by unrighteousness, where there was no one blind for wealth, and where no one was greedy for food; where there was no injustice, no chariot-warfare, and no enmity among the king’s men.
Punishment was meted out only with staffs, axes, ploughshares, water-skins, and rows of fans (36),
and nowhere else except for umbrellas and arrows; there was no expression of anger or restraint, nor was there any lamentation anywhere except among groups of gamblers (37).
There, only gamblers are seen with dice in their hands;
only those weak women who subsist on the news of their husbands' stupidity are found among the waters. There, the women are hard-hearted, while the men are humble. (38)

Where there is the application of *kuṣṭha* only among medicinal herbs and not among men; where piercing occurs only in precious gems and not in those who fashion images; and where trembling arises from a state of pure goodness (*sāttvika-bhāva*) and never from fear in anyone at all—(therein resides the Lord). 39–40.
The fever of desire arises where there is poverty and impurity,
and where that which is always difficult to obtain is not a result of one's own merit.
Only elephants are intoxicated in battle, while [other] fish are intoxicated in the water.
The loss of generosity is found only in elephants; thorns are indeed sharp only on snakes;
the separation from the string occurs only in arrows; the mention of binding is firm only in books; the abandonment of affection is found only among the wicked, and never among one's own kinsmen.
He protected that region, cherishing his subjects who were themselves cherished; establishing righteousness in the land, he was like a wielder of the rod of punishment toward the wicked.
(44) Thus, while protecting the surface of the earth with righteousness, he governed the country.
Eleven thousand years passed for the Lord.
There, having heard from low-born people about the insult to Sītā and his own reproach from the washerman, that scion of Raghu abandoned her.

Then, while the high-minded king was protecting the earth and its inhabitants according to dharma, Sītā remained alone, well-guarded by his command; once, as he sat in the midst of the assembly hall, O wise one—
The great sage Kumbhotpatti, the best of munis, arrived;
accompanied by Vasiṣṭha, he rose up taking the water-offering (arghya) as the people beheld the great king who had come to dry up the ocean. 48-49.
Having welcomed him with great hospitality and inquired after his well-being,
the joy of the Raghus, once he was comfortably seated and rested, spoke to him.
(50) Thus ends the section on Rāma’s Horse Sacrifice in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
The Fifth Chapter, titled "The Meeting with Agastya.
The Sixth Chapter. Śeṣa said:
Thus, the wise hero, the teacher of all the worlds, spoke to the sage who was content with such a welcome and who was a treasure-house of celibacy and austerity:
"Welcome to you, O highly fortunate one, O Agastya, O treasure-house of asceticism!"
By the sight of you, all of us, along with our families, have been purified.
Is your mind indeed engaged with the Vedas and the Shastras?
There is no one anywhere on this earth who can cause an obstacle to your ascetic penance.

O highly fortunate one, Lopāmudrā is a practitioner of dharma who, through her devotion to her husband, causes everything auspicious to come to pass; O highly fortunate one, embodiment of dharma, treasury of compassion, she is indeed praiseworthy. 4.
"O Lord of Sages, what task should I perform for you who are free from worldly desire?
Through the power of your penance and yoga, everything comes to pass according to your will in great abundance.
Nevertheless, O Lord of Sages, bestow your grace upon me."
Śeṣa said:
Having been thus addressed by the wise king of kings, the teacher of the world, he spoke to Rāma,
the lord of the world, in a most humble tone.
Agastya said:
O Lord, O ocean of compassion for kings, know that I have come here, considering your sight—which is so difficult to obtain even for the gods—to be attained. 8.
"The asura known as Rāvaṇa, that thorn of the world, has been slain by you. By good fortune the gods are now happy today; by good fortune King Vibhīṣaṇa [is established].
O Rāma, by the sight of you today, my evil deeds have indeed come to an end."
"O best of gods, my inner treasury is filled with joy," he said.
Having spoken thus, the one born from a jar (Agastya) quickly became silent, his mind overwhelmed by the delight of beholding Rāma. 10–11.
Rāma questioned that sage, who was expert in knowledge, saying:
"O Sage, you know everything—past and future—transcending the world in every respect;
tell me all of this in great detail as I ask."
"O great sage, who was this Rāvaṇa, the harasser of the gods, whom I have slain?
And who was this Kumbhakarṇa? Of what lineage were these evil-minded ones—were they gods, daityas, piśācas, or rākṣasas?"
"O Omniscient One, tell me everything; you know all in detail.
Therefore, having shown compassion toward me, explain it all to me.
(15) Having heard these words, the pot-born sage, a treasury of asceticism, [replied].
He began to relate that which had been asked by the King of the Raghus:
"O King, Brahmā is the creator of the universe; Pulastya was his son. From him was born Viśravas, who was highly proficient in the knowledge of the Vedas."
He had two wives who maintained the conduct of devoted wives;
one was named Mandākinī and the second was known as Kaikasī.
From the former was born Dhanada, who possessed the splendor of a world-protector.
By the grace of Śiva, he established his residence in Laṅkā.
To the daughter of Vidyunmālī, however, three great sons were born:
Rāvaṇa, Kumbhakarṇa, and the meritorious Vibhīṣaṇa.
O high-minded one, because he was born from the womb of a Rākṣasī and because of his birth at the time of twilight, the minds of both were skilled in unrighteousness.
Once, [he traveled] in the very beautiful Puṣpaka chariot.
Mounted upon a golden vehicle adorned with garlands of networks of tinkling bells, he set out, endowed with splendor, to see his father,
while being praised by his own attendants who were decorated with various jewel ornaments.

Having arrived and fallen at the feet of his parents, the son— his soul overwhelmed with joy and the hair on his body standing on end— spoke after a long time: "Today is a blessed day, the fruit of which is the dawning of great fortune."
"By the mere sight of your feet, we have attained great merit"—
having praised him with these and other words of praise, he went to his own home;
and the parents also became filled with joy through their affection for their son.
Seeing him, the wise Rāvaṇa said to his own mother:
"Who is this man—is he a god, or a yakṣa, or perhaps the best of men—who has come here after having served the feet of my father? (27)
A treasury of great fortune, well-surrounded by his own attendants, [he asked:
"By what austerity was this aerial chariot, which possesses the speed of the wind and is an excellent place for the pleasures of gardens, groves, and sports, obtained? (28-29)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words, the mother, distressed by anger and troubled in mind, spoke to her son with a slight change in her eyes. 30.

"O son, listen to my words, which are endowed with much instruction and superior in their discernment of his birth, deeds, and so forth. A destiny has come to pass for one dwelling in my womb by another wife."
By whom your mother’s stainless and great lineage was made to shine; yet you, O worm, are born from my womb— a sinner who merely fills his own belly,
just as a donkey knows its own burden but not its value.
Thus you appear as one ignorant, possessing beds, seats, and enjoyments; it is possible for you to be asleep, or to have gone somewhere, or to have fallen from your state.
By this austerity, which has brought about the satisfaction of Śiva, [all this has been attained].
The palace on Laṅkā, Manovega, and the splendors of his kingdom—35.
Blessed is his mother, fortunate and of great success, whose son, by his own virtues, has attained the station of the great. 36.
Having heard these words spoken in anger by that distressed woman, Rāvaṇa, the best among the evil-minded,
harbored a secret rage within himself and, firm in his resolve regarding her penance, spoke these words again. (37) Rāvaṇa said:
"O Mother, listen to my words, which are filled with pride:
'You alone are Ratnagarbhā (the Womb of Jewels), whose three sons we are. Who is that Kīṭa who possesses Kubera? And where is his meager penance? (38)
O Mother, that kingdom is now devoid of its splendor and possessed of but few servants.
O compassionate one, O you who are uniquely fortunate in this world, listen with enthusiasm to my vow, which has never been made by any other creator. 39-40.
If, by performing difficult austerities that bring satisfaction to Brahmā, I were indeed to bring the entire world under my control,
having forever renounced food, water, sleep, and likewise play; 41.
"In that case, sin would accrue to me from the killing of my father.
Kumbhakarna also, accompanied by Vibhīṣaṇa and having spoken thus to his brother Rāvaṇa, went to the mountain forest. 42–43.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Origin of Rāvaṇa," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padmapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
Chapter Seven.
Agastya said: Then the Daitya Ugra performed fierce penance for ten thousand years,
standing on his tiptoes and gazing at the sun with his eyes.
Kumbhakarna also performed an extremely difficult penance,
and the righteous Vibhishana likewise practiced supreme austerity.
Then the Lord, the God of gods and the Progenitor of creatures, became pleased.
Honored by the crowns of gods, dānavas, yakṣas, and others,
he bestowed a vast sovereignty that illumines the three worlds and assumed a beautiful form served by gods and dānavas.
Then his brother Dhanada, possessed of a righteous mind, was deeply distressed;
the celestial chariot was then forcibly led away from here to the city of Laṅkā.
The entire world was scorched, and even the gods departed for heaven.
He destroyed the families of Brahmins and was the uprooter of the sages.
Then the gods, including Indra, being exceedingly distressed, approached Brahmā;
those high-souled ones offered hymns of praise and prostrated themselves like a staff.
All the gods, filled with reverence, praised him with meaningful words;
then the Lord, being pleased, said, "What shall I do?
Thereupon, the deities presented their request before Brahmā.
Having meditated for a moment upon the distress arising from the Ten-necked one as well as his own defeat, Brahmā went to Kailāsa along with the gods;
they were filled with wonder at the various marvels on the side of that mountain.
Standing there, the gods, led by Śakra, praised Śambhu:
"Homage to Bhava, to Śarva, and to that Blue-necked One; homage to You! Homage to the gross, to the subtle, and to the one of manifold forms; homage to You!"
Having heard these words spoken with a face of total composure, Śaṅkara said to Nandin,
"Bring the gods into my presence.
In the meantime, the gods were summoned by Nandin.
Having entered the inner apartments, the gods beheld him with eyes wide with wonder;
then Brahmā arrived and saw Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world,
attended by thousands of millions of joyful Gaṇas.

Naked, deformed, crooked, soiled, and likewise hideous, they stood before the Grandfather after prostrating themselves along with their divine companions; then the Grandfather spoke to the Lord of the Gods of gods: "Behold the condition of the inhabitants of heaven."
"O Great God, compassionate toward those who have sought refuge, please exert yourself for the sake of slaying the wicked Daitya! 17.
Having heard those words, which were filled with wretchedness and grief, he too—
Accompanied by all the thirty gods, he arrived at the abode of Hari.
All the sages, along with the gods, serpents, and kinnaras, offered praise: "Victory to you, O Mādhava, Lord of Gods! Victory to you, O Destroyer of the suffering of your devotees! 18–19.
"Behold Mahādeva! Behold your own servants!
thus all the gods, led by Śarva, cried out loudly. Having heard what was said and having seen the distress of the gods, Viṣṇu, the lord of the deities, reflected upon it.
With a voice like a mass of clouds, he spoke as if bringing their sorrow to an end:
"O gods, led by Brahmā, Śiva, and Indra, listen to my words which are intent on your welfare.
I know the fear caused to you by the Ten-necked one; having now descended to earth, I shall destroy it."

That city, Ayodhyā, the ornament of the earth, protected by kings born of the solar dynasty who performed noble deeds such as great gifts and sacrifices, shines with its silver-plated grounds. In that city lived King Daśaratha, endowed with royal splendor, yet childless.
Now that all-pervading lord, having achieved victory over the circle of directions, protects the kingdom.
Desiring a son, that sacrificer, endowed with great strength, performed the Putreṣṭi sacrifice according to the prescribed rites after being requested by the venerable Ṛṣyaśṛṅga.
Then, O gods, having been previously unasked for by him through his ascetic penance, I,
out of affection for you, divided myself into four parts among his three wives:
[I became] endowed with the names Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Śatrughna, and Bharata.
"I shall effect the uprooting of Rāvaṇa along with his entire army and vehicles.
You too, descending here with your own portions, should move about everywhere upon the surface of the earth in the form of bears and monkeys. (27-28)
Having spoken thus, O Sage, he quickly ceased his speech in the sky;
and all the gods, having heard those great words, were delighted in their minds. They then performed exactly as they had been instructed by the wise God of gods.

O Great King, you are that very Lord Viṣṇu, the Mahādeva who destroys the suffering of the gods, who has assumed this physical form through his own various portions manifested in the forms of bears and monkeys, filling the earth. 30–31.
O high-minded one, Bharata, Lakṣmaṇa,
and Śatrughna were born from your portions, as was Daśagrīva, the tormentor of the gods;
and due to the persistence of an ancient enmity, he subsequently abducted Jānakī.
The Daitya Satvayā, who belonged to the species of Brahmarākṣasa, was struck down;
that lord of Daityas, the son of Pulastya and the sole thorn of all the worlds, was cast down, and Maheśvara obtained happiness over the entire earth. 33–34.
Today there is happiness for the brahmins and ascetic power for the sages;
all sacred fords are auspicious and all sacrifices are well-performed.
O King, with you as ruler, the entire world—including gods, asuras, and humans—is at peace.
"O Supreme among Men, O Soul of the Universe, O Source of the World, may you attain happiness.
(36) "O Sinless One, all this that was asked by you has been related by me according to my understanding: both the origin and the dissolution. (37)

Having thus heard this account, which resembled the lineage of the lords of the Daityas, the Great Being, the Lord, the Sovereign of renowned power, fell to the ground in the assembly with the lotus of his face drenched by suppressed and falling tears. 38.
Thus ends the [section] on Rāma’s Horse Sacrifice in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
The Seventh Chapter, titled "The Narration of the Birth and Destruction of Rāvaṇa.
The Eighth Chapter. Śeṣa said:
This story of the most excellent sage Vātsyāyana, which destroys sin,
concerns the God of gods who is devoted to Brahman and the sole protector of all dharma.
Seeing the king unconscious, the pot-born Agastya, a treasure-house of asceticism, [acted].
Slowly, slowly, touching him with his hand and shedding tears, he said: "O Rāma, take heart quickly; why do you despair?
You are the eternal Great Viṣṇu, the destroyer of the Daitya race."
"Whatever has been, whatever is to be, and whatever is currently existing—whether stationary or moving—there is no mover in this world other than you; for what reason, then, have you fainted here?
(4) Having heard these words uttered by the pot-born sage, the great king [recovered].
He rose up, his face filled with a stream of tears falling from his eyes;
with his body bowed under the weight of shame and turning away from any thought of hostility toward Brahmā, he spoke most piteously in words of distinct clarity and detail.
Śrī Rāma said:
Alas! Behold the ignorance of that deluded and evil-souled man, who, greedy for his desires, has slain one born into a lineage of brāhmaṇas. 7.
O Brahmin, for the sake of a woman, I— who was once possessed of discernment regarding the Vedas and Shastras—
became devoid of wisdom and, being exceedingly evil-minded, destroyed the lineage of the Vāḍavas. A Brahmin born in the family of the Ikṣvākus does not utter harsh words.
By performing such deeds, this body of mine has been stained with karma.
Those Brahmins who were worthy of worship through gifts, honors, and food—
those sages have been slain by me with volleys of arrows.
To which world shall I go? Even Kumbhīpāka is unbearable;
there is no such sacred place (tīrtha) that is capable of purifying me. Neither sacrifice, nor austerity, nor charity, nor even speech or vows can do so.
But those who are haters of Brahmins, who cause my purification to fail, and by whom the community of Brahmins has been provoked— those men, having gone to hell,
shall experience great suffering for a long time. 12–13.
The Vedas are the root of the dharmas for those who distinguish between the social classes and stages of life;
the Brāhmaṇa community is the root of those Vedas, being the sole branch of all the Vedas. What state will befall me, who through arrogance have cut off that very root? 14.
"What indeed must be done now so that welfare may come to me? Come here! (15) Śeṣa said:
To Rāma, the lord of kings, the bull among the Raghus, who was lamenting intensely—
The pot-born Agastya spoke these words to the one who possessed a body of illusory human form.
Agastya said: "O great-minded King of the Kurus, O highly intelligent one, do not despair."
For one who desires the destruction of the wicked, there shall be no sin of Brahmin-slaughter.

You are the ancient Puruṣa, the manifest Lord beyond primordial nature (prakṛti); the creator, the destroyer, the protector, and the witness; devoid of qualities, yet by your own will you possess qualities.
O high-minded one, by merely uttering your name, those who have drunk liquor, committed the murder of a Brahmin, stolen gold, or performed other great sins, indeed become purified quickly;
such is this goddess, the daughter of Janaka, the Great Vidyā.
By the mere remembrance of her, even those who have fallen from their state attain the supreme goal.
Even Rāvaṇa, that Daitya, the slayer of Danujas, became a servant of yours in Vaikuṇṭha;
he attained the state of a Daitya only due to the curse of the sages.
"You are the one who bestows grace upon him, not the slayer of this twice-born man; reflecting thus, you should not grieve for your own kin.
Having heard these words, Rāma, the conqueror of enemy cities, [acted accordingly].
He spoke these sweet words, uttered with a faltering voice.
Śrī Rāma said: "Sin is said to be of two kinds, distinguished as intentional and unintentional."
That which is performed intentionally is known, while that which is devoid of intention is unknown. An action performed intentionally perishes only through its experience;
other [actions] perish through remorse—this is determined by the scriptures. 24–25.
"Though I have intentionally committed the highly censurable murder of a Brahmin,
let the well-regarded praise of the virtuous be for the removal of my suffering. Tell me such a thing as that which burns away my sin."
Whatever vow, gift, sacrifice, pilgrimage, or great act of worship he performs,
by that alone his stainless fame shall purify the worlds— those who are defiled by sinful conduct, those whose splendor has been destroyed by the murder of a Brahmin.
Śeṣa said: To Rāma, who had spoken thus, that treasure of asceticism replied—Rāma whose feet were illuminated by the jewels in the crowns of the gods and demons bowing down before him. 29.
Listen, O great hero Rāma, who bestows grace upon the world;
I shall speak those words by which one may be liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin. Indeed, he who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice crosses over all sin.
Therefore, O Soul of the Universe, you should perform the beautiful horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha).
This seven-threaded rite must be accomplished by you, the lord of the earth, who are wise, endowed with great prosperity, and distinguished by great strength. (31-32)
Your ancestor, the great king Dilīpa, performed that horse sacrifice which removes the sin of killing Brahmins; likewise,
Śatakratu, that bull among men, performed it a hundred times.
The abode in Amarāvatī is well-served by gods and daityas. Manu, King Sagara, Marutta, and the son of Nahuṣa—
all these ancestors, having performed sacrifice, have gone to that place.
"Therefore, O Indra among the Kuru kings, you are capable in every respect; your brothers, who are like the world-protectors, will turn toward you with devotion.
Having heard these words of the sage, the fortunate best of the Raghus, fearing the killing of a Brahmin, [reflected].
Desiring to perform a sacrifice, he questioned Sumati regarding the procedure as it was being proclaimed by the ancient seers.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Instruction of Agastya to Raghunātha during the Horse-Sacrifice," in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
Chapter Nine.
Śrī Rāma said:
What kind of horse should be used there, what is the procedure for its worship,
how can it be performed, and who are the enemies to be conquered there?
Agastya said:
Auspicious in body with a complexion like the water of the Gaṅgā, he was dark in the ears, red in the face, and well-marked as yellow at the tail. 2.

Possessing the speed of thought, capable of traveling everywhere, and equal in luster to Uccaiḥśravas, this horse— marked with auspicious characteristics— is declared to be the sacrificial steed in the Aśvamedha.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, having worshipped it according to the prescribed rites, [one should proceed].
Having written a document and having looked at it, marked with his own name and seal, he should say:
"He must be released with effort even if guarded by guards;
wherever the sacrificial horse goes, there the well-guarded protector should go. 4-5.
Therefore, that horse who, arrogant in the power of his own strength, attempts to break free by force, must be brought back by those who provide protection; in such circumstances,
the agent must remain here according to the prescribed rules.
Having assumed the form of one bearing antelope horns and being endowed with celibacy,
he should satisfy the poor, the blind, and the wretched with wealth and other gifts as long as the year of his vow elapses.
"O noble one, food and wealth should be given in great abundance;
for whatever the wise man requests, that very thing one should indeed give.
By acting in this manner, the sacrifice of action attains completion. (9)
O destroyer of enemies, you are the destroyer of all sins;
therefore, you are capable in the tasks of performing, protecting, and worshipping.
O King, having established a most stainless fame, purify other people as well.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O best of the twice-born, look now at my horse-stable; are there any horses there marked with such auspicious characteristics?"
Having heard those words, Agastya, the mine of compassion,
rose up while looking at the auspicious horses that were worthy of sacrifice; then,
accompanied by Rāmacandra, he went there to the sacrificial hall.
He beheld horses of variegated limbs, swift as thought and possessed of great strength. Seeing them, he was filled with wonder in his mind, wondering:
"Are these the descendants of the king of horses fallen upon the earth? Or are they perhaps the massed glory of the lords of the Raghus gathered in one place?
Or is this a heap of nectar from the ocean in the form of horses? Thus did the sage experience amazement within his heart as he gazed.
On one side was an excellent row of horses with bodies red as blood; on another side were those with dark ears, possessing a luster like that of musk;
on one side were those with a golden hue, and on the other, those of blue color.
Surrounded by horses distinguished by their various variegated colors,
the sage, observing them all with a mind filled with curiosity, went elsewhere to see those other horses fit for the sacrifice.
There he saw hundreds of such-colored [beings] bound together;
seeing them, the sage was filled with wonder, his body bristling with joy.
Some had ears black on one side, while their entire bodies were white like milk.
Beholding on all sides those faultless horses— yellow-tailed with red mouths, endowed with auspicious marks,
resembling streams of pure water, graced by the speed of thought, and possessing the splendor of a mass of stainless fame—
the sage, his eyes and the radiance of his face brightened by the sight of the wondrous steeds, spoke to the Lord of Sītā regarding the drying up of the ocean.
Agastya said:
O best of the Raghus, as I behold these many auspicious sacrificial horses fit for the horse-sacrifice, my eyes find no satiety today. 22.

"O illustrious Rāmacandra, saluted by gods and asuras, perform the horse sacrifice, O great king, in its full extent. Like the lord of the gods, you shall perform all the assemblies of sacrifices; like the sun, you shall dry up the waters of the enemies of the gods."
"O highly fortunate one, having conquered the enemy hosts in battle, enjoy the pleasures of this earth!"—
with these words, his every sense gratified, he brought together all the charming materials required for the sacrifice. 24-25.
Accompanied by Munya, the great king arrived at the bank of the Sarayū and ploughed the vast earth with golden ploughs.
Having furrowed the ground many times over an area measuring four yojanas, he [proceeded].
That best of men had pavilions constructed for the sake of the sacrifice (27).
Having fashioned the sacrificial pit according to the rules, complete with a yoni and a girdle,
it was set with many jewels and endowed with every splendor (28).
The illustrious Lord of Sages, Vasiṣṭha, of great ascetic power,
caused all of that to be performed according to the injunctions of the Vedas and the Śāstras.
By that sage, his disciples were sent to the hermitages of the best of sages.
They spoke to the best of the Raghus, who was intent upon the horse sacrifice.
Then all the sages, the foremost among those who practice austerity,
being summoned, arrived, longing intensely for a vision of the Supreme Lord.
Nārada, Īṣitānāma, Parvata, the sage Kapila,
Jātūkarṇya, Aṅgiras, Vyāsa, Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, Atri, Āsuri, Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Saṃvarta, and the one known as Śuka. (32)
Thus, these and others went to the excellent horse-sacrifice of Rāma.
The high-minded King of the Raghus honored them all with rising to greet them, salutations, offerings of water (arghya), seats, and other such hospitality.
Having witnessed their prowess, he generally gave them cows and gold, saying:
"Great indeed is your good fortune today, that you have come into my sight.
Śeṣa said:
"O Brahmin, when the assembly of the best of sages was thus crowded together,
there arose a discourse on dharma that was highly esteemed by those of all social classes and stages of life.
Vātsyāyana said:
What news of dharma was there? Or what wonder was recounted?
And what did the virtuous say out of compassion for all the worlds?
Śeṣa said:
Seeing those sages assembled there, the great Rāma, son of Daśaratha,
questioned them regarding all duties appropriate for every caste and stage of life (varṇa-āśrama). Being thus questioned by Rāma, they proclaimed the dharmas of great merit.
"I shall declare them all; listen to them according to the prescribed rule.
The sages said:
"A Brāhmaṇa must always perform sacrifices, Vedic study, and other such duties."

Having studied the Vedas, one who has become dispassionate should not enter the life of a householder at all. A Brahmin must always avoid living by serving the low-born; even when fallen into distress, he should never live by the livelihood of a dog.

Approaching one's wife during her fertile period is the supreme duty of a householder; or, desiring offspring, he may do so out of regard for the excellence of women. Approaching her during the day is considered by men to be detrimental to longevity.

Since all festival days (*parvan*) and the day of ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) must be avoided by the wise, if one approaches a woman out of delusion on such occasions, he falls away from the highest dharma.
He who approaches his wife only during her fertile period (*ṛtu*) and remains devoted solely to his own wife [attains that dharma]. (43–44)
A householder should be known as one who practices celibacy at all times;
however, among the sixteen nights of the menstrual cycle, four are strictly forbidden. Among those, the even nights grant sons, while the odd nights grant daughters.
Having abandoned the defiled *candramasa* (the moon-constellation) and avoiding *maghā* and *mūla*, being pure, he should approach his wife especially under the *puṃnāma* (male-named) asterisms;
thus she shall give birth to a pure son who accomplishes the goals of human life.
In the Ārṣa form of marriage, the giving of a pair of cattle that has been prescribed is praised;
however, even a small bride-price for a girl is a sinful act on the part of the buyer of the girl. Trade, service to a king, and likewise the non-study of the Vedas [are censured]. 48.

An improper marriage and the neglect of sacred rites are the causes of a family’s downfall. (49) Furthermore, whatever merit is gained by one in the householder stage through the gift of food, water, milk, roots, or fruits, or even through the ritual gift of a cow to a worthy recipient according to the prescribed rules— (50) [that merit is lost through these aforementioned faults].
If a guest departs from one's house unhonored and with hopes frustrated,
that person is instantly excluded from the merit accumulated throughout their entire life.
A householder should eat what is like nectar (amṛta) only after having given portions to the ancestors, the gods, and human beings.

He who feeds only his own belly cooks for his own sake and eats sin alone. Sin enters [the body] on the sixth and eighth lunar days; it is always present in oil and meat. One should likewise avoid shaving and sexual intercourse on the fourteenth day and the new moon day.

One should not have sexual intercourse with a woman during her menses; one should not eat together with one's wife; one should not eat wearing only a single garment, nor should one eat while seated on a high seat (54).
A superior man who desires luster should not look at a woman while she is eating.
One should not blow on a fire with one's mouth, nor look at a naked woman; one should not warm one's feet over a fire, nor throw any impure substance into it;
one should not commit violence against living beings, nor eat during the two twilights.
One should not point out a cow that is suckling, nor should one display a rainbow;
one should not eat curd at night when its essence has risen upward. One should not salute a woman in her menses, nor should one eat until full satisfaction during the nights.
One who is fond of the triple symphony (song, dance, and instrumental music) should not wash his feet on a bell-metal vessel.
He should not wear clothing or sandals that have been used by another. He should not eat from a broken vessel, nor should he eat food that has been defiled.
One should not go to sleep with wet feet, nor should one go anywhere while still impure from eating; nor should one eat while lying down, nor touch the head while impure.
One should not offer praise to men, nor should one disparage oneself.
One should not bow down to one who has risen up [in anger], nor should one speak of the vital secrets of others.
Having thus entered the householder stage, one should proceed to the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) stage; whether with one's wife or having left her behind, one should thereafter become dispassionate.
Thus were these and other dharmas proclaimed at that time by the great Ṛṣi Śrutārāma, who desires the welfare of all the worlds.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Instruction on All Dharmas," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
The Tenth Chapter. Śeṣa said:
While he was thus listening to these duties, the spring season arrived.
When the commencement of the sacrificial rites and other ceremonies by those great-souled ones took place,
the wise Vasiṣṭha, born from a water-jar, having observed that occasion,
spoke appropriately to the great king Rāmacandra.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O mighty-armed Rāmacandra, the time has come for you, when the horse, duly honored for the sake of the sacrifice, is to be released."
Let the preparations be made there; let the best of the twice-born be summoned, and let the Blessed One perform the worship of the brahmins as is appropriate.
Let gifts arise from his own heart for the poor, the blind, and the wretched.
Having honored them with great respect, you should grant them their desires according to the prescribed rites.
You, O Kanaka, together with your virtuous wife and others, must observe a vow here:
sleeping on the ground, practicing celibacy, and abstaining from all sensual enjoyments.
"Let him, bearing a deer-horn at his waist and holding a girdle, a deerskin, and a staff,
prepare the sacrificial materials provided with all necessary substances.
Having heard these significant words of Vasiṣṭha, which were true to their meaning—
The wise one spoke to Lakṣmaṇa in words enriched with various meanings.
Śrī Rāma said:
"Listen, Lakṣmaṇa, to my words; having heard them, perform it quickly."
With great effort, he performed the rites appropriate for the horse sacrifice.
Śeṣa said:
Having heard the words of the Lord of the Raghus, Lakṣmaṇa, the conqueror of enemies, then [acted].
He spoke these words of various descriptions to the commander-in-chief. Lakṣmaṇa said: "O hero, listen to these very sweet words; having heard them, you will again be filled with haste."

By the command of Rāma, whose feet are rubbed by the crowns of the crests of kings, you must prepare that army— whose limbs are rendered powerful by the force of the wind-god Kālabala— and have it equipped with excellent chariots, elephants, infantry, and fine horsemen. 11.

Let the horses, swift as the wind, be readied— those whose graceful movements resemble the tossing of waves— and let them be mounted by excellent horsemen who carry many weapons and strike down the enemy forces.
Let the elephants, resembling mountains, be observed, accompanied by mahouts with spears and lances held in their hands.
Let the chariots—filled with heroes, weapons, and abundant offerings of gifts; intoxicated [with battle]; and fully equipped with all manner of arms and missiles;

shining with vast and widespread prosperity; yoked to horses as swift as the wind; and whose side-seats are laden with various weapons and missiles that call to mind the destruction of diverse enemies—be brought here by throngs of charioteers. 13–14.
"Hundreds of foot-soldiers are approaching me, weapons and fire in their hands, exerting every effort to protect the steed worthy of the horse sacrifice.
Having heard these words of the high-souled Lakṣmaṇa, [he spoke].
The commander-in-chief named Kālajit caused [the army] to be prepared for battle.

Then, that horse shone with the mass of rays from his raised foreleg; he was adorned with the beauty of ten *dhruvaka* marks on his forehead and fine, sparse hair; he bore a prominent pearl upon his neck within the hollow of his throat; he possessed bright luster on his face and dark luster on his ears.
With its face adorned with decorative ornaments, beautified by shimmering gems,
and graced with garlands of pearls, the horse went forth. It was provided with a white parasol and embellished by white chowries.
Then the king of horses, his limbs enveloped in great splendor, went forth;
meanwhile, some soldiers were in front, some in the middle, and others behind, serving Hari as was their wont, just as the gods used to serve him in the past. 19-20.
Then, having summoned his entire army— which was densely crowded with multitudes of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry— he issued all his commands at that time.
From here and there, the roar of the assembled troops was heard.
Then, at that time, the sound of kettledrums arose in that best of cities. By that great and beloved roar of the heroes,
the mountain peaks trembled and the palaces shook.

O King, there was a great neighing from the horses as they became bewildered; the earth, resounded by the clashing of chariot wheels, trembled violently. And the earth was obstructed on all sides by herds of elephants in motion.
But the dust rising there caused the people to disappear from view.
A great army, crowded with men and led by the commander-in-chief named Kālajit, marched forth, obscuring the sun with its umbrellas. 25–26.
Roaring, those foremost of the brave warriors, creating a festive bustle at the archway,
set out with joy, fully prepared for the sacrifice of Raghunātha. Adorning their limbs with unguents made of musk, their heads were beautified by pure garlands of flowers.
All of them, their limbs adorned with crowns, bracelets, and ornaments, set forth as urged by the lord of the earth.
Thus, O great king, those excellent soldiers marched toward the monarch—archers, noose-bearers, and sword-wielders of distinct prowess. 28-29.
Thus, gradually reaching the pavilion marked by the signs of sacrifice,
the horse, leaping into the sky and making the ground beneath its hooves scarred,
arrived; and Rāma, seeing Hari arrived, was filled with great joy in his heart.
He urged Vasiṣṭha toward the performance of the necessary rites.
Vasiṣṭha, having summoned Rāma together with his golden wife,
caused him to perform the ritual for the removal of the sin of Brahmin-slaughter.
Rāma, the conqueror of enemy cities, who observed the vow of celibacy and carried a deer-horn, caused that work to be performed;
he began the sacrificial rites by preparing a fire-pit commensurate with the sacrificial pavilion.
There, the wise sage Vasiṣṭha, the ancient family preceptor of Raghunātha and a knower of the deliberations of the Vedas and Śāstras, became the Ācārya;
and Agastya, a treasure-house of austerity, performed his sacred rites there, O Brahmā.
The sage Vālmīki was the Adhvaryu priest, and the sage Kaṇva was the gatekeeper;
there were eight gates there, truly adorned with beautiful archways.
O Brahmin, at each gate stood two gatekeepers who were knowers of the supreme mantras.
At the eastern gate were the two best of sages known as Udevala and Asita; at the southern gate were the two great ones, Kaśyapa and Atri, who were treasures of asceticism;
and at the western gate were Ṛṣabha, Jātūkarṇya, and Jājali.
At the northern gate were two sages, one of whom was a *dvita* and the other a *tāpasa*.
Having thus performed the ritual for the gates, Vasiṣṭha, born from a water-jar (*kalaśodbhava*),
O twice-born one, began to perform the proper worship of the excellent horse.

There, auspicious women adorned with garments and ornaments worshipped the honored one with turmeric, unbroken grains, perfumes, and other offerings; then, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and having incensed him with fragrant aloe-wood, they honored him. 40–41.
Then, by the command of Tāḍava, the courtesans performed the celebration of his growth;
having thus honored him whose forehead was stainless, smeared with sandalwood paste,
enriched with fragrances such as saffron, and endowed with every splendor.
He drew upon a leaf that was bound with bright threads and fashioned from refined gold (43).
Therein he depicted the exalted majesty and power of the Ten-headed One’s foe—
the archer who is the banner of the Solar dynasty and the preceptor of the initiation into archery (44).
He whom all the gods, together with the asuras, honor with their jeweled crowns—
his son is the scion of Raghu, Rāmacandra, the highly fortunate one who strips away the pride of heroic strength and the crest-jewel among all warriors. 45.
Born from the womb of the queen of the King of Kosala,
that mother’s very jewel— Rāma, the destroyer of enemies—
is performing a horse sacrifice, having been well-instructed by a Brāhmaṇa.
O best of Brahmins named Rāvaṇa, for the sake of removing the sin of killing, that foremost of horses, the best of steeds, was released by him;
it was well-protected by moats consisting of his mighty army and its retinue. 48.
His protector is his brother Śatrughna, the slayer of Lavaṇa.
Accompanied by a multitude of troops consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, he possesses such supreme pride in his own strength that it intoxicates him. 49-50.
"We are archers, heroes, the best and most formidable here;
seize by force this horse adorned with a jewel-garland, which possesses the speed of thought, the swiftness of desire, and is radiant in all its movements. (51)
Then Śatrughna, having liberated his brother,
playfully struck the horse with sharp-pointed calf-tooth arrows released from his bow;
thus did the great lord of sages describe and so forth.

He released [the arrow] which possessed the blazing majesty of the heroic strength of Śrī Rāmacandra’s arms, was a treasury of splendor, moved with the speed of the exceedingly swift wind, and traveled through the netherworld, the earth, and the heavens. 54
Then Rāma, the best among those who bear arms, commanded Śatrughna:
"Go behind the horse that moves at its own will for the sake of protecting it.
"Śatrughna, go; may prosperity be yours on the path of the horse."
May your two arms be victorious over enemies and capable of drawing them away;

may those warriors who have come against you in battle be warded off by you. Being endowed with the multitude of your own virtues, do not strike those who are sleeping on the great earth, those who have fallen, those who are naked, those who are terrified, or those who are bowed down, for the virtuous declare that such is the deed of one who has performed good works.
"Terrified and deprived of their chariots, they say to you:
'We are yours; you, who desire the merit of good deeds, must not slay us.
For he who would kill one who is devoid of pride, intoxicated, asleep, submerged, or overcome by fear—"
And he who speaks of you as his own goes to the lowest state. Do not set your mind on the property of others, nor on another's wife;
being filled with all excellent virtues, do not indulge in base pleasures.

O conqueror, do not first urge the elders to flee; endowed with compassion, do not neglect the worship of those worthy of honor. You should bow down to cows, Brahmins, and Vaiṣṇavas who are united with righteousness.
Having paid homage, as you go from there, you shall attain success.
O mighty-armed one, Viṣṇu is the Lord of all, the witness, and the one who assumes a body that pervades everything; indeed, those who belong to him wander about in his very form.
O descendant of Raghu, those who remember Mahāviṣṇu, who dwells in the hearts of all beings,
should be regarded as equal in form to Mahāviṣṇu himself. He for whom there is no "own" and no "belonging to another," and for whom an enemy is the same as a friend— [he is one with the Lord].

Indeed, those devotees of Viṣṇu purify even a sinner in an instant. Those for whom the Bhāgavata is dear and for whom the Brāhmaṇas are dear have been sent here from Vaikuṇṭha for the purpose of purifying the world.

He in whose mouth is the name of Hari, in whose heart is the eternal Viṣṇu, and in whose stomach is the food offering (naivedya) of Viṣṇu— even if he be an outcaste— he is indeed a Vaiṣṇava. Those for whom the Vedas are most dear, and not the pleasure born of worldly existence—
And those who are devoted to their own dharma—bow down with reverence to them.
There is no difference between Śiva and Viṣṇu, nor between Brahmā and Maheśvara; I carry upon my head the dust from their feet, which purifies and destroys all sins. 68–69.
Those men by whom Gaurī, Gaṅgā, and Mahālakṣmī are not perceived as separate [from Him] should be considered as having come here from the heavenly world;
they are protectors of those who seek refuge and are devoted to honor and charity. 70.
He who acts according to his ability for the pleasure of Hari should indeed be known as the best of Vaiṣṇavas (71).
He whose name quickly burns away a heap of great sins,
and he who possesses devotion to His pair of feet— he is truly a Vaiṣṇava (72).

Having paid homage to those whose senses are under control and whose minds contemplate Hari, one may be purified from birth until the end of death. By abandoning another's wife like a blade of grass, you shall become a ground for the prosperity of fame and ornaments.
"By acting according to this command of mine, you shall attain the supreme, praiseworthy abode of perfect yoga.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Instruction to Śatrughna," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* within the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
The eleventh chapter. Śeṣa said:
Having thus commanded, the Blessed One Rāma, the subduer of enemies, [departed].
Looking again at the heroes, he spoke once more with a voice full of fear:
"Who is following behind my brother Śatrughna, who is guarding the horse, acting as its protector and carrying out his command?"
"Let him who shall utterly defeat all the foremost heroes who have come against him with multitudes of vital-piercing weapons,
take this betel-roll, thereby spreading his own fame most extensively upon the earth.
When Rāma had spoken thus, Puṣkala, the son of Bharata, [replied].
From that lotus-like hand of the Raghu king, he took the betel-roll.
"O Lord, O Master, I shall go daily as the protector of Śatrughna’s rear,
fully equipped and bearing all weapons, missiles, bows, and arrows."
O high-minded Rāmacandra, by your majesty, this entire surface of the earth shall be conquered;
through your grace, O great-souled one, all that exists— including gods, asuras, and humans— shall be won.
"Since he has arrived ready for battle, I shall indeed endure his assault;
my master will know everything from witnessing my prowess.
Here I go, acting as a protector for Śatrughna’s rear."
As the son of Bharata was speaking thus, the Lord Hanumān, commending him and expressing his approval by saying "Excellent!",
praised all the foremost leaders among the monkey heroes, headed by the son of Pavana (Hanumān).
"O great hero Hanumān, listen with respect to my words."
"Through your grace, I have obtained this kingdom free from all thorns. O Lord of Monkeys, I know all that you did when you crossed the ocean for the sake of my union with Sītā."
"Go, acting as the protector of my army at my command;
my brother Śatrughna must be protected by you just as I am.
Wherever a lapse of mindfulness arises in Śatrughna,"
"In every matter, O high-minded one, my brother must be awakened. Having heard these great words of the wise Rāmacandra,
he then placed them upon his head and offered his salutation.
Then the great king commanded Jāmbavān, the lord of monkeys,
who possessed the supreme splendor of the best of monkeys, for the service of Raghunātha.
Aṅgada, Gavaya, Mainda, and likewise the monkey Dadhimukha [were also commanded].
Sugrīva, the lord of the monkeys; Śatabali, Akṣika, and Kapi;
Nīla, Anala, Manovega, and Aṅgadaja, the son of the monkey—O you, headed by these, be ready! 16–17.
Accompanied by all the elephants and excellent horses adorned with ornaments of refined gold,
and decorated with armor and helmets, they proceeded in great haste.
Śeṣa said:

Then Rāma, resplendent with strength and valor, summoned his excellent minister Sumantra; having called for the foremost of counselors, he said, "O Vādaka, summon men who are capable of protecting Ayodhyā.
Having heard what was thus spoken, the slayer of enemy heroes replied.
O Lord of Men, listen to these nine heroes of the Raghu clan, who are capable of protecting the horses, powerful, well-disciplined,
wielders of the bow, possessors of great knowledge, and experts in all weapons and missiles. 20–21.
He was a king of foremost prowess, a sapphire jewel, and likewise a treasury of prosperity; he was a scorcher of enemies, a subduer of the planets, and a king skilled in weapons.
This royal personage was a sapphire jewel, a great hero, and a leader of chariot-warriors.
He alone shall protect a hundred thousand and fight fearlessly against a hundred thousand;
with ten Akṣauhiṇīs for the protection of Yātudhāna, by my uplifted arms, armored and equipped with helmets.

He who is the foremost in prowess, who has shattered the pride of his enemies, who is a discharger of arrows from both the left and right hands, and who is the most skilled among all knowers of weapons—
let him come with twenty akṣauhiṇīs for the protection of the sacrificial horse. 25.
Armed with a staff-like bow,
that youth was intent on destroying his enemies; likewise, this best of kṣatriyas was a treasury of fortune, for he had propitiated Śatadhṛti through austerities and mastered the divine weapons.
The Brahmāstra, the Pāśupatyastra, the Gāruḍa known as the Nāga,
the Māyūra, the Nākula, the Raudra, the Vaiṣṇava known as the Megha,
the Vajra known as the Pārāvata, and likewise the one known as the Vāyavya. 28.
"Thus, he is skilled in the employment and withdrawal of these and other weapons.

"O fearless one, those who are adorned by the power of their own asceticism must not be disregarded by you.

Chapter Twelve.
Śeṣa said:

"Victory to you, O Goddess, Great Goddess, who are served exclusively by the multitude of devotees! (22)
O sinless Mother, whose pair of feet is served by Brahmā, Rudra, and the lords of the gods—this entire world of moving and non-moving beings shines as it is permeated by a portion of you.
Apart from you, nothing exists; O auspicious Mother, salutations to you!
O Great One, by you, through your power of support (*dhāraśakti*), the earth has been established, immovable and adorned with mountains, forests, groves, and the elephants of the quarters.
While the sun scorches the earth, burning it with his sharp rays, [you remain steadfast].

By your power, may the fire, which dwells within and without and draws up the moisture situated upon the earth, release it; O Great Goddess, worshipped by gods and asuras, may it bring peace to the worlds through your majesty. 26–27.
You are knowledge; you are the great illusion (Mahāmāyā) of Viṣṇu, the sole protector of the world. By your own power, O deluder, you create this universe and you also protect it.
From you alone all the gods obtain perfection and attain happiness.
Protect me, O compassionate Lord, who art saluted by all and beloved of your devotees (29).
O Mother, protect me, your servant, who has taken refuge at your feet;
grant me the fulfillment of my desires, O Primordial One of the Great Beings (30).
Sumati said:
"The Mother of the World, thus gratified, said to her devotee Sumada, whose body was emaciated by penance: 'Choose an excellent boon.'"
Having heard these words, King Sumada was overjoyed;
he chose back his own kingdom, from which the thorns of the wicked had been removed,
and unswerving devotion at the pair of feet of the Great Goddess.
Furthermore, she is the one who carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra to liberation at the end.
Kāmākṣa said:
"O you of great passion, obtain a kingdom where all thorns have been destroyed."
O you named Sumada, may there never be such defeat by enemies as that which befell him whose two lotus-feet were graced by the jewel of a woman;
for when the highly illustrious Lord of the Raghus had slain the afflicted Rāvaṇa, [he was so overwhelmed]. 34–35.
For he will perform the horse sacrifice, adorned with every requisite;
his brother, the great hero Śatrughna, slayer of enemy warriors,
will come here protecting the horse, surrounded by heroic men and others.
Therefore, entrust this entire prosperous kingdom, including its wealth and other assets, to him.
You shall protect it with your own formidable archer-warriors;
thereafter, O high-minded one, you will wander everywhere upon the earth.
Then, having paid homage to Rāma, who is served by Brahmā, Indra, Īśa,
and others, you shall attain liberation— difficult to reach even for yogis through the practice of *yamas*.
I shall remain here for as long as it takes until the arrival of the great sacrifice, O Rāma.
"But after I have uplifted you, I shall go to the supreme state.
Having spoken thus, the goddess, who is saluted by gods and asuras, vanished.
Sumada, too, having slain his enemies in Ahicchatrā, became king.

"Even though this king is capable and endowed with a powerful army, I, being well-trained in great illusions, will not allow him to seize it. Having heard that the excellent horse of the horse-sacrifice had arrived near the city, [he spoke thus].
And he, the omniscient king named Sumadana, will grant everything to you, whose feet are served by all the great kings and who possess great wisdom—
now, through the majesty of that great king Rāmacandra. 43–44.
Śeṣa said:
Having heard this account of Sumada, the highly illustrious and mighty one exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! and rejoiced exceedingly. 45.
The lord of Ahicchatrā, surrounded by all his own attendants and served by many kṣatriyas, sat comfortably in his assembly hall;
there were brahmins learned in the Vedas and vaiśyas prosperous with wealth. 46.
They waited upon the king, who was intoxicated with pride and endowed with both beauty and majesty.
Excellent Brahmins, learned in the Vedas and devoted to the practice of justice,
offered their blessings to that monarch, the sole protector of all the world.
At that time, someone approached and said to the king: "O Lord, a certain horse carrying a letter has arrived in the presence of Aja.
Having heard this, he quickly dispatched his chief servant.
"Know this: whose horse is this near my city?
(50) Then a servant went there, learned the events from the beginning, and reported them to the king: "O Great King, it belongs to one who has been served by you. (51)
Having heard this, the wise King, constantly remembering the horse of the Lord of the Raghus, commanded all his people:
"All these worlds belonging to me, which are filled with wealth and grain— "
Let auspicious archways and other decorations be fashioned here in the houses. Let thousands of beautiful maidens, adorned with every ornament and mounted upon elephants, proceed to meet Śatrughna.
Having thus issued all these commands himself, King Yauvanāśva,
surrounded by his retinue of sons, grandsons, queens, and others,
[departed] along with Śatrughna, great ministers, and excellent warriors such as Puṣkala.
He beheld the heroic king named Sumada, accompanied by elephants with their riders, by foot-soldiers who scorched their enemies, and by adorned horses;
he was joined by heroes and graced by valor. 56-57.
Then the great king, having arrived, joyfully bowed to Śatrughna, saying: "I am blessed; I have accomplished my purpose; my body has been truly honored.
"O Lord, this place is well-filled with great wealth such as rubies and pearls;
alas, I have been waiting for a long time for the arrival of that horse.
What was previously told by Kāmākṣā has now come to pass exactly so. (59-60)
"Behold my city and make its people fulfilled; purify our entire lineage, O King Rāmānuja.
Having spoken thus, he caused him to mount the elephant Candrasuprabha.

Then, O Great King, urged on by Sumada, Puṣkala and the great hero [Rāvaṇa] mounted [the chariot] themselves; at that time, the sound of kettledrums, cymbals, trumpets, lutes, and other instruments pervaded [the air]. 62–63.

The maidens, sent by Indra, approached the great lord of men, Śatrughna, whose feet are served by Indra and the other gods; seated upon an elephant, they offered him congratulations with heaps of pearls.
Slowly and gradually, having entered the midst of the city, they were received with joy by the people.
Having been celebrated with festive honors, the two of them reached a house adorned with arched gateways and other decorations (65).
Accompanied by the jewel among horses and likewise graced by heroes,
King Śatrughna, escorted by the king [his elder brother], reached the palace (66).
Having then worshipped the younger brother of Raghunātha with the *arghya* and other offerings,
he offered everything to the wise Rāmacandra.
Thus ends the [section] on the Horse Sacrifice of Rāma in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
Chapter Thirteen: The Entry into the City of Ahicchatrā by Śatrughna.
Chapter Fourteen. Śeṣa said:
Then the king, that bull among men, desiring to hear the most excellent stories of the Lord of the Raghus, spoke to Śatrughna, who was pleased by his welcome.
Sumada said:

Is Rāma, the crest-jewel of all the worlds, dwelling in happiness? He who has descended as an incarnation for the protection of his devotees and who bestows grace upon me—is he well? Blessed are these people in this city, for they behold the lotus-face of the Lord of the Raghus.
O bull among men, those who incessantly drink with the cups of their eyes, being thoroughly delighted by my entire collection of wealth—
O high-minded one, they have truly fulfilled the purpose of their family, land, and all other possessions.
"O compassionate one, I have previously obtained the grace of Kāmākṣā that whoever, along with their family, shall behold the lotus-face of Raghunātha [shall attain liberation].
When Sumada, the best of kings, had spoken thus, the hero [Rāma]— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the portion available.)

They related everything concerning the arising of the virtues of the Lord of the Raghus. Having stayed there for three nights, the high-minded younger brother of the Lord of the Raghus resolved to depart along with the king.
Knowing this, Asumada quickly consecrated his son in the kingdom,
with the approval of the great king Śatrughna and Puṣkala;
[he gave him] garments, many jewels, and various kinds of wealth.
There, the high-minded one bestowed [gifts] upon the servants of Śatrughna. Then he began his journey with ministers who were most wealthy,
along with infantry, horses, elephants, excellent steeds, and ten million chariots.
Accompanied by that archer Sumada, Śatrughna,
who bore the majesty of the Lord of the Raghus, proceeded along the path laughing;
having reached the bank of the Payoṣṇī river, he went on with his excellent horse.
All the warriors who protected the horse followed behind him.
Beholding various hermitages of sages who had performed great austerities, he heard here and there of the multitude of virtues of the Lord of the Raghus.
"This wise Hari goes forth, protected by tawny deer and repeatedly by tawny devotees who follow the best of lions.
Hearing these auspicious words of the sages all around him, the Lord [proceeded].
The Great One was gratified by those whose mental dispositions were overflowing with devotion;
he beheld the pure hermitage, teeming with people and living creatures, where all inauspiciousness was dispelled for the men listening to the resonance of the Vedas. 15–16.
The entire sky there was purified by the smoke from the oblations of the *agnihotra* sacrifice,
and it was beautifully adorned with many sacrificial posts erected for the various rites performed by the eminent sages; there, cows worthy of protection were tended by the sons of Tuhariṇa.
Out of fear of the cat, mice dig their burrows in this place.
Snakes sport with peacocks and mongooses throughout the night; here, elephants and lions dwell together constantly, having attained friendship. 18–19.

The deer there, intent on feeding upon wild grain (nīvāra), feel no fear, for they are protected by hosts of sages and by Kālāñjara. The cows, possessing bodies as beautiful as Nandinī, have udders resembling water-jars.

The best of sages, seeing that the mountain was being purified by the dust arising from his feet as he performed the ritual acts appropriate for dharma with sacrificial fuel held in their lotus-like hands,
questioned Rāma’s minister Sumati, who was omniscient.
Śatrughna said: "O wise one, whose hermitage shines before us—frequented by creatures free from enmity and crowded with throngs of sages? (23)
"I shall hear the news of the sage and I shall purify my own body through accounts and descriptions concerning him. Having heard these significant words of the high-souled Śatrughna, [he replied: 24.
The ministers of the wise Raghunātha spoke thus:
Sumati said,
"Know that the hermitage of Cyavana is graced by great ascetics."
It was crowded with creatures free from enmity and surrounded by the wives of sages.
That great sage, who—without distinguishing between Śakra and Manu—assigned portions to the physicians of heaven in the great sacrifice of Svāyambhuva, [is here]. 26–27.
"Who can possibly equal the power of this great sage, who is enriched by the strength of his asceticism and who bears the very form of the Vedas?
Having heard these words concerning the great sage Cyavana, Rāma’s younger brother [Lakṣmaṇa] spoke.

Out of respect, Śatrughna questioned Sumati, the destroyer of the pride of Indra: "When did he take his share among the ranks of the gods? Śatrughna said: "When did he take his share among the ranks of the gods?

"What was performed by the King of the Gods at the great sacrifice of Svāyambhuva?
Sumati said:
"In the lineage of Brahmā, there was a highly renowned sage known as Bhṛgu."
Once, having gone out in the evening to gather sacrificial fuel, the powerful Rākṣasa Damana arrived there to destroy the sacrifice and spoke these words, which caused great terror:
31-32. "At that time, for the destruction of the sacrifice, the powerful Rākṣasa Damana arrived and spoke these words, which were most terrifying."
"Where is the friend of the sages, and where is that sinless lady?
Thus he spoke again and again, his voice choked with rage.
Then Agni, perceiving the fear that had come upon him from the Rākṣasa, [acted].
He showed him his blameless wife, who was pregnant;
the Rākṣasa carried her away while she was crying out like a female osprey—O Bhṛgu, O Lord of the night-rangers, O protector, O treasure-house of asceticism! 34–35.

Taking hold of that distressed woman as she spoke thus, the wicked man went outside, awakening that virtuous lady of Bhṛgu’s lineage with a blow of his words. Then, terrified by great fear, the fetus moved from within her womb.
With his eyes blazing like fire, the son of Aṅga fell down.
He said: "O evil-minded one, do not go away quickly; you shall be reduced to ashes! For by violating a virtuous woman, you will not attain any well-being. (37-38)
Thus addressed, he fell down, his body reduced to ashes;
then the mother, taking her child, returned to the hermitage with a distracted mind.
Bhrigu, having learned everything that had been done by Agni, was overwhelmed with anger.
