"O you who eat everything, you have become a wicked betrayer of enemies!
Thus cursed, Agni, afflicted by extreme suffering, quickly grasped his feet and said: "O Lord, O great-minded ocean of compassion, grant me your grace. (40-41)
"I have spoken this untruth out of fear, not because I am a hater of my guru;
therefore, O crest-jewel of Dharma, show mercy toward me.
Then, bestowing his grace upon him, he said, "Though you are a consumer of all things, you shall become pure."

Having spoken thus to the fire-god, the ascetic sage, moist with compassion, performed the birth-rites and other ceremonies for his son who had emerged from the womb; the pure Brahmin, auspicious and holding *darbha* grass in his hand, performed them according to the rules. 43–44.
All the ascetics called him Cyavana because he had fallen from his state;
he grew gradually, like the moon on the first day of the bright fortnight.
He went to the river Revā, the sole purifier of the world, to perform austerities.
Surrounded by all his disciples, who were endowed with the power of asceticism,
that great sage went there and performed penance for ten thousand years;
on his two shoulders grew *kiṃśuka* trees, which shone atop anthills.
Deer, full of longing, came and scratched their bodies against his limbs;
yet, enveloped by irresistible ascetic power, he perceived nothing at all.
Once, the lord Manu prepared himself for a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā).
Accompanied by his family and surrounded by a great army,
he bathed there in that great river, offered libations to the ancestors and the gods,
and gave gifts to the Brahmins for the propitiation of Viṣṇu.
Then that maiden, wandering here and there in the midst of the forest together with her friends, adorned with beautiful ornaments of refined gold,
saw there an anthill graced by a great tree.
She beheld a certain light, devoid of blinking or opening;
having gone there, she pierced it with needles and blood flowed out.
Seeing the exhaustion of the King's body, she became overcome with extreme sorrow.
O King, though she was not her mother nor her father, that cow,
overwhelmed by grief, being afflicted by fear, quickly lamented for herself by means of herself.
At that time, O King, the earth trembled and meteors fell from the sky.
All directions became smoky and the sun was surrounded by a halo (55).
Then many horses and elephants of the king perished;
wealth along with jewels was lost, and there was mutual strife at that time (56).
Seeing that, the king became afraid and, with a somewhat agitated mind, asked the people: "By whom has this sage been offended?
Having learned through hearsay of his daughter's misdeed, he [inquired further].
Extremely distressed, he went there with his abundant army and vehicles.
Beholding that treasure-house of asceticism endowed with great austerity, he praised him and sought to propitiate him, saying, "O best of sages, show mercy."
Therefore, being pleased, that best of sages, a man of great asceticism, said to him:
"Know that all these portents and other omens have been brought about by your daughter; O Great King, the bursting of your eyes was caused by your own child."
Seeing you shedding much blood, she said:
"Therefore, O great king, this [daughter] must be given to me according to the prescribed rite;
then the pacification of the portent will occur, of this there is no doubt. (61-62)
Hearing that, the king was distressed; he gave his daughter Prajñācakṣuṣā, who was endowed with noble lineage, youth, beauty, good character, and auspicious marks.
When this lotus-eyed maiden had been given by the king, [the sage said: 63.
Then all the portents subsided, and the sages rose up.
Having given his daughter to that sage, the treasury of asceticism, the king returned to his own city,
once again filled with sorrow and overcome by grief.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Episode of Cyavana," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* within the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
Chapter Fifteen.
Sumati said:
Then the sage, having returned to his own hermitage with Mānavī and his wife—who was absorbed in yoga—attained joy, all his sins having been destroyed. 1.
Harimedhā attended upon that best of men, her husband, who was deprived of his eyesight and whose vigor had departed due to old age, yet who remained her chosen lord.
She served her husband, who was like a family deity who grants one's desires,
a man of great majesty and a treasure-house of asceticism, understanding his every gesture.
The virtuous Manoharā attained supreme joy, like Śacī intent upon serving Śakra; that slender woman, endowed with all auspicious marks, began to serve his feet.
The princess, possessing a beautiful form, subsisted on fruits, roots, and water;
she was constantly intent on carrying out his commands, devoted to his worship,
and spent her time dedicated to the welfare of all living beings.
Having abandoned desire, hypocrisy, hatred, greed, sin,
and pride, he, ever vigilant and diligent, constantly gratified Cyavana.
Thus, performing service for him through speech, body, and action, [he remained devoted].
O Great King, for a thousand years she cherished her desire in her mind.
Once, the two physicians of the gods arrived at the sage’s hermitage; having honored them with a welcome, she performed worship for them.
Their mental dispositions having been gratified by the worship, including water for the feet and offerings, performed by the daughter of Śaryāti,
those two handsome physicians, under the influence of affection, said to that woman of enchanting limbs, "Choose a boon.
Seeing them pleased, she requested a boon from the physicians of the gods.
The princess, the best among the wise, formed a plan. Having perceived her husband’s intention, the king’s daughter spoke these words:
"If you two gods are pleased with me, then let my eyes be given back to my husband."
Having heard these words, which were enchanting to the virtuous maiden,
and having observed her fidelity, the two best of physicians spoke as follows:
"If your husband offers a portion to the gods in the sacrifice,"
"Now, grant us the clear vision of our eyes," [they said]. Cyavana replied, "So be it," regarding the granting of the boon of vigor.

Then the two Aśvins, being delighted, spoke to that best of ascetics: 13–14. "Now, grant us the clear vision of our eyes. Cyavana replied, "So be it," regarding the granting of the boon of vigor. Then the two Aśvins, being delighted, spoke to that best of ascetics.
"Enter this lake created by the Siddhas for those who are sinking [in saṃsāra].
Thus addressed, Jarā, his body seized by old age and his veins throbbing,
was made to enter the lake by the two Aśvins, and he himself plunged into the water.

Three men rose up, exceedingly handsome and beloved by women; they wore golden garlands, had earrings, were identical in appearance, well-dressed, possessed of beautiful limbs, and shone with the luster of the sun.
Beholding them, the woman of noble hips was struck with wonder.
Not knowing her husband was dead, the virtuous wife sought refuge with the Aśvins;
having shown him to her, they, gratified by her devotion to her husband,
took leave of the sage and departed for heaven in a celestial chariot.
When the sacrifice was about to begin and he was joined by his own portion and the purpose of the rite,
he— afflicted by the long duration of time and emaciated by the practice of vows—
spoke out of compassion with a voice faltering with love.
O beautiful lady, I am pleased today by your supreme service and your singular devotion of heart;
for this body of yours is the most intimate friend to all embodied beings.
It was not considered appropriate for me to destroy them for your sake.

(21) Those blessings of the Blessed One—which were won by me through my own devotion to duty, and by means of austerity, meditative absorption, knowledge, and self-yoga—those very same blessings, which are not inconsistent with your service to me, I now bestow upon you; behold them with your vision, for they grant freedom from fear and sorrow. (22)
Others, however, said: "O Blessed One, why do you abandon these arrangements of wealth that have fallen from the knitting of Your eyebrows?
O You of wide strides, enjoy the divine riches produced by Your own dharma, which are unattainable for men through royal machinations.
To him who was speaking thus, the woman [said], who possesses all yogic powers...

Beholding him, who was discerning in wisdom, her mental anguish departed; overwhelmed by profound courtesy and affection, she spoke these words with a face radiant with a smile and a glance of modesty. 24.
Sukanyā said:
"O Lord, O bull among the twice-born, I know this: that you, O powerful one, are the master of unfailing yogic power (māyā).
O husband, I understand that the promise you made—that there shall be a single physical union—is fulfilled; for the offspring of virtuous women possesses even greater excellence. (25)
There, having trained in what was to be done according to the instruction, by means of that [practice],
she whose self was most emaciated through the desire for pleasure—
and who was overcome by the god of love— might attain success.
"O wretched one, behold that palace which is worthy of its lord.
Sumati said:
"Seeking to do what was pleasing to his beloved, Cyavana resorted to the power of yoga."
At that very moment, he caused a celestial chariot to appear— a king of vehicles that moves at will,
delightful, yielding all desires, endowed with every kind of jewel, resulting in the accumulation of all prosperity, and adorned with pillars of precious gems. 27–28.
It was provided with divine coverlets that bring comfort at all times,
adorned with colorful bands and banners,
and with garlands and variegated wreaths upon which bees hummed sweetly. 29.

It was resplendent with various garments such as *dukūla*, *kṣauma*, and *kauśeya*; it was lovely with couches, fans, and other furnishings, and with separate beds prepared in dwellings arranged one above the other.
Adorned here and there with various works of art placed in their respective locations,
it was graced by great emerald platforms and coral altars;
at its doors, the thresholds were made of coral, shining brightly, while the door-panels were of diamond.
On its sapphire peaks it was adorned with golden domes (33),
and it was graced by various canopies suspended from strings of pearls, fashioned upon diamond walls with exquisite, lustrous rubies (34).

Resounding here and there with flocks of swans and pigeons who, repeatedly alighting upon them, mistook them for artificial structures— [the palace] was filled with pleasure-grounds, resting places, sleeping quarters, courtyards, and open squares. (35)

Seeing her thus beholding the house, which seemed to amaze her with its arrangements made to her liking, he who knows the hearts of all beings spoke to her himself with a mind that was not entirely pleased. 36–37.
"O timid one, having bathed in this lake, ascend this celestial chariot," said the lotus-eyed woman of beautiful brows, taking her husband's word to heart;
she wore a garment still bearing dust and her hair was matted like a single braid.
With her limbs covered by the mud of filth and her breasts mottled,
she entered that lake, a reservoir of auspicious waters, with joy; while within the house situated in the middle of the lake, there were hundreds of maidens.
She saw that all of them were of youthful age and possessed the fragrance of blue lotuses;
seeing her, the women rose quickly and, with palms joined in reverence, said: "We are your servants; command us what we should do. (41)
Having bathed that high-minded woman with a most precious bath, O giver of honor, they gave her two spotless, new silk garments and excellent,
supreme ornaments that were radiant like the heavens.
There was food endowed with every excellence and a drink like the nectar of immortality; then he beheld his own self in a mirror, wearing a garland and clad in spotless garments,
having been honored by those maidens who had performed rites for his well-being.
Adorned with a highly precious necklace and a rucaka ornament, his neck was graced by a golden medallion and he wore bracelets; his ankles were decorated with tinkling golden anklets,
and his hips were encircled by a girdle set with many jewels.

When she remembered her beloved husband, the favorite of the sages, with her beautiful-browed face, her white, glossy eyes casting sidelong glances that vied with the lotus bud, and her dark locks of hair falling over her quivering countenance. (47)
And there he dwells with thousands of women, where that lord of sages resides.
Then, seeing herself before her husband surrounded by thousands of women, she fell into doubt regarding his yogic power.
Having performed her bath with the dust of the virtuous, she shone unlike before,
bearing her own form with its beautiful breasts revealed,
well-attired and being attended by thousands of Vidyādharīs.
Then the slayer of enemies ascended that celestial chariot;
in that vimāna, his majesty unimpaired, accompanied by his beloved and with his body attended by Vidyādharīs, he remained.
The lovely moon, situated in the sky and surrounded by stars, shone like a cluster of blossoming white water-lilies;

it was as beautiful as the lord of the night when accompanied by the wind, the friend of the god of love, amidst the valleys of the great kulaparvata mountains where the lords of the eight worlds sport. 52. In those valleys, which were graced by the breezes that are the companions of Ananga...
Accompanied by his host of women, he took delight for a long time like Kubera in the sounds of the Siddhas' songs and the auspicious roar of falling clouds;
he sported with Rāmā in the Vaiśrambha forest, the celestial Nandana grove, Puṣpabhadraka,
Mānasa, Caitraratha, and the lake Sārasa.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Cyavana’s Austerity and Enjoyment," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* within the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
Chapter Sixteen.
Sumati said: Thus sporting everywhere upon the surface of the earth, he did not perceive that hundreds of years, measured by their number, had passed.

Then, having understood that his most excellent beloved was returning at the appointed time and that her desires were fulfilled, the brahmin returned to his preeminent hermitage situated on the banks of the Payoṣṇī.
In that place, crowded with people free from enmity and frequented by deer, he dwelt together with his virtuous son and disciples well-versed in the Vedas;
constantly attended at his pair of feet, he performed supreme austerities. 3–4.
Once, Śaryāti desired to sacrifice to the gods;
then he dispatched his servants to bring Acyavana.
Summoned by them, that best of the twice-born, possessed of great ascetic power, arrived there.
Accompanied by his virtuous wife Sukanyā, who was firmly established in right conduct,
the highly illustrious king saw that best of sages approaching; he beheld the man, radiant as the sun, standing beside his daughter.

To the princess, who had performed a prostration at his feet, the king spoke as if his mind were not particularly pleased, withholding his blessings: "What is this that you wish to do? By you, [your] husband—"
The sage, who is honored by the world, has been deceived by you; having abandoned your husband—who was seized by old age and was unworthy—you have taken to this traveler, a paramour. 9.

"How have you come to such a thought? Otherwise, this would be a disgrace to your family, born as you are of a noble lineage, that you maintain a paramour who brings shame upon your father, your own husband, and your own conduct.
To her father speaking thus, she, with a pure smile, laughed.
He said, "O father, this son of Bhṛgu is your son-in-law. He reported all of this—the attainment of youth and beauty—to his father;
and being both amazed and exceedingly pleased, the father embraced his daughter.
With Soma, he caused the hero Cyavana to perform a sacrifice, and he took the draught of Soma for him;
though the Aśvins were not drinkers of Soma, Cyavana, endowed with the power of asceticism, compelled them by his own splendor to accept the draught.
Taking up his thunderbolt, Śakra prepared to strike the most excellent of Brahmins,
who was sanctifying those unworthy of the assembly by bringing even the two gods into the company of the row.
Seeing Śakra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, intent on killing him, the sage—
The wise one uttered the sound "huṃ" and paralyzed his arm;
Indra, with his arm thus paralyzed, was seen there by all human beings,
hissing in anger like a snake restrained by a mantra.
With his arm paralyzed, Śakra praised that sage, a treasure-house of austerity, whose inner heart was fearless as he was bestowing a share upon the two Aśvins.
He said, "O Lord, let the offering be given to the two Aśvins. (17–18)
"I have not restrained you, O father; forgive the great sin I have committed.
When addressed thus, the sage, that ocean of compassion, quickly abandoned his anger.
At that moment, O bull among men, Indra’s arms were restored.
Seeing this, all the people, their minds filled with wonder,
praised the power of the Brāhmaṇas, which is difficult even for the gods and others to attain.
Then the great king bestowed much wealth upon the Brāhmaṇas.

At the conclusion of the sacrifice, the scorcher of enemies performed the purificatory bath (avabhṛthasnāna) in the Cakra lake. Since you asked about the great prosperity of Cyavana, I have related it all to you in due order, together with his asceticism and yoga.
"Having paid homage to him whose very form is asceticism and having received these blessings for victory,
send him along with his wife to the delightful sacrifice of Rāma.
Śeṣa said:
While they were thus conversing, the horse reached the hermitage;
with the force of the wind, he made the earth tremble as he moved through that great hermitage, cropping the sprouts of *dūrvā* grass with the tip of his mouth.
While the sages, having taken darbha grass, had gone to the river to bathe,
Śatrughna— the scorcher of enemy armies and esteemed by heroes—
reached the exceedingly beautiful hermitage of the sage Cyavana.
Having gone to that hermitage, Vīra saw the sage Cyavana, who stood near Sukanyā like the very embodiment of asceticism;
he prostrated at his feet, announcing his own name. (27–28)
"I am Śatrughna, the brother of the Lord of the Raghus and the protector of horses.
Having heard these words, "I bow to you for the pacification of my great sins," the best of sages replied: 29-30.
"O Śatrughna, O bull among the best of men, may there be prosperity for you;
as you protect the sacrifice, may great fame accrue to you.
Behold, O brahmins, how wonderful it is that even Rāma has become a performer of the sacrifice!"
By the mere remembrance of whose name people effect the destruction of their sins;
even men burdened with great crimes and devoted to the wives of others, when intent on remembering his name, are liberated and attain the supreme goal. (32-33)
By the dust arising from his lotus feet, he who bore a form of stone instantly assumed a captivating appearance that became half of Gautama’s body;
Having consumed the entire heap of their sins, they attained a beautiful form;
beholding the Daitya’s enchanting form on the field of battle, they instead obtained his form, which was free from all deformity. 35–36.
Having meditated upon this steadfastness in the meditation of yogis and established themselves in yoga, they have departed for the supreme state, liberated from the fear of saṃsāra.
"I am blessed today; I shall behold the beautiful face of Rāma."
Her eyes end like lotus petals, her nose is beautiful, and her eyebrows are lovely and well-raised;
she, whose tongue is like the tongue of a serpent, performs the kīrtana of the name of Raghunātha with devotion. (38–39)
Today the merit of my asceticism has been attained, and today my desires are fulfilled,
since I shall behold the face of Rāmacandra, which is difficult even for Brahmā and the other gods to obtain.
With the dust of His feet, I shall purify my own body.
"May I purify my own tongue with most wonderful accounts [of you].
Thus, with speech faltering and tears flowing from the flood of love awakened by the remembrance of Rāma’s feet, he said:
"O Śrī Rāmacandra, bull among the Raghus, embodiment of Dharma, compassionate toward devotees, deliver me from the cycle of worldly existence! 42.
Then, speaking with his eyes filled with streams of tears before the sages, he remained absorbed in meditation and did not perceive there the distinction between self and other.
Śatrughna said to that sage: "O Lord, this is the most excellent sacrifice."
"Let this place be rendered most sacred by the dust of your feet.
It is a great fortune for the Lord of the Raghus that he, the mighty-armed one honored by all the worlds, dwells within the heart of your mind. 44–45.
Thus addressed, Cyavana, together with his retinue and surrounded on all sides by fires,
departed for that place, immersed in a lake of joy;
and Hanumān, beholding that devotee of Rāma approaching on foot, [welcomed him].
Endowed with humility, he spoke these words to Śatrughna:
"O Lord, O Great Being, if you will tell me of a beautiful devotee of Rāma who is an excellent sage, I shall lead him to my own city."
Having heard these great words of the monkey-hero, the slayer of enemies commanded Hanumān: "Go, and bring that sage here.
The swift Hanumān, having placed the sage upon his own back, [set out].
The all-pervading Wind quickly led him along with his family to Rāma.
Seeing that the sage had arrived, Rāma, the best among the wise,
being pleased and overwhelmed with affection, offered him the guest-offering (arghya), water for washing the feet (pādya), and other honors.
"I am blessed now by the sight of you, O best of sages;
my sacrifice, for which all the necessary materials have been gathered, has been purified.
Having heard these words, Cyavana, the most excellent of sages, [responded].
With his limbs bristling with horripilation from the intensity of his love and being exceedingly blissful, he said:
"O Lord, O God who is devoted to the Brahmins, this worship of the Vāḍava fire is indeed appropriate for you, O Great King, who protects the path of dharma. (53-54)

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Departure for Hayagriva's Hermitage," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana within the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter Seventeen.
Śeṣa said:
Then Śatrughna, having witnessed the inconceivable power of Cyavana’s asceticism, praised that Brahmanic austerity which is uniquely venerated by all the worlds. 1.
"O best of Brahmins, behold the perfection of yoga,
by which he caused that celestial chariot— so difficult to attain— to be fashioned in a mere instant!
Where, indeed, is such great attainment of worldly enjoyments for sages of pure soul?"
"Where is the desire for enjoyment among those human beings who are devoid of the power of austerity?
Thus reflecting to himself, Śatrughna stayed for a moment at Cyavana’s hermitage; having drunk water, he attained a state of pleasant enjoyment.
Having drunk the water of that river named Payoṣṇī, whose essence is meritorious water, the great [hero], possessing the speed of the wind in his gait, proceeded on his way;
and the warriors, seeing his departure, then followed after him.
Some with elephants, some with infantry, some with chariots, and others with horses— Śatrughna, accompanied by his chief minister named Sumati,
quickly followed behind in a chariot adorned with excellent horses.
Proceeding on, the horse reached the city of King Vimala,
known as Ratnātaṭa, which was crowded with people who were joyful and well-fed;
there he heard from the attendants that the excellent horse of the Lord of the Raghus had arrived.
Then he arrived in front, accompanied by all his warriors,
with seventy elephants having the luster of the moon,
along with ten thousand horses and chariots possessing the brilliance of gold.
Accompanied by a thousand [chariots], he went forth toward Śatrughna;
having paid his respects to Śatrughna and all the great chariot-warriors who had arrived, he offered him his entire treasury,
all his wealth, and his kingdom.
"What shall I do? the great king said to him as he stood before him; the king then firmly embraced him, who was bowing at his feet, with both arms.
Having heard the name Rāmacandra, which is enchanting to all who hear it, he went together with his sons, having entrusted his entire kingdom to them, surrounded by many archers. 13.
Having bowed down to him, they all gave him vast and great wealth.
Then, having honored the king with supreme joy, Śatrughna,
accompanied by his army, followed behind the horse.
Proceeding thus along that path, he beheld a preeminent mountain,
resplendent with ridges of crystal, gold, and silver, its surface composed of various minerals and echoing with the roar of waterfalls. 16.
It is resplendent with excellent minerals such as red chalk, lac, and vermilion;
there, the perfected women sport fearlessly with the perfected beings (siddhas), while gandharvas, apsarases, and nāgas play there with ease. 17–18.
Having beheld the mountain, which was cooled by breezes touching the waves of the Gaṅgā and graced by the beautiful sounds of lutes, swans, and parrots, Śatrughna spoke thus to Sumati: 19.
His mind filled with wonder arising from that sight, he thought:
"Who is this great, excellent mountain that astonishes my mind?
This marvelous peak, consisting of a true prastha of great silver, shines brilliantly upon my path."
"What deity resides here? This place, with its abundance of splendors, causes agitation to the mind of the gods as they sport here.
Having heard these words, Sumati then spoke.

O King, O protector of the earth, this Nīla mountain shines before you with its captivating great peaks, which have crystal summits on all sides, while the mind of Rāmacandra— the abode of virtues to be described hereafter— is fixed upon his lotus feet. 23–24.
Sinful men who take pleasure in the wives of others do not behold him;
those lowest of men regard him as something other than the multitude of Viṣṇu’s virtues.
Those who [reject] the dharma arising from the Śruti and Smṛti, which has been well-established by the virtuous—
Those who deliberate on the doctrines of causality based on their own intellect;
those who sell indigo, those who sell lac, and that Brahmin who sells ghee and other such items, as well as one who drinks liquor—[these are the ones excluded]. 26–27.
A father, deluded by sin and driven by greed for wealth, does not give his daughter—who is endowed with beauty—to one of noble birth and character, but instead sells her;
such a man defiles his wife, who is possessed of both noble lineage and virtuous conduct. 28–29.
He who eats very sweet food himself but does not give it to his kinsmen;

he who, while eating, makes a distinction in the cooking for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa; and that evil-minded man who does not cause the seeker to receive either kṛsara or pāyasa—[these are the ones who go to hell]. 29–30.

O Great King, those who disregard guests, those tormented by the heat of the sun, those who enjoy the atmosphere, and those who are betrayers of trust— those who turn their backs on the Lord of the Raghus do not see him. 31.
This most meritorious and excellent mountain, graced by Puruṣottama, purifies all beings by its mere sight;
it is enchanting, and here dwells He whose feet are worshipped by the crowns of the gods. 32–33.
The Supreme Person, the bestower of merit, is worthy of being beheld by those possessed of merit;
yet those who declare "not this, not this" according to the Vedas do not know Him,
whose lotus feet are sought after even by Indra and the other gods, and are exceedingly difficult to attain.
The wise know Him through such complete statements as the Vedānta;
that glorious Puruṣottama dwells here upon the Nīla mountain.
Having ascended it, having paid obeisance, and having worshipped Him with virtuous deeds and other offerings—35–36.
"By eating this offering, one indeed becomes a four-armed lord of the earth.
In this regard, they cite this ancient history;
listen to it, O Great King, for it is filled with every wonder. (37)
Whatever occurred regarding King Ratnagrīva and his family— how he attained the state of having four arms and other such marks, which are difficult even for gods and demons to obtain—
that took place in the great royal city of Kāñcī, renowned throughout the worlds. 38–39.
Abounding in a great multitude of followers and rich in troops and vehicles, in that city dwell the foremost of Brahmins, who are intensely devoted to the six duties,
engaged in the welfare of all beings, and deeply longing for devotion to Rāma. 40.
The Kṣatriyas were performers of the *araṇa* (sacrificial rites) and did not flee even in battle;
the Vaiśyas were averse to violating another's wife, seizing another's property, or committing injury, and were auspiciously engaged in the livelihoods of usury, agriculture, and trade. 41–42.
Constantly cultivating devotion for the lotus feet of the Lord of the Raghus, these Śūdras pass the intervals between day and night in the service of Brāhmaṇas;
they utter the words "Rāma, Rāma" from the tips of their tongues. 43.
Not even some common folk there commit sin with their minds or through their faults;
charity, compassion, self-restraint, and truthfulness abide there eternally.
Not a single person there, O sinless one, utters a word that causes harm to others.
They do not harbor greed for another's fuel, for that is indeed a sin;
thus, O Great King, is the people protected by Ratnagrīva.
Free from greed, he takes only the sixth part there, and nothing else.
While the king was thus protecting his subjects in accordance with dharma, many years passed for him who enjoyed every luxury.
O great king, on one occasion he spoke these words to Viśālākṣī: 47–48.
My lawful wife is devoted to her husband and dedicated to the dharma of a faithful spouse;
my sons have not yet been born, O large-eyed one, but they shall be capable of bearing the burden of protecting their subjects. My retinue is vast and free from all distress.

My elephants are like mountains, my horses are like the wind, and my chariots, yoked with excellent steeds, move about constantly for me; by the grace of Mahāviṣṇu, there is nothing lacking for me. 50–51.

Such is the single desire that remains in my mind: O most beautiful one, I have not yet visited that supreme holy place adorned by Govinda, which is capable of bringing an end to dwelling in the womb. 52.
"I have grown old; indeed, my body is now wrinkled and grey-haired.
I shall devotedly undertake the service of the heart-stealing holy fords (tīrthas). For that man who, until the end of his life, is merely a filler of his own belly..."
"One who does not perform the worship of Hari is considered a bull among men afflicted by disease;
therefore, O auspicious one, O beloved, I shall go on a pilgrimage to sacred sites,
having entrusted the burden of the kingdom to my son along with his family."
Having thus resolved during the twilight, while meditating on Hari throughout the night,
he beheld a single dream of a brahmin ascetic.
Rising in the morning, that king performed his duties, beginning with the twilight rituals.
The great king, having sat comfortably with the members of his assembly,
then beheld a brahmin ascetic of emaciated body,
wearing matted hair, bark garments, and a loincloth, and holding a staff in his hand. 58.
Seeing him, whose body was made meritorious through service at many holy fords,
the mighty-armed king bowed his head in salutation; with a joyful heart, the lord of the earth offered him water for his hands and feet, and other traditional honors.
When the twice-born man was seated comfortably and rested, he questioned him who was already known to him: "O Master, by the sight of you today, the sin of my body has been removed;
for the great go with reverence to the homes of the wretched to protect them."
Therefore, O elder Brahmins, tell me now:
which deity can destroy this pregnancy, and what holy place (tīrtha) might be effective?
You are all-traversing, most excellent, and devoted to meditative absorption and contemplation.
O you who are pure by virtue of the merit gained from bathing in all sacred fords,
please tell me in detail and with favor, O expert in all holy places, as I listen with faith according to the truth. (64)
The Brāhmaṇa said:
Listen, O Indra among kings, I shall explain that service to the sacred fords (tīrthas) which you have asked about—
by the grace of which deity does the removal of the womb (liberation from rebirth) occur?
That Śrī Rāmacandra, the destroyer of the fever of worldly existence, is to be served;
he alone is the worshipful Lord known as Puruṣottama.
Various cities have been seen by me, which bring about the destruction of all sins.
Ayodhyā, Sarayū, Tāpī, and the supreme gateway of Hari;
Avantī, Vimalā, Kāñcī, and Revā, which flows toward the ocean;
Gokarṇa, and the one called Hāṭaka, which destroys ten million sins of killing.

The great mountain named Mallikā bestows liberation upon men who behold it. There, on the limbs of men, water becomes dark or stainless; this sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), which removes all sin, was seen by me. 69–70.
By me was seen Dvāravatī, frequented by gods and asuras, where the auspicious Gomatī flows with water that is manifest Brahman;
there, sleep is declared to be dissolution and death is liberation—so says the Śruti. (71)
In that place, strife never arises among men who dwell together;
even the stones there are marked with the discus, and all humans are bearers of the discus, as are the beasts, insects, birds, and so forth—all possess bodies marked by the discus. (72–73)
That city, in which Trivikrama dwells as the sole protector of all the worlds,
has been brought within the range of my vision by great merits. Kurukṣetra, which removes the sin of killing all beings, has also been seen by me.
There is Syamantapañcaka, which destroys even the greatest of sins;
there, in Vārāṇasī, I beheld Viśvanātha, who has made his abode there,
where he imparts the liberating mantra known as Brahman.
In which [world], even insects, moths, bees, animals, or those of divine birth, having died, abandon the pleasure resulting from the enjoyment of their own karma.
Having transcended all suffering, they go to Kailāsa.
There is the Maṇikarṇika tīrtha where the northward-flowing river effects the severance of the bonds of saṃsāra even for those who have committed sins.
Wearing matted hair and earrings, adorned with excellent ornaments of serpents,
and clad in elephant hides, those who have transcended all suffering abide here;
by the mere name of Kālabhairava, the command of Yama is executed.
"Yama, the lord who wields the staff of punishment, does not even inquire about the livelihood of men.
O King, such is Kāśī, marked by the Lord of the Universe, which I have seen;
many other holy places as well have been seen by me."
"A single, supreme, and great marvel was seen on Mount Nīla in the presence of Puruṣottama; this has never come within the range of sight anywhere else.
(82) Thus ends the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Seventeen: The Assembly of Brahmins.
Chapter Eighteen.
The Brahmin said:
O King, listen to what occurred on Nīla, the best of mountains,
by having faith in which men go to the eternal Brahman.
While wandering about, I went there to that mountain named Nīla.
The courtyard there was repeatedly washed with the waters of the Gaṅgā and the ocean. There, on the mountain peak, I beheld Bhillas bearing bows,
their fatigue dispelled by eating roots and fruits, and possessing four arms.
Then, a very great doubt quickly arose in his mind:
"What are these four-armed men, bearing bows and arrows? Is this the form of the self-conquered inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha that is being seen?"
How was that which is difficult even for Brahmā and others to attain reproached by them?
With conch, discus, mace, Śārṅga bow, and lotus shining from their hands,
their bodies encircled by forest garlands, they were like devotees of Viṣṇu standing nearby.
O King, with my mind possessed by doubt, I did not then ask you: "Who are you, and how was the four-armed form obtained by you?
At that, they laughed heartily and spoke to me.

"This Brāhmaṇa does not know the wonderful greatness of the piṇḍa. Having heard this, I said: "O most righteous ones, who possesses four-armed bodies, tell me: what is the piṇḍa, and to whom is it given?"
Having heard those words of mine, all that had occurred there was related by those great-souled ones, beginning with the birth of the Four-Armed One.
The Kirātas said:

"Listen to the account of our brahmin: our young child, while constantly playing about, was eating jambu fruits and other such things. Once, while he was playing, [he climbed] a beautiful mountain peak."
Surrounded on all sides by children, he ascended;
then, right there, I beheld a wonderful temple of the gods, its golden walls inlaid with emeralds and other precious gems. 12–13.

Violently tearing apart the mass of darkness with its own radiance like the sun, [the sage] was struck with wonder upon seeing it and thought: "What is this? Whose house is this? (14) "I shall go and look," he thought; "What is this, the abode of the Great Ones? (15)
Having reflected thus, he entered the interior of the house due to his great good fortune.
There he beheld the Lord of Gods, who is saluted by both gods and demons, and who was resplendent with a crown, necklaces, armlets, a jeweled throat-ornament, and other ornaments. 15–16.
Wearing two exceedingly pure crest-jewels that captivate the mind, his lotus feet are intoxicated by the fragrance of tulasī, which attracts six-legged bees;
he is accompanied by the personified forms of the conch, discus, mace, Śārṅga bow, lotus, and other emblems.
They worshiped his lotus feet, which were the embodiment of glory and well-served by Nārada and others.
Some sang, some danced, and some laughed most wonderfully, pleasing the great king who is uniquely honored by all the worlds. 18-19.
O Sage, seeing Hari, my heart trembled with joy;
then the gods, having performed there an extensive worship complete with incense and other offerings,
prepared a food offering for the sake of the Beloved of Śrī, and thereafter performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
O King, they went each to their own home, looking back with respectful compassion.
By the power of great fortune, he obtained a single grain of the offered food (naivedya), which is difficult even for Brahmā and the gods, or for humans and demigods, to attain. 21–22.
Having consumed that and beheld the form of Śrī, Pṛthuka indeed attained the state of having four arms, appearing most beautiful.
Then, when we reached home, the boy was gazed upon by us again and again.

Having attained a four-armed form and bearing the conch, discus, and other emblems, the boy then spoke to us all regarding this most wonderful marvel that had occurred: "What is this wonder that has happened? (24–25)
Previously, the Lord of the Gods was seen by me there at the very peak of the summit;
there, I obtained a charming morsel of the food offering (naivedya).
By the mere act of eating that, for this present reason—
Having attained a four-armed form, he was filled with wonder. 27.
Having heard those words of his, we too, immediately struck with amazement, beheld that god who is exceedingly difficult to find. 28.
There, food and other things endowed with every kind of flavor were enjoyed;
and by the grace of the Lord, we have once again become four-armed.
O best of beings, you too should go and behold the Lord. 29.
"O Brahmin, having eaten even a single grain of rice there, you became four-armed;
O bull among the Vāḍavas, that wonder which was asked by you has now been told.
Thus ends the [section] in the *Śrī Padma Purāṇa*, in the *Pātāla Khaṇḍa*, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana, in the *Rāmāśvamedha*.
Chapter Eighteen, titled "The Instruction of the Brahmin. Chapter Nineteen.
The Brahmin said:
Having heard those wonderful words of the Bhills, and considering this to be a great marvel, I became truly delighted; indeed,
having bathed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, my body was purified by merit.
Then I ascended that peak, which was adorned with jewels and rubies.
There I beheld the Great King, the God worshipped by gods and others; having paid my respects, I felt my purpose fulfilled through this first feeding of solid food.

Having attained the state of having four arms, marked with the conch, discus, and other signs through the vision of Puruṣottama, I shall not enter a womb again. O King, you too should go quickly there to the mountain named Nīla.
"Make yourself successful and free from the suffering of the womb.
Having heard these words of that wise and foremost of Brahmins, he,
with his limbs thrilled with joy, questioned the sage regarding the procedure for pilgrimage.
The king said: "O sinless one, O foremost of virtuous brahmins, what you have spoken to me is well-said; the majesty of Puruṣottama destroys the sins of those who hear it. (7)
"Tell me the procedure for a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā) as prescribed by the Vedas;
by what rite may men obtain the full fruit [of their journey]?
The Brāhmaṇa said:
Listen, O King, I shall proclaim the auspicious procedure for the pilgrimage by which the God who is worshipped by gods and asuras is attained—
whether one's body be wrinkled and grey-haired, or even endowed with youth. 9.
Having realized that death is unavoidable, one should take refuge in Hari.
One’s mind should be directed solely toward chanting His names, hearing them, bowing to Him, and worshipping Him, and not toward women or other such things. 10–11.
Having observed that everything is transitory, existing only for a moment, and bestowing great suffering,
[one should seek] Acyuta, who is beyond birth, death, and old age, and is beloved by devotion.
Furthermore, from anger, desire, fear, hatred, greed, or hypocrisy, a man—
In whatever way one analyzes suffering as non-existent, one experiences it as equal [to joy].
Through association with virtuous people who are free from sin, that person is born as Hari; by their grace, men become free from unhappiness. (13–14)
O Great King, those virtuous ones who have stilled their passions and are free from desire and greed say that which brings about the cessation of saṃsāra;
such a virtuous person devoted to Rāmacandra is found at sacred fords (tīrthas). 15.
The sight of which is like a fire for burning away the heap of men's sins—
therefore, those men who fear saṃsāra should constantly go to sacred fords (tīrthas) that possess meritorious waters and shine with rows of virtuous people. 16–17.

O tiger among kings, those sacred fords, when visited according to the prescribed rite, destroy sin; therefore, perform that rite which is within the scope of the Vedas. First, one should cultivate detachment toward one's wife, family, and other worldly ties.
Knowing that to be unreal, one should remember Hari with the intention to seize it.

Having gone a distance of one *krośa* while crying out "O Rāma! O Rāma!", one who knows the ritual procedure should bathe in the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and other such places there and undergo a tonsure.
The sins of men follow them to the sacred fords; they remain clinging to their hair. Therefore, one should perform the shaving of the head.
Then, [one should take] a staff without a knot, a water-pot, and a deerskin.
A man who is free from greed may maintain the appearance of a pilgrim;
for those men who travel according to the prescribed rules, there is especially the attainment of fruit. Therefore, one should perform the ritual of pilgrimage with every effort. 22-23.
He whose hands, feet, and speech are well-restrained, and who possesses knowledge, austerity, and fame, enjoys the fruit of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrtha).
O Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of the Cowherds, you who are affectionate toward your devotees!
"O Lord Viṣṇu, refuge of all, protect me from this long cycle of transmigration.
Speaking thus with his tongue and remembering Hari with his mind, one of great fortune should proceed on foot toward the sacred ford (tīrtha). 25–26.
A man traveling by carriage shall obtain an equal share of the fruit;
by means of sandals, a fourth part; by means of a bullock-carriage, there is the sin of cow-slaughter and so forth.
One who employs [the vehicle] for business receives a third part, while one who uses it for service receives an eighth part.

If one goes there to the holy ford without such a desire, one obtains half the fruit. (28) A pilgrim should perform the visits to the holy fords according to their respective order; the destruction of sins certainly occurs, especially when performed according to the prescribed rules. (29)
There, one should pay homage to the virtuous through prostrations at their feet and service;
for by that means, devotion to Hari, the Supreme Person, is attained.
(30) Thus, the procedure for visiting sacred sites has been declared in brief, and not in detail.
"Resorting to this method, go to Puruṣottama.
O great king, Acyuta, being pleased with you, will grant you such devotion that the crossing over of saṃsāra will happen in an instant. 31-32.
"O bull among men, having heard the procedure for the pilgrimage to sacred sites (*tīrthayātrā*), which destroys all sins, one is liberated from all terrible transgressions.
Sumati said:
Having heard these words, the Great One, his mind overwhelmed by the eagerness to behold that sacred ford,
prostrated at [his] feet and commanded his own minister, who was most excellent and skilled in counsel.
Setting his mind on taking everyone with him out of a desire for a pilgrimage to sacred sites (tīrthayātrā),
he commanded all the ministers and the citizens by my order:
"For the sake of the joy of beholding the lotus feet of Puruṣottama."
"O best of men, let all the people in my city who carry out my commands depart from my city along with me. But those men who, having transgressed my word, shall remain in their homes— "
Therefore, these sinners who are the cause of unrighteousness should be punished with punishment; yet they have not been punished.
Of what use is that multitude of sons, or those kinsmen of wicked conduct, by whom Puruṣottama—the bestower of merit—has not been seen with their own eyes? 38–39.

The offspring of those who have not gone for refuge to Hari—the Lord who is capable of purifying all by His name alone—are like a herd of sows, devouring excrement; their sons and grandsons likewise [follow this path]. 40.
"O my subjects, quickly pay homage to him!
At these heart-stealing words, woven with the virtues of the Blessed One, the great minister Uttama, who bore the name Satya, rejoiced greatly. 42.

Having mounted his excellent elephant, he caused a drum to be sounded, proclaiming that which was commanded here by the king who desired to go on a pilgrimage to the sacred fords: "Let the people go quickly with the king to the great mountain."
Behold the destroyer of sins, who bears the name Puruṣottama!
Let the entire ocean of saṃsāra once again become a mere puddle for men, and let their own bodies be adorned with the marks of the conch, the discus, and other symbols. 44–45.
Thus did the minister, whose fatigue was dispelled by meditation on the feet of Raghunātha, proclaim that wonderful decree commanded by the king;
hearing this, all those subjects were submerged in the essence of bliss.
Having resolved in their minds to cross over their own misfortunes by beholding Puruṣottama,
the Brāhmaṇas there, well-attired, set forth along with their disciples,
bestowing blessings rich with the granting of boons upon the king. 47–48.
The Kṣatriyas were archers and heroes; the Vaiśyas were honored for their trade in goods;
the Śūdras delighted their own bodies with the joy of crossing over the cycle of existence (saṃsāra). There were washermen, leather-workers, honey-makers, Kirātas, and masons. 49.
Those who live by the profession of needlework,
those who trade in betel leaves, those who play the tala cymbals, those who subsist on the raṅga (stage), as well as those who sell oil and those who sell clothing; 50-51.
Filled with joy, the charioteers recounted the ancient news; the Magadha bards also emerged there by the king's command,
as did those who lived by the profession of physicians and those skilled in the art of dice.
Skilled in cooking and the flavors of food, delighting others with their humorous speech,
and likewise experts in the arts of illusionists and Vidyādharas,
they went forth from the center of the city, praising the great king. (53-54)
The king, having performed his morning twilight rituals and other duties there,
brought forth that most pure Brahmin, the best of ascetics. By the ascetic's command, the great king went out from the city.
Followed by his subjects, the king shone like the moon among the stars.
Having traveled for the distance of one *krośa*, he then had his head shaved according to the prescribed rites,
carrying a staff, a water-pot, and an auspicious deer-skin.
Endowed with an auspicious appearance, devoted to the meditation on Hari,
and bearing a mind free from desire, anger, and other such passions, that one of great fame [proceeded].
Then, kettledrums, war-drums, ānakas, and paṇavas likewise [resounded].
Conchs, lutes, and other instruments were repeatedly blown by their players;
saying, "O Lord of Gods, O Destroyer of Suffering, O You known as Puruṣottama, show Your body to me," the people went forth speaking thus. 59-60.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Departure of Ratnagrīva for the Sacred Fords," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* within the glorious *Padmapurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
Chapter Twenty.
Sumati said: Then, as the king set forth accompanied by all the people, the illustrious Vaiṣṇavas and singers chanted the praises of Kṛṣṇa.
On the road, the great king Aśoka heard the glorification of Govinda: "Victory to Mādhava! O Supreme Person, refuge of the devotees!
As he proceeded, he visited many sacred fords along the way, beholding great prosperity.
Then the king heard of their greatness from the ascetic brahmins; his mind delighted by various accounts of Viṣṇu,
he had singers sing the praises of Mahāviṣṇu at every stage along the way.

The wise Mahārāja, who had conquered his senses, gave gifts appropriate for the poor, the blind, the wretched, and the lame; he purified himself at many sacred fords and attained a state of auspiciousness. 5.
Performing these acts, the king, devoted to meditation upon Hari, proceeded with his own people. As he went along, he saw before him a river that destroys sins,
filled with stones marked by the discus, as pure as the minds of sages.

Having seen that [place], which was adorned by many rows of numerous groups of sages and graced by the warbling of birds such as cranes, he questioned a foremost brahmin ascetic who was skilled in the dharma.

"O Lord, what is this holy river, frequented by hosts of sages, that causes my heart to overflow with a weight of joy? It is blossoming with the specialized knowledge of the greatness of many sacred fords."
Having heard these words of that wise king of kings, the learned man began to speak of the supreme majesty of the sacred fords (tīrtha). 11.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
O king, this Gaṇḍakī is the queen of rivers, frequented by gods and asuras;
it destroys the accumulation of sins through its flow of meritorious waters.
By its sight, it burns away mental sin, and by its touch, it consumes the sin born of action.

Having previously observed that the entire multitude of subjects was unpurified by the accumulation of sins arising from their own speech and the drinking of their own water, the Lord of Creatures created this [river],
which destroys manifold sins, from the drops of sweat upon his cheek. 13–14.
Those men who touch this river of meritorious waters, which possesses beautiful waves, shall never again enter a womb, even if they are doers of evil.
Furthermore, those stones found within it that are adorned with the marks of the discus—
For those [images] are indeed the supreme Lords themselves, manifesting their own true forms.
That man who constantly worships the stone marked with the discus shall never again enter the womb of a mother.
The wise man who worships the excellent śālagrāma stone should be one of virtuous conduct,
free from hypocrisy and greed, and indeed a person who abstains from the wives and property of others. 18.
The Śālagrāma stone, marked with a discus, should be worshipped with great effort.
O Vīra, the discus originating from Dvāravatī and the stone originating from the Gaṇḍakī river instantly remove the sins of men accumulated over hundreds of births. 19–20.
A man may be the perpetrator of thousands of sins,
yet by drinking the water from a Śālagrāma stone, he becomes pure in an instant.
Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, provided he remains established on the path of the Vedas.

Having worshipped the Śālagrāma, a householder may attain liberation. A woman should never perform the worship of the Śālagrāma; whether she be widowed or fortunate, she who desires the welfare of the heavenly realm [should not do so]. 22–23.
Even by touching [these flowers] out of delusion, a woman endowed with birth, character,
and virtue would swiftly abandon her mass of merit and go to hell.
(24) [One should not place] flowers offered on a woman's hand upon a Śālagrāma stone.
The best of Brahmins declare that the additional footprints of the stone are like those of a serpent;
sandalwood becomes like poison, a flower like a thunderbolt, and an offering made for the Blessed One becomes like the Kālakūṭa venom. 25–26.
Therefore, the touch of a woman must be avoided by every means; for she who performs it upon a stone goes to hell for as long as the reign of fourteen Indras.
Even one of sinful conduct, or even one joined with the murder of a Brahmin, [is purified].
By drinking the water from a Śālagrāma stone, one attains the supreme goal.
Tulasī, sandalwood paste, water, a conch, a bell, a discus, a vessel of stone or copper, and the nectar of Viṣṇu’s names [are the eight auspicious things]. 29.
The peaceful sages, who are experts in the meaning of all scriptures, declare that the nectar of the [Lord's] feet, with its nine syllables, is the burner of heaps of sins;
O King, it is a wonder that merit arises at every single drop [of water offered];
where the Śālagrāma stone is worshipped by the most excellent of men, even an area of just one yojana there is endowed with ten million sacred fords (tīrthas). 31–32.

Śālagrāmas that are equal in size should be worshipped; two should not be worshipped among equals. Only those that are unequal should be worshipped; three should not be worshipped among unequals. Likewise, the discus originating from Dvārāvatī and that originating from the Gaṇḍakī [should be worshipped].
Wherever there is a confluence of both [rivers], there the Gaṅgā flows into the ocean.
(34) Rough [waters] make men harsh, devoid of longevity, prosperity, and strength; therefore, those that are smooth and possess enchanting forms bestow prosperity. (35)
O King, whatever man desires long life, or whatever man desires wealth,
by worshipping [it], he obtains everything pertaining to both this world and the next.
Furthermore, O King, at the time of death, such fortune shall belong to that man.
The merit of one who speaks the name of Hari is equal to that of one who carries a Śālagrāma stone upon his head or holds it near his heart.
For one on the path of life who, even by chance, perceives the manifestation of the Śālagrāma stone, there is liberation; of this there is no doubt. (37–38)
Formerly, it was declared by the Blessed One to the wise Ambarīṣa:
"O Brahmin, these three forms of mine—ascetics, affectionate friends, and likewise Śālagrāma stones—are present upon the circle of the earth. (39)
With joy, he acted to remove the sins of the wicked;
those sinners who even once revile the Śālagrāma stone are quickly cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as the dissolution of all beings lasts. 40–41.
The foolish-minded person who prevents another from preparing to perform worship,
his mother, father, and circle of kinsmen shall share in hell.
Or, O dear one, he who says, "Perform the worship of the Śālagrāma," [is blessed].
Having achieved his purpose, he swiftly leads his own ancestors to Vaikuṇṭha.
On this very point, sages who are free from passion and devoid of desire and anger cite this ancient history.
Formerly, in a region devoid of dharma known as Kīkaṭa, there was a man of the Pulkasa caste named Śabara;
he was constantly intent on killing living beings and frequently carried a bow.
He forcibly takes away the lives of those desiring to go to a sacred ford (tīrtha).
Always intent on killing many living beings, he is ever devoted to others' wives and possessed by passion and the like, as well as by lust, anger, and so forth. 46–47.
Wandering incessantly through the terrifying forest, he took the lives of living beings; with the tip of his arrow smeared with poison, he was ever-strained by the string drawn back upon his bow.
Once, as that hunter, who struck fear into all living creatures, was roaming about—
Though death has arrived, he of fierce mind does not realize it, even though it is close at hand. Then the messengers of Yama arrive, carrying nooses and mallets in their hands,
with copper-colored hair, long nails, and protruding fangs, appearing truly terrifying.
"Let these deluders bind this sinner—who causes fear to all living beings—with dark iron shackles; for he has never, even in thought, been a benefactor to any creature. 51.
"Never has he shown kindness to any living being, even in his mind."
"Devoted to adultery, the misappropriation of others' wealth, and violence toward others—52 from him I shall now extract his large tongue;
and as for this one who speaks alone, I shall pluck out his eyes. 53
One says, "I shall cut off the hands of this sinner," while another says,
"I shall cut off the ears of this evil-minded one. Speaking thus, they pressed their teeth together with great force.
Having arrived, those wicked-souled ones stood there in a state of frenzy, armed with weapons.
Then, one messenger, assuming the form of a serpent, bit him on the foot; as soon as he was bitten, his life-breath suddenly departed.
Then those servants of Yama bound her with iron shackles;
they struck her with whips and angrily beat her with mallets. "Alas! O wicked one, O evil-souled one, you never performed any virtuous deed! 57.
Even if we were to cast you into the Raurava hells with our own minds alone,
fierce crows would devour your skin and flesh in great wrath; for from birth until now, you have not performed service to Hari.
"By you, having made yourself free from wife, sons, and others, you have been well-nourished;
yet at no time was the Lord Janārdana, the remover of sins, remembered.
Therefore, you shall be cast into the Lohaśaṅku, Kumbhīpāka, and Raurava hells."
"By the command of the King of Dharma, we shall all bring him here with many beatings.
Having spoken thus, when the servants of Yama desired to take him away,
at that moment Mahāviṣṇu, who is solely devoted to the lotus-feet [of the Lord], arrived.
Then those hosts of Yama’s messengers, bearing wicked weapons such as nooses, mallets, and staffs, were seen by the high-souled Vaiṣṇava;
they prepared to depart after binding Pulkasa with iron shackles.
As he cried out, "Bind! Bind! Devour! Cut! Pierce!
Split!", the compassionate one, devoted to Padmanābha, then directed his mind toward him with extreme pity.
"Let not this great suffering from the wicked come into my presence;
I shall release him this very day even from the messengers of Yama.
Having formed this thought toward him, the lord of sages was filled with compassion.
Holding a Śālagrāma stone in his hand near the mouth of the Lord,
he placed the meritorious water from His feet, mixed with Tulasī leaves,
into his own mouth, while chanting the name of Rāma into his ears.
That Vaiṣṇava wore Tulasī upon his head, and having placed the stone of Mahāviṣṇu upon his heart, that Vaiṣṇava laughed.
"Go away, messengers of Yama, you who are intent upon inflicting torments! (69)

"The touch of a Śālagrāma stone burns away even great sin. When he had spoken thus, O King, the most wonderful attendants of Viṣṇu arrived in his presence, for he had been cleansed of his sins by the touch of the stone.
Clad in yellow garments and resplendent with conchs, discs, maces, and lotuses,
they arrived and liberated him from the difficult-to-overcome iron fetters. Having freed that Pulkasa man who had committed great sins, [they departed].
They said: "For what reason has this Vaiṣṇava, a venerable bearer of a body, been bound? Whose commands do you carry out, you who practice such unrighteousness?
Release this Vaiṣṇava; for what purpose indeed has he been held captive?"
Having heard these words, the servants of Yama,
who had arrived by the command of Dharmarāja and were intent on taking away the sinner, spoke:
"He never, even in his mind, performed a single act of assistance for any living being."
A perpetrator of the great sin of killing living beings, he bore a wicked body;
while many men were traveling on a pilgrimage, he plundered them.
Constantly devoted to the wives of others, he was the perpetrator of every kind of evil. (76–77)
"Therefore, we had come to take this sinful Pulkasa man;
why has he been released by you soldiers who arrived here unexpectedly?
The messengers of Viṣṇu said:
The touch of a Śālagrāma stone instantly consumes all sins, such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa or the slaughter of tens of millions of living beings.
If the name "Rāma" should reach the ears through trust, [it likewise destroys all evil].
It causes the burning of sin just as a spark of fire consumes cotton.
He on whose head is Tulasī, in whose heart is the charming Śāligrāma stone,
and from whose mouth or ear the name of Rāma has been released— he is liberated at that very moment.
Therefore, because he formerly held the Tulasī on his head, heard the name of Rāma, and firmly retained it in his heart like nectar,
the mass of his sins has been burnt away and his body has become composed of merit.
He shall go to the supreme abode, which is very difficult for sinners to attain.
Having enjoyed there for ten thousand years all manner of enchanting pleasures, he will obtain birth in Bhārata and, having fully propitiated the Teacher of the World, [attain liberation]. 83–84.
One shall attain the supreme abode, which is very difficult even for gods and demons to reach;
yet the greatness of this stone of the Supreme Lord has not been fully known.
When seen, touched, or even worshipped, it removes all sins in an instant.
Having spoken thus, all the attendants of Mahāviṣṇu remained silent.
O King, those southern servants reported the wonder to the Lord:
"The devotee of Viṣṇu, who is solely devoted to Raghunātha, has attained great joy. (86-87)
Once he was liberated from that noose, he would go to the supreme state;
then there arrived from the world of the gods a celestial chariot (vimāna), stainless, adorned with clusters of tinkling bells, enchanting to the mind, and most wonderful.
Having ascended there and gone to heaven, which is frequented by those of great merit,
he enjoyed vast pleasures and then returned to the surface of the earth;
having obtained birth in Kāśī within a pure and noble Vāḍava family.
Having worshipped the Lord of the worlds, that sinner, by the power of association with the virtuous and by touching the Śālagrāma stone, attained the supreme state;
freed from great suffering, he went to the highest abode. 91.
O King, I have thus related to you this great narrative of Gaṇḍakī.
By hearing it, one is liberated from sins and attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus ends the [section] in the *Śrī Padma Purāṇa*, in the *Pātālakhaṇḍa*, within the *Rāmāśvamedha*, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
The Greatness of the Gaṇḍakī, Chapter Twenty.
Chapter Twenty-One. Sumati said:
Having brought this incomparable majesty of the Gaṇḍakī within the range of his ears, that best of kings considered himself to have achieved his life's purpose;
having bathed in the holy ford and offered libations to all his ancestors, he rejoiced greatly.
Following the words of the brāhmaṇa, that best of kings performed the worship of the śālagrāma stones; having taken twenty-four stones from there,
he worshipped them with love using sandalwood and other offerings.
Having given gifts there, especially to the poor and the blind,
the king set out for the temple of Puruṣottama.
In this manner, he arrived in due course at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
Having brought that brāhmaṇa within the range of his vision, he joyfully asked him:
"O Master, tell me, how far away is the great mountain named Nīla,
the abode of Puruṣottama, which is worshipped by gods and asuras?"
Having heard those great words of King Ratnagrīva,
he was filled with wonder and spoke respectfully to the king:
"O King, this place is the site of the Nīla mountain, which is worthy of salutation."
"For what reason is this place, which bestows such great merit as its fruit, not seen?
He said this again and again: "O King, why is this site, the abode of Puruṣottama, not visible?"

"O King, having been properly bathed here, I ascended to the top of the mountain by this very path while remaining within the range of the eyes of the forest-dwellers. Upon hearing these words of his, the king was deeply pained in his mind.
Making his mind yearning by beholding the Blue Mountain (Nīlabhūdhara), he said:
"O Brahmin, how may Puruṣottama be seen?
Or how is Nīla seen? Tell us the means for that."
Having heard those words of King Ratnagrīva,
the astonished king, the ascetic Brāhmaṇa spoke these words:
"O Lord of the Earth, having bathed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean by us..."
One should remain right here as long as the Blue One is not seen.
The God known as Puruṣottama, the destroyer of sins,
who bears the name "the one who is affectionate toward his devotees," will swiftly show his grace.
"That crest-jewel of the gods of gods abandons those who are not devoted; many devotees have been protected by him—sing of him, O high-minded one!
(16) Having heard these words, the king’s heart was filled with distress.
Having bathed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, one should then undertake a fast.
If Puruṣottama shows mercy upon being seen, one may eat after performing worship; otherwise, the vow is fasting. 17–18.
Having thus made this vow, he sang of the multitude of Hari’s virtues on the shore of the Ganges and the ocean, and then observed a fast.
The King said:
Victory, O Lord who is a mine of compassion for the miserable! Victory, O You whose name is auspiciousness and who removes suffering!
Victory, O You who possess a form that destroys the afflictions of Your devotees! Victory, O Destroyer of the wicked!
[Then, seeing Ambarīṣa distressed, his every auspiciousness struck down by the curse of the Brahmins...]
Holding the Sudarśana discus in his own hand, you protected him from dwelling within the belly [of Hiraṇyakaśipu].
Afflicted by the tortures inflicted upon his father by the king of the Daityas— through impalement on a trident, drowning in a noose, and falling into water and fire—
you, assuming the form of Śrī Nṛsiṃha, protected him even as his father looked on.

Seeing the lordly elephant, whose feet had fallen into the jaws of a crocodile and who was tormented by extreme suffering, your mind became moist with noble compassion; you, Garuḍa, performed the act of tearing [the jaws] asunder.
Having abandoned the lord of birds, you took up your discus, shaking the garland of worlds and the garments of the sky with your speed.
You are sung of by the virtuous as the one who releases this man from his suffering and instantly destroys it.
O Lord, wherever there is the oppression of Your servants, You assume a physical form in those very places to protect Your own people with Your heart-stealing deeds that remove all sins. 24–25.
O Lord of the wretched, whose soles are rubbed by the diamonds in the crowns of the gods, O Beloved of your devotees, O Prabhū who burns away tens of millions of sins, show me your own vision!
If this person, though a doer of evil, has come before you with his mind, then show it to him accordingly.
O You who are worshipped by gods and asuras, we have indeed forgotten this destroyer of the flood of sins;
[for] those who utter Your stainless name cross the entire ocean of evil. If remembrance has been made by me, then let it be attained, O Protector from all suffering! 27–28.
Sumati said: Singing his virtues in this manner, whether by night or by day, the lord of the earth never rested for even a moment; he found no happiness nor did he obtain sleep. 29.
"O Puruṣottama, Lord of Mercy, show me Your own form day and night, whether I am singing, walking, speaking, or standing still.
Thus five days passed for the king at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
Then the Lord of the Cows (Brahmā), an ocean of compassion, thought with mercy:
"This king has had his sins removed by my song;
let him behold me, my most beloved, who am saluted by gods and demons. 31-32.
Having thus reflected, the Lord, his mind filled with compassion,
assumed the guise of a renunciant and went into the presence of the king.
O great king, having gone there, he appeared wearing the dress of a tridaṇḍī ascetic.
Having been seen by the ascetic out of compassion for his devotee, the best of kings said, "Oṃ namo viṣṇave," and bowed down;
with his mind fixed on Hari, he performed worship with offerings of water for the hands, water for the feet, and a seat. 34-35.
"Since you have come within the range of my vision, my good fortune is incomparable;
hereafter, Govinda will grant me his very own sight.
Having heard those words, the renunciant spoke to him:
O King, listen to my words as they issue forth;
I know through wisdom that which has been, that which is to be, and that which is present.
Therefore, I shall say something; listen with a one-pointed mind. 37-38.
Tomorrow at midday, Hari will grant you a vision difficult even for Brahmā to obtain;
together with five of your own kinsmen, you shall go to the supreme abode. You, your minister, Mahilāvatī, and the ascetic Vāḍava—[all shall go].
The virtuous weaver named Puretavakaraṃba—
by these five, you shall go upon this most excellent mountain Nīla, which is saluted by Brahmā and Indra and worshipped by the gods. 40-41.
Having spoken thus, the ascetic vanished and was no longer seen anywhere;
hearing this, the king immediately attained joy along with great wonder. 42.
The King said:
"O Lord, who was that person who came here, renounced this world, and spoke thus?
He is not seen again; where has that heart-gladdener gone?
The ascetic said:
O King, his heart drawn by great love for you,
this one named Puruṣottama, the destroyer of all sins, has arrived.
Tomorrow at midday, a great mountain shall appear before you.
"Having ascended that [vehicle] and seen Hari, you shall have achieved your purpose.
With the fever of his heart dispelled by this flood of nectar-like words,
the king attained such joy as even Brahmā could not know.
Then the kettledrums resounded, as did the lutes, small drums, and horn-like instruments; for at that time there was great bliss in the heart of King Rājāja.
Singing of Hari, he stood for a moment, laughing, talking, speaking, and bowing.
He attained a profound bliss that destroys all suffering. 48.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Vision of the Sannyāsin," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* within the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. 21.
Chapter Twenty-Two. Sumati said:
Then, having spent the entire day in the remembrance and chanting of Hari’s names, [he went to sleep].
During the night, while sleeping on the bank of the Gaṅgā which yields abundant fruit,
he beheld himself in the midst of a dream as four-armed,
bearing the conch, discus, mace, lotus, and the Śārṅga bow.

Seeing the Supreme Person dancing before Śarva and the other gods, together with the glorious Viṣvaksena and his excellent hosts of attendants— each accompanied by his own form and bearing weapons such as the discus, mace, conch, lotus, and thunderbolt— and seeing the Lord of Śrī constantly worshipped by them, he was struck with wonder that reached the world and with most extraordinary joy. 3.

"Grant me my heart's desire, O you who are known as Puruṣottama"; thus did the high-minded one consider himself a vessel of compassion. In this manner, the best of kings beheld [this] within the realm of his dream.
Having woken up in the morning, O Brahmins, he related the dream he had seen.
Upon hearing it, the wise son of a Brahmin, filled with wonder, said:
"O King, that being whom you saw is known by the name Puruṣottama."
"Hari will bestow his own body, marked with the conch, the discus, and other signs.
Having heard these words, the high-minded Ratnagrīva caused gifts to be given to the poor according to their desires.
Having bathed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, and having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods,
he beheld that vision while singing the multitude of Hari’s virtues; then,
at the time of midday, celestial drums resounded repeatedly.
Resounding with the loud noise of the blows from the hands of the gods, they struck [him];
and suddenly, a rain of flowers fell upon the king's head.
"O best of kings, you are blessed; behold Nīla within the range of your vision! (10-11)
When the king heard the words uttered by the god,
then there appeared before the king’s eyes a magnificent great mountain named Nīla, possessing a splendor exceeding that of ten million suns.
Resplendent on all sides with peaks of silver and gold, [they asked:
"Is this fire blazing? Or is it a second sun? Or is this a mass of lightning that has suddenly assumed a steady radiance? (13-14)
Having seen the beautifully adorned Nīlaprastha, the ascetic brahmin informed the king: "This is a great, meritorious mountain.
Upon hearing this, the best of kings bowed his head in reverence.
"I am blessed; I have accomplished my purpose, O bull among men, that Nīla has come within the range of my vision.
16. O best of men, the minister, the king’s wife, Karamba, and the weaver were all filled with joy at the sight of Nīla. 17.
These five, at the time of victory, ascended Mount Nīla while hearing the great sounds of kettledrums struck by the immortals;
they were upon its upper peak, which was adorned with variegated trees.
He beheld an unsurpassed temple bound with gold (19),
where Brahmā, having arrived, constantly performs worship of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) and offers food-oblations that bring satisfaction to Hari (20).
Then, having seen that supreme and stainless temple of the gods, he entered it surrounded by his five attendants. There,
he beheld [the image] fashioned of gold and adorned with great jewels.
Shining upon his lion-throne, four-armed and enchanting,
and attended by Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Vijaya, Jaya, and others,
the king, together with his wife and accompanied by his servants, prostrated before him.

Having prostrated before the Supreme Self, the Great King bathed that best of gods according to the rules with bathing mantras prescribed in the Vedas. With a joyful mind, the king also offered him water for the hands (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), and other honors.

Having smeared him with sandalwood paste and offered him fine garments, and having performed the incense offering and the waving of lights (ārārtika), the king then presented an offering of all kinds of delicious and delightful foods to the form of the Lord. 25–26.
Having prostrated, he offered praise along with the ascetic and the brahmin, using collections of hymns composed according to their intelligence and woven from a multitude of virtues. 27.
The king said:
You alone are the one Supreme Person, the Lord manifest, beyond primordial nature (prakṛti),
distinct from both cause and effect, and worshipped by the principles beginning with the Great Principle (mahattattva).
From the lotus of Your navel was born Brahmā, the expert in the work of creation.
Likewise, Rudra, who was born from your eye, is the agent of its withdrawal;
commanded by you, he performs all the activities of this universe.
From you was born in the past that which is ancient—the world, both stationary and moving. (29-30)

O Lord of the World, alas, you perceive this [universe] by entering into the power of consciousness; yet for you there is neither birth nor end. O All-pervading One, increase, decay, and transformation do not exist in you at all. 31
Nevertheless, for the sake of protecting your devotees and for the purpose of establishing dharma,
you indeed undertake births, actions, and qualities that are appropriate [to each occasion]. By you, having assumed the form of a fish, the asura Śaṅkha was slain.

O Brahman, O progenitor of the Great Being, the Vedas are well-guarded; even Śeṣa does not know them in their entirety, nor does the great goddess Bhāratī—how much less others like me, O Mahāviṣṇu, who possess but poor intellect? (33-34)
"Even with the mind one does not attain you, O Supreme Goddess; how then, O Lord, am I able to praise you? Having thus praised him, he repeatedly prostrated himself with his head bowed low.
His body bristling with horripilation and joined by a faltering voice,
the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, his soul delighted by this praise,
spoke these truthful and meaningful words to the king. (36-37)
The Blessed One said: O King of great intelligence, I was filled with supreme joy by your hymn of praise; know you that I am the Great King, transcendent beyond primordial nature (prakṛti). 38
"Indeed, quickly partake of this delightful food offering;
having attained the state of four arms, you shall go to the supreme abode.
Whatever man pleases me with this jewel of a hymn composed by you,"
"Even his sight shall grant the boon of enjoyment and liberation.
Having heard these words spoken by the Blessed One, the king partook of the consecrated food (naivedya) together with his four servants.
Then the righteous king beheld a celestial chariot named Puruṣottama, adorned with networks of tinkling bells, attended by throngs of apsarases, and endowed with every luxury. 42.

Having made himself a fit vessel for his compassion, he prostrated at his feet. Then, by his command, he ascended a celestial chariot accompanied by his wife and went to the wonderful Vaikuṇṭha in the sky even as he was looking on.
The minister, devoted to dharma and the supreme knower of all dharmas, went along with the king in a celestial chariot, attended by a multitude of women.
There was also a brahmin ascetic there who had bathed in all the sacred fords.
