Having attained a four-armed form, Karabha, O great king, went by means of his merit to the abode of the gods, which is difficult even for all the deities to obtain; he departed together with the gods traveling in their celestial chariots. 46–47.
All of them departed for the most wonderful realm of Viṣṇu;
they were four-armed, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
All possessed the splendor of clouds, pure, and held gently swaying lotuses in their hands. 48.
With their limbs adorned with necklaces, armlets, and bracelets, they ascended to heaven.
Seeing those rows of celestial chariots, the people and the subjects then brought the resonant sound of kettledrums within the range of their hearing.
At that time, there was a certain brāhmaṇa who was devoted to the lotus feet of Viṣṇu;
his mind being drawn by separation from Him, he became four-armed.
Seeing that marvel, those people praised that great manifestation.
Having bathed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, they returned toward that city.
"Oh, what great fortune belongs to the wise King Ratnagrīva!
By means of this very body, he has gone to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. (52-53)
O King, this is Nīlagiri, honored by Puruṣottama;
merely upon seeing it, people truly go to Vaikuṇṭha, the supreme refuge.
He who hears this greatness of Nīla is fortunate.
Whoever causes this to be heard by the worlds, those two shall go to the supreme state.
Having heard this, that bad dream perishes by the mere act of remembering;
in the end, Puruṣottama grants deliverance from saṃsāra.
He who dwells in Nīla, that Rāma, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama),
and Sītā, who is Mahālakṣmī herself— the cause of all causes—
having performed the horse sacrifice, will indeed purify the worlds.
Whatever penance is prescribed for the slaughter of a Brāhmaṇa, that has now arrived at your horse on this most excellent mountain, Nīla;
therefore, O high-minded one, pay homage to Lord Puruṣottama. 58–59.
"Having become sinless therein, we shall go to the supreme state,
by whose grace many have crossed over the ocean of worldly existence.
While he was speaking thus, his horse reached Mount Nīla.
By the force of his wind, he made the earth’s surface crumpled and its regions shattered.
Then the king, traveling upon his back, reached the mountain named Nīla; having bathed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, he went to Puruṣottama.
Having praised and bowed to the Lord of Gods, who is worshipped by both gods and demons,
the slayer of enemies considered himself to have achieved his purpose.
Thus ends the [section] in the *Śrī Padma Purāṇa*, in the *Pātālakhaṇḍa*, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana, in the *Rāmāśvamedha*.
The twenty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Nīlagiri.
Chapter Twenty-Three. Śeṣa said:

Having stood for a moment and having eaten some grass, the horse, swift as thought, went on, surrounded by a line of heroes, with a leaf held [before him] and a chowrie. He was accompanied by the brave Śatrughna and King Lakṣmīnidhi.
Protected by Puṣkala, Ugravāhana, and Pratāpāgrya,
O Lord, he went to the city of Sañcakrāṅkā, which was guarded by Subāhu and protected by many millions of heroes.

Then his son, Damana, who was a great man engaged in hunting, saw a horse adorned with a forehead-ornament and smeared with sandalwood paste and other unguents. Upon seeing it, he spoke to his attendant: "Whose horse is this that has come within my sight?"
"Is that a forehead-ornament worn, or is it a beautiful fly-whisk?
(5) Having heard these words of the king, the servant then went to where that horse with the beautiful forehead-ornament was located. (6)
Taking him, who was adorned with a garland of jewels amidst his mass of hair, he brought him before King Subāhu, the upholder of the lineage;
and he had the letter read aloud, which was beautified by its elegant characters.
And there was a powerful king, Daśaratha, who was the sovereign of Ayodhyā. His son was Rāmabhadra, the crest-jewel of all heroes; there was no other on earth equal to him in prowess as an archer.
Therefore, that horse, adorned with sandalwood paste and other unguents, was released by him;
the righteous Śatrughna, slayer of enemy heroes, protects it.
And we who are here are brave warriors, these very ones with bows in our hands.
Let them seize the horse adorned with a garland of jewels by force;
then Śatrughna, the crest-jewel of all heroes, will liberate it. Otherwise, let those archers prostrate themselves at his feet.
Perceiving this intention, the prince said:
"Rāma alone is the wielder of the bow; we are not considered Kṣatriyas. While my father remains on earth, what great pride is this in the world?"
"May he obtain the fruit of his arrogance through my released arrows.
Today, let my sharp shafts make Śatrughna, like a blossoming *kiṃśuka* tree, covered with wounds. (14-15)
Let them tear the cheeks of the rutting elephants with their arrows;
let them behold horses by the hundreds drenched in floods of blood;
and let the throngs of Yoginīs drink the blood from human skulls. 16.
May the jackals be satisfied by devouring the flesh of my enemies;
let them behold the great strength of my arms as I discharge millions of arrows released from the staff of my bow. 17–18.
Having spoken thus to the king, the powerful son named Udaman, being greatly delighted, sent him back to his own city;
then he said this to the commander-in-chief: "O high-minded one, make yourself ready."

Having quickly prepared an immeasurable army for me to repel the host of enemies, he stood ready on the battlefield facing them; while he remained there in his extreme ferocity, his horse and followers arrived.
"Where is that horse of the great king, marked with a mark on its forehead?
they asked one another repeatedly, greatly agitated.
Just then, Pratāpāgrya, the scorcher of foes, saw [the horse] before him.
The army was fully prepared and resounded with the shouts of heroes.
There, some people said: "O King, this horse has been led away by him;
otherwise, how could that hero, followed by his forces, stand facing us? (23-24)
Having heard this, Pratāpāgrya dispatched a servant;
having gone there, he asked, "Where is King Rāma? By whom was he taken, and from where was he taken? That dull-witted man did not know Rāma.
The great army of that King of Dharma, when provoked, will surely devour those gods led by Śakra who have come with offerings and bowed down, unless they submit in every way. (26–27)
Having heard what was thus spoken, the powerful son of the king,
being deeply distressed, reviled him with a web of words:
"The sacrificial horse, adorned with leaf-marks and other signs, has been brought back by me."
"Those Jesuras, having conquered me, have released me here by force.
Hearing those words, the servant, filled with rage, went away laughing and reported to the king exactly what had been described.
Hearing that, Pratāpāgrya, possessed of great strength and eyes copper-red with rage,
went forth to fight the prince who was preceded by great heroes,
riding in a chariot with golden parts and beautifully adorned with four horses. 31.
The powerful one, endowed with great strength, went forth with his quiver filled with all kinds of missiles; he made his bow twang and,
overcome with anger, laughed aloud again and again until tears welled up from his eyes.
Mounted on horses and elephants, with swords flashing in their hands,
they followed that foremost of heroes, whose eyes were agitated and filled with wrath;
there were also crores of elephants and foot-soldiers intent on battle.
Having had a gateway constructed for which he had long yearned,
the heroic prince, the foremost of warriors, surrounded by a great force, went out to meet the enemy army as soon as he perceived it approaching. 35-36.
Armed with armor, a sword, and a bow, the youth advanced to fight with effortless ease, like a lion toward a herd of elephants.
Then the warriors, provoked to anger, sought to slay one another.
Skilled in the duties of the gateway, shouting "Cut! and "Pierce!", the infantrymen were joined by groups of infantry; those mounted on elephants by elephant-riders;
those mounted on chariots by those staying in chariots; and those mounted on horses by those stationed on horseback. 38–39.
Elephants were split in two, horses were cut in pieces,
and the earth was indeed filled with the brains of many men.
Then King Pratāpāgrya, possessed of great strength, became enraged.
And seeing the prince intent on the slaughter of his own army,
he then said to the charioteer: "Drive the horses to where that great car-warrior, the prince, is engaged in the destruction of my forces."
Then the valiant prince, whose feet were bowed to by the crest-jewels of heroes,
went directly toward that Pratāpāgrya;
the charioteer brought the horses of Pratāpāgrya forward.

There, standing in a chariot polished with gold and holding a staff-like bow, he who was the hero Asaudamana— the crest-jewel of all heroes— went and challenged that prince who was intent on battle. 44-45.
O little prince, you have bound this most excellent horse, yet you do not know the great king who is served by all the lords of heroes;
it is he whose wondrous majesty even the lord of the Daityas was unable to withstand. 46.
Having led that horse away, you have come to this city;
know me to be an enemy in the form of Time who has arrived before you.
Release the horse, O child, go, and play with auspicious toys. 47–48.
"Whose son are you? Where are you from? How was this horse, which we were so short-sighted as not to see, seized by us? O child, compassion has arisen within me for you.
Hearing this, the high-minded Damana smiled.
And speaking thus, treating that preeminent prowess and his army as mere straw,
Damanaka said:
"The horse was forcibly bound by me and brought to my own city."

"O one of great strength, as long as I possess life, I shall not yield; fight with me today! O Great King, behold this play of mine at the forefront of the battle—this 'play' which you, a child, said I should perform by going there. (51-52)
Śeṣa said:
Having spoken thus and having strung his excellent bow, the son of Subhujāngama fixed a hundred arrows upon the chest of Pratāpāgrya. (53)
Aiming a hundred arrows, the majestic one blew his conch shell;
by that sound of the conch, fear indeed arose among the cowards.
He struck them in the heart with a hundred arrows.

The powerful prince, foremost in prowess and light-handed, cut down the well-jointed arrows; seeing his shafts thus severed, he became enraged and discharged sharp, heron-feathered *bhalla* arrows. 55–56.
In the sky, on the earth, and in between, arrows marked with his own name were seen drawn back,
beautiful with the fall of their sharp edges;
those arrows, having struck his chest and arms, emitted many sparks of fire.
As they were creating that great conflagration against the army, Pratāpāgrya, becoming enraged, cried out, "Stay! Stay!
and struck them on the head with ten arrows. 58-59.
Fixed upon the forehead of that prince Bāṇa,
those arrows shone like the ten branches of a tree on a mountain peak.
By that blow from Bāṇa, the high-minded one was deeply pained.
Just like a seven-year-old elephant struck by a goad-stick,
he fixed three hundred auspicious arrows to his bow and released them—
arrows adorned with golden feathers and resembling the great fire of cosmic destruction.
Those arrows of Pratāpāgrya, having pierced his chest and become smeared with blood, fell downward like those who are averse to devotion for Rāmacandra.
Then Pratāpāgrya, greatly enraged, released arrows by the thousands.
In that very instant, he swiftly rendered Subāhu’s son, Viratha, chariotless; with four arrows he struck down his four horses, with two he shattered his banner,
and with one he felled the charioteer’s head from his body to the ground.
Again, he struck the king’s son with four arrows, and at that very moment, he cut his bow— still strung— with one shaft.
He then mounted another chariot, beautifully adorned with excellent horses.
Taking up his bow and stringing it, the high-minded one replied: "O foremost of the valiant, you have displayed wonderful prowess;
now behold, O noble warrior, the power of my bow. (67-68)
Having spoken thus, he took up ten arrows;
with four, he sent the four horses to the abode of Yama.
With another four, the chariot, along with its wheels, was cut into pieces as small as sesame seeds.
With one arrow he pierced the heart, and with another, the charioteer.
Filling his conch shell, he roared, accompanied by the sound of the conch.
"Well done, O hero of great strength! they exclaimed, praising that deed.
Beholding such prowess, filled with intense rage, Pratāpāgrya mounted another chariot and went forth to fight the prince.
He said, "O hero, behold my wonderful valor!"
Having spoken thus, he swiftly released a torrent of sharp-jointed arrows.
Arrows were seen everywhere— upon the elephants and the horses—
pervading all things like the Supreme Brahman, yet remaining within the range of perception.

Having quickly covered that prince with millions of sharp arrows, the valiant one roared aloud; gladdening his own hosts while making his enemies utterly despondent in their hearts and deprived of life,
that prince [was overwhelmed] by the multitude of his sharp shafts.
Beholding himself fully restored, the enraged one of boundless prowess seized his weapons;
the great hero brandished his bow with his staff-like arms.

The mighty prince, his eyes copper-red with rage, cut down all those missiles and weapons as he discharged arrows capable of rending his enemies; having warded off that mass of weapons, the prince spoke to him.
"Forgive me this one blow, O noble one, if you are indeed a hero.
If I were to strike you down from your chariot with this [arrow], O hero, listen to my vow made without pride. (78-79)
"May the sin of those intoxicated ones who, being experts in the doctrine of causality, revile the Veda, be mine alone as I sink into the ocean of hell.
Having said this, he drew toward Bāṇa a bow resembling Death itself.
A sharp, excellent arrow, wreathed in garlands of flames and drawn from its quiver,
was discharged by that best of kings; aimed at his heart,
it flew toward him with great speed, possessing a radiance like the fire of cosmic destruction.
Seeing the arrow raised for his own slaughter, Pratāpāgrya then fixed sharp arrows upon his bow for the purpose of cutting that shaft;
indeed, with his own arrow already nocked, he cut all those arrows right through their middles.
The arrow, possessing supreme power and joined with fortitude, went toward his heart;
having lodged in the heart like a lotus stalk, it entered deep within. Struck by that blow, the king fell upon the surface of the earth.
Unconscious and deprived of his senses, he fell from the seat of the chariot to the ground;
the charioteer, taking him up, carried him away from the circle of the battlefield.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, and the army was broken and fled from there.
There, that prince named Śatrughna, surrounded by ten million heroes and having attained victory and preeminent prowess,
waited for King Śatrughna after having conquered him. 87-88.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Account of the Battle between the Two Princes," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana within the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter Twenty-four.
Śeṣa said: Śatrughna, overcome with rage, ground his teeth against his teeth,
shook his hands, and repeatedly licked his lower lip with his tongue.
Again and again he asked them: "By whom was my horse Pratāpāgrya led away? By whom was that crest-jewel of all heroes conquered?
Then those servants replied, "O slayer of enemies, by one named Damana."
The son of Subāhu, possessing supreme prowess, conquered and seized the horse.
Hearing that the horse had been taken by his enemy Damana, he arrived with great speed at the place where the circle of battle was located.
There, along with Śatrughna, he saw elephants with split temples,
resembling mountains whose peaks were dripping with blood and intoxicated with rut;
and there he saw horses wounded together with their riders.
Mṛtāvīra was seen by the enraged Śatrughna;
observing men, chariots, and elephants shattered, that slayer of enemies became exceedingly furious, like the ocean of dissolution at the end of an aeon.
Seeing before him the formidable tamer of horses,
who had surpassed his own strength and was the conqueror of even the greatest in prowess,
the king then replied to his warriors with eyes agitated by anger.
Who is this invincible one here who wields all weapons and missiles?
Let him, who will fearlessly conquer the heroic son of Virāṭa—skilled in the arts of war—by means of his weapon, now prepare himself. 9–10.
Having heard these words, Puṣkala, the slayer of enemy heroes,
prepared to conquer Damana and spoke this speech: "O Lord, where is this Damana, and where is your immeasurable strength?"
"I shall conquer through your majesty; I am going now, O high-minded one!
While I stand here as a servant for the sake of battle, by whom can the horse be led?
This majesty of the Lord of the Raghus will perform every task. (12-13)
"O Lord, hear this vow of mine which bestows joy:
I shall conquer this Rāmacandra, who is skilled in the arts of battle, for those who are deprived of tasting the nectar of his lotus feet."
If that sin were to exist, it would not overcome my self-control.
(15) If a son, regarding the feet of his mother as a sacred ford, should act in opposition to her, even that would not overcome my self-control. (16)
Pierced by the first arrow, the prince with his broad chest laid himself down upon the earth in battle;
indeed, he adorned the ground by his reclining there.
Śeṣa said:
Having heard this vow of Puṣkala, the radiant scion of Raghu rejoiced in his heart and directed him toward the battlefield. Thus commanded, he departed, surrounded by many troops.

Wherein that prince Damana, born of a heroic lineage, was staying; having learned of his arrival on the field of battle, Damana, the foremost of heroes, went out to meet him, surrounded by his own army. 19-20.
The two chariot-riders, standing upon their chariots and gracing them with their splendor, were locked in mutual combat;
were the Lord of the Gods and the Daitya come to the battlefield for the sake of war?
Puṣkala spoke thus to that mighty son of the King.
O best of beings, know that Prince Damana has arrived;
know him to be the formidable son of Bharata who has come for battle with a vow, distinguished by his own name, Puṣkala. 22–23.
"O high-minded one, prepare yourself; I shall conquer you, who are like a bee constantly devoted to the lotus-feet of Raghunātha, with a multitude of weapons.
Having heard these words, Damana, the slayer of enemy heroes, [prepared for battle].
Laughing, the eloquent and fearless one, who had witnessed his prowess, replied to Subāhu’s son Damana, whose sins were destroyed by devotion to his father:
"Know me to be the horse-keeper of King Śatrughna. (25–26)
"Victory! This arrow, discharged by fate, shall adorn him;
behold his strength at the forefront of battle.
Having spoken thus, he drew his bow with an arrow back to his ear.
He released sharp arrows that snatch away the lives of enemies. Those arrows, becoming dense, covered the sky,
where the radiance of the sun’s rays was obstructed by the shadow of the arrows.
The rows of arrows lodged in the temples of the elephants adorned them like the various mineral pigments that color the elements.
Men, horses, elephants, and chariots were seen fallen there.
Struck by the king’s son with a shower of arrows,
Puṣkala, the slayer of enemy heroes, beheld that prowess and saw the battlefield enveloped in the shadow of his shafts.
Having properly sipped water according to the rules, he drew an arrow charged with fire-mantras upon his bow and released that shaft.
Then, fire manifested there at the forefront of the battle.
Licking the sky with its flames like the fire of universal dissolution that has arisen,
he then utterly consumed his army on the field of battle; tormented by the tongues of fire, the host fell into terror and became intent on flight.
Furthermore, the umbrellas of the archers, burnt and shaped like the moon,
were seen there bearing a luster like that of refined gold (jātarūpa).
The horses of the enemies, though burnt, fled among their own manes.
Then the elephants, accompanied by chariots and yokes, carrying loads of gems,
rubies, and jewels, fled, tormented by the garlands of flames from the fire of the earth. 37–38.
In some places elephants perished; in some places horsemen;
in some places foot-soldiers perished, their bodies consumed by fire.
All the arrows discharged by the prince reached their destruction.
Reduced to ashes on all sides by the flames of the fire-god,
when his own army had thus been consumed, Damana, filled with rage,
then took up the Varuna weapon in order to quell that fire with all his knowledge of missiles.
For the sake of pacifying the fire, that king discharged the Vāruṇa weapon,
which flooded his army crowded with chariots and horses;
the chariots of his adversaries were seen submerged in the water.
The elephants, though scorched, also attained peace;
the fire, released by the fire-missile (agnyastra), was pacified, and his own army, which had been oppressed by the flames of the fire, also found relief.
Shaken by the cold water, the enemies whistled in pain; struck by showers of hailstones and tormented by the wind,
they then beheld their own army overwhelmed by the flood of water.
Shaken, agitated, and destroyed, it was driven away by the Vāruṇa weapon. Then Puṣkala, the son of Bharata, his eyes copper-red with extreme anger,
fixed a single great arrow upon his bow, charged with the Vāyavya weapon.
Then a great wind arose, impelled by the Vāyavya weapon;
with its force, it destroyed the approaching army of clouds.
Struck by the wind, the elephants collided with one another.
The horses, crowded together with one another and accompanied by their respective riders,
and the men— hair disheveled and breathless, tossed by the wind as they fell— appeared like vetālas (vampire-spirits) dwelling upon the earth. 49-50.
Seeing his entire army overwhelmed by Vāyu,
that prince fixed the mountain-weapon (*parvatāstra*) upon his bow. Then, mountains fell upon the heads of those who were fighting.
Shrouded by those [missiles], Vāyu could not move anywhere.
Then Puṣkala fixed a weapon named Vajra upon his bow;
cut by that Vajra, they were all instantly reduced to pieces as small as sesame seeds.
Having reduced the mountains to mere dust with arrows consecrated by mantras,
the prince fell from on high with a loud and violent roar,
his mind agitated by the being [within him], pierced in the heart, and severely wounded. (54)
The powerful hero was distressed and fell into a state of extreme dejection. Seeing him thus overwhelmed by dejection, the charioteer, skilled in policy,
drew the prince away from that battle for the distance of one krośa.

Then, the terrified soldiers of the prince fled and, having reached the city, reported that the king's son was overcome by dejection. Meanwhile, Puṣkala, the knower of dharma, having thus achieved victory at the forefront of the battle—
But remembering the words of the Lord of the Raghus, he was no longer able to strike him.
Then there arose the great roar of kettledrums and shouts of victory, and enchanting voices cried out, "Excellent! Excellent! (58–59).
Seeing Puṣkala victorious, Śatrughna attained great joy;
surrounded by his ministers, headed by Sumati, he praised him.
Thus ends the [section on] Rāma’s Horse Sacrifice in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
Chapter Twenty-four, named Puṣkalavijaya.
Chapter Twenty-five. Śeṣa said:
Then, seeing his own soldiers with their limbs drenched in a flood of blood, the king felt no sorrow for them as they attained peace; instead, he inquired about the actions of his son.
As [the minister] related all of his deeds, he explained how he had indeed recovered that excellent horse.
Tell me again, how great was the strength of those heroes, and how many came to fight?
(2) Furthermore, facing the enemy host, how did my hero Damana engage in battle; and having achieved victory, who indeed struck down that invincible hero? (3)
Having heard these words of the king, his servants— whose bodies, garments, and other belongings were drenched with blood— replied:
"O King, having observed the horse adorned with the marks of the leaf and other signs..."
Out of pride, he treated the best of the Raghus as if he were a blade of grass and caused him to be captured.
Then, followed by his horse and surrounded by a small force of troops, he arrived;
with him there occurred a tumultuous battle that made the hair stand on end.
Having then rendered him unconscious with his own arrows, while your son remained there,
Śatrughna arrived, surrounded by his own forces. Thereupon,
a great battle ensued, intensified by the discharge of weapons and missiles.
"O King, your son of great strength had many times attained victory;
yet now, having been addressed by that weapon by the brother’s son of Śatrughna,
your heroic son has been rendered unconscious in the battle."
Having heard these words, filled with rage and grief,
his limbs became as motionless as the ocean on a full-moon day;
with his lips quivering in anger, he spoke to the commander-in-chief.
Wasted by grief, he licked his lip with his teeth and his lip with his tongue.
"O General, quickly prepare my army;
I shall fight Rāma's great warriors who have struck down my son."
"Today, with my sharp arrows, I shall strike down this one who causes suffering to my son— my 'I' and 'mine'— even if Maheśvara himself were his protector.
These words were spoken by the commander-in-chief to King Subhuja.
Having heard this and having acted accordingly, he himself became ready.
He reported to the king that the fourfold army— resembling the power of Time itself and having destroyed tens of millions of wicked men— was prepared for battle.
Having heard the words of the commander-in-chief, Subāhu, the slayer of enemy heroes, then set out for the place where Śatrughna, the tormentor of his enemies, was located,
accompanied by elephants intoxicated with rut and horses swift as thought.
With chariots filled with all kinds of weapons and missiles that conquer the enemy, the earth then trembled under the immense weight of the army;
a great tumult arose as the host advanced.
Seeing the king set out in a golden chariot,
Śatrughna prepared his army, which was capable of striking down all enemies;
Suketu, his brother, was an expert in combat with the mace.
Filled with all kinds of weapons and missiles, he arrived on his chariot;
then Citrāṅga, the king’s son, who was skilled in every art of war,
quickly went forth on his own chariot toward the intoxicated army of Śatrughna.
His younger brother, named Vicitra, who was skilled in various modes of combat,
went forth on a golden chariot, tormented by grief for his brother.
Other heroes there were great archers, experts in all weapons and missiles.
Commanded by the king, they went to the battlefield filled with heroes.
King Subāhu, having arrived at the field of battle in great rage,
beheld his son unconscious and tormented by arrows.
Seeing his own son, named Damana, seated on the floor of the chariot and overcome with grief, the king repeatedly sprinkled him with water and fanned him with tender leaves.
Sprinkled with water and touched by the king’s gentle hand, he [revived].
Regaining consciousness after a short time, the hero Udamana, an expert in supreme weapons, rose up and cried out: "Where is my bow? Where has Puṣkala gone?
Having abandoned the battle, he has fled, tormented by the wounds from my arrows. (26-27)
Having heard these words spoken by his son,
Subāhu attained supreme joy and embraced his own son. Then Damana, with his head bowed low, beheld his father, the king.
With his body unharmed by rows of missiles, he fell at [the king’s] feet out of devotion.
Then the king, skilled in the arts of war, having stationed his own son upon a chariot, spoke again to the commander-in-chief.
"Form in battle the array called Krauñca, which is difficult for enemies to conquer;
entering it, you shall defeat the army of King Śatrughna.
Having heard those words of King Subāhu, [he did so].
He formed a specific and excellent array known as the Krauñca;
into it suddenly entered the hosts of the enemy, who were possessed of great strength and bore a multitude of weapons. 32.
In his front was Suketu, in his throat the one named Citrāṅga;
on his two wings were two princes, and on his tail was established Rājā. His great army, consisting of the four divisions, shone in the center.
Having formed the wonderfully variegated Krauñca array, he informed the king.
Seeing the well-constructed Krauñca array fully prepared, the king,
stationed at the front of Śatrughna's division, set his mind upon battle.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Arrival of Subāhu’s Army," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
Chapter Twenty-six.
Śeṣa said:
Śatrughna, seeing that army—which was as formidable in appearance as a cloud and surrounded by many elephants, horses, chariots, and foot soldiers—[was filled with wonder]. 1.
Sumati replied with these words endowed with profound sound,
attended by scholars who were experts in the investigation of various doctrines.
Śatrughna said:
Having reached the city of Sumateka, that most illustrious being beheld this army there, surging like the waves of the ocean;
"Whose is this exultant force, endowed with its four divisions?"
"Tell me all this exactly as it is, as I ask you, for it appears before me with respect, having arrived for battle;
knowing which, I shall direct my own soldiers to their positions in the arrangement of the fight."
Having heard these words, the wise and virtuous Sumati,
being delighted, spoke these words to Śatrughna, the scorcher of his enemies.
Sumati said:
Nearby stands the auspicious city of Cakrāṅka, O King,
where the people are free from sin due to their devotion to Viṣṇu.
This Subāhu, the foremost among those who know dharma, is the lord of that city.
This [city] shines before you, O son, surrounded by your sons and grandsons;
it is a place where one is constantly devoted to one’s own wife and turns away from the wives of others, and where the stories of Viṣṇu—which reveal no other purpose—reside in the ears. 8–9.
That righteous king does not take more than a sixth part as tax from the property of others;
by him, the Brāhmaṇas are honored solely through devotion to Viṣṇu.
Constantly engaged in service, he is like a bee at the honey of the lotus feet of Viṣṇu.
He is devoted to his own duty and averse to the duties of others.
Indeed, the strength of new warriors is nowhere equal to his strength.
Having heard of his son’s fall, he was overwhelmed with both rage and grief.

Accompanied by the fourfold army and having drawn up for battle, many heroes of yours as well— such as Lakṣmīnidhi and others— will quickly conquer these enemies, who are intent on the welfare of others, with a multitude of weapons.

Having heard those words, Śatrughna spoke to his excellent soldiers, whose minds were filled with a flood of great joy at the prospect of entering the battle: "Today, the Krauñca formation has been arranged by the troops of Subāhu. (14-15)

Who, skilled in weapons, will pierce those warriors stationed on the front and wings— [piercing] him by whose division one's own power is neutralized and who is intent on victory over heroes? May he take the betel-roll from my lotus-like hand.
Then the heroic Alakṣmīnidhi,
an expert in all weapons and missiles, surrounded by many warriors, spoke these words to the king: "I shall go to the Krauñca-bheda."
"Bhārgava was already the breaker of Krauñca, and so am I;
furthermore, he spoke to another hero, asking, 'Who will go with you? Thereupon, Puṣkala set his mind upon following behind him."
Riputāpa, Nīlaratna, Ugrāśva, and Vīramardana—all these went at the command of Śatrughna to break through that Krauñca mountain;
Śatrughna himself, the supreme warrior, stood upon his chariot bearing all his weapons. 20–21.
Then, followed and surrounded by many soldiers,
he set out; and those two oceans of armies were seen, like two great rivers with surging waves, intent on bringing about the dissolution of the world.
Then, sturdy battle-drums were struck in both armies;
the sounds of war-drums and the blasts of conchs were heard here and there.
There, the horses neighed and the elephants trumpeted loudly.
The foremost heroes uttered "huṃ, huṃ," and the rims of the chariot wheels rattled;
there, many enraged warriors, proud of their strength and mighty arms, were seen in the battle crying out, "Cut him down! Pierce him! (25)
While the army of the enemy of Śatrughna was thus engaged in battle,
Lakṣmīnidhi spoke to that Suketu who stood before him.
Lakṣmīnidhi said:
Know that the son of Janaka is remembered as Lakṣmīnidhi;
he is skilled in all weapons and missiles and proficient in every form of warfare.
Release the horse of Rāmacandra, the subduer of all demons.
To that foremost of heroes who was saying, "Pierced by my arrows, you shall go to the abode of Yama," Suketu quickly and impetuously drew his strung bow and,
discharging excellent shafts, stood firm.
Those arrows, with sharpened joints and golden feathers, were seen pervading all sides throughout the midst of the battle; they were difficult to withstand.
Having swiftly struck down that mass of arrows, [he...]
Then Lakṣmīnidhi,
having strung his bow, released six sharp arrows, adorned with polished joints, at his chest. 31.
Having pierced the heart of his strong-armed brother, those arrows were seen on the ground, stained dark with blood. With his heart split by those arrows, Suketu was filled with rage.
With twenty sharp arrows of straight joints, he struck them both; with their limbs pierced by shafts and drenched in blood,
they were beheld by the soldiers like two *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom.
Discharging millions of arrows and fitting swift shafts with such speed,
those two of great strength and light-handedness could not be perceived by anyone;
they held their excellent bows drawn into circles and rained down a torrent of arrows.
Like two fresh clouds in the sky executing the commands of Indra, they rendered the elephants,
horses, and men of their opponents headless; they were seen only as having already accomplished this, for no one perceived the aiming or the release of their arrows.

The earth was filled with excellent warriors wearing crowns and earrings, holding bows and arrows in their hands, and biting their lips in rage as those two, both experts in all weapons and missiles, fought out of pride. 38. As they were fighting out of pride, [both] being knowers of all weapons and missiles.
A great and terrible battle ensued, causing amazement even to the gods. There was an extreme carnage that tore apart millions of heroes;
nowhere could anyone see the sky through the dense network of arrows.
At that time, the heroic Lakṣmīnidhi, the crusher of enemies,
fixed eight firm and sharp arrows upon his bow;
with four of them, the hero brought Suketu’s horses to their destruction.
With one [arrow], he swiftly severed that most fierce standard;
with another, he struck the charioteer’s head from his body onto the ground; and filled with rage, with yet another he cut through the bow along with its string.
The impetuous King pierced Suketu with a single arrow;
beholding that wondrous feat, the heroes were struck with amazement.
With his bow severed, his chariot destroyed, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed, [he remained].
Grasping a massive mace and desiring to fight, he approached. Seeing him coming— skilled in mace-combat and equipped with a great mace—
he [Balarāma] descended from his chariot.
Taking up a massive mace made entirely of iron,
its body variegated with gold and endowed with every splendor,
Lakṣmīnidhi, violently enraged, swiftly struck Suketu in the chest.
He struck him in the heart with a mace that resembled a thunderbolt or fire.
O great sage, though struck by the mace, the hero did not tremble, like an elephant intoxicated with rut when struck on its temples with flower garlands by a young boy. 48–49.
Then that foremost of heroes said to King Lakṣmīnidhi,
"If you are a hero, O scorcher of foes, endure this one blow from me.
Having spoken thus, he struck him violently on the forehead with his mace.
Struck on the forehead by the mace, he vomited blood and became exceedingly enraged;
he then struck him on the head with a mace that resembled Death itself.
Suketu, however, who was well-versed in dharma, struck him on the shoulder.
Thus, exceedingly enraged and skilled in mace-fighting, the two engaged in a mace-duel, each desiring victory over the other;
they struck one another with force and were intent on slaying each other.
Neither of them was provoked to anger nor did either falter in the battle.
With their heads, foreheads, shoulders, hearts, and all their limbs drenched in streams of blood, those two remained possessed of great strength and prowess.
Then the powerful Alakṣmīnidhi, enraged, swiftly raised his mace and rushed toward the king’s younger brother to slay that mighty one. Seeing him approaching, [the other] held up his own great mace.
The king’s brother, with great speed, forcefully attempted to strike Balarāma;
however, Balarāma caught the mace thrown by him in his own hand, and with that very mace, the one of great strength struck him in the heart. 57–58.
Seeing him subdued by the end of his own mace, King Lakṣmīnidhi desired to fight that most powerful man with a wrestling match.
Then the king’s younger brother, filled with rage, seized him with both arms.
He fought in every battle, being the best among the heroic kinsmen. Then Lakṣmīnidhi struck him on the chest with his own fist;
then he too, raising his fist, struck him on the head.
With fists resembling thunderbolts and with terrible slaps of their palms,
the two, enraged and biting their sprout-like lips, struck one another—
fist against fist, tooth against tooth, hair against hair, and nail against nail.
Then a tumultuous battle, hair-raising and fierce, took place between the two.
At that moment, the king’s enraged brother seized the monarch by the foot, whirled him around, and then cast him down upon the ground.

Lakṣmīnidhi seized the younger brother of the king by the hand, whirled him high up a hundred times, and struck him down upon the back of an elephant. Having fallen to the ground at that time, he regained consciousness after a moment.
In that very manner, the valiant one whirled him about with speed in the sky. Thus fighting on, they again engaged in hand-to-hand combat,
foot against foot, hand against hand, chest against chest, and face against face.
Thus, locked together and each desiring the other's death,
both were valiant and both fainted away.
Seeing that, thousands of people were filled with wonder and offered their praise.
The king Dhanya was a treasure-house of Lakṣmī, and the powerful younger brother of the king was Dhanyarāja.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Mace-Fight," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padmapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
The twenty-seventh chapter. Śeṣa said:
Citrāṅga stood upon the neck of the Krauñca mountain, mounted on his chariot and graced by heroes.
He caused that army to plunge in, just as a boar plunges into the ocean;
drawing his very firm bow, which resounded like the roar of clouds,
he released sharpened arrows capable of scorching millions of enemies.

With all their limbs pierced by his arrows, those great warriors lay prostrate, still wearing their crowns and armor, their lips bitten in rage. While the battle was thus proceeding, Puṣkala went forth to fight.
Taking up his bow, which was adorned with jewels and scorched his enemies,
their united form appeared exceedingly beautiful,
like that of Skanda and Tāraka in the ancient battle of Tāraka.
Swiftly drawing his bow, the ambidextrous Savyasācī, filled with many arrows,
quickly struck him with straight-knotted shafts.
Citrāṅga, overcome by rage, [discharged] sharpened arrows from his bow.
Placing many arrows upon the tip of his bow-mandala,
he released them; yet neither the taking up, nor the aiming, nor even the releasing was seen— only those two were visible with their bows drawn into circles.
Then the enraged Puṣkala, that great warrior, pierced that formidable opponent in the chest with a hundred arrows;
Citrāṅga, however, cut all those arrows into pieces as small as sesame seeds in an instant.
He struck Puṣkala in his limbs with sharp arrows.
Puṣkala, by means of a brilliant whirling weapon (*bhrāmakāstra*), caused that divine chariot to spin in the sky; it was like a marvel.

Having wandered for only a moment, the chariot together with its horses and driver found it difficult to maintain its position on the battlefield, being held fast by the enemy. And seeing his prowess, Citrāṅga became exceedingly enraged.
The wise Puṣkala, who was skilled in all weapons, said:
Citrāṅga said,
"You have performed a deed well done, as esteemed by great warriors in battle."
"O Madraka, having been joined by a few arrows, you were made to whirl in the sky for a moment.
Behold my prowess as well, displayed by a great warrior! Though you move through the sky, let it be so, for you are honored by the gods. (14-15)
Having spoken thus, he who was the supreme knower of divine weapons and the best among those who understand all duties released a most terrible missile from his bow in the battle.
Pierced by that arrow, he whirled in the sky like a moth.
Along with his chariot, his companion, his banner,
and his charioteer, that best of car-warriors whirled through the sky with great speed; yet before he could regain his stability, another arrow was released.
Then, mounted on his chariot and accompanied by his charioteer, he wandered about;
seeing that deed of his son, the king was filled with wonder.
Puṣkala, the slayer of enemy heroes, somehow managed to regain his composure.
With his arrows, he struck down his chariot along with its driver and horses. When his vehicle was shattered, the hero mounted another,
but that too was quickly destroyed by Puṣkala’s shafts upon the field of battle.
Furthermore, as soon as he mounted his shoulder and came face to face with him,
he shattered that chariot again with sharp arrows. Thus was the son of King Daśaratha indeed broken.
Then Citrāṅgaka, standing upon a variegated chariot in that great battle, approached Puṣkala with great speed to fight him, O hero, who was distinguished in the great conflict. 23–24.
In that battle, Puṣkala struck him with five arrows;
severely wounded by those shafts, the son of Bharata was greatly pained.
Enraged, he raised his great bow and [fixed] ten sharp arrows.
He released at his heart arrows beautifully adorned with golden feathers.
Those most terrible arrows drank his blood and,
having drunk, fell to the earth like false witnesses of former times.
Then Citrāṅgaka, enraged, took up five broad-headed arrows (bhallas) and discharged them at the forehead of his son, the highly powerful Bharata.
Struck by those bhallas, he became furious and [fixed] an arrow upon his excellent bow.
He made a strange vow regarding the destruction of Aṅga:
"O hero, listen quickly to my vow concerning your slaughter; having learned that, you must indeed fight with full attention. 29–30.
If, having defiled this virtuous woman who is so radiant with her character and conduct, I were to deprive you of your life with this very arrow,
then you would go to that world which is reached by those people who remain under the sway of Yama. 31.
"May I attain the same world as you; my promise is true.
Having heard these excellent words, the slayer of enemy heroes laughed and, being wise and brave, spoke these auspicious words to Puṣkala.
Death is inevitable for all living beings everywhere and at all times;
therefore, O crest-jewel of heroes, there is no sorrow for me in dying. (34) Since you, who are adorned with heroism, have fulfilled your vow, O hero!
Let this further great declaration of mine, which is indeed true, be heard today:
"If I do not sever your arrow as it is intent upon my slaughter, then listen to my vow, O you who pride yourselves on being all heroes. (35-36)

May the sin of him who, desiring to go on a pilgrimage, causes his own heart to falter, and who considers any vow other than the Ekādaśī vow to be superior, belong to me alone— he who strikes down his own solemn pledge.
Having uttered these words, he became silent and took up his bow. Then, drawing an excellent arrow from his quiver,
he spoke these clear words intended for the slaying of the enemy.
Puṣkala said:
"If the pair of Rāma’s feet has been worshipped by me with a mind free from deceit, then let my word become true. (40)
"If I have enjoyed only my own wife and know no other woman even in my mind,
by that truth, let this very word of mine become true in battle. Having uttered these words, he fixed a terrible arrow upon his bow.
Seeing that arrow released, which resembled the fire of cosmic destruction and was capable of severing the head of a hero, the powerful son of the king took up another sharp shaft,
similar to the fire of cosmic destruction, upon his bow. 42–43.
Severed by that arrow, the shaft raised its own weapon for his destruction;
when that arrow was thus cut, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose.
Then the rear half fell to the ground, while the front half remained joined with the blade.
He instantly severed his neck like a lotus stalk.
Seeing him then falling to the ground, all of his soldiers raised a great cry of "Alas! and became intent on flight.
With its head touching the earth, adorned with a crown and earrings,
it shone exceedingly like the orb of the moon fallen from the sky.
Seeing him fallen, the heroic Puṣkala, son of Bharata, [beheld him].
He plunged into this battle-array, which was graced by all the heroes alone. 48.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Slaying of Citrāṅga," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. 27.
The twenty-eighth chapter. Śeṣa said:
Then, beholding his son fallen, lifeless, and uprooted, [he...]
Afflicted by grief for his son, the king lamented intensely;
overcome with extreme sorrow, he struck his head with both hands,
trembling violently and shedding tears from his lotus-like eyes.

Having seized the fallen head, which was as beautiful as the orb of the moon, drenched with blood from its many wounds, adorned with earrings, possessing a pair of excellent curved eyebrows, and with its sprout-like lower lip bitten;
3. [he beheld] that most excellent head with its curved pair of eyebrows and its bitten lower lip-sprout.
Kissing her lotus-like face while lamenting, he spoke these words: "Alas, my son Vīra! O hero, why do you not look upon me with your pair of bright eyes, I who am so full of longing for you?"
"What is the use of this conversation that provides no diversion? You appear to be one whose mind is indeed submerged in an ocean of wrath.
Tell me, my son, how can you speak to me thus while laughing again?"
"O son, delight yourself with these nectars of sweet flavor.
O Śatrughna, O high-minded one, take this horse adorned with white chowries and richly embellished with golden plates; abandon sleep!"
This Puṣkala, radiant with prowess, foremost in valor, a scorcher of foes and slayer of enemy heroes,
stands before us holding his bow;
restrain him with sharp arrows discharged from your bow.
"How is it that you, O hero, remain bewildered in the midst of battle?
Elephants, foot soldiers, and those mounted on chariots, afflicted by fear, are coming to you for refuge; look upon them, O high-minded one! (9-10)

"O son, how would you be able to endure on the field of battle the sharp arrows of Śatrughna, discharged from his fierce bow? Therefore, who indeed is capable of protecting me when I am deprived of you?"
"Since you have cast off sleep, you are now capable of conquering me.
Having lamented thus, the king, distressed by grief for his son, struck his own chest many times with his hand.
Then, seated upon their own various and wonderful chariots,
they bowed at the feet of their father and spoke words appropriate for the occasion:
"O King, while we are still alive, tell us what sorrow dwells in your heart."
In the great battle of heroes, death becomes desirable;
blessed indeed is this Citrāṅga who shines upon the earth of warriors—this lord, adorned with a crown and biting his lips with his teeth. 15-16.
"Speak quickly! Perform today itself the task you desire: destroy the entire army of Śatrughna, which is now left without a protector.
This very day, slay Puṣkala in battle, the one who caused his brother's death."
"Having severed [him] from his chariot—his head adorned with a crown—cast him down!
O high-minded one, why do you appear so afflicted by grief? Abandon your sorrow;
we two are worthy of honor, so give your mind to battle! (18-19)
Having heard these words of his two sons who pride themselves on their heroism,
the great king abandoned his grief and resolved to engage in battle.
Those two, intoxicated by the pride of war, also desired an opponent to fight.
The two went to the camp of the enemy of Kaṭaka, which was filled with infinite soldiers.
There, Riputāpana and Damana, like two clouds in the rainy season, fought as heroes against Nīlaratna and the other [Vīra].
Mounted upon a chariot yoked with horses adorned with gold, variegated with jewels,
and enriched by the beauty of its gem-studded pole, the powerful King stood holding his bow and went forth to fight Śatrughna, who was surrounded by millions of heroes.
Treating as mere straw even those great heroes who were experts in the science of archery, Subāhu,
filled with rage due to the death of his son, arrived to fight and began the slaughter of the entire army. (24-25)
Hanumān, moving by the side of Śatrughna, rushed toward him,
making a great roar with his claws as weapons, like a cloud in battle.
Subāhu [beheld] that Hanumān approaching with a mighty sound.
With eyes filled with rage, he spoke these words while laughing:
"Where has Puṣkala gone? Today, I shall swiftly strike down my son upon the field of battle, his head adorned with flaming earrings."
"Where is Śatrughna, the protector of the army? Where is Rāma? And where are the warriors?
Let them see me as I approach in battle to take their lives!
Hearing these words of his, Hanumān spoke to him.
Śatrughna, the slayer of Lavaṇa, remains as the protector of the army. O King, how could he fight in the forefront of battle while his servant stands at the front?
Having conquered me in combat, you shall go to him, O bull among men. (30-31)
When he had spoken thus, that [demon] pierced the exceedingly fierce Vānara— who stood like a preeminent mountain— with ten arrows in the heart; but [the Vānara],
having caught those incoming arrows in the hollow of his hands, [held them].
He pulverized those enemies of his, who were capable of rending foes, into pieces as small as sesame seeds. Having crushed those arrows while roaring with the thunder of clouds,
the one of great strength then encircled the chariot with his tail and carried it high up.
Then that best of kings, remaining right there in the sky,
repeatedly struck his tail with sharp-pointed arrows.
Being thus struck on the tip of his tail by those straight-knotted shafts, he—
Then he released that divine arrow, variegated with gold;
struck by it, he swiftly assailed Hanumān, the best of monkeys, with sharp shafts, his eyes filled with rage.
Pierced by arrows and drenched in blood on all sides, Hanumān,
the lord of monkeys, summoned a great rage toward the king;
seizing his chariot along with its horses by means of his fangs.
They crushed it with great force, and it was like a marvel;
seeing his own chariot being shattered, the powerful king quickly mounted another chariot and fought that one of great strength. 39–40.

The king, skilled in aiming his arrows and a master of supreme weapons, struck him on the face, the mouth, the chest, the arms, and the feet (41). Then the enraged leader of monkeys struck him on the chest.
Leaping up with speed upon the king, who was resplendent with brave warriors, he struck him with his foot; he fell to the ground, fainting from exhaustion,
vomiting warm blood from his mouth, and trembling with heavy breaths.
Then, extremely enraged on the field of battle, Hanumān crushed horses, heroes, and elephants by his sheer force.
At that time, Sukeśu, his brother, as well as King Lakṣmīnidhi—
Both of them, being well-armored, stood ready for battle.
Seeing the king unconscious, the men who had fled here and there were wounded by the showers of arrows discharged by Puṣkala. 45–46.
Seeing his own army being broken, the powerful prince Damana paralyzed it, just as a dam stops the surging ocean.
Then the king, having fainted, beheld a certain dream.
Struck by the blow of his heel in the midst of battle,
Rāmacandra was surrounded in Ayodhyā by many Brahmins, the best among sacrificial officiants, at a pavilion on the bank of the Sarayū river. 48–49.
There, Brahmā and the other gods, as well as millions of cosmic eggs, stood with palms joined in reverence, repeatedly praising him with hymns—
Rāma, the dark-complexioned one with beautiful eyes, who holds a deer-horn.
Nārada and others, with vīṇās shimmering in their hands, sang; and the apsarases, such as Ghṛtācī and Menakā, danced there.
Having assumed the forms of the Vedas, they waited upon Rāghava.
"Whatever collection of objects exists, endowed with all splendor— may he be the giver of all that to his devotees and the bestower of enjoyments.
Perceiving [the dream] in this way and other such manners, he regained the state of consciousness known as waking.
His knowledge struck down by the curse of Brahmā, saying "What have I seen?", he rose up and proceeded on foot toward the feet of Śatrughna,
surrounded by ten million servants and encircled by ten million chariots.
Having summoned Suketu and Vicitradamana,
the knower of dharma, the great king— righteous and endowed with virtue— restrained those who were intent on engaging in battle. He spoke to them.
"O brother and son, listen to these words endowed with righteousness:
do not engage in battle immediately, for a great injustice has occurred, in that you have seized the powerful Candravāha from me. (57-58)
This Rāma is the Supreme Brahman, transcending cause and effect,
the Lord of the moving and unmoving world, who has assumed a human form. Indeed, I have now realized this knowledge of Brahman.
O sinless ones, formerly my wealth of knowledge was stolen by the curse of Asitāṅga. Long ago, I went on a pilgrimage to the sacred fords out of a desire to know the ultimate truth;
there, I beheld many sages who were most eminent in their knowledge of dharma.
Then, desiring to know him, I approached the sage Asitāṅga; showing compassion toward me, the brahmin spoke to me:
"He who is the lord of Ayodhyā is designated by the term 'Supreme Brahman'."
His wife is known as Queen Jānakī, who is herself manifest consciousness (cit).
Yogis, desiring to cross the ocean of saṃsāra which is difficult to traverse and shoreless, worship her directly with the primary forms of yoga.
The one who has Garuda as his banner removes great sins by being remembered alone;
the wise man who serves him shall cross over saṃsāra.
Then, O Brahmin, I laughed and thought, "Who is this Rama? Is he a mere human?"
Who is this lady Sītā, overwhelmed by both joy and grief?
How can there be birth for one who is unborn? What is his purpose here, the creator of all?
O Sage, tell me how he transcends the suffering of birth and old age.
To me, who had spoken thus, the lordly sage, enraged because I had not recognized his true nature, uttered this curse: "O lowest of men, you respond to me while laughing, saying,
'This Rāma is a mere human,' and thus insulting him."
"Therefore, you shall become utterly deluded regarding reality and merely one who fills his belly.
Then, filled with compassion, I grasped his feet; and seeing my humility, that ocean of mercy spoke to me.
O King, when you cause an obstacle to Rāma’s sacrifice, then Hanumān will strike your foot with great force;
at that time, O King, you will understand this, and not otherwise by your own intellect. 71.
Formerly I was told this very thing by him, and now it has been seen by me:
when the enraged Hanumān struck me on the chest,
then I beheld the Lord of Ramā, whose nature is the fullness of Brahman.
Therefore, let the mighty ones bring a horse rich in beauty, as well as wealth, garments, and this very kingdom;
having seen Rāma at this merit-bestowing sacrifice, I shall have attained my life's purpose. 74.
"Bring the horse to me; that mirror pleases me.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Defeat of Subāhu," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* within the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
Chapter Twenty-nine. Śeṣa said:
Having heard those words of their father, they were delighted and prepared for combat.
"So be it," they said to the great king who was longing for a sight of Rāma.
The sons said:
"O King, we know nothing other than your lotus feet."
"Let that which has arisen from your heart come forth today with speed.
Let a horse be led there, adorned with white chowries,
enriched by the great splendor of jewel garlands, and anointed with sandalwood paste and other unguents."
O Lord, sovereignty is the fruit of your command; your treasuries are immensely prosperous;
your garments are most precious, fine, and of excellent quality;
and you possess sandalwood, camphor, and horses that are truly enchanting.
There were elephants agitated by rut, chariots with golden poles,
adorned with various ornaments of most wonderful colors; and there were hundreds of thousands of female servants and handsome male servants.
There were jewels resembling the sun, various kinds of gems, bright pearls produced from the frontal globes of elephants, and hundreds of thousands of corals— whatever objects were of great value. 7.

Having heard these words of his son, the lord of the earth became joyful and spoke to his heroic sons, who were intent on carrying out his command. 10.

Having heard these words of the king, Vicitra, Udama, Suketu, and the hero Samara set out for battle, prepared at his command. 12.
Having gone there, the heroes reached that most beautiful horse,
which was equipped with white chowries, adorned with golden plates and other ornaments,
enriched by a garland of jewels, and graced with variegated feathers. 13.

who were equipped with mighty weapons and missiles and endowed with every splendor (15).
A white parasol shines high above the head of this horse, and two beautiful chowries are repeatedly held before it;

He led the horse to the presence of the king for the well-performed Horse Sacrifice.
Seeing that brought horse, adorned with a garland of jewels, swift as thought and able to assume any form at will, the exceedingly noble king rejoiced.
Adorned with royal insignia and other ornaments, the most righteous king, accompanied by his sons and grandsons, went on foot toward Śatrughna;

To Sumati, who was inquiring about the narrative of Rāmacandra—which is free from reports of fear and adorned with heroic splendor—he replied:
"It is crowded with tens of millions of heroes who are eager to protect the horses. (22)
Surrounded on all sides by thousands of monkeys,

Seeing that affectionate king Udbhaṭa, Śatrughna rose from his seat and embraced him with both arms along with all the soldiers. Having honored Śatrughna firmly, the king, the slayer of enemy heroes, [welcomed him].

Subāhu said: "Today I am blessed, along with my sons, my family, and my mounts."
If these two feet of yours, praised by tens of millions of kings, have been seized by this ignorant son who has taken the best of horses, O Damana, please bring him back;
forgive him, O treasure-house of compassion! 27–28.

He did not know that the ornament of the Raghus was the presiding deity of all gods, the creator of the universe by his mere play, and also its destroyer and protector; [nor did he know] this kingdom with its flourishing components, its abundant forces, and its vehicles. 29.
"These treasuries are full of wealth; these are our sons; and here we are—30.
We are all Rāmanātha’s, the executors of your commands.
Accept everything as fruitful; there is nothing in me that is improper. 31.

Where is that Hanumān, the bee at the lotus-feet of Rāma, by whose grace I shall obtain a vision of the King of Kings? What indeed cannot be obtained on this earth through association with the virtuous? 32.
By whose grace I, though deluded, have crossed over the Brahmin’s curse;
having now beheld you, O Great King, with eyes like lotus petals, I shall obtain here the entire fruit of my birth, which is otherwise so difficult to attain. (33-34)

My life has already passed away, for I have been separated from Rāma for so long; only a very small portion remains, and how shall I behold the best of the Raghus? Show me that Rāma, who is skilled in the performance of sacrificial rites.
By the dust of whose feet the stone beloved of the Sage became purified;
by the mere touch of whose arrow the crow attained the supreme state;
and upon seeing whose lotus-face, many have gone to the state beyond reckoning. (36-37)
But those who respectfully utter the name of this Lord of the Raghus go to that supreme abode which is meditated upon by yogis.

Having drunk [the nectar] with the cups of their own eyes, they go happily to the great exaltation (mahodaya).
Having thus addressed the king, I offered him my kingdom, wealth, and everything else, and said: "O Lord of the Earth, what shall I do for you? (39-40)
Having heard these words of the king, Śatrughna— the conqueror of enemy cities, eloquent and skilled in speech— replied to that monarch. (41) Śatrughna said:
"O King, how can you say this, you who are an elder and honored by me?
Let him subdue everything belonging to you and your kingdom. For this is the duty of Kṣatriyas: that which ordains battle. (42)
"By my command, let this entire kingdom and all this wealth return [to me]. O lord of the earth,
just as Raghunātha is always to be honored by you in thought and word,
so too shall you be honored by me."
"May your lordship be ready today to follow him,
equipped with armor and sword, and accompanied by elephants, horses, and chariots.
Having heard these words of Śatrughna, the king—
Having consecrated his son in the kingdom and being highly honored by Śatrughna,
the king, surrounded by great chariot-warriors, performed the funeral rites according to the prescribed rules for his own son who had been slain by Puṣkala on the field of battle. 46–47.

The great chariot-warrior, a knower of reality, felt grief for a moment through the perspective of worldly views; however, by means of knowledge and by recollecting Raghunātha, he destroyed that sorrow.
Standing ready upon his chariot, surrounded by a vast army, he remained there.
He arrived accompanied by Śatrughna and preceded by great chariot-warriors. Seeing him arrive with his entire army, the king resolved to depart for the protection of that excellent horse.
That horse, released by him and marked with a leaf upon its forehead,
proceeded toward many eastern regions, circling in a counter-clockwise direction. There, it was honored by the local kings who were themselves great heroes.

Prostration was performed before him who was neither angry nor accepting [anything]: some brought variegated garments, some their own great kingdom, some wealth, and some people, and having brought these, they bowed down to him. 52–53.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Departure of Śatrughna with Subāhu," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* within the glorious *Padmapurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
Chapter Thirty.
Śeṣa said:
Then the horse, adorned with feathers, reached the city of Tejaḥpura,
where King Satyavān protects his subjects through truth.

Then the younger brother of Raghunātha, surrounded by a retinue of crores and followed by his horse, advanced ahead of him, subduing the city. Having seen that delightful city, adorned with variegated ramparts—

It was illuminated on all sides there by golden pitchers, and it shone everywhere with thousands of temples of the gods; moreover, monasteries for ascetics, filled with sages, were resplendent there. 3–4.
There flows the great goddess [Gaṅgā], who rests upon the head of the three-eyed Lord,
crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, and frequented by throngs of sages;
moreover, from every house of the Brahmins there arises the smoke of the *agnihotra* sacrifice.
There, the smoke purified those whose minds were submerged in great sins.
King Śatrughna, the scorcher of his enemies, whose mind was filled with joy and wonder at the sight of that city, spoke to Sumati.
Śatrughna said:
"O Minister, tell me whose city is this that has come within my sight;
it brings delight to the mind and is governed with righteousness. (8)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words of King Śatrughna, Sumati spoke everything exactly as it was, without arrogance. 9.
Sumati said:
"Listen attentively, O Lord, to the auspicious stories of the Vaiṣṇavas,
by hearing which one is liberated from sin, even from that equal to the killing of a Brahmin."
He remained as one liberated while living, a bee at the lotus feet of Rāma;
he was truthful, a knower of sacrifices and their constituent parts, a performer of rites, a great protector,
and the father who attained him after propitiating the Cow of Plenty with many vows.
Known as Ṛtaṃbhara, he was world-renowned and supremely righteous.
Prasannā gave birth to a son endowed with manifold virtues and refined qualities, Satyavān, who was richly adorned with great beauty; know him to be the best of kings. 12–13.
Śatrughna said:
Who was the king Ṛtambhara? For what purpose was the cow worshipped?
And how did his son become a Vaiṣṇava, a servant of Viṣṇu? 14.
"Relate all this narrative of the non-Vaishnava;
when heard, it removes the mountain of great sins for living beings.
Shesha said:
Having heard these highly significant words of Śatrughna,
Ṛtambhara related clearly the narrative of his origin:
"In ancient times, King Ṛtambhara was childless."

Although he had many wives, he did not obtain a son among them. Then, having approached by chance the sage named Jābāli, he, being intent on his welfare, questioned him regarding the cause for the birth of a son.
Ṛtaṃbhara said: "O Lord, tell me words that will bring about the birth of a son for me, who am barren;
by performing which a noble offspring shall be born to me as the sustainer of my lineage. (19)
"Knowing that,
O best of sages, I shall certainly perform whatever is beneficial for me— be it charity, a vow, a pilgrimage, or a sacrifice.
Having heard these words of the king, the best of sages spoke.
This speech, which brings about the birth of a son for one who bows down seeking offspring, has been spoken.
O Lord, for one desiring to obtain progeny, there are three means: the grace of Viṣṇu, or that of the Cow, or again, that of Śiva. 21–22.
Therefore, O King, perform worship indeed to the cow, whose body is the deity;
for upon her tail, mouth, horns, and back, the gods are established.
When she is satisfied, she will swiftly grant you your desire in accordance with dharma.
Knowing this, O sustainer of nectar, you should perform the worship of cows.
Indeed, for one who constantly worships a cow with barley and other offerings, both the gods and the ancestors remain perpetually satisfied. 24-25.
Whoever, observing auspicious vows, gives fodder for a cow according to the rule—
by that truth, may all his desires be fulfilled.
A thirsty cow tied in the house, or a maiden in her home during her menses;
The discarded garlands of the deities destroy previously accumulated merit. That man who forbids a cow from eating her own grass—
his ancestors tremble, facing their imminent fall.
That mortal of deluded intellect who strikes a cow with a staff goes to the city of Dharmarāja, deprived of his hands. Furthermore,
those of his ancestors fall into the lower realms.
"The fortunate son of Matsya will indeed deliver us.
In this very context, they cite this ancient history concerning the wonderful past of Janaka that occurred long ago in the city of Dharmarāja.
Once, King Janaka voluntarily relinquished his life-breaths;
at that moment, a celestial chariot adorned with a network of tinkling bells arrived. Having ascended it, the king departed, his physical body borne by his attendants.
He proceeded on the path toward the city of Saṃyaminī, in the presence of Dharmarāja.
At that time, those who had committed evil deeds, though being tormented in millions of hells,
attained happiness upon reaching the breeze from Janaka’s body.
The suffering born of burning and torment in hell became a source of happiness for them;
at that time, their great misery was destroyed by the breath from the body of the Father.
Then, seeing him emerged, the beings who were oppressed by sin [were relieved].
Terrified and unwilling to be separated from him, they cried out intensely (36).
They spoke these piteous words: "O doer of good deeds, do not go from here!

Having heard these words, the supremely righteous king,
filled with a flood of compassion, reflected in his mind:
"If only the happiness of living beings here could arise from me once again."
"Right here in this city you shall remain, and this delightful heaven is yours.
Having spoken thus, the king stood right there in front of the hell, his mind filled with compassion as he brought happiness to living beings. 39-40.
There, Dharma, having arrived at the gate of hell which inflicts suffering,
was inflicting intense torments upon those who had committed various sins;
then he saw King Janaka standing at the entrance.
To him, who had performed great meritorious deeds and was endowed with compassion, the Lord of the Dead (Yama) spoke suddenly with a voice from his celestial chariot:
"O King, crest-jewel of all dharma, from where have you come?"

Only those men who are intent on harming others come to this place.
Those who delight in slandering others, those intent on the wealth of others,
and he who would abandon his own devoted wife— who is righteous and dedicated to his service— without cause, that man shall go to the Samāvraja hell. 45-46.
That man who, enticed by greed for wealth, deceives a friend,
shall come here and suffer terrible torment from me.
He who [deceives] Rāma in thought, word, deed, or even through hypocrisy—

Whether out of hatred or through mockery, one of such deluded intellect does not remember Him; yet I bind him again and cast him into the fire, for He who is remembered is the Lord of Men and the warder-off of the sufferings of hell. 48–49.
O King, sin remains within the bodies of men for as long as a man of wicked intellect does not utter the name of Rāma;
O high-minded one, kings who commit great sins become [possessed by it].
"Your servants bring them here, for they are unable to even look upon those such as you.
Therefore, O Great King, depart; enjoy manifold pleasures.
Ascending this excellent celestial chariot, enjoy the merit you have earned. (51-52)
Having heard these words of her husband, the King of Dharma,
Janaka, filled with a flood of compassion, spoke to the King of Dharma. (53) Janaka said:
"I am going, O Lord, out of compassion for living beings;
indeed, by the wind from my body, they have attained happiness and remain at ease.
O King, if you would release all these who are situated in hell," so he said.
"Then, happy, I shall go to heaven, which is inhabited by meritorious people. Jābāli said: Having heard these words, he replied to Janaka.
Pointing out each of the individual living beings dwelling in various hells, Dharma said: "This man followed his trusted wife and friend."
Therefore, I have cooked him on an iron spike for ten thousand years;
thereafter, having cast this sinner into the womb of swine,
he shall be brought down among humans, marked with the sign of a eunuch.

Because he repeatedly embraced another man's wife by force, he is therefore being cooked here in the Raurava hell for a hundred years. This evil-minded one, however, having stolen the property of others, enjoyed it for himself.
Therefore, having cut off his hands, he was cooked in pus and blood.
When this guest arrived in the evening, afflicted by hunger,
he did not offer him even a word of welcome or honor.
Therefore, this man, who is shameless in loudly reviling another, shall be cast into the hell of Tāmisra filled with fuel and, tormented by bees, undergo agony for a hundred years.
62. This man, indeed, has been so shameless as to engage in the loud censure of another.
He too heard that [report], nodding his ears many times in approval:
"Therefore, these two have fallen into a blind well, tormented by misery;
and this betrayer of friends, filled with anxiety, is being severely cooked in the Raurava hell."
"Therefore, having caused these [beings] to experience their evil karmic results, you must release them as you go, O tiger among men, for you are the one who establishes a mass of merit.

Having thus pointed out the living beings who remained silent while performing their duties, he,
a devotee of Rāma with eyes filled with compassion, spoke.
Janaka said:
"How may the liberation from hell come about for these suffering living beings? Tell us that quickly, indeed, so that by performing it they may attain happiness. Dharma said:
Viṣṇu has not been propitiated by these, nor have the stories of Him been heard by them;
how, then, can there be liberation from hell for these evildoers?
If you would release even these perpetrators of great sins, [then please do so].
In that case, O Great King, I shall impart that merit; listen.
Once, having risen at dawn with a mind of pure intent, he meditated upon the illustrious Raghunātha, who is known as the remover of great sins. (69–70)
"Whatever was uttered by you with a pure mind, saying 'Rāma, Rāma,' offer that merit to these [beings] so that there may be their deliverance from hell.
Jābāli said:
Having heard these words of that wise Dharmarāja, O Great King, they gave him the merit accumulated from birth,
arising from the worship of the Lord of the Age performed through the merits earned since his birth. 72.
"May there be a delightful liberation from these hells for them here.
As he was speaking thus, the souls residing in hell were instantly freed from hell and assumed divine bodies.
They said to King Janaka: "O King, by your grace we have been liberated in an instant from this hell that gives rise to suffering; we shall go to the supreme state.
Having seen those men, who resembled the sun, emerged from hell, [the king was amazed].
He, who was devoted to compassion for all beings, rejoiced greatly in his heart.
They all departed for that world, heaven adorned by the gods,
while praising Janaka, the great king and treasury of mercy.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Liberation of Beings Dwelling in Hell by Janaka," within the *Satyavat-ākhyāna* of the *Rāmāśvamedha*, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana, in the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter Thirty-one.
Jābāli said:
Then, when those men had departed and remained in hell,
the king questioned Kīnāśa, the foremost among all knowers of dharma.
The king said:

"Therefore, relate all that to me from the beginning, including the cause of your sin.
Having heard those words, Dharmarāja, the scorcher of foes,
then related to him his arrival at the city of Yama.
The King of Dharma said:
O King, your merit is great; no one else on the surface of the earth has such as yours, for you are a bee at the nectar of the pair of feet of Raghunātha.
Your fame, like the celestial river Gaṅgā— bestowing supreme joy and ferrying across the wicked— purifies all sinners along with their impurities;
yet, O best of kings, even so, a trace of sin still remains within you.
Filled with merit, he arrived at the side of Saṃyaminī. Once, however, out of arrogance, he restrained a cow while it was grazing; as the ripening of that sin, he beheld the gateway to hell.

Now, liberated from sin and endowed with abundant merit, enjoy the many vast pleasures acquired by your own merit. While these oceans of compassion, the Lord of the Raghus, are taking away their happiness, [you have attained this]. 9.
On the great highway of Saṃyaminī, he indeed dispatched the Vaiṣṇava messenger:
"O you of excellent vows, had you not come by this path, how could there have been the liberation of those from hell? (10-11)
"O Great-minded One, those like you, who are pained by the suffering of others and are abodes of compassion, surely bring about the cessation of the suffering of living beings.

Having bowed to Śamana as he was speaking thus,
he departed for heaven in a divine celestial chariot adorned by hosts of Apsaras.
Therefore, cows should be worshipped constantly, and one should not revile them even in thought.

Therefore, O best of kings, perform the worship of cows;
when they are satisfied, they will swiftly grant you a son devoted to righteousness.

O King, she should be eaten by one who desires a son. When she drinks water, he should drink pure water;

"One should constantly ward off gadflies and personally provide fodder;
for one who acts in this manner, a son devoted to dharma will be granted.

Having heard these words, the righteous-souled Ṛtambhara, desiring a son, undertook a vow while performing the worship of the cow;

thus, as he honored the cow, many days passed while she grazed on grass and other fodder in the middle of the forest, free from fear from any quarter.
Once, the king, his eyes fixed upon beholding the beauty of that forest, wandered about it on all sides with great curiosity.
At that time, a five-faced lion emerged from within the woods and struck the cow.

Crying out piteously in many ways and distressed by the weight of the lion, she was then approached by the king; seeing his own mother slain by the lion, he wept, utterly overwhelmed with grief. 25-26.
Afflicted with grief, he approached Jābāli, the best of sages,
and asked for atonement for that act of cow-slaughter committed through negligence.
(27) Ṛtaṃbhara said:
"O Lord, while I was staying in the forest guarding the cow by your command,

"How indeed can my vow be fulfilled so that it may grant me a son?

consisting of *kṛcchra* penances, *cāndrāyaṇa* fasts, gifts, vows, along with observances and restraints.

for the one who intentionally kills a cow, and for the one who reviles Nārāyaṇa.
That lowest of beings who desires suffering for cows even in his mind goes to a place in hell for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras;
so too does that unfortunate man who should ever revile Lord Hari.
Even if one should see hell surrounded by sons and grandsons, O lord of men, he who,
