having known Hari, slanders Him and practices evil deeds, shall never attain liberation from hell. 35-36.
However, there exists an expiation for the unintentional killing of a cow; go therefore to the wise Ṛtuparṇa, who is a devotee of Rāma.
He indeed looks upon all enemies and friends with an equal eye.
He will soon tell you the atonement for this slaughter of a cow. You were formerly exiled from his territories;
therefore, casting aside your state of enmity, go to Ṛtuparṇa. 38–39.
"Whatever he shall say, do it quickly and with focused attention,
so that there may indeed be atonement for the sin committed by you.
Having heard those words, he went to Ṛtuparṇa.
He spoke to that devotee of Rāma—who looked upon enemy and friend with equal vision—of what had occurred, such as the killing of the cow;
and he too reflected upon a means for the expiation of that sin. 41–42.
Having meditated for a moment, the wise king, skilled in dharma, laughed and spoke these words to Ṛtuparṇa, who was devoted to truth:
"O King, who is it that speaks thus before sages who are knowers of the scriptures?"
"Having abandoned them, why have you come to me, a fool who fancies himself a scholar? (44) If you have faith in me, then I shall say something;
listen, O tiger among men, with respect to what I say. (45)
Worship the illustrious Raghunātha with your actions, mind, and speech;
O high-minded one, satisfy the Lord of the World with sincerity. When He is pleased, He will grant you every desire residing within your heart.
It will bring about the destruction of the sin of killing a cow committed through ignorance. O best of beings, O righteous-souled one, while remembering Rāma, protect the cow;
by giving gold to a twice-born, you shall obtain atonement for your sin. 47–48.
Sumati said:
Having heard those words, King Ṛtambhara then performed the remembrance of Rāma and, with his soul purified, observed the vow. 49
Protecting the cow as before, he went to the great forest,
constantly remembering the name of Rāma and devoted to the welfare of all beings.
Then Surabhi, being pleased and satisfied with him, spoke to him.
O King, as if choosing a boon from his own heart's desire,
the king then spoke to his son: "Grant me a beautiful son who is devoted to Rāma, devoted to his father, and a protector of his own dharma."
Having granted the boon requested by her son, the compassionate goddess Kāmadhenu vanished from sight; then,
in due time, he obtained a Vaiṣṇava son who was a servant of Rāma.
There, his father gave him the name Satyavān;
having obtained a son named Satyavān who was devoted to his father and possessed prowess equal to Śakra, the great man attained supreme joy. (54-55)
Having obtained his son as a righteous king, he was filled with intense joy; entrusting the great kingdom to him, he went to the forest for asceticism.
There, with a mind imbued with devotion, he worshipped Hṛṣīkeśa.
With his sins shaken off and his body [transformed], the king went to the abode of Hari.

57. Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Cow-Vow," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana concerning the narrative of Satyavat.
Chapter Thirty-Two.
Sumati said:
"O gentle one, this king renowned by the name Satyavān pleased the Lord of the World, Raghunātha, through his own dharma."
To him, the Lord Rāma, being pleased, granted unwavering devotion to his own lotus feet— a devotion difficult to attain even through millions of merits.
Free from all affliction, he constantly delighted in the narrative of the illustrious Raghunātha.
Endowed with compassion, he performs that which purifies all the worlds.
He who does not worship the Lord Raghunātha, the husband of Ramā,
is struck by the punishments of Yama, which inspire even him with fear.
From his eighth year until he reached eighty,
this man caused the Ekādaśī vow to be observed by all human beings; for at no time did the Tulasī, beloved of Viṣṇu, ever leave his neck.
This supreme garland for the lotus feet of the Lord of Ramā does not release [its fragrance];
how could this one, who is worthy of worship even by sages, not [be so] for others?
For he whose sins are shaken off and whose impurities destroyed possesses the joy of remembering the Lord of the Raghus.

"Having recognized this most wonderful horse of Rāmacandra, he will come and bestow upon you this kingdom free from all thorns. O King, that which was spoken by you has been told to you in its entirety."
"Furthermore, what do you ask, O Lord? Command me and I shall do it.
Śeṣa said:
"The horse, filled with various wonders, entered that city."
Seeing him, the people went to the king and informed him.
The people said:
"There is a certain horse, white in color, resembling the water of the Gaṅgā."
He arrived, shining with a golden plate upon his forehead.
Having heard those delightful words spoken so pleasingly to the hearts of the people, the king laughed and replied to them: "Let it be known whose horse this is."

And they told him: "The horse of the lord of the earth, Rāma, protected by Śatrughna, is entering the middle of the city. Upon hearing those two very beautiful syllables, the name of Rāma, he [was filled with joy].
His heart rejoiced exceedingly, marked by a faltering voice:
"That Rāma, who is constantly meditated upon in my heart as the Lord of Ayodhyā—
his horse, together with Śatrughna, has arrived at my city."
Hanumān shall be there as a servant of Rāma’s feet, he who never at any time forgets Rāma within his mind.
I am going where Śatrughna is, where the son of the Wind-god is.
There were others as well who were servants of the lotus feet of that man who delights in men.
Then he commanded his minister: "Take all the king's great wealth and come with me, moving with great haste."
"I shall go to protect the excellent horse of the Lord of the Raghus,
and to perform the service of Rāma’s lotus feet, which is so very difficult to attain.
Having spoken thus, he then set out toward Śatrughna with his soldiers.
Just then, Rāma’s brother arrived at the city with his army;
the heroes roared, their powerful chariots thundered,
the sounds of victory-conchs resounded there, and the notes of flutes arose on all sides.

Having arrived accompanied by his ministers, King Satyavān prostrated at his feet and offered him the kingdom along with great wealth. Then Śatrughna, recognizing that the king was devotedly following Rāma, [honored him].
They gave that great kingdom to his son named Rukma.
Having embraced Hanumān, the mighty-armed servant of Rāma,
and having also embraced the other devotees of Rāma, he of great fame [departed].

Endowed with truth, he considered himself as one who had achieved his purpose; accompanied by Śatrughna, his heart rejoiced at that time. Meanwhile, the horse, well-protected by the heroes, had traveled a great distance.
Accompanied by his heroes, Śatrughna departed with that king. 26.

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Meeting with Satyavatsa," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
Chapter Thirty-Three.
Śeṣa said:
While the many excellent kings, including Śatrughna and others, all great monarchs accompanied by ten million chariots, were departing...

Suddenly, an exceedingly terrible darkness arose on the path, in which neither one's own kin nor strangers could be distinguished by their relatives; the sky was shrouded in dust and filled with lightning and thunder.
Then, in such a tumultuous conflict that caused great terror,
the clouds rained down blood, pus, impure matter, and much else; those heroes, who were supreme enemies, became utterly overwhelmed.
"What is this? What is this state of affairs?"—thus the world was thrown into confusion.
The eyes of even those renowned for their prowess were enveloped in darkness;
for Rāvaṇa’s friend, dwelling in the netherworld (Pātāla), had carried off his horse.
Known as Vidyunmālī, surrounded by a host of Rākṣasas,
he mounted a celestial chariot that moved at will and was entirely made of iron; causing fear among the heroes, he carried her away.
In a moment, that darkness vanished and the sky shone forth pure;
those heroes, headed by Śatrughna, said, "Where is that horse?
As they all searched for the king of horses among one another, [the horse spoke].
They saw the flood of the river, and then a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose.
"Where has the horse of the horse-sacrifice been led by that evil-minded one?"—thus they spoke, until the lord of the Asuras arrived.
He was seen surrounded by all the brave warriors standing upon their chariots, adorned with valor,
and by the foremost of the Rākṣasas mounted upon excellent celestial vehicles;
they were hideous-faced, with gaping mouths and long fangs, and terrifying to behold.

Then Rākṣasas were seen there, intent on devouring the army. At that time, they informed Śatrughna, the best among the foremost of men: "We do not know where this horse has been led by one sporting in a celestial chariot in the sky."
Having thrown us heroes into confusion with his darkness, he approached;
O tiger among kings, seize the horse as is fitting!
(14) Having heard those words, Śatrughna was overcome with great rage.
"Who is this powerful rākṣasa who has seized my horse?
Let that celestial chariot fall today, struck down by the multitude of my arrows!
Let the head of that enemy of mine fall today, severed by my kṣurapra blades!"
"Let all the chariots, filled with great weapons and missiles, be readied; let the warriors go forth to capture that stealer of horses.
Having spoken thus, the two of them, their eyes copper-red with rage, addressed their own minister.
[To] that hero who knew right from wrong and was skilled in the conduct of war,
Śatrughna said: "O minister, tell me which of us should be appointed, as we are intent on the slaying of the Rākṣasa."

"O great warriors, O great heroes, supreme masters of the highest weapons—having reflected upon this, tell me quickly: 'I shall do as you say. Tell me of those heroes who are worthy of him and skilled in all weapons. (19-20)
Having heard this, the minister spoke these appropriate words,
pointing out with vigor those heroes who were fit for that preeminent battle:
Sumati said:
Let Puṣkala, the scorcher of enemies, equipped with great weapons and missiles, go forth to conquer that demon in battle, intent on victory;
likewise, let Lakṣmīnidhi go, accompanied by a multitude of weapons.
May he shatter that vehicle with his own sharp arrows.
O Lord, Hanumān, who performs bold deeds and is capable of fighting the Rākṣasas here, may he inflict blows upon the demons with his face and tail. 23–24.
And those heroic monkeys, skilled in forest warfare,
all set out to fight, impelled by your words—
namely Sumada, Subāhu, and Pratāpāgrya, the most excellent of beings. 25.
"Go forth with your sharp arrows to fight those lowest of Rākṣasas. You too,
standing upon your chariot surrounded by great weapons and intent on slaying the Rākṣasa, must achieve victory in battle."
"O King, this is my opinion: those heroes who are the destroyers of the enemy's warriors—let them go to battle; what is the use of many other soldiers?
When the chief minister named Sumati had spoken thus, [the king replied: 28.
Śatrughna spoke to the heroes skilled in combat:
"O heroes, Puṣkala and the others, you who are experts in all weapons and missiles,
make a solemn vow here before me for the destruction of the Rākṣasa."
"Having made a vast vow that shines with your own prowess,
come, you who are endowed with strength, into the midst of the battle!
Having heard these words of Śatrughna, those of great might—
Endowed with splendor, they each made their own great vows.
Thereupon, O Lord of the Earth, having heard the words of the king, the hero Puṣkala, filled with supreme enthusiasm, uttered this vow: 32–33.
Puṣkala said:
"Listen, O tiger among kings, to my vow made through my prowess, most wonderful, while all the worlds listen. (34)

I would strike the Daitya—who was overcome by fainting and whose face was disheveled with scattered hair—with sharp arrowheads released from my bow; [and I would endure] whatever sin belongs to one who consumes his own daughters, and whatever sin lies in the reviling of the gods. 35.
"May that sin be mine if I should make my own word false. O Great King, listen to my vow: if these soldiers of great strength, pierced by my arrows, do not fall, then let that sin be mine. (36-37)
"May that very sin which one commits by creating a distinction between Viṣṇu and Īśa, or between Śiva and Śakti, be mine—if my word does not prove true. 38.
"All this has been spoken by me regarding the lotus-feet of Raghunātha."
"Unwavering devotion alone shall make this true.
(39) Having heard that vow of Puṣkala, King Lakṣmīnidhi made his own vow true, adorned by his own valor. (40)
Lakṣmīnidhi said:
Having heard the censure of the Vedas, that man who, like a thief, would inwardly take pleasure in [such talk] while remaining silent, is excluded from all dharma. 41.

A Brahmin who is of evil conduct, who sells lac, dyes, and the like, and who, being a fool deluded by greed for wealth, sells even a cow; having drunk water from a well belonging to a Mleccha, he shall not perform any expiation. 42.
"May that sin be mine if I turn my face away from you. Having heard that vow, Hanumān, skilled in battle,
remembered the feet of Rāma and spoke these auspicious words.
My Lord, who is to be meditated upon constantly and repeatedly by yogis, and whom all the gods, including the asuras, salute with their jeweled crowns;
he is the glorious Rāma, the lord of Ayodhyā, worshipped by the guardians of the world. 45.
"Remembering that, whatever word I speak shall indeed become true.
O King, who is this insignificant and weak Daitya riding in the *kāmagama* chariot? Tell me quickly; I must alone bring about his downfall. (46-47)

Accompanied by Meru and the lord of the gods, I shall lift [the mountain] with the tip of my tail; I shall dry up the entire ocean, or I shall drink it all, by the grace of King Śrī Raghunātha and Jānakī. 48.
"O King, there is nothing on this earth that cannot be accomplished by him.
O Lord, if these words spoken by me should ever prove false, then may I be far removed from devotion to the Lord of the Raghus. 49–50.
O Śūdraka, if you should protect the river Pīlā with the thought that it is the Gaṅgā,
let the sin of that be mine alone, provided that I should speak a falsehood.
O Śūdraka, deluded by me, you have out of delusion gone to a Brāhmaṇa woman.
If I should speak a false word, let its sin be mine alone.
(52) Let him who, greedy for the taste on his tongue, drinks that wine which leads one to hell by smelling it and to Raurava even by touching it—let his sin be mine. (53)
"Whatever sin may arise from that, let it be mine alone;
provided that, by the power of Rāma’s grace, I do not fail to fulfill my vow with truth.
When this was said by the great heroes, the warriors were swiftly joined together.

They made a great vow, characterized by their own prowess. Śatrughna also, while praising those heroes skilled in battle with cries of "Excellent! Excellent!", made a vow there in the sight of all men.
I declare before you my own vow, adorned by its truth;
listen to it, O noble ones, endowed as you are with zeal for battle:
if I do not strike off his head with my arrows and cast it down, [then may I suffer the fate of one who has failed his word].
Whatever sin there is from destroying or severing the wheels and axles of celestial chariots on the ground;
whatever sin comes from false testimony, whatever sin from stealing gold, and whatever sin from reviling Brahmins—let all that be mine today, so be it my firm resolve. (58–59)
Having heard these excellent words of Śatrughna, those heroes who are honored by the brave said:
"O brother of Rāghava, you are blessed; who else could be superior to you?
By you indeed was the Daitya, the bringer of misery to gods and Dānavas, slain."
"Lavaṇa, the son of Madhu and lord of the world, is possessed of great strength.
Who is this wicked and hostile Rākṣasa, and where is his meager power? O high-minded one, you shall bring about his destruction in an instant."
Having spoken thus, those great heroes, having equipped themselves on the field of battle, went joyfully toward the Rākṣasa in order to fulfill their own immortal vow. 63.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Śrī Padma Purāṇa*, in the *Pātāla Khaṇḍa*, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana, in the *Rāmāśvamedha*.
Chapter Thirty-three: The Declaration of the Hero’s Vow.
Chapter Thirty-four: Śeṣa said:
They went toward that lowest of Rākṣasas in chariots richly adorned, yoked with excellent horses, filled with all kinds of weapons and missiles, and endowed with various jewels.
Seeing them, the Rākṣasa, standing in a vehicle that travels at will, spoke:
With a voice as deep as a thundercloud, as if threatening them repeatedly:
"O great warriors, go to your own homes to fight against Māyā;
do not abandon your lives, nor will you release this excellent horse."
Known as Vidyunmālin, he was a dear friend of Rāvaṇa;
he has come here to perform the funeral rites for my friend who has become a ghost.
Where is that Rāma, who, having struck down his friend Rāvaṇa, has departed?
"Where is his brother, that crest-jewel of all heroes? Having slain him, the younger brother of Rāma, I shall obtain retribution for him,
drinking the blood arising from his throat-tract like bubbles."
Having heard these words, Puṣkala, the most excellent among the foremost of warriors, spoke to him who was endowed with heroism and valor. 7.
Puṣkala said:
In battle, those brave warriors do not engage in boastful talk;
they display their prowess by discharging showers of their own weapons and missiles.
By him, Rāvaṇa was slain, though he was surrounded by his friends and kinsmen.
"Having seized his horse, where will you go, O evil-minded one?
You shall fall by the arrows of Śatrughna released from his bow; the jackals on the ground will devour you when you have fallen, deprived of life."
"Let them not roar while I, the servant of the wicked Rāma, stand present;
for great warriors roar in battle only after conquering the enemy and attaining great glory.
Śeṣa said:
As the hero Puṣkala, who is fierce in battle, was speaking thus,
that best of Rākṣasas struck him violently in the heart with a spear. As that great iron spear, adorned with gold, came flying toward him—
With three exceedingly fierce and sharp arrows, Puṣkala cut it down;
severed into three parts by those shafts and deprived of its luster, it fell to the earth, shining like the triple power (Śakti-trayī) of Viṣṇu as it descends.
Seeing those spears shattered, the Rākṣasa, the scorcher of his enemies,
swiftly seized a three-pointed iron trident.
The lord of the Rākṣasas released that sharp-edged weapon, which resembled a blazing fire.
As he approached, the one named Puṣkala,
the servant of Rāghava, cut his trident into pieces with arrows;
then Puṣkala took up his bow and fixed sharp, mind-swift arrows upon it.
The arrows of those [gods], having struck his heart, produced a redness like that of fresh lac, just as the captivating qualities of Viṣṇu produce passion within the heart of a Vaiṣṇava.
Afflicted by the pain of being pierced by those arrows, the exceedingly arrogant Vidyunmālin—
Intent on killing him, I seized a formidable and massive mallet.
That mallet, hurled by him who was named Vidyunmālin,
struck my chest and quickly caused me to fall into a swoon.
Struck by the mallet, the hero Puṣkala, the scorcher of his enemies, fell trembling and shuddering onto the seat of his chariot. Then his brother Ugradaṃṣṭra fought Lakṣmīnidhi.

When weapons and missiles of many kinds, capable of snatching away the lives of heroes, had been discharged, Puṣkala regained consciousness that very moment and said to the Rākṣasa: "O best of Rākṣasas, you are fortunate; your prowess is truly great."
"Now behold my lofty vow and my pride as a hero:
today I shall cast you from your celestial chariot onto the earth with sharpened arrows.
Having spoken thus, he seized a sharp and irresistible arrow.
While he, blazing with the brilliance of fire and endowed with great magnanimity,
was exerting his own prowess to counter that [attack],
at that very moment, an exceedingly fierce arrow with a sharp blade entered his heart. 25-26.
Stunned by that arrow, his mind reeling, the Rākṣasa fell from the seat of Kāmagopa to the ground, deprived of consciousness; indeed,
he was seen falling by Ugradaṃṣṭra, his own elder brother.
Seizing him and fearing his enemies, he brought him inside the celestial chariot.
Then, with great rage, he said to Puṣkala, the best among the strong:
"O evil-minded one, having struck down my brother, where do you intend to go? (28-29)

"Only after conquering me in battle shall you attain supreme victory; while I stand here, let your hope for victory be turned back. As he was speaking thus, [the opponent] swiftly struck him with ten arrows.
His eyes filled with rage at this wicked man, the evil-minded one was struck in the heart by ten arrows by the high-souled Puṣkala; he grew furious and set out to kill him. 31–32.
Grinding his teeth in rage, he raised his fist and struck him,
producing a sound in the heart that created the fear of a falling thunderbolt.
Struck by that fist, the heroic Puṣkala was a master of supreme weapons.
Desiring to crush him who did not tremble, that evil-minded one released extremely sharp calf-toothed arrows into his heart;
pained by those shafts, the Daitya seized a trident.
A terrible, three-pointed trident, blazing fiercely and terrifying with its garlands of flames,
struck the heart of the great hero Puṣkala;
struck by that spear, that best of archers fell unconscious.
Overcome by supreme dejection, he fell upon his chariot.
Perceiving that he had fallen into a swoon, Hanumān, the son of the Wind,
his heart agitated with anger, addressed that Rākṣasa.
"O evil-minded one, where are you going while I stand here as your deliverer?
I shall kill you with blows from my feet, for you have come as a stealer of my horse!
Having spoken thus, the great Daitya struck down the enemy soldiers.
Standing in the sky, he tore at those situated in their celestial chariots with the tips of his claws; some were struck by his tail, some were beaten by the soles of his feet,
and others were torn apart by the arms of the son of the Wind-god.
Some perished, some were slain, and others, struck down in groups, fell into a swoon;
then, tormented by the fear and pain of his foot-strikes, they fled.
There, many exceedingly fierce rākṣasas were killed.

Cut and split into two parts by the son of the Wind-god, that celestial chariot capable of moving at will had its walls and arches shattered, and it was surrounded on all sides by asuras crying out "Alas! Alas! (43-44).
The great hero Hanumān was seen on the ground and in the sky,
moving here and there, difficult to approach; wherever that celestial chariot went, there the son of the Wind-god was seen as well.
Striking [the enemy], the monkey, assuming a form at will, appeared right there;
thus, while the great multitude staying in the celestial chariot was thrown into such agitation, Ugradamshtra, the lord of the Daityas, approached Hanuman. 46–47.
"Having committed the great deed of slaying the warriors,
if you stand here for even a moment, we shall deprive you of your life! Having spoken thus to Hanumān, that evil-minded one struck him.
Then, with his trident— which was extremely sharp and possessed the luster of a blazing fire—
the valiant one seized the approaching trident in his mouth and pulverized it entirely, for it was made wholly of iron. 49–50.
Then the mighty Hanumān crushed that iron trident released by the Daitya and struck him with many slaps.
Struck here and there by the slaps of the lord of monkeys, he [fell].

Distressed, he unleashed an illusion that struck fear into all the worlds. Then a fierce darkness arose, in which no one could be discerned, nor could one's own kin or strangers be distinguished among the many people.
Rocks resembling mountain peaks fell upon the great warriors;
struck by them, they all then became utterly distressed. Lightning flashed there and the clouds thundered loudly.
They rain down pus and blood, and discharge foul water;
many headless trunks falling from the sky are seen, along with severed heads still adorned with earrings. 55–56.
Naked, deformed, with extremely disheveled hair and hideous faces,
the Daityas were seen everywhere, fierce and causing terror. At that time, the people became agitated, overwhelmed by fear of one another.
Defeated by the flight [of the enemy], they considered it a great portent (58).
Then the highly illustrious Śatrughna, standing upon his chariot, arrived;
having performed the remembrance of Śrī Rāma, he fixed arrows upon his bow (59).
Then, having completely shaken off that illusion with the mohana (stupefying) weapon,
the valiant one scattered showers of arrows from the sky and rained them down upon the demon in battle. At that time, the quarters became clear and the sun was surrounded by a halo.
Just as clouds have passed away and the lightning has come to rest, so too was it;
then a great celestial chariot, filled with Rākṣasas and extremely agitated by cries of "Cut! and "Pierce!", appeared before him. 61–62.
Hundreds of thousands of arrows, adorned with golden feathers, fell repeatedly upon the celestial chariot as it remained in the sky, moving at will.
At that time, the chariot was seen to have been shattered and could no longer be seen from above.
Then, like a portion of his own city with its limbs shattered upon the ground, the enraged Daitya fixed arrows to his bow;
roaring aloud, he scattered those arrows toward Rāma’s brother. 64–65.
Those arrows, by the hundreds, having struck his body in great numbers, attained a beauty as they flowed with streams of blood and possessed sharp points.
Śatrughna, endowed with supreme power, [discharged] the weapon presided over by Vāyu.
He took up a weapon upon his bow that caused the Rākṣasas to tremble.
By that weapon, the sky-dwellers were seen falling from their celestial chariots through the air with their hair disheveled, like throngs of Bhūtas and Vetālas.
Seeing that weapon discharged by his brother, the Lord of the Raghus,
the son of Danu fixed the Pāśupata weapon upon his bow.
Then, Vetālas, Bhūtas, Pretas, and Niśācaras began to emerge.

Equipped with skull-bowls and scimitars, they drank copious amounts of blood; with joy, they quaffed the blood of Śatrughna’s warriors, irresistible even while those men were still alive, adorned as they were with scimitars in hand.
Seeing that weapon pervading all the heroes and destroying their splendor, he released the weapon named Nārāyaṇa in order to repel it.
At that very moment, the Nārāyaṇa weapon warded off all of them.
All of them, dispatched by the night-stalker, met their destruction.
Then the enraged night-stalker Vidyunmālī took up a sharp,
terrible trident, a fierce weapon for slaying his enemies.
In the battle, as Vidyunmālin approached with a trident in his hand, he struck his arms—
which shone like the half-moon— with arrows;
with those shafts his arms severed, he prepared to strike with his head.
"Your protector, Śatrughna, will come after we have slain him.
As he was speaking thus, [Śatrughna] swiftly severed with sharp arrows the head— adorned with earrings— of that powerful hero.
Seeing his head severed, the powerful Ugradanstra began to strike Śatrughna— who is served by heroes— with his fist;
but Śatrughna cut off that head with a razor-edged arrow.
The remaining Rākṣasas, who had fled from the heroes skilled in all weapons and missiles and were now deprived of their lord,
approached Śatrughna; having prostrated before him, they then presented the horse that had been recovered.
Then, the sounds of lutes and the blasts of conchs were heard on all sides, along with the captivating shouts of victory from the brave warriors. 81.

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Defeat of the Rākṣasa Vidyunmālin," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* within the *Śrī Padma Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. 34.
The thirty-fifth chapter. Śeṣa said:
Having recovered that horse which had been carried off by the Rākṣasas, King Śatrughna...
Filled with Puṣkala, he attained extreme joy.
With their limbs drenched in blood, those warriors as well as Lakṣmīnidhi praised the great king, who was endowed with martial enthusiasm for battle.
O Sage, when that great and invincible Daitya Vidyutmālin had been slain, all the gods cast off their fear and attained great happiness;
the rivers became pure and the sun became clear.
Fanned by the wind, sprinkled with fragrant water, stainless,
and full of vigor— those great heroes, clad in armor, standing upon their chariots with spotless limbs and endowed with the fortune of victory, all spoke to the king.
The heroes said:
"O high-minded one, by good fortune the Daitya Vidyunmālī has been slain by you—
he from whose fear the gods were struck with terror and driven out of heaven."
"By good fortune, this magnificent great steed of Raghunātha has been obtained;
by good fortune, you shall go everywhere, may you be victorious throughout the circle of the earth!
O Master, release this mount, which is as swift as thought and delightful."
"O Mahāmati, let there be no delay regarding this agreement.
Śeṣa said:
Having heard those words of the heroes, which were appropriate for the occasion...
Having praised him as "Excellent! Excellent!", he released that best of horses.
Once released and well-protected, it then wandered toward the northern direction, accompanied by excellent chariots, infantry, and horses, all of whom were experts in every weapon and missile.
In this regard, O Vātsyāyana, listen to this captivating account of Śatrughna, which burns away heaps of sin:
having then reached the bank of the Revā, which is frequented by hosts of sages.
Was it the essence of a multitude of blue jewels, or was it water in disguise?
Bowing down to all those various eminent sages, he who was served by heroes proceeded on the back of that jewel among horses, which moved according to his will.
As he went there, he saw a dilapidated hermitage made of palāśa leaves,
sprinkled by the waves of the Revā river, a refuge that removes all sins.
Seeing him, Sumati spoke to the omniscient one, who was skilled in policy.
Śatrughna was skilled in performing all duties pertaining to dharma, artha, and action. The King said: "O minister, tell me, whose hermitage is this, so auspicious to behold?"
To me, who asked this as one most skilled in inquiry,
Śeṣa said:
"Having heard these words, Sumati spoke to that king."
Displaying his own friendship with words bright with a smile,
Sumati said:
"O Great King, having seen him, we have indeed been cleansed of our sins."
"O best of sages, we shall become devoted to all the scriptures.
Therefore, having bowed to him and inquired of him, he—who is intensely eager for the nectar of the lotus feet of Raghunātha—will tell you everything. (18-19)
"By name he is known as Āraṇyaka, a servant of the feet of Raghunātha,
perfected by most intense austerity, and skilled in the meaning of all the scriptures.
Having heard those words, which were enriched with righteousness and purpose, [he spoke].
Then, accompanied by a small retinue of servants, he went to see him:
Hanumān, the heroic Puṣkala, Sumati the best of ministers, Lakṣmīnidhi, Pratāpāgrya, Subāhu, and likewise Sumada. (21–22)

Surrounded by these, the noble-minded King Śatrughna reached the hermitage to pay homage to the best of the twice-born, Āraṇyaka. Having approached that foremost of ascetics, he then offered his salutations.
Accompanied by all those heroes whose necks were bowed in humility,

[Rāma] then offered the guest-offering (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), and other honors with fruits, roots, and the like, upon seeing all those kings led by Śatrughna standing before him in prostration.
He said to all those kings: "O sinless ones, where have you gathered? How have you come here? Tell me all of that.
Having heard these words of that best of sages, Vāḍava—
Sumati, skilled in debate, spoke these words: Sumati said,
"This horse indeed belongs to the king of the Raghu dynasty, and it is being protected by all."
"The hero will perform a sacrifice provided with all necessary materials.
Having heard those words of theirs, the best of sages spoke,
as if dispelling the entire terrible darkness with the luster of his teeth.
Āraṇyaka said: "What is the use of various other sacrifices, provided with all manner of requisites, which indeed yield little merit and bestow only perishable states? (30)

Foolish people, abandoning Hari—the Hero of the Raghus, Lord of Ramā, who bestows the state of eternal sovereignty—perform the worship of others. He, however, removes the mountain of sins merely by being remembered by men. 31.
Having abandoned that, the fool suffers through sacrifices, yogic practices, vows, and the like.
Alas! Behold the extreme delusion of people who, having abandoned the easily accessible worship of Rāma, practice that which is difficult to attain. 32–33.
It is meditated upon by yogis both with desires and those free from desire;
it bestows liberation upon men and destroys all sins merely by being remembered.
Long ago, while I was thoroughly investigating a man of knowledge who was a knower of reality, I [spoke this].
Many scriptures and numerous sacred fords exist, yet none among them has imparted the ultimate truth to me.
Then, by great good fortune, I encountered the sage Lomaśa, who had descended from the heavenly realm with the desire to perform a pilgrimage. 35–36.
Then, having prostrated before that great sage, whose two feet are served by great yogis and who possesses a long life, I questioned him:
"O Lord, today I have attained this human state, which is marvelous and difficult to find."
"O you who desire to cross the terrible ocean of saṃsāra,
having reflected upon what must be done— whether it be a vow, a gift, a recitation, a sacrifice,
or indeed some deity— who is there that can truly carry one across the ocean of worldly existence? (38-39)"

"O Lord of Yoga, O you who have reached the further shore of the meaning of all scriptures, tell me that which, having known from the ocean of your compassion, one may cross over this terrible and boundless cycle of existence.
Having heard these words of mine, the best of sages spoke.
Listen with a one-pointed mind, O Brahmin, endowed with supreme faith.
There are gifts, sacred fords, vows, observances, and restraints;
likewise, there are many yogas and sacrifices that bestow heaven. 41-42.

I shall proclaim the supreme secret that destroys all sins; listen to it, O highly fortunate one, for it is the savior from the ocean of saṃsāra. (43) It must not be told to an atheist, nor again to one who lacks faith.
It should not be given to one who is a slanderer, nor to one who is deceitful, nor to an enemy of devotion (44).
It should be spoken to one who is a devotee of Rāma, who is peaceful, and who is free from desire and anger; it is the supreme means for destroying all suffering (45).
There is no god higher than Rāma; there is no vow higher than Rāma. There is no yoga higher than Rāma, and no sacrifice higher than Rāma.
By remembering him, chanting his name, and worshipping him, a person attains the supreme state. 46.
He attains supreme prosperity both in this world and the next (47).
When remembered and meditated upon in the mind, He bestows the fruit of all desires;
He grants supreme devotion that carries one across the ocean of worldly existence (48).
Even a dog-cooker (outcaste), by remembering Rāma, attains the supreme goal; what then to say of those like you who are devoted to the Vedas and the Śāstras?
(49) The secret of all the Vedas and Śāstras has been revealed to you.
Indeed, may his true nature be realized exactly as he desires.
(50) Rāmacandra is the one God; his worship is the one vow;
his name is the one mantra; and this scripture is the one hymn of praise for him. (51)
"Therefore, with your whole being, worship the heart-stealing Rāmacandra,
so that this ocean of saṃsāra may become as trivial as a cow's footprint.
Having heard those words from me, he again put a question.
"How is the Lord meditated upon, and how is he worshipped by men?
O one of great intelligence, tell me in detail, O omniscient one, O best of sages; having known this, I shall have achieved my purpose throughout the three worlds."
Having heard these words of mine and reflected upon them, Lomaśa spoke everything to me with Rāma’s meditation foremost in his mind:
"Listen, O best of Brahmins, sinless one; I shall tell you that which was asked by you."
In order that the Lord of Mānasa, who burns with the fever of saṃsāra, may be pleased— 56—
one should meditate upon him at the foot of a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) which grants the fulfillment of all desires, in the beautiful city of Ayodhyā adorned with wonderful pavilions. 57.
Adorned with great emeralds, gold, sapphires, and other gems,
the lion-throne was heart-stealing and, by its splendor, dispelled all darkness; upon it sat the charming King of the Raghus.
His body was dark-green like a blade of *dūrvā* grass; he was worshipped by the Lord of the Gods, the Indra of gods.
His face surpassed the luster of the full moon on the night of the new moon (*rākā*), and he bore a forehead mark as beautiful as a crescent of the eighth-day moon.
Abounding in the beauty of dark-blue locks, adorned with the gems of his crown,
and resplendent with two earrings of exquisite beauty shaped like sea-monsters; he shone with lips possessing the lovely luster of coral.
It is beautifully adorned by the king of the twice-born (the moon), whose form resembles that of the lord of stars;
its face is graced by a tongue as dark as the *japā* flower, and within it dwell the Vedas, beginning with the *Ṛgveda*, together with the various scriptures. 62–63.
He was beautifully adorned by the splendor of a neck possessing the luster of a conch shell;
he bore excellent, high, and muscular shoulders like those of a lion,
and possessed long arms marked with armlets and bracelets.
His vital energy was adorned with the splendors of various mudrās, and his arms hung down to his knees (65).
He possessed a broad chest, beautified by being the dwelling place of Lakṣmī,
and was most enchanting, marked with the wonderful signs such as the Śrīvatsa (66).
He had a large belly and a prominent navel, and was graced by beautiful hips;
he was especially endowed with splendor by his girdle set with precious gems. He was further adorned with the beauty of his two pure thighs and his well-formed knees.
Adorned with feet marked by the lines of a thunderbolt, barley-corns,
and auspicious hooks— feet fit for meditation by yogis and tender to the touch—
having meditated upon and remembered [the Lord] thus, you shall cross over the ocean of saṃsāra.
By constantly worshipping Him with sandalwood paste and other offerings according to one's desire, one attains supreme prosperity in this world and the next.
O Great King, you have asked about the supreme meditation upon Rāma.
Therefore, this has been told; indeed, cross the ocean of saṃsāra.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Lomaśa and Āraṇyaka," within the "Story of Āraṇyaka" in the *Rāmāśvamedha* of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
The thirty-sixth chapter. Śeṣa said:
Having heard this most great [account] from Lomaśa, the lord of brahmins was indeed amazed.
He questioned that omniscient sage, the best among yogis, once again. Āraṇyaka said:
"O best of sages, O high-minded one, tell me this which I ask of you."
The gurus, endowed with compassion, spoke everything to their servant:
"O highly fortunate one, who is this Rāma whom you constantly meditate upon? O best of the twice-born, tell us of his deeds."
"For what purpose has he descended, and why has he assumed human form? Tell me all of that quickly, so as to dispel my doubt. Śeṣa said:
Having heard these most excellent words of the sage,
Lomaśa recounted the wonderful life-story of Rāma;
the Lord of the Lords of Yoga, having perceived that the worlds were submerged in hell, [acted].
"By which [act] my terrible [deeds] will be extinguished and my fame spread throughout the world.
Having understood this, the Supreme Lord, the charming ocean of compassion, took an incarnation there in four forms, accompanied by Śrī.
When the Tretā Yuga arrived after the previous age,
the lotus-eyed Rāma, the delighter of the Raghus, was born in the Solar dynasty;
he was a youth accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, wearing side-locks of hair.
At their father’s word,
those two princes, self-controlled, heroic archers, and devoted followers of Viśvāmitra, were given by the king for the purpose of protecting the sacrifice. (9–10)
As they were traveling along that path, the terrible Rākṣasī Tāṭakā encountered them for the purpose of creating an obstacle;
with the permission of the sage, Rāma [dispatched] Tāṭakā to the torments of Yama.

Rāghava entered [the hermitage] through his practice of the science of archery (dhanurveda). By the touch of whose soles, Ahalyā— the wife of Gautama— was restored to her own form, having been released from her state of dwelling within a stone brought about by a yogic curse.
While Viśvāmitra’s sacrifice was proceeding excellently, that lowest of sinners slew both Mārīca and Subāhu with his supreme arrows.
Furthermore, the bow of Īśvara, which had been kept in the house of Janaka, was broken.

In his fifteenth year, Rāma married the lovely Sītā, the daughter of the King of Mithilā, who was six years old and not born of a womb. Having obtained Sītā, the descendant of Raghu then felt that he had accomplished all his life's purposes.
Then Rāma sported with her for twelve years;
in his twenty-seventh year, he was installed as the crown prince. Then Kaikeyī asked the king for two boons.
Of these two, let one— Rāma, together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa—
go forth into exile wearing matted hair for fourteen years here; and let Bharata, by means of the other, be my sovereign heir-apparent.
The king, sending forth Rāma— who was accompanied by Jānakī and Lakṣmaṇa—
remained for three nights subsisting on water and on the fourth day ate only fruit;
on the fifth day, he established Rāma’s residence at Citrakūṭa.
Then, O great sage, in the thirteenth year at Pañcavaṭī,
Rāma disfigured the night-stalker Śūrpaṇakhā while he was wandering in the forest together with Jānakī.
Then, due to the ripening of his evil karma, the Rākṣasa arrived to carry her away;
consequently, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, during the muhūrta known as Vṛnda,
the Ten-necked one (Rāvaṇa) abducted Sītā in the absence of the two descendants of Raghu.
Thus being carried away by him, she cried out like a female osprey:
"Rāma, Rāma! Protect me, protect me, who am being snatched away by this Rākṣasa, just as a hawk overcome by hunger might carry off a crying quail!"
Thus, having fallen under the power of passion, Rāvaṇa was carrying off the daughter of Janaka; at that moment, Jaṭāyu, the king of birds,
fought with the lord of the Rākṣasas and, struck by Rāvaṇa, fell down.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, Sampāti informed the monkeys that Vasantī was in the abode of Rāvaṇa; on the tenth day of the month,
he leaped one hundred yojanas from the peak of Mount Mahendra on the eleventh day.
Hanumān searched throughout Lankā during the night; indeed, it was at the end of that night that Hanumān beheld Sītā. On the twelfth day, Hanumān took his stand beneath a Śiṃśapā tree.
On that night, a conversation took place for the sake of Jānakī’s confidence;
then, on the thirteenth day, the battle commenced with the [throwing of] dice and other games.
On the fourteenth day, the monkey was bound by Śakrajit using the Brahmāstra.
With his tail set ablaze by fire, the burning of Laṅkā was accomplished;
on the full moon day, the monkey’s return to Mount Mahendra took place. Within five days from the first day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, he traversed the path.
Having returned on the sixth day, Madhuvana was reportedly destroyed; on the seventh day, there was the granting of recognition and the presentation of everything;
and on the eighth day, under the constellation Uttaraphalgunī, during the hour known as Vijaya.
When the thousand-rayed sun reached the meridian,
Rāghava made his vow and set out toward the southern direction;
having crossed even the ocean, I shall slay the lord of the Rākṣasas.
Sugrīva also became his companion as he set out toward the southern direction.
Within seven days, from the first day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa until the third, he reached the encampment on the shore of the ocean.
On the fourth day, Vibhīṣaṇa, having joined with Rāma, became the attendant of Rāghava and his army. On the fifth day, he applied himself to the counsel for the purpose of crossing the ocean.
The four Rāmas performed a fast unto death (prāyopaveśana).
Then followed the obtaining of boons from the ocean along with the demonstration of the means [to cross it].
Thereafter, the undertaking took place on the tenth day and its completion on the thirteenth.
On the fourteenth day, Rāma encamped his army on Mount Suvela;
by the end of the second day following the full moon, the crossing of the army was completed over three days. Then, accompanied by the host of the lord of monkeys, Rāma crossed the ocean.
For the sake of Sītā, he besieged the city of Laṅkā together with Lakṣmaṇa.
The encampment lasted for eight days, from the third day until the tenth;
on the eleventh day, Śuka and Sāraṇa arrived there.
On the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa, there was the counting of the army by Śārdūla, as well as the sudden description of the leaders of the monkeys;
on the thirteenth day, [the crossing began], and by the three days until the new moon, they reached Laṅkā.

Rāvaṇa then made a reckoning of his army and displayed his zeal for battle (45). On the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, Aṅgada went as an envoy; thereafter followed the display of the illusory head of Sītā’s husband and other such sights (46).
For seven days beginning from the second day of the month of Māgha until the eighth,
there was a tumultuous battle between the Rākṣasas and the monkeys. On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, however, Indrajit was slain in the conflict during the night.
It is said that Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa were bound by the serpent-noose (nāgapāśa). While the monkey leaders were agitated and utterly dispirited on all sides,
Pavana (Hanumān) recited prayers on the tenth day for the sake of releasing them from the serpent-noose.
Then, on the eleventh and twelfth lunar days, Karna heard the true nature of Rama and the arrival of Garuda; on the twelfth day, the slaying of Dhumraksha was accomplished,
and on the thirteenth day, Kampana was likewise killed by him in battle.
From the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha until the first day of the dark fortnight (51),
the slaying of Prahasta was accomplished by Nīla in three days;
from the second day of the dark fortnight of Māgha until the fourth (52), [the remainder] was done in three days.
In that tumultuous battle, Rāvaṇa was driven from the rampart by Rāma; then,
from the fifth day until the eighth,
Kumbhakarṇa, having been awakened by Rāvaṇa, took his meal for four days.
Within six days from the day Kumbhakarṇa fell— from the ninth to the fourteenth—
he, the devourer of many monkeys, was slain in battle by Rāma;
on the day of the new moon (amāvāsyā), the withdrawal [of the army] took place out of grief.
From the first day of the month of Phālguna until the fourth, in four days,
the five Rākṣasas beginning with Bisatanu were slain;
likewise, from the fifth until the seventh, the killing of Atikāya took place.

From the eighth day until the twelfth, five days were spent in battle; then Nikumbha and Kumbha fell, and Makarākṣa was slain by Indrajit in three days on the second day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna. 57–58.
From the third day until the end of the fifth day,
there was a cessation of activity because everyone was occupied with bringing the medicinal herbs.
Then, on the thirteenth day, after five days had passed, Indrajit—
Slain by Lakṣmaṇa in battle, he who was renowned for his strength and prowess—
the ten-necked Rāvaṇa— received the initiation on the fourteenth day and set out for the fight on the new moon day.
During the five days from the first to the fifth of the bright fortnight of Caitra,
while Rāvaṇa was engaged in battle, there was a great slaughter of the Rākṣasas;
and from the sixth until the eighth of Caitra, Mahāpārśva and others were slain.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the piercing of Lakṣmaṇa’s vital force occurred;
by Rāma, who was overcome with wrath, the ten-necked Rāvaṇa was routed,
and by him (Rāma), Mount Drona was brought for the sake of Lakṣmaṇa.
On the tenth day, there occurred at night a slaughter of the Rākṣasas caused by the battle;
on the eleventh day, however, Mātali, acting as charioteer, drove the chariot toward Rāma at the command of Vāsava, and the King presented it with devotion.
Then, filled with wrath, Rāma fought Rāvaṇa in a duel of chariots for eighteen days, from the twelfth day until the fourteenth of the dark fortnight;
in that tumultuous battle, Rāma achieved victory.
From the second day of the bright fortnight of Māgha until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra—
thus, within eighty-seven days, there was a cessation of hostilities for fifteen intermediate days;
the actual battle lasted for seventy-two days.
On the new moon day, the consecration of Saṃskāra, Rāvaṇa, and the others took place;
on the second lunar day of the month of Vaiśākha, Vibhīṣaṇa was consecrated in the kingdom of Laṅkā at the sacred bathing sites of Rāma.
On the third day, there was the purification of Sītā and the obtaining of boons from the gods; then,
having slain the Lord of Laṅkā without delay, that elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa took back the virtuous Jānakī, who had been made miserable by the Rākṣasa.
Taking Jānakī with him out of supreme affection, he turned back;
on the fourth day of the month of Vaiśākha, Rāma, having ascended the Puṣpaka chariot,
returned through the air once more toward the city of Ayodhyā.
When his fourteenth year was complete, on the fifth day of the month of Mādhava, Rāma, accompanied by his followers, arrived at the hermitage of Bharadvāja.
On the sixth day, he met with Bharata in Nandigrāma.
On the seventh [night], that scion of Raghu was consecrated in Ayodhyā.
Maithilī, however, remained for ten months and fourteen days in Rāvaṇa’s residence, deprived of Rāma.
Rāma ruled the kingdom for forty-two years,
at which time thirty-three years had passed for Sītā.
At the end of those fourteen years, the Lord entered the city.
Delighted by the slaying of Rāvaṇa in battle, Rāma returned to Ayodhyā;
there, together with his brothers, he then ruled the kingdom.
While he was governing the realm, the preceptor, the best among speakers, addressed him.
Agastya, born from a jar, will come to you, O Lord of the Raghus;
at his word, that Lord of the Raghus will perform the horse sacrifice.
O you of virtuous vows, his horse will indeed come to your hermitage.
His warriors, filled with joy, will come to your hermitage. Before them, you shall recount the enchanting stories of Rāma;
together with them, O bull among the twice-born, you shall indeed go to Ayodhyā. 81–82.
"Upon seeing the one with eyes like lotus petals in the garden of Ayodhyā,
you shall at that very moment become a means of crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra.
Having spoken thus to me, the best of sages, Lomaśa, who possesses all-encompassing wisdom, [departed].
He said, "What should be asked? Then I spoke what was beneficial:
"By your grace, the entire wonderful life-story of Rāma has been known; by your favor, I shall attain the lotus-feet of Rāma today. (84-85)
After I had paid my respects, that lord of sages departed;
through his grace, I attained the worship of Rāma’s feet. Day after day, I repeatedly remembered those two beautiful feet of Rāma.
Without weariness, I repeatedly sang the life-story of him who is praised by songs;
I purified other people with that song which captivates the heart, while joyfully remembering the words of that sage through his grace. 87-88.

"I am blessed, I have accomplished my purpose, and I am fortunate upon this earth, for I shall behold the lotus feet of Rāmacandra. Therefore, with all one's being, the enchanting Rāma should be worshipped. (89)
"He is indeed worthy of veneration by all who desire to cross the ocean of saṃsāra.
Therefore, for what purpose have you arrived? And who is this lord of monkeys, this righteous-souled one, who performs the great sacrifice, the horse-sacrifice (hayamedha)? (90-91)
"Tell all that here and remain for the protection of the horse;
let them remember the feet of the Lord of the Raghus, remembering them again and again.
Having heard these words of the sage, they were filled with wonder.
Remembering Raghunātha, they spoke to the sage Āraṇyaka. 93.

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of Rāma’s Life Story," within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, specifically in the dialogue between Lomaśa and Āraṇyaka during the Horse Sacrifice of Rāma.
Chapter Thirty-Seven.
Śeṣa said:
Questioned by that best of sages regarding the wonderful life-story of Rāma, they, considering themselves blessed and fortunate, spoke with reverence about themselves. 1.
The people said:
"We have all been purified now by the sight of you, since you, O Rāma, are purifying us people here today with your speech."
Listen to these truthful words; you are the most excellent of Brahman-sages.
Whatever has been asked of us by you, all of that we shall indeed relate.
At the word of Agastya, Śrī Rāma [acted] for the removal of the sin of killing a Brahmin.
O high-minded Brahmin, know this: all those great ones, having gathered every requisite for a sacrifice, have come to your hermitage along with the horse, and they are guarding it. 4–5.
Having heard these words, which were like a captivating elixir,
the Brahmin, a devotee of Rāma, attained extreme joy:
"Today the tree of my desire, endowed with the glory of its fruit, has borne fruit."
Today my mother, who has been blessed with fortune, has given birth to me;
today I have attained a kingdom free from thorns;
today the treasuries are well-filled; and today the gods are thoroughly propitiated.
Indeed, the fruit of the Agnihotra sacrifice has been attained by me today through this oblation of clarified butter,
since I shall behold the pair of lotus feet of Rāmacandra,
the Lord and Sovereign of Ayodhyā, who constantly meditates upon them within his own heart. 9.

Surely he will be delightful to behold, sharing the same field of vision as me. Hanumān, embracing me, will inquire after my welfare; seeing my great devotion, that most excellent being will attain joy.
Having heard these words, Hanumān, the best of monkeys,
grasped the two feet of the sage Āraṇyaka.
"O Lord, O brahmin-sage, I am your servant standing before you."
"O Lord of Sages, know Rāmadāsa to be like a particle of dust [to you].
When he had spoken thus, the sage was indeed filled with supreme joy;
he embraced Hanumān, who was beautifully adorned by devotion to Rāma.
Both of them, pierced by mutual love and drenched in nectar, remained there as if they were motionless figures in a painting.
Seated there, they engaged in most enchanting conversation.

Hanumān spoke these words, beautiful in every way, to that best of sages, the forest-dweller who was filled with the meditation on Rāma’s feet and whose mind was overflowing with love for the lotus-feet of Raghunātha. 16–17.
"O Lord, this great and heroic brother of Rāma, Śatrughna—the diamond-studded sprout of Daśaratha’s lineage—bows down to you;
he by whom Lavaṇa, the terror of all the worlds, was slain. (18)
And all the sages, whose wealth is their excellent penance, have been made happy.
This one named Puṣkala, served by the most eminent [warriors],
bows to you— he by whom the great heroes have now been conquered on the field of battle.
Know this man to be a minister of Rāma, possessed of many virtues and great strength; he is dearer than life to the Lord of the Raghus, omniscient, and skilled in dharma.
This Subāhu is exceedingly fierce, a forest fire to the lineage of his enemies.
O Pārvatī, even this Sumada, who was once bowed down by his mind hanging upon the lotus-feet of Rāma,
has now attained the great crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra through the service of Rāma’s feet. 22–23.
"This is Satyavān, who, having heard from his servant that the horse had been recovered,
offered you the kingdom and bows down to you upon the ground.
Having heard these words, he embraced him with great affection.
The forest-dwelling sage offered a welcome with fruits and other offerings.
Delighted, those best of sages took up residence there in the hermitage; having performed their daily rites at dawn on the banks of the Revā, they remained there with great diligence.
Then Śatrughna, having placed the sage along with his attendants upon the Nārāyaṇa chariot, brought him to Ayodhyā, the city where Rāma had made his abode.
Seeing from afar that city inhabited by the kings of the Solar dynasty, [he proceeded further].
Out of a longing to see the Lord of the Raghus, he became a foot-soldier in haste;
having reached the beautiful city of Ayodhyā, which was adorned with people, his heart had grown through thousands of desires for the sight of Rāma. 28–29.
There, on the bank of the Sarayū, adorned with pavilions, he beheld Rāma— dark as a blade of dūrvā grass, with eyes possessing the luster of lotuses,
holding a beautiful deer-horn upon his shoulder, and endowed with splendor. 30.
He was surrounded by hosts of sages headed by Vyāsa and well-served by heroic men; he was encircled by Bharata, the son of Sumitrā,
and was bestowing upon the multitudes of the poor whatever gifts they requested.
Beholding him, who is known as Āraṇyaka,
my eyes— equal to lotus petals—
considered their purpose fulfilled; today, my mastery of all the scriptures has become truly meaningful.
"By whom Śrī Rāma was recognized, he has arrived at this city of Ayodhyā.

Hearing such words and many others, his body radiant with the great joy of beholding Rāma’s feet, he proceeded toward the presence of the Lord of the Raghus—a distance so remote that it was inaccessible even to other masters of yoga devoted to contemplation. 34–35.
"Today I am blessed; I shall place the two feet of Rāma within the range of my sight," he said, gazing at Rāma with a most beautiful face.
Rāma, for his part, [beheld] the best of brāhmaṇas, blazing with his own splendor.
Seeing him bearing the very form of austerity, the great Rāmacandra then rose to greet him; bowing for a long time at his feet, he said,
"O God who is devoted to Brahmanas, my body has been purified today."
Having spoken these words, the Lord, whose feet were illuminated by the jewels in the crowns of gods and demons bowing down, fell at his feet.
O best of kings, the great ascetic, the lord of the Vāḍavas, [spoke] to that prostrate king.
Taking his beloved Lord between his two arms, he embraced Him;
then, having seated the son of Kausalya upon a high jeweled throne, the Lord washed His pair of feet with water.
Hari himself placed the water for washing the feet upon his head,
saying, "Today, along with my attendants and my family, I have been purified. Then, having anointed [him] with sandalwood paste, he gave him a milch cow.
And he, served by the lords of the gods, spoke these charming words:
"O Lord, let the horse-sacrifice (vājimedha) be performed by me;
today it shall be completed, having come to your feet."

"Today this Aśvamedha sacrifice, purified by your foot, shall effect the destruction of the sin arising from the slaughter of a Brahmin. To him who was speaking these words, the lord of kings, who is served by [the gods], [replied].
The sage Āraṇyaka, laughing, spoke these words in a honeyed voice:
"O Lord of the Earth, it is indeed fitting that you speak thus, for you are devoted to the Brahmanas.
O Great King, the Brahmanas who have mastered the Vedas are your very own embodiments. (46-47)
O King, when you perform auspicious deeds such as the worship of Brahmins, then all the monarchs will likewise honor the Brahmin, O Lord of the Earth.
As for what was said by you, O Great King, regarding the removal of the sin of killing a Brahmin—
I perform this pure sacrifice; these words of mine are indeed laughable.
(49) O fool, by the mere remembrance of your name, even one devoid of all sacred scriptures may cross the ocean of all sins and attain the supreme state. (50)
It is clear that this is the essential meaning of all the Vedas and Itihāsas;
for when the remembrance of Rāmanāma is performed, it delivers one from sin.
To that extent, even sins equal to the killing of a Brahmin continue to roar.
O Rāmacandra,
it is clearly proclaimed by me that upon hearing the thundering roar of your name, the elephants of great sins flee,
O Great King, seeking a place anywhere to hide. 52-53.
Therefore, O Rāma, whose sight bestows great merit, how can there be any talk of killing for you? Upon hearing your auspicious story, one shall immediately become purified.
Formerly, in the Kṛta Yuga, [I spoke] to those dwelling on the banks of the Gaṅgā.
This speech from the mouths of the sages, who are knowers of antiquity, was heard by me in the past:
(55) "Fear of sin remains for men who are cowardly and great sinners only so long as they do not utter the heart-stealing name of Rāma. (56)
"Therefore, I am blessed now; for the destruction of this cycle of worldly existence has become easily attainable through the sight of you, O Rāmacandra.
To the sage who had spoken thus, he indeed paid homage there.
"All the people among the sages exclaimed, 'Excellent! Excellent!
" Śeṣa said:
"A great wonder occurred there; listen as I relate it to you."
O best of sages, Vātsyāyana, who was solely devoted to the worship of Rāma,
having beheld the great king Rāma exactly as he appeared within the scope of his meditation, attained extreme joy and spoke to the lords of sages: 59–60.
O lords of sages, listen to my most enchanting words:
who in this world has been as fortunate as I, and who will ever be so? There is no one like me; none has been born before, nor shall there be in the future.
Or rather, when Mābhadra, having bowed to me, inquired after my welcome;
he, whose lotus-feet’ dust is ever sought by the Vedas, today considered himself purified by drinking the water from my feet. 62–63.

As he was speaking thus, a burst of Brahma-energy occurred; that splendor which emerged then entered the Leader of the Raghus, while all the worlds looked on from the pavilion on the banks of the Sarayū. 64.
She attained the liberation of union (sāyujya-mukti), which is difficult even for yogis to achieve.
At that time, the sound of celestial drums arose and the resonance of lutes was heard; a rain of flowers fell before them as they beheld this wonderful and marvelous sight. 65-66.
Even the sages, having witnessed this, praised the Lord of Sages:
"This best of sages has achieved his purpose, since he has beheld the form of Rāma.

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Departure of the Forest Sage for the World of Viṣṇu," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
The thirty-eighth chapter.
Sūta said:
Having heard this narrative, Vātsyāyana, of noble intellect, [spoke].
He attained supreme joy and spoke to the Lord of Serpents.
Vātsyāyana said:
O Lord of Serpents, as I listen to this story, I am not yet satiated.
There was a most blessed sage named Āraṇyaka, a supreme upholder of the Vedas, who, upon beholding Raghunātha— the one whose fame dispels the suffering of his devotees—
cast off his transient body. 2–3.
"Then, O Lord of Serpents, where did the king’s horse go, and by whom was it restrained?
How did the fame of the Lord of Ramā arise there?
Tell me all this truly, for you are omniscient."
"Assuming the form of the Earth-bearer (Śiva), he directly bears his very own nature.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words, with a heart full of joy...
He spoke of the life of Rāma, which gives rise to the narration of his various virtues.
Śeṣa said:
"O Brahmin-sage, you rightly ask again and again about the virtues of the Lord of the Raghus."
Acting as if he had not heard what he had heard, and concealing his longing for them,
he then departed on horseback, surrounded by many soldiers,
to go to the charming bank of the Revā river, which is frequented by hosts of sages.
Then all those soldiers, skilled in battle, moved here and there, keeping watch and following the path of the horse. Then,
the horse went to a deep-watered lake on the banks of the Revā river.
Wearing a leaf made of gold upon his forehead, his body was honored with worship.
Then that excellent horse of Rāmacandra submerged itself in the water;
at that moment, all the great heroes there were struck with amazement.
They said to one another: "How can there be a meeting with the horse?
Who here will go into the water to bring back that great treasure?
While they were thus consulting one another in agitation, [the horse appeared].
Then the lord of the Raghus arrived together with hundreds of heroes.
Seeing them all despondent, that crest-jewel among heroes, known as Śatrughna, questioned them in a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
"Where is he now staying with all of you in this body of water?
Where is the horse of the Lord of the Raghus, adorned with its golden leaf? Is it submerged in the water, or has it been seized by some proud man? (15)
"Tell me that quickly; how have you been so deluded?
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words of the king, the best of the Raghus...
All those heroes told everything to that crest-jewel of the brave.
The people said: "O Lord, we did not know; for a moment we were submerged in the water."
Then, having plunged into the water, that horse of yours was lost; it is most heart-stealing. 18.
"Go there yourself and bring this horse back with speed. O high-minded one, we must go there along with you. 19.
Having heard these words of the soldiers, the scion of Raghu felt distress upon seeing the people intent on crossing the water;
he then spoke to his chief minister: "What should be done after this?"
Tell me how the recovery of the horse will come about; speak of that.
Who are the heroes there who, having joined together, shall search for the horse in the water?
Or who will bring back the steed, and by what means? Tell me that. (21–22)
Having heard these words of the king, Sumati, the best of ministers,
spoke what was appropriate for the occasion, as if gladdening Śatrughna:
"O Lord, O illustrious one of wondrous deeds, you possess power."
The power to go to the netherworld (pātāla) from the midst of water and so forth is clearly manifest;
furthermore, there is the power of the great-souled Puṣkala, and even that of Hanumān, who was devoted to the service of Rāma’s feet. 24–25.
"Therefore, you three must go and certainly bring Hayagrīva, so that there may be a mount for the wise Lord of the Raghus.
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words, Śatrughna, the slayer of enemy heroes,
entered the water himself, accompanied by Hanumān and Puṣkala.
As soon as he had entered the water, the city became visible.
That immeasurable city was enriched with the beauty of many gardens. There, he saw Rāma’s horse tied to a pillar made of gold and adorned with rubies, beautifully decorated with golden leaves.
There, excellent women possessing captivating beauty attended upon that one beautiful woman as she sat comfortably on a couch.
Seeing them, all those women spoke to their mistress.
"These men, though small in stature and age, possess bodies well-nourished with flesh;
this shall be the great and excellent fruit of your abundant food. The blood of these men, whose life-span has reached its end, will be delicious."
Having heard these words of her maidservants,
the faultless and excellent woman laughed slightly, making her face dance with her eyebrows.
Just then, those three arrived, resplendent with the beauty of their armor.
Seeing those women there, endowed with beauty and splendor, putting on helmets and possessed of heroism and valor, the brahmin spoke in wonder:
"What is this great thing that is seen? (34-35)
Then all those high-souled ones, the excellent wives of the gods, offered their salutations,
their pair of feet illuminated by the radiance of the jewels in their crowns. Thereupon, that beautiful woman questioned those foremost of men.
"O Keyūyamatra, how have you arrived here, you men bearing weapons?
This place of mine is inaccessible to all the gods and is a great delusion; for one who has reached this place, there is indeed no turning back. (37-38)
"Tell me how King Ayaka’s horse was fanned with chowries and adorned with a beautiful golden plate.
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words of hers, which were full of delusive conduct,
Hanumān, free from fear, replied to her as if laughing:
"We are the servants of the King, the crest-jewel of the three worlds."
"The three worlds bow down to this crest-jewel of all the gods.
Know him to be Rāmabhadra, the performer of the horse sacrifice.
Release my horse; O beautiful woman, how has it been bound?"
"We are skilled in all missiles and experts in every weapon and projectile;
we shall forcibly carry off the horse after slaying its protectors.
Having heard these words of the monkey, the beautiful woman—
Standing at the opening, she who was skilled in speech replied with a laugh:
"I have brought him here; no one is capable of releasing him, even with ten thousand years of sharp arrows and millions of blazing shafts. (44-45)

"I shall not accept the horse of that wise king of kings, for I am a servant performing the duties of the lotus-feet of Paraśurāma. A great impropriety has arisen on my part as the minister of this excellent steed."
"O Moon, may he forgive you; for he is the refuge of all and is affectionate toward his devotees.
You have been afflicted by his servants; therefore, O best of beings, beg from that protector a boon that is unattainable even by the gods."
"Just as Puruṣottama forgives my most terrible sin,
you too, casting aside all shame, should choose an excellent boon.
Having heard her supreme words, Hanumān spoke to her.

By the grace of Raghunātha, everything of ours has become prosperous. Nevertheless, I beg for one supreme boon: fulfill this desire of my heart—that in birth after birth, may the Lord of the Raghus be our master, and we his servants performing his work.
Having heard these words of the monkey, his wife then laughed and spoke these sweet words, which were honored for their excellence:
"That which you have requested is difficult to obtain even for all the gods."
"O servants, that will undoubtedly happen for the sake of that lord of the Raghus;
nevertheless, I shall grant one boon, even though I have committed an offense— may these words of mine prove true for the purpose of pleasing Raghunātha."
The king Agravīramaṇi, accompanied by Mahāvīra and protected by Śiva, will seize your chariot. Therefore, O you of great strength,
take up this great weapon for the sake of his victory.
"In a duel, you must fight that great enemy with Śatrughna.
When you discharge this weapon in battle, Rāma’s true nature will be known again through it. 56–57.
"Having recognized that horse and having offered it, he will fall at [your] feet;
therefore, take up that weapon of mine which rends enemies.
Having heard that from the Lord of the Raghus, his brother took up the weapon.
Facing north, his body purified, he received that wonderful weapon bestowed by the Yoginī. Having obtained that weapon, he became possessed of great splendor, the crusher of enemies,
invincible, difficult to propitiate, and a goad for the elephants that were his foes.

Having bowed to her, Śatrughna, the best of the Rāghavas, took that excellent horse from the water and went to the banks of the Revā, which were pleasant to behold. Seeing him, all the soldiers were delighted and filled with joy.
Praising the virtuous one after another, they asked about the departure of the horse.
Hanumān related the great arrival of the horse and the obtaining of the boon from those two; having heard this, they too were filled with joy.

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Attainment of the Horse from the Midst of the Water upon Seeing the Yoginīs by Śatrughna," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
Chapter Thirty-Nine. Śeṣa said:
While the drums resounded and the sounds of lutes arose on all sides,
he was released from his vehicle and proceeded toward the city of the gods, fashioned by the gods,
where the houses of the inhabitants were adorned with structures of crystal walls. 1.
They laugh at the pure Vindhya mountain frequented by serpents;
for here are seen palaces of silver, adorned with various gems and featuring gate-towers of rubies, which even Nature herself could not create. 2–3.
In that place, there were charming lotus-women in every house who captivated the hearts of men with their gaze fixed upon their lotus-like faces;
and in every house, upon the beautiful floors, there were rubies.

Bound as if in rivalry with the lips of the women there, does it appear like a prisoner? The pleasure-mountains constructed of sapphires in every house cause the suspicion that they are clouds to the long-tailed peacocks.
Confined within crystal dwellings that serve as cages for swans,
men do not fear the clouds nor do they remember Lake Mānasa;
for in the abodes of Śiva, darkness is perpetually destroyed by the moonlight.
There, among men, there is no distinction between the bright and dark fortnights.
There, the great King Vīramaṇi, a leader among the righteous,
rules over a vast kingdom endowed with all enjoyments.
His son, a great hero named Rukmāṅgada, powerful and possessed of a beautiful body, went to the forest to sport with women.
There was the tinkling of their anklets as well as the sound of their bracelets.

O Lord, what need is there to speak of others? He, whose desire was for that which captivates the mind, went to a vast forest filled with flowering trees—a place established by Sadāśiva, resplendent with the six seasons. 11–12.

The *caṃpaka* trees, adorned with many blossoming buds, cause pain to the hearts of lovers when beheld there (13). The mango trees, bent down by fruits and joined with millions of flower-clusters, [bring joy].
There were *nāga* trees, *puṃnāga* trees, *śāla*, *tāla*, and *tamāla* trees; there,
the cries of cuckoos were within the range of hearing, and the *mallikā* jasmine flowers never slept, being constantly awakened by the humming of bees.
There were clusters of pomegranate trees accompanied by karṇikāras,
and the forest was adorned with rows of wild trees such as the ketakī,
kānakī, and vanya; in that forest, his mental state filled with joy, he sang sweetly and loudly with a melodious voice, desiring to perform [the dance].
The one whose body was a treasury of splendor, free from fear, entered surrounded by women with uplifted breasts.
Some pleased that beautiful one with the art of dance; some with the skill of song; and others with words appropriate to their eloquence. 17–18.

Some women, intoxicated with passion, gratified him with gestures of their eyebrows, while other women made him rejoice with their skill in embracing. Having gathered flowers from them, those women adorned him.
With tender speech, he offered blessings to the one who had assumed a form of desire. While this was occurring at that time for the wise king of kings,
a most magnificent horse arrived at that forest region.
His forehead was adorned with a single ornament fashioned from gold leaf;
his body was tawny like the Gaṅgā, saffron, and beeswax;
and his gait surpassed the speed of the wind.
Seeing her body, which was the abode of supreme wonder, those women—

whose complexions were as tawny as the interior of a lotus, whose lower lips shone like coral struck by their brilliance, whose faces were made beautiful by smiles revealed by rows of teeth, and who possessed the power to enchant with eyes like the arrows of Kāma— spoke to their husbands. (22–23)
The women said:
"O beloved, who is this great man, adorned with a single golden leaf? To whom does he belong, appearing so rich in splendor? Take him for yourself, O strong one. 24
Śeṣa said:
Having heard those words, he whose beautiful eyes were playful with charm effortlessly seized the horse with one lotus-like hand. 25
Having read the golden leaf endowed with clear letters, he laughed in the midst of the women and spoke these words again.
Rukmāṅgada said:
"On this earth, there is no one equal to my father in valor or in prosperity; how then can that king Rāma display such arrogance toward him,
he for whose protection Rudra, the wielder of the Pināka bow, always stands ready?"
"Let the immensely powerful Janaka perform the horse sacrifice, which even the gods, dānavas, and yakṣas honor with their jewel-adorned crowns.
Let my warriors indeed bind this horse in the stable."
Having heard these words, those enchanting women, their faces filled with great joy, embraced their beloved;
and the great son of King Vīramaṇi, having taken the horse—
Accompanied by his wife, he entered the city with great enthusiasm (31).
As the sounds of mṛdaṅga drums were struck loudly on all sides,
he proceeded to the great palace of his father, being praised by bards (32).
He told him that the horse of the lord of the Raghus had been brought back—
that wonderful steed, moving at its own will, which had been released for the horse sacrifice and was protected by the slayer of enemies accompanied by a host of great strength.
Having heard those words of his, the great and highly intelligent King Vīramaṇi did not praise that deed much,
for it was like the conduct of a thief who returns after having taken something away.
They spoke to their son-in-law Śiva, whose deeds are wondrous,
who wears half of a woman's body as his own ornament, and who bears the moon;
with him, the great King Vīramaṇi took counsel.
"The great deed performed by your son is censurable in the eyes of the great," [he said]. Śiva said:
"O King, a most wonderful deed has been performed by your son."
The wise Rāmacandra yoked that great steed.
Today a great battle appears, which will bewilder both gods and demons,
between the great king Śatrughna and the protector of ten million heroes.
"That Rāma, whose very heart and tongue are devoted to me— he is the one whose sacrificial limb your son has seized. In this battle, there will surely be a supreme and great gain for us."
Or rather, we shall behold my own lotus-feet served by him.
