(41) A great effort must be made here in the protection of this horse; they will forcibly lead away this steed, even though it is protected by me. (42)
"Therefore, O Great King, bowing down along with your kingdom, give fodder and food to this horse, and then behold its pair of hooves.
Having heard these words of Śiva, that best of kings—
He spoke to those lords of the gods, whose two lotus-feet were worthy of worship.
Vīramaṇi said:
"This is the duty of Kṣatriyas, that they protect the distressed through their prowess."
Therefore, he was intent on departing by means of the sacrifice known as Hayamedha (Horse Sacrifice).
For this reason, one who possesses pride should protect his own prowess by performing whatever action is possible, even at the cost of his body's destruction. 45–46.
"O Lord, since this horse has been seized by that son who has accomplished everything, appease King Rāma, who has been provoked, in a manner befitting the occasion;
for this act is not worthy of being performed by Kṣatriyas. (47)
When one bows at the feet of an enemy out of sudden fear, trembling with dread, his enemies laugh at him, saying: "This lowest of kings is a coward;
he has acted like a base, mean-spirited, and lowly man, bowing down, overwhelmed by fear. (48-49)
Therefore, O Bhavānī, when the time for battle has arrived as is appropriate, you must reflect upon what ought to be done and then protect your devotees.
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words, the moon-crested Lord (Śiva), laughing, spoke these words in a voice as deep as a thundercloud, utterly bewildering the mind:
"Even if the thirty-three crores of gods were to assemble here..."
Nevertheless, by whom can a horse be seized from you, my protector?
(52) If Rāma comes and reveals himself to me, then I shall bow down at his very tender feet. (53)
A master must not be fought; it is called a great impropriety.
Other heroes are like blades of grass, incapable of accomplishing anything.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, fight while I stand firm as your protector.
"If she were to seize the horse by force, the three worlds would be united.
55 Śeṣa said:
Having heard these supreme words of the moon-crested Lord, the king [acted].
His mind was exceedingly delighted, for he was eager for the act of battle. 56.

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Seizing of the Horse by the Son of Vīramaṇi" in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
Chapter Forty.
Śeṣa said:
O Great King, the scouts of the army, endowed with great strength, arrived there while observing that horse of King Rāma. 1.
"Where is that horse? By whom was it led? Or how is he seen?
Who is this person of very dull intellect who, having abducted me from the city, is now departing?"—thus they spoke while searching his path as far as the roar of the army was heard.
Then the great king, surrounded by a vast army, arrived and questioned all his servants: "Where is my horse now?
Why is the mount, so beautifully adorned with golden plates, not to be seen?"

Having heard those words, the attendants following the horse said to their lord: "O Master, this horse, swift as thought, has been carried off by someone in the forest; he is not to be seen by us, though we are experts in tracking."
"Therefore, O Lord, an effort must be made toward their attainment.
Having heard their words, King Śatrughna, the destroyer of enemies who had assumed a charming form, questioned Sumati.
Śatrughna said:
"Who is the king who dwells here, or how did you come to meet him? What is the strength of this lord of the earth, by whom this horse has been taken away today? (8)
Sumati said:
"O King, this is indeed the city of the gods, fashioned by the God himself;
like Kailāsa, it is difficult to approach even for hosts of enemies joined together in great strength. (9)
In this realm, the king Vīramaṇi, a great hero and possessor of majesty, rules according to dharma, protected by Śiva;
he who was the bringer of universal destruction has been brought under control through devotion.
Candracūḍa always displays partiality toward his devotee;
therefore, if he is captured here, a great battle will surely ensue. Let the virtuous ones remain vigilant and protect the camp.

Having heard this, the highly illustrious Śatrughna, the crest-jewel of all kings, drew up his army in battle formation and remained there. Then, as he sat comfortably consulting with his excellent minister, [the messenger spoke].
The divine sage arrived, filled with curiosity for the battle.
Seeing that the sage, a treasure-house of asceticism, had arrived, Śatrughna rose,
offered him a seat, and then presented him with the madhuparka offering.

Satisfied by the welcome, he who was skilled in speech and discourse spoke with pleasing words to Nārada, the best of sages. Śatrughna said: 16. [Śatrughna said: "Welcome! he said, delighting the most excellent of sages, Nārada, with his words. 16. Śatrughna said:
"O high-minded one, tell me where my horse has gone; its track is not seen by my skilled attendants. Tell me which proud kṣatriya has taken it away. (17)
"O ascetic, how will the attainment of the two [brothers] come about here?
Having heard these words of Śatrughna, Nārada spoke,
repeatedly playing his lute and singing the story of Rāma.
Nārada said:
O King, this is the city of the gods; there, the great king Vīramaṇi’s sovereign horse was seized by his son who had retired to the forest.
"A great and most terrible battle will take place there today;
heroes endowed with strength and valor will fall therein.
Therefore, O one of great power, you must remain here with great effort."
"Arrange a battle formation difficult for enemy troops to penetrate.
Victory shall be yours, O King, even through hardship against this best of monarchs;
for who in all the world could defeat Rāma? (22-23)
Having spoken thus, the Brahmin vanished and remained stationed in the sky,
desiring to witness the most terrible battle, like that between the gods and the Dānavas.
Śeṣa said:
Then King Vīramaṇi, the crest-jewel of all heroes,
caused a great-sounding drum to be beaten in the midst of his own city and summoned his commander-in-chief, the highly exalted hero of his enemies.
He spoke quickly with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
Vīramaṇi said:
"O General, give me the command for the drum in this beautiful city."
Having heard that, they donned their armor and set out toward Śatrughna.
Then, having heard these words of King Vīramaṇi, he had a drum beaten with a great resounding noise.
The sound of kettledrums is heard in every house along the streets: "Let all those heroes residing in the royal city who consider themselves brave go forth to slay Śatrughna!
Let those who, regarding themselves as heroes, have transgressed the king's command [go forth]! 29.
"Whether they be sons or brothers, they must be slain by your command, O King.
"Let the heroes listen!"—thus it was proclaimed again with the sound of beaten drums—"Having heard this, let what is to be done be performed quickly; do not delay! (30-31)
Śeṣa said:
Thus, hearing the sound of the drum within the range of their ears,
those foremost of men, the best of heroes, approached the most excellent of kings.
With their own bodies adorned with golden armor,
their hearts and minds delighted by the great festival of battle, some went forth wearing beautiful helmets upon their heads. 32.
Richly adorned with armor and beautifully embellished by hundreds of millions [of gems], they went,
intoxicated with joy at the king’s command, in a chariot yoked to two horses and shining with jewels and gold to the abode of the best of men.
Some went on rutting elephants, others on magnificent horses; all of them, carrying out the king's command, proceeded to the royal palace,
resplendent in their polished golden armor and helmets.
Rukmāṅgada also, standing upon his own chariot swift as thought, set out for the festival of battle;
his younger brother Śubhāṅgada followed him, wearing upon his body his own excellent armor made of great jewels.
The king’s brother, Vīrasiṃha, who was skilled in all weapons and missiles,
went there by the king’s command to carry out the monarch’s decree.
The king’s nephew, known as Mitrasena, also went with him.
Armed with armor and a sword, he went to the king’s palace.
Then that great commander, the subduer of enemies, having made that fourfold army ready, reported it to the king.
Then King Vīramaṇi ascended an excellent chariot, filled with all kinds of weapons and missiles, which was lofty with great wheels fashioned from jewels.
Then, there arose the sound of conchs on all sides, like the roar of the ocean of heroes.
The kettledrums, sounded by skilled players, were heard on all sides as if urging on the timid heroes in battle; they resounded where the armies stood ready to advance for the fight. 42–43.
Having performed all auspicious rites and adorned with every ornament,
they went to the field of battle fully equipped with all weapons and missiles;
the mountain caves were filled with the sound of kettledrums and conchs.
"Has he gone to summon those residing in heaven?
Amidst that clamor, the great King Vīramaṇi, filled with martial zeal, proceeded to the field of battle.
Having arrived and halted there,
that force, teeming with chariots and infantry, came as if to submerge those stationed there like the ocean; then, seeing that army arrive, [the enemy was met] by chariot-warriors skilled in weapons.
When everything was filled with clamor, the king spoke to Sumati.
Śatrughna said:
"The powerful Vīramaṇi has arrived as my horse-keeper."
To fight me once again with a vast fourfold army—
how should the battle be conducted, and who among those fierce in strength will engage?
Direct all those heroes toward that direction so that my desired victory may be achieved.
Sumati said: "O Lord, this great king has arrived, surrounded by a vast army, for the purpose of battle, yet he is endowed with devotion to Śiva. (51)
"Now let the hero Puṣkala, who is skilled in supreme weapons, fight;
and let the other warriors, such as Nīlaratna and the rest, who are experts in combat, also fight.
O sinless one, you, the king, must also fight with Śiva."
"He who possesses great strength and prowess must be conquered through a duel. O King, by this method you will achieve victory here.
Afterwards, O high-minded Lord, do whatever pleases you. (53-54)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words, Śatrughna, the slayer of enemy heroes, having resolved upon battle, then commanded his excellent warriors. 55.

"Effort must once again be made so that Jaya may quickly be mine, along with all the kings skilled in weapons and their armies for the sake of battle. Having heard this for the sake of Raghava's victory, those experts in combat [prepared].
Filled with great enthusiasm, they went forth with their soldiers to do battle. 57.

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Decision for Battle with Vīramaṇi," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the *Śrī Padma Purāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
Chapter Forty-one.
Śeṣa said:
Fully prepared for battle and endowed with valor, the mighty followers of Śatrughna marched into the midst of Vīramaṇi’s army. 1.
Discharging arrows and piercing many soldiers,
those men bearing bows were seen stationed within the ocean;
there, numerous elephants and chariots adorned with jewels were slain.
Those whose mounts were broken were seen upon the field of battle;
hearing of the slaughter wrought upon them, the mighty Rukmāṅgada,
standing in a chariot adorned with jewels, went forth to fight those soldiers.
Placing arrows upon his bow and holding two inexhaustible quivers,
he was terrifying with blood-red eyes and filled with great wrath,
agitating thousands of heroes with his many shafts. 5.
Causing a great cry of lamentation,
the powerful prince Ūrmikāṅgada, who was equal to him in strength, fame, and splendor,
challenged Śatrughna, Bhāratī, and Puṣkala.
Rukmāṅgada said:
"Come, O you of heroic deeds, great strength, and prowess!
Fight with me, a powerful and radiant prince."
"What is the use of these other terrified men, slain by the millions? Achieve victory by engaging in a great battle with me!
When he had spoken thus, the powerful Puṣkala laughed heartily and [attacked] with speed.

He struck him in the middle of his broad chest with sharp-jointed arrows. Unable to endure that, the prince fixed arrows upon his great bow and struck the hero Puṣkala in the center of his chest with ten shafts.
Both, equally impetuous and both desiring victory, shone in that battle like the two princes, Kumāra and Tāraka.
Fixing ten great, sharp arrows upon their bows, they stood ready.
The heroic Puṣkala rendered the prince chariotless;
with four arrows he struck down the four horses, with two he felled the charioteer, with one his standard, and with two the protectors of the chariot. 13–14.
Vegavān pierced the prince in the heart with a single arrow; seeing that miraculous feat, all the heroes were greatly delighted.
With his bow broken, his chariot destroyed, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed, he [remained there].
Overcome with extreme anger, he ascended his excellent chariot. Having mounted that superior chariot, which was adorned with precious gems,
he took up a great bow that was very firm and strung with a cord.
Rukmāṅgada spoke these words to the heroic Puṣkala:
"O scorcher of enemies, having displayed such great prowess, where will you go? Behold today my own valor, which has been fashioned by my own strength."
"O hero, O lord, stand with effort; do not lead my chariot into the sky!
Having spoken thus, he fixed an exceedingly fierce arrow upon his bow, and after consecrating it with mantras, he discharged that wheel-turning weapon at the chariot of Pauṣkali.
He discharged a sharp arrow, beautifully adorned with a single golden feather;
by that arrow, his chariot was driven a distance of one yojana.
Held with great difficulty by the charioteer, the chariot reeled upon the surface of the earth.
Having with great difficulty reached his own abode, Puṣkala, the master of supreme weapons,
spoke these words to Bāṇa while holding [his bow] upon the string:
"O foremost of heroes, attain heaven, which is served by all the gods!"
"O best of kings, those like you are not fit for the earth; rather, you are worthy of the assembly of Śatakratu. Therefore, go to the abode of the gods.
Having said this, he released a great weapon capable of reaching the sky.
By that arrow, the chariot, together with its horses and charioteer, went forth in accordance with the direction of the hair (anuloma).
Passing beyond all the pores of the skin, it entered the solar orb;
there, the chariot, along with the horses and the charioteer, was consumed by its flames.
With his body mostly consumed by those rays, he fell down in great misery, holding to the moon-crested Lord who removes the suffering of the heart;
there, with his body burnt by the rays, he collapsed upon the ground.
Having fallen into extreme agony, he fainted within the circle of his refuge (28).
When that prince had fallen upon the ground in a swoon, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose there at the front of the battle (29).
The enemies, led by Puṣkala, attained the fortune of victory,
while the horse-protectors among the foes were defeated and fled.
Then, seeing his son’s fainting spell, King Vīramaṇi—
Filled with rage, he advanced toward Puṣkala, who stood in the midst of the battle.
Then this earth, along with its mountains and excellent forests, trembled; the heroes attained great joy, while the cowards were tormented by fear.
Bearing his great bow and even his two inexhaustible quivers, he,
releasing a breath of rage, challenged his enemy.

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Defeat of Rukmāṅgada and the Victory of Puṣkala," in the *Aśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
Chapter Forty-Two. Śeṣa said:
To King Puṣkala, who was calling out from the ocean of his great army—
Even Hanumān, having clearly identified the lord of monkeys, rushed toward him,
raising his massive tail and stretching it with a roar like the thundering of clouds.
The lord of monkeys went toward that jewel among heroes, the king of men, who stood upon the battlefield;
seeing Hanumān approaching, the formidable Puṣkala [prepared for battle].
Beholding him with eyes deeply reddened by the wrath of his enemy,
Puṣkala, an expert in supreme weapons,
addressed Hanumān in a voice as deep as a thundercloud, making the entire battlefield resound.
Puṣkala said:
"O great monkey, why have you come to fight in battle?
How small is this strength of yours compared to the vast power of King Vīramaṇi?"
Do you wish to go there to fight in sport, where all the three worlds have assembled face to face? Who is this King Vīramaṇi, and how small is his meager strength?

"O Lord of Monkeys, it is not conceivable that your arrival here will be anything less than most formidable. By the compassionate glance of Raghunātha, I have crossed over this impassable [ocean] in an instant; therefore, do not harbor any fear regarding the battle."
Just as you crossed the ocean of rākṣasas by virtue of the abundance of Rāma’s compassion,
so too shall I cross over this difficult-to-traverse [ocean] by remembering Rāma well.
Whoever, having encountered what is difficult to cross, remembers the Lord of the Raghus, [they shall likewise cross].
The ocean of their suffering will surely dry up; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, O mighty Mahāvīra, go to the presence of Śatrughna; having defeated King Vīramaṇi in an instant, he shall arrive here. 10–11.
Śeṣa said: Having heard these wise words spoken by Puṣkala, the slayer of enemy heroes spoke again to Puṣkala. 12.
Hanumān said:
"O King, do not act with such rashness toward King Vīramaṇi;
he is a donor, a protector, and endowed with strength and heroism. (13)
"You are a youth, while he is an aged king, the most eminent among all those skilled in weapons and missiles;
many heroes, resplendent in their valor, have been conquered by him in battle. Know that Sadāśiva is always his protector by his side. (14)
"By his devotion, he has subdued Sthāṇu and Soma, who reside in this city.
Therefore, O Puṣkala, I shall fight with this king alone; you, however, should attain great fame by conquering other heroes. (15-16)
Puṣkala said:
Having brought Śiva under his control through devotion, he established him in his own city; thus Maheśvara remains there with a heart most intent on [his] welfare. 17
This Sadāśiva, having worshipped [Rāma] and attained the supreme state,
has abandoned both Rāma and his own mind and does not go anywhere else.
Wherever Rāma is, there is the entire universe— both the stationary and the moving.
Therefore, I shall conquer King Vīramaṇi in battle;
you go to fight other eminent kings, such as Vīrasiṃha and the others—O Lord, do not harbor anxiety on my account. 19–20.
Having heard these words spoken in such a spirited manner, Hanumān went to the battle to fight the younger brother of the king, that lion among heroes;
while Lakṣmīnidhi went with his son, who was well-known by the name Śubhāṅgada.
Skilled in the knowledge of great weapons and missiles,
Sumada, the son of the king, who was exalted by his own prowess and strength, moved about the battlefield armed with weapons to fight in a duel with Balamitra. (22-23)
Seeing the king challenging him, Puṣkala, skilled in battle,
stood upon a chariot adorned with gold and advanced toward his foe.
Seeing that Puṣkala, who was an expert in combat, had arrived, the king—
In the midst of the forest, he spoke with a fearless and eloquent voice.
Vīramaṇi said: "This boy is a deceiver; he is enraged and possesses fierce wrath in battle."
"Go, if you desire to preserve your life; do not engage in battle with me. Kings like me show compassion toward children such as you;
they certainly do not strike them. Therefore, depart from this place of refuge. (26-27)

"As long as you have not been seen by my eyes, so long has my mind been unsettled; now, however, my mind desires to strike you down. Since my son was pierced by your arrows and rendered unconscious once more,"
"O you of childish intellect, everything that has been said by me today has been forgiven. Having heard these words, Puṣkala spoke to him.
Puṣkala said:
Though a child, he was unslayable, exceedingly aged, and skilled in all weapons and missiles.

(30) Furthermore, among Kṣatriyas, those who are endowed with superior strength are considered the elders; it is they alone who are the foremost of kings, for in them true old age resides, even if they have not reached advanced years. (31)
"My son, who was intoxicated by the pride of his heroism and strength, has been rendered unconscious by me;
now, I shall strike you down with weapons in this battle.
Therefore, O King, stand with diligence at the forefront of the fray."
"Is there some devotee of Rāma who stands at the feet of Jayatīndra?
Having heard these words spoken by Puṣkala, the foremost of kings laughed upon seeing the boy, and then he became filled with anger once more.
Perceiving him to be enraged, the son of Bharata, driven by intoxication,
struck the king in the chest with twenty sharp arrows. Seeing those arrows released by him approaching, the king—
Extremely enraged, he cut [the opponent's weapons] into many pieces with sharp arrows.
Seeing that his arrows were being severed, Bhāratī, the slayer of enemy heroes, became exceedingly angry in his heart and struck the king with three arrows.
The prince named Puṣkala pierced him in the forehead;
did those arrows, fixed there, not shine like the peaks of Mount Trikūṭa?
Afflicted by those arrows, the king struck back with nine shafts.
Filled with great rage, he struck the heroic Puṣkala in the heart;
by those calf-toothed arrows, much blood was drunk from the body of Rāma’s younger brother's son.
Like venomous serpents, they remained fixed within his body as if enraged.
Having fallen into a state of supreme distress, Puṣkala again pierced Bhūmipa with a hundred sharp-jointed arrows;
by those arrows, his armor, crown, and helmet were shattered.
His great chariot bow, strung and ready, was shattered by the agitation of his grief; drenched in blood, his body pierced by arrows,
he mounted another chariot and went toward the son of Bharata.
"O bee at the lotus-feet of Vīrarāma, you are blessed!
A great deed has been done by you today, in that I have been deprived of my chariot.
O hero, protect your life now, for I am fighting against you. (43-44)
"Life is easily obtained when I, in the form of Time,
am present," having said this, he who was skilled in weapons struck him with countless arrows;
yet on the ground and in all directions, those arrows were not seen there.
Thousands of elephants and horses were pierced on all sides;
chariots, along with their charioteers, were cut and split in two by him,
and there a river of blood flowed across the courtyard of the arena.
There, the hair of living beings resting upon their heads appeared like the peaks of mountains, while the moss-like *śaivala* was visible;
there, the severed hands of heroes were seen, beautiful as if they were jeweled seals. 48.548–549.1.
There, smeared with sandalwood paste and other unguents, they appeared like snakes;
the heads of the foremost warriors indeed bore the likeness of tortoises, and from them flowed the flesh of the great heroes like mud. 49-50.

When this event had thus occurred, hundreds of yoginīs drank the blood of the creatures fallen in battle with their cups in the arena; filled with joy and curiosity, they likewise devoured their flesh.

Having drunk blood there and devoured flesh, the Piśācas, intoxicated with joy, danced, laughed loudly, and sang aloud on the battlefield; they indeed carried away the heads of living beings in that conflict. 52–53.
Holding them with both hands like cymbals,
the intoxicated Śivās were intent on playing them; having devoured the great flesh of those fallen upon the battlefield, they roared in their frenzy, striking terror into the cowards.
Terrified and weaponless, they entered the hollows of elephants and were devoured by the yoginīs; there is no place of refuge anywhere for such sinners.
Observing this slaughter of his own army, the leader of the chariots [acted].
Puṣkala also wrought carnage there upon the field of battle;
the heads of elephants were split asunder and pearls fell like rain, while that river appeared filled with hair like the Tāmraparṇī. 57.
The arrows discharged by Puṣkala, having struck the limbs of his enemies, brought about the severance of the lives of even the heroes on all sides;
all [the enemies] had their limbs drenched in blood, and all had their own bodies mangled.
In that moment, like *kiṃśuka* trees on a battlefield, the warriors were seen [falling].
Then, at that time, the enraged [opponent], overflowing with a flood of fury, addressed the lord of the earth and struck him with many arrows.
With his limbs pierced by those arrows and his armor shattered, the king,
perceiving him to be possessed of great strength, struck him with millions of shafts.
From his armor, which had been released by those arrows, much blood flowed forth.
His body became beautiful as it lay within the cage of arrows;
staying in the midst of that cage of arrows, his mind was overwhelmed,
and even the son of Bharata was unable to take up or aim his arrows.
Remembering Rāma, he took up his great and firm bow, made it ready,
and discharged sharpened arrows capable of repelling the host of enemies.
O bull among sages, with those arrows he dispersed that net of shafts.
Blowing his conch in the battle, he, free from fear, spoke to the king.
Puṣkala said:
"A great deed has been performed by you, in that you have placed me within the cage of Bāṇa's arrows."
The hero made the formidable Vīratāpana his target. "Because of my old age, you are now honored by me on the field of battle; O King Vīramaṇi, behold today my great prowess."
"O hero, do not cause me to faint with these three arrows; otherwise, listen to my vow, which shall stupefy all warriors.
Even having reached the Gaṅgā, he who disparages her, the remover of sins—"

"O King Bhūpa, if I do not strike down that great sinner, whose conduct is that of a great fool, in the arena of battle by means of a swoon, then let his sin be mine; O Hero, prepare yourself! (69-70)
Having heard these words of Puṣkala, the best of kings became greatly enraged and agitated; he fixed sharp arrows to his bow.
Those arrows, having pierced his great heart, entered the earth, O Bhārata.
Those who were averse to devotion to Rāma fell upon the earth like moths;
then, aiming at his broad chest which was as expansive as the surface of a great door-panel, he discharged a sharp arrow blazing with the luster of fire.
Cut in two by the king with an arrow,
he fell in the middle of the chariot, blazing like the orb of the sun;
then [the king] took up another arrow born of devotion to his mother.
Having deposited his merit elsewhere, he then once more severed that great [tree].
Then, distressed and reflecting in his heart on what ought to be done, that master of supreme weapons released [the arrow] into his own heart, remembering Rāma, the destroyer of his suffering.

That arrow, resembling a venomous serpent and blazing with a radiance equal to the sun, struck his heart; it caused him to fall into a swoon. Then everyone raised a cry of "Alas! and became intent on flight.
When the queen had fallen into a swoon, Puṣkala achieved victory.

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Defeat of Vīramaṇi," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
The forty-third chapter. Śeṣa said:
Having approached Vīrasiṃha, Hanumān spoke these words.

"Stay! O you who are free from passion, I shall come to you here this very moment. Having heard these great words of the monkey, he was overwhelmed by a flood of anger and [took up] his bow, which rumbled like a rain-cloud.
Roaring fiercely and discharging sharp arrows in battle,
he appeared as beautiful as a rain-cloud pouring down torrents during the month of Āṣāḍha.
Seeing those sharp arrows deeply embedded in his own body, [he remained undaunted].
Hanumān, the son of Añjanī, became exceedingly enraged in his heart;
he struck him in the chest with a fist as hard as a thunderbolt.
Struck by that fist, the hero fell to the surface of the earth.
Beholding his paternal uncle thus unconscious, Rukmāṅgada, accompanied by Śubhāṅgada,
also cast off his swoon and entered the field of battle,
raining down arrows like two great-sounding clouds.
Causing a terrible carnage, they advanced against the monkey.
Seeing those two heroes arrived in battle, the lord of the monkeys,
having encircled both the chariot-bearers and their bow with his tail, [seized them].
We shall burst open that place on the earth; at that very moment, both of them became unconscious and motionless, their bodies stained red with blood.
Having fought for a long time against Sumada, Balamitra—
He indeed brought him to a swoon with arrows of very sharp joints; and in an instant, Puṣkala reduced him to a state of unconsciousness devoid of sentience,
while the army of Śatrughna, the crusher of enemy warriors, achieved victory.
At that time, Śiva, mounted upon his excellent chariot and wielding his divine bow,
rushed toward these warriors;
the Great One bore the crescent moon within the mass of his matted locks.
Wearing a serpent as an ornament and holding his bow Ājagava, which is pleasant to the touch of the mind,
Maheśvara— the destroyer of the distress of his devotees— beholding his own kinsmen unconscious,
set out with his great armies to fight these soldiers of Śatrughna.
Accompanied by his attendants and retinue, shaking the surface of the earth,
he came for the sake of protecting his devotees, just as [Śiva] did to Tripura in ancient times;
bringing about the dissolution of the world, he bore eyes of a deep red hue from anger.
Beholding the many esteemed heroes, the wielder of the Pināka bow, who is adored by the gods, arrived.
Seeing that Maheśāna had come, the powerful younger brother of Rāma went forth in battle to fight the crest-jewel of all the gods.
Then, seeing that Śatrughna had arrived, Rudra, the wielder of the Pināka bow who bears the excellent bow, spoke while overcome with supreme wrath:
"A great deed has been performed by Puṣkala, the servant of Rāma’s feet."

"Having slain my two devotees, you have come to the field of battle. Where is that supreme hero Puṣkala, the knower of the highest weapons? Having killed him—the oppressor of my devotees—I shall find happiness in this war. (19-20)
Śeṣa said: Having spoken thus, he dispatched Vīrabhadra along with Puṣkala, saying, "Go, you two,
to fight in battle against Puṣkala, the crusher of his own servants."
He dispatched the exceedingly powerful Hanumān, as well as Nandin,
Kuśadhvaja, Pracaṇḍa, Bhṛṅgin, Subāhuka,
Sumada, and his own attendant named Caṇḍa.
Seeing the great gaṇa Vīrabhadra, the attendant of Mahārudra, approaching, the high-minded Puṣkala went forth to fight;
in the battle, he struck him with five arrows.
With his limbs wounded by those arrows, he hurled a trident;
but having cut down that trident in an instant, the mighty one roared aloud.
Seeing his own trident severed, the powerful follower of Rudra [acted].
O twice-born one, he swiftly struck Bhāratī on the head with his khaṭvāṅga staff (26).
Struck by that khaṭvāṅga, the formidable warrior fainted for a moment; then, regaining consciousness, the noble hero Puṣkala, an expert in supreme weapons, rose up (27).
At that very moment, with arrows, he severed the khaṭvāṅga staff held in Vīrabhadra’s hand;
when the khaṭvāṅga held in his hand was thus cut down, Vīrabhadra was overcome with supreme rage and shattered the chariot of the charioteer.
Having shattered the chariot of the hero and reduced him to a mere foot-soldier,
he fought with the high-souled Puṣkala in hand-to-hand combat; meanwhile, Puṣkala abandoned his chariot, which had been pulverized by him through sheer force.
The one of great strength struck Vīrabhadra with his fist;
thus they struck each other with fists, thighs, and knees, intent on killing one another and desiring victory over the other. 31.
Thus, for four days and even nights, the two lords remained there;
he could not be provoked to anger, nor could that one of great strength be slain.
When the fifth day had arrived, the mighty Vīrabhadra [acted].
Having seized the great hero Puṣkala—who was not fleeing—the battle between the two of them took place there, bewildering even the gods and asuras;
it was a great conflict fought with fists, kicks, arms, and knees. 34.
Then Puṣkala, becoming extremely enraged, seized Vīrabhadra by the neck and struck him against the ground;
pained by that blow, the exceedingly powerful Vīrabhadra [fell].
Seizing Puṣkala by the foot, the one of great strength struck him repeatedly; having beaten him against the ground, he swiftly severed Puṣkala’s head,
which was adorned with glittering earrings, with his trident.

Having slain Puṣkala as he was roaring, the exceedingly powerful Vīrabhadra [advanced]. Terrified by that roaring son of Śarva, the fierce warriors were struck with fear; a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose when Puṣkala fell in battle. 38–39.
All the people present in the midst of the battle, though highly skilled in warfare, were struck with terror;
they saw Śatrughna and Puṣkala fallen on the field,
slain indeed by Vīrabhadra, the attendant of Maheśvara.
Having heard of the slaughter of Puṣkala at that time, the great hero Āśrutimān experienced extreme sorrow in battle;
trembling greatly with grief, the mighty one perceived Śatrughna to be distressed and spoke these words. 41–42.
"O Puṣkala, do not grieve for the heroic Śatrughna slain in battle; O one of great strength, do not harbor sorrow for Śatrughna in this war.
For the falling of heroes in the midst of battle is recorded as a source of fame."
Blessed is the hero named Puṣkala,
who fought against Vīrabhadra, the cause of the great dissolution,
by whom Dakṣa— who had acted with pride and contempt— was slain in an instant. 44-45.

"O great king, O mighty one, since the Daityas and the soldiers of Tripura have been struck down in an instant by him, abandon your grief and fight! O foremost of heroes, stand with effort while I remain here to do battle."
Abandoning his grief, the heroic Śatrughna became enraged at Śaṅkara;
with his ready bow grasped and arrows drawn, he covered Maheśvara with shafts that struck the head and body of the god, wounding him here and there. 47–48.
As he performed great wonders for the sake of protecting his devotees,
the arrows of those [enemies], though remaining in the sky, were met by the arrows of Śaṅkara,
Beholding the martial prowess of those two archers, everyone everywhere considered it to be the dissolution itself—
the cause of the world's destruction and the deluder of all. Meanwhile,
those residing in their own cities took refuge in celestial chariots in the sky.
Having come to behold them, they praised those two greatly:
"This one is the cause of the dissolution and creation of these three worlds;
this other is the younger brother of the great king Rāmacandra."
"What will happen here? Who will conquer on the circle of the earth? Or which hero will suffer defeat at the forefront of the battle?
Thus did the mutual combat continue for eleven days.
When the twelfth day arrived, the lord of men, filled with rage, discharged the great weapon known as Brahmā in order to slay Mahādeva. Recognizing that great weapon released by his enemy, Śatrughna—
Even while laughing, he drank that great *Brahmaśiras* weapon which had been discharged;
having attained extreme astonishment, he reflected, "What should be done after this?"—
and as he was thus engaged in reflection, [the weapon] blazed like fire within his heart.
The crest-jewel of the gods discharged an arrow;
by that shaft, Śatrughna fainted at the archway. A cry of "Alas! Alas! arose throughout the entire camp inhabited by warriors.
All the heroes, led by Subāhu and Sumada, were struck down to the surface of the earth by all the hosts of Rudras;
seeing Śatrughna fallen and unconscious, tormented by arrows, they were filled with pride in the strength of their own arms. (59–60)
Having stationed Puṣkala in the chariot and protected him with attendants, Hanumān arrived to fight Śiva, the agent of universal destruction;
he [also] brought about the remembrance of Śrī Rāma for his warriors, who were greatly delighted by the brāhmaṇas. 61.
Acting thus, he became violently enraged and lashed his tail.

62. Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Defeat of Puṣkala and Śatrughna," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
Chapter Forty-Four.
Śeṣa said:
Having approached Rudra at the forefront of the battlefield,
the heroic Hanumān spoke, desiring to subdue the lord of the gods.
Hanumān said:
"O Rudra, since you are acting in opposition to dharma and are intent on slaying the devotees of Rāma, I therefore desire to punish you."
"O Lord, I have previously heard it stated many times by the sages that Rudra,
the wielder of the Pināka bow, is a constant rememberer of Raghunātha’s feet;
yet all of that has proven false as he fights against Śatrughna."

The hero Puṣkala has been slain, and Śatrughna too has fainted. Therefore, I shall strike you down today—you who are intent on the destruction of the three worlds! Stay firm with effort, O Śarva, you who have turned your back on devotion to Rāma.
Śeṣa said:
To the monkey who had spoken thus, the Great Lord replied:
"Blessed are you, O best of heroes; what you say to us is not false."
Śatrughna, the slayer of enemy heroes, brought back that horse for his master Rāmacandra, who is saluted by both gods and asuras;
he had come for the purpose of guarding it, being completely won over by devotion to him.
In whatever way possible, this self of mine must be protected by my devotee; such is the established rule.
May Raghunātha, having shown compassion, look upon me shamelessly; may the Great One, though feeling some anger at the extreme suffering of his own devotee, [forgive me]. 8-9.
Śeṣa said: While Caṇḍīśa was speaking thus, Hanumān became exceedingly enraged;
seizing a massive rock, he struck him with it on that very chariot. 10.
Struck by the stone, his chariot— along with its driver, horses, standard, and banners— was shattered into pieces;
all the deities stationed in the sky praised the lord of monkeys.
"O Lord of the Plavagas, you have performed a great deed worthy of one blessed with fortune! 12.
Seeing Śrī Śiva deprived of his chariot, Nandī ran toward him and said to the illustrious Mahādeva, "Please proceed to my back. 13.
Then Hanumān, becoming exceedingly enraged at the Lord of Beings who was seated upon the bull,
uprooted a rock with great force and struck him in the heart. Struck thus, the Lord of Beings then took up a sharp trident.
Seeing that great trident approaching, blazing with a fiery luster and equal in radiance to flames of fire,
he seized it in his hand and in an instant violently shattered it into pieces as small as sesame seeds.
When the Lord of Monkeys had his trident shattered by the other [Rāvaṇa], Śiva instantly took up a spear fashioned from all kinds of metals and hurled it at Kesarin.
Released by Śiva, that spear struck the heart of that wise one.
At that moment, the lord of the monkeys was momentarily overwhelmed;
but having overcome that distress in an instant, he seized a massive tree and struck him in the heart, which was adorned with great serpents.
Struck by that hero, the lords of serpents were seized with terror;
abandoning him, they fled swiftly here and there to the netherworld (Pātāla).
When that mountain had been released from his chest, Śiva gazed intently at him.
Enraged, he brandished a terrible mace with both hands:
"O lowest of monkeys, you are slain! Go from this battle and flee!
Here I am, the destroyer of your life, with this mace in an instant!"
Seeing the pestle indeed released by the enraged Śiva,
Kīśa dodged it while remembering Hari; that pestle, cast by Śiva and made of great iron, fell down below with great velocity.
Tearing asunder the entire earth, he went to the subterranean realm of Rasātala.
Then Hanumān, the servant of Rāma, becoming exceedingly enraged,
seized a mountain in his hand and struck him in the chest.
Just as the husband of Satī resolved to cut down the mountain,
he was struck by the lord of monkeys with a many-branched śāla tree.
Just as he prepared to cut that [tree] down, he was struck by a rock.
As Mṛḍa (Śiva) exerted himself to split his own heart with those stones,
he then brought down a rain of rocks and mountains;
and wrapping [the demon] with his tail, he struck that lord of spirits.

With rocks, mountains, and trees, and by the frequent lashing of his tail, Nandin caused great terror; even the moon was shattered into fragments. Maheśāna, the wrathful one, became utterly overwhelmed with agitation.
To the lord of the monkeys, who was making him extremely agitated by striking him blow after blow, he said:
"O follower of Raghupati, you are fortunate;
today you have performed a great deed, for I am well-pleased with you."
"I am not easily attained by one who lacks generosity, who is ignorant of the path, or by even slight austerity;
I am possessed of great speed. Therefore, pray for a boon.
Śeṣa said:
Seeing him speaking thus, Hanumān spoke to him,
laughing with a fearless voice and greatly pleased with Maheśāna.
Hanumān said:
"O Maheśvara, by the grace of Raghunātha, everything is mine; nevertheless, I beg this boon from you, who have been propitiated by my battle. This one named Puṣkala has fallen, slain in combat."
Likewise, Śatrughna, the younger brother of Rāma, fainted at the gateway; many other heroes were also struck down by arrows, wounded,
some fainting and others fallen— protect them along with your hosts of attendants.
Just as these great elements are not seized or devoured by vetālas, piśācas, dogs, jackals, and the like,
so too you must act so that no such disintegration of their bodies occurs. 37.
"O Indra, until I have conquered the host and brought Mount Droṇa here,
and until I have revived all the soldiers stationed there by bringing the medicinal herbs and establishing them, you must protect [us] in every way. (38-39)
"Come, let us go to lead him to that best of mountains,
upon which dwell medicinal herbs that restore life to living beings. Having heard these words, he replied to him, "So be it."
"Go quickly so that you may protect my soldiers who have died.
Having heard those words of the Lord, he went to Mount Droṇa;
crossing all the continents, he went to the Ocean of Milk.
There, the great Śiva protected that cremation ground with his own hosts, who possessed great strength and prowess; meanwhile,
Hanumān approached the great mountain named Droṇa.
Placing his tail upon it, he quickly set out for the field of battle.
As Vipra prepared to lead him away, that mountain trembled;
seeing it shaking, the hosts of deities who protect it were struck with fear.
Crying out "Alas! Alas!", they said, "What is this that has happened on the mountain?
Who is this hero of great strength and prowess who leads him away?
Having spoken thus, all the asuras gathered together and beheld the monkey.
"Release him!"—saying this, they struck him with millions of weapons and missiles.
Seeing them all attacking, the heroic Hanumān became exceedingly enraged and, in an instant, slew them just as Śakra destroyed all the Asuras. 47-48.
Some were struck by his feet, some crushed by his hands,
some beaten by his tail, and others struck by his horns;
all of them, struck by that monkey, met their end in an instant.
Some fell upon the ground, drenched in blood;
others, terrified by the fear of the monkeys, fled to Śakra, the lord of the gods,
their bodies mangled by wounds and streaming with blood from their injuries.
Seeing them thus terrified with fear and drenched in blood, Śakra, the best of all the gods, spoke to the deities with a troubled mind:
"Why are you so stricken with fear? Why are you drenched in blood?"
"By which Daitya or by which base Rākṣasa has she been slain? Tell me all this truly so that, having learned it, I may go there;
having struck down and bound that intoxicated slayer of yours, I shall bring him back. (53-54)
Having heard these words, the best of the gods spoke with piteous voices to Turāsāha, who is honored by both gods and asuras. (55) The gods said:
Having come here, we do not know who this being is, assuming the form of a monkey and intent on carrying away Droṇa; he is wrapping the mountain with his tail.
Meanwhile, let us all remain well-united, having resolved to go [to his aid].
Well-armored and raining down all manner of weapons and missiles, they waged war.
By him, who was preeminent in strength, we were all defeated in that battle;
many of those excellent gods were slain there and fell to the ground.
"By our many merits we have been restored to life and have come here,
our limbs well-sprinkled with blood and still beset by the pain of our wounds.
Having heard these words of the gods, Indra, together with Purandara, [responded].
He commanded all the gods, endowed with great strength:
"Go to the great Droṇa mountain to bind the mighty Kapi;
having bound him, you must bring back that source of calamity for the gods in battle."
Thus commanded, they went to Mount Droṇa, the best of mountains,
where the powerful hero Hanumān, the best of monkeys, was staying. Having arrived, they all struck the mighty Hanumān.
Struck by Hanumān with his fists and palm-blows,
they fell there in an instant, their bodies wounded and dripping with blood;
others, defeated, fled toward the Lord of the Three Heavens.
Having heard that, Śakra, the best of the gods, became incensed and commanded all the foremost immortals regarding the great hero, the lord of the monkeys.
Thus commanded, they indeed went to where the powerful lord of the monkeys was.
Seeing them all approaching, the best of monkeys said:
"O heroes, I shall forcibly withdraw this illusion in battle; I will now lead you into the presence of Yama."
Thus addressed, they all, endowed with great strength, equipped themselves for battle and struck the monkey with various weapons and missiles discharged in many ways;
some with spears and axes, others with swords and pattisas.
Some, defiled by anger, [assailed him] with maces and spears;
though struck by those foremost of immortals with various weapons, that powerful one quickly struck all those best of gods with rocks. 69–70.
Some fled and said that they had gone into the presence of Śakra;
having heard those words, the lord of the gods was seized with fear toward Bṛhaspati, the chief of the gods and minister of the inhabitants of heaven.
Having approached the presence of the excellent preceptor of the gods and bowed down,
Indra asked: "O Lord, who is this man who has come to lead Droṇa away?"
"By whom were these heroic, weapon-bearing immortals slain?
Śeṣa said: Having heard those words spoken by the great descendant of Aṅgiras, he [replied].
To Turāsāha, the lord of the gods, who was terrified by the fear of the world,
Bṛhaspati said:
"He who slew Rāvaṇa in battle and utterly consumed Kumbhakarṇa..."
By him all his enemies were slain, and he alone is his servant;
by him the city of Laṅkā on Mount Trikūṭa was burnt with the fire from his tail,
and Akṣa was killed while Hanumān looked on.
Therefore, having been defeated by all [of us],
this best of the powerful, the great king, has now prepared for a horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) for the sake of Droṇa.
However, the great King Vīramaṇi, a devotee of Śiva, [has seized] his horse.
There, a battle took place that was truly bewildering to the gods;
Śiva himself slew the numerous heroes of Rāma’s army in great numbers.
To restore them to life, the mighty Droṇa will surely come there.
"Endowed with such strength as this, he cannot be conquered by you even in a hundred years;
therefore, appease the monkey and give him the medicine found there.
Thus ends the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*, on Mount Droṇa.
The forty-fourth chapter, named "The Defeat of the Gods.
Chapter Forty-Five. Śeṣa said:
Having heard the words spoken by his preceptor, the self-ruling enemy of Vṛṣaparvan realized that the son of the Wind had come for the sake of Rāma’s mission;
he perceived that the fear arising from the monkey was present in his mind.
With a heart greatly rejoicing, he spoke to Vācaspati.
Indra said:
"O Lord of the Gods, how should it be done if Droṇa is to be led away?"
Tell me how the life of the gods may be restored;
now, appease Pavana exactly as he is, so that Rāma may attain supreme joy and the gods may find happiness. 4.
Having heard the words of the lord of the gods, Vācaspati then,
placing Śakra at his head and surrounded by all the deities,
went to that place where the fearless monkey Hanumān was.
Having forcibly conquered all the gods who were dwelling in happiness, he roared aloud. Then,
led by Bṛhaspati, they went into his presence and,
having bowed at the feet of that son of the Wind-god, they prostrated themselves.
Bṛhaspati, the best among speakers, being impelled by that lord of the gods, the preceptor of the world, spoke thus to that hero:
"The gods, acting out of ignorance, have committed an act against your prowess."
"O high-minded one, you are a servant of the feet of Śrī Rāma.
For what purpose is this undertaking? How did your meeting with him come about?
We shall all do exactly as you have commanded. (9-10)
"Abandoning your anger and showing compassion, O Lord of Gods, look upon the son of Pavana, who bears a form that strikes terror into the Daityas.
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words spoken thus by the gods and his preceptor,
the one of great fame spoke in this manner to all the gods and the guru:
"In the battle against King Vīramaṇi, many were slain by Śarva."
I shall take Droṇa to the mountain to restore those soldiers to life;
and those who, arrogant in their own heroism and strength, attempt to stop him,
I shall send them to the abode of Yama in an instant.
"Therefore, tell me that which is immeasurable— either Drona or that medicine— by which I shall restore to life the heroes who have died on the field of battle.
Shesha said:
Having heard these words of the high-souled son of Vāyu,
they all bowed down and gave him the life-restoring herb (saṃjīvanauṣadha). Casting aside their fear, those gods, the inhabitants of heaven, were themselves filled with joy.

Accompanied by happiness, they went forth with the Lord of the Gods at their head. Hanumān, having taken that medicine, arrived at the gateway while being praised by all the hosts of gods who were eager for his great deed.
Seeing Hanumān arrive, all the enemies praised him, saying "Excellent! Excellent!", and they regarded that crow as something marvelous.
The monkey, having arrived, was filled with great joy.
Puṣkala, the foremost warrior who had arrived dead but was protected by Śiva within the fierce maṇḍala,
went into the presence of Śrī Rāma’s heart. 20.
Having summoned his minister Sumati, who possessed the wisdom of the great, he said,
"Today I shall restore to life all the heroes who have died in battle. Having spoken thus, he applied that medicine to the broad chest of Puṣkala.
Joining her head to her body, she spoke these auspicious words:
"If I recognize Rāghava as my husband in thought, word, and deed, then by this medicine may he live forthwith. (22-23)
As soon as these words were spoken, Puṣkala rose up;
that crest-jewel of heroes, out of rage, bit his teeth on the field of battle.
"Where has Vīrabhadra gone? He has fainted on the field of battle, deprived of flesh."
"I shall strike him down this very instant; where is my supreme bow?
To the hero who was speaking thus, the lord of monkeys said:
"O hero, you are blessed that you speak so boldly against him on the field of battle."
"O Vīrabhadra, you have been slain; by the grace of the Lord of the Raghus, you are restored to life here again. Come now to Śatrughna, who has fainted!
Having spoken thus, he proceeded to that foremost front of the battle.

Sighing, Śatrughna, afflicted by Śiva’s arrow, lay there. Having gone near that high-souled Śatrughna and applied the medicine to his chest once he had regained his breath, [the physician remained there]. 28–29.
Hanumān said to him: "O Śatrughna, best of men, why have you fainted on the battlefield, O you of great strength and prowess?
If I have been diligent in my vow of celibacy from birth until this life..."

"O hero, protect him; let Śatrughna live for even a moment! As soon as this was said by him, he was restored to life in an instant. Where is Śiva, and where has Śiva gone, having abandoned the field of battle? 32.
Those many heroes who had been slain in battle by the illustrious Rudra,
wielder of the Pināka bow, were all brought back to life by the high-souled Lord of Monkeys.
Then they all, their minds filled with rage, stood well-prepared for combat.
Established in their respective positions, they advanced against the enemies with their bodies wounded in battle.
Puṣkala went against Vīrabhadra, Kuśadhvaja against Caṇḍa,
the heroic Hanumān against Nandin, and Śatrughna against Śiva in the conflict.
The king approached Śatrughna, the best among the strong, who was drawing his bow and standing in battle having challenged Śiva;
the heroic King Vīramaṇi, the powerful Śatrughna, [stood] in the fray. 36.
They engaged in a battle with one another that caused wonder even to the sages.
O twice-born one, more than a hundred chariots of King Śatrughna, the lord of men, were reduced to pieces as small as sesame seeds in an instant by Vīramaṇi. 37–38.
Then, extremely enraged on the field of battle, Śatrughna discharged the Āgneya weapon to burn him along with his army.
Seeing that great burning weapon released by the enemy, [the opponent... 39.
The king, becoming exceedingly enraged, took up the Vāruṇa weapon (40).
Seeing that [the enemy] was afflicted by cold due to the Vāruṇa weapon, the powerful younger brother of Rāma discharged the Vāyavya weapon at him;
by that, a great wind arose (41).
The clouds, driven by the wind, moved in all directions;
having dispersed here and there, that entire army appeared comfortable.
While the army was distressed by the affliction of the wind, the great king Vīramati—
He took up the mountain-weapon (*parvatāstra*) against his enemy and fixed it upon his bow.
By means of the mountains, the wind was paralyzed and could not move in that battle. Seeing this, Rāma’s younger brother then took up the thunderbolt-weapon (*vajrāstra*).
Struck by the Vajrāstra, all the mountains were reduced to pieces like sesame seeds and turned to dust in that battle honored by the best of heroes.
With their limbs shattered by the Vajrāstra, the warriors were adorned with blood.
At the edge of the battle, a wonderful combat took place. Then the great King Vīramaṇi, becoming exceedingly enraged,
took up upon his bow the marvelous Brahmāstra, which consumes enemies.
Śatrughna took up an arrow and recalled that enchanting weapon given by the Yoginī, which bewilders all enemies;
that Brahmāstra, released from his hand, flew toward the foe.

Then, that deluding missile (mohanāstra) was released by the one named Śatrughna. In an instant, that Brahma-missile was split in two by the deluding missile; it then quickly struck the king’s heart, causing the monarch to fall into a swoon.
Hundreds of arrows released by King Śatrughna struck all those hosts of Rudra’s heroes, who then fell unconscious;
bewildered, they collapsed upon the surface of the earth at the feet of Śiva.
Then Śiva, becoming enraged, stood ready to strike the king. As he suddenly arrived at the courtyard of the archway to fight with Śiva,
Śatrughna, having strung his bow and made it ready, engaged in battle.
Between the two of them there occurred a terrible battle that tore asunder their enemies;
with various weapons and missiles discharged in many ways, the quarters of the sky were set ablaze by the impact of missiles and counter-missiles, and by blows and counter-blows.
Neither among the gods nor among the Daityas had there ever been such a circle of combatants.
Then, utterly overwhelmed in that battle with Śiva, Śatrughna remembered his master there, following the instruction of Pāvani.
O brother of Hānātha, the exceedingly fierce Śiva, raising his iron-tipped bow upon the circle of the earth, effects the taking away of life;
yet you have crossed the ocean of manifold miseries by means of that which is called Rāma.
"O Rāma, O Rāma, O ocean of compassion, lift me up as well from this state of suffering!
While he was speaking thus, Rāma— dark as the petal of a blue lotus and possessing eyes like lotuses— was beheld within the archway.
Holding a deer-horn and a sword, and bearing a consecrated body,
Śatrughna was struck with wonder upon seeing him on the field of battle.
Thus ends the [section] in the *Śrī Padma Purāṇa*, in the *Pātāla Khaṇḍa*, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana, in the *Rāmāśvamedha*.
The forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Meeting with Śrī Rāma.
Chapter Forty-Six. Śeṣa said:
O best of the twice-born, seeing his brother Śrī Rāma— who removes the suffering of those who bow before him— approach, Śatrughna was liberated from all his grief;
and Hanumān, beholding Rāma’s feet, was filled with joy despite his agitation.
She bowed down and spoke to him who had arrived for the sake of protecting her devotees:
"O Lord, this protection of your own devotees is indeed worthy of you,
in that you have released all those conquered in battle and bound with nooses."
"But we, O descendant of Raghu, are indeed fortunate that we shall behold your feet;
by your grace, we shall conquer our enemies in an instant.
Śeṣa said:
Then Sthāṇu, falling at the feet of Rāma— who has arrived as the object of meditation for yogis and who grants fearlessness to those who bow before him—
spoke: "You alone are the manifest Supreme Person, moving beyond primordial nature (prakṛti)."
You, who by a portion of your own self create, sustain, and destroy the universe; you are formless, the supreme cause of the entire world,
yet alone you assume a threefold form, accompanied by your illusory power (*māyā*).
In creation, you exist in the form of the Creator; in preservation, you are yourself;
and at the dissolution of the world, you directly assume the state known as Śarva.
Whatever sacrificial rite of the horse-sacrifice (hayamedha) belongs to you, O Supreme Lord—
That imitation of him, which serves to dispel even the sin of killing a Brahmin, is truly wonderful.
Since I carry upon my head that stainless water from his feet, known as the Gaṅgā, for the sake of pacifying my own sins, how could there be any transgression in you?

"O compassionate one, please forgive that deed which I clearly committed against you, who have been so greatly helpful; let it not be an obstacle for you. What can I do? I did this for the sake of upholding the truth."
Knowing your power, he has come for the sake of protecting your devotees.
Formerly, in Ujjayinī at the abode of Mahākāla, he performed most wonderful penance after bathing in the river known as the Śiprā. 12-13.
Then, having become pleased, I spoke to the lord of the earth: "O great king, ask for this wonderful kingdom as your boon.
I said: "Your kingdom shall be in Devapura."
"From the moment that the sacrificer arrives in the city of Mahāya, I shall remain here, intent on guarding you;
for by virtue of my own truth, O Rāma, I am your servant, having been granted this boon. (15-16)
"I have now been favored by the king, along with my sons, cattle, and kinsmen;
the horse is being surrendered, and the king will perform service at your feet.
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words of Maheśa, the best of the Raghus, his eyes filled with compassion, spoke with a steady voice. 18.
Rāma said:
This indeed is the duty of the gods: the protection of their devotee.
You have performed a noble deed in that the devotee has now been protected by you.
O Śarva, you are in my heart, and I am in your heart.
"There is no difference between us; only the foolish and the evil-minded perceive such a distinction.
Those men who truly create a division between us, who are of one and the same form, shall be cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hells for a thousand kalpas."
"Those who were your devotees became my devotees endowed with righteousness;
even those who were my devotees now bow down to you with even greater devotion.
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words thus spoken, the Lord Śarva restored King Vīramaṇi,
who had fainted, to life by touching him with his hand; he likewise revived his other sons, who were unconscious from the pain of the arrows.
The prosperous, capable, powerful Lord restored him to life;
then the Lord of Beings, having prepared that king—who was surrounded by his sons and grandsons—to bow at the feet of Śrī Rāma, caused him to do so. 24–25.
The fortunate King Vīramaṇi beheld the best of the Raghus,
who is difficult to attain even for tens of thousands of yogis established in yoga. Having seen that Lord of the Raghus, his very body was rendered fulfilled.
O best of the twice-born, they became most worthy of worship by Brahmā and the other gods; then,
having been praised by Śatrughna, Hanumān, Puṣkala, and other formidable warriors, the king gave that excellent horse to Rāma.
Then, impelled by Śarva, King Vīramaṇi gave away everything— including his kingdom, along with his sons, cattle, and kinsmen.
Thereafter, Rāma was praised by all his enemies and his own servants.
Especially by Śatrughna and the others who were exceedingly eager,
he remained seated upon a chariot made of jewels and became completely invisible;
when Rāmabhadra had thus vanished, they all were filled with great wonder.
"Do not consider him a mere mortal; that Rāma is praised as the sole refuge of the world.
He always exists and abides everywhere, both in water and on land.
Then the heroes, exceedingly delighted, embraced one another.
A truly great festival took place with the auspicious sounds of musical instruments. Then the horse was released, followed by all the heroes who were skilled in weapons and missiles,
and who were filled with joy and wonder.
Śarva, whose vow is true, having taken leave of that servant and having declared Śrī Rāma— the one difficult to attain for all the worlds— to be his refuge,
vanished there himself, he who is the cause of both dissolution and creation.
Accompanied by his attendants, Śarva went to Kailāsa; King Vīramaṇi, meditating upon the lotus-feet of Śrī Rāma,
went along with Śatrughna and Bālī, joined by a great army.
O best of men, those who hear this account of Rāma’s deeds shall never again experience the suffering born of saṃsāra. 38.
Thus ends the section on Rāma’s Horse Sacrifice in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
Chapter Forty-Six: The Departure on Horseback.
Chapter Forty-Seven. Śeṣa said:
O twice-born one, at the end of Bhārata lies Hemakūṭa;
it is protected by many thousands of warriors and adorned with tied chowries. It extends for many yojanas in width and length on all sides.
With ten thousand beautiful horns made of silver, gold, and other precious materials,
there was a great and excellent garden there,
adorned on all sides by trees such as śālas, tālas, tamālas, and karṇikāras.
With *hintāla*, *nāga-punnāga*, *kovidāra*, and *bilvaka* trees;
with *campaka*, *bakula*, *megha*, *madana*, *kuṭaja*, and others;
as well as with *jātikā*, *yūthikā*, and *navamālikā*. 4.
The forest was adorned with mangoes, *mādhava* trees, grapes, and pomegranates;
it resounded with the cries of many flocks of birds and was made to echo by the humming of bees.
Filled with the cries of peacocks, O horse, it provided pleasure in all seasons.

Accompanied by Śatrughna and endowed with the speed of thought, he entered while bearing a beautiful golden leaf upon his broad forehead. As that horse of the horse-sacrifice proceeded at that time, [it moved]— 7.
O best of the twice-born, listen to that wonderful event which occurred suddenly:
a stiffness came over his limbs and, though standing on the path, he did not move;
that excellent horse became as immovable as Mount Hemakūṭa.
Then all the guards struck him with lashes of whips;
yet even though thus beaten, the excellent horse stood firm and did not move.
The horse-keepers, having approached Śatrughna who was nearby, cried out to him.
"O Lord, we do not know what happened to that best of horses.
O King, O high-minded one, as that excellent steed was traveling with the speed of thought, a sudden stiffness of the limbs came over it."
Though struck by us with whips, he did not move at all;
having reflected thus, O best of kings, perform whatever action is required. Then the king, filled with wonder, [departed] along with his soldiers.
Accompanied by all of them, he went into the presence of that great horse.
Then Puṣkala, seizing its two legs with his arms, attempted to uproot it from the ground, but they did not move at all.
Then the horse, though attacked by one who was weak in strength, did not tremble;
thereupon the high-minded Hanumān resolved to lift it up. Enveloping it with his tail, that best among the strong exerted his power.
He pulled at the horse with all his might, yet it did not move;
then Hanumān, the best of monkeys, filled with wonder,
spoke to Śatrughna, the foremost of the strong, while the heroes were listening.

"Just now, this mountain was effortlessly uprooted by me with the tip of my toe; yet, what a great marvel it is that even this small horse does not tremble! Indeed, the cause for this has been seen by the powerful and arrogant heroes."
Though pulled, he did not move even a single sesame seed from his place.
Hearing these words of the monkey, Śatrughna, the best among speakers, was filled with wonder and spoke to Sumati, the foremost of his ministers.
Śatrughna said: "O sinless minister, what was the cause of the horse's paralysis? What remedy should be applied here so that the horse may regain its movement? (22)
Sumati said:
"O Lord, some sage who is expert in all branches of knowledge must be sought;
I know one born in this country, known through direct perception and not through hearsay. (23)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words of Sumati, the one skilled in dharma, together with his attendants, searched for that auspicious sage. 24.

Having gone everywhere, those soldiers searched for the Sage who knows the Dharma, but they did not see the Lord of Munis anywhere. However, one follower of the Brahmin had gone a distance of about a yojana.
Exerting himself toward the eastern direction, he beheld a great hermitage (26),
where all animals and people were free from enmity, exceedingly beautiful, and with all their sins destroyed by bathing in the Gaṅgā (27).
There, some performed supreme austerities with fires;
facing downwards, they sustained their bellies with smoke, leaves, and air.
There, the smoke arising from the agnihotra sacrifice constantly purifies everything.
With its many sages rejoicing and its excellent creepers shedding fallen leaves,
he recognized that charming hermitage of the sage Śaunaka and informed the king, whose mind was filled with wonder.
Hearing that, Śatrughna was exceedingly delighted; accompanied by his servants and joined by Hanumān, Puṣkala, and others, he then went to that hermitage.
There he beheld the best of sages, who had duly offered oblations into the sacrificial fire.
Having prostrated like a staff before his feet, which remove all sins,
he [Rāma]— recognizing that King Śatrughna, the best among the strong, had arrived—
prepared the guest-offering (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), and so forth, becoming joyful at the sight of him.
When the king was seated comfortably and rested, the lord of sages said to him:
"O King, for what purpose is this wandering of yours? Your journey is truly great. If kings like you did not wander over the entire earth," 34.
Then wicked people harass the virtuous who are free from all distress.
(35) O Mahīpāla, best among the strong, tell me everything regarding your travels and so forth; may it all lead to your well-being. (36)
Śeṣa said:
To the Brahmin who had spoken thus, the lord of the earth replied with a voice faltering with emotion, his own body thrilled with joy. 37.
Śatrughna said: "O best among the knowers of truth, listen: it was a wondrous thing that occurred suddenly; Rāma’s horse, having captivated his mind, was not far from your dwelling."
In that garden, rich with the beauty of its trees, by chance and through the power of destiny,
the horse's limbs suddenly became stiff at its edge.
Then, my powerful and heroic warriors, Puṣkala and others, fierce in their pride, [arrived].
They forcibly pulled at the vehicle, yet it did not move;
you are remembered as a boatman for those of us submerged in an ocean of boundless suffering.
Having been seen by fortunate ones through destiny, tell us the cause of this.
Śeṣa said:
Thus questioned, the best of sages, possessed of great intelligence, meditated for a moment; then, through reflection, he held two views supported by their respective reasons. 42
In an instant, having attained that state of knowledge, his eyes blossomed with wonder;
he spoke to the king, who was distressed and filled with doubt.
Śaunaka said:

Listen, O King, I shall proclaim the cause of the horse-stupor, by hearing which one is liberated from suffering; it is a most wonderful narrative. (44) In the Gauḍa country, in a great forest adorned by the banks of the Kāverī river...
The Vāḍava, named Sātvata, performed supreme austerity:
for one day he consumed only milk, for one day he subsisted on air, and for one day he remained without food; thus he continued for three days. 45–46.
While he was thus engaged in his vow, Time, the destroyer of all, seized him with its fangs; the observer of the great vow met his death.
[He ascended] into a celestial chariot (vimāna) rich in every splendor and adorned with all kinds of jewels.
Playing with the Apsarases, he went to the peaks of Mount Meru.
There stood a great tree named Jambū, whose juice was worthy of being enjoyed; from it flowed a river named Jāmbavatī, filled with liquid gold. 48–49.
In that place, sages endowed with merit through manifold austerities and possessed of all happiness sport with their desires, filled with curiosity.
There, he too, sporting at his own will with the Apsarases, was filled with joy.
Exalted by the intoxication of his own pride, he acted in opposition to them.
Then, cursed by the sages, that Rākṣasa became deformed;
thereafter, being deeply distressed, he spoke to the sages whose wealth was their knowledge and asceticism.
"May all you compassionate Brahmins favor me. Then, when he was thus favored by them, the hearing of the story of Rāma will swiftly bring about the immobilization of you, O horse. 53.

"O Lord, liberation from this most terrible curse of the sage shall come to you later," so said the gods to him. "O Lord, having fallen into the state of a Rākṣasa, [the sage] paralyzed him; [Rāma] then released the horse through the chanting of sinless hymns."

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Curse," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* within the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
Chapter Forty-Eight.
Śeṣa said: Having heard what was thus spoken by the sage, that slayer of enemy heroes experienced wonder in his heart and spoke to Śaunaka. 1.
Śatrughna said:
"O you who bear the name Sātvata, the course of karma is profound;
for even though you reached heaven by great deeds, you have been turned into a Rākṣasī by the power of karma."
"O Lord, O great sage, please tell us how the destiny of one's own actions unfolds, and by what ripening of karma such-and-such a hell comes to be. Śaunaka said:
O best of the Raghus, you are blessed that you possess this auspicious resolve;
for though you know the truth, O Lord, you speak for the sake of the world’s welfare.
I shall describe the various outcomes of diverse and wonderful karmas.

Listen to them, O Great King, by hearing which one may attain liberation. That evil-minded man who, with the intent to enjoy them, seizes by force the wealth of others, the children of others, or the wife of another.
Bound by the noose of Time and led by the mighty messengers of Yama,
he is cast into the Tāmisra hell for as long as a thousand years;
there, the servants of Yama inflict beatings upon him with uplifted weapons.
Tormented by the ripening of his evil deeds, he will then enter a sow’s womb;
having experienced great suffering there, he will attain human status marked by diseases and other signs that proclaim his own infamy.
He who, devoted to sin, nourishes only his own family while inflicting injury upon living beings, shall fall into the Andhatāmisra hell.
Furthermore, those men who commit the slaughter of creatures through falsehood [shall likewise suffer].
They are cast down and torn apart by the Great Ruru hell with great fear.
He who clearly commits the slaughter of living beings for the sake of his own belly is cast down into the one named Mahāraurava by the command of Yama himself.
The evil-doer who hates a Brahmin who is a merchant or a progenitor is cast into the extremely wicked Kālasūtra hell, which extends for ten thousand yojanas;
he remains there as long as there are hairs on the bodies of cattle upon whom he has harbored hatred.
For that many thousands of years, this person is tormented by the servants of Yama:
he who, having become a king on earth, punishes one who is unworthy of punishment, and being greedy, inflicts corporal punishment even upon a Brahmin. 14–15.
This [sinner] is tormented by wicked servants with the faces of boars;
afterwards, for the sake of expiating his sin, he is born in wicked wombs.
As for those who seize even a small amount of wealth or property belonging to Brahmins or cows—
Out of delusion, men seize the livelihood of others and rob them by their own strength;
they are cast into the blind well in the next world, greatly tormented.
He who, being greedy for sweets, personally brings food [for himself] while [neglecting others], [is likewise punished]. 17–18.
One who gives wealth to a non-devotee or an unfriendly person falls indeed into the hell known as Kṛmibhojana;
likewise, he who takes away gold and other riches from one who is not in distress.
O great sinner, one who misappropriates the property of a Brahmin shall fall into the Saṃdaṃśa hell.
That fool of deluded intellect who nourishes only his own body and knows no other shall be cast into the most dreadful Kumbhīpāka, where oil is heated.
Out of delusion, he who desires a woman who should not be approached— be she his mother or a female ascetic—
his servants cause him to be embraced by her with a glowing iron rod.
Those who, arrogant in their own strength, forcibly violate the boundaries of the Vedas, [suffer this fate].
Those who consume flesh and blood fall into the Vaitaraṇī river.
He who makes a Śūdra woman his wife and practices the life of a householder with her falls into the Pūyoda hell, overwhelmed by great suffering. (23-24)
Those rogues who resort to this deception to cheat the world fall,
struck by Yama, into the Vaiśasa hell, O fools;
and those fools who cause their own semen to be drunk by a woman of the same caste.
Those who are intent on drinking semen, who are wicked thieves,
arsonists, poisoners, and plunderers of villages— possessed of such sins, they are cast into the Sārameyādana hell. 26–27.
A person burdened by sin who speaks false testimony indeed, or he who, being powerful, forcibly seizes another's property—
that sinner falls headlong into the Avīci hell.
Having experienced great suffering there, he enters a most sinful womb. That fool who drinks liquor for the sake of its taste,
the servants of Dharma make him drink molten iron.
A man who, arrogant due to his own learning and conduct, disregards those superior to him in yoga,
is cast head-first into the Kṣāra hell while still alive.
Those men devoid of dharma who commit treachery against those who trust them [suffer likewise].
The slanderer is cast into the Śūlaprota hell, where there are many torments;
having terrified all men with his speech, he falls into the Daṃdaśūka hell and is bitten by venomous serpents. 32–33.
Thus, O King, there are many hells for evildoers;
having committed sin, they go there and undergo most terrible suffering.
This is the fate of those by whom the stories of Rāma have not been heard and who have not performed service for others.
All those sufferings of theirs occur within the midst of hell.
Here, it is explained that for whom there is happiness in heaven, they are those who have come from hell while afflicted by disease and suffering. 35–36.
Śeṣa said:
Having heard this, the protector of the earth, trembling moment by moment, questioned that Brahmin again for the sake of dispelling all his doubts. 37.
"O great sage, tell me the signs of each respective sin;
by what sin does what sign arise in the world of mortals?
Having heard those words, the sage spoke to the king.
"Listen, O King, I shall declare the signs of those who commit evil deeds.
Śaunaka said:
"A drinker of spirituous liquor is born with black teeth at the end of his stay in hell."

One who eats what is unfit for consumption is born with abdominal tumors and enlargement of the abdomen (gulmodara). Having eaten food looked upon by a woman in her menses, one is born with worms in the abdomen (krimilodara).
Having eaten food touched by dogs, cats, or similar creatures, one becomes foul-smelling.
A man who eats without first offering food to the gods and others becomes afflicted with diseases of the stomach, miserable, and tormented by great ailments;
indigestion arises from creating obstacles for the food of others. 42.
One who gives food only occasionally becomes one whose digestive fire is weak;
one who gives poison suffers from vomiting and disease; one who obstructs the path has diseases of the feet; and a slanderer is born at the end of hell as one afflicted by asthma and cough.

A deceitful person shall suffer from epilepsy, as shall one who causes pain to others; and one who sets fire to a forest shall suffer from bloody diarrhea. Furthermore, he who casts excrement into a temple or into water [shall likewise suffer]. 45.
He shall suffer from a most dreadful disease in the form of sin, such as a horse-disease (or a severe affliction).
Diseases arising from causing an abortion—such as consumption, urinary disorders, and dropsy—as well as one who destroys idols, become established without a firm foundation. 46-47.
One who speaks wickedly shall become afflicted with a skin disease; one who reviles others becomes bald;
and one who takes sides in an assembly becomes afflicted with hemiplegia (wasting of a side).
One who mocks the speech of others becomes one-eyed, and a thief of a Brahmin’s gold becomes one with deformed nails.
