A thief of a *tuṇḍīvarī* plant becomes one who steals copper; a thief of bell-metal becomes one who steals white lotuses. A man who steals tin is born with tawny hair, and a man who steals lead is born with diseases of the head. 49–50.
A man who steals ghee is born with eye disease;
a man who steals iron is born with deformed limbs.
A man who steals leather is born covered in fat. 51.
A man who steals honey is born with an odor emanating from his bladder. By stealing oil, a man becomes afflicted with severe itching.
And by taking uncooked food, he is born toothless.
From stealing cooked food, one becomes afflicted with diseases of the tongue;
and a man who approaches his mother is born devoid of virility.
From approaching the wife of one's teacher, dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra) arises.
By approaching a sister, one is born with yellow leprosy (pīta-kuṣṭha);
by approaching one's own daughter, one is born with blood-red leprosy (rakta-kuṣṭha);
and by approaching the wife of a brother, one is born with knotty leprosy (gulma-kuṣṭha). 55–56.

By having sexual intercourse with one's own master’s wife and others, a cluster of *jāyadru* trees arises; by having intercourse with the wife of a person who trusts one, an elephant hide is produced [as a growth].
By having intercourse with one's father’s sister, a wound appears on the right side of the body.
By approaching a maternal aunt, one shall have a wound on the left side;
by approaching the wife of a paternal uncle, leprosy arises on the chest;
and by approaching the wife of a friend, one is born with his wife dead.
Through sexual union with a woman of one's own lineage, bhagaṃdara (fistula-in-ano) arises;
through union with an ascetic woman, prameha (urinary disorder) arises in a man; and through union with the wife of a learned brahmin (śrotriya), a nasal ulcer arises.

Through sexual union with the wife of one initiated for a sacrifice, one becomes afflicted with foul hemorrhaging (duṣṭarakta-sṛk). By approaching the wife of one born of the same caste, one develops a heart-wound;
by approaching a woman of higher caste, one develops a wound on the head.
From approaching the womb of an animal, urinary obstruction arises;
these defects occur for men at the end of their stay in hell, without a doubt. These same [defects] also occur for women through union with such a man.
Thus, O King, have the signs of great sinners been proclaimed.
(64) By means of the merit of giving gifts, through rituals at sacred fords and the like, and by hearing the life-story of Rāma, one shall attain imperishability through austerity. (65)
The river of Hari’s praise washes away the mud of all sins for those sinful men; no deliberation is required in this matter.
(66) For him who disregards Hari, the sacrifices, rituals, and sacred scriptures are of no avail.
Even most meritorious sacred fords are not capable of purifying that person whose character,
when being recounted, causes laughter because of his weakness in knowledge;
for him, there shall be no liberation from hell even at the end of a kalpa.
"O King, for the sake of liberation, you should cause the life-story of Śrī to be heard along with your followers, so that the horse may regain its course.
Śeṣa said:
Having heard this, Śatrughna, the slayer of enemy heroes, became overjoyed;
having bowed to him and circumambulated him, he departed accompanied by his attendants.
Having gone there together with Hanumān, he stood beside the excellent horse.
He spoke the life-story of Rāma, which destroys great misfortune: "O god, go now to your own celestial chariot by virtue of the merit of chanting Rāma's name;
wander freely in your own world, for you have been liberated from birth in an evil womb. (71-72)
Having heard these words, while Śatrughna remained there, he beheld a stainless, excellent deity seated in a celestial chariot (vimāna). The deity said:
"I have been liberated because of my hearing the glorification of Rāma."
"O King, O high-minded one, command your own palace! Having spoken thus, the god departed, seated upon his celestial chariot;
at that moment, Śatrughna and his followers were filled with wonder.
Then, released from the paralysis of his limbs and from the ground, he went through that entire forest, which was teeming with birds, wandering about. 76.

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Liberation of the Horse," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. 48.
Chapter Forty-nine. Śeṣa said:
Seven months passed effortlessly for that excellent horse.
He traveled through the land of Bhārata, which was filled with many kings;
he was honored by the best of monarchs as he circumambulated the excellent Bhārata,
surrounded by the most eminent heroes, such as the formidable Śatrughna and others.
Remembering the power of Rāma, he subdued the horse that had not been provoked, after wandering through many countries near the Himālayas;
the horse was praised by the kings of Aṅga, Vaṅga, and Kaliṅga.
He went to the charming city of Suratha, the king’s capital;
there is the city named Kuṇḍala, where the earring of Aditi fell to the ground from her ears as she trembled with joy and fear.
Where the people never transgressed the dharma and daily performed the remembrance of Śrī Rāma with love;
where men daily worshipped the Aśvattha trees and Tulasī.
It is performed by the sinless servants of Raghunātha. There,
beautiful temples containing images of Rāghava are worshipped daily by those of pure mind and free from deceit.
Where the speech of those who speak consists of nothing but conversations concerning Hari, where meditation is fixed solely upon Him and not on the memory of the fruits of desire;
where there is sport with the bodies of those purified by the news of Rāma—[that is Ayodhyā]. 9.
Never indeed did those men who pride themselves on their devotion to truth suffer any calamity.
In that city dwelt the righteous-souled Suratha, truthful and powerful;
his heart was gladdened by the remembrance of the feet of the Lord of the Raghus, and he was intensely devoted.
How can I describe the excellent chariot of Rāma’s servant,
whose pervasive virtues, being the ground of all excellence, purify all sin?
Once, while wandering about, the servants of that king—
They saw the horse of the Ashvamedha sacrifice, anointed with sandalwood paste.
Having seen it, they were filled with wonder and looked at the horse’s hoof-print,
which was clearly inscribed with letters and smeared with sandalwood and other substances.
Having recognized that horse, so enchanting to the eye,
as one released by Rāma, they joyfully and eagerly reported it to the king seated in his assembly hall:
"O Lord, the master of the city of Ayodhyā is its Rāghava."
The horse, fit for the horse-sacrifice (hayamedha), having been released and wandering about, reached the vicinity of Satetapura accompanied by its attendants. [The messengers said:
"O Great King, seize this most beautiful horse! 16-17.
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words spoken by his own [son], he was overwhelmed with joy and spoke to his powerful heroes in a voice as deep as a thundercloud. 18.
Suratha said:
"Blessed are we, along with our servants, that we behold the face of Rāma;
I shall seize his horse, though it is surrounded by ten million warriors. (19)
"Then I shall surely release him when Ārāma approaches—
my devotee who has accomplished his purpose and has long been devoted to meditation.
Śeṣa said:
Having spoken thus, the protector of the earth personally commanded his servants:
"Seize the horse by force; no horse that has come within the range of my sight shall be released. By this means, a very great profit will accrue to me; this is my opinion. (21)
Or rather, he who beholds my feet— feet difficult even for Brahmā, Śakra, and others to attain—
is truly blessed, whether he be a kinsman, a son, a friend,
a beast, or even a mount, provided that through him the attainment of Rāma may come to pass. (22-23)
"Therefore, having taken the sacrificial horse, adorned with a golden plate, bind that beautiful Kāmavega in the stable. Having been told this, they then went and seized Rāma’s magnificent steed.
Having seized him by force, they all brought the auspicious-bodied one before King Atithi. Having obtained the horse, the king,
the subduer of demons and expert in righteous duties, spoke joyfully to his powerful servants.
O Vātsyāyana of great intelligence, listen with a one-pointed mind:
among his subjects, there was not a single man who took pleasure in the wives of others, nor one who delighted in the wealth of others, nor one who was greedy for sensual desires. 27.
One who is not devoted to the tongue should not proclaim [the name] on the wrong path due to the lack of chanting Rāma’s name.
A king who says to his servants, "You have come for the sake of service; being experts in righteous deeds, tell me of your activities," [is at fault]. 28–29.
Those warriors who observe the vow of having only one wife, who do not covet the wealth of others, who are not intent on slandering others, and who have not strayed onto the path of the Vedas,
perform the remembrance of Śrī Rāma and other such practices every day.
I protect them for the sake of serving Rāma, even while filled with wrath against Death himself.
Those men who possess qualities contrary to this and are joined with sin— I do not dwell those evil-minded ones within my own domain.
In that region, even the most wicked people committed sins only mentally,
for they were filled with the joy of having all their transgressions destroyed by meditation on Hari.
Such was the land when it was governed by a king endowed with righteousness.
Then all the inhabitants of that place, having died, attained liberation.
At that time, there was no entry for the messengers of Yama into the city of Sauratha;
instead, Yama assumed the form of a sage and approached the lord of the earth.
Wearing garments of bark and with his head adorned by matted locks, he saw Suratha, a servant of Hara, in the midst of the assembly;
on whose head was the name of Hari, supreme among all words, together with Tulasī.
While he was making his own people hear news concerning those devoted to dharma and righteous action,
the king, seeing the sage standing there like the very embodiment of austerity,
saluted his feet and then offered him water for washing the feet and other honors. 37-38.
When the sage was comfortably seated and rested, the foremost of kings said to him:
"Today my birth is blessed; today my home is blessed.
Tell me various excellent stories of Rāma."
"For those who hear this, there shall be the destruction of sins at every step.
Having heard what was thus spoken, the sage laughed heartily,
showing all his teeth and clapping his hands.

To that laughing sage he said, "What is the reason for your laughter? Please tell me out of your grace so that there may be happiness in my mind. Then the sage said to the king, "Listen, O King, with an attentive mind."
"Since you have asked me, I shall explain the supreme reason for my smile.
You said, 'Tell me about the glory of Hari'; but who is Hari, and whose is his glory? All men are subject to their own karma. (43-44)
By action heaven is attained; by action one goes to hell;
by action alone all things—sons, grandsons, and many others—come to be.
Having performed a hundred sacrifices, Śakra went to the supreme state.
Even Brahmā, having attained through his karma this wonderful world known as Satya, [enjoys it];
likewise, the lords such as the Maruts and others, perfected by manifold karmas and served by hosts of Apsarases, experience the happiness of enjoyment. 46–47.
"Therefore, perform sacrifices and the like; worship the gods so that your stainless fame shall spread across the surface of the earth.
Having heard these words, his mind was agitated with anger.
With a single-minded focus, he spoke to the Brahmin who was skilled in ritual action:
"Do not speak to me of that karma which yields only perishable fruits; go outside the vicinity of my city, for you are despised by the world."
Indra will fall swiftly, and even the Lotus-born Brahmā will fall;
but those humans who are eager to take refuge in Rāma shall not fall.
Behold Dhruva, Prahlāda, and the wonderful Vibhīṣaṇa.
And those others who are devotees of Rāma, they never fall [into this state]. But those wicked ones who revile Rāma—
my servants here shall strike them with iron mallets and with bonds of nooses.
"O lowest of the twice-born, because you are a Brāhmaṇa, I shall not inflict corporal punishment upon you;
go, go from my sight, otherwise I shall strike you.
When the excellent king named Suratha had spoken thus—
Then, as the servants seized him by the arm and prepared to cast him out, Yama assumed his own form, which is worshipped by all the world, and said to the king:
"I am well-pleased; ask for a boon, O servant of Hari."
"O you of noble vows, though tempted by me with many words, you have not wavered from the service of this king, which is practiced by the virtuous.
Then the lord of the earth, seeing Yama well-pleased, spoke.
He said: "If you are pleased with me, grant me this supreme boon:
let there be no death for me until the arrival of Rāma; O Dharmarāja, may I never have any fear from you."

Then Dharma said to the king, "O Lord of the Earth, all that you desire shall truly come to pass; the Lord of the Raghus will fulfill it. Having spoken thus, Dharma vanished and departed toward his own city.

The conduct of that praiseworthy one, whose soul was devoted to Hari, [was celebrated]. That righteous king, a servant of Rāma, having seized the horse with supreme joy, replied to his servants who were themselves devotees of Hari.
"This vehicle has been taken by me; O you who are skilled in battle, prepare yourselves in every way! Having been addressed thus, all those mighty warriors of the king [prepared].
Having prepared themselves, they went to the assembly hall in an instant, full of eagerness.
The king had ten heroic sons: Campaka, Mohaka, Ripuñjaya, Atidurvāra, Pratāpin, and Balamodaka.
Haryakṣa, Sahadeva, Bhūrideva, and Sutāpana—
these ten sons of the king, fully prepared on the field of battle,
possessed of great enthusiasm, desired to set out.

The king also, filled with enthusiasm for battle and surrounded by his entire army, summoned his own wonderful chariot— which was fashioned with the splendor of gold and adorned with swift, well-ornamented horses. 67–68.
The lord of the earth sat in the assembly hall, directing all his attendants.

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "King Suratha’s Seizure of the Horse" in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* within the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
Chapter Fifty.
Śeṣa said:
Then Rāmānuja, having arrived with speed, asked his own servants, "Where is that most charming sacrificial horse? 1.
Then those of great strength spoke these words to Śatrughna:
"O soldiers, we do not know which of us brought the horse and returned to the city;
indeed, we have all been humiliated by the powerful royal servants."
"The Blessed One is not an authority regarding what ought to be done.
Having heard those words of theirs, Śatrughna became exceedingly enraged;
gnashing his teeth out of fury, he repeatedly licked them with his tongue.
The hero said: "Having seized my horse, where will you go?
Now I shall strike down both you and Purañjana with my arrows. Having spoken thus, he said to Sumati: "Whose is this city?"
"Who exists as its sovereign, whom I have thus deprived?
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words of the king, which were filled with anger—
The minister spoke with sweet words, endowed with clear syllables:
"Know this most enchanting city to be named Kuṇḍala.
In this city dwells the righteous and powerful Kṣatriya Suratha."
Constantly devoted to dharma and a servant of the pair of Rāma’s feet—
Hanumān is such a servant in thought, deed, and word.
Hundreds of accounts of his righteous deeds exist.
Suratha, who possesses a vast retinue of great strength and is preeminent in all splendor—
(10) if this best of steeds were to be carried off, a great battle would ensue here, and many heroes skilled in the art of war would fall. (11)
Having heard what was thus spoken, Śatrughna, the best among speakers, addressed his minister once again with these words.
12 Śatrughna said:
"What should be done here if Rāmāśva has been captured by him? He does not come to fight, even though this powerful army is frequented by heroes.
Sumati said:
O Great King, an eloquent messenger has been dispatched to the king,
by whose word that best of the powerful will come with his army; unless, indeed, he has been led astray through ignorance or seized by some arrogant man.

"He will surely bestow upon us that excellent, auspicious horse, the most noble of sacrificial offerings. Śatrughna said:
"Go indeed to the great city of Suratha which is nearby;
having gone there as a messenger, speak thus to the king."
Whether intentionally or unintentionally, you have carried away Rāma’s vehicle;
therefore, either restore it or come forth for battle accompanied by your heroes.
(18) As for that mission to Laṅkā which was undertaken by Rāma against Rāvaṇa—
He went into the midst of the assembly, which was filled with rows of heroes;
there he beheld King Suratha, who wore a cluster of *tulasī* blossoms and was addressing his own servants with his tongue [speaking] to Rāmabhadra. 20–21.
The king, seeing the monkey who possessed a captivating form and thinking him to be Śatrughna’s messenger, spoke to the son of Vālī.
Suratha said:
"O Lord of the Monkeys, from where have you come here? Who are you?
Tell me everything according to the facts; having understood it, I shall act accordingly.
Śeṣa said:
As the king was speaking thus, the lord of monkeys, his mind filled with great wonder at the monarch who had performed service for Rāma, replied to him:
"O best of kings, know me to be the son of Vāli and the lord of monkeys."
And Śatrughna has been sent by you as a messenger to my presence.
O King, some of his servants have now arrived and, acting out of ignorance, have suddenly seized my horse—an act which is a great injustice. (25-26)
Filled with joy, take the horse along with the kingdom and your sons;
fall at Shatrughna’s feet and quickly grant him permission to depart. Otherwise, his body will be wounded by the iron arrows released by Shatrughna.

Adorning the surface of the earth with your severed head, you shall lie there; for where will you go after having stolen the sacrificial horse of him by whom the Lord of Laṅkā was brought to destruction in an instant as if in play? 28-29.
Śeṣa said:
To him who was speaking these words and others, the Lord of the Earth replied: "Everything you say is true; nothing false has been spoken by you. (30)
"Furthermore, listen to my words, O servant of Śatrughna’s feet:
I have taken up the great bow of the wise Rāmacandra.
I shall by no means abandon it out of fear of Śatrughna or anyone else."
If he himself comes and grants me an audience,
then, together with my son, I shall bow at his feet and offer him my entire kingdom, my family, my wealth, my grain, and my great army.
"O King, having conquered him, I shall bind him in my own palace if Indra should come here.
Śeṣa said:
Having heard this, the wise Aṅgada then laughed at the king.
He spoke these great words, endowed with immense fortitude.
Angada said:
"Devoid of wisdom, you speak thus because of your old age and your attachment."
O powerful one, it is a shame that you, with such a mind, should despise King Śatrughna—
he who effortlessly slew the Daitya Lavaṇa, the enemy of Māndhātṛ,
and by whom many powerful and arrogant foes were conquered in battle. (37-38)
"O hero among heroes, you appear to me to be devoid of intelligence, for you seek to bind that Rākṣasa Vidyunmālī, who stands upon his wish-fulfilling chariot;
he whose brother Puṣkala is exceedingly powerful and a master of supreme weapons."
O Rudra, how can I describe the prowess and the formidable strength of this Vīrabhadra, by whom the host of Gaṇas was so well-pleased?
On this earth, there is no one equal to him in power, in fame, or in splendor.
Hanumān, near whom dwells the mind fixed upon the lotus-feet of the Lord of the Raghus, whose many heroic deeds shall be heard of;
by him, the city of the Rākṣasas along with Trikūṭa was forcibly consumed in an instant. 42.
The son of the evil-minded lord of the Rākṣasas was struck by Akṣauhiṇī;
he is the mountain named Droṇa, who, with the tip of his tail, has repeatedly brought [the enemy] there for the sake of the soldiers' livelihood. 43-44.

Rāma alone knows his conduct; no other of deluded intellect knows it—this lord of monkeys, your servant, whom you do not forget for even a moment from your heart. (45) Those lords of monkeys, Sugrīva and the others, who swallow up the entire earth today...
All of them, eager for the spectacle, waited upon King Śatrughna.
Kuśadhvaja, Nīlaratna, Riputāpa—who was skilled in great weapons—and Pratāpāgrya, as well as Subāhu, Vimala, and Sumada [were there]. 46–47.
King Vīramaṇi, endowed with truthfulness and a servant of Rāma—
these and other kings, lords of the earth, wait upon him there. O hero, who are you, appearing like a mere gnat in that ocean?
Knowing this, come with your sons to the compassionate Śatrughna; having entrusted your horse to him, you shall go to the lotus-eyed Rāma,
and upon seeing him, you will make your own limbs and your very birth successful.
Śeṣa said: The king spoke to that messenger who was speaking in many ways:
"Show these to me quickly; let them all come within my range of vision. 51
Such is my strength as a messenger, yet such is not the strength of Hanumān,
who went to protect the sacrifice while keeping Rāma at his back.
If I, filled with curiosity, [had acted] in thought, word, and deed—
"Let me worship Rāma; he will surely show me his own form within a short time.
Otherwise, O heroes headed by Hanumān, bind me by force or seize me, for I am filled with devotion to Rāma."
"Go, O King, and speak to Śatrughna what I have said:
'Let your excellent warriors prepare themselves; this powerful one is coming to the battle. Having reflected, he will act as is appropriate on the field of combat."
"Release the great horse; do not seize it from us. Śeṣa said:
Having heard this and smiling, the hero went to where the king was.
Having gone, he reported exactly what had been said by Suratha.

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Suratha and the Messenger," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* within the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
The fifty-first chapter. Śeṣa said:
Having heard those words spoken by Suratha from the mouth of Aṅgada, [he spoke].
All those skilled in chariot warfare stood ready with their chariots in the arena;
the sound of kettledrums arose, as did the blare of war-drums,
and the roars of the heroes manifested throughout the courtyard of the arena.
That entire universe was pervaded by the rattling sound of chariots and the trumpeting of elephants; that great roar reached even unto heaven.
The heroes, skilled in battle, were filled with martial enthusiasm.
They raised various cries that were terrifying to the cowardly.
While such a clamor was occurring, the king named Suratha,
surrounded by his sons and soldiers, then advanced onto the field of battle.
Seeing the earth filled with elephants, chariots, horses,
and throngs of foot soldiers, the warriors beheld it as if being flooded by the ocean;
it resounded with the blast of conchs and likewise with shouts of victory.
Seeing him prepared for battle, the king spoke to Sumati.
Śatrughna said:
"This king has arrived, surrounded by a vast army."
"In this matter, O high-minded one, tell us what must be done by us.
Sumati said:
"In this matter, we must fight against many heroes who are skilled and experienced."

Let Subala, the son of Mīra, who possesses supreme heroism and is highly skilled in combat with others, engage in battle along with Puṣkala and the other extremely fierce warriors, all of whom are experts in every kind of weapon and missile. 9–10.
Śeṣa said:
Even as the great minister was speaking thus, the sons of the king, filled with arrogance, loudly twanged their bows upon the field of battle. 11.
Seeing them, the very powerful warriors Puṣkala and the others, fierce in battle,
advanced in their own chariots with bows and arrows in hand.
The great hero Puṣkala, an expert in supreme weapons, [advanced] with Campaka.
The son of Janaka, along with Kuśadhvaja, fought with Mohaka in a duel of chariots against that illustrious great hero;
Subāhuka fought with Ripuñjaya, Vimala, and Durvāra. 13–14.
Pratāpin fought with Apratāpāgrya, Balamoda with Aṅgada,
Haryakṣa with Nīlaratna, and Sahadeva with Satyavān.
The powerful King Vīramaṇi fought with Bhūrideva.
Asutāpa, fierce and endowed with great strength, fought [against him];
those experts in combat, all skilled in weapons and missiles and proficient in warfare, engaged in a great duel on chariots. 16–17.
O best of sages, as the battle thus proceeded with the sons of Suratha, a great slaughter took place there.
Then Puṣkala said to Caṃpaka, "What is your name, O prince?"
"You are fortunate to have entered into battle with me.
Stay now; what do you intend to do? How shall your life continue?
Come and fight with me, O master of all weapons and missiles! (19-20)
Having heard these words spoken by him, the powerful and heroic prince spoke to Puṣkala with a voice as deep as a thundercloud. 21.
Campaka said:
"This battle here will not take place between two families of different names;
nevertheless, I shall speak my own name preceded by my strength:
My mother is known as Rāghaveśī, and my father is remembered as Rāghava."
Rāmacandra is my kinsman; Rāghava is my own person. 23 My name is Rāmadāsa, and I am a constant servant of Rāma.
Rāma, who is compassionate toward his devotees, will deliver me from the ocean of worldly existence. 24
Adopting the common view of the world, I shall now speak to you:
I am the son of Suratha, and my mother is Vīravatī;

Deluded by honey, they abandon their abode of sweet nectar. (26) Know me, O Vīra, as the one who deludes them; I am named after that very [abode], possessing a body with a waist like gold in color. (27)
"Fight with your arrows in battle; for who is capable of conquering me? Now I shall display my own wonderful prowess.
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these great words, Puṣkala was delighted in his heart;
considering him difficult to conquer, he remained in battle discharging arrows.
As Puṣkala discharged a multitude of arrows in ten million ways, [the opponent] advanced toward him.
Then Campaka, filled with rage, strung his bow;
he released sharp arrows capable of rending hosts of enemies,
each marked with his own name and provided with golden-feathered shafts.
The great hero Puṣkala cut them down on the field of battle,
discharging stone-sharpened arrows that created a darkness of shafts everywhere.
Seeing his own arrows thus severed by the hero, Campaka—
Filled with rage, he challenged the powerful Puṣkala,
saying repeatedly in the battle, "Do not flee, abandon your chariot! Then,
acting with haste, he pierced Puṣkala in the heart with ten arrows.
Those arrows of Puṣkala, possessing intense velocity, having arrived, struck deep into his heart and drank his abundant blood. Afflicted by those arrows, the hero took up five shafts.
Holding back those arrows with their extremely sharp points as if they were great mountains of wrath,
those powerful shafts of his and the other’s arrows were then cut into hundreds of streams by the son of the King in the sky.
Having cut through those arrows with extremely sharp points, the powerful one born from the limbs of Suratha took up a hundred arrows to strike Puṣkala in the heart.
Those arrows were severed into a hundred pieces by the high-souled Puṣkala.

Not falling, though afflicted by the force of the arrows at the edge of the bowstring, he remained firm. Then, seeing that great feat of the king, the powerful son struck him clearly in the chest with a thousand arrows.

Puṣkala, who was an expert in supreme weapons, swiftly cut those down as well; then once more he quickly fixed ten thousand arrows upon his own bow. (41) Puṣkala, who was an expert in supreme weapons, swiftly cut those down as well.
Then, becoming exceedingly enraged, he unleashed a shower of arrows.
Perceiving the approaching shower of arrows, Caṃpaka, the slayer of heroes, struck Puṣkala as he was praising him, saying, "Excellent! Excellent! (42-43).
And Puṣkala, an expert in all weapons, seeing Campaka endowed with great heroism, fixed the Brahmāstra upon his own bow. That great weapon, released by him, set the ten directions ablaze.

Seeing that *caṃpaka* weapon, which was intent on bringing about the dissolution of the entire universe pervading the sky and the earth, he who is skilled in all weapons discharged that very same weapon to destroy it as it rose against his enemy. 45–46.
The people considered it to be the dissolution of one of the two splendors;
then that supreme weapon, having become unified with the other weapon, withdrew.
Seeing that wonderful feat, Puṣkala said, "Stay! Stay! 47.

Speaking thus, he struck Campaka with unerring arrows in a fit of rage. Campaka, however, being high-minded, disregarded those discharged shafts and then released the exceedingly terrible Rāmāstra against Puṣkala.
Seeing that weapon released, as the high-souled Campaka resolved to cut it down, he was instantly seized by an arrow; then, bound by the hero Campaka, he was placed back upon his own chariot.
The high-minded one then resolved to send him back to the city.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose when the one named Puṣkala was bound;
the warriors, intent on flight, fled toward Śatrughna.
Seeing them broken, Śatrughna said to Hanumān: "O hero, by which warrior has my army, adorned with heroes, been shattered?
Then the slayer of enemy heroes spoke to Puṣkala, the lord of the earth.
"Having bound him, this hero Caṃpaka, who is firm in his own station, brings him here.
Hearing these words of his, Śatrughna, filled with anger, said to Pavanodbhūta: "Release him quickly from the king’s son!"
"O foremost of heroes, his son Mahābala has bound the warrior Puṣkala with iron; release him from there! Why do you remain standing in the midst of battle?
Hearing these words, Hanumān replied, "So be it."
He went from Campaka to liberate Puṣkala from the warrior; then, seeing Hanūmat arrived to set him free, he,
filled with supreme rage, struck him with hundreds and thousands of arrows.
That great-souled one shattered those arrows discharged by him; yet, as he continued to discharge even more inauspicious arrows at him, he became truly formidable.
He pulverized all those iron-tipped shafts (nārāca) released by his enemy.
Seizing Śālaṅkāyana with his hand, the mighty one crushed the prince like sesame seeds; then Hanumān, released by him,
hurled the elephant onto the head of the prince.
Struck by Campaka, he fell dead upon the ground;
then Hanumān, the knower of supreme weapons, unleashed those rocks,
but Campaka pulverized all those rocks completely in an instant.
O Brahmin, this was a great marvel produced by the catapult:
seeing all those stones discharged by him pulverized, Māruti became exceedingly angry in his heart, remembering that he possessed great heroism. 63–64.
Having arrived, seized him, and placed him upon his back, the monkey leapt into the sky;
then, with great speed, he passed above the range of vision.
Campaka, remaining in the air, fought with Hanuman.
Struck by that great hand-to-hand combat, the bull among monkeys became enraged in his mind;
he who was as formidable as a mountain of pride seized Campaka with his foot and dashed him against the ground.
Struck by the lord of monkeys, that powerful one rose up in an instant,
seized Hanumān by his tail, and whirled him about in every direction. Seeing that strength of his, the lord of monkeys laughed and seized him again by the foot.
Having whirled him around a hundred times, he threw him onto the back of the elephant. Subala’s son, Campaka, fell to the ground,
unconscious, still adorning the field of battle with his heroic ornaments.
Then the worlds, following Campaka, cried out, "Alas! Alas! And Puṣkala released Campaka, who was bound by the snares [of the enemy].
Thus ends the section on Rāma’s Horse Sacrifice in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
The fifty-first chapter, named "Puṣkalamocana.
Chapter fifty-two. Śeṣa said:
Seeing the Campaka tree fallen, the powerful Kṣatriya Suratha,
his body overwhelmed with grief for his son, set out in his chariot. Then,
filled with rage, Suratha summoned the lord of monkeys.
Releasing a torrent of breath, endowed with great strength,
and seeing his own king challenging him, that heroic lord of monkeys,
possessed of immense speed, rushed toward him. 2-3.
To Hanumān, who had arrived and was treating the fierce warriors as if they were mere blades of grass,
King Suratha, whose voice was as deep and resonant as a thundercloud, spoke.
(4) Suratha said:
Blessed indeed is this Ikṣvāku, endowed with great strength and prowess,
by whom such a great task was accomplished in the city of the Rākṣasa;
you are his servant at Rāma’s feet, filled with devotion.
"By you, a coward, my son, the powerful Campaka, was struck down. Now, having bound you, I shall go to my city;
stay here with effort, O Lord of Monkeys, for I have spoken the truth as I remember it."
Having heard these words spoken by Suratha,
the Lord of Monkeys spoke with a steady voice to Rāṇā, who was adorned as the sole hero:
Hanumān said:
"You are a reminder of Rāma's feet, while we are the servants of Rāma;
if you bind me by force, my Lord will surely set me free. O Hero, fulfill the true promise residing within your heart."
"Remembering Rāma, one goes to the end of all suffering; thus the Vedas declare.
10 Śeṣa said:
Having praised the son of the Wind-god as he was speaking thus, Suratha—

He pierced him with many sharp arrows, terrible because they had been whetted on a grindstone. Disregarding those blood-dripping arrows that had been released, he then took up in his hand a bow equipped with a string and provided with an arrow.
Seizing the bow with both hands, the enraged monkey broke it,
letting out a roar that terrified the heroes while rending the warriors with his claws. Seeing his own bow, along with its string, thus shattered by him, [he was filled with anger].
Furthermore, he took up another great bow adorned with a magnificent string;
the monkey seized that as well and broke it out of rage. He took up yet another bow, and the one of great strength shattered that too.
When that bow was broken, he took up another bow;
he too, endowed with great speed, broke that bow as well. In this manner, eighty bows of the king were shattered.
Moment by moment, out of great rage, he uttered various cries.
Then, becoming exceedingly provoked, he seized a fierce spear;
struck by that spear, the hero fell for a moment, overcome with distress.
Rising up in great fury, he seized the king’s chariot;
having taken hold of it, he flew into the ocean with extreme speed.
Beholding him thus flying away, Suratha, the slayer of enemy heroes—
He struck the advancing Māruti in the chest with iron clubs;
by that blow, his chariot was instantly pulverized at a distance.
Mounting another chariot, he then rushed with speed toward the son of the Wind.

Hanumān, having coiled his tail around that chariot on the field of battle, shattered it along with its horses, charioteer, and banners. Then the exceedingly powerful king, mounting another chariot, departed.
The son of the Wind-god, his limbs trembling with rage, shattered the chariot by its momentum.
Seeing that chariot broken, Suratha mounted another;
yet he too was suddenly destroyed along with his horse and charioteer by him.
In this manner, forty-nine chariots were shattered by Hanumān;
beholding that feat, the king, along with his army, was filled with wonder.
Enraged, he said to the lord of monkeys, "O son of the Wind, you are fortunate!"
Exerting his prowess, he will perform this deed and shall do it no more.
Wait for a single moment, O bee at the lotus-feet of Rāma stirred by the wind, until I string my bow. 26–27.
Having spoken thus, his eyes overflowing with rage, he strung his bow and fixed upon a fierce arrow the weapon named Pāśupata.
Then there arose bhūtas, vetālas, piśācas, and those led by the yoginīs.
Suddenly, [weapons] appeared, terrifying the son of the Wind;
the monkey was bound by the Pāśupata missiles while the worlds looked on, crying out "Alas! Alas! even as the son of the Wind [was being struck]. 29–30.
Remembering the grove in his mind, he instantly tore it down; with his limbs thus released, he suddenly fought against King Suratha.
Seeing him with his limbs freed, Suratha, who was a supreme knower of weapons—
Considering himself possessed of great strength, he took up the Brahma-weapon;
but the powerful son of the Wind-god swallowed that Brahma-weapon while laughing.
Seeing it swallowed, the king, the lord of the earth, remembered Rāma.
Remembering Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, he fixed the Rāma-weapon upon his bow and spoke this: "O bull among monkeys, you are bound!
As soon as he heard that, he set out; meanwhile, [the other] was already bound on the field of battle.

Then the heroic Hanumān, the servant of Rāma, who had been struck by the king’s arrow, spoke to the monarch: "O lord of the earth, what shall I do? I am bound by my master’s weapon, and certainly not by any ordinary one. (35-36)
"Therefore, O King, I shall honor you; lead me back to your own city.
My lord, that ocean of compassion, will come and release me. When Samīraṇa was thus bound, the enraged Puṣkala went toward the king.
As Puṣkala approached, he pierced him with Vasu arrows;
the powerful one struck the king with many thousands of shafts, and numerous elephants were cut down by the king on the field of battle. 38–39.
When the chariot of Samarasankruddha was thus completely [overwhelmed] by arrows, the entire world— both the stationary and the moving— was pervaded by shafts;
beholding their exertion in battle, the celestial soldiers were struck with amazement.
As the men were seized with terror at every moment,
a tumultuous battle ensued between the heroes, hair-raising and characterized by the discharge of missiles countered by counter-missiles, accompanied by the chanting of great mantras. 41–42.
Then the king, provoked to anger, took up an iron shaft (nārāca), but it was cut down by the vatsadanta arrows discharged in fury by the Bharatas, O Bhārata.
When that arrow had been cut, the king, out of rage, took up another.
As long as the arrow remained embedded in his heart, he was wounded;
the highly effulgent and great-minded Puṣkala fell into a swoon after engaging in that most wonderful and great battle with the king. 44-45.
King Śatrughna, the son of Puṣkala and scorcher of his enemies,
mounted upon his chariot and, filled with rage, advanced against Suratha.
The mighty brother of Rāma spoke to King Suratha.
"A great deed has been performed by you, in that the son of the Wind-god has been bound;
likewise, the great hero Puṣkala and my other soldiers, possessed of immense strength and prowess, have been struck down in this terrible battle. (47-48)
"Now, having struck down these heroes on the field of battle, where will you go, O lord of the earth? Withstand my arrows!
(49) Having thus heard the speech of the hero, the powerful Suratha—
He spoke, fixing the beautiful lotus-feet of Rāma in his heart:
"In battle, I have already struck down heroes who were as fierce as the wind;
now, I shall strike you down as well upon the field of combat."
"O Hero, that one who remembers the sound of my name comes and protects me;
otherwise, O scorcher of enemies, there is no life for me in your presence.
Having spoken thus, the lord of the earth struck him with thousands of arrows.

Śatrughna placed another supreme weapon within the cage of his mass of arrows. Śatrughna then discharged the *Vahni-daivata* (Fire-god) weapon for the purpose of burning those straight-knotted arrows that were being released.
Then, beholding that weapon released, the great king Śura neutralized it with the Vāruṇa weapon and pierced him with ten million arrows.
Thereupon, he fixed upon his bow that weapon which had been bestowed by the Yoginīs.
It was a wonderful weapon that brought sleep and deluded all heroes.
Seeing that great deluding missile, the king, who was skilled in all weapons and missiles, remembered Lord Hari and spoke to Śatrughna. 56–57.
"O Śrīmat Rāma, for me who am thus deluded, nothing else appears as a source of enchantment, nor even a state of fear or calamity, except for the remembrance of you.
When the hero had spoken thus, he released a great weapon.
Cut by that arrow, it fell upon the circle of the battlefield. Seeing that great deluding weapon rendered fruitless,
the king was overcome with extreme astonishment and fixed an arrow upon his bow.

The crusher of great demons took from his quiver that terrible arrow, which, by its brilliance, possessed the luster of fire. Seeing it, the king said: "This is the arrow [that resides] in the hearts of the wicked."
"Even in the presence of one who is a devoted worshiper of Rāma, he does not shine.
As he was speaking thus, the slayer of enemies (Rāma) swiftly pierced Bāṇa in the heart with an arrow that possessed a brilliance equal to a flame of fire.
Afflicted by that arrow and overcome with great agony, that scorcher of enemies fell into a swoon for a moment upon the seat of his chariot;
having endured that pain for a moment, he went before the foe.
"Endure a single blow from me; come before me!
Having spoken thus, O great multitude, he fixed upon his bow an arrow whose body was encircled by garlands of flames and which was equipped with a golden feathered shaft.
Released from his bow by Śatrughna, an arrow struck him as he stood in the path;
though severed at its tip, it quickly entered his heart. Fainting from that arrow, he fell upon his chariot.
Then the entire army, crying out "Alas!", was broken and fled in all directions.
Suratha, the servant of Rāma, achieved victory in the battle;
ten heroes were felled somewhere, rendered unconscious by his ten sons.

Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Victory of Suratha," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* within the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
[Chapter Fifty-Three]
Śeṣa said:
Having seen that army broken on the field of battle and his master even rendered unconscious, Sugrīva went forth to fight against the king. 1.
"Come, O King! Having overwhelmed all these beings, from where do you come? Go quickly; give me battle, O hero skilled in combat!
Having spoken thus, he [climbed] a certain large tree provided with branches.
Endowed with great strength, he uprooted [the tree] and struck him on the head. By that blow, the mighty king,
having looked at Sugrīva, then [fixed it] upon his own bow.
Taking up sharp arrows with great fury,
the exceedingly valiant and powerful one struck him in the chest; but Sugrīva, laughing, suddenly warded off all those arrows.
The exceedingly powerful one struck Suratha in the heart with mountains, peaks, and trees the size of great elephants; he struck him with force,
tearing at Suratha with his claws.
From that most terrible and swift-binding noose, which was difficult to perceive,
the monkey-king Hanumān thought himself bound;
he was like an elephant caught in an iron chain hanging from its feet, while Suratha remained a servant of Rāma.
Having attained something, he was unable to do anything else; for it had indeed become so.
That great king Suratha, who possessed a virtuous son, was victorious; having placed all the heroes upon his chariot, he departed toward his own city. 8–9.
Having gone to the assembly hall, the great one spoke to the bound Māruti:
"Remember the compassionate Raghunātha, the protector of his devotees,
so that he, being of excellent intellect, may immediately release you from your bonds."
"I shall not release you from bondage otherwise than after ten thousand years.

Having heard this spoken, Samīraja then beheld himself tightly bound; seeing his warriors unconscious and tormented by the impact of the enemy's arrows, he remembered [his vow] for the sake of their release from bondage.

With all his senses free from sorrow, he remembered Śrī Rāmacandra— the one born of the Raghu dynasty, the husband of Sītā, whose eyes are like lotus petals, and who is compassionate enough to liberate even himself from bondage.
(13) Hanumān said:
O Lord of Hāna, supreme among the best of givers, most compassionate one; O Lord of Sītā, whose face is adorned with beautiful locks of hair;
O you who possess a charming form that burns away the suffering of your devotees!
Release me from this bondage immediately, without delay! For by you were the preeminent elephants and others liberated,
as well as the gods who were being consumed by the fire of the host of Dānavas.
O abode of compassion, remember me; you have released the hair-braid resting upon the head of Suṃdarī.
O Lord of Sages, you are devoted to the rites of sacrifice; O King whose feet are worthy of praise, you contemplate the Dharma. 15.
O Mahāpuruṣa, O Śuddhadeva, today I am bound by the deep noose of Asuratha; release me! 16.

If you do not release me because of excessive forgetfulness, then the world would laugh at you, whose lotus feet are worshipped by the best of all gods; therefore, do not delay here, release me quickly! 17.
Having heard this, Raghuvīra, the Lord of the World and ocean of mercy,
set out in the swift-moving Puṣpaka chariot to liberate his devotee. He was then accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa as his follower and graced by Bharata.
The monkey saw him accompanied by hosts of sages led by Vyāsa.
Seeing that his own lord had arrived, he said to the king:
"O King, behold Hari, who has come out of compassion to liberate you."
"Having previously liberated many of his own servants through remembrance,
he has likewise come to release me who am bound by the noose. Seeing Śrī Rāmabhadra approaching, Suratha, in that very moment—

Overwhelmed by a flood of devotion, he prostrated himself hundreds of times. Then the four-armed Śrī Rāma embraced him with his own arms, repeatedly drenching his head with tears of joy for his own devotee.
"O blessed one, you have performed a great deed;
Hanumān, the lord of monkeys who possesses strength in every limb, has been bound by you.
Thus spoke Śrī Rāma, and he released that best of monkeys from his bonds.
Seeing all those soldiers unconscious, he restored them to life with his glance. Having seen Rāma, the servant of the gods, they abandoned their fainting;
having risen, they beheld the beautiful and charming Śrī Rāmacandra.
Having bowed down to the Lord of the Raghus, they were asked about their well-being;
the kings, having become happy, told the monarch that all was well with them. Then Suratha, seeing Rāma for the sake of compassion toward his own servant, spoke.
He offered his entire kingdom along with his horse to the most noble Śrī Rāma; he propitiated him with manifold services and said,
"O Raghava, forgive the injustice committed by me."
Then Śrī Rāma said to him: "The protection of those who have come for refuge has been accomplished.
This is the duty of Kṣatriyas: to fight alongside their master. You have performed a noble deed; heroes are well-pleased by death in battle."
Having spoken thus, Śrī Rāma, honoring Nṛhari along with his son,
stayed for three days and then departed after taking leave of him, traveling in a great celestial chariot that moves at will, accompanied by sages.
Seeing him, they were filled with wonder and recounted his charming stories.
Having installed Campaka in his own city, the powerful Kṣatriya Suratha,
possessed of great strength, set his mind on going together with Śatrughna.
Having recovered his own horse, Śatrughna caused kettledrums to be sounded and had various kinds of conch shells blown everywhere. Then the hero released the sacrificial horse along with Suratha.
Wandering through various other lands, that powerful one did not capture anyone; wherever the horse went,
he roamed there, followed by a great army and by Śatrughna along with Suratha.
Once, at dawn, he went to the excellent hermitage of Vālmīki on the banks of the Jāhnavī, a place frequented by the best of sages and marked by smoke.
Thus ends the [section] in the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana concerning Rāma’s horse sacrifice (*Aśvamedha*).
Chapter Fifty-Three: The Meeting with Raghunātha.
Chapter Fifty-Four. Śeṣa said:
Having performed his morning rites, Lava, the son of Janaki, was chosen by the sons of the sages to fetch the sacrificial fuel required for those rituals;
there he beheld the sacrificial horse, marked with a golden leaf.

Perfumed with the divine fragrance of saffron, agallochum, and musk, he beheld it; filled with curiosity, he spoke to those sons of the sages: "By chance, Arvāk, whose speed is like that of thought, has arrived at my hermitage."
"Come with me and behold; do not be afraid," having said this, Lava quickly went near Vāhasya.
The descendant of Raghu, who was standing near the king of the lake, [spoke] to Vāhasya.
Bearing a bow and arrows upon his shoulder, as invincible as Jayanta,
he went together with the sons of the sages and read the excellent document,
which was adorned with rows of clearly defined letters and placed upon his forehead.

The great lineage of Vivasvat is renowned throughout all the worlds; therein not even one person was a harasser of others or a coveter of another's property. He was a banner of the Solar dynasty, a bowman, a preceptor in the initiation of archery, and a venerable teacher.
He whom all the gods together with the immortals honor with their jeweled crowns—
his son is Rāmacandra, the upholder of the Raghu dynasty, who humbles the pride of heroic strength, the highly fortunate one, the crest-jewel of all heroes. 8–9.
His mother was the daughter of the King of Kośala, born from a jewel;
Rāma, the destroyer of enemies, who is that jewel born from her womb, performs the horse sacrifice, being well-instructed by a Brāhmaṇa. 10.
For the removal of the sin of killing the eminent brahmin named Rāvaṇa, that chief sacrificial horse was released by him;
it was well-guarded by a great force of attendants and by moats. 11–12.
His protector is his illustrious brother Śatrughna, the slayer of Lavaṇa,
accompanied by an army consisting of hosts of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry;
for such a king as he, pride would never arise from self-conceit.
"We are heroes, we are the best of archers, and we are fierce here.
Let them seize by force the horse adorned with a jewel-garland—swift as thought, moving at will, capable of going everywhere, and radiant in all its movements. (14-15)
Then Śatrughna, having effortlessly and forcibly liberated his brother from the pain caused by the calf-tooth released from the bow,
[addressed] those kṣatriyas regarding the kṣatriya maiden.
Those born into noble families and virtuous lineages should accept that [state], while those with bodies of the opposite nature should offer their kingdom to Raghava and bow down. 17.
Thus addressed, the enraged Lava, bearing sword and bow, spoke to those sons of the sages with words faltering from rage:
"Behold quickly the audacity of this kṣatriya!"
The king inscribed his own prowess and strength upon the leaves of their foreheads:
"Who is this Rāma? Who is Śatrughna? They are mere insects relying on little strength.
We are the superior ones, born in the lineage of Kṣatriyas. (19-20)
The mother of this hero is Janaki, the progenitor of Kusha,
who bore the jewel named Kusha just as the fire-drill produces fire.
Now, I shall demonstrate his kshatriya nature in every respect.

"If he becomes a Kṣatriya and a slayer of enemies, he shall seize me bound, for I am fit for the performance of sacrifice; otherwise, having abandoned his Kṣatriya status, he will become a worshiper at the feet of Kuśa. (22-23)
"Now he shall fall asleep by the arrows released from my bow,
as well as other great heroes who are the ornaments of the battlefield.
Having uttered these words, Lava seized that horse.
Treating all kings as mere blades of grass, that excellent wielder of the bow and arrows then spoke to the sons of the sage, who were desirous of seizing Lava,
saying: "Rāma, the king of Ayodhyā, possesses great strength and prowess."
"Even Śakra, though arrogant in his own power, does not seize this [sacrifice] of his;
do not seize it, but listen to these words of mine which are fraught with benefit.
Having heard what was thus spoken, he restrained himself and spoke to the sons of the virtuous brahmin.
"O best of the twice-born, you do not know the strength of Kṣatriyas.
Kṣatriyas are distinguished by their heroism and prowess, while Brāhmaṇas are distinguished by their food.
Therefore, go home and eat what has been brought by your mother. (28-29)
Thus addressed, those sons of the sages became silent as they watched Lava’s prowess; they remained standing at a distance outside.
While this occurrence was taking place, the servants of that king [were likewise present].

Having arrived and seen that horse bound, they then spoke to Lava: "Who, being exceedingly enraged, has bound this horse? Is it Dharmarāja? Or who, standing amidst a multitude of arrows, shall suffer supreme agony? (31-32)
Then Lava spoke quickly: "The best of horses has been bound by me;
he who releases it, his brother Kuśa is great and swift.
Even though the Lord Yama himself has arrived, what will he do? Do not be deluded. 33.
"Having bowed, he will quickly arrive, satisfied by the shower of arrows.
Śeṣa said:
"Having heard these words, they said, 'He is but a child.'"
To liberate the horse that had been bound by those who were followers of Hari,
he took up his bow in his hands and discharged razor-sharp arrows at the servants of Śatrughna who had arrived to set it free.
With their arms severed, they approached Śatrughna out of grief; when questioned, they all told him how Lava had lopped off their own arms.
Thus ends the section on Rāma’s Horse Sacrifice in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
The fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Binding of Lavaṇa," ends here.
Chapter Fifty-Five. Vyāsa said:
Having heard this delightful account of Lava and Bali, the sage,
filled with doubt, questioned the thousand-faced Nāga.
Śrī Vātsyāyana said:
You have said that long ago, Rama, being greedy for women, abandoned Sita all alone in the forest due to the harsh words of a washerman.
Where are the two sons born of Janaki, and where has their mastery of the bow gone?
And how did the learned Avidyā bring about the great destruction?
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of the sage, the high-minded serpent Śeṣa—
The world praised the wonderful life-story of Rāma, the eminent Brahmin.
Śeṣa said:
Rāma ruled the kingdom in Ayodhyā together with his brothers.

Protecting the entire realm of the earth according to dharma with his own wife, Sītā bore that seed for five months. Then the goddess, like the Earth supporting the personified Vedas, shone exceedingly.

Once, at a certain time, Rāma asked the daughter of Videha: "O virtuous lady, what longing do you have? I shall surely fulfill it for you. Being questioned thus in private, that chaste woman, feeling bashful, spoke to her husband.
With her voice faltering from shame, she spoke these words, which were like nectar:
Sītā said:
"By your grace, everything has been enjoyed by me, and I shall continue to enjoy what is auspicious."
Indeed, there is no object whatsoever that exceeds the singular focus of her mind;
for her, whose lord is one like you— whose holy feet are praised by the gods—
nothing remains that does not already exist in abundance.
"Out of persistence you ask me about this longing residing in my mind; O charming master, I shall speak the truth before you.
For a long time I have truly known Lopāmudrā and other such women."

Having seen those beautiful women eager to behold their own master’s mind, I, who have attained a kingdom and dwell in manifold pleasures with you, am ungrateful; for even now my mind is intent on bowing down to them. 12–13.
Having gone there, one should worship the treasuries of asceticism with garments and other offerings,
and present radiant jewels as well as ornaments;
thus propitiated, those truthful ones bestow delightful blessings.
"This is my longing for fatness, my mind being completely filled with my beloved.
Having heard these most charming words of Sītā, Rāmacandra, feeling supreme joy, spoke to his beloved.
"O ascetics, you are blessed; you shall go tomorrow morning.
Let Janaki be seen by you so that you may have fulfilled your purpose, and then you shall come into my presence.
Having heard these words of Rama, she attained supreme joy.
"In the morning, my meeting with the female ascetics will surely take place.
Then, at night, the spies sent by Rāma to observe his own fame as it was being proclaimed heard of it; indeed, they arrived there slowly in the dead of night.
Every day, listening to the most enchanting stories of Rāma, they went on that particular day to the great house of a wealthy man; there,
seeing a lamp burning brightly and perceiving a human voice, [they entered].
The spies stationed there heard another’s speech very clearly at that moment.
There, a certain beautiful-eyed woman, greatly delighted, sang these most charming words to her suckling infant: 21–22.
"O son, drink my charming breast milk as much as you desire;
later, O my child, it will become very difficult for you to obtain.
This Rāma, who possesses the luster of the petals of a blue lotus, is the lord of this city."
Indeed, for the people residing in that city, there shall be no further birth (24). Since there is an absence of birth, how can the drinking of breast milk occur on earth?
Therefore, drink breast milk repeatedly; it is difficult to obtain, and one should keep another [thought] in the heart (25).
"Those who shall remember Śrī Rāma, meditate upon him, and speak of him— even for them,
there shall never again be the drinking of water [in this world].
Having heard these words, which were like the nectar of Śrī Rāma’s glory...

Filled with joy, they proceeded to another great house belonging to a fortunate man. Meanwhile, another spy, perceiving this charming house to belong to Rāma, remained there for a moment out of a desire for his fame.
There,

a certain beautiful woman, richly adorned with the sound and splendor of her bangles and perfumed with camphor and agallochum incense, sat comfortably upon a couch while chewing betel-leaf affectionately offered by her husband. (29)
Beholding her beloved of such amorous form, she with trembling eyes said:
"O Lord, you appear to me as you did when you were the husband of Raghu, bearing an exceedingly beautiful and most delicate body. (30-31)
"Your pair of eyes has the beauty of lotus petals, your chest is expansive and enchanting, and you bear arms adorned with armlets; you are truly Rāma himself before me.
Having heard these most captivating words of his beloved, [he was moved]. 32.
Making the corners of his eyes dance with desire, he who was beautiful as the god of love said:
"Listen, O beloved; what you have spoken is virtuous and very charming.
It is indeed fitting for wives devoted to their husbands that Rāma alone is their own beloved. (33-34)
Where am I, so unfortunate, and where is Rāma, the great and fortunate one?
Where am I, as insignificant as an insect, and where is he, worshipped by Brahmā and the other gods? Where is a firefly, and where is the jewel of the sky? Where is a moth, and where is a god?
Where is this lion, the king of beasts, and where is this dull-witted rabbit? (36) Where is the goddess Gaṅgā, and where is the water of a roadside ditch flowing out of its course?
Where is Meru, the abode of the gods, and where is a mere heap of guñjā seeds? (37)
"Such is he, the one who delights in the 'I' and the 'mine,' by the dust of whose feet this woman has become like a stone in an instant, having assumed a form that deludes even Brahmā.
Speaking these words, she embraced her own husband.
Having heard such words as, "Her eyebrows, acting as bows, quiver with a love brought forth by the desire for union," he went to another dwelling; there,
he heard the speech of another spy, which was endowed with glory.
One woman, having prepared a bed made of flowers, sandalwood, and saffron—
everything worthy of the God of Love— spoke these words to her husband: "O Lord,
prepare a bed upon this flower-couch, fit for enjoyment."
Anoint yourself with sandalwood paste and other unguents, and likewise enjoy various kinds of pleasures;
only those like you are worthy of such enjoyments, for we have not turned our backs on you.
Enjoy everything as it is, having obtained it through the grace of Rāma.
A beloved woman like me, sandalwood that removes all heat,
and a couch adorned with flowers— all this has come about through the grace of Rāma.
Those who will not worship Rāma shall themselves become the womb of a king.
"Those who are deprived of clothing, food, and other necessities are truly unable to support their husbands.
To the woman speaking thus, her husband, filled with joy, replied: "Everything you say is true; it has come about through the grace of Rāma toward me."

Having thus heard the fame of Rāmabhadra, a spy arrived; meanwhile, another spy staying in the house of someone else overheard these words: "A certain woman, intent on playing the lute upon her bed with her beloved... (47)
Singing the excellent fame of Rāma, Kāntā spoke to her husband:
"O Lord, we are most fortunate, for Śrī Rāma, the sovereign and protector of our city, protects his subjects like his own sons. (48-49)

He who performed that great deed so difficult to accomplish—that which was not easily achieved—built a bridge across the ocean using monkeys as the material; and having slain his enemy Rāvaṇa, he enjoyed Laṅkā with those monkeys. 50.
"He abducted Jānakī at night and practiced a most great transgression.
Having heard these words spoken in such sweet syllables, the husband smiled and then spoke this sentence again to me: 51-52. "He abducted Jānakī at night and practiced a most great transgression.
Having heard these words spoken in such sweet syllables, the husband smiled and then spoke this sentence again to me: 52.
O beautiful lady, this great deed of Rāmacandra—
the slaying of the ten-headed Rāvaṇa, the subduing of the ocean, and so forth—
was performed by that Great One who, though requested by Brahmā and others, descended to the earth as if in sport, appearing as if deluded. 53.

Know me to be that man Rāma, the bestower of joy upon Kauśalyā, whose true deeds remove even great sins. Having assumed human form through his divine play, he creates, protects, and destroys this universe. 54–55.
"Blessed are we, who behold the lotus-face of Rāma, which is difficult even for the gods beginning with Brahmā to see; we are doers of great merit.
Thus he heard the life-story of Rāmacandra, which bestows happiness upon the ears.
Standing at the water's edge, he repeatedly heard such words as these (57).
One after another, having gone to various houses, they stood there to hear the glory of Hari;
there too, they heard the beautiful fame of Rāmabhadra (58).
Playing at dice with her husband, the beautiful woman spoke these sweet words while dancing, her bracelets jingling: "O beloved, I have won everything by my swiftness! (59)
"Will you do this with such a dejected mind?"— having spoken these words preceded by a jest,
she joyfully embraced her beloved. 60.
The beloved said, "O beautiful one of lovely limbs,
for me who constantly remembers Rāma, there is no defeat anywhere. Now, however, having remembered the enchanting Rāma, I shall conquer you."
"O gods, as in the past, having remembered the sons of Aditi, he conquered them in an instant.
Having spoken thus, he performed the turn of the dice;
at that moment, he achieved victory and, filled with joy, spoke these words.
"O you who have conquered old age, what has been spoken by me has become true; you are in the prime of youth.
O son, may Rāma never again be afflicted by the pain of longing for his wife.
Thus did those two speak to one another, filled with eagerness.
Then, having embraced him firmly with deep affection, they returned home from the palace.
Having thus heard the five great conducts of the king, Vainya’s subjects praised one another and went to their respective homes with joy.
The sixty-first traveler, having observed the houses of artisans, went there desiring to hear about the fame of King Yaśas, the lord of the earth.
The washerman, touched by anger because his wife was staying in another's house, [said]: 67.
Kicking her with his foot and looking at her with bloodshot eyes, he said:
"Go from my house to that house where you have stayed for the day; I will not accept you, a wicked woman who has transgressed my word. (68-69)
Then her mother said, "Do not abandon her, who has come to our home, who is free from offense and devoid of wicked deeds.
Thereupon, the washerman, filled with rage, replied to his mother.

"O Rāma, I do not take as my own beloved woman who dwells in the house of another; whatever that king does is indeed consistent with moral conduct. I do not take a wife who resides in the house of another. (71-72)
Again and again he said this: "I am not King Rāma, who protected Jānakī while she resided in the house of another rākṣasa. Having heard these words, the spy was overwhelmed with anger.
Taking a sword in his hand, he set his mind on killing him; but remembering what Saramā had said— that no human being is unslayable by him—
the high-minded one, realizing this, withdrew his wrath.

Having heard that, he was afflicted with great sorrow; standing there with his five spies, he then departed, enraged, sighing and gasping repeatedly. Those five, having met together there, spoke to one another.
Having heard that account of Rāma’s life, which is uniquely honored by all the world and which they themselves had heard, they consulted with one another:
"What was spoken by wicked people must not be told to the Lord of the Raghus. (77-78)
Having thus consulted together, they went home and slept with eager anticipation;
at dawn, they were resolved in their minds that they would offer praise to the king.
Thus ends the [section] concerning Rāma’s Horse Sacrifice in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
The fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Observation of Spies.
The fifty-sixth chapter. Śeṣa said:
Having performed his daily morning rites and having gratified the Brahmins, who were most learned in the Vedas, with gifts of gold according to tradition, he proceeded to the assembly hall.
All the people came to pay homage to Raghunātha, the lord of the earth.
They went to the assembly hall where he was protecting all his subjects like his own sons.
At that time, Lakṣmaṇa held the royal parasol over the head of the king,
while Bharata and Śatrughna held a pair of chowries.
There, the sages headed by Vasiṣṭha sat in attendance,
as did the ministers headed by Sumantra, who were administrators of justice.
While things were proceeding in this manner, those six spies, well-adorned, arrived at that time.

They gathered to pay homage to the lord of men as he sat in the assembly hall. Observing those spies who were eager to speak, that best of kings, filled with curiosity, entered the inner chamber of the assembly in private.
In private, King Sumati questioned all those spies:
"O subduers of enemies, tell me truly as spies:
what do the people say of me, and what do they say of my wife?"
"What kind of conduct do people say the ministers possess, and how is it?
Having heard these words, they then spoke to Cārurāma as he questioned the leader of the Raghus with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
The spies said:
"O Lord, your fame now purifies all people on this earth;
we have heard it in every house, praised by both men and women. (10)
The great lineage of Vivasvat was brought by you, O Supreme Lord,
to adorn this earth, and your vast fame has been spread abroad.
Many others, such as Sagara and his kin, were renowned and possessed of great strength.
Their fame was not such as yours;
indeed, with you as their protector, all the subjects have been made fulfilled,
for them there is no untimely death nor any affliction from passion and the like.
Just as the moon appears in the sky and just as the river Jāhnavī flows, so does your virtuous fame illuminate the earth.
Hearing of your fame, even Brahmā and the other gods were greatly moved with wonder.
The fame of Lord Sarvavratī now purifies all people.
O King, we are all most fortunate who, as your spies, behold your charming face moment by moment. (15–16)
Having observed these and other words of the five spies, Rāghava questioned the sixth spy, whose face was marked with an expression of dejection. 17.
Rāma said:
"O one of great intelligence, speak the truth regarding what was heard during the confusion of the worlds;
may all of that be praised by me as it is, otherwise it would be like committing a sin.
Thus Rāma questioned him again and again in detail.
Nevertheless, he did not speak any worldly words to Rāma.
Then Rāma replied to Cāra, his face showing signs of embarrassment:
"I swear to you by truth; tell me everything exactly as it is."
Then the spy spoke these words slowly to the king,
like a father speaking that which ought not to be told, yet was uttered by his own servant.
The spy said:
O Master, your fame for fulfilling all vows—beginning with the slaying of the Ten-Faced Rāvaṇa—is truly great;
Seeing her staying at another's house, he rebuked her and struck her.
Her mother replied to her: "Why do you strike this innocent woman? Take her back; do not utter such reproach; follow my word."
Then Sarayū said: "I am not King Rāma;
it was he who accepted Sītā after she had dwelt in the house of a rākṣasa.
O Lord, every deed performed by a king becomes characterized by wisdom."
"Even for other doers of meritorious deeds, such conduct is unwise.
He spoke this again and again: "I am not King Rāma. O King, at that moment, when he remembered your words, he became enraged.
Then, having severed his head, I cast it down upon the surface of the earth; yet again, I reflected: "Where indeed is this washerman, Kvarāma?
This man is wicked and speaks falsehood; this which is said is not the truth. (28)
"If you command me now, O King, I shall kill him. Though this is improper, it has been spoken because of your insistence.
Let the King, who is the authority here, consider what is appropriate."
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words, whose syllables were like a great thunderbolt, he sighed repeatedly, took deep breaths, and fell down unconscious. 31.

Seeing the king thus unconscious, they were overcome with grief according to custom; for the sake of dispelling his suffering, they fanned him with the hem of their garments. After a moment, the king regained consciousness and spoke to them.
"Go quickly to Bharata and send him back to me. Those sorrowful spies, carrying the message, went swiftly to Bharata's house and delivered Rāma's command.
Having heard Bharata’s message, the wise one went to the assembly hall;
hearing that Rāma was staying in private, he approached him with great haste.
Having arrived, the high-minded one replied to that doorkeeper:

"Where is that Rāmabhadra, my gentle brother, the ocean of compassion? (36) Having been directed there, the hero went to that house, enchanting with its jewels; and upon seeing Rāma so distressed, fear arose in his heart. (37)
"Is Rāma angry, or is there some sorrow for the Lord?
Thus he spoke to the king, who was sighing again and again:
"O Master, why is your face, which is so easy to please, cast down?"
"By your tears it is seen that your body is seized by grief, like the moon [eclipsed] by Rāhu.
Tell me the truth, what is the cause of all this? What shall I do for you?
Abandon your sorrow, O Great King; why are you a vessel for grief? (39-40)
Thus addressed by his brother in a voice faltering with emotion,
the heroic and righteous Rāmacandra spoke to his brother:
"Listen, O brother, to my words regarding the cause of my sorrow."
"O high-minded brother, perform that cleansing this very morning.
In the lineage of Vaivasvata, there has been no king wounded by infamy; today my own fame, once turbid, has been joined by the Gaṅgā-Yamunā. (42-43)
Only those men whose fame exists on earth have truly lived; for those whose reputation is wounded by infamy, life is equal to death.
Those whose fame shall endure on earth will attain eternal worlds.
May those bitten by the serpent of ill-repute fall into a downward state.
Today, my singularly defiled infamy has become world-renowned as the celestial river Ganges; hear now my words regarding what was said today by the washerman. (45-46)
"O brother, today in this city the washerman has spoken something concerning the birth of Jānakī; what then shall I do on this earth?
Shall I kill myself today, or shall I kill this woman, Jānakī?"
"What must I do for both of you? Tell me the truth, O venerable one.
Having spoken thus, with tears flowing and his limbs trembling with agitation, that crest-jewel of the righteous fell upon the ground. 48–49.

Seeing his brother fallen, Bharata was overcome with grief; looking at him, he slowly restored Rāma to consciousness. Seeing that Rāmacandra had regained consciousness, yet remained deeply distressed, [he spoke].
He spoke these most enchanting words for the destruction of his sorrow:
"Who is this washerman, and what were the words he spoke? I shall cut out the tongues of those who speak ill of Jānakī. 51-52.
Then Tāḍakārāma spoke these words that had issued from the mouth of the washerman;
the high-souled Bharata heard all of that through his spy.
Having heard it, Bharata spoke to his brother, who was grieving with sorrow.
Jānakī was purified by fire in Laṅkā and honored by the heroes.
Brahmā said: "She is pure; Daśaratha is your father.
How can she, who is honored by the world, be abandoned on the mere word of a washerman?"
Indeed, your fame, praised by Brahmā and others, purifies the worlds;
how then could it become defiled by the words of a washerman? Therefore, abandon this great sorrow arising from Sītā’s reproach.
O King of the Kurus, together with your highly fortunate wife who is pregnant,
why do you wish to abandon your own beautiful body? We have all been destroyed today without you, the destroyer of our sorrow.
"O Sītā, this great prosperity would not have lived for even a moment without you;
therefore, let that devoted wife enjoy vast fortune together with him. Hearing these words of Bharata, the righteous [Rāma]—
Then that best among those skilled in speech spoke these words again:
"O brother, everything that you have said is consistent with dharma; however, perform this further word which I speak, by my command. (60-61)
"I know her to be pure, purified by fire, stainless, and honored by the world; yet, fearing public scandal, I abandoned my own Janaki.
Having said this, he took up a most terrible sword held in his hand.
"Either cut off my head, or release Jānakī in the forest.
Having heard these words of Rāma, Bharata fell down unconscious; his body trembled and he was filled with tears.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Speech of Bharata," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana within the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padmapurāṇa*.
Chapter Fifty-Seven.
Vātsyāyana said:
O observer of noble vows, tell me how the Lord, whose pure fame purifies the world, performed the recitation of the unspeakable with Jānakī.

O Śeṣa, act in such a way that there will be most beautiful happiness for my mind; for by drinking the nectar issuing from your mouth, there shall be such satisfaction as cuts through the cycle of worldly existence.
Śeṣa said:
In the great city of Mithilā, there was a king named Janaka; he ruled that kingdom righteously, gratifying his subjects. 3.
As Saṃkarṣaṇa was plowing the earth with the long-tailed Sītā, a most beautiful maiden indeed emerged from the furrow of Sīradhvaja.
Then King Sīraketu attained the utmost joy.
He gave the name Sītā to her, the enchantress who was the very fortune of the world.
Once, while that most beautiful woman was playing in the grove of a garden,
she saw a pair of parrots— a male and a female— speaking of their own beloved.
Filled with extreme joy and intensely greedy for sensual pleasure,
that couple spoke to one another with affectionate and auspicious words; then, as they were sporting, they were swiftly cast down from the sky.
As he was rising up, he uttered this sound from his throat:
"Rāma, a captivating lord of the earth, shall be born upon the ground; and a great woman named Sītā shall be his wife."
The wise and powerful one, subduing other lords of the earth, shall rule for ten thousand years, which constitute a single yuga of six million years.
Blessed is that lady Janaki, and blessed is he known as Rama.
"Those two who have come together here on earth shall sport with joy.
Hearing this conversation, Sītā realized that the pair of parrots was actually a pair of deities, and she observed their speech.
"But this pair of parrots makes my delightful stories their own;
having taken them, I shall ask every word until its meaning is fully understood.
Having reflected thus, she spoke to her own female companions.
"Seize this charming pair of birds slowly! 14.
Having gone to that mountain, those friends captured the excellent pair of birds and presented them to their friend out of a desire to do what was pleasing to her. 15.
Seeing him making many various sounds that were captivating to the mind,
Sītā then comforted him and spoke these words: Sītā said:
"Do not fear, O beautiful ones; where have you both come from? Who is that Rāma, and who was that Sītā? And from where has this knowledge been remembered?
Tell me all of that quickly, so that the fear which oppresses you may pass away. (17)
Thus questioned by her, the pair of birds praised everything.
Vālmīki said to the pair of birds: "There dwells a great sage, the most excellent among those who know the Dharma."
In that most beautiful hermitage where we both reside,
the sage— who is devoted to the welfare of all beings and who daily remembers that supreme state— caused his disciples to sing the future *Rāmāyaṇa*. (19–20)
At that time, we both heard the entire great future Rāmāyaṇa as it was being sung repeatedly and recited in its proper sequence.
We shall tell you who Rāma is and who Jānakī is once we have heard it.

Whatever is destined to happen, Hari— the glorious one whose virtuous deeds are sung by celestial women— will manifest through the sacrifice performed for Ṛṣyaśṛṅga by him who delights his soul in the pleasure garden, having entered into a fourfold state. 22–23.
Accompanied by his brother and with bow in hand, he will reach Mithilā through skill; then,
