having broken that bow which is difficult for other kings to grasp,
he will win the most enchanting daughter of Janaka.
"O best of those who have heard the Vedas, it has been heard by us that she will rule over a great kingdom together with him.
This and other matters were heard by us while we were standing there; O lady of beautiful limbs, tell this to those two who desire to go, so that they may release us."
Having held those very charming words in their ears, that pair of birds spoke again these words in response:
"Where does Rāma dwell? Whose son is he? And how is he? (27)
"What kind of form will that supreme man assume who will take me as his wife?
Tell me all this that I have asked exactly as it is;
afterwards, I shall do everything that is pleasing and agreeable to your minds. (28-29)

Having heard that and seeing Jānakī tormented by the weaver, the wise and powerful King Paṅktiratha— the banner of the Solar dynasty— realized what was in her heart and then recited [the verse] before her. 30.

Relying upon him, the gods shall conquer all their enemies in every respect. He shall have three wives who assume forms enchanting even to Śakra, and from him there shall arise four offspring of great strength.
Rāma shall be the eldest of them all; Bharata is remembered as following him;
after him, the illustrious Lakṣmaṇa; and then Śatrughna, who is powerful in every way.
This high-minded one shall attain the renown of "Raghunātha."
O friend, the face of that powerful one, whose names are infinite and who is free from passion, is as beautiful as the interior of a lotus bud,
with long eyes resembling lotuses.
Her nose was prominent, broad, and charming;
her eyebrows were beautiful, well-proportioned, and lovely; and her arms were enchanting, reaching down to her knees. 35.
His neck is short and as beautiful as a conch shell; his chest is broad like the surface of a fine door-panel, stainless and marked with auspicious signs. 36.
His pair of stainless knees, endowed with the beauty of lovely thighs and hips,
is always attended by all his own lotus-feet.
I have served the most beautiful Lord of the Raghus (Rāma). Though Rāma assumes this form, how can he be fully described even by me?
Even one with a hundred faces cannot reach [the end of describing him], so what need be said of birds like us? 37-38.
Beholding whose form was graceful and captivating, Lakṣmī herself was infatuated; she who, when she appears on earth, causes even him who is not subject to delusion to be bewildered.
He possessed great strength, great heroism, and bore a form capable of causing great delusion.
How can I describe Śrī Rāma, who is endowed with all sovereign powers and virtues?
Blessed is that Goddess Jānakī, who assumes a form so intensely enchanting that she shall rejoice with him in joy for ten thousand years.
"O Kāśikī, who are you? By what name are you known, O beautiful one, that you thus inquire of me with such skill and devotion regarding the fame of Rāma?
Having heard these words, the pair of birds [addressed] Jānakī.
She spoke, describing her own enchanting birth:
"I am that very Janaki whom you mentioned; when the most handsome Rama comes and finds me, [he shall take me]. 43-44.
"Then I shall truly release you both; otherwise, enticed by my words, I shall dote upon you with pleasure while you remain in my lap, O sweet-eyed ones.
Having heard what was thus spoken, they trembled and were overcome with fear.
With their vigor mutually aroused, they spoke thus to Jānakī:
"We are indeed birds, virtuous ones who dwell in the forest and range among the trees;
we wander everywhere, for there is no happiness for us in a home."
"Having gone to my own place while pregnant, I shall give birth to sons and then return to your abode; this word spoken by me is the truth.
Having been addressed thus by her, she herself did not release the parrot.
Then her husband, free from anxiety, spoke to her with humility:
"Sītā, release my charming wife;
how can you keep her? Let us go and wander happily together in the forest."
"My beautiful wife is pregnant; O auspicious one, after bringing her to term, I shall return to you.
Having been addressed thus, she said to him, "Go happily, O high-minded one."
"I shall protect this happy woman, who does what is dear to me, by my side.
Having been addressed thus, the bird, filled with compassion, spoke to her in distress:
"Indeed, these words spoken by the yogis are truly so."
"It must not be spoken, it must not be spoken; let us remain resorting to silence.
Otherwise, like a mad elephant, he will strike the tethering post with the fault of his own words. (54) "And if we do not speak a word here against the cowherd..."
"How could there be imprisonment for us? Therefore, one should practice silence.
Having said this, he replied to her: "O beautiful one, I do not live without this wife, Sītā; therefore, release her, O charming lady. (55-56)
Then, having been addressed with many kinds of words by her,
the wife, enraged and distressed, cursed the daughter of Janaka:
"Just as you separate me from my husband here, [so shall it be for you]."
"Even so, though separated from Rāma, she became pregnant.
When she had spoken thus, repeatedly pained by grief and filled with sorrow for her husband, her life-breaths departed out of misery. 58–59.
As she repeatedly remembered Rāma and spoke of him again and again, a celestial chariot arrived; having departed for heaven, the female bird shone brilliantly.
When she had died, her husband, the king of birds, was afflicted with grief.
Overcome by supreme anger, he fell into the Ganges in distress.
Likewise, O Rāma, in this city filled with people,
she has become agitated and deeply sorrowful due to separation from me because of my words.
Having spoken thus, he fell into the Ganges, which was beautified by its foam and clouds;
distressed, enraged, and terrified, he trembled due to separation from her,
and because of his anger, his sorrow, and his humiliation at the hands of Sītā.
Having attained the state of an outcaste, there was a washerman named Krodhana (64).
O best of the twice-born, that man who, through anger and committing wicked deeds against the great, would give up his own life, goes upon dying to the state of an outcaste (65).
O Brahmin, she was censured by the washerwoman because of her birth, and she was separated from him due to the washerman's curse; thus she went to the forest.
This which you asked regarding the daughter of Videha has been told to you.

Furthermore, hear another account here; listen as I relate it. (67) Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Washerwoman's Previous Birth," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* within the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. (57)
The fifty-eighth chapter. Śeṣa said:
Seeing Bharata unconscious, Raghunātha was deeply distressed.
He said this to the doorkeeper: "Bring Śatrughna to me quickly.
Having heard those words spoken, he brought Śatrughna in an instant to where his own brother Rāma was staying together with Bharata.
Seeing Bharata unconscious and Raghunātha distressed, he bowed down and, filled with grief, said: "What is this great and terrible calamity?
Then Rāma spoke these words, which were condemned by the world, as if they were the utterances of an outcaste.

He replied to that Śatrughna, who was serving at his feet: "O brother, listen to my words today; perform this with diligence and speed. (4-5) With his face cast down, his voice weak and faltering, and his body trembling, he spoke. (5)
Just as her stainless fame has spread across the earth like the Ganges, having heard these incomparable words of reproach regarding Sītā uttered by an outcaste,
I desire to abandon my own body, or indeed this Jānakī herself.
Having heard these words of Rāma, the slayer of enemies— the destroyer of foes—
fell to the earth in great distress, trembling violently. Regaining consciousness after a moment, he spoke to the Lord of the Raghus.
Śatrughna said:
"O Lord, why is this harsh thing being said regarding Jānakī by these heretics of wicked mind who are excluded from all dharma? (9)
The Ganges, which destroys all sins and removes misfortune, became censured and unfit to be accepted by those of the highest birth; yet she, who removes the sins of all the worlds,
was touched by sinful men while remaining worthy of contact for the virtuous.
"Alas! The sun rises in the world to illuminate the world;
yet it causes no harm to the owls for whom it holds no appeal.
Therefore, you should accept this blameless woman, the wife of a minister."
"O Śrī Rāmabhadra, out of compassion, please do as I say.
Having heard these words of the high-souled Śatrughna,
he spoke again and again that which had been said regarding Bharata.
Hearing those words of his brother, overwhelmed by a flood of sorrow,
he fell unconscious upon the ground like a tree severed at its roots.
Seeing his brother Śatrughna fallen, he was deeply afflicted with grief.
He said this to the doorkeeper: "Bring Lakṣmaṇa into my presence. Having gone to Lakṣmaṇa’s house, the doorkeeper delivered these words. (16) The doorkeeper said:
"O Master, Rāma is summoning you with speed. Having heard that summons from Rāmacandra,
he went swiftly and with great haste to that place where his sinless brother was.
Seeing Bharata unconscious and Śatrughna also unconscious,
the sorrowful [Vasiṣṭha] spoke these words to the grief-stricken Śrī Rāmacandra:
"O King, what is this terrible sight that is seen, such as this fainting and so forth?"
Then, O sinless one, as he was thus speaking of the primary cause of everything while expressing his hope,
the king quickly related the entire account from the beginning to Lakṣmaṇa, who was overwhelmed by a flood of sorrow.
Having heard those words of Sītā concerning her abandonment, Lakṣmaṇa sighed repeatedly and stood with his limbs paralyzed;
he trembled again and again while his brother stood motionless.
Seeing him speaking thus as if he were a man possessing nothing, Śoka, overcome with grief, said:
"What shall I do, standing upon this earth, stained by infamy? Afflicted by sorrow and fearing the world, I shall cast off this glorious body."
"Always eager to carry out my word, they were like brothers to me;
now, even they act with contrary speech due to fate.
Where shall I go? To whom shall I go? The kings here on earth will treat me with contempt."

"O kings, in former times, those born in Manu’s lineage were endowed with beauty and possessed of superior virtues; yet now that I have been born, all of that has become the opposite, for I am marked by ill-repute and am devoid of form. (26)
Seeing Rāmabhadra speaking thus, he steadied his profuse tears and, with a faltering voice, said:
"O Master, do not despair; how has your mind become so despondent?"
"O learned one, why do you not abandon Sītā, who is blameless? Let me call the washerman; I shall question him regarding her.
"How could that Jānakī, the best among women, have been blamed by you?"
By the force of your commands, not even a single person is being oppressed.
Therefore, act in such a way that he may have confidence in his own mind; for what reason is this timid woman, devoted solely to her husband's vows, being abandoned?
The daughter of Janaka knows no other through mind or speech;
therefore, accept her, do not abandon this Janaki.
Having shown compassion toward me, quickly take refuge in what I have said.
To him who was speaking thus, Rāma, emaciated by grief,
replied, seeking to awaken Lakṣmaṇa with words of dharma and relinquishing his resolve.
Rāma said:

"How can you speak thus to me? Do not abandon me, who am blameless. Even if I were a sinner, I would abandon my life out of fear of public scandal; for the sake of my own reputation, I shall cast off this wretched body."
I shall even abandon you, my brother, if you are censured by public opinion;
how much more so other houses, sons, friends, and beautiful wealth?
For the sake of my own fame, I would renounce everything—why then not Maithilī?
Neither my dear brother, nor my wife, nor my kinsmen are as beloved to me as this stainless fame, renowned throughout the world. Now, it is certain that the washerman is no longer to be questioned.
In time, everything will come to pass; the coloring of the world-mind is like a disease that cannot be cured on earth except through the ripening of time and medicine. (39–40)
"Thus, at this opportune time, do not delay;
either abandon this virtuous woman in the forest, or strike me with your sword.
Having heard these words spoken, he then became greatly distressed.
And Lakṣmaṇa, emaciated by grief, reflected within his heart:
"The son of Jamadagni, though commanded by his father, even killed his own mother; for the command of a guru must never be transgressed, whether it be right or wrong in every respect. (42-43)
"Therefore, desiring to do what is pleasing to Rāma, I shall indeed abandon her.
Having reflected thus in his mind, he spoke to his brother.
Lakṣmaṇa said:
"Even if it were an improper act, one must never transgress the command of a superior;
therefore, O you of virtuous vows, I shall do whatever word you speak.
To Lakṣmaṇa, who was speaking thus, he replied:
"Excellent, excellent! O one of great wisdom, you have pleased my mind.
This very night, Jānakī has a longing to see female ascetics;
under that pretext, place her in the chariot and release her into the great forest."
Having heard these words, his face completely parched, he went to his own residence weeping and shedding a stream of tears.
Then, having summoned Sumantra, he spoke these words to him. 48.
"Prepare a chariot, O Kuru, adorned with the finest horses.
Having heard those words, he then brought the chariot.
Seeing that the chariot had been brought, Lakṣmaṇa was overcome with grief. 49-50.
Having reached a state of supreme distress, he climbed onto his excellent chariot and,
sighing deeply, set out for Jānakī’s residence accompanied by his brother and his attendants.
Having entered the inner apartments, the brother [beheld] Rāma’s wife, the daughter of Mithilā.
Sighing and overwhelmed by a flood of sorrow, he replied with these words:
"O Mother, Janaki has been sent to your dwelling by Rama; you must go to the female ascetics for the sake of obtaining the object of her longing."
Having heard these words of Lakṣmaṇa, the daughter of Videha was filled with supreme joy and replied to Lakṣmaṇa. Jānakī said:
Blessed am I, Queen Maithilī, who remembers the feet of Rāma; for the sake of fulfilling her pregnancy longing, he sent Lakṣmaṇa [to me].
Today, I shall see those forest-dwelling female ascetics who regard their husbands as deities.
"I shall pay homage and worship these enchanting ones with garments.
Having said this, he offered beautiful clothes, highly precious ornaments,
gems, pure pearls, and fragrant substances such as camphor.

Desiring to please her beloved, Sītā’s consort took up thousands of various items, such as sandalwood and other fragrances; having taken them all, she repeatedly placed them into the hands of her maidservants. 58.
As she was going toward Lakṣmaṇa, she then stumbled at the threshold.
Without reflecting on that, out of eagerness for her beloved’s sake, she said to Lakṣmaṇa: "Where is the chariot by which you will take me?"
Sighing deeply, he entered the golden chariot together with Jānakī;
then, addressing Sumantra, he said, "Drive the horses, which are as swift as thought. At Lakṣmaṇa’s word, he summoned the well-prepared chariot.
Seeing Lakṣmaṇa with his face bathed in tears again and again,
[the charioteer] struck the horses with a whip;
yet when the horses did not move on the path, he then spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
Sumantra said:
"O Master, the draft animals move not even when urged with effort; I do not know what to do or what the cause is for the failure of the vehicle."
To him who was speaking thus, Lakṣmaṇa, his voice faltering, replied:
"O charioteer, summoning your courage, strike them with whips and the like!
Having heard these words spoken, the driver somehow managed to move [the chariot] along.
Then Jānakī’s right eye throbbed, foreboding sorrow;
at that very moment, grief arose in her heart, signaling misery;
and at that same instant, even the auspicious birds began to wheel about.
Having observed her thus, Vaidehī then replied to her brother-in-law:
"O descendant of Raghu, why do you wish to go for the sake of practicing asceticism? May there be great prosperity for Rāma, and likewise for his younger brother Bharata."
"May all misfortunes and adversities for those subjects everywhere cease to exist.
Seeing Jānakī speaking thus, he, along with Lakṣmaṇa, said nothing; his throat was choked and he was overwhelmed with tears.
Seeing deer approaching and turning to the left—a sign that portends a mass of suffering—he spoke:
"Today the deer are turning to my left; this is not desired. (71)
"For a woman departing after leaving the feet of Śrī Rāma, this was indeed appropriate;
for the supreme duty of women is the worship of their husband's feet. For me, departing elsewhere after leaving those feet, whatever may happen is indeed appropriate. (72-73)
While she was thus reflecting on the path in accordance with the ultimate truth,
the goddess Jāhnavī, who is uniquely served by hosts of sages, appeared to her; in her,
the waves of water were seen to resemble milk.
Where the waves are seen bearing the very form of a staircase to heaven;
by the touch of whose water-drops the accumulation of great sins flees away, seeking no place for itself anywhere around.
Then, having reached the Gaṅgā, the son of Sumitrā spoke to Jānakī, who was seated in the chariot: "O Sītā, come down from the chariot to the ground," as his tears flowed forth.
Hearing those words, Sītā descended instantly.
Held by Lakṣmaṇa by the arm, she stumbled along the path due to its thorns. 78.

Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "Jānakī’s Vision of the Gaṅgā," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. 58.
Chapter Fifty-nine. Śeṣa said:
Then, having crossed the Gaṅgā by boat, Lakṣmaṇa [proceeded].
Taking Jānakī by the hand, he went to the forest from the opposite bank. As she walked along the path, her face quickly became parched;
her beautiful feet were wounded by thorns, and she stumbled at every step.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, carrying out the command of Rāghava, caused her to enter that most terrible forest which brings such sorrow;
there, the trees were most fearsome— arbūlas, khadiras, and ghanas.
There, *śleṣmātaka* and *ciñciṇīkā* trees were scorched by the fire of the dried-up forest;
great serpents dwelling in their hollows hissed, being greatly provoked to anger,
while owls, terrifying to the minds of people, shrieked there.
Tigers, lions, jackals, and extremely terrifying leopards are seen there,
as well as straightforward man-eaters who are prone to sudden anger; there are also buffaloes and wicked boars distinguished by their two tusks.
Arrogant with pride, they cause torment to the minds of living beings. Beholding such a forest, her fever of fear subsided;
though her feet were bitten by thorns, she spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa.
Jānakī said:
"I do not see the hermitages frequented by heroic sages and seers that grant delight to the eyes, nor do I see their wives, who are rich in ascetic merit. (9)
I see only terrible birds and withered trees;
this entire forest is being consumed by a forest fire.
And I see you, afflicted by grief, your eyes clouded and filled with tears.
"May thousands other than Śakuni arise at every step for me! O foremost of heroes, tell me that: how was that evil-hearted one swiftly released by the high-souled Rāma? Tell me that quickly."
Having heard these words, Lakṣmaṇa, emaciated by grief and with his face choked with tears, said nothing at that time.
Accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, she proceeded toward that very same formidable forest.
Again she beheld the face of the hero, who had been struck down and was afflicted by suffering; even then, eager to see him, he spoke something to her as she bowed before him,
and she questioned him with extreme persistence.
When Lakṣmaṇa was questioned with persistence by Sītā,
his throat choked and grieving repeatedly, he spoke of the cause of her abandonment.
O best of sages, having heard those words, which were like a thunderbolt—
With her roots severed by the axe of scandal, she became devoid of all support;
at that very moment, fearing that Rāma might not abandon this sinful Sītā, the Earth did not accept her as her daughter. 17–18.
Seeing Vaidehī fallen there, the son of Sumitrā became anxious; he then restored her consciousness with the breeze from the tips of the young shoots.
Having regained her senses, she spoke these words: "O Lord, please smile."
"How can the scion of the Raghus abandon me, who am free from sin?
Having lamented thus at length, she beheld Lakṣmaṇa, who was overcome with grief; then, fainting and deeply distressed, she fell upon the ground.
Regaining consciousness after a mere moment, she, overwhelmed by suffering and wounded by grief for her beloved, spoke to Rāma’s feet:
"How could the great and highly intelligent Lord of the Raghus abandon me?"

"How could that great hero, who crossed the ocean for my sake accompanied by monkeys, abandon me—though I am sinless—merely because of the words of a washerman? Here, it is surely my own destiny that has turned against me. (23-24)
Speaking thus, the daughter of Videha fell once more into a swoon; seeing her unconscious, he then wept with a piteous voice.
Having regained consciousness again, she spoke thus to the son of Sumitrā:
Beholding him afflicted by suffering with his throat choked, she, deeply distressed, said:
"O son of Sumitrā, go to Rāma, the embodiment of dharma and the treasury of glory;
speak these very words of mine in the presence of that storehouse of asceticism."

Why indeed have you abandoned me, even though you know I am a sinner? Is this consistent with your lineage, or is it the fruit of your knowledge of the scriptures? (28) For I am constantly devoted to your feet and eat only what remains from your meals.
Your honor has abandoned all of that; indeed, fate alone is the cause here.
O best among the foremost of heroes, may all prosperity be yours everywhere. As for me, I shall sustain my life in the forest by remembering you.

O Lord of the Earth, through mind, deed, and speech, may you alone be my supreme husband; all others have been rendered insignificant by my mind, O scion of Raghu’s lineage. In birth after birth, may you alone be my lord.
"O Lord of the unchaste women whose many sins were destroyed by the remembrance of your feet, tell all my message to your mother-in-law, O best of the Raghus;
that virtuous woman has been abandoned by Rāma on this most terrible earth, though she is free from sin. (32-33)
I remember your feet in the forest filled with herds of deer, when you, that great-souled one, abandoned the grove because it was inhabited by pregnant animals.
O Saumitri, listen to my words; may all be well with the best of the Raghus.
Now, while carefully guarding the prowess of Rāma, you may even sacrifice your life.
Whatever truthful word of Rāma you perform for your own welfare must be carried out by one who serves the lotus feet of Rāma, being dependent upon Him.
"Go to the presence of Rāma; may your paths be auspicious.
You must show compassion toward me, and I must be remembered by you from time to time.
Having spoken thus, she then fell unconscious upon the ground before him.

Seeing Jānakī unconscious, Lakṣmaṇa was overcome with grief; he fanned her with the edges of his garment until she regained consciousness, and then the son of Sumitrā repeatedly consoled her with sweet words.
Lakṣmaṇa said: "I am going to Rāma; having gone there, I shall report everything to him. Near you is the great hermitage of the sage Vālmīki."
Having spoken thus, he circumambulated her, distressed and filled with tears;
shedding a stream of tears from grief, he went toward King Rāma.
Seeing his brother-in-law departing, Jānakī’s eyes were wide with astonishment.
"This illustrious brother-in-law of mine, Lakṣmaṇa, is laughing!
How could Rāghava have abandoned me, who am sinless and dearer to him than his own life?
Thinking thus, she gazed at him with unblinking eyes.
Knowing that Jāhnavī had completely crossed over, that her own destruction was certain,
she then fell into a swoon, reaching a state where her life was in danger.
Then I, with my two wings, brought water from all sides.
A sweet breeze, fragrant with the scent of flowers, blew;
and elephants arrived from all sides, as if to wash their dust-covered bodies with their trunks filled with water. 45–46.
The deer, having reached his presence, stood there with eyes wide in wonder;
even the trees, though devoid of spring at that time, became laden with flowers. While this was occurring, the virtuous woman regained her consciousness.
Afflicted by intense sorrow, she lamented, crying out, "Rāma! Rāma!
(48). "Alas, O Lord, friend of the distressed, O embodiment of compassion, why do you abandon me here in the forest, even though I am free from any offense? (49)
Speaking thus and lamenting again and again,
looking here and there, and fainting repeatedly—
then the venerable Vālmīki arrived at the forest accompanied by his own disciples.
There he heard weeping uttered in a piteous tone;
then he addressed his disciples: "Look into the middle of the forest!
Who is this crying out with a voice of distress in this most terrible wilderness?"
Dispatched by the sage, they went to where Jānakī was, crying out "Rāma, Rāma! while overwhelmed by a flood of tears. Upon seeing that woman, they approached the sage Vālmīki with great eagerness.

Having heard those words spoken by him, that sage then departed. Seeing him—a mass of asceticism, an embodiment of the Vedas, and a treasury of vows—the goddess Jānakī, whose deity is her husband, exclaimed: "Salutations to the sage! 54-55.
To Sītā, who had spoken thus, he greeted her with blessings:
"May you live long with your husband; may you obtain two handsome sons. "Who are you? Why have you come to this terrible forest? Why are you in such a state?"
"May you know everything that is the cause of my suffering. Then Rāma’s wife,
sighing with compassion and her voice trembling, replied to the sage.
Listen to my words, which speak the truth regarding the cause of all suffering:
know me to be a servant of Aghunātha, the lord of the earth.
I do not know the reason why I was abandoned there without any offense.
"By the command of Rāghava, Lakṣmaṇa has gone there leaving me behind.
Having said this, Vālmīki spoke to the lotus-eyed Jānakī, consoling her as she bore a lotus-face filled with a flood of tears.

"Know me, O Vaidehī, to be the sage Vālmīki, the preceptor of your father; do not grieve, for come to my hermitage. Know the house of your father to be in a different place, O you who hold your husband as a deity."
"O Lord of the Earth, let there be no anger toward him for such an act.
Having heard these words, she whose deity is the husband of Janaki,
her face filled with tears of sorrow, obtained a measure of comfort.
Śeṣa said:
Having consoled her, whose eyes were agitated by a flood of grief, Vālmīki led her to his own holy hermitage, which was filled with throngs of female ascetics. 65.
Following behind that treasure-house of asceticism, Vālmīki,
she shone as beautiful as the starry Vaitaraṇī following the moon.
And Vālmīki, having reached his own hermitage filled with sages, [saw her].
She informed the female ascetics that Jānakī had gone to her own hermitage.
The high-minded Vaidehī paid homage to all the female ascetics, and they, greatly delighted, engaged in mutual embraces.
Vālmīki, that treasure-house of asceticism, replied to his own disciples:
"Alas! Let a beautiful leaf-hut be constructed for Jānakī.
Having heard these most pleasing words spoken by Vālmīki, [they acted accordingly].
With leaves and wood, he constructed a most beautiful hall;
there the princess of Videha, devoted to her husband, resided, subsisting on fruits while performing service for Vālmīki.
Mentally and verbally chanting "Rāma, Rāma" herself,
Janakī, who held her husband as her deity, passed her days there. In due time, she gave birth to two sons of enchanting form.
"O Rāmacandra, you two are like the twin Aśvins, and Jānakī is like Sūryā.
Hearing that news of the birth of Jānakī's son, the sage was delighted; being the most skilled in mantras, he performed the *jātakarma* and other purificatory rites.
The sage Vālmīki performed his religious rites with *kuśa* and *lava* grass;
hence the names of his two sons became clearly known as Kuśa and Lava.
Wherever Vālmīki performed that auspicious and stainless rite, [it was established].
Her lotus-like eyes became exceedingly joyful.
On that day, having slain Lavaṇa with a small force of soldiers, Śatrughna arrived at the hermitage of Vālmīki during the beautiful night.
Then Śatrughna, instructed by Vālmīki, praised the leader of the Raghus, saying:
"I shall describe before you the two sons of Janakī. There, the two sons of Janakī grew up, delightful to the mind.
When they had grown strong on bulbs, roots, and fruits, the two excellent youths became intoxicated with vigor;
like the moon and the flower, beautiful to behold, they were consecrated by time and, having received the sacred thread ceremony, became truly enchanting.

Having initiated his two sons, the sage taught them the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches (*aṅga*), and he instructed Rāma in the science of archery (*dhanurveda*) together with its secret doctrines (*rahasya*); furthermore,
Vālmīki presented him with two bows beautifully adorned with gold.

Then, he gave to the two sons of Jānakī quivers filled with arrows, inexhaustible swords, and impenetrable shields— [swords] possessing indivisible and supreme qualities for the destruction of hosts of enemies. 82–83.
The two archers, masters of the science of weaponry (dhanurveda), moved joyfully about the hermitage and shone there like the two beautiful Aśvins;
seeing these two excellent sons bearing swords and shields, Jānakī [was filled with joy].
Overcome with supreme joy, she did not abandon the grief born of separation.
O Brahmin, this birth of Jānakī’s son has been told to you;
now hear what occurred regarding the lopping off of Vīra’s arms.

Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Birth of Kuśa and Lava," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana within the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padmapurāṇa*.
Chapter Sixty.
Śeṣa said:
Beholding the severed arms of his own warriors, Śatrughna, deeply distressed and with his lips bitten in rage, spoke to them. 1.
"O sirs, why did you not cut off the arms of that hero? O soldiers, I shall now cut off the arms of this man who is protected by the gods.
That great fool does not know the mighty power of Rāmacandra."
Now I shall demonstrate my own strength through valor:
Where is that hero? Where is the charming horse? And what fool, knowing his prowess, has seized sleeping serpents? 3-4.
Having heard this, the heroes were astonished and deeply distressed;
they praised the boy who was the representative of Rāmacandra.
Hearing that the horse had been seized by the boy, his eyes became copper-red with rage.
Desirous of battle, he commanded Vaikartana, the conqueror of time, who was the commander-in-chief:
"By my command, marshal the entire army;
the enemy, possessed of great strength and prowess, must now be encountered."
"This boy cannot surely be Hari, the steed-bearer;
or perhaps he is the enemy of Tripura, for otherwise my pride would not have been taken away. A great slaughter of my powerful army is certain to occur."
"Playing with his own will, the thief-like child moves about with a fearless mind.
Having heard these words of Śatrughna, the commander of the army [replied]: "We must go there, fully prepared and invincible to our enemies. 9-10.
He prepared that fourfold army, which was poorly arrayed;
seeing it ready and excellent, consisting of the four divisions, Śatrughna then ordered it to go to where the boy Hayaṃdhara was.
Then that army, endowed with its four divisions,
marched forth, shaking the regions of the earth and terrifying the enemies by its might;
then the commander beheld that boy in the form of Rāma.
Reflecting upon Rāma, he spoke these beneficial words: "Release the excellent horse of the powerful Rāma, O child! [Thus spoke] the haughty Kālajit, the commander-in-chief of that king.
"Seeing you, who are equal to Rāma, compassion arises in my heart. Otherwise, due to your misfortune, my life would not continue. Having heard these words of the soldier Śatrughna—
With a slight show of anger, he spoke these extraordinary words:
"Go, O messenger, and tell the white-horsed Rāma what has been said;
I do not fear you, O hero, for your words are full of statesmanship."
If there were as many crores of people here as there are grains of sand in the Ganges,
they would undoubtedly become like cotton-wool through the grace of my mother's feet,
O conqueror of time, by means of your name alone which is so pleasing to the mind.
Like a ripe bimba fruit in color but not in strength, display now your power, marked by the might of your own name. Having conquered me, who am like Death, you shall become one whose name is true.
Śeṣa said:
Pierced by words equal to thunderbolts, that crest-jewel of great warriors became exceedingly enraged in his heart and spoke these words again.

"In what family were you born, and what is your name, O child? I do not know your name, nor your lineage, your character, or your age. How can I, standing in a chariot, conquer one who moves on foot through unrighteousness? (22)
Then, extremely incensed, he spoke these words again:
"What is the use of lineage, conduct, or even a heart-stealing name?
I am Lava; I shall conquer all the enemy soldiers, who are themselves like mere blades of grass."
"Now I shall make even you a foot-soldier," having spoken thus, the powerful one strung his bow with a *lava* measure of effort;
he then caused it to ring out, making the heroes tremble in their hearts.
First remembering Vālmīki and then his mother Jānakī, Lava immediately released sharp arrows that snatch away life. Kālajit, filled with rage, fixed his bow with a string.
The younger brother of Kuśa, who was skilled in battle, swiftly cut those arrows into a hundred pieces with speed, and in an instant,
deprived the commander of his chariot with eight of his own excellent shafts.
Deprived of his chariot, he was brought by his own warriors and mounted an elephant that was intoxicated with rut,
possessed of great speed, and exuding ichor from seven streams. Seeing him mounted upon the elephant, [the opponent struck] him with ten arrows discharged from bows.
Laughing, the victorious one pierced all the hosts of enemies with arrows;
and Kālajit, his mind struck with wonder upon seeing his prowess,
hurled a massive mace fashioned from great iron.
With his arrows,
Lakṣmaṇa swiftly cut into three pieces that mace, fashioned from ten thousand bhāras,
as it came flying with great force; he also shattered the sharp and terrible iron club said to take the lives of enemies.
Lava, filled with impetuosity, again swiftly cut down that [missile];
having severed that terrible iron club, he, with eyes bloodshot with rage, became enraged as he perceived [the opponent] mounted upon the elephant's back. 34.
At that very moment, he swiftly severed the trunk of that elephant with his sword; then,
grasping the two tusks with his feet, he climbed onto the head of the elephant,
shattering the crown into a hundred pieces and the armor into a thousand.
Having seized the commander by the hair, he threw him down upon the ground; once thrown from the back of his elephant, the commander, filled with rage,
struck him again on the chest with a fist as hard as a thunderbolt.
Striking with his fists, he who held his bow drawn into a circle quickly released sharp, razor-edged arrows at the heart [of his foe] on the edge of the battlefield,
his bow encircled. 38–39.
Wearing a helmet and armor impenetrable even by millions of arrows,
he took up his sword to slay him, though he was pierced by sharp shafts;
biting his own teeth in rage, he sighed and gasped repeatedly.

As the heroic general approached with sword in hand, Lava cut off his arm; the hand, still clutching the sword, fell down. Seeing his hand severed while holding the blade, the commander of the army was filled with rage.
With his left arm, he attempted to strike him with a mace;
however, that arm of his, along with its armlet, was severed by sharp arrows.
Then the enraged hero struck Lava with both his feet.
Struck by Lava's foot, he did not stir on the field of battle; though struck by the garland like an elephant, he performed a severing of the foot.
Then, with his head, he began to strike him back.
Then, regarding him as the lord of the army and one of supreme prowess,
he took up a sword resembling the fire of cosmic destruction in his hand and severed his head, which was adorned with a great crown.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose when the commander of the army was struck down.
The soldiers, filled with rage, rushed forward to kill Lava; but Lava, with the blows of his own arrows, rendered them intent on flight. 47–48.
Some with their limbs severed or mangled departed from the field of battle, while others,

The earth, filled with pearls produced from the temples of elephants split open, became impassable for the foremost warriors, as if it were covered by mountains. The horses, beautiful with golden saddles and resplendent with jewels, [shone forth]. 50–51.
Splashed with blood and adorned by their fallen bodies,
the chariot-warriors, graced by the staffs of their bows held in their hands,
lay upon the floorboards of their chariots like gods bound for heaven. 52.

With their faces marked by the beauty of their rolling eyes and their lips bitten together, the heroes skilled in battle were seen fallen there; a river of blood flowed, with the heads of horses for its turtles. 53–54.

Causing fear to those who sported in the great torrent, the arms of some were severed, the feet of others were cut off; the ears and noses of some were gone, as were the armor and earrings of others. 55.
Thus, when the commander had fallen in battle, a great slaughter occurred;
all the heroes fell, though some remained alive.
Then Lava, having attained victory in the fray and having conquered the host of his enemies, [remained].
Fearing the arrival of others, he did not look back;
some who had survived the battle by chance went to Śatrughna’s presence to report the wonderful event. 58.
Having gone there, they related exactly what had occurred on the field of battle:
the death of Kālajit by the boy and the extraordinary prowess in combat.
Upon hearing this, Śatrughna was filled with wonder and spoke to them.
Laughing in anger, he bit his teeth while remembering the horse Bālagrāha, saying:
"O sons of Revā, are you intoxicated with pride, or are you practitioners of deception?
Or has some calamity occurred; how could Kālajit have died?"
"How could a mere child conquer him, who is as fierce as a multitude of countless enemies and victorious in battle, and who is difficult even for Yama to approach?
Hearing these words of Śatrughna, the heroes, drenched in blood, spoke.
"O King, know this as the truth: our defeat was not due to intoxication with pride or any such trickery, nor was it through divine intervention; rather, our death at the hands of Time was inevitable.
Our entire army has been crushed by that boy of incomparable prowess. (64)
"Therefore, O best of men, whatever task must be done hereafter,
you servants should know me to be a child and not commit any act of forceful violence.
Having heard these words of those heroes, the slayer of enemies then [acted].
He spoke to Sumati, the best of the wise, regarding the cause for his departure. 67.

Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Death of the Commander-in-Chief Kālajit at the Time of the Defeat of the Army in the Battle between Kuśa and Lava" within the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. 60.
The sixty-first chapter.
Śatrughna said:
"Do you know, O great minister, which boy seized the horse?"
"By whom has this entire army, resembling the ocean, been destroyed?
Sumati said:
"O Lord, this is the great hermitage of Vālmīki, the best of sages."
O scorcher of enemies, there is no place for Kṣatriyas to dwell here.
Either Indra will become extremely enraged and seize this horse, or perhaps the enemy,
or someone else on your side, will take it away.
Since the most terrible Kālajit has met his destruction by him, Śrī Mahārāja Puṣkala will go against him from here, surrounded by all you heroes, warriors, and kings. 4.
And you [should follow], surrounded by all the heroic soldiers and kings.
Go there with a great army, O destroyer of enemies! Having gone and bound that heroic Sajīva, I shall show him to Rāma, who desires to see him; this is my firm resolve.
Having heard these words, he commanded all the heroes: "Come with a great army; I shall follow behind you. Thus directed, those heroes arrived in an instant where the powerful Lava was.
There, stretching his bow which was firmly strung with a cord,
and seeing that great force approaching filled with heroes,
the powerful Lava did not fear anything in his mind.
Lava, like a lion, sprang up, perceiving all the warriors to be deer;
stretching his bow in rage, he discharged arrows by the thousands. Being tormented by those arrows, they were filled with great fury.
Then, considering themselves to be heroes, they rushed forward to face him.
Seeing thousands of warriors surrounded by whirlwinds, Lava, filled with rage, fixed his arrows with great speed.
The first [encirclement] was with a thousand warriors, the second with a number of ten thousand,
the third with two tens of thousands, the fourth with five tens of thousands, the fifth with a hundred thousand warriors, and the sixth with more than ten thousand warriors.
Surrounded by seven whirlpools consisting of seven pairs of lakṣas [of yojanas],
with an *ilāvarta* region pervading the center, it then moved like fire and utterly consumed all the soldiers who had created those whirlpools. 14–15.
One was struck by swords, another by arrows, another by spears, some by *kuṇtala* weapons, and others by *paṭṭiśas* and iron clubs; all were shattered by the high-souled one.
Released from seven whirlpools, the king of the Rākṣasas, along with his younger brother Kuśa, [remained].
Like the moon released from a mass of clouds at the arrival of autumn,
he struck the warriors in every way, piercing many elephant trunks,
and severing the great heads and brows of heroes with his discus.
Afflicted by Lava’s arrows, many fallen heroes fainted in the battle;
some were destroyed, while others were cowardly. The army, tormented by Lava’s shafts, was intent on flight.
Seeing Vīra, the one named Puṣkala went forth to fight him;
saying "Stay! Stay! with eyes filled with rage, the powerful one, standing in his chariot adorned with fine horses, advanced against Lava.
Then Puṣkala, the supreme knower of weapons, replied to Śalava:
"Stay here on this chariot of mine, which is adorned with excellent horses;
how can I fight with you on foot in this battle?"
"Therefore, stay behind on the chariot; I shall fight with you.
Having heard these words, that son of Lava spoke to Puṣkala:
"Standing on the chariot given by you, I shall engage in battle in the fray."
In that case, there would be only sin for us, for victory is indeed uncertain.
O hero, we brahmins are not intent upon accepting gifts;
rather, we are kshatriyas who are constantly devoted to the performance of acts of giving.
"Now, out of anger, I shall break your chariot; day after day you shall indeed travel on foot, and only afterwards will you engage in battle.
Having heard these words of Puṣkala, which were endowed with righteousness and fortitude, [he replied].
Wondrously amazed for a long time in his mind, he then strung his bow.
Seeing him with the bow taken up, Lava, filled with rage,
cut the bow held in his hand while aiming an arrow.
To whatever extent he drew his bow with its string, to that same extent the powerful one acted with arrogance;
laughing in the battle, he shattered the other's chariot.
Seeing his own chariot broken and his bow severed by the high-souled one, [he was struck with wonder].
Considering himself a great hero, he fled on foot in the battle;
both were heroic archers, both were covered with arrows, both were drenched in blood, and both had their armor shattered.
With their bodies marked by wounds from each other's arrows,
desiring victory and seeking to slay one another,
they fought like Jayanta and Kārttikeya against the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva).
Thus engaged in mutual combat upon the field of battle,
Puṣkala then replied to Bāla: "O crest-jewel of heroes, no one like you, a crown-jewel among warriors, has ever been seen by me."
"Today I shall strike down your head with my sharp-jointed arrows;
do not flee from the battle, but protect your life with self-restraint.
Having spoken thus, he trapped the heroic Lava within a cage of arrows.
Puṣkala’s arrows remained stationed, pervading the sky and the field of battle.
Standing in the midst of that cage of arrows, Lava said to Puṣkala:
"O hero, you have performed a great feat, for you have afflicted me with your shafts. (36-37)
Having spoken thus, the hero, skilled in aiming his arrows, severed the mass of shafts and spoke again to Puṣkala:
"Protect yourself while standing in battle, for you will be afflicted by the impact of my arrows."
"You shall fall upon the surface of the earth, drenched in blood.
Having heard these words, Puṣkala, filled with rage,
engaged the mighty hero Lava in battle.
Enraged, Lava seized from his quiver a sharp arrow capable of rending enemies,
like a venomous serpent in its fury;
that blazing shaft was then released by Lava from his bow.
Intent on piercing his heart, he was swiftly cut down by Bhāratī with an arrow that takes away life.
When he had been struck by Bhāratī’s life-destroying arrow,
he became exceedingly enraged and took up another terrible shaft.
A sharp arrow, released from a bow drawn back to the ear, pierced the heart of that Puṣkala in the great battle. With his chest thus pierced by the hero with a swift-moving shaft, [he fell].
The crest-jewel of great heroes fell upon the surface of the earth.
Seeing that Puṣkala had fallen, the son of the Wind-god took him up, though he was overcome by fainting, and gave him to his brother, the descendant of Raghu. 45–46.
Beholding him unconscious, his mind overwhelmed with grief and filled with rage, he commanded Hanumān to slay Lava.
Enflamed by anger, Hanumān [confronted] the exceedingly powerful Lava in battle.

Raising a śālmali tree, the powerful Hanumān rushed forward with speed to conquer Lava; he struck him on the head with the tree. As Lava was charging with force, Hanumān cut him into a hundred pieces.
Not becoming angry again even though his arm was severed, the one of great strength uprooted trees from their very foundations and struck him on the chest and the head;
whatever trees the son of the Wind-god brought forth, he used them to strike him.
The powerful one swiftly cut them down with his straight-jointed arrows.
Then the monkey Māruti, uprooting boulders resembling great crags, hurled them with great speed at his head.
Struck by masses of rocks, he raised his single bow and pulverized them with his arrows, as if they were mustard seeds from mechanical devices.
Then, the son of the Wind-god became exceedingly enraged at the binding of his tail.
The skillful and powerful son of the Wind-god, having performed his ritual ablutions at the conclusion of the sacrifice,
saw his own tail being pulled by the mighty Lavasura; remembering his mother in his heart, the strong one struck the monkey-tailed demon with his fist.
Stricken by the pain of that fist-blow, Māruti released him;
once released, he became powerful in battle as he discharged arrows from his tail.
With his body tormented by the irresistible impact of those arrows, the monkey—
Perceiving the heavy rain of arrows in battle as unbearable, he thought:
"What should be done by us from this point? If we flee, then shame would strike me; here, my young master would strike me. (57-58)
"Because of the boon granted by Brahmā, there is no fainting or death for you;
however, the pain from this unbearable arrow—what should I do now?
Let Śatrughna go to the battlefield and obtain victory over Bālaka."
Desiring to conquer his pride, he lay down in a feigned swoon;
having thus resolved in his mind,
he fell upon the field of battle under the pretext of fainting, while all the heroes were looking on.
Perceiving that the mighty Hanumān had fainted, he,
who was skilled in the discharge of arrows, struck all the kings.
Thus ends the [section] in the *Śrī Padma Purāṇa*, in the *Pātālakhaṇḍa*, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana, in the *Rāmāśvamedha*.
The sixty-first chapter, titled "The Leaping of Hanumān.
Chapter Sixty-Two. Śeṣa said:
Hearing that Māruti had fainted, Śatrughna was overcome with grief, thinking:
"What must I do? This child is exceedingly powerful. Standing himself upon a golden chariot along with his foremost heroes, he [proceeded].
Lava, skilled in diverse modes of combat, went forth to fight where he was.
He beheld Lava, who had attained the state of childhood like Rāma upon the earth,
holding bow and arrow in hand and casting down the heroes at the front of the battle.
Then he who had assumed the form of Rāma reflected:
"He who bears a body as dark as the petal of a blue lotus and is so captivating must be the son of the daughter of Videha; it cannot be otherwise."
Having defeated us in battle, he will depart like the king of beasts;
victory must belong to us whose souls are devoid of power.
Being powerless, what shall we do in battle, even though we are skilled in the art of war?
Having reflected thus, he then spoke these words to the boy,
who was causing a spectacle of battle and felling millions of heroes to the earth:
"Who are you, that you cause our heroes to fall upon the ground in this battle?"
Do you not know the power of King Rāma, the destroyer of the sons of Danu?
Who is your mother, who is your father, and what fortunate man has won you as his wife?
What is your name, renowned in the world, O one of great strength, that I might know it?
"O Munjavaha, how can you be bound? Because of your youth, I forgive this;
come and see Rama, and he will grant you much.
Thus addressed, the heroic boy spoke these words to Shatrughna:
"What is the use of that name, or of your father, or of such a state of youth? (11) Fight in battle, O hero, if you possess strength!
Having bowed at the feet of the heroic Kuśa, go; not otherwise! (12)
"O hero, brother of Rāma, you are not the strongest among us;
release my horse by force if you have the power!
Having said this, the formidable one fixed an arrow and struck him.
On his heart, head, and both arms, within the circle of his chariot,
the king then became enraged and strung his bow,
making it sound as deep as a thundercloud as if to terrify the boy.
The best among the strong released countless arrows, but Bāla,
by his own strength, cut down all those volleys of shafts.
The surface of the earth was covered by the many arrows discharged by Lava.
Like gifts bestowed during the *vyatīpāta* yoga, they became inexhaustible. Those arrows, released with a firm aim, pervaded the entire sky;
reaching the solar disc, they spread out in every direction. 17–18.
Where even the wind did not enter because it was within the range of the cage of arrows, what talk can there be of men who live for but a moment, proclaiming their own lives?
Seeing those widespread arrows, Śatrughna was filled with wonder.
Skilled in discharging hundreds of thousands of arrows,
the younger brother of Kuśa, seeing all those shafts of his cut down,
swiftly severed the bow of King Śatrughna.
As soon as he took up another bow and began to release his arrows, [the other] shattered that chariot with sharp-jointed shafts;
he cut down the very firm bow, which was already drawn to the string, from his hand.
The heroes stationed in the circle of the battlefield did not honor that deed.
With his bow broken, deprived of his chariot, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed,
Lava mounted another chariot and went forth to fight with force.
Pierced by many arrows, his body streaming with blood,
he shone in the midst of the battlefield like a blossoming *kiṃśuka* tree;
struck by Śatrughna’s arrows, he attained the highest state of fury.
Skilled in aiming his arrows and with his bow drawn into a circle, he rendered Śatrughna’s body—
its armor shattered, its head and crown severed,
and drenched and soaked in flowing blood.
Then Rāmānuja, enraged and extremely agitated, released ten sharp-pointed arrows capable of destroying life;
having cut those [arrows] into pieces as small as sesame seeds with his own sharp-jointed shafts.
He struck Śatrughna in the heart with eight arrows.
(29) Afflicted by the extreme pain of those shafts, yet remembering the powerful Lava and considering him difficult to overcome, he then continued discharging his own arrows. (30)
Then, pierced in the broad chest with a sharp arrow resembling a crescent moon, beautiful at its joints,
he was struck by that shaft and experienced a most terrible pain.
He fell upon the seat of his chariot, looking magnificent with the bow in his hand.
Seeing Śatrughna unconscious, King Suratha and the other monarchs then rushed toward Lava, intent on securing victory in the battle.
Suratha, Vimala, Vīra, King Vīramaṇi,
Sumada, Riputāpa, and others surrounded him in the battle;
some with razor-sharp arrows, some with clubs, and some with most dreadful shafts.
Some kings struck him from all sides with spears and axes;
seeing them eager for battle through unrighteous means, that crest-jewel of heroes struck each of them with ten arrows in the encounter.
Struck by that shower of arrows in the midst of the forest, some became enraged, some fled, and others were bewildered on the field of battle.
At that moment, King Śatrughna cast off his fainting spell in the fray.
Endowed with great strength, he approached the mighty hero Lava to fight him.
Having arrived, he said to Lava: "Blessed are you, appearing like a child;
yet you are not a child, but some god who has come to deceive me."
"O hero, I have never been struck down by anyone else at the gateway; yet you have brought me to a swoon right before my very eyes while I looked on.
Now behold my prowess; I shall cast you down in battle."
"O child, withstand even a single arrow; do not flee!
Having spoken thus in the battle, Lavaṇa took up a single arrow as terrible as the mouth of Yama, by which [the demon] was slain. 41-42.
Aiming an arrow that was fiercely blazing and capable of piercing the heart, he fixed his mind upon it— an arrow that, like fire, would always consume thousands of heroes.
That flaming arrow suddenly illuminated the ten directions.
Seeing the powerful Kuśa, the slayer of enemies, he thought:
"If at this very moment my heroic brother were here, strong as I am, then this terrible danger from Śatrughna would not come under my power."
While the high-souled Lava was thus reflecting,
a great and terrible arrow, resembling the fire of cosmic destruction, struck him in the heart; then that hero, struck by the king’s shafts, fell into a swoon.

[It was] adorned with the heads of all the heroes in the battle. 47. Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Fainting of Lava," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. 62.
The sixty-third chapter. Śeṣa said:
Having seen Lava, the destroyer of Bali’s enemies, rendered unconscious, [the gods...]

The mighty Śatrughna achieved victory at the head of the battle. Then, having placed Lava— the boy who was his very image of Rāma and adorned with a helmet and other ornaments— upon his chariot, he desired to depart.
Overwhelmed with grief because their own friend had been seized by the enemy,
they quickly informed Sītā, who was like a young girl, of what had occurred. The young girls said:
"O Mother Janaki, your son forcibly carried off the horse of a certain eminent king who was both powerful and proud.
Thereupon, a terrible battle ensued between him and that king's army, O Janaki."
Then everything was struck down by your son Āvīra;
subsequently, your charming son also achieved victory,
having rendered that king unconscious on the field of battle.
Then, having recovered from his swoon, that most cruel king,
becoming enraged, struck down your son upon the field of battle.
Previously, we had restrained him, saying, "Do not seize this excellent horse."
"Having insulted all of us Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas"—
having heard these most cruel words of the children, she fell upon the surface of the earth and wept in great distress.
Sītā said:
"O King, how can one who is devoid of compassion, who acts unrighteously, who is evil-minded, and who struck down my child, fight with a mere boy?"
"Where is that exceedingly powerful Lava-vīra?
How did you, a mere child, seize the excellent horse of that merciless king? Alas! You are all overcome by evil; yet you are experts in every weapon."

"O father, how can a battle be equal when one is stationed in a chariot and the other is without a chariot? O Rāma, because of your abandonment, I have lost my happiness; now, deprived of you, how shall I live in the forest? (12-13)
"Release this sacrificial horse; let this lord of the earth depart.
You do not recognize my grief, you who ought to be the one to wipe it away.
If Kuśa, that crest-jewel of heroes, had been here, he would have [acted] at once."
"He would have liberated you this very moment from the presence of the king;
yet he too is not here because of my fate. What can I do now? Thus, destiny alone is the cause of the arising of my misery."
Thus she lamented at length with many such words,
scratching the ground with her big toe and shedding tears from both eyes; that young child, who was also the king, spoke to the children.
"Where will my son go after falling into battle?"—
thus spoke Jānakī, who regards her husband as a deity; at that moment, Kuśa arrived in Ujjayinī along with the great sages.
Having worshipped Mahākāla on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha and obtained many boons from him, he returned to the presence of his mother.
Seeing Jānakī overwhelmed and distressed by tears welling in her eyes, [he approached her].
While he was speaking eagerly to her, whose limbs were distressed and miserable with grief,
his own arm throbbed, portending battle;
for the heart of that great car-warrior was filled with the zeal for combat.
He replied to his mother, who was speaking with a piteous and faltering voice: "O Mother, your sorrow has vanished now that I, your son, am present.
As long as I live, tears shall not fall from your eyes upon the earth."
He spoke to his mother, who was drenched in tears and speaking with a piteous, faltering voice:
"O Mother, my mind is steady; where is my brother Lava, the crusher of enemies, now that he has suddenly become so distressed by grief? (24-25)
Knowing that he had arrived, she went into his presence with great joy, thinking:
"How is it that the hero is not seen? Where has the mighty one gone to play? And with whom has he gone to look for me, out of childishness? (26)
"But why do you weep, O mother? Where does Lava dwell?
Tell me all that which is the cause of your sorrow.
Having heard her son's words, she, being distressed, spoke to Kuśa.

There, he was captured by a certain horse-guardian of King Lavodhṛta, who bound the boy, that steed worthy of the sacrificial rite. The powerful one, alone, conquered many guards, as a hero overcomes numerous enemies.
The king, having rendered him unconscious, bound him upon the surface of the earth.
"He is but a child," they said to me, and indeed they were my companions as well. Then, hearing that Lava had been seized, I became filled with sorrow.
"Release me from that power of the best of kings; the time has come.
Hearing the words of his distressed mother, Kuśa was filled with wrath;
biting his lips and grinding his teeth against his teeth, he spoke to her. 32.
Kuśa said:
"O Mother, know that Lava has been released from the bond of the noose;
now I shall slay him with my arrows, along with his entire army and vehicles. (33)
"Even if it were a god or an immortal, or even if Śiva himself had arrived, he would still be released by me with my sharp-jointed arrows.
O Mother, do not weep; this is the battlefield of heroes."
"Fleeing from here would lead only to infamy; let it be celebrated instead.
O Mother, give me a divine armor, a bow equipped with a string, a helmet, and likewise a sharpened sword. (35-36)
"Now, in this battle, I shall strike down that great force and release my own brother, who has fainted in the midst of the fray. O mother, I will not release your son from the great battle today."
"Then, at that time, may your two feet become enraged upon the earth.
Śeṣa said: "Satisfied by these words, Jānakī, who possesses auspicious marks,"
He bestowed the entire collection of weapons upon him, enjoining them with blessings for victory.
"Go to battle, my son, and liberate Lava who has fainted," thus commanded, the powerful Kuśa, clad in armor and wearing earrings, entered the fray.
Wearing a crown, carrying a sword, a shield, and a bow,
and having placed two inexhaustible quivers upon his lion-like shoulders,
that foremost of chariot-warriors went swiftly on foot to the feet of his mother.

While he was proceeding swiftly to the battle, moving quickly toward the fray, those great warriors beheld the hero Kuśa approaching, bringing about the downfall of the enemy host; they saw Svalava himself. 42–43.
Seeing his brother Kuśa arrived with great strength, Lava blazed up intensely in battle like fire fanned by the wind, as if Kṛtānta himself had appeared to destroy the entire universe. 44.
Having unyoked himself from the chariot, he emerged for battle.
Kuśa cast all the heroes stationed in the eastern direction toward the western direction, while Lava, out of anger, drove them all back. 45–46.
The entire army, though filled with heroes, found no protection;
that force, broken here and there and terrified again and again, did not desire to fight, even though possessed of strength, as it failed to stand its ground anywhere on the battlefield. 48-49.
At that time, King Aśvatthāman, the scorcher of enemies,
went forth to fight the heroic Kuśa, who was like Lava himself.
Seeing Kuśa, who was endowed with strength and possessed a splendor equal to the form of Rāma, [he advanced].
Standing upon his golden chariot, the slayer of enemy heroes spoke:
Śatrughna said:
"Who are you, who resemble my brother Lava in appearance and possess such great strength?"
"What is your name, O great hero? Who is your father, and who gave you birth? How is it that you, O bull among men, dwell in this forest frequented by the twice-born?
Tell me everything so that I may fight with you, O one of great strength. (52-53)
Having heard these words, Kuśa spoke to the king, filling the arena of battle with a voice as deep as a thundercloud:
"Sītā gave birth to only two sons who were devoted to their duty as wives."

O sinless king, those two, ever intent on worshipping the feet of Vālmīki in the forest, were devoted to serving their mother and were experts in all branches of knowledge; thus they became renowned as Kuśa and Lava. 55–56.

"Who are you, O hero, who boasts in battle? For what purpose has this best of horses been released by you in the midst of the fray? Go and conquer him who is endowed with great strength. Fight with me, O lord of the earth, if indeed you are a hero."
"Now I shall strike you down at the head of the battle! (58) Recognizing that son as one born of Sītā and Rāma, Śatrughna was struck with wonder; yet, out of anger, he himself took up his bow. (59)
Seeing him with his bow drawn, Kuśa, filled with rage,
stretched his own very firm and excellent bow.
Śatrughna, who was skilled in all weapons, released sharpened arrows.
Kuśa, laughing in the battle, effortlessly cut all of them down.
O Sage, hundreds of thousands of arrows belonging both to Kuśa and the king filled the entire world; that was truly marvelous. 61-62.
The powerful Kuśa swiftly burnt them all with the fire-weapon (agnyastra),
but the heroic king quelled it with the rain-weapon (parjanyāstra). The king of exceeding prowess then quelled that [fire] with the wind-weapon (vāyavya).
Then a fierce wind arose from all sides of the circle of arches;
the king, with the mountain-weapon (*parvatāstra*), enveloped that wind as it agitated everything. In the battle, he cut down the mountains and clouds with the thunderbolt-weapon (*vajrāstra*).
Then the formidable Kuśa discharged the Nārāyaṇa weapon;
yet that Nārāyaṇa weapon was unable to afflict King [Nārāyaṇa]. Then Kuśa became exceedingly enraged, devoted entirely to his anger.
He spoke to King Śatrughna, who possessed great strength and prowess:
"I know you, O great hero, to be one who brings victory in battle;
yet that terrifying Nārāyaṇa weapon did not subdue you."
"Now, O King, if I do not strike you down to the earth with my arrows this very day,
then hear my vow:
that whoever, having attained a human body so difficult to obtain even through millions of merits— "
"One should not heed that out of delusion; let there be sin for me in this matter.
Be vigilant here on the field of battle; I shall immediately cast him to the earth," having said this, [he fixed an arrow] upon his own bow. (69–70)
He fixed an arrow, terrible and blazing like the fire of time,
aiming it at the enemy's broad, hard, and massive chest.
Seeing that arrow aimed, Śatrughna was overwhelmed with rage.
He discharged sharp arrows capable of piercing even the skin of a goad; with those arrows, he indeed advanced to pierce his heart,
possessing a terrible form like fire and hissing like a venomous serpent.
Recognizing him instantly as Rāma by the excellence of his archery,
that best of kings cut down the sharp-jointed arrow released by Kuśa.
Then, Kuśa became exceedingly enraged at the severing of his shaft.

Furthermore, as he, impetuous with great strength, took up another sharp-jointed arrow upon his bow to pierce that chest, [the Lord] instantly cut down his arrow, which blazed like the fire of cosmic destruction. 75–76.
Then, remembering the feet of his mother Akūśā, filled with rage,
he fixed a third wonderful arrow upon his bow;
Śatrughna quickly took up another shaft to cut that one as well.
Pierced by that arrow, he fell to the surface of the earth.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose when Śatrughna was struck down;
there, Kuśa, proud of the strength of his own arms, achieved victory.
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Fainting of Śatrughna," within the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Śeṣa-Vātsyāyana-saṃvāda* in the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter Sixty-Four.
Śeṣa said:
Seeing Śatrughna fallen, Suratha, the preeminent king,
proceeded with the chariot created by Maṇi, while that great marvel stood still.
Puṣkala, having previously struck Turaṇa down, then reflected and went forth to fight Lava, who was exalted by the strength of a great hero.
Suratha, having encountered Kuśa, discharged arrows at him in many ways.
That crest-jewel among great heroes caused him distress in battle;
with ten upward-flaming arrows, he deprived Suratha of his chariot and swiftly severed his very firm bow, which was strung with a cord.
Through the discharge and withdrawal of missiles and counter-missiles, and through hurling and counter-hurling,
there arose a tumultuous battle among the heroes that caused the hair to stand on end,
while the king, seated upon his invincible celestial chariot, remained intensely engaged in the conflict.
Kuśa reflected, "What must be done by me in this battle?
Having deliberated, he, endowed with great strength, took up a sharp and terrible arrow for the purpose of slaying this king.

Seeing that arrow approaching, radiant like the fire of universal destruction, the heroic Vīra, possessed of great prowess, quickly resolved to cut it down; however, as he reached out with his hand, that great arrow struck him, and he fainted on the battlefield.
The charioteer leaped from the seat of the chariot and rescued him.
Seeing Suratha fallen, Kuśa, accompanied by Jaya, was terrifying the hosts of heroes; then the son of the Wind-god advanced.
Seeing the powerful son of the Wind approaching as a monkey, he laughed, baring his teeth as if to provoke him with anger. He said to Hanumān: "Come here, stand before me!"
"You shall be pierced by a thousand arrows and go to the night of death.
Having been addressed thus, Hanumān, recognizing the son of Rāma to be of great strength,
resolved that he must accomplish his master's task and rushed forward.
Having violently uprooted a massive *śāla* tree with its hundred branches,
the mighty one, beholding Kuśa upon his chest, went forth to fight;
he was the exceedingly powerful Hanumān, who had come forward with a *śāla* tree in hand.
The powerful one pierced him in the heart with three crescent-headed arrows resembling the moon.
Pierced by those arrows, Māruti, exerting his speed, crushed his tusks and struck him in the chest with a spear as formidable as a śāla tree.
Struck by the *śāla* tree, the boy did not tremble even slightly out of pride;
then the heroes offered him praise for his childhood valor. Struck by the *śāla*, that hero took up the *saṃhāra* weapon.
Desiring to destroy his enemy out of anger, Kuśa, who was a master of supreme weapons,
took aim at Durjaya with the Saṃhāra weapon. Then,
in his mind, he meditated upon Rāma, the destroyer of the obstacles of his devotees.
Then that well-aimed goad, having struck the heart of the Wind-god's son with great pain,
caused him to fall into a swoon once again.
Seeing the monkey fallen into a swoon, the powerful one [approached].
He pierced that entire great army with sharp arrows.
Broken by his tens of thousands of shafts on the field of battle, the whole force, consisting of all four divisions, became intent on flight.
Then Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys and great protector, rushed toward many mountains in a fit of rage and uprooted them; Kuśa,
laughing, effortlessly cut down all those formidable mountains with ease.
Furthermore, the powerful one swiftly cut down the trees that came toward him again.
Sugrīva, pained by many arrows on the field of battle,
seized a formidable mountain by its middle from the tip of its trunk.
Seeing Kuśastambha approaching, he crushed him in many ways with arrows and brought about a state of great Rudra-like prowess. 26.
Sugrīva, having witnessed that great feat performed by the boy, [was amazed].
His hope for victory was extinguished on the field of battle.
In the midst of the fray, seeing Kuśa—who was difficult to assail—striking him with his tail, the exceedingly intolerant [Gaja] was overcome by rage and seized a mountain to kill him. 27–28.
Seeing Sugrīva intent on killing himself,
he respectfully struck him with many sharp-jointed arrows. Being struck by those various kinds of shafts, he was filled with pain.
Having begun to slay Kuśa, he went toward Śāla and took it up;
then the heroic Kuśa also took up the Vāruṇa weapon,
and that elder brother of Lava bound him with a firm noose.
Bound with smooth nooses by the powerful Kuśa,
he fell into the midst of the battle, which was adorned by great heroes.
Seeing Sugrīva fallen, the warriors fled in every direction.
The elder brother of Jayamāpa, the crest-jewel of great heroes, having conquered the Lava warriors— namely Puṣkala, Aṅgada,
Pratāpāgrya, Vīramaṇi, and other kings as well— [remained victorious]. 33–34.
Having achieved victory in battle, the hero Lava approached his brother,
who had been the victor in the conflict and the one who struck down millions of enemies; both,
greatly delighted, embraced one another.
Having attained victory, the two of them, intoxicated with pride, then addressed the sage with these words.
Lava said:
"O brother, by your grace, we have crossed the ocean of battle."
"Now let us purify the beautifully adorned Vīraraṇaka," having said this, the two heroes Kuśa and Lava went quickly;
there they seized the king's wonderful crest-jewel, set with gold. 37–38.
The heroic Lava took the beautiful crown of Puṣkala,
as well as the two highly priceless armlets of Śatrughna and his other [brother]. Having seized that collection of weapons, he [addressed] Hanumān, the lord of monkeys.
Having gone into the presence of Sugrīva, they both bound him.
Then, having seized the tail of the son of the Wind-god, the younger brother of Kuśa spoke thus to his brother: "I shall take him to my own abode."
"Out of affection for our mother, I took hold of your tail for the sake of playing with the sons of the sages and for my own amusement.
Having heard these words, Kuśa then spoke to Lava.
"I shall capture this powerful and sturdy monkey"—
speaking thus, those two foremost of the strong bound him; seizing him by his tail, they both departed toward their own hermitage.
Seeing those two best of monkeys departing for their own hermitage,
they spoke to one another in voices trembling with fear;
then Hanumān, his mind drenched in terror, replied to the king of the monkeys.
"These two sons of Rāma will lead us back toward our own hermitage. Previously, while I was going toward Jānakī, I performed a certain rite;
there, the enchanting Goddess Jānakī appeared before me."
The King of Videha will behold me bound by the enemy’s noose; then that wicked woman will laugh, saying, "He is here.
What must I do in this situation? My life shall come to an end.

"O great monkey, having heard those words of Sugrīva, [Rāma will think], 'If he does not take me away even though I am in such a state, then my death will surely come. 49–50. "And what will Rāma do when this great suffering has fallen upon him? 49. Having heard those words, [Sugrīva said]:
"O great monkey, if he does not take me away even though I am in such a state, then my death will surely come. 50.
While the two of them were thus conversing with one another, both filled with fear,
Kuśa and Lava reached their mother’s dwelling with great speed. Upon seeing that they had arrived, the mother of those two rejoiced.
With supreme mutual affection, they embraced their two sons.
Seeing those two monkeys—Hanumān and Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys and a hero among all—holding the tail of Jānakī with them, [Rāma was moved]. (52–53)
Seeing those two bound by the noose of the snare, the beautiful woman spoke these excellent words for the sake of their liberation:
"O monkeys, release my two sons, who are great heroes and possess immense strength. (54)
"If these two swelling [with rage] look upon me, they will give up their lives. This is indeed the heroic Hanumān who burnt the city of Danu;
this also is the king of the bears, the sovereign of all the monkeys."
"For what purpose were you two held? Where? And what was done by you out of disrespect?
You two have been held; this causes me great wonder. Having heard these gentle words of his mother, O son, they then looked at one another.
Those two best of disciplined ones, endowed with great strength, said:
"O Mother, there is a certain powerful king named Rāma, the son of Daśaratha;
he has released this horse, which is beautifully adorned with a golden leaf upon its forehead. (58-59)

"O Mother, it was written there in this way: 'Let those Kṣatriyas take me, the mother of Ekavīra, or else let them be worshippers at my feet. O devoted wife, then a troubled reflection arose within my heart."
"O lady, why would you not be the mother of heroes?
Having observed that audacity of the king, the horse was seized by me by force;
the army was conquered by the hero Kuśa and struck down in battle. (61-62)
Know this crown to belong to the lord of the earth, O goddess who regards her husband as a deity;
know that this other crown, resplendent with jewels and pearls, belongs to the high-souled Puṣkala, another hero.
"O King, know that this horse, which captivates the mind, belongs to my brother Bali, the best among the strong; it has been brought here for him to mount.
And these two monkeys, the best among the powerful, have been brought by me for sport. (64–65)
"Out of curiosity, these two have engaged in battle against you. Hearing these words, the wife of Janaka, whose deity is her husband, said again and again: "Release those two heroic sons!"
Sītā said:
"By you two, a great injustice has been committed; the great Rāma has been taken away. Many heroes have been struck down, and these two lords of the monkeys are bound."
"By him, your father’s horse was released for the sake of the sacrifice. Why have you both seized even his horse during this most excellent of sacrifices?
Release these two monkeys; release the best of horses! 68–69.
Hearing those words of their mother, the two powerful brothers, Śatrughna and the king’s brother [Lakṣmaṇa], who were prone to great anger, spoke to her:
"In accordance with the duty of a Kṣatriya, we have conquered that powerful king. (70)

"It was previously proclaimed by Vālmīki before us that for those who fight according to the future duty of the kṣatriyas, there shall be no [sin] for us. Having assumed the form suitable for sacrificial rites at Kaṇva’s hermitage..."

Therefore, a son may even fight with his own father, and a younger brother with his elder brother; likewise, a disciple may even fight with his preceptor. Consequently, there is no possibility of sin in this.
Now, by your command, we two shall give you this excellent horse.

"We two shall liberate these two monkeys and fulfill your word," having said this to their mother, the two heroic lords of the monkeys went to the arena and released the horse fit for the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha).
Having heard that her army had been struck down by her two sons, Queen Sītā meditated upon Śrī Rāma in her mind and gazed at the Sun as her witness:
"If, in thought, word, or deed, I have [ever been unfaithful] to the Leader of the Raghus... (76-77)
"O Lord of the worlds, let this king,
his entire great army which was forcibly destroyed,
and these two sons of his live by my truth; I worship no other in my mind."
While Janakī’s husband, whose deity she was, was speaking these words,
that entire army and its very life-force [perished] at the forefront of the battle.
Thus ends the section on Rāma’s Horse Sacrifice in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
The sixty-fourth chapter, named "The Life of the Army.
Chapter Sixty-Five. Śeṣa said:
In an instant, the hero Śatrughna cast off his fainting spell on the field of battle; other powerful warriors who had also fainted were restored to life.
Then Śatrughna beheld the best of horses standing before him.
Seeing himself without his helmet and the army deprived of life,
