he felt this wonder within his heart and then spoke to Sumati, the best of ministers, who had now recovered from his swoon.
"Having shown compassion, he gave this horse for the completion of the sacrifice;
let us go quickly to Amara, who is longing for our arrival.
Having spoken thus, he stood upon the chariot and took up the horse with speed.
Then he departed from the hermitage to a great distance, free from the sound of kettledrums and conchs.
Behind him, the great army, complete with its four divisions, marched along,
causing the lord of serpents to bend under its weight.
Having swiftly crossed the Ganges, which abounds with surging waves,
the king, accompanied by Puṣkala and joined by Suratha, proceeded to his own kingdom, which was adorned by his own people.
Standing in a chariot made of jewels, wielding a great bow;
having placed a horse adorned with a garland of gems before him, a white parasol decorated with chowries was held over his head. 8–9.
Surrounded on all sides by thousands of chariots and powerful kings who were graceful with raised bows and adorned by heroic shouts,
he reached in due course the city graced by the Solar dynasty.
Adorned with many excellent banners and shining with fortresses,
Rāma, hearing that the horse had arrived along with Śatrughna, this sage,
and the heroic Puṣkala, experienced manifold joy. 11–12.
He assigned a fourfold great army to Kaṭaka,
and dispatched his brother Lakṣmaṇa, the best among the strong.
Having gone with the army, Lakṣmaṇa met his returning brother.
Overcome with joy, he embraced him whose limbs were adorned with wounds;
having been asked about his welfare in every respect, Śatrughna, filled with supreme delight, engaged in conversation with him in gladness. (14–15)
Standing upon his own chariot together with his brother, the high-minded and heroic son of Sumitrā set out toward his own city with a vast army.
The Sarayū, with its holy waters, purifies the three worlds.
Purified by the dust of Rāma’s feet, it possesses a luster equal to the autumnal moon;
it is crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, graced by *cakravāka* birds,
and resounds intensely with the cries of birds of most diverse colors.
There, many pavilions were caused to be built by Rāmacandra,
resounding with the distinct recitations of Brahmins learned in the Vedas.
There, many Kṣatriyas were present, beautifully adorned with bows in their hands.
Making the surface of the earth resound with the great twanging of their bowstrings,
the Brahmins there partook of various delightful foods; looking at one another, they engaged in charming conversation.
There were white milk-rice dishes, radiant like the luster of the moon,
abundant with milk and ghee, and mixed with sugar;
and there were many cakes there, equal in splendor to the orb of the moon.
Scented with the fragrance of camphor and other perfumes, they were most enchanting;
there were *phenikās*, *ghaṭakas*, and smooth *viraṃdhrakas* with a hundred holes;
there were *śaṣkulis*, *maṇḍakas*, and polished sweets accompanied by sweetened foods. 23–24.
The rice, resembling white water-lilies and mixed with green gram sprouts, was endowed with fragrance and gave great pleasure; it was served with curd and accompanied by Bhīmasena. 25.
Odana (rice) was joined with curd and accompanied by Bhīmasena.
It was prepared by those skilled in cooking delicious foods and served in vessels by the waiters.
There, some twice-born ones, seeing the milk-rice (pāyasa) placed in their bowls, said to one another, "What is this wonder that is seen? (26-27)
"Furthermore, has the lunar orb fallen from the sky out of fear of darkness?
For here is nectar, wondrously capable of destroying death.
Hearing that, another excellent brahmin, his eyes copper-red with rage, spoke.
And yet, the orb of the moon does not exist as something flooded with nectar.
How is it that this single body of the moon is seen as identical, vessel after vessel, for each of a thousand Brahmins? (29–30)
"Therefore, know this: it must be either a white lotus or camphor; do not mistake it for the orb of the moon, endowed as it is with brilliant splendor. 31.
Meanwhile, another [man], overcome by passion, likewise shook his own head.
Foolish brahmins, lacking the discernment to know what is truly sweet, do not recognize this.
Know that it has been cooked with the juice of the kṣaudra-kanda root and the sweet flowers of the śatapatra lotus. 32–33.

O Sage, while the brahmins, subsisting on roots, tubers, and fruits, were thus conversing with one another— delighted, discerning of flavors, and intensely greedy— a certain other twice-born man said: "The birth of kṣatriyas is the best."
"They shall eat such food as this, prepared through great merits.
Then the Brahmin said to him, "Such is the fruit of giving:
those who give to the twice-born obtain their desires. (35-36)
For those by whom Hari has not been repeatedly worshipped with various kinds of food offerings (naivedya), such food as this would never even come within the range of their vision.
(37) By those men who have fed the Brahmins with various flavors...
While those sinners were eating that food of delicious flavor, which was devoid of sight,
the best of the twice-born, who were experts in the Brahman of Sound, were fed with such sweet delicacies in the pavilion as they recited [the scriptures]. 38-39.
Some were dancing, some were laughing, and others, filled with joy, were singing;
a great festival was unfolding there when Śatrughna arrived.
Rāma saw Śatrughna approaching, accompanied by Puṣkala.
Then, unable to check the joy that had arisen within him as he gazed [at them],
Rāma was about to rise toward his brother, the horse-keeper,
when Śatrughna, who was devoted to his brother, clung to Rāma’s feet. 41–42.
Seeing his brother fallen at his feet, full of humility, Rāghava, filled with affection, embraced him firmly;
He attained an exceeding and supreme joy that transcended words;
overwhelmed with humility, he drew Puṣkala— bowed at his feet—
firmly into the middle of his arms and pressed him tightly.
Likewise, [he honored] the heroic Hanumān, Sugrīva, and Aṅgada;
Lakṣmīnidhi, Janakaja (Sītā), Pratāpāgrya, Ripuñjaya, Subāhu, the heroic Sumada, Vimala, and Nīlaratnaka. 46.
Then Raghunātha himself firmly embraced Satyavanta, Vīramaṇi, Suratha, and Rāmasevaka—
those other illustrious kings who were affectionate and prostrated at his feet. 47–48.
Sumati, filled with joy, embraced the illustrious Lord of the Raghus— who bestows grace upon His devotees— firmly, and stood before Him with uplifted countenance.
Then Rāma, seeing his own minister arrived in his presence, [spoke].
The best among speakers, with supreme affection, said to the minister:
"O Sumati, best of ministers and foremost of those who speak, tell me—who are all these kings, and how have they gathered here? (50-51)
"From where and from where was the horse obtained? By whom and by what means was it restrained?
And how indeed was it liberated by his brother, who is so greatly powerful and illustrious?
Śeṣa said:
Thus addressed by the minister, the wise Sumati, the best among counselors, laughed and spoke to Raghava with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
Sumati said:
Today, how can I speak before the Omniscient One?
You ask according to worldly custom; you are all-seeing and know everything. Nevertheless, always bearing your instruction upon my head, [I shall speak]. 54.
I speak this, so listen now, O crest-jewel of all kings:
by your grace, O Lord, I have indeed wandered everywhere upon the surface of the earth, adorned with the leaf of the forehead [as a royal mark]. (55-56)
No one, arrogant with the power of his own name, could restrain his mind;
then, having surrendered their respective kingdoms, they bowed at his lotus feet.
Who indeed, O Rāvaṇa, lord of the Daityas, could restrain the best of horses? || 57 ||

Desiring victory and free from old age and death, he seized it. At that moment, O Lord, your charming horse arrived at Ahicchatrā; hearing that the horse had reached you, King Sumada [was moved]. 58–59.
Accompanied by his sons, powerful, and surrounded by a mighty army,
he surrendered the entire kingdom, now cleared of all thorns.
He [offered it] to the Mother of the Universe, the Ambika of the world, who is the eye and guide of the worlds.
Having propitiated [the deity], he quickly obtained long life and a kingdom free from thorns.
This very Sumada, who has been longing for a vision of you for a long time, bows down to you, O Lord; accept him with a glance of compassion. 61-62.
Then, in the city of King Subāhu, which was filled with troops, his son Damana seized that excellent horse.
A great battle took place between him and Damana.
Puṣkala attained victory after rendering Subāhu unconscious;
then the enraged Subāhu fought by force in battle against the son of the Wind-god,
the supreme among those who possess strength and serve his lotus feet.
Having obtained knowledge that was previously obscured by a curse through being struck by his foot,
he offered it all to you and became the protector of horses. This king of noble arms and tall stature bows down to you.
"Consecrate Subāhu, who is skilled in policy, with your glance of compassion.
Thereupon, having been released by the two horses, he plunged into the lake.
Then, the powerful Śatrughna employed the bewildering weapon (*mohanāstra*) against him.
Then he went to Devapura, adorned by the dwelling of Śiva; you should know what occurred there when you arrived,
and how the Daitya Vidyunmālī was slain and Satyavān was reunited with him.
"O high-minded one, you know that the battle with Suratha was equal [in intensity].
Then, released from Kuṇḍalaka, the horse wandered everywhere;
no one, arrogant in his own prowess and strength, could restrain him."
O best of men, hear now of the wonder that occurred there when that beautiful horse arrived at the lovely hermitage of Vālmīki. There, a youth of sixteen years bore a resemblance to you.

Seeing the horse marked with the leaf-design, that most powerful one seized it. O best of men, a great battle then took place there against Kālajit; he was slain by that hero with a sharp-edged weapon.
Many mighty warriors, such as Puṣkala and others, were slain by him;
then that crest-jewel of heroes rendered Śatrughna unconscious.
At that time, the king, reflecting upon his great sorrow in his heart during the battle, [acted].
The hero, the best among the powerful, rendered him unconscious with a blow. While he remained unconscious, O King, another arrived; by that other, he was revived and your army was destroyed.
Having seized the weapons and ornaments of all those who had fainted, the two monkeys bound them and departed toward their own hermitage;
out of compassion, he then gave them a great sacrificial horse.
The entire camp, whose life had been lost, was restored to life.
Having taken that horse, we have arrived in your presence; this is exactly what I understood, and thus those words were spoken by me before you.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "Sumati’s Report," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana within the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter Sixty-six.
Śeṣa said:
Having been told by Sumati that the two boys were his own sons in the hermitage of Vālmīki, he recognized them as such and spoke to Vālmīki. (1)
Śrī Rāma said: O Kauśika, why do you two, who bear a form similar to mine, who are the best among the powerful, and who are experts in the science of archery, remain there?
Having heard what was said by the minister, astonishment has arisen within me,
for those two [demons] effortlessly bound Śatrughna and Hanumān.
Therefore, O Sage, tell me everything regarding the deeds of those two boys.
"May this supreme joy become for me as much as it is desired"—
having heard that which was spoken by the wise king of kings,
he spoke these most excellent words, composed of clear syllables.
Vālmīki said:
"How can there be knowledge of You, the inner controller of men?
Nevertheless, I shall speak here for the sake of your satisfaction."
These two princes, the best among the strong, are in my hermitage; they possess a form resembling yours and bear bodies beautiful in their every limb.
Since Jānakī, though innocent, was abandoned by you in the forest— (7) [they have come here.]
Seeing your beloved, the virtuous daughter of Janaka, crying out again and again like a female osprey afflicted by grief in that dreadful forest, I then brought her to the hermitage. 8–9.
A beautiful leaf-hut was constructed for her by the sons of sages;
in it, she gave birth to two sons who illuminated the ten directions. I clearly gave them the names Kuśa and Lava.
There they grew incessantly, like the moon during the bright fortnight.

In due course, O King, I performed for them all the rites beginning with the sacred thread ceremony (*upanayana*), and I caused them to master all the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches (*sāṅga*).
Listen from my own mouth to all these along with their secret doctrines:
Ayurveda, the science of archery, the science of weapons, as well as the Jālandharī lore; and you two have been made skilled in music.
On the banks of the Gaṅgā, and in the groves and forests of creepers where they were singing,
those two— restless and fickle-minded yet experts in all branches of knowledge—
then brought me the greatest satisfaction, O best of the Raghus.
Having bestowed all the weapons and placed his hand upon [the sage's] head, those two,
who were highly skilled in singing and proficient in the distinctions between the notes Ṣaḍja, Madhyama, and Gāndhāra, caused the people to marvel upon seeing them. 16.
Beholding them in such a state, I caused them to sing the beautiful and auspicious *Rāmāyaṇa*, which I had composed through the power of my knowledge of the future;
they were both experts in the mṛdaṅga, paṇava, and other instruments, as well as in the vīṇā. 17.
Singing in the forest and enchanting the deer and birds,
Varuṇa brought those two boys, Tāraka and Rāma, back for the night so that they might hear the wonderful sweetness of their song.
There, at the command of Lokeśa, the two Kumāras— masters of the ocean of knowledge regarding captivating youth, beauty, song, and dance—
sang your most supreme, sweet, delightful, and purifying life-story in full measure. 20.
Varuṇa, together with his family and singers, listened;
even as he heard, Varuṇa along with Mitra found no satiety.
O descendant of Raghu, his conduct was sweeter than even nectar.
With the functions of his life-force and senses stolen by the great greed for the joy of singing, he commanded Kumāra and Nahuṣa to return;
yet the two boys were enticed by those delightful and magnificent pleasures.
And as I remembered the lotus feet of my own mother, the wife of the preceptor of the gods,
I too subsequently went to the supreme abode of Varuṇa; there,
O Lord, Varuṇa, filled with love, performed worship for me.
To Varuṇa, who was questioning me regarding the births, deeds, and all other matters concerning the two children, I related everything concerning their birth, learning, and arrival.
Having heard this, the Lord, along with Sītā and her sons, adorned them with garments and ornaments.
"Devadatta" is to be understood as such because of the weight of my words;
that which was given by Varuṇa was brought by the two princes, for he was pleased with their qualities of instrumental music, singing, knowledge, and youth.
Then the virtuous Varuṇa spoke to me concerning Sītā:
"Sītā is the foremost among women devoted to her husband, endowed with beauty, character, and youth; she is the mother of a hero and highly fortunate—she ought never to be abandoned. (28-29)
O descendant of Raghu, there is great loss in abandoning this;
for this is your supreme, imperishable perfection among all perfections.
Indeed, its greatness is not understood by the vulgar who are defiled by ignorance.

The hearing and chanting of her name, which brings about the attainment of *kāhāni*, is meritorious. (31) With us as witnesses, her conduct is ever purifying; those who meditate upon Sītā’s feet attain perfection immediately. (32)
By her mere volition,
these lords constantly perform the functions of the worlds— creation, preservation, and dissolution.
She is death to Sītā, nectar to this [world], and she rains down for the one who suffers.
Heaven, liberation, austerity, yoga, and charity—these are yours, O Jānaki;
this Sītā, your beloved, creates Brahmā, Śiva, and the other world-protectors such as myself, and she alone creates them, no one else exists. 34–35.
"You are the father of all the worlds and Sītā is the mother; therefore, a wrong view regarding this matter is never suitable for your welfare.
The Blessed One himself, being omniscient, knows Sītā to be eternally pure."
Therefore, O Lord of the Earth, you too must honor Jānakī, who is dearer to you than life itself and pure; for there shall be neither a curse nor any humiliation for Sītā, nor for you, O Sovereign.
"O best of sages, Vālmīki, you must speak these words— words that are beyond description— to Rāma, the Lord of the worlds, in person.
Having been addressed thus by Varuṇa for the purpose of recovering Sītā, I spoke.
In this very way, O Lord, the singing of the Rāmāyaṇa by your two sons was heard by all the world-protectors, as well as by the gods, the asuras,
and all the gandharvas, whose minds were filled with wonder.
All of them, being delighted, praised those two sons; the three worlds were enchanted by their beauty, song, youth, and virtues.
Whatever was offered by the guardians of the world was accepted by the two sons.

43–44. By the sages, by the two excellent ones, and by others, fame alone was [attained]. Previously, the entire world was seen by the sage as having one Rāma; now it has become three Rāmas, as it is perceived by you both together with your sons.
O Indra among kings, this form, which was previously seen in the world as the embodiment of a single desire, now arises here and there through all four desires;
and everywhere else, O Indra among kings, are the two sons of Rāma, Kuśa and Lava.
O wise one, why is this contraction [of praise] being sung here regarding you?
For it is heard that a great eulogy is bestowed upon all your deeds, O crest-jewel of those of meritorious fame, except for the abandonment of Sītā. (46–47)
O Lord of the three worlds, you who are emulating the life of a householder must accept two sons endowed with learning, virtue, and good qualities;
having bowed to their mother, they shall remain in your presence. 48.
"Therefore, you should bring those two sons here along with their mother. By her now restoring the army to life,
she will provide proof for all people, purifying even those who have fallen."
"O giver of honor, there is nothing unknown to him, nor to us, nor to the gods;
whatever has perished in the worlds of that pure one is certainly restored here.
Śeṣa said:
Thus addressed by Vālmīki, Rāma, though omniscient, was further enlightened;
having praised and bowed to Vālmīki, he replied to him along with Lakṣmaṇa:
"O Father, go now to bring back Sītā, my partner in dharma."
O friend, mounting the chariot with Sumantra and accompanied by my sons, proclaim these words of mine and those of the sage; then,
having alerted this city, quickly bring back Sītā.
Lakṣmaṇa said: "O Lord, O All-pervading One, at your command I shall go;
if the Queen comes to this pilgrimage of ours, then it will become fruitful for all of us."
"O noble lady, my previous fault was indeed due to malice toward me; since that has passed, please forgive this transgression of mine.
Having spoken thus to Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, by the king's command, took his place in the chariot.
Accompanied by Sumitra and the two disciples of the sage, he went to the hermitage of the Earth-born (Anasuya). [He thought:
"How may the divine Sita be propitiated by me, since she knows of my former transgression and is always dependent upon Rama?"
Thinking thus, with joy and distress contending within him, Lakṣmaṇa reached Sītā’s hermitage, which dispels all fatigue; then,
descending from the chariot, he approached it with eyes choked with tears.
Repeatedly saying, "O Noble One! O Worthy One! O Blessed One! O Auspicious One!
he fell at her feet with all his limbs trembling;
and he was raised up by that goddess, who was overwhelmed with affection for him.

"For what purpose have you come, O gentle one, to this forest beloved by the sages? Is the Lord—the pearl from the oyster-shell of Kausalyā—faring well? Is he free from anger and free from fear, honored solely by his own glory?"
He is proclaimed by all the worlds as an ocean of auspicious qualities.
Fearing infamy, he appointed you to abandon me;
consequently, his stainless fame has spread throughout the worlds.

"Even after death, you shall remain steadfast in performing what is pleasing to your husband; may you attain proximity to your husband, O goddess. Even though I have been abandoned by him, he has not abandoned me even in the slightest."
For the fruit depends upon the means, but the cause does not depend upon the fruit.
(66) O my dear one, she who is free from the thorn of sorrow regarding Kausalyā, who is ever full of compassion, and who remains well—she whose son is the protector of the three worlds. (67)
"Are all my kinsmen, Bharata and the others, well?
And is the highly fortunate Sumitrā well—she for whom I am dearer than her own life?
But why have you abandoned me as well, like me, for the sake of fame throughout all the worlds?"
"What is difficult for that king to renounce, he for whom even his own self is not dear?
Thus questioned in many ways by her, the younger brother of Rāma replied: "The Lord is well; He asks after your welfare. (69-70)
Kausalyā, Sumitrā, and the other wives of the king asked the queen about her welfare with affection, along with blessings;
for they had first inquired after her well-being and then offered salutations at her feet.
"O auspicious one, I report that Śatrughna and Bharata have performed their duties;
O auspicious Jānakī, all the elders and their wives have bestowed blessings upon you and inquired after your welfare. (72–73)
The self-possessed god, free from guile, gazes upon you;
O beautiful woman, you find no pleasure in anyone other than him anywhere.
O daughter of Janaka, all the directions are truly empty without you.
Seeing the one who weeps, the Lord did not cause the others to weep as well.
(75) Wherever the Goddess was present, Rāghava constantly remembered her;
he considered that place to be never empty of her, O Daughter of Videha. (76)
"Blessed is this hermitage where Janaki dwells, speaking of my news," he said while weeping slightly;
O Master, hear from me what he then spoke.
Without a doubt, that which is in the heart of the speaker becomes manifest.
(78) The world says of me alone, "I am the Lord of all lords," yet I declare that for them, the unseen alone is the independent cause. (79)
Even the Lord follows after his effects only through the unseen (adṛṣṭa);
why then would those subject to his rule not follow him in their experiences of pleasure and pain?
[This is so] in the breaking of a bow, in the loss of mind, in the abandonment of one's own, or even in the death of a father.
In going to the forest, in seizing that [Sītā] there, in crossing the ocean,
in slaying the lord of the rākṣasas in battle, and in being my ally among the bears, monkeys, and rākṣasas— (81–82)
O beautiful lady, while the truth of your vow remained intact, and while you had regained your connection with your kinsmen and obtained the kingdom,
what was the unavoidable cause for your subsequent separation from your beloved?
"Be gracious, O Lord; let there be a reunion for us two as before.
Since the Veda was composed by you, and since the origin and dissolution of the worlds proceed from you, I am therefore the primary cause who follows after the worlds. (84-85)
People who possess true understanding follow what is unseen;
that unseen merit is worn away by experience, and all of that has been experienced by you, O Vani.
O Sita, this causeless affection for me toward you is ever-increasing.

Disregarding the world’s lack of vision, he calls out to you with earnest respect. Even when a fault is suspected, the purity of affection is never submerged; thus, that [affection], being entirely pure, is always to be savored by the wise. 87–88.

"O blessed lady, this purification by means of oil has been performed by you; otherwise, even though this world is protected by one who follows the conduct of the virtuous, it would be considered as defiled by the reproach of us two, O Goddess, in all circumstances for the sake of purity. (89)
The world would not perish, for this deluded man has acted according to the ways of the great. Our fame is radiant; our passion is radiant;
our lineages are radiant; our deeds are radiant.
"May our fame be sung by radiant singers upon the earth; and those who possess devotion to us, may they at the end cross over the ocean of existence.
Thus was she addressed by him, who was delighted by her virtues.
May she set her compassionate mind upon beholding the lotus-feet of her husband.
93 Delightful garments, magnificent ornaments, as well as body-unguents and pleasing perfumes have been prepared for you. 94
Chariots, elephants, and horses, beautiful with auspicious umbrellas and chowries, moved like a festival, sent forth by Rāma;
they were being praised by the best of the twice-born, as well as by sūtas, māgadhas, and bards. 95.
Being honored by the city women and attended by the warriors,
the Goddess was covered with flowers by the celestial nymphs and others;
she gave wealth to those twice-born ones according to their desires.
Placing Kumāra, who was mounted upon an elephant, at our head, O Queen of Men,
and followed by me, you shall go to Ayodhyā, your own city;
for when you have arrived there, you will be reunited with your beloved.

"Let there be a great festival today with auspicious instrumental music, songs, and the like for all the royal women who have arrived from every direction, as well as for all the wives of the sages and those of Kosala. (99-100)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard this petition, the goddess Sītā said to him, "O King, I am not one who brings fame; indeed, I am disgrace itself. 101
What could be accomplished by one who is devoid of dharma, pleasure, and wealth?
Such being the case, O ladies, why do you place such unrestrained trust in him? Whether manifest or hidden, the faults residing in the mind of your husband [are evident].
At the time of taking her hand in marriage, the form of that woman—born of an ignoble lineage, resembling a low-born woman, and hailing from an inauspicious family—stood fixed within my heart;
that very form never departs from my heart. (103–104)
O Lakṣmaṇa, these two delicate ones, born from a portion of my own splendor,
are the sprouts of our lineage, great heroes, and experts in the science of archery;
having brought them to their father’s presence, they must be cherished with great care.
"Remaining here, I shall propitiate Rāma through ascetic penance.
O highly fortunate one, you must go from here on my behalf and offer salutations at the feet of all those worthy of honor, and inquire after their welfare. (106-107)
Sītā commanded her two sons: "Go to the presence of your father;
he, who has bestowed his own station upon you, must indeed be served by you both.
Although thus commanded, the two youths Kuśa and Lava were unwilling to go.
At the word of Vālmīki, they both went there with Lakṣmaṇa;
having arrived near the lotus-feet of Vālmīki himself, those two sons approached him,
and Lakṣmaṇa also, accompanied by the boy, paid his respects.
Vālmīki and Lakṣmaṇa praised them; having learned that Rāma was seated in the assembly hall, these who had gathered together went there full of eagerness.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, having prostrated himself, [related] everything beginning with Sītā’s words.
Filled with both joy and sorrow, the wise one spoke (verse 112).
From the words of Sītā’s message, Rāma experienced a faint; regaining consciousness, he spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, who was skilled in statecraft (verse 113).
"Go once more to that place with great effort and bring her back quickly; may it be well with you. Having delivered my words, ask her:
'What are you practicing penance for in the forest? Has some other course been considered by you? ||| 114 ||
"O Jānakī, did you not come here by hearing or seeing [of me], or perhaps by water? By your own will you went to the forest dear to the sages;
there you honored the wives of the sages and beheld the hosts of sages. (115-116)
"O beautiful woman, your desires are fulfilled today; why do you not come?
You should see no fault in me, for you have beheld your own desire. Or rather, O lovely-thighed one, going again and again is the very path of a woman toward her husband. 117

Though devoid of qualities, he is an ocean of virtues; how much more so when desired by the mind! (118) Whatever action noble women perform, each and every one is for the gratification of their husband. I was already pleased with you before, but now I am even more so. (119)
Sacrifice, recitation, austerity, charity, vows, pilgrimage, compassion, and so forth—the gods themselves abide within me; when I am satisfied, all this is undoubtedly satisfied.
(120) Śeṣa said:
Taking this message from the Lord of the World,
Lakṣmaṇa spoke to Sītā with humility and affection toward Hari,
saying: "Regarding the bringing of Sītā, you have spoken with favor."
"I shall speak those words endowed with humility. Having said this and bowing at the feet of Raghunātha, Lakṣmaṇa went quickly to Sītā, standing upon a chariot of great speed.
Vālmīki, beholding the two illustrious sons of Rāma endowed with great majesty,
smiled and, making his face charming, said:
"O sons, sing the wonderful life-story of Rāma."
Playing the lute and beautified by sweet singing,
those two illustrious sons sang the life-story of Rāma, which bestows great merit and is adorned with excellent words and phrases. 125–126.
In this [city], the ordinances of Dharma are manifest, and therein resides the virtue of devotion to one's husband;
there, brotherly affection is great, and likewise is devotion to one's elders;
indeed, the conduct between master and servant exists there in embodied form. (127)
There, the descendant of Raghu personally bestowed a punishment for unrighteousness.
The world was pervaded by his singing; even the gods in heaven and the Kinnaras fell into a swoon in an instant upon hearing his song.
Hearing the resonance of the lute, beautified by rhythmic timing and measure,
the entire assembly there became as if painted in a statue;
likewise, Rāma and the other kings shed tears of joy.
Enchanted by the fifth note (*pañcama*) of their singing, they became as if painted in a picture.
Seeing his two sons there, who were utterly captivated by the great music, Rāma gave each of them one hundred thousand pieces of gold individually.

Then, seeing Vālmīki, the best of sages, intent on taking that [gift], those two, with their eyebrows slightly arched, said while laughing: "O Sage, a great offense is being committed here by this king. (133)
When he desires to give us gold, tempting us with it—though the acceptance of gifts is praised for Brahmins, it is not so for others; a king intent on receiving gifts leads only to hell. 134–135.
"By our grace, this lord of the earth enjoys his kingdom;
why does he, who is endowed with all blessings, desire to give away gold? Seeing them speak thus, Vālmīki was filled with compassion.
"O you two most skilled in policy, know that your father has passed away.
Having heard these words of the sage, the two boys, exceedingly pure through devotion to their mother and endowed with humility, fell at the feet of the king.
Embracing the young Rāma firmly upon his own body, he was filled with joy;
then he thought that Dharma and Adharma had arrived in embodied form.
Beholding the beautiful faces of both Rāma and his son, the assembly [was moved].
"O Lord of Sages, it is true that devotion to the husband of Jānakī is [supreme]," [said Śeṣa].
Having heard what was spoken from the mouth of Śeṣa, Vātsyāyana, desiring to hear the Rāmāyaṇa endowed with all virtues, spoke thus. (140–141)
Vātsyāyana said: "O Lord, at what time was this great Rāmāyaṇa composed? For what reason did he create it, and what is described therein? Please tell me that. (142)
Śeṣa said:
Once the brahmin Vālmīki came to a great forest where there were palmyra trees, tamāla trees, and kiṃśuka trees in full bloom. 143
Making the forest fragrant with the pollen of *ketakī* flowers, a great white-eared one is seen, radiant as the moon; there are also *campaka*, *bakula*, *kovidāra*, and *kuraṇṭaka* trees. 144.
In that beautiful forest, many flowering and tall trees resounded on all sides with the cries of cuckoos and the humming of bees; it was delightful, charming, and filled with various birds. 145.
There, a pair of lovely curlews, tormented by the arrows of love, rejoiced together, standing close with affection and delighting in one another.
Then a hunter approached and [killed] one of that charming pair.
Then a certain merciless man, greedy for the taste of flesh, killed her husband;
seeing her husband slain by the hunter, the female curlew was overcome with grief and lamented intensely,
letting out loud cries of woe.
Then the sage, becoming enraged at the Niṣāda who had killed the krauñca bird,
performed the purifying and auspicious ritual ablution in the river and cursed him: "O Niṣāda, may you remain in this state for eternal years!"
"O twice-born ones, because you killed one of the two krauñca birds while it was deluded by passion, a continuous composition of verses has arisen from that;
therefore, being delighted and praising him, they said to the sage, 'Excellent! Excellent! (151)
"O Lord, Sarasvatī has composed this verse in response to your words.
(152) "O best of sages, this verse is exceedingly enchanting.
Then the sage, that bull among speakers, became joyful in spirit.
At that time, Brahmā, accompanied by his sons, arrived and spoke these words to Vālmīki: "O lord of sages, you are blessed;
for the Goddess of Speech (Bhāratī), having resided within your mouth, has attained the state of being a verse."
Therefore, O Rāmāyaṇa, compose that which is delightful and sweet-syllabled,
by which your stainless fame shall endure until the end of the kalpa.
Blessed indeed is this speech when it is joined with the name of Rāma.
For those who speak of other matters against their will, it surely produces sin.
Therefore, relate the world-renowned life of Rāma, by which there may be the destruction of the sins of sinners at every step. 156-157.
Having spoken thus, the Creator vanished, accompanied by all the gods;
thereafter, he became absorbed in meditation on a delightful riverbank, pondering how the Rāmāyaṇa might come to be. 158.
Then, a captivating Rāma appeared in his mind—Rāma, dark as the petal of a blue lotus and lotus-eyed;
and he beheld Rāma’s conduct, past, future, and present. (159–160)
Then, having attained extreme joy, he composed the Rāmāyaṇa,
endowed with beautiful words and various poetic meters. O sinless one, that Rāmāyaṇa consists of six most delightful kāṇḍas.
The Bāla, Māraṇya, and another, Kiṣkindhāsundara,
as well as Uttara and another— O Great-minded One, the man who hears these six [sections] is liberated from all sins through merit. 163
There, being satisfied with the *Bāla* sacrifice, Paṅktiratha obtained four sons through the *Putreṣṭi* rite; he directly attained Hari, the eternal Brahman.
Having gone to the sacrifice of Kauśika and having married Sītā, the descendant of Bhṛgu [performed the rites].

Having arrived at the excellent city, the appointment to the position of crown prince was made. At his mother's word, he previously went to the forest; having crossed the Gaṅgā, he reached Mount Citrakūṭa accompanied by his wife and Lakṣmaṇa.
Having heard of him in the forest, Bharata went to his brother;
not finding him there, he himself established his residence in Nandigrāma.
Listen now to another account concerning this boy, arising from the forest.
The description of his dwelling in various hermitages of sages (168);
the cutting off of Śūrpaṇakhā’s nose; the destruction of Khara and Dūṣaṇa;
the slaying of the illusory Mārīca; and the abduction of Sītā by the demon Rāvaṇa (169).
The wandering in the forest by one separated from his beloved,
the encounter with Kabandha, the journey to Pampā, and the meeting with Hanumān— this is the section known as the Araṇya-kāṇḍa.
Furthermore, O Sage, listen; I shall relate it to you in brief:
the division of the seven palm trees, the wonderful slaying of Vālin, the granting of the kingdom to Sugrīva, and the description of the mountain. 171–172.
From Lakṣmaṇa came the commission of the task; then the exile of Sugrīva, as well as the mobilization of the army and the search for Sītā;
there followed the sighting of Saṃpāti and likewise the leaping across the ocean.
The attainment of the single monkey on the opposite shore;

the wonderful Kiṣkindhā-kāṇḍa—listen now to the beautiful Sunda-ra-kāṇḍa, wherein the marvelous story of Rāma unfolds, including the monkey’s wandering from house to house and the sighting of Citra. 174–175.
Therein is the sighting of Sītā and likewise the conversation with Jānakī;
the destruction of the grove by the enraged [monkeys] and the binding of the monkey;
then the burning of Laṅkā and subsequently the reunion with the monkeys.
The granting of the token of recognition to Rāma, the dispatch of the army, the construction of the bridge across the ocean, the meeting with Śuka and Sāraṇa—
thus has been narrated the beautiful [section] ending with the reunion with Sītā in battle. 177–178.
The dialogue with the sages in the north and the commencement of the sacrifice,
as well as the stories of various gardens there which destroy the sins of those who hear them—
thus has the sixth section been described, which removes the sin of killing a Brahmin. 179.
In brief, I have related to you this most captivating work;
it is known as the Vālmīki-Rāmāyaṇa, consisting of twenty-four thousand verses, divided into six sections, and it destroys even the greatest of sins.
Having heard that, Rāghava was delighted; he seated his two sons upon a throne, embraced them firmly, and then remembered his beloved Sītā. 182.
Thus ends the [section on] Rāmāśvamedha in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
The sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Singing of the Rāmāyaṇa.
The sixty-seventh chapter. Śeṣa said:
Then Saumitri, having approached, bowed repeatedly to Jānakī and,
with a voice faltering with affection, delivered the message sent by Rāma.
Seeing that Lakṣmaṇa had arrived, full of humility, Sītā—
Having heard the message from his mouth, she spoke, overcome with shame:
"O son of Sumitrā, how could you come here, leaving Rāma in the great forest?
I remain here at the hermitage of Vālmīki, remembering Rāma."
Having heard those words uttered from her mouth, the son of Sumitrā said: "O mother, Rāma, devoted to his wife, repeatedly summons you;
a woman devoted to her husband does not take to heart any fault committed by her husband."
"Therefore, come; we shall stay here in this excellent chariot.
Having heard these words, Jānaki, whose deity was her husband, abandoned her mental resentment and stayed in the chariot with the son of Sumitrā.
Having bowed to all the female ascetics and the sages radiant with Vedic knowledge,
and remembering Rāma in her mind, she stood upon the chariot and proceeded toward the city.
Endowed with highly precious ornaments, she reached the city in due course.
She reached the river Sarayū where Rāma himself was staying.
Alighting from the chariot together with Lakṣmaṇa, she, devoted to her husband, fell at the feet of Rāma. 8-9.
Seeing Jānakī arrive, overwhelmed with love, Rāma said: "Excellent! Now, together with you, I shall complete the sacrifice.
Having paid homage to Vālmīki and likewise to the other most excellent brahmins, [he spoke].
Eager to perform a prostration at her mother's feet, she approached.
Then Kausalyā, having greeted her beloved Jānakī, the mother of heroes, as she arrived with blessings, experienced manifold joy. 11–12.

Seeing the daughter of Videha bowing at Kaikeyī’s feet, she bestowed the blessing: "Live long with your husband and your son. Seeing the daughter of Videha bowing at Sumitrā’s feet, [she likewise blessed her].
He bestowed upon her a blessing that grants sons and grandsons.
O Vāḍava, Sītā, the virtuous beloved of Rāmacandra, having bowed down to him from all sides, became filled with supreme joy. 14–15.
Seeing his wife arrived, the pot-born Agastya disregarded the golden wife and bestowed that status upon her who was a follower of dharma.
Then Rāma shone resplendently in the midst of the sacrifice together with Sītā.
Just as the moon followed by Tārā shines with intense radiance in autumn, so too,
when that delightful time had arrived, he performed a ritual there for the removal of all sins of his lawful wife, Vaidehī.
Beholding Rāma together with Sītā deeply engaged in the sacrificial rites, those present there rejoiced, filled with wonder.
At that excellent sacrifice, Rāma spoke to Sumati, the son of Vasiṣṭha.
"O Master, what must I necessarily do hereafter?
Having heard Rāma's words, the high-minded Guru said:
"One must perform worship of the Brāhmaṇas that brings them satisfaction. (20-21)
Formerly, Marutta had prepared the sacrificial requisites and released [the horse];
at that time, the Brahmins were gratified there with wealth and other offerings. Indeed, the Brahmins were unable to carry away such an immense accumulation of wealth.
The twice-born, unable to bear the burden of wealth, cast it away in the region of the Himalayas.
Therefore, O best of kings, you too, possessing the preeminent fortune of royalty,
should give gifts and other offerings to the brahmins so that there may be supreme satisfaction.
Having heard this, that foremost of kings, regarding the pitcher-born Agastya as worthy of worship, first honored that son of Brahmā, whose wealth was his asceticism,
with multitudes of various jewels and many loads of gold.
Surrounded by regions and people who bestowed extreme joy,
he worshipped the charming Agastya together with his wife,
likewise with jewels, gold, and various kinds of lands.
In the same way, he honored Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī,
and likewise honored Cyavana along with his wife with excellent jewels;
he also honored all the other sages and officiating priests, who were repositories of ascetic power.

He worshipped [the deities] with floods of jewels and many loads of gold in various ways. Then, at the sacrifice, Rāma gave abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins— one hundred thousand pieces of gold to each member of the twice-born.
He bestowed various kinds of gifts upon the poor, the blind, and the wretched, using wealth and enchanting jewels acquired through righteous means; he also gave them diverse garments and soft foods.
There, he bestowed upon everyone gifts that bring joy, in accordance with the scriptures.
The city, crowded with people who were thrilled and well-nourished, and filled with all living beings, became exceedingly joyful, teeming with both men and women.
Seeing everyone bestowing gifts during that most excellent sacrifice, the twice-born sage born from a jar (Agastya) attained a state of supreme and intense joy.
Then, for the purpose of the consecration bath, there was water comparable to nectar.
And he summoned sixty-four kings along with their wives to bring [the water]. Rāma, together with Sītā, went to fetch the water,
carrying a golden-colored pitcher adorned with every ornament.

The son of Sumitrā married Ūrmilā; King Bharata, the son of Aṅgada; Śatrughna, the son of Nṛpa; Puṣkala, the son of Śatrughna; and Satyavān, the son of Subāhu, married Śrutakīrti, Kāntimatī, and Vīrabhūṣā respectively.
There, King Sumada was with Satkīrti; and King Vimala was with Rājñī;
there, King Vīramaṇi was with Manojñā; Lakṣmīnidhi was with Komalā; and Ariputāpa was with Aṅgasenā. (38–39)
Vibhīṣaṇa was mounted on a horse of great stature, foremost in majesty and well-known;
Ugrāśva on one that could go anywhere at will and was exceedingly beautiful with its dark-blue jewels;
Suratha on one that was most captivating; and the monkey (Aṅgada) on one that was enchanting.
The brahmin sage Vasiṣṭha sent these and other kings away.
Having gone to the Sarayū river, which was flooded with auspicious and holy waters, Vasiṣṭha, the knower of mantras, consecrated the water with this mantra.
"O Purifier of Waters, purify this man with water drawn by Manoharā for the sake of the sacrifice of Rāmacandra, the sole protector of all the worlds.
(43) Then all the kings, headed by Rāma, touched that water which had been touched by the sage.
On the floor of the pavilion, which was praised by the foremost of brahmins, they bathed the horse, who was white as milk, with pure waters;
then the son of the Pot-born Sage (Agastya) consecrated it with mantras in the hand of Rāma. 44–45.
"O great-armed one, purify me in this assembly of Brahmins;
may all the gods, fully gratified, be pleased by your sacrifice.
Having spoken thus, King Rāma touched [the ground] together with Sītā.
Then all the twice-born ones marveled with great curiosity;
they said to one another, "Aho! What is this that men are saying—that by the mere remembrance of his name, people are liberated from even the greatest sins? (47-48)
When the lord of the earth had spoken thus,
the sage born from a jar (Agastya) consecrated a sword with mantras and placed it in Rāma’s hand.
As soon as the sword was grasped and touched by Rāma at the sacrifice, the horse [was released].
Having quickly cast off his state as a beast, he attained a divine form (50).
Mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot, surrounded on all sides by Apsarases,
fanned with chowries, and adorned with the Vaijayantī garland (51).
Then, seeing that excellent one who had cast off his mortal form and assumed a divine body, all those present at the sacrifice were filled with wonder. At that time,
Rāma, knowing the truth himself, made it known to all the people from every side.
The most virtuous one questioned that god of divine form:
"Who are you who have attained this celestial body? Why have you come here, O winged one? How is it that you are accompanied by a celestial woman? Tell me, what do you intend to do? (53-54)
Having heard Rāma’s words, the God, laughing, spoke to the lord of the earth; he uttered a most charming voice with the resonance of a thundercloud:
"Nothing remains unknown to you, who move both outside and within everything."
Nevertheless, since you ask, I shall tell it to you exactly as it happened. O destroyer of enemies, in a former life I was a most righteous brahmin, yet I acted in opposition to the Vedas. (56–57)
Once in the past, he went to the bank of the Dhutapāpā river,
which was graced by many trees and delightful in every way with its beautiful flowers.
Having bathed there, satisfied his ancestors, and given gifts according to the prescribed rites, [he remained].
O mighty-armed one, he performed a meditation in accordance with the Vedas.
At that time, O King, many people gathered there;
for the sake of deceiving them, I practiced this hypocrisy.
The supreme courtyard was filled with the materials for numerous sacrifices;
it was beautiful, vast, covered with cloths, and provided with sacrificial sheds (caṣāla) and other structures.
The smoke arising from the *agnihotra* fires spread in all directions toward the sky.
Bearing a body that was beautiful, incomparable, and wondrous to behold, he performed [the rite].

(62) With his limbs adorned by the splendor of many sectarian marks (*tilaka*), and possessing great austerity, he was resplendent with *darbha* grass; with sacrificial fuel (*samidh*) in hand, was he perhaps Dambha (Hypocrisy) personified? (63)
Wandering at will across the surface of the earth, the highly effulgent Durvāsas arrived there on the bank of the river Dhūtapāpā and saw me before him, practicing hypocrisy while observing silence.

Seeing me, who was acting like a madman of priceless deeds and offering no word of welcome, that great-minded sage, overcome with intense anger like the ocean during a full moon, cursed me, the deceitful one, with fierce words.
"O evil-minded one, if you practice hypocrisy even after crossing this river,
then, O lowest of ascetics, you shall attain the state of a beast, which is beyond reproach.
Having heard the curse thus bestowed, I became distressed at that time.
At that time, O Rāma, the twice-born Durvāsas indeed bestowed a supreme favor upon me, saying:
"O ascetic, may you attain the state of a horse in the sacrifice of the king of kings. 68–69.

Thereafter, having assumed a divine and heart-stealing form, free from all pretense, through contact with his hand she attained the supreme state. Thus, even the curse pronounced by him became a source of grace for me.
That I have obtained the delightful touch of his hand—
which is difficult even for gods such as Varuṇa and Indra to attain through many lifetimes—
I have here attained that very touch of his hand, which is so difficult to obtain.

"Command me, O Great King! By your grace, I shall go to that great, eternal abode, free from all suffering and the like—where there is neither sorrow, nor old age, nor death, nor the confusion of time. (73)
"O lord of men, by your grace, I shall go to that place, O God.
Having spoken thus, he circumambulated him and ascended an excellent celestial chariot,
inlaid with many jewels and worshipped by all the gods.
By the grace of Rāma’s feet, he has gone to that eternal abode,
which is free from rebirth and devoid of sorrow and delusion.
Having heard what was told by him and having recognized Rāma, the other people [were filled with joy].
They all attained a state of wonder, intoxicated with joy toward one another.
Listen, O highly intelligent twice-born one: even when remembered through hypocrisy, Hari grants liberation; how much more so when remembered by abandoning hypocrisy! (77-78)
"By whatever means possible, O Rāma, one must practice remembrance as the supreme [duty], through which one attains the highest state, difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Seeing that wonder, the sages considered themselves to have achieved their life's purpose.
Or rather, when that god had previously departed for heaven in the form of a horse, having been purified by the sight of my feet and the touch of my hand,
Rāma spoke to those foremost knowers of the Vedas, who were treasures of asceticism. 80–81.

"O Brahmin, what should be done by me now that the horse has been lost? How shall the future sacrifice proceed, which satisfies all the deities? How may there be complete satisfaction for the gods, and how may my sacrifice become supreme? (82)

"O sages, act in such a way that my desire may be fulfilled according to the injunctions of the Vedas. Having heard these words, Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages and an expert in discerning the thoughts of all the gods, spoke.
"Bring camphor quickly, so that the gods themselves, now impelled by my word, may receive the oblation upon obtaining it. Having heard these words, Rāma brought it forth immediately.
For the sake of pleasing many gods, that camphor was exceedingly beautiful. Then the sage, with a delighted soul, summoned the wondrous deities;
they all arrived at that very moment, surrounded by their own retinues.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Commencement of the Sacrifice," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* within the *Śeṣa-Vātsyāyana Saṃvāda* of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter Sixty-Eight.
Śeṣa said:

Thereupon, Indra, together with the gods, partook of the sacrificial oblation purified by Rāmacandra; yet, even though he was joined by the deities, he did not attain satisfaction at the sacrifice. 1.
Nārāyaṇa, Mahādeva, the four-faced Brahmā, Varuṇa, Kubera, and likewise the other world-protectors were there;
having tasted the unctuous sacrificial oblation prepared by Vasiṣṭha, they remained there.
Then, O best of Brahmins, like one afflicted by hunger desiring food,
that treasury of compassion, having gratified all the gods with the sacrificial oblation (havis),
performed every duty as urged by Vasiṣṭha.
Satisfied with the gifts from the Brahmins, the best of gods were pleased;
having taken their respective portions, they all went to their own abodes, fully contented.
He bestowed upon the sages, headed by the chief Hotṛ priests, sovereignty over the four quarters.
Being satisfied, those twice-born ones gave auspicious blessings to Rāma;
then, having performed the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), Vasiṣṭha said to the virtuous women,
"May they congratulate the supreme lord of the earth, who has completed the sacrifice."
Hearing those words, the women joyfully showered him— who had surpassed Kāmadeva in beauty and was adorned with great jewels— with parched grains (lāja).
Then, he urged the king to perform the purificatory bath (avabhṛthasnāna).
Accompanied by his own powerful forces and surrounded by many millions of kings traveling on foot, Rāma went to the excellent bank of the Sarayū,
which was filled with flocks of birds and was the best of rivers. 9–10.
Just as the moon, the lord of the stars, shines resplendent when surrounded by his wives,
so too did Rāma shine, surrounded by the hosts of kings.
Having learned of that festival, the people went there with great haste.
With their eyes fixed motionlessly upon the face of Sītā’s husband,
the people— delighted at the sight and longing for a long time to behold him— beheld the lord of kings proceeding with Sītā toward the river.
Many actors and gandharvas, singing of his radiant glory,
followed the Lord of the Earth, who is honored by all the worlds. There, dancing girls were dancing, agitating the mind of their lord.
Sprinkling water with mechanical devices, they went to serve Śrī Rāma.
Anointing the great king with turmeric, saffron, and other substances, and anointing one another, they attained supreme joy. 15–16.
Adorned with pearl necklaces resting upon their pairs of breasts and distinguished by golden earrings shimmering on their two ears, they proceeded along a path crowded with many men and women. 17.
He beheld the river Sarayū as it truly was, flooded with auspicious and holy waters. Having gone there with Vaidehī and Rāma, the lotus-eyed one,
accompanied by Vasiṣṭha and the others, entered the sacred water.
All the kings and the people likewise entered that water, which was purified by the dust of his feet and honored by the world alone; they sprinkled one another with beautiful water-machines. 20.

With their eyes reddened by joy, they all experienced exceeding delight. Having sported for a long time with Sītā amidst the waves of the holy waters, Rāma, endowed with righteousness, emerged from the lake.
Clad in fine *dukūla* silk, wearing a crown and earrings, adorned with the splendor of armlets and excellent bracelets,
and bearing the beauty of ten million gods of love, the king shone while being praised by the most eminent of monarchs.
Having constructed a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) resplendent with excellent colors upon a choice riverbank, that high-minded one—
Seizing with his own arms that wondrous glory of the three worlds, which was difficult for others to attain, the king—
thus performing three horse-sacrifices with the daughter of Janaka—
attained incomparable fame throughout the three worlds, which is very difficult even for the gods to achieve.
Thus, O dear one, that virtuous story of Rāma which you asked about has been narrated by me at length; O wise brahmin, what more do you wish to ask?
He who listens with devotion to this account of Rāmacandra, as if it were a sacrifice, [attains the highest goal].
Having instantly crossed over the sin of killing a Brahmin, one shall attain the eternal Brahman.
One without a son obtains sons; the destitute obtains wealth.
One afflicted by disease is freed from disease, and one who is bound is released from bondage.
By hearing whose story even a wicked outcaste attains the supreme state; how much more so a preeminent Brahmin who is devoted to Rāma?
By remembering the illustrious Rāma, even sinners reach the highest abode. (29)
They shall attain the supreme heaven, difficult even for Śakra and the gods to reach.
(30) Those men in this world who remember the best of the Raghus are blessed;
having crossed the ocean of worldly existence in an instant, they go to imperishable bliss. (31)
Each individual syllable is a forest fire for the lineage of the sin of killing a Brahmin;
the wise man who causes this to be heard should fully honor that teacher. Having heard the story, one should present a pair of cows to the reciter.
Having honored them along with their wives with garments, ornaments, and food—
Rāma and Sītā, who shone with two earrings and were adorned with rings— he gave them excellent, beautiful golden images.
O best of the twice-born, when this is performed and given to the reciter,
then the gods and the ancestors shall attain Vaikuṇṭha. The story of Rāma, which you asked about, has been told by me to you as it was in the past.
O Brahmin, what else may be told before you, who are so wise?
Those who hear this narrative which destroys the flood of sins arising from the killing of a Brahmin,
they go to the supreme abode which is very difficult even for the gods to attain.
Even a killer of a cow, a killer of a son, a drinker of liquor, or one who violates the teacher’s bed becomes purified in an instant; there is no room for doubt in this matter.
(38) Thus ends the section on Rāma’s Horse Sacrifice within the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
The sixty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Merit of Hearing and Reciting," is concluded.
Thus ends the section on the Horse Sacrifice of Rāma.
The sixty-ninth chapter begins.
The sages said: O highly fortunate one, we have duly heard from you concerning Rāma’s horse-sacrifice;
now speak of the majesty of the great-souled Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Sūta said:
O tigers among sages, listen to the nectar of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s deeds;
that which Pārvatī asked of the Lord of Beings, I shall now proclaim to you. 2.
Once, the goddess Pārvatī, her mind full of affection for Śiva, bowed with love and spoke these words: Pārvatī said:
The supreme abode of Viṣṇu, situated both inside and outside of infinite millions of cosmic eggs, is the foremost, most excellent, and highest among them;
it is the unsurpassed, delightful place that is dear to Kṛṣṇa. 4.
"I desire to hear all of that; please tell it to me, O Great Lord.
The Lord said: "This is a secret more secret than the most secret, which brings about supreme bliss."
It is a most wonderful secret place, supreme and ultimate bliss; the most difficult to attain among all things difficult to attain, supremely enchanting,
consisting of all powers, O Goddess, and hidden from all other locations.
The preeminent abode of the Sātvatas, which is exceedingly difficult even for Viṣṇu to attain,
is the eternal place named Vṛndāvana, situated above the cosmic egg;
it possesses the fullness of Brahman’s bliss and sovereignty, and is eternally imperishable joy.
Vṛndāvana itself on earth is a portion of a portion of Vaikuṇṭha and other realms.
Whatever sovereignty belongs to Goloka is established here in Gokula;
and whatever majesty belongs to Vaikuṇṭha is established in Dvārakā.

That supreme sovereignty of Brahman which is eternal and centered in Vṛndāvana— the supreme abode of Kṛṣṇa for them, especially within that forest— is found there. Therefore, among the three worlds, the earth is renowned as blessed.
Because the region named Mathurā is the singular favorite of Viṣṇu; it is his own preeminent abode, the domain of Mathurā, containing various secret locations situated within the city. 12–13.
The Mathurā-maṇḍala has the form of a thousand-petaled lotus;
through the revolution of Viṣṇu’s discus, it is the wonderful abode of Vaiṣṇava. Its expanse of pericarp and petals is declared to be the secret tree.
The greatness of the twelve principal forests has been described in sequence:
Bhadra, Śrīloha, Bhāṇḍīra, Mahātāla, Khadīraka, Bakula, Kumuda, Kāmya, and likewise Madhu-vṛndāvana. 15–16.
Twelve such Kalpas have passed; in the west there are seven and in the east five forests are proclaimed, among which lies the supreme secret:
the great forest named Gokula, as well as Madhu-vṛndāvana. 17.
Furthermore, another grove is proclaimed as the place for the essence of Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes:
the Kadamba-khaṇḍana, Nandavana, Nandīśvara, and likewise the Nandanandana-khaṇḍa, along with Palāśa, Aśoka, and Ketakī. 18–19.
Sugandhamānasaka, Amṛtabhojanasthala,
Sukhaprasādhana, Vatsaharaṇa, Śeṣaśāyika, Śyāmapūrvodadhigrāma, and likewise Cakrabhānupura. 20.
It was a place of conventions and two-footed creatures, grey with the dust of children’s play;
a lovely grove of wish-fulfilling trees, full of longing, a site for various kinds of amorous sports and the essence of diverse playful pastimes. (21–22)
It is said to be the secret tree that restrains the expansion of the serpent [of worldly existence],
the great abode called Gokula which possesses a thousand-petaled lotus; its pericarp is that great splendor, the supreme station of Govinda.
There, upon a golden pedestal above, it is adorned with a pavilion of jewels (24).
In the pericarp, the petals are said to be arranged in order toward the cardinal and intermediate directions;
that petal which is declared to be in the south is the supreme among the supremely secret (25).
In that petal is the great sacred seat (mahāpīṭha), difficult to access through the Nigamas and Āgamas, hard for even the lords of yogins to attain, which is Gokula, the soul of all.
The second petal is in the southeast; it is likewise the secret petal.
Saṃketa, Dvipada, and Kuṭī—these two reside in that lineage.
The third part, the foremost and most excellent place, is remembered as being a hundred times more meritorious than the touch of all sacred fords such as the Gaṅgā. 27–28.
On the fourth petal in the northeast, at the Siddha-pīṭha, that very state is bestowed;
by practicing there, one obtains a husband who is dark-complexioned, young, and a protector.
The stealing of clothes and ornaments is said to occur on that petal.
The fifth petal, declared to be the best of all petals, is said to be in the north;
here, the twelve Ādityas reside, and this petal is equal in size to the pericarp.
In the northwest, however, is the sixth petal, where the lake of Kālī is remembered to be.
The supreme among the supreme is declared to be the primary station;
the petal that is the best of all is remembered as the seventh in the west, which grants the desired boons to the hosts of sacrificial wives. 32.
Here, even the Asura attained Nirvana, which is difficult for the gods to achieve.
Here too is the petal that deludes Brahmā and brings about the Brahmahrada;
in the southwest is declared the eighth petal, the destroyer of the sky.

There, the slaying of Śaṅkhacūḍa is the place for the flavor of various pastimes; it is said to be the eight-petaled lotus situated within the Vṛndā forest. The beautiful and glorious Vṛndāvana lies to the right of the Yamunā.
The Śiva-liṅga known as Gopīśvara was seen as the foundational seat (adhiṣṭhāna).
Outside of that is the sixteen-petaled [lotus] filled with splendor; that Lord is proclaimed to be in all directions, proceeding in due order by way of circumambulation. 36–37.
The great station, the great abode, known as Svadhāma,
the foremost and excellent single-petaled lotus whose majesty is equal to the pericarp—
there, on Mount Govardhana, the delightful refuge of eternal rasa.
In the pericarp [of that lotus] are Mahālīlā and Tallīlā, who are the depths of the essence of divine play (līlā-rasa).
There, Kṛṣṇa is eternally the Lord of the Vṛndā forest;
Kṛṣṇa has attained the state of Govinda—what is the use of further words? 39–40.
The third petal is declared to be the most excellent of all the best;
the fourth petal is declared to be the place of the most wonderful sentiment (rasa). There lies the delightful Nandīśvara forest, where the abode of Nandin is remembered to be.
The fifth circle is said to be the greatness of the pericarp and petals (karṇikā-dalamāhātmya).
Here, Gopāla, who is intent on tending the cows, is the presiding deity.
That which is called the sixth petal is known as Nandavana. 42–43.
The seventh petal is proclaimed as the beautiful Bakula forest;
there, the eighth is the Tāla grove, where the slaying of the cow is recorded to have occurred.
The ninth petal is proclaimed as the beautiful Kumuda forest.

The forest of Kāmāraṇya is the tenth, the primary cause of all. Therein lies the accomplishment of Brahman and the manifestation of Viṣṇu’s disguise; it is called the primary seat of the essence of Kṛṣṇa’s play and his retinue. 45–46.
The eleventh petal is said to be the cause of grace for devotees;
it is the site of the construction of the Setubandha, a place consisting of various groves.
The twelfth petal is the delightful and enchanting forest of Bhāṇḍīra.

There, Kṛṣṇa, delighting in play, is surrounded by Śrīdāma and others. (48) The thirteenth petal is excellent; there, Bhadra-vara is remembered [to be]. The fourteenth petal is declared to be the place that bestows all spiritual perfections. (49)
The Śrīvana forest is beautiful and the cause of all sovereignty; it consists of the petals of Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes and increases fortune, splendor, and fame.
(50) Therein, the fifteenth petal is remembered as the excellent Lohavana.
The greatness of the sixteen-petaled lotus, equal to the pericarp, has been told.
There, the Great Forest is celebrated; there lies the supreme secret.
There, He is engaged in childhood play, surrounded by cowherd boys.

The slaying of Pūtanā and others, as well as the breaking of the twin *arjuna* trees; there, the presiding Lord was the young cowherd boy of five years, known by the name Dāmodara, an ocean of the essence of the nectar of love. (53)
The petal is well-known as the most excellent of all supreme petals (54).
The filament is said to be the petal of the Kṛṣṇa-play garden,
and it is also declared to be the petal of the filament of the preeminent Siddhas (55).
Pārvatī said:
"O Great Lord, I desire to hear the greatness and the wonderful secret of the Vṛndā forest; please tell it to me. (56)
Īśvara said:
O most beloved one, I have told you that which is the secret of secrets, the highest of the high, the mystery of mysteries, and the most difficult to attain among all things difficult to attain. 57
This place is protected by the three worlds, highly honored by the Lord of the Gods, desired by Brahmā and others, and served by the gods, siddhas, and the rest;
for the lords of yogis are always devoted with bhakti, intent solely upon its meditation. 58.
With Apsarases and Gandharvas engaged in incessant dancing and singing,
the glorious Vṛndāvana is delightful, the refuge of the essence of perfect bliss;
its waters are like abundant Cintāmaṇi gems, filled with the nectar of rasa.
There, the tree was a great sandalwood tree frequented by swarms of fragrant bees;
the woman was Lakṣmī and the man was Viṣṇu, born from a tenth part of that [tree].
There, he was of youthful age and eternally an embodiment of bliss.
That forest was constantly filled with Vaiṣṇavas of pure being who were full of love, whose movements, dances, playful speech, and smiles were uninterrupted;
it was immersed in the bliss of the perfect Brahman, radiant with His form, and identical with Him.
It was enchanting with the warbling of intoxicated cuckoos, bees, and other birds; it resounded with the song of parrots upon its banks and the humming of thousands of frenzied bees.
It was enriched by the dancing of peacocks—the enemies of serpents—and possessed the intoxicating grace of every season.
It was filled with pollen from flowers of various colors;
it possessed the eternal rising of the full moon and was graced by the gentle rays of the sun;
it was free from suffering, a cessation of all pain, and devoid of old age and death.
Free from anger and devoid of envy, undivided and without egoism;
a full ocean of the bliss of perfect love, filled with the nectar-essence of complete joy;
transcending all qualities, the great abode whose very nature is perfect love.
Where even the trees and other plants experience horripilation and shed tears of the nectar of love (68),
what then can be said of those endowed with consciousness who are devotees of Viṣṇu?
By the touch of the dust of Govinda’s feet, Vṛndāvana is eternally [holy] on this earth (69).
Vṛndāraṇya is the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus;
by the mere touch of it, the earth becomes blessed throughout the three worlds.
Situated within Vṛndāvana on this earth, it is more secret than the secret and most enchanting.
The syllable *akṣara* is supreme bliss, the imperishable abode of Govinda. It is non-different from the body of Govinda and is the refuge of the bliss of the perfect Brahman.
Liberation occurs there by the mere touch of its dust; how can its greatness be described? 71-72.
Therefore, with your whole being, make that forest dwell within your heart— Kṛṣṇa, whose youthful form sports in Vṛndāvana,
around the pericarp of whose lotus feet Kālī performed circumambulation. 73.
Its waters were profound with playful tranquility and enchanting with fragrance;
they were blended with the nectar of bliss and abounded with thick clusters of flower-nectar.
It was brilliantly radiant with various colors from blossoms such as lotuses and water-lilies. 74–75.
The water was beautiful, graced by birds such as ruddy geese with sweet and melodious calls, and its waves were exceedingly enchanting; both its banks were lovely, fashioned as if from pure gold. 76.
It is said that where even a single cowrie shell [offered] has ten million times the merit of the Gaṅgā (77),
there, in the pericarp, Hari delights in play with ten millionfold merit;
Kālindī, the pericarp, and Kṛṣṇa are one inseparable form (78).
Pārvatī said:
"O treasure-house of compassion, what is so wonderful about Govinda’s form, which possesses such beauty? I wish to hear that; please tell me. (79)
Īśvara said: In the midst of beautiful Vṛndāvana, which is adorned with charming anklets and embellished by the branches and sprouts of excellent trees extending for many yojanas— (80)
In the center of that [palace] is the brilliantly radiant yoga-pīṭha in the Mañju-bhavana; its construction consists of eight corners and is enchanting with various splendors.
Upon it is a beautiful lion-throne made of rubies and jewels.
Upon that [lotus] is an eight-petaled lotus, with a pericarp that is a seat of bliss;
it is the supreme abode of Govinda—how can its greatness be described?
It is served by the multitude of cowherdesses residing within the glorious mantra of Govinda. 82–83.

Kṛṣṇa, the lord of Vṛndāvana, possessing divine youth and beauty, the sovereign of Vraja with eternal sovereignty, the sole beloved of the children of Vraja, whose childhood was blossoming into youth and whose form was wondrous by virtue of his age. 84.
The beginningless origin of all, the beloved son of Nanda the cowherd; sought by the Vedas, unborn and eternal, the heart-stealer of the gopīs;
the supreme abode, the supreme form, two-armed Lord of Gokula. (85–86)
One should meditate upon the son of the cowherdesses, the sole cause of the attributeless [Brahman],
who is exceedingly glorious, fresh, pure, possessing a charming dark luster,
and adorned with beautiful earrings as lovely as a row of fresh rain clouds. 87.
Possessing the beautiful luster of a blooming blue lotus, it was pleasant to the touch and brought happiness;
it was dark and enchanting, with the appearance of a mass of crushed collyrium, smooth, and adorned with very glossy, dark, curly locks of hair that were entirely fragrant. 88–89.
Above that, on the right, was the Kāleśyā [mountain], enchanting with its crest,
shining with various colors, adorned with a royal tuft of leaves,
and possessing a beautiful crest of a soft, lovely cow’s tail as its ornament. 90.
In some places it was adorned with a crown of rows of large leaves;
in other places, it was decorated with crests and ornaments of many gems and rubies; in others, it was veiled by dangling locks of hair, its face resembling ten million moons of silver.
He has a shining tilaka-mark of musk combined with beautiful gorocana;
his eyes have long, very smooth petals like blue lotuses;
he possesses a smiling gaze with arched brows that seem to embrace one another in a dance. 93.
Extremely captivating with the tip of her nose possessing exquisite, elevated beauty;

enchanting the three worlds with the luster of the pearls on the tips of her elephants [or the pearls atop her nose]; and most beautiful with lips as lovely as flowers, glistening and reddened by vermilion (94–95).
His earrings, shaped like golden makaras, shimmered with various colors;
their radiance shone brilliantly upon his cheeks, which resembled mirrors made of a mass of light.
He was adorned with ear-lotuses, jasmine flowers, and makara-shaped crest-ornaments. 96.
His chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem; his throat gleams with a pearl necklace;
he is adorned with shimmering divine rubies interspersed with beautiful gold; his hands bear bracelets and armlets, and his waist is graced by tinkling bells. 97–98.
He is resplendent with feet graced by the beauty of tinkling anklets,
and his divine body is adorned with fragrant unguents such as camphor, aguru, musk, and sandalwood, mixed with gorocanā and other substances. 99.
With the soles of his feet shining like smooth yellow sandalwood and his eyes like rolling collyrium; with a deep lotus-like navel and a garland of curved lines of body hair;
with a pair of well-rounded knees and enchanting lotus-feet. 100–101.
Adorned with hands holding a banner, a vajra, a goad, and a lotus, and with the soles of his feet graced by rows of moon-like rays from his fingernails— the sole cause of Brahman—
some declare him to be a non-dual portion of that [Brahman] whose nature is consciousness. 102.
The wise declare that Mahāviṣṇu is one-tenth of that [Brahmā].
He is meditated upon in the heart by the lords of yogis, such as Nara and others, as having three bends (tribhaṅga), fashioned from the essence of all graceful creation. 103–104.
His neck was curved like that of a swan, surpassing the beauty of infinite millions of Cupids;
on his left shoulder rested a beautiful golden earring shimmering against his fine cheek, while he smiled with sidelong glances, more lovely than ten million gods of love. 105.
Enchanting the three worlds with the sweet, resonant sounds of the flute placed against his pursed lips, he was immersed in an ocean of the nectar of love.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
The supreme cause, Kṛṣṇa, known as Govinda, the great state, the eternal Lord of Vṛndāvana, the sole cause of the attributeless— one—
what wonderful and beautiful majesty of His various secrets [is there]? 107–108.
"O Lord of the gods, O Master, tell me that which I desire to hear. The Lord said:
"The limit of the majesty of the moonbeams from the nails of whose feet cannot be reached. (109)
O Goddess, listen with joy as I describe how great that majesty is:
within infinite millions of cosmic eggs, which possess an infinite expansion of the three qualities,
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are but infinitesimal fractions— parts of a hundred-millionth part— of His power.

The manifestations of His glory, engaged in the creation, maintenance, and so forth [of the universe], abide as such; portions consisting of millions upon millions of His forms, possessing bodies like those of Kandarpa, they bring about the delusion of the world while remaining within His cosmic egg. 111-112.
The omnipresent Lord is but a ten-millionth part of a ten-millionth part of the splendor shining from his body; the rays of his light are like sparks of fire.
With the rays of his own body, which are the nectar-essence of supreme bliss, [he nourishes others].
They consist of the nature of supreme bliss and consciousness, being the sole cause of that which is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
They are composed of rays that are like the living souls (jīvas), each being a ten-millionth part of a ten-millionth part of His portion.
They are the radiance of the moon-like jewels of the nails on the pair of His lotus feet.
They say that even the Perfect Brahman has a cause that is difficult for the Vedas to comprehend;
an infinite croreth part of a portion of that [Brahman] is the Enchanter of the Universe.
From the touch of that [Brahman], there arises the manifold fragrance of flowers and other scents.
Her beloved’s own nature is that of Ādyā Rādhikā, the consort of Kṛṣṇa (117).
From even a ten-millionth of a ten-millionth part of her power, Durgā and others, who consist of the three qualities, arise;
by the touch of the dust of Her feet, ten million Viṣṇus are produced (118).
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter [and begins the seventieth chapter] in the Vṛndāvana-māhātmya, within the Kṛṣṇacaritra of the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Seventy.
Pārvatī said:
O Lord, I desire to hear that which was heard by the attendants of the Master; tell it to me, O ocean of compassion. 1.
Īśvara said:
[He saw] Govinda seated upon a golden lion-throne together with Rādhā, possessing the previously described form and beauty, and adorned with divine ornaments, garments, and garlands. 2.

On a golden lion-throne situated upon a yogic seat outside that [palace], there were the principal beloveds of Kṛṣṇa, who were intensely absorbed in the passionate embrace of his every limb, their bodies tender with the sweetness of his three-fold bending posture (tribhaṅgī), and captivating like the pupils of the eyes of the gopīs. 3.
Lalitā and the others are portions of Prakṛti, while Mūlaprakṛti is Rādhikā. Goddess Lalitā is in front; Śyāmalā is in the northwest corner;
Śrīmatī is in the north; Dhanyā is in the northeast; and Śrī Haripriyā is in the east.
Viśākhā is likewise in the east, Śaibyā in the southeast; thereafter Padmā is situated in the south, and subsequently in the southwest, in the Nairṛta direction.
On the Yogapīṭha, at the tip of the filaments, is the beloved Cārucandrāvatī.
There are eight auspicious primary Prakṛtis who are dear to Kṛṣṇa.
The first among these primary Prakṛtis is Rādhā, who is equal to Candrāvatī;
[the others are] Candrāvalī, Citrarekhā, and Candrāmadanasundarī.
Priyā, Śrīmadhumatī, Candrarekhā, Haripriyā, and the sixteen primary Prakṛtis who are the beloveds of Kṛṣṇa;
likewise Rādhā, the Queen of Vṛndāvana, and Candrāvalī, his beloved.

There were thousands of other cowherd girls ahead of them, possessing undivided qualities of grace and beauty, with lovely eyes, charming and innocent attire, and radiant with the bloom of youth. 10–11.
Resembling masses of pure gold, they were serene and possessed beautiful eyes;
with that form ascended upon their hearts, they were eager for her embrace,
immersed in the nectar-like essence of Śyāmā, and their minds vibrated with her state of being.
