Their minds were offered at the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, which are worshipped by the blue-lotuses of their eyes;
then, the daughters of Śrutadeva, numbering thousands and tens of thousands,
with forms that enchant the world and hearts longing for Kṛṣṇa, stood to his right.

Then, celestial maidens, resplendent in divine attire and radiant with the essence of passion, stood to her left; they had enchanted the three worlds with their various vocal melodies and conversations, and, overwhelmed with love, they sang of the hidden secrets therein. 15.
Endowed with a multitude of various clever arts and divine dispositions,
rich in supreme beauty and possessing most enchanting side-glances,
they were shameless there, striving to touch the limbs of Govinda.
With their minds immersed in that state, their gazes fixed on her smiling face,
they then went outside the palace, which was surrounded by their beloved;
they were equal in dress and age, and equal in strength and prowess.
Possessing identical qualities and activities, fond of the same ornaments,
and devoted to singing and playing the flute in unison,
Śrīdāmā was at the western gate and Vasudāmā was at the northern gate. 19–20.
To the east is Sudāmā, and likewise Kiṅkiṇī is to the south;
outside of that, on a golden pedestal surrounded by golden mansions,
situated within a golden altar and adorned with golden ornaments.

Accompanied by tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of cowherd boys—Subhadra and others—who were slightly dark-complexioned, and who possessed horns, lutes, flutes, and canes, and who matched him in age, dress, appearance, and voice;
who were absorbed in meditation on His qualities and were singing while overwhelmed with emotion. (22-23)

It was surrounded by countless Govindas depicted in various forms within the paintings, who were showering tears of constant bliss, their entire bodies bristling with horripilation like astonished lords of yogis. It was filled with Govindas from whom nectar was flowing.
Outside of that is a golden rampart, blazing with the brilliance of ten million suns; in its four directions are great gardens, enchanting with their exquisite fragrance,
and facing west, there is a magnificent abode sheltered by a Pārijāta tree.
Beneath that, upon a golden pedestal adorned with golden ornaments,
and in its center, resplendent with a divine lion-throne of jewels and rubies (27),
there [sat] Vāsudeva, the Lord of the universe, who is supreme bliss.
The form of consciousness transcending the three qualities (guṇas), the cause of all causes;
dark blue like a sapphire or a rain cloud, with dark, curly locks of hair;
with large eyes like lotus petals and earrings shaped like sea-monsters (makaras). 28–29.
Four-armed, bearing the discus, sword, mace, conch, and lotus as weapons;
devoid of beginning and end, eternal, the primordial Pradhāna, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama);
the form of light, the great abode, the ancient one, adorned with a garland of forest flowers.
He wore yellow garments, was gracious, and adorned with divine ornaments;
he was smeared with divine unguents, his limbs were radiant and variegated, and he was enchanting to behold.
Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, Nāgnajitī, and Sulakṣaṇā [were there]. 31–32.
Then there were eight women dear to Vāsudeva: Mitravindā, Anuvindā, Sunandā, Jāmbavatī, Priyā, and Suśīlā.
Furthermore, the attendants of the two [brothers] were resplendent and devoted to their service.
In the great northern garden, resting upon Haricandana trees,
there was a golden pedestal adorned with a jeweled pavilion;
in its center stood a brilliant lion-throne fashioned of gold.
Right there he saw Saṃkarṣaṇa, whose weapon is the plow, together with Revatī—
the beloved of the Lord, who is non-different from him in qualities and form—
resembling pure crystal and having eyes like the petals of a red lotus. (36)
Wearing a smooth blue silk garment, adorned with divine ornaments, garlands, and fine raiment;
ever addicted to drinking wine, his eyes rolling from intoxication;
he was situated in the beautiful inner part on the right side of the hero.
At the foot of the tree of the lineage, adorned with a palace of jewels,
in its center, upon a resplendent divine throne of gems and rubies,
the god Pradyumna moves, seated there in comfort.
He whose essence consists of the stream of the finest beauty that deludes the world;
who has the luster of a cluster of blue lotuses and eyes like the petals of a lotus;
who is adorned with divine ornaments and anointed with divine perfumes.
[He beheld] that body which was a wonder of beauty, enchanting the entire world;
there, beneath a great forest tree in the eastern garden, which resembled a celestial tree, upon a golden pedestal adorned with a golden pavilion— 42.
In its center, upon a divine lion-throne radiant with royal splendor,
sat the Lord of the World, the illustrious Aniruddha, together with his divine consort;
he was dark like a dense mass of bliss, exceedingly tender, and possessed of beautiful, dark-blue locks of hair.
With eyebrows possessing the graceful curve of a bow, beautiful cheeks, a fine nose, a handsome neck, and a chest that was lovely and captivating;
he wore a crown and earrings, and was adorned with ornaments upon his neck. 45.
Whose form is exceedingly beautiful due to the sweetness of his tinkling anklets;
who is worshipped by a host of dear servants; who delights in musical performances; who is the fullness of Brahman, eternal bliss, and the very nature of pure being. 46–47.
Above him, in the intermediate space, he beheld Viṣṇu, the Lord of all lords,
beginningless yet the source of all, whose nature is consciousness, the supreme pervasive Lord,
beyond the three qualities, unmanifest, eternal, imperishable, and immutable. 48.
His body was dark-complexioned with a sweetness and beauty like a mass of clouds;
he was exceedingly handsome with a mass of dark, curly, and very glossy hair, and possessed long, beautiful eyes as lovely as lotus petals. 49–50.
It was surrounded by those whose very selves were pure sattva, adorned with crowns, earrings, and prominent cheeks;

who delighted in the Self, whose nature was consciousness, and who were intent on meditating upon His form (51); whose meditation on Him had ascended into their hearts, and whose eyes were fixed on the tip of the nose.
Devotion without cause is performed through the body, heart, actions, and speech (52),
by those including the Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and Vidyādharas, and by beautiful throngs of Apsarases intent on dance and song (53).
Then, desiring to worship His limbs and longing for Kṛṣṇa,
all the Vaiṣṇavas stood before Him in the sky upon comfortable seats, along with Prahlāda, Nārada, and others, as well as Kumāra, Śuka, and other devotees of Viṣṇu.

With Janaka and others, whose radiant states of being were intent on the manifestation [of the Divine] both within and without, whose every limb was bristling with horripilation, who were overwhelmed by throbbing love,
and who were drenched in the nectar of the secret [teaching], the mantra of the half-couple of syllables [was recited]. (55–56)
It is declared to be the crest-jewel of mantras, the sole cause of all mantras;
it is the youthfulness of the mantras of all the gods, having the mantra as its source.
This mantra, the crest-jewel, is the cause of all mantras that possess the quality of youthfulness.
Taking refuge in the bliss of perfect love, they perform their recitation (japa) with the mind;
they desire that lotus-foot as the firm means for attaining love.
Outside of that, within a beautiful enclosure made of high walls of crystal and other precious materials, (they remain). 58–59.
In the four directions, crowded with saffron, white, red, and other colors,
one should place Viṣṇu, white in color and four-armed, as the guardian of the western door,
adorned with a conch, discus, mace, lotus, crown, and other ornaments.
To the north is the red, four-armed gatekeeper, radiant with a crown and earrings, bearing the weapons of the lotus, conch, discus,
and mace; and [further] the fair-complexioned, four-armed Viṣṇu, bearing the weapons of the conch, discus, and mace.
Adorned with a crown, earrings, and other ornaments, and wearing a garland of forest flowers— this is proclaimed to be the fair-complexioned Viṣṇu, the gatekeeper at the eastern gate.
He is dark-complexioned, four-armed, and adorned with the conch, discus, and other emblems.
The guardian of the southern gate is Śrī Viṣṇu, who is dark-complexioned. Indeed,
he who, being restrained and pure, reads this account of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, or he who hears it with devotion, attains delight in Govinda.
Thus ends the seventieth chapter in the Kṛṣṇacarita of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa. Chapter seventy-one.
The Holy Goddess said:
O Blessed One, Lord of all beings, Soul of all, Source of all, Lord of gods, Great God, Omniscient One, Mine of Compassion!
I have already been favored by you; once again, out of compassion, please speak to me.
O Lord, you have recounted to me the mantras known as Trailokyamohana;
tell me now by what specific means that god, who possesses a form of great enchantment, sported with the gopīs. (2–3)
Mahādeva said:
Once, Nārada, the bull among sages, playing his lute and having learned of the incarnation of Kṛṣṇa, went to the cowherd settlement of Nanda. 4.
Having gone there to the house of Nanda, he beheld the Lord, the all-pervading and infallible Master, who consists of great yoga, who wears the dance of a child, and who is the vision of the gods,
seated upon a very delicate golden couch spread with cloth. 5.
He was being watched by the cowherd girls as he lay down, ever bringing them joy; his limbs were exceedingly delicate, he was charming with a lovely gaze,
and the circle of his face was framed by loose, dark, and curly locks of hair.
Beholding him, who was clothed in the directions (naked), whose single tusk was slightly revealed by the sprout of a faint smile,
and who illuminated the interior of the palace on all sides with his own radiance,
he attained extreme joy.
Having addressed Nanda, the lord of cowherds, he who is dear to all masters said:
"The life of those devoted to Nārāyaṇa is indeed very difficult to attain;
no one here understands his incomparable power. (9-10)
Even Brahmā and the other gods desire eternal delight in this child; they sing with joy, listen, and offer praise to his exploits, which bring joy to everyone. 11. Such are those who do so.

O best of cowherds, men whose minds are affectionate toward this son of yours, who possesses inconceivable power, shall never suffer any loss of prosperity; therefore, O most excellent of cowherds, abandon all desires for this world and the next.
"O child, show your affection toward him with single-minded devotion and with a focused heart.
Having spoken thus, the bull among sages departed from the abode of bliss.
Honored by him as Viṣṇu, he bowed down and was dismissed.
Then the sage, a great devotee of the Lord, reflected:
"The blessed Lakṣmī, the beloved of Nārāyaṇa Hari, having assumed the form of a cowherd girl for the sake of sporting with the wielder of the Śārṅga bow," ||| 15-16 ||
"She must certainly have descended; of this there is no doubt.
Having reflected thus, the best of sages searched the houses of the residents of Vraja today, house by house.
Having entered as a guest and being worshipped with the thought that he was Viṣṇu,
the best of sages mentally prostrated before all of them— the cowherds and others— upon seeing the supreme joy of everyone toward the son of Nanda. 18–19.
In the house of the cowherds, he saw a girl with a white complexion; having seen her, he reflected, "This is undoubtedly Rāmā. Then the wise one entered the home of the high-souled friend of Nanda.
He went to the great house of a certain eminent cowherd named Bhānu.
Having been honored by him according to the prescribed rites, that high-minded one also asked:
"O virtuous one, you are renowned on earth for your steadfastness in dharma."
I perceive your abundance of wealth, grain, and other riches;
do you have a worthy son, or perhaps a daughter of auspicious marks, through whom your fame shall pervade the entire world? (23)
Having been addressed thus by the best of sages, Bhānu brought his son—
who was possessed of great luster and pride— and introduced him to Nārada.
Seeing him, who was peerless on earth in beauty, the excellent sage [was struck with wonder].

Having embraced him with both arms— he whose eyes were as broad as lotus petals, who had a beautiful neck and lovely eyebrows, whose teeth and ears were exquisite, and who was handsome in every limb— she shed tears of affection.
Then, with affection, the great sage spoke with a faltering voice.
Nārada said: "This child shall be a dear friend to Rāma and Kṛṣṇa."
He will dwell there day and night, free from sloth.
Then, as that bull among sages was about to depart, he addressed the best of cowherds,
and Bhānu spoke to him thus.
O most blessed one, may this dull-witted younger sister of mine, who resembles a wooden doll or the wife of a god, and who has the appearance of one who is dull, blind, and deaf,
go forth with zeal to beg a boon from you for the sake of her child's growth.
"By a mere glance with a gracious look, make the sprout of my lineage firm.
Having heard these words of Nārada, his mind drawn by curiosity,
he then entered the palace and saw his daughter rolling upon the ground.

Raising him up and placing him on his lap, the sun, his mind overwhelmed with excessive affection, approached the presence of the best of sages with his body bowed in devotion. Then, that foremost of devotees, the sage who was exceedingly dear to Kṛṣṇa—
Having beheld her supreme form— wonderful, never before seen or heard—
the great sage, who was previously bewildered by love for Hari,
became immersed in the ocean of supreme bliss, that singular elixir.
For two muhūrtas, the sage remained there like a stone;
but the lord of sages, Pratibuddha, slowly opening his eyes, was filled with great wonder and remained silent. (36)
Within his heart, the one of great intelligence reflected thus:
"I have wandered through all the worlds, moving according to my own will; yet, nowhere have I seen anyone whose form is equal to hers. (37-38)
In the worlds of Brahmā, Rudra, and Indra, no one possesses even a ten-millionth part of her splendor; nowhere has such beauty been seen.
O Lord of Mountains, the Blessed Mahāmāyā, the daughter of the Mountain King, has been beheld.
By whose form the entire universe, with its mobile and immobile beings, is deluded;
even she [the goddess Lakṣmī], with her delicate limbs, never attains a fraction of her splendor.
Nor do Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Kānti, Vidyā, and other excellent women ever reach her beauty.

Even the shadow of this [form] is never seen, for it was Viṣṇu’s Mohinī form by which Hara was utterly deluded; even that was seen by me—how could anything be its equal? 42. And how could anything be similar to this?
Therefore, I have no power whatsoever to know her true nature;
nor do others generally know this beloved of Hari, from the mere sight of her, [one knows] the lotus-feet of Govinda. 43-44.
That supernatural power which we previously never possessed has now appeared;
having displayed this supreme majesty exclusively for us, Kṛṣṇa’s form arises for our ultimate satisfaction. 45.
Having reflected thus, the sage sent the preeminent cowherd somewhere else; then, in a secluded place, he praised the girl of divine form:
"O Goddess, sovereign of great yogic power and illusion, O you of great luster! (46-47)
O you who shower the divine limbs of great enchantment and supreme sweetness,
whose mind is softened by the bliss of the most wonderful aesthetic flavor— by some great fortune, you have come within the range of my vision. 48
O Goddess, your gaze is always perceived as turned inward;
thus, within you, you appear entirely satiated with great bliss.
This beautiful face of yours is adorned with a serene, sweet, and gentle expression.
O most beautiful one, you are the power of the primordial seed-syllable (kalikā-śakti) associated with *rajas*, which manifests an extraordinary wonder and the arising of internal bliss;
you are established as the embodiment of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
The supreme power, whose essence is knowledge (*vidyā*), is the reality of pure being (*viśuddhasattva*);
she bestows the supreme mass of Viṣṇu’s bliss, O You of wondrous majesty, who are difficult to fathom even for Brahmā, Rudra, and the others. (52–53)
O Lord, you never touch the path of meditation of even the foremost of yogis;
yet the will-power, the knowledge-power, and the action-power of the Sovereign proceed from you as nothing more than your own portions—such is the conviction that arises in my mind. 54.
The inconceivable manifestations of Māyā belong to that Lord who is the master of Māyā and the Child;
they are all but portions of the portions of Mahāviṣṇu, the Supreme Lord. O Sovereign Lady, you are the power whose very nature is bliss; of this there is no doubt.
"Kṛṣṇa surely played with you in the forest of Vṛndāvana while you were still in your maiden form; for you are the enchantress of the entire universe.
Now that you have reached the age of youth, what kind of wonderful beauty is yours?"
O beloved of Hari, what kind of splendor and beauty does that form possess, endowed with playful smiles and glances?
Adorned with the wonder of a human-like body through its desire for men, I wish to behold that form of yours, O dear one to Hari. (58-59)

O Maheśvarī, out of compassion for me now, you ought to reveal your own true form to this son of Nanda, Kṛṣṇa, who is about to fall into delusion, so that he may behold it as he bows down and seeks refuge in you.
Thus addressed by the best of sages, whose mind was devoted to her,
she bowed to the supreme Mahāmāheśvarī, who is composed of great bliss,
whose auspicious eyes were agitated with the intense longing of great love.
As he stood gazing at Govinda and describing him thus:

"Victory to you, O Kṛṣṇa, captivator of the mind! Victory to you, beloved of Vṛndāvana! Victory to you, charming with the playfulness of your eyebrows! Victory to you, filled with the sound of your flute! (63)
Victory to You, the crest-jewel who bestows victory, O Enchanter of the Gopīs! Victory to You, whose limbs are smeared with saffron and who are adorned with jewels!
When, by Your grace, shall I [be united] with her of this divine form? 64–65.
"O Lord of the World, I shall behold you, the youth who enchants the world, endowed with the beauty of a body that captivates through fresh youth.
Even as he was thus praising her, at that very moment she appeared once again.
She became possessed of a divine form that was exceedingly enchanting,
appearing as a most graceful maiden of fourteen years;
at that very moment, other girls from Vraja of the same age also appeared.
Arriving there, adorned with divine ornaments, garments, and garlands, they surrounded him;
yet that lord of sages remained motionless, stupefied by wonder.
At that time, those friends of the girl [sprinkled] the sage with drops of water from their feet.
Having sprinkled him with water, they awakened him and spoke, filled with compassion:
"O most excellent of sages, O highly fortunate one, O Lord of the great masters of yoga! By your supreme devotion alone, the Blessed Lord Hari, the Sovereign, [was propitiated]. (70-71)
Surely the God who fulfills the desires of his devotees has been propitiated,
since he— who is difficult to behold and difficult to attain— has been seen by Brahmā, Rudra, and other gods, as well as by the lords of perfected sages and other great devotees. (72)
The beloved of Hari, who deludes with her most wonderful youth and form, has come within the range of your vision through some inconceivable fortune.
Arise, arise, O brahmin-sage; quickly summoning your fortitude! 73–74.
Circumambulate her and bow down to her again and again; do you not see this lady of beautiful limbs, who appears utterly distressed?
At this very moment, she will surely vanish from sight.
O best of the knowers of Brahman, you will not have any conversation with her by any means, nor will you obtain a sight of her again; however,
even now, a beautiful Aśoka creeper shines forth in Vṛndāvana.
Abounding in flowers at all times and possessing a fragrance that pervades every direction,
on the bank of the lake named Kusuma, not far from Govardhana— at its very base, at midnight— you shall behold us in our entirety.
Having heard these words of theirs, whose hearts were overwhelmed with affection,
the sage was about to circumambulate and prostrate himself like a staff before the young girl, who was beautiful with her various divine manifestations, when two muhūrtas passed.
Having summoned Bhānu, Nārada spoke these auspicious words:
"O daughter, she possesses such power that she cannot be subdued even by the gods;
however, whatever house is adorned with her footprints—"
There, the god Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava himself, dwells;
and Lakṣmī always resides there together with all perfections and accomplishments.
Today, [he beheld] this woman of beautiful hips, adorned with every ornament.
"O best of men, protect this goddess-like woman with supreme effort," having said this, that most excellent devotee of the Lord entered the dense forest, keeping her very form in his mind.
Having reached the foot of an Ashoka creeper, the best of sages remained right there at night, awaiting the arrival of the Goddess;
overwhelmed with love, he stood there contemplating his beloved Kṛṣṇa. 85-86.
Then, during the middle watch of the night, having previously seen those most wonderful young women and others adorned with various ornaments and garlands,
he was bewildered in his mind and fell prostrate upon the ground like a staff.
Surrounding the Sage, all those beautiful women entered;
though the Sage desired to ask something dear to his own heart, he was unable to do so, being overwhelmed by their love, beauty, and charming speech. 88-89.

Then, filled with compassion, she spoke right there to the most humble one, who stood before the Supreme Sage with palms joined, his neck bowed under the weight of devotion, and filled with wonder and agitation.
The goddess of the Aśoka grove,
named Aśokamālinī, said: "O great sage, I dwell within this bud of the Aśoka tree."
She is eternally clad in red garments, adorned with red garlands and red unguents;
she wears a crest-jewel of red sindūra and a red utpala lotus as an ear-ornament, and is decorated with armlets, a crown, and other ornaments made of red rubies. 92–93.
Once, while sporting with my beloved at the spring festival,
the cowherd girls, dressed in variegated garments, gathered there;
and I [saw] Hari, wearing the guise of a cowherd, adorned with garlands of *aśoka* flowers.
I worshipped all of them, who were the forms of Ramā, with perfect devotion. From that time forward, I have always remained in their midst, pleasing the Lord of Ramā with various ornaments. 95–96.
"I know everything here from every perspective, even that which is higher than the highest, including the secret of the cows, the cowherds, and the gopīs;
everything you wish to know has been spoken within my heart."
How shall I behold that Goddess of wondrous form, who bestows marvelous bliss;
the beloved of Hari, radiant as gold, with her fingers adorned by rings blazing like diamonds—how shall I see her tremulous eyes, or how her lotus feet? 98–99.
"O Brahmin, you have reflected that [the Lord] is propitiated by you with supreme devotion;
therefore, I shall relate to you the account of those great-souled ones who, dwelling at Lake Mānasa, engaged in intense austerity. (100)
While those sages of great luster—
numbering seventy-one thousand— were reciting perfected mantras and meditating on Hari, the Lord, they constantly longed for her very lotus feet. (101–102)
"Therefore, I shall tell you today of that supreme laughter in the forest.
(103) Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Greatness of Śrī Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa," in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
[Chapter Seventy-Two]
Īśvara said:
O goddess of beautiful countenance, listen with a one-pointed mind.
There was once a certain sage of firm vows, known as Ugratapā (the One of Fierce Austerities). 1.
Maintaining the sacred fires and subsisting on fire, he performed most wonderful penance; he recited the supreme mantra of fifteen syllables,
which is encased within the Kāma-mantra and bestows the boon of desire.
The word "Kṛṣṇāya" accompanied by "Svāhā" is the supreme bestower of perfection.
He meditated upon the dark-complexioned Kṛṣṇa, intoxicated with the rāsa dance and eager for the bridegroom's choice;
he wore yellow silk garments and held a flute to his lips with his hand.

At the end of a hundred kalpas, while thus absorbed in meditation, that great sage cast off his body as he was drawing his beloved toward him with his hand, she being endowed with the bloom of fresh youth.
That great sage became the daughter of the cowherd named Sunanda.
There was one renowned as Sunandā, who held a lute in her hand;
another sage, famous as Satyatapas and observer of great vows,
who ate only withered leaves and recited the supreme mantra.
The best of sages meditated upon Hari, who wears diverse garments and whose fifteen-syllable mantra is encased by the seed-syllables of Rati and Kāma;
he held the two creeper-like arms of Ramā, which were radiant with bracelets. 8.
Dancing and becoming intoxicated, he embraced [her] again and again;
laughing loudly with waves of bliss within the expanse of his belly, he held a flute reaching to his knees and was adorned with a Vaijayantī garland. 9-10.
Having repeatedly abandoned his body through asceticism, with his face framed by a forehead drenched in drops of perspiration,
this great sage was indeed born here from Nandavana after the interval of ten kalpas.
The daughter of the cowherd named Subhadra was widely renowned as Bhadrā.
On the surface of her back, a divine fan was visible.
There was a certain great sage named Haridhāman.
He too performed severe penance, eating only a single leaf daily,
and recited the twenty-syllable mantra which brings swift accomplishment. Immediately thereafter, he [recited] that very same mantra mounted upon the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja).
Beyond the city of Māyā, he beheld the Lord, who was like a moon possessing the luster of blood and the brilliance of a swan in the sky;
thereafter, in the beautiful Madhavī bower of Vṛndāvana, he meditated upon the Lord, preceded by the ten-syllable mantra joined with "namaḥ" and beginning with "smara. 15-16.
And [he saw him] lying on his back upon a beautiful bed of sprouts,
while a certain female attendant, her eyes reddened by excessive passion,
repeatedly covered his broad chest with the pair of her breasts. 17.
With his cheeks being kissed and his lips being caressed, he embraced his beloved with both arms in a most wonderful and joyful manner.
Then the sage, having abandoned many bodies over the course of three kalpas, [attained liberation]. 18–19.
The cowherd named Sāraṅga had a daughter endowed with auspicious marks,
renowned as Raṅgaveṇī, who was highly skilled in the art of painting;
on the tips of her fingers, red dots were seen painted.
A certain sage who discoursed on Brahman, renowned as Jābāli,
a yogi of great austerity and devotion, was wandering this earth when he reached a vast wilderness extending for ten thousand yojanas.
Arriving there by chance, he beheld a single, most beautiful pond, its banks bound on all sides with crystal, filled with sweet water,
and fanned by breezes fragrant with the scent of blooming lotuses. (23)
In the western direction of that place, at the foot of a banyan tree, he saw a certain female ascetic performing severe penance;
she was endowed with the bloom of youth and was exceedingly captivating in her beauty. (24-25)
Having placed her left hand upon her hip and her right hand on the right side, she— whose radiance resembles the rays of the moon, whose every limb is beautiful,
who bears the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā), and whose eyes do not blink— [was visualized]. 26.

Having abandoned food and movement, she remained perfectly motionless. Desiring to test her, the excellent sage stood there for a hundred years; at the end of that time, the sage raised her up as she began to move with humility.
He asked, "O you of wondrous form, who are you, and what will you do? If it is appropriate, you should please tell me.
(29) Then the young woman, emaciated by severe asceticism, spoke softly.
I am that Brahma-vidyā which is sought after by the lords of yogis who are beyond compare;
desiring the lotus feet of Hari, I perform penance for a very long time in this formidable forest, meditating upon Puruṣottama. 30–31.
Filled with the bliss of Brahman and my intellect satisfied by that bliss,
nevertheless, without the delight in Kṛṣṇa, I consider myself empty;
now I am utterly despondent regarding the casting off of this body.
"I desire to perform [this] right here in this very meritorious pond.
Having heard those words of hers, the sage was exceedingly amazed;
falling at her feet, he [requested] the auspicious rite for the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
Filled with supreme joy, having abandoned his internal contemplation (*adhyātma-virocana*), he asked [his preceptor];
and having received the mantra spoken by her and obtained her permission, he departed for Lake Mānasa.
Thereafter, he performed an ascetic penance (*tapas*) that was exceedingly difficult to practice and caused wonder.
Standing on one foot and gazing at the sun with unblinking eyes,
he muttered the supreme mantra consisting of twenty-five syllables; with a state of supreme devotion, he meditated upon Kṛṣṇa, whose very form is bliss.
Moving through the streets of Vraja with a playful and variegated gait,
making his anklets tinkle with graceful steps, and displaying diverse amorous gestures along with smiling sidelong glances— 38.
With his flute, which was called "the Deluder," variegated with five red stripes,
kissing the bimba-fruit-like lips of the women of Vraja with charming, sweet sounds, he captivated both the minds and the bodies of the cowherd maidens. (39–40)
His body was suddenly embraced by women who approached with their waist-knots loosened;
he wore divine garlands and garments, was anointed with divine perfumes and unguents, and, filling the three worlds with the radiance of his dark-complexioned limbs, he enchanted them all. 41.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of the Universe for many days,
she was born within nine kalpas in Gokula as a girl of divine form to the highly illustrious cowherd named Pracaṇḍa.

Behold this auspicious maiden, renowned as Citragandhā, who possesses a beautiful countenance and delights the ten directions with the various fragrances of her own limbs. She is like a bee drinking the nectar of the Vṛnda forest. 44.
Having made her lord rest upon her limbs, she was overwhelmed by the onset of passion;
in the embrace of her breasts, her chest was struck by all her necklaces, which fell away from her bosom, scattering their various fragrant scents. 45–46.
Other excellent sages, whose minds were perpetually pure,
performed austerities while subsisting on air alone, chanting the supreme mantra.
Smara [offered worship] to Kṛṣṇa, who possesses the manifestation of the arts of love and desire.
Having joined the fifteen-syllable mantra with the Āgneyī [vidyā],
the best of sages meditated upon the form of Kṛṣṇa, adorned with divine ornaments,
his full and fleshy waist encircled by a divine, variegated silk garment. 48–49.
Her crest was fashioned from peacock feathers, and she wore radiant earrings;
taking her right lotus-foot with her left leg,
she whirled about while bringing together her two beautiful lotus-hands in a hollowed gesture.
With a flute tucked into the region of her waist and her fingers moving gracefully over its holes, she delighted the eyes and minds of the gopīs;
she entered the performance arena in a form of supreme wonder. 51-52.
And being filled on all sides by the cowherd girls with showers of flowers—
those who, having cast off their bodies in another kalpa, have now been born here,
and in whose ears are seen earrings illuminated by rays of light.
Jeweled garlands were upon their necks and jeweled flowers upon their braided locks.
There was a sage named Śuciśravas and another named Suvarṇa;
these two sons of the Brahman-sage Kuśadhvaja had mastered the Vedas.
With their feet raised upward,
performing severe penance, those two, with restrained minds, chanted the three-syllabled mantra *hrīṃ haṃsaḥ* repeatedly while meditating upon Kṛṣṇa as a ten-year-old child in Gokula.
With forms as beautiful as the god of love and charming in their youth, they incessantly enchanted those women of Vraja with their bimba-like lips;
having cast off their bodies at the end of the kalpa, they were born again in Vraja. 57–58.
To the two most beautiful sons of the cowherd named Suvīra—
Jaṭila, Jaṅghapūta, Ghṛtāśin, and Karbu— the sweet-voiced Sārikā appeared in their hands. 59.
Four sages were fortunate, being free from desire for both this world and the next;
having surrendered with single-minded devotion to the Lord of the Cowherdesses, they remained submerged in the water, chanting his mantra alone. 60–61.
In forest after forest, the gopīs meditated with intense devotion upon the ten-syllable mantra beginning with "Smara," which was encased within three repetitions of the name of Ramā (Rāma-rāma-rāma).
They beheld Him wandering about, enchanting them with His dancing, singing, and other arts.
With all their limbs smeared with sandalwood paste and adorned with *japā* flowers as ear-ornaments,
they were garlanded with strings of white water-lilies and clothed in blue and yellow garments;
those endowed with auspicious marks were born in Gokula at the end of three *kalpas*.
These are those lovely women seated before me, with their brows slightly bent;
on their forearms, they wear bracelets made solely of dharma,
adorned with various jewels and divine pearls.
In a previous kalpa, Vyāsa was a sage among those of long austerity (dīrghatapas).
His son was the eminent and wise sage known as Śuka; even as a child, he was possessed of great intelligence and constantly recollected the supreme state.
Leaving behind his father, mother, and others, he went to the forest and meditated upon Kṛṣṇa; there,
without food, he worshipped the Lord Viṣṇu in the form of a cowherd with divine mental offerings day and night.
Chanting the eighteen-syllable mantra encircled by the *ramā* (Lakṣmī) seed-syllable, he meditated with supreme devotion upon Hari beneath a golden tree,
within a golden pavilion, and upon a golden lion-throne.
Seated, he held a golden flute with the tips of his golden hands,
while with his right hand he whirled a golden lotus;
his body was adorned with variegated ornaments fashioned by his beloved, who was of golden complexion and dear to him.
Seeing his own hermitage with exceeding joy, he laughed;

then, his eyes filled with tears of delight and his limbs covered in horripilation, he cried out loudly, "Be gracious, O Lord! and fell trembling upon the ground to offer a prostration like a staff before the Creator of the three worlds.
To him who had fallen upon the ground longing for devotion, saying aloud "I am weary," Hari took his two arms as he prostrated like a staff and touched him with eyes overflowing with joy.
Then Hari spoke to Śuka, who had attained a form dear to Him.

"O auspicious one, you are my most beloved; always remain by my side, contemplating my form and having become the very object of my love. And there are two other excellent gopīs, beautiful and of the same age as you. (75-76)

She who observes a single vow, who has a single goal, whose name is that of a single constellation, who resembles molten gold, and who possesses the luster of lightning; she who is solitary, whose eyes are like those of a Yama-animal, and who is supremely gentle with long eyes.
With supreme devotion, he worshipped those two [forms] of Hari on the left and right;
at the end of his life, having cast off his body, he became the daughter of the high-souled Upa-nanda in Gokula, possessing the luster of the petals of a blue lotus.
This very woman, the consort of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, whose garments consist of a yellow silk cloth, has breasts like jars of refined gold filled with a red bodice;
she wears red vermilion as a veil for her entire body. 80.
Her cheeks were radiant with golden earrings, making her exceedingly beautiful;
she was adorned with a garland of golden lotuses, and her lovely breasts were smeared with saffron;
in her hand was seen a morsel of food offered by Hari, which appeared ready to be chewed. 81–82.
Exceedingly skilled in the playing of the flute and devoted to Keśava, she was once, when Kṛṣṇa was well-pleased during a performance of song,
adorned with a beautiful garland of guñjā berries placed by him around her conch-like neck.
Even when Kṛ�让你的 beloved is out of sight, she remains tormented by love;
while her friends play instruments and sing most melodiously, she causes this young bride—who has been dressed in the attire of her lover—to dance. 84-85.
Again and again, with deep devotion, that beloved woman embraced and kissed Govinda; she was most dear to all the gopīs and to Kṛṣṇa as well.
(86) There was a certain son of Śvetaketu who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
Having renounced everything, he undertook fierce asceticism (87).
He [sought] the nectar-like splendor of the dust of Murāri’s feet, the sweet-sounding beloved power of Govinda, which is difficult even for Brahmā, Rudra, and others to attain (88).
Devoting himself with single-minded devotion to Śrī alone, who is so enchanting,
he meditated upon her and constantly recited the eleven-syllable mantra. Having performed all the prescribed rites and laughter, he engaged them in the observance of the vow.
Perfuming the world on all sides with her laughter and other qualities such as beauty, she dwells here in spring;
constantly contemplating this very meaning of the mantra, he too attained birth here, having become perfected through two kalpas. 90–91.
This daughter appears like a young girl, with slender limbs and bud-like breasts;
her neck is radiant with a string of pearls, she is clothed in pure silk, and her anklets, bracelets, armlets, and rings are inlaid with pearls. 92.
She wore two divine, auspicious earrings that dripped with nectar (93).
Upon her rounded forehead, amidst a streak of musk-unguent, she bore a dot of vermilion like a speck of sindūra, together with various decorative patterns of sandalwood paste (94).
She who was seen thus, peaceful and chanting the supreme state— there was a royal sage named Candraprabha, who was pleasing to behold. By the grace of Kṛṣṇa, he had a son of sweet appearance.
Known as Citradhvaja, that Vaiṣṇava who had been devoted to the Lord since his youth, commanded his excellent son Saumya— who was twelve years old and very steady—
to learn from the twice-born the supreme eighteen-syllable mantra. 96–97.
Being consecrated with the nectar-like waters of mantras while still an infant,
he bowed with love to the king at that very moment, his eyes filled with tears. On that day, the child, wearing pure garments, remained himself pure.

Adorned with necklaces, anklets, threads, and other ornaments, as well as neck-chains, armlets, and bracelets, he touched upon devotion to Hari; then, having gone to the temple of Viṣṇu and standing there alone, he reflected with a pure heart. (99–100)
"How shall I approach this devotee, the deluder of the cowherd women,
who is always sporting with them on the banks of the Kālindī in the forest? (101) Thus the boy, his mind extremely agitated, remained lost in thought.
Then he attained the supreme knowledge and experienced a dream.
Before him appeared a beautiful image of Kṛṣṇa made of stone, seated upon a golden pedestal and endowed with all auspicious marks.
She was dark-complexioned like a blue lotus, radiant with smooth beauty, adorned with peacock feathers whose forms were gracefully curved in three places;
she joyfully played the flute while holding a golden one to her lips. 104.

Seeing Kṛṣṇa, adorned with such attire and playful gestures, attended by two beautiful women standing at his right and left, who were increasing their passion through kisses, embraces, and other endearments, Citradhvaja— (105-106)
Bowing his head before them with a mind overcome by shame,
Hari then spoke with a smile to his beloved seated at his right side—
she who was filled with supreme bashfulness as she sat upon his own body.

"O fawn-eyed one, create a divine and wonderful form of a young woman equal to yourself, and contemplate it as non-different from your own body; then, touched by the splendors of your limbs, he will attain your very form. 108-109.
Then that lotus-eyed woman, having gone near Citradhvaja,
stood meditating on the non-difference between her own limbs and his limbs. Then her own splendors completely filled his body.
From the light of her breasts were born her full and beautiful breasts;
from the light of her hips was born her charming orb of the buttocks; from the light of her tresses arose the mass of hair, and from the light of her hands, her two hands. 111–112.
Everything—ornaments, garments, garlands, and so forth—was thus perfectly prepared;
she was born with an inner fragrance that arose from her being highly skilled in the arts.
Beholding that beautiful maiden on earth, as if seeing one lamp from another, [he was filled with wonder].

Taking her by the hands with love, he joyfully removed her fatigue; she was enchanting, with the beauty of her smiles and the graceful movement of her variegated banner-like garments, as he embraced his beloved standing at Govinda’s left side. 114–115.
He said, "Let her be yours; give her a name, and let this beloved woman perform service for you with affection according to your liking. Then, by his own will, she gave her the name Citralekhā.
She also took up the lute (vipaṃcikā) for the purpose of serving [him] with song:
"O you whose essence is virtue, remain always near me and sing with various melodies; this is the duty ordained for you, the lord of my life. (117-118)
Then, having received permission through her art of painting, she bowed to Mādhava;
and taking hold of the feet of His beloved, she sang a very sweet song that was the cause of their joy. 119.
Then, while he was embraced with love by Kṛṣṇa, whose form is bliss,
Citradhvaja— overwhelmed by great affection and intent on remembering Him— remained unconscious for as long as he stayed immersed in that ocean of happiness.
Then, having spoken thus to Harivicāraka, he wept with a loud voice, wailing for that supreme bliss; from that time on,
even when addressed by his father and others, he did not speak a single word.
Having stayed in his home for only a month, at midnight he took refuge in Kṛṣṇa;
departing, he practiced in the forest an austerity difficult even for sages.
At the end of the kalpa, that great sage cast off his body through that very austerity.
The daughter of the cowherd named Vīragupta was born as Aśubhā, whose beautiful shoulder was adorned with a lute (*vīṇā*) called Citrakalā,
which was constantly embellished with the seven musical notes. 125.
A wondrous jeweled water-pot stood near Agni,
and in his right hand he held a jeweled spittoon;
formerly, he was saluted by all the ascetics.

His father was the sage named Puṇyaśravas Kāśyapa, a knower of all dharmas; he was a devotee of Śiva, who daily praised the Lord of the gods, the Sovereign of the Universe, who is compassionate toward his devotees, by reciting the Śatarudrīya. 128.
The Blessed Lord Śaṅkara, together with Pārvatī, being pleased, appeared in person at midnight on the fourteenth lunar day and granted him a boon:
"O Kṛṣṇa, even as a child, you shall indeed possess devotion. (129–130)

Having initiated him in the eighth year, you should teach him this perfected mantra; it is declared that this mantra named Gopālavidyā, which bestows the perfection of speech, consists of twenty-one syllables. 131.
This wondrous and playful conduct upon the tongue of the practitioner brings the one of infinite forms himself as the bestower of boons;
Kāma, Māyā, Ramā, Kaṇṭha, Indra, and others, radiant with Dāmodara, [attain this]. 132–133.
Having recited the ten-syllable mantra in the middle, one should again point to those very same [limbs].
I shall now declare the seers (ṛṣis) and other attributes, as well as the meditation (dhyāna), for this ten-syllable mantra:
one should meditate upon an island consisting of light in the midst of the ocean of full nectar.
There, in the forest of Vṛndāvana, one should meditate upon Him encircled by Kālindī,
surrounded by coral-like creepers dripping with the flowers of all seasons, and filled with the cries of dancing, intoxicated peacocks and the songs of cuckoos and bees. 135–136.
In its midst stands a single great pārijāta tree,
rising a hundred yojanas high with the expansion of its branches and sub-branches; beneath it, on the spotless ground, is a circle of cows.
Within that was the circle of cowherd boys with their flutes and horns;
and within that, the beautiful circle of the fair-browed women of Vraja, their hands bearing various offerings and their minds unsteady with intoxication.
One should contemplate the circle of those with palms joined in reverence, clad in white garments,
adorned with white ornaments, their souls overwhelmed with love,
as they receive the dear words of the daughters of the Vedas. 140.
Then, upon a jeweled altar, one should meditate on Hari, clothed in silken garments (141),
reclining upon the thighs of Rādhā which rest atop a plantain stalk, gazing at her beautiful face which is as radiant as the moon and captivating to the mind (142).
With his left foot slightly bent and his left hand holding a flute, he embraces his beloved;
with his right hand, he touches her chin.
He possesses the luster of a great emerald and the radiance of pearls.
His eyes were as large as lotuses, and he was clad in pure yellow garments;
his head shone with a mass of peacock feathers, and he was enchanting with a pearl necklace and beautiful makara-shaped earrings shimmering upon the edges of his cheeks.

One should meditate upon Him who is exceedingly delicate, endowed with the age of a youth, and adorned from His feet upward with garlands of *tulasī*, bracelets, armlets, anklets, rings, and a girdle. 146.
"The worship is exactly as described in the *Daśākṣara*, and the preliminary rite (*puraskriyā*) consists of one hundred thousand recitations.
Having said this, the God vanished; and the virtuous Goddess Girijā, having returned, likewise instructed her son.
Upon merely receiving those mantras from Puṇyaśravas, Keśava himself,
having defeated all the sages, described [the Lord] who possesses the wondrous characteristics of form, grace, eloquence, and beauty. 149.
Then, with a joyful heart, the boy departed from his own home and,
subsisting on air alone, performed austerities for thirty thousand kalpas.
At the conclusion of that time, he himself was born in the house of Nanda’s brother in Gokula.
Lavaṅgā is she whose name is so called because she observes the gestures of Kṛṣṇa;
in her hand may be seen a face-cleansing instrument.
Thus have some of the principal beloveds of Kṛṣṇa been described to you. 152–153.

The person who here reads with devotion this chapter, endowed with various mellows such as *hara* and others, along with the daughters of the best of the Vraja who possess beautiful smiles and glances, or causes it to be read, goes to the abode of the Blessed Lord Śrī Vāsudeva.
154. Thus ends the seventy-second chapter in the Śrī Kṛṣṇa-māhātmya of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa. 72.
The seventy-third chapter.
The Lord said: That wonder which was asked by you has been narrated by me in due order.
Even Brahmā and the other gods are bewildered by that; who then would not be bewildered?
Nevertheless, O Great King, I shall relate what was spoken by the supreme ṛṣi concerning Ambarīṣa, the devotee of Viṣṇu who was endowed with devotion to Śiva.

Having reached the hermitage of Badarī, the king bowed down and offered praise to the self-controlled Vedavyāsa— who was seated there, the highly fortunate, omniscient, and supreme among men— in his desire to learn the dharma of Viṣṇu.
"You ought to protect me here in this ocean of saṃsāra, which is so difficult to cross. I am detached from these sense-objects; salutations to them all!
Salutations to that state which is free from agitation and whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss."
The Supreme Brahman is the supreme ether, formless and free from ailment;
by directly realizing which, sages indeed cross the ocean of worldly existence.
How then can I ever attain a path for my mind to reach that state?
Vyāsa said:
"What you have asked is extremely secret, which I did not previously tell Śuka;
however, since you are my own son and a beloved devotee of Hari, I shall speak it to you here."

This entire universe existed as that supreme form, established as that which is unmanifest and undisturbed; hear now of that which consists of the Lord. Formerly, I performed austerities for many thousands of years.
Then, as I subsisted on fruits, roots, leaves, water, and air, and remained devoted to my own meditation, the Blessed Lord Hari said to me:
"O high-minded one, what object do you desire to accomplish, or what do you wish to know? (10)
"I am pleased; choose a boon from me, O best among the givers of boons.
'The cycle of worldly existence ends with the sight of me'—this I tell you as the truth.
Then, my body bristling with horripilation, I spoke to Kṛṣṇa.
O Madhusūdana, I desire to see you with my own eyes—
you who are that supreme Brahman, the truth, the light of the world, and the Lord of the universe,
whom the Upaniṣads describe as the wondrous Master of sight. 13.
The Blessed Lord said:
Just as I was formerly questioned and entreated by Brahmā in the past,
that which I spoke to him is now being told to you as well.
Some call me Prakṛti, and others Puruṣa and Īśvara; some [call me] Dharma, some Wealth, and some Liberation free from fear. Some call me Śūnya, some Bhāva, some Śiva, and some Sadāśiva. (15–16)

Behold today that one eternal reality, situated at the head of the Vedas, which is devoid of modification and whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss— this very nature of mine, which has been hidden by the Vedas, which I shall now reveal. 17.
Then I beheld that prince, who possessed the luster of a dark rain-cloud;
he was a cowherd surrounded by cowherd girls, laughing with the cowherd boys, seated at the foot of a kadamba tree, wearing yellow garments, and most wonderful to behold. 18-19.
I saw the forest named Vṛndāvana, adorned with fresh sprouts,
resounding with the cries of cuckoos and bees, and enchanting to the god of love;
there I beheld the river Kālindī, possessing the luster of blue lotus petals.
Then I beheld Govardhana, which had been lifted up by Kṛṣṇa and Rāma;
it brought happiness to the cows and cowherds, destroyed the pride of Mahendra, and was gladdened by the union with the cowherd women as he played the flute. 21–22.
Seeing him, who is the ornament of all ornaments, I became exceedingly joyful;
then the Blessed One himself, the dweller of Vṛndāvana, spoke to me:
"This divine and eternal form of mine which you have seen—"
Partless, actionless, peaceful, the embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss;
full, with eyes like lotus petals—there is nothing higher than this for me.
These Vedas declare this alone to be the cause of all causes.
Know my Mathurā to be eternally true, supreme bliss, a mass of consciousness, perpetual, and auspicious;
likewise, know Vṛndāvana forest to be eternal. Know also the Yamunā, the cowherd girls, and the young cowherd boys. 26.
This incarnation of mine is eternal; do not entertain any doubt in this matter.

For I am the beloved, the ever-worshipped, the omniscient, and higher than the highest; I am the fulfiller of all desires, the Lord of all, the embodiment of all bliss, and the supreme beyond the supreme. 27–28.
"Since this entire universe appears as a manifestation of Māyā, I then spoke to the Lord, the cause of the cause of the world:
'Who are these gopīs? Who are these cowherds? And what kind of tree is this considered to be?'"
"What forest is this? What are these cuckoos and other birds? And what mountain is this? Who is this most fortunate flute, the sole vessel of joy for the worlds? [Thus asked.
Then the Blessed Lord, pleased with me, spoke with a serene lotus-face. 31.
The Gopīs should be known as the Śrutis (the Vedas), and the daughters of the cowherds as the Ṛks;
O Indra among kings, the celestial maidens were those endowed with austerity who sought liberation.
All the cowherds were sages, the very embodiments of the bliss of Vaikuṇṭha.
This *kadaṃba* tree is a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*), the sole vessel of supreme bliss.
The forest named Ānanda destroys even the greatest of sins; there, the Siddhas, Sādhyas, Gandharvas, Kokilas, and others dwell without a doubt. (33–34)
Some say his heart is filled with bliss, while others say he is the Yamunā herself in bodily form;
this mountain is the beginningless servant of Hari—of this there is no doubt.
Listen, O brāhmaṇa, to that which is known as the flute, and you too shall understand it thus.
There was a twice-born man named Devavrata, whose mind was tranquil and who was devoted to austerity and peace;
he was self-controlled, an expert in the ritual section of the Vedas, intent on his duties, and lived in the midst of a multitude of Vaiṣṇava devotees. 36–37.
O King, having once heard that there was a Lord of Sacrifice (Yajñeśa), a twice-born man, firm in his resolve, went to his abode;
he was a devotee of Śambhu who sometimes performed worship with *tulasī* leaves and water. 38.1–2.
He prepared some fruit and roots in that house and offered them [to him]. The wise man gave him some water for bathing and a little fruit;
with a smile and without faith, he too accepted it from the twice-born man.
By that evil deed, he was born as a most dreadful bamboo;
yet by that merit, he then attained my state of being dear to me.
O Indra among kings, by this [merit], he shines like Ketumān.
At the end of the age, having become devoted to Viṣṇu, he shall attain the state of Brahman.

Alas! Men of evil intent do not know my supreme and eternal city, that ancient Mathurā, which is beautiful and praised by the lords of the gods, the lords of the serpents, and the lords of the sages. 42-43.
Although cities such as Kāśī exist, among them Mathurā alone is blessed, for through birth, the investiture of the sacred thread, death, and cremation, she bestows liberation upon men in four ways.
(44) When people become purified by austerity and other means, possessing the wealth of meditation with pure intentions, they remain constant [in that state].
O best of the twice-born, at that very moment they beheld this most excellent city, and not otherwise even in hundreds of kalpas;
those inhabitants of Mathurā are blessed and worthy of honor even by the gods, for all of them possess immeasurable majesty and are four-armed. 45–46.

Those men who perceive faults in the residents of Mathurā do not perceive the fault arising from thousands of births and deaths; even those who are destitute are truly fortunate if they remember Mathurā. 47.
There dwells the Lord of Beings (Bhūteśvara), the God who grants liberation even to sinners.
(48) The supreme Lord Bhūteśvara is eternally most dear to me; out of affection for me, he never abandons that city. (49)

A man of evil conduct who does not bow to, worship, or even remember Bhūteśvaranana, and who does not behold this Mathurā of mine—which is self-luminous and known as the Supreme Deity—how can that sinful person ever obtain devotion unto me? 50. Those lowest of men whose intellects are deluded by my māyā generally do not worship Śiva, who is my supreme devotee;
they neither bow to the Lord of Beings, nor remember him, nor praise him. 51–52.
Even as a child, Dhruva, intent upon my worship, reached that supreme and pure place which had been attained with great effort by his ancestors.
Having reached that city of Mathurā, which is difficult even for the gods to attain— my own abode— 53.
Even if one becomes lame or blind, one should rather give up one's life;
O highly fortunate Vedavyāsa, do not entertain any doubt regarding this secret of the Upaniṣads which has been revealed by me to you. 54-55.
Whoever, being pure, recites this chapter spoken by the Blessed One, or even listens to it with devotion, for them there is eternal liberation. 56.
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of Vṛndāvana and Other Places in Mathurā," in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. 73.
The seventy-fourth chapter.
The Lord said: Once, in private, the illustrious Uddhava, who was dear to the Blessed One and possessed of divine knowledge, [spoke].

In private, an attendant asked the Lord Sanatkumāra: "O Master, where is that supreme place where Govinda eternally sports with the cowherd women, that eternal abode of the gods? Where is it, and what is it like?"
If you have learned any other wonderful account of those various pastimes, it should be told to me if affection for me exists in you. Sanatkumāra said:
Once, on the bank of the Yamunā beneath a certain tree,
while seated comfortably, that high-souled son of Pṛthā experienced the same realization as the divine attendant [Nārada].
Whatever has been seen and whatever has been done by me has been recounted here in this context;
I shall now tell that to you—listen with supreme attention.
However, this must never be disclosed anywhere at any time.
Arjuna said:
O Lord, ocean of mercy, please out of compassion explain all of this which has never been seen nor heard by Śaṅkara, Viriñci, and the other gods. 7.
But what did you previously say regarding those Ābhīrī women who are your beloveds?
O God, how many kinds are they, and what is their number? What are their names, and where are they situated?
O Lord, what will be their speech, their rituals, their age, and their dress?
O Master, with whom and where will You sport day after day, in forest after forest, which is eternally blissful and eternally prosperous? (9-10)
What is that place like, where is it, and how is it eternal, supreme, and great?
If you have such compassion, you ought to tell me all of this here, even that which I have not asked about and which remains unknown to me, as well as that which is known to you. 11.
"O illustrious one, you who destroy the suffering of the distressed, you shall tell me all of that.
The Blessed One said:
"That place is dear to me; such is my pleasure-ground there."
"Even for those whose vital breaths are equal to their own life-force, truth remains beyond the reach of men.
(13) O child, you will surely have a longing to see that which is invisible even to Brahmā and the other gods; how much more so for any other person? (14)
Therefore, O Vira, why do you remain thus without him? Having heard these most terrible words from the Blessed One,
Arjuna, dejected, fell prostrate like a staff at His pair of lotus feet.
Then the Lord, the All-pervading One, who is affectionate toward His devotees, laughed and raised him up with both arms; out of supreme love for His devotee, He said:
"What is the use of speaking of that here? For whatever it is that you wish to see, behold it!"

Having propitiated with supreme devotion that Goddess Śrī Tripurasundarī, in whom everything has arisen, in whom it remains even today, and into whom it shall go to its dissolution, offer yourself to her. 18.
"Without her, I am never able to bestow this state.
Having heard these words of the Blessed One, Arjuna, his eyes overflowing with joy,
went to the ground of the glorious Śrīpādukā of the divine Tripurā.
Having gone there, he beheld that altar of the Śrī-Cintāmaṇi,
exceedingly beautiful with staircases fashioned from various jewels; and there he saw the Kalpa-tree, bent down by the weight of various flowers and fruits.
It was made radiant by sprouts that were tender in all seasons, dripping with droplets of honey-nectar, and trembling in the wind;
and it was filled with parrots, flocks of cuckoos, mainas, and pigeons.
It resounded with the charming cries of playful cakora birds and was filled with the tumultuous humming of the king of bees; it was enchanting,
like a blazing forest fire made radiant by shimmering jewels.
Beneath that [palace] was the divine and most wonderful Śrīratnamaṇḍira;
there was a jeweled throne made of great gold, utterly enchanting.
There [he saw her], resembling the rising sun and adorned with various ornaments.
Endowed with fresh youth, her four creeper-like arms shining with the goad, noose, bow, and arrows, she was exceedingly gracious and captivating;
[she was adorned] by the rays from the jewels in the crowns of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and others.
To the goddess whose lotus feet were resplendent, adorned with the *maṇi* jewel and other ornaments, whose face was serene, who grants boons, and who is affectionate toward her devotees—
Arjuna, having identified himself as such, bowed down again and again. 28–29.

Standing in a secluded corner with palms joined in reverence and filled with the weight of devotion, she perceived that he had been worshipped; then the Goddess, a treasure-house of mercy, knowing his state, spoke out of compassion, overwhelmed by the memory of him.
The Blessed One said:
"O child, what gift, so difficult for others to obtain, was given by you to a worthy recipient? What sacrifice was performed here, or what austerity was practiced?"
Was this devotion to the Immaculate Blessed One acquired by you in a previous life?
Or what is difficult to obtain in this world, or what great auspicious deed was performed, by which this grace has been bestowed upon you who have sought refuge with such joy? (32-33)
This [teaching], most secret and unattainable by others, was established by the Blessed One;
such a thing exists neither for those in the world of mortals, nor for those dwelling on the surface of the earth, nor even for the inhabitants of heaven, the gods, ascetics, lords, or yogis. 34.

Upon seeing me, the divine Gautama fell to the surface of the earth.
"Rise up, my child, my dear one," he said to me; "for it is I myself.
"How is it that you are called 'the wise one' (Manasvin)?"—let this be told, if it pleases you.
Gautama said:
From your own mouth, I have heard many times such secrets concerning the true nature of Kṛṣṇa, namely those known as Dvārakā and Mathurā. (22)
"O true guru, the secret of Vṛndāvana has not been heard from your lotus-like mouth, for by that my mind will attain stability.
Nārada said:
But this is the supreme secret, a mystery within mysteries.
O Lord of Gods, my father, tell me that very secret concerning the origin of Vṛndāvana, which was formerly told to me by Brahmā regarding the birth of Vṛndāvana. 24-25.
Having heard this which she desired to know, he remained silent for a moment; then he said to me, "O child, go to my lord, the Great Viṣṇu.
I too must go there along with you, without a doubt."
Having spoken thus and taken me with him, he went to the abode of Viṣṇu. Whatever I had said was indeed related by me to Mahāviṣṇu;
and having heard that, Mahāviṣṇu then commanded Svayambhū.
"By my command, take the sage Nārada yourself and direct him to bathe in the lake known as Amṛta.
Thus instructed by Mahāviṣṇu, Svayaṃbhū did exactly so.

There, having entered the lake of nectar (Amṛtasaras), I performed my ablutions. At that very moment, I appeared on the shore of that lake in the presence of women, endowed with all auspicious marks and possessing a female form that caused great wonder.
Seeing me approaching, they asked again and again; the women said: "Who are you? From where have you come? Tell us of your own deeds. (32)
Having heard their pleasant words, I said: "Listen to that—whence has this person come, or how is it that he has the form of a woman?
Everything appears like a dream; am I perhaps deluded on this earth? (33)
Having heard those words of mine, the goddess spoke with sweet tones:
"This city named Vṛndā is always dear to Kṛṣṇacandra;
and I am the goddess Lalitā, who transcends the fourth state and is partless."
Having spoken thus, the Great Goddess, her mind overflowing with compassion, spoke to me again: "O Goddess, come back with me;
all these other women are solely devoted to the feet of Kṛṣṇa."
They spoke thus to me: "Come together with her.
Then, out of compassion, the fourteen-syllable mantra of Kṛṣṇacandra was revealed to that noble-souled goddess.
At that very moment, she attained equality with Him through various similes;
she went there along with them, to where the eternal Kṛṣṇa resides—the Lord who is pure existence, consciousness, and bliss, and who has Himself become composed of women. 39.
Her heart overflowing with joy, the woman looked at me and said repeatedly: "Come, my dear beloved; embrace me with devotion.
And there, O best of the twice-born, she took her pleasure for the duration of a year.
Thus it was said by Ramaṇeśa to that goddess Rādhikā:
"This is my Prakṛti; there, assuming the form of Nārada, he took me to the delightful Amṛtasara lake and directed me to bathe."
She spoke these affectionate words at the end of their amorous play:
"I am the goddess Lalitā, and I am celebrated as Rādhikā; and I am known as Vāsudeva, eternally consisting of the essence of the arts of love. 43–44.

It is true that I am the eternal female form, and yet I am not a woman; I am the goddess Lalitā, whose body is Kṛṣṇa in male form. There is no difference between us; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Nārada. 45.

He who thus knows this reality, as well as the Samaya and Anu [Tantras], along with the conduct and conventions, is as dear to me as Lalitā herself. This place named Vṛndāvana is my own secret abode. 46–47.
This must never be disclosed, nor spoken of anywhere, nor even to an animal;
therefore, having brought this goddess Anurādhikā to that lake and remained there, she returned once more to the presence of the feet of Kṛṣṇacandra.
Immediately upon emerging from that immersion, I, Nārada, arrived there;
with a lute in hand and intent on singing, I repeatedly and joyfully bowed to the Self-born Brahmā and went there as an attendant of Viṣṇu. 49-50.
Furthermore, nothing was seen or said by the Self-born (Brahmā) at that time; thus,
O child, I have told you this which is most secret,
for you are but a portion of the consciousness-light of Kṛṣṇacandra.
It should be guarded with great effort, like a lover by a mother for her beloved.
Just as this secret was spoken by me to my disciple Gautama, so has it been told to you in its entirety and in its most highly protected form. 52-53.
O bulls among sages, O brahmins, wherever, whenever, and by whomever this may be revealed, the fulfillment of that person's desires from Kṛṣṇacandra is certain.
This is the supreme chapter, endowed with the divine sports of Kṛṣṇa.
Whoever reads or even hears this attains the supreme state.
Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Conciliation of Nārada," within the "Glorification of Vṛndāvana" in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The seventy-sixth chapter.
The Lord said: Having heard that Śiśupāla had been slain there by Kṛṣṇa, Dantavaktra came to Mathurā to fight him. 1.
Having heard this praise of Kṛṣṇa, he mounted his chariot and went with him to Mathurā.

Then, having slain him (Kaṃsa), crossed the Yamunā, and gone to the cowherd settlement of Nanda, he saluted his parents and comforted them; embraced by them, he greeted all the elder cowherds, consoled them, and gratified everyone residing there with many garments, ornaments, and other gifts.
He dwelt there for three nights, enjoying the pleasure of play day and night with the cowherd women on the lovely banks of the Kālindī, which were filled with sacred trees.

There, by the grace of Vāsudeva, all the people such as Nanda Gopa and others, along with their sons and wives— even the beasts, birds, and wild animals— assuming divine forms and mounting celestial chariots (vimānas), attained the supreme realm of Vaikuṇṭha.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, having granted his own stainless abode to all the inhabitants of Nanda Gopa’s settlement, entered the glorious Dvārāvatī while being praised by hosts of gods.

There, daily honored by Vasudeva, Ugrasena, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Akrūra, and others, he—assuming his universal form (viśvarūpa)—delighted himself within bowers of celestial jewel-creepers upon exceedingly smooth couches strewn with flowers from the wish-fulfilling trees, in the company of his sixteen thousand and eight queens.

Thus, for the benefit of all the gods and for the destruction of the entire burden of the earth, Vāsudeva descended into the lineage of Yadu; having brought about the destruction of all the rākṣasas and removed the great weight of the world, and having liberated all beings—both stationary and moving—dwelling in Nanda-vraja and Dvārakā from the bonds of worldly existence, he established them in his supreme, eternal, and beautiful abode which is meditated upon by yogis. There, eternally served by his divine queens and others, Vāsudeva spoke to all of them: "In the beginning, there was the unmanifest Brahman, like clarified butter within a water-pot."
"Released from the qualities of his material nature, having become fluid, he went to heaven.
Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter in the Vṛndāvana-māhātmya of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Pārvatī and Śiva.
Chapter Seventy-Seven.
Pārvatī said:
"Explain in detail the gravity of the meanings of the names and words, as well as the true nature of the Lord, his abodes, and his manifestations."
"O Lord of the Suras, that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, as well as the various manifestations (vyūha) of Hari, and that which is called Nirvāṇa— all these exist as my own true essence. The Lord said:
There, in Vṛndāvana, Kṛṣṇa was surrounded by millions of gopīs;
there also was the Gaṅgā, the supreme Śakti, and situated therein was Ānandakānana, made fragrant by breezes carrying the scent of various beautiful flowers. 3.
It was cooled by the reddish hue of the waves from the daughter of Kalinda (the Yamunā),
frequented by the foremost sages such as Sanaka and other devotees of the Lord,
and adorned by herds of cows with their delightful and sweet lowing.
Surrounded by dancing boys adorned with beautiful garlands and ornaments,
there stood the glorious Kalpa tree,
its foliage made of gold, enriched with various gems and corals, and radiant with fruits of diverse jewels.

At its base was a jeweled altar illuminated by the radiance of gems; there stood an unsurpassed lion-throne composed of the three Vedas. Seated upon it was the Lord of the World, beyond the three qualities (guṇas) and immutable.
Resembling ten million moons, radiant as ten million suns,
and illuminating the ten directions with the beauty of ten million Kandarpas;
he has three eyes and two arms, is fair-complexioned, and possesses the luster of refined gold.
He is constantly embraced on all sides by women,
and he is meditated upon by Brahmā, Sanaka, and the others; he is brought under the power of his devotees,
while they dance with great festivities, their eyes perpetually rolling.
Surrounded on all sides by millions upon millions of Vedic personifications (Śrutis), who had attained the bodies of gopīs and were repeatedly kissing, laughing, and embracing Him,
their minds were intoxicated by the honey of His lotus feet. 12.
Among them, however, was that goddess who possessed the luster of molten gold; illuminating all directions and making them blaze like lightning,
she is the primordial Bhagavatī by whom all this is pervaded.
She who consists of the forms of creation, maintenance, and dissolution; she who is beyond the triad of ignorance and knowledge;
she who is the power of one's own nature (*svarūpa-śakti*), yet also takes the form of *māyā* and is composed of non-consciousness (*acit-mayī*);
she is the cause of the causes of the bodies of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others. (15)
The entire world, both moving and unmoving, is embraced by his Māyā.
Out of affection for Rādhā, the mistress of Vṛndāvana, he dwells in joy within the forest of Vṛndāvana, embracing her who bears the name Vṛndāvaneśvarī and who resembles his own creator. 16–17.
One should meditate upon Lord Kṛṣṇa thus— as reeling from the intoxication of mutual kissing and embracing— and he shall attain perfection.
The knower of mantras [should likewise meditate upon] this secret king of mantras and his mantra.
A high-souled person who would recite, write, or even hear [this] is very rare to find.
Rādhikā, Citrarekhā, Candrā, Madanasundarī, Śrīpriyā, Śrīmadhumatī, Śaśirekhā, and Haripriyā—[these are her names]. 19–20.
She is adorned with the splendor of gold, bewildered by passion, and marked by horripilation; she is joined with paleness and perspiration, intent on the state of love, and sweet-spoken.
(21) She wears a golden garland, is tranquil, and likewise delights in wine.
Compassionate toward all women and their livelihoods, she possesses a stainless disposition;
she is celebrated as the one who holds the essence of the nectar of the Name that has been drunk in;
she is endowed with a very long smile and possesses the luster of molten gold. 22–23.
She is the collyrium for the eyes that veil Rādhā, whose river of love flows in a fainting swoon;
she whose life is the sovereignty of giving, joined with the power of illusion and freedom from envy;
she who is celebrated as a wondrous line in the battle of the festival of amorous play. 24.
Fair-limbed and not too tall, she is ever intent upon playing [the flute];
25. She is overwhelmed by dejection, passion, dancing, fainting, and horripilation;
she stands on the right side of Hari and likewise loves all mantras. 26.
She is celebrated as Candrā because of her limbless greed and sweetness;
she moves with a graceful, slow gait, her eyes are beautiful with lovely lashes, and she is radiant with a stream of love, adorned with the splendor of crushed collyrium. 27.

Delighting in the aesthetic flavor of devotion to Kṛṣṇa and yearning for the sound of His flute, he possesses a face that puts the moon to shame; endowed with self-confidence, he is skilled in sweet speech and is the crest-jewel among those who have conquered their senses. 28–29.
Endowed with a beautiful smile, she is more lovely than Rati; she delights in secluded amorous play, and being dark-complexioned, she is enchanting to the heart.
With her love and her loving sidelong glances, she captivates the mind of Hari. 30.

She who had conquered her senses and subdued her anger was not proclaimed as beloved [by others]; (31) her limbs were fair like well-refined gold, she was beautiful in her graceful gait, and her form was sweet with the wonderful thrill of horripilation born of love for Smara. (32)
Her face, endowed with a beautiful smile, puts the moon to shame;
she is a jewel among those who have conquered their senses through skill in sweet conversation, and she is intent upon the practice of love for the one celebrated as Madhumatī. 33.
Accompanied by the fever of infatuation, horripilation, and a stream of love;
she who sports in the dust of giving and is the great dancer of the sound of truth—she should always be known as Śaśirekhā, the beloved of the cowherd. 34–35.
Kṛṣṇātmā, the most excellent Śyāmā, with honey-tawny eyes, was in some places kissed by horripilation due to the delirious love for his feet;
she was Śivānandā, delighting in the Śivakuṇḍa on the bank of the Dehikā. 36.
Rukmiṇī in Dvārakā, Rādhā in the forest of Vṛndāvana;
Devakī born in Mathurā, O Supreme Goddess, and likewise Sītā on Candrakūṭa and Vindhyavāsinī on the Vindhya mountains. 37–38.
In Vārāṇasī, at Viśālākṣī-vimalā-puruṣottama,
sovereignty over Vṛndāvana was granted to her by Kṛṣṇa, who was pleased with her; elsewhere, O Goddess, Rādhā [was likewise honored] in the forest of Vṛndāvana.
Śauri, whose body is eternal bliss, is described as being "bodiless.
The presiding deities of air, fire, ether, and earth are likewise established as the very form of Govinda, even for Brahmā. 40-41.
Just as the sun, though possessing sense-organs, cannot be perceived by its own brilliance,
so too Kṛṣṇa, endowed with splendor, certainly deludes Time itself. His form is not composed of flesh, blood, or bone like that of ordinary beings.
The yogi and the Lord are indeed distinct; [the latter] is the soul of all, possessing an eternal form.
Through divine yoga, hardness arises like that of hailstones or ghee;
yet the sole deity is the foot of Kṛṣṇa, whose true nature is immeasurable. 43–44.
In the mass of dust from Vṛndāvana, ten million Viṣṇus might tremble;
for this storehouse of all arts pervades the universe with rays of bliss.
O Self, just as living beings are composed of the qualities (guṇas), so too are those [beings] whose bodies are formed from His rays.

Kṛṣṇa is always enveloped by two arms and never possesses four; there he sports at all times, surrounded by a single gopī. Govinda alone is the Supreme Person (Puruṣa), while Brahmā and the others are indeed women.
Therefore, this very nature is the Lord;
the Puruṣa and Prakṛti are the two Lords of Vṛndāvana from the beginning. Everything other than the Lord of Vṛndāvana is a transformation of Prakṛti. 48–49.

This world, having attained differentiation through its very manifestation, would indeed cease to exist upon its destruction; for just as there is no destruction of gold, so too there is no loss of Kṛṣṇa even when the fish and other forms perish.
This entire phenomenal universe, consisting of the three qualities and the rest, belongs to Him who sports in Vṛndāvana.

Just as the ocean does not arise from its own waves, nor the waves from the ocean; 51 A woman is not superior to, equal to, or like Kṛṣṇa among men; youth is nothing beyond adolescence, and nature is beyond its own inherent character. 52
One should meditate upon the youthfulness of His adolescence; one should meditate upon the forest of Vṛndāvana as the forest;
the dark-complexioned Supreme Form, the Primordial God, is the highest essence.
Childhood lasts until the end of the fifth year, and boyhood extends up to the tenth year.

From eight years up to the limit of fifteen is the period of *kaishora*; that which emerges from *kaishora* is called fresh youth (*navayauvana*). That age is his entire essence; all other ages are merely worldly manifestations (*prapañca*). 54–55.

I bow to the one whose childhood, youth, and adolescence are enchanting; who is the protector of the cowherd boys and the protector of the cows; who possesses the form of Gopāla that captivates the mind;
and who is Madanagopāla, possessing a wondrous adolescent form. 56.

Victorious is the secret form of the Lord of Śrī, manifesting as a youth, which those call the enchanting Madana whose beauty blossoms with youth; it is a great ocean of bliss consisting of the flavor of unbroken, incomparable nectar. (57-58)
Though He is one, immutable, and previously situated in the midst of the cowherd women,
