those of diverse intellects perceive Him differently according to their distinct inclinations (59)— He whose toenail-lustre is the object of meditation for Brahmā and the other gods.
I bow to that Lord of Vṛndāvana, who has transcended the three qualities (guṇas).
There is no abandonment of Vṛndāvana by Govinda; whatever form He assumes elsewhere is artificial, of this there is no doubt. 60-61.
That which is easily accessible to women on their way [to their husbands] is difficult to attain for those seeking liberation;
one should worship that son of Nanda, the splendor of whose toenails is the supreme Manu.
Pārvatī said:
"As long as the demoness of longing for worldly enjoyment and liberation dwells within the heart, how can there be the arising of the bliss of divine love here? 63. The Lord said:
"O auspicious lady, you have asked well; I shall tell you everything that dwells in my mind. Listen attentively.
Remembering his virtues, I shall chant his name, which delights Vāmana."
He awakens himself by himself and is constantly absorbed in love.

Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa," in the Vṛndāvana-māhātmya of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Pārvatī and Śiva.
The seventy-eighth chapter. Pārvatī said: "Tell me truly everything regarding the dharma of the Vaiṣṇavas."
"By performing which all the immortals indeed cross the ocean of worldly existence.
1. The Lord said: "Now, the twelvefold purification of the Vaiṣṇavas is described here."
Smearing the house with cow-dung, following after Hari, circumambulating him with devotion, and likewise cleansing his feet;
and lifting up leaves and flowers for the sake of worship with devotion alone—these are the duties of Hari. 2-3.
Among all purifications of the hands, this is distinguished as the highest:
the chanting of His name and the chanting of His qualities.
Through devotion to the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the purification of speech is desired.

Listening to his stories and beholding his festival are said here to be the complete purification of the ears and the eyes. Furthermore, there is the drinking of the water from his feet, the wearing of his used garlands, and the wearing of flower garlands as well. (5–6)
It is said, O beloved, that the purification of the head occurs by bowing before Hari,
as well as by smelling His flowers and other such offerings (nirmālya); likewise,
the purification of the internal sense and even of the sense of smell is ordained.
Whatever flower and so forth is offered at the pair of Kṛṣṇa’s feet, that alone is purifying in the world; it indeed purifies everything.
Worship is said to be fivefold; hear from me the distinction between them.
Approaching (abhigamana), taking up materials (upādāna), yoga, and likewise self-study (svādhyāya),
as well as sacrifice (ijyā)— I shall describe to you this fivefold worship in its proper order. Among these, approaching is defined as the cleansing of the deity’s place.
The removal of smears and the clearing away of withered flower offerings; likewise, "appropriation" (upādāna) is the gathering of names, perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
and "yoga" is the contemplation of one's own deity as being identical with one's own self. 11–12.
The worship of the deity through sacrifice and through one's own name according to their true meaning—
thus, O lady of virtuous vows, the fivefold mode of worship has been described to you, which bestows, in sequence, the states of Sārṣṭi, Sāmīpya, Sālokya, Sāyujya, and Sārūpya. 14–15.
In this context, I shall describe the worship of the Śālagrāma stone.
Keśava is known by the sequence of his four arms, beginning from the upper right hand;
he holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and is the bearer of the mace (Gadādhara).
Nārāyaṇa is characterized by the lotus, mace, discus, and conch as his weapons in sequence;
Mādhava is formed by the discus and conch along with the lotus and mace; and he who holds the mace and is known as Govinda possesses the mace, lotus, conch, and discus. 17–18.

Salutation to Him who has the form of Viṣṇu, holding a lotus, a conch, a sword, and a mace; salutation to the form of Madhusūdana, possessing a conch, a lotus, a mace, and a discus. Salutation to Trivikrama, endowed with a mace, a sword, a conch, and a lotus.
Salutations to the form of Vāmana, who holds the *sārī*, the *kaumodakī* mace, the lotus, and the conch;
salutations to the form of Śrīdhara, who holds the discus, the lotus, the conch, and the *gadā*;
salutations to you, Hṛṣīkeśa, who hold the *sārī*, the *gadā*, the conch, and the lotus.
Salutations to you, whose own form possesses the lotus, conch, mace, and discus, and who has the lotus as your navel;
O Dāmodara, salutations to you who possess the conch, mace, discus, and lotus.
Salutations to Saṃkarṣaṇa, who holds the conch, lotus, discus, and mace.

Salutations to you, Vāsudeva, who holds the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus. (23) Salutations to him who possesses the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus, who has assumed the form of Pradyumna;
salutations to Aniruddha, the bearer of the mace, the conch, the lotus, and the enemy-slaying [discus]. (24)
Salutations to the form of Puruṣottama, who holds the lotus, conch, mace, and discus;
salutations to the form of Adhokṣaja, who bears the mace, conch, discus, and lotus. Salutations to the form of Nṛsiṃha, who carries the lotus, mace, conch, and discus.
Salutations to the form of Acyuta, who holds the lotus, the enemy [of Madhu], the conch, and the mace.

Salutations to the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who bears the mace, the lotus, the enemy [of Madhu], and the conch, and who possesses two wheels fixed upon the surface of the entrance of the Śālagrāma stone. 26–27.
Śrī Gadādhara is rich in splendor, adorned with white lines, accompanied by deities, marked with two joined discs, red-hued, and his eastern portion is abundant.
Then there is Saṃkarṣaṇa and Pradyumna; the latter has a subtle disc and is yellowish.
Indeed, it has very long hollow openings, is unobstructed, and perfectly circular (29).
It has a blue-colored opening with three lines; furthermore, Nārāyaṇa is dark-hued, with lines in the shape of a mace in the middle and a highly elevated lotus at the navel (30).
He who is Pṛthucakra and Nṛsiṃha, he who is Kapila and Tribinduka,
or rather the worship of Pañcabinduka for the celibate student (brahmacārin);
[he who is] Varāha with three marks and two uneven cakras.
Nīla has three lines, is thick, and has the form of a tortoise with a dot;
Kṛṣṇa is black, has circular whirlpools, is pale on the back, and holds [the earth];
Śrīdhara has five lines, wears a forest garland, and is marked with a mace. 33.
Vāmana is round, with a discus in the center and blue;
Ananta has many forms of various colors and the coils of a serpent.
Sthūla is large-bellied, dark-blue, with a discus in the center and blue.
He is Saṃkarṣaṇa, the gateway, the two Dvārakas, the weapon, Brahmā, and the deep red one (35).
He is the very long line, the cavity, the single wheel, the lotus,
the broad one, the broad wheel, the maker of thick apertures, Kṛṣṇa, the dot, and the possessor of dots (36).
The Hayagrīva [mark] is shaped like a goad, has five lines, and is accompanied by the Kaustubha; Vaikuṇṭha appears like a wrestler, being dark and consisting of a single wheel.
Matsya is long, shaped like a lotus, has long lines, and is white.
Salutations to the dark-complexioned Trivikrama, who possesses the lines of the Rāmacakra;
salutations to the mace-bearer Gadādhara, who resides in Śālagrāma and Dvārakā and is marked by the single Sudarśana discus. 38–39.
May Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa protect with two, Trivikrama with three,
Caturvyūha with four, Vāsudeva with five,
Pradyumna with six, and Saṃkarṣaṇa with seven.
May Puruṣottama protect us with eight [forms], and the ninefold Navavyūha with nine;
may Aniruddha, the ten incarnations, protect us with ten, and then the twelve-fold Ātmā with twelve; beyond that, may the Infinite One (Anantaka) protect us. 41-42.
Brahmā has four faces and holds a staff and a water-pot, adorned with a garland;
Maheśvara has five faces, ten arms, and the bull as his emblem.
Gaurī, Caṇḍikā, and Sarasvatī likewise possess the same weapons.
Mahālakṣmī, the Mothers, the Sun-god with lotus in hand,
Gajānana, Gajaskandha, Ṣaṇmukha, and the various Gaṇas—
these should be present, installed, propitiated, or worshipped. 44–45.
Dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa are to be attained by a person at the end [of their journey]. 46.
Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Determination of Śālagrāma," in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Seventy-Nine.
Īśvara said:
The worship of Śrī Hari should always be performed in the Śālagrāma stone, a gem, a yantra, a maṇḍala, or an image, but never in an earthen vessel alone.

In a certain part of the Gaṇḍakī river, there is a great region known as Śālagrāma; the stone produced there is established as being called Śālagrāma. By the touch of a Śālagrāma stone, the sins of ten million births are destroyed.
How much more so, then, is the worship performed there the cause for the presence of Hari?
By worshipping a single Śālagrāma stone, one obtains the fruit of a hundred liṅgas.
If, through the merits of many births, one should obtain a Kṛṣṇa-śilā stone, [one attains the supreme goal].
By that mark of a cow’s footprint, one's birth is completed.
First, one should examine the stone: it is best when it is glossy and deep blue-black;
it is said to be middling when it is black; and when it is variegated, it yields mixed results.
Just as fire, which exists eternally within the six kinds of wood, is made manifest through friction,
so too is the all-pervading Hari perceived in the Śālagrāma stone.
He who worships twelve Śālagrāma stones every day [attains the highest goal].
One who possesses a stone from Dvāravatī is honored even in Vaikuṇṭha; however,
a man who perceives a cavity within a Śālagrāma stone causes his ancestors to remain satisfied in heaven until the end of the kalpa.
There, where the stone of Dvārāvatī is located, lies the abode of Vaikuṇṭha;

one who dies there goes to the city of Viṣṇu. That sacred site extends for three yojanas, and all acts performed there—recitation, worship, and fire-offerings—become ten million times more efficacious.
There is no doubt that even a mere worm, having reached the distance of a krośa from the place most desired by the mind, goes to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha upon death;
this applies to any man who would assign a price to the Śālagrāma stone.
The seller, the one who consents to it, and he who approves of the examination—
all these go to hell for as long as the sun and moon endure.
Therefore, O Goddess, one should avoid the buying and selling of the discus.
The deity originating from Śālagrāma and the deity originating from Dvārakā—wherever there is a union of these two, liberation is attained; of this there is no doubt.
[14] That which originates from Dvārakā is enriched with a discus and marked by many discs.
The stainless one, whose nature is consciousness in the form of the stone of the *cakrāsana*—salutations to you who are the form of the syllable *Oṃ* and whose nature is eternal bliss;
O highly blessed Śālagrāma, grant grace to your devotee. 15–16.
O Lord, for me who am desirous of your grace yet bound by debt,
I shall hereafter joyfully proclaim the rite of the *tilaka*,
hearing which all human beings may attain the same form as Viṣṇu. 17.
One should know Keśava to be on the forehead and Śrī Puruṣottama on the neck;
likewise, one should know the god Nārāyaṇa at the navel and Vaikuṇṭha in the heart, Dāmodara on the left side, and Trivikrama on the right. 18–19.
One should place Hṛṣīkeśa on the head, Padmanābha on the back,
Yamunā and Gaṅgā on the two ears, and likewise Kṛṣṇa and Hari on the two arms;
thus the twelve deities are pleased when placed in their respective positions.
One should recite these twelve names in the Tilaka-vidhi;
one whose soul is purified of all sins goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
On whose forehead an upward-marked vertical line (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) is seen... [21-22]

Even a Cāṇḍāla whose soul is purified is indeed worthy of worship; of this there is no doubt—provided that the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) is seen upon his forehead. One should not even look at such a person; having seen him, one should gaze at the sun.
If the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) is not seen on the forehead of a Brahmin who possesses the triple horizontal mark (*tripuṇḍra*),
one should perform a bath with one's clothes on upon seeing or touching him.
The *puṇḍra* should be made with intervals between the lines and in the shape of the feet of Hari.

If the lowest of the twice-born should draw an uninterrupted vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) on his forehead, there is no doubt that a dog’s footprint is always present upon it. A beautiful vertical mark should extend from the nose up to the hairline.
One should know that which is joined with a central aperture to be the temple of Hari (Viṣṇu).
Brahmā resides on the left side, while Sadāśiva is always on the right;
one should recognize Viṣṇu as being in the middle; therefore, one should not apply plaster to the middle. 27–28.
O highly fortunate one, he who, having looked [at his reflection] even in a mirror or in water, diligently applies the upright *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, attains the supreme goal.
Fire, water, the Vedas, the moon, the sun, and likewise the wind—
These [deities] always reside here on the right ear of the Brahmins:
Gaṅgā in the right ear and Hutāśana (Fire) in the nose;
by the touch of both, one becomes pure at that very moment.
Having performed the water libation for the high-souled Vaiṣṇavas with conch shells,
one should offer [the water] mixed with Tulasī, drink it, and honor them by bowing one's head; furthermore,
one should consume it, sprinkle one's own body, and [sprinkle] one's sons, friends, and dependents.
The water from Viṣṇu’s feet, when drunk, destroys the sins of ten million births. That very same water becomes eightfold sinful by the falling of even a single drop upon the ground.
Having placed the water-vessel and the conch in one's hand, one should offer praise, prostration, and circumambulation.
The fruit of birth is truly attained by one who constantly maintains [these items] at hand;
for he in whose house there is no conch, nor a bell accompanied by Garuḍa before Vāsudeva, is not a Bhāgavata in the Kali age. (35)

Traveling in vehicles or on sandals to the house of the Blessed One; not attending during festivals for the deity; failing to prostrate before him; and performing salutations and other rites to the Blessed One while one is impure due to food remnants or physical uncleanness—(these are offenses). 36–37.

Prostrating with only one hand before him, circumambulating to his left, stretching out one's feet in his presence, as well as sitting in a cross-legged posture (paryaṅka), lying down, eating, and speaking falsely— 38.
Speaking loudly, whispering with one another, weeping, quarreling, (39) as well as punishing and favoring others, speaking harshly to women,
being exclusively conceited, censuring others, and praising others; (40)
Speaking indecorous words, the emission of downward wind (flatus),
using secondary metaphors when one is capable of the primary meaning, eating without having first offered [the food],
and failing to offer fruits and other such items that have appeared at their respective seasons. 41.
Giving away the remainder of a seasoned dish that has already been served (verse 42);
eating while making it obvious; censuring others and praising oneself; remaining silent toward one's guru; praising oneself; and likewise, reviling the deities (verse 43).
Likewise, thirty-two offenses of Viṣṇu have been proclaimed.
(44) Thousands of offenses are committed by me day and night; considering me as "I am yours," O Madhusūdana, please forgive me. (45)
Having recited this mantra, one should prostrate like a staff upon the ground;
Hari always forgives thousands of offenses.
Likewise, for the twice-born, eating in the evening and morning is as prescribed by the Vedas.

One who eats the remnants of food from a devotee of Viṣṇu is liberated from the sins of the day. Reciting "Brahmā is the food, Viṣṇu is the essence," while eating meat, he who eats with this knowledge is not tainted by the defects of the food. 47–48.
A Vaiṣṇava man should not eat a round gourd, lentils with their husks, white palmyra fruit,
or eggplant; nor should he eat from the leaves of the banyan, the holy fig tree, the arka, the kumbhī, or the tinduka.
A devotee of Viṣṇu should not eat kovidāraka, kadamba, or cane-seeds.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should avoid leafy vegetables; in Bhādrapada, one should renounce curd; in the month of Āśvina, milk; and in Kārttika, one should give up meat. (50–51)
Food that has been burnt, citron not offered to Viṣṇu,
pomegranate, leafy vegetables, and likewise salt that is visible—
if one should eat these by chance, then one should remember His name.
Winter rice, white kidney beans, mung beans, sesame seeds, barley,
53 kalāpa, kangu, nīvāra, and the vegetable hilamocikā, as well as kālaśāka, vāstūka, radish, and red or other [colored] potherbs; 54

Salt from the Indus and the ocean, cow's curd and clarified butter, milk from which the essence has been extracted, the jackfruit, the mango, and the harītakī; long pepper, cumin, and likewise the nāgaraṅga and the tiṃtiḍī.
Sages declare that plantains, lavalī fruits, and dhātrī fruits, along with jaggery and sugarcane products, when not fried in oil, constitute *haviṣyānna*.
A man who wears a garland made of tulasī leaves, flowers, and the like, [attains great merit]. 56-57.
One should know that even Viṣṇu is present there; this is the truth, the absolute truth, of this there is no doubt.
By planting a Dhātrī tree, a man becomes equal to Viṣṇu. One should recognize Kurukṣetra as extending three hundred and fifty cubits.
Having placed around one's neck a rosary fashioned from beads made of Tulasī wood or carved from Rudrākṣa, one should begin the worship;
likewise, one may use a rosary of Āmalaka fruits or a well-crafted rosary of lotus seeds.

The worshiper of Viṣṇu should diligently wear a garland around his neck, and he should also place the remains of the offering (nirmālya) and a tulasī garland upon his head. He should mark his body with the sandalwood paste from the offering while reciting the names of that Lord.
On his forehead he bears the mace, and likewise on his head the bow and arrow;
Nandaka is in the center of his heart, and the conch and discus are upon his two arms.
O Brahmin, if one who is thus endowed with the conch and discus dies in a cremation ground, [he attains liberation]. 62–63.
The path to Prayāga is said to be his certain destination—he who, devoted to Viṣṇu, holds a Tulasi leaf upon his head and performs all his duties; he attains imperishable fruit. 64.
Adorned with garlands made of Tulasī wood while performing one's duties,
the merit offered to the ancestors and the gods becomes ten millionfold.
Having offered a garland fashioned from Tulasī wood to Keśava, [the same result follows].
The sin of that man who carries [the Ganges] with devotion perishes; having honored her with water for the feet and other offerings, one should then recite this mantra:
"O you who, when seen, pacify the entire multitude of sins, and when touched, purify the body! (67)

Salutations to this Tulasī, who is worshipped as the dispeller of diseases, who sprinkles terror upon Death (Antaka), who brings about proximity to the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, and who, when planted and placed at His feet, bestows the fruit of liberation. 68.
Thus ends the dialogue between Devī and Īśvara in the Vṛndāvana-māhātmya of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Tilaka and Other Marks," is concluded.
Chapter Eighty.
Pārvatī said:
O Lord, now that the terrible Kali age has arrived, which is teeming with the crocodiles of sensory objects,
how can it be sustained by those afflicted by sons, wives, wealth, and the like?
O Mahādeva, O ocean of compassion, tell me the means for that.
Īśvara said: "The name of Hari, the name of Hari, the name of Hari alone is everything.
'Hari, Rāma, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa'—this is auspicious."
Thus they speak constantly: "The Kali age does not oppress those who are devoted.
Having performed various actions at intervals, one should remember the names; one should say "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa" again and again.
By joining my name with yours and performing [the rite] without transgression,
he too shall be liberated from sin, just as fire consumes a heap of cotton.
Or, you may obtain this victory and so forth, preceded by the word "Śrī."
By chanting this auspicious name, one is liberated from sin.
One should remember it day and night, at the twilights, and at all times;
by remembering Rāma and Kṛṣṇa day and night, one beholds them with one's own eyes.
Whether impure or pure, at all times and in every way,
by the mere recollection of the Name, one is instantly liberated from saṃsāra.
Even for one burdened with various offenses, the Name alone removes their sin.
In the Kali age, sacrificial rites, vows, austerities, and charity do not bear fruit in their entirety;

however, bathing in the Gaṅgā and the name of Hari—this pair is unfailing. Even ten thousand killings, a thousand fierce sins, and the violation of ten million preceptors' wives [are destroyed by it].
O beloved, there are no other thefts [as grave as] the stealing of the name "Govinda," O auspicious one.
Whether impure or pure, or even if situated in any state whatsoever,
he who remembers the lotus-eyed Lord is pure both internally and externally.
Merely by recollecting the name and reflecting upon its meaning,
one should fashion an image made of gold, silver, or even flour in the shape of a garland,
marked with the feet [of the deity], and then commence the worship.
He who bears a discus at the base of the big toe of his right foot—
for the severing of the cycle of existence even for those humble beings there— and Acyuta bears a lotus at the base of his middle toes. 14–15.
To attract the bees of the meditator’s mind, he held beneath the lotus a most beautiful banner, a victory-banner over all misfortunes;
from the base of his little finger, he bore a vajra that shatters the flood of the sins of those who have partaken [of the offerings]. 16.
In the middle of his side, he bears a goad—the cause of delight for those whose minds are devoted—consisting of the perfection of enjoyments;
and at the joint of his thumb, he holds a mace at its base, which shatters the mountain of sins of all embodied beings. 17–18.

The unborn Blessed One bears all the emblems that illuminate every branch of knowledge; furthermore, that treasury of compassion bears upon his right hand the lotus and other such signs, while on his left foot he likewise bears them.

Therefore, one who constantly hears and recites this majesty of Govinda, which is beautiful with the essence of bliss, shall undoubtedly be liberated from all bonds. I shall now declare the monthly rites that bring supreme pleasure to Viṣṇu.

Being pure, one should diligently perform the ritual bathing of Śrī Viṣṇu during the month of Jyeṣṭha; it destroys daily sins as well as those born of the fortnight, the month, the season, and the year, and even thousands of killings of Brahmins committed knowingly or unknowingly. 22.
The theft of gold, the drinking of liquor, violating the teacher’s bed, and tens of thousands of crores of secondary sins—
all these perish on the day of the full moon. 23–24.
Then, one should sprinkle that water from the pitcher upon the head of Acyuta with the Puruṣasūkta mantra and indeed with the Pāvamānī verses;
likewise, with coconut water and the juice of the palmyra fruit.
Having worshipped with the five offerings according to the extent of one's means— using water containing jewels, scented water, and likewise water with flowers—
one should offer the ringing of the bell while reciting "Ghaṃ Ghaṇṭāyai namaḥ. 26–27.
"Protect me, a sinner fallen upon the great path where a multitude of sins has been cast, and plunged into the terrible ocean of saṃsāra.
Thus does the learned, pure Brāhmaṇa, well-versed in the Vedas, act.
One shall be liberated from all sins and go to the world of Viṣṇu.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, one should perform the great festival of the Lord’s sleep;
in Āṣāḍha, one should perform the chariot festival, and in Śrāvaṇa, the rite associated with the Śravaṇā constellation.
In the month of Bhādrapada, one should be intent on fasting on the day of one's birth;

in the month of Āśvina, one should perform the ritual of turning over the Lord as He lies asleep. One should perform the awakening of Śrī Hari; otherwise, one becomes a committer of offense against Viṣṇu.
In the auspicious month of Āśvina, one should worship Mahāmāyā.
She may be fashioned of gold or silver, having the form of Viṣṇu; for a righteous soul who worships Viṣṇu, there should indeed be no violence or hatred toward strength. 32–33.

In the months of Kārttika and Puṣya, one should perform meritorious acts according to one's desire; one should offer a lamp to Dāmodara in a prominent place. That lamp should be four fingers in height and consist of seven wicks.

And at the end of the fortnight, a beautiful row of lamps should be offered. On the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship the Lord of the Universe with white garments, and especially Brahmā.
One should avoid the flower-ablution in the month of Pauṣa and avoid soft sandalwood paste.
During the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti) and in the month of Māgha, one should offer as an oblation (naivedya) to Viṣṇu rice that has been consecrated (sādhivāsita), while reciting this mantra: 37.

One should devoutly feed the Brahmins standing before the God of gods (38). Having honored the twice-born devotees of the Lord with the thought that they are the Lord himself, when one devotee is fed, it is as if ten million have been fed (39).
Merely by feeding a Brahmin, one will certainly become free from physical defects and possessed of all limbs;
having bathed Keśava on the fifth day of the bright fortnight and worshipped him according to the prescribed rite with mango sprouts, [one attains this].

With various powdered fruits, scented and prepared on cloth, the beautiful grove was made radiant and illuminated by lamps. There were grapes, sugarcane juice, rose-apples, citrons, oranges, and betel nuts.
With coconut trees, dhātrī trees, jackfruit trees, and harītakī trees, as well as with other groves of trees endowed with flowers of all seasons,
and with various others likewise provided with fruits and blossoms.
Adorned with canopies profuse with flowers, with jars filled with water, and with the branches and twigs of mango trees, as well as with umbrellas and chowries;
having remembered "Victory to Kṛṣṇa! and preceded by a circumambulation—44–45.
Specifically in the Kali Yuga, the festival of the swing (dolotsava) is observed on the fourteenth day of the month of Phālguna, known as the eighth watch (yāma);
or alternatively, on the full moon day, at the junction known as the *saṃdhi* with the first lunar day (*pratipad*).
One should worship according to the prescribed rites with devotion, using four kinds of powders—
white, red, pale-yellow, and yellow— blended with camphor and other substances,
and rendered beautiful and captivating by the application of colors through the addition of turmeric dye. 47–48.
Or one should gratify the Supreme Lord with other beautiful forms;
beginning on the eleventh day, one should complete it by the fifth.
A festival of the *dolā* (swing) lasting five days or three days is thus ordained.
Having seen Kṛṣṇa swinging on the swing facing south even once, men are liberated from their multitudes of offenses; of this there is no doubt.
And having placed [the image] in a water-vessel known as Mādhava... 51.

O highly fortunate one, the merit of one who worships the deity originating from Śālagrāma, whether it be an image or a stone, while it is situated in water within a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay, cannot be calculated.
Having performed the offering of *damanaka* flowers, one should present them to Śrī Viṣṇu.
This offering may be made in the months of Vaiśākha, Śrāvaṇa, or Bhādrapada;
or it may be performed on each preceding day during the rites involving *damanaka* and other such materials.
It must be performed according to the prescribed injunctions; otherwise, it shall be fruitless.
Specifically on the third day of the month of Vaiśākha, one should perform it in the midst of water, or else in a mandala, or in a pavilion, or in a great forest.
Day by day, one should diligently apply fragrant sandalwood paste to nourish the body,
just as one would provide nourishment for a person with a lean frame; likewise,
[one should use] sandalwood, agallochum, hrīvera, black saffron, and gorocana.
They know *jaṭāmāṃsī*, *māṃsī*, and *murā* to be the eight-fold fragrance (*gandhāṣṭaka*) of Viṣṇu;
one should smear the limbs of Viṣṇu with these various fragrant substances.
Furthermore, one should apply powdered *tulasī* wood combined with camphor and *aguru*.
Alternatively, it is said that yellow sandalwood (haricandana) should be mixed with saffron filaments (kesara).
Those men who, at the time of the festival procession, behold Kṛṣṇa with devotion,
shall not undergo rebirth even after hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Those who bathe the God of gods with waters scented with fragrances,
or else place the Lord of the World amidst flowers; having gone there to Vṛndāvana, they should offer fruits as well.
One should feed it entirely to a worthy devotee of Viṣṇu.
Having extracted the seed-vessel from a coconut fruit, one should offer it; having extracted the seed-vessel from a *ghoṇṭā* fruit and a jackfruit (*panasa*), one should offer them. 62–63.
One should cause food mixed with curd to be given after sprinkling it with ghee;
likewise, one should offer cooked flour-cakes and eighteen types of fried cakes with ghee,
and offer ripe fruit with oils mixed with sesame.
Whatever is pleasing to oneself, that very thing one should offer to the Lord.
Having offered it with food offerings, clothing, and so forth, one should never take it back;
rather, having renounced it for the sake of Viṣṇu, one should especially give it to His devotees.
Thus, O Maheśvarī, O Pārvatī, I have related something to you in brief; it must be guarded with great effort, like one's own private parts.
If one possesses the qualification for understanding the class of scriptures that describe the form and qualities of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, then enough with the study of other texts.

If the mind indeed delights in the great necklace of the playful devotion to the essence of that love, what need is there for beautiful women? (68) For those who worship with their hearts the Lord of the boys of Vraja, the land of Vṛndāvana, and the waters of the Yamunā—bodies smeared with the dust from the lotus feet of that Lord of the World—sandalwood and other unguents are truly useless. (69)
Thus ends the eightieth chapter in the Vṛndāvana-māhātmya, within the Umā-Maheśvara-saṃvāda of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa in the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter eighty-one.
The Sages said:
O Sūta, long live you, O virtuous one! You have revealed the entire nectar of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s deeds, which brings liberation to all devotees.
O Lord, tell us the entirety of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s daily pastimes.

"O most fortunate one, you are indeed our supreme friend; tell us separately the characteristics and the ritual procedure for the preceptor, the disciple, and the mantra, by hearing which devotion to Kṛṣṇa increases in those who are not yet perfected."
Sūta said:
Once, having prostrated before the Teacher of the World, Sadāśiva, the God of gods, who was seated on the banks of the Yamunā, Nārada spoke. 4.
Nārada said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, omniscient Lord of the universe, knower of the true essence of the Lord’s dharma, and best among those who know the mantras of Kṛṣṇa! 5.
O supreme father, all those Kṛṣṇa-mantras that were unattainable by me have been mastered by me from you through the water [you gave], as well as the King of Mantras and others,
while I subsisted on vegetables, roots, and fruits for many thousands of years.
Subsisting on dry leaves, water, wind, and so forth, remaining without food, avoiding the sight and conversation of women, sleeping upon the ground,
and having conquered the six qualities beginning with desire, one should restrain the external senses. 7–8.
Even when this has been done, O Śaṅkara, my soul is still not satisfied; therefore,
O Lord, tell me that by which the supreme fruit may be obtained even without purificatory rites and the like, simply through a single recitation.
"If I am worthy, O Lord of Gods, then speak out of compassion for me.
Śiva said:
"O highly fortunate one, you who desire the welfare of the world have asked well."

I shall speak to you this *Mantracintāmaṇi*, which is most worthy of being guarded as a secret. It is the secret of secrets, the supreme mystery among mysteries; it was not previously told by me even to the Goddess, nor to my elder brothers, before you.

I shall speak to you of the unsurpassed Kṛṣṇa-mantra couplet, known as the Mantra-cintāmaṇi, which consists of exactly two pairs; furthermore, the synonyms for this mantra include the term "pañcapadī" (the five-worded). 13.
"Ending with *gopījana-vallabha* and preceded by *tad-caraṇau*, one should take refuge in these five words. This sixteen-syllabled great mantra is declared to be the Cintāmaṇi of mantras. (14-15)
Having uttered "namo gopījana," one should then say "vallabhābhyām";
this mantra, consisting of two words, is said to have ten syllables. Having chanted these five words even once with faith, [one attains the goal].
One attains the presence of those dear to Kṛṣṇa; of this there is no doubt.

(17) There is no requirement for preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*), nor is there any need for the sequence of ritual installations (*nyāsa*); there is no restriction regarding place or time, nor any purification concerning enemies, friends, and so forth. (18)
O Lord of Sages, all are eligible for this, even those down to the Caṇḍālas,
as well as women, Śūdras, and others, including the dull-witted, the mute, the lame, and so forth; likewise the Hūṇas, Kirātas, Pulindas, and Puṣkasas.
The Ābhīras, Yavanas, Kaṅkas, Khasas, and others of sinful birth (20)—
who are devoted to hypocrisy and egoism, who are wicked and intent on backbiting,
who are slayers of cows and Brahmins, and who are possessed of great and minor sins (21).
Those devoid of knowledge and dispassion, those who have abandoned hearing [the scriptures] and so forth—
these and all others may become qualified for the Manōratha [mantra],
provided they possess devotion toward Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the lords of all.
Therefore, O best of sages, all these persons are qualified [to perform the rite], and not otherwise:
a performer of sacrifices, one devoted to giving gifts, a follower of all the Tantras, a speaker of truth, an ascetic, or even one who has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences. 23–24.
One who is devoted to the Brahman, well-born, an ascetic, or intent on vows—
even such a person would not be qualified here if they are devoid of devotion to Kṛṣṇa.
Therefore, [this is not for] one who lacks devotion to Kṛṣṇa, who is ungrateful, or who is conceited.

It should not be told to one devoid of faith, nor to an atheist (26). It should not be told to one who does not wish to hear it, nor to one who has not served for a year; but it should be told to one who possesses exclusive devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa and is free from hypocrisy and greed (27).
This should be bestowed with great effort upon one who is liberated from desire and anger;
I am the seer (ṛṣi) of this mantra, and Gāyatrī is declared to be its meter (chandas). The beloved of Ballavī is proclaimed as the deity (devatā) of this mantra. 28.
The employment [of the mantra] as service to Hari together with His beloved has been described.

(29) One should then perform the assignment of the five limbs (pañcāṅga) using the mantras beginning with "ā cakrāya," or else one should perform the assignment of the hands and limbs (karāṅganyāsa) using one's own seed-syllable (bīja). (30)

The first syllable of the mantra, adorned with a bindu on its head, becomes the seed-syllable (bīja) "gaṃ"; here, "namaḥ" is declared to be the power (śakti). With the final syllables, the ten limbs (aṅgas) are formed, and likewise, worship is performed with them.
That [worship] should be performed with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, or even with water alone if these are unavailable, preceded by the ritual of *nyāsa*, for the pleasure of Hari.
For this very reason, others prescribe other rites such as *nyāsa* for this mantra.
Although it grants the fulfillment of all duties through a single utterance,
one should nevertheless arrange [the syllables] in ten ways for the purpose of constant recitation (*japa*) and so forth.
Now, O best of the twice-born, I shall describe the meditation (*dhyāna*) upon this mantra.
Wearing yellow garments, dark as a rain cloud, with two arms and a forest garland;
having a crest made of peacock feathers, a face resembling ten million moons, with rolling eyes and an ear-ornament of karṇikāra flowers. 35–36.
He bore on his forehead a circular tilaka, fashioned with sandalwood paste on the outer edges and a drop of saffron in the center;
he resembled the rising sun and was resplendent with two earrings. 37.
His cheeks shone like mirrors with glistening droplets of perspiration;

his eyes were fixed upon the face of his beloved, while his playful side-glances and raised eyebrows were directed toward her; and his prominent nose was made radiant by a pearl set upon its tip. 38–39.
His lower lip, like a ripe bimba fruit, shone with the moonlight of his teeth;
his arms were radiant with armlets and bracelets set with excellent gems; he held a flute in one hand and likewise a lotus in his left hand. 40.
His waist was shimmering with a girdle, his feet were radiant with anklets;
restless in the passion of amorous play, with flickering eyes, he laughed together with his beloved and repeatedly made her laugh. 41-42.

Thus, one should remember Kṛṣṇa seated upon a jeweled lion-throne at the foot of the wish-fulfilling tree in the Vṛndāvana forest together with his beloved; then, one should remember Rādhikā standing at his left side. 43.
Clad in a blue tunic, she possessed a luster like molten gold;

her lotus-face was half-covered by the hem of her silk garment and was beautifully smiling, while her eyes, as restless as those of a female cakora bird, were fixed upon the face of her beloved. 44-45.

With her thumb and forefinger, she was offering a betel nut together with leaf and lime into the lotus-face of her own beloved; her full, high breasts were beautiful and shimmering with a pearl necklace. 46.
She has a slender waist and broad hips, adorned with a network of tinkling bells; she wears jeweled earrings, armlets, rings, and bracelets,
along with jingling anklets and jeweled toe-rings.
They are to be served with fly-whisks, fans, and other such articles.
Now, O Nārada, listen as I declare to you the meaning of the mantra:
through the external limbs of the phenomenal world, by means of His own portions, the powers such as Māyā and the rest. 50–51.

Because she protects [the Lord] through those internal, eternal, and all-pervading attributes such as consciousness (cit) and the rest, she is called Gopī; Rādhikā, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, is declared to be the Goddess who consists of Kṛṣṇa, the supreme deity Rādhikā. 52

Since she is the embodiment of all prosperity and the nature of Kṛṣṇa’s bliss, she is therefore called Hlādinī by the wise, O Brahmin. Durgā and others, who consist of the three guṇas, are but a ten-millionth of a ten-millionth part of her power.
Sātū is Mahālakṣmī herself, and Kṛṣṇa is the Lord Nārāyaṇa;
O best of sages, not even the slightest difference exists between these two.
She is Durgā, she is Rudrāṇī, she is Śacī, and she is Śakra. (54–55)
Sāvitrī is this Lakṣmī, Hari is Brahmā, and Dhūmorṇā is that Yamunā;
O best of sages, what need is there for much? Without these two, there is nothing at all.
The entire world, characterized by both the conscious and the unconscious, is composed of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa.
O Nārada, know that everything in this manner is the manifestation of those two alone (57).
It is not possible for me to describe it even in hundreds of millions of years.
Within the three worlds, the earth is the most venerable; among the continents, Jambūdvīpa is superior to that (58).
Therein lies Bhārata-varṣa; therein lies the city of Mathurā;
therein lies the place named Vṛndāvana; therein lies the assembly of gopīs; therein lies the circle of Rādhā’s friends; and therein, moreover, is the supreme Rādhikā. 59.

Due to the superiority of her presence, there is a progressive increase [in excellence] among the elements beginning with earth; nothing else has been stated here. This very [earth] is the serpent-king Śeṣa, and the multitude of cowherd women (gopīs) are his circle of friends. 60–61.
"Thus, this serpent has come for refuge;
whatever belongs to me, let all that be for the sake of these two, for that is what is to be enjoyed by them, for there is neither 'I' nor 'mine'.
O Brahmin, such is the meaning of the mantra explained in brief.

The meaning of the couple, as well as the other placement, self-surrender, seeking refuge, and the offering of oneself—these five synonyms have been declared by me to you. This alone should be meditated upon day and night by those who are free from sloth. 65–66.
Thus ends the eighty-first chapter in the Vṛndāvana-māhātmya of the Pātālakhaṇḍa in the glorious Padma Purāṇa. Chapter Eighty-two.
Śiva said:
Now I shall describe the procedure for initiation (dīkṣā); listen, O Nārada, according to the truth. By merely hearing this, one is liberated even without performing its ritual application. 1.
O best of sages, having realized that the entire world up to Brahmā is impermanent,
and having experienced the threefold suffering— namely, that which is internal and so forth—
and because all pleasures are transitory, the wise man [should seek liberation]. 2.3.1–2.3.2ab.

Having cast aside the side of suffering and being liberated from those [afflictions], one should become dispassionate toward saṃsāra; for the sake of its abandonment, one should contemplate the means [to liberation], being intensely at peace even upon the attainment of unsurpassed bliss. (3–4)

Having realized the difficulty for men [to attain this], the one of great intelligence, being deeply distressed, should then go for refuge to his preceptor, the Brahmin. He should be peaceful, free from envy, devoted to Kṛṣṇa, and having no other purpose.
Possessing no other means of accomplishment, glorious, and free from desire and greed (6),
he was a knower of the essential truth of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s rasa, the best among those who know the Kṛṣṇa-mantras,
eternally taking refuge in the Kṛṣṇa-mantra, devoted to mantra, and always pure (7).
One who constantly teaches the True Dharma, always enjoins others to right conduct, is a transmitter of tradition, full of compassion, and free from passion— such a person is called a Guru.
One who possesses such qualities as these, and who generally desires to serve at the feet of the Guru, [is a disciple].
A disciple is said to be one who is intensely devoted to the guru and seeks liberation (mumukṣu). By serving him directly with love, one becomes a true devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata);
this is declared by the wise who know the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences to be equivalent to liberation itself.
Having taken refuge at the feet of his own guru, he should report his own conduct;
having repeatedly cleared away his doubts and brought him to understanding,
[the guru should look upon] him who is prostrate at his feet, peaceful, and desirous of service at his feet.
With a deeply delighted mind, he should teach the supreme mantra to the disciple.
O Brahmin, he should mark the base of the left and right upper arms with sandalwood paste or soft clay, drawing a conch and a discus respectively.
Then, one should apply the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) on the forehead and other parts according to the prescribed rule;
thereafter, one should recite two mantras into his right ear. One should also explain the meaning of those mantras to him exactly and in proper sequence.
One should diligently bear a name for him that includes the word "dāsa" (servant).
Then, with great devotion and affection, the wise person should feed the Vaiṣṇavas and worship the venerable Guru with garments, ornaments, and other offerings.
O great sage, one should give all one's possessions to the guru, or half of them; even casting aside one’s own body, those who possess nothing should remain at the service of the guru.
A wise man who has been consecrated by these five purificatory rites [becomes a true disciple].
One shall belong to the state of servitude to Kṛṣṇa; it cannot be otherwise even in tens of millions of kalpas.

Marking [the body], the vertical tilaka (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), the mantra, the bearing of the Name, and the fifth, sacrifice—these are declared as the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) by the ancient sages. 18–19.
Marking with the conch, discus, and so forth, along with the sacred *puṇḍra* marked with a central hole, is prescribed;
the name joined with the word "servant" (*dāsa*) is known as the pair of mantras.
Worship of the Guru and the Vaiṣṇava is designated as sacrifice (*yāga*). 20.
These have been proclaimed as the supreme purificatory rites (saṃskāras).
Now, O Nārada, I shall declare to you the duties for those who have sought refuge in me, by adhering to which men in the Kali age shall go to the abode of Hari. 21–22.
Thus, having received the mantra from his guru, the wise disciple, devoted to service of the guru, should constantly serve him and contemplate his grace.
One should constantly satisfy the Vaiṣṇavas with the thought that they are one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadeva).
Just as women accept beating and rebuke as objects of enjoyment for those who desire them,
so too should the wise accept whatever is offered by the Vaiṣṇavas.
One should never at any time harbor anxiety regarding this world or the next; rather, one should always attend to the concerns of this life through the karma performed in previous lives.
As for the matters of the hereafter, Kṛṣṇa himself will take care of them.
Therefore, men should by all means abandon the effort directed toward that which is not beneficial;
they should renounce all other means and worship with Kṛṣṇa as their very self, just as a woman devoted solely to her husband when he has been away on a long journey. 27–28.
One who is devoted to her beloved, distressed by separation, and desiring only union with him, should constantly contemplate his virtues, sing of them, and listen to them;
one should act in this way by recollecting the virtues, pastimes, and other qualities of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. 29.
That [state] is never again to be accomplished as something that needs to be proven anew;
just as a woman, upon finding her beloved who has returned after a long absence, thinking "it is my lover," kisses him, embraces him, and even drinks him in with the corners of her eyes. 30-31.
Just as one who has attained the bliss of Brahman serves with supreme joy, so too should one serve Hari through the glorious arcāvatāra (the manifested form). Thus,
one should always have no other refuge and likewise employ no other means.
Because it has no other means of accomplishment, it should have no other purpose (33).
One should not worship another deity, nor bow to them, nor remember them, nor look upon them, nor sing their praises, nor ever censure them (34).

One should not eat the leftovers of others, nor should one keep the remnants of others; one should avoid conversation, salutation, and other such interactions with those who are not Vaiṣṇavas (35). One should never listen to the censure of the Lord or of Vaiṣṇavas.
One should proceed while covering one's ears; if capable, one should administer punishment.
O twice-born one, adopting the "cātaka" way of life until the fall of the body, one should remain intent upon the welfare of both [self and others]; such is my opinion. 36–37.
Just as a thirsty cātaka bird, having abandoned lakes, oceans, rivers, and the like, either dies or begs from a cloud,
even so should one contemplate the means [of attainment] with diligent effort. 38.
"May you always be my refuge, my chosen deity; thus [he prays].
(39) One should always remain in favor with one's chosen deity, its attendants, and especially with the guru; one should avoid being contrary to them. (40)
I shall describe the auspicious qualities of these two;
reflecting upon them, one should place one's trust in them, for they will deliver me from this ocean of worldly existence, which is crowded with masters, friends, sons, and homes. 41.
O protectors, I have sought refuge in you two alone, the destroyers of fear. Whatever belongs to me— whether in this world or the next—
all that is today offered at the feet of you both.

I am a repository of offenses, abandoned by all means of protection, and without refuge; therefore, O Lord, you two alone are my refuge. 44 O Beloved, I am yours through my actions, my mind, and my speech.
O Beloved of Kṛṣṇa, I am yours alone; you two are my only refuge.
I have come to you for shelter—you who are the source of a multitude of mercies—grant me your favor and accept the service of this wicked and offending servant. 45-46.
O best of sages, one who desires that [state] should constantly remain reciting these five verses; before long, that state will be granted.
These external dharmas have thus been described by me in brief.
Now, the supreme internal dharma for those who have taken refuge is being declared:
having diligently assumed the state of a female friend of Kṛṣṇa’s beloveds, one should perform service to the two of them day and night without weariness. 48–49.

O Nārada, I have thus described the mantra, its constituent parts, the qualified practitioner, his duties, and the fruit resulting from them for the mantra; you too should practice this, and you shall attain service to those two.

There is no doubt whatsoever here regarding the exhaustion of one's own office (svādhikāra). To one who has surrendered even once and entreats, "I am yours," Hari grants His own service; there is no deliberation on this point. 51-52.
In this regard, O best of sages, I shall describe to you this most wonderful secret, which I previously heard directly from the Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa; this internal dharma has now been declared to you.

This most secret of secrets, to be concealed with great effort, is the jewel among mantras; formerly, while reciting it on the summit of Kailāsa and meditating upon the god Nārāyaṇa, I dwelt in a dense forest. 54–55.
Then the Blessed One, being pleased, appeared before me;
when he said, "Choose a boon," I opened my eyes and beheld the Lord seated upon Garuḍa together with his beloved.
Having prostrated, I spoke to the Lord of Kamalā, the bestower of boons:
"O Ocean of Mercy, what is that form of yours which grants supreme bliss, which is the eternal refuge of all joy, embodied, and superior in every respect? (57-58)

"O Supreme Lord, I desire to see with my own eyes that Brahman which the wise know as being devoid of qualities, actionless, and tranquil. Then the Blessed One, the Lord of Kamalā, spoke to me who had sought refuge in him.
"Therefore, you shall see today that form which your mind has long desired.
Go to my Vṛndāvana on the western bank of the Yamunā.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the world vanished along with his beloved.
Then I too arrived at the auspicious bank of the Yamunā,
and there I beheld Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the lords of all gods,
wearing the attire of a cowherd, lovely and endowed with youthful vigor.
With his left hand gracefully resting upon the shoulder of his beloved, he was enchanting;
laughing and causing her to laugh in the midst of the assembly of cowherdesses,
he possessed a luster like a gentle cloud and was a temple of auspicious virtues.
Then Kṛṣṇa, whose speech is nectar, laughed and said to me:
"O Rudra, having known your desire, I have appeared before you. This extraordinary form which you have seen today is mine."

The multitudes of Upaniṣads describe this very one as my sinless refuge: the embodiment of solidified, pure love, existence, consciousness, and bliss; formless, devoid of qualities, all-pervading, free from action, and higher than the highest. (66-67)

Because of the absence of qualities arising from primordial nature (prakṛti), because of my infinity, and because my qualities are not established [in that way], they indeed call me "devoid of qualities" (nirguṇa);
for this form of mine is invisible to the physical eye.
"O Maheśvara, all these Vedas declare me to be formless;
because of my pervasiveness through the aspect of consciousness, the wise know me as Brahman;
and because I am not the agent of the phenomenal world, they indeed call me actionless. (69-70)
"O Śiva, because they perform the acts of creation and so forth through the qualities of my *māyā*, I myself do nothing at all regarding creation and the rest;
O Mahādeva, I am overwhelmed with love for these gopīs."
"I know no other activity, O Nārada, nor even myself;
I sport eternally with her, being completely captivated by her love.
Know this Rādhikā, my beloved, to be the Supreme Deity. (72-73)
O friends, look all around this place by the hundreds and thousands;
all these are eternal, O Rudra, just as I am eternally embodied. The cowherds, the cows, the cowherd women, and Vṛndāvana itself are always mine.
All this is indeed eternal, consisting of the essence of consciousness and bliss.
Know this to be my Vṛndāvana, called the "Root of Bliss" (Ānandakanda), by the mere entry into which one shall not enter into worldly existence again. 75-76.
O God, that fool who, having reached Madavana, goes elsewhere again, would be a destroyer of his own soul; this which I have spoken is the truth, the absolute truth.
I shall never go anywhere else after abandoning Vrindavana.
"I always dwell right here together with her.
Thus has everything that resides in your heart been told, O Rudra;
now tell me, what else do you wish to hear?
Then I said to that god, "O best of sages, how can one such as you be obtained? Tell me the means for that.
Thereupon the Blessed One said to me, "O Rudra, you have spoken well."
This is most secret; it must be guarded with great effort.
O Lord of Gods, he who has once taken refuge in us and worships us, having abandoned all other means, by virtue of the state of being a *gopī*, attains equality with me, and no one else. 81–82.
If one has once taken refuge in me, he undoubtedly attains me alone; or if he serves my beloved alone with single-minded devotion, he likewise attains me—of this there is no doubt.
And he who has taken refuge in me alone, as well as in my beloved, O Maheśvara...
He never attains Me; thus have I declared to you.
Even he who, having surrendered but once, should say, "I am yours," attains Me even without spiritual practice—of this there is no doubt.

Therefore, with every effort, one should go for refuge to those who are dear to me; O Rudra, having taken refuge in me, who am dear to him, you ought to bring him under your control. This supreme secret has been proclaimed by me to you.
O Mahādeva, you too must protect this with great effort.
(87) You also, having taken refuge in this Rādhikā, my beloved, and chanting my couple-mantra, should always remain in my abode. (88)
Śiva said:
Having spoken thus into my right ear, that ocean of compassion for me instructed me in the supreme mantra and performed the purificatory rites. 89
Accompanied by his attendants, O Brahmin, he vanished right there while I was looking on;
from that time forward, I have remained here without interruption.
All of this has been narrated by me to you in its entirety.
"Now, O best of Brahmins, what more do you wish to hear? 91.
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter in the Vṛndāvana-māhātmya of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa in the glorious Padma Purāṇa. 82.
The eighty-third chapter. Nārada said:
O Blessed One, O Guru, everything that was asked by me has been explained.
"Now I wish to hear about the unsurpassed path of bhāva. Śiva said:
"Excellent, O Brahmin! You have asked this out of a desire for the welfare of all the worlds."
I shall also speak of a secret; listen to me as I declare it.
O best of sages, here all the servants, friends, parents, and beloved consorts of Hari dwell eternally, endowed with virtuous qualities. 2–3.
Just as they are celebrated in the Purāṇas in their manifest pastimes,
so too do they exist in their eternal pastimes on the earth in Vṛndāvana; He constantly performs coming and going between the forest and the cowherd settlement.
The tending of the cows with his companions, the destruction of the demons,
and likewise those beloved women who take pride in being his handmaidens—
they delight their own beloved with a hidden affection.
There, in their midst, he should contemplate himself as a charming young woman, endowed with beauty and youth, possessing the form of a maiden,
skilled in various arts and crafts, and suited for the enjoyment of Kṛṣṇa. 7.
There, although she was sought after by Kṛṣṇa, Rādhikā’s attendant— who was averse to worldly enjoyment and solely intent on serving her—
displayed a love for Rādhikā that was even greater than that of Kṛṣṇa himself.

Thinking thus of herself— being one who brings about their union through daily effort with love, and being exceedingly tranquil through the state of bliss arising from the pleasure of serving them— one should perform service to them. 10.
"From the *brāhma-muhūrta* until the great nightfall," Nārada said,
"I wish to hear the daily pastimes of Hari according to their true nature."
"How can Hari be served by one who, through his mind, does not understand His divine play (līlā)?
Śiva said:
"O Nārada, I do not know that play of Hari in its true essence."
Go from here to Vṛndādevī; she will relate her divine play (līlā) to you.
Not far from this place, near the Keśī-tīrtha, she stands surrounded by a multitude of companions as an attendant of Govinda. 13–14.
Sūta said:
Having been addressed thus, Nārada, the best of sages, circumambulated him and, bowing down again and again with joy, then departed for Vṛndāśrama. 15.
Vṛndā, having seen Nārada and bowing down to him again and again, said:
"O best of sages, how have you come here?
Nārada said:
"O beautiful one, if I am worthy, then tell me from the beginning how I may learn of the eternal conduct of Hari.
Vṛndā said:
I shall speak even a secret, O Nārada, for you are a devotee of Kṛṣṇa;
yet this must not be disclosed by you, for it is a great mystery, more secret than the secret.
Within the beautiful Vṛndāvana, adorned with fifty forest groves (kuñjas), [there lies]... 18.
In a house made of divine jewels within a grove of wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa), they lay sleeping on a couch, closely embracing one another;
even when awakened later by birds acting according to my command, [they remained there]. 19–20.
Fearing the interruption of the bliss born from their firm embrace,
they did not even slightly incline their minds toward rising from the bed.
Then, [they were surrounded] on all sides by flocks of sarika birds, parrots, and others, repeatedly—
Awakened by various words, they rose from their bed (verse 22).
Then, seeing them seated upon the bed and filled with joy, their female companions entered and performed for them the service appropriate to that time (verse 23).
Then, by the words of the sārikā bird, they both rose from their beds and departed for their respective homes,
agitated by fear and longing. Then,
in the morning, awakened by his mother, he rose quickly from his bed.
Having used his tooth-stick, which was not black, accompanied by Baladeva and with his mother's permission,
he went to the cow-pen surrounded by his friends.
Rādhā also was awakened from her bed by her Brahmin companions.
Having risen and performed her dental cleansing and other morning rites, she should apply anointing oil.
Then, having gone to the bathing pavilion, she was bathed by her female companions. She would then proceed to the dressing room, where her friends adorned her with ornaments.
With various divine ornaments, perfumes, garlands, and ointments,
Yaśodā then, having diligently entreated her mother-in-law with her circle of female companions, summoned her to prepare a meal for herself along with those friends.
Nārada said:
O Goddess, how was she summoned by Yaśodā for the purpose of cooking, even though there were other cooks present, headed by Rohiṇī? 30
Vṛndā said:
O great sage, I previously heard from the mouth of Kātyāyanī that a boon had been granted to her by Durvāsas in the past. (31)
"O Goddess, whatever food is cooked by you shall, through my grace,
be as sweet as nectar and bestow long life upon the eater. Thus Yaśodā, who was devoted to her son, would daily invite her [to eat].
"If I were to have a long-lived son, then [I shall do so] out of greed for sweetness.
Having heard this, she was delighted and rejoiced; then, accompanied by her circle of friends, she went to her home and prepared the food. 33-34.
Kṛṣṇa, too, having milked some cows himself and having others milked by people,
returned to his own home surrounded by his friends at the command of his father;
and after having an oil massage and a rubbing down performed, he was joyfully bathed by the servants.
Wearing washed garments and adorned with garlands, his body was anointed with sandalwood paste (36).
With hair tied in two tufts at the forehead, it shimmered above his neck and face;
he was graced by a radiant tilaka mark on his forehead that had the form of the moon (37).
With hands radiant with bracelets, armlets, upper-arm ornaments, and jeweled rings, his chest shimmering with a pearl necklace and his ears adorned with makara-shaped earrings,
he would enter the dining hall whenever he was repeatedly summoned by his mother.
Supporting his friend's hand and devotedly following Baladeva, he enjoys various foods surrounded by his brother and friends;
making them laugh with various jokes, he himself laughs along with those companions. 39–40.

Having eaten thus and sipped water accordingly, Kṛṣṇa, wearing the dress of a cowherd and preceded by the herd of cows, rested for a moment upon a celestial couch and distributed and ate the betel-leaf offered by his attendants. 41.
Followed affectionately on the path by all the inhabitants of Vraja,

he should bow to his father and mother, dismiss that assembly with a mere glance from the corner of his eye, and likewise turn back the others as is appropriate, before proceeding to the forest. 42-43.
Having entered the forest and played with his friends for a moment,
he then sported joyfully there in the woods with various diversions.
Then, having left everyone behind, surrounded by only two or three dear friends, [he departed].

Eager to see his beloved, he went to the rendezvous out of joy. She too, seeing that Kṛṣṇa had gone to the forest, returned to her own home and likewise gathered flowers under the pretext of performing worship to the Sun and other deities.
Having deceived their elders out of a desire for union with those they dearly loved,
they then met together in the forest with great effort;
there, they spent the day joyfully sporting in various diversions.

Sometimes mounted upon a swing, he was rocked back and forth by his friends (48). At another time, Hari, searching for his flute which had slipped from his hand and been hidden by his beloved, was scolded by the groups of his beloveds who were teasing him. (49)
Laughing in many ways with loud laughter, he remains there;
somewhere, he joyfully enters a grove of trees fanned by the spring breeze, sprinkled with sandalwood water and waters scented with saffron and other fragrances. 50.
Sprinkling one another with water discharged from syringes and smearing each other with that mud, their friends likewise sprinkled them, and they in turn sprinkled those friends,
everywhere in the forest groves fanned by the breezes of spring.

O twice-born one, O best of sages, having become weary from various diversions appropriate to those respective times, the two of them, accompanied by their attendants, reached the foot of a tree in a certain place and,
sitting upon a divine seat, partook of honey-wine.
Then, intoxicated by honey-wine, their eyes closed in sleep,
they grasped each other’s hands; overcome by the arrows of Kama and desiring to sport, they entered the bower on the path with their speech and minds faltering.
As they were sporting and wandering there like a herd of female elephants with their leader,
even their friends, intoxicated by honey and their eyes heavy with sleep,
all lay down together within the lovely groves.
Although Kṛṣṇa is one, the omnipresent Lord, urged repeatedly by his beloved, would simultaneously go into the presence of all of them with a single body;
and having delighted them all, he was like a lordly elephant among female elephants.
Then, for the sake of sport with his beloved, he went to the lake;
there, accompanied by his attendants, the two of them played with one another, splashing each other with water.
Adorned with divine garments, garlands, sandalwood paste, and ornaments, they remained there.

O Sage, on that very shore of the lake, in a house made of divine jewels, Hari had already prepared fruits and roots; having first eaten them while surrounded by his beloved, he remained there. 60-61.
Served by two or three women, he should go to a bed fashioned of flowers;
there, being attended with betel leaves, fans, and the massaging of his feet and so forth,
he rejoices while laughing and remembering his beloved.
Rādhikā too, her heart filled with joy while Hari slept with his attendants, would go there and eat some of his leftovers; having eaten that, she would then return to the bedchamber. 63–64.
Like a female cakora bird desiring to behold the moon, she longed for the lotus-face of her beloved;
there, the women of that place offered him betel to chew,
and he ate the betels while distributing them among his dear friends.
Kṛṣṇa, desiring to hear their private conversation, appeared as if he had fallen asleep, though he was wide awake and covered by his cloth; they, for their part,
looked at him with a sidelong glance, inferring from some sign that he was there.

Tasting the nectar of their lips with their teeth and gazing at one another’s faces, they were as if submerged in an ocean of shame; for a moment, they said nothing at all. Then, in an instant, they removed the garments from their bodies.
"You have fallen into a sound sleep," they said, laughing as they laughed;
O best of sages, thus, while sporting with those various groups of attendants, he experienced for a moment the bliss of sleep. 69-70.
Seated joyfully upon two expansive, divine thrones, the two hosts played at dice with mutual affection, preceded by playful conversation, while staking necklaces, kisses, embraces, and garments.

Even though he had been defeated, saying "I have been conquered by my beloved," he proceeded to seize her necklace and other ornaments; being struck by her in this manner, Kṛṣṇa seized her lotus-like hand with his own.
Becoming despondent in mind, he set his heart on departing and said, "O Goddess, if I have been defeated by you, let that which was staked be taken;
what I gave you, such as the kisses and so forth, is yours. Having spoken thus, she acted accordingly.
They wished to behold the crookedness of her eyebrows and to hear her threatening words;
then, having heard the mutual cries of the mainas and parrots, they desired to go home and were departing from that place. (75-76)
Having taken leave of his beloved, Kṛṣṇa should proceed toward the cows,
while she, accompanied by a circle of her female friends, should go to the house of the Sun.
Having gone some distance, he should then turn back toward Hari.
Assuming the guise of a Brahmin, he went toward the house of the Sun;
there, at the request of his friends, he worshipped the Sun with Vedic hymns composed on the spot, which were infused with jesting.

Then, O Sage, having understood that beloved command, those wise ones were immersed in an ocean of bliss; they knew neither themselves nor anything else. Thus, with various diversions, two and a half watches of the night passed away.
Having led them home, they would depart, while Kṛṣṇa would go toward the cow-pen;
O Sage, having met his friends and gathered the cows from all sides, Kṛṣṇa would joyfully return to Vraja, sounding his flute.
Then Nanda and all the others, having heard the sound of Hari’s flute and seeing the sky enveloped in a mass of dust from the cows,
abandoned all their activities— including the women, children, and everyone else.
Eager for the sight of him, they went toward Kṛṣṇa at the entrance of the road where all the inhabitants of Vraja were gathered;
Kṛṣṇa also approached them and greeted them one by one in due order. 84-85.

O Nārada, [he honored] his father and Rohiṇī as well with sight and touch, with words preceded by smiles and glances, with prostrations to the elder cowherds, and even with physical and verbal acts of reverence, including falling on the ground in the eight-limbed *praṇāma*.
Thus he honored his beloved with a modesty indicated by the very corners of his eyes (87).
In this manner, having been duly worshipped by those cowherd folk, he entered the cow-pen along with the cows on all sides (88).
Requested by his parents, he goes to his own home with his brother;
having bathed there, drunk some water, and eaten,
he is permitted by his mother to go back to the cow-pen, desiring to milk the cows' milk.
Having milked them, caused them to be milked, and having made some drink [the milk], she goes to the house together with her father; there, she follows hundreds of dispositions along with her father,
her paternal uncles, their sons, and Bala.
While he was enjoying various foods, such as those to be chewed and sucked,
Radhika, whose mind was already longing for him, immediately sent cooked foods to his abode through her female companions.
Praising those [offerings], Hari, having eaten together with his father and others, would go to the assembly hall frequented by them, the bards, and so forth.
Those female friends who had previously arrived there, taking the cooked foods, [departed]. 93–94.
Furthermore, many of those were given by Yaśodā; her friends brought there what had been given as the remnants of Kṛṣṇa’s meal,
and having gathered it all, they presented it to Rādhikā.
She too, having eaten in the company of her circle of friends in due order,
should remain adorned by her companions, intent upon going to meet him;
then, I shall dispatch a certain friend from right here.

Led by her to this house made of divine jewels within a grove of *kalpa* trees near the Yamunā, she was surrounded by her close female companions, dressed in attire suitable for both bright and dark nights. 98.
Then Kṛṣṇa, having witnessed various wonders there and having heard the charming musical performances by Kātyāyanī,
gratified them according to the prescribed rites with wealth, grain, and other gifts.
Having been honored by the people, he went to the home of his very dear friend;
and when his mother had departed, he fed her and then went home. There, he would meet with his beloved at the appointed place, remaining unobserved.
Having joined together, the two of them sported there amidst the rows of forest groves (102),
engaging in various pastimes preceded by dancing, singing, and laughter; thus they spent two and a half watches of the night in such diversion (103).
Desiring to sleep, they entered the bower unobserved by the female birds; there,
upon a charming bed for dalliance fashioned with flowers in a secluded spot, they remained asleep, attended by their own swarms of bees.
Thus, O Nārada, the daily conduct of Hari has been entirely narrated;
even sinners are liberated by hearing this. Nārada said:
"I am blessed and I have been graced by you, O Goddess; of this there is no doubt. Today, the daily pastimes of Hari have been revealed to me.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus and circumambulated him, and having been honored by her as well, O Brahmin, Nārada, the best of sages, vanished from sight;
all of this has been recounted by me in its proper sequence.
One should daily recite with effort this unsurpassed pair of mantras, which was obtained in the past from the mouth of Kṛṣṇa by Rudra through great exertion.
It was spoken by him to Nārada, and by Nārada it was declared to me. 109.
"Having performed these preparatory rites, I have likewise declared this to you.
You too must keep this most wonderful secret hidden.
Śaunaka said:
"O Guru, by your direct grace I have become one who has accomplished his purpose;
for you have revealed to me that which is the secret of all secrets.
Sūta said:

"By adhering to these dharmas and reciting the mantra day and night, you will before long attain that state of servitude; of this there is no doubt. O Brahmin, I too go daily to the abode of the All-pervading Lord. (112-113)
This supreme and most purifying account, which bestows great spiritual merit, was told by Maheśa on the banks of the Yamunā, the river of the Guru’s Guru, and near Gopīśvara.
Those men who listen to it with devotion shall eternally go to the abode of Acyuta.

Those men devoted to Viṣṇu who daily recite this with devotion obtain wealth, fame, long life, health, and the fulfillment of their desires; it is the cause of attaining heaven and liberation, and it destroys all sins. 116.
"For them, there is no return from the world of Viṣṇu by any means whatsoever.
(117) Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Greatness of Vṛndāvana," in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. The Greatness of Vṛndāvana is complete.
The eighty-fourth chapter.
The Sages said:
O Sūta, O highly fortunate son of Romaharṣaṇa!
The discourse you have narrated is delightful and bestows joy upon the world.
We have heard the entire great and most wonderful account of the illustrious Kṛṣṇa as told by you, and we have attained peace through it.
Oh, how great is the majesty of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, which bestows the ultimate goal upon his devotees;
for what fortunate person would not attain liberation through it?
Therefore, once again, the great life-story of the glorious Kṛṣṇa [is told].
We wish to hear further about other matters such as vows, gifts, and worship (4).
O highly fortunate one, tell us in detail everything regarding how and by whom the ritual bath was performed in the past, so that we may attain peace of mind (5).
Sūta said:
O best of the twice-born, you have asked well concerning that supreme means of salvation for the worlds;
you have achieved your purpose, for your minds are filled with devotion to Kṛṣṇa.

O best of the twice-born, I shall proclaim the meritorious and supreme account of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s deeds, a great and excellent narrative that brings the highest joy to the virtuous. Once, Nārada, the beloved of the Lord, was wandering through the worlds.

In Mathurā, the best of sages saw the highly fortunate Ambarīṣa, who was devoted to the worship of Kṛṣṇa and intent upon his vows. Having honored that excellent sage who had arrived, the best of sages [spoke].
With a joyful mind, His Holiness himself questioned him with faith.
Ambarīṣa said:
"O Sage, that which is called the Supreme Brahman by those who proclaim the Vedas—" (10)
How can that Hari be meditated upon—he who is with the gods, the lotus-eyed, Nārāyaṇa himself, the Supreme;
who is formless yet possesses form, the Lord, unmanifest yet manifest, eternal, consisting of all beings, and inconceivable? 11.
In which this entire universe is woven across and lengthwise, firmly established;

that which is unmanifest, one, supreme, and renowned as the Supreme Self (Paramātman); from which the birth and so forth of the world proceed, the self-existent source of illusion—[that is Brahman]. 12–13.
He grants the Vedas which are established within the Self itself;
how can that Lord, the bestower of all human goals, be propitiated?
He is difficult to reach even for yogis; therefore, speak of this out of compassion.
One who has not propitiated Govinda does not know the arising of true welfare.
(15) He who has not tasted the nectar of the lotus feet of Govinda does not obtain the supreme fruit of penance, sacrifice, or charity. (16)
One cannot conceive of a fruit more abundant than that which transcends the path of one's desires,
yet which surpasses the propitiation of Hari— the dispeller of the flood of sins. O Sage, I see no other supreme atonement for living beings.
Since all supernatural powers (siddhis) are heard to abide within the dancing of his eyebrows, how is that Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, to be propitiated?
How is that Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa to be worshipped by men? (18-19)

O Maitreya, tell me all this with joy; for that Blessed Lord is fond of devotion—by what kind of devotion does He become pleased? (20) How may devotion toward Him arise, and how is He worshipped by all?
"You are a Vaiṣṇava, you are dear to that Hari, and you are a knower of the supreme truth.
Therefore, O Brāhmaṇa, best among the knowers of Brahman, I ask you about that person of Hari who is both the listener and the speaker, as well as the questioner. (21-22)
A question: Just as the water from Kṛṣṇa’s feet purifies, so too is this human body—fleeting as a moment—difficult for embodied beings to obtain;
In this cycle of existence, even half a moment spent in the company of the virtuous is a treasure for human beings.
For from that, all four aims of human life are obtained.
O Blessed One, may your journey be auspicious for all embodied beings.
Just as the conduct of the gods brings both suffering and happiness to living beings who follow the path of their parents, O Child of Illustrious Fame,
the conduct of the virtuous— such as yourself, whose souls are fixed on Acyuta— brings only happiness.
Just as the gods worship those [who serve them], so too do they worship those [who worship the gods].
Like shadows, the virtuous who are compassionate toward the distressed are companions in one's actions;
therefore, O Blessed One, instruct me in the Vaiṣṇava dharma.
"By giving instruction on this, one obtains the fruit born of the Vedas.
Nārada said: "O protector of the earth, you who possess devotion to Viṣṇu have asked well. (29)
Knowing that the supreme dharma is the singular service of Mādhava—
in whom, when propitiated, Viṣṇu is propitiated, and when Hari, who embodies all the gods, is satisfied, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings is satisfied— 30.

By the mere remembrance of whom the collection of great sins perishes in that very instant—he alone, Hari, is to be served. O King, who among those possessed of senses would not worship the lotus feet of Mukunda? 31-32.
