Death does not come from all sides to one who honors, reveres, recites, studies, meditates upon, respects, and rejoices in the True Dharma—which, when heard, chanted, and contemplated by seers and deities, immediately purifies even those who have done harm to the entire world. 33. The Heroic True Dharma indeed purifies instantly.
He who is this cause of causes and effects, the cause even of the cause; the yogi who has no other cause, the life-force of the world, identical with the world;
minute, vast, lean, and gross; devoid of qualities yet the bearer of qualities; the Great One. (34-35)
Hari, who is beyond birth and dissolution, should always be meditated upon;
O bull among men, you have rightly resolved this matter by inquiring about the Bhāgavata duties that sustain the universe.

Incidentally, for the virtuous, the pure stories of Kṛṣṇa—who is worthy of being glorified—become an elixir for the ears, mind, and soul (37). For this Lord is to be realized through devotion; indeed, Your Majesty knows this yourself (38).
Nevertheless, for the welfare of the world and out of respect for you, I shall speak:
that which they call the Supreme Brahman, beyond Pradhāna and Puruṣa;
by whose Māyā all this is pervaded, and who bestows everything—that is Acyuta. 39.
The Unconquered One (Ajita), when worshipped with devotion, bestows sons, a wife, long life, sovereignty, heaven, and liberation— indeed, everything desired—
upon those men who are intent upon him through action, mind, and speech. 40-41.
O best of kings, for your pleasure I shall describe their vows:
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and freedom from desire;
these are said to be the mental vows for the satisfaction of Hari. 42.
Eating once a day, eating at night, fasting, and eating only what is unasked for—
O Lord of Men, thus has the physical vow of men been described.
Furthermore, the study of the Veda, the chanting of Viṣṇu’s names, and the speaking of truth [constitute the mental vow].
O King, this absence of backbiting is the supreme vow regarding speech:
one should always and everywhere proclaim the names of the wielder of the discus weapon (Viṣṇu). There is no impurity in chanting His name, for by doing so, one's hands become purified.
By a person who follows the conduct of their caste and stage of life, the Supreme Person, Viṣṇu, is propitiated; there is no other path that causes such satisfaction.
And by women who are devoted to the pleasure and welfare of their husbands, through the restraint of mind, speech, and body, [He is likewise propitiated].
Vāsudeva, the ocean of the rising moon, is propitiated by women through vows;
even by women and śūdras, worship must be performed for Kṛṣṇacandra, who possesses the most excellent form of a twice-born, according to the path taught in the Āgamas. 48.

The three castes, however, should be intent on propitiating [the Lord] through the path prescribed in the Vedas (49). Women and Śūdras, on the other hand, should be intent on propitiating Him by means of His Name alone; Mādhava is not [attained] through ritual worship, nor through sacrifices, nor even through vows (50).

He is said to be pleased solely by devotion; he is proclaimed as one who loves devotion. Indeed, for women who are devoted to their husbands, the husband alone is the deity. He, moreover, is to be worshipped with devotion to Viṣṇu through the actions of mind, speech, and body.

Having meditated upon Viṣṇu as their husband within their hearts, they should perform their duties with faith; for Śūdras, the worship of the deity is by means of His name alone. All should perform it according to the path of the Āgamas, which follows the pattern of the Vedas.
Women also have the right to perform the worship of Viṣṇu and other rites, provided they are devoted to pleasing their husbands; this is the eternal Vedic injunction.
(54) Whatever vow has been prescribed for anyone according to the dharma appropriate to their own family—
One should perform whatever action by which Keśava is pleased; the wise constantly worship Hari with oblations in the fire, with water, with flowers, and through meditation in the heart,
while others worship him in the solar orb through silent recitation.
Non-violence is the first flower; the second is the restraint of the organs; the third is compassion for all beings, and the fourth is indeed forbearance.
Tranquility is the fifth flower, and self-control is the sixth and seventh.
Meditation, truth, and the eighth, [namely, non-violence]—by these Keśava is pleased.
O best of men, Hari is indeed satisfied when worshipped with these eight flowers alone; there are other external flowers as well.
Viṣṇu is thoroughly pleased by those who have performed worship with devotion; water belongs to Varuṇa, flowers to Soma, ghee,
milk, and curd to Prajāpati, while incense and lamps belong to Agni.
Fruits, flowers, and so forth constitute the fifth, namely the *vānaspatya* offering.
That which consists of *kuśa* grass, roots, and the like is called *pārthiva*; fragrant sandalwood is *vāyavya*.
The flower known as faith (*śraddhā*) is *vaiṣṇava*, and it is remembered as the station of Viṣṇu (*viṣṇupada*).
Viṣṇu is indeed pleased even when worshipped with these flowers:
the sun, fire, a brāhmaṇa, cows, a Vaiṣṇava, the sky, the wind, water, the earth, the self, and all living beings— these are the places of worship for Hari.
Then, one should worship with the recitation of the Sūryya-mantra and with oblations in the fire (64).
One should worship through hospitality toward the foremost of Brahmins, by providing mouthfuls of food and liquids to cows,
by honoring kinsmen as Vaiṣṇavas, and by steadfastness in meditation within the heart (65).

With the understanding that air is the primary element, one should worship the pervasive Lord— the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña)— within oneself by means of water preceded by wine, upon the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) with mantras and heart-essences, and through enjoyments, while regarding him with equanimity in all beings. 66.
In these sacred seats (dhiṣṇyas), one should worship with a concentrated mind, meditating upon that peaceful form endowed with four arms and bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
by worshipping [the Brahmins], He is undoubtedly worshipped. 67–68.
When these four [scriptures] are censured, the Lord censures even the king;
for when they are established, they uphold the Vedas and the Dharmaśāstras.
Those Brahmins are indeed considered the supreme, purifying form of Viṣṇu. 69–70.
Everything auspicious in the world is obtained through the very nature of dharma; O King, the path to dharma is found in the Vedas and the Dharmaśāstras.
Indeed, the path to those two as well is the Brahmins on earth; when they are honored here, the Lord of the World is honored.
Not by sacrifices or yogic practices, nor by other austerities, nor by the application of yoga, nor by worship.
The God of gods is so pleased by the propitiation of the deities of the earth that he is not otherwise so satisfied.

Brahmā—the friend of the Brahmins, the knower of Brahman, the creator of the Veda, and the promulgator of the Vedas—is pleased only by the Brahmins; when the Brahmins are gratified, the deity Brahman is gratified.
Even those ancestors who have long been submerged in hell go to heaven at that very moment when a son worships Hari;
what is the use of their life here, lived like that of a beast? 74.
For those whose minds are not inclined toward Vāsudeva, who pervades the universe—
I shall declare that meditation which has never been seen by anyone;
O King, listen to this absolute liberation, which is entirely free from impurity.
Just as a lamp standing in a windless place, motionless and free from air,
burning brightly, O Mahāmati, would dispel all darkness;
even so, the Self, when freed from defects, becomes truly free from affliction.
Free from hope, the hero remains motionless; likewise, he has neither friend nor enemy.
He is liberated from sorrow, joy, dejection, greed, envy, and delusion, as well as from agitation, idle chatter, infatuation, and pleasure and pain.
When one is liberated from all sense objects and the senses as well,
then one becomes a possessor of absolute knowledge (kevalajñānī), and the state of isolation (kaivalya) arises. Just as a lamp, through the process of its flame, dries up the oil.
O Indra among kings, supported by the wick, free from duality and devoid of wind, it subsequently emits soot even from the oil, O great-minded one;
a black line is seen before the lamp, O great-minded one. 81–82.
Just as that oil, having been drawn out by itself, becomes stainless through its own brilliance,
so too does [the Self], abiding within the body, dry up the oil of karma.
Having turned the objects of the senses into lampblack, it reveals them directly before one's eyes.
Having become stainless like a flame, it shall shine by itself (84).
Freed from the winds known as anger, greed, and the rest,
and having become desireless and motionless, its own radiance shall blaze forth (85).
Remaining in his own place, he beholds the entire three worlds by his own splendor;
he who is of the nature of absolute knowledge (kevalajñāna) has thus been described to you.
Now I shall explain the two kinds of meditation belonging to that wielder of the wheel.
He is perceived by the eyes of others in the form of absolute knowledge (kevalajñāna).
Great-souled ones, disciplined in yoga and devoted to the supreme reality, behold Him; but the deluded do not see Him, the omniscient one who perceives all things. 87–88.
Though devoid of hands and feet, he moves everywhere and grasps everything—the three worlds, both the stationary and the moving—O King; and though devoid of nose and mouth, he smells and eats. 89.
Though earless, he hears everything; he is the witness of all, the Lord of the universe.
Though formless, he is connected with forms; though subject to the fivefold group [of senses], he is the life-breath of all the world, worshipped by all that is moving and unmoving. 90–91.
Though tongueless, he speaks everything in accordance with the Vedas and Shastras; though skinless, he perceives the touch of all beings.
Ever blissful, with senses withdrawn, he is of a single form and independent of external support.
He is devoid of qualities, free from the sense of "mine," all-pervading, possessed of qualities, stainless, and sinless.
He is independent, yet the self that brings all under control; he is the giver of everything and the supreme knower of all.
He has no mother, nor indeed does he have a father; he is everything, consisting of all, and all-pervasive.
He who, with undistracted mind, perceives this meditation which consists of all things, goes to the supreme abode, which is formless and like unto the immortal.
(95) Now I shall proclaim the second; listen to it, O you of great intelligence.
He who possesses form yet is formless, who is without blemish,
and by whose latent impression (vāsanā) this entire incomparable universe is permeated— he, O prince, is therefore called Vāsudeva. 96–97.
From the radiance of that raining cloud, there appeared the Lord of the Gods with four arms, resembling the splendor of the sun;
on his right side shone a conch shell adorned with gold and jewels. 98.
The Kaumodakī mace, the destroyer of great asuras, shines in the left hand of that heroic, high-souled one;
and in his right hand is a great lotus, rich with fragrance. 99–100.
He remains eternally resplendent, bearing weapons and possessing the beauty of a lotus;
with a neck like a conch, a well-rounded face, and eyes resembling lotus petals,
Hṛṣīkeśa shines forth with teeth as white as jasmine buds.
He whose lower lip is like coral—the lotus-eyed Guḍākeśa—shines with his radiant crown;
Keśava, moreover, possesses a broad chest and a truly beautiful form. 102-103.
Janārdana shines with the Kaustubha gem as his very mark, and he glows with two earrings that resemble the brilliance of the sun;
Hari always radiates splendor with the auspicious Śrīvatsa mark. 104.
Vijaya, the best among victors, shone with his body adorned with armlets, bracelets, and pearl necklaces resembling stars;
Govinda, too, shone with a garment of golden hue. 105–106.
Hari shines upon his fingers with various mudrās, fully endowed with all divine weapons and celestial ornaments;
mounted upon Vainateya, he is the creator of the worlds and the Lord of the universe. 107.

The man who thus meditates constantly with a one-pointed mind is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. Thus, O Lord of the World, this entire classification of meditation upon the Lord has been recounted to you.

Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Meditation upon the Blessed Lord," in the Vaiśākha-māsa-māhātmya of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Nārada and Ambarīṣa.
The Sages said:
O Sūta, O highly fortunate son of Romaharṣaṇa, a delightful story that bestows joy upon the world has been narrated by you.
O illustrious one, the life-story of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is truly great and wonderful.
You have heard everything that was spoken, and by that you have attained peace.
Oh, how great is the majesty of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who grants the ultimate goal to his devotees;
for what fortunate person would not attain peace through him?
Therefore, once again, we wish to hear the great life-story of the illustrious Kṛṣṇa, as well as other matters such as vows, gifts, and worship (4),
or even the bath, O fortunate one, and how it was performed by whom in the past.
"Tell all of that in detail, so that we may attain peace.
Sūta said:
"O best of the twice-born, you have asked well; this is the supreme means for the salvation of the worlds."
You have achieved your purpose, your minds being fully satisfied by devotion to Kṛṣṇa.
O best of the twice-born, I shall proclaim the meritorious life-story of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, which brings supreme joy to the virtuous— the great and most excellent narrative.
Once, while wandering through the worlds, Nārada,
the beloved of the Lord and best of sages, beheld the highly fortunate Ambarīṣa in Mathurā, who was devoted to the worship of Kṛṣṇa and intent upon his vows.
Having honored the best of sages who had arrived, that most excellent of sages,
with a joyful heart and faith, questioned him just as Bhagavān had done.
Ambarīṣa said:
O Sage, that which is called the Supreme Brahman by those who proclaim the Vedas—
that God is the lotus-eyed one himself, the supreme Nārāyaṇa; he who is formless yet possesses form, the Lord, manifest and unmanifest, eternal.
How is that Hari to be meditated upon—he who consists of all beings, who is inconceivable, and in whom this entire universe is woven like warp and woof and established?
He is the one unmanifest, supreme, and renowned as the Supreme Self (Paramātman). 12.12–13a.
Since He, having brought forth the world from its very origin, bestowed upon the Self-born (Brahmā) the Vedas which reside within His own self—
how is that Lord, the bestower of all human goals, to be propitiated?
Tell me this out of compassion, for it is difficult even for yogis to comprehend; those who have not worshipped Govinda do not know the source of true welfare.
One does not obtain the supreme fruit of austerities, sacrifices, or gifts [without him]. 15.
And he who has not tasted the nectar of the lotus feet of Govinda will not perceive the abundant fruit that transcends the path of desire,
having abandoned the worship of Hari, which wards off the flood of misfortunes. 16–17.
"O Sage, I see no other supreme expiation for living beings than that by which all supernatural powers (siddhis) are heard to be attained, even while moving within the dance of the eyebrows.
How is this Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, to be propitiated?"
How is that Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa worshipped by men?
Tell me all this for my benefit; how does that Blessed One, who is fond of devotion, become pleased through what kind of devotion? (19–20)
How may devotion toward him arise? How indeed is he worshipped by all?
You are a Vaiṣṇava, you are dear to Hari, and you are a knower of the supreme truth.
Therefore, O Brahmin, best among the knowers of Brahman, I ask you this very thing.
The question concerning Hari purifies the listener, the speaker, and the person who asks,
just as the water from His feet purifies;
yet a human body, fragile and momentary, is difficult for embodied beings to obtain.
Even there, I consider the sight of Vaikuṇṭha to be difficult to obtain;
in this cycle of worldly existence, even half a moment of association with the virtuous is a treasure for men,
from which all four goals of human life are attained.
O Blessed One, your journey is for the well-being of all embodied beings; yet, just as the conduct of parents is for the benefit of children who follow the path of the Illustrious One,
so too the conduct of the gods brings both suffering and happiness to living beings.

For indeed, for the sake of the happiness of virtuous ones like you, whose souls are fixed on Acyuta, the gods likewise honor those who worship them; for such virtuous ones, compassionate toward the distressed, follow one’s actions like a shadow.
Therefore, O Blessed One, instruct me in the Vaiṣṇava dharma,
by the imparting of which one obtains the fruit born of the Vedas.
Nārada said:
Well asked, O protector of the earth, by you who possess devotion to Viṣṇu (29)!
You know the supreme dharma, which is the singular service of Mādhava; when Viṣṇu is propitiated in this way, the entire universe becomes propitiated (30).
When Hari, who embodies all the gods, is pleased, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings is pleased;
by the mere remembrance of him, the mass of great sins perishes in that very instant. Therefore, Hari alone is indeed to be served. 31.
O King, what person possessed of sense-organs would not worship the lotus feet of Mukunda, which are to be meditated upon by sages and deities from all sides,
and which have been heard, recited, contemplated, honored, and approved?
The Heroic True Dharma instantly purifies even those who have committed every offense;
for that which is the cause of causes and effects, the non-dual cause, the yogi, the life-force of the world, and the essence of the world—[that is the True Dharma]. 34.
He is minute, vast, subtle, and gross; devoid of qualities yet the bearer of qualities; the Great One.
He is unborn, beyond birth and dissolution—that Hari should always be meditated upon.
O bull among men, this has been correctly resolved by you. 35–36.
Since you ask about the Bhāgavata dharmas that sustain the universe— dharmas which, through association with the virtuous, are an elixir for the ears and minds of the self-realized—
the stories of Kṛṣṇa, who is worthy of being glorified, become pure. (37)
"O Lord, this God is indeed to be accomplished through devotion; Your Majesty knows this yourself.
Nevertheless, out of respect for you and for the welfare of the world, I shall speak.
That which they call the Supreme Brahman, beyond both Pradhāna and Puruṣa," (38-39)

He by whose māyā all is pervaded, and who bestows everything—that Acyuta, when worshipped with devotion, grants sons, a wife, long life, sovereignty, heaven, and liberation; that unconquerable one shall grant every desired object. 40.
O best of kings, for the pleasure of those men who are devoted to that [practice] through deed, mind, and speech, I shall describe their vows:
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and freedom from desire. 41–42.
"These mental vows are said to be for the pleasure of Hari:
eating once a day, eating only at night, fasting, and eating only what is unasked.
Thus, O Lord of Men, has the bodily vow of men been described.
The study of the Veda, the chanting of Viṣṇu’s names, speaking the truth, and refraining from slander— O King, this is the supreme vow regarding speech.
One should always and everywhere chant the names of the one whose weapon is the discus.
There is no impurity regarding the chanting of his name, for he is the purifier of hands;
by a person who follows the conduct of their caste and stage of life, the Supreme Person Viṣṇu is propitiated— there is no other path that causes such satisfaction.
Vāsudeva, the ocean of compassion, is propitiated by women through vows consisting of restraints of mind, speech, and body that are pleasing and beneficial;
likewise, worship may be performed even by women and śūdras according to the path declared in the Āgamas. 47–48.
The three castes, being intent on following the path prescribed by the Vedas, must perform the service of Kṛṣṇacandra, who has assumed the form of the most excellent among the twice-born;
whereas women, Śūdras, and others should be intent on worshipping him by means of his Name alone. 49.
Mādhava is not pleased by worship, nor by sacrifices, nor even by vows;
he is declared to be one who loves devotion alone.
For women who are devoted to their husbands, the husband indeed is their deity.
He, however, is to be honored through devotion to Viṣṇu by means of mind, speech, body, and action;
having meditated upon Viṣṇu with faith while keeping him as the Lord within the heart, the worship of the deity for Śūdras indeed occurs through His name alone. 52.
All should perform [these rites] according to the path of the scriptures that follow the Vedas.
Women also have the right to perform the worship of Viṣṇu and other such acts, provided they are devoted to pleasing their husbands; this is the eternal Vedic injunction.
Whatever vow has been prescribed for each person according to the dharma appropriate to his own family, he should perform that very thing; for by that alone Keśava is pleased.
One may worship Hari with oblations in the fire, with water, with flowers, or with meditation in the heart.
The wise constantly worship within the solar orb through silent recitation (japa).
Non-violence is the first flower, the restraint of the senses is the second, compassion for all beings is the third, and forgiveness is indeed the fourth.
Peace is the fifth flower, self-restraint the sixth, and meditation the seventh; truth is indeed the eighth, for by these Keśava is pleased.
Worshipped with these very eight flowers, Hari is truly satisfied.
O best of men, there are indeed other external flowers by which Viṣṇu, when worshipped with devotion, is thoroughly pleased:
water from the ocean, flowers, Soma-juice, ghee, milk, and curd. (59–60)
Food and the like belong to Prajāpati; incense and lamps belong to Agni;
fruits, flowers, and so forth are the fifth, belonging to Vanaspati; items such as *kuśa* grass and roots belong to Pṛthivī; and perfume and sandalwood belong to Vāyu. (61)
Faith is known as the flower of Viṣṇu, and music is remembered as the station of Viṣṇu.
When worshipped with these flowers, even Viṣṇu becomes pleased.
The sun, fire, brāhmaṇas, cows, a Vaiṣṇava, the sky, the wind, and water—[these are the objects of worship].
The self is the earth and all beings are the objects of worship for Hari;

thereafter, one should worship Him in the sun through the recitation of mantras, in the fire with oblations, in the foremost of Brahmins with hospitality, and in cows with mouthfuls of fodder and the like. 64.
In the Vaiṣṇava [element], one worships through honoring kinsmen; in the heart, through steadfastness in meditation (65);
in the wind, with the thought of its primacy; in water, with substances preceded by water; on the sacrificial mound, with the essence of mantras; and within the self, through enjoyments. (66)
One should worship the all-pervading Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) with equanimity within all beings;
meditating with a concentrated mind upon that form as endowed with four arms, peaceful, and bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus within these abodes, one should perform worship.
When the Brahmins are honored, he too is undoubtedly honored;
when they are reviled, O King, the Lord is likewise reviled.
For upon them as their foundation rest both the Vedas and the treatises on Dharma. (68–69)

O King, those Brahmins are indeed considered the supreme, purifying form of Viṣṇu. All that is auspicious in the world is obtainable through dharma alone; dharma is understood from the Vedas and the Dharmaśāstras.
Indeed, on this earth, the very path to both of these is the Brahmins; when they are honored here, the Lord of the Universe is honored.

The Lord of Gods does not become so pleased by sacrifices, nor by other austerities, nor by the application of yoga, nor by ritual worship, as He is by pleasing the deity of the earth (the Brahmins). He is the friend of the Brahmins, the knower of Brahman, Brahmā himself, and the promulgator of the Veda of Brahman.
One should be satisfied with the Brahmins alone; when they are satisfied, the deity Brahmā is satisfied.
Even those ancestors who have long been submerged in hell in both lineages go to heaven at that very moment when a son worships Hari. 73–74.
Of what use is life for those whose minds are not inclined toward Vāsudeva, who pervades the universe, and what is the use of their animal-like behavior here?
I shall now describe his meditation, which has never been seen by anyone.
Listen, O King, to the state of absolute liberation, which is solitary and free from all impurity.
Just as a lamp standing in a windless place, steady and devoid of air, burns brightly and destroys all darkness, O high-minded one. (76–77)
In the same way, the self, freed from defects, becomes truly free from affliction—hopeless, immovable, a hero, neither friend nor foe;
likewise, it is devoid of sorrow, joy, despondency, greed, envy, and delusion. (78)
He is liberated from agitation, speech, delusion, and from pleasure and pain;
he is also released from all objects of the senses.
Then, becoming possessed of absolute knowledge (*kevalajñāna*), he attains the state of isolation (*kaivalya*). 79–80.
O King of kings, through the process of its flaming activity, the lamp dries up the oil by means of the wick as its support— being free from duality and sheltered from the wind;
thereafter, O Great-minded One, it emits soot even from the oil.
O Great-minded One, a black line is seen at the tip of a lamp;
having drawn up that oil by itself through its own radiance, it becomes pure.
In the same way, [the light] situated within the body dries up the oil of karma.
Having turned the objects of the senses into collyrium, he should display them directly;
becoming pure like a flame, he shall manifest himself by his own power. (84) He is entirely devoid of the winds known as anger, greed, and the rest.
Becoming free from desire and unwavering, one's own splendor shall blaze forth spontaneously.
Standing in one's own place, one beholds the entire three worlds by means of that splendor; this is what I have described to you as the nature of absolute knowledge (kevalajñāna). 85–86.
I shall now describe the two-fold meditation of that Wielder of the Wheel (Cakrin),
which is perceived by the eye of another through the form of absolute knowledge (kevalajñāna).
The great-souled ones, disciplined in yoga, are devoted to the supreme reality.

But the deluded do not see him who is all-knowing and all-seeing. (88) Though devoid of hands and feet, he moves everywhere; moreover, he grasps the entire triple world, both the stationary and the moving. (89)
O King, though devoid of nose and mouth, he smells and eats;
though without ears, he hears everything—the Lord of the Universe who is the witness of all.
Though formless, he is connected with forms and has come under the sway of the fivefold group [of senses]. 90.
He who is the life-breath of the entire world is worshipped by all things, both moving and unmoving.
Though tongueless, he speaks everything in accordance with the Vedas and the Shastras; though skinless, he perceives the touch of all beings. 91–92.
Ever-blissful, with senses withdrawn, of a single form, and without support;

devoid of qualities, free from the sense of "mine," all-pervading; possessing qualities yet stainless and sinless; independent, yet the self that brings all under control; the giver of everything, and the supreme knower of all. (93)
He has no mother, for he is indeed the all-pervading Lord who consists of everything.
He who, with undistracted mind, perceives such meditation consisting of all things, goes to the supreme station, which is formless and like unto the immortal.
But I shall now declare the second; listen to it, O Mahāmati: it has a formal appearance yet is with form, and it is formless and free from affliction (nirāmaya).
It is the incomparable cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) which is permeated by its latent impression (vāsanā). 96.
Therefore, O prince, he is called Vāsudeva;
for when it rains, the light of that [cloud] becomes like the splendor of the sun, and he is the four-armed Lord of the Gods. 97–98.
On the right, a conch shell adorned with gold and jewels shines;
his mace, Kaumodakī, is the destroyer of great asuras.
And on the left, O hero, it shines in the hand of that Great-Souled One. 99.
A great lotus, rich in fragrance, was always held in his right hand;
it shone constantly, endowed with its stalk and possessing the beauty of a lotus.
He had a neck like a conch shell, a well-rounded face, and eyes resembling lotus petals. 100–101.
Hṛṣīkeśa shines with teeth resembling kunda flowers, and the lip of Guḍākeśa, which has the appearance of coral, is resplendent; thus the lotus-eyed one is beautiful even with his radiant crown. 102.
Janārdana Keśava, however, shone with his broad and well-formed chest marked by the Kaustubha gem;
he also gleamed with two earrings that resembled the splendor of the sun. 103–104.
Hari shone with armlets, bracelets, and pearl necklaces resembling stars;
and Vijaya, the best among victors, also shone with a body resplendent in a golden-colored garment—Goviṃda himself. 105–106.
Adorned with the appropriate finger-rings, Hari shines upon his fingers, which are fully equipped with all divine weapons and ornaments;
mounted upon Vainateya, he is the creator of the worlds and the Lord of the universe. 107.

Thus, the man who meditates constantly with an undistracted mind is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. All this, the various types of meditation on the Lord of the World, has been recounted to you.

Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Meditation on the Lord," in the Vaiśākha-māsa-māhātmya of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Nārada and Ambarīṣa.
Chapter Eighty-Five. Ambarīṣa said:
"Excellent, excellent, O best of sages, you who bestow grace upon the world!
You have described the meditation on Viṣṇu, both with attributes and without attributes. Now, O compassionate one, tell us the characteristics of devotion."
"In whatever manner, by whom, how, where, and when it is performed.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of the best of kings, the sage was delighted and spoke to the monarch.
Listen, O King, I shall properly proclaim to you that devotion to Hari which removes all sins.
Now I shall explain the various forms of devotion that destroy evil; devotion is said to be of many kinds, arising from mind, speech, and body.
That which is worldly, Vedic, and likewise spiritual—
the recollection of the names through meditation, concentration, and the intellect—
is indeed called mental devotion (mānasī-bhakti), which brings pleasure to Viṣṇu. 5.

Vocal devotion is said to consist of the uninterrupted recitation of mantras and the Vedas, constant contemplation, and the chanting of *jāpyas* and *āraṇyakas*. It also includes vows, fasts, observances, and the conquest of the five senses.
Devotion directed toward the physical form is taught as the means for accomplishing all goals,
through ornaments marked with gold and gems, and likewise through various words,
garments, amulets, threads, and the raising of fire-fans.
Whatever worship is performed by men with dance, instrumental music, song, and all kinds of offerings, as well as with various foods, edibles, meals, and drinks,
directed toward Nārāyaṇa— that is considered worldly devotion (laukikī bhakti). 9–10.
Devotion directed toward the body is declared to be the accomplisher of all goals;
when the recitations of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as the study of the Saṃhitās,
are performed with Viṣṇu as the objective, that is called Vedic devotion.
The medical procedure is considered to consist of Vedic mantras, oblations, and sacrifices (12).
On the new moon and the full moon days, the Agnihotra rite must be performed,
as well as the ritual of consuming [the remnants], the giving of sacrificial fees, and the preparation of the *puroḍāśa* cake and the *caru* oblation (13).
Sacrifices, fortitude, the drinking of soma, and all sacrificial rites performed in every way—
whether directed toward Agni, Earth, Wind, Space, the Sun, Śaṅkara, or Bhāskara—
all such actions have Viṣṇu as their presiding deity.
O King, there are various kinds of internal devotion to Brahman; listen now, O ruler, as it has been declared, to that which is known as Sāṃkhya and born of Yoga.
By enumeration, there are twenty-four principles beginning with Pradhāna.
The twenty-fifth principle, Puruṣa, is conscious; he is declared to be the enjoyer of these insentient objects. He is the agent and the experiencer of actions.
The Self is eternal and immutable, the presiding controller and the impeller.

The Puruṣa is unmanifest and eternal, and Maheśvara is the cause. In truth, there is the creation of the principles (tattva-sarga), the creation of states (bhāva-sarga), and the creation of the elements (bhūta-sarga). Through enumeration and thorough calculation, Pradhāna consists of the qualities (guṇas). 18–19.
Having understood the similarity and dissimilarity, as well as the primary nature and the contrary nature,
this is called the causality of Brahman;
the state of being directed [by another] is said to be the dissimilarity of Pradhāna.

The universal agency of the Puruṣa as Brahman, and yet his lack of agency—this is said to be his similarity to the insentient Pradhāna; furthermore, it is a distinct principle among the principles, being indeed both cause and effect. 21–22.

Having understood the purpose and the state of being employed through the enumeration of the principles (tattva-prasaṃkhyā), he is called "one who has completed the enumeration" by the wise who contemplate for the sake of victory.
Thinking thus, one should understand its true existence, its reality, and its enumeration according to the truth.
The wise know that the reality of the elements (bhūtatattva) is even superior to the reality of Brahman.
This devotion established by the Sāṃkhyas is remembered as spiritual devotion (ādhyātmikī bhakti). O King, listen now to the devotion born of Yoga (yogajā), which I shall describe to you. 24-25.
Constantly devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma), possessed of meditation, with senses restrained, subsisting on alms according to his vow, and having withdrawn all his senses,
he should perform mental concentration (dhāraṇā) in the heart while meditating upon Maheśvara. 26.
Seated upon the pericarp of the heart-lotus, wearing yellow garments and possessing beautiful eyes (27),
beholding his face illuminated, with the sacred thread reaching down to his hips,
white in complexion, four-armed, and with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness (28).
The perfection of the mental faculty born of yoga is remembered as supreme devotion to Viṣṇu;
he who possesses such devotion is called a devotee of Viṣṇu.
Thus, O prince, various kinds of devotion have been described.
These [energies] of Viṣṇu, who possesses immeasurable splendor, are to be understood as being of various kinds— namely, sāttvikī, rājasī, and tāmasī— according to their distinctions.
Just as a fire with well-kindled flames reduces fuel to ashes, so too does he act.
Devotion to the Lord burns away sins at that very moment (32).
As long as a person on earth does not hear of devotion to Viṣṇu— which is manifest nectar, the singular essence of all flavors—
for so long do they experience the sufferings arising from hundreds of births, deaths, and old age, produced by many bodies (33).

The Lord Ananta, whose fame is celebrated and contemplated within, and whose majesty has been heard, destroys sin on all sides— just as the wind disperses a cloud or the sun dispels darkness— not merely by chanting his names,
but through the practice of giving, worshiping the gods, bathing at sacred fords, hearing the scriptures, proper conduct, and the performance of austerities. 34.
In such a way does the inner self attain purity as it does when the infinite Lord resides within the heart.

(35) O King, those very stories of the Lord are pure and true; they are wholesome and true when the holy name of Hari is proclaimed therein, and when the virtuous fame of that one of sacred form is heard and listened to. (36)

O bearer of the steady earth, you are blessed, O leader of the Dharma, whose heart is one-pointed in meditation; for this supreme devotion of yours toward the Supreme Person is the very glory of your auspicious fortune, brought about by the merit of hearing the name of Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
(37) Without having propitiated Hari through devotion—the immutable Viṣṇu who grants boons—[how could such a thing be possible?]

Whence could there be any higher good for a man of the king who considers himself [the master]? O King, this person is born of illusion, yet he is not illusory; that virtuous man is accomplished through non-illusory devotion—this you yourself know. 38–39.

"O King, this reality of Dharma was not known by me; yet you have asked me about this stainless truth regarding the Lord whose feet are the source of all sacred fords, out of a sense of devotion to Viṣṇu and the pleasure of this discourse.
I see no greater merit than this, which nourishes a special satisfaction and is mutually appropriate."
The virtuous, by virtue of their superior disposition, forcibly enjoy those who possess infinite qualities and are repositories of endless welfare;
for Brāhmaṇas are the very limbs of Lord Hari—consisting of the cow, truth, faith, the dust that has settled [upon them], the Vedas, the Smṛtis, compassion, initiation, and peace. 41–42.
The Sun, Moon, Wind, Earth, Water, Ether, the Quarters,
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra— the all-pervading Lord who consists of all beings—
himself, in his universal form, created this world of the moving and the unmoving. 43.
Having entered the bodies of Brahmins themselves, they always partake of food.

Then, they worship the dust of the feet of those who dwell in sacred fords— those whose nature is the earth, who are the gods upon the earth, who are the supreme Self, who are the very essence of all meritorious fortune, and who are the self of all beings.

He who perceives a learned Brāhmaṇa as Viṣṇu himself is indeed a Vaiṣṇava, as is he who is solely devoted to his own prescribed duties. This much of the secret has been told by me; this is my solemn pledge.
There is no further occasion for talk of going to the Gaṅgā to bathe;
this meritorious month of Mādhava, beloved of Mādhava, has arrived, and even within it, the seventh day of the bright fortnight at the Gaṅgā is exceedingly rare. 47–48.

In ancient times, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, Jahnu drank the Gaṅgā out of anger and then released her from his right ear-canal; on that very day, one should worship the Goddess Gaṅgā, whose girdle is the sky.
A fortunate and virtuous man who, having bathed there according to the proper rite,
offers libations to the gods and the ancestors as prescribed—
Gangā herself beholds that mortal who has bathed in her and whose sins have been destroyed.
The month of Madhava has arrived, and there is a river resembling the Ganga;
indeed, this yoga is difficult to attain and is obtained only through devotion to Hari.
Arising from the water of Vishnu’s feet, it has come down from the world of Brahma.
Through three streams, she tirelessly purifies the three worlds. She is a ladder for ascending to heaven, a constant bestower of bliss,
a remover of the outpouring of manifold evils, and a deliverer from misfortune.
Dwelling within the matted locks of the illustrious Maheśa, she is the destroyer of suffering;
she is the one who destroys the amorous play within the hearts of those who worship her.
She is the cause of liberation for the lineage of Sagara and the upholder of Dharma.

The Goddess who wanders the three paths, who acts as the ornament of the world, purifies thousands of men— both meritorious and non-meritorious— through being seen, touched, bathed in, praised, meditated upon, and served. 56–57.

If the name "Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā" is uttered during the three junctions of the day even by those standing at a great distance, it destroys the sins accumulated over three lifetimes. That man who remembers the Gaṅgā while thousands of yojanas away [is likewise purified].

Even one who has committed evil deeds attains the supreme goal on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha; O protector of the world, that [attainment] is especially difficult to obtain, yet it is secured through the grace of Hari, the Brahmins, and the ancestors. 59–60.
The month of Vaiśākha is equal to Nārāyaṇa, and the all-pervading Lord is equal to the month of Vaiśākha;
for He is the one who has gone [to the rescue] of people sinking in the ocean of misfortune.
Whatever is given, chanted, offered in sacrifice, or used for bathing during the month of Mādhava is performed with devotion.
O King, that merit shall become inexhaustible, exceeding even a hundred crores;
just as among the gods Viśvātman, Lord Nārāyaṇa Hari is supreme,
as Gāyatrī is among prayers, and as the Jāhnavī is among rivers.
Just as Umā is among all women, as the sun is among those that give heat,
as the acquisition of health is among gains, and as the Brāhmaṇa is among bipeds; so is service to others among meritorious deeds, and the Veda among branches of knowledge.
Just as the Praṇava is among mantras, and reflection on the Self is among meditations;

just as truthfulness is the best of one's own duties, and austerity is the best of ascetic practices; just as purity of purpose is the best of purities, and the gift of fearlessness is the best of gifts. (65-66)
Just as among all virtues, the destruction of greed is considered the foremost virtue,
so too is the month of Vaiśākha regarded as the most excellent of months.
Whatever śrāddha, sacrifice, gift, or fasting is performed therein [is of supreme merit].
Austerity, study, worship, and so forth are recorded as having inexhaustible fruit.
Sins end with Vaiśākha; darkness ends with the sun;
and good deeds end with the injury of others and malicious speech.
O King, whatever bathing, giving of gifts, and other such acts are performed in the month of Kārttika while the sun is situated in Libra, they become ten million times (parārdha) more meritorious;
therefore, when the sun is in Capricorn during the month of Māgha, the merit is a thousand times greater than that.
Even more than that,
those men are truly blessed and virtuous who, in the month of Vaiśākha when the sun is in Aries, bathe at dawn according to the prescribed rites and worship the Slayer of Madhu. (71–72)
O King, morning ablutions, sacrificial offerings, fasting, the consumption of *haviṣya* food, and celibacy in the month of Vaiśākha destroy even the greatest sins;
yet in the Kali age, O King, this [practice] will become something to be kept secret.
Because the greatness of Mādhava consists of the Aśvamedha and other rites,
and since the meritorious Aśvamedha sacrifice does not take place in the Kali age,
this ritual for the month of Mādhava is equal to the horse-sacrifice.
In this Kali age, sinful people of wicked intellect will not know that merit of the horse-sacrifice (Aśvamedha), which bestows the fruits of heaven and liberation;
by those sinful men born in that time, the ocean of hell must be traversed.
Therefore, its practice has become very rare, by which it was brought forth.
77. Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter in the Vaiśākha-māsa-māhātmya of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa in the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Eighty-six.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of the high-souled Nārada,
the royal sage Ambarīṣa, filled with wonder, spoke these words.
Ambarīṣa said:
O great sage, why do you praise Vaiśākha as superior to all other months, setting aside the meritorious months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa?

Why is Mādhava, the beloved of Mādhava, superior even to all? What is the ritual injunction there, what is the gift, what is the austerity, and who is the deity? O Sage, for me who am purified by the dust of Your lotus feet—
"By the grace of your instruction, you ought to grant me favor.
O great sage, you are the knower of dharma and the upholder of the paths of righteousness;
you alone are the one who knows the meaning of all truths and the teacher of dharma."
O best of sages, those who perform an act, those who instruct, those who approve, and even those who instigate it, are remembered by the knowers of the scriptures as sharing equally in the result;
indeed, whatever fruit is obtained through vows, sacrifices, austerities, and gifts— [all these share in it].
By the teaching of the Dharma alone all this is obtained.
O Sage, even he who performs bathing at sacred fords, austerity, sacrifice, or ritual action shall partake of its fruit if he becomes an initiator [of the teaching]. (7–8)
Whatever a great man practices, that very thing other people do;
whatever standard he sets, the world follows it. Therefore, it is fitting for you to teach the dharma; that would be wonderful.
Rare are the awakening from a teacher, the right place, the right time, and a favorable birth;
indeed, there are no such conditions that cool the mind as this meeting with you has done for me, even more so than the acquisition of a kingdom and the like. (10–11)
Sūta said:
Then Nārada, the best of sages, followed by the radiance of his teeth shimmering in a gentle, soft smile, replied to Ambarīṣa. 12.
Nārada said:
Listen, O King, I shall declare to you the ordinance for the month of Mādhava, which was formerly heard by you from Brahmā for the sake of the welfare of the world. 13.
Birth in the land of Bhārata-varṣa is difficult to obtain; therefore, human status is rare.
In this world, where human status is so difficult to attain, the practice of one's own specific duty is rare. Even more difficult than that, O King, is devotion to Vāsudeva.
Even there, the month of Mādhava, dear to Mādhava, is difficult to obtain.
Those fortunate and virtuous men who, having obtained that month, perform bathing, giving, recitation, and so forth according to the prescribed rules, are truly blessed. 15–16.
By the mere sight of them, even sinners become cleansed of their taints;
permeated by the divine nature of the Lord, they become seekers of dharma. Those who, joined with self-restraint, bathe at dawn during the month of Mādhava, [attain this state].
They sported in the Nandana grove for a period of ten million years;
just as there is no other body of water in the world equal to the new ocean,
so too there was no month like Vaiśākha, which is dear to Mādhava.
Sins remain within the bodies of human beings only so long as Mādhava, the destroyer of impurities, has not yet arrived. Indeed,
only the remaining days of that fifth month [are left].
Beginning from Ekādaśī, throughout all the months of the year,
O Indra among kings, those by whom the Lord Mādhava, the slayer of Madhu, was worshipped with various offerings in the month of Vaiśākha have attained the true fruit of their birth.
What indeed is more difficult to obtain than that which is attained by bathing and worshipping the Supreme Lord according to the prescribed rites during the month of Mādhava?
Neither has been given, neither offered in sacrifice, neither chanted, nor has death been met at a sacred pilgrimage site.

O King, it should be known that the birth of those men in this world is fruitless who have not meditated upon Nārāyaṇa, the destroyer of all sins. That man who remains miserly despite possessing wealth is likewise so. (24-25)
He who dies without having given away his wealth finds that property to be useless;
through penance such as bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha), one obtains birth in a noble family.
O King, nothing whatsoever is attained without the giving of gifts.
Even from the greatness of the Vaiśākha bath consisting of five days,
one obtains birth in a noble family, as well as various forms of prosperity— such as a virtuous son, a good lineage, kingship, wealth, grain, and excellent women. (27–28)

Auspicious birth and death, excellent enjoyments, and happiness as well; constant delight in giving, generosity, and supreme fortitude—these arise from the grace of that god, the high-souled Viṣṇu. 29.

The perfections desired by kings arise from Nārāyaṇa. Having bathed with devotion in the month of Kārttika, in the month of fasting, and in the month of Vaiśākha, which is dear to Mādhava, one should worship Dāmodara, Mādhava, and Madhusūdana.
Having honored him with special devotion and given gifts according to one's ability,
a person, after attaining worldly happiness, shall go to the state of Hari. By bathing in Mādhava, the multitude of sins accumulated over many lifetimes is dissolved.
Just as darkness at sunrise is dispelled by the king, so did the Self-Existent One (Brahmā) command me;
Viṣṇu then set this word of Yama into wide circulation during the month known as Mādhava, making it reach the world of men in a secret and inconceivable manner. 33–34.
Therefore, when this month of Mādhava has arrived, O great king, Vaiṣṇavas should bathe in the purifying waters of the Gaṅgā, which sanctify men,
or in the Revā, or the Yamunā, or the Śāradā.
In the morning, O best of kings, before the sun has risen, having worshipped according to the prescribed rite the Lord of Gods, Mukunda Madhusūdana,
one obtains sons, grandsons, wealth, prosperity, desired objects, and happiness. (36-37)
Having experienced the fruits of your penance, you shall attain imperishable heaven;
knowing this, O highly fortunate one, worship Madhusūdana. Having bathed according to the proper rite, especially during the month of Vaiśākha.
Having propitiated the god Govinda, Nārāyaṇa, who is free from all ailment,
you shall obtain happiness, a son, wealth, and the abode of Hari.
Having paid homage to Mādhava, the god of gods and the destroyer of sins— (39-40)
O King, one should begin this vow on the full moon day of the month of Madhu, endowed with restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas), giving some gift according to one's capacity,
eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), sleeping on the ground, and remaining established in the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya). 41.
Having performed austerities such as the Kṛcchra penance and meditating on Nārāyaṇa within his heart,
he should thus reach the full moon day of Vaiśākha and devoutly give honey, sesame seeds, and other offerings, as well as food to the foremost of the twice-born, along with a cow and a monetary gift.
O Brahmins, one should pray for the flawlessness of the performed bath,
so that Lakṣmī may become as dear to the Lord of the World, Mādhava, the King, as she is to him; and likewise, Mādhava shall be as dear to Mā, the daughter of Madhu, as she is to him.

A mortal endowed with such a procedure, having bathed for twelve years, should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) according to his capacity for the gratification of Madhusūdana. Thus has the majesty of the month of Mādhava been recounted to you. 45–46.
"O King, that which was formerly heard by me from the mouth of Brahmā.
Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter in the Vaiśākha-māsa-māhātmya of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa in the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The seventy-eighth chapter.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of Nārada, that lord of the earth...
Having prostrated, he spoke with wonder, reflecting on Hari in his mind. 1.
Ambarīṣa said:
O Sage, how is this? We are truly bewildered that such a thing was accomplished with so little effort.
"By merely bathing, even that fruit which is exceedingly difficult to attain is obtained.
Nārada said:
"O King, you have spoken the truth; how great is this [fruit] achieved with so little effort!"
The fruit will be attained there; have faith in what has been spoken by the Ordainer.
The courses of dharma are subtle and difficult to comprehend even for the lords of gods; even the wise are deluded regarding the inconceivable power of Hari’s actions. 3–4.

O King, through their excellence in dharma, Viśvāmitra and others who were born of the kṣatriya order attained the status of brahmins; therefore, the course of dharma is subtle. Even Ajāmila, O protector of the earth, was known as the husband of a slave woman.
Though he had abandoned his lawful wife and was constantly established on the path of sin,
as he was dying, out of affection for his son he cried out, "Nārāyaṇa!
By uttering that name first, he attained a station that is very difficult to reach.
Just as fire, when touched, burns even against one's will,
so too does that which is uttered under the pretext of the name of Govinda burn [the sinner].
[This was said] regarding the grandson of the sage Kānīna, who had approached his brother’s wife.
And the sons of the wise Gola and Paṇḍu were likewise Kuṇḍas;
those five Pāṇḍavas were devoted to the Goddess Padī on the mountain.
From that arose their status as Puṇyaślokas and the subtle course of dharma.
Diverse are the actions, diverse are the manifestations of the elements,
diverse are the beings, and diverse are the potencies of karma.
Sometimes, a well-performed action remains fixed and stable.
O King, by some unwholesome action, [the merit] increases;
it yields a very great fruit even in another birth.
Dharma is subtle and exceedingly profound; it is measured in various ways according to its nature.
No certainty is heard regarding the king's determination in the granting of this fruit:
that whatever meritorious deed has been performed, even if concealed by other sins, comes from somewhere or other and bestows its own fruit. 14.
There is no destruction of what has been done, whether it be merit or evil;
nevertheless, O King, through many merits, even terrible evil departs, as you have stated that it arises from an excess of exertion. 15–16.
Hear from me the reason why there is great merit even in that [small act]: it is because the smallness or greatness [of the result] depends on whether the exertion is slight or great.
Therefore, farmers and others would possess great merit at all times.
Furthermore, there is the recitation of mantras and the great exertion involved in [the worship of] lions and other such beings;
moreover, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are highly recommended as an ancillary part of the vow for us.
Thus, there is a great deal of ritual activity and magnitude, whereas that [other path] is of little consequence. 18–19.
The entry into water, fire, and so forth would follow from another vow;
that "this is small" and "that is great" is not a restrictive rule at all. O King, whatever fruit is prescribed in the scripture, that alone shall be great.
Just as the destruction of great things occurs through small means, so too does the destruction of small things occur through small means.
(21) Indeed, even by a tiny spark, a heap of grass is consumed by fire.
(22) Ten thousand killings, a thousand fierce sins, and the violation of ten million preceptors’ wives—[all these are destroyed].
Sins such as theft and the like, born of ignorance, are completely swept away by those devoted to Kṛṣṇa.
O hero, whatever small amount of virtuous deed is performed by one who possesses devotion to Viṣṇu, that wise person shall obtain its inexhaustible fruit. 23–24.
No doubt should be entertained in this matter: the man who worships Mādhava with devotion during the month of Mādhava shall obtain whatever he desires—
offspring, wealth, jewels, a wife, a mansion, horses, and elephants.
Happiness, heaven, and liberation are not far off through devotion to Hari (26).

Thus, according to the method prescribed in the scriptures, even by a very little [practice], there is no doubt that there will be the destruction of even great sin and the increase of virtuous deeds (27).
An abundance of results arises from the excellence of the lordship of the house and its karma; however, the movement of subtle dharma is to be understood through various means.
This month of Mādhava is dear to the great-souled Ādhava.
Even if performed by a single person, it bestows all that is desired upon the world.

O King, my view is this: even one who is devoted to bathing in the holy water of the Ganges at the proper time and place, yet remains a giver [of gifts] while being driven by worldly motives from birth, does not attain purity. 29–30.

Living beings dwell constantly at holy sites such as the Gaṅgā, and flocks of birds reside eternally in temples; yet, even if they observe fasts, they meet with destruction if they are devoid of devotion, and they do not attain a higher state.
Therefore, one should place the glorious Mādhava within the lotus of the heart with devotion during the month of Mādhava.
One who is purified by being intent on bathing in the sacrificial fire— his merit is such that it is impossible to describe.
Having kindled the fire at the proper time with offerings of ghee and oil, one whose flames turn clockwise,
if a person of corrupt intent enters and is burned, he attains neither heaven nor any other fruit.
Therefore, O King, have faith in the fruit of Mādhava;
even a very small auspicious deed destroys hundreds of misdeeds.
Just as all multitudes of evils, O King, perish through fear of Hari’s name.
Surely, when dawn has arrived with the sun in Aries, through bathing at a sacred ford and through hymns to Hari,
sins certainly flee away by the power of the Vaiśākha bath at daybreak, just as serpents flee before the splendor of Garuḍa. 35–36.

O King, having bathed in the Gaṅgā or the Narmadā when the sun has entered Aries, whoever recites this hymn for the pacification of sins with a spirit of devotion— whether once, twice, or at the three junctions of the day— 37.
One who is free from all sins attains the supreme state;
O Kuru, for the sake of obtaining great merit, one should behold Ambarīṣa and perform a morning bath in the month of Vaiśākha, established in religious observances. 38-39.

O King, listen now to the ancient account regarding this matter: that which was said to take ten million years for those dwelling in the city of Anarta is obtained here by a single morning bath in the month of Madhava. 40.
The conversation of the twice-born Devaśarman with his wife took place on the very meritorious bank of the Revā at the holy site of Amarakaṇṭaka.
There, the son of Kauśika was born as Devaśarman, the best of the twice-born. 41–42.
Deprived of wealth and sons, he was beset by manifold sufferings;
oppressed at all times by the great misery of poverty, he pondered day and night on the means to obtain both sons and wealth. 43.
Once, however, his beloved wife named Sumanā, who was devoted to her vows,
observed that her husband was filled with anxiety and had his face cast downwards; then, looking at her husband, the illustrious woman spoke to him.

O high-minded one, your mind has been dragged down by countless nets of suffering and utterly deluded by confusion; therefore, abandon this anxiety. Tell me your sorrow, become composed, and attain happiness.
There is no suffering equal to the anxiety of "it does not exist," for it truly withers the body.
Abandoning that [anxiety], one should proceed; thus one finds happiness and rejoices.
O Lord, tell me, the cause of this anxiety, which is far-reaching. 47–48.
Nārada said:
Having heard those affectionate words, the high-minded Devaśarman, though distressed, spoke these words with joy, accompanied by his virtuous wife. 49
Devasharman said:
"O blessed lady, whatever cause of distress you have reflected upon, I shall explain it all to you; having heard it, let it be well considered. (50)
"I do not know by what sin, O lady of excellent vows, I have become destitute of wealth and likewise bereft of sons; this is the cause of my suffering.
Sumanā said:

Listen, I shall declare that which destroys all doubt: the true nature of instruction, which reveals all knowledge. (52) Contentment alone is the supreme merit and the cause of happiness and other virtues.
"Discontent is the supreme sin," said the Blessed Lord Hari. Greed is the seed of this sin, and delusion is its root; untruth is its trunk, which spreads out with great branches.
Its leaves are intoxication and crookedness; it is always in bloom with evil intellect.
Falsehood is its fragrance, and ignorance is its fruit indeed.
Heretics, thieves, the cruel, the deceitful, and sinners are its walls. 55.
Birds take refuge upon its great branches, which are the tree of delusion.
Ignorance is its excellent fruit, and the essence of that fruit is indeed dharma.
Its growth is nourished by the water of worldly existence, and faith is dear to it as a ritual sacrifice.
Through the overflowing juices of unrighteousness, that tree of greed becomes sweet; and by such fruits, the tree of greed indeed bears fruit. That man who dwells taking refuge in its shade—
Day after day he eats fruits that have ripened on their own;
yet, though nourished even by the juice of those fruits, that mortal remains emaciated by unrighteousness and hastens toward his downfall. 59-60.
Therefore, having abandoned anxiety, one should not harbor greed for a master;
one should not entertain this concern for wealth, sons, and wife.
For if a wise man does not follow the path of fools, he indeed remains steadfast.
Deluded, he constantly thinks day and night: "How may I find auspicious means? How shall I obtain sons?
Thus he constantly thinks day and night, utterly bewildered.
For a single moment one may behold great happiness amidst anxiety, yet consciousness returns once more and one is tormented by great suffering.
O twice-born one, abandon both anxiety and delusion, and follow that [path].
O Mahāmati, what connection can there be with saṃsāra?
Friends, kinsmen, sons, fathers, mothers, daughters, as well as sisters, relatives, wives, and so forth—these all come into being [only through such associations]. 65–66.
Devasharma said:
"O blessed lady, tell me in detail what kind of connection it is, by which all those kinsmen—wealth, sons, and so forth—are produced. (67)
Sumanā said:
"O husband, five kinds of sons are born; I shall describe them to you: one is the appropriator of a deposit, and another is the one connected by debt. (68)
"An enemy, one who is attainable, and a neutral party—these, O Lord, are said to be your beloveds.
I shall describe their characteristics to you individually:
sons, friends, dear wives, fathers, mothers, and kinsmen."
On this earth, they are born with their own respective kinsmen through the bond of relationship.
By virtue of the act of misappropriating a deposit, whoever has taken what was entrusted to them on earth shall become the son of that depositor, endowed with virtues and beauty upon this earth.
For by him the deposit was stolen; there is no doubt that it remained in his house.
Having experienced the terrible suffering caused by the theft of the deposit, he departed after having given it back. The owner of the deposit became a good son to the one who had stolen the deposit.
Possessed of virtues, endowed with beauty, and complete with all auspicious marks, he shall show devotion to him day after day; having become his son,
he shall speak kindly, use sweet words, be eloquent, and display great affection.

Having seized his own wealth and produced incomparable joy, he gave it back to him; yet, due to the theft of that deposit, O highly fortunate one, such terrible suffering arose, resulting even in the loss of life. 75.
Becoming his son endowed with great virtues, he would bestow such [merit] upon him;
yet, having become short-lived, he likewise meets his death.
Having thus inflicted suffering and struck [him] again and again, he departs.
When someone utters the lamentation "O son! O son!", he merely laughs at that; for who is a son, and to whom does he belong? By this evildoer, my deposit has been stolen.

"Indeed, even by the seizure of my property, my life-breaths were formerly taken away by you with great and unbearable suffering; therefore, having inflicted that same suffering upon you, I shall now recover my excellent wealth. (79-80)
Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter in the Vaiśākha-māhātmya of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Eighty-eight.
Sumanā said:
"I shall describe before you the son who is connected by debt—
that one who, having incurred a debt, departs unto death."
Having become a donor of wealth, or appearing as a son, a brother, a father,
or a beloved friend, he always remains inwardly wicked;
that cruel one of harsh appearance never perceives any virtue.
He always spoke harsh words even to his own kinsmen; he constantly ate only the sweetest things and perpetually enjoyed sensual pleasures;
he was ever devoted to gambling and longed for the deeds of thieves.
When forbidden, he steals property from the house and becomes angry;
day by day he reviles both his father and his mother. In this way his wealth is exhausted, and he speaks in this manner as well.
"Without a doubt, everything— house, field, and so forth— belongs to me alone.
Day after day, he indeed harms both my father and mother with severe punishments, pestles, and the terrible plucking out of their hair."

When that father and mother have died, he becomes exceedingly cruel, devoid of affection, and indeed harsh; of this there is no doubt. He never performs the ancestral rites (śrāddha) nor does he ever give gifts.
O Lord of the Earth, such are the beloved sons that come into being.
O best of the twice-born, I shall now describe to you the son who is an enemy: one who, having reached the stage of childhood, always remains in the state of a son [only in name]. 11–12.
While playing, he would strike his father and mother;
having struck them, he would go away laughing in this manner again and again. Then he would return there once more to his father and mother.
He was constantly full of anger and reviled [others] day after day; thus he always engaged in acts of enmity with great intensity. Furthermore, he struck both his father and his mother. (14-15)
Thus, that evil-minded one proceeds by the power of former enmity;
therefore, I shall now explain how one may obtain what is dear. One should act kindly toward a person as soon as they are born, and during childhood, through play and gentle blows.
Upon reaching maturity, one should immediately do what is pleasing to one's mother and father;
one should constantly satisfy them with devotion and please both of them with affection, kind words, and pleasant conversation. 17–18.
Recognizing his deceased elders, he weeps again out of affection;
though afflicted by great sorrow, he performs all the śrāddha rites, including the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and other ceremonies, and provides for their journey to the next world.
He who, being resolute, would liberate from the three debts out of affection—whatever may be obtained from that [debt], he bestows it upon his beloved;
having become a son, O highly wise one, indeed by this method. 20–21.

I shall now describe the indifferent one (udāsīna) before you, who is dear to me; he always conducts himself with an indifferent disposition. He neither gives nor takes, and he neither becomes angry nor is he pleased.
O best of the twice-born, having abandoned new undertakings and remaining indifferent, these are declared to be one's dependents:
cattle, horses, elephants, buffaloes, female slaves, and those bound by debt. (23-24)

"O beloved, listen: by one [birth] through the power of illusion, this was taken from us both; indeed, no such deposit was ever made by either of us in a previous birth. Nor was even a single moment [of it] ever enjoyed by Rādhā."
"O best of Brahmins, even though he was treated with hostility by me in a previous birth, my husband was not abandoned by me from childhood onwards.
Knowing this, attain peace and abandon this useless anxiety. (26-27)
"It was neither stolen by anyone, nor was it given away by you again; O Lord, how has this wealth come to you? We are filled with great wonder. For it has arrived right where it was being guarded."
Knowing this, one should attain tranquility and abandon useless anxiety.
Whose are sons? Whose is a beloved wife? Whose are kinsmen and relatives?
O best of the twice-born, there is no one who belongs to another in this saṃsāra; there is no such relationship. 29–30.
Men, deluded by the confusion of illusion and possessed of sinful intentions, think: "This is my house, these are my sons, and this indeed is my wife.
This false perception is seen as the very bond of worldly existence, O beloved.
Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter in the Vaiśākha-māsa-māhātmya of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
[The eighty-ninth chapter follows.]
Nārada said:
Thus enlightened, the brahmin Devaśarman, the best of the twice-born,
spoke again to his beloved wife, who was endowed with wisdom.
"What you have said, O blessed lady, is true and destroys all doubt;
for indeed, virtuous men who are wise in truth desire a lineage,
just as they care for a son, O dear one."
"By whatever means possible, I shall produce a son.
Sumanā said:
"Through a son one conquers the worlds; a son delivers the family."
O fortunate one, father and mother live through a good son.
A single son who is excellent and beloved is better than many who are devoid of virtue; one such son delivers the lineage, while others only cause distress.

Previously, I have declared this: others who share in the bond [of kinship] obtain a son through merit, and a noble lineage is obtained through merit. A virtuous conception is attained through merits, and likewise, a miserable death is brought about by sins.
I declare the truth itself, O beloved: it is the accumulation of all happiness.
Through celibacy, truth, austerity, constant observances, charity, restraints, forbearance, and purity—O dear one. (7–8)
One proceeds by means of non-violence, or according to one's capacity, and also by non-stealing;
through these ten limbs, dharma is thus brought forth.
Dharma becomes complete through its limbs, just as a fetus is formed within the womb.
The righteous-souled one creates Dharma through three kinds of action alone. To him, Dharma—being a serene self—bestows merit and happiness;
whatever that wise man contemplates, even if it be difficult to attain, he obtains it. 10–11.
Devaśarman said:
"O Goddess, you have fully explained the supreme knowledge known as Dharma; how then may I obtain a son who is a Vaiṣṇava endowed with all virtuous qualities? (12)
"Speak to me, O highly fortunate one, if you know, O lady of virtuous vows:
O sinless one, was the entire path of dharma obtained by you from your father in the past? This is known to me, O beloved, that you are a speaker of Brahman."
"In former times, by the grace of Cyavana and through the satisfaction of Viṣṇu, [this was granted].
Sumanā said: "Go to Vasiṣṭha, O knower of dharma, and entreat that great sage."
"Therefore, O son, you shall obtain that son who knows the Dharma and is devoted to the Dharma.
When these words had been spoken by her, Devaśarman, the best of the twice-born, replied:
"O auspicious lady, I shall do exactly as you have intended; of this there is no doubt."
Surrounded by a blaze of splendor like a second sun, that high-souled one shone resplendent as a lion of Brahman, the best of the twice-born;
having prostrated himself like a staff before that sage again and again with devotion, [he stood there]. 18–19.
The son of Brahmā, possessed of great splendor, said to that stainless one:
"Sit down comfortably on these auspicious seats, O high-minded one.
Nārada said:
Seated there, that lord of yogis spoke again to the ascetic: "O illustrious one,
is all well with your household, your sons, your wife, your servants, and always with your meritorious deeds and the sacred fires?"
"You are free from ailment in your limbs and you always protect the Dharma.
Having spoken thus, the one of great wisdom spoke again to the Brahmin:
"O best of the twice-born, what dear and most beloved wish shall I fulfill for you?"
Nārada said:
Having thus spoken these auspicious words to that brahmin, he became silent;
then the highly fortunate brahmin [addressed] Vasiṣṭha, the bull among sages.
He spoke to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, the best among those who practice austerities:
"O Blessed One, O best of the twice-born, please listen to these words that will bring an end [to my suffering]. How indeed can there be no happiness from a son due to the state of poverty?"
"O father, tell me this which is my doubt: from what sin did this arise? (26) O twice-born one, utterly bewildered by great delusion, I was awakened by my beloved;
sent by her, O father, I have come here to your side. (27)
"Tell me all of that, which destroys every doubt; may you become the giver of liberation for me from the bondage of saṃsāra.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Sons, enemies, as well as brothers and other kinsmen and relatives— these five types of relationships belong to a man.
These have already been described by Sumanas previously in your presence.
O best of the twice-born, all those who are connected to debt are but bad sons;
I shall now describe before you the meritorious characteristics of a true son—
one whose soul is devoted to merit and who is always intent upon truth and righteousness.
Pure, endowed with knowledge, ascetic, the best among those skilled in speech,
well-restrained in all his actions, and devoted to the study of the Vedas;
he was a master of all scriptures and a worshiper of the gods and Brahmins.
He was a performer of sacrifices, a giver of all sacrifices, a renouncer, and one who spoke kindly;
he was constantly devoted to the meditation on Viṣṇu, ever peaceful and self-controlled, always a friend, eternally devoted to his father and mother, and affectionate toward all his kinsmen. 33–34.
A wise son who rescues his family and nourishes his own kin—one endowed with such qualities is a true son and a bestower of happiness;
others who are merely connected by kinship cause only grief and torment. 35.
"O sinless one, what should be done by you who are indifferent and devoid of fruit?
O best of the twice-born, they all come and go after inflicting most terrible suffering upon you in the form of sons within this worldly existence."

I shall indeed relate everything regarding the karma performed and maintained by you in a previous birth; listen once more to this wonderful account. O highly wise one, you were a Śūdra in your former life, and not otherwise.
A farmer, devoid of knowledge and possessed by great greed, having only one wife yet always full of hatred, he had many sons but gave nothing away;
indeed, you do not know dharma nor the firmly established truth. 39-40.
"No gift was ever given by you, nor was any scripture ever heard; no sacred ford was visited by you, nor was any pilgrimage undertaken, O high-minded one.
In this way, you have repeatedly traversed the path of misfortune."
O best of the twice-born, in the past you went about tending cattle, and likewise you tended female buffaloes and mares again and again;
such was the work performed by you alone in former times, O best of the twice-born. (42-43)
That vast wealth was accumulated through greed;
yet, when it came to its expenditure, you never once spent it on merit.
Indeed, seeing it to be weak and fleeting, you did not give even a single gift to a worthy recipient.
Indeed, by practicing agriculture, wealth was acquired even though nothing had been given;
and by selling all this cow-dung and the entire collection of livestock, O Brahmin, a vast amount of wealth was accumulated by you. 45–46.
Buttermilk, ghee, milk, and curd were constantly sold;
thus, O best of Brahmins, a time of great scarcity was brought about by me, deluded as I was by the Māyā of Viṣṇu, making this wealth exceedingly precious. 47.
Indeed, at that time, you gave no gift out of your mercilessness;
O Brahmin, you never performed the worship of the gods, nor did you ever offer wealth to the Brahmins upon reaching the auspicious festival days. 48-49.

"When the time for the *śrāddha* had arrived, your virtuous wife said to you, 'O high-minded one, the time for the *śrāddha* of your father-in-law and mother-in-law has come during the middle of the day. (50)
Having heard those words of theirs, you have abandoned your home and fled;
indeed, the path of dharma has never been seen nor even heard by you.
Greed is mother, father, and brother; greed is one's kinsmen and relatives.
Having always abandoned unrighteousness, you were indeed possessed solely by greed for wealth;
therefore, you have become miserable, excessively tormented by poverty. Day after day, great craving continues to arise within your heart.
Whenever you acquire wealth, it always leads to further increase;
yet, consumed by thirst—which is like fire—you think even more intensely of greed while you are asleep at night. 54-55.

When day arrives, he is indeed always pervaded by great delusions; will there ever be a thousand, a hundred thousand, ten million, or even a hundred million [of such days] in my house? Or will there ever be a billion or ten billion? 56.
In this way, thousands, lakhs, crores, arbudas, kharvas,
and nikharvas are produced, yet thirst does not depart;
thus, even as time passes, it always continues to increase.
"Neither has this been given away, nor offered in sacrifice, nor eaten by Brahmins; it has certainly never been cast into the depths of the earth, for my sons do not know of it.
Therefore, seek another means for the recovery of the wealth."
O wise one, you always wander through various regions and ask questions;
yet, though alone and utterly deluded by craving, you continue to roam about inquiring after spades, collyrium, or even the alchemy of minerals. 60-61.
You constantly contemplate all the kalpas that bestow accomplishments,
and you inquire about the entrance into the multicolored [realms] and the wish-fulfilling gem;
yet, consumed by the fire of craving, you find no happiness at all.

"O best of Brahmins, you have become like a lion inflamed by the fire of thirst, devoid of consciousness; having thus come under the sway of time, you did not respond when your wife and sons questioned you about that wealth. (63-64)
"It was indeed spoken, but it was not given; having abandoned his life-breaths, he has gone to Yama.
Thus I have related to you this entire account from the beginning, O Brahmin;
by this karma, you have become penniless and impoverished."
In this cycle of existence, those who possess virtuous sons who are always devoted, well-behaved, endowed with knowledge, and ever-delighted in truth and righteousness,
arise in the home of that person for whom Viṣṇu is pleased.
He whose Viṣṇu is pleased indeed enjoys inexhaustible wealth, grain, a wife, sons, and grandsons in the world of mortals;
without the grace of Viṣṇu, neither wives nor sons come to be.
"O Brahmin of noble birth, that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
