69. Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Devaśarman," within the "Glorious Greatness of the Month of Vaiśākha" in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Ninety.
Devaśarman said:
"O best of brahmins, you have told me of the sin committed by you in a previous birth; for it was by me alone, O lord of brahmins, that this wealth was acquired while in the state of a śūdra. (1)
"O best of the twice-born, how was this status of a Brahmin attained by me?
O scholar in knowledge and realization, tell me the cause of all that.
Birth in the land of Bhārata is difficult to obtain; from that, human status [is even more so]."

Human birth is rare, and being a Brahmin born of a noble lineage is even rarer. Furthermore, how did she come to have such a wife—one who is all-knowing, sweet-spoken, virtuous, and endowed with every excellence, for she is difficult to find? (3-4)
Vasiṣṭha said:
O twice-born one, I shall fully relate that which was performed by you previously as a righteous deed; listen, if you so desire. 5.
There was a certain Brāhmaṇa, a man of pure character, of virtuous conduct, and highly learned;
he was a devotee of Viṣṇu, righteous-souled, and eternally dedicated to Viṣṇu. He wandered alone over the earth for the sake of bathing in sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrthas).
Wandering about, that high-minded one arrived at your home;
by the mere sight of him, wisdom arose within you,
for the arrival of the virtuous occurs in the house of one who is established in dharma.
O Brahmin, what indeed is not obtained by serving a Vaiṣṇava?
Whatever may be difficult to attain in this world, even the stable state of liberation— O best of beings, he requested a single place for the sake of his livelihood.
"It was given by your very own wife, and you should eat it together with your sons.
"Come here, come here, O Brāhmaṇa; stay happily in my house," he said again and again to that meritorious Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇa.
"O you of firm vows, remain here at ease; this is my home. Today I am blessed and meritorious, for today I have come to a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha).
Today, by the sight of you, O Brahmin, I have obtained the fruit of that pilgrimage."
The supreme and most meritorious abode of the cows has been shown as their dwelling place.
Their limbs were properly massaged and their feet rubbed; they were then washed again with water, and he himself bathed with the water from their feet. 13–14.
Fresh ghee, curd, and milk—each one gave these to the other brahmin;
thus, impelled by the unseen power, you satisfied that brahmin along with his wife. 15. Thus was the brahmin gratified by you together with your wife.
Accompanied by his sons, that illustrious devotee of Viṣṇu, learned in wisdom,
then set out for the Gaṅgā at dawn during the month of Mādhava to bathe; being pleased, he approached the Lord with compassion.
The greatness of the Vaiśākha bath has been taught before you; you, together with your wife and son, have performed it according to the prescribed rules.
Indeed, there is no reservoir of water in this world equal to the great ocean.

Likewise, the month of Vaiśākha is similar to Māsa and is dear to Mādhava. Sins remain unimpeded within the body only so long as the month of Vaiśākha, which destroys even great evils, does not arrive. 19-20.
Having heard his words, Madhusūdana was worshipped by the Brahmin with a satisfied mind for the practice performed during Vaiśākha; indeed,
he remained so for the remaining days of that month.

Beginning from the eleventh day, you performed your ritual bath according to the rules; and by association with the Brāhmaṇa, you have daily performed your morning bath in the Revā river throughout the month of Vaiśākha, O twice-born one. (22-23)

The Lord of the gods of gods, the Supreme Sovereign who slays Madhu, was not worshipped by you at all during that entire month for the sake of ritual bathing as before. Thus, although you have performed the bath for five days, it has been incomplete.
"By that merit, and especially through association with a brāhmaṇa,
you have attained the state of a brāhmaṇa by the grace of Govinda;
this great lineage was obtained by you through the conjunction of that month."
O gods, it is rare to find one endowed with truth and righteousness;
yet even a wife was obtained who was virtuous, auspicious, possessed of all good qualities, born in the house of Cyavana, omniscient, and a knower of Brahman. 27.
O great sage, physical beauty alone is the primary ornament of women;
second is virtuous conduct, third is truthfulness, fourth is constant nobility, and fifth is supreme merit. (28-29)
Sweetness is the sixth, and greatness of purity is the seventh;
these three, along with all ornaments, are always present in women both outwardly and inwardly. The eighth, however, is the disposition toward the husband, and the ninth is indeed service.
Forbearance is the tenth, and likewise, delight is the eleventh;
O best of Brahmins, devotion to her husband is remembered as the twelfth among women.
Adorned with these qualities, such a wife is virtuous and a knower of Brahman.

By the merit earnestly obtained through the practice of the Vaiśākha bath, what indeed is difficult to attain in the month of Mādhava? Through bathing and the worship of the Supreme Lord according to the prescribed rites, [all things are attained]. 33.
Now, your mind, utterly deluded by ignorance and pervaded by craving, accumulated wealth alone in your previous birth;
indeed, it was not given by you to the Brahmins, nor to the poor, nor to others. (34-35)
Neither toward your circle of kinsmen nor toward your sons and wife did you ever feel attachment while dying; indeed, nothing but greed was entertained by you.
You gave no gifts, you offered no oblations, you chanted no prayers, and you did not die at a sacred pilgrimage site.
Lord Nārāyaṇa is the destroyer of all sins through meditation.
(37) A man becomes a miser even while wealth is present;
what indeed could be more painful than for one to die without having given anything? (38)
O Brahmin, through penances such as bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha*), one merely obtains birth;
nothing whatsoever comes to pass without having first been given. Due to the presence of that sin, he has fallen into poverty.
"You have become childless and are constantly tormented by suffering;
yet, through the greatness of the Vaiśākha bath for even five days, and likewise through the merit of the worship of Hari and the company of a brāhmaṇa, [you shall attain liberation]. 40-41.
Birth in a noble family has been obtained, and even the status of a Brahmin is difficult to attain;
likewise, a virtuous son, a noble lineage, wealth, grain, clothing, women, a good birth, a peaceful death, excellent enjoyments, and happiness itself [have been attained]. 42.
A superior intellect regarding constant giving constitutes magnanimity and supreme fortitude (43). Through the grace of that god Viṣṇu,
the high-souled Nārāyaṇa, the perfections desired by the brahmins arise (44).

Having bathed with devotion in the month of Mādhava (Vaiśākha), which is full of vigor, austerity, and dear to Mādhava, one should worship Dāmodara, Mādhava, and Madhusūdana with special care, and having given gifts with devotion, [one attains the highest state]. 45.
Having attained worldly happiness, a person then goes to Hari.
By immersion in Mādhava, the multitude of sins accumulated over many births dissolves, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun; thus the Self-born One himself commanded Indradyumna. 46–47.
Viṣṇu performed a pure investigation regarding the month of Mādhava at the very beginning;
it was hidden from Yama, inconceivable even by the mind, and inaccessible to the world of men in the celestial realm.
Therefore, when this month of Mādhava has arrived— 48. In this month of Mādhava...
Having bathed in the holy waters of the sacred ford before the sun has risen,
and having worshipped Mukunda Madhusūdana according to the prescribed rite,
one obtains sons, grandsons, wealth, prosperity, desired objects, and happiness.
Having experienced this, you will at last attain imperishable heaven;
all that was performed by you through your efforts in previous births has been related by me before you, O Brahmin. 51. All that was performed by you has been told by me in your presence.
Having understood this, O highly fortunate ones, especially during the month of Vaiśākha,
one should bathe according to the proper ritual and worship Madhusūdana; having propitiated the god Govinda, Nārāyaṇa, who is free from all ailment.
"You shall obtain happiness, a son, wealth, and here, the imperishable Hari.
Nārada said:
"That noble and best of Brahmins was indeed thus enlightened by the son of Brahmā."
Filled with joy, that noble-souled one prostrated there before Vasiṣṭha with devotion;
having taken leave of the Brahmin, he went home and spoke to his wife Sumanā: "O Great Seer, all this has indeed occurred through my former deeds and by the grace of that very Brahmin."
"O blessed lady, my delusion has been dispelled this very day by Vasiṣṭha.
I shall worship Madhusūdana, having bathed with devotion during the month of Śrī-Mādhava.
Nārada said:

Having heard those most sacred, auspicious, and highly propitious words that are the cause of all blessings, she was filled with joy and said to her beloved: "Blessed are you, for you have been enlightened by the Brahmin.
Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Devaśarman," within the "Glorification of the Month of Vaiśākha" in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The Ninety-First Chapter.
Nārada said:
O highly wise one, Devaśarman lived together with that Sumanas.
At the highly renowned holy site of Gaṅgā in Nakhala,

during the month of Vaiśākha when the sun was situated in Aries, he performed his ritual bath according to the prescribed rules and worshipped Madhusūdana, the infallible Acyuta, in accordance with the injunctions.

Endowed with restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas), he then gave whatever he could according to his capacity; subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya), sleeping on the ground, and established in the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya),
he delighted in penance such as the Kṛcchra, while meditating upon Nārāyaṇa within his heart.

There, having reached the full moon day of Vaiśākha, he gave honey, sesame seeds, and other offerings to the Brahmins; and after providing them with food along with a cow and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
he requested the twice-born ones to declare the ritual bath to be complete and flawless.
That virtuous woman of beautiful hips, devoted solely to her husband's service,
constantly attended to him after bathing and worshipping Keśava. Then that couple went to their own home, filled with the joy of the righteous.
Then, considering themselves without doubt to have accomplished all that was to be done,
by the power of that merit, after some time, his wealth, grain, and riches became indeed immeasurable.
His four sons were endowed with discipline, proficient in the Vedas,
knowers of dharma, constant devotees of Viṣṇu, and devoted to their father and mother; possessed of immeasurable wisdom, they were awakened for the sake of the goals of human life.
Those renowned ones, who know the truth of the injunctions, who know Brahman, and who are devoted to Brahman—
endowed with all virtues, their glories remain firmly established.
Then, after a long time, that couple, having enjoyed the full happiness of prosperity along with their son, which arose from the dawning of merit, [departed].
By means of their devotion to Śrī Mādhava and through the favor of the king, they both attained the supreme station of merit.
Just as Mādhava is remembered as the manifest husband of Vidyā and Lakṣmī, so too is Mādhava-Māsa the beloved of Madhusūdana. 12–13.
"O sinless hero, this greatness of Mādhava has been recounted by me to you in brief, which I formerly heard from my father.
(14) Thus ends the section on the Greatness of the Month of Vaiśākha in the Dialogue between Nārada and Ambarīṣa within the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Ninety-first chapter;
Ninety-second chapter.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of Nārada, the lord of the earth,
filled with wonder, bowed down and spoke while meditating upon Hari in his mind.
Ambarīṣa said:
"How can we be deluded by this, O Sage, that a Śūdra, through such slight effort, attained the supreme status of a Brāhmaṇa?
For the status of a Brāhmaṇa, dear one, is difficult to obtain even through various kinds of meritorious deeds."
O Lord, how is it that even the lowest of sinners, by merely bathing in the month of Mādhava,

do not become like us— wealthy kings who, despite performing sacrifices, giving gifts, practicing fierce austerities, or other meritorious deeds, have never attained the status of being deities upon this earth? 3–4.
Even after performing various and most terrible austerities incessantly for a long time,
Sagara’s son obtained [the boon] only with great difficulty after a full hundred years, alas, through many strenuous efforts.
How is it that this sinful man, the lowest of his own caste, devoid of his own duty, wealthy yet uncharitable?
"Depart from here quickly, for this truth is obtained from that merit which is achieved without effort, even if it be small.
Nārada said:
"O King, you have spoken the truth; the status of a brāhmaṇa is exceedingly difficult to attain."

Nevertheless, the destinies are subtle and difficult to understand from the perspective of the true nature of phenomena (dharmatattva). The karmas are diverse, as are the various formations of the elements;
the elements themselves are diverse, as are the powers of karma.
O King, sometimes a well-performed deed that was performed and remains fixed increases through some other auspicious action,
and it yields a very great fruit even in that very same birth.
This subtle and profound nature of phenomena is led here and there according to its own course;
no fixed time for the ripening of its fruit is heard of,
whether it be some virtuous deed hidden even by internal evils.
Then, arriving from some unknown place, it bestows excellent fruit; herein there is no destruction of what has been done, whether it be merit or evil.
Nevertheless, through many merits, even terrible evil comes to an end.

O King, as for what was said by you—that the result would depend on the greater degree of exertion—hear now the truth spoken by me: whether there is little or great effort, it is the absence of exertion or the presence of great exertion that determines the result in each respective case. (13–14)

Consequently, they would be constant performers of great vows (mahāvrata), such as [the consumption of] the urine and other excretions of lions, tigers, and so forth; therefore, there would be an abundance of hardships. Thus, the excellence of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) would be established within the context of these vows.
If greatness were to consist in the abundance of duties to be performed, then [the vow of] entering water, fire, and so forth would result in being greater than other vows;
yet there is no such rule that "this is small" and "that is great. (16–17)

The fruit described in the teaching shall indeed lead to great prosperity; just as the destruction of the great occurs through the small, so too does the destruction of the small occur through the small.
However, the destruction of grass by a tiny spark is clearly observed.
Ajāmila was known as the husband of a king’s maidservant;
having abandoned his lawful wife and constantly remaining on the path of sin,
while dying he called out the name of his son, "Nārāyaṇa."
Just as one attains a state so difficult to reach by merely uttering his name,
and just as fire burns when touched even against one's will,
so too does Govinda burn away [all sins] when his name is uttered even under a pretext. 21-22.

Ten thousand murders, a thousand curses, a thousand fierce acts, the violation of ten million teachers’ wives, and all manner of thefts—these are instantly destroyed by the name of Govinda, which is dear to Hari.
O Hero, whatever even the slightest act is performed, if it is permeated with devotion to Viṣṇu, [it becomes infinite]. 23.
A well-performed act done by a wise person shall yield inexhaustible fruit.
One should not entertain any doubt; by worshipping Mādhava with devotion during the month of Mādhava, a person shall obtain whatever they desire. 24–25.
Offspring, wealth, wives, mansions,
horses, elephants, happiness, heaven, and even liberation are not far off through devotion to Hari (26).
Thus, according to the rules prescribed in the scriptures, there is no doubt that [these results are attained] even by a small amount [of devotion].
Even great evil may be destroyed through the correct performance of rites;
O learned one, there may even be an increase in the fruit due to the excellence of intention and action.
The subtle movements of dharma are difficult to comprehend even for the gods.
This month of Mādhava is dear to the high-souled Ādhava; even alone, it bestows all desired objects throughout the three worlds.
A wise man, by some means, should be intent on bathing at the proper time and place with the meritorious water of the Gaṅgā.
"It is my view that even a donor who has been struck down by [evil] intentions since birth does not become pure.

Having kindled a fire sprinkled with ghee and oil, whose flames turn clockwise, one who is corrupted in intention and enters it at the proper time is indeed not attained to heaven, nor to any other fruit. (30-31)

The gods reside eternally at holy sites such as the Gaṅgā, and hosts of yakṣas dwell in temples; yet those who observe fasts while devoid of devotion go to destruction, and thus they do not obtain the fruit.
Therefore, having placed the glorious Mādhava within the lotus of one's heart with devotion during the month of Mādhava (Vaiśākha), [one attains the fruit].
One who is purified by being intent on bathing in the *Yajeta* [river] becomes pure; it is not possible for me to describe its merit.
O Lord of the Earth, listen to an ancient account regarding this very matter; I shall relate a wonderful story concerning the various fruits of actions.
By the grace of Mādhava and during the month of Mādhava,
even a certain unchaste Brāhmaṇa woman obtained an auspicious fruit. Long ago, there was a lord of Kāñcī renowned as Divodāsa.
Her offspring was a great jewel, always the most excellent among women (36). Endowed with virtue and beauty, well-behaved, lovely, and auspicious,
she was renowned as the divine goddess Divyādevī, peerless in form upon the earth (37).
Beheld by her father, endowed with beauty and grace, that divine daughter then appeared like a celestial goddess to the virtuous;
"To which noble and great-souled suitor shall this maiden be given? [he wondered].
Having become absorbed in these reflections, that best of men gazed about;
then the lord of the earth, having correctly identified the king of Rūpadeśa, the high-souled Citrasena, summoned him. 39–40.
Divodāsa gave his daughter to the wise Citrasena;
O King, when the time for her marriage had arrived,
that Citrasena indeed died according to the law of time.
Then the righteous King Divodāsa, O prince, began to reflect;
having summoned the Brāhmaṇas, he questioned them: "At the time of her marriage, Citrasena has departed for heaven. (42-43)
"What kind of karma will befall her? Tell me.
The Brahmin said:
"O King, the marriage of a maiden occurs according to the prescribed rites. (44)
A husband surely goes to death, or he who practices renunciation; having become terrified by great mental or physical illness, he departs after having made his renunciation.
O King, it is seen in the treatises on dharma that one may become a wandering mendicant (pravrājita).
And while she is in her menses, another husband is ordained for her.
The father, however, should perform the primary marriage ceremony; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, O King, has it been instructed in the Dharmaśāstra by auspicious people.
"Let her marriage be performed," said those best of the twice-born.
And the righteous King Divodāsa, urged by the brāhmaṇas, O King, made up his mind for the purpose of the wedding.
48. Thus did the great king prepare his mind for the marriage.
O best of kings, because of the failure to give back what had been given, the divine goddess Puṣpasenā, who was meritorious and high-souled, issued a command to him;
at that very moment of the wedding, the king fell subject to death.
Whenever the illustrious lord of the earth, being deeply distressed, makes an effort for the marriage of the divine goddess,
at that very time her husband also dies when the appointed moment arrives. 51.
Then, one after another, twenty-one husbands died in due course.
Thereupon, the king, renowned for his valor, became deeply distressed; gazing [upon the situation], he stood motionless and summoned his ministers. (52-53)

Then the lord of the earth made up his great mind for a *svayaṃvara* (self-choice marriage). Thereupon, many kings and various rulers, devoted to righteousness, were summoned by him for the sake of her *svayaṃvara*.
Agitated by her beauty, kings sent by Death waged war against that foolish woman;
O lord of men, thus the destruction of those kṣatriyas occurred. 55–56.
Then Divyādevī, afflicted by grief, wept piteously; and the king, beholding that young girl weeping and deeply distressed,
[addressed] the priest, who was a knower of dharma, possessed of wisdom, and an ascetic.
Having first bowed to Jātūkarṇa with his neck bent in humility,
Divodāsa said: "Tell me, by your grace, what was this man's sin?"
"O hero, I shall describe to you the conduct of that Divyādevī, my daughter, which has been performed.
Jātūkarṇa said:
"I shall indeed tell you of her conduct, O hero."
Listen as I relate everything done in my previous births.
There is a holy city named Vārāṇasī, which destroys all sins;
in that city lived one of great wisdom known by the name Suvīra.
Born into the Vaiśya caste, he was well-provided with wealth and grain;
his wife, named Citrā, was highly intelligent and very beautiful, yet she abandoned the family traditions and lived according to wicked conduct. 62.
She disregards her husband and engages in fierce deeds;
devoid of virtuous actions, that evil-minded woman commits sins. Always scolding her husband, she is an unchaste woman who delights in quarreling.
Constantly delighting in dwelling in the houses of others, she wanders about excessively;
she always perceives the faults of others and is ever wicked toward living beings.
Devoted to censuring the virtuous, that sinful woman is always prone to much laughter.
"Devoted to bad company,
speaking untruths, fond of people of evil conduct, deceitful, causing hatred among righteous people, and a speaker of falsehood—
having recognized her to be thus, O Suvīra, you should marry another woman after this one. (66–67)

Accompanied by his wife Anavīnaya, that hero constantly enjoyed sense-objects dear to the mind as he pleased; for he was a meritorious soul who always practiced righteous conduct and possessed a mind devoted to truth and virtue. 68.
Propitiated by Satyā, Amitā, Asatyā, and Sumati, he shone forth.
By him, that woman Citrā was cast out—she who was of variegated appearance, wanton, and a hater of the dharma resulting from the cultivation of virtues. (69–70)
One who is characterized by wandering and joined with the passion of old age, who has abandoned proper conduct and is overcome by shamelessness,
who is intent on sinful acts and devoid of affection— such a woman is skilled in the arts of a procuress and is superior to other women in the practice of such deeds. 71.
With a crooked mind intent on the ruin of the household and impurity,
she would summon a virtuous woman and incite her with sinful words— words intended as jests, ploys for gain, or playful banter, serving as causes for the arousal of doubt. 72–73.

She agitates the minds of wicked men and women; however, virtuous women who are destined for excellence bestow themselves upon others. She causes them to practice deceit and the abandonment of the village of Dharma.
Having thus enjoyed [pleasures] for a hundred years, she later lived according to the ways of a courtesan;
eventually meeting her death in the course of time, she who was constantly resolved upon evil was born as your daughter, this divine girl known as Devī.
"Endowed with a beautiful form, she was seen by him in the city and urged [to come].
Nārada said:
"Having heard these words of his, Divodāsa was greatly amazed."
The king spoke these sweet words to the sage Jātūkarṇa: Divodāsa said:
"If she is such as this—always engaged in the practice of evil and devoted to wicked conduct—then let her depart."

"How is it that a daughter worthy of me—whose deity is the Lord of Śrī and who am of noble lineage—has obtained this most difficult-to-attain and auspicious birth in a vast royal family? O holy sage, by what pure and wondrously varied karma was she, the performer of deeds, brought forth? (78–79)
Nārada said:
Having heard these words of the king, the wise sage then smiled slightly and spoke these truthful and pleasant words. 80.
Jātūkarṇa said:

Having practiced the drinking of poison for a time in the great and famous city of the Nāgas, she became a courtesan; there, through various and manifold amorous dalliances, she deceived hidden lovers and parasites who were destitute of wealth and intellect. (81)
A certain Brahmin, afflicted by distress and tormented by hunger, arrived there in the evening;
being bewildered and finding no other place in the city named Nāga, that pure-souled man went to the painted house (citrāgṛha). 82.

Utterly deluded by that courtesan through the power of her gaze, he was gratified by her massaging his feet, bathing him, offering betel, providing a seat, and serving food; thus, through her amorous charms, he too became free from all weariness. 83–84.
Then, served by her through various amorous attentions with a mind that had lost its discernment, the Brahmin,
greedy for the particularity of her passion, passed the entire night.
At dawn, as he was about to depart, his heart being deeply attached, he spoke these strange words to her with some difficulty.
Satisfied by her own conduct, her self-performed duties, and her words, she was then focused with one-pointed mind.
The Brahmin said:
"O beloved, since I have been satisfied by you, I must now perform a service in return."
I shall relate my own deep and personal suffering without omission.
(87) Listen with respect to that auspicious ancient tale told by Brahmins on the banks of the Narmadā, which destroys all sins. (88)
He who diligently bathes for even three days when the sun has entered Aries,
during the month of Mādhava before the sun has risen, is liberated from heaps of sins.
Furthermore, he who performs an external bath throughout the entire month of Vaiśākha [attains the same].
One should worship the god named Ādhava according to the prescribed rites; he too is a destroyer of sins.
(90) Especially by means of bathing, giving gifts, and other such acts at a holy pilgrimage site, a human being shall be liberated from great sins during the month of Mādhava. (91)
"A great accumulation of sin remains within the body of the embodied being without fear only so long as he does not joyfully bathe at dawn when the sun has risen over the mountain of rams.
Thus was I heard by me from those Brahmins as they were speaking.
It is the supreme boat for crossing the ocean of manifold misfortunes. That best of rivers is not far from the body of Śiva; I shall go there to bathe and to destroy the mass of my accumulated sins.
"If it pleases you, or if your mind has become dispassionate toward worldly things, then come with me for the sake of the Vaiśākha bath. This life is impermanent, and youth is exceedingly beautiful."
He would become an irresistible cause for dwelling in hell;
yet by you I have been propitiated and cast into the ocean of misfortune—truly, this is the nature of even great beings when they encounter wicked persons. 96–97.
"What is the use of much speaking here? There is no moment for delay. I shall rescue you as well, if there is detachment in your heart.
Citrā said:

"O Master, by the power of my unseen destiny (adṛṣṭa-yoga) and through the nature of our meeting with you, my mind has certainly become detached from this censurable worldly existence. Indeed, I have heard this very thing in the scriptures: that the company of the virtuous (sādhu-saṅgama)..."
"Salutations to the inconceivable one, and again to the one who is beyond all determination.
Jātūkarṇa said:
Having spoken thus, he then departed together with him toward Citrā.
Taking whatever wealth was available, she was urged by the sage;
thereafter, that twice-born man, being compassionate, immediately gave his own body for the sake of bathing the deity Śiva during the month of Vaiśākha, so that the Sun-god might bathe. 101–102.
Then this compassionate brahmin bathed Citrā, who spoke so wonderfully, according to the prescribed rites;
there, with great joy, he heard the majesty of the Vaiśākha bath. 103.
While the Brahmins were reciting the Purāṇas individually,
by the mere hearing of which the darkness of sin is destroyed,
just as the mass of gloom perishes at the rising of the sun. (104–105)

By bathing again according to the prescribed rite in the waters of the Śiva-Śivā (the Gaṅgā), which produce auspicious results, her mind became stainless; she shone forth as pure as the radiance of the sun.
There, devoted to the service of Hari, they immersed themselves in the river Revā.
In the month of Vaiśākha, those who desire the infinite light of the worlds perform various rites here at the Narmadā, which bestows happiness;
by doing so, even those of impure bodies purify themselves, especially during the month of Mādhava, and mortals become like the playful lords of the world of immortals. 107–108.

By the mere remembrance of her, even from birth, men destroy the sins born of ten lifetimes; moreover, one who has bathed here somehow destroys the sins born of a hundred births. Having served her, he attains the world of Rudra.
Furthermore, by [bathing] in the waters of the Narmadā during the entire month of Mādhava under the Citrā constellation...
He bathed and constantly gave some gift according to his ability to the Brahmins.
Through the association with those twice-born ones who were reciting there, he listened with faith to the hymn of Hari which removes all sins. 110-111.

Having immersed himself in the waters of the Revā on the full moon day of the month of Āśvina, that lord of the earth (Sudeva) performed the *acchidra-vrata* for the sake of the Brahmins according to the prescribed rites; there, too, he celebrated the month of Citrā.
Having constructed a new hut, that very Sudeva, who was like a god upon the earth, [continued his practice].
Immersed in the waters of the river Uvāsara and constantly moved by compassion due to his attachment to Citrā, he remained there.
Then, after some time, O King, that brahmin passed away; and Citrā, following him, died before long. 113–114.
Surely, by virtue of the merit she performed on that very day of the month of Mādhava,
she became your daughter, having not seen this suffering;
for such is the ripening of her karma that she has entered the family of a king.
O best of men, the divine goddess named Varā gave birth here to that Vaiṣṇava realm, which is pure and difficult for those of sinful deeds to attain;
she also bestowed upon it food, objects of enjoyment, happiness, and comforts. (116–117)
Although she was a courtesan, she associated with that Brahmin;
having bathed and sipped water during the month of Mādhava, she gave him something there as well.
She now enjoys the fruit arising from that gift and that ritual bathing. 118.
They drink cool water and likewise enjoy sweet food constantly;
partaking in divine pleasures, they dwell in the abode of the Lord,
yet they eat what is allotted by fate, afflicted as they are by misery, grief, and other torments.

This is the ripening of that karma which she previously committed by delighting in the destruction of the homes of men and women; now it has come upon her, yet without the torments of Yama, due to the greatness of the Mādhava-bath. 121.
Vīrasundarī became pregnant with a son despite having committed great sins.
All this—the conduct of your daughter throughout all her births, arising from both virtuous and wicked deeds—has been narrated to you. 122-123.
Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "The Story of Citrā," in the Vaiśākha-māsa-māhātmya of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
[Chapter Ninety-three]
Nārada said: Having heard these wonderful words of Jātūkarṇa, the king,
having offered salutations to that wise sage, spoke to him with reverence.
Divodāsa said:
"O sage, how might she now be released from this suffering?
Jātūkarṇa said:
We shall relate a great merit by which she may become happy; though it is generally not to be disclosed, I shall nevertheless speak it before you—
a wondrous deed, even if small, which destroys hundreds of misdeeds.
Just as all great evil is utterly destroyed by the power of meditation upon Hari,
so too does even the most terrible sin go to its dissolution through the morning bath and the gift of mādhava flowers.
Just as all the multitudes of serpents perish from the fear of Hari’s terror, so it is likewise here.
5. Indeed, when the sun has entered Aries, Hari shines forth through bathing at a sacred ford (tīrtha) and through hymns of praise.
6. Just as serpents flee at the sight of the splendor of Garuḍa, so certainly do sins flee away by means of the Vaiśākha bath at dawn.
Therefore, O King, even though she was to be given away, the divine queen herself, having performed the Vaiśākha-śravaṇa rite and heard the sin-destroying hymn,
shall become a partaker in the blissful enjoyment of union with her husband.
That powerful lord of the Pāṇḍya country is indeed born as Sudeva.
O King, by the merit of bathing in the Revā river during the month of Vaiśākha,
give your pure daughter to him, who has likewise purified himself through that bath.

O King, behold this wonder: by hearing the hymn of praise to Mādhava once again, no doubt should be entertained regarding the fruit of that meritorious deed, which is equal in both this world and the next. 10.
Nārada said:
Having heard all this that was thus spoken,
the king then had his daughter perform the rite as instructed by Jātūkarṇa.
Long ago, that divine lady was married by Vīrasena, the ruler of the Pāṇḍya country, who had been her sole friend since their previous birth;
having observed her vows well, she enjoyed manifold pleasures for a long time.
This has been related to you in brief by your friend Vīrasena, on account of what was performed in a previous birth;
this is the majesty of the Vaiśākha bath—what else do you wish to hear? 14–15.
Thus ends the ninety-third chapter, titled "The Narrative of Citrā," in the Vaiśākha-māsa-māhātmya of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
[Chapter Ninety-Four]
Ambarīṣa said:
O Lord, I wish to hear that hymn which pacifies sins, by the mere hearing of which a heap of sin is dissolved. 1.
I am blessed, I am favored, and I have been made to hear the auspicious rite,

by the mere hearing of which that which was acquired through evil deeds is destroyed. What wonder is there in this regarding the month of Mādhava, whose deity is Madhusūdana, and which is filled here with meritorious sacrifices?
The destruction of heaps of sins occurs through baths that are necessarily prescribed; yet the world of Him [is attained] even by the mere recitation of His name.

That which is called the name "Keśava" is indeed the supreme merit, the ultimate purifier, heart-pleasing, and obtainable in this world only through virtuous deeds; O wise one, I consider it auspicious in the month of Mādhava.
Blessed are those who remember the name of Madhava, the slayer of Madhu, during this month of Madhava; they shall again recount some of His pure and world-renowned deeds.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of the beloved of Hari, the sage was pleased with that best of kings; though eager for the ritual bath of Mādhava, he was captivated by the essence of the story of Mādhava.
Nārada said:

O King Satyamahīpāla, this pure practice of conversing with one another on the nectar of the stories of Mukunda is superior even to the ritual bathing prescribed for the month of Mādhava when performed together with you, whose deity is Hari— [you] whose life is for the sake of dharma, and whose dharma is solely for the sake of Hari.
(7) [And he] whose life is for the sake of dharma, and whose dharma is indeed for the sake of Hari.
O King, regarding the merit for the sake of which people on earth consider themselves Vaiṣṇavas day and night,
I shall tell you something of the fruit arising from the Vaiśākha bath;
even our father is not able to describe it in its entirety at length.
In the month of Mādhava, even by merely immersing themselves in the waters of the Narmadā, sinners attained liberation from the state of a preta; this was told by another brāhmaṇa who,
while wandering in connection with ancient holy sites, happened upon it.
He was renowned as Muniśarman, a righteous soul, truthful and pure; he was endowed with tranquility and self-restraint, possessed of forgiveness and contentment,
devoted to the rites for the ancestors, and observant of the injunctions of the Śruti and Smṛti.
He was skilled in sweet speech, devoted to the worship of Hari,

intent on the company of Vaiṣṇavas, a sage possessing knowledge of the three periods of time, delighting in his own duty, wise, compassionate, and impartial toward the pleasant and the unpleasant. 13.
Compassionate, exceedingly wise, a knower of reality, and fond of brāhmaṇas,
he was traveling toward the Revā river in the month of Mādhava for the purpose of bathing when he saw five men before him who were in extreme distress. 14–15.

Seeing those dark-complexioned figures seated together, having taken refuge in the shade of a banyan tree and remaining there without interacting with one another, their minds were agitated by sin as they looked in all directions. 16.
Beholding them, the best of the twice-born was struck with wonder and reflected:
"Here in this forest, these men, terrified and acting dejectedly, appear to have joined with thieves of hideous form. (17-18)
While they were thus conversing with one another— emaciated and possessing the dark luster of Kṛṣṇa’s body— the wise and foremost of Brahmins reflected in this manner;
at that very moment, they all approached the sage from afar with great reverence.
Having joined their palms in reverence and bowed down, they spoke clearly as follows.
The five men said:
"O Blessed One, you are a supreme person, resplendent and worthy of honor for your conduct."
We consider you to be the foremost among the compassionate, for you are friendly upon hearing our words.

(21) The virtuous are destroyers of the distress of those who are suffering—such as those whose wealth and status have been lost through fate or who have become sinners—and they do so merely by their presence. (22)
"I am a Kṣatriya from the land of Pañcāla named Vīravāhana;
out of delusion, I killed a Brāhmaṇa with a sound-aimed arrow.
Deprived of my topknot and sacred thread, and bereft of my sectarian mark," so he said.

Wandering over this entire earth while declaring, "I am a slayer of a Brahmin," I have come here after roaming through all the sacred fords (tīrthas), saying to the most sinful slayers of Brahmins, "Let alms be given to me. 24–25.
"O best of sages, even the sin of killing a Brahmin perishes;
thus, O Lord, one year passed for me as I performed this, while being consumed by sin and my mind overwhelmed with grief. (26)
"O twice-born one, this other brahmin who is seen here, Candraśarman, is a slayer of his guru, O Brahmin, his mind being agitated by delusion;
because his heart is overwhelmed by delusion, he is called a killer of his guru. (27-28)
O Sage, having been abandoned by his own kinsmen while living in the Magadha country, he too, wandering about by the turn of fate, arrived here;
though devoid of the topknot and sacred thread, he was nevertheless stripped of the marks of a Brahmin.
Though not questioned by me, the brahmin spoke the entire account exactly as it was;
he related how, while living in the house of his guru with a mind agitated by anger and overcome by great delusion, he had indeed slain his guru.
Burned by that evil deed, he wanders about, tormented by grief.
Furthermore, O Master, this third one, Vedaśarman, was once composed and focused;
yet, through delusion and association with a courtesan, he became a Brāhmaṇa who drank liquor.

Questioned by me, he, afflicted with mental anguish and cast out by all the world, as well as by his wife and kinsmen, related to me everything regarding his own conduct exactly as it had occurred. 33–34.
Smeared with that sin, wandering about, this man has come here; he is a Vaiśya named Vidhura, the fourth [in this group], who violated his guru’s bed.
Out of delusion, for as long as three months, he treated his mother as a prostitute.

Then, having realized the truth, he wandered through the land of Videha and enjoyed himself; thereafter, wandering again, that miserable man returned to this earth. This fifth person is a great sinner who associates with the wicked.
Day after day, out of greed for wealth, he committed sins such as theft; overcome by these great crimes, the Vaiśya was himself abandoned by his people.
With a despondent mind, he happened by chance to meet a man named Nandana.
Thus, all five of those most wicked ones came together to one place.
O highly fortunate one, O best of the twice-born, not one of them would have any contact with another—whether through food, clothing, or otherwise—except for conversation. 39–40.

They enter together upon a single seat and do not sleep upon a single bed; thus, O best of sages, those who have gone to various sacred fords (tīrthas) are overcome by suffering, yet our terrible sin does not depart.
Seeing you shining thus, their minds became serene;
they said, "O holy one, by the sight of your merit, the end of our misfortunes has come. O Lord, please tell us the means by which our sins may indeed be destroyed."
O Lord, we recognize you as compassionate toward us—toward these brahmins who know the meaning of the Vedas, who are distressed, seeking [a way out], and have fallen into remorse;
you are certainly the one who will deliver us from the sins acquired through delusion. 44.
Nārada said: Having heard their words, the sage Muniśarman,
an ocean of compassion, reflected upon this and then spoke as follows.
Muniśarman said:
"Since you have incurred sin through ignorance yet speak the truth and are filled with remorse, you should now be shown favor by me."
Listen to my true words; with arms upraised, I speak them.
(47) That which was previously heard by me in the assembly of sages from Aṅgiras, as well as seen in the Vedas and Śāstras, and likewise heard from the mouth of my guru—(48)
In the beginning, this was spoken in its true essence by Viṣṇu himself when he was propitiated:
"There is no satisfaction other than that from food; there is no teacher greater than one's father.
There is no vessel superior to the Brahmins, and no god higher than Keśava. (49)

There is no holy ford equal to the Nāgaṅgā; there is no gift equal to that of Surabhī. There is no recitation of mantras equal to the Gāyatrī; there is no vow equal to that of the Dvādaśī. There is no friend equal to a wife; there is nothing equal to the arising of righteousness (dharma).
There is no stage of life superior to the householder’s state for attaining happiness equal to independence;
there is no conduct higher than truth, and no happiness greater than contentment.
There is no month equal to Mādhava (Vaiśākha) as a supreme remover of great sins.
When performed with devotion according to the prescribed rite, this [rite] is dear to Madhusūdana;
it is especially difficult to attain even at sacred fords such as the Gaṅgā. All expiations, beginning with those lasting twelve years, [are surpassed by it]. 53–54.
Sins roar only so long as Mādhava has not arrived; [but for him] who,
devoted to Hari, bathes throughout the entire month of Vaiśākha in the water originating from the feet of Hari, his heart becomes pure.
He alone is seen by sinners as the destroyer of all evils;
indeed, the Kinnaras must declare that he is the very expiation for the flood of their own sins. For he who bathes during this month known as Vaiśākha is truly liberated from all sins.
Now that the sun is situated in Aries, the waters of the Narmadā—which bestow happiness and ward off sin—are difficult to obtain everywhere during the month of Mādhava.
Even more difficult to obtain than those are the Gaṅgā, Revā, and Yamunā. 58–59.

"Among these three [months], he who bathes with devotion even in one of them during the month of Mādhava becomes free from sin and shall go to Hari. Therefore, oh, what a wonder! You two have come to the Revā river during the month of Vaiśākha, which is the singular essence of all meritorious deeds."
"Even for one who has committed the sin of drinking liquor, the water of this river—frequented by hosts of sages—is sufficient to remove the fear of all sins.
(61) Having been addressed thus, they all then departed with the sage, joyful and praising the Revā, the performer of wonders, as far as the portion belonging to the two sinners. (62)
Then Muniśarman, proceeding along with those men following him, saw on the path eight terrifying piśācas,
who were wandering here and there while uttering various cries. (63)
Seeing those with upstanding hair, upward-pointing red eyes, black teeth, and emaciated bellies—
running toward him in a forest overrun by thorns and devoid of trees or water— with his mind agitated by fear, [he spoke]. (64-65)
"Salutation to Nārāyaṇa! Protect us, protect us! he cried out.

(66) Hearing this high-sounding name "Salutation to Nārāyaṇa," which is the singular treasury of Dharma, those ghosts—who had been obtained by the power of their own past karma—vanished even from his mind in another birth. (67)

Seeing them, Muniśarman, whose mind was endowed with discipline and who spoke sweetly, said: "Who are you, deformed men? What deed has been committed by whom that you have come to this state of deformity? (68)
"How is it that all these beings are thus suffering, so exceedingly terrifying? (69) The pretas replied:
"We are constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst, agitated by a multitude of various miseries."

With our intellects destroyed and cruel hearts, our senses lost and our minds bewildered, we did not know the directions; we were like deluded men-slayers. This is what has been described as suffering, and this indeed is misery once again.
Upon hearing your soft voice loudly uttering "Nārāyaṇa," it was as if dawn had broken at the sight of the rising sun;
and having seen you, O Brahmin, we have attained a state of pure being.
"O Brahmin, by the mere sight and hearing of the name of Hari, we have attained this other birth as compassionate ones;
it destroys ill-repute and clarifies the intellect. (73-74)
For the most part, the Vaiṣṇava doctrine establishes itself among men;
I am named Paryuṣita, this second one is Sūcaka, another is Śīghraga, Rodhaka is yet another, and this fifth is Lekhaka. 75.
"This sixth one is corrupted by speech; this seventh is presided over by the Viśvedevas (76).
And this eighth, who causes constant suffering, is a performer of sacrifices.
Muniśarman said:

"Whence come the names of you *pretas* born of your own karma? With what cause in view do you possess these names? I have always eaten what was delicious, yet I gave stale food to the twice-born (78).
While clarified butter was available, I offered it without ghee; because of that, I have become one who is subject to decay.
By nature, I am a seeker of faults and vital secrets in others, and that too is false, false (79).
Because he had thus betrayed him, that informer— impure and afflicted— perished quickly when entreated by the agitated Brahmin;
O best of the twice-born, this was the reason for his swift destruction.
This wicked man, who ate delicious food alone in the assembly hall above the house with an evil mind, is known as Raudhaka;
though he always remains in silence, he scratches the earth with his foot. 81–82.
Even for us, this most wicked scribe is associated with the world;
he hates the virtues of the virtuous, yet perceives the presence of virtue in the meritless.
He is ignorant of consciousness yet claims to be a yogi of knowledge; therefore, he is remembered as one whose speech is corrupt.

Due to his state of atheism, he constantly fails to honor his ancestors, deities, and men (84). Devoid of gods, he does not respect virtuous deeds; he is always a beggar, a liar, and one who displays his own miserable condition as false (85).
This man was once a beggar who caused agitation and was greedy for gain;

having experienced the torments of hell due to these previously committed sins, we have now been reborn as hungry ghosts (pretas), yet by the mere sight of him today, we have become well-established once more. 86.
"All this has been narrated to you, arising from my own life's history.
If you have faith in the question you asked, I shall tell you something else.
The Brahmin said:

"All living beings that exist are rooted in food. [Yama said: "I also wish to hear about your food from you. The pretas replied: 88. "All living beings that exist are rooted in food. We also wish to hear about your food from you.
The pretas said:
Listen to our food, which is despised by all beings;
hearing of which, O Brahmin, you will surely and constantly revile it again and again—[food] consisting of phlegm, urine, excrement, and the impurities of a woman's body. (89–90)
In that place, they indeed eat those things which have been abandoned as impure,
including women who have been cremated, scattered items, and scattered iron filings (91).
There, the deceased eat even these contemptible and filthy things.
Where they do not worship Mādhava, where households are ruled by women, where there is a lack of compassion and forbearance—there the deceased spirits feast.
Where there are inauspicious words in the home and where the women are devoid of purity. (92–93)
Where there is constant quarreling, there the pretas eat;
where sisters-in-law are not honored in the house, there we shall eat. Where there is association with the wicked, there we shall eat.
Where there is no service to Hari, nor any talk concerning Viṣṇu;
where there is no love for Viṣṇu—there the pretas (ghosts) eat.
But in whosever house they are thus pleased, even they eat with haste.

Through such evil, they become hungry ghosts who bring about the destruction of their own lineage; O Brahmin, as I speak, my own food vanishes. Nothing else more sinful than this can possibly be said.
"Disgusted with my state as a preta, I ask you, who are firm in your vows:
how is it that one is not born again as a preta, and how is there liberation from the condition of being a preta?
The Brāhmaṇa said:
By meritorious vows such as Ekādaśī, by chanting the praises of Acyuta,
by the worship of deities and guests, as well as by the worship of gurus and other such practices,
and by days spent in conduct practiced by the virtuous as prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti; 99–100.
Thus, by means of ancestral rites and gifts performed according to the rules,
and through compassion, charity, self-restraint, patience, virtuous conduct, and saluting the learned—
by such dharmas as these, they indeed cause the deceased to attain a high state within their own family.

He who, being humble toward his kinsmen, repeatedly pays homage to cows, brahmins, sacred fords, the supreme mountain Amaraparvata, rivers, streams, and the Aśvattha tree—such a person certainly does not become a preta in this world;
rather, being disciplined, that man gradually worships them with particular distinction. 102–103.
The merit of that person at holy pilgrimage sites such as the Gaṅgā is infinite;
even the omnipresent Lord himself would not be able to describe it in thousands of years.
Merely by the sight of him, one shall be liberated from the state of a preta.
The month of Ūrja, the month of Ūrjasvala, and the one dear to Dāmodara;
the supreme month of austerities, the month of austerity, and the one beloved by Mādhava; the month of Vaiśākha, the month of Mādhava, and that which has Madhusūdana as its presiding deity. (105–106)
The sages know this one month to be the best of all months, by means of which alone every rite is accomplished;
it is considered the knowledge of Brahman, and that Lakṣmī, the creator of the universe, is attained through it. 107.

Since Mādhava is his abode, he is therefore remembered as Māsa (the month). Just as it is certain that no god among the gods is equal to Mādhava, so too among all months, no month is as dear to Mādhava as Māsa. 108–109.

By hearing with devotion even the greatness of that month of Mādhava, one is liberated from the state of being a ghost; how much more so by conversing with the virtuous or by resorting to holy pilgrimage sites! 110.
By reciting the name "Nārāyaṇa" or even by hearing it,
a person devoted to bhakti is liberated from all sins.
I shall strive for this so that you, though currently ghosts, may also attain liberation.
Since merit born from helping others cannot be attained even through sacrifices,
one should therefore bathe in the waters of the Revā during the month of Mādhava,
when the sun is situated in Aries, accompanied by these men. 113.
Furthermore, these five, having accumulated a mass of sins through delusion,
come here to bathe solely by the command of me, the compassionate one.
Therefore, you all should remain right there in that forest, free from sorrow, according to my instruction.

Having gone to the waters of the Śrī Narmadā and setting aside his own ritual bathing, he was bound by compassion, thinking: "I shall cause even men who have not performed their rites to immerse themselves here in the Narmadā during the days of the month of Mādhava according to the prescribed rule. (116-117)
"Thus, by merely bathing as a *darbha*-boy for three days, your liberation from the state of a ghost will occur; of this there is no doubt. Nārada said:

Having been addressed thus, Muniśarman was honored by them as they were pleased; then, followed by those five, he departed. Having gone there, he then bathed at dawn and performed the prescribed rites.
He caused those deceased spirits to be bathed by name using [water] prepared with darbha grass.
When remembered by the sage and thus bathed at the sacred ford, those meritorious spirits were immediately liberated and went to heaven.
Even those five sinners, submerged in the water at the command of the Lord, instantly became as radiant as pure gold, their previously discolored bodies transformed in that very month of Śrī Mādhava.
[122] This hymn for the pacification of sins was recited by Muniśarman.

In the presence of all the worlds, those of most excellent beauty were born there; O lord of kings, the humans dwelling there do not touch those who are free from passion (virajas) even by the mere act of bathing, for they harbor no fear of contact with the sinful.
Then, at the request of Muniśarman and according to the authority of the Dharma, a divine voice immediately spoke:
"These people shall be freed from sin, having bathed in the month of Mādhava with their hearts fixed on Mukunda. (125)
For those who listen here with reverence to this hymn that pacifies evil, what wonder is there that purification arises from the accumulation of sins?
This is the supreme atonement for all evils whatsoever. (126–127)
Because of that immersion in the sacred ford with devotion during the month of Mādhava at dawn,
those sinful ghosts were liberated by that meritorious one, Muniśarman, merely by being remembered. 128–129.
Having thus heard those most wonderful words from the sky, the men immediately praised these five meritorious ones, as well as the month of Vaiśākha, the sage, and the river Carmanvatī.
Then the king, having heard that hymn which destroys all sins, [proceeded].
Upon hearing this with devotion, a person is liberated from heaps of sins.
Merely by hearing it, sinners have attained purification, and many others have been freed from the sins born of ignorance. 131–132.
When the minds of men engage in such acts as adultery, the theft of others' property, and violence toward living beings, then praise [of the deity] serves as their atonement:
"To Viṣṇu, to Viṣṇu, always to Viṣṇu, salutation to Viṣṇu. (133)
I bow to Viṣṇu, to Hari who resides in the mind and has entered into the ego;
134 To the Lord residing in the mind, the unmanifest, the infinite, the unconquered, the adorable Viṣṇu of all beings, the pervasive one without beginning or end. 135
That Viṣṇu who has entered my heart, that Viṣṇu who has entered my intellect,
that Viṣṇu who is within my ego, and that Viṣṇu who is established in me— he,
acting as the agent, creates all that is moving and stationary.
That sin goes to destruction as soon as he is thought of.
I bow down to that beloved Upeṃdra Mahāviṣṇu, who, when meditated upon or seen even in a dream, removes whatever sin exists. 137–138.
In this world which is without support, I salute Madhusūdana, the infallible Acyuta, Viṣṇu, the Supreme beyond the supreme, as my hand-held support—
O Lord of the lords of all, O All-pervading One, O Supreme Self, O Adhokṣaja! 139
O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Hṛṣīkeśa, salutations to you!
140 O Nṛsiṃha, Ananta, Govinda, Bhūtabhāvana, Keśava; may whatever was ill-spoken, ill-done, or ill-thought be pacified; salutations to you! 141

O Keśava, O God of the Brahmins, O Govinda, O supreme refuge of the ultimate truth, please bring to rest that wicked, most terrible sin and improper act which was conceived by me while under the sway of my own mind. 142.
O Jagannātha, O Creator of the World, O Acyuta, pacify my sin—
whatever sin has been committed by me through body, mind, or speech, whether unknowingly during the afternoon, the evening, midday, or at night. 143–144.
O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Puṇḍarīkākṣa, O Mādhava,
by the utterance of these three names, let all my sins go to destruction;
O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Puṇḍarīkākṣa, may my body and mind be purified.
O Mādhava, may the evil committed by my speech be pacified.
Whatever sin I have committed for the sake of wealth—with body, mind, or speech—while eating, drinking, standing, sleeping, waking, or remaining engaged in activity; [may it be pacified].

May even that great or small sin, which generally leads to rebirth in evil wombs or hell, be pacified by the chanting of the name of Vāsudeva. (148) He is the Supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, and that which is most pure.
When that Viṣṇu has been thus glorified, may whatever sin exists be utterly destroyed.
May that very state of Viṣṇu— which the wise, devoid of smell, touch, and other sensations, reach and from which they do not return— bring all this to peace.
The person who recites or hears this hymn for the pacification of sins is liberated from the evils committed through body, mind, and speech;
freed from malevolent planets and other afflictions, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. 151.

Therefore, for the sake of purifying evil deeds, the *japya* hymn that crushes all sins should be recited by the best of men as an atonement for floods of transgressions; through such excellent hymns of atonement and vows, sin is destroyed. 152–153.

Therefore, O Lord of Men, for the sake of accomplishing one's tasks, or indeed for the sake of worldly enjoyment and liberation, the sins accumulated in previous births as well as those of this life are dissolved instantly by listening to this hymn. (154)
O King, this hymn of praise— which is an axe to the tree of evil, a forest fire to the fuel of sin, and a sun to the mass of darkness that is the heap of wickedness—
has been revealed by me to you out of compassion for the world. 155-156.

O lord of men, even Hari himself would be unable to describe the merit and majesty of that person who listens to this holy history (itihāsa), which I have respectfully received as a secret from my father.
"May you be well, O Great King! I am going quickly to bathe in the Gaṅgā;
this great month of Āṣāḍha has arrived.

Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Pacification of Sin," within the Narrative of the Preta, in the Vaiśākha-māhātmya, in the dialogue between Nārada and Ambarīṣa, in the Pātāla-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The ninety-fifth chapter.
Sūta said:
O King, then, with joy, [the sage] bowed to him who was prepared to depart.
He asked about the concise procedure appropriate for the rites of bathing and giving gifts.
Ambarīṣa said:
"O Sage, what is the ritual in this month of Vaiśākha, and what is the superior austerity?"
Furthermore, O Brahmin-sage, please tell me out of compassion: what is the gift, how is the bath performed, and how is the worship of Keśava conducted? O beloved of Hari, you are omniscient;
therefore, explain specifically the procedure for worship at Tīrthapada.
Nārada said: O best of beings, during the month of Mādhava, when the sun enters Aries,
at a great river, on a riverbank, in a land, or by a spring— 4.

Or, having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Madhu, one should bathe in a natural pool, or in whatever reservoir of water is available— such as a long pond, a well, or a large tank— while self-restrained and remembering Hari.
On the fifteenth day, or even during the transit of the sun into Aries,
one should perform the vow for the Vaiśākha bath preceded by a thorough ritual bath, having worshipped Madhusūdana with the permission of Brāhmaṇas.

"Throughout the entire month of Vaiśākha, when the sun is in Aries, I shall bathe at dawn with my observances; may Madhusūdana be pleased. By the grace of the Slayer of Madhu and through the favor of the brāhmaṇas..."
May my daily meritorious Vaiśākha bath be free from obstacles.
O Mādhava, O Murāri, O Madhusūdana, when the sun is in Aries, grant me, through this morning bath, the fruits as they have been described. 9–10.
"O Madhusūdana, just as this month of Mādhava is dear to you,
may you, the bestower of fruits and destroyer of sins, become so through this morning bath.
Having recited this at that sacred ford and having washed his feet while restraining his speech—
Remembering the god Nārāyaṇa, one should perform the ritual bath according to the prescribed rules.
The wise man should prepare the sacred bathing site (tīrtha) while reciting this root mantra:
"Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya. This is declared to be the root mantra. 12–13.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules, with darbha grass in hand and bowing down upon the ground,
a person should prepare a square space measuring four cubits on all sides and invoke Gaṅgā with this mantra: 14.

Born from the foot of Viṣṇu, the Vaiṣṇavī [weapon], whose deity is Viṣṇu—protect us from that sin which begins at birth and ends with death! Vāyu has declared that there are thirty-five million sacred fords (tīrthas). 15–16.
O Jāhnavī, those [names] exist in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space;
in the Vedas, they are known as Nandinī and also as Nalinī. You are Dakṣā, Pṛthvī, Vihagā, Viśvagāthā, and Śivapriyā.
Vidyādharī, Mahādevī, as well as Lokaprasādinī,
Kṣemaṃkarī, Jāhnavī, Śāntā, and Śāntipradāyinī—
one should recite these auspicious names at the time of bathing. (18–19)
O King, the Ganges, which flows through the three paths, becomes present there when one places water joined in the hollow of the palms— over which the mantra has been recited seven times—
upon the head four, five, or seven times.
Having performed his bath with earth in the same manner, he should address it according to the prescribed rite:
"O Earth, traversed by horses, traversed by chariots, and traversed by Viṣṇu; O Clay, take away my sin, whatever evil deed has been committed by me. (21-22)

"Salutations to you, O Goddess of excellent vows, the source and progenitor of all the worlds, who were raised up by Viṣṇu in his form as the Boar with a hundred arms. Having bathed in this manner, one should thereafter perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the prescribed rules.
Having risen, one should cause him to put on two pure white garments. Then, for the sake of nourishing the three worlds, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa),
first offering it to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Prajāpati.
Gods, yakṣas, as well as nāgas, gandharvas, apsarases, and asuras;
cruel serpents, suparṇas, trees, indeed all creatures, and birds;
vidyādharas, cloud-bearers, and likewise those who travel through the sky.
For those living beings who are without support and those who are devoted to sinful deeds, I offer this water for their nourishment.
A man should wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītī*) when offering to the gods, and over the right shoulder (*nivītī*) when offering to humans. (27–28)
One should satisfy humans with devotion, as well as the sons of Brahmā and the sages:
Sanaka, Sanaṃdana, and the third, Sanātana;
Kapila, Āsuri, Voḍhu, and likewise Pañcaśikha.
May they all find constant satisfaction with the water offered by me:
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada. 30–31.

One should satisfy all the gods, Brahmanical sages, and others with water and unbroken grains (akṣata). Then, one should perform the rite with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), placing the left knee upon the ground. [One should offer to] the Agniṣvātta, Saumya, Haviṣmat, and Uṣmapā ancestors.
Likewise, one should again satisfy with devotion the Kavya-analas, the Barhishads, and the Ajyapas with water mixed with sesame seeds and sandalwood paste;
and [one should offer] to Yama, Dharmaraja, Mrityu, and Antaka.
Salutations to Vaivasvata, to Kāla, to the destroyer of all beings, to Udumbara, to Dadhna, to Nīla, and to Parameṣṭhin; salutations indeed to Vṛkodara, to Citra, and to Citragupta.
Then, with *darbha* grass in hand, he should duly satisfy the ancestors;
having satisfied all of them, including the father and others by name and lineage, as well as the maternal grandfathers, according to the prescribed rule, he should recite this mantra: 36–37.
"May those who were my kinsmen or not my kinsmen, and those who were my kinsmen in another birth— whoever desires water from me— attain complete satisfaction.
(38) Having sipped water according to the rule, one should properly draw a lotus in front.
One should diligently offer the *argha* with unbroken grains, flowers, water, and red sandalwood, while reciting the names of the Sun:
"Salutations to you who have the form of Viṣṇu; salutations to you whose form is Brahmā. (39-40)

Salutations to the thousand-rayed Sun; salutations to you, the embodiment of all splendor. Salutations to you, O Rudra, whose form is majestic; salutations to you, O lover of your devotees. Salutations be to Padmanābha, adorned with earrings and armlets.
Salutations to you, the Lord of all worlds, who awakens those who sleep.
You always behold all good and evil deeds; O God of Truth, salutations to you, O Bhāskara, be gracious to me. 42–43.
"Obeisance to you, O Maker of Day; obeisance to you, O Maker of Light.
Having thus paid homage to the Sun and circumambulated him seven times, and having touched a twice-born man, a cow, and gold, one should then proceed to one's own home.
Then, having honored those residing in the hermitages, one should also worship the images;
O King, a householder who has restrained his self should first worship Govinda with devotion, and then worship both [the images and the ascetics] according to the rules. 45–46.
Especially in the month of Vaiśākha, whoever worships Madhusūdana,
by him Mādhava has been worshipped for the duration of an entire year. When the month of Mādhava has arrived, while the Sun, the witness of all actions, is situated in Aries (Meṣa).
For the pleasure of Keśava, one should perform the collection of Keśava-vows;
one should also give various gifts, such as sesame seeds and clarified butter, which bring an end to the sins accumulated over ten million lifetimes. 48–49.
Gifts such as water, food, sugar, a cow, sesame seeds, and a "sesame-cow" (tiladhenu) should be given according to one's wealth for the attainment of desired goals.
One who has conquered the senses should perform daily ablutions throughout the entire month of Vaiśākha.
One who eats only *haviṣya* food in the month of Mādhava is liberated from all sins.
Furthermore, he who, free from sloth, observes eating once a day, or eating only at night, or eating only what is unasked for during the month of Mādhava, obtains everything he desires. (51-52)

In the month of Vaiśākha, one should perform two baths according to the prescribed rite outside [the home] in rivers and other such places; observe the consumption of sacrificial food (haviṣya), celibacy, sleeping on the ground, and adherence to the rules of discipline;
and practice vows, charity, recitation of mantras (japa), fire-offerings (homa), and the worship of Madhusūdana.
It burns away even the terrible sins arising from thousands of births; just as Mādhava destroys evil when meditated upon,
so too does a bath performed according to the rules during the month of Mādhava.

One should perform daily bathing at a sacred ford (tīrtha), the libation for the ancestors with sesame seeds, the giving of "Dharma-pots" and other gifts, and the worship of Madhusūdana during the month of Mādhava; this brings satisfaction to Madhusūdana. (56)
One should give sesame seeds, water, gold, food, sugar, garments, ornaments,
sandals, an umbrella, a water-pot, and other gifts to the twice-born; and with devotion, one should worship the Lord Madhusūdana at the three junctions of the day.
With a concentrated mind, one who is endowed with the goddess Vimalālaksmyi in person should satisfy many Brahmins according to his capacity with vessels of gold and sesame seeds,
as well as with vessels of water; such a person destroys even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Having bathed in the morning in a river during the month of Vaiśākha with a concentrated mind,
and having worshipped Hari with devotion using flowers and fruits produced in season, one should— avoiding conversation with heretics— worship a Brāhmaṇa according to one's ability.
One should gratify [the deity] with gifts of clothing, cows, jewels, and stores of wealth;
or otherwise, according to one's ability, one should practice this little by little. Afterwards, when the man has become destitute, he should worship Mādhava in the month of Mādhava.
One should worship Madhusūdana according to the prescribed rite of flower-offering;
liberated from all sins, one shall deliver a hundred ancestors and shall not experience the fruit of sorrow for hundreds of thousands of births.
He shall have no fear of disease, nor poverty, nor imprisonment;
For that long, O hero, he shall dwell in heaven and then become a king once more.
Having enjoyed various pleasures as a king according to his desire, he shall then merge into Mādhava through the grace of Mādhava.
Listen, O King, I shall describe in brief the worship of Mādhava—
whether Vedic, Tantric, or mixed— which destroys all sins.
For there is no end to this worship-rite, O King, whose boundaries are limitless.
Now, it shall be stated briefly and correctly in due order:
the sacrifice to Śrī Viṣṇu is threefold—Vedic, Tantric, and Mixed.
One should worship Hari according to whichever of these three methods one desires. 70.
The Vedic [initiation] is prescribed for the Brahmins and others,
while the Tantric is proclaimed even for a Śūdra who is a devotee of Viṣṇu.
Just as it has been stated in one's own Veda, a person, having attained the status of the twice-born, [should proceed].

A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī), being composed, should worship Viṣṇu according to the prescribed rules. He should worship Him on the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), in the fire, in the sun, in water, in the heart, or in a Brahmin, with materials offered with devotion; and by His permission, he should likewise worship his own guru.

First, one should perform the bath with cleansed teeth for the purification of the limbs; both [the teacher and the disciple] should likewise perform the bath with mantras, beginning with the application of clay (74). Indeed, the rites such as the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsti) are proclaimed in the Vedas and Tantras.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should properly form a resolve that purifies the ritual action.
An image is said to be of eight kinds: made of stone, wood, metal, plaster, painting, sand, mind, or gemstone. 75–76.
The consecration (pratiṣṭhā) of the temple of the living soul is of two kinds: mobile and immobile.

In the worship of Mādhava, the rite of dismissal (udvāsana) and invocation (āvāhana) are omitted in the case of a stationary [image]. In the case of a non-stationary [image], there is an option; however, in the case of a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), both rites should be performed.
Bathing is prescribed for images that are not made of clay; for others, it is merely wiping.
Worship with well-known materials should be performed by one free from deceit toward the deities, their images, and so forth, using whatever is available and with a spirit of devotion. 78–79.
O King, bathing and adorning [the deity] is the most excellent for worship in an image;
likewise, for worship on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), it is the ritual placement [of the deities], and for fire-worship, it is the offering of oblations of clarified butter.
For the Sun, worship with water and other offerings upon a sacrificial mound is the most excellent.
O Hara, even water offered with faith by a devotee is most excellent;
how much more so then perfumes, incense, flowers, lamps, food, and other offerings?
Being pure and having prepared the necessary materials, one should first arrange a seat made of darbha grass.
Seated facing either east or north, or facing the image during worship,

having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), he should touch with his hand the image of Hari upon which the nyāsa has been performed. He should then duly prepare the water-pot (kalaśa) and the sprinkling-water (prokṣaṇīya).
Having sprinkled the sacrificial ground for the gods and oneself with those waters (verse 84), one should place the three vessels with their respective substances;
one should provide three vessels for the purpose of the foot-water, the guest-offering, and the water for sipping. 85.
One should consecrate the *piṇḍas* with the *Gāyatrī* mantra, whose head and crest have been removed;

then, within the *piṇḍa* perfected by the wind and fire, one should meditate upon the subtle particle of the Lord’s life-force (*jīvakalā*), which resides in the heart-lotus and is realized at the end of the *nāda*. 86.

Having pervaded the image with that [deity] who has become one's own self, and having worshipped it as being composed of that essence (tanmaya), one should invoke [the deity] into the icons and other objects, establish it, and worship it through the placement of the limbs (nyastāṅga).
One should then present the ritual services (upacāra) such as water for the feet, the arghya offering, the bath, and the respectful salutation (arhaṇa). 87–88.
Having fashioned a seat for Hari with the nine [syllables] beginning with *dharma*, one should place there an eight-petaled lotus, radiant with its pericarp and filaments;
by means of both the Vedas and the Tantras, this is for the attainment of both goals for Hari.

One should worship Sudarśana, Pāñcajanya, the mace, the sword, the bow, the plow, the pestle, the Kaustubha gem, the garland, and the Śrīvatsa mark; as well as Nanda, Sunanda, Garuḍa, Pracaṇḍa, and Caṇḍa. 90–91.
One should worship Mahābala, Bala, Kumuda, Kumudekṣaṇa,
Durgā, Vināyaka, Vyāsa, Viṣvaksena, the gurus, and the gods,
facing them in their respective places with sprinkling and other rites.

One should daily bathe [the deity] with waters scented with sandalwood, uśīra, camphor, saffron, and agallochum, using mantras, or whenever possible, with the *Svarṇadharmānuvāka* and the *Mahāpuruṣavidyā*. 93–94.

A devotee of Viṣṇu, filled with love, should appropriately adorn [the deity] with the Pauruṣa Sūkta, Sāmans, the Nīrājana rite, and so forth, as well as with garments, sacred threads, ornaments, leaf-plates, garlands, perfumes, and ointments. (95)
The worshipper, with faith, should offer water for the feet, water for sipping, fragrance, flowers, and unbroken grains; likewise, perfumes, incense, and various offerings,
as well as jaggery, milk-porridge, clarified butter, fried cakes, flour-cakes, and sweetmeats.
One should offer milk-rice, curd, and ghee as the sacrificial food (naivedya), along with various other offerings;
daily there should be oil-baths, massages, the viewing of mirrors, cleansing the teeth, ceremonial ablutions, food and drink, dance, and song. 98.

Having established the fire in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) constructed according to the prescribed rules, complete with its girdle, circular path, and altar, one should sprinkle water around it with the hand; then,
having strewn grass around it, sprinkled water again, and offered fuel according to the rule— 99–100.

Having set out the materials for sprinkling with the *prokṣaṇī* water, one should sprinkle the clarified butter (*ājya*) with that same *prokṣaṇī* water. [One should meditate on the Lord] who resembles molten gold, possessing four arms shining with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus; who is peaceful, and whose garment is the filaments of a lotus. 101.
Meditating upon Him who possesses a shimmering crown, bracelets, a waist-band, and excellent armlets; whose chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark and the radiant Kaustubha gem;
and who wears a garland of forest flowers—one should worship Him with offerings of wood, oblations, and clarified butter.
Having offered the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*) and the two libations (*āghāra*), and having presented the oblation soaked in clarified butter,
one should then worship and pay homage to the attendants (*pārṣada*) and offer the sacrificial gift (*bali*).
O Brahmin, one should recite the root mantra while remembering that its essence is Nārāyaṇa.
Having offered water for sipping (ācamana), one should offer the remnants to Viṣvaksena.
One should then present fragrant mouth-fresheners such as betel-leaf and the like, while constantly singing and reciting the eternal deeds with pleasing syllables. 105–106.
Causing others to hear or listening himself to sacred discourses, he should remain attentive for even a moment;
having praised [the Lord] with various hymns and praises, whether from the Purāṇas or even in the vernacular, he should prostrate himself like a staff, saying, "O Blessed One, be gracious."
Placing his head at the Lord's feet and embracing him with both arms, he said:
"O Lord, protect me, who have sought refuge, from this ocean of the jaws of death. Thus speaking, he respectfully placed upon his own head the remnants offered by Hari.
