If one should perform the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*), one should dismiss the light into the light of the Self;
wherever there is a footprint [of the deity] in images and the like, there the person of faith should worship.
One should perceive the Universal Self abiding in all beings and in oneself.
Thus, by means of the paths of ritual action and yoga, both Vedic and Tantric,
a person should worship so that he attains the desired perfection from Hari;
having consecrated that image, he should have a firm temple constructed.
By giving delightful flower gardens, as well as offerings, processions, festivals,

and so forth— both on great holy days and daily— for the sake of maintaining the continuous flow of worship and other rites, one who gives fields, marketplaces, cities, and villages shall attain union [with the Divine]. (113)
Through consecration, one attains the status of a universal sovereign; through a temple, the three worlds;
and through worship and other rites, the world of Brahmā. By means of these three, one may attain equality with Him;
yet it is only through the yoga of devotion, characterized by independence from all else, that one truly finds Him.
Thus, he who worships Hari attains indeed the yoga of devotion (bhaktiyoga).
That body which is whitened by the dust from prostrating before Kṛṣṇa is auspicious;
by means of those two beautiful eyes earned through penance, Hari is beheld.
That intellect which is as white as the spotless moon, a conch, or the *āyāma* flower, and which pervades Mādhava;
that tongue which speaks softly and which repeatedly praises Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Men—by such [means], worship may be performed even by women and Śūdras using the root mantra. 117.
With faith, following the path indicated by your own guru and others, you, a Vaiṣṇava, have been told all this purifying worship of Mādhava;
O King, perform this especially during the month of Mādhava. 118–119.
Sūta said:

Having thus heard these wonderful, meritorious, and purifying words of the son of Vidhi (Brahmā), the king—who was a foremost devotee of the Bhāgavata and filled with curiosity—bowed down with palms joined in reverence and spoke. 120.
Ambarīṣa said:

I am the sovereign of the entire circle of the earth, my command unimpeded, a servant of the gods, one who has fixed his mind upon the lotus feet of Govinda, and one who has satisfied the Brahmins with the contentment of his own heart. 121.

I am a jewel of a lineage fit for a renowned king, constantly delighting in dharma, illustrious, possessing the rise of beauty and valor, endowed with the virtue of generosity, blessed with excellent sons, and having conquered the host of my enemies.
By some merit, I have become pure-minded; thus has such auspiciousness of virtuous qualities been born within me.
"Moreover, from where has this beloved woman been obtained, who is like the goddess Śrī herself, a personification of merit, and so radiant?
O Sage, O ocean of compassion, O omniscient one, please explain to me correctly all these good deeds I performed in my previous birth. (123-124)
Nārada said: "In another birth, she was a courtesan named Rūpavatī; now, through her virtuous conduct, she has become your most beautiful wife. (125)
The noble lady conducted herself according to the profession of a courtesan as prescribed,
performing auspicious rites at the command of the twice-born.
You were known as Devadāsa, a goldsmith by trade.

In a previous birth, her husband was a serpent; because of that lack of affection, this beautiful woman now serves you. Furthermore, for the sake of expenditure, she resorts to virtue, while in her steadfastness lies supreme wisdom.

And having once heard the dharma arising from the Vaiśākha bath, Dharmavatī performed her bath in the waters of the Meṣa transit when the sun was in Aries; the clever courtesan Rūpavatī always gave gifts as well. (129)
Preceded by devotion and respect,
you, Devadāsa, having been awakened by truth and constrained by affection, performed the ritual bath with a devoted mind during the month of Mādhava. 130–131.
There, at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, having reached the third [day] which was pure, the courtesan spoke with respect to that goldsmith Devadāsa. (132) The courtesan said:
Having worshipped the supreme golden Madhusūdana, the infallible Acyuta, with these offerings, and having gratified the sacrificial fire,
I shall give [this] to a Brāhmaṇa with the permission of the Brāhmaṇas.
This gift is described in the Purāṇas as being inexhaustible therein;
I have heard from Brāhmaṇas that on the third lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha, it bestows imperishable fruit. 134–135.
"In this [image], I shall fashion the golden, imperishable Madhusūdana.
Nārada said:
Having heard these sweet words of his, the goldsmith—136.
Free from theft, with a sincere intention for the sake of dharma, he [made] a beautiful golden image of Acyuta on a discus,
as well as an image of Candra as described, endowed with all auspicious marks. 137.

Having bathed according to the prescribed rites and having worshipped that beautiful woman, O King, he gave her to a Brahmin on that inexhaustible lunar day (Akṣayā Tithi). After some time, that prostitute died, firmly established in righteousness.
Devadāsa also died truly at the exhaustion of his own lifespan.
By that merit, O King, in another birth you have become this goldsmith, a sovereign endowed with all virtues. (140-141)
By that dharma, she became like a courtesan endowed with beauty; known by the name Kāntimatī, she was lovely and overflowing with affection.
She possessed various latent impressions (*vāsanā*) arising from heroic deeds performed in previous births.
O Father, its various movements are known even by the wise;
this month of Mādhava must certainly be observed, for it has been concealed by that Lord and by Brahmā, the Mādhava. 143–144.

The dharma of the month of Mādhava cannot be attained by those who associate with the wicked, those who have not acquired knowledge, those who are unrestrained, those who lack the duties of their stage of life, those who have not visited sacred fords, and those who have not observed vows— by such as these,
[O] Govinda, Keśava, Mukunda, Hara, Murāri, Lakṣmīnivāsa, Madhusūdana, Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu! 145.
Those who dwell within the mouths of the best of speakers—the wise—observe the vow of the month of Vaiśākha; for them, there is no lack of merit.

(146) Those who do not listen to the abundant and virtuous words of the holy, nor to the nectar-like accounts of Hari’s deeds, and who do not behold the temples of the Lord of Kamalā, do not obtain the fruit of the vow of the month of Vaiśākha. (147)

Those who have served their parents and elders, who have bestowed their daughters upon worthy husbands at the proper time according to the sacred tradition, and who have instructed their sons in discipline and other duties, do not suffer the loss [of their merit] by observing the vows of the month of Vaiśākha. (148) Sūta said:
Having thus addressed the lord of men, the sage, foremost among those who know the mantras, departed for the Gaṅgā to bathe during the month of Vaiśākha; and then those brahmins were honored by him.
The king also performed the ritual of the month of Vaiśākha as prescribed by the sage.
With a mind focused on that very [merit] equal to his wife’s, he whose fame purifies the world reflected thus.
150. Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Nārada and Ambarīṣa," in the Vaiśākha-māhātmya of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Ninety-six.
The sages said: O Sūta, O Sūta of great wisdom, live for a hundred lives! We have been made to hear that meritorious account which is beneficial to the world. (1)
"O Sūta, even though we drink your words— which are for the most part abundant and most excellent— again and again, we are not satiated. Sūta said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
the dialogue between the primordial being and the Lord of the worlds regarding the worlds.
Its height is six thousand [yojanas], and its width is three thousand.
Having thus fashioned [the earth] at nine thousand yojanas,
the Earth was grasped and lifted up by his left tusk;
indeed, for a thousand divine years, the great Earth was supported by that tusk.
In the course of explaining the Dharma, she spoke with humility to the Lord.
The Earth said:
"These are indeed twelve months, six hundred and thirty days."
"O Keśava, among these, which is the most meritorious and dear to you?
The month of Kārttika is purifying when the sun is situated in Libra (tulā),
and the month of Māgha is remembered in the Purāṇas as purifying when the sun is situated in Capricorn (makara)."
The month of Caitra, when the sun is situated in Aries, is proclaimed by the wise;
Mārgaśīrṣa also is celebrated as the purifier among months. Thus these months are sacred; which days, then, could be otherwise? 8–9.

The beginnings of the ages (yuga-ādi), the ends of the ages (yuga-anta), and likewise the beginnings of the kalpas—all these are surpassed by this month; tell me that which is most purifying among them all.
O glorious one, consisting of all sacrifices, having determined it as the one [supreme], please speak.
Varāha said:
"Whether by prescribed rites or even without rites, those lowest of men who worship me with devotion in the month of Mādhava— I am always to be honored by them."
O fair-faced one, you slew Hiraṇyākṣa and the sweet-sounding Madhu;
having slain both these primordial Daityas, you were indeed uplifted.
In the Tretā Yuga, the dharma of the three Vedas, as well as the system of knowledge and the social orders, [shall prevail].
Because he was born in the month of Mādhava, therefore Mādhava is dear to me;
and in the third [Tretā] Yuga, on the third day of the bright fortnight in the month of Mādhava,
the dharma of the three Vedas commenced, and those [duties] were set in motion and increased.

Akṣayā is renowned in the world as the third [lunar day] dear to Hari. Those who bathe, give gifts, perform worship, offer śrāddha, recite prayers, and satisfy their ancestors, and who diligently perform the śrāddha for Viṣṇu with barley, [attain imperishable merit]. 15–16.
To them, I grant everything that is most desired by their minds; those men who give gifts are blessed and righteous, as are those who constantly worship Hari with various sacrifices. 17.
O Mādhavī, for one who worships at the end of my month, the fruit is even greater than that.
O Goddess, hear now the meritorious fruit of whatever bathing, giving, recitation, fire-offering, austerity, sacrifice, vow, and so forth is performed in Vaiśākha. 18–19.
For fifteen and seven crores of Manvantaras,
they remain in my presence, free from fear.
Even if all the planets should be malefic, situated in the eighth or twelfth house from their birth sign;
By means of the morning bath in Vaiśākha, all those people indeed become gentle. O Brahmins, for one who is devoted to feeding [Brahmins] in the month of Vaiśākha,
there shall be satisfaction for the ancestors for as many yugas as there are grains of rice in each mouthful.
Those who offer there sweet and abundant foods, or even meals of barley and water mixed with sesame,
as well as umbrellas and garments that provide protection for their feet— they alone are blessed, for they bring supreme satisfaction to Viṣṇu.
In this regard, sesame seeds combined with honey should especially be given here.

For the sake of Dharma, for the vast [liberation], and as a cause for the destruction of long-standing sins; (24) as for the merit that is obtained by those men who have performed this [rite] in such a manner—who could possibly calculate it, even in hundreds of millions of years? (25)

One obtains here, as desired, the attainment of sons, grandsons, and so forth, along with long life; and in the hereafter, one attains Me alone. The multitude of sins accumulated over many births dissolves by bathing in Mādhava.
Just as people resort to a sacred bathing place at dawn according to the prescribed rules, so too [should one act].
He who, having abandoned the Vaiśākha vow, performs another vow,
is like one who discards a great jewel held in his hand and begs for a clod of earth.
Sūta said:
Thus did the Blessed One, the primordial God, the all-pervading upholder of the world, formerly speak on this earth concerning the month of Mādhava.
O brāhmaṇas, what is the use of speaking much more on this matter?
There is nothing that cannot be attained by worshipping Mādhava in the month of Mādhava.
Listen now to a most wonderful ancient account regarding this very subject.
This is the conversation between the Brāhmaṇa and the high-souled Yama.
(31) In the Middle Country, there was a great village of Brāhmaṇas situated between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, at the foot of the Yamunā mountain. (32)
At that time, many learned Brāhmaṇas were residing there;
then Yama dispatched a certain man who was dark-brown,
red-eyed, with hair standing erect, and with shanks, eyes, and nose like those of a crow.

"Go to the great village of Ambha; having gone there, bring a Brāhmaṇa named Yajñadatta, born of the Vasiṣṭha lineage, who is established in tranquility, learned, and skilled in sacrificial rites. (34-35)
And you should not bring another from his side who belongs to the same lineage,
who is accompanied by such qualities, equal to him in learning and birth, and who is likewise a most excellent man in appearance and all his characteristics. (36)

"Bring him here so that the worship required for my purpose may be performed. Having gone, he carried out that command of mine which was contrary [to his wishes]; though forbidden by Yama, he brought that very man. 37–38.
Yama, the knower of dharma, rose up, paid him homage, and said: "This one is fit to be led away;
let another be brought.
Sūta said:
When these words had been spoken by the King of Dharma, the virtuous twice-born man,
despondent at the prospect of departure, spoke to that Dharmarāja.
(40) The Brāhmaṇa said:
"Why have I been brought here, and why do you urge me again to go?
O Lord, I have no desire at all to return to that world of mortals.
Yama said:
For men whose lifespan here has been exhausted, residence shall be among the meritorious;
this world of Dharmarāja is proclaimed to be the realm of Dharma.
This entire land is a ground of happiness, and I am Dharmarāja, the Lord.
Bestowing happiness and suffering upon living beings according to their merit and demerit,
he appears here in the form of Yama to sinners, granting them hell;
likewise, for the meritorious, he is the embodiment of Dharma, bestowing happiness and heaven.
Go this very day to your own abode as a vipra, just as you came;
even now, a lifespan of ten years remains for you.
When your life-span is exhausted, your arrival in this world will take place.
"Indeed, you must ask something else; ask it, and I shall explain it to you. (46) The Brāhmaṇa said:
"Tell me that by performing which great merit one may attain heaven."
"For you alone possess authority in the determination of dharma and adharma.
If it is indeed my duty to go properly to my own abode, then tell me: by what action do men fall into hell?"
"O Vrajanika, please tell me all about that new heaven.
Yamu said:
"Those men who are averse to dharma in deed, thought, or speech... (49)

Those who are devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu surely go to hell; those who perceive Brahmā, Śaṅkara, and Hari with a sense of duality [also go there]. Men who are indifferent toward the knowledge of Viṣṇu likewise go to hell.
That man who, out of desire or even through delusion, abandons the duties appropriate to his family and country and performs other acts, shall go to hell; likewise,
he who officiates at sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice, and he who rejects those fit to sacrifice.
One who abstains from the true knowledge of Viṣṇu partakes in many hells;
likewise, a sinner who dies wealthy without having given to the ancestors, the gods, the brahmins, or his fellow mortals, shall go to many hells. 53.
He who prepares various cooked foods for himself alone,
without performing the Vaiśvadeva rite, shall go to hell for a long time.
O twice-born one, those who acquire wealth through great cruelty toward living beings [meet the same fate].
Those wealthy men who,
out of atheism, greed, or delusion— according to the time that has arisen—
do not perform the ancestral śrāddha offering with devotion, become partakers of suffering and go to the depths of hell. They are cooked in those very hells.

That man who creates an obstacle when wealth is being given to Brāhmaṇas is a doer of evil and shall go to hell; likewise, he who, out of delusion, takes for himself a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) that belongs to all [the priests] shall also fall into hell. 57–58.
A man who is devoted to the sentiment of nihilism shall dwell in the abode of hell; his intolerance toward virtues becomes the cause for that great sin which arises and serves as the cause of hell.
59. That great sin has arisen and is the cause of hell.

He who, in the course of time, abandons his blameless wife and his friends, shall fall into hell; such a man incurs ninefold infamy. Furthermore, he who, having fallen under the sway of delusion, speaks of unrighteousness as righteousness, [shall likewise fall].
That man who is a rationalist and a nihilist, whose abode is hell,
and who with a different intent in his mind speaks otherwise in his words—
he would make his heart turbid and that man shall dwell in hell.

Those men who, while looking upon the gateway of the Blessed One and the collection of scriptures known as the *Nāma-śāstra*, should nevertheless despise and disregard the chanting of the Blessed One’s names, go to a terrible hell because of that sinful deed. 63–64.
Those men who go to dwell in hell for failing to offer salutations to them,
and those men who, without cause, take a second wife and abandon a virtuous spouse, they too go to hell. 65.
That man who does not listen to the words of his guru nor to the scriptures of dharma shall go to hell;
he who causes distress to the minds of others will likewise fall into hell.
He who eats delicacies while his kinsmen and children look on with longing shall suffer.
He who performs the morning bath during the zodiacal signs of Libra, Capricorn, and Aries would otherwise go to a terrible hell, were he merely intent on filling his own belly;
provided he is not an atheist, his abode shall not be in hell.
That man who, out of pride or lack of affection, does not rise to greet a Vaiṣṇava upon seeing him, O Brahmin,
becomes a guest of hell;
he is pierced with wooden stakes, spikes, or even with thorns and hair.
Those who obstruct the paths of righteousness are indeed destined for hell;
those who do not contemplate Viṣṇu— the primordial Puruṣa, the Lord, the Great Sovereign of all worlds— are indeed destined for hell.
Those men who destroy fields, livelihoods, and homes, and who destroy the joy [of others],
as well as those who destroy the hopes of Brāhmaṇas emaciated by want of means who have come for the sake of food— those men become inhabitants of hell. 72–73.

That fool who would examine [with contempt] one who is helpless, a devotee of Viṣṇu, the distressed, the diseased, or even the aged, should be known as a guest of hell. Those fools who do not show compassion are indeed destined for the underworld.

But those who, having undertaken the religious observances (*niyama*), later violate them because their senses are unsubdued, surely go to hell. Listen, O Brahmin, how compassionate men go to heaven. 75–76.
Out of respect for you, I shall speak briefly;
those who worship the eternal Lord Hari, the victorious Viṣṇu—
Nārāyaṇa, the unborn Kṛṣṇa, Viṣvaksena, the four-armed one.
Those who meditate upon the divine Puruṣa and remember the Infallible (Acyuta) attain the station of Acyuta; this is the ancient Vedic revelation.
This alone is indeed auspiciousness, and this alone is the acquisition of wealth.
This is the fruit of life: the chanting of the name of Dāmodara;
for through the chanting of Viṣṇu, the God of gods, who possesses immeasurable splendor, all sins dissolve like darkness at the rising of the sun. 80.
Those men who, endowed with faith, constantly sing the verses of Viṣṇu,
who are ever devoted to the study of the sacred texts, and who, having abandoned all afflictions, praise Viṣṇu alone, go to heaven. 81-82.
Firmly established and devoted to their own duty, those men go to heaven;
even the messengers of Yama, though they be terrible, do not approach those people who are intent on the chanting of Vāsudeva, even if they have been doers of evil.
O best of the twice-born, they see nothing else for living beings except the chanting of Hari’s glory, which is the expiation that pacifies all sins;
those who, when solicited, rejoice and speak kindly after giving what is pleasing. 84–85.
Those men who have renounced the fruits of their giving go to heaven;
those men who avoid sleeping during the day and endure all things go to heaven;
and those mortals who act as a refuge on sacred festival days go to heaven.
Those men who never speak of the faults of their enemies, but rather proclaim their virtues, go to heaven;
likewise, those who, upon seeing the prosperity of others, do not burn with envy. 87–88.

Those men who are joyful and offer praise, who follow both the path of worldly engagement and the path of renunciation exactly as declared in the Vedas and the scriptures, and who act with reverence and clarity of mind, go to heaven. 89.
In whatever family they may be born, those who are compassionate, illustrious, merciful, and of virtuous conduct go to heaven; likewise,
those who are pure and refrain from the wives of others in deed, thought, and speech.
Those men who delight in not being established in the quality of passion (rajas), and who always perform their prescribed duties as they have been ordained, go to heaven.
Furthermore, those men who understand their own capacity go to heaven.
He who always maintains faith in the qualities of mind, speech, and body,
and who is esteemed by the virtuous, shall become a guest of the gods.
He who [restrains] the impulse of speech, the impulse of mind, and the impulse arising from the stomach— 93–94.
That man who endures the impulse of sexual desire becomes a dweller in heaven;
those whose contentment lies in virtues, whose speech is directed toward sacred learning, and whose minds are fixed on the supreme truth—those refined ones go to heaven. (95)
Those who protect their vows from anger, their prosperity from envy, their learning from honor and dishonor, and themselves from negligence;
those who protect their intellect from greed and their mind from desire—[they alone attain success]. 96–97.
Those men who protect the Dharma from evil association go to heaven;
those who, O Brahmin, are devoted to fasting according to the rules on the eleventh lunar day, whether in the bright or the dark fortnight, go to heaven. 98.99.
Like a mother to all children, like medicine to the sick, the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) was created for the protection of all the worlds;
there exists no footwear equal to Ekādaśī. 99–100.
Having fasted according to the prescribed rite, men go to heaven.
O twice-born one, whatever sin has been committed by the eleven senses, a man quickly shakes it off and, being gratified, attains the path to heaven. (101)

Thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Rājasūya sacrifices do not equal even a sixteenth part of the fast on the eleventh day; so too, all sacrifices together with all sacred fords and austerities [do not equal it]. (102–103)
On one side is the Vaiṣṇava vow consisting of great gifts and other forms of charity;
on the other side is the merit born of the Vaiṣṇava vow and the merit arising from sacrifices and the like.
When these two were weighed together by the Creator, the former proved to be the heavier.

I am not the ruler over those who are devoted to the day of Hari and who speak of Acyuta as infinite; I am especially afraid of them, O Brahmin, whose sons and grandsons have likewise fasted on the Ekādaśī. 105–106.
He forcibly delivers a hundred men along with himself;
therefore, one should observe a fast during both fortnights.
On the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), one who has saved others becomes a single vessel for both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, and Pāpanāśinī;
Trispṛśā, Vañjulī, Pakṣasaṃvardhinī, Varā, Tiladugdhā, Aparā, and Akhaṇḍadvādaśī—these are the twelve. 108–109.
Likewise, there are the Manorathākhyā, Aparā, Bhīmā, Dvādaśikā, and so forth; there are numerous such varieties of the Dvādaśī [fast].
Those who are capable of these vows should be known as established in Brahman.

Those who listen to the Dharmaśāstras, who are endowed with faith in the Dharma, and who act for the benefit of children, go to the heavenly world. Those men who observe the vow of Śrāddha on the new moon day (darśa) once every month [attain the same]. (111–112)
Those whose ancestors are satisfied are blessed and go to heaven—those who, when food is served, offer it with respect;
those whose facial expression remains unchanged are disciplined and go to heaven. 113–114.
Those who possess devotion for Madhusūdana, Nārāyaṇa, the leader of all—even if they are devoid of truth and joined with passion—go to that heaven of infinite merit;
[so too do those who bathe] in the Vitastā, Yamunā, Sītā, and the holy river Godāvarī. 115.
Those of virtuous conduct who devote themselves to bathing and giving gifts never behold the path to hell, for they bathe here in the Narmadā,
the bestower of happiness, and are even satisfied by the mere sight of her. (116–117)
Having shaken off their sins, they go to the world of Maheśa and rejoice there for a long time.

(118) Men who bathe on the bank of the Carmanvatī river for three nights, remaining self-restrained—especially at Vyāsa’s hermitage—are remembered as being equal to those who possess celestial vehicles (*nākinaḥ*). (119)
Those who die at Prayāga in the waters of the Gaṅgā, at Kedāra, at Puṣkara, at Vyāsāśrama, or at Prabhāsa, go to Viṣṇu. Likewise,
those who die at Dvāravatī or Kurukṣetra through the practice of yoga [attain the same].
Those who utter the syllables "Hari" do not undergo rebirth (121).
Those Brahmins who stay for even three nights in the city of Dvāravatī and bathe on the banks of the Gomatī are blessed and beloved by Keśava (122).
Those who have resided for three nights at the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa,
and those who dwell for six months in the presence of the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) in the mortal world at Nandā— blessed are they, for they are dear to Keśava. 123.
Surely those whose souls are undecaying, having seen this remover of sins, must be such persons;

they who bathe in the waters of Maṇikarṇikā—the waters of merit acquired over many births—and having reached Kāśī, bow to the Lord of the Universe, are indeed worthy of my veneration here as well. 124–125.
Having worshipped Hari on the ground with darbha grass and sesame seeds, having scattered sesame seeds and given iron and a milch cow,
those men who die according to the prescribed rite go to heaven along with the Brahmin.
Having procreated sons and established them in the station of their fathers and grandfathers, those who are free from possessiveness and egoism—even when dead—are followers of Śiva;
they constantly refrain from theft and are content with their own wealth. 127–128.
Those men who live according to their own good fortune go to heaven;
those men who address others with gentle, harmless speech, free from deceitful means, and with words of welcome, go to heaven. 129–130.
Those men who understand the ripening of the accumulation of fruits of both auspicious and inauspicious deeds, O Brahmin, go to heaven;
they are those engaged in wealth and righteousness, and those who follow the path of dharma. 130–131.
Those men who increase the encouragement [of others] and rejoice in heaven,
as well as he who gives fire in the winter and likewise gives water in the summer,
and he who provides a hermitage during the rains— he rejoices in heaven for a long time. 132.

He who performs a śrāddha with devotion during all auspicious times—whether regular, occasional, or otherwise—is surely destined for the world of the gods. Charity is the duty of the poor; forgiveness is that of the powerful; silence is the duty of the young, and likewise of those possessed of austerity and knowledge.
The cessation of desire for those accustomed to pleasure, and compassion toward all beings, lead one to heaven.
(135) The connection with karma arising from sin and merit is of two kinds; indeed, it is by relying solely on truth that this determination is made here. (136)

That which is joined with austerity and meditation is for the sake of crossing the ocean of existence; however, that which is joined with force, service, and valor is said to lead to downfall—this is the truth, there is no doubt. 137. Even for one endowed with strength, attendance, and heroism.

For a man devoid of merit, even that [power] is overcome as if by force. (138) In the lofty mountain fastnesses there are trees that are well-nourished; yet, even though they are massive, they fall with the force of the wind along with their very roots. (139)
Those who are devoid of truth and dharma go thus to the abode of Yama;
for dharma alone is the strength common to all living beings, by which a creature crosses over in this world and the next. 140.
All of this, which correctly bestows the path to heaven, has been fully related by me in brief. What more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the Vaiśākha-māhātmya in the Pātāla-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The ninety-sixth chapter;
the ninety-seventh chapter.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
Even a fool knows this: a man who performs auspicious deeds goes to heaven, while one devoted to sinful actions goes to hell;
[this is achieved] through various sacrifices, desired vows, gifts, recitations, and so forth.

Through truth and those skilled in right conduct, the happiness of heaven is attained. By ṛṣis who have mastered the Vedas and are endowed with knowledge, conduct, and wealth, heaven is reached through the power of merit and sacrifices; therefore, it is never found otherwise.

A gift cannot be given in abundance even by one with wealth, nor by one whose mind is attached to the family, even though he possesses riches. Furthermore, rites such as the *agnihotra* are not practiced specifically in the Kali age.
"O Blessed One, even the practice of giving that is difficult to perform is considered difficult.
Yet, by means of a dharma that requires little effort, a great accumulation of merit is obtained.
Therefore, O Revealer of Dharma and Adharma, please explain this to me in detail."
Therefore, let that one Dharma be told— the most supreme among all Dharmas—
by the performance of which alone here all sins may be destroyed,
and by which wealth, grain, fame, righteousness, and longevity increase. (7)
By this, friendship may exist even in the mortal world, through which heaven becomes imperishable;
by this, Nārāyaṇa himself, the bestower of fearlessness upon his devotees,
is pleased, and by his grace, every desire rests in the palm of one's hand.

"O Vaivasvata, if there is any fruit superior to all sacrifices, austerities, gifts, and visiting sacred fords, then declare it to me. For I am indeed worthy of being favored by you through the instruction of dharma."
O Compassionate One, please speak of that single essence of all religious practices (11).
Just as the wise have remembered and declared various expiations corresponding to specific sins, so [should they be applied] (12).
"O Lord, it is not possible for men to perform them individually;
if there exists a single meritorious act that removes all sins, please tell me that.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus to Yama, who is the very embodiment of Dharma, that best of brahmins,
becoming composed and desiring to understand the subtle nature of dharma, offered praise.
The brahmin said:
Salutations to you, the pacifier of all; salutations to you, the Lord of the worlds.
Salutations to you who possess a divine form and bestow the path to heaven. Salutations to you, O King of Dharma, whose very nature is the scripture of righteousness. 15.
By you the earth is protected, O God, as well as the intermediate space and the great heaven; Janas, Tapas, and Satya—all this universe is protected by you.
There is nothing in the world, whether stationary or moving, that is devoid of you.
If, however, it were not grasped by you, the world would surely perish instantly;

you are the Self of all beings, possessing the nature of pure goodness (*sattva*) for the virtuous (18). You are likewise passion (*rajas*) for those characterized by passion, and darkness (*tamas*) for those characterized by darkness.
O God, you are the source of four-footed creatures, possessing four horns and three eyes;
homage to you who have seven hands, are bound in three ways, and take the form of a bull! Dharma, consisting of all sacrifices, has taken bodily form within you. 19-20.
O Lord Lokeśa, you have been seen directly; salutations, salutations to you!
You abide in the hearts of all beings as the witness of their merit and demerit. Therefore, O God, you are the teacher of beings, the giver, and the sovereign ruler.
"For he is the promoter of Dharma on earth, the wielder of the divine rod of punishment.
Tell me with certainty that one essential truth which consists of all dharmas.
Yama said:
"I am well-pleased with you, O Brahmin, especially by this hymn of praise.
Nevertheless, O best of beings, you are worthy of my favor according to the dharma of the scriptures;
for that which has not been told to anyone is my supreme secret."
Having extracted the essence from all [teachings], that which has been determined by me as the supreme means for the expulsion [of beings] from the multitude of great hells—
O Brahmā, though it is unspeakable, I shall speak of it because you have pleased me with your humility. 25–26.

Let those ancient scriptures and traditions of the world of moving and non-moving beings speak of whichever supreme deity they may; yet, when all the activities of the various scriptures have been brought into harmony by the discerning, it is determined that the Lord Viṣṇu alone is the one [reality] in the final conclusion (siddhānta). (27) Bhava, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu—this triad is considered to be the triple Veda itself.
Just as a lamp consists of fire, a wick, and oil, so too is Hari.
(28) By worshipping Hari with devotion, one shall attain the auspicious realms of Goloka; when Hari is propitiated, all desires rest within the palm of one's hand. (29)
O twice-born one, among all meritorious acts, giving alone is supreme and most excellent;
by giving, all sin is destroyed, and by giving, everything is obtained.
[This includes] the obligatory, the occasional, the optional, and that which consists of prosperity.
Furthermore, another supreme gift is remembered as being of five kinds.
Whatever little may be given with effort during the three times— morning, midday, and afternoon— is proclaimed as a constant duty.
A day should not be made empty by those who desire their own welfare;
for whatever is given in a family, it remains present right there.
He who, being devoid of intelligence, eats himself out of delusion without having first given [to others], [incurs sin].
I shall produce a disease that obstructs his enjoyment;
it shall be satisfied with those tasks, inflicting great torment, joined with a dull digestive fire, and causing a burning sensation at the gateways [of the body]. 34-35.
Those by whom nothing was given to Brahmins or to the gods during the three times of day, yet who themselves enjoy what is desirable—they have committed a great sin;
I shall purify them through a formidable expiation. 36.
Through fasts such as those that wither the body of a god on earth (the Brahmin), O pitiless one,
just as a leather-worker might clean a leather bag with whips and the like, or as he would beat a wicked person until it bursts; 37–38.
"In the same way, I shall undoubtedly purify the evildoer through the excellent application of medicinal herbs, pungent decoctions,
and certainly through hot water and heat, assuming the form of a physician and not otherwise. (39)
Others enjoy before him all the pleasures desired by his mind. What can I do, though I am capable? That supreme gift has not been bestowed.
One should surround him with a great form of disease. 40–41.
O Mahīdeva, just as one does not give oneself to sinners through faith and according to one's own power during the time of the eternal [ancestors],
so indeed shall he burn those who have arrived by means of terrible methods.
I shall now declare before you the occasional [types of] giving and the proper times for it:
when a great festival has arrived, likewise upon reaching a sacred ford (tīrtha), on the anniversary of a father’s death, and with diligence during the month of Vaiśākha and others. 43–44.
Giving on auspicious days such as the months and lunar phases is known as occasional (naimittika) giving.
I shall now describe the time for optional (kāmya) giving, which bestows specific fruits, intended for the fulfillment of particular desires through vows and the like. 45.

Whatever desire is correctly expressed, being consistent in all its parts, a human being enjoys a corresponding fruit through the power of that gift, as it is permeated by meditative cultivation and by grace from that [deity]. (46–47)

I shall now declare that which is remembered as pertaining to prosperity (ābhyudayika) in sacrifices and other rites, in ceremonies such as the birth-rite (jātakarman), in the rites of investiture with the girdle (mauñjī) and marriage,
and with great care in the consecrations of temples, banners, and deities.
Such is the gift to the gods of the earth (land), which consists of prosperity;
it increases progeny and bestows enjoyment, fame, and the happiness of heaven.
O best of the twice-born, listen as I shall now describe the final gift. 49–50.
Having realized the destruction of desire and being tormented by old age,
one should give gifts with diligence and should not place hope in anyone.
And when I have died, O sons, my wife, kinsmen, and brothers—
"How will these friends of mine fare without me? Or how shall I myself continue to live, deprived as I am of wealth?"—realizing this, he indeed gives nothing at all. (52-53)
Bound by hundreds of snares of hope, the foolish-minded man goes toward death through the power of fate; then his sons weep, afflicted by sorrow and their minds agitated by some delusion. 54.
They somehow contrive to give even a very small gift; yet when this time has arrived and great suffering has set in, they either forget that gift or, out of greed, do not give it at all. 55–56.
Knowing that this father has died, the bond of affection ceases;
yet he who is dead is still bound by my snares, O god on earth, overcome by thirst and hunger and tormented by manifold sufferings. (57)
He will undoubtedly be cooked for a long time in a terrible hell;
therefore, one should give gifts oneself, without doubt. For whose sons and grandsons are they? And whose wife or wealth is it? 59.
To whom can one who is an atheist regarding *saṃsāra* personally give drink, food, betel, water, gold,
clothing, a cow, land, an umbrella, or various kinds of vessels? (60)

O Brahmin, various fruits and gifts of land should be given according to one's own capacity; O god among men, no hesitation should be felt in this matter. O Brahmin, I shall now describe the characteristics of sacred fords (tīrthas) before you.
This Gaṅgā shines with excellent bathing-ghats, as do the meritorious Sarasvatī,
Revā, Yamunā, Tāpī, and likewise the river Carmaṇvatī;
also the Sarayū, Varā, Veṇī, and the Pūrṇā, which destroys all sins.
The Kāverī, the Kapilā, and another, the Viśalyā, which delivers all; the river known as Godāvarī, the Tuṅgabhadrā, and the Gaṇḍakī;
and the Bhīmarathī, remembered as the river that constantly strikes fear into sinners. 64–65.
The Devikā, the Kṛṣṇagaṅgā, and other excellent rivers—
these indeed exist as numerous sacred fords (tīrthas) during auspicious times.
Whether in a village or in a forest, rivers are purifying everywhere.

In each respective place, rites such as bathing and giving gifts must be performed. O twice-born one, when the name of that holy ford (tīrtha) is not known, one should utter the words: "This is a great Viṣṇu-tīrtha. 67–68.

Viṣṇu is the presiding deity of every sacred ford (tīrtha); of this there is no doubt. When a practitioner at sacred fords remembers the name "Nārāyaṇa," the fruit of that sacred ford arises perfectly through the name of Viṣṇu alone.
Without a doubt, for unknown sacred sites and deities,
a human being should proclaim their names using the name of Viṣṇu alone; for all meritorious accomplishments are indeed sacred sites, as is the ocean.
Lakes such as Mānasa, waterfalls, ponds and the like,
even small streams— all of these are holy places (tīrtha) by virtue of the name of Hari. Mountains are of the nature of holy places, as are sacrifice and the sacrificial ground.
Even those Brahmins who were learned in the three Vedas remained there out of curiosity.
That very place is remembered as a most great sacred ford (tīrtha) that removes all sins;
it is the site for ancestral rites (śrāddha), the ground for śrāddha, the hall of the gods, and the ground for fire-offerings (homa).
Where the sound of the Vedas resounds properly, and where the auspicious stories of Viṣṇu are told,
one’s own home is joined with merit, and even a cow-pen becomes purifying. Where there is the holy Aśvattha tree in the forest, even that dwelling is purifying.
Such places as these are holy fords (tīrtha), as are one’s father and mother;
where the Guru himself resides for the sake of dharma,
that is a holy ford, and wherever a virtuous wife dwells, there too is a holy ford— of this there is no doubt.
"Wherever a wise son constantly takes delight in dharma,
there that sacred ford (tīrtha) is established for his welfare and for his crossing over [to liberation]. Thus [are described] these and other sacred fords, as well as the royal palace.
In such sacred places (tīrthas), especially on the occasion of festival conjunctions (parva-yoga),
it is certain that one who has not propitiated Hṛṣīkeśa— the giver of all things to all embodied beings— will not obtain anything whatsoever anywhere at all. 79–80.
Offspring, wealth, wives, spacious mansions, horses,
elephants, happiness, and even heaven and liberation are not far off through devotion to Hari.
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme deity, the personification of truth, Janārdana.

The Blessed Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, divided himself threefold. The all-pervading one became joined with rajas and tamas, while rajas was predominant over sattva; he then created Brahmā, whose seat is the lotus, within the navel-lotus.
The omnipresent Lord created Rudra, who is possessed of passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas).
These three—sattva, rajas, and tamas—are thus called the triad.
By sattva, a living being is liberated; sattva has Nārāyaṇa as its essence.
One endowed with passion (rajas) and goodness (sattva) shall be prosperous and preeminent in fame.
That Vedic statement which one studies while aiming for dharma is declared by men to be the distinguished [portion] known as the Rudra. 85–86.

Therefore, O King, let the world not be filled again with passion and darkness— that which is devoid of passion and consists solely of darkness brings misfortune to men both in this world and in the next.
He who is Viṣṇu is himself Brahmā; he who is Brahmā is himself Hara.
O best of the twice-born, he who creates a distinction among these three gods—who are eternally worshipped as deities in this sacrifice—is a sinner. 88–89.
One who commits evil deeds and is evil-minded shall attain an undesirable state of existence.
O twice-born one, Viṣṇu alone is the Supreme Brahman, and Viṣṇu alone is the world;
this month of Mādhava is dear to him in all ritual acts.
It is proclaimed as the bestower of the fruits of great sacrifices such as the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha),
and it excels the fruits of bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha), austerity, charity, recitation, and ritual worship.
When the sun is in Aries, one should regularly bathe in a river every morning without ceasing.
Those who perform even this worship of the Brahmins do not become subject to my rod.

Having repeatedly struck down the throng of my servants before me, having repeatedly erased the records of Citragupta, and having bathed again and again in the sacred ford during the month of Mādhava, they deliver their ancestors here from sin. 93–94.

This supreme secret, which cuts through fear, must not be revealed; it is the cause of expulsion from my abode, hell, and the reason for the exhaustion of my authority. [The rivers] Bhāgīrathī, Narmadā, Yamunā, and Sarasvatī... 95.
The Viśokā, the Cavitastā, and those situated to the north of the Vindhya range;
the Godāvarī, Bhīmarathī, Tuṅgabhadrā, Devikā, Tāpī, and Payoṣṇī are proclaimed to be to the south of the Vindhya range. 96–97.

These twelve great rivers have been constantly bathed by him; whoever performs the ritual morning bath in a river during the month of Vaiśākha [attains merit]. All rivers flowing to the ocean are holy, and all excellent mountains are holy.
All sacred sites (āyatanas) are meritorious, and all meritorious places are worthy of refuge.

Having plunged into them, beheld them, bowed before them, and frequented them extensively, one should regularly perform ritual bathing during the month of Vaiśākha when the sun has half-risen. 99–100.
O best of the twice-born, even if one were to possess thousands upon thousands of mouths and if the lifespan of Brahmā himself were short, no one would be able to describe his merit. (101)
Then, it would be possible to describe the fruit of the month of Mādhava:

just as Mādhava [the Lord] is the fire that drags one out of the great hell, so too does Mādhava [the month] [burn away] sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and approaching those who should not be approached. 102–103.
Sins committed intentionally or unintentionally, as well as mortal transgressions (*pātaka*), secondary sins (*upapātaka*), secret sins, those that cause loss of caste (*saṃkarīkaraṇa*),
the terrible ones that cause loss of caste (*jātibhraṃśakara*), and likewise those that render one unworthy of receiving gifts (*apātrīkaraṇa*). 104.
The month of Mādhava, when properly observed according to the prescribed rites, burns away the impurities arising from speech, mind, and body— whether scattered or accumulated—
for thousands of millions and hundreds of millions of kalpas. 105–106.
The illustrious one who worships Hari during the month of Mādhava shall dwell in the city of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Greatness of Vaiśākha," in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The Ninety-eighth Chapter.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of that Dharmarāja, the Brahmin...
Again he asked about the auspicious ritual for the month of Mādhava.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O illustrious Dharmarāja, the secret has been correctly revealed."

The merit born from bathing in Mādhava bestows supreme liberation upon men. Having bathed in the month of Mādhava at dawn with a concentrated mind, how should one worship the Lord, and with what flowers? Tell me that procedure.
The King of Dharma said:
"Among all species of trees, tulasī is dear to Keśava;
likewise, Puṣkara and other holy fords, as well as the Gaṅgā and other rivers [are dear]."
The gods, beginning with Vāsudeva, always dwell upon the leaf of the tulasī at all times; indeed, tulasī is the beloved of Viṣṇu.
Abandoning the mālatī flower and setting aside the lotus, [one should offer tulasī].
Having taken a Tulasī leaf, one should worship Mādhava with devotion;
even Śeṣa would not be capable of describing the fruit of his merit.
Having cut a Tulasī leaf for the sake of a deity or for ancestral rites without having bathed— [7]

All that becomes fruitless; one is purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), even from many sins such as the experience of poverty and suffering. Tulasī quickly removes [these], just as harītakī removes diseases.
One should worship the Slayer of Madhu with Tulasī, known as both dark and fair;
especially so, for a man who is a devotee of Hari becomes Nārāyaṇa himself.
For he who worships Mādhava with Tulasī throughout the entire month of Vaiśākha [becomes so].
For one who worships the Slayer of Madhu at the three junctions of the day, there is no rebirth;
even in the absence of flowers and leaves, one should worship Hari with food and other offerings,
or always with śāli rice, wheat, or barley.
Having bathed in the morning according to the prescribed rite during the month of Mādhava, which is dear to Mādhava,
one should satisfy the ancestors, gods, and humans, as well as all things moving and stationary.
He who always waters the root of the Aśvattha tree with abundant water [attains great merit].
One should then perform circumambulations until the end; he who worships the divine Aśvattha tree with water on all sides will undoubtedly have uplifted ten thousand generations of his lineage. 14.

O dear one, by the libation offered to the Aśvattha tree, misfortune, Kālakarṇī, bad dreams, and evil thoughts— all such sufferings dissolve away. By that act, the ancestors are gratified, and Viṣṇu is worshipped.
The hero who worships the Aśvattha tree has thereby worshipped the planets themselves.
(16) One should touch white horse-flowers, as well as the Śamī tree, fire, sandalwood, the orb of the sun, and the Aśvattha tree; thereafter, one should perform the duties of one's own caste. (17)
By scratching [the cow's body], giving a mouthful of grass to a cow, performing the libation of *pippala* fruits after bathing,
and worshipping Govinda, one shall not meet with misfortune.
On the thirteenth, the fourteenth, and the three days of the month of Vaiśākha, [one should likewise act].

Even one who is entirely incapable, whether woman or man, by following the prescribed rule and being endowed with the previously mentioned observances, having bathed in the morning according to his ability,
is liberated from all sins and attains imperishable heaven. 19–20.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one who has risen for three nights, having bathed, being restrained and pure, should feed ten Brahmins according to his capacity—
Having given [these] to twelve Brahmins, he should have them recite the benediction (*svasti*) with those very words:
"May Dharmarāja, my ancestors, and the gods be pleased. Whatever sin has been committed throughout his life perishes at that very moment. 22–23.
He shall dwell in the heavenly realm for ten billion years at his own pleasure;
honored by all the deities, he shall not even perceive me [as distinct from himself].
[This applies to one who offers] cooked food, water-jars, and so forth, for the satisfaction of the ancestors and the gods.
On the thirteenth, the fourteenth, and the full moon day— for these three days—
he who gives with devotion to Brahmins according to his capacity vessels of gold and sesame seeds is liberated from great sins. (25-26)
One should satisfy [the ancestors] with vessels of water; thus one indeed removes the sin of killing a Brahmin.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, sesame seeds should be offered with devotion by the one created from the lotus-womb (Brahmā), for the sake of prosperity and the continuity of the lineage.

In this regard, O observer of noble vows, listen to an ancient account concerning the most wonderful fruit of the month of Mādhava on its full-moon day; starting from the sun's entry into Aries (Meṣa-saṃkrānti), there are thirty excellent lunar days. 28–29.
These three, proclaimed in the Purāṇas as meritorious and superior to all sacrifices, are especially pure and difficult for sinners to attain.
Even among those, the full-moon day of Mādhava (Vaiśākha) is meritorious and dear to Mādhava.
This first lunar day of the Vārāha-kalpa is one that yields great fruit.
In ancient times, on this very day, Nārāyaṇa deluded the two primordial Daityas;
Hiraṇyākṣa and Madhu were defeated, and the Earth was lifted up by the Brahmin.
On the thirteenth, the fourteenth, and the full moon day, this all-pervading Lord sequentially performed these three acts during the bright fortnight of this month of Mādhava.
From that time forward, O best of Brahmins, the full moon day became especially significant.
The beginning of the eon is proclaimed as the purifier, the witness of the eon for one whose actions are pure.

O Brahmin, what is the use of the birth of that man who, though established in religious observances, does not perform his bath in the morning during Vaiśākha? Surely such a person brings harm upon himself.
Especially on the thirteenth, the fourteenth, and the full moon day,
whether it be a woman or a man, by bathing in the morning according to the proper rite and observing the prescribed restraints, one is liberated from all sins.

He for whom Vaiśākha has passed without the merit of bathing, giving, worship, śrāddha rites, and so forth, will surely have his abode in hell. There is no scripture equal to the Vedas, and no sacred ford equal to the Gaṅgā. 37–38.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha,
he who is devoted to Viṣṇu should give a water-cow; such a gift is equal to the gift of rivers, oceans, and clouds,
and is especially dear to the three gods as a fourth.
The killer of a mother, the killer of a father, the killer of an embryo, and one who violates the teacher’s bed—
by beholding the Water-Cow (Jaladhenu), they are liberated from all sins;
they deliver ten ancestors and ten descendants from hell.
Those who, on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, offer a water-cow according to the prescribed rite to the Three-eyed Lord (Śiva),
as well as sugar, fruit, betel, sandals,
and leafy vegetables to the foremost of the twice-born— they are proclaimed here as truly fortunate.

He who gives jeweled water-pitchers, cooked food, and golden sacrificial fees on the full moon day of Vaiśākha shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. In this regard, they also cite this ancient history.

O sinless one, in ancient times there was a Brāhmaṇa named Dhanaśarman in the Middle Country; he went to the forest for the sake of Kuśa grass and other items, and then beheld this wonder in the great forest: his conversation with the ghosts (pretas).
Terrified, he saw three wicked and most dreadful pretas—
those with upstanding hair, bloodshot eyes, black teeth, and emaciated bellies— who were running here and there while uttering various shrieks. 46-47.
Seeing them, the Brahmin, terrified with fear, fled with speed;
then they, crying out, pursued him.
Being thus assailed by those ghosts, he spoke these sweet words:
Dhanaśarman said: "Who are you, from where have you come, and how did you fall into this state so suited for hell?
You ought to protect me, who am afflicted by fear, pitiable, and distressed."
"Keśava will surely grant prosperity even to you—this Vaiṣṇava, who has many dependents, is destitute, and is a Brahmin who has come from the forest.
For the Lord Viṣṇu, who is devoted to the Brahmins, is pleased with me out of compassion. (50-51)
Viṣṇu, Hari, who resembles the flax flower and wears yellow garments—
he by the mere hearing of whose name the great darkness departs;
he is the God without beginning or end, the bearer of the conch, the discus, and the mace.
The imperishable Puṇḍarīkākṣa is the bestower of liberation upon the deceased.
Yama said:
"Merely by hearing his name, you have been fully satisfied by Viṣṇu."
The Piśācas, who abide in a state of merit and are restrained by compassion and courtesy, being pleased by his words and impelled by that which was commanded,
those Pretas— afflicted by a flood of hunger and thirst— then spoke thus to the twice-born man: (54-55)
The pretas said: "O Brahmin, by the mere sight of you and by hearing the name of Hari, we have attained another state of being and have become compassionate. (56)
Association with Vaiṣṇavas surely dispels evil, bestows prosperity, and swiftly spreads one’s fame;
it is like an elixir, cooling and bestowing supreme bliss. 57.
The one named Anandayitika is a Vaiṣṇava; this second one is named Kṛtaghna, who is devoted to the gods;
and this third one is Avaiśākha, a sinner among all three. 58–59.
Because this wicked man has always practiced extreme ingratitude,
his name, derived from his actions, was established as "Kṛtaghna" (the Ungrateful).
In a previous birth, he was a Śūdra known by the name Sudāsa.
"O twice-born one, this state has been reached by that ungrateful, sinful thief.
For the extreme sinner, the rogue, and even for one who acts against his guru or master, there is a means of expiation; but for the ungrateful man, O Brahmin, there is no expiation. (61-62)
"O twice-born one, having experienced this final state with bodies capable of enduring the torments of various hells and conflagrations,
you have reached this end because you always ate food without performing the worship of the deities."
Because he did not give [offerings] to his gurus and Brahmins, this king, who is devoted to the deity Viṣṇu, was born as such.
This king, the lord of ten thousand villages, was known by the name Harivīra in his previous birth. (64–65)
Out of anger, egoism, and atheism, he was intent on transgressing the command of his guru;
without having performed the great sacrifices, he ate while reviling the Brahmins.
By that sinful action, he [fell into] the peril of a great hell.
Having experienced that, he was born as a preta named Vidai-vata (Vidai-devata).
On the third day of Vaiśākha, he became a doer of evil toward all three [of his kin].
Because of that karma, a brahmin established for him the name A-havya (Non-offerer). 67–68.
Born in the Middle Country, I am Gautama by name and also by lineage; in my previous birth, I was a Brahmin residing in Vāsapura who maintained the sacrificial fires.
By me alone, following solely the path of the Śruti, [this was accomplished].
If one has not bathed during the month of Mādhava dedicated to Lord Mādhava,
nor given anything in charity, nor offered oblations— especially on the full moon day of Vaiśākha— and if the Slayer of Madhu has not been worshipped there, the wise have not been gratified. (70–71)
The ancestors and deities were gratified by gifts of jeweled water-pots and jars, as well as offerings of sesame seeds mixed with honey for those seeking long life;
they were further honored with flowers, fruits, betel, sandalwood, fans, and garments. (72)
The learned have not been honored there for the satisfaction of the ancestors and the gods.
Not even a single full-moon day of Vaiśākha—which bestows complete fruit—has been observed by me through the meritorious acts of bathing, giving, ritual performance, and worship. (73–74)
"Consequently, all my Vedic rituals have become entirely fruitless;
therefore, I have been born everywhere as a preta named Vaiśākha.
Thus, I have related to you the cause of all three."
You are our deliverer from the ocean of worldly existence, for you are indeed a virtuous Brahmin; and since the holy sages declare that the sacred ford of Brahma is supreme,
they rescue those who have taken refuge there even from great sins and from the hells.
For the man who always bathes at holy pilgrimage sites such as the Gaṅgā, and he who cultivates the company of the virtuous— the company of the good is superior to both.
Or else, I have a son well-known by the name Dhanaśarman.
"Go to him, O Lord, and awaken him; you have made an effort for our sake.
When an undertaking has been initiated and others approach, one who exerts effort obtains abundant fruit, even greater than that of sacrifices and acts of charity. (79-80)
Having heard those words of the deceased, Dhanasharman was deeply distressed; he recognized that his own father had fallen into hell. 81.
Reproaching himself on all sides, Dhanaśarman spoke these words: "O Lord, I am your son, yet I am as useless as Gautama. (82)
But that son who, being diligent, does not bring about his father's deliverance, does not purify himself;
he is not one who possesses pure wealth.
For dharma is profound and difficult to understand, even for a wise person despite their effort.
Just as you have reached this miserable state because of me,
so too, when you obtain a continuous stream of happiness from me, you shall be considered a true son in both worlds. (84–85)
According to the Dharma, both the father and the mother are the gurus of a person in this world;
yet between those two, the father is superior, as it is observed that the seed is the primary factor. "What shall I do? Where shall I go? O Father, what is your destination?"
"I do not know the true nature of dharma; I rely upon your word. The Preta said:
"Listen, my son, to these truthful words, by the power of which the future matter shall be revealed."
"Perhaps by some merit, a happy rebirth will be mine;
yet while I was performing the rites prescribed by the Vedas, I acted out of pride, disregarding the words of my guru and showing him contempt. (88-89)
Through disrespect toward gurus, and through excessive joy, anger, and pride,
one's merits perish just as fame does through improper conduct;
whatever ritual action is performed according to the Purāṇic injunctions must not contradict the Śruti.

Only Vedic rites were performed by me out of ignorance. Not even a single Vaiśākha Pūrṇimā— the axe for the tree of sin and the forest fire for the fuel of evil— was observed according to the prescribed rule, O son.
That man who does not observe the vow on the Vaiśākhī day becomes a non-Vaiśākha;
thereafter, he is born in the wombs of animals for ten lifetimes. Having experienced suffering for a long time, he eventually becomes a preta at the end.
One somehow attains a human birth, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain.
(94) I shall tell you the supreme means that brings about liberation for the deceased, which I myself heard previously in a former birth from the mouth of my own guru. (95)
"O son, go home and bathe in the Yamunā according to the prescribed rites;
for from today until the end of the kalpa, this Vaiśākha full moon day— which grants all goals— has arrived, and it is beneficial for the worship of the ancestors and the gods on that final day."

If one should devoutly offer even water mixed with sesame seeds, along with water-pots, food, and fruits to the ancestors here, by that the Śrāddha offered always becomes equal to one given for a thousand years. (97) He who,
on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, should feed the gods of the earth (Brāhmaṇas), [attains great merit].
For every grain of rice offered, the ancestors remain satisfied for a number of ages equal to the grains.
(98) Having bathed according to the prescribed rite on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should feed ten Brahmins with milk-rice; one is liberated from all sins—of this there is no doubt. (99)
Having given white or black sesame seeds mixed with honey to ten Brahmins, one should have them pronounce a blessing with those very words:
"May Dharmarāja be pleased," and one should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods.
Even the sin committed throughout one's entire life perishes at that very moment.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, O twice-born one, sesame seeds were created by the Lotus-born [Brahmā]; they should be given with devotion and touched upon all parts of the body. 101–102.

Then, for one who bathes with sesame seeds mixed with barley over all their limbs, Brahmā and Dharma grant here the desired boon. Furthermore, he who gives water-pots for the pleasure of Dharmarāja [attains the same]. 103.
By this, seven times seven families shall be delivered; of this there is no doubt.
(104) On the thirteenth, the fourteenth, or the full moon day, one intent on devotion, having bathed, recited mantras, offered oblations, given gifts, and worshipped Mādhava, (105)
"O Lord, bestow upon us that fruit which arises from having a son; for I shall not resort to the path of heaven while abandoning these two deceased ones who are so familiar to me.
Indeed, the end of their suffering has now arrived. (106)
Yama said: Having said "So be it," that twice-born man returned and performed everything accordingly;
being pleased by his supreme devotion, he performed the ritual bath and the giving of gifts on the full moon day of Vaiśākha.
Having bathed with devotion on the full moon day of Mādhava,
he gave many gifts to them and bestowed merit upon each individually;
at that very moment, they all ascended celestial chariots and departed for heaven.
O best of the twice-born, through the connection of that gift of merit, Dhanaśarman— himself a lord of brahmins and a knower of the Vedas, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas— became joyful and,
after enjoying pleasures for a long time, attained the world of Brahmā.
Therefore, O Brahmin, this Vaiśākhī, the most meritorious and the purifier of the entire universe,
is described by me in brief due to its extreme gravity.
Blessed indeed are they, successful indeed are they, truly born into this world are they, and truly men endowed with the goals of human existence are they.
Those whose minds are purified by bathing according to the rule worship Madhusūdana in the month of Vaiśākha at dawn.

(113) That man who, having bathed at daybreak in the month of Vaiśākha, worships the Lord of Ramā while endowed with the restraints and surrounded by all the observances, surely destroys his sin here. (114)
By them alone has time been conquered; they alone among men are blessed and freed from sin;

they alone enter the womb no more, while those who are joined with the month of Mādhava sink back down again. When the month of Mādhava thunders, it is due to its connection with sacrifice, its connection with the performance of austerity, and its connection with the practice of giving.

Whatever small merit has been performed in any way during the month of Māsa shall become equal to a kalpa once again for one who bathes at the break of day in the month of Mādhava, because even a person of darkness attains purity in every limb through contact with a single drop of water [offered] for the worship of Mādhava. 116–117.
Embodied beings wander about in this body only so long as they commit sins,
until that Virāṭ appears— He who is called Samādhi, the beloved of Śrī Ramā’s lover.
Even if their fierce sins are as numerous as the Meru and Mandara mountains, [they are destroyed by His sight].
The month of Mādhava is burning [with heat], and the one beloved by Mādhava has bathed. 120.
This greatness of the Vaiśākha bath, which destroys the sins of the listener, has been told by me to you in brief out of favor, O twice-born one. 121.
But whoever shall listen to this history spoken by me with devotion,
he too, liberated from sin, shall behold my face.
Even sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, though committed many times over—
By the performance of the Vaiśākha rites, those [sins] are certainly destroyed.
One who has bathed according to the prescribed rule in Vaiśākha shall deliver thirty ancestors, thirty descendants, and thirty more of both lines from hell. 123–124.
On one side are all the holy fords and all sacrifices accompanied by ritual fees;
on the other side is the month of Mādhava, observed with disciplined observances, because it belongs to that Blessed Lord Hari of exalted deeds. (125)

"O Brahmin, do not entertain any doubt whatsoever regarding my statement concerning the month of Vaiśākha; indeed, the month of Mādhava is dear to me, being the most excellent and superior of all. (126-127)
In this regard, listen to this wonderful ancient account;
though it is not something that should be told, I shall nevertheless relate this narrative at the end.
Thus ends the Vaiśākha-māhātmya in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The ninety-eighth chapter.
The ninety-ninth chapter.
Yama said:
In former times, there was a renowned king named Mahīratha,
who had attained abundant sovereignty and prosperity as the fruit of his past merits;
he remained solely devoted to the charming company of women for the sake of sensual pleasure.
Addicted solely to that [pleasure] and not established in virtue or worldly purpose,
the king entrusted the glory of the kingdom to his ministers and enjoyed sensual objects, turning away from the affairs of state while accompanied by his beloved.

He did not understand wealth, dharma, nor purpose; he perceived only that which was appropriate for the amorous play of his beloved, for such was his sole mental impression. Then, after a long time, his family priest Kaśyapa [arrived].

He spoke words consistent with dharma, reflecting thus in his mind: "If a preceptor, out of delusion, does not restrain a king from unrighteousness, he too partakes in that sin; therefore, the king must be enlightened by the priest. (5-6)
If, even after being awakened, he disregards the words of his domestic priest,
then the priest would be faultless and the king would bear all the blame.
Listen, O King, to the words of my preceptor, which are consistent with dharma and artha.
It possesses an undivided meaning and a meaningful purpose, and is free from desire, passion, and the like.
This alone is the supreme dharma: to abide by the word of the guru. Obedience to the guru’s command increases one’s lifespan, prosperity, and happiness, just as obedience to a king does.
Brahmins were not gratified by you with gifts, nor was Viṣṇu propitiated by you; no vow, no austerity, and indeed no pilgrimage was performed by you.
Under the sway of desire, the name of Hari was never even contemplated by you.
Alas! By associating with you, O fearless one, I have failed to cultivate the company of the wise. To whom are beloved women, who carry the fly-whisks of Love, not dear?
Yet they are as fickle as the leaves of a plantain tree tossed by the wind. 11–12.
Noble-minded men are not satisfied with objects as flickering as waves, with enjoyments as transient as the play of eyebrows, or with youth that can be drunk up in a mere moment.
Of what use is learning, or austerity, or renunciation, or even statesmanship? 13.
Of what use is a secluded mind to one whose mind has been stolen by women?
Dharma alone is a friend who follows one even in death;
everything else will perish along with the body.
One should gradually accumulate merit, just as termites build up an anthill;
for with merit as one's companion, one crosses over the darkness that is so difficult to traverse.
(16) [The world is] as fickle as the surging waves of water tossed by the wind.
O Indra among kings, do you not know the instability of human life?
(17) For those whose crown-jewel is humility, whose earrings are truth and righteousness, and whose bracelet is renunciation—what need have they for the ornaments of the dull-witted? (18)
Having cast off the dead body upon the earth like a piece of wood or a clod of earth, the kinsmen turn away; only Dharma follows him.
While all things are passing away and life itself is thus wasting away, (one must practice virtue). 19.
When life itself is being snatched away, why do you rise up and run about?
Family, children, wife, and the like; the body and the accumulation of wealth—these are all alien and impermanent. What, however, is truly one's own? Only one's good and evil deeds. 20–21.
Since one must inevitably depart, abandoning everything,
why are you attached to what is useless and do not practice your own duty? [It is] without rest, without support, without provisions for the journey, and without a guide.
"Once dead, how will you travel alone through the wilderness on the road?
For no one at all will follow behind you as you set out; only your good and evil deeds will follow you as you go. (23-24)

Diligently practice the conduct of the virtuous, which is declared in the Śruti and Smṛti, appropriate for your family and region, beneficial, and rooted in Dharma. One should abandon wealth and pleasure if they are devoid of Dharma.
Everything—wealth, desire, and all other forms of happiness—is attained through righteousness.
One should practice the yoga of self-restraint over the senses day and night;
for only one who has conquered his senses is able to establish his subjects on the right path.

The fortunes of kings, made restless by the side-long glances of excessively bold women, endure for a long time only through their commitment to discipline. This is so because those whose character is defined by lust and pride act without reflection. 28.
The prosperity of those with deluded minds perishes along with their very life.
Great-souled ones dance amidst ashes whose vision has vanished;
the ocean is neither increased by rivers that have arrived, nor diminished by those that have departed.
Between calamity and death, calamity is said to be the more grievous; the king who is addicted to vice sinks lower and lower, whereas the king free from vice ascends to heaven.
Vices born of passion, in particular, are difficult to overcome.
Therefore, O Great King, abandon desire, which is opposed to dharma.
Even for the dull-witted, the undiscriminating, the evil-minded asuras, and those who act contrary to policy, there exist kingdoms to be enjoyed through their good fortune. (32-33)

These [impurities] are not stable here; they dissolve through the practice of austerities, just as pieces of wood are consumed by contact with fire—whether one is walking or standing, waking or even sleeping. 34.
He whose mind is not intent on inquiry is as good as dead;
for it is said that the teacher of those who have heard the scriptures is called a "guru," yet for you,
whose calamities are imminent, even your own hair serves as such instruction.
Having cast off the fever of sense-objects, the wise man accomplishes his own purpose through a mind that is equanimous and healthy, and through reasoning that remains consistent in worldly conduct.
(37) That which has moved away from the inauspicious proceeds toward the auspicious, and from that [state] again toward the other.
A person’s mind is like that of a child; therefore, one should restrain it by force.
O King, having ascertained the intellect of the elders who perceive the Dharma, one should control with supreme wisdom the mind that has strayed onto a wrong path.
Neither wealth, nor friends, nor kinsmen provide assistance;
there is no movement of hands or feet, nor travel to other lands (40); there is no affliction from bodily toil, nor resorting to sacred fords or shrines.
The state is attained through recitation by one whose mind is focused solely on that;
therefore, O King, a wise man should exert effort in restraining the mind from its objects, just as one restrains horses in training. 41–42.
O King, you should do whatever was done by those by whom you were deceived—both by the sages and by various fruits; therefore, listen now further.

Whatever they may say when questioned, that should be done as is appropriate. One who seeks his own welfare must restrain both desire and anger by every possible means, for those two are intent upon destroying one's well-being. 44-45.
O King, desire is powerful and is a great enemy residing within the body;
therefore, a person who desires their own welfare should come under its control.
By that very god Śiva, the wielder of the trident, was Kāma formerly [subdued] by the God of Gods himself.
It is established that the Bodiless One (Kāma) was not consumed by the fire of the forehead [of Śiva].
Whenever that Mind-born One desires to slay a woman, he resorts to the bodies of men and reveals his own form. 47–48.

When a man repeatedly contemplates the form of a woman, she, taking hold of him while he is thus unobserved, drives him mad. In the very same way, O dear one, she drives a man insane; of this there is no doubt.

O King, from the mere remembrance of his name, Smara (the God of Love) was born; whatever his form may be, he takes refuge in the garment of Vīra. Through the radiance of his own splendor, he becomes one who drinks the streams of tears.
Having mounted the form of a woman, it may delude even a steadfast man;
yet, having taken refuge in a man, it causes the woman to wither away. O King, that very same [principle], which is innate, bodiless, and yet residing within the body, is the sovereign.
How can sin be attributed even to the body?

(53) Since even the most pure things, such as the five products of the cow and sacrificial offerings, attain impurity for a moment upon reaching it, who else could be more impure than that [body]? (54)
Even while smelling its own foul odor and seeing its own filth, this world does not become dispassionate, even though it afflicts the nose;
for it attains delicious foods, drinks, and fragrant things. 55.
Impurity quickly reaches another, and from that, one becomes impure.
For the food that has entered someone's stomach abandons its own natural form;
indeed, it is known to quickly become a foul mixture of worms and excrement. (56–57)
Even so, one who abandons their own form as a protector of the earth in this body will later attain the state of a dog in a place crowded with worms and foul odors;
there, indeed, they are born as lice or worms— of this there is no doubt.
The worm produces a blister accompanied by a most agonizing itching;
it further causes pain and makes the entire body tremble.
When rubbed with the tips of the fingernails, that itching becomes subsided. 59–60.
In that same way, pleasure indeed arises from sexual union; of this there is no doubt.
Thus a mortal enjoys flavors, eats good food, and drinks again.
There, the fire situated within digests it and causes the waste to be cast out through the anus.
There, the essence that has become the core is produced as pure and free from dross; being stainless and possessing pure potency, it proceeds to the station of Brahmā,
drawn upward by the *samāna* wind and carried by that very air.
It finds no stable place and exists in a state of instability;
indeed, there are five types of worms within the skulls of living beings. These two [worms] are at the base of the ears, and then again in the location of the eyes.
O King, those with red tails are measured by the span of the little finger;
those with black tails have the color of butter, without a doubt.
Listen as I declare their names, beginning with Bhadra. 65–66.
Two worms named Piṅgalī and Śṛṅgalī reside at the roots of the ears;
another, Śṛṅgalī—also known as Jaṅgalī—is situated between the eyes.
Of such worms, there are one hundred and fifty; of this there is no doubt.
All those residing within the forehead, measuring the size of a mustard seed, are sufferers of skull-disease; they cause transformation [of the body], of this there is no doubt.
I shall now describe another: the great worm belonging to Prajāpati.
O King, listen: there is no doubt that he has two hairs on his face, each the size and color of a grain of rice;
at that very moment, the intellect of living beings perishes, without a doubt.
Even when situated in its own place, if the Prājāpatya [fire] is turned away, that semen falls in the form of fluid;
of this there is no doubt. One drinks the semen with ease, and by that, one becomes intoxicated and procreates.
