Having pierced the location of the palate, it moves with restlessness; therein reside the channels (nāḍīs) known as Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā. By its own power, that very [channel] causes the other channels to tremble for a moment.

O King, it is said that the itch of desire exists in all living beings. O Lord of the Earth, the male organ of a man and the womb of a woman swell; then, those two, the woman and the man, being intoxicated by passion, engage in union.
By rubbing body against body through sexual union, pleasure arises there for but a moment, yet thereafter there is such itching;
indeed, this is the nature of the heroic state seen everywhere. 76.
The ripening of an object that is not one's domain is undoubtedly bitter;
however, Dharma alone, when practiced according to the prescribed rules, leads to the highest good. Therefore, summoning fortitude, practice Dharma alone.
This breath is fickle; within a single moment it performs hundreds of arrivals and departures.

Since the life of embodied beings depends upon it, who would delay the practice of Dharma? O King, even for one who has reached the tenth stage [of life], the mind does not yet turn [to virtue] today.
One should restrain the restless mind from forbidden objects;
for desire is never appeased by the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, but like a fire fed with clarified butter, it only increases all the more. 80–81.
Who else is capable of liberating a mind stolen by a harlot,
except for the Blessed Lord Mādhava, the Sovereign who delights in the Self?
Therefore, everything has become fruitless due to the defilement of lust.
O King, I shall now tell you my own conduct, which is beneficial for you and is the most excellent of all; for I am your priest, and thus I partake in both your good and evil deeds. (83-84)
On one side are all the merits for the destruction of the sins of sinners;
on the other side is the month of Mādhava, which is always dear to Mādhava.
[The sins include] the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, and violating the teacher's bed.
These alone have been proclaimed as the great sins (mahāpātakas) by the lords of sages.
Among them, the month of Mādhava destroys all that has been committed by men through mind, body, or even through vows—the great darkness of sin. 86-87.
Just as the sun destroys darkness in every direction,
so too does the illustrious Mādhava-māsa destroy [sins] according to the prescribed rules. O King, having abandoned those terrible and great misdeeds committed even since birth, mortals—
By the merit arising from the power of performing the practices prescribed for the month of Vaiśākha, people attain the joyful city of Hari.
(89) Even those who are sinful, if they perform even a single [act] of Vaiśākha according to the rules and with devotion, go to the abode of Hari. (90)
Therefore, O Indra among kings, you too, having bathed this morning according to the prescribed rite in this month of Mādhava, should now worship the Enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu).
Just as the husk is removed from rice and the blackness from copper, [so too is sin removed].

Just as the husk of a grain of rice is destroyed by the act of threshing, so too is even great innate impurity destroyed; there is no doubt about this. Therefore, perform the actions prescribed by your duty. 92–93.
Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter [and begins the hundredth chapter] in the Vaiśākha-māhātmya of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
King Śrī said: I have been awakened by you with words that are like the waters of the Ocean of Milk— cool, pure, truthful, and wonderful.
O gentle one, you have caused me to drink the nectar that does not arise from the ocean, the non-material medicine for calamities, which wards off the disease of worldly existence;
it bestows joy upon men, destroys their sins, and is the elixir of life. 2.
Indeed, association with the virtuous removes old age and death; whatever things on this earth are difficult to obtain yet desired,
all those are attained solely through the company of the righteous.
For one who has bathed in the Gaṅgā of association with the virtuous— which removes all sin—
what need is there for gifts, what need for sacred fords, what need for austerities, or what need for sacrifices?
It is the supreme refuge for men who, sinking and surfacing, struggle within the ocean of worldly existence.
O Lord, just as those who know the Dharma and are peaceful sink into a solid mass of water,
so too has my former disposition— which was once intensely eager for the pleasure of desire—
become its opposite today through your sight and your words.

For the sake of the happiness of a single birth, a wise person may destroy thousands [of future births], yet through that single birth, he accumulates thousands of births. Alas! With a mind craving the pleasure of tasting the flavor of sensual desire, [one ruins one's future].

"O twice-born one, nothing beneficial for my own self was performed by me while I was deluded. Alas! What a delusion of my mind, that for the sake of women, I have cast myself into a terrible calamity, full of suffering, difficult to overcome, and hard to escape."

O Blessed One, I am thoroughly satisfied by these words concerning enlightenment; you ought to deliver me here by granting this instruction. Since I have performed meritorious deeds in the past, I have been awakened by you.

O best among the eloquent, tell me the ritual of the month of Mādhava, which you have proclaimed to be the destroyer of all sins, and which has been purified by the contact with the dust of your feet. 12–13.
"What is the gift there, what is the bath, who is the deity, and what are the observances?
O brahmin-sage, tell me this for the sake of crossing over my sins.
(14) Yama said:
Thus addressed, the Blessed Kaśyapa, a treasury of compassion, spoke these words that were righteous for a brahmin, beneficial to all, and auspicious.
Kaśyapa said:

O King, that which is asked by a wise person possessing an intellect capable of reconciling the preceding and the following should be spoken; it should not be told to one of base and sinful mind. Thus, O King, having bestowed auspicious wisdom upon one who is engaged in sinful conduct—
The fruit of the gift of knowledge is fully attained by him; of this there is no doubt.
One should not speak to anyone unless asked, nor to one who asks in an improper manner.
Even though he knows, the wise man should behave toward the world like one who is dull-witted. 17–18.
Even for learned disciples and sons who perform their duties,
that which is beneficial and conducive to the welfare of those possessed of faith should be spoken, even if unasked.
At present, you have become pure-hearted because of my words.

O Great Lord of the Earth, by the merit accumulated in a previous life by someone, that body of yours which had fallen into a state of sin became established in righteousness through its reliance on me and through the hearing of the Dharmaśāstra. (20–21)

That which is known as unrighteousness (adharma), characterized by evil states and devoid of knowledge of dharma, is the other [type of] good vow; that indeed should be understood as righteous (dhārmika).
The third, which is beyond the senses, exists for the purpose of experiencing dharma and adharma.
Indeed, those who know the Dharma declare that this body here is threefold (23).
To the extent that there is the experience of dharma and liberation, these constitute its three divisions.
That body which is in a state of sin is called by the name "sin" (24).

Now, as you practice devotion to your guru and listen to my words which are the very form of dharma, your body has become established in that dharma; by that alone, a stainless purity has arisen, fit for the performance of righteous deeds. 25.
By fate, the minds and actions of embodied beings,
as well as their bodies, undergo transformation from time to time.
At present, your mind is surely set upon dharma.
"Therefore, I shall cause you to perform this supreme Mādhava-bath.
Yama said:
"Then it was performed by him [Yama] with Kaśyapa as his domestic priest. (28)

The sage replied to the king with the following account of the procedure for bathing, giving gifts, and worship performed during the month of Vaiśākha, together with Nṛpa and Mādhava, exactly as it was seen in the ancient scriptures. 29.
The essence of the hymn was made heard to him, and he was taught [the hymn] of Harimedhas (Viṣṇu).
By hearing this and by studying it, one obtains the full fruit. Then, with a purified heart, the king also performed that [rite] according to the prescribed rules.
Then, with great reverence, he related that venerable ordinance of the month of Mādhava exactly as it had been heard from Śrī Mādhava.

That best of kings performed the morning bath, the offering of water for the feet, the respectful oblation (arghya), the worship of Hari, and the presentation of food offerings (naivedya) with a spirit of devotion.
He who performs the rites of the month of Vaiśākha with devotion, according to the rules and with care— such as charity and the observance of vows—
and does so daily for every year, that foremost of Brahmins goes to the abode of Hari.
Now, in the other months, he is devoted to the dalliance of playing with the breasts of his beloved.
Thus, becoming excessively devoted solely to sensual enjoyments according to his own whim, he—
under the sway of desire— performed neither religious duty nor restraint, and showed no consideration for royal affairs, having abandoned Māsa along with Samādhu.
O foremost of brahmins, even for the great, the mind-born passion is difficult to restrain;
indeed, the succession of latent impressions (vāsanā) is innate to the body and beginningless.
[The hair] is beautiful with its dark curls, yet it is difficult to touch while being dear to the eyes. 37.1–2.

For the ignoble flame of desire, like fire, burns a man like straw; this terrible enemy resides within the bodies of men. Consisting of the smoke of delusion, by whom has this evil not been blinded with darkness? 38–39.
Thus ends the one hundredth chapter in the Vaiśākha-māsa-māhātmya of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa in the glorious Padma Purāṇa. Chapter one hundred and one.
Yama said:
Then, marked by the sidelong glance of Kālaka, the king died; his body wasted away by consumption arising from excessive indulgence,
he was led away by the hosts of Yama while being beaten again and again.
Crying out with a great roar and remembering his own sin,
he was approached by the messengers of Viṣṇu; having struck my followers and declared, "This man is righteous," he was then placed upon a celestial chariot.
The king, his sins diminished by the morning bath in the month of Vaiśākha, was led to the city of Hari while being praised by hosts of apsarases.
Then, thinking that he was devoid of dharma, they [again]—
Then, by the command of the divine messengers acting on Viṣṇu’s behalf, the lord of the earth proceeded with focused mind along the path to hell, which was not far away;
even as he went, he heard the cries of living beings wailing again and again.
Then, hearing the various cries of those being cooked in hell,
and the most terrible wailing of the sinners as they were being boiled,
the brahmin king was filled with wonder and became exceedingly distressed.
He said, "O messengers, what is this dreadful wailing that has been heard?
Let it not be heard again; you ought to tell me the cause of it.
The messengers said:
Those living beings who have abandoned the bounds of propriety, who are sinful and devoid of right conduct,
are cast into the terrible hells such as Tāmisra and others; indeed,
those who have committed sins here [fall there] immediately after the relinquishing of their life-breaths.
Resorting to the southern path, they experience terrible suffering;
dragged here and there by the fierce servants of Yama, they fall into darkness and are devoured by most dreadful creatures. 10–11.
They are [tormented] by dogs, jackals, carnivorous beasts, crows, vultures, cranes, and the like;
by fire-mouthed wolves, tigers, serpents, scorpions, and so forth;
being burned by fire and pierced by thorns.
Being split apart by saws and tormented by thirst,
oppressed by hunger as well as by terrible hosts of diseases, they faint at every step from the stench of pus and blood.
In some places they are boiled in oils; in some places they are beaten with pestles;
and in some places they are cooked upon iron slabs. In some places they eat vomit, and in some places pus and blood.
In some places there was excrement, and in others flesh, foul-smelling and dreadful;
in various spots they were being devoured by worms with mouths like fire,
amidst heaps of hair, blood, flesh, gore, fat, and bones.

The corpses lie unheeded, strewn about and clearly devoured by worms; they are desecrated by the beaks of crows, vultures, and great eagles, amidst hundreds of millions of fissures filled with the foul stench of excrement.
In the saws, the stone-slab blades, and the heated oilless cauldrons;
in the iron, the oils, the marrow, the pillars, the kūṭa-śālmali trees, and the dwellings;
and in those resplendent with razor-sharp thorns, wedges, and blazing pillars of flame.
In the various hells filled with the pus of the heated Vaitaraṇī river,
and where the breasts of men and women were lacerated by the forest of sword-leaves,
they repeatedly experienced the terrors of seizing hold of them amidst a dreadful darkness.
Being tormented and crying out due to various cruel executions,
they have nooses tied around their necks and are sometimes entwined by serpents;
likewise, they are crushed by machines and dragged by their knees.

O King, with their backs, heads, and necks broken, and their throats constricted, these most dreadful evildoers, devoid of merit, are made to wander within peaked-roofed chambers with bodies capable of enduring torment, while they are tormented and cry out in lamentation.

Accompanied by the relish of sense objects, they perform such wailing; and all living beings experience the consequences of what was previously done. Attachment formed toward the wives of others brings pleasure at first, but it results in suffering.

O King of kings, the taste of the pleasure derived from a single moment of the morning bath in the month of Mādhava, when performed according to the purifying rite, brings suffering for many years; yet even the wind, having touched these [waters], attains purity. 27.
Having obtained happiness for a moment, they were nourished by your splendor;
because of that, they became free from crying while remaining in hell.
Even the name of those of virtuous character is proclaimed as a source of happiness when heard. 28–29.
The touch of the wind from his body would arise as a source of great comfort.
Yama said: Having heard these words of the messenger, that king, a treasure-house of compassion, [acted accordingly]. 30.
He replied to the messengers of Viṣṇu, whose deeds are miraculous:
"The heart of the virtuous is surely as tender as fresh butter;
when heated by the fire's torment, it clearly melts away. (31)
The king said:
"I do not venture to go and afflict any living being who is not distressed. Fie on that most wicked man who, though capable, does not remove the suffering of those in distress!"
If even living beings have become happy by the touch of the wind rendered impure through contact with my limbs, then lead me there; for by that [wind],
men purify their mother and the earth as well.

Those who remove the distress of others are like sandalwood trees; indeed, it is the virtuous who are oppressed for the sake of helping others. Only they are truly "good" (santaḥ) in this world who tear away the suffering of others.
Those men who strive for the welfare of others, for whom life is as insignificant as a blade of grass, sustain this earth by destroying the suffering of the afflicted.
That constant happiness which is found in the mind is like heaven; [any other] is comparable to hell.

Therefore, the virtuous are always happy only through the happiness of others; better here is a fall into hell, better even is the loss of life, than the happiness found in the mere removal of the suffering of those in distress for even a moment. 38.
The messengers said:
"Those sinful beings are cooked in the terrible hell;
they subsist solely upon their own karma, for there is no place for delusion there."

O King, those by whom nothing was given in charity, nor offered in sacrifice, nor performed as a ritual bath at a sacred ford (tīrtha); by whom no service was rendered with devotion, nor any supreme merit performed; by whom no sacrifice was offered, no austerity practiced, and no mantra recited with a joyful heart—[they go to hell]. 40–41.

In the other most terrible hells, those of evil character, wicked conduct, and censurable dwelling and diet— those who harm others, commit sins, and lead depraved lives— are made to ripen [for their karma]. 42.
Indeed, those wicked ones who pierce the vital organs of others with their speech and those who dally with the wives of others are cooked in hell;
come, O protector of the earth, let us surely go to the abode of Hari. 43–44.
"It is not fitting for one who possesses merit to remain here any longer.
The King said:
"O messengers, if I am a man of good deeds, why [do you treat me thus] in the midst of this great terror?"
"Have I been brought to the path of hell? What supreme merit have I performed? Even though I was filled with desire, I did not perform such merit.
How shall I go to the city of Hari? I am indeed full of doubt."
The messengers said:
"Truly, no good deed has been performed by you, whose soul is under the sway of desire.
You have neither sacrificed with sacrifices, nor have you consumed the remnants of sacrifice."
However, three years ago, in the month of Mādhava,
you bathed in the morning and, impelled by the words of your guru, worshipped Viṣṇu— the Lord of the Universe and Madhusūdana— with devotion according to the prescribed rite. 48-49.
O Lord of Men, he who destroys the flood of great sins and even greater evils, who is affectionate toward his devotees,
and who is the sole essence of all dharmas— by him alone,
being honored by the hosts of gods, one is led to the abode of merit.
Even great sins are destroyed when Mādhava is worshipped;
likewise, Mādhava, impelled by the ritual injunctions, consumes mortals just as a mass of grass is set ablaze by a single spark. 51-52.

Even a flood of sins is consumed by the morning bath in the month of Vaiśākha; indeed, great sins persist in the body only so long as one does not immerse oneself at dawn in a sacred bathing place during the month of Mādhava.
The man who is engaged in the month of Vaiśākha according to the prescribed rules,
being liberated from the multitude of his sins through devotion to Hari alone, shall go to the abode of Acyuta.
Whatever merit you have previously performed since birth— 55.

Therefore, O Lord of Men, you have been led by us—the hosts of Maruts—onto the path to the abode of hell; now, being praised by us, go quickly to the residence of Govinda by means of a celestial chariot (vimāna). 56–57.
Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter in the Vaiśākha-māsa-māhātmya of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa in the glorious Padma Purāṇa. Chapter One Hundred and Two.
Yama said:
Then the king, an ocean of compassion, afflicted by grief for them,
spoke with humility to the messengers of Śrī Hari: "O Brāhmaṇa,
[regarding] sovereignty, noble birth, virtues, and merit..."

For the virtuous count as their fruit only the protection of those who are afraid. (2) If I have any merit whatsoever, O living beings, by that alone may you go to heaven in multitudes; remain here yourselves, for I shall dwell among you. (3)
Having heard these words of King Satyavat, which were for his own welfare, they meditated upon truth and magnanimity and spoke these words to the king.
The messengers said: 4. Having heard these words of that truthful king, which were for his benefit, they, reflecting upon truth and generosity, spoke these words to the monarch.
The messengers said:

O King, by this act of compassion and these words, there was an increase in his accumulated merit, especially so; for bathing, giving, recitation, burnt offerings, austerity, worship of the gods, and so forth— Please note that the provided text fragment ends mid-sentence. The translation reflects the portion available. If you require a continuation, please provide the subsequent text.
Whatever is performed in the month of Mādhava, they know that to yield infinite fruit.
The sacrificer and the donor sport in heaven together with the gods, amidst golden lotuses in ponds and beneath the shade of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa).
He who gives food and water attains the auspicious realm of Varuṇa, where he finds joy as the hosts of celestial nymphs sing his praises.
The giver of cows effortlessly delivers seven generations of his lineage across [the ocean of rebirth].
By giving a horse, a man goes to the world of the Sun; by bestowing knowledge, he goes to the world of Brahmā. Likewise, by the gift of gold, he goes to the abode of the gods;
and he who gives a maiden in marriage likewise goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Having bathed in the month of Mādhava, having given gifts, and having worshipped Mādhava,
one attains all desires and proceeds to the imperishable state.
Even on one side [of this merit] stand such acts as austerity, charity, and the performance of sacrifices.

The great month of Mādhava was observed according to the rules for one day; O King, whatever merit was performed during even a single day of that month of Mādhava was formerly declared to be superior to all other gifts.

O Lord of the Earth, O treasure-house of compassion, bestow upon me today the merit of giving [even] a single day’s [gift] to those suffering while being cooked in hell. There is no dharma equal to compassion; there is no austerity equal to compassion. (14)
There is no gift equal to compassion; there is no friend equal to compassion.
A person who bestows merit always obtains a hundred-thousandfold merit; through compassion in particular, O Dharma, an increase in righteousness shall arise from that.
Indeed, he who removes the suffering of beings who are afflicted is alone to be known as a man of meritorious deeds in this world, born from a portion of Nārāyaṇa.
On the full moon day of the month of Vaiśākha, bathing, giving gifts, and other such acts were performed by you.
O hero, having performed according to the prescribed rite that act which destroys all sins—performed at a sacred ford (tīrtha)—and having made Lord Hari the witness, give this body to these men;
so that by your threefold declaration, they may attain heaven from hell. 18–19.
In the past, Śibi, a treasure-house of compassion and an ocean of fame, gave his own flesh out of pity for the sake of a pigeon and now shines in heaven; likewise,
the royal sage Dadhīci, having given his own collection of bones, [attained the same state].
Having attained fame that served as a moonlight for the three worlds, he reached imperishable heaven.
The highly illustrious royal sage Sahasrajit,
having renounced his dear life for the sake of a Brahmin, went to the unsurpassed worlds.
O King, it is my conviction that a person does not obtain in heaven nor even in liberation that happiness which arises from granting relief to a distressed being; for you,
O Lord of the Earth, were born in ancient times as the foremost among all givers.
Having applied this number through my action and having observed your unwavering wisdom, righteousness, compassion, and generosity, we too, as proponents of dharma, shall exert our enthusiasm. 24–25.
"O King,
if you so desire, then give that merit— which burns away the suffering of hell— to these [beings] without delay.
Thus addressed, he then made Gadādhara his witness and did as he was told.

The compassionate one bestowed upon them merit arising from three verbal utterances according to the prescribed rite. When that [merit] produced by a single day in the month of Mādhava was given, those beings were freed from the torments of Yama.
Having ascended excellent celestial chariots, they all went to the third heaven,
bowing, praising, and gazing upon him with great joy;
having obtained that merit bestowed by the king, which was produced by a single day in the month of Vaiśākha.
By that, they were all liberated from hell and attained various celestial chariots in heaven. (30) Indeed, the multitude of beings on earth is diverse; their existence is manifold and varied;
likewise, the application of all their actions is diverse, and the accumulation of the power of those actions is manifold. (31)

Being praised by hosts of sages and gods, he—having acquired even greater merit through those specific [deeds] and being saluted by the hosts of the Lord of the World—attained that supreme state unattainable even by the best of yogis. 32.
Thus ends the [section on] the Greatness of the Month of Vaiśākha in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter One Hundred and Two;
Chapter One Hundred and Three.
Yama said:
O best of the twice-born, this greatness of the full moon day of the month of Mādhava has been briefly recounted in its entirety;
and he who reads this history, which is dear to Madhusūdana, during the month of Vaiśākha, [attains the highest goal].
Having quickly purified himself from his dwelling in black deeds, he rejoices here for many kalpas.
This [narrative] is auspicious, conducive to fame, long life, and great well-being; it leads to heaven, bestows prosperity, brings mental serenity, is highly praised, and is a purifier of sins.

Having heard, read, and duly rejoiced in this greatness of the month of Mādhava— which is dear to Mādhava— as well as the life-story of that king and our own dialogue, one's heart becomes beloved [of the Lord]. 4.
May there be devotion to the Blessed One by which the destruction of one's sins may occur.
Now go, O Mahīdeva, to the world of the gods as you wish;
having cast Vaidehī down to earth, her kinsmen still weep even today.

"Until my body has been cast into the fire by those weeping kinsmen, alas, I shall not wake up from this sleep; rather, I remain as if fast asleep. By my grace, you have heard this method for attaining merit here; perform it exactly as it was taught."
"According to the prescribed rite, at the appointed time, there shall be a meeting with the gods at the end.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of the god and having bowed to the Lord of Dharma, he then—
Then, with a heart full of contentment, that twice-born man fell back down here;
by the grace of Dharmarāja, he then rose up upon that ground, surrounded by his circle of kinsmen, as if from a deep sleep.
Every year, that twice-born man himself performed this rite on the earth,
and he personally caused the people to perform the ritual bathing of Mādhava. This dialogue between Yama and the Brāhmaṇa has thus been fully narrated by me.
In connection with the meritorious ritual bathing during that month of Mādhava,

a wise person should constantly perform ritual bathing in the month of Vaiśākha, which is dear to Hari; and by offering gifts with devotion and likewise performing fire-sacrifices and good deeds, for such a person, the abode of Hari will never be difficult to attain.
He who listens with a single-minded focus to this majesty concerning me, born of the Sun,
shall be liberated from all sins and go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. (14) The Sages said:

O Sūta, O most wise one, you who are of a deeply compassionate nature have proclaimed the greatness of the month of Vaiśākha, which destroys all sins. You have also described the religious observances for the Slayer of Madhu that are to be performed during Mādhava.
Worship, bathing, giving gifts, and so forth, according to the injunctions of the Śruti and Smṛti—just as by these the Lord Mādhava, the destroyer of sins, is pleased;
now we wish to hear the meditation (dhyāna) upon that Great Soul. 16–17.
The incarnation of Kṛṣṇa, who is dear to the multitudes of his devotees.
Sūta said:
Listen, all you sages, to [the account] of Kṛṣṇa, the soul of the universe.

O best of the twice-born, once Nārada was questioned by Gautama; I shall now relate to you that which he spoke in reply, which destroys all sins. (19–20) [He is] the life-breath of the cowherds and cowherdesses, and the one who wanders in Vṛndāvana. (19) Once Nārada was questioned by Gautama; O best of the twice-born, I shall tell you that which he spoke in reply, which destroys all sins. (20)
Nārada said:

One of steady mind should constantly remember the beautiful Vṛndāvana, which possesses the splendor of bowing branches laden with clusters of fresh sprouts and honey-sweet *mādhvīka* flowers falling from their abundant fragrance; it is entwined by lovely creepers bearing blossoming new clusters of blossoms. 21.
Its interior was made resonant by the humming sounds emerging from the mouths of wandering bees as they tasted the nectar of blooming jasmine flowers;
it was filled with the cries of pigeons, parrots, mynas, cuckoos, and other birds here and there, and was agitated by the dancing of peacocks, the enemies of serpents.
It was greyed by the clouds of pollen from the bellies of blossoming lotuses, carried by the spray of the moving waves of the Yamunā.

One should meditate upon that exalted Kalpa-tree within his heart, which is constantly attended by breezes that incessantly flutter the garments of the playful women of the host of ignited Manobhavas (Cupid);

which possesses sprouts of fresh coral and leaves of emerald; whose buds are clusters of pearl-like radiance; which bears various fruits with the hue of lotuses; and which, being the granter of desires, is perpetually served by all the seasons. 23–24.

The wise man, free from the six waves [of affliction] and unwearied, should again meditate upon that golden ground below the mountain of excellent golden peaks, radiant like the rising sun, showering sprays of nectar, with its floor of blazing jewels made brilliant by heaps of flower-pollen— [the ground] devoid of the six waves.
Having visualized there an eight-petaled red lotus upon a most magnificent yoga-seat situated on that jeweled floor...
Then, one should meditate upon Mukunda seated comfortably in the midst of that [light], stealing the splendor of the rising sun;
possessing a luster equal to a fresh blue lotus or a mass of clouds as black as crushed collyrium;
with a mass of very glossy, dark-blue, thick, and curly hair; and adorned with a crest of peacock feathers, beautiful and shining like those of the lovely-throated Śiva. 26–27.

Adorned with an ear-ornament of a blooming fresh blue lotus from the son of the celestial tree (Pārijāta) cherished by the *rolamba* bees, his forehead shone with a mark of yellow pigment (*gorocanā*) shimmering with hovering bees, and he possessed a brilliant bow of eyebrows;
his face was as beautiful as the orb of the full autumnal moon, and his large eyes were like lotus petals. 28.
His cheeks were like mirrors, radiant with the light from jeweled crocodile-shaped earrings; his nose was high and beautiful.
His lower lip was made lovely by vermilion, and the quarters of the sky were illuminated by the luster of his gentle smile, which was like the moon, jasmine, and mandāra flowers.
His conch-like neck was brilliant and captivating, adorned with a necklace fashioned from a cluster of wild sprouts and blossoms. 29–30.
His shoulders were adorned with a trailing garland of *saṃtānaka* flowers resounding with the humming of intoxicated, wandering bees;
his broad chest shone with a necklace of many strings of pearls and the radiant Kaustubha gem gleaming upon it.
He was beautifully marked with the Śrīvatsa sign, possessed of uplifted shoulders, and had well-formed, thick, rounded arms reaching down to his knees. 31.21–22.
With a belly marked by folds, a broad and deep navel, and a line of hair as beautiful as a swarm of female bees;

with arms adorned with bracelets set with various jewels, and wearing wave-like armlets, necklaces, girdles, anklets, and a waist-band; with his slender body stained yellowish-red by divine unguents, and his rounded hips wrapped in saffron-colored garments. 32–33.
With beautiful thighs and knees, and lovely calves that follow their natural curve; with lovely, elevated forefeet that put to shame the beauty of a tortoise;

with lotus-feet made beautiful by toenails shining like rubies and mirrors, and toes adorned with red lac-dye; and delightful with the soles of his hands and feet marked by the fish, goad, lotus, banner, barley-corn, lotus, and thunderbolt—34.

His limbs were fashioned from the very essence of all that is beautiful, and the splendor of his body surpassed the loveliness of the god of love; (35) with divine melodies constantly produced by the movements of his trembling fingers as they filled the holes of his lotus-like mouth’s flute, he caused all the multitudes of living beings to bow down, and he is an ocean of infinite bliss. (36)

Then he was surrounded by cows whose eyes were fixed upon his lotus-like faces, who moved slowly and languidly, stumbling under the weight of their udders, with tips of grass still held between their teeth and their vine-like tails hanging down;
they were lovely with the thick, frothy milk trickling steadily from their teats, which were adorned by the ornaments of their flowing udders. 37.1–2.
It was also filled with young male and female calves, whose pairs of ears were pricked up by the charming, slow songs set to flutes;
whose hooves struck the ground with a restless intensity born of the impulse to nuzzle the soft heads of their mothers with their fresh horns;
and whose necks were thick with dewlaps and tails held erect. 38–39.
With great bulls whose lowing agitated the circle of the quarters, who were weary from the burden of their massive humps,
and whose broad nostrils expanded with joy as they drank the nectar of the flute’s sound through upturned ears;
accompanied by cowherds whose qualities, character, age, grace, and dress matched his own, and who played flutes and lutes with a sweet, resonant melody.
It was surrounded by children who were skilled in performing graceful dances with their swaying vine-like arms while singing in low, high, and sharp tones;
who wandered about making sounds from the clusters of dangling bells fastened to the slopes of their thick hips at the ends of their shanks;
and who, though innocent, wore beautiful ornaments fashioned from the claws of hyenas and spoke indistinct yet sweet words. 41–42.

Then, [he beheld] the exceedingly graceful cowherd beauties, slow-moving due to the weight of their broad hips and heavy tresses, their slender waists bent under the burden of their full breasts, and displaying lines of hair that had blossomed with the expansion of their three folds;
they were like the sprouting branches of the God of Love, whose feet were moistened by the nectar-like essence of the music of his most beautiful and lovely flute. 43.1–2.
Their vine-like bodies were adorned with the emergence of hair that had grown lovely and pure like flower buds;

they were drenched by a dense succession of perspiration droplets, resembling a spray from the breaking waves of the most tremulous ripples of the ocean of passion stirred up by the moonlight of their exceedingly beautiful, gentle smiles. 44–45.

[They were] overwhelmed by the piercing shafts of glances discharged from the exceedingly lovely bow of her slightly arched eyebrows; their entire vital organs shattered by that rain of arrows, their limbs were afflicted with the pain of unbearable trembling spreading through them.
They were longing for the act of drinking the nectar-essence of the beauty of her exceedingly radiant attire and form. 46. 47.
Of those whose lotus-eyes were languidly trembling as they flowed with the waters of affection;

who were repeatedly attended by swarms of bees greedy for the honey dripping from the blossoming flowers falling from their loosened tresses; whose soft voices faltered with the intoxication of passion; and whose hips shone with the glow of silken garments slipping down from their shifting girdles and loosened waistbands. 47–48.
Of those whose faces fill the quarters with the tinkling of jeweled anklets set in motion by the gentle impact of lotus-feet stumbling in playful gait;
whose lower-lip petals quiver; whose two lotus-eyes are like blossoming buds with thick lashes; whose earrings shimmer;
and whose sprout-like red lips wither from the heat of their most rapid sighing.
He is constantly attended on all sides by rows of [goddesses] whose lotus-hands shine with various offerings;

his entire body is worshipped by the blossoming lotus-garlands of their long, tremulous, dark-blue eyes; he is the abode of manifold charms; and out of affection, he wears a captivating garland of bees—his own eyes—that taste the honey-dew trickling from the lotus-faces of those lovely women. 50–51.
One should visualize in front of him, outside, the host of gods led by Viriñci, Trinetra, and Śatamanyu, who are intent on praise and desirous of wealth;

likewise, to the right, a multitude of sages devoted to the sacred tradition (Samāmnāya) with a firm longing for Dharma; and behind him, the lords of yogis such as Sanaka and others, seeking liberation through meditative absorption (Samādhi). 52–53.
Then he [beheld] the yakṣas, siddhas, gandharvas, vidyādharas, and cāraṇas,
along with the kinnaras and the foremost apsarases who, desiring love, were engaged in dancing, singing, and instrumental music;
[he saw him] white as a conch, the moon, or a kunda flower, a knower of all scriptures, with a mass of matted hair tawny like a flash of lightning.
[He saw] him who desires pure devotion directed toward his lotus feet, having utterly abandoned all other attachments;

who gladdens [the world] with delightful modulations (*mūrchanās*) belonging to the three scales (*grāmas*) endowed with the seven notes and various qualities of the Vedas; and who, through supreme devotion, meditates upon this [Goddess] born of Brahmā in the sky. 55–56.

Having thus meditated upon himself, a man of sharp and clear intellect should worship the Son of Nanda with his own understanding through blameless offerings beginning with the removal of sins, and furthermore, with devotion, through external riches within his own body. O best of Brahmins, all that was desired has now been declared.
(57) Thus ends the one hundred and third chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Month of Vaiśākha," in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. (103)
The one hundred and fourth chapter.
The sages said:
O highly fortunate one, tell us once more the wonderful life-story of Rāma.
The entire essence of Rāma’s greatness, which bestows joy upon his devotees.
Sūta said:
Just as the son of Daśaratha performed the horse sacrifice, the most excellent of rituals.
Engaged in worldly affairs and skilled in the performance of scriptural duties,
the high-souled Śaṅkara, desiring to go to Ayodhyā,
dwelt on the bank of the Sarayū together with Pārvatī and Devasena.
The sages, Kaśyapa and others of great soul, approached Śaṅkara, who possesses universal form and immeasurable splendor, and asked him:
"Welcome, O best of sages! Where have you come from, and with whom? (4-5)
"What is the purpose of your coming? You appear ready to go to another region. Śaṅkara said:
"I am a brahmin known as Śambhu, residing on the Himālaya mountains."
"I shall go to see the descendant of Raghu; therefore, this is my great duty.
That king, who is devoted to listening to the Purāṇas, is summoning me. You all should also come, so that Rāghava may be well-pleased."
Then those sages and Śambhu departed with the desire to see Rāma.
Knowing that they had arrived, Vasiṣṭha informed Rāma;
thereupon, rising quickly, he went forth accompanied by his family priest.
The subduer of enemies honored all those sages with offerings of water for the hands (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), and other rites;
then he caused them all to enter the king of houses (the palace). Having offered a seat to each one, he welcomed them as they took their places.
In due order, that tiger among the Raghus honored those sages;
pleasing them with sweet words while they sat upon their seats,
Śrī Rāma spoke as follows.
Today the fruit of my birth has been attained; today the fruit of my penance has arrived.
Today the time has come for the fruit of my practice of the sciences.
Today my parents are satisfied, and my kingdom has become fruitful.
To the king who was speaking thus— "Today the fruit of my vows has been realized; today the fruit of my vows has been heard"— the brahmins, Kaśyapa and the others,
spoke these most pleasing words to the lotus-eyed Rāma.
The sages said:
"This Śambhu, a twice-born man who has arrived here, is an expert in all the scriptures;
he knows the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary branches, and is devoted to the welfare of all living beings."
Dwelling constantly on Mount Kailāsa, he was firmly resolved upon austerity;
equal to Brahmā in sacred luster, he was the best among the knowers of Brahman;
like Hari in his affection for the Brahmins, and comparable to Śaṅkara in his graciousness.
Such is this Śambhu, a bull among Brahmins, possessed of great luster;
he is a knower of the eighteen Purāṇas and an expert in Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya.
It is solely due to the weight of your good fortune that this best of sages has arrived here.
"O Lord, the best of sages, having been summoned by you, has arrived from Kailāsa.
Therefore, O illustrious one, descendant of Raghu, we have come to you today desiring to hear the supreme narrative of the Purāṇa; please ask [him about it]. (19-20)
"For a man who has mastered the Vedas and knows the meaning of all the scriptures, even if he has not heard the Purāṇas, there is no failure in his vision of the ultimate goal.
Sūta said:
Thus addressed by the sages who perceive the truth, the best of the Raghus,
eager to hear the Purāṇa, experienced incomparable joy.
Śrī Rāma said:
The method of worshipping the *liṅga*, the majesty of the *liṅga* itself, the majesty of the name of Maheśa, the majesty of worship,
the majesty of prostration, and the majesty of sight.
O most excellent one, [he spoke] of the majesty of the gift of water, the gift of incense,
the gift of lamps, perfumes, and so forth, as well as the majesty of flowers, and various stories from narratives and histories that destroy all sins.
"O observer of excellent vows, O best among the foremost of sages, I desire to hear from you all of that— dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, as well as the means to attain them.
Śambhu said:
O Rāma, O Rāma, O mighty-armed Rāghava, you who possess merit,
through service to the great and by frequenting sacred pilgrimage sites, a devotion to hearing the Purāṇas has arisen in you, even though you were previously attached to the kingdom. (27)

That tongue which sings the praises of Śiva, and that mind which is offered to Him—those two alone are praiseworthy hands that perform His worship; that alone is a truly noble birth and body throughout all future lives. 28–29.
"Since I have become one who has accomplished his purpose by chanting the name of the Lord whose splendor causes my hair to stand on end, O Great King, my mind is now intent upon His questions.
(30) Immediately thereafter, messengers arrived, weary from their swift journey.
Then, having taken the leaf from his hand, Raghunandana reflected in his mind, "How has this come to be?
At that moment, Śambhu, wearing the guise of a brahmin, spoke to Rāma in the presence of the Goddess.
"What are you thinking, even while the sages are seated before you?
Having heard those words, Rāghava questioned the preeminent sages.
Śrī Rāma said:
"How was Bibhīṣaṇa not bound with chains by the men? Alas!
Having seen the auspicious Liṅga Rāmeśvara installed by me, he has been released by those crooked and wicked Dravidians; let this be reflected upon by yourself. 34.

"O best of sages, you should investigate; by that, the Lord will be known even in part. They replied to Rāma, "We do not know it. Then Rāma said, "O most excellent ones, having examined the Purāṇas according to the prescribed method, speak of all that."
Thereafter, the cause of your ignorance must be investigated: which Purāṇas should be studied, and likewise, which ones should be avoided?
What kind of verse is commendable, and what kind would be otherwise? (37)
"In what kind of rites, and likewise, what kind of worshipper [should be],
and by what kind of devotees should the worship be performed according to the revealed determination?
Having heard these words of Rāma, those best of the twice-born— 38–39.
They replied to that best of the Raghus, whose mind was agitated by anxiety:
"O Rāma, we are not speakers of such boons; rather, let one who knows the Purāṇas look upon us.
Having heard that, Rāghava, filled with humility, questioned Śambhu.
Having heard those words, the high-minded one replied.
Śambhu said:
"One who lives according to the Purāṇas, is worthy of worship, studies his own Vedic branch, and is pure—"
He possessed a thorough knowledge of the principles of Mīmāṃsā, was a learned Vedic scholar, and a censurer of falsehood.

Then Rāma spoke these words: "O Blessed One, O Lord, I shall go."
Then, permitted by Hari, Rāghava,
together with the sages, Śambhu, and Nārāyaṇa, departed; having quickly reached Lokāloka, he then proceeded to Svādūdaka.
Then, having traversed the islands and oceans, he returned once more to Jambūdvīpa and stayed at the hermitage of Bharadvāja on the bank of the Gautamī.
Then, having bathed in the great river, the lord of sages, Bharadvāja—
Surrounded by his disciples, the illustrious sage beheld the Puṣpaka chariot;
having duly honored the mighty-armed Rāma there, as well as Śiva, Nārāyaṇa, and the sages, the great muni spoke to them.
"O most excellent ones, you should partake of food in my hermitage.
Rāma, however, at the word of Manu, agreed to do so in every way.
Then, having bathed in the great river and performed the libations for the gods and others, he ate.
Vasiṣṭha spoke these words to him who was desirous of eating and fond of that [food]:
"O King, if a Śrāddha is performed with meat, there would be an abandonment of Dharma.
Śrī Rāma said:

"O Blessed One, if a Śrāddha that was already performed on the new moon day, during an eclipse, at a sacred ford (tīrtha), on the Vyatīpāta yoga, or at the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti), is performed again,
you have stated that one should not perform the daily Śrāddha (nitya-śrāddha) once more. (61–62)
Just as it was for me, so too when the death of my mothers occurred and the period of impurity had arrived, the daily *śrāddha* was not omitted; however,
on occasions such as the *vyatīpāta*, it was performed according to your word.
Vasiṣṭha said: "All these sages, as well as this twice-born Śambhu,
will provide you with the complete and definitive resolution from their own mouths."
Having all reached a firm conclusion, the sages spoke to Śambhu:
"Tell us everything, O best of the twice-born; you are great.
Śambhu said:
I shall now describe what must be abandoned and what must be performed again when a birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) occurs or when obstacles arise:
the monthly rites, the water-pots, and all the *śrāddha* ceremonies. (66–67)

The wise know that the annual *śrāddha* is to be performed immediately after the period of impurity (*sūtaka*). All other [rites] that were postponed during the occurrence of an obstacle due to *sūtaka* are indeed to be performed immediately thereafter; of this there is no doubt. (68)

The monthly *śrāddhas*, the annual *śrāddha*, and likewise [the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*] should be performed after the period of impurity (*sūtaka*) has ended; however, in the event of an obstacle, it may be done otherwise. One who desires auspiciousness should perform [the annual *śrāddha*] on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight.
If there is an obstacle on that new-moon day (amāvāsyā),

then it should be performed on the subsequent days, provided there are no further hindrances; however, during the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), the rite performed by Rāma must be observed on the new-moon day itself.

If the month of the day of death cannot be known by any means whatsoever, it is prescribed that the śrāddha be performed on that same day in either the month of Mārgaśīrṣa or Māgha. However, when the day is known but the month itself is unknown, [the śrāddha should be performed on that day in the month of Kārttika]. 72–73.

The annual *śrāddha* for one who has been away on a journey or who has died should be performed on the new moon day of that very month. However, if the specific lunar day (*tithi*) is unknown, that day [of the new moon] should be taken; this is the rule when such knowledge is available. (74)
The three days beginning with Āśvina, Mārgaśīrṣa, Māgha, and Āṣāḍha—
any one of these should be selected according to the month at hand—
for the rites of Vṛddhi-śrāddha, Sīmantonnayana, Preta-śrāddha, and the monthly Anvāṣṭakā śrāddhas. 75–76.

The daily water-vessel rite (nityodakumbha), the monthly śrāddha, and even the rites for eclipses, the birth of a son, and propitiatory ceremonies— when all such acts are intended to be performed, the intercalary month does not cause any defect.
When a human being becomes ill when the time for the śrāddha rite has arrived,
he should appoint his wife, a brother, or even a disciple;
otherwise, in their absence, there would be a failure of the rite known as śrāddha.

One should appoint a recipient for the daily *śrāddha* according to one's capacity, as well as for that performed on the new moon day and the monthly [ancestral rites], provided they are distinct from those for the anniversary of death (80). If one is unable to perform the rite oneself, one should appoint a son or a Brahmin.
For one appointed to royal service who is occupied with the management of slaves,
when all calamities have occurred, he should have the Śrāddha performed by a Brāhmaṇa;
however, the best of the twice-born do not perform the Śrāddha during the morning time.
In the case of occasional *śrāddhas*, no restriction regarding time is prescribed. For one who is away from home and other such places, the *kutu-pa* (the specific auspicious time) is prescribed;
or else, it may be that which occurs shortly before the *kutu-pa*. 83–84.

Just as the afternoon is prescribed for the monthly śrāddha, so too when the new moon (amāvāsyā) spans both days, it should fall within the afternoon. However, in the case of a lunar decrease (kṣaya), the śrāddha should be performed on the earlier day; in the case of an increase (vṛddhi) or equality (sāmya), the later day is traditionally taught.

If the new moon (amāvāsyā) should coincide with two afternoons, it occurs during a waning; in cases of increase or equality, the latter [afternoon] should be taken. Where the moon has waned, there the śrāddha is pārvaṇa.
If this [lunar day] is not present during even one-eighth part of the subtle [period] following the eight parts of the day,
then that lunar day which extends through midday shall be the one for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite;
and that lunar day which extends through the evening shall be the one for the *pārvaṇa* rite.
In the case of those such as the *aśrāddha* (the rite for one who died before the afternoon), it should occur when the tithi is still present during a small portion of the afternoon.

If the tithi lasts for three *muhūrtas* at the time of sunset on the day of death, it is [the tithi] for that purpose; however, where it has set on the previous day and remains for three *muhūrtas* on the following day, it is as stated previously.
In that regard, if a Śrāddha performed on the following day results in the destruction of the eldest son,
one should perform the Amā-Śrāddha when the anniversary of death (mṛtāha) has arrived;
for it is prescribed for a twice-born man that [the rite] should take place when it overlaps with midday.
Rāma said:
"You should explain in its entirety the sequence of the śrāddha rites, as well as the sequence of mortal duties, and the determination of those dharmas that are incidental."
Śambhu said:
When the day of the śrāddha has arrived, one who is observant of the rules on the preceding day should invite the best of Brahmins, those endowed with the characteristics of a Brahmin.

One should observe eating only once a day, celibacy, and refraining from speaking with outcastes and others (94). One who performs the rite should do so on the previous day— brushing the teeth, applying oil, and cutting the nails and hair— and then abandon these activities on the following day (95).
One should adopt the prescribed observances and abandon all else;

if one performs worship at the three times of day, one should worship one's own deity in the morning at the time of dawn. (96) If one performs the worship at the hour of sunrise, [it is most auspicious].
Sleeping on the ground in that manner, rising at dawn and knowing his duties, he performs the morning rites preceded by bathing;
thus liberated from the three debts, he shall go to the supreme Brahman. 97-98.

He who performs the worship of Śiva at the time of sunrise becomes as radiant as the sun and is glorified in the world of Śiva. (99) Worship performed even within one *ghaṭikā* after the sun has risen [is likewise effective].

One who performs the worship of Śiva during the third ghaṭikā becomes equal in splendor to Rudra and is glorified in the world of Śiva. (100) One who performs the worship of Śiva during the third ghaṭikā becomes equal in splendor to Kubera and is glorified in the world of Śiva. (101)

In the third ghaṭikā, one should perform the worship of Śiva; possessing splendor equal to Kubera, he is glorified in the world of Śiva. As for he who [performs it] during the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh ghaṭikās...

One who worships Śiva with devotion becomes equal to the Maruts in the world of Śiva (103). Worship should be performed at the very time prescribed; or else, one should sacrifice according to one's vow or having undertaken a specific observance (104).
One should observe the rules of restraint according to one's capacity during the ritual services;
for even if there is a transgression of the rules, the sacrifice of the All-pervading Lord would still take place.
Śrī Rāma said:
Where is the worship of Śaṅkara, the God of gods, who possesses immeasurable splendor;
he who, through remembrance, destroys sin and grants liberation; Śiva, whose form is auspicious, and who knows the true meaning of the principle of Śiva? (106)
To the one adorned by Soma, whose eyes are Soma, the sovereign;
to the embodiment of the Veda who is formless, the essence of the Veda, the knower;
to the yogi who knows the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, and who is both the object of knowledge and that which is beyond being known. 107–108.
To Gopālī, who possessed a body as white as cow’s milk, who delighted in bathing with cow’s milk,
who has three eyes, whose eyes are the triple Veda, and who is the master of illusion— while he was in the midst of answering the question, he then imparted the knowledge of Śiva concerning Rāma.
Remaining as motionless as a pillar, with his eyes fixed upon the tip of his nose,
his cheeks moistened by streams of tears flowing from his eyes— an outpouring of bliss—
he bore the divine Giriśa within the lotus of his heart, whose limbs were exceedingly beautiful and smooth like cow’s milk.
Then, the reflection of Rāma was seen upon the thigh;
as soon as they saw Śambhu reflected there with four arms and three eyes, all the sages and lords of monkeys were struck with supreme wonder. (112)
Seeing Rāma, auspicious and of radiant form, situated upon the chest of Śambhu,
they remained silent for half a watch; then, looking toward Rāma and reflecting upon their own question, they laughed and spoke everything.
Śambhu said:

Worship should always be performed at an immovable [liṅga], or otherwise, as one desires, at a movable one; the worship of the liṅga is primary, though it may be performed in images and the like when a liṅga is unavailable. 115.
Due to the distinction of one's qualification, even in those various cases, the worship of the *liṅga*—whether deficient in qualities or complete in them—is fruitful.
However, worship performed toward an image (*pratimā*) and the like, if deficient in qualities, is certainly not fruitful. (116)
Worship is praised for both the immovable and the movable [liṅga].
(117) I shall now describe the worship of the movable [liṅga], as well as its installation and removal; no one—not even a sage—understands these two in their entirety anywhere. (118)
The yogis always install the Lord of Gods, Śaṅkara, within the lotus of their hearts, protect him, worship him, and eventually bid him farewell;
for the officiating priests, however, the ritual action consists of worshipping the three-eyed God in the fire.
For all worshippers without exception, Maheśvara resides within the Śiva-liṅga.
The installation of the liṅga, its worship, its dismissal, and even its wearing—Śaṅkara, the Great Lord, is indeed the liṅga itself. (120–121)

The *sajjikā* should be made of the most excellent gold, or it may be fashioned from silver or copper; likewise, that which is made of silver or bamboo, or even constructed from creepers, threads, or wood. 122.
It may be fashioned from cloth or else made of clay (123). Having wrapped it there with cloth and provided it with fragrant substances, [one should place it] upon a pair of clean,
washed garments and a soft seat (124).

Free from cold and heat, provided with four legs, equipped with a cover to ward off rain, and devoid of worms and insects— [one should] wrap that auspicious [liṅga] on all sides with a clean, soft cloth. (125)
Having placed [the deity] in the midst of the *sajjikā* and having again covered the Lord,
this indeed is proclaimed as the *sajjikā* situated before the god Rāma;
and the installation of that Great Lord is described in the *Pāṭha-rahasya*.
Alternatively, it may be at the base of a wall or upon a sacrificial altar (devavedī);
likewise, in a well-protected location, one should appoint a guardian.
One should ensure an inseparable connection between the vital breaths (prāṇa) and the like, along with the observances (niyamas).
This is declared to be the supreme installation of the Paramātman by the wise king. Sāttvika placement is that which is situated near oneself;
tāmasa placement, on the other hand, is the touching of the limbs and the protection of the entire body. 129–130.

The wearing [of the mark] on the crown of the head is primary, and it was likewise performed by Brahmā; its wearing at the edge of the crown is said to be auspicious. Wearing it on the forehead is recommended, just as the auspicious [mark] was worn by Lakṣmī.
Furthermore, Bāṇa held [the spear] to his head or again to his right breast; then,
by the sage Karṇa, that supreme ṛṣi, it was severed at the ear, and having thus pierced his body, it was fashioned into a place for iron.
Some superior rākṣasas carry the *tathāliṅga* (the form of the Tathāgata) on their heads;
for mortals who are homeless and powerless, bearing it upon the head is declared to be the lowest of the low, such as wearing it around the waist or in similar ways. 134.
If they happen to receive the leavings [of food] from them, they must wear it upon their heads (135).
For those of the lowest-of-the-low conduct, there is always the wearing of the *vairiṇa* mark;
and for sinners, it is a wonder that exists even in the world of Yama (136).
Śrī Rāma said:
Since the firm script written by Citragupta upon the forehead is fixed, how can one go to hell otherwise? (137)
"How does the worship of Karoti destroy sin?
Śambhu replied: "It destroys all sin, even that accumulated over hundreds of lifetimes. (138)

Through the scorching away of all sins by its remembrance, the Great Lord, the word "bhasma" (ashes) is so designated; its wearing is supreme, performed according to the rules upon the forehead through the application of the primary potency of fire. 139.
It destroys [sin] just as the fire consumes what is written on a cloth;
sin committed above the ears is destroyed by wearing it on the face, and by wearing it on the neck, the sin committed through enjoyments of the neck and so forth is destroyed. 140–141.
Sin committed with the arms, sin committed in the chest through the mind, sin committed at the navel, and likewise sin committed at the anus on the back;
O Rāma, [these are purified] by wearing [the ashes] on the sides, as well as that born from embracing another's wife and so forth. 142.
The wearing of that sacred ash as the *tripuṇḍra* mark everywhere is highly commended.
It is the wearing of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, as well as the three fires;
by it, the three worlds are indeed protected. (143-144)
Pure ashes, consecrated with mantras, should be held in fifteen locations:
on the two sides of the chest, on the two arms, and likewise on the pair of shoulders above the chest.
Wearing [ashes] on all parts of the body for the sake of worship is approved by Dharma. (145)

Those who eat ashes, sleep on ashes, and have their bodies smeared with ashes, and who perform ablutions with ashes, are always liberated from sins; of this there is no doubt. At the beginning of the Brāhmaṇa initiation, it is traditionally taught that one should recite the mantra "Tryāyuṣam."

This is indeed a means for all— whether a Vaiṣṇava mortal or any other person— for protection against possession by spirits among men, and for the destruction of the venom of snakes and other creatures. (148)
"One who bathes in ashes and is joined with ashes indeed becomes qualified for ritual acts.
Śrī Rāma said: "Tell me first the greatness of the ashes; for whom indeed is the ash-grace (bhasmāyuṣya)?"
"How indeed does one protect all this? Tell me that.
Śambhu said:
"It is the cause for increasing the lifespan of every embodied being in its threefold state."
It destroys sin, and by its touch, it bestows both coolness and heat, as well as the state of Śiva.
(151) In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient history:
there was a twice-born man named Dhanañjaya belonging to the lineage of Vasiṣṭha. (152)
He had a hundred wives endowed with beauty and grace;
among them, O Sage, one gave birth to Śamāka, who was compassionate toward all beings.
By the number of those wives, there were also ascetic sons of Rāma.
The division of their paternal inheritance was arranged unequally;
at that time, a great bond of enmity arose among the brothers. Indeed, for men born of the same lineage, enmity is inevitable. 154–155.
Then, moved by compassion, he went to the bank of the Bhavanāśinī river together with various groups of sages, desiring to behold Narasiṃha;
indeed, for the purpose of seeing Narasiṃha, he was accompanied by a certain Brāhmaṇa.
Having brought a superior fruit of the *jaṃbīra* tree, endowed with excellent form and fragrance, Karuṇa then took that most excellent fruit and smelled it;
the groups of brahmins present there then afflicted him with a curse. (157–158)

"O you whose nature is sinful due to becoming a fly, the end of this curse shall come after a hundred years through the high-souled Dadhīci. (159) Then, having attained the state of a fly, he spoke thus to his wife:
"O auspicious one, protect me who has attained the state of a fly!
Having spoken thus, he became such [a fly] and wandered here and there.
Then, having learned of this situation, his kinsmen, whose resolve was set upon evil—
Having made that effort, she cast him into the midst of oil;
then, taking her deceased husband, that sorrowful woman of slender waist [was found].
To alleviate her grief, the goddess Arundhatī spoke.
"O lady of pure smiles, I shall restore this man to life this very day with these ashes alone.
(163) Then he presented the ashes produced from the *agnihotra* sacrifice to Arundhatī; likewise, by means of the *mṛtyuñjaya* mantra, he cast them upon the deceased being. (164)
Then, with a fan, she of the pure smile created a gentle breeze; thereupon, by the power of that ash, the creature rose up.
Then, when a hundred years were complete, a kinsman killed him.

Her husband having died, that virtuous woman, sorrowful yet possessing a pure smile, sought refuge with the eminent brahmin sage named Dadhīca, a great devotee of Maheśvara. That virtuous woman approached him, and the brahmin, whose wealth was his asceticism, spoke to her.
He restored to life the aged Jamadagni, a treasury of asceticism, who was deprived of his triple lifespan,
and likewise Kaśyapa, who was in such a state;
he did the same for the gods who were in that condition, and even for me, who was like this in the past.
"Therefore, O sinless one, I shall restore this creature to life with my ashes.
Having spoken thus, the blessed Dadhīca went for refuge to Maheśvara;
then, having consecrated the ashes with mantras and taken them in his hand, he restored the husband of that virtuous woman to life.
Through the touch of Maheśa’s hand, Karuṇa was freed from his curse;
having returned to his true form, he went to his own hermitage. That virtuous woman also brought Dadhīca to her home for a meal.
Then that virtuous twice-born one requested the brahmin-sage; and when the lord of brahmins had finished eating, ten million disciples arrived,
followed by the gods whose bodies were smeared with ashes.
Having paid homage to Dadhīca, they questioned him out of a desire for auspiciousness.
The gods said:
"O high-minded one, our knowledge was previously lost. (174)
But having seen Gautama’s wife, we became afflicted with lust;
thus the goddess, who had performed the auspicious marriage rites, was violated by us. As we lusted after her, our spiritual knowledge was utterly destroyed.
Then we all went to the sage Durvāsas and said:
"Now we shall remove all this impurity by means of the Śatarudriya mantra, consecrated by Śambhu himself. 176-177.
"By him alone has this been given even to me for the pacification of the sin of killing a Brahmin and other such offenses.
Having spoken thus, Durvāsas gave him the excellent sacred ash. Then, because of those words, all of us became agitated in mind.
With their bodies smeared with ashes by means of the Śatarudriya mantra,
they were all instantly cleansed of their sins;
we recognize this as a marvel— such is the power of the sacred ash.
Dadhīca said: We shall describe to you briefly the power of the ash of Śiva;
it is not possible to describe it in detail even in hundreds of years. 181
In this regard, I shall proclaim to you the ancient account of the two gods,
Hari and Śaṅkara, which destroys all sins such as the killing of a Brahmin.
Long ago, when the dissolution of Brahmā had occurred and there was a single, terrible ocean, [the Lord appeared].
The Blessed Lord Mahāviṣṇu was lying in the waters of the dissolution;
having reached both his sides were two hundred brahmāṇḍas,
twenty on the sides of his feet, and twenty within the space of his head.
The Lord fashioned the cosmic egg from the nature of the pearl of His nose;
within the circle of its navel, certain lords of sages such as Lomaśa and others perform great austerities and worship the Supreme Lord. 185.
Then Viṣṇu, possessed of great splendor, fell into anxiety due to his desire to create.
Becoming intent on the yoga of meditation, he perceived nothing at all;
then, with great sorrow, he wept aloud again and again.
In the meantime, a certain radiance, unlike anything seen in the world, was perceived; upon seeing it, Hari closed his eyes out of fear.
Then, one possessing a physical form and a luster equal to cow's milk approached.
Holding in his two hands a pair of garments woven from millions of cosmic eggs,
and upon his chest bearing a single cosmic egg fashioned from millions of worlds,
he causes one cosmic egg to fall and another to spring up from his two feet.
Seeing him thus, adorned with all ornaments and imperishable, Viṣṇu was pleased and spoke for the sake of his manifestation. Viṣṇu said:
Salutations to you, O Lord of the lords of gods; salutations to you, O eternal and imperishable one.
O Blessed One, I do not know you, but you know everything; salutations again and again. I do not understand your true nature, for your splendor is difficult to behold.
Adorned with ruby earrings and a network of golden chains,
he wore beautiful jeweled rings and ornaments upon his forearms; his long, radiant eyes were cast toward the excellent lady who was slightly reddened.
The Lord, who resembles a lotus in his eyes, possesses an eye upon his forehead; he is imperishable, and his eyebrows produce the illusion of Cupid’s bow.
His lovely face has smooth, high, and beautiful ears and symmetrical, even cheeks. 195.

I have taken refuge in You, the All-pervading Lord, who possesses a gentle smile and a serene countenance, whose appearance is like that of the young moon, who is clothed in garments red with consciousness, and whose ornaments are fashioned from the Vedas; O Lord, let my eyes be granted to me.
"Be the refuge for the wretched, the blind, the miserable, and the ignorant who have lost their way;
now grant me divine vision, the power to behold my own Self.
Then Hari beheld Śambhu, the three-eyed Lord, standing before him.
"O Kopa, who are you? he asked; then the one of great fame replied, "I do not know you. "In this state, I am only capable of offering a prostration, not of knowing [you]," he said.
Sadāśiva spoke:
"I shall bestow that knowledge upon you; first perform the ritual bath with water (vāruṇa-snāna), and after that, the bath with ashes (bhasma-snāna); thereafter, I shall declare the knowledge.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Water fit for my bath does not exist anywhere," he said;
thus addressed, Brahmā sat down with his body resting upon the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa), yet even in water reaching up to his thighs, it was not suitable for Hari to bathe.
Śambhu laughed, saying, "Oh, the water for bathing and sacrifice is indeed too much!
Then Dadhīca spoke;
thereafter, Lord Śiva gazed at Viṣṇu with his eye on the forehead.
He gazed with his left eye at Viṣṇu, whose subtle limbs had dissolved away. Then Śambhu said to Viṣṇu, whose body was now subtle and cool: "O Viṣṇu, bathe in this lake which has been prepared."
Then Hari, wishing to bathe,
was unable to enter that deep lake which had been prepared on the lap of Hara.
Hari said, "There is no path for entering this lake."
Then Śambhu said to the deity, "Let a path be made;
formerly this great water was a fathom deep, O Lord, but now that you have settled here, the water has reached only up to your thighs. (207)
"Now, even as you stand here, how is it that there is no entry into the lake?
This thigh of mine is only eight finger-breadths in measure; I see it within that lake. Enter it, and I shall give you the touch of my foot."
Hari said: "This single sentence, which is a staircase issued from my own speech, is the Veda; however, no one here possesses the capacity to ascend these words. (210)
"How is it possible to grasp that which has form, or how can there be a grasping of the Veda?
Śambhu said:
"A man's power does not lie in the holding or climbing of physical objects. (211)
"Take this great Veda," [said Śiva]; then Hari also took it, his hand bent low as if falling from exhaustion, O Janārdana. "I am not able to hold it," Hari said to Śiva.
Śiva, laughing, said: "O King, descend into this very great lake;
having ascended its steps, O Keśava, you ought to bathe.
Dadhīca said:

Having bathed there according to the prescribed rite in waters reaching up to the thighs—which serve as a staircase to the Vedas—and having emerged outside, he said, "I have bathed; what should be done next? Thereupon, Śambhu spoke to Hari.
"What are you meditating upon here in your heart? Speak, for you say nothing.
Hari replied, "Nothing. Then Śambhu said to him:
"Once purified by the bath of ashes, you shall know the supreme auspiciousness."
"Whatever is desired for the benefit of one who has been initiated, that I shall provide for his protection.
Dadhīca said:
Taking a bit of ash from the ash situated upon his own chest with his fingernail, Śaṅkara—
Then, having consecrated it with the *praṇava* and the *gāyatrī* which has become Brahman,
Śiva took it up with his two fingers and, using the five-syllabled mantra, scattered it over all the limbs and the head of Hari.
Then, looking at him with a peaceful gaze, Hara said to Hari, "Live!
and [asked], "Meditate; what is in your heart? He became intent on meditation, and in his heart he saw a lamp, long in shape and exceedingly brilliant.
Hari said to Śiva, "I have seen the lamp directly, O Māyā. Śiva replied, "O Hari, that knowledge is not yet fully ripened;
once you consume the ashes, that knowledge will become complete in its entirety."
Hari said:
"Having previously bathed in ashes and having seen the Lord who is accessible through devotion, I shall eat the auspicious ash; thus Acyuta ate the ash."
In that regard, it was truly a marvel: Vāsudeva, who previously possessed a luster like that of a ripe *bimba* fruit, in an instant became the color of pure pearls.
From that time forth, this Vāsudeva remained white and gracious.
Furthermore, becoming intent on meditation, one should [visualize] Śiva in the midst of a lamp—
resembling pure crystal, three-eyed, two-armed,
the all-pervading Lord, granting boons with his right hand and granting fearlessness with his left.
With a body like that of a five-year-old child, possessing a luster equal to the autumnal moon,
adorned with ruby earrings and a network of golden chains,
beautiful with jeweled rings, and well-adorned with ornaments on his forearms and wrists.
With thin reddish lips and long, wide eyes reaching to his ears;
with an imperishable eye upon his forehead resembling the eye of Bāṇa;
the Lord whose eyebrows produce the illusion of the bow of Kandarpa. 228–229.
The Lord has smooth, elevated, and very beautiful limbs, with symmetrical cheeks; he possesses a gentle smile and a serene face, appearing like the young moon;
he wears garments dyed with saffron and has anklets fashioned according to the Vedas.

Śucismitā said:

"Unseasonable conduct certainly gives rise to suspicion in everyone;
and here in this house, there is mutual talk and secret laughter between those of youthful age. (9)

The Brahmin said:

The state of mind that arises from touch is not the same as that which arises from sight; likewise,
the state of mind that arises from sight is not the same as that which arises from touch (verse 21),
due to the sight and touch of one's own genitals, the armpits, and the pair of breasts.
"Whose mind would not falter, and whose seed would not be spilled?

departed by the path they had come; meanwhile, they beheld a Rākṣasa approaching—
Pañcaṣeḍhra, of massive body and endowed with ten arms.

while the lord of the rākṣasas was thus reflecting, he seized that monkey, who remained in such a state, with a single effort.

The immeasurable-souled one devoured [his foes] and let out a lion’s roar;

"You ought to perform penance at that sacred ford, Syamantapañcaka.

Having bound him with iron fetters at the ankles and the ends of the feet,
