the Blessed Lord, the husband of Ambikā, rose up from the midst of the fire.
Resembling pure crystal and adorned with the crescent moon, Maheśvara beheld him with his head hanging down and said:
"Do not act rashly, O Rākṣasa; I am the giver of boons—choose a boon."
The Rākṣasa said:
"O Maheśvara, you are surely the giver of many boons;
[grant me] the resurrection of my severed head as well as the restoration of life to one who has been swallowed. (75)

May the power of Viṣṇu in his boar-form be fourfold; by me, Hiraṇyākṣa shall be slain, and may he always remain in my presence. Through the plucking out of your matted hair, one Puruṣa shall come into being.
"Therefore, let this death come from no other than him; may this be my chosen fate.
"It shall be exactly so," having said this, Hara vanished.
Thus was the sinful Rākṣasa, who had obtained the boon, slain by you.
Then Hari, Śaṅkara, and Pitāmaha,
along with the wives of the gods and others, departed as they had come;
having prostrated themselves on the ground like a staff before Vīrabhadra, they then spoke to him.
"Salutations to you, O Lord of the lords of gods; salutations to you, O mine of compassion!
Salutations to you, the eternal and infinite; salutations to you, be a granter of boons.
Vīrabhadra said:
"I shall restore to life the gods, along with the sages and monkeys, by means of my ashes. You must be satisfied; you should not grieve now.
Having spoken thus, Vīrabhadra restored them all to life with his ashes.
Then the sages, the gods, and the monkeys rose up;
delighted, they spoke these words with their heads bowed and palms joined in reverence:
"O Father, we have been restored to life by you; O Father, you are our protector according to dharma."
O Śaṅkara, source of all existence, be our eternal refuge.

Having seen the wicked conduct of these children, please instruct them accordingly, and protect them from the afflictions caused by others and from diseases, just as you would your own biological sons. 84-85.
"O sinless one, we who committed an offense at Dakṣa’s sacrifice have been disciplined by you; now, O Lord, we are protected by you like children.
Vīrabhadra said:

This is true, there is no doubt: wherever you may encounter an obstacle, remember me quickly, and the destruction of that obstacle shall come to pass. Furthermore, those who recite the "Vīrabhadra-pada" one hundred and eight times—
Likewise, accompanied by the *praṇava* at the beginning and *namaḥ* at the end, along with the dative case ending,
there shall be the destruction of those afflictions caused by *rākṣasas*,
as well as in cases of affliction by *brahmarākṣasas* and fears of *piśācas* and other such beings. 88–89.
By the mere recollection of his name, all afflictions are destroyed.

[One should meditate on] the Lord, whose eyes are as brilliant as lightning, who is fierce, whose lower lip is beautified by the redness of the crescent moon, whose body is deep blue, who wears a garland of matted locks, and who bears white sectarian marks (tripuṇḍra) upon his limbs. 90–91.
This recollection has been proclaimed for the sake of liberating the Brahmarākṣasa;
all of this has been declared within the mantra of Vīrabhadra. 92.
Dadhīca said:
Thus have the sages, gods,
and Tathāgatas declared this supreme majesty of the sacred ash (bhasma), which destroys the sins of one who reads it, hears it, or even remembers it throughout their entire lifespan. 93.
"It bestows devotion to Śiva, is meritorious, and increases longevity and health.
Śucismitā said:
"I am fulfilled, blessed, and the most excellent among women."
"O bull among sages, likewise, let there be obeisance to Hatapāpa here.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava," in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The one hundred and eighth chapter.
Śrī Rāma said:
O highly fortunate one, [please tell me] the origin of the sacred ash (bhasma) and also its greatness.
Tell me the merit of wearing the ashes and likewise the merit of giving them.
Śambhu said: I shall proclaim the origin of the ashes, which destroys all sins.
Listen, O lord of men, to the greatness [of Him] from remembering and chanting [His name]:
He who is the one eternal God, Śiva, who is worshipped by Brahmā, the three-eyed one, the substratum of qualities, yet transcending qualities, imperishable and immutable. 2–3.
Then, desiring to create, he beheld the three qualities residing within himself;
for this which is to be known as the three Vedas is indeed these three qualities. Having separated those qualities from himself and having divided their respective locations, O dear one...
From his right side he created Brahmā, and from the left, Hari;
from the region of his back, the omnipresent Lord created Maheśāna—thus the all-pervading one created three sons.
As soon as they were born, these three gods were Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
They spoke these clear words: "Who are you, and who are we? Śiva said to those sons: "You are my sons; I am the father.
O sons, partake of these three qualities which have karma as their cause."
The sons said:
"O Lord, whom or what quality should one worship, for how long a time?
And how may there be the cessation of the qualities? Tell us this."
Śiva said: "As far as your knowledge extends, or even as long as your lifespan may last,
so far shall there be the retention of each individual quality."
"Let Brahmā worship *sattva*, Viṣṇu *rajas*, and Maheśvara *tamas*.
As soon as this was said by the Lord of Gods, Brahmā then grasped *sattva*; he was not even able to move it, so how could he have been capable of sustaining it?
But having set aside that quality, he then grasped the quality of passion (rajas);
yet, unable to move it, he then grasped the quality of darkness (tamas).
Unable to move it either, he fell down and wept.
Viṣṇu held the quality of Rajas with his left hand; Maheśa also held the quality of Tamas with two fingers;
and he placed the quality of Sattva upon Viṣṇu with one finger.
He placed Brahmā upon his footstool and danced.
Beholding Śiva dancing with an exceedingly graceful form, white as cow’s milk, youthful, three-eyed, assuming all [forms], and full of playful charm, the Giver of Boons spoke to his sons. 15–16.
Śiva said:
"O son, I am pleased with you; choose a boon as you desire. Then the son said to his father, "Grant me this boon. 17.
"O Śiva, may the worship performed with me in mind become worship of yourself; may you always abide within me, for you and I are indeed the immutable one.
Śiva said:

"O highly fortunate one, it shall be exactly so; there is no doubt. These two sons of mine, Brahmā and Viṣṇu, are indeed red and fair-complexioned, and their body hair at the base of the arms is likewise like my own form, O sinless one."
Then he said this to Brahmā: "May you resort to one quality.
Brahmā replied:
"O Lord, I am not able to maintain the quality designated by you."
"O King, you shall uphold [the portion]; let Hari indeed worship the divine being.
This Lord Śambhu will also uphold the remaining quality. Thus spoke Śambhu.
Having taken up the qualities (guṇas), the gods were unable to maintain them eternally;
for the sake of the power to sustain them, they spoke again to Śiva, saying, "We are not capable of maintaining the connection with the qualities at all times. (22-23)
"O Blessed One, if you are a granter of boons, let power be given to me.
Having heard those words, Śiva spoke these words. Śiva said:
The power of knowledge is called "power" (śakti) for all things;
ignorance (avidyā) rests upon the three qualities (guṇas), and non-ignorance (vidyā) rests upon that [knowledge].
Only after burning away the three qualities are you worthy to uphold their essence.
"Whatever may be there, let that which is beneficial be maintained by you.
Then they said to his son's words: "There is no burning without fire.
Śiva replied: "Indeed, fire exists within the eye of Maheśa."
This triad of qualities (guṇas) is the cow; knowledge is its auspicious dung, and the Upaniṣads are said to be its urine. One should then produce the ashes.
The Smṛtis are its calves, and from them is produced the dung.
One should consecrate the cow there with the mantra "Āgāva" (Come, O Cows). Then, with the mantra "Gāvo gāvo gāva," one should feed her grass and water.
Having fasted on the fourteenth day of either the bright or the dark fortnight, the observer of the vow [should proceed].
Having risen early the next morning, being pure and composed, having bathed and put on clean clothes, he should go to a cow for the sake of cow-dung.
Having raised her with effort while reciting the Gāyatrī, he should collect her urine.

One should hold [the materials] in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or clay; or one should place cow’s urine in a lotus leaf, a Palāśa leaf, a water-pot, or even a cow’s horn. One should apply cow dung with the mantra "Gandhadvārā. (32–33)

One should collect [the earth] without letting it fall to the ground into the previously mentioned vessel; the wise one should then purify it with cow dung while reciting the mantra, "May prosperity attend me," and perform the wiping away of the cow dung with the mantra, "The misfortune consisting of me. (34)
One should pour cow’s urine onto the cow dung while reciting the mantra "saṃ tvā siñcāmi," and then,
having dried them with the rays of the sun, one should prepare fourteen balls (piṇḍas) using the mantra "pañcānāṃ tvā" and carry them away. 35–36.
Then, having placed balls of cow-dung in the previously mentioned vessel and having established the fire according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra, one should kindle it;
one should cast the balls into that [fire], offering each ball to the deity corresponding to its respective syllable.
The wise one should offer the two Āghāra libations and the two Ājyabhāgas, and then perform two Homa offerings.
Thereafter, thirteen offerings beginning with Jaya should be made to Nidhanapati; then the five Brahmans should be offered to Namah Hiraṇyabāhave. 38–39.

Having offered all the oblations with mantras ending in the dative case, the wise one should then offer them with these: "To Śarva," "To Rudra," and "To Yaśasvin," as well as with the three "Anājñāta" mantras. 40.
Then, having offered the *vyāhṛti* oblations, one should offer the *sviṣṭakṛt*.
(41) Having set aside the remainder of the fuel-sticks, one should then augment the water in the full-vessel with other water while reciting the *pūrṇamāsa* formula. (42)
One should place that water, [reciting] "The nectar is in the Brahmins," upon one's head;
then, with the indicative marks of the directions such as "In the east," one should pour water toward the various quarters.
Having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmin, one should perform the rite of the auspicious horripilation (pulaka).

"I shall bring [the fire] for the protection of the ritual actions of all the gods. Having brought it with the mantra "O Jātavedas, lead you," he should then cover the fire within the *pulāka* (grain-offering) with this mantra: "Cover [it], O Yama. Thus, he should cover that fire in the *pulāka*.
It is taught that for three days one should remain standing in the fire and cover oneself with horripilation (pulaka).
One should devoutly feed the Brahmins and eat oneself while remaining silent. If one desires an abundance of ash, one should collect an even greater amount of cow dung.
Whether over three days or on a single day,
having bathed at dawn on the third or the fourth day, wearing white garments, a white sacred thread, and white garlands and unguents; 47–48.
The knower of mantras, having smeared his teeth with white ash and having uttered "So be it" (tadvat) along with this mantra, should not abandon the truth that is the ash.
Then follow the sixteen services, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana).
Having offered the oblation that is to be performed, he should then withdraw the fire.
With the mantra "O Agni, you are ashes," he should take up the ashes produced therefrom;
then, after wiping [the vessel] with the mantra "I am Agni," he should proceed further.
Having mixed it with the waters of the Gaṅgā or with the milk of a Kapilā cow,
one should grind together camphor, saffron from Kāśmīra, uśīra, sandalwood,
and the two types of aguru into a fine powder.
One should cast that powder into the ashes with the Brahma-mantra "Oṃ.
Then, for the sprinkling of milk, the Kapilā-mantra is prescribed:
"O Goddess, this milk is nectar; it is pure and increased here. 53-54.
"By your grace, let all men be liberated from every sin.
Then, the wise man should bring down the balls of ash with the *praṇava* (Om), using the mantra 'aṇor aṇīyān' for the discerning one. 55.
Śambhu said:
Having thus prepared the ashes and taken them while dry, the knower of mantras should then rub them with the *praṇava* (Om) and consecrate them seven times with the *praṇava* mantra.
One should consecrate the head with Īśāna, the face with Tatpuruṣa (57), the chest region with Aghora, the private parts with Vāma,
the feet with Sadyojāta, and indeed all the limbs with the Praṇava. (58)
Then, having smeared his entire body from the soles of his feet to the top of his head with ashes, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and put on a clean, white garment.
Having sipped water once more, he is fit to perform all his duties in every respect.
Then, having taken up the ashes and wiped [the body] with the *praṇava* (OM),

one should apply the *tripuṇḍra* mark on the forehead while reciting "Oṃ namaḥ śivāya," meditating upon the all-pervading Lord who has three eyes, who is the substratum of the three qualities (*guṇas*), and the progenitor of the three.

Having said "Namaḥ śivābhyām," one should apply the Tripuṇḍra on both arms; with "Aghorāya namaḥ," on both forearms (prakoṣṭha); then with "Bhīmāya," on the back and likewise on the nape of the neck (śirodhi) at the rear.
One should offer [the water] to Nīlakaṇṭha on the head with the mantra "Salutation to you, the Soul of All" (sarvātmane namaḥ).
Then, having washed both hands, one should perform the ritual action.
Śiva said:
"Only after you have thus reduced [the earth] to ashes and rubbed it clean will you be able to sustain the qualities; thereafter, indeed, you shall create progeny.
Śambhu said:
Thus commanded by Śiva, the gods— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—
having then acted according to the prescribed rite with competitive zeal, yet being unable to understand one another's intentions, bowed to Śiva and spoke.
Who would wear the *kaṅguṇa* [garland], and who is Śiva? Then he spoke to his sons:
"Action-power as well as knowledge perishes just like a mouthful of dust.
Brahmā is seen to have a short lifespan, and his life is measured by *manus*."
I, who am adorned with garlands of cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) and am the protector of Brahmā—
when you did not know me while relying upon the quality of passion (rajas),
it was because Viṣṇu possesses greater strength than Brahmā, and his lifespan is longer than that of Brahmā.
May the Great Lord (Maheśa), whose ornament is a garland of cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍa), be mine alone;
for the lifespan of Viṣṇu is said to be merely four breaths [of Maheśa].
Because he possesses a superior quality of sattva compared to Brahmā, Hari takes recourse in that very sattva.
He knows me at all times and shall never forget me.
His worship is exclusively *sāttvika*; it is neither *rājasa* nor *tāmasa*.
Śiva is peaceful and of the nature of *sattva*, yet he is perceived through the mouth of *rajas*. 71–72.
Likewise, Śambhu partook of the quality of space (nabhas) as well as blue;
indeed, he formerly assumed the bodies of sattva, rajas, and tamas.
Therefore, various forms of worship are prescribed for this Śaṅkara.
That which is joined with *rajas* and *tamas* is proclaimed to be cruel (74).
Even though it is cruel, worship directed toward Śaṅkara is said to grant the ultimate goal;
it is joined with *rajas* and *tamas*, yet it is fully capable of setting forth the scriptures (75).
Even when interrupted, worship directed toward Śaṅkara is said to grant fruit;

likewise, that which is joined with both darkness (tamas) and purity (sattva), as well as that which is mixed, is productive. However, mixed worship toward Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, yields no fruit.
"O Lord, whether it be of such a kind or that kind, the worship of Śaṅkara performed according to rule bestows fruit immediately upon any embodied being whatsoever.
Śambhu said:
O sinless one, this procedure for the sacred ash has been declared in brief;
it destroys all the sins of both the speaker and the listeners.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Origin of Sacred Ash," in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava.
The one hundred and ninth chapter.
Śambhu said:
Here I shall narrate to you a story that destroys all sins.
Having heard this, the righteous-souled one attained unsurpassed devotion to Śiva.
There was a preeminent Brahmin named Ikṣvāku, possessed of great learning and high intelligence,
proficient in many scriptures and an expert in the science of ethics.
He was neither a sacrificer nor a giver, nor a worshiper of the gods; he was neither a teacher of the Veda nor an expounder of what has been heard,
nor [an expounder] of the Purāṇas, the Itihāsas, the Śrutis, or the Āgamas.
With effort, he acted as the sole promoter of the refinement of the body for the enjoyer; then,
for such a twice-born man, his life passed away after observing [this state],
at which time one year had elapsed and five months of that year remained.
On the night of the third day, he heard this ancient account:
that the wealth acquired by oneself becomes utterly exhausted if it is not given away as a gift,
for it will surely become worthless even as it is consumed day after day.
For that many years, he will certainly be cooked in hell;
thereafter, having experienced a thousand births as a worm,
he becomes poor, diseased, friendless, possessed of a wicked wife, and burdened with many children.

Living day by day through begging and soliciting, yet never seeking out seeds that have been submerged anywhere; living on what is obtained is the livelihood of those who subsist on labor. 9. Living on what is obtained is the livelihood of servants.
Deaf in his middle ear and blind in one eye, with impurities trickling from him—
having thus heard the Purāṇa, that descendant of Ikṣvāku was deeply distressed;
remembering [the sage] again and again, that lowest of the twice-born reflected thus in his mind.
With the flowers of form, she who is made of buffalo [skin] and Durgā is devoid of fruit;
likewise, she who is devoid of the Purāṇas shows the way to liberation through knowledge.
Having thoroughly studied many scriptures and the Vedas with their extensive commentaries, [she reveals this].
"For a man who has not heard the Purāṇas, there is no vision of the true path.
Śambhu said:
"As he was reflecting thus, his untimely death occurred."
Then, having gone to the realm of Yama, he was rebuked by Yama.
Yama said:
"You are possessed of many sins; you have no great merit at all."
"The sin incurred from teaching the Vedas is known to you; O twice-born one, your residence in hell shall last for ten million years.
Your lifespan here is extremely short; go back to your former body. (15-16)

Perform meritorious and beneficial acts of charity, worship of the deities, and the recitation of mantras; engage in the study of the Vedas with their auxiliary sciences, feed the Brahmins, and wear the sacred ashes.
Worship the Lord Viśveśvara, the God of gods and the consort of Umā.
By the mere effort of that [listening], you shall go to the stainless world.
O sinner, listen daily with devotion to whatever Purāṇa there may be; then, by that very hearing, you shall not behold my torments. 18-19.
Having heard the words of Yama, the brahmin returned to his own body;
then, applying himself with effort to the worship of the Lord, that virtuous twice-born man went to Jābāli, the best of sages and a devotee of Śiva.
He was perfected in austerity and Vedic study, a discerning judge of the Śruti and Smṛti;
he was a knower of the truth of the Purāṇas, surrounded by a hundred thousand disciples,
his entire body loosened by old age, and one who had reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
Desirous of seeing it, he went to Mount Mandara, which possessed beautiful caves,
was filled with various birds, and was covered with various flowering creepers;
it was endowed with the blossoms of all seasons and adorned with diverse fragrances.
The great cave was filled with the songs of pairs of kinnaras;
its trees were graced by women endowed with many forms and beauties, and it was adorned by those various women hanging from the branches. 24-25.
Awakening the bees that had fallen asleep from the fatigue of passion, the cuckoos warble at will; indeed, they cry out for the union of those who are separated.
[This place] is crowded with various groups of sages, tranquil, and frequented by deer.
It was crowded with throngs of Apsarases and frequented by hosts of Gandharvas; its interior forests were filled with songs emerging from the mouths of various Siddhas;
it was replete with diverse fruits and endowed with many temples of the gods. 27–28.
It was crowded with hundreds of palaces and provided with various dwellings,

[guarded] by lions-faced, elephant-faced, and owl-faced beings, as well as by those with hideous faces, those with distorted faces, fierce ones, those with half-faces, and those with the faces of does.

[He was surrounded] by the lords of the Gaṇas, whose faces resembled the mouths of all living beings, including those with the heads of deer, elephants, goats, lizards, snakes, monkeys, and bears (30), as well as those with the snouts of tigers, scorpions, bears, camels, dogs, and donkeys.
It was adorned with faces like creepers, faces like trees, faces like rocks, and faces like iron;
with faces like conch shells, pearls, and other aquatic creatures;
and with beings possessing extra limbs, bodiless forms, those with matted hair, and those with shaven heads. 31–32.
With faces like birds, with twelve faces, and even with three bodies and multiple faces;
with faces like bells, with faces, ears, and feet like winnowing baskets,
and even with faces like bells, faces like flutes, and faces like tinkling bells.
Some had faces like iron maws, corresponding to the nature of the objects that exist in the world; others were characterized by hidden passion, beauty,
and tenderness, resembling ten million suns and possessing a splendor equal to ten million moons.

It was joined by [beings] of various colors, with faces in every direction, possessing universal forms—with four faces, two faces, five faces, three faces, and even six faces; some had one or many faces, were peaceful, and were always happy. 36.

The Mount Mandara was frequented by those endowed with various riches and equal to the gods of desire, such as Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, whose forms were like those of Umā and Īśa, as well as by others assuming various forms. 37–38.

Where the cows are the Vedas joined with the calves of Mīmāṃsā, and Dharma and the others are present in bodily form; where the Purāṇas are the actions, and the Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Āgamas have taken on physical bodies. (39)
Where Mount Mandara, the destroyer of sins, stands together with its peaks; in its center is a most meritorious city, supremely beautiful,
adorned with hundreds of ponds, lakes, groves, and palaces.

It was surrounded by seven walls and moats, provided with jeweled watchtowers, endowed with nine gate-towers, and filled with various wonderful mansions; its splendor was peerless and free from heat, cold, and other such extremes. 42.

In the midst of that was a holy city, and in the center of that was an auspicious assembly hall (43). In its center was an excellent throne adorned with the feet of the Vedas, and it possessed a beautiful footstool fashioned from all the Upaniṣads (44).
The Purāṇas and Āgamas proclaimed "May it be well" at the feet of Śiva;
there sat the Great Yogin, whose form was like cow's milk,
the Lord with a beautiful face and a gentle smile, appearing to be sixteen years of age.
Wearing a garland of Rudrākṣa beads fashioned from precious gems around his neck (46),
bearing a sacred thread, possessing a luster equal to the Karṇikāra flower, adorned with fine jeweled earrings, the Lord wore a crown and golden garments (47).
Adorned with various ornaments and anointed with various fragrant unguents,
he held the Daughter of the Mountain upon his left lap and gazed at her face— she who was charming, fair-faced, youthful, and radiant with the bloom of fresh youth. 48.

Adorned with ornaments on all her beautiful limbs and holding a golden lotus, the Goddess was embraced by him with his left hand; lifting her face with his right hand, the Lord touched her head with his left hand and applied a tilaka mark upon it with his right. 49–50.

Devotion fans the Lord with the fan of the *praṇava*, while Worship, bearing a garland of lovely flowers for the God, stands by; Wisdom and Dispassion stand as two female attendants holding the fly-whisks of yoga. 51.
Samādhi is his agent of action, and dhāraṇā is his wife; the yamas and niyamas are proclaimed as his servants,
while prāṇāyāma is his priest and pratyāhāra is his treasurer.
Dhyāna is the lord of the moon, and Satya is likewise the commander-in-chief;
from Brahmā down to the smallest insect, all are cattle, and Śiva is their Lord.
Dharma is the protector of these cattle, while Adharma is the thief.

One should constantly meditate upon Umāpati, the God of gods, who is like the death that liberates those bound by the noose of Māyā; indeed, ten million living beings should thus remember such a Lord of Umā. 55–56.
Having obtained his desired enjoyments, he is then glorified in the world of Śiva;
for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and others are the gatekeepers of that city, while the goddesses Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī are seen as the deities of the threshold and other parts of the shrine. 57.

The gods, the celestial sages, and the wives of the gods were appointed as handmaidens to that great-souled one; indeed, all the gods were his female servants and his male servants. Ikṣvāku beheld such a magnificent mountain.
Then, having bowed to the sage Jābāli, he spoke these words: "O Sage, I wish to go to the great mountain; are you able to accompany me there?
My lifespan was previously declared to be short by the wise Yama. (60-61)
"Since hell has been described as so vast, how will there be any well-being?
Jābāli said:
"All of this has also been known by me through my divine vision."

O Brahmin, though he was learned, he performed no religious duty for ten days of his life; for neither penance nor yoga can be achieved through lack of practice, nor can they be attained in a short time.
There was no charity due to the absence of wealth, and likewise no honoring of guests because of incapacity.
For one whose life-span is exhausted, there is no merit from sacrifices, nor from vows, nor from charitable works;
nor is there merit from teaching or service at sacred fords, due to the lapse of time.
Therefore, no expiation exists for the destruction of that sin.
"O Muni, go or stay according to that dharma which grants one's destination.
Ikṣvāku said:
"O twice-born one, whatever vow is made for as long as one lives, that is the bull [of dharma]. (66)
"Therefore, tell me with certainty that dharma by which my sin will be destroyed,
and by what connection of merit the state of heaven shall be attained. (67)
"For one who is greatly terrified of hell, O eminent sage, refuge is the protection of those who have come for shelter; they say this is the fruit of all dharmas. Jābāli said:
Truly, such a bull [of dharma] is not obtained in so short a time.
It is possible to speak of truth even amidst falsehoods, even within dreams; however, a certain secret is never told to just anyone. 69-70.
Ikṣvāku said, "O Sage, protect me as a refuge; Kāla will depart.
Jābāli said:
O Brahmin, this secret, which is dearer to me than life itself and enjoined by the Vedas—
namely, the worship of the Śiva-liṅga, practiced by Brahmā and the other gods—
is the pacifier of all sins and the destroyer of all calamities. 71–72.
Therefore, O sage, perform the worship of Śiva, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
for if one does not neglect the auspicious worship of the Śiva-liṅga,
my head shall be severed by him who interrupts the worship of Śambhu.
Better is the thrusting of a trident, better is the dragging through the *śālmalī* thicket;
better is the abandonment of life than the transgression of worship. Better is leaping into fire, and better is having one's head turned downward.
It is better to suffer the loss of one's livelihood or the neglect of the worship of the Lord than for that lowest of men who eats without having worshipped Īśāna;
for his eating is said to be the consumption of sins in the form of food.
If one utters the unpronounceable name of Śambhu while eating,
or if the auspicious name "Śivā" proceeds from one's speech,
millions of his great sins are instantly reduced to ashes. (77–78)
Whatever merit a person obtains by circumambulating the earth, they obtain that same merit by circumambulating Śiva and bowing down to him.
Having performed three circumambulations, one should offer five prostrations.
By performing circumambulation once more and bowing down, one shall be liberated from sins.
He who plays all kinds of musical instruments or causes them to be played in the temple of Śiva,
being endowed with great power, becomes a servant of the Vedas.
He who causes the Purāṇas to be heard concerning the three-eyed God of gods shall be liberated from all sins and, being successful, shall dwell in the city of Śiva.
To him, the Lord always speaks pleasant words with constant respect.
This supreme worship of the Lord has been briefly described.
O Brahmin, you who are short-lived, perform the worship of Śiva three times a day, twice a day, or even once a day. 83–84.
Perform the worship of Śiva for a watch or even half a watch;
having entered the stage of the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) and taking refuge in the life of a forest-dweller, worship Śaṅkara in the morning with the flowers produced in the forest. 85.
With *śrīphala* fruits, *śatapatra*, *padma*, and *saugandhika* lotuses;
with *nīpa*, *japā*, *punnāga*, *karavīra*, and *pāṭala* flowers; and likewise with *tulasī*, *cāra*, *vidala*, and *aparājitā*—86–87.
With leaves of *apāmārga*, *rudrajaṭā*, and *damanaka*;
with all these in equal parts, along with *bilva* leaves, *dhūrta* fruits,
*droṇa* flowers, *śirīṣa* flowers, *śakta* flowers, and even the buds of *dūrvā* grass— 88.
One should worship Śiva in the morning with *naṃdyāvarta* flowers, unbroken grains mixed with sesame seeds, or even plain unbroken grains;
one may also worship Śiva with other flowers according to one's ability, such as golden *karṇikāra* or *dūrvā* grass. (89–90)
One should not worship the deity with buds, except for *caṃpaka* flowers and water-born lotuses; nor with the leaves of any water-born plants, nor with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*),
nor with *kuśa* grass flowers, nor even with those made of silver or gold.

O King, if anything else is prepared differently than prescribed, even if it has been cooked in oil, it is not declared to be "stale"; this applies to cakes and similar items that have been sprinkled with fruit juices, oil, salt, sour liquids, and cumin. (92–93)

O King, roots, fruits, vegetables, and the like that have been sprinkled with this water are not said to be stale; nor are the waters of the Gaṅgā, the ocean, all the waters of great rivers, or the waters of Kedāra. 94.
O Raghava, whatever water from a holy place, a well,
a pond, a tank, a reservoir, or a lake one might offer with the *hna* form, all that water from those sacred sites shall not become stale.

Water for the night should be fetched at night, while water for the day should be prepared during the day; likewise, it should be kept with sand and must not be stale. Having understood this, perform worship to the linga of Śiva.
Śambhu said:
Having been addressed thus by the sage, Ikṣvāku, who was devoted to Brahmins,
became intent on the worship of Śiva and remained so for eight days.
Then, when the ninth day had arrived, having performed his morning worship at the hour of death, he offered his own vital breaths as a sacrifice to the Great Lord Śiva. 99-100.
Then, having recognized him as dead, the messengers of Yama arrived; those who lead one to the world of Yama took their positions and stood ready.
(101) Furthermore, the messengers of Śiva, such as Vahnimukha and others, also arrived.
Among them, a mutual dispute arose: "He is mine! He is mine! (102). Then Yama, noose in hand, struck Śiva’s messenger;
thereafter, the messenger of Yama, whose mouth was fire, became enraged at the hundred messengers of Yama. (103)

Having assumed a massive body, he seized them with one hand; then, pressing down with the other, he cut off their heads like blades of grass. Having slain those messengers, he then took [the head] and went toward the descendant of Ikṣvāku.
Vīrabhadra reported that to the wise one;
and then Maheśvara said to Śaṅkara:
"O Kṛṣṇa, you have performed worship for only eight days, day after day. (105-106)
"O Aninda, because you previously called my *liṅga* 'the tip of the penis' (*śiśnāgra*), by that very connection with sin you shall have a penis for a mouth.
There shall be a hole at the tip of the penis, like a wheel, and you shall be devoid of a tongue, a nose, and so forth. (107)
"Because you previously spoke my name, you shall also become a speaker.
108 Then, by the word of the Lord, he likewise became so in an instant.
Śambhu said:

Whoever should constantly hear this supreme ancient narrative (purāṇa) shall be liberated from the bonds of sin and become a devotee of Śiva; he shall go to the abode of Śiva, and the narrator likewise shall become so. 109-110.
And whoever says, "Who would be equal to Hara?"—
having previously spoken this story, a king named Adhīra, though he had committed sins, went to heaven along with his wife. (111-112)
Thus ends the one hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Vibhūti," in the dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava within the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
[Chapter 110]
Śrī Rāma said: This fire named Agniśikha is indeed a follower of Śiva; how did he become such as that? Tell me that, for I bow before you.
Śambhu said: In ancient times, there was a certain kṣatriya who was always prone to anger;
he was deeply distressed, having lost his wife, lost his army, and lost his kingdom. 2.
Having obtained a pair of rams, he engaged in agriculture with his sons;
yet, burdened by a great debt, he became once again exceedingly distressed. Furthermore, the king was filled with grief due to the loss of his son caused by a serpent.
The protector of the earth, having become such as he was, abandoned even agriculture;
having renounced his two sons and ceased taking food, he wept.

Then the two sons, having approached, spoke thus to their father: 4–5. "The protector of the earth, having become such as he was, abandoned even agriculture; having renounced his two sons and ceased taking food, he wept. Then the two sons, having approached, spoke thus to their father."
"O father, why do you weep? He who is lost will not return from weeping; rather, your grief today will lead to the withering of your body.
By this grief, both your eyes are ruined and your throat is likewise ruined."
The performance [of duty] has not been lost; why then do you grieve?
One is lost, yet another does not come; protect the five lives that remain.
To protect many is meritorious, especially those who have sought refuge.
"How can you grieve for this enemy who depends on another?
The father said:
"How can a son be an enemy? O son, how can both of you be enemies to me?"
"How did you speak of your son, who is exceedingly happy, as an enemy?
The two sons replied:
"Upon being born, he takes away one's wife; upon growing up, he takes away one's wealth. (10)
For one who is dying, the vital breaths likewise become enemies; what could be more so than this?
O King, all that you have described as pleasure—through touching, embracing, and so forth—I tell you is entirely destined to result in suffering.

At the time of childbirth, there is the anxiety regarding the loss of one's son; and even if the wife remains alive, there is the destruction of one's own happiness. Furthermore, when impurity of the womb has arisen, sexual union is no longer possible.

Even when her body is drenched by the breast-milk of a woman intent on a firm embrace, if there is still union [with another], the child cries; thus, the mind fixed upon the child becomes intensely distressed, and from that, only a sense of world-weariness arises.

Furthermore, if a child falls [during intercourse], or if there is an ejaculation midway through the act, or if the interruption occurs during the height of passion, there arises a certain unpleasantness resembling suffering;
for even when all time is limited, the occurrence of sexual pleasure happens only occasionally.
At that time there is no food, no sleep with one's wife,
and the hardship of protecting children from disease, thirst, malevolent spirits, and the like.
That which is considered happiness by them is as strange as a father climbing onto a hook.
O Lord of Men, the pleasures derived from embracing, kissing, and so forth, as well as those arising from exceedingly sweet speech and the like,
do not equal even a sixteenth part of the pleasure found in the cessation of sexual union. (18–19)

"There are thousands of other sorrows as well regarding sons; what will you do here with this one who brings opposition both in this world and the next? Therefore, abandon this grief, for we two, your parents, remain here. (20)
The illustrious King said:
"I shall abandon this irresistible grief which obstructs all my duties;
for my two sons are what must be accomplished for my own welfare in this world and the next."
"I shall go to this unprecedented great preceptor, Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, who is always my refuge.
Having spoken thus, he went to the brahmin preceptor residing in Vārāṇasī.

Then, having prostrated like a staff, he was honored by the sage; embraced, kissed on the head, and offered a seat to occupy. He was asked, "What is the reason for your arrival? What service may I truly perform for you?"
The king said:
"O Brahmin, grant me a refuge from this worldly existence;
for I am perpetually exhausted by karma and have come to you for shelter. (25)
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Great King, behold the path to liberation; here stands the Great Liṅga, Viśveśvara.
Worship him, O Indra among kings, the God of gods who wields the Pināka bow."

Having propitiated whom in the past, the sage who was the son of Arundhatī and possessed of power was devoured by a *rākṣasa*; though he had gone to the world of the gods, he did not remain there for long, but thereafter went to the world of Brahmā. 27–28.
"O Great King, that son of mine remains sporting in the world of Viṣṇu, having come from the world of Brahmā.
Behold him, this hunter who wanders the forest, yet worships the Lord of the Universe with merely the leaves he has gathered himself. (29)

Behold him worshipping Maheśāna with these: flowers produced from the Śamī tree, as well as nutmeg blossoms, Kadamba flowers, Arka flowers, and those born of the Yūthikā; worship him with these and others. 30–31.
"In only half a watch from now he will perish; that is a marvel!
When the time of death has arrived, even a hunter becomes truly auspicious. Having said this, he saw a water-pot by his side for the purpose of making an offering.
That [fruit] was filled with mangoes, discarded by a dog, and thus contemptible;
yet, due to the absence of the intended offering, the hunter likewise uttered these auspicious words, indicative of his devotion toward the world. 33–34.
In the absence of flowers, Harinetra [is the substitute]; in the absence of fruits, Aṅgula and Ravi; likewise, when the liṅga falls away, Jamadagni the Ṛṣi [is the remedy].
And in the case of a fracture between the liṅga and the pedestal, he pierced his own body and gave [the marrow].
"Another supreme act of daring has been performed by other great lords;
I too must act in that same manner, otherwise I shall be a partaker in the fault.
In the meantime, a certain madman approached Śiva.
Then, having taken the offerings made by the hunter, he consumed them in an instant;
and the hunter likewise performed an act of vomiting at the sacred seat (pīṭha) of Śiva.
He thought, "I shall kill this one who has harmed Śivā."

Then Śaṅkara, exerting effort for his own destruction, performed the worship of Śiva like one intoxicated; indeed, this was the covering of the *liṅga* by him who possesses no sense of "this is mine" or "I am the body. 39–40.
"This skin-covering must now be quickly cast off by me;
for the sake of its release through worship and to prevent the loss of its fruit, one should let it go.
Having thus made this resolve, he [then] with a sharp and wondrous axe—
Having cut the skin from his right foot below the hip, he quickly placed it upon the discus;
likewise, he cut the skin from his left foot as far as the hip.
Then, both thrilled and trembling, he cut [the rest] upwards.
Having pierced the skin of his hands, shoulders, belly, heart, throat, and neck, the hunter,
filled with joy, also pierced the skin of his head.
Then, having torn through the body from between those two [joints], he emerged in a circular shape.
Having cut off his finger and taken it, he offered his own skin to the god.
Then, from nearby, the divine son of Śaṅkara appeared in the sky, possessing a celestial form, beautiful eyes, four arms, and adorned with various ornaments. 45–46.
Then hundreds of thousands of Śaiva messengers arrived, wearing various types of crowns and adorned with all ornaments;
they all held tridents in their hands and were as pure as crystal. 47.
They were four-armed and handsome, seated upon excellent celestial chariots (vimānas).
All were as radiant as the sun, peaceful, and accompanied by their beloved wives; they were endowed with sons, wives, strength, energy, and hundreds of playful women. 48–49.
Resembling the sun in their splendor, they showered down a rain of flowers;
summoned by them, the hunter arrived and said to them:
"Come here with your wife and kinsmen, or else go to the forest."
Having heard those words, the Śaivas then spoke this sentence:
"By whomsoever merit or sin has been committed, by him indeed must its fruit be experienced.
The hunter said:
The impurities of all [other] dharmas belong to a single agent (52),
whereas the fruit of the dharmas of the Māheśvaras belongs to two or even many;
in the meantime, the heroic Bhadraśaḥ arrived with his young son (53).
Accompanied by many millions of followers and joined by your kinsmen, O hunter,
everything you have said shall come to pass; together with your wife and your circle of relatives,
ascend this celestial chariot and go to Śiva— may there be auspiciousness for you all.
Then, having reached the world of Śiva by means of a celestial chariot due to those words, Vasiṣṭha said:
"You have seen everything; now perform the worship of the Lord."
"Released from the bonds of sin, you shall go to the world of Śiva.
O King, if sovereignty is desired by you, cleanse the courtyard of the Lord and always perform the smearing with cow-dung and water. (56-57)

By this much, the kingdom of the earth shall certainly be yours for as long as your life lasts; at the end, the state of Śiva shall be attained. However, in this [kingdom], there can be no perfect success until death.
"Therefore, having attained another body through the power of serving Śiva,
your kingdom shall be restored and your devotion to Śiva shall likewise become firm.
Śambhu said:
Then, having failed to perform that worship, he died and went to heaven;
subsequently, having attained birth as a king once more, he ruled the kingdom with devotion to Śiva.
Then, on one occasion, the king went to the temple of the God.
Then, as the king descended upon the single island amidst the throng of soldiers— which was like the king of serpents adorned with various jewels— the king became enraged and quickly seized a lamp.

Filled with rage, he cast [the fire] into the beautiful city of Devālayapura. By him, the temple was burnt, and thus his own ruin was brought about. Then, by him once again, the houses and dwellings there were set ablaze.
Then the king had [an image of] Maheśāna fashioned and worshipped him;
having propitiated Śaṅkara, the king, who bathed in ashes, slept on ashes, and was muttering the Rudra-mantra, passed away on the day his death was due.
Having gone to the world of Śiva, he was addressed by Vīrabhadra:
"Become a tiger among the Gaṇas and my attendant;
by my command as the son of Śaṅkara, bring him into my presence."
He shall become headless and possess a face of flames;
then he spoke to the high-souled Vīrabhadra, the lord of the Gaṇas:
"The eyes, ears, tongue, nose, mouth, and the collection of heads—"
"Without these, how will my worldly affairs be possible?
O Lord, what sin have I committed that my head should be absent?
Vīrabhadra said:
By you alone was the supremely beautiful Goddess previously accepted;
she who constantly adorns the abode of Maheśa with auspicious designs such as the *svastika*, *sarvatobhadra*, and *naṃdyāvarta* using colored powders. 70–71.
A lotus, a blue lotus, a swinging foot, a fly-whisk,
a trident, a conch, a discus, a mace, and likewise a bow;
a trident, a hand-drum, a sword, a bull, Bhṛṅgiriṭi, and Śiva.

Thus, fashioning another eight-petaled lotus as well as other yantras and such every day, she served the Bull-bannered Lord (Śiva). Then, on one occasion, that prostitute arrived at the temple of the God.
A certain jailer entered the royal palace;
having seen her there, he spoke these words. (75) The jailer said:
A woman may abandon a man who stands alone, or one who is a courtesan, a youth, or an old man; one who is aged, diseased, impotent, incapable, destitute of wealth, has a short penis, or is miserable.
One should avoid from afar a woman who is beardless, covered in filth, dull-witted, and tainted by foul odors; one who is meager and free from passion.
Therefore, O courtesan, give yourself to me in sexual union; quickly restore my life! 77–78.
The courtesan said:
"We have heard that for women, devotion to one's husband is the supreme dharma, which is constant and bestows happiness both in this world and the next. (79)
"Since she is under his control and dependent upon him, and since she has never been united with another, she is renowned as a devoted wife (*pativratā*); therefore, one should protect her.
Kārāṅkikā said:
"If death should thus come so soon, there is no doubt;
then, having gone into the presence of the king, he spoke this to the king:
'It is not fitting for you to say, "A courtesan is indeed a courtesan, she is not my wife. (81)
Having thus spoken to the king, he took a small portion of the *maṇḍa* made from rice-gruel and went to her palace; then,
perceiving that it was time for sleep, he stretched out his hand.
There, the evil-minded man threw the cake into a fold of his garment;
having done this, he then went and said this to the king:
"O King, go out and approach that foremost of courtesans."
"Having raised her up, you ought to examine that courtesan's entire body; or else, look carefully at her garment once its fastenings have been loosened.
Then the king went to the courtesan's house and spoke these words to the keeper of the establishment: 85–86.
"O King, this is what was said while I was asleep: 'Whomever you see here, whom I also see, that king should be summoned there. O King, this is not appropriate;
therefore, appoint either his mother or his father to come for an audience."
Upon seeing her, all this will clearly become auspicious.
Then, brought by the king’s command, his mother prepared to look upon her; yet, at the king's very word, she was as if cleansing her garment.
Then, perceiving that the *maṇḍa* was situated there, he crushed it from the outside.
Because of the crushing, his garment became wet; the King asked, "What is that?
She replied, "Nothing, O Lord; nothing at all," and so did the prostitute's mother.
Then the king, having observed the garment with suspicion due to many reports, said, "Look at this garment, which is soaked with semen!
Then those standing nearby, having seen it, spoke these words to the king: "It is so."
Then the king, having gone to his own palace, spoke to the magistrate: "Without hesitation, cut off the head of the courtesan this very moment;
her head must be presented to me within the span of a single ghaṭikā."
At the king’s command, Daṇḍaka did exactly so and presented it to him.
Vīrabhadra said:
"You have done this before, and now you have received the fruit of it today."
"By means of fire alone you shall speak; through hearing and seeing, you shall smell;
you shall know taste and possess intelligence, yet you shall become exceedingly wrathful.
Śambhu said:
Thus was Jvālāmukha born, a king devoted to Maheśvara yet devoid of patience.
Therefore, one who desires happiness in this world and the next should cultivate patience.
Whoever constantly hears this unsurpassed, meritorious narrative [shall attain it]. 96–97.
"And being liberated from the bonds of sin, he shall dwell in the world of Śiva.

(98) Thus ends the one hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of the Worship of Śiva," in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava. 110.
The one hundred and eleventh chapter. Śrī Rāma said:
[Tell me] the greatness of the name of Maheśa, as well as the greatness of his worship.
O Guru, tell me of the greatness of the prostration (namaskāra) and the greatness of the vision [of the deity],
as well as the greatness of the gift of water, the gift of incense, O best of men,
and the greatness of the gift of lamps, perfumes, and so forth.
Śambhu said:
"It is not possible to describe the greatness of each individual name in detail; therefore, I shall speak to you in brief. Listen with respect, O Rāghava."
In ancient times, during the Tretā Yuga, there was a powerful king named Vidhṛta.
When his father died, he was consecrated as the ruler of the earth while still a child. He placed all those of equal age who were near him in positions of authority.
Those who were elderly and those who were learned were not honored by him; rather,
the young men were esteemed— those who were wicked, performers of improper acts, skilled at abducting beautiful women, and experts in the work of thieves.
Those skilled in the trade of vessels, in rhythm, and in dance were esteemed by him;
likewise, those who knew the mantras for subjugation, as well as those conversant with garments and medicinal herbs,
were dear to him— those whose nature was inclined toward song and dance, and who were clever gamblers.
That king abandoned those who acted according to his father's wishes;
having deliberated with those wicked men, he had their work carried out,
and likewise joined them with other such wicked people.
Adhering to this teaching, he abandoned his remaining friends; those who would clench their fists against his chest and emit cries of "pheṭ" were dear to him.
They were knowers of the reality of the characteristics of the *bhaga* and experts in the *Rati-tantras*.
At that time, the kingdom became devoid of statesmanship.
Whatever elephants, horses, chariots, camels, goats, cattle, buffaloes, and so forth there were, all of them met with destruction through plunder here and there. 11-12.
Then, treasures such as gold were no longer seen in the city;
subsequently, having been defeated by another king, he fled.
Then, having entered a great forest, he established a fortress in the mountains.

There, having a small retinue and adopting the livelihood of a thief, he would point out gold, clothing, grain, jewels, perfumes, and other such items here and there, thereby bringing together thieves who were deceivers. 14–15.
When food was not available for the performance of the ritual recitation due to their abstention from causing the slaughter of animals and so forth, he then provided that food.
If food could not be obtained through the meat of cows, buffaloes, and other such animals, [he provided it otherwise].
He prepared a meal consisting of the flesh of horses and men.
Such was the conduct that occurred, devoid of the twilight prayers and other rites;
however, he had one minister, a Rākṣasa named Surāpa.
"Appoint him at all times to seize and strike down;
thus, remaining under your protection, O Rakṣas, he shall take men from various lands, surrounded by a retinue of a thousand men, for he is a home of mercilessness. 19.
Having identified his own desired women, whether he knew them or not, he seized them;
and after enjoying them for some time, he devoured their flesh.
Thus, having slain men and women, he ruled a kingdom that was most difficult to endure.
Having ruled the kingdom in this manner for a thousand years, that lowest of men— his entire body now loosened by old age and defiled by wrinkles and grey hair—
passed away, and the region for ten yojanas in every direction became lifeless.
Then the day of death arrived for that high-souled king.
When the time of death had come, the king bathed and lay upon the ground;
all his attendants stood surrounding him.
The liquor-drinking minister said, "Command me; what must I do?
Then the king, thus afflicted and his life-force departing, being unable [to speak], somehow uttered these words from below his navel as his vitality failed: 25. "How... [he spoke].
"O Lord of Daityas, strike, strike back, seize! Seize!"—having spoken thus at all times, the messengers of Yama arrived before me;
intent on inflicting blows, they made every effort to bind me with various fetters.
The binding nooses were crushed and the weapons and staffs were shattered;
by the mere touch of his body, it was as if a miracle had occurred.
Then Death himself arrived and bound him with a noose.
Seeing even the noose of Death severed, Death reflected:
"The death of all mortals has been seen, yet never anywhere has such [a death] been witnessed.
While Death was thus absorbed in thought, the powerful Jvālāmukha appeared.
Suddenly commanded by Vīrabhadra, the wielder of the trident (Śiva) approached;
then, beholding the flaming mouth, Death fled swiftly.
Seeing Death thus fleeing, Vahnimukha then—

"O thief! O thief! Stay, stay! Where will you go? (32) "The thief is released from his sin merely by being impaled upon the stake. Having addressed Death in this manner, he caused him to be transfixed upon a stake. (33)
Having placed the stake upon his shoulder and bound the messengers with a rope,

he took them, their feet fettered in chains, into the midst of the king's assembly; then, having mounted them upon a magnificent celestial chariot beautifully adorned with song and instrumental music, [he departed].
Then, having approached Vīra, he reported everything to him; and Vīrabhadra likewise reported all of that to Śaṅkara, the immeasurable Self,
who was accompanied by various hosts of sages and gods, with Brahmā and Viṣṇu at the forefront.
Having prostrated before the Lord who was being served by Pārvatī and having offered up Mṛtyu himself upon the trident,
Viśvātman Vīrabhadra, filled with fervor, became silent.

Seeing Agnyānana, Śiva reproached him, saying: "How was this act of audacity committed by you against my attendants? Why do you not fear Death, who is under the authority of Yama? Tell me everything according to the ultimate truth.
Bowing down to him, Vahnimukha, filled with extreme rage, beheld Death and danced out of joy.
And he said, "Theft has been committed by Death; therefore, this man has been impaled upon the stake by me. Śiva then released Death and rendered all the messengers free from disease.
Beholding Death, Śiva spoke: "My name resides in their death."

"Whether it be deficient in syllables or endowed with extra letters, for those of focused mind and superior intellect, I truly bestow my own world; for it has been said that by this [name] one shall destroy [sin]. Even a mere fragment of sound destroys [evil], for they say that a word indeed bestows a state. (42)
O Ārāda, you should repeatedly recite "namas" and speak my words to Yama.

Those who have taken refuge in obeisance, self-restraint, fame, service, and devotion, as well as those who perform the five-syllable mantra and the recitation of the *Śatarudriya* for Śiva—they are not to be questioned by you. 43–44.
Those who wear the ashes of Rudra, who recite the *Upaniṣads*, and who are speakers of the Purāṇas—even when all these sins are present, I alone shall govern them; Yama has no authority over them.
(45) And those men who, though possessed of sin and deceitful, eat the food, clothing, and wives of others...
The inhabitants of Vārāṇasī who are intent on transcending death, as well as the mortals of Śrīśaila, are not to be questioned [regarding their destiny].
(46) Even lice, gadflies, bedbugs, deer and other wild animals, insects, ants, reptiles, scorpions, and pigs—having died in Kāśī, they attain Śaṅkara. (47)
He who indeed meditates upon the three-eyed, multiformed Lord, adorned with the crescent moon, while reciting His name—
Him who has three eyes, whose eye is the triple Veda, and whose eyes are the moon, the sun, and the fire— within the temple of his heart-lotus. 48.
"Having paid homage to him, Death stood at a distance by my command.

Having said "So be it," Sunaya then went to the sage Aṅgiras, the best of men, who was skilled in the Purāṇas and proficient in all the Śāstras.
Having paid homage to him who was learned in all the Āgamas and Purāṇas and who always practiced virtuous deeds, we, whose lives have now borne fruit, spoke thus:
"O Brahmin, O Sage, we have accomplished our purpose, since you have been seen by us in person. (16)
Aṅgiras said: "I shall perform whatever task you have come here for to accomplish.
Since you have gathered here desiring to hear the Purāṇa,"
I shall proclaim to you the ritual procedure which destroys all sins;
it bestows all knowledge, arises from the realization of reality, grants devotion to Śiva, is heart-pleasing, and auspiciously grants devotion to Viṣṇu. 18–19.
It bestows the knowledge for attaining various celestial realms and grants delightful pleasures;
it reveals the *Rati-tantra* consisting of manifold auspicious wisdom, and is the primary source for enjoyment and liberation, illuminating the vision of the ritual rules. 20.
It contains descriptions of various modes of devotion and the proclamation of the daring acts of devotion; it reveals the rules for vows, consecrations, gifts, and the worship with sacred ash;
thus is the Padma Purāṇa proclaimed, which is like a lotus arising from the Brahma-Purāṇa.
This description of the forms of the Pramathas was told by Maheśvara;
it was also told elsewhere, specifically in the Padma Purāṇa. Formerly, when asked by Dilīpa, Vasiṣṭha spoke this.
"Listen to that, O best of sages; it shall bring all knowledge.
Then, at those words, the brahmins, who were devoted to hearing the Purāṇas, said to the sage: "How should we listen now, and what must we do? (24-25)
He too shall relate everything; listen to the eternal Dharma.
Having paid homage to the knower of the Purāṇas, one should then offer him water for the feet (argha) and a seat.
Saying, "Please sit there," one should worship him with perfumes and flowers.
One should offer them betel-leaf along with a self-prepared mixture or even more;
one should say, "O Brahmin, tell us a meritorious story from the Purāṇas," but without mounting a couch or a high seat. 27–28.
One should listen while seated on a low seat for the sake of attaining dharma, kama, and artha;
having been told "Listen," one who knows the Purāṇas should recite this mantra:
"Salutations to Hari, Hara, and then to Gaṇeśa, and thereafter to Bhāratī. (29)
Having paid homage to one's chosen deity, one should proceed to recite the Purāṇa. This may be done for half a watch every day, or as desired.
Having heard the completion of the recitation in this manner, one should perform the prescribed rites.
The listener should either remain silent while reflecting or listen in silence;
otherwise, the Goddess of Speech becomes angry, and from that anger, muteness may result.
Therefore, the listener of the Purāṇa should offer betel leaves and other such gifts.

Furthermore, according to the capacity of the speaker’s livelihood and duties, one should give a set of garments including an undergarment (*udgamanīya*) within the context of the Purāṇa recitation; or else, one should offer fine cloth or even a pair of garments. (33–34)
One should likewise give a seat that is great, variegated, delightful, powerful, soft, and golden; or else one should give cows, land, houses, and so forth.
O best of Brahmins, all of this was [taught] by Dakṣiṇāmūrti in the past.
This was spoken by Śaṅkara to the sages and the inhabitants of heaven.
Then all those sages, having bowed to him as he sat upon his seat and having each offered him betel-leaf, stood waiting with a desire to hear.
He too related everything—the ancient lore that bestows all things—up to the final chapter; thus it was heard by those best of the twice-born.
Dilīpa said:
A celestial chariot, moving at will, endowed with every prosperity and filled with all forms of happiness, arrived at that holy place.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O King, it is not enough that you have asked; they will play with even greater wonders than these, by which that merit is described.
Having whitened the temple of Śiva on all sides with lime, [they will play].
There were women rich in the beauty and grace of feminine form, adorned with every ornament;
they were skilled in various beautiful songs and proficient in various dances.
There were four, eight, or six women who provided the sound of the maddala drum.
Vaśinī, Audvegā, Avarjikī, Koṇikā, and Dhamanī—these two; Lāsikī makes four; then there is Saṃtuṣṭā and Gāyikā.
Ekā and Dvevā are proclaimed as those skilled in song, while Amukharā is likewise celebrated.
When the drummers struck the corners [of the instruments], six or eight of them became silent;
all were women of exquisite beauty, with breasts that had not yet fallen [to the ground], highly skilled in the arts of love, and for that very reason, they were free from apprehension. 44–45.

O King, on a certain day, Vatsara traveled by means of a celestial chariot and witnessed a dance performed by such women, who were dressed in extremely fine garments and possessed glances as flickering as lightning. 46.
His face was gazed upon by hundreds of women, and he was honored by many;
filled with the nourishment of bliss, he was devoid of anger, envy, and other such passions; his limbs were smeared with the five fragrances, and his face was like a moon with its full orb. 47-48.

Resembling the sun, all those women were endowed with teeth; they wore garlands made of *pārijātaka* flowers that had just blossomed and emitted fragrance. All wore garlands made of blooming *aroha* flowers with reddish joints.
Wearing garlands of *dhammilla* on their breasts and possessing smiling lips,
he wanders accompanied by such women who delight in dance and song; thus, having become a lord of celestial chariots (*vimāna*), he dwells there for an inexhaustible period of time.
Having acted thus once more, a king shall subsequently be born;
having enjoyed the fruit of sovereignty which is heaven, he will become a devotee of Śiva. (52) Śambhu said:
Vasiṣṭha spoke it to Dilīpa, and Aṅgiras spoke it to the sages;
they performed those three cycles of the Lord of Umā accordingly,
and having heard the entire Padma Purāṇa, they became happy.
Indeed, they are seen dwelling in excellent celestial palaces in the Brahmā-world, happy and always joyful in mind;
all this has been declared as established in the Purāṇas. 54-55.

"O Rāghava, what more do you wish to hear beyond this? (56) Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava," in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. 113.
The one hundred and fourteenth chapter.
Rāma said:
"Who is this seen in the sky, adorned with all ornaments?"
Seated in his celestial chariot, he was like another sun at the height of its blazing midday,
difficult for all mortals to behold; upon his lap sat five beautiful women, O Brahmin, smiling sweetly like other goddesses of fortune.
They sang sweet songs with the movements of their beautiful eyebrows and glances,
with gentle smiles, the clapping of palms, and the snapping of fingers; in some places they sang with voices faltering from emotion, while striking one another’s hands.
Gazing at one another's faces with alluring songs preceded by singing, the great yogi, resembling the filaments of a lotus, remains playing;
tell me, by what merit of conduct does he act thus? (4-5)
Śambhu said: "O Brāhmaṇa, formerly this man was endowed with all prosperity and possessed various kinds of happiness; he was devoted solely to the maintenance of his wife."

One who has no sons, who is devoid of giving gifts, who has abandoned the worship of the deities, who is bereft of the five great sacrifices, who has completely forsaken the private recitation of the Vedas,
and who is impure, being solely intent on eating in the morning, at midday, and in the evening.
Once, he went to the home of the great-souled Gautama on the sacred mountain of Tryambaka,
which is inhabited by hosts of sages;
there too was a beautiful house constructed with crystal pillars.
Its walls were anointed with aguru, musk, camphor, and saffron,
and possessed the exquisite fragrance of santāna flowers;
its floor was sprinkled with the essence of musk and floral nectar.
The courtyard was adorned with various fine and brilliant white canopies (vitāna),
beautified by magnificent plantain trees and areca palms, and graced by honeybees warbling sweetly as they emerged from the nearby lotus pond. 11–12.
The quarters of the sky were filled with the fragrance arising from sandalwood trees, and the quarters of the sky were filled with songs that brought delight through the singing of the precepts;
it was a machine constructed to destroy the heat produced by the summer season. 13.
Its roof was fashioned from fire concealed beneath layers of plantain leaves;
its door-panels were made of dense, smooth sandalwood;
and its inner walls were composed of highly fragrant *saugandhika* flowers.
In the northeastern quarter, there was a beautiful altar fashioned for the sake of pleasure, its surface adorned with gold and its various platforms decorated with jewels;
it was situated at the foot of a banyan tree that provided dense and very refreshing shade. 16.
Its borders were beautified by lakes filled with clusters of flowering plantains; its clouds of mist clung to the tops of great banyan trees;
and it was adorned with various groves as magnificent as the pleasure gardens of heaven. 17–18.
In that house, which was graced by many groves and adorned with ponds, wells, and tanks, a breeze blew very gently, bestowing happiness;
and beautiful women with lovely limbs played musical instruments that were the very wealth of the god of love. 19.

Excellent women played the vīṇā, the flute, and the triple-flute; likewise, women performing the triple symphony (tauryatrika) were present in the four directions as well as above. Auspicious balls of rice mixed with ashes were placed in vessels made of gold and other precious materials.
They were perfumed with all kinds of fragrances and incensed with excellent incense; there were millions of rosaries strung with *kuśa* grass,
and thousands of black antelope skins placed at the outer boundary.
In such an excellent house, the lord of sages, who is worthy of worship by the gods,
established camphor and other substances in the four directions; the lord of sages fashioned a camphor throne upon a sandalwood pedestal.
Having bathed Śaṅkara with milk— subtle, white, very smooth, and covered with camphor— and having bathed Sadāśiva with other Vedic mantras using water scented with fragrances; 25.
Having placed a cloth-seat upon a wooden seat, one should place a vessel in front; having thus established it, one should place these [substances] upon the petals:
in one vessel, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and in another, unbroken rice grains mixed with sesame seeds.
In one vessel, place the five fragrances, and in another, the eight fragrances—
namely saffron, musk, camphor, and sandalwood—
and having arranged them in separate vessels, establish them at the place of worship.
Worship is performed there by way of various paths;
the five-faced Lord Sadāśiva resides within the liṅga.
His covering is the liṅga, and Śakti is prescribed as his [covering].
Viṣṇu is the covering of Śakti; Brahmā is the covering of Viṣṇu. The Moon is the covering of Brahmā, and the Sun is the covering of that [Moon]; after that is the Veda (Śruti).
The protection of that [Veda] is by the deities of the directions, and the covering of those [deities] is the quarters themselves. 30–31.
Śambhu is the covering of the directions, and his qualities are the covering of that;
this auspicious worship of the Śiva-liṅga indeed consists of these ten coverings. This may be the opinion of some; now follows another covering.
The veil of knowledge (vidyāvaraṇa) has been described; that is remembered as the veil of Umā (umāvaraṇa).
Viṣṇu is her veil, and Brahmā is the veil of Viṣṇu. The moon is the outer covering of Brahmā, and the sun is his covering. 33–34.
If the covering of the Sun is also included, O Lord, it is remembered as the sixfold enclosure (ṣoḍhāvṛti);
otherwise, it is declared as the excellent fivefold enclosure (pañcāvaraṇa).
This threefold enclosure belongs to the Moon, Viṣṇu, and Śakti.
The enclosure of Ambika has been declared as the single, supreme enclosure (36).
Alternatively, the world-protectors may serve as the enclosure in the worship of Soma;
or else, O Śivā, worship without any enclosure is praised (37).
One should worship Śiva with substances placed upon the eight petals of the *patrikā*.
I shall now describe the characteristics of the *patrikā*, which is useful for all ritual acts. It may be fashioned from gold, silver, or copper.
One should fashion an auspicious eight-petaled lotus leaf resembling a pearl oyster-shell (39).
One should design it with eight corners equal in shape to a lotus petal; a weight of one pala is recommended for that well-finished and broad base (40).
One should fashion it as being neither thick nor thin, with an upper lotus-shape having eight petals;
or else, by way of the Śakti-path, one should conceive of it as having five petals;
or alternatively, one may make it three-petaled according to the view of the Śakti-state. 41.

The wise man should fashion it so that its bowl is beautiful. A splendid sacred thread (mālā-upavīta) should be fashioned with one hundred and eight auspicious rudrākṣas interspersed according to his capacity, or with thirty-eight. 42–43.
Then, by that supreme rishi, one bead was placed on each forearm, two were bound upon the two wrists, one was held on the head, and another was worn on the neck;
thus fashioned was the rosary made of rudrākṣas, crystal, and precious gems. 44.

Having prepared a seat of tiger skin and himself assuming the lotus posture, the sage performed the rites of invocation, the offering of the seat, the water for the hands (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), and the water for sipping (ācamanīya);
then, with the waters of the Gaṅgā, he bathed Śaṅkara.

With Bakula and Pāṭala flowers mixed with the eight fragrant substances (aṣṭagandhaka), placed in golden vessels, purified with a cloth, and strongly scented; at the entrance, there should be an auspicious copper cauldron and a well-fastened droṇī.
Sometimes with the horn of a cow, or likewise with the horn of a gavaya;
or with a right-spiraling conch, or even with vessels of jewels, or of gold, silver, copper, or even bell-metal. 48–49.
One should bathe [the deity] according to one’s desire with golden or small silver pitchers;
or alternatively, one may do so with earthen ones, or even with lotus leaves,
or with vessels made of Palāśa, mango, Jambū, and other such materials, one should bathe the Lord.
Of all types of baths, the shower-bath (dhārā-snāna) is the most excellent.
With the mantra beginning with "namaste," known as the Śatarudriya, and with the Anuvāka beginning with "śaṃ ca," which is of the nature of peace, one [should bathe] the Lord. 51–52.
Having performed the circumambulation according to one's capacity, one should place [the offerings] behind [the deity] and so forth;
then, one should worship with beautiful flowers, leaves, and bilva fruits (53),
as well as with tulasī, maruvaka petals, kalhāras, and great lotuses.
With blue lotuses, utpalas, and all other varieties, with karavīrakas, karṇikāras, white lotuses, and likewise with aparājitā;
with sesame seeds, unbroken grains (akṣatas), and śrīpatra leaves mixed with sesame.
In this manner, Gautama worshipped the Great Lord Īśāna with camphor, agallochum, musk, sarja, agarwood, and sandalwood;
he also offered other incenses and sixteen lamps.
Placed upon a lamp-stand joined with camphor wicks, the supreme food offering was presented to Maheśa:
well-cooked rice-flour cakes, along with foods to be chewed, licked, and sucked. 57–58.
It was endowed with sweet flavors and the like, provided with five kinds of edible foods,
rich in many varieties of cooked vegetables, and mixed with many different preparations;
the drink consisted of twenty ingredients, including grapes and mango fruits.

The sage presented as an offering food prepared with the eight kinds of soups and the like, combined with roots, fruits, and so forth; it was provided with whatever else was available, accompanied by the finest flowers. 60–61.
Having offered a thousand lamps for the lustration ceremony placed in golden vessels,
along with sacrificial offerings, to the God and having bowed down to him,
[he presented] pieces of betel nut that had been crushed and leaves that had been washed.
With its leaf-stalks removed, its tip intact, and covered with a beautiful white cloth;
this auspicious betel leaf, together with camphor powder and three other leaves, is placed in a golden vessel for the Lord. 63–64.
Then, after performing circumambulations and offering salutations,
eight women arrived there, carrying lutes, flutes, and other instruments; playing various musical instruments, they approached the presence of the sage.
Taking up a pair of small cymbals, she herself began to sing. When Gautama was intent on singing, the women there made rhythmic claps, while others played musical instruments very softly.
As the sage Madhuranga assumed a form with a melodic voice and danced before Maheshvara, it was as if a miracle had occurred.
In that interval, the venerable sage Narada arrived.
Gautama, having honored him upon his arrival and prostrated before him, said to him:
"My purpose has been accomplished; there is no one equal to me. What is the reason for your coming, and from where have you come?"
Śrī Nārada said:
"I have come here from Pātāla after eating in the palace of Bāṇa;
the high-souled ones, Bāṇa, Śukra, and others, will come to my house."
Then, in an instant, Bāṇa, the conqueror of enemy cities, arrived mounted upon an elephant; that asura was accompanied by twenty akṣauhiṇīs.
Śukra [was on] another elephant, and Prahlāda [was on] a supreme chariot.
Bali [took] Vṛṣaparvan’s excellent chariot and the supreme horse.
Then, having learned that they had all arrived, Gautama, together with his disciples, went out in haste, taking with him the water for honoring (arghya) and other offerings. 73–74.
Seeing Gautama there as well, the Daityas descended from their elephants and other mounts and paid him homage; then, having offered salutations to that descendant of Bhṛgu,
they embraced all the Rākṣasas and honored them according to the prescribed rites.
The bull among sages arranged the encampment of the army;
having washed Śukra’s feet, the sage likewise placed the water upon his head and offered him an honoring gift consisting of various fruits.
Having performed their rites preceded by bathing in ponds, lakes, and pools,
they entered that auspicious hermitage of Gautama situated at the confluence,
while the Rākṣasas along with their priest entered his house.
All of them performed worship and surrender to the gods in the house of the twice-born;
on an altar prepared instantly, Śukra sacrificed to Śiva, while on his left side Prahlāda sacrificed to Acyuta. 79–80.
Soma, Bali, and other preeminent asuras did likewise;
then Bāṇa worshipped the one and only god, Tryambaka,
and Śukra also worshipped that Blessed Lord, the husband of Umā.
Then Gautama also worshipped Śaṅkara at midday.
All [the sages] wore white garments, their bodies smeared with ashes, having applied the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) in every place with white ash. 82–83.
Having bowed to Bhārgava, they all proceeded with the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Within the hollow space in the center of the heart-lotus, there is the pentad of elements;
in the midst of those is the great ether, and from that ether, pure fire.
In the midst of that, one should meditate upon the auspicious Maheśāna, who is full of radiance.
One should burn that body—which is composed of ignorance, impure, and attached to all things—within the lamp of the ether by means of the fire of knowledge. 85–86.
Having burned away the obstruction of space, one should then burn space itself;
having burned space, one should then burn the wind that has become fire;
and after that, having burned that which has become water, as well as that which has become earth.
Having burned away the qualities (guṇas) dependent upon that [body], one should then consume the body itself.
Having thus burned the elements with the fire of knowledge regarding them, the embodied soul beholds Viṣṇu, who abides in the center of the crest-lock and is filled with the essence of bliss.
The auspicious [fire] possessed rays resembling the rays of the full moon;
then, by the rays produced from Śiva’s body which were joined with liquid nectar, the flames became very cool and were extinguished like the rays of the moon. 90.
One should contemplate the supreme dissolution, which has become dense with the rays of spreading nectar,
gradually submerging the entire collection of elements.
Having thus performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), the mortal becomes truly pure through the ritual fire-offering (kriyā-homa).
After performing worship and the rite of recitation (jāpya), there is the destruction of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin through meditation on the God.

Having thus meditated upon Him who possesses the brilliance and luster of the moon, and having quickly projected [the deity] onto the Linga of Śiva through meditation, one should contemplate Sadāśiva in the midst of the lamp and perform the imperishable worship with the five-syllabled mantra. 93-94.
