Having likewise performed the ritual services beginning with the invocation (āvāhana), the bathing of Śaṅkara is done as before.
Having placed an udumbara, silver, or golden pedestal covered with cloth and so forth— all such a pedestal—
here at the end of the shower of bubbles, one should place a single image upon the pedestal in front.
One should place a pair of serpents on the pedestal, one above and one to the right and left near the deity.

Having placed a hibiscus flower (*japāpuṣpa*) between the two serpents, one should place a cloth in the center; then, upon that very center, one should worship Maheśa in the form of a *liṅga* together with its pedestal, using twelve times as much pure white [flower] for each quality. 96–97.
Having performed this, and having offered or not offered the five fragrances or the eight fragrances to the Lord of the Gods, beginning with Bāṇamukhya,

one should worship Him with flowers, leaves, auspicious sesame seeds, unbroken rice grains, and either those mixed with sesame or alone; then, having offered incense prepared according to the rules and having offered the lamp and the aforementioned food offering.
Having completed the remainder of the worship, they all then performed singing and dancing here and there.
(99) Now, in the meantime, a disciple of Gautama named Śaṅkarātman arrived; he was dressed like a madman, naked, and had assumed many disguises. (100)
In one place he was like the most eminent of the twice-born, and in another he resembled a caṇḍāla;
in some places the yogi appeared equal to a śūdra, and in others he was even a tāpasa.
He roared, leaped up, danced, praised, and sang.
He wept, heard clearly, fell down, and rose up at times;
endowed solely with the knowledge of Śiva and overflowing with supreme bliss, he arrived at the time for the meal and went into the presence of Gautama. (103)
In some places he ate only the leftovers together with his guru;
in some places he licked that vessel; in some places he went away silently;
and in some places, taking the hand of his guru, he ate by himself.
Seeing that in one part of the house there was urine and in another it was smeared with mud, the Guru always took Tāmragupta by the hand,
led him into the temple, seated him upon his own seat, and fed him.
The sage Gautama himself ate that [food] from his own vessel.
Then, on one occasion, the auspicious Sundarī Ahalyā, desiring to ascertain his state of mind, summoned her disciple and said, "Eat. 107–108.
Having placed food in a golden vessel and drinks and so forth in another cup, he then placed fire in one [vessel] and a heap of charcoal and a mass of thorns in the other. 109.
"Set it down and eat; eat," he said, and the sage ate.
Just as the twice-born one had drunk water, so too did he consume fire; having eaten even the thorns, he remained just as he was before.
Formerly, invited daily by the daughters of sages for a meal,
he ate with joy and delight the clods of earth, water, cow dung, mud, and wooden sticks that were offered to him. 112.
This sage, whose appearance was like that of a caṇḍāla,
holding a pair of well-worn sandals in his hand,
approached Vṛṣaparvan while speaking in the dialect appropriate for those of the lowest caste.
Vāsava stood between Vṛṣaparvan and Īśa;
not recognizing him as Vṛṣaparvan, he struck and severed his head.
When that best of the twice-born was slain, this entire world, both moving and unmoving, [was filled with grief].
Those sages residing there became exceedingly distressed;
likewise, great sorrow arose within the high-souled Gautama, and water flowed from his eyes as if manifesting his grief. 116–117.
Gautama spoke these words in the presence of all the Daityas:
"What sin has been committed by this man, that his head has been severed—he who was always a yogi of Śiva and dearer to me than my own life? (118)

My death is also certain, for the Guru has come to me in the form of a disciple. (119) Wherever the death of those devoted to the Śiva-dharma and ever-abiding in Śiva is seen, there our death is likewise certain. (120)
Śukra said:
"I shall restore this one to life—he who is without lineage and dear to Śiva. Why does he die, O Brāhmaṇa? Behold the power of my asceticism!"

When that lord of sages had spoken thus, Gautama also died; and when he too was dead, Śukra likewise gave up his life through yoga. Having learned that he too was slain, the lords of the Dānavas [fled] from Prahlāda.
In an instant, everyone was dead; it was like a miracle.
Then the army of that wise Bāṇa lay slain, while Ahalyā, tormented by grief, wept aloud again and again.

Honored by Gautama through the worship of Maheśa, the all-pervading Vīrabhadra, the great yogi, became enraged upon seeing everything: "Alas, what a tragedy! What a tragedy! Many devotees of Maheśa have perished! (125)
"I shall inform Śiva; I will do whatever he says.
Having thus resolved, he went to the imperishable Mount Mandara, and after bowing to Virūpākṣa, he then related all of this. 126–127.
Seeing that act of daring committed there by my devotees while Brahmā and Hari were present, Śiva, the bestower of boons, spoke these words:
"O Viṣṇu, let us go and see; you two shall also come."
Then the Lord, having mounted his bull, with fly-whisks fanned by the wind,

shone resplendently as a beautiful umbrella was held by Nandīka in fine attire— a magnificent white umbrella with a golden handle, held not for any other purpose but for the sake of the All-pervading One.
Having obtained the permission of Maheśa, Hari stood ready for the destruction of the Nāgas;
he shone brilliantly with his two red and blue umbrellas, while the Kaustubha gem was clearly visible upon his chest.
At that time, by the consent of Śiva, Brahmā also mounted his swan.
The Creator shone with two umbrellas having the luster and form of indragopa insects.
Then all the gods, beginning with Indra, accompanied by their respective vehicles and cheered by various musical instruments, set forth. 132–133.
Surrounded by hosts numbering in the millions of crores, they went to the hermitage of Gautama; having seen that supreme wonder, Brahmā, Viṣṇu,
and Maheśāna saw that he had restored his own devotee to life by glancing at him from the left corner of his eye.
Śaṅkara said to Gautama: "I am pleased; choose a boon that is not forbidden.
Gautama said:
"O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to me..."
"O Maheśvara, may I always possess the capacity to worship your liṅga;
this is the boon chosen by me, O God—listen to it, O Three-eyed One!
May my disciple be highly fortunate and free from the distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted. (136-137)
He does not perceive with the eye that which is to be seen as "mine," nor that which is to be smelled with the nose, nor that which is to be given, nor anything else.
Having understood this and acting accordingly, that yogi of great renown— ||| 138 ||
"O Śaṅkara, he is proclaimed as one whose form is transformed by madness. Let no one hate him, nor let anyone harm him;
O Lord, grant me this, as well as immortality for these [beings]. (139-140)
The Blessed One said:
"May these live until the end of the kalpa, and thereafter attain liberation.
This house, which you have constructed, is vast, wonderful, and auspicious. (141)
"Let us stay for just a moment, and then we shall go to my home.
Gautama said: "O Lord, I am asking for what is improper; yet a seeker does not perceive his own fault. (142)
"O Lord of Gods, if it pleases you, let that which is unobtainable even by Brahmā and the others be granted.
Then Īśa, looking at Viṣṇu and taking the hand of Hari,
Sadāśiva, whose eyes resemble lotuses, spoke thus while smiling.
"O Govinda, why do you not give food to these who are emaciated and suffering from hunger?
Either enter yourself and eat as if in your own home, or go to the house of Pārvatī, whose womb shall fill yours. (144-145)

Having spoken thus, the omnipresent Lord, terrifying in his form, went to a secluded place after instructing Nandī, the guardian of the gate, as previously directed. Then Viṣṇu spoke this reply to Gautama.
Sadāśiva said:
"O Sage, prepare food for all of us, for we desire to eat.
Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara went into a secluded place with Vāsudeva.
Having ascended a soft bed, the two supreme deities lay down;
after conversing with one another, they both rose up.
Having gone to a deep lake, those best of gods prepared to bathe.

Having separately engaged in drinking water from each other's hands in both instances, the sages and the rākṣasas alike performed their water-sports. Then Viṣṇu and Maheśa quickly [performed] the splashing of water.
Śaṅkara and Hari both scattered handfuls of lotus filaments into the face of that [child], whose eyes were like blooming lotuses;
at which Keśava closed his eyes due to the falling of the pollen.
In the meantime, Maheśvara climbed onto the shoulder of Hari;
seizing Hari’s head with his two arms, he submerged him.
Having raised him up again and again, over and over once more, [he did so repeatedly].
Afflicted by him, Hari cast Śaṅkara down with subtle force;
then, seizing his feet, he dragged him, whirled him around,
struck him upon the chest, and threw Acyuta to the ground.
Then Hari, having risen, took water in his joined palms and sprinkled it over Śambhu; then Śambhu likewise sprinkled it over Viṣṇu.
Thus a water-sport ensued in the midst of the assembly of sages.
Due to the agitation of their water-sports, the binding of their matted locks became loosened;
then, in that flurry, those lords of sages tied each other’s matted locks together, so that their matted locks were bound to one another.

The powerful ones dragged the powerless with great pain, throwing them down elsewhere while they cried out and wept; thus did that tumultuous conflict arise during the work involving the waters. 159. Thus did that tumultuous conflict arise during the work involving the waters.
Delighted by the sound of the sky, Ārada danced and sang; making the lute resound, he sang a charming song of rhythm.
With beautiful melody, he sang ten verses in praise of Lalitā.

Śaṅkara, the creator of the world, heard a sweet song; he himself then began to sing it gracefully and very slowly. As the Lord of Gods sang himself, the auspicious Kaiśikī melody was blended with it.
While Nārada was dancing and singing with various modulations of tone, [the Lord],
adopting the *dhruva* melody endowed with all auspicious characteristics and joined by the nectar of his own stream [of voice], then delighted him through that very song. 163–164.
Vāsudeva struck this mṛdaṅga drum with his two hands; meanwhile, Tumburu, the four-faced one, shone forth resonant as he immersed himself in song.
Tānaka, Gautama, and the others remained silent, while Vāyu provided the accompaniment for the singing.
When Hanumān, the lord of monkeys, sang his sweet song,

[the other singers] became withered and faded, while those who were emaciated then became nourished; for all of them, having utterly surpassed their own respective songs, were thus overcome with ecstasy.
All the hosts of gods, sages, and dānavas became silent;
Hanumān alone was the speaker, while they were all listeners, as the time for the midday meal had spread out. (168)
Hearing the song, Maheśvara put on a pair of *dukūla* garments;
Viṣṇu took two yellow cloths, and Caturānana (Brahmā) took a reddish one. Then, having all performed their respective duties, they all assumed the attire appropriate for themselves. 169–170.
Having mounted their respective vehicles, all the deities departed. Maheśa, who is fond of song, spoke to the Lord of the Monkeys:
"I have commanded you to become a monkey; mount the bull without hesitation."
"Facing me, sing a song that leaves nothing unsung.
Then the tiger among monkeys said to the Blessed Maheśvara:
"The capacity for mounting the bull belongs to you; it does not belong to anyone else."
"O Lord, having mounted your vehicle, I shall become a sinner;
O Lord of Gods, let this bird, the vehicle of Śiva, mount me instead. Behold, I shall go toward you. 174.
Then the Lord mounted Hanumān as one mounts a bull.
Once the god Śaṅkara had ascended, Hanumān severed his neck and head, turned over the skin, and sang from the mouth just as before. 175–176.
Hearing the nectar-like song of Śambhu, Gautama went to his home,
and all the hosts of celestial sages and dānavas also arrived there; then,
when it was time for the meal, they were honored by Gautama.
All the household utensils and other items made from dry wood sprouted forth while Hanumān was singing; as he sang,
everyone’s gaze remained fixed upon that wondrous sight.

Having two arms, he prostrated at the feet of the Lord; endowed with ornaments upon all his limbs, he was of pleasing form and youth, praised by the gods who stood with palms joined over their heads and gazed upon his slender waist.
Then, taking Hanumān’s head with both hands, Śaṅkara turned his face toward the east.
Seated in the lotus posture, Hanumān placed one foot in his joined palms and the other upon his face;
then the Lord, with great affection, very gently grasped his nose with two of his toes.
He touched him on the shoulder, the face, the armpit, the neck, the chest, between the breasts, and the heart.

Then Śaṅkara placed his hand upon Hanumān’s belly, then on the region of his navel, and then a second time upon his joined palms; taking hold of his head and bending it down, he touched Hanumān’s back with his own mouth, making a sound.
And Śiva placed around Hanumān’s neck a necklace fashioned of pearls.
Then Viṣṇu spoke these words to Maheśāna:
"In the entire expanse of the Brahmāṇḍa, there is no one equal to Hanumān;
for he stands at your very feet, a station inaccessible even to the Vedas, the gods, and others."
Your state, which is unmanifest even to all the Upaniṣads, is joined by all the monkeys;
yet Your state does not abide for even a moment within yogas practiced with means such as *yama* and the rest.
O Hanumān, the pure power [of that state] resides in the lotus-heart of the great yogis.

"Even after performing difficult austerities for thousands of millions of years, those lords of sages do not recognize your form; how then could they know your foot? Oh, how wondrous is this fortune! For even a fickle monkey is a deer [in comparison]. (187-188)

O Lord, although I have worshipped you with devotion for a thousand years, and even for a thousand aeons day after day, you have not shown me your feet, which are pleasing to the heart of a yogi. 189.
"Indeed, the worldly renown of Śambhu is very great and dear to Nārāyaṇa;
likewise, Hari is dear to Śambhu. But I do not possess such fortune.
Sadāśiva said:
"O Blessed One, O Hari, there is no one equal to you who is dear to me;
nor is there anyone else like Pārvatī who is equal to you for me.
Then the great Gautama, having prostrated before the god, [spoke].
"O immeasurable soul, O ocean of compassion for the world,
midday has already passed and it is the time for everyone to eat. Then the omnipresent Mahādeva, having sipped water (performed ācamana), together with Viṣṇu—
Having entered the house of Gautama, he proceeded to take his meal.
[He was adorned] with jeweled rings, anklets, a silk garment, a beautiful girdle of lightning-bright gold, many necklaces, as well as a golden breast-plate, a sacred thread, and an upper robe.
With his shimmering jeweled earrings dangling, his excellent hair beautifully flowered, anointed with the five-fold fragrant unguents, and adorned with armlets, bracelets,
and rings— Śiva, thus decorated, sat upon an excellent seat and likewise seated Hari upon a superior seat facing him.
When the two best of gods, Hari and Īśa, stood facing one another, Gautama then presented golden vessels;
the sage prepared thirty varieties of solid foods, four kinds of excellent milk-rice (*pāyasa*), two hundred types of well-cooked preparations,
three hundred mixed raw and cooked dishes, and likewise a hundred each of roots, tubers, and vegetables.
He gave twenty-five [offerings] consisting of vegetables and the like mixed with ghee, as well as excellent sugar and other sweets, along with fresh pomegranates and so forth; furthermore,
plantain fruit, *gostanī*, excellent *kharjūra*, *nāgaraṅga*, *jambū* fruit, *priyāluka*, and *vikaṅkata* fruit—
these and other such items were offered according to the prescribed ritual.
Having offered the *āpośana* water, the Brahmin said, "Eat.
While they were all eating, Gautama himself took a fan made of fine cloth and fanned Śiva and Viṣṇu.
The Supreme Lord desired to make a jest:
"Look at Viṣṇu; how does that monkey eat?
Look at the monkey Hara eating a frog in Viṣṇu’s vessel."
Maheśvara cast it among the assemblies of sages and even watched over them himself.
He gave his own leavings, such as milk-rice and other foods, to Hanumān, saying: "O Lord, by your very word, these leavings of yours are not to be eaten."
"Whatever food offering, leaf, flower, or fruit is unfit for me, once offered to me, one should cast it all into a well.
Whether you have not yet eaten or whether you have already eaten, this is surely by your grace. (205)
Sadāśiva said:

When the self-manifested Bāṇaliṅga is present in the form of the moon-stone (candrakānta), the consumption of Śambhu’s food offering (naivedya) is known to be equal to the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. || 206 ||
"This is the time for eating; the distaste for that [other] matter comes from another story.
Having eaten, I shall tell it; eat that without hesitation. Then the sage Gautama performed the consecration with water.

He filled water-jars with those waters from the lake—waters which had been cleansed by rubbing seeds within them and thoroughly purified; the waters were slightly reddened, very smooth, and flowed through extremely fine channels, having their bodies repeatedly washed and well-dried.
Then, having covered a brand-new sand altar of the river with pure, most white, fine cloths, he placed the jars full of water upon it.

Having cast into it the powder of *anālaka*, *māsta*, *puṭaka*, *kaṅkolaka*, and musk, one should place within the vessel a garland as bright as sandalwood and moonbeams. Then, having purified it again with water for a watch (*yāma*), one should pour it into a jar; thereafter, having placed a *caṃdra-granthi* flower, and likewise having cast in *bakula* and *pāṭalā* flowers, one should then place a cluster of *śephālī* and water therein, beginning first with the purification of the water.
Then, having wrapped it with a piece of very soft and fine cloth, one should cover the opening of the *sṛṇikā* with a fine cloth resembling the moon; then,
having placed the water-crystals (*karakāḥ*) in a shaded place, provided with a gentle breeze and fanned by a fine fan.
Then, O King, having consecrated even a blade of grass with water from the ocean, one should sprinkle it there; and having performed the purificatory rites, men and women, or the king himself,
along with his daughters, should bathe and put on clean, washed garments.

Having smeared thick honey-colored resin and a dense flow of agallochum at the base of the arms and on the neck, and having applied the five fragrances as an ointment upon the head while performing the placement (nyāsa) of the mantra to be recited.
With hair beautifully bound with flowers, praised, with auspicious faces and perfectly pure, likewise noble and worthy, their bodies anointed with saffron;
these young women, whose every limb was lovely, were further adorned with ornaments. 217.
One might cause such women or monkeys to fetch water;
at the time of giving it, observe whether they have wrapped it in fine cloth or placed the water-jar in their left hand. 218–219.
Then, having removed the water placed upon the *dorikā* (staff), he should cause it to be offered;
in this manner, the venerable sage Gautama caused [the rite] to be performed when all the great-souled ones, beginning with Maheśa, had finished eating. 220.
When the hands and feet of the God of Gods, Maheśvara, had been washed and his hands were rubbed with fragrant unguents, and when he was seated upon his throne,
the gods along with the hosts of sages likewise sat down on low seats.
Having wrapped well-scented pieces of betel nut in jeweled vessels—
pieces that are without corners, circular, large, neither too small nor too thin—
and having cleaned white leaves and placed pieces of camphor within them; 223.
Then, O Gautama, he offered the powder to Śaṅkara;
when the sage had spoken these words, "Accept the betel," [Śiva said] to the monkey, "Accept the betel and give me unbroken areca nuts. 224–225.
The monkey said: "O Maheśvara, there is no impurity in me;
for how can a monkey be impure when he eats many kinds of fruit? Sadāśiva said:
By my word all is purified; by my word nectar becomes poison.
By my word all the Vedas exist; by my word the deities and others arise.
By my word there is the knowledge of Dharma; by my word liberation is proclaimed.
"The Purāṇas, the Āgamas, and the Smṛtis are all from the words of Maheśvara;
therefore, accept this betel leaf and give me pieces of sugar.
Hari took the betel leaf and the pieces of areca nut with his left hand.

Then, having taken the leaves and offered the pieces [of betel nut], Śiva took the camphor placed before him and chewed it. When the Lord had finished with the tāmbūla, Pārvatī [departed] from Mount Mandara.
Taking the hands of Jayā and Vijayā, he went to the hermitage of the sage. Then, having bowed at the feet of the God, she stood with her face cast down.
Raising her face, the Three-eyed One spoke this to her.
"O Goddess of the lords of gods, this offense was committed by me for your sake;
that I ate while leaving you aside—listen further, O beautiful one. Then, having established [the deity] in my own home, which was devoid of the God of gods..."

"O Lord of Gods, you who are liberated from all bonds, a great sin has been committed by me; you ought to forgive it. Having spoken thus with her anger cast aside, she looked at him and departed with Arundhatī. 234–235.
Knowing that she was departing, the sage prostrated himself like a staff;
from that time forward, he performed prostrations like a staff and offered hymns of praise to Maheśa.
Then Śivā said to Gautama, "What do you desire? (236)
Gautama said:
"O Lord of Gods, I have accomplished my purpose if a boon is to be granted to me;
O highly fortunate one, you ought to eat at my house for a long time."
The Goddess said:
"O Sage, with the permission of Śaṅkara, I shall eat here in your house. Having gone to the Lord and obtained his consent, the brahmin Gautama returned.
They fed the goddess Girijā as well as Arundhatī.
Then, having eaten everything, Pārvatī— adorned with perfumes, flowers, and ornaments—
went to Hara along with her thousand attendant maidens.
Then Śaṅkara said to the Goddess: "Go to the hermitage of Gautama;
having performed my twilight devotions, I shall return home again.
Having been addressed thus, the Goddess departed for the very abode of Gautama.

Desiring to perform the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā-vandana), everyone indeed went forth. Having performed the twilight rites at the lake, Maheśa and all the others in their entirety [returned]; then Śambhu, facing north, performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) and recited the mantra.
Then Viṣṇu, of great splendor, spoke this to Maheśa:
"He who is saluted by all and worshipped by all, he in whom all sacrifices are offered—what will you recite? (244)
With palms joined in reverence, they all worship you alone.
O Lord of the gods of gods, to whom else would they offer salutations with joined palms?
O Maheśvara, you are the bestower of the fruits of all meritorious acts such as prostrations and other offerings.
"Who is more worthy of worship than you, who bestows the fruit of your own devotion? Tell me. Śaṅkara said:
"One should meditate upon Govinda in some way, and one should offer salutations to him in some way. (247)
"I shall not worship anyone, O Hari, nor shall I mutter any mantra;
however, this has been displayed by me for the sake of engaging those beings who are nihilists, otherwise they would become evildoers. (248)
"Therefore, for the sake of benefiting the world, all this has been performed by me.
Having said "Om," Hari then bowed to him and remained standing.
Then those hosts of gods and sages arrived at the house of Gautama.

Then they all performed worship to the God of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow; meanwhile, the Lord, the best of the Raghus, remained seated with Hanumān chanting the five-syllabled great mantra (pañcākṣarī). At that time, everyone was reciting it.
Taking hold of Hanūmat’s hand, Hara approached the presence of the Goddess.
Seated together on a single bed, those two divine spouses remained there while Hanūmat, Tuṃburu, and Nārada sang.
The Supreme Lord performed various kinds of playful sports; having summoned Pārvatī, the Lord spoke these words. (254) Śrī Sadāśiva said:
"O auspicious one, it is not proper for a woman to arrange her hair in the presence of her husband;
in the act of adorning the hair, some misfortune might befall her. (255)
If the entire process of grooming the hair is not desired,
then, after the binding [of the hair] has been performed, one should wipe the edges of the shoulders and remove any remaining hair, flowers, or other items clinging to the body. 256–257.

While this is occurring, O Great-Souled One, when those who praise you from heaven have arrived here, what answer can be given to them? Or else, O Lord, if they do not come, fear will go to its destruction.
While she was speaking thus, Śaṅkara drew her toward him with his hand, placed her upon his own thighs, loosened the binding of her hair,
and with both hands, he parted it and even tore at it with his fingernails.
Having taken the pārijāta garland given by Viṣṇu, though it had fallen upon her hair, she fashioned it into a braid; then,
taking a jasmine wreath, she bound it within the knot of her tresses.
Maheśvara took the garland of Kalpa flowers given by Brahmā and placed it upon Pārvatī’s garment, which was rich with hidden fragrance;
then the Lord performed a wiping motion against her shoulder and back.
When the Lord’s waist-knot had slipped down due to the downward pull of the Goddess’s garment, he said, "What is this? and tied his waist-knot once more.
Then, out of intoxication, he said, "I see this nose-ornament of yours."
Having spoken thus, the virtuous woman herself took up a lusterless pearl;
for when combined with turmeric, a pearl becomes devoid of brilliance. "Let this pearl, which is dear to me, be held by you. (265-266)
Pārvatī said:
"Oh, how wonderful! Śambhu’s abode is enriched with every kind of object; previously, I had already recognized all these things by their ornaments. (267)
Oh! The attainment of beauty is recognized by ornaments:
the head of the god [Śiva] is adorned with the skull of Brahmā as a garland; likewise, the garland of Naraka is an ornament for the region of his chest. 268.
Śeṣa and Vāsuki are your two venomous bracelets;
the quarters of the sky are your matted hair, and white ash is your body ointment.
A great bull is your vehicle, and your lineage and family remain entirely unknown.
"O Girijā, you do not recognize these two fathers, nor do you recognize Virūpākṣa, whose body is such as this.
To her who was speaking thus, Viṣṇu, becoming exceedingly angry, said:
"O Goddess, for what reason do you revile the God of gods, the Lord of the universe?"
"O blessed lady, I shall surely give up my dear life-breaths because of your lack of restraint;
O blessed lady, our vow is that death occurs wherever there is the reviling of the Lord.
Having said this, Hari then moved toward his head to cut it off with his two claws.
Maheśa, taking his hand, said:
"O Pārvatī, do not act so rashly; everything you have said is dear to me, yet it is unpleasant to you.
O Hṛṣīkeśa, whatever you desire to do that is unpleasant to me—"
Having said "Om," Lord Hari became silent.
Then Hanumān addressed these words to the God:
"I request that my vow of worship be likewise fulfilled without desire for reward."
"I shall go for the sake of worship; you ought to grant me permission.
Śaṅkara said: "Whose worship? Where is the worship? What is the flower? What is the offering? Speak! (277)
"Who is your preceptor? What is your mantra? And what is your mode of worship?
Thus spoke the Lord of Gods, while Hanumān was trembling violently, his entire body shaking, as he proceeded to offer praise.
Hanumān said:
"Homage to the great god Śaṅkara, the immeasurable Self;
homage to the yogi, the source of yoga, and the teacher of yogis."
Salutations to the one accessible to yogis, to the god, to the lord of the ignorant. 280.
Salutations to you, the lord of the Vedas, to the lord of the gods;
salutations to the one who is meditation itself, who is accessible through meditation, and who is the preceptor of the sustainers of the world. 281.
Salutations to the one who is accessible to both the disciplined and the undisciplined, and who is the lord of the earth and other realms;

salutations to Him who is the treasury of Vedic statements such as "namaste" (salutations to you) and so forth; salutations to Him who is propounded by the words beginning with "ātanuṣva" (spread yourself).
Salutations to you, the eight-formed one; salutations to the Lord of Creatures. 283.
Salutations to the three-eyed Tryambaka, whose eyes are the Moon, Sun, and Fire, and who is fond of the Bhṛṅgarāja, Dhattūra, and Droṇa flowers. 284.
Salutations to you, beloved of the *bṛhatī* groves, the *puṃnāga*, the *caṃpaka*, and others;
salutations to you, salutations to you, again and again, salutations, salutations! (285) Then Śiva said to Hari: "Do not fear; tell me everything."
Hanumān said:
"The worship of the Śiva-liṅga must be performed by one whose body is smeared with ashes (286),
using waters collected during the day and likewise flowers and other offerings."
I shall inform Your Majesty of the auspicious procedure for the worship of Śiva.
When evening has arrived, one should perform a head-bath;
having put on clean, dry clothes and sipped water, one of clear intellect should perform the rite twice.
Then, having taken up the ashes, one should perform the fire-related bath (āgneyasnāna),
either consecrating them eight times with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), or else with the five-syllabled mantra, or with whatever name [of the deity] one chooses. 289.
Holding darbha grass in his hand, he should collect the ashes consecrated seven times while reciting "Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām" and cast it upon his head; then,
reciting "Tatpuruṣāya vidmahe," he should sprinkle the ashes on his face.
One should place [the ashes] on the chest with "To the non-terrible and to the terrible ones";
one should place them on the secret parts with "Salutation to Vāmadeva";
and then one should place them on the feet with "I take refuge in Sadyojāta."
The wise one should dust his entire body with the *praṇava*.
This supreme procedure for bathing and other rites has been declared for those of the three twice-born classes; now I shall explain that which was likewise taught by the Guru for Śūdras and others.
The wise one, having uttered the word "Śiva," should consecrate the ashes seven times; then, taking them, he should apply them to the head with the mantra "To Śiva.
It is taught that he should apply them to the mouth with "To Śaṅkara" and to the heart with "To the Omniscient One."
Having uttered "Sthāṇave namaḥ" and "Svayambhuve," one should then place pure ashes on the secret parts; thereafter,
having recited "Namaḥ śivāya," the smearing of all the limbs with ashes is prescribed.
Having washed his hands and sipped water, with darbha grass in hand and composed in mind—where darbha is unavailable, gold may be used; in its absence, cow-hair;
in its absence, dūrvā grass; and in its absence, silver. (298)

Having performed the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsti) and the recitation (japa) to the Goddess, one should proceed to the temple of the deity. Then, one should prepare either a divine altar (devavedi), or a consecrated mound (sthaṇḍila),
or a pure earthen structure fashioned for the purpose, adorned with designs such as lotuses.
Furthermore, there are variegated lotuses made with the four colors or even with white alone, as well as svastikas and the like;
likewise, there are blue lotuses (utpala) and so forth, maces, conchs, tridents, and hand-drums (ḍamaru).
Furthermore, there is the five-prasāda mentioned previously, as well as the Śivaliṅga;
likewise, the Sarvakāmaphala tree, the Kulaka, and the Kolaka;
and also the hexagon, the triangle, or even the nonagon. (302–303)

The wise man should fashion upon the altar, or even within the temple, a swing with twelve corners, sandals, fans, a pair of chowries and umbrellas, as well as Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the other deities, using colored powders. 304.
Wherever there may be worship of the Deity, the wise man should arrange it in this manner:
that which is fashioned with one's own hand is primary; that which is purchased is middling; that which is obtained by request is inferior; and that which is taken by force is the lowest. 305–306.
However, that which is performed for those unworthy by force is fruitless.
[One should perform it] with red *śāli*, *japā*, *sthāṇa*, *kalamā*, and white and red grains, using rice-grains the size of *vrīhi* and ears of grain, respectively. 307.
One should properly perform this sacrifice by means of those described as superior, middling, and likewise inferior, through the installation of the lotus and other [mandalas];
one should face either the northeast or the east. 308–309.
I shall now describe the seat as it has been seen and heard: one made of kuśa grass, of leather, equal to cloth, wooden, or of palmyra leaf;
likewise, one made of wool, gold, silver, or copper.
One should prepare a seat from either cow-dung or the wood of the Arka tree.
The fourfold skins to be known are those of the tiger, the Ruru deer, the black antelope, and the common deer; or alternatively, the skin of the Bandhūka. 311–312.
One should prepare a seat among these as is appropriate;
having assumed either the lotus posture (padmāsana) or the auspicious cross-legged posture (svastikāsana), seated upon *darbha* grass and ashes, one should restrain the breath and remain silent.
For that long, one should practice meditation internally upon the form of the deity;

[one should meditate on] Śiva, who resides at the end of the twelve-finger space of the crest-lock (*śikhā*), whose body is subtle, who moves within all beings, and who dwells in the cave of the heart within those of universal form. 314–315.

Having meditated upon Him as endowed with all ornaments and possessed of qualities such as the power of atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, one should hold Him in the mind and fill the body through His pervasive presence.
By that radiance, the evil residing within the body goes to destruction.
Just as gold becomes red or white through contact with mercury, so too,
having prepared a pure seat— either surrounded by twelve petals or five, eight, or three— and having placed the *liṅga* there; 317–318.
One should likewise meditate upon Maheśāna, who resides in the cave,
within the purified liṅga; then, having placed fragrant flowers into the purified water scented with perfume in the consecrated jar, one should empower it with the Praṇava.
Prāṇāyāma and the Praṇava are not prescribed for Śūdras.
(320) Meditation on the word "Prāṇāyāma," the recitation of the mantra "Oṃ Śiva," and whatever materials for worship there may be, such as sandalwood paste, flowers, and unbroken rice grains— (321)
Having placed those [implements] nearby, he will then make the formal resolve (saṃkalpa):
"I shall perform the worship of Śiva for the sake of pleasing Śiva alone. Having thus made the resolve, he should then proceed with the invocation (āvāhana) and the other rites.

Having performed everything up to the ritual bath for the deceased, one should then perform the bathing ceremony with the mantra beginning with "namaste" according to the procedure of the Śatarudriya. That stream which flows without interruption is celebrated as the "Stream of Liberation."
With that [mixture], one should bathe an iron [image] for a month while muttering the Rudra-mantra either in a whisper (*upāṃśu*) once,
three times, five, seven, nine, or eleven times,
or even eleven times accompanied by another eleven.
This should be known as the "liberation bath," which bestows liberation for an entire month;
it consists of bathing with the Śaiva-vidyā, the pure *praṇava*, and likewise with earthen [pastes], coconut shells, and waves. 326–327.
One should bathe the Lord of the gods with bell-metal, pearl, food, flowers, and the like, or with the pollen of flowers, using whatever materials are available as prescribed.
(328) Now I shall describe the procedure for the horn so that it becomes fit for bathing.
Having first purified the interior, one should then purify the exterior.
Having made the serpent very smooth and light, one should by no means cut it; rather, it should be placed in two well-rounded leather buckets (droṇīs) situated in a low-lying area. 329–330.
One should offer a bath to the deity with water mixed with *kuśa* grass;
thus the form of water from the horn of a gavaya is described.
At the door, half of the prohibited metal is provided along with the jointed door.

One should fashion the curved joint of the *yogavakra* in the shape of a serpent's staff (*nāgadaṇḍa*). At the position of the fruit, however, there should be a cup (*caṣaka*) with a hole equal in size to that of the staff.
Therein one should cause the water situated in the upper vessel of the machine to fall. 332–333.

Then, having caused [the water] to fall with either the other hand or the left hand alone, a stream of liberation is thereby created; that purifier destroys sin. 334. Having thus installed the Lord of Devas, one should likewise [bathe him] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Then, having bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the three sweets,
and having adorned the Lord with ornaments, one should bathe Maheśvara once again;
then, having performed the cooling services, one should proceed with the water for sipping (ācamana) and so forth.
One should worship Śivaliṅga with a garment, a sacred thread (upavīta), the five fragrances (pañcagandha),
camphor, agallochum (aguru), and sandalwood (pāṭīra),
or both of these mixed together.

The entire pedestal should be filled with fragrance, or according to the extent of one's wealth; then, one should silently perform the ritual service or offer the *kāliya* flower, the *śrīpatra*, and the *maruci* flower, as well as all other items according to one's capacity and as prescribed.

Incense made from many substances, as well as pure guggulu mixed with the clarified butter of a tawny cow, is recommended for all types of incense offerings. (340) Having offered incense according to one's capacity, one should offer lamps of tawny cow's clarified butter.
Alternatively, having offered lamps with mere clarified butter as an oblation (upahāra),
and having given whatever is available according to one's capacity along with flowers, one should then perform the purification of the mouth and respectfully offer betel.
Thus indeed is the worship completed through circumambulation, prostration, and offerings; thereafter, I shall describe those five limbs of song (gītāṅga-pañcaka) to you:
song, instrumental music, Purāṇas, dance, and humorous speech. 343.
The waving of lights (nīrājana), the offering of handfuls of flowers, and the total surrender of everything (akhilārpaṇa) are proclaimed as the ritual services (upacāra).
Likewise, the ornaments, the parasol, the chowrie, and the fan [are also included]. 344-345.
Service as the sacred thread for Śiva and service consisting of the six offerings to the Lord—
whosoever worships Śiva with these thirty-two modes of service,
there is certainly the destruction of all sins in a single day. (346)
The worship consisting of thirty-two services is indeed the most excellent of the excellent.
Sadāśiva said: "O best of monkeys, it is even so; I shall now describe your worship."
"Worship my pair of feet and become the performer of all worship.
Having propitiated me in this manner, perform my service through physical union.
Hanumān said:
"O Lord, I shall first perform the worship of the divine Śiva-liṅga as ordained by my guru,
and afterwards I shall perform the worship of your feet.
Having spoken thus, he bowed to the Lord and became intent upon the worship of the Śiva-liṅga.
Then, having gone down to the shore of the lake and constructed a small altar of sand, he should prepare a seat fashioned from palm leaves.
Having washed his hands and feet and sipped water for purification, he should remain composed in mind.
Then he performed the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna), and having sipped water again while remaining silent,
he arranged beautiful lotuses upon the altar of the deity.
Immediately thereafter, the monkey sat upon a lotus-seat with a palm-leaf [as a fan].
Having restrained his breath and performed renunciation, endowed with pure meditation,
and having prostrated before his guru and the Lord, he sat down thereafter reciting [mantras];
then he applied himself to the effort of performing the worship of the deity.

Having placed the pure water brought in two leaf-cups made of *palāśa* into the water-pot on his head, he should perform the invocation and other rites, including everything up to the ritual bathing, after consecrating the fire with the three mantras.
Then, having taken the god in the hollow of his palms in order to bathe him, the monkey looked at the deity but did not see the pedestal;
seeing only the *liṅga* held in his hand, he was filled with fear.
"What sin have I committed, O great yogi?
Since this Śiva-liṅga remains in my hand without its pedestal, my death today is certain if the pedestal does not arrive. (358-359)
"Then I shall recite the Rudra-hymn; at that time Maheśvara will surely arrive," he resolved in his mind and thus recited the Śatarudriya.
(360) Yet even so, Maheśa did not arrive; then Kapīśvara [acted].
Vīrabhadra, having arrived, cast Rudra down upon the earth. "O devotee, why are you weeping? Tell me the reason for your weeping.
Hanumān said:
"Behold this linga, which is devoid of its pedestal; behold my accumulation of sin.
Vīrabhadra said:
"If your linga does not come to the pedestal, then perform an act of daring."
"I shall burn the world if the pedestal does not arrive. See whether the liṅga and the pedestal have arrived or not.
Then, seeing that the pedestal had not arrived, Vīrabhadra [looked at] the liṅga. 364-365.

Desirous of burning all the worlds, the powerful Vīrabhadra cast fire upon the earth; at that moment, the world was consumed by flames. Then, having burnt the seven nether regions (saptatala), he moved upward once again.
The Lord burned the five upper worlds inhabited by the denizens of Janaloka;
having taken up with his nail the fire produced from the eye on his forehead—
resembling a jambīra fruit— the omnipresent one held it in the palm of his hand.
"If you do not come to the sacrificial seat, these worlds will undoubtedly be consumed by fire.
Then, seeing that they had not arrived, the high-souled Sanaka and others, possessing great ascetic power, understood through yoga that Vīrabhadra had come. 368.
Having arrived at the excellent hermitage of Gautama,
the twice-born ones did not see the Lord of gods, even though he was present;
nevertheless, they praised him with hymns originating from all the Vedas.
Oṃ, salutation to that God of gods, to him of pure radiance and inconceivable form; salutation to him, the sovereign of the gods; salutation to him, the secret of the Vedas and the pure one.
Salutation to Śiva, the primordial god; salutation to him who has a serpent as his sacred thread.
Salutations to Him, the supporter of the universe, who rains down the essence of the three Vedas—the mass of bliss for the gods.
372 Salutations eternally to that Śaṅkara, who is accessible through knowledge, whose eight forms are earth, water, wind, ether, fire, moon, sun, and the Self. 373
Then, having heard this hymn of praise, Śiva, the restorer of Bhaga’s eyes, said to Viṣṇu: "Go and bring those brahmins here. They were brought by Hari and prostrated themselves before the God.
To them, Śaṅkara spoke these words: "For what purpose have you come? (375) The sages said:
"O Lord, heaps of ashes belonging to twelve worlds are seen."
"Behold this single forest standing as the destruction of the world.
Sadāśiva said:
"When the five worlds situated above are being consumed by fire, we have no doubt at all."
"How did the rain of embers occur, and how did that great sound arise?
(377) The sages said:
"O Vīrabhadra, fear of him now prevails within us."
Then that very god Bhava, as if thirsty for a rain of burning coals, summoned Vīra and said, "O Vīra, why was this done? Vīra replied,
"This was done because there was no *liṅgapīṭha* (pedestal) for Hanumān."

In order to fully understand the mind of the monkey, I performed this great [deed]; then the Lord, that ocean of compassion, restored all the worlds to their former state, even though they had been burnt, making them beautiful as before. 380. The All-pervading One made them so.
The Soul of the Universe, Hara, having embraced him and smelled his head, gave him betel; then Vīrabhadra spoke thus.
Then that Hanumān performed the worship of the Lord.
There, I spoke thus to a certain forest-dwelling gandharva who was accompanied by a lute-player:
"Let this great vīṇā be given to me. The gandharva replied, "This vīṇā, which is as dear to me as my own life, must not be abandoned by me."
"The lute is as dear to me as my own life," said the lord of monkeys (384).
Then, when the Gandharva had fallen by the blow of his fist,
the monkey took up the great lute, which was equipped with its strings and sounds (385).
Having fashioned a gourd into the shape of a *rājavṛkṣa* fruit and placing it upon his chest, he went toward Śiva singing;
he worshipped the feet of the God with pure *bṛhatī* flowers. 386.
Then he granted him a boon: furthermore, life lasting until the end of the kalpa (387). Then he granted another boon: the power to cross the ocean (388).
His limbs were beautifully adorned with all ornaments, and his own radiance eclipsed the brilliance of the gods.

With a serene form, youthful, and possessing limbs as auspicious as Śiva’s, he honored all the gods. Taking a yellow garment, Maheśvara said: "O Hari, accept this auspicious yellow cloth, O God. 389–390.

Brahmā gave a pair of red garments, and Vasudatta likewise gave a pair of garments to all— the celestial sages, the Dānavas, and the others. Having heard this, Rāma also offered a pair [of garments] to Śambhu.
And there was also very fine and highly valuable golden ornamentation.
Then, having eaten and being seated comfortably on the bank of the Gautamī, he was accompanied by his ministers, his family priest, various groups of sages, kings, and monkeys.
Rāghava spoke these words to Śambhu, the knower of the truth of the Purāṇas:
"You alone know everything that dwells within the secret cave of all dharmas;
O Brahmin, tell me what is distinguished in each respective age."
Śambhu said:
"In the Kṛta age, meditation alone is supreme; in the Tretā, sacrifice; in the Dvāpara, worship; and in the Kali age, charity and the chanting of Hari's names."
And all [virtues] are praised everywhere, yet meditation is not [possible] in the Kali age (396).
O Lord of the Earth, because the minds of men are deluded and they are situated in hardship, their intellect is not fixed upon dharma, nor is it fixed upon the Veda or the Smṛti (397).
Neither by the *nakṣatra*, *tīrtha*, or *svadhākāra* rites, nor in the Purāṇas, nor in the Śruti;
neither by sacrifice, nor at sacred fords (*tīrthas*), nor by service to the virtuous (398); neither by the worship of deities, nor by the duties pertaining to one's own caste.
O King, neither by the recollection of the gods nor even by the bull [Dharma] can this be achieved;
therefore, O men, you are incapable of performing meritorious acts that require a long duration of time,
whereas a human being is able to perform a gift (dāna) because it takes only a short time.
Therefore, for those who have committed evil deeds, no expiation exists;
however, for some, the destruction of sin may occur through expiations, and not otherwise.
(401) One who possesses knowledge of Brahman, one who performs the śrāddha at Gayā, one who goes to Kāśī, and one who is devoted to the Vedas—[these are exempt].
O Raghava, these [sages] are knowers of the Puranas and are devoted to hearing them;
for they discern the meaning according to the sequence of the Yugas, generate conviction in themselves and others, and illuminate the Supreme Brahman. (402–403)
A Brāhmaṇa who recites the Purāṇas is distinguished above all others;
even the sin committed by him does not cling to him, much less that of anyone else.
For some others as well, the Purāṇa is the destroyer of sin.
He who has faith in the Purāṇas, who regards the speaker as his guru,
and who recognizes the bestower of the knowledge of Brahman as superior to his own kinsmen—
all his sins undoubtedly go to destruction. (405-406)
Now follows the journey of the worshipper to Śrīśaila, the Great Lord;
this ancient narrative destroys the sins of men in the Kali age. Listen as I relate what occurred in the past during the Kali Yuga, O Rāma.
There was a Brāhmaṇa named Gautama who was devoid of Vedic knowledge (408).
He had two brothers, Puṣṭi and Paśu, who were likewise devoid of Vedic knowledge;
together with them, he practiced agriculture and attained prosperity therein (409).
Then the king gave him some wealth, grain, and other possessions, and spoke these words: "Appoint some office for me;
I shall send wealth, as my two brothers are capable."
The king said:
"The entitlement of a Brāhmaṇa indeed lies in Vedic religious rites;
for one who is appointed to anything other than that, his status as a Brāhmaṇa perishes."
Gautama said: "In other ages, this dharma was different; the dharma of the Kali age is not like that. For kingship, O protector of the earth, is indeed declared to be the duty of kings."

A Brahmin who is utterly destitute does not incur sin by performing such work; however, for Śūdras, agriculture is their duty, and it is not permitted for one born of the first caste even in times of distress.
Therefore, I shall subsist as a Kṣatriya; point out some villages to me.
"Otherwise, I prefer that my livelihood be conducted through the office of a *kṣattṛ* (steward), and not otherwise," he said;
thus addressed, [the king] gave villages to the twice-born. However, for one corrupted by the authority over those villages, his conduct became quite different.
I ate meat and drank liquor; I spoke wicked words;
likewise, I approached the wives of others, seized the property of others, and was hostile toward my enemies;
I played at dice repeatedly and ate forbidden food such as *kalañja*. (416–417)
Neither Śiva nor Viṣṇu, the lords of the worlds, was worshipped; thus, after some time, the king spoke these words to the one of evil conduct:
"O Brahmin, having abandoned your status as a Brahmin, you have attained the state of a Śūdra."
Therefore, by means of the law of compulsion, I shall cause you to fall from your status.

Let there be no Brahminhood for you this very day; O Śūdra, even being a Śūdra is better for me than having you as a Brahmin, for otherwise they would eat [the food] belonging to a Brahmin, which is better for me.
"O Lord of the Earth, I am not able to renounce all of this.
Śambhu said: "While the wicked Brahmins were speaking thus, the king remained silent. (421)
Equal to a butcher and a Śūdra, he ate food along with meat;

once, that man of evil conduct, while standing in a pavilion on the main road, heard this verse being recited by a twice-born man: [Verse follows] 422. [The verse was: "He who eats the food of one who eats dog-meat, or eats the food of a dog-eater, becomes a dog-eater himself after three births. Hearing this, he became terrified and thought, "I have indeed become a dog-eater. Then, having made a vow, he went to the city of Ayodhyā. There, he saw a certain Brahmin who was a master of the Vedas and a knower of the Purāṇas. He bowed down to him and spoke these words: "O best of the twice-born, I am a dog-eater. Tell me, O holy one, how may I be purified? Hearing his words, the Brahmin said: "O son, go to the city of Mathurā. There dwells the Lord of the World, the Supreme Person, the remover of all sins. By worshipping Him, you will attain purification. Having heard his words, he went to Mathurā and worshipped the Lord of the World. By the grace of the Lord, he attained supreme liberation. Therefore, one should never eat the food of a dog-eater. One should always avoid such a person, for he is equal to a dog. Thus it is told. ||| 423 || ||| 424 || ||| 425 || ||| 426 || ||| 427 || ||| 428 || ||| 429 || ||| 430 || ||| 431 || ||| 432 || ||| 433 || ||| 434 || ||| 435 || ||| 436 || ||| 437 || ||| 438 || ||| 439 || ||| 440 || ||| 441 || ||| 442 || ||| 443 || ||| 444 || ||| 445 || ||| 446 || ||| 447 || ||| 448 || ||| 449 || ||| 450 || ||| 451 || ||| 452 || ||| 453 || ||| 454 || ||| 455 || ||| 456 || ||| 457 || ||| 458 || ||| 459 || ||| 460 || ||| 461 || ||| 462 || ||| 463 || ||| 464 || ||| 465 || ||| 466 || ||| 467 || ||| 468 || ||| 469 || ||| 470 || ||| 471 || ||| 472 || ||| 473 || ||| 474 || ||| 475 || ||| 476 || ||| 477 || ||| 478 || ||| 479 || ||| 480 || ||| 481 || ||| 482 || ||| 483 || ||| 484 || ||| 485 || ||| 486 || ||| 487 || ||| 488 || ||| 489 || ||| 490 || ||| 491 || ||| 492 || ||| 493 || ||| 494 || ||| 495 || ||| 496 || ||| 497 || ||| 498 || ||| 499 || ||| 500 || ||| 501 || ||| 502 || ||| 503 || ||| 504 || ||| 505 || ||| 506 || ||| 507 || ||| 508 || ||| 509 || ||| 510 || ||| 511 || ||| 512 || ||| 513 || ||| 514 || ||| 515 || ||| 516 || ||| 517 || ||| 518 || ||| 519 || ||| 520 || ||| 521 || ||| 522 || ||| 52
This lotus in the heart, uttered by the twice-born, remained [there].
Those who are devoted to Nārāyaṇa go to that which is higher than the highest;
those who hate Maheśvara shall not go there.
Having heard the explanation as well, he spoke regarding the Purāṇas:
"What is Nārāyaṇa said to be like? And what is Maheśvara like? What is declared to be the supreme refuge? And how is hatred described?"
"What is that which is known as the Supreme, and what is even higher than that?
The Purāṇika said:
"The Supreme is that abode of Brahmā, characterized solely by bliss and manifestation."
Beyond that is the abode of Viṣṇu, which is superior even to that of Brahmā;
because of its indestructibility, it is proclaimed as the supreme state (*parama-pada*).
Within that [abode] is the Person, Viṣṇu, the all-pervading Lord who is the supreme limb of that [state].
Because they were born from the waters (nārāḥ), they are called *nara* by the wise;
and because those waters (*nārāḥ*) are his abode (*ayana*), he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa. Those for whom that [Nārāyaṇa] is the supreme goal are called *tatparāyaṇa*.
Those principles beginning with Mahat—He who is their Lord;
He whose eyes are the sun, fire, and moon; He is Maheśa, the husband of Umā.
Indeed, hatred and enmity are to be understood as residing in Īśvara, the Supreme Self. 430–431.
Śambhu said: Having reflected upon these words thus uttered by the Paurāṇika Bhaṭṭa, I spoke once more: "What is the destiny for one such as I? (432)
Then the Paurāṇika said to him: "Listen, I shall tell you the way forward; with all effort, O Kuru, perform atonement according to the rules.
Practice dharma according to your ability, at the proper time, and according to the prescribed rites."
Freed from sin, you shall thereafter attain the highest state.
Alternatively, listen with focused attention to the eternal Purāṇa;
or, free from desire, worship Maheśāna, the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Or else, be ever devoted to the knowledge of Brahman through renunciation (saṃnyāsa) toward the lotus-eyed Lord Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions;
or else go to the Lord of Kāśī and attain either liberation or death.
"Or else, go to Gayā there and perform a śrāddha with great effort;
or rather, daily recite with devotion the Rudra, which is the essence of all the Vedas, the destroyer of sins, and dear to Rudra."
Or go to Śrīśaila, or to Kedāra according to your desire; or else, perform the Māgha bath every year. What is the use of much speaking on this matter? Always remain devoted to dharma.
"O lowest of the twice-born, you shall not dwell in hell in this manner.
Gautama said:
"Having heard everything from your mouth, I shall perform the Purāṇa."
"Tell me also the cause for trusting the scripture and that which is to be avoided.
The Purāṇika said:
"Meat, liquor, the enjoyment of other women, gambling, and boastfulness are to be avoided."

Harsh speech, falsehood, deceit, and the reviling of the God of gods; the censuring of gurus, the gods, the elders, and those who speak the Purāṇas and Smṛtis; white eggplant, and the cultivation of artificial bottle-gourds—these are forbidden. 442–443.
The citron, safflower, red lotus, and likewise the śṛṅga;
the araru, the coconut, and similarly the pumpkin; the kovidāra fruit, food cooked in oil, and human milk. 444.
The milk of a female rhinoceros, of a female donkey, of a woman who has recently given birth, and of a ewe;
the milk of a female camel, of animals with uncloven hooves, and of a female deer, goat, or human;
the milk of a cow whose calf has died or of one in heat; and salt—these are what the Yogin [should avoid]. 445–446.
One should never cause coconut juice to be offered in vessels made of bell-metal, copper, bronze, honey, lead, glass, earthenware, or clay;
however, the oblation (homa) may be performed in an earthen vessel, and the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) in a silver one. 447.
A wise person seeking merit in the next world should not associate with others [in such ways]:
applying powder or ointments inside a vessel, eating from it, as well as chewing betel nut and indeed chewing the leaf of the powder. 448–449.
The eating of even ripe betel nut by a Krami-yogin,
as well as milk-rice with salt or anything placed directly into the hand, [is forbidden];
likewise in Sindhu, Saurāṣṭra, Kāmbhoja, Māgadha, and Siṃhala.
In that case, milk mixed with salt would not be harmful;
indeed, all types of milk and salts, when combined, may be used in other regions without harm, yet here [in this land], there is no doubt that drinking them leads to illness. 451–452.
"What is the use of saying much more here? One should avoid that which is censured by the virtuous.
Śambhu said:
"Having thus heard these words of that high-souled brāhmaṇa... (453)
Having gone to his own abode, he reflected in distress:
"Neither at night nor by day does even a great man know when death will come; there is happiness in the next world, while here there is only the diversion of sensory enjoyments."
Through worms, insects, humans, and so forth, pleasure and pain are experienced individually;
indeed, for every single living being, the distinction among causes is well-established, for there is no uniform state even for a single soul. (455–456)
At the time of birth, there is great ignorance; in infancy, there is slight awakening;

in the stage of faltering steps (early childhood), there is little discernment; and likewise, in boyhood, it remains slight. In youth, one is intent on play, and in adolescence, on sensual objects and women.

When youth has ceased, the desire for the acquisition of wealth is stilled; and in old age, one is no longer able to enjoy even the objects of desire, due to tears, phlegm, saliva, wrinkles, gray hair, and trembling. (458–459)

With his senses agitated and impaired by breathlessness, coughing, and wind disorders, he is unable to hold anything back and knows nothing at all; even when other women are present, he exposes his private parts. 460.
One intent on scratching his scrotum is cruel according to the signs of life;
461 while eating, he scratches his buttocks, lifting and shifting his garment, yet he is unable to swallow his mouthful of food due to phlegm. 462
When there was space, then the wind arose, and the wind possessed sound;
there was also the exit of impurity and the discharge of phlegm.
There was the scolding of daughters-in-law and others, and the display of childish palm-clapping laughter.

Reflecting again and again upon the departure of his guru and other matters (464), when summoned for the sake of food and such, he reviled the food and other items offered; and having long reproached [the host] regarding the hot food, he fell once more into deep reflection. (465)
"I have committed most wicked deeds; how shall I eat, how shall I sleep, how shall I stand, how shall I walk, and what will become of me in the next world?
Thus, constantly agitated by such thoughts, he was never free from great anxiety.
O Raghava, having gone to the house of a twice-born man who was learned in the Puranas, he,
with a face cast down in shame, asked, "What shall I do? But that twice-born man, a knower of the Puranas, said nothing at all then.
Realizing, "This man is a sinner," Gautama caused his disciple to drive him out;
having gone outside, Gautama stood right at the doorway.
Then, perceiving that [the other] was seated upon the ground, a contemplator of the meaning of the Purāṇas—
With great difficulty he reached the seat, but once it was offered, he did not sit upon it;
instead, sitting on the ground, he spoke to the knower of the Purāṇas of Rāma:
"I shall perform an expiation; let that be prescribed right here."
The Brahmin said: "Declare all the sins you have committed in every way," but he replied, saying, "Not even a single sin has been committed by me. (472)
Weeping and tormented, he fell to the ground, crying out, "O father! Then the Brāhmaṇa said to him: "If this great sin has been committed three times, there is no atonement. (473)
Gautama said:
O illustrious knower of the Purāṇas, even though I am burdened by sin, how could my meeting with you, O best of the twice-born, be fruitless? 474.
The Paurāṇika said:
"The scripture is the authority for all in determining expiation (prāyaścitta). Whatever one might say as beneficial without that [scripture], that would not constitute expiation."
If committed once, it is said to be single-fold; if a second time, it becomes double;
if a third time, it is said to be triple; but for the fourth time, there is no atonement.
Yet you have performed all four types of sins many times, according to your own will.
"How am I able to prescribe an expiation for one such as you?
Gautama spoke again, "Where must I go? [He replied:
"Having observed three fasts, he attained Śivarātri. 480
Deeply distressed, he observed the fourth fast;
on the full moon day, he broke his fast with fruits and bark garments.
Then that virtuous twice-born man performed a circumambulation of Śrīśaila.
He then went to his home, sighing and exceedingly emaciated by anxiety:
"How will my cessation of sin succeed while I remain silent?
What is this infinite, inconceivable, and most grievous sin? (482-483)
Having heard this, he said to me, "Let an expiation be prescribed;
however, once which Purāṇa has been heard will this knowledge be attained?
Having formed this thought, he then spoke to the knower of the Purāṇas.
"O Blessed One, please explain this one Purāṇa to me.
(485) "Perform for me quickly the purificatory rites beginning with the birth-ceremony;
having become a twice-born, I shall listen today and thereafter perform my atonement. (486)
"The Purāṇa that has been proclaimed shall be my means of instruction;
therefore, having ascertained the meaning of the Purāṇa, I shall perform what is possible. Thus spoke the Paurāṇika.
I shall proclaim this ancient Purāṇa, which destroys all sins, according to my knowledge, according to my ability, as purely as possible, and according to the prescribed rules.
Or rather, what specific Purāṇa do you desire that I should proclaim?
Gautama said:
"O Ruci, tell me the entire Purāṇa; speak that which is beneficial, by hearing which no distinction whatsoever arises between Hari and Īśa."
The Paurāṇika said: That Purāṇa which was spoken by Kūrma proclaims the non-difference between the two deities;
whoever hears it first, his sin is destroyed. 490.

If a sinful person considers that which comes from the mouth of such a brahmin as something to be heard, obstacles will arise for him; moreover, his wife shall perish. Furthermore, I shall state one thing that is difficult to do: not censuring either the listener or the speaker. 491–492.
When there is such devotion toward the expounder— who reveals the Dharma from the Dharma itself—
and skill in observing right conduct, which shows the path to liberation and other goals, then Maheśa shall be pleased and Viṣṇu will bestow the desired fruit. (493)
"By him the ancestors are delivered, and they go to the supreme goal.
Thus ends the one hundred and fourteenth chapter in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava. 114.
The one hundred and fifteenth chapter.
Śrī Rāma said: How is it that in a base Brāhmaṇa there occurs such a convergence of multitudes of sins?
"O best of the twice-born, how did the knower of the Purāṇas explain it?
Śambhu said: "In teaching and in studying, a connection is established."
O knower of the Purāṇas, O descendant of Kakutstha who knows the meaning of all truths: even the mass of sins committed by a great sinner perishes upon meeting Rāma for a year. 2–3.
Just as a mass of smoke from a great fire is not capable of extinguishing that fire, nor is a moth capable of extinguishing the flame for the sake of destroying it,
so too the reciter of the Purāṇas is not capable of destroying the sins committed by others.
Just as one who possesses the mantras can release mortals seized by spirits and the like from the fear of those spirits,
yet does not himself become afflicted, so too the reciter of the Purāṇas does not deserve to incur any sin whatsoever.
The knower of the Purāṇas destroys the extremely wicked sin committed by himself as well as that committed by others, or even his own past karma;
O Īśa, Hṛṣīkeśa, you are impartial and possess discernment.
O Rudra, you are a knower of the world, the Vedas, and ritual action; you are free from desire through the recitation of mantras.
You are contented, peaceful, skilled in ritual, abundant, a practitioner of yoga, self-controlled, and like the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha, who was formerly a knower of the Purāṇas.

O protector of the earth, by your command he remained in Ayodhyā; while you were protecting the entire world, a Rākṣasa assailed you. And that Rākṣasa, following the instruction of Śukra, then approached you.
"I shall kill him while he is fast asleep; otherwise, it is not the right occasion.
Then the brahmin Vasiṣṭha, who was devoted to your welfare, realizing this, [warned you that] the Rākṣasa would undoubtedly kill the descendant of Kakutstha while he was sleeping and heedless.
Thinking, "Since he has obtained a boon from Brahmā, this task of mine to ward him off is impossible," the brahmin-sage set out, taking his army with him;
yet, being unable to slay the Rākṣasa who was devoid of death, the sage [despaired].
Having himself become a rākṣasa, the great sage spoke these words:
"For what purpose have you come here to this forest frequented by sages? He replied, "O King, I am a slayer of rākṣasas; I have come here to kill him. 14–15.
The sage also said: "What is the use of that life, or even death, if after eating my flesh you go forth victorious having fought a battle?
The two Rākṣasas said:
"How will you, a Rākṣasa, become my food?
Then Vasiṣṭha, assuming a human form, stood in the sky;
spitting upon his head, he struck him with his fist.
Struck by that Rākṣasa, the thief fled, and the Ṛṣi pursued him.
As they both fled toward one another, they entered the ocean;
there, the Rākṣasa was then seized by a crocodile dwelling within it.
The sage remained once again in Ayodhyā, established as before.
Śambhu said:
"Therefore, one who knows the Purāṇas and is free from envy should act according to his own inclination. (20)
I shall now describe the auspicious procedure for listening [to the scripture]; listen carefully.

On a pure day during the bright fortnight, in conjunction with a favorable weekday, lunar mansion, and yoga, and when the *karaṇa* and the ascendant are endowed with the strength of the planets and stars.

One should listen to the Purāṇa, endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics, when one is free from delusion, not a child nor an old man, when Jupiter is situated in its exaltation, not during the dark fortnight, not during an eclipse, and not in the presence of an atheist. Thus it is said. (22-23)
O Lord of the Gods, [this may be performed] in a pure house, or on an impure altar, in a monastery, or on a riverbank, in a temple, or in an assembly hall;
or on a street, in a monastery, or in a beautiful, meritorious hall.
One should personally pay homage to the best of Brahmins, especially those who are knowers of the Purāṇas (25).
One should prepare a seat that is specially elevated above all others and address them with gentle words, saying, "Come, please sit upon this seat of Dharma" (26).
On the day of commencing the Purāṇa, one should proclaim the task at hand;
one should honor the expounder of the Purāṇa with garments and other offerings. Having given auspicious, fine, and new garments, [one should proceed].
The water-pot, the ornaments for the neck and so forth, the vessel, and the seat—

these should be worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), and after offering betel-leaf, one should meditate upon Viṣṇu, who wears white garments, is moon-colored, and possesses four arms. 28–29.
One should meditate upon the one with a serene countenance for the pacification of all obstacles; then, having honored the members of the assembly, one should pray to Gaṇeśa.
(30) Worship is performed with the mantra beginning "Oṃ namaḥ," followed by a hymn of praise to Sarasvatī.
One should begin the commencement of the Purāṇa at the time of dawn (verse 31). On the day of commencement, fifteen verses are auspicious;
on the second day, twice that number are auspicious (verse 32).
On the third day, it is desired that the discourse and its listening continue for even longer;

as long as there is no interruption of the days, so long should the explanation and the hearing proceed. When the arrangement has been established, then [one should approach] the teacher who is learned in the Purāṇas.
Then, on the following day, after offering betel leaves and other gifts, one should listen to the Purāṇa;
for such is the scriptural injunction that it should be heard daily. Any man whatsoever who listens to the Purāṇa in the form of a religious vow [attains great merit].

When this Purāṇa is thus [recited], one undoubtedly attains that [state]; for one desiring to hear the Purāṇa, even if a single verse is heard, it will undoubtedly destroy whatever sin was committed on that day. (36-37)

Whoever thus hears this Purāṇa is liberated from the bond of sin consisting of the killing of a Brahmin, from the addiction to drinking liquor, from stealing gold, and from approaching the wife of a preceptor;

In this case as well, whatever has been acquired over a hundred years perishes for both the listener and the speaker. (39) In the Kali age, omniscience does not exist among any of the brahmins; nevertheless, even an explanation devoid of qualities yields fruit, like the act of giving. (40)
I know the intention of the Purāṇas more specifically than Vyāsa or even Brahmā;
nor do my Vedic study, penance, mantras, or oblations [hold such power].
The hearing of the Purāṇa does not bear fruit in the same way as [other acts]; for by hearing it even once, a great sin is undoubtedly destroyed, just as by residing at Śrīśaila. 42–43.
The Guru who knows the Purāṇas, who is worthy of reverence by his listeners, and who destroys sin—
there is no other Guru superior to him for bestowing the ultimate goal.
Those who are considered Gurus in mantras and those who are esteemed in the Vedas and Śāstras [are all subordinate to him].
They are unable to impart all-encompassing knowledge; therefore, they are not enlighteners.
(45) For the most part, there are Piśācas known by the names of Rākṣasas and Brahma-rākṣasas; those who know the Vedic mantras are seen, but not those who know the Purāṇas. (46)
One who is averse to the Purāṇas does not see anything at all; however, one who knows the Purāṇas sees everything. Therefore, that Lord is the destroyer of sins.
Worship of Him is the worship of all, and His protection is the warding off of harm from all.
"Just as among all gifts, the gift of knowledge is praised (48), so too is the reciter of the Purāṇas blessed; in that regard, the gift yields great fruit.
Rāma said:
"What should be given, how much, and of what kind? What kind of Purāṇa is to be avoided, and what kind of knower of the Purāṇas is to be avoided?
Śambhu said:
One should cause food and drink of the six flavors, as well as oily substances,
and a house with its furnishings to be given to a knower of the Purāṇas, O Rāma; all these should be sufficient, or even more, for the sake of greater fruit.
One should give abundant material wealth; one should present soft garments adorned with ornaments, as well as perfumes and flowers every day, or even perfume alone, according to one's capacity. 52.
At the time of the fruiting, one should likewise offer only flowers and fruits; one should also give betel-leaf and pay obeisance with devotion.
At the conclusion of the Purāṇa, one should likewise give gifts and other offerings.
Furthermore, O King, land, gold, and other such things should be given [to the witness] in excess;
no one should remain silent when the matter is being introduced. And whatever honor has been bestowed by the members of the assembly must be conferred by the litigant as well. 55.56ab.
At a temple of the gods, worship by all according to their capacity is desired (56).
Furthermore, O Rāghava, at a sacred ford, in a grove, or in holy shrines, one who knows the Purāṇas should perform worship according to his own ability (57).
O King, I have previously described the characteristics of the listener;
now I shall tell you the characteristics of every kind of narrator of the Purāṇas.
One who is of low birth, afflicted by a great disease, a great sinner, or one who is despised—these are to be avoided.

One who is devoid of purity and proper conduct, one who has abandoned the Vedas and the Smṛtis; one who worships another deity, one with foul speech, one who is deficient in limbs, or one with redundant limbs; the husband of a woman previously married to another, a thief, a killer of living beings, and one who is an outcast—[these are those from whom one should not accept food].
Furthermore, O best of kings, I shall relate to you the Varjya Purāṇa,
which was spoken by ancient knowers and proclaimed by supreme sages;
one should recite that which the eminent sages such as Vyāsa and others have declared.

One should read the text contained in the Purāṇas, explaining it while reflecting upon it (verse 62). Whether by means of any language whatsoever, or according to the local dialect, one shall obtain the fruit [of the merit] upon hearing a text composed in that local dialect (verse 63).
"Having explained the Ākāpikākutstha Purāṇa for the sake of [discerning] what is beneficial and what is harmful,
you should therefore, O Goddess, request that I explain this Purāṇa.
Śambhu said:
Having heard what was thus spoken by the reciter of the Purāṇa, Gautama himself gave three garments to that high-souled Brāhmaṇa;
we have heard that he was the first to hear the Kūrma Purāṇa.
He gave away abundant gold as well as auspicious garments. Then he listened to the Liṅga Purāṇa, the Vaiṣṇava, the Vāmana,
the Padma, the Gāruḍa, the Saura, and the Brāhma Purāṇas.
In this way, Gautama listened to the eight Purāṇas,
as well as the Rāmāyaṇa and the Kūrma Purāṇa; moreover,
he constantly performed the recitation of "Śiva-Nārāyaṇa."
Having reached the state of Brahman with "ava" as its nidhana, he attained the abode of Brahman (verse 69). That Brahmin, having been worshipped by Brahmā, then went to the world of Viṣṇu;
and honored by Viṣṇu, he then departed for the temple of Śiva (verse 70).
This Gautama, the best of sages, is indeed worthy of veneration by all. Furthermore, these rules for the hearing of the *Bhārata* have been declared by me;
that auspicious work which was composed three years ago by the sage Vyāsa— [71] —[is now to be heard].
He who has heard that entire Bhārata in its full extent and can expound it—
save for the most excellent yogi— to no brahmin whatsoever should he bow;
for he who expounds the Bhārata is worthy of veneration by all.
The Brahmin who daily explains or reads the great Mahābhārata is superior to all others; he should indeed propagate it among men.
He may explain a single parva or even several.
One who is liberated from all sins excels in the offerings to the gods and the ancestors (havya-kavya).
One should bow down to that very brahmin, honor him as one worthy of worship,
feed him constantly, and offer everything to him.

O twice-born one, the procedure for his worship has been declared; at the time of the exposition, he should be honored and worshipped according to the prescribed method with garments and other offerings.
Furthermore, upon the completion of the Ādi-parvan, one should give three fine garments.

O bull among kings, gold, garments, and whatever else one can afford should be offered according to one's capacity during the Sabhāparvan (78), as well as during the Ānuśāsana, Āraṇyaka, Svargāroha, and Ādi parvans, for such is the worship [prescribed] therein. (79)
In the sections concerning Karṇa, Aśvamedha, Vairāṭa, Śalya, Droṇa, and Iṣu,
one should offer three pieces of fine, pure cloth or two niṣkas;
in the other minor sections, one should likewise bring one niṣka.
In the Harivaṃśa, one should indeed give three garments and a gold coin (niṣka);
at the conclusion of the entire Bhārata, one should be a giver of land;
and during the hearing of the Rāmāyaṇa, one should perform worship at the end of each Kāṇḍa. 81–82.
Or one may cause a field or even gold to be given;
this [gift] destroys all impurities for the teacher of the Guru’s words.
Through hearing this explanation, all those of excellent intellect attain success;
even the sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are destroyed by hearing this but once—something never heard on earth even by the Kinnaras. 84–85.

One should constantly honor this expounder with vehicles, wealth, gold, and other gifts, for he is the destroyer of the entire mass of one's sins. Furthermore, those other Purāṇas spoken by the sages—
This is for the destruction of the sins of the listeners, and especially for that of the speaker.
Whoever should recite or listen to all thirty-six Purāṇas, there shall never be any cutting of his heart (or mental distress). 87-88.
The first is the Brāhma Purāṇa; the second is called the Pādma; the third is indeed the Vaiṣṇava; and the fourth is called the Śaiva.
Then the Bhāgavata is proclaimed as the fifth; the sixth is now being mentioned.
