The Bhaviṣya and the Nāradīya are proclaimed as the seventh;
the Mārkaṇḍeya is declared the eighth, and likewise the ninth; the Āgneya and the Brahmavaivarta are proclaimed as the tenth. 90–91.
The Liṅga, Vāmana, Skānda, Mātsya,
Kaurma, Varāha, Gāruḍa,
and Brahmāṇḍa— these are known by the wise as the eighteen Purāṇas. 92.
And so, hereafter I shall describe the Upapurāṇas:
first that named Sanatkumāra, then the Nārasiṃha, the third is designated as the Āṇḍa, and likewise the Daurvāsasa. 93–94.
Then there is the Nārada-purāṇa, as well as the Kāpila, the Mānava,
and likewise that which was proclaimed by Uśanas; after that, the Brahmāṇḍa,
the Vāruṇa, the one called Kālikā, the Māheśa, and the Sāmba.
The Saura, Pārāśara, Mārīca, and that called Bhārgava,
along with the Kaumāra— these eighteen Purāṇas have been proclaimed;
indeed, Manu shall be the expounder of these eighteen Purāṇas.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of the Purāṇas," in the Dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava within the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter One Hundred and Sixteen.
Sūta said:
"O Rāma, let the rite of the twilight prayer be performed," the sage said to him;
for even as the sun was setting, this flock of birds was returning to its nest.
Desiring to perform the twilight prayers himself, he proceeded toward the northern direction, leaving his vehicle behind;
his glory was proclaimed by bards and celebrated with the songs of the *hāhā* and *hūhū* celestial musicians.
Having reached the bank of the Gautamī, Rāghava’s pair of feet were thoroughly washed by the son of Vāyu (Hanumān).
Taking the hand offered by Jāmbavat, he reached the excellent river Gautamī.
Holding kuśa grass in both hands, Rāghava then proceeded toward the northern direction;
having offered the three-fold oblation according to the rules, his hair standing on end with joy, he chanted "Oṃ" within himself.

Having offered prayers to Varuṇa in due order, Rāghava bowed down to Śambhu and Vasiṣṭha; having received their blessings, his mind reached its state of tranquility, and with his lotus-feet washed by Hanumān,
he then offered oblations to the sacred fires and, being extolled by panegyrists and bards, went forth.
The sky, as if smeared with nectar by the laughing rays of the moon, appeared on all sides like a canopy of blossoming, radiant stars.
Then he ascended to the palace roof, which had been prepared by the elder minister.
The king went to the assembly hall, which was furnished with various seats. Then, having seated the sage, Rāghava himself took the foremost seat;
the hosts of monkeys, possessing massive bodies, took their positions surrounding him in an orderly arrangement.
Beholding the king seated comfortably, the virtuous brahmin Śambhu then spoke these appropriate words:
"How is it that you, who are honored by all while staying here, now dwell in a cave, O best of kings?
Hearing the brahmin's speech, the scion of Raghu became desirous of hearing the story; standing there, he skillfully silenced [others] so that his words were heard by everyone at that very moment.
"How is it that this service, which is so greatly wondrous, has become centered upon my own self, rather than speaking of the destruction of the Rākṣasa? To this, the King said:
"In the past, the slaying of Kumbhaśrotra occurred, and the Ten-faced one met his death. (10)
"Later on, this man speaks of a Rāmāyaṇa composed otherwise;
who is this best of brahmins that, having approached the presence of kings, proclaims something that causes all people to fall into atheism—is he to be punished according to the law or honored?
Then Jāmbavān spoke to that best of the Raghus regarding the story.
This Rāmāyaṇa is not composed by you; rather, it is considered to have been fashioned by me.
Listen, O God, as I shall relate its entirety in detail, for it was heard by me in the past from the son of Paṅkeruha (Brahmā). 12.
Having addressed Jāmbavanta, Rāmacandra spoke these words:
Śrī Rāma said: "Proclaim the Purāṇa to me; desiring to hear it out of curiosity, I ask by whom it was composed and by whom it has been understood."
Then Jāmbavān spoke: "Salutations, salutations to the Creator, and likewise to Viṣṇu, who is adorned by the moon.
Now, I shall relate the ancient Rāmāyaṇa, by the hearing of which the destruction of all sins committed throughout one's entire life is brought about.

Nevertheless, Daśaratha, possessing a chariot equal to that of Daśaratha [Indra] and a superior force, desiring to conquer the city named Sumānasana, summoned Vasiṣṭha, the son of the Lotus-born [Brahmā]. Having paid his respects and received the sage’s permission, he mounted a horse whose body was like the moon and, filled with great wrath, set out on a military expedition after propitiating Viṣṭaraśravas (Viṣṇu) with an army of one hundred akṣauhiṇīs. One named Sādhya, surrounded by his own army, came toward Daśaratha to fight, and a battle took place between them.
After fighting for one month, Daśaratha captured that Sādhya.
Then Sādhyasūnu, named Bhūṣaṇa, with a small retinue, fought against Daśaratha.
Daśaratha, too, upon beholding Sādhyasūnu, who was an ornament of the earth, did not even wish to fight him. [He thought:
"How can I kill such a one? And if he is killed, how will his father fare? How will his mother? And what of his beloved wife, who is in the prime of her youth?"
Upon his body, marks like fresh petals of lotuses—seen from embracing, kissing, and turning about—are visible.

(24) "A son of similar complexion and age, so handsome and a great increaser of joy, has been eaten by a bear and is dead; yet even as he comes to my path of memory, he seems to wish to protect me, changing my heart. Having thus reflected in her mind, she began to take up the very young child.
(25) And though he was one who could be mastered, he became dependent on another. (26)
Together with Prince Cakrī, he dwelt in happiness, disregarding even the weariness caused by his defeat. 27.
Daśaratha also, having remained there for some time and beholding the joy of seeing his son, reflected: 28.

"Aha! This gazing upon his face, which is capable of dispelling all suffering, is indeed called 'the nurturing of a son. For me, this victory over the entire kingdom results only in sorrow as I remember my separation from my son. 29.
Therefore, I shall ask him: "How is such a son born?"—thus reflecting, he questioned him. Sādhya also instructed the lord of the earth in the entire path to liberation.

Having fasted on all the Ekādaśīs that are to be honored by Hari, Īśāna, and Soma, and having gratified the Brāhmaṇas on the Dvādaśīs; having righteously procured food, side-dishes, flowers, and fruit appropriate to each respective time; having bathed Keśava with the ghee of a tawny cow (kapilā); having smeared him with powdered green gram (mudga-cūrṇa); having bathed him with sweet water; and having personally rubbed fragrant sandalwood paste, musk, or aloe-wood essence upon the entire body of the Lord, [one should worship Him] with Tulasī leaves, Yūthikā, Karavīra, Nīlotpala, Kamala, Kokanada, and Droṇa...

Having worshipped [the deity] with *na-kusuma*, *maruva*, *damana*, *girikarṇikā*, *ketakī* petals, and so forth, as available—with either the twelve-syllable mantra, the *Puruṣasūkta*, or the deity’s name—having propitiated him with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), having prostrated and performed a dance, one should ask the God for forgiveness. (32) Likewise, one should perform various vows (*vrata*) for the pleasure of Nārāyaṇa.
(33) "The blessed sage, being pleased, will grant you a desired son; therefore, worship him," he said to Daśaratha. (34)
Even though the object to be accomplished was located there, he went to Ayodhyā and performed everything accordingly.

(35) Then, when the Putra-kāmeṣṭi sacrifice was completed, the embodiment of the sacrifice, bearing a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, arose from the Āhavanīya fire and said to the king, "Choose a boon. (36)

The king requested, "Grant me four sons who are exceedingly righteous, long-lived, and benefactors of the world. (37) Then the four queens—Kauśalyā, Sumitrā, Surūpā, and Suveṣā—spoke to the king: "O Lord, it should be so that there is but one son for each of us. (38–39)
Then Kauśalyā said: "If the Lord is pleased with me, then let this [son] be born to me. (40) The King said:
"If it is my own desire, then Hari is being entreated for this."

"O Viṣṇu, be gracious! O Lord of gods, O Consort of Kamalā, O Wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, O Terrifying One, O Eternal Hari, whose pair of feet are worshipped by the entire creation, the world-protectors, and others—salutations to you, salutations to you! Thus praised, the Blessed One then spoke to the king.
Mādhava said:
"I shall become your son through Kauśalyā."
Then Hari entered the sacrificial porridge (caru); having divided that caru into four parts, he gave them to his wives.
Then Rāma was born of Kauśalyā, Lakṣmaṇa of Sumitrā, Bharata of Surūpā, and Śatrughna of Suveṣā; and a rain of flowers fell from the sky.
Then the Four-faced One (Brahmā) himself approached and performed the birth-rites and other ceremonies for him.

Because he was the delight of the three worlds, he gave him the name Rāma; because he possessed the excellence of beauty, valor, and other virtues, he gave the other [son] the name Lakṣmaṇa; and because he would rescue the earth from its burden, he named him Bharata, and because he would slay his enemies, Śatrughna. Having thus given these names, Brahmā returned to his own abode, and the infants attained growth.
Then, as he began to walk on his feet like the young moon...

His face was like a mirror; his lower lip was like a bimba fruit; his nose was as prominent as a sesame flower; a jeweled leaf-ornament hung from the crest of his head; earrings dangled and swayed upon his ears; a thick pearl necklace trembled against his chest; he wore many glistening golden armlets; his wrists resounded with jeweled bracelets and gem-studded rings; a girdle fashioned of gold and gems encircled his hips; his feet were adorned with tinkling anklets; the spaces between his toes were beautified by toe-rings; the soles of his broad feet were graced with the auspicious marks of the thunderbolt, the goad, and the lotus; and his calves were like quivers.

King Daśaratha, seeing Rāma—the youth whose thighs were like the trunk of an elephant, with broad hips, a slender waist, and rounded, whorled limbs; whose deep navel was like a sapphire stone, whose chest was as expansive as a slab of indranīla, and who possessed a conch-like neck and a face resembling the orb of the moon; whose forehead was like a half-moon, and whose dark, curly hair was dusted pale by the pollen clinging to his breast; whose restless eyes were as red as the petals of a blooming lotus; who resembled Maheśvara covered in sacred ash, and like Maheśvara himself, was naked—King Daśaratha, his heart overflowing with joy, embraced his son, kissed him, and pressed him firmly to his chest. 46.
Then the prince also, having placed him on his lap by his side and his eyes filled with affection, said something or other;
looking here and there for those who were begging, he cried out, "Father, go! O Father, let us play! and so forth. Experiencing the joy of fatherhood again and again, he attained great contentment.

Then once, when King Nṛga had come to eat, Rāmacandra, his heart intent on childhood play and holding many toys in his lotus-like hands, jumped and ran about. Having caught with his left hand some food from a golden vessel set with jewels that stood before the king, he threw it at the king.
The king considered this also to be a source of unhappiness;
Rāmacandra performed other such deeds as well.
(49) Then, once while Rāma was playing, Vātyārāma caused him to fall, and Rāma fell down weeping. (50)
In the meantime, a Brahma-rākṣasa seized Rāma, and Rāma fell into a swoon.
Then his young companion, crying out here and there, informed the king that Rāma was in such a state.
Thereupon, the king took Rāma and said to Vasiṣṭha, asking, "What is this with Rāma?"
Then Vasiṣṭha, taking some ashes and consecrating them with mantras, liberated the Brahmarākṣasa.

[Vasiṣṭha] asked, "Who are you? and he replied, "I am a Brāhmaṇa who was arrogant because of my Vedic learning; having repeatedly stolen the wealth of others, I have become a Brahmarākṣasa. Consider a means for my atonement. Vasiṣṭha said:

"Now, beyond this, you shall experience the state of a *rākṣasa* for one hundred years and suffer in hell; however, by bathing once in the Bhāgīrathī and offering a hundred *bilva* leaves to Śiva, you will then be bathed and liberated from sin.

(56) "Perhaps, having performed such merit, you may attain my own station; thereafter, you shall enjoy a superior destiny"—having heard these words of Vasiṣṭha, the *brahmarākṣasa*, through the power of the merit instructed by Vasiṣṭha, assumed a divine body, offered his salutations, and departed for heaven. (57)

Then, when the time had arrived, Vasiṣṭha initiated Rāma and taught him the Vedas along with their six auxiliary limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), as well as the two systems of Mīmāṃsā and the science of polity (nītiśāstra).

Next, he taught him the science of archery (dhanurveda), the science of medicine (āyurveda), and various treatises on the arts of Bharata, music (gāndharva), architecture (vāstu), augury (śākuna), and warfare.
Then, King Daśaratha, desiring to arrange his son’s marriage, dispatched messengers to the lords of various regions.

Then, someone arriving quickly spoke thus to the king: "O King, there is a king named Videha, the lord of the Vidarbha country; he has a daughter, Vaidehī, who was obtained through a fire-sacrifice. She is equal to Lakṣmī in beauty, endowed with all auspicious marks, and worthy of Rāma. That king is intent on giving her to Rāma; therefore, let us go there quickly."

Then he dispatched Vasiṣṭha and the others; they went there, and having observed her, determined an auspicious moment, and returned to Ayodhyā. Having informed the King, they set out together with Rāma and the Lord of the Earth. They traveled swiftly by means of various elephants, horses, carts, palanquins, and swing-cots, accompanied by Gandharvas who were highly skilled in the arts of beautiful form, sensual enjoyment, and amorous play, well-versed in diverse gestures and extremely proficient in the science of love—women whose necks were pressed against their soft, firm, and full breasts.

They possessed broad, delicate foreheads, lips like the bimba fruit, and lotus-like faces; their hair was gathered into long, curly braids, and they wore golden leaf-ornaments on their ears. Their teeth were as red as *japā* flowers, beautified by the bristling of body hair that arose from the act of bathing. Their eyes were clear and shimmering like saphari fish, and their ears resembled oyster shells. Their nostrils were adorned with large pearls like stars, their cheeks were like mirrors, and their noses were like sesame blossoms. Their nipples were situated at the center of their sunken waists, O Indra.

Their lower lips were marked by the bites of teeth resembling those of a cowherd; their limbs were long and displayed with evenness, and all parts of their bodies were rounded. Their lumps of flesh were not overly fleshy, yet possessed knots and folds at the base of the arms; because the hair had grown for not very long, it was yellowish like turmeric.

In terms of their complexion, they had armpits resembling the petals of the *karṇikāra* flower; their waist regions were soft, smooth, rounded, and slender; their chests were adorned with various necklaces made of gems dangling over breasts that were firm, thick, rounded, with deeply set nipples, which vied with one another to occupy each other's space; and because these [necklaces] found their place all around the breasts, they were gazed upon by a continuous succession of youthful eyes.

Her abdominal region was adorned with a line of hair above an uneven navel, while her waist—its middle part appearing as if it were being pinched—was graced by three folds; her hips were like the trunk of an elephant; her thighs were smooth, soft, glossy, stainless, and hairless, resembling the trunks of plantain trees; her shanks were slender, without prominent kneecaps or round protuberances, and her ankles were not protruding; her feet possessed long, delicate, and smooth toes, and she moved with the gait of a swan or an elephant, summoning the God of Love with the tinkling sound of her anklets.

Women came repeatedly to perform the auspicious marriage rites, their slender bodies adorned as they touched the tips of their hair with their right thumbs; having arranged their lower garments (nīvī) over their hips, they left the region of their breasts uncovered by both hands, while the other part of their dress covered the rest of their bodies; with the hem of their garment draped over their left shoulder, it reached down to their right side and was tucked into the waistband at the navel, thus gracing their forms. 63.

Young girls, their slender bodies illuminated by the rays of lightning, their chests adorned with various necklaces upon budding lotus-like breasts, speaking only a few words and moving with an exceedingly swift and gentle gait, as well as elderly women, were coming forth. 64.

Now, in Videha, at a distance of only one *krośa* ahead, there was a mango grove where the ears of forest deer were fixed upon hearing the warbling of various birds amidst regions of spreading branches; its grounds were adorned with high and low palaces fashioned from great silver; it contained various birds and rows of trees graced by throngs of matted-haired sages whose bodies were smeared with ashes and clothed in golden bark-garments, intent on meditation and worship; and it possessed lakes with rippling waves stirred by the weight of the breasts of various Vidyādhara women.

On the banks of that lake, where young men were being summoned by young women—the *sairandhrīs*—who had gathered there; where every region was perfumed with the fragrance of flowers of various colors; where courtesans with bodies radiant with luster moved about here and there, their eyes flickering like large fish due to their desire for pleasure; and which was filled with manifold wonders, Daśaratha dwelt happily together with his ministers, his family priest, and his beloved sons, Rāma and the others.

Then the King of Videha also entered Mithilā—a city adorned with various banners; graced with diverse palaces, gate-towers, gardens, and temples; thronged by young women clever in their mutual sports; its streets beautified by people enjoying water-sports at great drinking-stalls fashioned from *uśīra* grass;

its roads lined with various wares; its monasteries resounding here and there with the chanting of the Vedas (*brahmaghoṣa*); and where in every house the study of the *Mīmāṃsā* commentaries and the *Sāman* chants was flourishing.

It was adorned by attendants who had acquired their fine garments, betel, and red lips through entering and departing from the dwellings of many lords—where the sounds of the *sāman* chants, the fragrance of most meritorious sacrificial offerings, and the recitation of the *padakrama*, *śruti*, and *brāhmaṇa* texts resounded; it was graced by those wearing the attire of *adhvaryu* priests with agallochum and saffron, and by women whose soft speech, harsh words, hand gestures, and firm replies were accompanied by the bringing of various gifts; and it was further beautified by the central region of their breasts, which were smooth, round, and pressing against one another, visible above the white, soft garments draped over their hips.

He beautified that city, which was adorned with the left shoulder of Aśobhita and graced by Vainateya; whose lips were like a string of various pearls and the *japā* flower and who wore a gentle smile; which was a temple for the preparation of meritorious wine; which had various archways here and there and pure streets; where wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*) were planted in various places and the gates were decorated with celestial nymphs (*raṃbhā*). 66.

Then, for the purpose of the auspicious procession (*abhikalanā*), the king went forth accompanied by women and other beautiful people. The women bore auspicious substances—clarified butter, *guggulu* resin, fruits, and so forth—contained in golden vessels; these were intended as offerings of good fortune for their faces, noses, and various ornaments, which were adorned with diverse decorations. Their hair was braided and fashioned into matted locks (*jaṭā*) at the ends, secured with *niśā*, *dūrvā* grass, unhusked rice, mantras, and auspicious collyrium (*kajjala*). Their foreheads were graced by these braids, and they wore various head-ornaments. At that time, the sounds of auspicious musical instruments arose—the resonance of divine drums (*dundubhi*), kettledrums (*bherī*), *niḥsāṇa*, *mardala*, and conch shells—and the singers sang auspicious songs.

The Vedic Brahmins, reciting auspicious Vedic mantras, and the family preceptors, filling the entire sky with the sound of kettledrums, [proceeded]. Then, accepting one another’s greetings with parched grain (akṣata), they entered the city while being praised by bards, panegyrists, and others. 70-71.
Daśaratha entered the palace constructed on the western side of the city of Videha;
the others entered their respective dwellings as was appropriate. Then, at that very moment, Nārada arrived in Mithilā.
Videha, having honored the celestial sage and seeing that he had arrived, provided him with food;
once the sage was comfortably seated, he gave him betel-leaf with camphor and addressed him:
"Since the wedding is tomorrow, you ought to remain here to preside over the marriage ceremony."
Nārada said:

"Tomorrow is the asterism of Śvina, the same as that of the sun; therefore, the marriage should not be performed then. (77-78) Then the king, having summoned the astrologer Vṛddhagārgya, asked: "When is the auspicious moment for the marriage? (79)
Śvaitigārgya said: 80. Then the king, looking at Nārada and Gārgya, asked, "O sirs, what is this, and how is it? 81. Thereupon, Nārada spoke to Gārgya. 82.
"How can you say, 'I will give the lagna'?
(83) Then Gārgya said, "Setting aside the poisonous hours (*viṣaghaṭikā*), I shall give the lagna.
(84) Nārada also said to Gārgya, "Do you not know the words of Brahmā? (85)
Gārgya, being pleased, recited those defects:
"The meteor, the staff of Brahmā, the futile [missile], and likewise trembling—these were indeed seen by Brahmā in the past for the destruction of all undertakings. (86-87)
In the consecration of temples, marriages, the tying of the sacred thread (mauñjībandha), royal inaugurations,
and all other undertakings, one should avoid the poison-veins (viṣanāḍī). Beyond this, by performing such tasks, one incurs no fault.
Therefore, I shall now describe the defects regarding rites such as marriage:

a meteor (ulkā) would burn the entire family; the staff of Brahmā (brahmadaṇḍa) would cause destruction; a futile thunderbolt (mogha-astra) leads to death; and an earthquake portends the failure of the undertaking. 89–90.
Having heard these words spoken by Nārada, the sage Gārgya became intent on observing a vow of silence.
He reflected: "Let the marriage be performed, setting aside the planet Jupiter and the poisonous *nāḍīs*.
Nārada said:
How is the word of Brahmā [to be understood]? 93.
The Sun said: "The rule has been declared according to the distinction of regions; therefore, in this region, the marriage must indeed be performed, excluding the 'poison-hour' (viṣaghaṭikā). 94.
Nārada also consented and said: "Tomorrow afternoon the Kṣatriya wedding shall take place; therefore, let the kings come for the svayaṃvara. Send out the king's messengers for that purpose.
Then, with the approval of King Daśaratha, [Vasiṣṭha] summoned all the kings and reflected.
"How could she have gone to Rāma, completely disregarding all the princesses of Videha?
Thus, sighing repeatedly during that night, he was unable to find sleep, though he longed for it.

Then, in the middle of the night, the king, having purified himself, beheld the Three-Eyed Lord with Ambikā, clad in auspicious silken garments, whose lotus feet were served by all the gods headed by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra; by the foremost sages headed by Bhṛgu; by the Gandharvas headed by Hāhā and Tumburu; by the personified Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇas; by the hosts of Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and Mātṛkās; and by the Gaṇas headed by Nandin—the deliverer from all inauspiciousness, who was being bathed by the stainless Gaṅgā with its exceedingly meritorious waters.

His head was adorned with a crescent moon; he was smiling as the Daughter of the Mountain, seated upon his left lap, offered him betel-leaf; he gazed at her with amorous and affectionate looks; his body was white like cow’s milk, while his throat was dark like musk; his matted hair was fashioned into a crown-lock, soft, fine, and glossy; his cheeks were beautified by earrings of pure gold; he appeared sixteen years of age, and his head was wrapped in a cloth the color of saffron, adorned with large pearls as white as cow’s milk.

He beheld him whose chest was adorned with gold fashioned from various jewels, whose body was graced by an exceedingly white sacred thread (*upavīta*), and whose fragrant form was reddened by the saffron clinging to Ambikā; he saw him as one who seemed to be threatening the arrows of Kāma and resembled ten million gods of love (*kaṃdarpa*). Thus he meditated in his mind.
(99) He recited the *Śatarudriya*, offered oblations to Kāma with that very mantra, and praised him with the *Puruṣasūkta*.
(100) Then, Maheśvara appeared there in exactly such a form. (101)
Then, having paid homage to the King, he praised him.
The King said:

"O Eight-formed One (*aṣṭamūrti*), whose forms are earth, water, sky, wind, fire, sun, moon, and the sacrificial priest; O Universal Form, Form of the World, Form of the Three Worlds, Form of the Vedas and Purāṇas, Form of Sacrifice, Form of Hymns, Form of the Scriptures, Form of the *Svadha* offering, Form of Nārāyaṇa, Form of all Deities! O You who consist of the Triple Veda (*trayīmaya*), whose authority is the Triple Veda, whose eyes are the Triple Veda, who are dear to the Sāman-chanters, who are fond of the earth, fond of devotion, easily accessible to devotees, fond of the praises of those far from worldly ties, fond of incense, fond of lamps, fond of ghee and milk, and fond of the *drona* tree..."

Salutations to You, who are fond of the *nakara*, *vīra*, *priya*, *śrīpatra*, *priyaka*, *kamala*, *kahlāra*, *naṃdyāvarta*, *bakula*, *yūthikā*, *kokanada* flowers; who are fond of dwelling in water during the summer; who are fond of self-restraint (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*); who are fond of those with controlled senses; who are fond of recitation (*japa*), ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), singing, the *gāyatrī* mantra, and the five *brahmans*; who are fond of virtuous conduct; whose lotus feet are worshipped by the eyes of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva; who grant victory; who were requested by Hari (Viṣṇu) and manifested the discus from the waters; who bestow memory and reasoning; who grant auspiciousness when remembered; and who are the conqueror of death (*mṛtyuñjaya*). Salutations to You! Salutations to You! 103.

Having heard this hymn of praise, the Lord Bhava, the bestower of boons, said to the king: "Choose a boon. The king said: "O Illustrious One, my daughter Vaidehī was intended to be given to Rāma at the svayaṃvara. In that assembly of all living beings—including kings, rākṣasas, brahmins, and others—endowed with lineage, beauty, strength, and prowess, if one who possessed greater strength than Rāma had taken her, then my word would have become false and I would have incurred sin."

On the contrary, even Daśaratha is capable of conquering all those who have arrived; yet Rāma, the destroyer of the kṣatriyas, if he were to come, what would he do with my daughter, or whom would he send, or what kind of thing would he cause to be made for me, or what would he do to me? For that king possesses abundant forces and vehicles and could destroy even the entire three worlds, let alone this woman of little strength. What more need be said? You alone are my refuge; tell me a means so that there will be welfare at the wedding and Rāma shall become my son-in-law. (106) Śambhu also said, "I shall do so," and [declared] that Rāma alone shall be the lord of Sītā. (107)
"Having performed the auspicious rites for Rāma, I shall do so this very day; take up this bow, Ājagava.
The King said:
"What is the use of this Ājagava bow? At the svayaṃvara, let Sītā obtain Rāma."
Śaṅkara said: "To whoever shall string this bow of mine, which is currently unstrung, I shall give Sītā; act according to this promise. (110)
Having spoken thus, Lord Hara vanished along with his attendants;
then the king was unable to take up the bow despite his greatest efforts.
Then, having summoned a brilliant force of a hundred thousand elephants, he said, "Take it! 111–112.
Even after bowing to his maternal uncle and letting out a loud laugh, he leaped up and seized the bow with both hands down to the knee;
meanwhile, Mārīca, the maternal uncle, having heard this, assumed the guise of a Brahmin alone and begged for the body of Viśvāmitra, saying:
"Know me to be a guest who has arrived at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice. (113)
The king said, "Welcome, O Brahmin! Here is a seat; please sit upon it. (114) Having replied, "So be it," that guest sat down. (115)
Then the king, having taken water and washed his feet, worshipped him with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains; having offered a great animal to him, he requested him for a meal.
And he, while gazing at that food endowed with the six flavors contained in a golden vessel, looked here and there.

At that very moment, Sītā appeared, adorned with garments slightly reddened like the filaments of a lotus; her forehead graced by dark, curling locks of hair that moved as they drew the minds of young men, as if showing women’s hearts to be thus broken by the gaze of a lover; her face further beautified by a bow-like brow, eyes as red as lotus petals, a nose like a sesame flower, soft, smooth, and hairy cheeks, lips as red as a ruby seat or a pomegranate, and a lower lip as lovely as a hibiscus flower.

With ears like those of a conch, long necks, and very fleshy chests; with full, budding breasts adorned by many necklaces, possessing beautiful forms; with lovely, long, and symmetrical fingers whose tips were like red lotus petals, adorned with various many-jeweled finger-ornaments; with waists graspable by a fist, deep navels marked by a line of hair, broad hips, thighs like elephant trunks, shanks like quivers, and lotus-feet adorned with anklets and other ornaments; and wearing blooming fragrant flowers—these women approached the front of the one who was enjoying the company of Mārīca. 118.
Seeing her, he thought, "How shall I abduct her? How shall I embrace her? What else shall I do? Finding no such opportunity, he departed in silence.
(119) Then, as the gods were striving to string their bows in a competitive race for precedence, each seeking to outdo the other, Mahendra was unable to bend his supreme bow beyond its two ends.
(120) Then Sūrya, having taken up his bow, fell down while even attempting to bend it. (121)
Vāyu is the best among the powerful; he seized the Ājagava bow with his own hand and, lifting it upward, let it fall down, while the bow itself fell upon Vāyu, and everyone then laughed. 122.
In the meantime, the thousand-armed Bāṇāsura, mounted upon his excellent horse and surrounded by Daityas of many various heads, arrived at the city of Videha together with Prahlāda. 123.

Then, illuminating the quarters of the sky with the splendor of his own ornaments and making the gods shameless by his own brilliance, he listened to various kinds of songs and stopped [the bow] at a distance of only two finger-breadths. 124.
Prahlāda and Bali both ran forward and then stopped.
(125) Then, when the Rākṣasas had become silent, the exceedingly powerful kings who had assembled, being unable to bind the sacrificial ghee, withdrew and stood aside.
(126) Then the Brāhmaṇas assembled. (127)

Then Viśvāmitra, having taken up the bow and strung it so that it was bent by only a single finger’s breadth, desisted; and the others also turned back. (128) Then, when the day had passed and the bow remained silent, Rāghava, accompanied by his younger brothers, arrived, and having gazed at the bow, he touched it. (129)
Then hundreds of princes assembled;
though adorned with all their ornaments, they merely touched the bow upon seeing it, for they were not capable of moving it.
Then the princes, headed by the son of Daśaratha, arrived.
Alternatively, those with *vetra* staffs and *jharjhara* drums in their hands approached and drove everyone away.
Then Rāma, adorned with all his ornaments, took Lakṣmaṇa by the hand, approached the bow, touched it, bowed to it, circumambulated it, and taking up the bow, drew it back.
At the moment of its being drawn, everyone exclaimed with laughter, "The great chariot-warriors have been broken here!"
Then Rāma, having lowered the position of the bowstring and placed his knee upon the bow, while drawing it with one hand, bent it at the tip.
Then, seeing that the bow was strung, everyone stood with their fingers placed upon the tips of their noses.
Rāma also caused the string to resound.
By that sound, the minds of all were agitated (137).
The report arose everywhere that the bow had been strung by Rāma (138).
Janaka also gave Sītā to Rāma; having fought with the kings and defeated them, he returned to his own city (139).

Then, on one occasion, after Daśaratha had consecrated Rāma as the heir apparent (*yauvarājya*), he became happy; and because he delighted all his subjects, there arose a public proclamation among all the people that "King Rāma is approved by [the will of] the King.

(140) Now, the daughter of the lord of the Kaikeya country, who was poorly dressed and unable to endure King Rāma, said to the King, "This is the occasion for granting my boon. The King reflected, "What should be given?
(141) The Queen said:

Rāma entered the forest for fourteen years, while Bharata protected the kingdom. 142 The King, out of fear of the fault of speaking an untruth, accepted [the situation] with great difficulty. 143 Then, having reflected on what might happen to him as Rāma was departing for the forest, Vasiṣṭha spoke to Bhavitā regarding the auspicious and inauspicious [outcomes].
"Speak!
Vasiṣṭha, having reflected with joy, said to the king:
"Having gone to the forest, the slayer of all the heroic Dānavas performs various kinds of worship of Śambhu."
Enraged by the separation from Sītā, Rāma crossed the ocean with an army of monkeys and slew the ten-faced Rāvaṇa.
Having returned, the joy of the Raghus ruled his kingdom for many years;
possessing celebrated fame throughout the entire world, he dwelt there for a long time together with Lord Śiva.

"Endowed with a virtuous son, performing many sacrifices, a sovereign, and pre-eminent in all qualities"—having heard these words of Vasiṣṭha, Daśaratha, recollecting the virtues of Rāma, spoke thus: "Death would be better for me than the departure of Rāma. Then Rāma, having paid obeisance to his mother, his father, his guru Vasiṣṭha, and the wives of his father, departed for the forest.

Then, having stayed for one day in the grove, he had his matted locks fashioned, donned bark garments, and put on a single sacred thread (*upavīta*). Having purified his teeth with one [twig], he tied his matted hair with that same thread; his entire body was smeared with ashes, his frame made rugged by the ash-powder, and he wore upon his chest a rosary of *rudrākṣa* beads interspersed with strings of pearls and gems as ornaments. Adorned with few decorations, accompanied by Sītā and followed by Lakṣmaṇa, he entered the interior of the forest. 151.

Then, having slain many rākṣasas there as you had done in Bhava’s forest, and having performed everything from the abduction of Sītā onwards exactly as it occurred, Rāma went with Lakṣmaṇa to Sugrīva’s hermitage on Mount Ṛṣyamūka; reaching a mango tree with dense shade, he prepared a shelter.

Having mounted his bow upon a tree, with his head resting on the lap of the seated Lakṣmaṇa, reclining on a bed of tiger-skin, and listening to the song of a woman whose limbs were visible, he observed a single monkey. The monkey was adorned with jeweled earrings, was tawny as gold, wore a firmly tied loin-cloth of muñja grass and a clean sacred thread, and was exceedingly restless. Taking fruit, he tossed it to himself; he scattered clusters of flowers and mimicked the singing. As he climbed a branch, he fanned Rāma with a fan and likewise fanned him while perched there. Seeing the monkey carrying only mango fruits, Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa: "Lakṣmaṇa, who is this monkey? (152–153)
Lakṣmaṇa also did not know him and spoke;
then Rāma, having summoned him, asked, "Who are you? What is your name? (154) And he replied, "I am Hanumān, [the servant] of Sugrīva. (155)

Having bowed to Rāma and approached Sugrīva, he saw another person like the divine Nārāyaṇa—a youth, dark as a rain-cloud, with matted hair and arms reaching to his knees, exceedingly illustrious, who sat there together with another man resplendent like the sun.
(156) Then, seeing those two princes endowed with all auspicious marks seated beneath the shade of a tree, he was told by them, "Inform Sugrīva," and so you have informed me.
(157) Thereupon Sugrīva rose quickly, took flowers, water, and other articles, performed the washing of their feet and other rites, offered fruits, and made this request: (158)
Hearing Sugrīva’s words, “O princes, for what purpose have you two ascetics come here? Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa:
“We two are the sons of Daśaratha, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa; we have come to the forest for the sake of subduing the wicked and protecting the virtuous.
Then Sugrīva said, “It appears that there is some service or injury to be done by you two.”
Lakṣmaṇa said: "They will arrive accompanied by an army; however, there is another matter at hand.

It is not known by whom his wife has been abducted, so we have come here to search for her. That alone is our primary task; everything else is incidental. For that purpose, we shall cross the ocean, even enter the netherworld (pātāla), conquer the bow of Śiva (nāka), topple Mahendra, slay Bala, and accomplish whatever else may be required. (162)

Sugrīva said, "I have collected some ornaments that were dropped by a certain woman who was being carried away by Rāvaṇa; she came here while being abducted and left them behind. Having spoken thus, he led Rāma to his residence and showed them to him.
(163) Rāma, having examined them and reached a certainty, wept and asked, "Where has that Rāvaṇa gone? and he replied, "He has gone toward the southern direction. (164)
Then Rāma formed a friendship with him and asked, "For what reason do you remain here deprived of your wife?
Sugrīva replied:

"My brother Vālin, having seized my wife and my kingdom, dwells in Kiṣkindhā; I have been defeated by him in battle. Therefore, I am entirely preoccupied with his slaughter so that he may be slain by you. Once I have bridged the ocean and reached Laṅkā on the opposite shore, I shall restore to you Sītā, who was abducted by Rāvaṇa. Having spoken thus and made this solemn oath, Sugrīva fought with Vālin, who was exceedingly powerful, when challenged to combat. (166) Rāma, however, did not slay Vālin immediately due to uncertainty.
(167) Then Sugrīva, having fled, spoke this to Rāma: (168)
"Without knowing your mind, I have set out for my own death.
(169) "Rāma too, because he did not know the distinction between you two, remained silent; therefore, look at me marked with the sign and kill me.
(170) Then Sugrīva, having made the mark, challenged Vālin to battle and stood his ground. (171)
Tārā spoke to Vālin:

"Sugrīva appears as if he has allies; otherwise, he would not have challenged you in this way. I have realized that Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, the sons of Daśaratha and portions of Nārāyaṇa, have arrived together to remove the burden of the earth, and they have become his allies.
Vālin said:

"I have heard that Rāma is possessed of statesmanship; such a person does not abandon the strong to resort to the weak. Let Rāma come here; having accepted our challenge, that hero will surely fear nothing. If Rāma himself comes for battle, then we must fight. Having addressed Tārā in this manner and prepared for combat, Sugrīva set out for the fray. (174) Then, a fist-fight ensued between them. (175)
Rāma also struck Vālin; 176.
And Vālin fell from the chariot in that weaponless combat, his entire body becoming drenched in blood from the impact of the arrows. 177.
Then Tārā and Aṅgada, having arrived, became deeply distressed. 178.
Then the monkeys, having arrived, fell down near the foot of the banyan tree and wept.
Then Tārā spoke to Rāma: "O Raghava, you who are skilled in the scriptures, heroic, and righteous—how could you have committed such a sinful act against Rāma in the past?
You do not know the duty of the stars (nakṣatra-dharma), which is served by the hosts of kings."

When two people fight each other in battle, victory may belong to one or death may come; if one of them kills the other, he is declared a slayer of a Brahmin. (182) Did you kill Vālin out of enmity, or was it out of a desire for monkey flesh? (183)

If you consider monkey flesh to be unfit for consumption because it is unpleasant to yourself and lacks pleasure, and thus think the same applies to others—alas, what delusion is this that you have undertaken this vow of a single wife in order to seize me? 184.

If it was indeed necessary to bring back Sītā, who had been abducted by Rāvaṇa, with Sugrīva as an ally, then why was such a great difference made? By the exceedingly powerful Vālin, who increased his strength through virtue, who was capable of bringing back Sītā from within the solar orbit, and who was able to remember and counter the gifts of Rāvaṇa, the task would have been accomplished for his own purpose with an army of fifty parārdhas of monkeys and bears. Why then was the task accomplished by the monkey Sugrīva, who possesses little prowess and commands an army of only seven parārdhas?
"Aha! It is understood; all is well with the gods, since you have been addressed thus. 185–186.

The messenger said: "O Lord of the Earth, the suppression of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous must be carried out by me. Vālin seized Sugrīva’s wife Ruma and his kingdom; therefore, there is no fault in killing such a person. Tārā said:

"Sugrīva too ought to be killed. While Vālin was engaged in battle with Dundubhi and had entered his cave, Sugrīva lived there for a year. During that interval, he abducted me and took over the kingdom. He should be killed first, and only afterwards [Vālin]."
Rāma said: "Tell me, how long ago did this happen?
Tārā said:
Sixty thousand years ago, in the eightieth year, Sugrīva was deprived of his kingdom during a battle with the Rākṣasas (190).
Furthermore, when Vālin returned after an interval of years, Sugrīva fled (191);
his wife and his kingdom were both seized by him (192).
On that very day, there was the consecration of your father, Daśaratha.
Rāghava said:
"By my father's command, I have carried out the suppression of the wicked within the kingdom."

Because the word of a guru must not be transgressed, at the time of his abduction, you were seated upon the royal throne (194). Alternatively, wild animals are independent; Vālin was killed by a hunter, and there is no loathsomeness in wild animals tearing one another apart (195). Since this is my hunting, or rather, [the behavior] of wild animals...

"For those who were moving, stationary, or bound; for those who were fleeing, wandering, or retreating—I have pursued them without restraint and abandoned the hunt as prescribed by the treatises on hunting. 196. "This hunt was conducted by me according to the rules of the science of hunting."
Through seeing and not seeing, and likewise through pursuing and not pursuing,
the supreme state of those characterized by sattva is distinguished from that of kings whose dharma consists of hunting and the consumption of meat. (197–198)
Then, having heard Rāma’s words, they all shook their heads;
Vālī, placing his joined palms upon his head, spoke to Rāma: "Salutations to you, O Rāma! Listen to my words.
[I am] the teacher of the world, with conch, discus, and mace in hand, clad in yellow garments."
"I have heard that you are Nārāyaṇa himself, manifest in person. Yogis meditate upon you, and sacrificers worship you;
you alone consume the offerings to gods and ancestors, assuming the forms of both the Pitṛs and the Devas. (201-202)
"For one like you who contemplates death, liberation is not far off; you have attained my sight, O Rāma, and my sins are destroyed.
O descendant of Kakutstha, take this arrow; I am greatly tormented. 203–204.
Then Rāma, saying "So be it," took up the arrow and said to Vālin, "Tell me what you desire; let it be given.
The monkey said:
"If the Blessed One is pleased with me, grant me a good rebirth."
"This Sugrīva, as well as Aṅgada and Tārā, must be protected by me; thus, having committed this offense as a sinner, I have experienced its fruit.
(207) Then, even while looking at Rāma, Vālī went to heaven.
(208) Thereafter, having consecrated Sugrīva in the kingdom, he himself entered the forest. (209)
Then, having gone near the ocean with that companion, Rāma asked Sugrīva, "Where is Laṅkā? Where is Sītā? And where is the enemy?

(210) Then Hanumān said, "Having entered Laṅkā and searched for Sītā, and having understood the full truth of the matter, we must decide whether to wage war or make peace. Therefore, may your lordship give some instruction regarding the crossing of that ocean.
(211) Then Rāma spoke to Sugrīva.
"How is this possible? [the king asked].
The monkey replied:
"I have tens of millions of followers, headed by monkeys and bears. (212-213)
"Having appointed one person and having considered everything, it should be done accordingly.
Then Jāmbavān said:
"Let Hanumān go alone; let him discover Laṅkā."

Then Hanumān went to the city of Laṅkā; having searched for Sītā and found her seated in the Aśoka grove, he conversed with her, gained her confidence, and destroyed the grove as well as the forest guards.
Having been bound by the Rākṣasa, he burnt Laṅkā, went to the northern shore, saw Rāma, related the news, and remained silent.
Then Rāma deliberated with everyone; Jāmbavān said, "Nārada told me that Laṅkā would be destroyed by the monkeys on behalf of Rāma."
Then, one must remain resolute in the effort to cross the ocean.
Then Rāma, having propitiated Śaṅkara and reported everything, said, "I shall do as you have instructed," and after worshipping Śiva and bowing down, he made this request.

O Mahādeva, who devours the great elements; O Great Rudra, the cause of the great dissolution; O Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord adorned with great serpents, whose sacred thread is a serpent, whose garment is an elephant hide, who is adorned with a garland of skulls including the head of Brahmā, who is decorated with ornaments of human bones, who is smeared with ashes, who is dear to the supreme Nārāyaṇa, whose conduct is auspicious, who is the five-faced lion among the gods beginning with the Five Brahmas, who is known through the four Vedas, who is easily accessible to devotees yet difficult for non-devotees to attain, who is supreme bliss and consciousness, who is capable of felling the teeth of Pūṣan and severing the head of Dakṣa.
O beloved of Pārvatī, who took the fifth head of Brahmā; O Śarva, three-eyed one, whose auspicious deeds are sung by Nārada.

Salutations, salutations to you, O wielder of the trident, who holds the *pināka* bow in hand, the one with matted hair, the bearer of manifold forms, whose vehicle is the bull, who resembles pure crystal, the four-armed one, the Lord of diverse weapons, Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the Lord of gods, Īśvara, the bearer of the Gaṅgā, the destroyer of Tripura, the dweller on Śrīśaila, the Lord of Kāśī, Kedāreśvara, Bhūṣaṇasiddheśvara, Gokarṇeśvara, Kanakhaleśvara, Parvateśvara, the giver of the discus, the destroyer of Bāṇa and Ciṃtāpāda, the remover of Mura, the one whose lotus feet are worshipped, the one adorned by the moon, the omniscient one, the embodiment of light, and the soul of the universe. 221.
As Rāma was thus offering praise, a form composed of radiant light appeared before him amidst the circle of attendants.

Then Rāma beheld the Lord, who grants fearlessness, seated upon a lotus throne with Umā resting on his lap; he was adorned with all ornaments, wore a beautiful crown, and the touch of the daughter of the Himalayas was felt at his waist. With his two hands, he bestowed the gestures of fearlessness and boons; he was full of splendor, pervading many directions with his shimmering radiance, possessing a smiling face and a gracious countenance. 222–223.
Having bowed to the Supreme Lord with palms joined in reverence, he then prostrated himself like a staff.
224 Then the Supreme Lord said to Rāma, "Choose a boon; I am the giver of boons.
225 Rāma said:
"I shall go to Laṅkā; O Śambhu, grant me a single means for crossing the ocean.
Śambhu said:
"I have a bow, the Ājagava, which at that time becomes formless and free from conceptual construction."
"Having ascended that [chariot] and crossed the ocean, obtain Laṅkā.
Rama, having resolved "So be it," called to mind the Ājagava bow. Then the bow arrived, and Rāma worshipped it.
Then, taking up his bow, he gave it to Rāma;
Rāma, for his part, cast it into the ocean.
All the monkeys, as well as Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, climbed [onto it]; and when sixty parārdhas of those innumerable monkeys had mounted the bow, it proceeded at great speed.
Then the monkeys went to the bank of the Dhanuṣkoṭi and surveyed it. (233) Then a Rākṣasa named Atikāya, having observed the monkey army, reported it to Rāvaṇa.
(234) Rāvaṇa also said, "What is the use of these monkeys, those mere tree-dwellers? What is the use of the two humans, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa? A great feast has arrived by fate! (235)

Then Sugriva, accompanied by Hanuman, Jambavat, and other mighty ones of immense stature, went to the side of Lanka with countless great forces trailing behind him like the sun. Having entered the grove, they ate various fruits and drank water; then, having put the Rākṣasa guardians of the grove to flight, they seized the entire forest one by one and rushed toward the city of Lanka. Reaching the gateway of the city, some climbed the palace and, having shattered it, took pillars one by one and fought with the Rākṣasas.
Some broke down the halls and reduced the houses to powder; they slaughtered everyone—children, the elderly, women, and all others alike.
Then, perceiving that one rampart had been conquered, Rāvaṇa commanded Indrajit.
Having engaged in battle with Indrajit, the monkeys became terrified and fled.

Then Hanumān, realizing that everyone had gone out and knowing Rāvaṇa’s intention, summoned the monkeys, rebuked them, formed a great army, and having assumed the form of the Ten-faced one, he caused him joy.
Then, while still in the air, the monkeys beheld Indrajit with Jāmbavān.
(241) Then Hanumān and Jāmbavān, leaping up into the sky, struck Indrajit from both mountain peaks.
(242) Then he fell to the ground, and Lakṣmaṇa dispatched him to the realm of Yama. (243)

Then Atikāya and Mahākāya, having slaughtered much of the monkey army, afflicted Lakṣmaṇa, fought with Rāma, and defeated Sugrīva, engaged in combat with Hanumān and Jāmbavān. Having been vanquished, those two warriors were seized and taken before Rāma, where they informed him of their deeds. Rāma addressed Atikāya:
"Tell me of the battle with Rāvaṇa, and of the other ministers who are a source of great fear."
Atikāya said:

"This was certainly decided by us long ago: having divided the army into sections, a rākṣasa named Vidyunmālī, who is of great strength and a versatile warrior, fights alone against all the monkeys—fighting whether they are seen or unseen.
Other powerful and great warriors, skilled in weapons, have arrived; we two shall fight with you two, while Rāvaṇa, mounting the Puṣpaka chariot, will slay you from the other side."
Other Rākṣasas, headed by Kumbhakarṇa, will assume their own forms, surround and seize you, show you to Sītā, and kill you right there in her presence.
Rāma said: "Alas! What is impossible for the powerful? Such is the crooked course of destiny. Sugrīva, being extremely irascible, looked at Rāma with anger and spoke.

"These two should be executed," [said Rāvaṇa]. "They are not to be executed; they are to be released," Rāma said. "Bring their garments and ornaments. As soon as this was said, Hanumān brought them, and Rāma gave them to the two.
"Having bowed down, this wooden five-faced [statue] which is seen at the gate of Laṅkā was described by Śuka: 'By this being cut, Rāvaṇa shall be slain.'"
Furthermore, the instruction spoken by Bhārgava was inscribed [on the bow]: "Immediately upon the cutting of the wood, you must go to Pātāla.
(254) Therefore, cut this wood into five pieces with a single effort and a single discharge of an arrow; then, having ascertained your power, we shall engage in a most firm battle.

(255) Then, understanding the words of Bhārgava, Rāma made the bow ready by merely touching its upper end, fixed an arrow upon it, and discharged that arrow while making it heard by the two Rākṣasas and Hanūmat. (256)

As the two Rākṣasas watched the path of the arrow discharged from Bāṇa’s bow, they saw it cut into five pieces by Dāru-bāṇa; they then informed Rāma, "Our two children must be protected by you," and Rāma replied, "So be it. The two Rākṣasas then entered Laṅkā. (257) Then the monkeys, having gone to engage in a battle against the rampart, covered the entire wall on all sides with their heels, feet, knees, hands, and backs, making it level with the ground; they then proceeded to the second rampart. At that time, Rāvaṇa arrived and, having driven them all away with his arrows, pursued them and went toward Rāma. (258)
Then he pierced Rāma with five arrows (259);
then Rāma made Āvaṇa wounded with ten arrows (260).
A most terrible battle took place between these two (261).
Rāvaṇa pierced him with ten arrows;
then, his body wounded by Rāma’s shafts, the Rākṣasa became intent on flight. The monkeys and Lakṣmaṇa slaughtered crores upon crores of Rākṣasas.
Then, on the following day, Vibhīṣaṇa, having reflected, said this to Rāvaṇa:
"This is the time for the third expedient; do not consider the fourth.
The fourth is contrary and is not praised for one who seeks to accomplish his purpose."
Having ascertained the strength of the enemy and knowing one's own power to be superior, then war would be commendable; otherwise, it leads to destruction.
(267) You are weak, and there can be no war for you with the mighty Rāma.
In the past, you recognized him as the slayer of Ekeṣu and Vālin; even you fled from Mārīca with a single arrow. The heroic Rākṣasas were slain, and Indrajit, his son, was killed.
"Your three boons have been broken; therefore, either engage in battle with me, or else, having surrendered Sītā, attain the state of a slave.
Likewise, [strike] the wooden five-faced [statue] standing at the city gate with an arrow."
"He will cut it into five pieces; by that means, Rāma will kill you.
For your sake, many have perished, and others shall perish as well. O brother, there is but one path to happiness, and not folly. (271-272)
Having honored your wife— who is human, subject to death, unwilling, and devoted to her husband— even though she belongs to a powerful man, release her;
for from union with one who is unwilling, there will arise a succession of miseries.

Association with women is loathsome, being joined with foul odors and impurities. (274) If detachment has arisen, then engaging in such improper conduct leads to suffering; if passion persists, it leads to death and thereafter to hell. (275)
"O dear one, my own death would be in vain upon her union today;
otherwise, there would be either the abandonment or the death of my lawful wife.
Such things and other similar misfortunes will come to pass. (276)
I shall tell you another word that is dear and beneficial to all:

having gone into the presence of Rāma, having bowed and praised him, and having made this request to the descendant of Raghu—"Forgive me, O Rāma, great hero, you who are compassionate toward those who seek refuge. (277–278)
"All of us Rākṣasas are of a tamasic nature and are great sinners;
setting aside the fault born of abducting Sītā, consider us as your sons.
O Rāma, we are dependent on you; protect us or kill us as you wish."
"Having spoken thus, we stood before that descendant of Raghu, saying:
'O Ten-faced One, we shall have long lives and a stable kingdom.
Then Rāvaṇa spoke these words: 'Ah! Are you not a Rākṣasa?'"
You are no hero, nor do you understand the eternal duty of kings,
because of your pursuit of another's wife, another's wealth, and another's kingdom.
The supreme dharma belongs to heroes, not to eunuchs such as yourself.
"O King, if you desire peace, you should go forth embracing the enemy's side.

(283) Then Vibhīṣaṇa, having gone to his residence and approached Rāma, sought refuge with him. (284) Then Rāvaṇa departed from the city; Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and the monkeys fought, and the Rākṣasas also fought. (285)

Then Rāma, unable to slay the immensely powerful Rāvaṇa, looked toward the face of Vibhīṣaṇa; having identified him by the signs and marks described by him, he pierced him with an arrow and killed him.
(286) Then Kumbhakarṇa, seizing a great mace and accomplishing everything, devoured numerous monkeys and struck the head of Rāma with his mace.
(287) Then Rāma struck him with hundreds of sharp arrows, and Kumbhakarṇa died. (288)

Then, having caused Vibhīṣaṇa to perform the funeral rites (*śrāddha*) for Rāvaṇa and the others, and having had a temple of Śiva built in his name, he consecrated Vibhīṣaṇa himself in the sovereignty of Laṅkā. Having caused Sītā—who was purified by her entry into the fire—to bow before Umā and Maheśvara, and having been granted all immortality, strength, and longevity by Purahara (Śiva), he mounted the excellent Puṣpaka chariot, crossed the ocean, and stationed his army on the shore of the sea. Having performed the installation of Śiva there, he returned to Ayodhyā, honored by sages and gods. 289

Then, accompanied by Bharata and others, and honored by the citizens, Vasiṣṭha, and the sages, he went to his own home. Having honored Indra and the other gods who had come in person with seats and other offerings, and having fully worshipped the monkeys, he unbraided his matted locks and was consecrated in the kingdom. Delighted by the slaying of Rāvaṇa, the gods said to Rāma: "We have been established in our own kingdoms by you; protect us always. You are the primordial Lord Nārāyaṇa, descended for the sake of subduing all the wicked; having slain Rāvaṇa along with his kinsmen, you are the protector of the three worlds. May you be happy together with Śrī. Having spoken thus, they departed for heaven.
Then the inhabitants of Ayodhyā, filled with joy, said to Rāma:
"Having slain the enemies, you have returned; having seen [the truth], you have indeed attained auspiciousness. By good fortune you shine, O Rāma; by good fortune you protect the subjects."
"Yajñas will be performed by you; through you, dharma shall increase"—
having heard these words of the citizens, the lotus-eyed Rāma then honored all the townspeople with garments and other gifts.
Having honored him with all the people, the righteous-souled sage said to the sages:
"Is your austerity flourishing? Is your sacrifice well-performed? Are you devoted to your own wives? And is the Lord worshipped? (296-297)
"Are their wives blessed with good offspring? Is everything exceedingly well? 298.
The sages said:
"O King of the Kakutsthas, all is well for the ascetics under your rule."
"O King, let us go from here to that place; what do you think? (299) Rāma said:
"He with whom the Brahmins are pleased, with him Śambhu is pleased."
"Whomever Īśāna is pleased with, for him there shall be prosperity.
(300) Having performed that [rite], you ought to come here immediately after taking food.
Saying "So be it," the hosts of sages took excellent food. (301)
Having honored him with blessings, they departed for their respective homes filled with joy;
Rāma too, exceedingly pleased along with his wife and younger brother, ruled the kingdom without any thorns, beloved by all the people. 302.
Whoever, even if they be a sinner, hears this narrative,
shall be liberated from all sins and attain the Supreme Brahman;
and that man who remembers this shall never fall into an evil state of existence.
And whoever should proclaim this which has been thus uttered [to him]—305.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Rāmāyaṇa from a Previous Kalpa," in the Śiva-Rāghava Saṃvāda of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter One Hundred and Seventeen.
Sūta said:
Having eaten at the house of Bhāradvāja, Rāmacandra, his mind full of joy, was accompanied by the lord of sages (Brahmā), Viṣṇu, and the monkeys and bears. 1.
When the sky was thus covered by clouds and a gentle breeze was blowing,
there appeared in a certain part of that forest an excellent and divine palace (2),
provided with pillars of gold and fashioned with golden fillets.
It was joined with jewels and pearls, provided with silver jars,
made fragrant with sandalwood, camphor, musk, and saffron, covered with mud, provided with lattices, and enclosed above by stone slabs.
The entire floor within the house was illuminated by the moonlight of the moon, which surpassed the sun, and was adorned with moon-flowers sprinkled with nectar; likewise,
the northern direction was entirely devoid of any constructed walls.
At every pillar, there were painted figures of birds fashioned from crystal; its courtyard measured a hundred cubits and was likewise fashioned from crystal;
and within that courtyard stood the great Pārijāta tree, casting a shade even greater than that of the house itself.
There was a dense plantain grove, completely enveloped,
joined with a plantain forest and surrounded by a grove of ketaki trees;
it was filled with the cries of peacocks and the sweet humming of bees.
Resounding with the calls of flocks of pigeons, adorned with various groves, crowded with hundreds of palaces, echoing with the songs of intoxicated cuckoos,
and featuring many trees beautified by great jewels hanging from their branches.
The excellent bank of the Gautamī, filled with the sounds of the songs of kinnara women filling the quarters of the sky, beautiful with many groves,
and the meritorious home of Bhāradvāja, which is frequented by infinite virtues. 11.
The auspicious house of Bhāradvāja was filled with hundreds of male and female servants resembling Rati and Kandarpa, and was equipped with various implements; within it stood a palatial mansion,
and inside that were garden courtyards.
In the midst of those eight, there was one house that was most magnificent,
adorned with the palaces and temples of Mahādeva in the four directions.
Each temple was beautifully graced by three archways (toraṇas) of dark stone.
It was fashioned solely for the repose of the excellent women dwelling in heaven.
Then, departing from the house of Bhāradvāja with his entire retinue, Rāma went to that very man's great mansion situated in the middle of the forest. 15–16.
Then he entered [the hall], where a single lion-throne was situated in the center, covered with a woolen blanket and provided with separate cloth seats; likewise,
many seats for sages were present, as well as the incomparable seat of the Purāṇic scholar and the excellent seat of the king’s tiger and bear.
Then, having first seated the Paurāṇika, followed by Vasiṣṭha and the foremost of sages,
as well as Nārāyaṇa and the lords of the earth and the monkeys on lower seats, he himself took his place;
the sky was covered with clouds, the quarters were serene, and the surface of the earth was strewn with beautiful flowers like sown seeds.

Then, having beheld Śambhu—whose courtyard was neither hot nor cold, who possessed flowers that were eternal and a fragrance that moved through the air—Rāma spoke these words: "O best of sages, I have not yet reached satiety while listening to this narrative of Maheśa, which destroys the multitude of sins. Please recount the stories of Śaṅkara."
Or what did Maheśvara do at the hermitage of Gautama, surrounded by the hosts of gods?
Śiva said:
Having taken up his great lute (vipaṃcī) and settled there, that son of Vāyu questioned Śiva.
O Lord, tell me, what kind of fruit would there be from worshipping the All-pervading One with wealth earned through righteous means, as opposed to that born of improper conduct?

(22) Furthermore, O Śambhu, tell me quickly the answer to each of these questions: what is the fruit when offerings are made through theft, or when the offering consists of goods obtained by extortion? Speak at once! (23)
Then Īśvara spoke to the monkey: "I shall tell you everything; listen with concentration.
O Gautama, by worshipping Sadāśiva with wealth acquired through righteous means, he indeed attained this sovereignty.
Long ago, there was a twice-born man named Akatha, the son of Maṅkaṇa, who approached an excellent and virtuous woman."
Draḍhidra alone was endowed with compassion; he ate on the sixth day and avoided meat. Having fasted for five days, he was about to eat when a mendicant arrived.
The mendicant then spoke sweetly: "How is it that you, who observe a month-long fast, have come here to eat? (25-26)

"O Sage, stay here; if you wish to eat, I shall provide for you, for I have no hunger to eat at another's house. He replied: "O best of the twice-born, there is no eating for me for five days; on the sixth day, my meal has arrived. 27.
"Then, the effect of that disease need not be considered; I shall wash your feet here.
Saying "Om," the yogi then washed his pair of feet and desired to take his meal.
He ate that food—which had been prepared and cooked with clarified butter—from the leaves of a plantain tree.
Then, with great care, he served him forest-grown foods, leaving not even a morsel of food remaining.
(29) Then, seeing that the sage was well-pleased, the ascetic, together with his wife, was filled with joy;
and having eaten, that mendicant Ākatha, his mind contented, then performed his recitation of prayers. (30)
The sage, who was a virtuous man living like a pigeon and whose wife was covered by the sun’s heat,
then placed that Śiva, the Lord of Umā, upon a pedestal along with his attendants, and having worshipped the Liṅga, he sat down.
Then, while gazing at the Liṅga, he beheld a twice-born man of unknown identity and emaciated form.

Then he saw his master approaching his home— naked, footless, one-eyed, and with a withered arm and no ears— yet exuding fragrance and having mastered many scriptures. Then Akatha spoke these words to his beautiful wife:
"Indeed, this Brahmin with a distorted appearance is approaching.

(35) Half of the food should be given to him, and half should be kept for protection; otherwise, when this sixth day has passed, it is my conviction that your life will not endure due to the lack of food—what do you think? Speak.
(36) She, Śobhanā, said:
"What is written on the forehead by destiny does not perish midway.

He replied, "For example, even the head of Yajña, though his life was firmly bound, was severed by Vīrabhadra—how much more so for embodied beings who are sinful? Therefore, you may enjoy him after setting him aside; however, if I were to give food to him..."
"Whatever I must do shall be according to your wish.
(38) How can I eat when you have not eaten? What was eaten by me previously? Listen to this other [reason]:
food is indeed the life-breath of all embodied beings; it is evident to everyone. (39)
Therefore, he who bestows food is declared to be a giver of life.
Since all beings are born from food and indeed grow through it,
there is no gift superior to food that yields such great fruit.
If one should give away their life—which is as transient as a drop of water clinging to the tip of a trembling leaf of the holy fig tree—then that person's birth is useless.
For dharma alone is the companion in the next world; wife, sons, and kinsmen are not.
Wife, son, father, and kinsmen do not follow one as long as life lasts; wealth, youth, and friends remain only here in this world.
O best among the upholders of dharma, you alone enjoy that dharma which is beneficial both here and in the hereafter—what else is there for us two? 43-44.
Having heard these words of his wife, Ākatha, a treasury of compassion, gave him powerful food without any hesitation, saying: "This is the god Śaṅkara himself, who has arrived in various guises. 45.
Having thus resolved in his mind, he washed her limbs—which destroy all sin—beginning from the feet up to the knees;
then the lower shanks, and below that, the ankles; thereafter, he caused the twice-born one to sip water for purification.
Then Akatha led the sage, whose joints were aching, to the courtyard of his house;
having released the sage's stiff joints, he seated him upon a provided seat. After honoring him properly, Akatha fed the sage a full meal.
In the meantime, a certain madman arrived at the house;
seizing the joint of a pillar, he dragged it outside the house,
then set that house on fire and beat the husband and wife as well.
Though reviled and beaten, the brahmin then entered his burning house in order to quickly retrieve the Lord Īśāna.
Then, having taken Maheśāna, whose worship had been consumed by fire, that best of the twice-born—
Having gone out and seen that very distress on his face,
and having observed the burnt offering and his own scorched body as well,
the righteous-souled one spoke to his wife regarding the worship of the Great Lord exactly as it had been performed.
"In that way, you must perform the worship with all your limbs without hesitation.
Vyaṅgī said:
"Even if performed later, your worship shall become fruitful. (54)
"Just as people offer such things for the burning of other substances,
so too let this worship be performed for his burning. Thus spoke Ākaṭha.
"Even with wealth acquired through theft, worshipping Him would be beneficial;
however, O Brahmin, worship of Śambhu performed with ill-gotten gains does not bestow auspiciousness.
Having said this, he immediately began to burn his own body.
Then, having seized that burnt Linga, the madman vanished in an instant.
Thereupon, Hara became deformed and restrained him, saying, "O Brahmin, why do you grieve? I am the granter of boons; choose a boon. 57-58.
Ākaṭha also chose unwavering devotion at the feet of the Lord.
Sūta said:
Having heard this story, Rāma, surrounded by the sages, was greatly delighted.

Having paid homage to Bhāradvāja, he requested permission for his departure. (60) Then the sage Bharadvāja, being pleased, bowed to Śambhu, Vasiṣṭha—the bull among sages—as well as Nārāyaṇa and the hosts of seers, and dismissed them; they too departed after bowing down. (61)
The residents of Naimiṣa said:
Having gone to Ayodhyā accompanied by all the sages, what did the highly effulgent Rāma do thereafter, and what did that illustrious Śambhu do?
Sūta said:
On the following day, Rāghava, desiring to perform the monthly śrāddha for Kausalyā, invited the most eminent brahmins who were like ṛṣis.
Then Rāma, devoted to the vow of eating only once a day, slept upon the ground strewn with grass, his senses undisturbed, after having paid homage to Śambhu, Nārada, Romaśa, Bhṛgu, Viśvāmitra,
and likewise to Ekabhaktavratin.
Then, when the next day had arrived, he who was knowledgeable in the ritual rules bathed in the morning and caused pure food,
such as vegetables and the like,
as well as various wonderful foods, including those to be sucked and so forth, to be prepared by his servants.
He prepared thirty-eight kinds of foods such as *vaṭaka* cakes and others,
six varieties of milk-rice (*pāyasa*), two hundred kinds of cooked vegetables,
and three hundred kinds of raw, mixed, and cooked dishes.
Having had vegetables such as *kālaśāka*, various fruits, roots,
tubers,
and bark prepared, Rāghava went to the river together with his brother and the family priest.
Having bathed in the waters of the Sarayū, offered oblations into the fire, and welcomed the twice-born,
the king, having performed the worship of the gods, greeted them with a welcome; then,
having restrained his breath and made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), he granted them the opportunity for their meal.
Rāma invited Romaśa and Nārada for the Vaiśvadeva rite;
he then invited Śambhu, Bhṛgu, and Kauśika for the Mātṛ-sthāna rite.
Having then prepared a mandala with cow dung, he worshipped those worthy ones.

He washed their feet with water he had brought and, having caused those brahmins to sip water for purification, was then preparing to go home when an elderly man of deformed appearance arrived as a guest.
Emaciated, with trembling limbs and quivering feet and head (74),
afflicted by labored breathing, coughing, and the like, with sagging skin,
with cheeks moistened by rheum, and with a beard smeared with saliva; (75)
He said to King Rāma, "I am a single brahmin standing here;
food must also be given to me, for I am old and emaciated.
Having heard those words, Rāma spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa.
"I shall wash the feet of the brahmin and honor him. But the guest spoke these words to me with agitation:
"If your feet have not been washed, I do not wish to eat. (77–78)
"O Brahmins, what is it to you that I am superior, such that you disregard me?
You do not know the dharma of the Śrāddha, which is practiced by hosts of great sages. By insulting me, you insult all Brahmins. (79)
"Furthermore, your ancestral rites (śrāddha) will be obstructed, and you shall go to hell.
Then Rāma himself washed the feet of the brahmin; having offered him water for sipping (ācamana), he then led him into the house.
Then Rāma himself, having sipped water for purification, offered a seat;
and when the brahmins were seated, he restrained his vital breath (prāṇa).
Then, having obtained permission to perform his duties, he [offered] water along with sesame seeds.
One should scatter [the grains] at the doorway with the mantra "Apahatā" (83);
likewise, one should scatter them on the place for the ancestral vessels with the mantra "Udīratām";
and one should scatter unbroken rice and water on the place for the divine vessels with the Gāyatrī mantra.
Having likewise sprinkled that which has been cooked, one should utter this mantra:

"Having meditated upon the sacrificial ground as Gayā, having meditated again and again upon the Lord Janārdana, and having meditated upon the ancestors beginning with the Vasus, one should then proceed with the śrāddha. (84–85)
One should perform the worship of the Viśvedevas with barley or rice; having taken darbha grass joined at the roots and tips along with unbroken grains (akṣata),
one should offer water into the hand of a twice-born man while the right knee touches the ground.
"O Purūravas, O Ārdravāṇas, this is the seat for the Viśvedevas.
(87) Having thus offered them a seat, the giver of the śrāddha should request a moment’s pause.
(88) Then, having performed the *arghya* offering, he should [place it] upon kuśa grass with its tips pointing north.
Then, having turned the vessel face down and placed a knot of kuśa grass upon it,
he should turn it face up again, sprinkle it with water from golden vessels,
and pour water into the vessel— which is covered by a purifier— reciting the verse "śaṃ no devī."

All ritual acts, as far as they are enjoined by the rules, belong to the Vaiśvadeva; one should then place barley grains into the vessel with the mantra, "O barley, you are the king of grains. Thereafter, one should offer water-pots mixed with honey, along with fragrances and flowers.
Having said, "O twice-born one, let there be arghya," and then saying, "Let there be arghya," from the north;
having asked, "Shall I invoke these deities? and having received the answer thereto;
and having recited, "viśvedevāsaḥ... (RV 1.2.2), he should cast kuśa grass upon the head of the Brahmin.
One should mutter the mantra: "O Viśvedevas, hear this; may you come.
Then, once they have arrived and are seated, one should take a vessel containing Darbha grass and, having poured the water from that principal vessel onto their right foot, [proceed]. 94.

Then, while the *pavitra* grass-blades with tips pointing eastward rest in the right hand of the Brahmin, he should pour water from the vessel into it with the mantra "yā divyāḥ" (95). Having said, "This water is for the *argha*," he should then place the *argha* water to the north (96).

Having taken the water for the removal of evil (aghatoya) in that vessel, one should place that vessel somewhere. Then, having poured water into the hand, one should worship them with barley grains. Having asked, "Worship! Worship!", one should then [proceed] from the north.

Having worshipped [the deity] from the feet up to the head and offered water, he should then say "So be it" with the mantra *gandhadvārām*. Then, standing to the north, he should perform the worship of the ancestors in the same manner, but with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*). 98–99.

Having made the twice-born person wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder (upavīta), and having placed broken kuśa grass mixed with sesame seeds upon his left knee on the ground, one should then offer him a seat.
Then, facing the south, one should ask for his readiness to receive the guest.
One should place three vessels face-down upon Darbha grass with their tips pointing south (verse 101).
Then, one should arrange them face-up, joined with knots of triple Kuśa grass;
thereafter, having sprinkled water over the vessels along with the Pavitra grass and sesame seeds (verse 102).
Having poured water with the *śaṃ no devī* mantra, one should scatter sesame seeds with the *tilo 'si* mantra;
then, having offered fragrance and flowers, one asks, "Svadhā-argha? (103). Having been answered, "Let there be svadhā-argha," one should then invoke the ancestors (*pitṛs*).
Standing with sesame seeds, flowers, and *kuśa* grass, he should prepare the *argha* offering;
with the mantra "uśantas tvā," he should offer the *argha* water three times.
At that time, their worship should be performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), as before. 104–105.

Having washed the vessel, one should provide a golden one for the gods and a silver one for the ancestors, or whatever is available; in their absence, however, bell-metal is excellent, provided it has not been used by another.
In the absence of those [earlier-mentioned] vessels, those made of *pālāśa* leaves are middling;
