likewise, those of *rambhā*, mango leaves, *jambū*, *puṃnāga*, *parāka*, *campaka*, *madhūka*, and *kuṭaja*. 107–108.
The leaves of the mātuluṅga fruit should indeed be offered by men at the śrāddha;
furthermore, the food should be served with a ladle, and the clarified butter (ājya) with both hands.
Then, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta), he should ask the twice-born for permission to place it [on the fire].
"I shall perform the offering into the fire"; "Do so," he replies.

(110) Having served the food, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (upavītī), and having sprinkled it with clarified butter, he should collect [the portions] and offer them while uttering: "To Soma accompanied by the ancestors, svadhā namaḥ. (111)

Having offered the second oblation with the mantra, "To Yama, to Aṅgiras, to Pitṛmat; svadhā! Namas! and having sprinkled it with clarified butter, he should then offer the unbroken rice grain (akṣata) with the words, "To Agni Kavyavāhana; svadhā! Namas! thereafter.
Having offered the oblation and performed the rite with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), he should serve the food and approach the twice-born guests.
Then, using the stirring-spoon (mekṣaṇa), he should repeatedly pour [the ghee] into the vessel for the ancestors.
After that comes the vessel for the funeral cakes (piṇḍa), the remnants, and finally the washing of the ladle (darvī).
Then, having placed the stirring-spoon into the fire, one should arrange the vessels;
immediately thereafter, one should place food on the right side of the vessels, providing all kinds of eatables, foods, and vegetables. 115.
Then the guest, a very old man, looking here and there, spoke to Rāghava: "Offer salutations immediately;
hunger is afflicting us, and we shall eat at your command. (116-117)
Rāma spoke these words: "O Sage, wait for a moment;
the gods and the ancestors are now being honored by me.
Having said this, Rāghava then gave the food contained in the vessel.

In the rite for the gods, one should place *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing eastward and northward; in the rite for the ancestors, the tips should point westward and southward. Then, for the sake of purification, they offer *darbha* grass, barley, and sesame seeds, while making the offering of food with the mantra beginning "pṛthivī" (Earth).
Having touched [the food] with his thumb while reciting "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," he should first give it to the gods while reciting "ye devāḥ";
thereafter, he should give to the ancestors, and then he should give to the guest.
Having uttered the names of the deities beginning with "Aitīmukha," one should give the *āpośana* water.
Having recited the Gāyatrī mantra three times while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītī*) and facing east,
one should thereafter recite the "Three Honey" verses (*madhutraya*) while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*).

Having said to them, "Eat," while the twice-born were eating, he had them recite mantras that destroy demons as he caused various kinds of food and drink to be served. In the meantime, a certain Brahmin guest arrived there. 124. Just so.
He performed a great marvel; I shall describe it briefly:
he swallowed everything contained in the vessel with a single mouthful and said, "Let enough be given for the offerings of the vital breaths. 125–126.
"If you are unable to give even this much, how can you be intent on performing the *śrāddha* rite?
O Rāma, if you are incapable of giving to me alone, why exert yourself in vain? O Rāma, why do you strive in vain to provide food for many?"
Those who perform actions impulsively do not reach completion.
What you have done is sufficient for all of them; it is not enough for my offering of life-breaths. Tell me, how can there be enjoyment for me, and how for them? (128–129)
The heroic Rāma said to him, "Eat as you please," and having spoken thus, he observed his most wonderful deed. Then, summoning Śambhu, he said, "You serve the food."
"It is my conviction that you are the father and the goddess Śivā is the mother;
it is my conviction that the goddess Annapūrṇeśvarī is indeed Bhavānī. To her, she who belongs to Śambhu replied: "That is sufficient; I shall grant it."
Then, taking a golden vessel filled with food and adorned,
and holding a golden ladle, he offered the fragrant and lustrous milk-rice (pāyasa),
saying, "May this be inexhaustible for him."
With joy, she respectfully placed it into the right hand of the twice-born man;
shaking his head and gazing upwards, he then extended his hand and took the milk-rice from the vessel.
"Let this deliciously cooked milk-rice be given; what is this?
Śambhu’s wife said to him, "Eat it from my hand," and then she gave it to him. Then the Brahmin ate that which remained in her palm.
Then, knowing that it was inexhaustible, she extended her other hand;
indeed, the virtuous lady placed the milk-rice upon that palm and gave the cooked food, which remained imperishable, to the other brahmins as well. 137–138.
Then, perceiving that there was inexhaustible milk-rice in his two hands, the virtuous brahmin extended his other hand and said, "Excellent food should be given, along with soup and ghee. (139)
Likewise, Śivādevī, the beloved of Śambhu, bestowed that which was inexhaustible;
whatever that virtuous woman gave at that time, all of it became imperishable.
Then, yet another hand was created, and again and again it was filled to completion.
Having performed a thousand such acts, he desisted;
the brahmin spoke these words: "O auspicious lady, I have been gratified by you with mouthfuls of water, as I was never before by Nara, Nami, or Sītā. (142)
Śambhu said:
"That which was given by Rāma and Sītā has indeed been given by me as well; tell me, what more remains to be given? Is it complete? 143
The twice-born said:
"I am satisfied with this; no more should be given. O learned one, that which has already come into my hand can by no means be taken back. (144)
Seated there, he reflected for a long time: "How is it that all this has been done by me alone? This entire act was performed for my own enjoyment, not for the sake of any other karma.
Therefore, because it was created by another [selfish motive], all of this will become void."
Having thus resolved in his mind, he smeared his limbs and became a guest;
while all the gods looked on, it was as if a miracle had occurred.
Then Rāghava, the knower of the supreme truth, perceiving that the twice-born were satisfied— (146–147)
Having asked according to the prescribed rite, "Are you satisfied?",
and having been told by the lords of brahmins, "We are satisfied," he should scatter the food with mantras and offer the *piṇḍa* near the vessel while facing the south.
He should provide mouthfuls of water for the Brahmins right there.
They performed the rinsing of their mouths using the leaf-plates that had held their leftovers; meanwhile, those Brahmins entered the interior of the house without even waiting for a guest.
"O Lord of the Twice-born, the guest must be sent outside by me;
O Raghava, I am unable to rise, for my hand is paralyzed.
Then Rama gave him his hand, yet that best of the twice-born did not rise.
Then Hanumān also offered his powerful hand;
but seizing the eminent brahmin with his other hand, the lord of monkeys pulled him along, while the brahmin cried out in protest. 152–153.
The twice-born said: "One pillar is clearly being cut; therefore, lift up another from elsewhere," he said, covering that pillar along with its base up to its head with his tail. 154.
Then the twice-born man ran toward him from that spot, yet he did not move;
or rather, the heroic monkey tore up the earth with his feet, and planting them firmly, he struck the head of the twice-born man.
The house fell into ruin, and likewise all the twice-born men were outside;
then Hanumān, together with the elderly twice-born man, went outside and placed the aged, emaciated Brāhmaṇa upon a seat. 156–157.
Taking water for the twice-born in an earthen pot, Jāmbavān said: "O Brahmin, you must provide clear water along with a vessel;
Sītā shall wash her limbs, and Lakṣmaṇa shall be the giver of the water. (158)

Jāmbavān related to Rāma everything that had been told by the brāhmaṇa. Then, at the brāhmaṇa’s request, Rāma commanded his younger brother to wash his beloved; accordingly, Saumitri took water for the purpose of washing the brāhmaṇa’s body.
He washed every limb [of Sītā], as if she were the statue of a king;
then, by Rāma’s instruction, they both performed the rite in that very same manner.
Then the guest released his own mouthful of water into Sītā’s mouth.
Then that virtuous woman washed [the vessel] with water mixed with ornaments;
she thoroughly cleansed the Brahmin’s mouth, which was filled with abundant phlegm and saliva, and having washed it again, she wiped it until the nasal mucus was entirely removed.
Having offered water for rinsing the mouth, the son of Sumitrā said to the twice-born, "Arise.
The twice-born replied, "It is not possible. Then Hanumān arrived; the guest, that brahmin, said to him, "I am being tormented by Hanumān."
Having been seized and lifted up by the monkey, or even cast down, Jāmbavān then said to him: "O Brahmin, my body-hair is soft;
you are being held by me, and no pain shall occur."
Having spoken thus, Ajaṃbava took hold of the brahmin with both arms and lifted him up;
then, taking the edge of the twice-born one's garment, he established that sage [in his place].
Then Rāma performed a circumambulation of the lords of the twice-born.
Even after the lords of serpents had offered their blessings and presented betel-leaf before him, Rāma, along with his brothers, placed his feet in their hands and said:
"O Sītā, this guest's body has not been washed by you. (168–169)
The twice-born man thoroughly washed the pair of legs of the guest, which were free from dirt, and his own face, which was covered in grime; for a brahmin cannot endure impurity.
Sītā said: [170]
"Now that it has come out properly after being washed, Rāma said again:
'Wash it once more; otherwise, there would be a fault for me. (171)
Then Sītā, having done so, remained silent.
And the twice-born one, filled with supreme rage, seized both Sītā and Rāma;
O Indra among kings, he intended to seize those two feet of theirs by which Sītā had been supported.
May Bhavānī grant me my seed;
may Bharata be the one who combs the mass of my hair;
and may Śatrughna wipe away my phlegm with his own garment. 173–174.
Sūta said:
Then those brahmins, monkeys, and rākṣasas performed for the guest everything exactly as it had been described, and they were filled with great wonder. 175

Śivādevī and Śambhu gazed upon him with a knitting of their brows, and they both spoke to the guest mentally; indeed, Śambhu was that very guest. And the guest, bearing the conch, discus, and mace, became gracious.
Clad in yellow garments, adorned on all his limbs, and exceedingly radiant;
he who was formerly propitiated as Śambhu became pleased— the three-eyed one,
resembling pure crystal and decorated with every ornament.
Resembling ten million suns, wearing a crown, and a treasure-house of compassion,
Sadāśiva took hold of the hand of the wielder of the discus and stood there;
Rāma, whose soul was supremely righteous, his body covered with horripilation.
Falling prostrate upon the earth like a staff, his eyes overflowing with joy, he bowed down;
his brothers likewise stood upon the ground prostrate like staffs.
Śiva raised the descendant of Kakutstha, embraced him, and smelled the crown of his head.
Śiva spoke these sweet words to the lotus-eyed Rāma:
"Choose a boon; I am pleased, [a boon] difficult even for Brahmā and others to obtain. (182)
"There is nothing whatsoever that you cannot give; choose [a boon] from me without delay.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Lord of the Universe, I have no request at present; my kingdom is already mine. (183)
Heaven was attained through ritual acts, but devotion arose from the sight of your feet;
O Sītā, best among women, behold my health and prosperity as I enjoy this day, having brought all kings under my control and my subjects endowed with righteousness. (184)
O Acyuta, having attained such joy from your arrival, I nevertheless choose this one boon:
let my devotion toward you be firm, and likewise, O Lord, O God, please stay in my house for three years. (185-186)
O Śaṅkara, as you speak of all these dharmas through this form, Śiva said: "So be it; O Rāma, everything shall come to pass for you exactly as you have said. (187)
Then the discus-king spoke to Rāma, the lotus-eyed one:
"O illustrious one, I am pleased; choose a boon, for that which you desire is mine.
Śrī Rāma said: "There is indeed nothing for me to request."
"Whatever portion was to be obtained from Śambhu has now been received; everything else has been declared.
Furthermore, O Viṣṇu, choose one boon, and may you always remain gracious.
Then Hari, being pleased, said to Sītā: "I have now slain [the demon] and am gratified. 189–190.
"Choose a boon; I shall grant it. Then Sītā said this: "A boon was already chosen by my husband long ago, and no other boon is to be chosen.
If you would grant me a wish, [grant that] my mind never turns toward another man."
"Your meal has been prepared; salutations to you, O lord of the twice-born!
(192) Then all those sages bowed down to the two supreme deities.
Thereupon, he said to Rāghava, "Eat together with your kinsmen. (193)
In a beautiful, secluded temple, I dwelt together with the Goddess;
there Viṣṇu, the creator of all, remained accompanied by the Daughter of the Ocean, for he was full of longing for her.
194. They both resided in that single temple, for he was indeed filled with desire.
Then, in a pure and spacious hall provided with many seats and numerous vessels,
the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha sat down before the two of them;
all the other ṛṣis and kings likewise sat according to their seniority.
King Rāma, together with his brothers, faced them and seated them upon young and equal thrones. Then Rāma,
consoling them, summoned his servants headed by Hanumān.
"Sirs, please wait here; afterwards you may eat, and not otherwise.
Then they all offered water for the feet and respectful offerings (arghya) in due order, and all those who were attendants of Rāma partook of the meal.
Having given them betel-leaf, he fed the lord of monkeys and the others.
When they had all finished eating, Rāma, whose eyes are like lotuses,
[fed] the poor, the blind, the wretched, and so forth, as well as the beasts, birds, and deer.

Having given food to the snakes, he indeed began to perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā). Having performed the twilight prayers and recitations, and having bowed to them, King Rāma then sat upon his throne along with the citizens, country-folk, and others.
Being served while seated in the assembly hall, Rāghava shone like the Lord of Śacī,
the god, surrounded by all the deities;
together with his brothers, he attended to every royal duty in its entirety.
Then Rāghava dismissed them all one by one by name;
he sent forth his brothers, as well as the monkeys and others.
Then the highly effulgent Vasiṣṭha addressed these words to Rāma.
O Raghava, whatever task must be performed this morning, do not forget it;
for the Blessed Lord Śambhu, the Master of the Universe and Consort of Ambikā, is present.
That Blessed One should be remembered and worshipped with diligent effort.
Having said "So be it," the king bowed to his guru and dismissed him;
he himself then united with his wife while meditating upon the God of gods.
The sages said:
"O best among the wise, having risen in the morning, what did Āmo do for his guru? Tell me that, for we have a great curiosity to hear it. Sūta said:
Then, beholding Śambhu, Rāma spoke: "O best of sages, recount the story of Śaṅkara;
no satiety has arisen in me as I listen to the majesty of Maheśa, which destroys the multitude of sins.
Śambhu said:
Now, I shall proclaim to you the answer to the remainder of the question as spoken by the Lord: those who worship Īśvara with wealth acquired through unjust means are born as *vyaṅga* (deformed).
For example, a certain *rākṣasa* named Rūpaka, having propitiated Śaṅkara with wealth acquired unjustly, made a bell out of that very wealth for the pleasure of Īśvara.
His son was known as Saṃpāti;
he worshipped Śaṅkara with wealth acquired through theft.
On one day, both of them died and went to the world of Śiva, where they were addressed by Vīrabhadra: 212–213.

"O Devata, worship was performed by you with wealth acquired through the unjust means of *bhorūpaka*, and because of that disposition toward the bell and other items, you shall become a member of a group of thieves after being born as a eunuch.

By the word of Śiva, it is evident that from hearing his name, one's sense of hearing is destroyed by its sound, and likewise one's sight; yet, to this extent, O Devata, the worship of the Lord has been properly performed by you. (214–215)
"Therefore, O Vīrabhadra, there shall be devotion [to me]; however, you must wander somewhere with a group of people known as the Anaśanas. Thus he commanded.
Both of them remained in that manner in the world of Śiva.
Śambhu said:
Now I shall relate the account of the worship with impaired materials as spoken by Maheśa to Hanumān (218).
Listen, O Rāghava, to the life-story of the Pramathas; I shall describe the ripening of the karma for each one of them (219).
Thus questioned by Hanumān, "Let an explanation of the group of those with impaired limbs be given," Śiva said: (220).
The water of his knowledge, having been defiled by that [impurity], would have perished; therefore, listen to what was said by the wise ones: "221.

This man is perspiring on all his limbs at all times; he is dripping with sweat, his clothes are soaked with perspiration, his body has small streams produced by the sweat, drops of sweat are falling from the tip of his nose, and he is seen to be unfit for touch. 222.
Previously, when he performed the worship of the Lord, he had caused himself to perspire.
In this regard, I shall relate an ancient history:
there was a Brāhmaṇa known as Cekitāna who became a farmer;
having constantly produced crops through agriculture, he would always bathe in the morning.
When midday had arrived, that Brāhmaṇa, while engaged in his recitations, said to his wife, "Bring food quickly. With the food brought by her, he performed the worship of Śiva with haste.
He was constantly heated by the sun and perspired at all times. Then,
when evening arrived, having washed his limbs and being beautifully adorned with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and other offerings mixed with drops of sweat— 226–227.
He worshipped the Lord of Gods with offerings appropriate for the time, and then that one of great intelligence died and went to the world of Śiva.
He was then addressed by Vīrabhadra: "Become a Gaṇa in my retinue."
"In the past, Śambhu was worshipped by objects touched by sweat;
because you were constantly associated with sweat, you have therefore become the host of sweat-beings (Svedagaṇa).
Śambhu said:
Then, commanded by Vīra, this host of Rāma’s followers arrived.

"Behold this Ghaṇṭāmukha! Formerly, he was a virtuous Vaiśya named Vibhāvasu, a performer of great gifts who constantly fed Brāhmaṇas and performed his religious duties. In the morning, having bowed to Śiva and worshipped him with flowers, he would smear a certain spot with cow-dung, prepare lotuses and other offerings, present them to the God, and then ring the bell with a loud sound.
Rāma said:
"How was his bell damaged?
Śambhu said:
"In ancient times, there was a certain powerful man well-known as Soma."
His son, named Cāṇḍa, was ten years of age.
O King, he would throw boiled *kulmāṣa* grains cooked over fire into a bell and eat them; yet he was not harmed by that. (233–234)
Then, striving to seize that Vaiśya, he said this;

or rather, the Vaiśya himself, having determined there the purification of the substance, established it as a subject of legal procedure in the worldly realm. 235. He made it a matter of worldly transaction in the world.
By this sinful connection, Ghaṇṭāmukha became a member of the Gaṇa host.
Rāma said:
"How can she, who is completely pure through the purity of her substance, be the cause of sin?"
Śambhu said: "It has been correctly stated how the purification of substances is achieved;
however, one will not become a devotee through worldly transactions. (237)
And Śiva’s abode shall always belong to him, and he too shall become a speaker [of the truth].
Sūta said:
And whoever speaks this narrative, he is equal to Him upon the earth.
O Brahmins, this is the most secret of secrets; it bestows the knowledge of Śiva.
This which has been told to you, O Brahmins, is a great merit that grants the longest life. Whoever hears this with devotion is glorified in the world of Śiva. 239–240.
To the reciter of the Purāṇa, one should give clothing, cows, gold ornaments,
and land endowed with crops and fruit, according to one's capacity.
[This is] the dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava, which destroys the entire multitude of sins.
Whoever reads or even hears this attains the supreme state. 242.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "The Liberation of Rāma," in the latter portion of the Śiva-Rāghava Saṃvāda within the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The fifth book, the Pātālakhaṇḍa, is complete. 5.
Thus ends the fifth section, the Pātālakhaṇḍa, in the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
